In doing so, it provides a comprehensive examination of state-of-the-art technologies across the entire marine plastics value chain in Europe, from detection and recovery to separation, identification, and recycling.
authors: Eimear Magee; Matheus C. dos Santos; Meriem Stimade; Jose Alvarez; Gerard Dooly; Vincent Mallet; Michel Bakni; Douglas Marques; Giordano Pierozan Bernardes; David Tormey

title: Adversarial domain adaptation for false-positive reduction in hospital-to-robotic echocardiographic screening under limited target-domain data.
abstract: Hospital-trained deep learning models for echocardiographic wall motion abnormality detection achieve strong performance under standard clinical acquisition conditions but often degrade substantially when deployed on autonomous robotic acquisition systems. Most existing models are developed and validated under controlled clinical acquisition conditions, limiting their robustness when deployed in emerging autonomous imaging systems. A hospital-trained wall motion abnormality detection model trained on 10,000 hospital echocardiograms achieved 92.3% accuracy (94.0% sensitivity, 90.6% specificity) when applied to an independent hospital test data set of 500 studies. However, direct deployment on 150 robotic echocardiograms from 15 healthy subjects reduced the normal-case specificity to 65.7%, representing a 24.9 percentage-point drop compared to the performance when applied to the hospital-acquired data. No statistically significant difference in SNR was observed between domains (p = 0.31; d = 0.12), with similarly small standardized differences in contrast and sharpness, although formal equivalence was not established. Acquisition-geometry measures differed descriptively between domains, suggesting that geometry-associated factors may contribute to the observed domain shift. We propose an adversarial domain adaptation framework built upon a 3D ResNet-18 backbone with a gradient-reversal domain discriminator for aligning hospital and robotic feature representations while retaining the hospital-trained classification objective. This design enables adaptation to the robotic domain without requiring labeled robot-acquired pathological cases, which are particularly difficult to obtain during early-stage robotic system development. Under leave-one-subject-out validation across robotic subjects, Mixed-DANN improved specificity to 86.1% ± 4.3%, while Normal-only DANN improved specificity to 89.3% ± 4.8% (p < 0.001 versus direct transfer), recovering 94.8% of the hospital-to-robot specificity gap. Because the robotic cohort comprises only healthy subjects, evaluation is appropriately restricted to specificity and false-positive rate; sensitivity evaluation requires future acquisition of robot-acquired pathological cases. These findings suggest that acquisition-associated domain shift substantially impacts cross-platform deployment. The proposed adversarial domain adaptation framework provides a potential pathway for adapting hospital-trained cardiac AI models to autonomous robotic ultrasound under conditions of limited target-domain data, although validation using robot-acquired pathological cases remains necessary before clinical translation.
authors: Hsu Thiri Soe; Yamauchi Yuki; Hiroyasu Iwata

title: Agreement and reproducibility of intraoral scan- versus CBCT-based three-dimensional implant position assessment in the posterior mandible — a paired in vitro method-comparison study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Three-dimensional postoperative implant assessment is increasingly performed using intraoral scan (IOS) superimposition as a radiation-free alternative to cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT). However, it remains unclear to what extent IOS- and CBCT-based measurements agree and how reproducibility changes across posterior mandibular configurations. METHODS: In this paired in vitro method-comparison study, based on the experimental platform of a previous study, 60 implants placed at Fédération Dentaire Internationale (FDI) positions 35, 36, 45, 46 and 47 in bounded edentulous spaces (BES) and distal extension situations (DE) underwent three IOS-based and three CBCT-based postoperative assessments relative to the virtual plan using the Treatment Evaluation Tool of the planning software. Angular, mesiodistal, buccolingual, apico-coronal, and three-dimensional (3D) deviations at implant base and apex were recorded, resulting in 180 paired measurements. Agreement was assessed by Bland-Altman analysis, and within-method reproducibility by the within-implant standard deviation (Sw). IOS variability was additionally separated into within-scan and between-scan components. Non-parametric analyses were used for comparisons by indication and FDI position. RESULTS: Mean absolute IOS-CBCT differences were 0.73° ± 0.55° for angular deviation, 0.22 ± 0.20 mm for the 3D base offset and 0.26 ± 0.22 mm for the 3D apical offset. Bland-Altman bias (CBCT - IOS) was small (- 0.35°; -0.05 mm; -0.07 mm) with 95% limits of agreement of [- 2.01°; +1.31°], [- 0.62; +0.53] mm and [- 0.73; +0.58] mm. Within-method reproducibility was superior for IOS in 8 of 9 parameters (e.g., Sw 0.20° vs. 0.55° for the angle), and IOS variability was dominated by scan-to-scan rather than within-scan re-evaluation. Discrepancies were larger in DE than in BES sites in 7 of 9 parameters (all p < 0.001 for the principal apical and buccolingual components) and were larger at position 47 than at position 35 (3D base p = 0.004; 3D apex p = 0.011). CONCLUSIONS: In this in vitro setting, IOS- and CBCT-based implant assessment in the posterior mandible showed good agreement with small overall differences, and IOS demonstrated lower within-method variability than CBCT. IOS-based superimposition may therefore serve as a radiation-free complement to CBCT for the postoperative evaluation of single implants in bounded posterior sites. Agreement decreased in distal extension situations and at more distal positions; in these configurations, and whenever clinical decisions depend on sub-millimeter or sub-degree precision, CBCT remains the reference technique. Confirmation in vivo is required before routine clinical use.
authors: Georg Hoene; Shabnam Shahpasand; Felix Karl Waffenschmidt; Frederik Holdorf; Robert Stünkel; Alexander-Nicolai Zeller; Philipp Kauffmann

title: Amelanotic Jejunal Malignant Melanoma Presenting as Overt Small-Bowel Bleeding and Mimicking a Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumor: A Case Report
abstract: BACKGROUND: Small-bowel bleeding accounts for a minority of gastrointestinal hemorrhage and may pose a diagnostic challenge after negative bidirectional endoscopy. Malignant melanoma involving the small intestine is usually metastatic, whereas a true primary small-bowel melanoma is exceptionally rare and remains controversial. CASE REPORT: We report the case of a 76-year-old female patient who presented with severe symptomatic iron-deficiency anemia and recurrent overt gastrointestinal bleeding. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy and colonoscopy did not identify a bleeding source. Cross-sectional imaging demonstrated a large necrotic mass in the inter-gastro-jejunal region, initially interpreted as a possible gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST). Endoscopic ultrasound showed a heterogeneous lesion exceeding 100 mm and enabled fine-needle biopsy. Histopathology demonstrated a malignant epithelioid amelanotic melanoma with diffuse SOX10, S100, and Melan-A expression and a high proliferative index. Concomitant CD117 positivity represented a potential diagnostic pitfall given the initial suspicion of a GIST. Enteroscopy subsequently documented a large ulcerated jejunal lesion with friable mucosa and stigmata of recent bleeding, demonstrating luminal involvement and ascertaining it as the likely source of blood loss. Dermatologic and ophthalmologic examinations revealed no alternative primary melanoma. CONCLUSIONS: This case illustrates the complementary roles of cross-sectional imaging, EUS-guided tissue acquisition, and enteroscopy in a tumor that mimicked a GIST, while emphasizing that absence of an identifiable extraintestinal primary does not by itself prove a primary intestinal origin.
authors: Diana‐Elena Floria; Ana-Maria Buzuleac; Andrei Vasile OLTEANU; Răzvan Constantinescu; Dana Mitrică; Gheorghe Gh Bălan

title: An Anatomy-guided 3D Segmentation Pipeline for Prostate Surgical Phantoms from CT Scans
abstract: Full autonomy has been a long-term goal in robotic surgery and a near-to-medium-term goal for prostatectomy. Due to the relatively closed structure of the procedure, its standard-of-care robotic/laparoscopic solutions, and procedure economics, prostate procedures are an optimal early target for surgical automation. Prototyping and testing of possible solutions is done in constructed laboratory phantoms, either synthetic tissues or animal phantoms. To enable measurement of perceptual and robotic motion error, phantoms undergo volumetric imaging; these images are critical to both a potential deployed automatic system, used in planning motion and treatment (cutting, ablation, suturing, etc.), as well as post-hoc assessment of system performance. Rapid iteration on these phantom models yields small, inconsistent datasets, while the current workflow for human annotation is often anatomically unreliable and prohibitively time-consuming, rendering deep learning unsuitable at reasonable scales. To address these limitations, we present an automated 3D segmentation pipeline that uses classical medical image-processing techniques to encode the known anatomy of the phantoms as explicit geometric and intensity priors, which requires no training corpus and is transferred to each new phantom revision without re-annotation. Across 57 scans spanning multiple phantom revisions, our pipeline recovers the capsule interior at 0.83 median Dice on 11 contrast-suppressed scans and detects all 32 annotated focal lesions without false positives, completing a full scan in 2-8 minutes on commodity CPU hardware versus 1-2 hours by hand.
authors: Iven Chen; Kuan-I Chung; Ayberk Acar; Susheela Sharma Stern; Alejandro Chara; Jie Ying Wu; Daniel Moyer

title: An Enterprise AI Assurance Framework for Biomedical Diagnostics: Integrating a Human Validation Boundary and a Multidimensional Assurance Score into a Lifecycle Governance Model
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems for biomedical diagnostics are usually evaluated on predictive performance, yet clinical adoption also depends on reliability under distribution shift, interpretability, safety behaviour, equity across subgroups, clinician oversight, and post-deployment monitoring. Existing guidelines and governance frameworks address these requirements separately; few link them to a measurable readiness assessment and a defined human decision rule. This paper presents the Enterprise AI Assurance Framework for Biomedical Diagnostics (EAIA-BD), a design science artefact comprising a five-layer architecture with an AI Assurance Intelligence Layer between model output and clinical use; a Human Validation Boundary that specifies, as an explicit decision rule, when and by whom AI outputs must be reviewed; the Biomedical AI Assurance Score (BAAS), a composite indicator with a non-compensatory gate on safety-critical dimensions; and a seven-stage assurance lifecycle with a maturity model. The framework was evaluated analytically through an author-rated comparison with eleven healthcare-AI frameworks and standards, a component-level mapping to NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001, ISO 14971, IEC 62304, Good Machine Learning Practice principles, FDA change-control guidance, CHAI guidance, and WHO guidance, a worked example of the decision rule and score, and a sensitivity analysis of the BAAS. Among the eleven frameworks compared, none combined a formal human decision boundary, a gated composite readiness score, and lifecycle governance in one artefact; this comparison has not been independently validated. The framework specifies mechanisms; the analytical evaluation establishes internal consistency and coverage, not effect, and no improvement in clinical safety, decision-making, or regulatory readiness is claimed. EAIA-BD has not been validated empirically; an operational specification of all indicators, a retrospective assessment protocol with an independent second rater, and a Delphi protocol are supplied for that purpose.
authors: Rakesh Kumar Agrawal; Ather Husain; Wasim Mohammed Amin Tambe; Pankaj Kumar Yadav; Anjan Chatterjee

title: An ingestible bioelectronic capsule for in vivo DNA monitoring in the gastrointestinal tract
abstract: Early detection of gastrointestinal pathogens and disease-associated DNA sequences is critical for timely clinical intervention, yet current diagnostic workflows rely on ex vivo stool analysis or invasive biopsy, which delays diagnosis and compromises trace DNA integrity. Here, we report an ingestible bioelectronic capsule embedded with a paper-based CRISPR/Cas system for in vivo sampling, on-board lysis, sequence-specific DNA sensing, and wireless signal readout. By performing thoroughly in situ, the capsule mitigates the degradation and dilution of target DNA that occur during ex vivo handling. It enables detection of the Salmonella invA gene in simulated gastric fluid, real gastric samples, and the stomachs of large animal models (canine and porcine). We further validate the capsule strategy for detecting Helicobacter pylori DNA in human volunteer samples. This CRISPR/Cas-embedded bioelectronic capsule offers a non-invasive, point-of-care approach for in vivo monitoring of specific DNA sequences in the gastrointestinal tract, with potential for personalized health management.
authors: HANJIE WANG; Guijie Bai; Xin Huang; Xinran Li; Yinli Bao; Hui Liu; Hongxiang Li; Leilei Wang; Xinyue Cao; Maoxing Yang; Zhanpu Bin; Xufei Teng; Meng Song; Jiachao Cao; Jiazhen Lu; Yi Zhang; Yanning Zhang; Long Li; Hanyan Zhou; Zhen Yang; Yue Jiang; Chao Zhang; Xi Jiang; Dawei Sun; Yihao Wang; Haihan Yao; Tiantian Hao; Cuiqin Huang; Zhijie Feng; Duo Liu

title: Applications of Artificial Intelligence in the Diagnosis and Management of Keratitis and Conjunctivitis: A Review
abstract: Ocular surface diseases, such as conjunctivitis and keratitis, are an important global health concern because of their socioeconomic burden and potential for visual impairment. Early diagnosis and appropriate management are key to preventing complications, yet traditional diagnosis based on clinical examination and investigations is resource-intensive and varies among clinicians. Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly machine learning and deep learning, has shown promise in image-focused specialties such as ophthalmology. This narrative review summarizes published studies evaluating AI in the diagnosis and management of keratitis and conjunctivitis, including image-based diagnostic models, chatbots, natural language processing tools, and smartphone applications, along with future directions and ethical considerations. Convolutional neural networks applied to slit-lamp, anterior segment optical coherence tomography, in vivo confocal microscopy, and smartphone images showed high performance in detecting infectious keratitis, with areas under the curve above 0.96 in large multicenter datasets. Performance was lower for differentiating causative organisms, with accuracies of approximately 76% to 92% for bacterial, fungal, and Acanthamoeba keratitis and fungal subtypes. In allergic conjunctival disease, an AI pipeline achieved a diagnostic accuracy of 86.2%, compared with 60.0% for board-certified ophthalmologists. Chatbots correctly answered 51% to 68% of questions on corneal and conjunctival diseases, and incorrect AI suggestions significantly reduced the diagnostic accuracy of non-specialist ophthalmologists. Ensemble learning, mobile imaging applications, and chatbot-supported triage may extend tele-ophthalmology to under-resourced areas. However, most models rely on retrospective, single-center datasets, and concerns remain regarding generalizability, accountability, transparency, and clinician trust. Prospective multicenter validation and explainable, multimodal systems are needed before AI can be routinely adopted as a supportive tool in clinical practice.
authors: Ashneet Sandhu; Jana Saleh; Rodrigo Carvalho de Olivera; Chia Ying Tsai; Mohammed Khan; Aaron Samuel; Noora Khalid Alhamid

title: Applications of Fairness Training in Artificial Intelligence to Ophthalmic Disease Diagnosis using External Eye Photographs
abstract: Diabetic retinopathy (DR), age-related macular degeneration (AMD), and glaucoma are leading causes of preventable blindness, yet whether external eye photographs carry phenotypic information about posterior segment disease remains unclear, and methods to mitigate demographic disparities in such models are largely unexplored. We developed and evaluated deep learning and vision-language models for binary classification of vision-threatening DR (VTDR), advanced AMD, and glaucoma using 40,687 external eye photographs from 9,878 patients at Massachusetts Eye and Ear. Convolutional networks (WResNet, EfficientNet), a vision transformer (ViT), and a finetuned vision-language model (LLaVA) were assessed by area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), with fairness across sex, race, and ethnicity quantified by the equity-scaled AUC (ES-AUC). Five fairness-training strategies were applied to the best models. LLaVA achieved the highest baseline AUC for VTDR (85·4%, comparable to ViT 82·6%); advanced AMD was similar across architectures (EfficientNet 86·3%; LLaVA 84·8%; ViT 84·7%), whereas glaucoma was substantially worse (67-74%). Fairness training improved VTDR and AMD AUCs to 86·3% and 85·9% while partially mitigating demographic disparities. In summary, although AI models that rely on external eye photography to detect posterior segment disease may not yet be suitable for clinical deployment, the fairness methods demonstrated in this proof-of-concept study could be applied to other AI systems to decrease performance disparities and potentially improve model performance.
authors: В. В. Костин; Sung-Hoon Yoon; Jimmy S. Chen; Seungjoo Baek; Jesse Seid; Nathan Quyang; Edward Li; Eric Li; Min Shi; Mengyu Wang

title: Artificial Intelligence Applications in Pediatric Dentistry: A Systematic Scoping Review With Visual Evidence Mapping
abstract: Background and Aims: Artificial intelligence is increasingly applied to pediatric dental imaging, caries detection, orthodontic decision support, age estimation, and risk prediction. However, pediatric evidence remains fragmented across clinical tasks, model types, validation strategies, and reported metrics. This systematic scoping review mapped the clinical applications, methodological characteristics, and reported performance of AI in pediatric dentistry. Methods: PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar were searched for English-language studies published from January 2010 to May 2026. Original studies evaluating AI, machine learning, or deep learning in pediatric dentistry or pediatric-relevant dental tasks were included. Screening was performed using Rayyan. Data extraction captured study characteristics, pediatric relevance, AI method, clinical task, outcomes, and validation approach. Risk of bias was assessed using QUADAS-3 for diagnostic/classification studies and PROBAST + AI for prediction and model-development studies. Findings were synthesized descriptively according to PRISMA-ScR. Results: Thirty-five studies were included, comprising 19 (54.3%) pediatric-only studies and 16 (45.7%) broader or mixed-age studies with separately identifiable pediatric or pediatric-relevant evidence. By primary application, 15 (42.9%) addressed orthodontic or craniofacial assessment and decision support, eight (22.9%) risk prediction or biomarker modeling, five (14.3%) diagnostic imaging or dental-anomaly detection, five (14.3%) dental age estimation, and two (5.7%) caries or plaque detection. Validation was internal or test-set based in 26 studies (74.3%), observer- or manual-comparative in five (14.3%), and not clearly defined in four (11.4%); none reported independent external validation. For QUADAS-3, non-low-risk judgments were most frequent in the analysis domain (8/19, 42.1%), whereas for PROBAST + AI they were most frequent in the participants and data-sources domain (5/16, 31.3%). Conclusion: AI shows promising pediatric dental applications, especially in image-based and decision-support tasks, but evidence remains heterogeneous, task-specific, and limited by variable validation, incomplete reporting, and scarce external testing.
authors: Aref Zarei; Amirhossein Ehsani; Amir Ebrahimzedeh Pasha; Mansour Gorjizad; Majid Aryannejad; Seyedeh Sara Rezazadeh Shojaee; Maedeh Barkhordari Dashtkhaki; Sharif Ebrahimi; Mohamad Mahdi Aghajany; Hamidreza Mousavi; Masoud Kiany; Mahsa Asadi Anar; Farzaneh Sadeghi Mahounak; F. Khosravi; Sara Zamani; Sepehr Ramezanipour; Nima Dehghan Banadaki

title: Artificial Intelligence Approaches for Gastrointestinal Bleeding Detection in Capsule Endoscopy: A Systematic Review and Critical Analysis.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding is a common, potentially life-threatening condition, and capsule endoscopy (CE) is the principal investigation for suspected small-bowel bleeding after non-diagnostic upper endoscopy and colonoscopy. Because manual review of thousands of CE frames is labor-intensive, artificial intelligence (AI) has been proposed to automate bleeding detection. Methods: Following PRISMA 2020, this systematic review synthesizes 15 peer-reviewed journal studies (2020-2025) applying traditional machine learning, convolutional neural networks, transfer learning, attention-based or hybrid architectures, segmentation, or object detection to GI bleeding detection in CE. Methodological quality was appraised with an AI-adapted risk-of-bias framework informed by QUADAS-2 and PROBAST. Results: Frame-level classification accuracy ranged from 90.6% to 99.9% (median 98.5%; 13 studies), with the lowest values from evaluations closest to clinical practice; the segmentation and detection studies reported a mean intersection-over-union of 86.9% and an mAP@0.5 of 79.0%. Only two studies (13%) were at low risk of bias for validation strategy, none reported patient-level separation of training and test data, only four (27%) used clinical patient data, and none compared AI with conventional endoscopy or clinical outcomes. Conclusions: Current evidence demonstrates high performance on curated datasets but not yet generalizability or clinical readiness; patient-level, external, and prospective multicentre validation is required.
authors: Helal NM, Regala JZ, Rahman M.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Imaging Technologies in Orthodontic Assessment, Referral and Care Pathways: A Scoping Review
abstract: Abstract* Background Artificial intelligence (AI), integrated with imaging technologies, is increasingly applied across orthodontic assessment and care pathways. However, the evidence remains scattered across imaging modalities, clinical applications, AI methodologies, and stages of clinical translation. Methods A scoping review was conducted in accordance with the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and reported in line with the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. PubMed, Scopus, and IEEE Xplore were searched for studies published between January 2016 and June 2026, with searches supplemented by Google Scholar, OpenAlex, grey literature sources, and citation searching. Eligible studies were mapped descriptively and synthesised thematically using Braun and Clarke’s framework. Results Fifty-four studies were included. AI applications used intraoral and facial photographs, cephalometric radiographs, CBCT, intraoral scans, three-dimensional dental models, and multimodal imaging. Applications ranged from landmark localisation, segmentation, and malocclusion classification to treatment-need assessment, screening, referral support, treatment planning, and remote monitoring. Evidence was strongest for bounded, anatomically verifiable image-analysis tasks, whereas applications involving referral, triage, treatment-need decisions, longitudinal prediction, and workflow integration were less mature. Common limitations included retrospective, single-centre designs; heterogeneous reference standards; limited external validation; inconsistent reporting of calibration and uncertainty; and insufficient evaluation of patient-centred, equity, and service-level outcomes. Conclusions Imaging-based AI in orthodontics has evolved from automated image interpretation to clinician-assisted decision support across the care pathway. Current evidence most strongly supports AI for structured image-analysis tasks, but does not yet support autonomous referral, triage, or treatment-planning decisions. Future research should prioritise prospective multicentre validation, transparent reporting, explainability, fairness, uncertainty handling, and workflow-integrated evaluation to enable safe and clinically useful implementation.
authors: Kayali S, Bernabe E, Golkari A.

title: Artificial Intelligence as a Catalyst for Cell-Based Therapies in Retinal Disease
abstract: Retinal degenerative diseases, including age-related macular degeneration (AMD), retinitis pigmentosa (RP), and Stargardt disease, represent leading causes of irreversible vision loss worldwide, collectively affecting hundreds of millions of people. Cell-based therapies, particularly those leveraging induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) transplantation, and CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing, have emerged as promising treatment modalities that may preserve, replace, or partially restore retinal function. However, these approaches face significant challenges in patient stratification, manufacturing consistency, surgical precision, and long-term outcome monitoring. Artificial intelligence (AI), encompassing machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and computer vision, is increasingly being integrated across the cell therapy pipeline to address these limitations. This review comprehensively explores the role of AI in enhancing cell-based retinal therapies, spanning disease diagnosis and patient selection, stem cell quality control and differentiation optimization, CRISPR off-target detection, retinal organoid characterization, scalable manufacturing, and post-transplantation monitoring through multimodal retinal imaging. Throughout, we distinguish direct retinal cell-therapy evidence from retinal-adjacent, cross-domain, and conceptual evidence. We also propose an AI-powered end-to-end pipeline that connects patient profiling through gene editing, cell production, and transplantation to longitudinal outcomes tracking (a forward-looking framework that needs to be clinically validated in future). While AI offers powerful tools to enhance efficacy, reproducibility, and personalization, it does not replace the clinical and biological foundations of cell therapy. Critical challenges remain, including data scarcity, algorithmic interpretability, regulatory compliance, and clinical validation. This review concludes that the strategic integration of AI has plausible potential to become supportive infrastructure for scalable and reproducible cell-based treatments for retinal diseases, although its necessity has not been demonstrated and prospective clinical validation is still required, and biological insight and rigorous empirical verification remain fundamental.
authors: Girish Kumar Srivastava; Priyank Shukla; Sara Crespo Millas; Yogeswaran Lokanathan

title: Artificial Intelligence for Benign Esophageal Stricture Dilation: An Evidence‐Transferability Framework and Safety‐First Roadmap
abstract: Background Endoscopic dilation is first‐line therapy for symptomatic benign esophageal strictures but remains operator‐dependent. Artificial intelligence (AI) could support assessment, risk stratification, and documentation; however, evidence from adjacent tasks is often mistaken for procedure‐specific validation. Aim To map the evidence for AI in benign esophageal stricture dilation, assess transferability and methodological quality, and propose a translational pathway. Methods We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Europe PMC from inception through June 28, 2026, using prespecified searches in adults and children. Studies were classified by evidence provenance and appraised using design‐adapted domain considerations. Results Within the search date and eligibility criteria, no AI system was identified that guided, monitored, or assessed dilation itself; two retrospective single‐center studies applied machine learning in the target population for other tasks. Adjacent neoplasia and engineering studies support component feasibility, while clinical cohorts identify candidate predictors. Functional lumen imaging probe technology provides non‐AI measurement and potential reference labels. Recurrent concerns included selected or retrospective samples, limited external validation, and high concern about applicability to dilation. Performance cannot be transferred across mismatched target tasks, acquisition physics, reference standards, populations or operating contexts, or consequences of error. Conclusion Adjacent evidence can justify candidate components. Procedure‐specific calibration and validation remain necessary. Priorities are calibrated morphometric variables with prespecified reference standards and reproducible documentation using synchronized multimodal and outcome data. External validation should be followed by human‐controlled advisory testing before intraprocedural automation.
authors: Ahmed Salman; Mohamed Abdalla Salman

title: Artificial Intelligence for Colorectal Cancer Diagnosis: A Comprehensive Survey of Modalities, Frameworks, and Clinical Tasks
abstract: The diagnosis of colorectal cancer encompasses nine complementary modalities: stool-based screening, blood-based biomarkers, cross-sectional imaging, endoscopic evaluation, histopathology, liquid biopsy, molecular and genetic profiling, microbiome analysis, and nanotechnology-based diagnostics. This narrative review synthesizes 160 references spanning seven task-specific artificial intelligence domains, including computer-aided detection, optical diagnosis, invasion depth prediction, computational pathology and radiogenomics, metastasis forecasting, neoadjuvant treatment response prediction, and surgical workflow analysis. We propose a conceptual multimodal pipeline comprising data ingestion, preprocessing and harmonization, feature representation, multimodal fusion, forecasting, explainability, and validation. A structured evidence grading framework classifies each clinical task by evidence level, consistency, and clinical readiness. We further catalog public datasets, challenge benchmarks, and five reporting standards: TRIPOD-AI, CONSORT-AI, SPIRIT-AI, DECIDE-AI, and CLAIM. Computer-aided detection and optical diagnosis demonstrate the highest maturity with Level 1 evidence from randomized controlled trials, while computational pathology, radiogenomics, and metastasis prediction remain at Level 2 with retrospective validation (internal or external). Microbiome screening, nanotechnology diagnostics, and surgical phase recognition are exploratory. The principal barriers to clinical adoption are domain shift, data scarcity, calibration, prospective validation, and workflow integration. We conclude that clinically useful artificial intelligence requires robust external validation, uncertainty quantification, explainable outputs, standardized reporting, and a structured translational pathway from retrospective evidence through regulatory clearance to post-deployment monitoring.
authors: Bassant El-Mosalamy; Hossam Magdy Balaha; Sohayla El-Moursi; Dibson Dibe Gondim; Khaldon Y. Lweesy; Jawad Yousaf; Mohammed Asaad Ghazal; Ayman S El-Baz

title: Artificial Intelligence in Bioengineering: Innovations, Challenges, and Future Directions: A Narrative Review
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming bioengineering, with applications ranging from diagnosis and biomedical imaging to wearable technologies, rehabilitation, biomaterials, biofabrication, and digital twins. This narrative review aims to examine the major innovations, challenges, and future directions of AI-enabled bioengineering, with particular attention to its clinical and translational development. The literature was searched in Scopus and PubMed, with emphasis on systematic reviews and meta-analyses and consideration of other relevant secondary literature across the main bioengineering domains. A total of 57 secondary publications were included in the principal evidence base. The review process was additionally informed by the ANDJ Narrative Review Checklist and an established qualification and scoring methodology applied to the selected secondary literature. The reviewed evidence shows a broad expansion of AI applications and increasing integration of intelligent technologies into bioengineering systems. However, important challenges remain, particularly regarding data quality and representativeness, validation and generalizability, reproducibility, safety, human oversight, ethical responsibility, equity, and regulatory requirements. Future developments are expected to increasingly involve multimodal, adaptive, connected, and human-centered systems integrating AI with sensing technologies, robotics, digital twins, and longitudinal data. Overall, AI-enabled bioengineering is progressing from promising technological applications toward increasingly integrated and translational systems. Its successful evolution will depend on combining technological innovation with robust clinical evidence, responsible development, and appropriate ethical and regulatory frameworks.
authors: Daniele Giansanti

title: Artificial Intelligence in Eye Disease: A Systematic Review of Screening, Diagnosis, Prognosis, Treatment-Response Prediction, and Clinical Decision Support
abstract: Background/Objectives: Artificial intelligence (AI) is expanding eye care beyond image-based detection toward prognosis, treatment-response prediction, monitoring, triage, and clinician-facing decision support. We evaluated AI across eye-disease screening, diagnosis, prognosis, treatment response, and decision support, emphasizing validation, explainability, and clinical readiness. Methods: This PROSPERO-registered review followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement. Six databases plus supplementary routes identified English-language literature published from 1 January 2015 through 10 August 2026. Included studies underwent design-mapped Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI)/adapted-JBI item-level appraisal; heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis. Results: The evidence base comprised 270 studies. Diabetic retinopathy/diabetic macular oedema was the largest clinical area (82), followed by retinal/multi-disease AI (52), glaucoma (46), and age-related macular degeneration (AMD)/macular disease (29); convolutional neural network (CNN)/convolutional deep learning was the largest primary method group (136). External validation was confirmed in 130 studies, including 95 with a clinical/geographic/prospective/real-world external-validation component (86 clinical-only and nine mixed clinical + technical); 49 had a strict direct clinical comparator and 90 used explainability. Pediatric/pediatric-relevant evidence accounted for 30 studies, while explicit optometry/optometrist involvement appeared in only three. Conclusions: Ophthalmic AI spans diagnosis through clinical management, but translation remains limited by heterogeneous outcomes, incomplete independent validation, few direct comparators, and sparse evaluation of safety, workflow effects, and patient outcomes.
authors: Manal M Alharbi; Emtenan M. Alharbi; Alanoud S Alsalamah; Hanan Asiri; Najla Beati; Renad AlAtawi; Amr A. Arafat

title: Artificial Intelligence in Ocular Surface Oncology: A Narrative Review of Multimodal Imaging, Smartphone-Based Screening, and Clinical Decision Support
abstract: Ocular surface malignancies include ocular surface squamous neoplasia (OSSN), con-junctival melanoma, and conjunctival lymphoma. These rare disorders may threaten vi-sion and, in some cases, life. Early identification may be difficult because malignant le-sions can resemble benign ocular surface conditions. Artificial intelligence (AI), including machine learning and deep learning, has emerged as a potential aid to detection, classi-fication, and referral. This structured narrative review, organized with reference to SANRA principles, synthesizes PubMed/MEDLINE literature on AI applications in ocular surface oncology available through 29 August 2026. We examine slit-lamp photography, anterior segment optical coherence tomography, in vivo confocal microscopy, ultrasound biomicroscopy, and smartphone imaging. Deep-learning models have shown promising performance in selected binary OSSN tasks, whereas multiclass studies report lower sen-sitivity for rare malignancies such as conjunctival melanoma and lymphoma. Smartphone-based screening has also been evaluated in a prospective referral pathway, although the reference standard and verification process limit interpretation of popula-tion-level sensitivity. Dataset imbalance, image-acquisition variability, limited external and prospective validation, explainability, and workflow integration remain barriers to implementation. Future work should prioritize multicenter datasets, standardized acquisition, calibrated thresholds, and prospective human-AI evaluations. Current evidence supports further evaluation of AI as an adjunct for detection and referral, not as a re-placement for specialist assessment or histopathology.
authors: F. Cappellani; Marco Zeppieri; Longo Antonio; Cosimo Giuseppe Mazzotta; Irene Gattazzo; Fabiana D’Esposito; Caterina Gagliano; Matteo Capobianco

title: Artificial Intelligence in Paediatric Dentistry: A Scoping Review
abstract: This review scoped artificial intelligence (AI) in paediatric dentistry to summarize current applications and limitations. A comprehensive literature search was completed across PubMed, Google Scholar, Scopus, Embase, IEEE Xplore, and medRxiv/aArXiv. The preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) checklist was used for reporting the present study. Studies concerning paediatric dentistry and utilizing AI, machine learning (ML) or large language models (LLMs) were included. Two independent reviewers screened and three extracted data on AI methodologies, performance metrics, and clinical applications. Fifty-nine studies were included. Computer vision studies (n = 32) most often used panoramic radiographs (n = 14), mainly for tooth detection, numbering and segmentation (n = 10) and caries detection (n = 9). Non-imaging ML studies (n = 18) primarily used clinical variables and questionnaire data (n = 8) or salivary/biological samples (n = 10). Accuracy ranged from 50% to 100%, with sensitivity reaching 100% in biomarker-based studies. LLM accuracy varied widely (33%-96%). Computer vision and non-imaging ML show promise for paediatric dentistry, particularly in the detection of dental structures and diseases, as well as risk stratification. Variable LLM performance underscores the need for standardized evaluation before clinical integration. CLINICAL RELEVANCE: AI-based tools may support paediatric dentists by improving tooth detection, dental structure assessment, caries detection, disease prediction and risk stratification. Computer vision and non-imaging machine learning approaches appear to have potential, but their clinical value depends on robust external validation, transparent reporting and integration into paediatric dental workflows. Given their variable performance, AI tools should be used only as adjunctive tools or a second reviewer.
authors: Rata Rokhshad; Antonín Tichý; Jung‐Wei Chen; Sadaf Taheri; Salar Motamedi; Falk Schwendicke

title: Artificial Intelligence in Uveitis: Where Are We on the Translational Pathway?
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has transformed several areas of ophthalmic practice, most notably diabetic retinopathy screening, where autonomous systems have achieved regulatory approval and real-world deployment. Uveitis, by contrast, remains at an earlier stage in translation. Its heterogeneity, longitudinal disease course and reliance on multimodal clinical reasoning present distinct challenges, compounded by small, fragmented and geographically restricted datasets. This review examines the landscape of AI applications in uveitis and maps them to the established ophthalmic AI validation pipeline, from algorithm development through to clinical deployment. Evidence varies between individual studies: selected vitritis detection and aetiological classification models have undergone independent external testing, while anterior chamber inflammation quantification includes small single-centre feasibility studies. Emerging applications, including recurrent-course prediction, treatment-response modelling, fluorescein angiography segmentation, natural language processing and foundation model fine-tuning, remain predominantly at proof-of-concept stages. Despite encouraging algorithmic performance, the studies discussed have not demonstrated clinical actionability: evidence that an AI output changes a clinical decision, leads to an appropriate management intervention and ultimately improves a patient-relevant outcome. We argue that the principal translational bottleneck is therefore not algorithmic capability alone, but the absence of harmonised longitudinal datasets, geographically diverse validation, prospective evaluation and, critically, studies linking AI output → clinical decision → management intervention → patient outcome. International collaborative registries offer a pathway towards addressing these gaps. The next phase of uveitis AI must move beyond model performance towards clinically actionable systems that improve diagnosis, disease monitoring, treatment selection and relapse prediction, ultimately delivering meaningful benefit to patients with ocular inflammatory disease.
authors: Agklinta Kiosia; Atharva Hudlikar; Tushar Kale; Kai Jin; Ao Lu; Guannan Su; Peizeng Yang; Rupesh V. Agrawal

title: Artificial intelligence as a diagnostic tool using lateral cephalometric imaging
abstract: Purpose To evaluate the accuracy and reliability of a newly developed artificial intelligence (AI)-driven system in identifying cephalometric landmarks, comparing its performance to manual tracing by orthodontists. Material and methods A total of 506 lateral cephalometric radiographs of patients aged 14 to 40 years were collected from Dubai Dental Hospital, United Arab Emirates. After applying exclusion criteria, 473 radiographs were included in the final analysis. Manual tracings were performed using Dolphin Imaging software, identifying key landmarks including Sella, Nasion, A-point, B-point, Menton, Glabella, and others. The AI-based cephalometric system (AI Ceph) was trained on these radiographs to locate the same landmarks. Its performance was compared to manual tracings to assess accuracy and reliability. Results The AI Ceph system demonstrated high concordance with manual tracing. The Menton point showed the highest agreement (96.6%), while Nasion had the lowest (86.6%). The majority of landmark deviations were within 2 mm, the predefined clinically acceptable range, while a small proportion exceeded this threshold and were classified as discordant (> 2 mm) according to the prespecified binary criterion. Sensitivity was above 80% for all landmarks, except Nasion (72.7%) and A-point (78.8%). A statistically significant improvement in concordance after model retraining was observed only for the Glabella landmark (p < 0.0213). Conclusions The AI system provided accurate and reliable cephalometric landmark identification. While most deviations fell within the clinically acceptable 2-mm tolerance, landmarks exceeding this threshold were clearly identified and quantified using the binary discordance classification (> 2 mm), ensuring transparent reporting of all errors.
authors: Amani Idres; Ahmed Ghoneima; Mohammed Osman

title: Artificial intelligence for kinematic (procedural motion) analysis in gastrointestinal endoscopy: A systematic review
abstract: BACKGROUND Artificial intelligence (AI) in gastrointestinal endoscopy has focused on computer-aided detection (CADe) for recognition errors; AI addressing endoscope motion, coverage, workflow, and skill – collectively kinematic analysis – has not been systematically synthesized. AIM To map kinematic AI evidence across eight predefined domains and assessed its quality relative to CADe and surgical AI. METHODS MEDLINE/PubMed, EMBASE-OVID, Cochrane, and IEEE Xplore were searched following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses checklist (CRD420261320279). Studies applying AI to kinematic data in gastrointestinal endoscopy were eligible. Risk of bias used Cochrane Risk of Bias 2, Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies-2, and PROBAST + AI; certainty of evidence used GRADE. RESULTS Fifty-eight studies were included. Evidence generation was asymmetric: (1) Randomized controlled trial ratio approximately 5:1 (> 40 vs 8); (2) Patient ratio approximately 4:1 (> 27000 vs approximately 6200); (3) Annual publication ratio approximately 12:1; and (4) ≥ 6 vs 0 regulatory approvals favoring diagnostic AI. Withdrawal speed monitoring and coverage/blind-spot mapping reached moderate GRADE certainty, but all 8 randomized controlled trials were from China and 6 of 8 used the ENDOANGEL platform. The remaining six domains have not reached moderate certainty: (1) Workflow recognition and skill assessment are approaching clinical readiness; and (2) Autonomous navigation, robotic control, simultaneous localization and mapping/three-dimensional reconstruction, and instrument tracking remain at the engineering stage. Comparison with surgical AI indicated that the gap reflects ecosystem-level factors – absence of open datasets, benchmarking challenges, and regulatory pathways for motion-acting AI – rather than technical immaturity. CONCLUSION Kinematic AI addresses exposure errors that CADe cannot correct and has shown additive benefit alongside CADe. Two domains are ready for geographically diverse validation; six remain at the engineering stage. Priorities are open datasets, benchmarking infrastructure, and dedicated regulatory pathways for motion-acting AI.
authors: Eun Jeong Gong; Chang Seok Bang; Jae Jun Lee

title: Artificial intelligence for ophthalmic vessel segmentation: from multimodal imaging to clinical translation
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-based vessel segmentation converts color fundus photographs, scanning laser ophthalmoscopy (SLO), optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA), structural OCT, and anterior-segment images into quantitative vascular biomarkers. Strong performance within individual datasets has not consistently yielded reliable clinical measurements because errors can arise during acquisition, anatomical preprocessing, vessel extraction, biomarker calculation, and deployment. This structured narrative review compares segmentation tasks involving retinal vascular trees, OCTA capillary plexuses, the structural choroid and choriocapillaris, macular neovascularization, corneal neovascularization, and conjunctival microvasculature. We assess modern architectures in relation to vessel geometry, severe foreground-background imbalance, scale variation, crossings, and susceptibility to artifacts. The methods considered include multiscale feature pyramids, deformable and directional operators, Transformers, state-space models, diffusion approaches, and foundation models. We organize the synthesis around five evaluation levels: pixel overlap, centerline recovery, vascular topology, biomarker agreement, and clinical actionability. Public fundus and OCTA datasets are catalogued with their acquisition and annotation characteristics, and gaps in public anterior-segment vessel benchmarks are discussed. Because devices, data splits, labels, and post-processing differ substantially, reported metrics are summarized without ranking studies against one another. The review distinguishes structural OCT choroidal vascularity index from OCTA choriocapillaris flow-deficit mapping, as well as true vessel segmentation from global hyperemia grading. Clinical translation will require ocular-magnification correction, quality control of retinal layers and projection artifacts, external testing across devices and populations, out-of-distribution rejection, DICOM/PACS interoperability, prospective impact studies, and regulation as software as a medical device. We conclude that clinical utility depends on an auditable pipeline that measures structural error, biomarker uncertainty, and failure states throughout the workflow.
authors: Lingyan Wu; Jiahao Tang; Shanping Zhao

title: Artificial intelligence for vascular minimally invasive surgery: techniques, clinical integration, and challenges
abstract: Introduction: Minimally invasive surgery (MIS), including endovascular and robot-assisted procedures, is widely used for vascular pathologies but remains limited by technical complexity, cognitive workload, and postoperative complications. Artificial Intelligence (AI) may help address these challenges through predictive analysis, decision support, image analysis, and automation. Methods: A structured Google Scholar search was conducted from February 21, 2025, to January 1, 2026, and updated through September 2026. Peer-reviewed studies applying AI to vascular MIS were included, with additional targeted searches addressing clinical translation, deployment, regulation, and ethical considerations. Results: Thirty primary studies were analyzed, including eight on machine learning, nine on deep learning, four on natural language processing, and nine on robotics or reinforcement learning. Machine learning supported risk stratification and outcome prediction, deep learning enabled imaging and segmentation applications, natural language processing facilitated clinical information extraction, and robotic systems supported navigation and procedural assistance. Discussion: AI demonstrates substantial potential across the vascular MIS pathway, but broader clinical adoption requires stronger validation, prospective multicenter studies, standardized reporting, health-economic evaluation, and careful consideration of regulatory, liability, and accessibility challenges.
authors: Cenk Jiang; Bogdan Bortnovskii; Ijaz Gul; Mehmed Özkan; Lian Zhang; Dongmei Yu; Vijay Pandey; Runming Wang; Jian Wu; Peiwu Qin

title: Artificial intelligence in chronic atrophic gastritis: A comprehensive review
abstract: Chronic atrophic gastritis (CAG) is a significant precancerous condition associated with gastric cancer, and its accurate diagnosis and comprehensive management are of great importance for reducing the risk of gastric cancer. In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has advanced rapidly in the field of digestive diseases, offering new approaches for the intelligent diagnosis and treatment of CAG. Early studies suggest that AI may improve diagnostic performance and assist in risk stratification. However, whether these systems reduce clinician workload or improve patient outcomes remains to be established. Most evidence comes from retrospective diagnostic accuracy studies, and no AI system has yet been incorporated into clinical guidelines. This review summarizes the research progress of AI in CAG, focusing on five key aspects: Assisted diagnosis, pathological interpretation, Helicobacter pylori infection diagnosis, risk prediction, and patient management. It aims to provide a reference for research on CAG and to highlight priorities for future research and clinical translation.
authors: Nuoya Zhou; Qi Luo; Wei Liu; Xiang-Lei Yuan; Huan Jiang; Bing Hu

title: Artificial intelligence in diabetes: Clinical applications across the disease continuum.
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly shaping the landscape of diabetes mellitus (DM) care by enabling data-driven approaches to prediction, diagnosis, classification, and management. The growing availability of continuous biometric data from wearable technologies, combined with advances in machine learning, has created new opportunities to overcome limitations of traditional diabetes metrics and population-based care models. This review summarises current clinical applications of AI in DM, with a focus on translational relevance and, critically, on the level of validation and clinical readiness of each application. AI-based models have demonstrated improved performance in predicting DM onset and diabetes-related complications by integrating electronic health records, imaging data, and longitudinal clinical variables. In diagnosis and screening, AI offers non-invasive and scalable tools, including automated retinal screening systems and emerging digital biomarkers. Data-driven clustering approaches have further refined diabetes classification. In diabetes management, AI supports personalised glucose monitoring, insulin titration, pharmacological decision-making, and lifestyle interventions. Crucially, these applications differ markedly in maturity: autonomous retinal screening and closed-loop insulin delivery are approaching or have reached routine clinical use, whereas voice-based biomarkers and simulation-evaluated lifestyle systems remain proof-of-concept. Addressing challenges of generalisability, data quality, interpretability, and ethical governance through robust validation and explainable AI will be essential to realise the full potential of AI in precision, patient-centred diabetes care.
authors: Serena Shih Yin; Viola Viola; Paolo Pozzilli
venue: Journal of diabetes and its complications

title: Artificial intelligence in diabetic retinopathy: From deep learning to foundation models, clinical translation, and real-world deployment.
abstract: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) remains a leading cause of preventable vision impairment worldwide, with its burden increasing in parallel with the global diabetes pandemic. As a progressive microvascular disorder with neurovascular unit involvement, DR is driven by retinal ischemia, inflammation, and pathological neovascularization, while diabetic macular edema (DME) continues to represent a principal cause of vision loss. This structured narrative review provides a critical synthesis of advances in diabetic retinopathy diagnosis, retinal imaging, treatment strategies, and artificial intelligence(AI)-enabled screening published from January, 2020, through March, 2026, while selectively incorporating earlier landmark studies to provide clinical and methodological context. We summarize contemporary screening pathways and emerging retinal imaging modalities, including ultra-widefield photography (up to ∼200° field of view), optical coherence tomography (OCT), and OCT angiography, examining how complementary structural and vascular biomarkers are reshaping disease severity assessment and DME characterization. We then review the evolution of AI methodologies, highlighting a transition from task-specific convolutional neural network pipelines toward transformer-based and self-supervised representation learning, including retina-specific foundation models designed to reduce annotation burden and improve robustness and generalizability under domain shift. Beyond algorithmic performance on curated benchmarks, we emphasize key translational requirements for clinical adoption, including model calibration, uncertainty-aware triage, image quality control, and external validation across imaging devices and diverse populations. Recent prospective and implementation studies across diverse healthcare systems demonstrate that the real-world effectiveness of AI-enabled DR screening depends not only on diagnostic accuracy but also on image gradability, clinically appropriate operating thresholds, uncertainty management, external validation, referral capacity, and integration with established care pathways. Evidence from the Asia-Pacific region provides important examples of these implementation challenges in heterogeneous and resource-constrained screening environments. Specific attention is given to the identification and mitigation strategies for fundus pigmentation-related performance disparities and the governance of autonomous versus hybrid human-AI screening models within evolving regulatory frameworks. Finally, we examine emerging work in oculomics for systemic risk stratification and propose a pragmatic clinical readiness framework centered on validation hierarchy, safety monitoring, and workflow integration. Particular emphasis is placed on the translational readiness of foundation models, multimodal retinal intelligence, and emerging technologies for large-scale screening, therapeutic decision-making, and longitudinal disease monitoring.
authors: Basanta Haobijam; Tourangbam Harishore Singh; Puyam Tondonba Singh; Wei-Chi Wu; Eugene Yu-Chuan Kang; Sinam Ajitkumar Singh; Anzila Laikhuram; Cheng-Ming Huang; Wei-Che Huang; Peng-Po Chun; Zhou-Yu Qin

title: Artificial intelligence in digestive diseases: Current evidence and clinical perspectives
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming the field of gastroenterology, providing new ways to diagnose, risk-stratify, and therapeutically manage a wide variety of gastrointestinal diseases. Machine learning and deep learning algorithms are among the AI-based models that have shown promise in non-invasive fibrosis assessment, early detection of hepatocellular carcinoma, prediction of disease severity in pancreatitis, and polyp detection during endoscopy. We searched major databases, including Scopus, EMBASE, PubMed/MEDLINE, and Web of Science, and analyzed current studies on AI in gastroenterology. The integration of AI with imaging modalities, electronic health records, and multi-omics data has led to greater diagnostic accuracy and individualized patient care. Yet, these advances have not addressed issues of data quality, algorithm generalizability, interpretability, and clinical integration. Future research will focus on prospective validation of AI, regulation, and implementation to maximize the clinical utility of AI in digestive diseases. AI has the potential to improve patient outcomes, enable personalized medicine, and optimize the overall efficiency of processes involved in gastroenterological care. In this paper, recent literature concerning the use of AI in gastrointestinal endoscopy and the treatment of various gastrointestinal disorders, such as liver and pancreatic diseases, inflammatory bowel disease, and malignancies, was reviewed.
authors: Mehmet Ali Kösekli; Gülali Aktaş

title: Artificial intelligence in gastroenterology practice: Current perspectives and emerging prospects
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly changing the landscape of gastroenterology by improving disease detection, diagnosis, risk stratification, prognostication, and clinical decision-making. Machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, large language models, and multimodal data integration have facilitated the development of accurate diagnostic and predictive algorithms for a wide spectrum of gastrointestinal and hepatopancreatobiliary diseases. In upper gastrointestinal diseases, AI has enhanced the detection and characterization of gastroesophageal reflux disease, Barrett’s esophagus, esophageal cancer, gastric neoplasia, and gastroesophageal varices. The use of AI in capsule endoscopy has facilitated small intestinal mucosal lesion detection and reduced reading time. Computer-aided detection and diagnosis systems have improved adenoma detection and polyp characterization in colorectal diseases, while AI is increasingly being applied to molecular profiling and prognostic modeling in colorectal cancer. In inflammatory bowel disease, AI facilitates more objective endoscopic and histologic assessment, as well as prediction of disease outcome and treatment response. Promising AI-based radiomics, digital pathology, biomarker discovery, and risk prediction models have been emerging in pancreatic, biliary, and liver diseases. Large language models and multimodal AI may further enable integration of heterogeneous information and support personalized decision-making. Computer-aided quality assessment represents an emerging application for standardizing procedural quality in endoscopy. Several AI-assisted platforms have received regulatory approval with ongoing integration into clinical practice. However, limited external validation, population and device-related heterogeneity, dataset bias, interpretability, workflow integration, and uncertain cost-effectiveness remain important barriers to generalizability and clinical adoption. Robust multicenter prospective validation and responsible implementation will be essential to optimize its clinical impact.
authors: Sujata Roy; Arghya Samanta; Arka Banerjee

title: Artificial intelligence in gastrointestinal endoscopy: Current applications, clinical impact, and future perspectives
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy by supporting lesion detection, characterization, and clinical decision-making.This narrative review summarizes current evidence on AI-assisted GI endoscopy, focusing on clinical applications, diagnostic performance, implementation challenges, and future directions.Machine learning and deep learning underpin computer-aided detection systems that identify suspicious lesions and computer-aided diagnosis systems that support their characterization.In colorectal cancer screening, the reviewed evidence highlights improvements in adenoma detection and the potential of AI to support optical diagnosis of colorectal polyps.In upper GI endoscopy, promising applications include the detection of Barrett's esophagus-associated neoplasia, early gastric cancer, and other premalignant lesions.Integration with image-enhanced endoscopy further supports real-time tissue characterization and risk stratification.Beyond lesion recognition, AI applications extend to procedural planning, quality assessment, and clinical decision support.Across these applications, data quality, external validation, and algorithm transparency remain central considerations when interpreting diagnostic performance and assessing clinical applicability.The review therefore emphasizes that successful implementation requires both technical development and careful evaluation within clinical workflows, alongside appropriate ethical and regulatory oversight.AI has substantial potential to advance precision endoscopy; however, its contribution to improved patient outcomes requires further clinical evaluation.
authors: Mirza Kovačević; Asmira Ljuca; Jasmina Smajić; Selma Sijerčić; Ferid Krupic; Semir Klokić

title: Artificial intelligence in ischemic retinopathy: from diagnostic and predictive performance to clinical translation
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being applied to retinal imaging for the detection, characterization, monitoring, and prediction of ischemic retinal disease. This narrative review examines the clinical applications and translational development of AI across retinopathy of prematurity (ROP), diabetic retinopathy (DR), and retinal vein occlusion (RVO). A structured literature search identified 18 primary studies spanning diagnosis and disease characterization, predictive and longitudinal applications, and clinical implementation. AI demonstrated strong performance across several imaging tasks, including plus-disease detection, DR detection and grading, RVO classification, angiographic interpretation, vascular quantification, and image-quality assessment. Predictive evidence of future clinical outcomes was more limited, with studies addressing ROP risk and short-term treatment response in RVO, while separate studies evaluated longitudinal vascular severity assessment in ROP. Translational maturity differed across diseases: DR had the strongest prospective and autonomous screening evidence, ROP had progressed toward quantitative assessment, prediction, and telemedicine support, and RVO remained predominantly at the retrospective development stage. Across all three diseases, high model performance did not necessarily indicate clinical readiness. Generalizability, image quality, interpretability, prospective validation, workflow integration, and evidence of downstream benefit remain important barriers to translation. The clinical value of retinal AI will ultimately depend not on achieving the highest performance metric, but on performing meaningful tasks reliably across settings and improving how patients are evaluated, referred, monitored, and treated.
authors: Fapianey J. Alexandre; Aleah J. Brokemond; Ronny Amamoo; Sewedo B. Ajisegiri; Briah Bailey; Pamela Moore Martin; Ravirajsinh Navalsinh Jadeja; Menaka Chanu Thounaojam

title: Artificial intelligence in odontology education
abstract: Introduction: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being explored in dental education as a tool to support teaching, learning, assessment, and clinical decision-making. This systematic review synthesized current evidence on the implementation and educational impact of AI technologies in undergraduate, postgraduate, and continuing dental education. Methodology: A PRISMA-guided systematic review was conducted using Scopus, PubMed, and IEEE Xplore. Studies published between 2020 and 2025 evaluating AI applications in dental education were identified using predefined PICO criteria. Educational outcomes included knowledge acquisition, diagnostic accuracy, clinical reasoning, procedural skills, learner engagement, and perceptions of AI-assisted learning. Results: The included literature reflects an expansion from machine learning, deep learning, and computer vision systems primarily evaluated for diagnostic support toward generative AI platforms, including large language models and retrieval-augmented generation systems. Across the included studies, AI applications were frequently associated with favorable diagnostic and examination performance and, in selected educational contexts, with supportive findings related to clinical reasoning, technical competency, feedback, and self-directed learning. However, the evidence was predominantly based on technical performance assessments and observational or cross-sectional designs. Discussion: AI is increasingly being explored as a potential complementary educational resource, with applications including interactive tutoring, adaptive learning, and support for clinical reasoning. Nevertheless, heterogeneous methodologies and limited longitudinal evidence indicate the need for standardized educational evaluation and responsible curricular integration. Conclusion: AI shows potential as a complementary resource in dental education. Its integration should remain pedagogically guided and ethically supervised while future research establishes its educational effectiveness through standardized and longitudinal evaluation.
authors: María Belén Morales-Cevallos; Canva Byron Ma Lam; Kathy Violeta Serrano Avalos; Mónica Jimena Concha Guailla; Diego Fabián Vique López

title: Artificial intelligence-driven imaging in sickle cell retinopathy: Advancing early detection, risk stratification, and precision ophthalmology
abstract: Sickle cell disease (SCD) is a disorder of genetically inherited red blood cells (RBCs), wherein it is manifested clinically as sickling of RBCs, due to polymerization of hemoglobin S. SCD patients frequently face RBCs clumping, blocking of blood vessels and capillaries along with persistent hemolysis.Sickle cell retinopathy (SCR), is a SCD associated disorder in the peripheral retina, responsible for several features like vasoocclusion, ischemia, vitreous hemorrhage and neovascularization within the retina and adjoining regions.While these are manageable features, some severe cases report retinal detachment and ultimately vision impairment in patients.As early signs of SCR are not usually manifested visually, its early diagnosis becomes the limiting factor for devising effective management strategies in patients.Artificial intelligence (AI) assisted deep learning models have very recently being utilized and provides a promising alternative in assisting early diagnosis, staging, and monitoring disease progression.Traditional retinal imaging methods like fundus photography, fluorescein angiography, optical coherence tomography and optical coherence tomography angiography scans have always assisted ophthalmologists to make clinical decisions for patients.Recently, these methods were being used to train AI models for easy and efficient analysis of such scans.As a growing field, works in this area have transitioned our understanding of image analyses and promises a fast, objective and efficient interpretation.This review discusses; how traditional methods captures structural damages to peripheral retina and summarizes recent research work done in this field to integrate AI driven models based on deep learning and machine learning.We summarize here AI based strategies for SCR screening and diagnosis, while underlining their clinical applicability, utilities and future translational promises towards ascertaining personalized ophthalmology.
authors: Tarun Sahu; Deepankar Mondal; Yashwant Kumar Ratre; Henu Kumar Verma

title: Artificial intelligence-driven precision management of Helicobacter pylori: an integrated framework from endoscopy and multi-omics to vaccine design and digital care
abstract: Helicobacter pylori ( H. pylori ) infection, affecting half of the world’s population, is the principal cause of peptic ulcer disease and gastric cancer, yet its clinical management is increasingly undermined by the rapidly escalating global burden of antibiotic resistance, the suboptimal accuracy of conventional diagnostic methods, and the declining efficacy of empirical therapeutic regimens. Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly reshaping this landscape, but existing research remains fragmented across single modalities. We propose a conceptual five-module framework that integrates AI approaches across the H. pylori care continuum: (1) global disease burden and the evolutionary dynamics of H. pylori drug resistance; (2) the application of multimodal AI, from convolutional neural networks to vision-language foundation models, for endoscopic early screening, pathological identification, and functional assessment; (3) the harnessing of machine learning (ML) on genomic and electronic health record data to decipher resistance mechanisms and generate personalized eradication regimens; (4) AI-driven vaccine target discovery and generative design, spanning reverse vaccinology to de novo immunogen creation; and (5) a digital closed-loop patient management platform that leverages new media and reinforcement learning to enhance adherence and eradication rates. We further delineate the core challenges of data bias, cross-scenario generalization, and the critical absence of prospective randomized evidence, and propose a future direction anchored in multimodal foundation models, federated learning, and continuous AI quality improvement. Rather than an established clinical pathway, this framework is proposed as a conceptual blueprint that, once prospectively validated, could upgrade AI-enabled H. pylori care from isolated image recognition toward an end-to-end “perception–reasoning–intervention” system, offering a blueprint for precision prevention and control.
authors: Minglin Zhang; Nuonan Lv; Yanghui Cao; Lingqiao Lou; Ting Cai; Jiaxing Zhu; Yingting Xu; Xuelin Zhao; Zhiyuan Ma; Xuemei Liu
venue: Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology

title: Assessing Clinical Reasoning in Dentistry: Proposal of a Multimodal Framework and Rubric‐Based Assessment Tool
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Clinical reasoning represents a core competence in dental education, enabling students to translate theoretical knowledge into patient-specific diagnostic and therapeutic decisions. Despite its importance, assessment in dental curricula often focuses on final outcomes rather than on reasoning processes that lead to them. This paper proposes a structured framework designed to make clinical reasoning explicit, observable and potentially assessable in educational settings. MATERIALS AND METHODS: A conceptual model for assessment of clinical reasoning in dentistry was developed based on contemporary theories of clinical reasoning in health professions education. It integrates multimodal clinical cases (anamnesis, clinical findings, diagnostic imaging), a structured Clinical Reasoning Sheet guiding students through reasoning steps and a rubric-based assessment system. Six dimensions of reasoning are evaluated using a four-level performance scale, generating both dimensional profiles and an overall reasoning score. A complementary taxonomy of cognitive errors is included to support educational interpretation of students' reasoning difficulties. RESULTS: The proposed framework operationalises clinical reasoning into defined and observable components intended to support systematic evaluation of how students identify findings, interpret clinical data, integrate information, generate and revise hypotheses, align diagnostic reasoning with treatment planning and justify their decisions. DISCUSSION: By combining structured case analysis, rubric-based evaluation and cognitive error identification, the model provides educators with a transparent tool to analyse reasoning processes rather than final answers alone. This approach could support formative feedback, targeted remediation and integration of reasoning assessment across the dental curriculum. CONCLUSIONS: The proposed schema offers a structured and educationally grounded approach to assessing clinical reasoning and provides a foundation for future validation and multicenter implementation.
authors: Giorgia Lanzaretti; Thiago de Oliveira Gamba; Leopoldo Forner; Marius Gheorghe Bud; Ada Gabriela Delean; Francesca Zotti

title: Assessment architecture, scoring, and evidence of quality in objective structured clinical examinations in dental education: a scoping review
abstract: This scoping review mapped the design, scoring, implementation, and quality assurance of objective structured clinical examinations (OSCEs) in dental education. The review followed Joanna Briggs Institute guidance and the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews. Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, PubMed/MEDLINE, ERIC, Embase, and LILACS/BVS were searched through July 25, 2026. Of the 940 records identified, 129 full-text reports were assessed and 63 studies were included. The most frequently reported evidence concerned station design, blueprinting, scoring, examiner calibration, reliability, and psychometric performance. Fewer studies examined standard setting, fairness and potential construct-irrelevant variance, classification accuracy, economic feasibility, or the consequences of high-stakes decisions. Virtual and electronic OSCEs supported assessment continuity and structured evaluation of diagnostic reasoning, interpretation, communication, and decision-making; however, they should not be assumed to replace direct observation when technical or psychomotor performance is the main target. The dental OSCE literature now encompasses both isolated station-based examinations and broader assessment systems. Future research should establish which combinations of assessment design, scoring, examiner preparation, psychometric evaluation, fairness analysis, and decision rules provide defensible evidence for specific educational purposes.
authors: Fernando Mauricio Espada-Salgado; Tatiana Ramírez-Mora; Bogdan Oprea; María Mihaela Iuga
venue: Journal of Educational Evaluation for Health Professions

title: Augmenting colonoscopy with artificial intelligence and robotic assistance: a human-factors scoping review toward a task-based shared autonomy paradigm
abstract: Colonoscopy is central to colorectal cancer prevention but remains a high-demand psychomotor and cognitive procedure, characterized by operator dependency, variable performance, and substantial physical and mental workload. Increasing evidence links procedural quality and safety to clinician-related factors, including musculoskeletal strain, fatigue, and non-technical skills. Concurrently, artificial intelligence (AI) and robotic technologies are emerging as potential tools to address these limitations. We conducted a scoping review with narrative synthesis of literature on human factors, ergonomics, AI, robotic technologies, and shared autonomy in colonoscopy and surgical robotics. Evidence synthesis: Colonoscopy performance remains limited by non-negligible miss rates and variability driven by both technical and human factors. Ergonomic constraints and cognitive workload contribute significantly to operator strain and may affect vigilance and decision-making. AI systems-including computer-aided detection (CADe), diagnosis (CADx), and quality monitoring-have demonstrated improvements in detection metrics and procedural standardisation, although concerns regarding cognitive offloading and potential deskilling persist. In parallel, emerging robotic and soft-robotic platforms aim to enhance navigation, improve procedural ergonomics, and reduce operator musculoskeletal strain, although clinical evidence remains limited. These technologies converge within a task-based shared-autonomy paradigm integrating physical, perceptual, and cognitive augmentation, with different procedural tasks operating at different levels of human-system control. A task-based shared-autonomy framework may provide a coherent model for integrating AI and robotics into colonoscopy while preserving human supervision and clinical judgement. Future developments should prioritise human-centred design, workflow integration, and multidimensional evaluation strategies to ensure safe and effective clinical implementation.
authors: Luigi Manfredi; Alfredo Annicchiarico; Gianpiero Gravante

title: Author’s Reply: “PREFERENDO: a preference for the full picture in pediatric capsule endoscopy”
abstract: We thank Koulaouzidis and colleagues for their thoughtful and constructive comments on the video capsule endoscopy (VCE) domain of the PREFERENDO consensus [1,2]. Their proposals provide useful additional granularity to several reporting elements already included in the framework and offer an opportunity to clarify the intended scope of the PREFERENDO recommendations.
authors: Andrea Chiaro; Sara Renzo; Paolo Gandullia

title: Automated Dental Calculus Mapping and Burden Estimation Using Deep Learning
abstract: Background Dental calculus is a primary etiological factor in periodontal disease, disproportionately affecting underserved populations with limited access to professional dental care.
