Automated photographic oral disease screening tools may help bridge this access gap by enabling early identification of calculus burden in community, school-based, and remote settings. Methods A ResNet-50 encoder integrated within a U-Net segmentation architecture was trained on intraoral photographic images sourced from a public dataset. The dataset was partitioned into training (1,361 images; 66.5%), validation (584 images; 28.5%), and an independent held-out test set (103 images; 5.0%), with the test set withheld from all model development decisions. Manual polygon segmentation masks were created using CVAT. A pixel-area calculation technique was developed to estimate the percentage of tooth surface covered by calculus. Architecture comparisons were conducted against a standard U-Net (no pretraining), VGG16/U-Net, and EfficientNet-B4/U-Net under identical training conditions. Results On the held-out test set, the model achieved a Dice coefficient of 0.731 (95% CI: 0.706–0.756), IoU of 0.698 (95% CI: 0.671–0.724), recall of 0.714, and specificity of 0.971. The pixel-level ROC-AUC was 0.931 (95% CI: 0.918–0.944) however, this value is inflated by background pixel dominance and should be interpreted alongside Dice and IoU as primary segmentation metrics. The proposed architecture outperformed all three comparators. Validation-set metrics (Dice 0.743, IoU 0.712) were modestly higher than test-set values, as expected given reduced optimization bias on unseen data. Conclusions This proof-of-concept study demonstrates that deep learning can support automated dental calculus screening from photographic images. Findings are preliminary and subject to important limitations including non-clinician annotation and a single public dataset source. With further clinical validation, such tools may contribute to scalable oral health monitoring in tele-dentistry workflows, school dental programs, and community health initiatives.

title: Automated Lewis Score Estimation for Small Bowel Crohn Disease Using Capsule Endoscopy: Retrospective Cohort Study
abstract: Background Small bowel capsule endoscopy (SBCE) is widely used to evaluate small bowel involvement in Crohn disease (CD); however, manual Lewis score calculation is time-consuming and susceptible to interobserver variability. Objective This study aimed to develop and preliminarily validate a multitask deep learning system for automated Lewis score estimation in patients with small bowel CD undergoing SBCE. Methods We developed Eval-Model, a multitask framework integrating You Only Look Once (YOLO)–style lesion detection and localization for ulcers and edema, a stenosis classification branch, and a long short-term memory–based temporal regression module. The primary dataset comprised SBCE examinations from 814 patients at the Children’s Hospital of Fudan University. In this dataset, 725 (89.1%) cases were included for lesion-level annotation, and 89 (10.9%) cases with expert-consensus Lewis scores were used for scoring model development and internal testing. These 89 cases comprised 49 (55.1%) training cases and 40 (44.9%) internal test cases. All splits were performed at the patient level. A retrospective same-center temporal validation cohort of 20 consecutive cases from 2026 and 5 control cases were used for preliminary assessments of temporal robustness and specificity. Results In the 40-case internal Lewis score test set, Eval-Model achieved a mean squared error of 14.693 (95% CI 8.72-22.15), root mean squared error of 3.833 (95% CI 2.95-4.71), mean absolute error of 2.9 (95% CI 2.1-3.8), R2 of 0.82 (95% CI 0.70-0.90), and explained variance of 0.83 (95% CI 0.72-0.91). For lesion recognition, the model achieved an overall mean average precision of 0.94 with an inference time of 15 ms per frame. In the 20-case same-center temporal validation cohort, the mean squared error was 26.848 (95% CI 12.51-45.33), the root mean squared error was 5.182 (95% CI 3.54-6.73), the mean absolute error was 3.3 (95% CI 2.2-4.6), R2 rounded to 1.00 (95% CI 0.98-1.00), and the explained variance rounded to 1.00 (95% CI 0.98-1.00). These temporal estimates require cautious interpretation because of the small, same-center cohort. Conclusions Eval-Model demonstrated preliminary feasibility for automated Lewis score estimation from SBCE in small bowel CD. The system may serve as a standardized adjunct to expert review, but larger multicenter prospective validation with independent external annotation is required before clinical deployment.
authors: Yingying Meng; Min Gao; Jie Wu; Ying Huang

title: Automatic Trajectory Planning from Preoperative MRI images Using the AI-Optimized RRT* Algorithm for Robotic Breast Ultrasound
abstract: Ultrasound imaging is the most widely used technique for detecting and diagnosing breast cancer, as it provides real-time images in a non-invasive and inexpensive manner. However, performing ultrasound examinations requires experienced and well-trained operators either for probe manipulation during acquisition or during image interpretation, which makes this technique dependent. This dependency requires the employment of sonographers with extensive training and experience, which may limit access to this technique in remote areas and also expose experts to serious health issues due to repetitive movements. To overcome these difficulties, robotic ultrasound systems have emerged in recent years to enable conventional ultrasound examinations to be performed in an automated and standardized way. Our study contributes to this field through an integrated approach to automated planning of robotic breast ultrasound trajectories. This approach is based on the application of a developed version of the rapidly-exploring random tree (RRT) trajectory planning algorithm to pre-operational threedimensional (3D) magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) images. We performed simulations with the three versions of the algorithm RRT, RRT* and RRT* with 30% reinforcement learning (RL) on two different patients. The results obtained demonstrate the potential of the RRT algorithm with 30% RL to obtain optimized trajectories with high fluidity and a short path while ensuring total and homogeneous coverage adapted to different complex breast morphologies.

title: Autonomous Reconfigurable Modular Conductive Hydrogels for Adaptive and Degradable Bioelectronic Interfaces
abstract: Bioelectronic interfaces are increasingly used in medical devices for tissue stimulation and sensing. Transient bioelectronics seek the same functionality in temporary systems, yet most available materials are nondegradable, stiff, and require surgery or external removal. Achieving tissue‐like softness, smooth injectability, stable mixed conductivity, and reliable short‐term bioresorption within a single biocompatible matrix remains challenging. Here, we decouple injectability from bulk conductive performance using a modular reconfiguration strategy. High‐filler‐content hydrogels are converted into lyophilized modules that can be resuspended, injected through a standard syringe, and then autonomously reassemble in situ into a cohesive conductive network, recovering 90% of conductivity after freeze–drying, fragmentation, and reconfiguration. The platform uses a fully degradable tannic‐acid‐crosslinked poly(vinyl alcohol) matrix with molybdenum and molybdenum trioxide nanoparticles as co‐functional fillers. Mixed ionic/electronic conduction arises from redox‐active tannic acid–Mo(VI) complexes (ionic transport) and semi‐percolated Mo nanoparticles (electron hopping). The optimized formulation matches extracellular‐matrix mechanics (Young's modulus 0.03 MPa; failure strain 998%) and fully degrades within 120 h under simulated physiological conditions. In a human skin explant wound model, conformal integration enables charge transfer, reaching 0.02 A at across a 1 cm defect.
authors: Matthew K. Burgess; Zofia B. Wolny; Zekun Liu; Karolina Cysewska; Malavika Nair

title: Autonomous navigation of multiple reconfigurable ferrofluid droplet robots in complex environments
abstract: Ferrofluid-based soft robots with extreme deformability have emerged as promising manipulation tools for diverse biomedical applications. Their unique properties to navigate irregular terrains and access otherwise unreachable regions within confined spaces have enabled new opportunities in targeted drug delivery, microfluidic logistics, and lab/organ on-a-chip. However, achieving dynamic motion planning and intelligent behavior for multiple reconfigurable ferrofluid droplet robots (FDRs) is still one of the major challenges yet to be solved. In this paper, we develop a novel framework that integrates dynamic path planning with adaptive motion control for teams of deformable FDRs to autonomously navigate through diverse scenarios involving moving obstacles. We first introduce a distributed magnetic field actuation platform capable of generating a series of local magnetic field sources to enable discrete locomotion and extreme deformation of multiple FDRs. Subsequently, an incremental version of the conflict-based search (CBS) algorithm, called the ICBS, is presented, which aims at finding conflict-free paths for more than one agent (i.e., FDR) and updating the plan according to changes in the environment or missions. To quantitatively describe different behaviors of FDRs and realize adaptive morphology transition, an image-guided motion-deformation controller combined with a finite state machine (FSM) is then designed. The physical and actuation constraints associated with the system are also considered for FDRs in close proximity so that they can smoothly traverse the planned waypoints in the form of localized step-by-step. Finally, extensive simulations and experiments are performed under different conditions to validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the deployed FDRs are capable of fully automated navigation with adaptive morphology transitions (stretching, splitting, and merging) in various complex environments.
authors: Guangming Cui; Xianrui Zhang; Zhenping Yu; Ang Liu; Juntian Qu

title: Autonomous osteogenesis in autotransplanted teeth in areas with severe bone deficiency: a case series
abstract: The aim of this case series is to demonstrate the clinical efficacy of autotransplantation across three distinct scenarios of severe bone insufficiency: congenitally missing teeth with tooth impaction in the upper left quadrant (Case 1), a complete unilateral cleft (Case 2), and an extensive horizontal and vertical bone defect associated with lower second premolar agenesis (Case 3). All cases demonstrate the regenerative potential of the periodontal ligament, which promotes osteogenesis around autotransplanted teeth. This biological mechanism enables new bone formation and soft tissue remodeling around the transplant without requiring additional bone grafting or guided bone regeneration membranes, even in areas with pre-existing significant bone atrophy. This unique effect is documented on the post-treatment cone-beam computed tomography images in all cases.

title: Awareness and Acceptance of AI In Dental Radiology Among Undergraduate Dental Students in Telangana
abstract: Aim : This study was done to know the awareness and acceptance of AI in dental radiology among undergraduate dental students in Telangana. Objectives :To assess the awareness, perception, acceptance, knowledge of the benefits and limitations, and willingness to adopt artificial intelligence (AI) in future dental practice among undergraduate dental students. Materials and Methods: A structured questionnaire of 15 questions was made, online google form were circulated to all the dental colleges in Telangana, students were asked to fill the forms and the responses were recorded, the questions are categorized in to 3 sections under knowledge, Attitude/ Acceptance and Future. Results: After the survey the total number of responses were 293, among them number of Third year students were 115, Final year students were 94, Internship students were 84. Conclusion: This study concluded that dental students have good awareness and a generally positive attitude towards Artificial Intelligence in dental radiology among undergraduate dental students.

title: BGAFS-UNet: adaptive feature fusion via boundary guided sampling for retinal vessel segmentation
abstract: Introduction Retinal vessel segmentation is difficult because fundus images contain branching structures, scale variation, uneven illumination, lesions, and weak vessel boundaries. Methods We propose BGAFS-UNet, combining Boundary Perception Module (BPM), Lightweight Wide Gated Attention (LWGA) with Dynamic Channel Allocation (DCA) and Adaptive Branch Fusion (ABF), Cross-Stage Fusion (CSF), Contextual Mixing (ContMix), and Attention-Guided Dynamic Sampling (AGDS). We evaluate three prespecified image-disjoint runs on DRIVE, STARE, and CHASE and use image-level paired tests with Holm correction on DRIVE. Results The full model obtains F1 scores of 80.61% on DRIVE, 76.15% on STARE, and 79.53% on CHASE. On DRIVE, corrected improvements are metric- and vessel-scale-specific: boundary F-score, clDice, and large-vessel Dice are significant, whereas Dice and small-vessel Dice are not. Discussion BGAFS-UNet is parameter-efficient but not unconditionally more efficient, with higher FLOPs and latency than U-Net; the findings support structure-aware segmentation while motivating broader cross-device validation and optimization. The code and reproducibility materials remain available at https://gitee.com/Zhangguoce/bgafs-net.git , fixed at commit 477b217990f68d43d5c1c8f3a818d8cf2c8af384.
authors: Guoce Zhang; Zhezhe Zhu; Aizimaiti Xiaokaiti

title: BOPPPS Instructional Framework Embedding Case‐ and Problem‐ Based Strategies in Oral Pathology Education: A Teaching Reform Study
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Oral pathology education requires students to master both foundational theoretical knowledge and clinical diagnostic reasoning, yet conventional lecture-based instruction provides limited opportunities for structured participatory learning that actively engages both dimensions. This study evaluated the pedagogical effectiveness of the BOPPPS instructional framework-a six phase teaching model comprising bridge-in, objective, pre-assessment, participatory learning, post-assessment, and summary-within an oral pathology curriculum. Within this framework, case-based learning (CBL) and problem-based learning (PBL) were integrated as complementary and overlapping pedagogical strategies and incorporated into phases of the BOPPPS framework, forming a unified, discipline-adapted teaching approach. METHODS: A total of 206 undergraduate oral medicine students were randomly assigned to the reform group (the BOPPPS instructional framework integrating case- and problem-based strategies) or a traditional lecture-based control group. Outcomes and learning experience were assessed through theoretical examination scores, experimental diagnostic image-recognition performance, and student satisfaction questionnaire respectively. RESULTS: Compared with the control group, students in the reform group achieved significantly higher average scores on the oral pathology theoretical examination (adjusted p < 0.001). In the pathology experimental course, the reform group also demonstrated improved overall performance, particularly on items assessing clinical reasoning skills (adjusted p < 0.05). Students also reported high satisfaction with the instructional experience, with the mean overall learning outcome self-assessment score reaching 4.5 out of 5. CONCLUSIONS: The BOPPPS instructional framework with embedded case- and problem-based strategies was associated with improved theoretical examination performance and diagnostic image interpretation in oral pathology. Students also reported high satisfaction with the learning experience.
authors: Jiaxin Yang; Yanan Sun; Li Wang; Shaodong Yang; Jiali Zhang

title: Beyond Conventional Endoscopy: The Diagnostic Challenge of Small-Bowel Angiodysplasia
abstract: Introduction Identifying the source of gastrointestinal bleeding remains challenging when conventional endoscopic investigations yield negative results. In elderly patients, small-bowel vascular lesions represent an important but potentially overlooked cause of significant blood loss. This case highlights the diagnostic value of video capsule endoscopy in revealing a suspected bleeding source despite an otherwise inconclusive conventional workup. Case Presentation A 71-year-old woman with a medical history of arterial hypertension, treated with perindopril and receiving antiplatelet therapy with low-dose acetylsalicylic acid (Aspenter), presented with melena and severe anemia, with a hemoglobin concentration of 6.0 g/dL. The clinical presentation raised concern for significant gastrointestinal blood loss, prompting further diagnostic investigations to identify the underlying bleeding source. Initial evaluation included upper gastrointestinal endoscopy and colonoscopy, neither of which revealed an identifiable source of bleeding. Contrast-enhanced abdominopelvic computed tomography was subsequently performed but showed no significant gastrointestinal abnormalities that could explain the severity of the anemia. Despite this extensive conventional diagnostic workup, the origin of the gastrointestinal bleeding remained undetermined. Given the discrepancy between the severity of the patient's clinical presentation and the absence of identifiable lesions on conventional investigations, further evaluation of the small bowel was pursued using video capsule endoscopy. The examination revealed two angiodysplastic lesions located in the jejunum, visualized approximately 3 hours and 28 minutes after capsule ingestion. These findings provided a plausible explanation for the patient's melena and profound anemia, suggesting jejunal angiodysplasia as the most likely source of gastrointestinal bleeding. Conclusion Severe gastrointestinal bleeding with negative bidirectional endoscopy should prompt consideration of a small-bowel source, particularly in elderly patients. This case demonstrates how video capsule endoscopy can reveal clinically relevant vascular lesions after an inconclusive conventional workup, highlighting the importance of a systematic diagnostic approach to suspected small-bowel bleeding.

title: Beyond Discrete Tokens: Preserving Numerical Continuity in Medical Vision-Language Models
abstract: Objective: To develop a unified vision-language model for prompt-conditioned quantitative ultrasound measurement that addresses the mismatch between continuous measurement targets and discrete token-based numerical prediction. Methods: This article presents HAD-VLM, a hybrid autoregressive-diffusion framework that combines autoregressive text generation with continuous measurement prediction within a shared backbone. Visual prompt tuning adapts the vision encoder to ultrasound images. A diffusion process predicts a five-component representation comprising caliper endpoint coordinates and measurement length. A post-processing strategy combining the proposed coordinate-length consistency mechanism with ensemble prediction is introduced to refine measurement estimates. We evaluate four echocardiographic measurement tasks on EchoNet-LVH, with additional assessments of medical question answering and X-ray vertebral measurement. Results: HAD-VLM achieves mean absolute errors of 1.36, 2.77, 3.05, and 1.16 mm for IVSd, LVIDd, LVIDs, and LVPWd, respectively, reducing errors by 21.4-37.6\% relative to the Vicuna-based autoregressive baseline. It also outperforms fine-tuned Qwen3-VL and direct MLP regression across all four tasks. Medical question answering performance is preserved on the evaluated dataset. For X-ray vertebral measurement, HAD-VLM reduces mean absolute error from 11.4 to 6.7 pixels. Conclusion: Integrating autoregressive language generation with diffusion-based continuous prediction improves quantitative medical image measurement while retaining prompt-conditioned task flexibility. Significance: HAD-VLM provides a unified approach to combining language interaction with anatomically grounded numerical prediction for quantitative medical image analysis.
authors: Dianye Huang; Jiamei Guo; Yue Zhou; Mingde Li; Yi Xiong; Wei Wang; Nassir Navab; Zhongliang Jiang

title: Beyond the Antibiotic Paradigm: A rare case of Hospital-Acquired Clostridioides difficile Infection without Antibiotic Exposure
abstract: Introduction Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI) is classically recognised as a major healthcare-associated complication, directly tied to prior systemic antibiotic therapy. However, emerging evidence highlights that host immunosuppression and prolonged hospitalization can occasionally also trigger CDI in completely non-antibiotic-exposed patients. This case report aims to highlight an atypical and deceptive presentation of CDI, highly representative of significant diagnostic and infection-control challenges. Case Presentation A 67-year-old female, with no other recent hospitalization, was admitted in October 2025 with primary hypertension for rectorrhagia and severe anemia (hemoglobin concentration, 7g/dL). A comprehensive diagnostic workup, including abdominal ultrasound, thoracoabdominal CT, upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, video capsule endoscopy, colonoscopy and rectosigmoidoscopy, was performed after bowel preparation with Macrogol 4000. The investigations revealed congested, ulcerated internal hemorrhoids, colonic diverticula and small gastric and jejunal angiodysplasias, though no active bleeding site was found. Notably, the patient received no systemic antibiotic therapy neither during hospitalization, nor before being admitted. On day 13 she developed acute diarrhea (>3 stools/24 hours) and through antigen detection and nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT/PCR), followed by toxin A/B enzyme immunoassay (EIA), the CDI diagnosis was established. Prompt contact isolation protocols and oral vancomycin (125 mg four times daily) were initiated. The patient experienced rapid clinical resolution of diarrhea within seven days, showed significant recovery of hemoglobin levels to 10 g/dL at discharge and no recurrence occurred at 30 days. Conclusion This case challenges the dogma that CDI requires antecedent antimicrobial exposure, initial hospitalization for gastrointestinal bleeding can be complicated by an infectious pathology, independent of the reason for presentation. Clinicians should maintain a high index of suspicion in regards to acute-onset diarrhea and prompt immediate evaluation for CDI, regardless of antibiotic administration history to ensure prompt diagnosis, timely targeted treatment and stringent institutional outbreak prevention.

title: Beyond the duodenum and the ampulla: addressing the classification and diagnostic challenges of jejunal and ileal tumours
abstract: Primary tumours of the jejunum and ileum are uncommon despite the distal small intestine representing most of the length and mucosal surface area of the gastrointestinal tract. Their relative rarity, limited endoscopic accessibility and often non-specific clinical presentation mean that many lesions are diagnosed only after symptoms, complications or surgical resection. This review summarises the principal tumour-forming conditions of the distal small intestine, including developmental heterotopias, hamartomatous and syndromic polyps, benign epithelial precursors, adenocarcinoma, neuroendocrine neoplasms, mesenchymal tumours and lymphoid proliferations. Emphasis is placed on malignant epithelial, neuroendocrine, stromal and haematolymphoid neoplasms, with discussion of their characteristic gross, histological, immunophenotypic and molecular features. Attention is given to diagnostic pitfalls, including pseudoinvasion in Peutz-Jeghers polyps, dysplasia arising in chronic inflammatory or immune dysregulation settings, differences of small intestinal adenocarcinoma from colorectal carcinoma, grading of neuroendocrine tumours and separation of aggressive intestinal T-cell lymphomas from indolent lymphoproliferative disorders. Integrated assessment using morphology, targeted immunohistochemistry and molecular testing is essential for accurate classification, prognostication and therapeutic stratification. Improved endoscopic, imaging and genomic approaches are likely to refine diagnosis and management of these challenging and anatomically remote neoplasms.

title: Bibliometric Data and Validation-Evidence Mapping of Robotic Ultrasound-Guided Biopsy, Ablation, and Access (2000–2025)
abstract: This repository provides supporting data and reproducibility materials for a bibliometric analysis and publication-level validation-evidence map of robotic ultrasound-guided biopsy, ablation, and access. The analysis integrates PubMed and Web of Science Core Collection records, comprising 857 unique bibliographic records after deduplication. The focused Master corpus includes 197 publications, of which 184 were classified as direct-validation reports. The deposited materials include publication-level classification matrices, application categories, V0–V3 validation settings, ablation technology pathways, supplementary data tables, and available plotting scripts and TXT data matrices. Validation settings describe the highest reported experimental or human evaluation within each publication. They should not be interpreted as clinical maturity, independent clinical trials, or unique patient cohorts. The deposited data and scripts are provided to support transparency and reproducibility. Redistribution of proprietary Web of Science records and copyrighted full-text articles is excluded.

title: Bibliometric Mapping of Transforaminal Research in Clinical Neurology: Publication Trends, Intellectual Structure, and Global Collaboration Networks
abstract: Objective: This study aimed to reveal the bibliometric profile, conceptual structure, and scientific collaboration patterns of articles containing the term “transforaminal” in their titles in the Web of Science (WoS) Clinical Neurology category. Methods: The title field was searched for “transforaminal” in WoS (data retrieved on 23 September 2026); 1,430 records restricted to the Clinical Neurology category and Article document type were analyzed. Publication distributions by year and journal and the most cited studies were assessed through performance analysis; keyword co-occurrence and institutional and country-level co-authorship analyses were performed using VOSviewer. Results: Publication output increased particularly after 2013 and peaked at 129 publications in 2025. World Neurosurgery was the most productive journal, with 222 publications (15.524%). Most of the highly cited publications concerned transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion (TLIF). In the keyword network, “transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion” was the most central concept, with 476 occurrences and a total link strength of 1,226. The United States stood out at the country level with 594 publications, 18,910 citations, and a total link strength of 122; China and South Korea were also major centers of output. Conclusion: Although transforaminal research has historically centered on TLIF, minimally invasive/endoscopic surgery, decompression, radiculopathy, and interventional pain management are prominent themes, with selected endoscopic keywords more frequently represented in recent publications. The findings show that publication productivity, citation impact, and international collaboration represent distinct bibliometric dimensions.
authors: Eylem Burcu Kahraman Özlü

title: BioMARS 2.0: a robotic biologist for formulating and adapting biological experiments
abstract: Biological experimentation is not reducible to a single optimization problem, but requires decisions at multiple levels of abstraction: translating scientific knowledge into experimental procedures, adapting culture conditions to measured phenotypes and selecting interventions that test biological hypotheses. Automating experimental execution does not, by itself, determine which experiments should be performed next or how they should change in response to biological feedback. Here we introduce BioMARS, a human-in-the-loop multi-agent robotic system that connects knowledge-guided experimental decision-making with robotic execution and biological feedback. At the procedural level, BioMARS generated literature-grounded protocols and traceable action plans, improving expert-reviewed protocol quality scores across four model backends. At the parametric level, BioMARS used image-derived phenotypes from robotic retinal organoid culture to select subsequent experimental conditions, with higher reported scores in later rounds of the three-round experiment. At the intervention level, BioMARS nominated drug-repurposing candidates from biomedical evidence and advanced six candidates to wet-lab testing by researchers. Together, these studies demonstrate feedback-driven robotic biological experimentation within a framework that supports decisions about experimental procedures, culture conditions and biological interventions.

title: Biodigital Transformation in Dentistry: From Diagnosis and Biological Preservation to Multidisciplinary Rehabilitation
abstract: Advances in digital technologies have expanded diagnostic and treatment possibilities in dentistry while making the preservation of biological tissues and collaboration among specialties increasingly important. This book, *Biodigital Transformation in Dentistry: From Diagnosis and Biological Preservation to Multidisciplinary Rehabilitation*, was prepared to address these developments from an integrated perspective. It follows a scientific progression from biodigital diagnosis and clinical decision-making to preventive care in pediatric dentistry; from the preservation of the pulp and natural dentition to periodontal and orthodontic treatment; and from digital prosthetic planning to implant-supported rehabilitation. Written by contributors from different dental specialties, the chapters examine both the clinical applications and the limitations of current technologies. We hope this book will serve as a valuable resource for dental students, residents, academics, and clinicians, and we thank all the authors for their knowledge, time, and contributions.

title: Bioinspired soft enteroscopic robot for intestinal locomotion, steering, and intervention
abstract: Diagnosing and treating small intestinal disorders such as bleeding, inflammatory bowel disease, and tumors present challenges because of limited access to this anatomical compartment. We present BIOSENTER, a bioinspired soft enteroscopic robot for deep procedures in the small intestine that addresses locomotion, steering, and intervention constraints of existing soft robotic systems. BIOSENTER features a hollow cylinder architecture comprising a linearly deformable soft pneumatic actuator as the body, two radially expandable soft pneumatic actuators wrapped with kirigami sleeves as the head and tail, a central hollow channel for accessory endoscopic tools, and a control box for navigation. Inspired by snake locomotion, the robotic body incorporates a fiber-reinforced actuator with four embedded inflatable chambers, enabling steering and axial expansion. The dynamic kirigami sleeves generate an anchoring force of ∼1.5 newtons on intestinal mucosa while requiring substantially less radial expansion than the corresponding nonkirigami configuration. A reinforced central channel supports tool passage for diagnostic and therapeutic interventions. The control box enables locomotion and steering at autonomous speeds of ∼100 millimeters per minute in vitro and ∼43 millimeters per minute in tissue-covered tubing. BIOSENTER successfully navigated the collapsed, tortuous small intestine for 2 meters in 11 minutes, with gentle forward pushing forces of 2.2 to 6.4 newtons in pig studies. In vivo pig studies demonstrated technical feasibility of tissue biopsy, localized fluid delivery as a model for future drug administration, and real-time visualization of the deep intestine, without macroscopic overdistention or visible tissue damage under the tested conditions.
authors: Binbin Ying; Ahmad Mujtaba Jebran; Sahab Babaee; Karen Jiang; Brenda D. Fernandez Martinez; Haniyah Shareef; Mohammed Talha Faiz; Andrew Pettinari; Kailyn Schmidt; Niora J. Fabian; Alison M. Hayward; Giovanni Traverso

title: BronchoVR: An Immersive VR Simulation for Bronchoscopy and Fibreoptic Intubation Training
abstract: Fibreoptic intubation (FOI) is an important airway-management skill that requires anaesthetists to navigate a flexible scope through patient-specific anatomy using an indirect, monitor-mediated view. Developing proficiency requires hands-on practice, yet opportunities for clinical training are limited. We present BronchoVR, an immersive VR training prototype developed through consultation with practising specialist anaesthetists and informed by the FOI literature. BronchoVR provides an operating-theatre environment and integrates a patient-specific airway model reconstructed from CT, monitor-mediated scope navigation, and a gamified precision task for practising scope-control skills. These features address requirements for anatomical realism, indirect visual guidance, and psychomotor training. BronchoVR supports rehearsal of FOI navigation and scope handling while preserving the monitor-mediated viewing and hand–eye coordination used during FOI.
authors: Muhammad Saad Khan; BRIAN J. ROBINSON; Stuart Marshall; Joaquim Armando Jorge; Craig Anslow

title: Bronchoscope Tip Localization With Learned Airway Constraints and an Open Source Simulator
abstract: Accurate bronchoscope localization is challenging because airway images contain limited texture and similar views across branches. We present BronchoLoc, a learning‐based framework that combines monocular video with a preoperative CT centerline graph to estimate the 3D bronchoscope tip position. Local visual tracking and global sequence context constrain predictions to the airway anatomy. The accompanying open‐source BronchoSim simulator generates synchronized images, depth, and trajectories (Traj) for training and evaluation. Averaged across Traj, localization RMSE was 5.65 mm in simulation with 82.8% branch selection accuracy and 8.72 mm in the physical phantom. Together, BronchoLoc and BronchoSim provide a framework for developing and evaluating image‐based airway localization.
authors: Emanuele Nicotra; James Davies; Bibhu Sharma; Adrienne Ji; Kefan Zhu; Phuoc Thien Phan; Nigel Hamilton Lovell; Thanh Nho Do

title: CAD/CAM Technologies, Three-Dimensional Printing, and Contemporary Dental Materials
abstract: CAD/CAM technologies have transformed the production of fixed prosthodontic restorations from a craft based on manual skill into a standardized and measurable digital process. This chapter addresses, for dental students in their clinical years and for early-career clinicians, the fundamental principles of CAD/CAM systems, digital and artificial intelligence-assisted restoration design, milling and three-dimensional printing technologies, contemporary restorative materials, the factors influencing material selection, accuracy and quality control in digital manufacturing, and the biocompatible and smart materials of the future, in the light of the current and verified literature. The digital workflow comprises three interdependent links—data acquisition, design, and manufacturing—and the quality of the final restoration is limited by the weakest link in the chain. Although milling remains the gold standard for definitive restorations, additive manufacturing has become established for interim restorations, models, and surgical guides, and it is a rapidly maturing alternative for definitive restorations. On the material side, the rise of monolithic zirconia, the diversification of lithium silicate glass-ceramics, and the establishment of resin-matrix ceramics in minimally invasive applications offer the clinician a broad range of options with varying levels of evidence. Current systematic-review and meta-analytic evidence shows that AI-assisted design shortens design time and improves reproducibility, but that human oversight remains indispensable. Clinical success depends on manufacturing the right material with validated parameters for the right indication and applying it with an appropriate adhesive or conventional cementation protocol. Accuracy should be defined by its trueness and precision components, marginal fit should be evaluated against clinical acceptability thresholds, and quality control should be maintained at every link of the digital chain. The graded, bioactive, self-healing, and stimuli-responsive materials of the future, together with additively manufactured ceramics, signal a transition from passive to smart materials in restorative dentistry.
authors: Muhammed Mustafa Akar; Alptuğ Kendirci

title: CBAM-Enhanced MaxViT-Tiny for Gastrointestinal Endoscopy Image Classification: Robustness, Explainability, and External Validation
abstract: Automated classification of the huge number of images generated during gas-trointestinal (GI) endoscopy is required for reliable and interpretable diagnosis but there is concern about the vulnerability of deep models to adversarial perturbations. In the current study, a MaxViT-Tiny backbone and a Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) head are used for 8-class classification of the Kvasir endoscopic images. After deleting the duplicate images, there are 3,996 images, which were split into 3 sets: 70% as the training set, 15% as the validation set, and 15% as the test set; the model was compared with 5 backbones with the same CBAM head under 3 random seeds. This resulted in the highest test accuracy of 94.33%, a macro F1 score of 0.9431, and a macro area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.9975, with a mean accuracy of 93.72 1 ± 1.06% across all the seeds. The attacks of white-box FGSM, PGD, CW-L2, and MI-FGSM greatly affected the accuracy, and the adversarial fine-tuned accuracy under FGSM attack was 74.17%, adversarial accuracy under PGD attack was less than 4% and adversarial accuracy under MI-FGSM attack was less than 4%, showing poor cross-attack generalization. A preliminary attack detector has been able to obtain an AUC of 0.857. Sometimes, clinically relevant regions were identified by Grad-CAM++, Score-CAM, and GradientSHAP, which also sometimes focused on non-anatomical artefacts. This means that achieving focused attention-augmenting and high accuracy on clean images does not necessarily mean that the accuracy of the adversarial images is also high, and that the explanation is good without adversarial training; it needs to be further verified by independent datasets and multi-center validation before applying to the clinical environment.

title: CROPS: Cosserat-Rod-Based Co-Design of Soft Slender Programmable Material Systems for Biomedical Applications
abstract: Programmable slender structures that deform in response to external stimuli represent a class of emerging material systems, with applications in soft robotics, minimally invasive surgery, wearable electronics, and deployable structures. In biomedical applications, the on-demand design of slender structures, encompassing both their material layout and actuation, is instrumental in leveraging their large deformation and multiphysics actuation for meeting patient-specific design requirements. However, owing to geometric and material nonlinearities, their structure-actuation-response relationship is highly non-intuitive and entails resource-intensive computation. This renders trial-and-error and conventional design approaches largely intractable for addressing patient-specific needs. To this end, we present a Cosserat-rod-based design optimization framework for the autonomous design of programmable slender structures. Capitalizing on the Cosserat rod representation, the end-to-end differentiable framework is demonstrated on two case studies: (i) design of swellable stents that morph to the shape of carotid vessels; (ii) co-design of the remnant magnetization and the applied field of magnetically-active catheters to reduce the force exerted on the patient-specific vessel wall during insertion. As the actuation types, the swelling of gel-elastomer composites and the magnetic actuation of hard-magnetic composites are considered. Additionally, the contact of the rod with itself and its surroundings is accounted for. The proposed framework presents an autonomous design platform for material-structure-actuation co-design of soft slender material systems that support large deformation and multiphysics actuation, with contact addressed.
authors: Aaditya Chandrasekhar; Lee, Dex Doksoo; Kwon, Hyunwoo; Li, Shicheng; Chen, Wei

title: Capsule Endoscopy Practice Patterns in Africa and the Middle East: A Multinational Assessment of Access, Utilization, and Diagnostic Yield أنماط ممارسة التنظير الداخلي بالكبسولة في إفريقيا والشرق الأوسط: تقييم متعدد الجنسيات لإمكانية الوصول والاندماج
abstract: Capsule endoscopy (CE) is the reference non-invasive modality for small bowel evaluation, with established roles in obscure gastrointestinal bleeding, iron deficiency anemia, and inflammatory bowel disease. Despite its clinical utility, access and utilization remain uneven globally, particularly in low- and middle-income regions. Aim: To evaluate the availability, utilization patterns, quality indicators, diagnostic yield, complications, and barriers to capsule endoscopy across Africa and the Middle East.Methods: A multinational cross-sectional web-based survey was conducted among physicians involved in small bowel disease management The questionnaire assessed demographic and institutional characteristics, CE availability, clinical indications, procedural practices, quality metrics, diagnostic outcomes, and perceived barriers. Results: A total of 407 physicians from 17 countries participated, the majority being gastroenterologists (80%). Obscure gastrointestinal bleeding was the most common indication. Quality monitoring was inconsistent, with limited reporting of optimal mucosal visualization and completion rates, and diagnostic yield was not routinely audited in most centers. The majority reported diagnostic yield in the range of 30–50% for obscure bleeding. Capsule retention was encountered by 16.7% of respondents, with most cases managed conservatively. Centers with CE were significantly associated with tertiary care settings and gastroenterology specialization (p<0.001). Higher diagnostic yield was associated with longer program duration, better mucosal visualization, higher completion rates, and greater clinician experience. Major barriers included high cost, limited availability, lack of insurance coverage, and insufficient trained personnel.Conclusion: Capsule endoscopy remains underutilized across Africa and the Middle East, with significant disparities in access and variability in quality practices.

title: Capsule endoscopy: Emerging technologies and future clinical applications
abstract: Capsule endoscopy has evolved from a diagnostic tool for small bowel evaluation into a complex platform with expanding diagnostic and prognostic potential. This mini review aims to summarize recent advances in capsule endoscopy and explore potential clinical applications and future directions of this technology. The introduction of pan-enteric capsule endoscopy has enabled comprehensive evaluation of the entire gastrointestinal tract in a single, minimally invasive examination, supporting treat-to-target approaches and improving disease phenotyping in inflammatory bowel disease. Artificial intelligence (AI) represents one of the most important recent developments in capsule endoscopy. Deep learning algorithms have demonstrated high accuracy in lesion detection while reducing reading times. More recently, AI has been applied to automated inflammatory activity scoring, bowel cleansing assessment, and computer-assisted reporting, facilitating standardized interpretation and improving report quality. Magnetically controlled capsule endoscopy has further expanded the role of capsule technology by enabling active navigation within the upper gastrointestinal tract. Recent innovations include detachable-string systems for esophageal examination, remote 5G-assisted capsule navigation, and integration with AI-assisted image analysis, opening new perspectives for noninvasive evaluation from mouth to anus. Experimental robotic capsule prototypes have explored the feasibility of interventional functions, including tissue sampling and targeted drug delivery. These technologies remain at the preclinical stage, and their potential clinical applicability requires further investigation.

title: Carbon dots derived from traditional Chinese medicines: a novel therapeutic strategy for ocular diseases
abstract: and in acute animal studies. They also exhibit distinctive optical properties and diverse pharmacological activities. Synthesized via eco-friendly green routes using traditional Chinese medicines (TCMs) and their extracts, TCM-derived carbon dots (TCM-CDs) display distinct properties compared to conventional nanocarriers. Benefiting from their inherent nanostructures, abundant surface functional groups, and nanozyme-like activity, TCM-CDs can deliver intrinsic therapeutic effects without loading exogenous drugs or relying on residual herbal ingredients. They possess multiple bioactivities, including antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antibacterial and neuroprotective effects, which make them potential non-invasive therapeutic candidates for refractory ocular disorders. A growing body of studies has validated the promising therapeutic efficacy of TCM-CDs in animal models against autoimmune uveitis, retinal lesions, and optic nerve injuries, highlighting their encouraging preclinical findings that warrant further investigation toward clinical translation. Focusing on the intrinsic therapeutic capacity of TCM-CDs, this review systematically summarizes their core functional mechanisms and research progress in ocular disease intervention, discusses prevailing academic controversies and unresolved research bottlenecks in this field, and proposes prospective developmental directions. This work intends to offer comprehensive theoretical evidence and guidance directions for subsequent mechanistic investigations and clinical translation of TCM-CDs in ophthalmic research.

title: Catalytic Design Logic of Nanozymes for Periodontitis: Linking Enzyme-Mimetic Activity to Antibacterial, Immunomodulatory, Regenerative and Diagnostic Outcomes
abstract: Periodontitis is a chronic inflammatory disease caused by the dental plaque formed due to bacterial imbalance. It is widespread and a major cause of tooth loss. Existing standard methods (mechanical debridement and systemic antibiotic administration) still have considerable limitations in clearing the biofilm, combating drug resistance, or managing the complex, multifactorial inflammatory microenvironment. Nanozymes, as a class of nanomaterials with intrinsic enzyme-mimicking catalytic functions, have many advantages: greater stability, lower cost, scalability, and wide applicability. The discussion links nanozyme design and catalytic mechanisms with periodontal immunopathology, including Th17/regulatory T cell imbalance, dendritic cell maturation, and inflammaging. The five therapeutic dimensions involved—antibacterial activity of reactive oxygen species, antioxidant cascades (superoxide dismutase–catalase–glutathione peroxidase multi-enzyme system and the Ce 3+ /Ce 4+ redox cycle), macrophage-mediated immune regulation, stem cell–guided tissue repair, and biosensing—are all related to nanozymes. Besides periodontitis, the review also summarizes the potential therapeutic effects of nanozymes on other oral problems, according to the latest research progress. All studies of nanozyme-based periodontal therapy discussed in this review are preclinical, and no registered interventional clinical trials of nanozymes for periodontitis were identified. Clinical translation remains constrained by substrate availability, local retention and biofilm access, together with long-term biosafety, reproducible production and regulatory requirements. Further development requires aligning catalytic activity with periodontal conditions and validating therapeutic benefit and safety under clinically relevant conditions.
authors: Zeng Fan; Yi Li; Huiya Huang; Jili Chen

title: Chronic Ileoileal Intussusception Causing Abdominal Pain in an Adolescent
abstract: Background and Clinical Significance: Intussusception is a condition in which part of the intestine slides into another adjacent section and causes obstruction. It classically presents with acute, intermittent abdominal pain and is typically diagnosed with abdominal ultrasound. However, the intussusceptum can be missed if the patient is outside of an acute episode. Case Presentation: A 15-year-old male presented with 5 weeks of intermittent periumbilical pain with associated 10-pound weight loss. Abdominal exam revealed a non-tender, non-distended abdomen without hepatosplenomegaly. Cardiorespiratory exam and labs were normal. Over the next 7 months, his abdominal pain worsened and required multiple hospitalizations. Capsule endoscopy revealed small intestine inflammation and magnetic resonance enterography (MRE) showed intestinal loop invagination. Subsequently, exploratory laparoscopy identified an ileoileal intussusception; ileal resection and end-to-end anastomosis were performed and the patient fully recovered. Conclusions: Intussusception in older patients can present atypically with a more chronic course. Diagnostic imaging provides only a single snapshot in time with the potential to miss transient disease processes; thus intussusception should remain on the differential diagnosis for unexplained chronic abdominal pain.
authors: Nicole P. Mirabadi; Jessica Chen; Lawrence Ma

title: Classifier-Pruned Bayesian Optimization for Particle Accelerator Tuning: Exploring Temporally Structured Manifold of 6D Beam Phase Space
abstract: Complex dynamical systems, such as particle accelerators, require tuning over high-dimensional, nonlinear state and parameter spaces while experimental measurements and high-fidelity simulations can be expensive. Learned latent representations provide a compact domain for such optimization, but poorly supported regions of the learned manifold may decode into unrealistic physical states and yield deceptively favorable objectives. To address this challenge, we propose the Classifier-pruned Bayesian Optimization-based Latent-space Tuner (CBOL-Tuner), which performs Bayesian optimization over a temporally structured latent representation of 6D beam phase-space dynamics. The CBOL-Tuner integrates a conditional variational autoencoder for latent space representation, a long short-term memory network for temporal dynamics, a lightweight neural network for parameter estimation, and a classifier-pruned Bayesian optimizer to adaptively search and filter the latent space for optimal solutions. This framework enables feasibility-aware exploration of learned scientific representations for accelerator tuning.
authors: Mahindra Rautela; Alan Williams; Alexander Scheinker

title: Clinical and CBCT Based Evaluation of Residual Ridge Length in Posterior Partially Edentulous Mandibular Arches for Dental Implant Planning
abstract: Dental implants have proved to be one of the most reliable methods for treating partially edentulous patients.Successful placement of dental implants in posterior regions of the mandible requires careful evaluation of ridge length, width, and height of residual bone relative to the inferior alveolar nerve and mental foramen.Clinical examination alone does not give an exact idea of the residual ridge anatomy due to morphological variations and ridge resorption following tooth extraction.Cone Beam Computed Tomography (CBCT) is an important diagnostic tool providing high-resolution, three-dimensional images of the alveolar bone with minimal distortion and radiation.This research discusses the significance of residual ridge length analysis for implant therapy in posterior partially edentulous mandibular arches, the anatomy of ridges, methods for evaluating ridge length, importance of CBCT in implantology, patterns of ridge resorption, measurements, clinical application, disadvantages, and prospects of digital planning in implant therapy.The article concludes by comparing clinical examinations with radiographic techniques in ridge length determination and concludes that radiographic examinations prove better than clinical methods.Importance of digital workflow integration, guided implant surgery, and artificial intelligence-based imaging to enhance implant treatment results is also pointed out in the article.Evaluation of the residual ridge length becomes vital in defining the size of the implant, its inclination angle, number of implants, and necessity of performing bone augmentation.

title: Clinical characteristics and prognosis of emergency enteroscopy for small bowel bleeding in hospitals of different levels: A real-world study based on 297 cases from provincial, municipal, and district hospitals
abstract: Background and aims: This study aimed to compare the clinical characteristics, diagnostic efficiency, lesion detection spectrum, and follow-up outcomes of emergency enteroscopy for obscure small bowel bleeding among provincial, municipal, and district hospitals. Methods: This was a multicenter retrospective analysis of 297 consecutive patients who underwent emergency enteroscopy for obscure small bowel bleeding at a provincial hospital (n = 240), a municipal hospital (n = 25), and a district hospital (n = 32). Baseline data, ward type on admission, pre-procedural examinations, enteroscopy completion rate (total enteroscopy), endoscopic diagnoses, treatment modalities, complications, and follow-up data were collected and compared. Results: The provincial hospital admitted the highest proportion of patients to the intensive care unit (ICU) (21.3%) and performed more comprehensive pre-procedural examinations. The total enteroscopy completion rate was significantly higher at the provincial hospital (87.92%) than at the municipal (68.0%) and district (46.88%) hospitals. In terms of disease spectrum, the provincial hospital predominantly managed Crohn’s disease (33.3%), Meckel’s diverticulum (16.7%), and small bowel vascular malformations (12.5%), whereas municipal and district hospitals showed a narrower disease spectrum. Endoscopic therapy was the most common treatment across all levels. Follow-up data indicated that the provincial hospital had a lower rebleeding rate and better long-term prognosis. Among cases of incomplete enteroscopy, “bowel loop tortuosity” was a significantly more frequent cause of failure at the municipal and district hospitals. Conclusions: Significant differences exist in the diagnostic and therapeutic capacity of emergency enteroscopy and patient composition across hospital levels. Provincial hospitals demonstrate clear advantages in procedural efficiency, lesion detection, and treatment outcomes. Establishing standardized care pathways for small bowel bleeding and strengthening technical support for primary hospitals are crucial for improving overall clinical care.

title: Cognitive digital twins: A state-of-the-art review
abstract: Digital twins are a key enabling technology for Industry 4.0/5.0 that provide digital representations of physical systems for monitoring and decision-making support. However, the increasing complexity, autonomy, and connectivity of modern industrial systems challenge traditional digital twin approaches focused on simple replication. Therefore, advanced capabilities that go beyond mirroring physical assets are required to enable simulation, optimization, prediction, and adaptive behavior. Cognitive digital twins extend the capabilities of traditional digital twins by integrating cognitive functions such as perception, attention, memory, reasoning, problem-solving, and learning through artificial intelligence techniques, including machine learning. This review considers the differences between cognitive and traditional digital twins, and investigates the operationalization of cognitive functions. It examines how algorithms, software, tools, and frameworks are implemented for cognitive digital twins through a systematic literature review conducted using the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) methodology. Moreover, it identifies current advancements; maps cognitive functions to applications; highlights underrepresented functions and implementation gaps in interoperability, validation, and learning infrastructure; and establishes opportunities for standardized evaluation and modular cross-sector designs.
authors: Naveed Shahzad; William Dias Ferreira; Bassant Selim

title: Colon capsule endoscopy and cost-effectiveness across colorectal care: a valuable filter, but a poor universal substitute.
abstract: Colon capsule endoscopy (CCE) is a patient-friendly, minimally invasive alternative to conventional colonoscopy, but its value depends on pathway performance rather than diagnostic accuracy alone. This narrative review examines the cost-effectiveness of CCE across colorectal cancer screening, symptomatic investigation, incomplete colonoscopy, post-polypectomy surveillance, inflammatory bowel disease monitoring, and AI-supported implementation. Targeted literature searches were performed in PubMed and official guidance sources through 6 July 2026. Across broad screening populations, CCE is not yet cost-effective compared with biennial faecal immunochemical testing (FIT) or 10-yearly colonoscopy; contemporary Dutch MISCAN modelling found all CCE screening strategies dominated at full adherence, largely because unit cost and follow-up colonoscopy burden remained high. The dominant economic problem is pathway duplication: a 2025 meta-analysis found a pooled follow-up endoscopy rate of 42%, and contemporary UK/Scottish service data showed that about half of patients required further optical endoscopy or sigmoidoscopy. CCE may offer conditional value after incomplete colonoscopy, in lower-risk symptomatic triage, and in carefully selected surveillance pathways where a negative or low-risk capsule result may avoid, defer, or focus colonoscopy. Evidence from Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis monitoring is encouraging but should not be extrapolated uncritically to colorectal cancer screening or dysplasia surveillance, where biopsy and therapy remain decisive. AI-assisted CCE may reduce reading time and improve polyp detection, but robust lifetime cost-effectiveness models are still needed. The current evidence supports CCE as a pathway-dependent filter, not a universal substitute for colonoscopy.
authors: Anastasios Koulaouzidis; Ian Io Lei; Ramesh Arasaradnam; Rami Eliakim

title: Colonic diseases: epidemiology, risk factors, diagnosis, and prevention (Global trends and data from Kazakhstan). A literature review
abstract: Relevance. Colorectal cancer, Crohn’s disease, ulcerative colitis, and colonic polyposis are major public health problems. These diseases reduce quality of life, increase disability and healthcare costs, and affect screening policy. Population aging, urbanization, and lifestyle changes have altered their incidence and age distribution in many countries. This burden makes their epidemiological assessment particularly important for public health planning, prevention, early detection, and organization of appropriate healthcare services. Objective. To summarize recent evidence on the epidemiology, risk factors, diagnosis, and prevention of major colon diseases worldwide and in Kazakhstan, with attention to regional differences and gaps in knowledge. Evidence was considered globally and nationally to provide comparative perspective. Methodology. A structured narrative literature review was conducted using PubMed, Scopus, eLibrary, and Google Scholar. The initial literature search was performed from June to August 2025, and the evidence base was subsequently updated to include relevant publications available through October 2026. The review primarily covered literature published between 2015 and 2026, with earlier landmark studies included where appropriate. Eligible sources comprised original research articles, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, clinical guidelines, authoritative reference materials, and official epidemiological and statistical reports. A total of 89 sources were included in the final narrative synthesis. Results. Colorectal cancer remains a major contributor to cancer incidence and mortality worldwide and in Kazakhstan. According to GLOBOCAN 2024 estimates, colorectal cancer accounted for 3,598 new cases (12.1% of all estimated cancer cases) in Kazakhstan. National statistical data demonstrated regional differences in colorectal cancer incidence and the continued occurrence of advanced-stage disease. Colorectal carcinogenesis involves chromosomal instability, microsatellite instability, and serrated neoplasia pathways, while hereditary syndromes contribute to increased individual risk. Advances in image-enhanced endoscopy, artificial intelligence-assisted colonoscopy, capsule endoscopy, and molecular testing offer additional diagnostic opportunities. However, gaps remain in population-based epidemiological data on inflammatory bowel diseases and colonic polyposis in Kazakhstan. Conclusions. The reviewed evidence highlights the importance of risk-factor modification, organized colorectal cancer screening, early detection and removal of precancerous lesions, and risk-adapted surveillance of individuals with hereditary predisposition. For Kazakhstan, priorities include improving screening quality, strengthening national cancer registration and epidemiological monitoring, expanding access to diagnostic services, and developing population-based research on inflammatory bowel diseases and colonic polyposis. Modern diagnostic technologies should complement established clinical pathways rather than replace colonoscopy and histological examination. Keywords: colorectal neoplasms, Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis, intestinal polyposis, epidemiology, Kazakhstan.

title: Community-based implementation and feasibility of portable ophthalmic diagnostic devices: a quasi-experimental pre-post study in underserved areas
abstract: Portable ophthalmic diagnostic devices have emerged as promising tools to improve access to eye care in underserved communities; however, their agreement with conventional equipment and real-world implementation feasibility remain insufficiently evaluated. This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic agreement of two portable ophthalmic devices and their real-world implementation feasibility in an underserved rural community. We conducted a two-phase study consisting of an in-hospital agreement study and a community-based implementation study. In the in-hospital phase, a smartphone-based portable slit lamp (TopSlit) and a handheld all-in-one imaging device (Reticapture) were compared with conventional stationary equipment in 72 patients with ocular diseases. Agreement was assessed using Cohen’s κ, intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC), and Spearman’s correlation. In the community-based phase, 124 residents aged ≥ 60 years from 10 underserved rural villages underwent baseline ophthalmic screening and a 6-month follow-up assessment. The primary endpoint was the 30-day hospital-visit completion rate among referred participants; secondary outcomes assessed implementation feasibility and participant acceptability, while longitudinal visual-acuity and patient-reported outcomes were exploratory. TopSlit and Reticapture showed moderate to almost perfect agreement with conventional reference equipment (κ = 0.535–0.944). Among 60 participants referred for further evaluation, the 30-day hospital-visit completion rate was 53.3% (32/60; 95% CI, 40.9–65.4%), exceeding the prespecified 40% feasibility threshold (exact p = 0.047). No upload/network or image-quality failures occurred during field implementation, and no additional image reacquisition or remote-grader requests for additional images were required. Participant satisfaction with the program was high (92.9%). These findings support the feasibility and acceptability of integrating portable ophthalmic devices into a community-based eye-care program in an underserved rural setting. The observed agreement with conventional reference equipment, operational performance, and linkage to follow-up care support further evaluation in larger, rigorously controlled studies. The study was approved by the Dankook University Hospital IRB (DKUH IRB 2022-10-016 (Date of Registration: 2022-10-13; Date of Approval: 2022-11-10) and DKUH IRB 2024-06-016 (Date of Registration: 2024-06-13; Date of Approval: 2024-08-02)). The study was registered at the Clinical Research Information Service (CRIS), Republic of Korea ( https://cris.nih.go.kr ; KCT0012177).
authors: Hoon Kim; 김진호; Sun Kwon Kim; Kyungsun Na; Seok Bum Lee; Won-Cheoul Jang; Kyong Jin Cho

title: Comparative Accuracy of a Commercial Multimodal Large Language Model Versus Clinicians in Dental Age and Sex Estimation from Panoramic Radiographs: A Benchmark Study
abstract: Background/Objectives: Routine dental imaging captures cumulative dentoalveolar and periodontal changes, offering a non-invasive window into both chronological aging and physiological senescence. While task-specific deep learning models have been widely explored in dental radiology, the zero-shot diagnostic performance of commercial Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) in adult populations remains underinvestigated. The aim of this study was to benchmark the zero-shot diagnostic accuracy and repeatability of a commercial MLLM against human clinicians of varying experience levels in estimating adult dental age and biological sex from panoramic radiographs (OPGs), using documented chronological age and biological sex as the ground truth. Methods: From 216 initially screened records, this retrospective single-center study included 127 standardized, anonymized OPGs from patients (74 men, 53 women; mean chronological age 55.5 ± 15.8 years, range 18–90 years) treated at the Clinical Department of Cranio-Maxillofacial Surgery, Military Institute of Medicine—National Research Institute in Warsaw. Each radiograph was independently evaluated across three trials by Gemini 3.1 Pro (Google, Mountain View, CA, USA) and once by two clinicians—a maxillofacial specialist (>10 years of experience) and a resident (<3 years of experience)—all blinded to clinical metadata. Results: Gemini 3.1 Pro demonstrated excellent repeatability across the three trials (ICC(A,1) = 0.926, ICC(A,3) = 0.974; p = 0.156) and moderate agreement with chronological age (ICC(A,1) = 0.604), but systematically overestimated age by a mean of 6.23 years. Mean absolute error (MAE) ranged from 12.91 to 13.03 years across the AI trials. The specialist achieved a significantly lower MAE (10.39 years) than all AI assessments (adjusted p ≤ 0.003), whereas the resident (MAE = 11.19 years) did not differ significantly from the AI (adjusted p = 0.282). In biological sex classification the specialist (66.1%) significantly outperformed all three AI trials (41.7–49.6%), while the resident (62.2%) significantly outperformed the first two AI trials (41.7% and 43.3%), but did not differ significantly from the third trial (49.6%). Across all runs, the AI exhibited significant directional asymmetry (p < 0.001), frequently misclassifying male patients as female. Conclusions: While Gemini 3.1 Pro demonstrated high internal repeatability and age-estimation accuracy comparable to a junior resident, its wide limits of agreement, systematic age overestimation, and poor sex-classification accuracy preclude its autonomous use in clinical or forensic workflows. Future studies incorporating healthy control cohorts and validated clinical indices are required to determine whether the observed age overestimation reflects inherent algorithmic miscalibration or sensitivity to cumulative dentoalveolar pathology in hospitalized patients.
authors: Dominika Zawadka-Modras; Maria Sobol; Kevin Du; Dariusz Jurkiewicz; Aldona Chloupek

title: Comparative Evaluation of Multiple Deep Learning Models for Six-Class Keratitis Classification
abstract: Purpose: Keratitis can be classified as infectious or noninfectious, with infectious keratitis being a major cause of blindness. In this study, multiple deep learning (DL) models were applied to perform six-class classification of corneal lesions, and their diagnostic performance was systematically compared. Methods: We analyzed 3797 slit-lamp images from six categories: normal cornea, bacterial keratitis, fungal keratitis, viral keratitis, Acanthamoeba keratitis, and non-infectious keratitis. Convolutional neural network (CNN), transformer, self-supervised, and vision-language models were evaluated at image and patient levels using patient-level splits, with clinician comparison on a 240-image test subset. Results: RegNet had the best image-level performance (accuracy, 76.8%; macro-F1 score, 75.7%; macro-AUC, 0.946), and EfficientNet_B0 had the highest patient-level accuracy (77.5%; macro-F1 score, 76.6%; macro-AUC, 0.954). On the same 240-image subset, RegNet accuracy was 75.4% versus 72.7%, 56.3%, and 44.4% for senior corneal specialists, junior corneal specialists, and junior general ophthalmologists. Conclusions: CNN-based models showed stable performance under the present image-based evaluation pipeline. RegNet achieved the most balanced image-level results, whereas EfficientNet_B0 showed the strongest patient-level performance. On the same 240-image subset, RegNet showed numerically higher accuracy than clinician-group means. However, performance remains insufficient for autonomous diagnosis and requires external and prospective validation. Translational Relevance: This comparative DL framework could serve as an adjunctive image-based decision-support tool for six-class keratitis classification after further external and prospective validation, which may assist clinicians in early diagnosis and improve decision making in clinical management.
authors: Qian Tan; Yingnan Xu; Yang Zhang; Yuning Wang; Yanwu Xu; Weihua Yang

title: Comparison of Retinopathy Screening Performed Using Conventional Methods and an Artificial Intelligence-Assisted System in Prediabetic and Diabetic Patients: A Single-Center Prospective Analysis
abstract: Background and Objectives: AI-assisted retinal imaging is increasingly proposed to expand diabetic retinopathy (DR) screening capacity, but most validation studies use reading-center standards, exclude prediabetes, and assess macular edema against photographic surrogates rather than optical coherence tomography (OCT). We compared an AI-assisted retinal screening system with routine ophthalmological examination in an unselected internal medicine screening population. Materials and Methods: In this prospective, cross-sectional diagnostic accuracy study, consecutive adults with prediabetes or diabetes underwent AI-assisted retinal imaging (index test) followed by masked ophthalmological examination (reference standard), with OCT as the reference for macular edema. Analyses were performed at the eye level (n = 714) and patient level (n = 357) using Wilson score 95% confidence intervals and Cohen kappa (κ) for agreement. Results: Among 357 patients (714 eyes; 83.8% diabetes, 16.2% prediabetes), DR prevalence by ophthalmological examination was 15.0% (eyes) and 17.9% (patients), versus 24.4% and 33.1% by AI (McNemar p < 0.001). Eye-level and patient-level sensitivity and specificity were 70.1% and 83.7% and 75.0% and 76.1%, respectively. Negative predictive value was high (93–94%) but positive predictive value was low (41–43%); agreement was moderate at the eye level and fair at the patient level (κ = 0.428 and 0.384, respectively). False-positive AI calls were associated with higher HbA1c and albuminuria (adjusted odds ratio for log-transformed ACR 1.23, p = 0.040); false negatives had milder disease. In prediabetes, DR prevalence was 1.7% and agreement was absent (κ = −0.03). AI sensitivity for OCT-defined macular edema was 45.5% (κ = 0.197), with no significant central macular thickness difference by AI status. Conclusions: The AI system showed high negative predictive value but systematically over-called DR, with only fair-to-moderate agreement and performance below accepted screening benchmarks, particularly in prediabetes and for macular edema. These findings support its use as a rule-out triage adjunct with ophthalmological confirmation of positive results, rather than an autonomous substitute, and argue for local recalibration before deployment.

title: Compartment-specific roles of gasdermin D and E in photoreceptor degeneration: evidence and pharmacological implications
abstract: Photoreceptor degeneration arises from diverse genetic and acquired insults, yet oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and sterile inflammation repeatedly converge on membrane injury and irreversible cell loss. Inflammasome activation is frequently described as retinal pyroptosis, although upstream markers alone neither establish gasdermin-dependent lysis nor identify the executing cell. Rather than treating retinal pyroptosis as a single cell-autonomous pathway, we distinguish a myeloid gasdermin D (GSDMD) inflammatory relay from a photoreceptor-intrinsic gasdermin E (GSDME) lytic amplification program and evaluate potential interventions according to direct retinal evidence, cellular specificity, and translational readiness. GSDMD is best supported in microglia and subretinal macrophages, where inflammasome-caspase-1 signaling promotes cytokine and extracellular-vesicle release and can worsen secondary photoreceptor injury. Recent evidence in TREM2-deficient rd10 retina further supports GSDMD as a functional disease modifier, while remaining context specific. By contrast, GSDME has direct loss-of-function support in all-trans-retinal overload, in which caspase-3-dependent cleavage increases membrane rupture and is associated with mitochondrial oxidative burden and ferroptotic susceptibility. We compare NLRP3/caspase-1, interleukin-1, GSDMD pore, GSDME, and redox-directed strategies against five translational gates: target engagement, ocular exposure, cell specificity, delivery feasibility, and safety. This evidence-graded framework identifies promising pharmacological entry points while preserving the distinction between mechanistic plausibility and retinal target readiness.
authors: Ying Deng; Yasha Zhou; 派 周; Li Xiao; Jing Lu; Qinghua Peng; Yijing Yang

title: Complementary Roles of Intestinal Ultrasound and Capsule Endoscopy in Crohn’s Disease: A Prospective Blinded Comparative Study
abstract: Background and Aims: Precise and longitudinal assessment of small-bowel inflammatory activity is essential in Crohn’s disease (CD). Capsule endoscopy (CE) provides comprehensive mucosal evaluation but is limited for routine use by cost and availability. Intestinal ultrasound (IUS) has emerged as a non-invasive, accessible, and complementary imaging modality. This study compared the diagnostic performance of IUS with CE for detecting terminal ileum inflammation. Methods: In this prospective blinded study, adult patients with suspected or established CD referred for CE underwent same-day IUS. Inflammatory activity was quantified by the International Bowel Ultrasound Segmental Activity Score (IBUS-SAS) for IUS and the Lewis score for CE. Results: Ninety-eight patients were included with a mean age of 42±14 years, 42% male. IBUS-SAS showed a significant association with the 3rd tertile Lewis score (ρ=0.515, p<0.001). This association differed according to inflammatory burden, as among patients with a Lewis score <350, the correlation was weak and non-significant (ρ=0.149, p=0.198), whereas a stronger correlation was observed in those with a Lewis score ≥350. IBUS-SAS demonstrated excellent discrimination for a Lewis Score ≥350 (AUROC 0.889; 95% CI 0.807–0.972), and an IBUS-SAS cut-off of ≥13.7 yielded 90.5% sensitivity, 76.3% specificity, and 96.7% negative predictive value. Discriminative performance remained high across suspected and established CD. IBUS-SAS was the only predictor of capsule-derived inflammation, when adjusted for clinical and laboratorial biomarkers (OR 1.149 per point increase; 95% CI, 1.070–1.234; p<0.001). Conclusions: IUS accurately detects clinically significant ileal inflammation (Lewis score ≥350) and performs best in patients with higher inflammatory burden. In contrast, its performance was lower in patients with absent or low-grade inflammation, in whom the correlation between IBUS-SAS and Lewis score was weak. These findings support a complementary approach, with CE remaining the reference standard for detailed mucosal assessment and IUS serving as a practical, non-invasive tool for the assessment of clinically significant ileal inflammation.
