title: Comprehensive Competence of Dental Hygienists: A Mixed‐Methods Systematic Review
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Dental hygienist's original purpose was to prevent oral diseases and promote oral health. Over the decades, the profession has evolved massively and its role in oral healthcare has increased. The aim of this study was to identify and describe the areas of competence of dental hygienists internationally, including clinical competence and other requirements set by a diverse working environment. METHODS: This is a systematic mixed-method review that examined international studies. The literature search was conducted in the following databases: PubMed, CINAHL (EBSCO), Scopus, Web of Science and Medic. The review followed the JBI protocol and a narrative analysis was performed to analyse the data. The qualitative and quantitative studies in the review were analysed and reported separately. RESULTS: The review included 54 studies. A total of 23,216 dental hygienists participated in the studies. The methodological quality of the studies was mostly moderate or good. The areas of competence for dental hygienists are primarily related to clinical and professional competence and knowledge. Dental hygienists' comprehensive competence also included patient guidance, interaction, ethical and cultural competence, multiprofessional collaboration, lifelong learning, application of evidence-based knowledge and safe working practices. In many respects, dental hygienists' competence was significantly linked to education and clinical experience. CONCLUSIONS: Clinical skills and knowledge were at the core of a dental hygienist's competence, but they are only part of the whole. Other workplace skills also play a major role. In addition to individual skills, dental hygienist education should focus more on comprehensive learning methods that simulate real-world situations.
authors: Kati Annika Karjalainen; Anni Laura Naukkarinen Lammi; Anne Oikarinen; Heli‐Maria Kuivila

title: Concept-Based Explainable AI in Retinal Imaging: Core Concepts, Techniques, and Challenges
abstract: In high-stakes domains like healthcare, establishing trust in AI-assisted decisions is critical for fostering confidence among experts and researchers. However, standard explanation methods may not fully meet clinical needs, offering raw data, such as saliency maps, rather than human-readable text and auditable, transparent reasoning. To bridge this gap, researchers are increasingly adopting concept-based approaches that express model reasoning through human-readable concepts grounded in expert-backed clinical knowledge. Although this field has advanced rapidly in recent years, retinal C-XAI remains methodologically heterogeneous, with limited agreement on taxonomy, evaluation, and clinical validation. This review identifies recurring reliability gaps in retinal C-XAI and synthesises potential directions for addressing them, including independent concept-level auditing, robustness testing, and clinician-informed validation. As an illustrative example, we discuss how the established SMILE methodology could be adapted for concept-level auditing in retinal C-XAI; this is presented as a candidate research direction rather than a new or clinically validated framework.

title: Context-dependent requirement for neutrophils in retinal regeneration
abstract: Innate immune responses shape Müller glia (MG) reprogramming and retinal regeneration, yet the contribution of individual immune cell type remains poorly defined. Neutrophils enter the blood-retinal-barrier (BRB)-damaged retina within hours of injury, but their role in retinal regeneration is unknown. Here we report that neutrophils are required for the regenerative responses in needle-poked, but not NMDA-injured, zebrafish retinas. Pharmacological ablation of neutrophils with Erbb2 inhibitors suppresses MG proliferation, progenitor formation, and subsequent neuronal regeneration after stab injury, whereas neutrophil depletion has no significant effect in the BRB-intact NMDA model. We further show that Cxcl12-Cxcr4b signaling retains neutrophils at the stab injury site, and manipulating neutrophil retention correspondingly alters the regenerative responses. Mechanistically, neutrophils may modulate MG reprogramming and proliferation by regulating microglial reactivity and by secreting a regeneration-promoting factor Hb-egf. These data identify neutrophil as a previously unrecognized regulator of retinal regeneration and establish that their contribution is injury context-dependent. Significance Statement Immune cells are increasingly recognized as active participants in tissue regeneration, but whether individual cell types promote repair or merely accompany it remains unclear. This study identifies neutrophils as previously unrecognized regulators of retinal regeneration—required after stab injury but not after NMDA injury—and reveals Hb-egf as a neutrophil-derived factor that supports this process. These findings establish that neutrophil participation in retinal regeneration is injury context-dependent, with implications for immune-based strategies to repair the mammalian retina.

title: Cross-Dataset Generalization of Deep Learning for Retinal Vessel Segmentation in Fundus Images: External Evaluation from DRIVE to CHASE_DB1
abstract: Automated retinal vessel segmentation can support quantitative analysis of fundus photographs and facilitate measurement of vascular characteristics associated with ocular and systemic disease. Although deep-learning methods achieve high segmentation performance on benchmark datasets, their reliability may decrease when applied to images obtained under different acquisition conditions. This study evaluated the cross-dataset generalizability of a U-Net segmentation architecture incorporating an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet34 encoder. Sixteen images from the DRIVE dataset were used for model training and four were retained for in-domain validation. Images were resized to 256 × 256 pixels and processed using a consistent normalization pipeline, while spatial and photometric augmentation was applied during training. Without target-domain retraining or domain adaptation, the trained model was subsequently evaluated on the independent CHASE_DB1 dataset. Segmentation performance was assessed using the Dice coefficient, intersection over union (IoU), and sensitivity, together with qualitative examination of predicted vessel maps. On the held-out DRIVE images, the model achieved a Dice coefficient of 0.7263, IoU of 0.5703, and sensitivity of 0.7201. On CHASE_DB1, performance decreased to 0.6269, 0.4573, and 0.5502, respectively. The disproportionately larger reduction in sensitivity indicated an increased frequency of missed vessel pixels under cross-dataset evaluation. Qualitative examination showed greater fragmentation and omission of fine and peripheral vascular structures in CHASE_DB1 images. These findings demonstrate that within-dataset performance may overestimate the robustness of retinal vessel segmentation models when transferred to a different imaging domain. External evaluation should therefore form an important component of retinal imaging artificial intelligence research. Future work should investigate higher-resolution processing, vessel-width-specific evaluation, multi-domain training, domain-adaptation strategies, and larger multicentre datasets to improve model generalizability.

title: Cryptogenic multifocal ulcerous stenosing enteritis diagnosed and managed with intraoperative enteroscopy: a case report
abstract: Background Cryptogenic multifocal ulcerous stenosing enteritis (CMUSE) is a rare small intestinal disorder characterized by multifocal superficial ulcerations and short-segment circumferential strictures. Because the lesions are discontinuous and confined to the mucosa/submucosa, preoperative assessment of disease extent is often inadequate. Intraoperative enteroscopy may enable direct mucosal visualization and guide segmental resection, yet its role in CMUSE remains inadequately described, and whether it confers any advantage over conventional surgical assessment cannot be established from a single case. Case summary A 58-year-old Han Chinese man presented with recurrent small-bowel obstruction for 20 years. Each episode had resolved with conservative management, but the cause had never been identified. He was admitted to our hospital with recent symptom exacerbation; he had no musculoskeletal or joint disorder and no chronic use of aspirin, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), or over-the-counter analgesics, and his only remote exposure was a 1–2-week course of an over-the-counter analgesic taken two years earlier after operative fixation of a left shoulder fracture. Contrast-enhanced CT enterography revealed localized ileal wall thickening, routine endoscopic examinations were unremarkable. Capsule endoscopy was performed after thorough counseling regarding the risk of retention, with the understanding that retention, should it occur, would confirm and localize obstructive strictures. Two stenosing ulcerations were visualized while the capsule was retained between them. The patient subsequently underwent exploratory laparoscopy. Intraoperative enteroscopy through a limited enterotomy provided direct visualization of the entire small bowel and identified four circumferential strictures, all of which were included in a tailored segmental resection. Histopathology showed superficial ulcerations confined to the mucosa and submucosa with fibrotic stricture formation, consistent with CMUSE. The postoperative course was uneventful, and he remained symptom-free at 10-month follow-up. Conclusion In this patient, intraoperative enteroscopy enabled intraoperative mucosal assessment of the entire small bowel, defined the extent of disease, and guided tailored segmental resection; these observations are limited to a single case and do not establish a bowel-preserving advantage over conventional surgical assessment. Capsule endoscopy in suspected stricturing small-bowel disease requires caution and patency assessment; if retention occurs it may provide localizing information, but this does not justify its use in patients with suspected strictures.

title: Current Diagnostic Approaches to Pulpal and Periapical Diseases
abstract: The success of endodontic treatment largely depends on establishing an accurate diagnosis and selecting an appropriate treatment strategy based on the available diagnostic findings. Pulpal and periapical diseases may present with overlapping clinical and radiographic features, while certain non-endodontic conditions can also mimic endodontic disease. These similarities may complicate diagnosis, particularly when symptoms are nonspecific, pulpal tests provide inconclusive results, or radiographic findings are limited. Therefore, endodontic diagnosis should be based on the integration of the patient’s history, clinical examination, pulpal and periapical tests, and radiographic findings. When necessary, advanced diagnostic methods, including cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) and histopathological examination, can provide additional information. An accurate differential diagnosis is essential not only for identifying the underlying condition but also for avoiding unnecessary endodontic or surgical procedures and establishing an appropriate treatment plan. When the expected healing does not occur after treatment or the clinical course is inconsistent with the initial diagnosis, the diagnosis should be reconsidered. In recent years, the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in endodontics has introduced new opportunities to support diagnostic assessment. AI-based applications have increasingly been investigated for tasks such as radiographic image analysis, detection of periapical lesions, assessment of root canal morphology, determination of working length, and identification of vertical root fractures. However, AI should not be regarded as an independent diagnostic method that replaces clinical assessment. Rather, it should be considered a supportive tool that may facilitate a more systematic and objective interpretation of clinical and radiographic data . Integrating clinical expertise with contemporary technological advances may improve diagnostic accuracy and contribute to more appropriate treatment planning in endodontics.

title: DIABETIC RETINOPATHY: CURRENT APPROACHES TO SCREENING, DIAGNOSIS, AND PERSONALIZED MANAGEMENT
abstract: Diabetic retinopathy remains a major cause of preventable visual impairment, despite the availability of effective screening and sight -preserving therapies. Contemporary care is moving from episodic eye examinations towards integrated pathways that combine retinal imaging, risk -based follow -up, systemic risk -factor optimisation, and timely treatment. This narrative review summarises recent guidance and evidence published predominantly during 2022- 2026 on screening, diagnostic assessment, artificial intellig ence, and individualised management. Retinal photography remains a scalable screening method, while dilated examination and optical coherence tomography support clinical confirmation and assessment of diabetic macular oedema. Validated autonomous AI systems can improve access, but require reliable image acquisition, quality assurance, referral pathways, and evaluation across diverse populations. Management is determined by disease severity, macular involvement, visual function, treatment burden, pregnancy s tatus, comorbidities, and the likelihood of adherence. Anti -vascular endothelial growth factor (anti -VEGF) therapy is a central treatment for vision-impairing centre-involving DME and an option for selected proliferative DR; panretinal photocoagulation rem ains important when durable treatment or reduced dependence on repeated injections is prioritised. Optimal glycaemic, blood- pressure, and lipid management remains foundational. A personalised model should link screening results to an actionable care plan rather than treating image classification as an endpoint.

title: DIAGNOSTIC ACCURACY OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCEBASED SYSTEMS FOR DETECTION OF DENTAL CARIES COMPARED WITH CONVENTIONAL DIAGNOSTIC METHODS
abstract: Objective: To evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of an artificial intelligence (AI)-based dental caries detection system compared with conventional clinical and radiographic diagnostic methods in patients presenting for routine dental examination. Methods: This comparative diagnostic accuracy study included 210 patients undergoing dental examination. Each participant received a standardized clinical examination followed by digital intraoral bitewing radiography when indicated. Dental caries were assessed using conventional visual-tactile examination and radiographic interpretation by experienced dentists. The same radiographic images were independently analyzed using an AI-based caries detection system based on deep-learning image analysis. A consensus diagnosis established by two experienced dental clinicians, with adjudication by a senior oral and maxillofacial radiologist in cases of disagreement, was considered the reference standard. Sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), diagnostic accuracy, F1-score and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) were calculated. Results: Among the 210 patients, 126 (60.0%) were male and 84 (40.0%) were female, with a mean age of 34.8 ± 12.6 years. Carious lesions were identified in 118 (56.2%) patients according to the reference standard. The AI system demonstrated a sensitivity of 91.5%, specificity of 90.2%, PPV of 91.5%, NPV of 90.2% and overall diagnostic accuracy of 90.9%. Conventional clinical examination demonstrated sensitivity of 82.2%, specificity of 86.9% and diagnostic accuracy of 84.3%. Radiographic interpretation alone demonstrated sensitivity of 87.3%, specificity of 89.1% and diagnostic accuracy of 88.1%. The AUC was 0.934 for AI, compared with 0.846 for conventional clinical examination and 0.882 for radiographic interpretation. AI performance was highest for dentinal lesions and somewhat lower for early enamel lesions. Conclusion: The AI-based system demonstrated high diagnostic accuracy for dental caries and performed better than conventional visual-tactile examination and comparably or better than conventional radiographic interpretation. AI may serve as a useful adjunct to conventional dental diagnosis, particularly for improving consistency and identifying lesions that may be difficult to detect clinically. AI should complement rather than replace professional clinical judgment until validated prospectively in larger, multicenter populations.

title: Dasatinib-Associated Gastrointestinal Bleeding and Colitis: A Narrative Review with Illustrative Cases
abstract: Dasatinib, an oral tyrosine kinase inhibitor used for chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML), is increasingly linked to gastrointestinal (GI) toxicities that remain under-recognised in clinical practice, ranging from mild, self-limiting symptoms to clinically significant GI bleeding and inflammatory colitis. This narrative review synthesises the published literature on dasatinib-associated GI bleeding and colitis, examining the mechanisms involved, including Src-family-kinase-mediated platelet dysfunction, endothelial barrier disruption and immune-driven T-cell infiltration, together with evidence on diagnosis and management. Dasatinib-associated colitis is far more extensively reported than non-colitis bleeding, has been reported across a broad adult age range and in both sexes, and has onset ranging from immediate to 9 years after initiation. Haematochezia, diarrhoea and abdominal pain are the most common presentations; endoscopic and histopathological findings are typically nonspecific and often mimic inflammatory bowel disease. The review is illustrated by two cases from a tertiary referral centre: delayed bleeding after cold-snare polypectomy of a diminutive 3 mm colorectal polyp, and chronic active colitis on combination asciminib-dasatinib therapy; formal causality assessment rated a dasatinib contribution as possible and probable, respectively. Dasatinib-associated GI complications, from delayed mucosal bleeding to chronic colitis, are clinically significant and warrant early recognition and multidisciplinary, individualised management. Standardised diagnostic criteria and peri-procedural guidance are needed to better balance bleeding risk against leukaemia control.

title: Deep Convolutional Neural Networks For Diabetic Retinopathy And Glaucoma Screening From Retinal Fundus Images: A Literature Review With Emphasis On Rural India
abstract: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) and glaucoma are major causes of preventable blindness, and both can be picked up on a colour fundus photograph before the patient notices any symptom. In rural India, though, ophthalmologists are few compared with the number of people at risk, so many patients are seen late or not at all. Convolutional neural networks (CNN) have been reported to grade fundus images about as well as trained graders, and a number of studies have tested them in Indian hospitals and community camps. This paper reviews that literature from a computer engineering perspective. It covers the clinical background, public datasets and preprocessing, the development of CNN architectures, published DR and glaucoma detection studies, and the practical problems of deploying such systems with smartphone-based cameras and poor connectivity. The review finds that DR detection is considerably more mature than glaucoma detection, that most of the evidence comes from well-resourced centres, and that image quality, dataset shift, explainability, joint multi-disease screening and regulatory readiness are still open problems. A framework for a rural screening pipeline and an evaluation plan are outlined to guide future work.
authors: Sanika Kolhe; Abhijit Banubakode

title: Deep learning in dental image analysis: A systematic review of datasets, methodologies, and emerging challenges
abstract: Efficient analysis and processing of dental images are crucial for dentists to achieve accurate diagnosis and optimal treatment planning. However, dental imaging inherently poses several challenges, such as low contrast, metallic artifacts, and variations in projection angles. Combined with the subjectivity arising from differences in clinicians’ expertise, manual interpretation often proves time-consuming and prone to inconsistency. Artificial intelligence (AI)-based automated dental image analysis (DIA) offers a promising solution to these issues and has become an integral part of computer-aided dental diagnosis and treatment. Among various AI technologies, deep learning (DL) stands out as the most widely applied and influential approach due to its superior feature extraction and representation capabilities. To comprehensively summarize recent progress in this field, we focus on the two fundamental aspects of DL research—datasets and models. In this paper, we systematically review 260 studies on DL applications in DIA, including 49 papers on publicly available dental datasets and 211 papers on DL-based algorithms. We first introduce the basic concepts of dental imaging and summarize the characteristics and acquisition methods of existing datasets. Then, we present the foundational techniques of DL and categorize relevant models and algorithms according to different DIA tasks, analyzing their network architectures, optimization strategies, training methods, and performance. Furthermore, we summarize commonly used training and evaluation metrics in the DIA domain. Finally, we discuss the current challenges of existing research and outline potential future directions. We hope that this work provides a valuable and systematic reference for researchers in this field. All supplementary materials and detailed comparison tables will be made publicly available on https://github.com/zhenhuanZ/DIA-Review.

title: Defining specialised expertise in dental education
abstract: Dental education is a broad, multifaceted, and interdisciplinary scholarly field encompassing key domains, including curriculum design, teaching and learning, assessment, leadership, programme evaluation, and educational research. However, the definition of expertise in dental education remains ambiguous. In many settings, individuals are recognised as “ dental education experts ” or “ dental educationists ” primarily based on teaching experience and educational contributions, sometimes without formal academic preparation in education. While experience provides valuable practical insights, it may not fully equip dental educators with the theoretical and methodological foundations required for contemporary educational practice. This paper reflects on the evolving nature of dental education and argues that expertise should be understood more broadly than teaching experience alone. It highlights the key domains that require specialised knowledge in education. Drawing on developments in medical and health professions education, this paper emphasises the growing role of academic qualifications in education to support educational competence and leadership in dental education. While experience remains indispensable, this paper emphasises formal postgraduate academic preparation as an important foundation for specialised expertise in dental education, complemented by continued educational practice, scholarship, faculty development, and institutional support.

title: Design and Comparative Evaluation of Two Low-Cost Analog RF Transmission Approaches for a Wireless Capsule Endoscopy Prototype
abstract: Capsule endoscopy provides a pain-free, non-surgical alternative to conventional gastrointestinal (GI) tract examination, yet its high commercial cost restricts adoption in resource-constrained healthcare environments. This paper presents the design and comparative evaluation of a low-cost wireless capsule endoscopy prototype built entirely from commercially available analog components. Two radiofrequency (RF) transmission solutions are implemented and compared: Solution 1 employs the MC1373 TV modulator integrated circuit (IC) configured as a 67.25 MHz carrier generator, while Solution 2 uses a discrete-component NPN transistor (2N2222) Colpitts-type oscillator circuit tuned to 61.2 MHz. Both solutions share a common miniaturized analog CMOS camera (8×8 mm, 600 TVL, CVBS output) and a custom-wound 0.1 µH air-core inductor forming the LC tank resonator. Breadboard prototyping, Proteus-based PCB design, and physical fabrication were performed for both solutions. Solution 1 produced a stable RF carrier confirmed on an oscilloscope but encountered video reception failure on available digital television receivers due to PAL/NTSC format incompatibility. Solution 2 successfully delivered clear real-time wireless video on an analog PAL television receiver, with a fabricated PCB footprint of 25×25 mm satisfying the esophageal lumen size constraint. The work provides a documented engineering baseline for low-cost capsule endoscopy development in developing-country contexts and identifies PAL/NTSC format incompatibility as a critical design constraint not previously reported in the prototype literature for this region.
authors: Ali Amir; Muhammad Ahmad

title: Diabetic Retinopathy – A New Understanding of Causation, Screening, and Intervention
abstract: The science of diabetes has progressed to provide a better understanding of the pathophysiology leading to the degeneration of the retinal and choroid multi-level neurovascular units, resulting in oxidative and inflammatory lesions. Within clinical offices, screening via physician examination has been replaced by fundus photography. However, this imaging, with coherence tomography imaging (OCT) layer analysis, only detects diabetic retinopathy when sufficient lesions occur later in the disease process, with neuronal apoptosis of the inner retina and photoreceptors resulting in progressive vision alterations. As such, screening and interventions have been primarily focused on more advanced disease stages. Furthermore, although clinical trials sometimes demonstrate a slowing of disease progression, generally only a modest reduction in microvascular and neuronal loss over time is observed. Similarly, vision measurement, assessed primarily for centuries with charts, only detects visual function impairments later in the disease process, as the ischemic and inflammatory processes most often begin parafoveally and within the peripheral macula and mid-peripheral retina, endangering the functional field of view. While visual acuity and standard contrasted spot perimetry have long been used for visual function endpoints in clinical trials, these methods are imprecise and poorly correlate with patient-reported outcome measures. This chapter reviews newer imaging techniques and visual function testing methods, as well as emerging systemic, topical, and applied laser treatments to reduce or reverse ischemia and prevent neurodegeneration and inflammatory processes within the eye. Earlier detection and evaluation of ischemic injury and inflammation, with appropriate therapy applied earlier in the disease cascade, potentially will result in improved outcomes, including normalization of function.
authors: Stephen H. Sinclair; Stanley S. Schwartz

title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Two Multimodal Artificial Intelligence Systems Versus Dental Students in Endodontic Radiographic Classification
abstract: Objectives: Multimodal artificial intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly used to support image interpretation in dentistry, but evidence regarding their diagnostic performance on endodontic radiographs remains limited. This study compared the diagnostic accuracy of two general-purpose multimodal AI systems with that of undergraduate and postgraduate dental students and evaluated whether image cropping influenced AI performance. Methods: Fifty anonymized periapical radiographs were retrospectively selected, with 10 cases in each of five predefined endodontic diagnostic categories. Reference diagnoses were established by consensus between two experienced endodontists. ChatGPT version 5.2 and Gemini version 3 independently classified each case using both full-size and tooth-cropped images and a standardized prompt. Twenty-five fifth-year undergraduate dental students and 20 postgraduate students in clinical endodontics classified the full-size images. Overall and category-specific accuracies were calculated, and agreement with the reference standard was assessed. Results: Overall accuracy was highest among postgraduate students (84.9%), followed by undergraduate students (78.7%). Gemini achieved accuracies of 72.0% with full-size images and 82.0% with cropped images, whereas ChatGPT achieved 68.0% and 50.0%, respectively. Cropping significantly reduced ChatGPT accuracy (p = 0.0117) but did not significantly affect Gemini performance (p = 0.3018). Diagnostic accuracy varied substantially across categories. Agreement with the reference standard for the AI systems ranged from 50.0% to 82.0%. Conclusions: Diagnostic performance depended on the evaluator, AI system, image format, and diagnostic category. Postgraduate students showed the highest overall accuracy, while AI performance was heterogeneous and did not consistently exceed that of trained human observers. General-purpose multimodal AI may support supervised radiographic interpretation and education, but it should not replace comprehensive clinical assessment or professional judgment.
authors: Andrea Spinelli; Emanuele Charles; Maria Giovanna Gandolfi; Carlo Prati; Fausto Zamparini

title: Diagnostic Performance of Artificial-Intelligence Algorithms in Video Capsule Endoscopy for Small-Bowel Lesions: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
abstract: Background and aims Video capsule endoscopy (VCE) exams of the small bowel generate tens of thousands of frames per exam, making lesion detection labor-intensive and error-prone. Artificial intelligence (AI) may improve performance and efficiency, but reported results vary across targets and architectures. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to benchmark diagnostic accuracy by lesion type and algorithm class. Methods Following PRISMA 2020, we searched five databases to February 2025. From 1,128 records, 825 were screened, and 83 full-length studies were included. We extracted contingency data by lesion and algorithm (standard CNN, hybrid/ensemble/feature-fusion, detection-localization) and pooled sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy using random-effects restricted maximum likelihood models; heterogeneity (I 2 ) and between-group differences were assessed using random effects meta-regression analysis. Risk of bias was appraised with QUADAS-2. Results A total of 83 studies yielding 74 datasets were included in this study. The pooled accuracy of all models across targets ranged between 93% to 97%. Sensitivity was highest for tumor (0.96; 95%CI: 90%-98%), ulcers and bleeding (each 0.95; 95% CIs 0.93–0.97 and 0.93–0.98, respectively), specificity peaked for angiodysplasia (0.98; 95% CI 0.97–0.99) and bleeding, ulcers, and protruding lesions (0.97; 95% CI 0.95–0.98; 95%CI 0.96-0.98), and accuracy was highest for bleeding and protruding lesions (each 0.97; 95% CI 0.95–0.98). After removing heterogeneity, Hybrid CNN (HSNN) produced the highest accuracy for bleeding (97%), Crohn's disease (94%), angiodysplasia (96%), protruding lesions (96%), and mucosal erosions (95%). However, Standard CNN (SCNN) yielded the highest performance without heterogeneity for normal mucosa (96%) and ulcer (96%). The performance of AI models for bleeding, Crohn's disease, and ulcers did not vary across studies. However, models trained on higher-resolution images achieved higher accuracy for angiodysplasia and protruding lesions. Conclusions AI for VCE achieves clinically strong accuracy (over 95%) with hybrid models, especially for bleeding, angiodysplasia, and protruding lesions, whereas standard CNN models yield greater accuracy for normal mucosa and ulcers without heterogeneity. Guidelines should define when to use AI (triage vs second reader), set target operating points with local recalibration, and be supported by prospective trials showing lower miss rates, shorter reading times, and cost-effectiveness.
authors: Shivangini Duggal; Lakshmi Katamuri; Sakar Khattar; Alok K. Dwivedi; Sherif E. Elhanafi; Marc J. Zuckerman

title: Diagnostic Performance of Claude AI Sonnet 4.6 in Interpreting Conventional Intraoral Periapical and Digital Radiovisiographic Images: A Retrospective Comparative Study
abstract: Background: Multimodal artificial intelligence and vision-language models are increasingly being evaluated for medical image interpretation. Recent radiology studies indicate that these systems can generate clinically relevant diagnostic suggestions, while performance varies according to model, task, and imaging context. Dental radiographic applications, particularly direct comparison of conventional intraoral periapical (IOPA) and digital radiovisiographic (RVG) images, require further evaluation. Aim: To evaluate and compare the diagnostic performance of Claude AI Sonnet 4.6 in interpreting conventional IOPA radiographs and digital RVG images. Materials and Methods: A retrospective comparative observational study was conducted on 100 intraoral radiographic images comprising 50 conventional IOPA radiographs and 50 RVG images. Eligible images were of acceptable diagnostic quality and had a confirmed reference-standard diagnosis. Each image was uploaded individually to Claude AI Sonnet 4.6 using a standardized prompt. The AI-generated diagnosis was compared with the clinician-established reference diagnosis. Prompt requirement and processing time were recorded, and data were entered into Microsoft Excel and analyzed using SPSS. Results: Sixty images (60%) represented the mandible and 40 (40%) the maxilla. Claude demonstrated 79% overall diagnostic concordance when full or partial agreement was considered. No statistically significant difference in diagnostic agreement was observed between RVG and IOPA images (p=0.908). RVG images required fewer prompts than IOPA images (mean 1.53±0.50 versus 2.13±0.57; p<0.001). Mean processing time documented was 15.4±5.5 seconds for RVG and 21.64 ± 1.91 seconds for IOPA. Conclusion: Claude AI Sonnet 4.6 demonstrated moderate diagnostic concordance across both conventional and digital intraoral radiographs. The findings support further evaluation of multimodal AI as a clinical decision-support technology, while emphasizing the continued need for expert clinical and radiographic interpretation.
authors: Mrudula Raju. B

title: Diagnostic accuracy of multidetector CT in predicting esophageal varices in cirrhotic patients: A comparison with endoscopy as the gold standard.
abstract: Objective: To determine the diagnostic accuracy of multidetector CT in predicting the presence of esophageal varices in patients with cirrhosis taking endoscopy as gold standard. Study Design: Cross-sectional study. Setting: Department of Radiology, Pakistan Kidney and Liver Institute and Research Centre (PKLI &RC), Lahore. Period: July 2025 to December 2025. Methods: Sample size (n) of 168 patients has been calculated with 95% confidence level taking prevalence of esophageal varices 10%, multidetector CT sensitivity of 98.9% and specificity of 100% in predicting presence of esophageal varices. Sampling Technique was non-probability consecutive sampling technique. Data selection included inclusion criteria as diagnosed case of Liver Cirrhosis on gray scale ultrasound, patients of both sex, patients of age 15 to 70 years. Results: In this cross-sectional study conducted at Pakistan Kidney and Liver Institute & RC over one year, 168 cirrhotic patients (mean age 52.3 ± 10.7 years; 61.3% male) underwent both multidetector CT (MDCT) and upper endoscopy for esophageal varices (EV) evaluation. Using endoscopy as the gold standard, MDCT demonstrated exceptional diagnostic performance: sensitivity 97.1% (95% CI: 92.3–99.2%), specificity 98.4% (94.1–99.8%), positive predictive value 97.7%, negative predictive value 97.9%, and overall accuracy of 97.6% (all p < 0.001). Inter-modality agreement for variceal grading was almost perfect (Cohen’s κ = 0.91, p < 0.001). Furthermore, MDCT-detected features including paraesophageal collaterals (OR 42.6, p < 0.001), gastric varices (OR 20.1, p < 0.001), splenomegaly (OR 14.8, p < 0.001), and portal vein dilation >13 mm (OR 13.2, p < 0.001) were strongly predictive of EV presence. These findings support MDCT as a highly accurate, noninvasive, and well-tolerated alternative to endoscopy for initial EV screening and risk stratification in cirrhotic patients, particularly where endoscopic resources are limited. Conclusion: This study demonstrates that multidetector computed tomography (MDCT) is a highly accurate, noninvasive, and patient-friendly imaging modality for the detection and grading of esophageal varices in patients with liver cirrhosis. With sensitivity and specificity exceeding 97%, and near-perfect agreement with endoscopy in variceal grading (κ = 0.91), MDCT proves to be a reliable alternative to upper gastrointestinal endoscopy particularly valuable in settings where endoscopic screening is limited by availability, cost, or patient tolerance. Future multicenter studies with larger cohorts are recommended to validate these findings across diverse populations and healthcare systems.
authors: Usman Farooq; Talat Ramzan; Hassan Javed Khan; Tahir Malik; Kanwal Shan; Sikander Abdullah

title: Digital Biomarkers and Artificial Intelligence for Early Detection and Risk Prediction of Diabetes-Associated Ocular Complications: Current Advances and Future Perspectives
abstract: Introduction: Diabetes-associated ocular complications, including diabetic retinopathy (DR), diabetic macular edema (DME), retinal neurodegeneration and ocular surface abnormalities, are major causes of visual impairment. Digital biomarkers combined with artificial intelligence (AI) offer promising opportunities for early detection, disease monitoring and individualized risk prediction.Methods: A structured literature search was conducted using PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and Google Scholar. A total of 289 records were identified, of which 136 studies were included following duplicate removal, screening and full-text eligibility assessment. Relevant evidence on digital biomarkers, AI technologies, clinical applications, limitations and future perspectives was critically reviewed.Findings: Digital biomarkers derived from fundus photography, optical coherence tomography (OCT), OCT angiography (OCTA), retinal electrophysiology and ocular surface imaging provide quantitative information about structural, vascular and functional abnormalities. Machine learning, deep learning and multimodal AI approaches demonstrate considerable potential for automated disease detection, severity classification and progression prediction. Longitudinal models, including DeepDR Plus, further support individualized screening strategies. AI-enabled clinical decision support may improve referral prioritization, treatment monitoring and ophthalmic care accessibility. However, dataset limitations, class imbalance, image quality, population bias, limited interpretability, inadequate external validation, privacy concerns and implementation costs remain important challenges.Conclusion: Integrating digital biomarkers with AI may transform diabetes-associated ocular care by enabling earlier detection, personalized risk assessment and more efficient clinical decision-making. Future research should prioritize multimodal integration, longitudinal validation, explainable algorithms and affordable implementation in resource-limited healthcare settings.
authors: Md. Al Amin

title: Digital Transformation and Multidsciplinary Treatment Approaches in Orthodontics
abstract: Digital transformation in orthodontics refers to the digitization of patients’ clinical, photographic, radiological, and surface data; the integration of these data within a common digital environment; and the management of the workflow from diagnosis to retention based on these data. Intraoral scanners, digital models, cone-beam computed tomography, three-dimensional cephalometry, virtual treatment setups, clear aligner systems, artificial intelligence, and remote monitoring platforms contribute to making orthodontic decisions more measurable, reproducible, and shareable. Nevertheless, it should be recognized that digital tools do not inherently guarantee clinical success and that data quality, biological boundaries, operator supervision, and the sequencing of multidisciplinary treatment are decisive determinants of outcomes. This chapter addresses digital diagnostic and record-taking methods in orthodontics, intraoral scanning, three-dimensional and artificial intelligence-assisted cephalometric assessment, digital treatment planning, clear aligner workflows, and teleorthodontics. In addition, decision-making and treatment sequencing are discussed in multidisciplinary clinical situations involving impacted teeth, endodontically treated teeth, patients with periodontal problems, missing teeth, and orthodontic preparation before prosthetic treatment. The monitoring of biological risks, particularly root resorption, using digital data; the limitations of digital orthodontics; and the future transition toward personalized treatment models are also evaluated. The fundamental approach is to use digital technology not as a substitute for clinical examination, but as a decision-support system that addresses the appropriate clinical question and strengthens communication among specialists.
authors: Ali Kağan Özen

title: Digital Twins in Dentistry: The Next Frontier in Personalized and Predictive Oral Healthcare
abstract: Digital dentistry is rapidly evolving from isolated digital workflows toward integrated, patient-specific systems capable of supporting diagnosis, treatment planning, simulation, and longitudinal monitoring. Digital twins represent an emerging concept in this transition, providing dynamic virtual representations of patients that can integrate multimodal and longitudinal data from CBCT, intraoral and facial scanning, clinical records, artificial intelligence, and other digital technologies. This review explores the concept and technological foundations of dental digital twins and examines their emerging applications across prosthodontics, implant dentistry, orthodontics, restorative dentistry, oral and maxillofacial surgery, periodontology, endodontics, maxillofacial prosthetics, and preventive dentistry.
authors: Ramsha Parwez; Urmi Reshamdalal; Sruthi Kalakota; Santosh; Mohammad Kashif Noorani; Shimoli Shah; Ridhi Bhola; Sandeep Singh

title: Digital planning and static guided surgery in a limited prosthetic space: a clinical case report
abstract: Dimensional reduction of the alveolar ridge after tooth extraction in the posterior mandible may limit available bone volume and prosthetic space, increasing the risk of improper implant positioning. Digital technologies (CBCT, intraoral scanning, virtual planning, and guided surgery) have enhanced three-dimensional control of the procedure and reduced clinical subjectivity. Objective: To report a clinical case in which digital planning and static guided surgery improved the predictability of a single-tooth rehabilitation in a posterior region with limited bone availability. Case report: A 51-year-old female patient with a root fracture and mobility of tooth 36 underwent extraction. After 12 months, a new CBCT scan and intraoral scan were obtained and superimposed for reverse planning and fabrication of a 3D-printed surgical guide. A 3.75 × 8.5 mm implant was placed using a guided protocol, with an insertion torque of 60 Ncm and an initial ISQ of 75. After five months, the ISQ increased to 80; an intraoral scan with a scan body was performed, and a zirconia crown cemented on a TiBase was fabricated and delivered without the need for occlusal adjustment. Results: Progressive implant stability was observed throughout clinical follow-up, with a functional definitive restoration and no reported complications. Conclusions: This case suggests that integrating digital planning with static guided surgery may support accurate three-dimensional implant positioning and increase the predictability of single-tooth rehabilitations in posterior regions with limited bone availability.
authors: Beatriz Cristina DE PAULO; Leandro César da Silva SIMÕES; Tatiana Cursino Pereira; Diana Pereira CUNHA; Guilherme de Siqueira Ferreira Anzaloni Saavedra

title: Digital twin technology in dentistry: A review
abstract: Digital twin technology (DTT) is an emerging innovation in dentistry that enables virtual representation of individual patients. It integrates intraoral scans, CBCT data, deep learning, sensor inputs and finite element analysis to create dynamic patient models. These models support personalised treatment planning, procedural guidance, error reduction and remote patient monitoring. Clinical implementation remains challenging due to high costs, data integration, privacy concerns, secure data transfer and real-time accuracy. Thus, DTT’s potential to advance predictive, personalised dental care while identifying barriers requiring further research is reviewed.
authors: Visali Priyankitha Bomidi

title: Dmcyp12c1 is required for eye development and retinal integrity during aging in Drosophila
abstract: Cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzymes regulate lipid metabolism and cellular homeostasis, yet their cell-type specific roles in the retina remain poorly understood. Using Drosophila melanogaster , we screened Cyp genes predicted to encode homologs of human CYP27A1 and identified Dmcyp12c1 as highly enriched in the retina and functionally critical in photoreceptors. Developmental photoreceptor-specific downregulation of Dmcyp12c1 gene reduces eye size and impairs pigmentation, while glial loss produces no phenotype. Adult-specific neuronal downregulation triggers progressive retinal degeneration characterized by ommatidial disorganization, retinal thinning, vacuole formation, and reduced retinal protein content. In contrast, glial downregulation produced no detectable phenotype. Surprisingly, degeneration occurred independently of cholesterol accumulation or lipid droplet formation, and dietary cholesterol supplementation does not reproduce retinal degeneration in control flies. Together, our findings identify the Dmcyp12c1 gene as a critical regulator of retinal integrity and suggest a mechanism independent of bulk cholesterol accumulation, pointing toward a mitochondrial mechanism underlying CYP-mediated neuroprotection.
authors: Jeanne Serrano; Lucy Martine; Louane Charvet; Gérard Manière; Yaël Grosjean; Niyazi Acar; Elodie A.Y. Masson; Georges Alves

title: Do Earth-Trained Humanoid Controllers Walk on the Moon? Gravity, Terrain, and Soil Transfer
abstract: Humanoid robots could aid lunar operations, but how to train their locomotion controllers for lunar gravity, terrain, and soil is unclear. We compare 12 strategies for a simulated Unitree G1 across gravity, terrain, and rigid or granular 3D resistive force theory (3D RFT) contact. Earth-trained policies keep 0.64 to 0.75 survival at the Moon on flat rigid ground in 10 s episodes, but falls continue, so longer episodes would see lower survival. Moon-trained and fine-tuned policies, in contrast, fall in every Earth episode, nearly all within 2 s. Rough-terrain training helps on uneven rigid ground only at training gravity. 3D RFT soil training helps on Earth sand but little on lunar soil. On three held-out soil models, Moon-trained policies lose no detectable progress at lunar gravity. Among tested strategies, only gravity-randomized rough 3D RFT training keeps mean survival above 0.83 at Earth and 0.95 at the Moon on all key tests up to 20 deg. Its ablation without soil training differs consistently only on soil at Earth gravity, falling in most sand episodes. These predictions depend on the contact model and soil stiffness, so lunar soil claims require agreement across soil models.
authors: Guillem Casadesus Vila; Sri Aditya Deevi; Grace X. Gao

title: Driving Factors of Remanufacturing Adoption for Diagnostic Radiology Medical Devices in Thailand
abstract: Remanufacturing medical devices has become a key strategy for improving resource efficiency, lowering healthcare costs, and promoting a circular economy. Despite this, the integration of remanufactured medical devices into healthcare systems faces obstacles, primarily due to stakeholder acceptance issues. This study aims to create and validate a structural model that explains the factors influencing the adoption of remanufactured diagnostic radiology medical devices in Thailand. The model being studied includes several factors, such as economic considerations, cost, environmental policy, environmental friendliness, attitude, social influence, facilitating conditions, regulatory aspects, quality, and information. Data were collected from a group of 400 experts and professionals involved in medical device management and then analyzed using Structural Equation Modeling (SEM). The findings reveal that the majority of the examined factors—including attitude, cost considerations, economic influences, governmental policy, environmental sustainability, social influence, quality, and information availability—exhibited statistically significant correlations with the adoption of medical devices. Conversely, the impact of enabling conditions and regulatory elements was found to be negligible. The model demonstrated a substantial capacity to elucidate the data, explaining 69.5% of the observed variance in adoption behavior (R² = 0.695). This study contributes to the existing body of knowledge by offering empirical evidence regarding the key determinants that shape the adoption of remanufacturing practices in the medical device sector. Furthermore, the findings provide actionable and policy-relevant recommendations for stakeholders, including policymakers, manufacturers, and healthcare administrators, thus supporting the enduring incorporation of remanufactured medical devices within Thailand's healthcare system.
authors: Paweenit Aim-on; Nuntachai Thongpance; Anantasak Wongkamhang; Anuchit Nirapai

title: Dynamic Digital Twins for trustworthy healthcare: Fusing multimodal EEG and endoscopic data for explainable clinical decision support
abstract: Background: Translating data-driven AI innovations into clinically meaningful solutions requires addressing biomedical data complexity and the need for explainable models. We introduce a novel approach to personalized medicine by leveraging Dynamic Digital Twins (DDT) to represent real-time patient states. Methods: This study proposes an explainable, multimodal architecture combining 1D physiological signals (EEG arrays for cognitive state) and 2D medical imaging (wireless capsule endoscopy). Utilizing a Graph Attention Network (GAT) integrated with a federated learning framework, the system processes cross-modal features while preserving data privacy across distributed clinical nodes. Results: In rigorous clinical validation protocols, the multimodal DDT model achieved a diagnostic accuracy of 94.8% (95% CI: 93.1%–96.4%), representing a 14.2% improvement over unimodal baselines. Processing latency was reduced by 31%, and clinician-assessed trustworthiness improved significantly, with SHAP-based interpretability scores reaching 0.89/1.0. Conclusion: By successfully synthesizing cognitive biomarkers and localized imaging into a unified digital twin, this framework provides a highly accurate, transparent, and privacy-preserving tool ready for real-world clinical implementation.
authors: Radhakrishnan Delhibabu

title: EBV-CAN: Vision--Language Grounding for Contact-Aided Endoscope Navigation
abstract: Flexible endoscopes exploit structural compliance to traverse narrow lumens, pipes, and cavities, where navigation involves distributed environmental contact. This compliance makes tip motion depend on the evolving support configuration. We present external bird's-eye-view contact-aided navigation (EBV-CAN), a vision-language policy that combines one initial global static bird's-eye image with evolving endoscopic observations and motor state. Three supervised semantic queries locate the tip, next waypoint, and instructed target on the cached global image; their residual representations predict bending and insertion commands. We introduce the Vision-Language Contact-Aided (VLCA) dataset, linking 517 demonstrations and 75k action samples to 958k spatial entries and 93k remaining-route records. On 50 held-out episodes, tip-coordinate and waypoint localization reach 97.5% and 94.8%. Swapping the target instruction under identical observations changes target attention and motor output across 17 dual-target episodes. Across 1,920 physical trials of eight policies trained under a shared protocol, EBV-CAN achieves 183/240 successes (76.25%) under automatic blue-area scoring. Gated recurrent unit behavior cloning (GRU-BC) achieves the lowest matched-task offline mean absolute error (MAE), 0.056, and 1/240 physical successes, establishing distinct rankings for action imitation and task completion. Successful multi-guide executions and representative failures connect spatial progress, steering transitions, and visibility to physical navigation.

title: EVALUATING THE ACCURACY AND RELIABILITY OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE CHATBOTS IN ANSWERING DENTAL SPECIALTY EXAMINATION PERIODONTOLOGY QUESTIONS
abstract: Background/Aim: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly utilized by dental students and specialty candidates as supplementary tools for examination preparation. However, their reliability in specialized clinical domains requiring analytical reasoning remains underexplored. This study aimed to comparatively evaluate the accuracy, reliability, and inter-model agreement of three contemporary reasoning-focused LLMs in answering Periodontology questions from the Turkish Dental Specialty Examination (DUS).Materials and Methods: In this cross-sectional in silico study, 100 multiple-choice Periodontology questions administered in past DUS sessions (2012–2026) were selected. The questions were presented in isolated sessions without prior contextual prompting to three models: OpenAI GPT-5.5 Thinking, Anthropic Claude Opus 4.7 (adaptive thinking), and Google Gemini 3.1 Pro. Responses were scored dichotomously against official answer keys. Overall accuracy rates were compared using Cochran's Q test, pairwise agreement was assessed via Cohen's Kappa (k) coefficient, and shared error distributions were analyzed using a two-tailed Binomial test (p 0.05), ChatGPT and Gemini selected the identical incorrect distractor in all 5 questions they mutually failed (100% shared error rate; p = 0.0625).Conclusion: Contemporary reasoning-capable LLMs demonstrate high accuracy and substantial inter-model consistency on specialty-level Periodontology questions. Nevertheless, the presence of concordant errors indicates shared algorithmic blind spots, underscoring that AI outputs must be supplemented by specialist oversight and evidence-based verification in dental education.
authors: Aysun Akpınar

title: Editorial: Cutting-edge technologies in digital dentistry
abstract: Digital dentistry including computer aided design and manufacturing (CAD/CAM), three-dimensional printing, virtual treatment plan, now extends well beyond replacing conventional impressions with digital files [1][2][3] . It connects image acquisition, interpretation, treatment planning, fabrication, and intervention, with artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly proposed as a layer of clinical decision support 4,5 . The Research Topic, "Cutting-Edge Technologies in Digital Dentistry," brings together 12 articles from Frontiers in Dental Medicine and Frontiers in Oral Health, including evidence syntheses, clinical investigations, methodological contributions, and conceptual work. Collectively, these papers address a central question: which digital innovations have demonstrated value in defined clinical tasks, and which remain promising but insufficiently validated? Their diversity offers an opportunity to examine the progression from technical possibility to reliable, patient-centered clinical use.Coronel-Zubiate et al. synthesized direct comparisons of AI-assisted and manual cephalometric analysis 6 . Across 22 studies, most parameter-level measurements showed small, generally non-significant differences, but heterogeneity and low-to-moderate certainty limit claims of interchangeability. Madfa et al. evaluated Manus, ChatGPT, and Claude using 117 case-based dental questions 7 . Claude and Manus achieved numerically higher accuracy and response consistency than ChatGPT; however, between-model differences in accuracy were not statistically significant. These findings illustrate why both reproducibility and independent clinical verification matter when assessing AI-based diagnostic support.Beyond diagnosis, Karnik et al. reviewed potential applications of AI and robotics in prosthodontics and implantology, including planning, automation, and operative assistance 8 . Ma proposed "oral implanomics," a framework integrating radiomics, quantitative imaging features, and AI to support individualized implant assessment and prediction 9 .Similarly, Drafta et al. described the Dental Unified CAD Utility (DUCU) as a conceptual framework for connecting digital smile design with functionally oriented restorative wax-ups 10 . Both proposals are relevant directions for research, but should not be read as evidence that these systems have achieved clinical effectiveness.Ramos-Morro et al. reviewed 10 clinical studies comparing intraoral scanning with conventional impressions 11 .Accuracy findings were mixed, with conventional impressions performing better in some full-arch comparisons; only two studies evaluated chairside time and patient comfort, both favoring digital techniques. Methodological heterogeneity and small samples restricted the strength of conclusions. Addressing an especially demanding anatomical setting, Petre et al. described a hybrid chairside workflow integrating an intraoral scan with a digitized conventional impression to model a partially edentulous mandible 12 . Its practical utility is promising, although the accuracy of the resulting composite model still requires clinical verification.In implant prosthodontics, Ma et al. reported a clinical case study comparing an extended Segma scan body with a standard SRA scan body for full-arch implant impressions. The extended design yielded lower deviations against a conventional-impression reference model, but a case report cannot establish generalizable superiority across patients, operators, or scanner systems 13 . In orthodontics, Alhazmi presented an electronic key-controlled palatal expander intended to permit asymmetric expansion. Its feasibility was explored using finite-element simulation, without bench or patient testing 14 . Together, these contributions show how digital design can address difficult clinical scenarios, while underscoring the distinction between a proposed solution and a validated workflow.Schnitzer et al. compared structured and narrative reporting of periapical radiographs. Structured reports received higher ratings for completeness, clarity, and information extraction, but did not significantly improve assessed therapeutic decision-making or the sufficiency of information for treatment planning 15 . In a different diagnostic domain, Li et al. integrated cone-beam computed tomography, intraoral scanning, and electromagnetic tracking to construct individualized incisal and condylar envelopes of mandibular motion 11 . The work illustrates potential intraoperative monitoring applications, although its simulated jaw positions do not demonstrate prevention of temporomandibular joint injury.Zhang et al. provided clinical evidence from a single-center pilot study of 30 patients undergoing temporomandibular joint gap arthroplasty. Patient-specific osteotomy and registration guides were associated with shorter registration times, lower target registration error, and modestly shorter operations than dental-surface registration; postoperative mouth opening at three months was similar between groups 16 . This distinction between technical precision and functional benefit is important for evaluating image-guided surgery.Three lessons emerge across the Research Topic. First, the maturity of the evidence differs substantially between contributions: systematic reviews and comparative clinical investigations sit alongside case reports, workflow descriptions, simulations, and conceptual frameworks. This diversity is valuable, but conclusions should remain proportionate to study design, sample size, and measured outcomes. Improvements in digital accuracy, reporting quality, or task efficiency do not automatically establish better diagnoses, safer procedures, or superior long-term outcomes.Second, evaluation should move beyond isolated technical metrics. Prospective, preferably multicenter studies should assess external validity, operator dependence, clinically meaningful error thresholds, patient-reported experience, treatment outcomes, and cost-effectiveness. For AI systems, transparent reporting of model versions, input data, reference standards, uncertainty, and performance across patient populations is essential. Comparisons with conventional care should test whether algorithmic or digital assistance changes clinical decisions and patient outcomes, not solely whether it reproduces intermediate measurements.Third, integration is as consequential as innovation. Scanner, imaging, design, and navigation systems must exchange information reliably without loss of accuracy or traceability. Interoperability, data protection, clinician training, and clear accountability for AI-assisted decisions require attention before routine deployment. Human oversight remains necessary, particularly when decisions involve irreversible treatments or safety-critical surgical steps. Education should therefore develop not only software proficiency but also the ability to recognize unreliable outputs, evaluate evidence, and communicate uncertainty to patients.The 12 contributions depict a field advancing through complementary pathways: quantitative evidence synthesis, digitally enabled clinical investigation, and proposals for future care. Their collective message is neither that technology should replace clinical judgment nor that technical progress alone guarantees better treatment. The priority is to establish when digital innovations offer reproducible, clinically meaningful benefits, and to integrate them into practice through rigorous validation, interoperable workflows, and responsible professional oversight.
authors: Sohaib Shujaat; Jinyang Wu; Hongyang Ma

title: Efficacy and Safety of String Capsule Endoscopy in Identifying Esophageal Varices: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
abstract: Background: Esophageal varices are a critical complication of liver cirrhosis, with significant mortality risk from haemorrhage. While esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) is the diagnostic gold standard, its invasiveness and resource demands limit frequent surveillance. String capsule endoscopy (SCE) offers a potential minimally invasive alternative. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the diagnostic accuracy and safety of SCE compared to EGD. Methods: We systematically searched for studies comparing SCE (including tethered and magnetically guided detachable-string variants) with EGD in adults with cirrhosis and portal hypertension. We pooled diagnostic accuracy metrics including sensitivity, specificity, positive likelihood ratio (PLR), and negative likelihood ratio (NLR) and assessed safety outcomes. Results: Five studies comprising 863 patients meeting eligibility criteria were included. SCE demonstrated excellent performance with a pooled sensitivity and specificity of 94% each. The high positive likelihood ratio (13.00) and low negative likelihood ratio (0.09) support its utility for both confirming and excluding varices. Moderate-to-high statistical heterogeneity (I² up to 76.8%) was noted, likely due to variations in device technology and study settings. No serious adverse events were reported. Conclusions: String capsule endoscopy demonstrated high diagnostic accuracy and a favorable safety profile for detecting esophageal varices and may serve as a less invasive pre-screening or surveillance option in appropriately selected patients. However, larger prospective studies are needed before widespread clinical implementation as an alternate screening method.
authors: Vineeth Potluri; Meghana Kakarla; Yashaswi Guntupalli; Rithish Nimmagadda; Umesh Bhagat; Ravi Medarametla; Satwik Kuppili; Pranathi Bandarupalli; Pradeep Yarra

title: Elastography in Endoscopic Ultrasound (EUS): Clinical Utility and Diagnostic Implications
abstract: Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) elastography has emerged as a valuable addition to conventional EUS by providing real-time information on tissue elasticity. Strain elastography (SE) and shear wave elastography (SWE) provide measurements of tissue elasticity via qualitative tissue deformation and quantitative shear-wave propagation, respectively. Both have shown value as adjunct tools in the characterization of solid pancreatic lesions as well as chronic pancreatitis. Beside its emerging applications including lymph node assessment, subepithelial lesions, liver fibrosis, portal hypertension, rectal lesions, and biliary diseases, elastography has demonstrated promising results regarding its functional diagnostic performance. Nonetheless, elastography interpretation is influenced by lesion heterogeneity, region of interest selection, depth, compression, and various motions, and it, therefore, should not be interpreted independently of clinical context; hence, its major advantage stems from its utilization along with conventional EUS B-mode, EUS contrast-enhanced imaging, and tissue histopathological examination.
authors: Ahmed Mohammed Elmeligui

title: Elastosynth—An Open-Source Software Package for the Generation of Realistic In-Silico RF Data for Ultrasound Elastography
abstract: Ultrasound elastography provides quantitative tissue information, yet displacement algorithm validation is hampered by lack of clinical ground truth and simplified phantoms. Current in silico FEA-FIELD II approaches are computationally prohibitive for large-scale data generation and lack heterogeneous tissue support. This paper introduces Elastosynth, an open-source package with modular architecture: procedural phantom generation, a custom lightweight finite element solver, and optimized FIELD-II RF simulation. The generator employs Monte-Carlo placement and superpixel heterogeneity workflows for complex stiffness fields with tunable inclusion properties. The bespoke C++/Armadillo FE engine supports heterogeneous 2D simulations, bypassing commercial preprocessing overhead while efficiently computing displacements under prescribed boundary conditions. A lateral windowing scheme reduces the RF simulation time 60-fold, enabling mass generation of reasonably realistic in silico phantoms. Supporting automated batch processing, Elastosynth facilitates statistically significant evaluation of displacement estimation techniques, addressing a critical gap in elastography and enabling advancement of tissue motion tracking and quasi-static ultrasound elastography techniques.
authors: Matthew Caius; Zhenbang Wang; Abbas Samani

title: Embedded Sim-to-Real Visual Servoing: Learned Reaching and Force-Guided Placement
abstract: Embedded perception-to-control systems must combine visual targeting with reliable contact handling under tight computational constraints. We present a shared architecture on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin controlling a Franka Research 3 through Cartesian impedance control. RealSense D435i observations, YOLO11-seg segmentation, depth back-projection, and hand--eye calibration provide metric robot-frame targets. We compare two strategies: compact proximal policy optimization (PPO) policies transferred from simulation for object- and hole-region reaching, and force-guided Cartesian placement using approximately 2 N normal contact and spiral search. The PPO policies achieved 87.2% and 83.1% success over 1000 simulation episodes each. Across 50 real-robot trials per strategy, the learned hybrid and force-guided analytical pipelines achieved 70.0% and 74.0% completion, respectively. Mean perception latency with TensorRT was 34.55 ms. These results support an embedded architecture combining learned free-space reaching with explicit contact correction.
authors: Dezhi Sun; Duy Khang Banh; Kenan Niu

title: EndoRSI: Physical-Evidence-Driven Recursive Improvement of Endoscopic Robot Policies
abstract: Artificial intelligence is beginning to automate scientific discovery, yet physical robot-policy research still relies on scientists and engineers to interpret experimental failures and decide how controllers should be revised. We present EndoRSI (Endoscopic Recursive Self-Improvement), a human-governed, self-improving robotic research system in which the embedded EndoForge coding agent iteratively develops and refines endoscopic robot policies using evidence from physical experiments. Physical execution remains isolated within a safety-constrained runtime under human authorisation. In motorised endoscopy, validation evidence first caused the agent to reject an initial action representation, while subsequent physical experiments falsified an offline-supported insertion strategy by revealing hazardous closed-loop behaviour absent from the source data. Failed physical rollouts were then incorporated into policy revision; insertion success subsequently increased from 2/21 in the first generation to 17/21 in the fourth. The frozen final policy retained competence across visual and hardware shifts and was the best performing autonomous policy across six independent ex-vivo porcine specimens. These results show that physical robot interaction can serve as experimental evidence for agent-driven robot policy research.
authors: Chi Kit Ng; Yidong Zhang; Tianchun Wu; Siu Hing Lui; Hanlin Zhao; Huxin Gao; Hongliang Ren

title: EndoVLA-OOV: Language-Conditioned Out-of-View Target Acquisition in Robotic Endoscopy
abstract: The scan-then-revisit workflow of upper gastrointestinal endoscopy requires bringing a previously observed suspicious region back into view for closer inspection. Acquiring such targets requires translating anatomical and appearance descriptions into camera motions from partial observations of a confined, deformable environment. We present EndoVLA-OOV, a language-conditioned vision-language-action policy for out-of-view target acquisition in robotic endoscopy. The policy adapts a pretrained backbone to continuous two-degree-of-freedom distal bending commands and combines initial, intermediate, and current images to guide search. To support policy learning, we provide an open-source VLA dataset containing 1,050 episodes across six tasks and approximately 262k observation-action pairs. Physical evaluation spans wet-lens and low-light conditions, two unseen stomach phantoms, and cross-embodiment transfer to an unseen ex-vivo environment. In the cross-embodiment evaluation, the full-data policy achieves 93.3% target acquisition success (28/30). In a controlled training-data comparison, expanding the corpus from 312 to 1,050 episodes increases acquisition success from 40.0% to 90.0% under the same model, training, and test configuration. Instruction and observation interventions further support the use of language and temporal context in the evaluated acquisition tasks. These results support language-guided endoscopic revisitation across the evaluated environments and robot embodiments and demonstrate the benefit of expanded task-specific demonstrations.
