title: Long-Term Outcomes According to a Device-Assisted Enteroscopy Strategy after Capsule Endoscopy in Patients with Small Bowel Bleeding: A Nationwide Population-Based Cohort Study.
abstract:
Background/aims

Although the use of device-assisted enteroscopy (DAE) has increased, few large-scale studies have examined long-term outcomes focused on small bowel (SB) bleeding. We analyzed National Health Insurance Service data to evaluate the clinical utility of DAE in patients with SB bleeding who underwent capsule endoscopy.

Methods

We included a cohort of 11,690 patients who underwent capsule endoscopy for SB bleeding (identified using ICD-10 codes) between 2014 and 2022. Patients were categorized into three groups: no DAE, diagnostic DAE, and therapeutic DAE. We assessed four major outcomes, including the probability and factors associated with SB rebleeding, severe SB rebleeding, rebleeding-related mortality, and all-cause mortality.

Results

Of 11,690 patients, 5,211 were included in the analysis (no DAE, n=4,960; diagnostic DAE, n=173; therapeutic DAE, n=78). The probability of SB rebleeding and severe SB rebleeding was highest in the therapeutic DAE group, followed by the diagnostic DAE and no DAE groups (p<0.001), with 7-year rebleeding probabilities of 19.8%, 15.8%, and 5.0%, respectively. Rebleeding-related and all-cause mortality were also highest in the therapeutic DAE group, followed by the diagnostic DAE and no DAE groups (p<0.001 for both), with 7-year rebleeding-related mortality probabilities of 9.3%, 5.9%, and 2.7%, respectively. Risk factors for both rebleeding-related and all-cause mortality included age, male sex, liver cirrhosis, and malignancy.

Conclusions

Patients who require therapeutic DAE for SB bleeding remain at increased long-term risk of rebleeding and mortality. These findings likely reflect their greater underlying disease burden and highlight the need for individualized long-term surveillance and careful management of comorbidities, even after therapeutic intervention.
authors: Song JH, Moon JR, Kim HG, Kim JO, Park JB, Jeon SR, Lee JS, Small Intestine Research Group of the Korean Association for the Study of Intestinal Diseases (KASID).

title: ML‐driven Early Detection of Retinal Diseases in Primary Care Settings
abstract: The common causes of preventable blindness mainly concern retinal diseases, including diabetic retinopathy (DR), age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and glaucoma. Machine-learning (ML) models are trained on large datasets of retinal images, demographics of patients and clinical information. This chapter looks at the potential of ML in facilitating the detection of retinal disease at an earlier stage in primary care. It explains the importance of early intervention, the ML methods applied in screening, clinical performance and implementation challenges, and also future trends that may change the way diagnostic processes work in the future. ML tools can help decrease preventable blindness, maximize resources and develop effective proactive eyecare by facilitating the connection between primary healthcare and specialist diagnostics. ML has been rapidly increasing in the detection of retinal diseases, particularly with the incorporation of deep learning. ML algorithms need to be rigorously validated before being deployed to real-world clinical applications to detect retinal diseases.
authors: Vijay Hari Karambelkar; N. Patil Ashish

title: Magnetic Resonance Imaging-Compatible Skull-Base Pin Fixation for Advanced Image-Guided Pediatric Neurosurgery Using Augmented Reality in Infants Younger than One Year: A Feasibility Study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Rigid cranial fixation in infants younger than 1 year is controversial because thin, incompletely ossified calvaria predispose to skull fractures, epidural hematomas, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leaks, and scalp injury. However, neuronavigation, augmented reality (AR), and intraoperative magnetic resonance imaging (iMRI) require stable head immobilization. METHODS: Four infants aged 5, 4, 7, and 10 months underwent surgery for choroid plexus papilloma, pineal atypical teratoid rhabdoid tumor, hemimegalencephaly, and occipital focal cortical dysplasia, respectively. An MRI-compatible head holder served as both fixation device and iMRI coil (prone position n = 3, supine n = 1). Low-pressure skull-base pinning (below 45 N; both lateral sphenoid wings and upper mastoid) avoided thin calvarial regions. Neuronavigation, microscope-based AR, and iMRI were integrated in all cases. RESULTS: Stable immobilization sufficient for neuronavigation (registration accuracy below 2 mm), AR-guided microsurgery, and repeated iMRI was achieved in all patients without loss of fixation. iMRI confirmed gross total resection in three cases and complete disconnection on diffusion tensor imaging after hemispherotomy. No fixation-related complications, new or unexpected neurological deficits, or wound-healing disorders occurred during a follow-up of 5-12 months (median 5.5 months). CONCLUSIONS: In this small technical series, low-pressure skull-base pin fixation with an MRI-compatible head holder provided stable immobilization without fixation-related complications in infants undergoing advanced image-guided neurosurgery. These results demonstrate technical feasibility but do not establish safety, which requires larger studies. Careful skull-base pin placement may reduce classical pinning complications while enabling multimodal neurosurgical techniques in infants.
authors: Julia Shawarba; Farjad Khalaveh; Johannes Zielke; Gregor Kasprian; Martin Bruno Niederle; Natalia Stępień; Amadeo Azizi; Andreas Peyrl; Johannes Gojo; Florian Mayer; Karl Rössler

title: Magnetically Actuated Microrobot for Drug Delivery: Current Progress and Challenges
abstract: Magnetically actuated microrobots have emerged as promising wireless platforms for targeted drug delivery, offering active navigation, deep‐tissue accessibility, and externally programmable therapeutic release at length scales inaccessible to conventional medical devices while reducing systemic exposure. This review summarizes recent progress in magnetically actuated microrobots for drug delivery, with an emphasis on how structural design, material selection, fabrication strategy, drug‐loading methodology, and release mechanisms collectively determine therapeutic performance. In addition, current imaging and localization modalities, navigation and control strategies, biocompatibility considerations, and translational barriers are critically evaluated. Finally, the review highlights remaining challenges in scalable manufacturing, controllable in vivo navigation, deep‐tissue imaging, biosafety, biodegradation, and regulatory translation and outlines future directions toward clinically relevant microrobotic drug delivery systems.
authors: Yang Yang; David J. Cappelleri

title: Magnetically gated millimeter-scale capsule power system for leadless electrotherapy
abstract: Temporary cardiac pacing is indispensable for bridging transient bradyarrhythmic indications over days to weeks, yet existing systems remain constrained by device dimensions, surgical complexity, patient burden, and intrinsic operational principles. Here, these challenges are addressed through a millimeter-scale capsule power system with magnetically gated activation via a reed switch, which eliminates the stringent orientation and implantation-depth requirements of optically controlled approaches. In contrast to conventional reed switch-based pacemakers, this capsule system extends the functionality of the reed switch by integrating electrode materials directly onto its surface, thereby enabling a monolithic miniaturized architecture. Pulsed magnetic fields wirelessly actuate intermittent switching, enabling controlled discharge, with robust cardiac pacing demonstrated in large animals. A proof-of-concept closed-loop system is further realized, establishing the feasibility of future integration with a wearable electronic module to enable autonomous electrotherapy upon arrhythmia detection. Collectively, this strategy addresses a key limitation in temporary pacing and may provide a versatile framework for the development of temporary electrotherapeutic systems across cardiac, neural, and regenerative applications.
authors: Feiyao Yang; Yu Tian; Enyi Zhang; Lixue Yang; Ziyue You; Puguang Peng; Qian Han; Yan Du; Haiwei Li; Yongquan Wu; Houfang Liu; Anfu Zhou; Tian‐Ling Ren; Weiping Sun; Zhong Lin Wang; Di Wei

title: Mapping Research on AI-Based Computer-Aided Diagnosis and Clinical Decision Support Systems: a Bibliometric Study Integrating Google Trends and Content Analysis
abstract: BACKGROUND: Research on artificial intelligence-based computer-aided diagnosis and clinical decision support systems (AI-CDSS) is expanding, but integrated evidence on publication patterns, keyword trajectories, online search activity, and methodological characteristics remains limited. OBJECTIVE: To characterize AI-CDSS research by integrating bibliometric analysis, Google Trends comparison, and structured content analysis of citation-ranked publications. METHODS: Scholarly interest was assessed using bibliometric analysis of Web of Science records from 2016 through August 2026, including author-keyword co-occurrence, bibliographic coupling, and reference co-citation, whereas Google Trends was used to characterize online search activity. A structured content analysis of citation-ranked publications was conducted to examine applications, methodological characteristics, and reported limitations. RESULTS: We analyzed 19,809 included publications from 2016 through August 2026. Output rose approximately 21-fold, from 193 records in 2016 to 4,082 in 2025. Output was geographically concentrated within the included corpus, with a Gini coefficient of 0.869. Among records with identifiable corresponding-author country or territory, China, the United States, and India accounted for 61.33%. Scientific Reports was the most frequent source (n = 916). Frequent artificial intelligence- and diagnosis-related keywords included machine learning (n = 5,666), deep learning (n = 4,022), and computer-aided diagnosis (n = 1,512). Bibliographic coupling identified 15 publication communities, and reference co-citation identified seven reference communities. In the monthly level-series comparison, 9 of 10 keyword concepts exhibited significant associations with Google Trends relative search interest, but none of the 10 first-difference associations remained significant after Bonferroni adjustment. Content analysis of 215 citation-ranked publications, including 191 empirical publications, showed frequent use of convolutional neural networks in diagnostic and radiology applications. Common limitations included limited external validation, infrequent calibration reporting, and sparse workflow-level or impact evaluation. CONCLUSION: AI-CDSS research has rapidly expanded around machine learning, deep learning, and diagnostic applications, but the analyzed citation-ranked publications provide more evidence of methodological development than of clinical deployment. Integrating bibliometric, search-activity, and content-based perspectives shows limited short-term correspondence between online search activity and scholarly keyword use and highlights the need to move beyond model development toward independent external validation, prospective workflow and patient-outcome evaluation, calibration, fairness, and postdeployment monitoring.
authors: Shuo-Chen Chien; Chien-Chu Huang; Chun-Chung Huang

title: Mapping the new frontier: Current perspectives on evolving gastrointestinal pathophysiology
abstract: With rapid advancement in cutting edge basic research in genetics, multi-omics, bioengineering and artificial intelligence focusing on improvement in precision medicine, the study of gastrointestinal (GI) pathophysiology has transitioned from describing GI conditions as isolated structural disorders to a systems-biology approach which recognize them as a complex network of interconnected systemic and functional diseases.It emphasizes the "interactome" -the complex crosstalk between the gut microbiome, the enteric nervous system, the mucosal immune system, and the enteroendocrine system -with associative effects on distant organs, metabolic, and immune function of the body.The gut is thus a central regulatory hub for metabolic health, immune education, and possibly neurocognitive function.Current perspectives emphasize three primary pillars in disease pathogenesis, namely the role of low-grade chronic inflammation and the integrity of the epithelial barrier (leaky gut), the metabolic influence of the microbiome, and its effect on functioning of distant organs.This narrative review will broaden the above perspectives highlighting the effect of smouldering inflammation affecting the epithelial barrier (its causative metabolomic signatures, the resulting epithelial plasticity, and its involvement in local and systemic diseases), the gut-microbiomedistant organ axis, the gut-metabolic axis (contributing to systemic inflammation and atherosclerosis), immuno-gastroenterology (related to GI cancers and other diseases), and advances in bioengineering (three dimensional in vitro modelling like organ-on-a-chip and personalized organoids) for better delineation of disease pathogenesis, biomarkers and precision therapeutics.Further, the utility of artificial intelligence in precision diagnostics (radiology, histology, multi-omics) and in shaping future therapies will be discussed as also the present limitations.

title: Micro- and Nanorobots in Cancer Therapy: From Active Drug Delivery to Clinical Translation
abstract: Micro- and nanorobotic systems represent an emerging approach to overcoming some of the limitations of conventional anticancer drug delivery. Unlike passive nanocarriers, these systems can exploit externally controlled or autonomous propulsion mechanisms to navigate through biological environments, transport therapeutic agents, and potentially improve their distribution within tumour tissues. Various platforms have been investigated, including magnetically actuated microrobots, chemically propelled Janus particles, acoustically responsive systems, and biohybrid devices incorporating bacteria, sperm cells, or microalgae. Recent preclinical investigations have demonstrated the feasibility of delivering therapeutic agents to poorly accessible anatomical compartments, including hypoxic tumour regions and pulmonary metastases. However, substantial challenges remain regarding physiological navigation, drug-loading capacity, pharmacokinetics, biodistribution, biocompatibility, pharmaceutical stability, manufacturing reproducibility, and regulatory evaluation. Importantly, the demonstration of successful propulsion or increased tumour accumulation does not necessarily establish therapeutic efficacy. This review critically examines the technological principles and experimental applications of micro- and nanorobots in oncology, with particular emphasis on pharmaceutical performance and the challenges associated with clinical translation.
authors: ASTIER Alain

title: Micro- and Nanorobots in Ophthalmology: Active Navigation Across Ocular Barriers for Precision Therapeutics—A Scoping Review of Technology Readiness, Clinical Applications and Therapeutic Gaps
abstract: This review concerns actively actuated miniaturised robotic systems investigated for ocular, adnexal and ophthalmic vascular applications. Its rationale is to distinguish such systems from passive drug carriers and conventional full-scale surgical robots, and to map how engineering capabilities relate to experimentally demonstrated ophthalmic tasks. Particular interests include movement across ocular barriers, precision delivery, surgical manipulation, tracking, retrieval, biocompatibility and translational readiness. A scoping review is appropriate to the stated objective of mapping a heterogeneous evidence base across engineering and biomedical disciplines, rather than estimating a pooled therapeutic effect. The methodological framework is the JBI approach to scoping reviews; reporting of the completed review follows PRISMA-ScR. JBI provides guidance specifically addressing protocol development, searching, data extraction and presentation. Primary objective To map the nature, extent, engineering characteristics, experimentally demonstrated applications and translational maturity of micro-, nano- and millirobotic systems investigated in ophthalmology. Review questions 1. What types of tethered and untethered miniaturised robots have been investigated for ophthalmic applications? 2. What device dimensions, materials, fabrication methods, propulsion mechanisms and actuation systems have been reported? 3. What imaging, localisation, tracking and control approaches have been demonstrated? 4. Which ophthalmic tasks and disease applications have been experimentally investigated? 5. What experimental models, comparators, efficacy outcomes and safety assessments have been used? 6. What evidence exists concerning retrieval, biodegradation, clearance and sustained ocular residence? 7. What provisional technology readiness has been demonstrated, and what gaps remain in the pathway toward clinical translation? These questions reflect the objectives and extraction domains reported in the manuscript.
authors: Islam Omar; Paria Malekahmadi; Mohamed Abosheisha; Ahmed Hafez; Tilemacos Zaimis; Meysam Keshavarz; Farid Froghi

title: MicroDLP: Microscope-Enabled Resolution-Switchable 3D Microprinting
abstract: Complex three-dimensional (3D) microarchitectures are increasingly important for microfluidics, microrobotics, organ-on-chip systems, biomedical devices, and architected materials. However, fabricating complex 3D microstructures with micrometre-scale precision remains a major manufacturing challenge. Integrating these fine features with larger supporting structures presents an additional challenge, requiring fabrication across multiple length scales within a single architecture. Although microscale 3D printing enables intricate geometries, the trade-off between resolution and build volume limits multiscale fabrication, while existing approaches often require complex optics and precise registration. Here, we introduce MicroDLP, a microscope-enabled digital light processing platform for versatile, resolution -switchable 3D microprinting. By integrating a projection module into a conventional inverted microscope, MicroDLP exploits its revolving objective turret to switch between 4×, 10×, and 20× objectives, provi ding projected pixel sizes from 1.89 to 0.378 µm. We characterize photopolymerization, voxel geometry, and lateral feature resolution across magnifications to establish suitable microscale printing conditions. MicroDLP enables the fabrication of diverse and complex 3D microarchitectures, including freestanding trusses with 170 µm struts, microvascular structures with 10 µm features, interlocking gears, suspended microbridges, and microneedles with 3–5 µm tips. Importantly, switching from 10× to 20× during fabrication produces monolithic 3D structures combining larger supporting foundations with fine micropillar arrays, without manual optical realignment. The shared optical pathway also enables coaxial in situ monitoring of photopolymerization. Together, these results establish MicroDLP as a versatile platform for microscale additive manufacturing, combining complex 3D microfabrication with resolution switching within a single monolithic structure.
authors: Dimitar Boev; Prajwal Sanjay Agrawal; Mahmoud Medany; 邓永; Gabriele Morlupi; Daniel Ahmed

title: Microvasculopathy in spinal muscular atrophy: The endothelium as a target of SMN deficiency and an amplifier of disease
abstract: Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is caused by deficiency of the ubiquitous survival motor neuron (SMN) protein. Degeneration of anterior horn motor neurons defines the disease, but many organs are affected, including heart, liver, kidney, and bone. The vascular compartment is among them: digital necrosis in infants with the fewest SMN2 copies, capillary rarefaction in SMA mice, and decreased von Willebrand factor with fibrinogen extravasation in human post-mortem spinal cord. Whether these reflect endothelial injury by SMN deficiency itself or capillary adaptation to atrophic, denervated tissue has not been examined systematically. SMN-depleted endothelial cells form defective networks and migrate poorly in neuron-free systems, but this is based on a single unreplicated study in macrovascular and progenitor cells, which do not recapitulate human spinal cord microvascular endothelium. Ventral horn hypoxia precedes or accompanies weakness. Retinal vascular abnormalities precede ganglion cell loss, but early SMN restoration prevents retinal vascular defects in mice and improves colony formation by patient-derived endothelial progenitors. Demand-matched regression, reduced cardiac output, post-mortem artefact, critical illness, autonomic dysfunction and measurement confounding account for part of the phenotype, not all. Throughout, we keep vascular abnormality distinct from impaired perfusion, only inferred in mice rather than directly measured. SMN has never been deleted from, or restored in, the endothelium alone in vivo. We therefore hypothesise, as a falsifiable model, not a proven mechanism, that the endothelium is injured cell-autonomously alongside other SMN-dependent lineages and amplifies rather than initiates disease, and we outline the genetic experiments required to falsify it. Retinal angiography and capillaroscopy are accessible readouts, neither visualising the cord.
authors: Stefania Paola Corti; Linda Ottoboni; Francesca Beatrice; Andrea D’Angelo; Filippo Marcotti; Martina D'Agostino; Federica Rizzo; Giulia Magni; Giacomo Pietro Comi

title: Misclassified and non-detected cancers by colon capsule endoscopy in screening participants: a case series from the CareForColon2015 trial
abstract: Background: Colon capsule endoscopy (CCE) has emerged as a minimally-invasive alternative to colonoscopy and has in several meta-analyses shown non-inferiority in detection rates of pathology. However, CCE is a reader-dependent technique and pathology can be missed, even though images of the lesions are captured. Furthermore, misclassification of pathology can lead to erroneous conclusions, and possible delays in correct diagnosis and patient management. Methods: We present a series of cancer cases from the Danish trial CareForColon2015. All participants were recruited from the screening program with a positive fecal immunochemical test. The cancers described in this series were detected at subsequent colonoscopy and patients were treated according to the findings. Results: We identified 4 cases of misclassified/misrepresented cancers (reported as non-neoplastic findings, such as inflammation or as a lesion significantly smaller than the actual size, as a result of suboptimal image reporting), and 1 case of a non-detected cancer (not reported by the reader, but captured in images). Conclusions: These cases prompt a discussion of the need for a unified terminology, reader training and implementation of artificial intelligence in the CCE reading process. This is necessary to improve the quality of CCE reporting and minimize the risk of missed pathology and misclassification of findings.
authors: Benedicte Schelde‐Olesen; Anastasios Koulaouzidis; Thomas Bjørsum‐Meyer; Lasse Kaalby; Gunnar Baatrup; Ulrik Deding

title: Mobile AI-Assisted Oral Lesion Triage for Community Oral Cancer Screening: Prospective Field Evaluation Study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Artificial intelligence (AI)-based tools for oral cancer screening have shown promising performance in curated or retrospective image datasets, although such evidence may not fully reflect performance in real-world mobile community screening workflows. In remote or resource-limited settings, intraoral images are often acquired by trained non-specialist personnel under variable field conditions, making workflow-integrated image quality assurance, risk stratification, and expert oversight essential for human-supervised AI-assisted screening. OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to evaluate the prospective field performance of a parameter-locked, mobile AI-assisted oral lesion triage system embedded within a human-supervised routine community oral cancer screening workflow. METHODS: We conducted a prospective community-based field evaluation in eastern Taiwan from June 17 to December 31, 2025. Trained non-specialist personnel acquired standard white-light intraoral images using handheld mobile devices during routine oral cancer screening activities. The AI system incorporated on-site image quality assessment and lesion-level risk stratification into green, yellow, and red triage categories. Images that remained technically inadequate after repeated acquisition attempts were classified as ungradable and excluded from performance analysis. Three board-certified oral and maxillofacial specialists established an operational clinical reference standard through structured image review and consensus adjudication. The primary outcome was lesion-level identification of high-risk lesions requiring specialist referral, defined as red versus non-red triage. Diagnostic performance was estimated with Wilson 95% confidence intervals; precision-recall performance and pre-consensus inter-rater agreement among specialists were also assessed. RESULTS: Among 602 screened participants, 4283 interpretable intraoral images were included in expert adjudication and lesion-level analysis. The AI system flagged 68 red lesions; 12 were confirmed as high risk by expert adjudication, and 4 additional high-risk lesions were identified during expert review, yielding 16 high-risk events for the primary red-triage analysis. For high-risk lesion identification, sensitivity was 75.0% (95% CI 50.5%-89.8%) and positive predictive value was 17.6% (95% CI 10.4%-28.4%); specificity, negative predictive value, and accuracy were 98.6%, 99.9%, and 98.5%, respectively. ROC-AUC values were 0.957 for red, 0.931 for yellow, and 0.964 for green triage; precision-recall analysis showed PR-AUC values of 0.8235 for red, 0.9052 for yellow, and 0.9476 for green triage. Pre-consensus specialist agreement was high, with a Fleiss' kappa of 0.921 and a Gwet's AC1 of 0.981. CONCLUSIONS: A parameter-locked mobile AI-assisted oral lesion triage system was feasibly integrated into a real-world community oral cancer screening workflow operated by trained non-specialist personnel. In this low-prevalence field setting, red triage showed moderate sensitivity and modest positive predictive value, supporting its potential role as human-supervised referral-prioritization support rather than autonomous diagnosis or standalone clinical decision-making. Further multicenter studies with blinded assessment, participant-level outcomes, workflow-efficiency measures, and longitudinal follow-up are needed before clinical impact and scalability can be determined.
authors: Hao-Yun Liu; Yucheng Huang; Si-Wei Chen; Ling‐Ying Wei; Cheng‐Ying Chou; Jang‐Jaer Lee; Shyh-Jye Chen; Chien‐Chang Lee

title: Monocular Depth Estimation for Three-Dimensional Reconstruction in Hysteroscopy Using Synthetic Data and Transfer Learning
abstract: Hysteroscopy provides direct visualisation of the uterine cavity, but conventional monocular imaging offers limited spatial information.Monocular depth estimation could recover threedimensional information without additional hardware, supporting future improvements in the procedure.This work investigates its feasibility for 3D reconstruction in hysteroscopy using synthetic data and transfer learning, addressing the lack of reliable ground-truth depth in hysteroscopic images.A synthetic hysteroscopic environment was developed to generate image sequences together with corresponding depth and camera information, allowing the behaviour of a pre-trained depth estimation model to be evaluated under controlled conditions.A self-supervised model that incorporates a geometric approach originally developed for gastrointestinal endoscopy was adapted to the hysteroscopic domain through fine-tuning on the generated data.Different training configurations were investigated, including learning rate, batch size, frame sampling and encoder freezing.Depth predictions were quantitatively evaluated on synthetic images and further analysed on real hysteroscopic images.The predicted depth was also used to reconstruct and fuse three-dimensional point clouds, providing an additional assessment of the spatial information recovered by the model.The needed computational time and resources were also addressed.Some fine-tuning configuration showed improved metric for depth estimation on the synthetic test data.The errors were computed on synthetic test images after adjusting the scale of each image, independently, using the ratio between the median ground-truth depth and the median predicted depth.The configuration with the lowest mean AbsRel achieved a value of 0.26 and an RMSE of 2.96 mm, compared with 0.30 and 3.48 mm, respectively, for the pretrained model.However, this model assumed a best performance at the first epoch, limiting the extent to which these improvements can be attributed to sustained fine-tuning.Conclusions for the real images depended on qualitative analysis with the addition of a reduced sensitivity to changes in image framing.The three-dimensional analysis revealed substantial frame-to-frame scale variation, demonstrating that improved depth estimation for individual images does not necessarily result in geometrically consistent reconstruction across a sequence.Overall, the results do not establish the viability of adapting a pre-trained monocular depth estimation model to hysteroscopy using synthetic data, but highlight sequence-level scale consistency and validation in the real domain as key challenges for future three-dimensional computer-assisted hysteroscopy.
