title: Mucosal protrusion angle measured on capsule endoscopy for the diagnosis of small bowel submucosal tumors: a preliminary exploration of diagnostic accuracy based on a case series.
abstract:
Introduction

Small bowel submucosal tumors (SBSTs) are rare, often asymptomatic in early stages, and difficult to detect due to the anatomical inaccessibility of the small intestine and limitations of conventional endoscopy.

Aim

We aimed to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of the mucosal protrusion angle (MPA) measured on capsule endoscopy for distinguishing SBSTs from benign bulges, and to compare its performance with the established smooth, protruding lesions index on capsule endoscopy (SPICE) scoring system.

Materials and methods

This case series study retrospectively reviewed 622 patients. Among them, 69 cases with smooth, protruding lesions were initially identified. After excluding lesions with alarm features and those without definitive follow-up confirmation, 31 cases were included in the final analysis.

Results

Mean MPA was significantly smaller in the SBST group than in the bulge cohort. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve for MPA in predicting SBSTs was 0.98, significantly higher than that of SPICE scoring. The optimal diagnostic cutoff for MPA was 88°, rounded to 90° for clinical practicality. Using a threshold below 90°, MPA achieved sensitivity of 100%, specificity of 95%, positive predictive value (PPV) of 91.7%, and negative predictive value (NPV) of 100%-all superior to SPICE scoring at a threshold above 2 points (sensitivity, 72.7%; specificity, 85%; PPV, 72.7%; NPV, 85%). A combined criterion (MPA <90° and SPICE >2) yielded 100% specificity and PPV, but lower sensitivity (72.7%).

Conclusions

MPA is a simple, highly accurate, and superior metric to SPICE scoring for differentiating SBSTs from innocent bulges on capsule endoscopy.
authors: Xue Z, Kang Y, Sun X.

title: Multi-modal Representation Fusion for Long-term Microsurgical Anastomosis Trajectory Anticipation
abstract: Microsurgical anastomosis is one of the most challenging and sophisticated procedures for surgical robotics, requiring accurate manipulation of surgical instruments within a limited space to achieve precise operations. Accurate surgical trajectory anticipation is essential for surgical scene understanding, intraoperative planning, robotic manipulation, and reliable behaviour analysis. However, existing approaches mainly focus on features extracted from surgical videos and historical trajectories, while overlooking rich semantic and motion information that can provide more discriminative multi-modal representations for complex surgical instrument-tissue interactions. In this work, we propose a cross-modal feature fusion framework for long-term 2D and 3D microsurgical anastomosis trajectory anticipation. The proposed framework consists of a multi-modal representation extractor and a cross-modal feature fusion network. Semantic recognition of surgical objects and consecutive motion estimation are incorporated as multi-modal visual cues, providing complementary spatial and temporal guidance for instrument-tissue interaction characterization. A coarse-to-fine progressive fusion strategy with a long-short-term memory mechanism is introduced to capture temporal dependencies step by step. The training and evaluation are conducted on our established robotic platform and a comprehensive dataset containing both phantom and ex-vivo surgical scenarios is constructed. Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate that the proposed framework consistently outperforms existing methods and exhibits improved robustness across different surgical scenes, highlighting its potential for both intelligent robot-assisted and autonomous surgical systems.
authors: Yuxuan Liu; Yating Luo; Yunfei Luan; Xinyao Zhou; Yuyang Zhuge; Yao Guo; Guang‐Zhong Yang

title: Multimodal 3D light-field and laser-speckle endoscopy
abstract: Minimally invasive surgery is a powerful technique that enables operations deep within the body while minimizing patient trauma and recovery time. Optical endoscopes are key to providing intraoperative vision but still face challenges due to the loss of essential senses, including depth perception and tactile feedback for tissue evaluation. Thus, it is critical to develop endoscopic imaging technologies that can augment operators with critical information. In this work, we explore a prototype multimodal 3D imaging endoscope that integrates volumetric light-field imaging with laser-speckle contrast imaging to simultaneously capture 3D structure and blood-flow information in a clinically relevant form factor.
authors: Corey Zheng; Shu Jia

title: Multimodal In-Process Risk Grading for Robot-Assisted Ultrasound-Guided Thyroid Nodule Puncture: A Phantom Study
abstract: To address the difficulty of quantitatively assessing the safety state during robot-assisted ultrasound-guided thyroid nodule puncture, this study proposes an in-process risk-grading method for experimentally defined process-risk states integrating force sensing, end-effector Z-position, and ultrasound imaging information. A phantom experimental platform was constructed to acquire force/torque signals, end-effector Z-position data, and ultrasound images during needle insertion, with window-level samples used as the basic analytical unit. Based on six observable risk factors-abnormal axial insertion force, abnormal lateral force, abnormal torque, loss of needle visibility, loss of nodule visibility, and blurring of ultrasound monitoring images-four-level in-process risk labels were constructed according to single-factor abnormality severity and multi-factor accumulation rules. Multimodal features derived from force sensing, end-effector Z-position, and ultrasound imaging were then extracted to develop an XGBoost-based four-level risk-grading model. A total of 536 valid window-level samples were obtained from 100 independent puncture trials. The results of 20 repetitions of five-fold cross-validation grouped by experiment ID showed that the model achieved an accuracy of 0.7318 ± 0.0489, a Macro-F1 score of 0.7005 ± 0.0755, a Macro-OVR AUC of 0.8998 ± 0.0311, and a quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) of 0.7293 ± 0.0975. The severe underestimation rate was 0.0272 ± 0.0232, and the Level IV recall was 0.8080. Algorithm comparison, modality ablation, and model interpretation analyses showed that the proposed method effectively integrated ultrasound visual-monitoring status, insertion-stage information represented by end-effector Z-position, and mechanical interaction information for window-level in-process risk discrimination. These results provide preliminary evidence for the feasibility of multimodal machine learning-based in-process risk grading for robot-assisted ultrasound-guided puncture under phantom conditions and provide a methodological basis for future research on online risk warning and in-process safety-state perception.
authors: 郭雅佩; Yao Wang

title: Multimodal Progress-Residual Fusion for Anticipating Navigation Retreat in Robotic Flexible Endoscopy
abstract: Flexible robotic endoscopes provide access through tortuous anatomy, where friction, deformation, and wall interaction separate commanded insertion from useful distal progress. Operators interpret this mismatch and retreat to recover a navigable configuration. Recognizing the approach to that decision requires relating motor intent to distal response and the local visual scene. We introduce Multimodal Progress-Residual Fusion (MPRF), a causal model that anticipates operator retreat from commands, electromagnetic (EM) tracking, and endoscopic video. A nominal-progress model predicts the response expected in normal or successful navigation; a temporal predictor combines its EM residual with all three observed modalities. In a 150-episode colon-phantom collection, MPRF achieves 0.580 +/- 0.007 AUPRC across three seeds, compared with 0.511 for the strongest reduced-modality control. Complete multimodal histories provide the principal ranking advantage, while the residual adds an explicit intent-response representation with a small, uncertain increment over raw fusion. Analysis of frozen alarms relates warning timing to the behavioral label and explains the increase in event recall under a longer matching window. These results establish a basis for behavioral assistance during operator-controlled navigation.
authors: Chi Kit Ng; Tianchun Wu; Jiatan Sun; Yuming Sun; Jianru Zhang; Hongliang Ren

title: Multimodal artificial intelligence and large language models in gastrointestinal endoscopy: From lesion detection to workflow-integrated report generation
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly transformed gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy, with most early applications focusing on computer-aided detection and diagnosis of lesions from endoscopic images. However, real-world endoscopic practice extends beyond image interpretation. Endoscopists must integrate real-time video, anatomical location, lesion morphology, procedural context, histopathological findings, clinical history, and standardized terminology to make diagnostic decisions and generate clinically meaningful reports. Recent advances in multimodal AI and large language models (LLMs) provide an opportunity to move beyond isolated endoscopic image analysis toward more comprehensive endoscopic workflow support. By integrating visual, textual, temporal, and clinical information, these models can support lesion characterization, anatomical navigation, procedure quality assessment, structured documentation, report generation, and patient-centered communication. Nevertheless, clinical translation remains limited by scarce high-quality multimodal datasets, heterogeneous reporting standards, insufficient external validation, hallucination risk, limited interpretability, real-time integration challenges, privacy concerns, and evolving regulation. This review summarizes current applications of AI in GI endoscopy, with particular emphasis on the emerging role of multimodal learning and LLMs in bridging lesion detection, context-aware interpretation, and automated report generation. Furthermore, the article analyzes future challenges and the methodological, clinical, ethical, and regulatory requirements for the reliable integration of these systems into clinical endoscopic practice.
authors: Hua-Wei He; In Neng Chan; Ye-Ying Qin; Tao Yan; Pak Kin Wong

title: Multi‐Scale Magnetically Controlled Soft Matter Robots for Tissue Interfacing Applications
abstract: Magnetically controlled soft matter robots (MSMRs) integrate remote magnetic control with soft matter adaptability, providing a promising platform for minimally invasive biomedical tasks at tissue interfaces across multiple scales. Although magnetic manipulability enables remote positioning of MSMRs, the intrinsic properties of soft materials are equally critical to their task‐specific performance at tissue interfaces, given that sustained interplay between MSMRs and host tissues persists throughout the entire tissue‐interfacing workflow. Both factors jointly influence the overall biomedical performance. This review systematically elaborates the constituent soft matter and magnetic manipulation strategies of MSMRs, together with medical imaging‐based perception and sensing, as the fundamental basis for tissue interfacing applications. Besides, the interaction mechanisms between MSMRs and tissue interfaces under three distinct stages—low‐interference delivery, target‐interface coupling, and post‐coupling regulation—are thoroughly dissected. Based on the dominant configurations formed by MSMRs at target tissue interfaces during tissue interfacing biomedical interventions, MSMRs are classified into five categories, including patch, stent, embolization, swarm, and non‐retentive MSMRs. Their performance evaluations are discussed through delivery, deployment, functional output, and biosafety. Furthermore, challenges and future perspectives of MSMRs for tissue interfacing applications are also discussed.
authors: Wenxin Lian; Yan Zhou; Dianhong Zhang; Yuanwen Liang; Zihao Tang; Zhuo Chen; Qichen Hong; Jiangfan Yu; Chi Zhang; Xiaopu Wang

title: Nanomotors: Preparation Strategies, Propulsion Mechanisms, and Applications in Cancer Therapeutics
abstract: Cancer remains one of the leading causes of human death globally. The capabilities of tumor cells for rapid proliferation, resistance to death, and metastasis have become major hurdles in the successful treatment of cancer. Nanomotors, with distinct advantages such as tumor targeting and excellent biocompatibility, have emerged as a crucial research area in cancer therapy. This type of nanoscale dynamic system can convert external energy sources like magnetic fields, light fields, and sound fields, as well as endogenous chemical energy such as hydrogen peroxide, into autonomously driven mechanical energy. These distinctive motion characteristics remarkably enhance the penetration efficiency of nanocarriers into tumor tissue. This offers a promising approach to overcome the physiological barriers of the tumor microenvironment and improve therapeutic efficacy. In this review, the latest advancements in tumor treatment using nanomotors are systematically summarized. The content encompasses the preparation strategies, driving mechanisms, and therapeutic applications, providing crucial references for the further development of nanomotors in the field of cancer treatment.
authors: Heyi Zhang; Ben Shi; Lianzhen Li; Qinrui Fu; Zeyu Jiang

title: Natural orifice transluminal endoscopic surgery: The true frontier of gastrointestinal endoscopy
abstract: Natural orifice transluminal endoscopic surgery (NOTES) remains a frontier that continues to blur the boundaries between surgery and interventional endoscopy. Since its inception as an idea, NOTES has witnessed remarkable progress, from early animal experiments to its gradual translation into human applications as a minimally invasive approach for various mediastinal, thoracic, peritoneal, retroperitoneal, and pelvic diseases. The initial phase of NOTES was met with significant technical and safety challenges, often requiring hybrid laparoscopic assistance. A decade after inception of the idea of NOTES, the first pure NOTES procedure, a transvaginal cholecystectomy, marked a turning point that demonstrated the feasibility of a completely incisionless surgical concept. Over time, major barriers such as safe access, reliable closure, and effective hemostasis have been steadily addressed through advances in endoscopic tunneling, suturing platforms, hemostatic materials, and flexible endoscopic systems. The evolution of third space endoscopy, endobariatric procedures, and organ preserving transluminal interventions has further strengthened the translational foundation of NOTES. Robotic are now providing greater stability, precision, and triangulation, bringing NOTES closer to daily clinical use. Now more than two decades since its conception, NOTES stands on the verge of redefining minimally invasive therapy. This review revisits its journey, summarizes the present achievements, and highlights the innovations and global collaboration needed to guide the next era of scarless surgery. Recent advances in magnetic-assisted platforms have also played an important role in improving exposure, traction, and anastomosis creation within NOTES.
authors: Saif Ullah; Faisal S. Ali; Yi-Lin Han; Bing-Rong Liu; Nirav C Thosani; Zhuan Liao

title: Neuro Inspired Robotics: What Robot Learning Can Borrow from the Sensorimotor Brain
abstract: Robot policies still fail at everyday manipulation: an unfamiliar task, an object never held before, a scene that changes mid-motion, a skill that should improve with use. They fail despite pretraining on over a million trajectories, pooled from dozens of robots at great expense, while a child acquires all of these abilities within a few years of learning from a single body. This survey argues that the gap is one of design, and proposes designs for the next generation of robot models, drawn from how the nervous system solves the same problems. From the body we take compliance: the policy commands stiffness alongside position, so the controller yields where the task allows and presses where it must, which greatly lowers the demand for precise position output. From the visual system, where a fast pathway for action runs in parallel with the slow pathway for recognition, we take a dedicated fast vision system for motor behavior: it precomputes the quantities the policy needs and drives a reactive policy at camera rate. From the cerebellum we take a predictor beside the policy that forecasts the consequence of each command and recalibrates from its own error. From motor cortex we take a single model that composes action units from primitives, verifies each at a sensory boundary, practices the weakest unit with a hypothesis in mind, and reasons each attempt closer to the goal. Proven primitives are then consolidated from code into weights, so they run fluently and respond quickly the next time. Together these describe a robot that acts on its own initiative, the basis of deployment and recursive self-improvement, and we offer each proposal as a hypothesis to be tested.
authors: Ruihan Zhang; Davy Deng

title: Neuromorphic Decoding and Dynamical Image Reconstruction from Populations of Spiking Retinal Ganglion Cells
abstract: Decoding visual stimuli from the spiking activity of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) informs both our understanding of the retinal code and the design of visual prostheses. Natural vision is dynamic, yet state-of-the-art decoders mostly reconstruct single frames with artificial neural networks that process dense, continuous-valued signals rather than the retina's sparse, asynchronous spikes. We asked whether dynamic scenes can be reconstructed and tracked entirely within the spike domain, and at what computational cost. We built an end-to-end spiking neural network (SNN) whose neurons integrate the recorded RGC spikes over time. Populations of up to 1836 RGCs were recorded ex vivo from mouse retina on high-density microelectrode arrays while flashed images, moving bars, drifting gratings and randomly moving handwritten digits were presented. For moving digits, one shared spiking encoder fed two readouts, one reconstructing the image and one decoding the digit's position. Compute energy was estimated from counted synaptic operations. The SNN decoded what and where at once. It reconstructed the stimuli with a structural similarity (SSIM) of up to 0.93, refining the reconstruction as spikes accumulated, and tracked a randomly moving target with a mean error of 1.33 pixels on a $32\times32$ grid. Its fidelity nearly matched that of the best of 17 larger spiking and artificial decoders (5.9 million to 1.7 billion parameters, versus 5.4 million), and at a mean firing rate of 14.2% it needed an estimated $\sim$70-fold less compute energy than a dense artificial network of the same architecture. Dynamic visual scenes can thus be decoded from retinal population activity in the spike domain, with a compact network and at a compute cost compatible with implantable and wearable neural interfaces, supporting spike-native decoders for visual prostheses.
authors: Ning Zhang; Arto V Nurmikko

title: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug-induced enteropathy, presenting with multiple small bowel strictures: A case report
abstract: Introduction: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are used commonly and are widely available, they have a significant association with gastrointestinal system morbidity including small bowel enteropathy that can lead to small bowel strictures. Case Report: We present a case of severe small bowel enteropathy in a 51-year-old woman with a history of multiple small bowel resections and a delayed diagnosis. She was admitted to our unit following a prolonged course of symptoms, multiple bowel resections, and an unclear underlying etiology. She underwent a laparotomy and on table enteroscopy revealing multiple diaphragm-like strictures. Balloon dilatation was done on amenable strictures and a bowel resection for the severe segment. A background history of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) was elicited with strong advise to discontinue, and a diagnosis of NSAID-induced small bowel enteropathy was made. She was subsequently discharged nutritionally well. Conclusion: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs-induced small bowel enteropathy represents a diagnostically challenging condition requiring a high index of suspicion. Advances in diagnostic modalities, including video capsule endoscopy and double-balloon enteroscopy, have significantly improved detection.
authors: Layla Lombard; Adam Boutall; Dominic Mutura; Nsizwenye Mkhwanazi

title: Novel magnetic tracking-based three-dimensional trajectory small bowel capsule endoscopy system for lesion localization: An in vivo animal study
abstract: BACKGROUNDCapsule endoscopy has become the first-line modality for small bowel diseases.However, lesion localization remains a significant clinical challenge for small bowel capsule endoscopy (SBCE).A novel magnetic tracking-based three-dimensional (3D) trajectory SBCE system has been developed for precise lesion localization. AIMTo evaluate the feasibility and efficacy of a 3D trajectory SBCE system for measuring pylorus-to-lesion distances in a canine model. METHODSIntestinal lesion models were surgically established in three dogs by suturing beads within the small bowel (three lesions per dog).Pylorus-to-lesion distances were intraoperatively measured as the reference standard.After one week's recovery, the three dogs underwent SBCE examinations, and the capsule localization system reconstructed 3D capsule trajectories to determine distances traveled by the capsule at lesion sites.Feasibility was defined as achieving complete small bowel mucosal visualization and uninterrupted 3D trajectory generation.Efficacy was assessed by lesion detection rate and accuracy of pylorus-to-lesion distance measurements against surgical standards. RESULTSAll three dogs successfully completed SBCE examinations with no adverse events.For feasibility evaluation, the localization SBCE system achieved full small bowel visualization and reconstructed continuous 3D capsule trajectories in all canine subjects.For efficacy assessment, the system detected 100% of lesions (9/9) and demonstrated a mean relative error of 5.03% ± 2.05% for pylorus-to-lesion distance measurement. / 23 CONCLUSIONThis animal study demonstrates the feasibility and efficacy of a novel magnetic tracking-based 3D trajectory SBCE system for accurate pylorus-to-lesion distance measurement, indicating significant clinical potential for precise lesion localization and guiding subsequent interventions.
authors: Yizhi Chen; Xi Jiang; Chao Xu; Chen He; Xiao-Ou Qiu; Saif Ullah; Qing Song; Zhao-Shen Li; Zhuan Liao

title: ORBIT: A Modular Multi-finger Robotic Hand Platform with Rotational Finger Reconfiguration
abstract: Despite the popularity of multi-fingered robotic hands for dexterous manipulation, there is no systematic platform to compare different hand morphologies against one another. We present ORBIT (Orbital Reconfigurable Base-actuated Integrated Theta-motion Hand), a modular platform designed to enable principled exploration of multi-fingered hand morphology. The core contribution of ORBIT is a rotating knuckle mechanism, where independent fingers travel around a cylindrical palm via a belt drive. This enables ORBIT to perform quick recon- figuration (< 1 s) of finger layout without hand disassembly. ORBITs a robust system, with finger average angular velocity of 1.57 rad / s1 and a root finger force resistance of 50 N. Using a three fingers instantiation of ORBIT, we demonstrate an initial pilot grasping study, comparing anthropomorphic, isometric, and Barrett-style finger layouts across eleven objects of varied size, shape, and texture. We further demonstrate how ORBITs nonanthropomorphic orbital DOF enables the achievement of tasks that would be difficult to perform with fixed-knuckle designs, such as cube face reorientation, lid threading, and precision pinching of sub-centimeter objects. These results establish ORBIT as a viable platform for direct apples to apples comparison of multi-fingered hand morphologies for specific manipulation tasks
authors: Benito Ribadeneira; Siqi Shang; Lillian Chin

title: Object Detection in Computer Vision: A Comprehensive Review of Algorithms, Datasets, and Evaluation Techniques
abstract: Object detection has evolved dramatically over three decades, transitioning from handcrafted features to deep learning, transformers, and now large language models. This paper provides a comprehensive systematic review of this evolution, covering traditional methods (SIFT, HOG, Viola-Jones), CNN-based single- and two-stage detectors (R-CNN family, YOLO v1-v12, SSD), transformer-based architectures (DETR, ViT, Swin), and emerging LLM-driven approaches (GPT-4V, Grounding DINO, YOLO-World). We benchmark and compare these methods using key metrics-mAP, IoU, FPS-and analyze over 50 datasets across generic, autonomous driving, medical, remote sensing, and agricultural domains. Our critical synthesis identifies persistent research gaps: lightweight edge deployment, sensor fusion for real-time systems, bias and fairness in AI, and multimodal vision-language integration. By consolidating three decades of progress and outlining future challenges, this survey serves as a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners seeking to develop accurate, efficient, and reliable object detection systems.
authors: Md. Faishal Rahaman; Li Xueyuan; Md Nagib Mahfuz Sunny; Muhammad Amjad; Xin Gao; Sakib Hasan

title: Optical See-Through, Video See-Through, and Screen-Based Guidance: A Three-Way Comparison for Close-Range Manual Tasks
abstract: Optical see-through (OST) and video see-through (VST) head-mounted displays promise to improve guidance for close-range manual tasks, yet prior comparisons often use a single display class, heterogeneous tasks, or lack a matched non-AR baseline. We report a within-subjects comparison of Microsoft HoloLens 2 (OST), Meta Quest 3 (VST), and a 24-inch screen baseline (N = 23) across three close-range tasks: object placement, trajectory tracing, and depth-bounded reaching, each tested under Visible and Occluded conditions on a shared apparatus with sub-millimetre optical tracking. The AR advantage over the screen increased with task depth demand, from near-equivalence in placement to the largest gain in reaching. The two headsets were similar in accuracy but differed in dynamics, comfort, and workload: VST was faster, had the lowest workload, and was rated most usable, but was least comfortable and showed a late decline in depth precision; OST was more comfortable and improved with practice despite the lowest self-perceived performance. These results provide task-specific guidance for selecting OST, VST, or screen-based guidance in close-range manual work.
authors: Sergey Strelkov; A. Bayrak; Supriya Supriya

title: Optical characterization of endoscopes for StoneSense™ compatibility
abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE: The StoneSense Module (SSM), integrated within IPG laser lithotripsy systems, uses endoscopic white-light illumination for real-time stone-tissue discrimination, enabling conditional laser firing only in the presence of a confirmed calculus. SSM performance depends on the endoscope's optical output falling within defined thresholds. We aimed to characterize commercially available flexible ureteroscopes and cystoscopes against predefined SSM compatibility criteria. METHODS: Twenty device-videobox combinations (15 flexible ureteroscopes, 4 cystoscopes, 1 semirigid ureteroscope; 7 manufacturers) with complete StoneSense-processed band data were included. Total power and spectral band power (Bands 1-3) were measured at three brightness levels in free-space configuration (no fiber inserted), and temporal profile was classified by oscilloscopy. Per-fiber band power was modeled from these free-space measurements, not measured with the fiber in the working channel. Predicted SSM band-power compatibility was assessed per device-brightness-fiber combination against predefined thresholds, with a minimum PWM frequency of 2 kHz as the temporal criterion. RESULTS: All 20 devices exhibited continuous-wave (CW) emission, conferring unconditional temporal SSM compatibility. Following recalibration of the SSM reference thresholds, the 200 µm and 365 µm fibers were predicted to meet SSM band power thresholds at medium/maximum brightness for 18 of the 20 devices, with the Karl Storz Flex XC and the Olympus CYF-VH cystoscope as the two exceptions at both fiber sizes. Additional saturation, restricted to the 550 µm and 940 µm fibers, was identified for six further devices (Table 1). Four Olympus platforms showed modeled sub-threshold power at minimum brightness. Four illumination archetypes were identified: blue-pump LED, red-shifted LED, Olympus intermediate LED, and LED-phosphor. CONCLUSIONS: The 200 µm and 365 µm fibers provide the broadest predicted compatibility (18/20 platforms), with the Flex XC and CYF-VH as the exceptions. Predicted incompatibilities are otherwise device-architecture-driven and manageable through fiber and brightness selection. A device-level compatibility reference matrix based on modeled estimates is provided.
authors: Nicola Nannola; Carlos Gonzalez-Gonzalez; Federico Zorzi; Pietro Scilipoti; Adèle Martin-Illac; Frédéric Panthier; M. Chicaud; Steeve Doizi; Iliya Yaroslavsky; Anastasia Kovalenko; James Childs; Igor Perchuk; Olivier Traxer

title: Optimizing Ophthalmic Surgery Outcomes Using Predictive ML Algorithms
abstract: Ophthalmic surgery has experienced tremendous progresses in the past two decades. It has all been due to new surgery techniques, improved imaging and the integration of digital health. Predictive machine-learning (ML) algorithms have the potential to be helpful in enhancing decisions and outcomes. In this chapter, the authors present a review of the recent predictive ML solutions in enhancing the outcome of ophthalmic surgery. They study algorithmic frameworks, analyze how to use them in particular areas of surgery, and explain what their advantages, disadvantages and prospects are. The authors leave evidence gathered in the recent past showing how predictive ML can complement precision ophthalmology and surgeons' custom-takes on procedures specific to the patient, and increase the overall success rates of the surgery. Combining ML and cloud technology with the electronic health records scale will ensure the availability of the tools in various environments.
authors: D.B. SHIRKE; V. Patil Zunjar

title: Oral Radiology and Diagnostic Imaging: The Most Mature Frontier of Dental Artificial Intelligence
abstract: Oral radiology is the most extensively studied domain of dental artificial intelligence (AI), accounting for more than a quarter of all dental AI publications between 2011 and 2021. Convolutional neural networks have been trained to detect caries, periapical lesions, alveolar bone loss, root fractures, cysts and anatomical structures on periapical, bitewing, panoramic and cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) images, often reaching sensitivity and specificity comparable to, or higher than, those of general dental practitioners. This chapter reviews the main applications of AI in dental imaging, the quantitative evidence behind them, the first randomized and economic evaluations, and the practical issues that determine whether a radiographic AI tool helps or harms patients: dataset heterogeneity, generalisability across equipment and populations, the risk of overtreatment and the need for prospective, real-world validation. Because many orthodontic, periodontal, endodontic, surgical and pediatric tools are built on the same image-analysis architectures, the maturity of oral radiology underpins much of what is discussed in later chapters. The chapter concludes that radiographic AI is ready to act as a second reader under clinical supervision, but not as an autonomous diagnostician.
authors: Paulo Vinícius de Oliveira Bastos; Pablo Lourenço Fernandes; Henrique Schultz Lacerda Guimarães; Marilya Roberta Ferreira de Melo; Anna Gabriela da Silva Pierre; · Luis Fernando Ferreira da Silva
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Oral ingestion versus endoscopic delivery of small-bowel capsule endoscopy in adults with surgically altered upper gastrointestinal anatomy: a systematic review and meta-analysis protocol
abstract: Small-bowel capsule endoscopy (SBCE) in adults with surgically altered upper gastrointestinal anatomy, such as Billroth II reconstruction, Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, oesophagectomy or pancreaticoduodenectomy, may be incomplete because the capsule can be retained in the gastric remnant or pouch, enter an afferent or biliopancreatic limb, or bypass small-bowel segments. Endoscopic delivery is often used to avoid these problems, but it adds a procedure, usually with sedation, and has its own risks. Direct comparisons between the two routes are scarce. This systematic review will estimate caecal completion with oral ingestion and with endoscopic delivery of SBCE in these patients. The primary outcome is caecal completion with the initially intended strategy, without endoscopic rescue. Secondary outcomes are caecal completion by the route actually used, retention, adverse events, delivery failure and endoscopic rescue, anatomical completeness and diagnostic yield. PubMed, Scopus, Europe PMC and Google Scholar were searched on 2 November 2026, together with targeted searches for conference abstracts. Eligible study designs include comparative studies, cohort studies and case series reporting outcomes for at least five adults with surgically altered upper gastrointestinal anatomy. Two reviewers independently select studies, extract data and assess risk of bias. Proportions will be pooled for each route with random-effects models when at least three clinically comparable studies are available. Because these estimates come largely from different studies, they will not be read as a comparison of effectiveness. Studies comparing both routes directly will be analysed separately, and results will be explored by type of surgical reconstruction. We will also examine how studies define anatomical completeness, particularly whether they assess visualisation of surgically excluded segments rather than caecal completion alone.
authors: Rui Vieira; Pedro Campelo; Bruno Joel Ferreira Rosa; José Cotter

title: Organoids as Building Blocks for Adaptive and Resilient Biohybrid Robots
abstract: Biohybrid robots combine engineered living tissues with synthetic materials and have emerged as a promising class of soft robotic systems capable of mimicking biological functions such as biodegradability, energy efficiency and flexible motions. By integrating biological and synthetic components, these systems leverage complementary properties to perform key robotic functions including locomotion and task execution. Despite rapid progress, important limitations remain, many of which arise from the biological components themselves, including limited longevity, adaptive behavior and challenges in control. In this review, we propose organoids as advanced biological building blocks for biohybrid robotics and examine their potential based on recent advances in organoid engineering, maturation and functional development. We summarize recent advances in organoid engineering relevant to robotic integration and discuss strategies for interfacing organoids with electronic and control systems. We also discuss key technical and conceptual challenges, including signal interfacing, long‐term viability, reproducibility and how these aspects of organoid research can benefit biohybrid systems. By integrating advances in stem cell biology, materials science and robotics, this review article examines how organoids could extend beyond their established roles as in vitro models and potentially contribute to a new generation of adaptive, resilient and biologically integrated machines.
authors: Antonia Georgopoulou

title: PREFERENDO: a preference for the full picture in pediatric capsule endoscopy
abstract: The PREFERENDO consensus provides a valuable framework for pediatric endoscopy reporting [1]. Its capsule domain already includes preparation quality, completeness, lesion description and interpretation. The opportunity for refinement lies in connecting these fields to the endorsed scores. We suggest an implementation principle: each reported score should include the information needed to understand what it measures and how examination quality constrains its interpretation.
authors: Anastasios Koulaouzidis; Ervin Tóth; Wojciech M. Marlicz

title: Paradigm shifts in prostate biopsy strategies in the era of precision medicine
abstract: The escalating global burden of prostate cancer necessitates continuous refinement of diagnostic strategies. Although prostate biopsy remains the gold standard for diagnosis, key procedural aspects, including biopsy template, guidance methods, and biopsy route, remain subjects of ongoing debate. Current approaches have yet to achieve the dual goals of high sensitivity and high specificity in diagnostic performance. In recent years, ongoing advancements in related fields have generated substantial clinical evidence, offering further insights into optimizing biopsy strategies. This review provides a synthesized framework for navigating the paradigm shift from traditional, standardized biopsy toward personalized, precision-based approaches. We not only trace the evolution of biopsy techniques but also offer a comprehensive, in-depth exploration of how patient-specific factors, such as prostate volume, prostate-specific antigen density, and Prostate Imaging Reporting and Data System scores, can inform individualized biopsy decisions, thereby providing practical clinical guidance. In addition to critically evaluating conventional biopsy paradigms, we systematically examine emerging biopsy strategies and synthesize high-quality studies at the forefront of this field. Finally, against the backdrop of the artificial intelligence era, we highlight the transformative potential of artificial intelligence and robotic platforms across the diagnosis. By integrating current development and future directions, this review offers a structured framework for personalized biopsy decision-making, ultimately aiming to achieve both high sensitivity and high specificity in individualized prostate cancer diagnosis.
authors: Chenhui Tang; Zhen Liang; Weigang Yan

title: Passive rotational substrate handling in three-axis gantry robots
abstract: Simple three-axis gantry-based robots are widely used in laboratory automation due to their low cost, ease of implementation and flexibility. However, solid sample manipulation tasks that are intuitive for human operators, such as positioning and reorientation, often require motion capabilities beyond those of standard gantry systems, limiting the implementation of more advanced, uninterrupted automated experiments. Dexterous movements can be achieved using robotic arms or advanced motor systems, but with substantially increased system integration complexity and cost. This work presents a low-cost substrate handling and rotation module that enables passive degree-of-freedom augmentation in existing three-axis gantry-based automated workflows, addressing a key manual handling bottleneck. The modular pick-and-place hardware leverages the existing linear motion of an Opentrons OT-2 gantry to drive a rack-and-pinion mechanism, thereby enabling repeatable 180° rotational motion about a horizontal axis without the need for additional motors, electronics, or an external robotic system. We demonstrate this module in the automated manipulation of contact lens hydrogels for wettability characterization assays, though this platform can be used in broader laboratory automation applications including sample repositioning for microscopy or coating formation.
authors: Tithi Choksi; Erin Ng; Mohammad Nazeri; Frank Gu

title: Path-breaking to Innovate: Patenting in Internet of Things (IoT) Technologies
abstract: This paper challenges conventional wisdom that core-technology competence and innovation persistence drive innovation success in architecturally distinct technologies. Using Internet of Things (IoT), we theorise its multi-layered architecture creates conditions where specialisation produces cognitive lock-in whilst breadth enables cross-domain integration. Analysing 93,777 patents from 2,619 UK firms (2008–2017), we find: (1) core-technology competence negatively predicts IoT patenting; (2) related and unrelated technological diversification positively influence IoT innovation, reversing absorptive capacity arguments; (3) innovation persistence strengthens IoT innovation through interaction with unrelated but not related diversification. Analysis across Big Data, 3D printing, and Robotics confirms generalisability. These findings identify architectural distinctiveness as a boundary condition requiring revision of core competence, absorptive capacity, and innovation persistence frameworks. Firms should prioritise technological breadth over depth; policymakers should foster diverse knowledge connections rather than supporting innovation champions.
authors: Jun Du; James H. Love; Xiaocan Yuan

title: Peer Review Report For: Artificial Intelligence and Imaging Technologies in Orthodontic Assessment, Referral and Care Pathways: A Scoping Review [version 1; peer review: 1 approved with reservations]
abstract: * Background Artificial intelligence (AI), integrated with imaging technologies, is increasingly applied across orthodontic assessment and care pathways. However, the evidence remains scattered across imaging modalities, clinical applications, AI methodologies, and stages of clinical translation. Methods A scoping review was conducted in accordance with the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and reported in line with the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. PubMed, Scopus, and IEEE Xplore were searched for studies published between January 2016 and June 2026, with searches supplemented by Google Scholar, OpenAlex, grey literature sources, and citation searching. Eligible studies were mapped descriptively and synthesised thematically using Braun and Clarke’s framework. Results Fifty-four studies were included. AI applications used intraoral and facial photographs, cephalometric radiographs, CBCT, intraoral scans, three-dimensional dental models, and multimodal imaging. Applications ranged from landmark localisation, segmentation, and malocclusion classification to treatment-need assessment, screening, referral support, treatment planning, and remote monitoring. Evidence was strongest for bounded, anatomically verifiable image-analysis tasks, whereas applications involving referral, triage, treatment-need decisions, longitudinal prediction, and workflow integration were less mature. Common limitations included retrospective, single-centre designs; heterogeneous reference standards; limited external validation; inconsistent reporting of calibration and uncertainty; and insufficient evaluation of patient-centred, equity, and service-level outcomes. Conclusions Imaging-based AI in orthodontics has evolved from automated image interpretation to clinician-assisted decision support across the care pathway. Current evidence most strongly supports AI for structured image-analysis tasks, but does not yet support autonomous referral, triage, or treatment-planning decisions. Future research should prioritise prospective multicentre validation, transparent reporting, explainability, fairness, uncertainty handling, and workflow-integrated evaluation to enable safe and clinically useful implementation.

title: Per-Patient Polyp Detection Rate of Colon Capsule Endoscopy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis with Exploratory Stratification by Referral Pathway.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Colon capsule endoscopy (CCE) is a minimally invasive alternative to optical colonoscopy, but per-patient polyp detection rate (PDR), the proportion of patients with at least one visually reported polyp, varies across referral populations. We estimated any-polyp and size-stratified CCE yield and explored between-study variation. Methods: MEDLINE, Embase, PubMed, and Cochrane CENTRAL were searched from 1 January 2004 to 29 July 2026. Proportions were pooled using random-intercept binomial-normal generalised linear mixed models. PROSPERO: CRD420261464937 (registration not prospective). Results: Of 44 retained studies (12,754 participants), 31 independent studies (11,310 participants) formed the primary pool. Pooled PDR was 53.2% (95% CI 46.1-60.1; prediction interval 19-85%), a descriptive average, not a performance target. Exploratory PDR was 81.2% after positive FIT (k = 4), 49.4% after incomplete colonoscopy (k = 4), and 39.9% in screening without prior FIT enrichment (k = 3); 14 studies had mixed pathways. Pooled detection was 32.7% for polyps ≥ 6 mm (prediction interval 8-74%) and 17.7% for polyps ≥ 10 mm (4-51%). Conclusions: CCE PDR is a visual yield measure, not adenoma detection or diagnostic accuracy. A global CCE PDR is not a portable quality threshold; referral-pathway estimates are descriptive and hypothesis-generating. Future quality metrics require standardised pathways, denominators, and linkage to downstream clinical outcomes.
authors: Lei II, Vigo GB, Arasaradnam RP, Koulaouzidis A.

title: Performance of Large Language Models Across Diagnostic Tasks in Oral and Maxillofacial Pathology: A Systematic Review
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly evaluated for diagnostic applications; however, studies in oral and maxillofacial pathology (OMFP) assess materially different diagnostic tasks and outcomes. This systematic review synthesized evidence according to the specific task evaluated. METHODS: PubMed, Web of Science, and Cochrane Central were searched without language or date restrictions, supplemented by gray-literature screening and citation tracking. Studies evaluating defined OMFP diagnostic tasks using task-appropriate outcomes were included. Screening, data extraction, and quality assessment were independently performed by 2 reviewers. Owing to clinical and methodological heterogeneity, evidence was synthesized narratively by diagnostic task. RESULTS: Sixteen studies published between 2024 and 2025 were included. Seven evaluated single-diagnosis identification, 6 differential-diagnosis generation or ranking, 5 binary or multiclass classification/detection, and 1 structured diagnostic report generation; counts were non-mutually exclusive. Exact-diagnosis performance varied considerably and did not demonstrate consistent specialist equivalence. Differential-diagnosis studies generally reported higher Top-k inclusion than Top-1 accuracy, but these outcomes did not establish exact diagnostic correctness. Classification studies frequently reported high specificity but variable sensitivity. The single report-generation study reported item-level rather than whole-case diagnostic outcomes. CONCLUSION: Large language models may support selected OMFP tasks, particularly differential-diagnosis generation. However, exact-diagnosis performance remains inconsistent, classification sensitivity is task-dependent, and evidence for structured report generation is limited. Current evidence does not support a single overall estimate of diagnostic performance or autonomous diagnostic use.
authors: Sohaib Shujaat; Marryam Riaz; Hisham Albrikeet; Hongyang Ma

title: Peroxisome dysfunction disrupts metabolism of photoreceptor outer segments in human retinal pigment epithelium
abstract: Retinal degeneration and blindness frequently develop in patients with peroxisomal disorders, yet mechanisms remain obscure. Peroxisomes are organelles that compartmentalize metabolic reactions including lipid catabolism and cellular detoxification. Here, we generated induced pluripotent stem cell-derived human retinal pigment epithelial cells (iRPEs) deficient in the essential peroxisomal proteins PEX1 and PEX6 to study the effects of peroxisome dysfunction in a disease-relevant cell type. Following a physiologically relevant photoreceptor outer segment (POS) challenge, PEX1 −/− and PEX6 −/− iRPEs demonstrated impaired polyunsaturated fatty acid retroconversion, lipid droplet accumulation, and reduced transepithelial electrical resistance. Additionally, PEX1 −/− and PEX6 −/− iRPEs exhibited a failure in the clearance of rhodopsin, the major protein in POS, which coincided with a broader defect in lysosomal function. These findings suggest that dysregulated POS metabolism in the retinal pigment epithelium is a potential mechanism driving retinal degeneration in patients with peroxisomal disorders and provide a basis for investigating lysosomal enhancement as a therapeutic strategy.
authors: Constantin Mouzaaber; Carly B. Feldman; Suzette M Huguenin; John Y.S. Han; Erin Trombly; Qitao Zhang; Aja M. Rieger; Hamed Hojjat; Brandon C. Huynh; Ehsan Misaghi; Alina Radziwon; Temesgen Fufa; Robert B. Hufnagel; Jason M. L. Miller; Matthew D. Benson

title: Physical AI in Medical Imaging and NVIDIA Isaac for Healthcare
abstract: Physical AI represents the convergence of artificial intelligence, robotics, simulation, sensing, and embodied reasoning systems capable of perceiving and acting within physical clinical environments. Within healthcare, medical imaging provides one of the most important and immediately transformative domains for Physical AI due to the increasing demand for imaging services, workforce shortages, rising operational complexity, and the need for precision-guided interventions. This chapter examines the emergence of Physical AI in imaging, with a particular focus on the NVIDIA Isaac for Healthcare ecosystem and its integration with digital twins, simulation environments, multimodal foundation models, robotic autonomy, and real-time edge AI. The chapter explores how Physical AI extends traditional AI beyond passive image interpretation toward autonomous and semi-autonomous imaging workflows, robotic ultrasound, image-guided intervention, and intelligent clinical environments. Technical foundations including sensor fusion, simulation-based training, reinforcement learning, synthetic data generation, and embodied healthcare robotics are discussed. The chapter further evaluates clinical opportunities, ethical considerations, infrastructure requirements, regulatory implications, and future research directions. Particular emphasis is placed on how Isaac for Healthcare enables the development of scalable healthcare robotics through digital twins, physics-based simulation, and deployment-ready architectures.
authors: Nilmini Wickramasinghe

title: Physics-informed computer vision-based prawn length measurement from mobile camera imagery: toward robotic aquaculture monitoring
abstract: This study presents a physics-informed computer vision framework using mobile camera imagery for non-invasive estimation of the body length of the giant freshwater prawn ( Macrobrachium rosenbergii ) in aquaculture ponds. Unlike previous systems that rely on static, geometrically constrained imaging setups, the proposed framework operates on images acquired from a mobile camera platform (floating or amphibious), enabling spatially distributed in situ sampling while maintaining a fixed camera-to-floor reference distance. The framework introduces three key innovations: geometric measurement algorithms tailored for mobile imaging with explicit correction of optical refraction at the air–water interface; a dual-validation strategy that evaluates measurement accuracy against human raters and a physical specimen; and a transparent error-decomposition framework that quantifies the major sources of measurement uncertainty. Pixel-to-length conversion combines trigonometric projection, Snell’s law-based refraction correction, and lens-distortion compensation. A YOLOv11-pose model detects anatomically meaningful keypoints to estimate carapace and total body length. The model achieved high pose-estimation performance across pond types (mAP@95 up to 0.98), while robustness analysis showed that simulated turbidity primarily reduced detection success rather than measurement accuracy. Comparison with repeated human measurements showed that model estimates fell within human measurement variability, with model-MAE/human-CR ratios of 0.3–0.7. Validation against physical specimens of known length yielded a median absolute relative error of 4.53% (7.09 mm; n = 90). Error decomposition revealed that pixel-localization uncertainty was the dominant error source, indicating that future accuracy gains depend mainly on improved keypoint localization. A database comprising 2,478 images from three RAS ponds is made publicly available.
authors: Gil Ben Or; Tair Carmon; Shai Avraham Shaked; Nisim Kachlon; Eliahu David Aflalo; Amir Sagi; David Zarrouk; Yael Edan

title: Pixels to precision: Deep learning in dental imaging
abstract: Dental imaging is fundamental to diagnosis, treatment planning, and follow-up in Oral Medicine and Maxillofacial Radiology. Although conventional radiographic interpretation remains dependent on professional expertise, diagnostic performance may be influenced by observer variability, image quality, workload, and the subtle nature of early pathological changes. The development of Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly deep learning (DL), has introduced new approaches for automated analysis of dental and maxillofacial images. This narrative review discusses the evolution, principles, applications, clinical relevance, limitations, and future directions of deep learning in dental imaging, with emphasis on intraoral radiography, panoramic radiography, cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT), and related imaging modalities. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have demonstrated applications in dental caries detection, periodontal bone assessment, periapical lesion detection, tooth identification and numbering, jaw lesion analysis, anatomical segmentation, and treatment planning. More advanced architectures, including U-Net, residual networks, object-detection models, three-dimensional CNNs, and emerging transformer-based systems, have expanded the scope of automated image interpretation. However, the rapid growth of research has also highlighted important limitations, including small and heterogeneous datasets, inconsistent annotation, retrospective study designs, limited external validation, algorithmic bias, and difficulties in explaining model predictions. Importantly, high algorithmic accuracy does not necessarily translate into clinical effectiveness. Future research should therefore focus on diverse multicentre datasets, external and prospective validation, explainable AI, multimodal systems, ethical governance, and meaningful human-AI collaboration. Deep learning is most appropriately viewed as an adjunctive clinical decision-support technology that complements rather than replaces professional diagnostic judgment.
authors: Ananya Sapra; Suman Sen

title: Polyp Matching Using Deep Learning
abstract: A key challenge in colon capsule endoscopy (CCE) analysis is accurately identifying whether multiple images depict the same polyp, which is critical to avoid over-counting and unnecessary clinical interventions. Additionally, this prevents prolonged follow-up colonoscopies where endoscopists search for duplicate polyps without precise localization. This study presents a novel contrastive learning-based approach to polyp matching using a Siamese neural network architecture. The model was trained on a dataset from the Danish CareForColon2015 trial. The dataset comprises 5,103 image pairs of confirmed same polyp and 5,103 pairs of different polyps, annotated by experienced clinicians. The proposed model employs ResNet variants (ResNet18, ResNet34, ResNet50), DenseNet121 and EfficientNet B0/B3 as backbones and utilizes contrastive learning with cosine vector distance metric for classification. Experimental results demonstrate high classification accuracies of up to 92% and AUC values close to 0.98. These results suggest that automated polyp matching has the potential to reduce polyp over-counting, improve patient risk stratification, and reduce unnecessary follow-up colonoscopies.
authors: Kristian Hindberg; Puneet Sharma; Benedicte Schelde‐Olesen; Ulrik Deding; Jakob Frederik Frokjaer Justsen; Jan-Matthias Braun; Esmaeil S. Nadimi

title: Polyzwitterion with Imidazole for Ultralow‐Power Organic Photoelectric Synaptic Transistors Achieving Multicolor Robot Vision and Dynamic Recognition
abstract: Neuromorphic in-sensor vision demands photoelectric synaptic transistors that co-localize optical sensing and electrically tunable plasticity in a compact device, thereby simplifying artificial visual sensing circuits. Electrolytes and ionic liquids are widely employed as dielectric layers for neuromorphic transistors; however, cation-anion pairs without covalent bonds typically suffer from ion-migration, ion replacement, and electrochemical reactions. These processes lead to current leakage, elevated power consumption, and irreversible drift, while photo-modulation is further attenuated by exciton-polaron quenching. Here, to stabilize ionic charges and suppress ion-migration, a polyzwitterion, poly(3-(1-vinyl-3-imidazolyl)-propanesulfonate), is used as a single medium to unify electro- and photo-synaptic functions, thereby simplifying the components and interfaces of the multilayer device. The aromatic conjugated imidazole ring stabilizes the cationic charge, and the covalently tethered cation-anion pair prevents long-distance ion-migration, ensuring strong cation-anion dipole polarization and reversible charge trapping. This enables robust multi-wavelength photo-synaptic modulation coupled with electro-synaptic plasticity. The resulting organic photoelectric synaptic transistors achieve ultralow event energy consumption down to 10.95 aJ and support application-relevant in-sensor demonstrations, including encrypted image decoding, color-guided robotic manipulation, pedestrian-speed recognition, and motion prediction. These findings are poised to accelerate the development of multifunctional photoelectric synaptic devices and integrated sensing-computing hardware architectures for artificial visual systems.
authors: Jingpeng Wu; Yi Zhao; Chaoxiong Guo; Pengyu Du; Xian Tang; Zechen Liang; Yiyu Chen; Xin Wang; Laju Bu; Guanghao Lu

title: Portable medical imaging in modern healthcare: Fundamentals, AI-based taxonomy, image quality, and open challenges
authors: Hamza Kheddar; Yassine Habchi; Muhammad Ali Qureshi; Azeddine Beghdadi

title: Portal Hypertensive Enteropathy in Cirrhosis: A Systematic Review of Prevalence, Predictors, and Bleeding Outcomes Detected by Capsule Endoscopy
abstract: Portal hypertensive enteropathy (PHE) is the small-bowel counterpart of portal hypertensive gastropathy; however, its frequency, determinants, and relevance to bleeding remain poorly defined. This systematic review, conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement, synthesised evidence from original studies evaluating PHE using small-bowel capsule endoscopy (SBCE) in adults with cirrhosis. PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, CINAHL, and IEEE Xplore were searched from January 1, 2016, to October 18, 2026. Of the 420 records identified, 224 remained after deduplication and were screened by a single reviewer, resulting in the inclusion of nine observational studies (898 participants overall). Six studies were conducted in Japan, and five originated from a single Japanese centre with overlapping enrolment; therefore, the estimated number of unique patients ranged from 586 to 898. Risk of bias was assessed using an adapted Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS). In four cohorts evaluating patients with anaemia or suspected small-bowel bleeding, PHE was present in 59% to 95% of patients. In elective cohorts, small-bowel lesions were identified in 84% of 31 transplant candidates, and villous oedema was observed in 36% of 363 patients referred for PHE assessment. Markers of advanced portal hypertension, namely Child-Pugh class B/C or decompensation, oesophageal varices, portal hypertensive gastropathy, portal vein thrombosis, and splenomegaly, were the most consistent factors associated with PHE. In three single-centre serial SBCE cohorts, PHE progressed in 35% to 48% of patients. In one cohort (n = 42), worsening was more frequent after endoscopic injection sclerotherapy than after band ligation (90% vs 50%), whereas in another (n = 55), splenectomy was associated with a lower frequency of worsening (adjusted odds ratio (aOR): 0.069, 95% confidence interval (CI): 0.006-0.789). Bleeding was predominantly associated with the vascular phenotype: in one single-centre cohort of 165 patients with suspected small-bowel bleeding, the small bowel was identified as the bleeding source in 66% of patients with vascular PHE, compared with 3% of those without vascular PHE, and one-year rebleeding rates were 33% versus 0%, respectively. Active or recent small-bowel bleeding was documented in 11.6% of a prospective cohort (n = 43). Four studies were rated as having a low risk of bias and five a moderate risk of bias. Despite the limitations of a small and geographically concentrated observational evidence base, PHE appears common in cirrhosis, is associated with surrogates of portal pressure, and exhibits considerable clinical heterogeneity. Vascular lesions appear to identify the subgroup at greatest risk of bleeding. Further studies incorporating standardised grading and prospective multicentre designs are required before SBCE-based surveillance can be recommended.
authors: Nazar Abdelgabar

title: Pou2f2 enhances retinal ganglion cell survival and axon regeneration after optic nerve injury
abstract: Retinal ganglion cell (RGC) degeneration and the limited regenerative capacity of mammalian central nervous system axons result in irreversible vision loss in optic neuropathies. Identifying intrinsic regulators that promote both neuroprotection and axon regeneration is critical for developing effective therapies. This study identified POU domain class 2 transcription factor 2 (Pou2f2) as a previously unrecognized regulator involved in RGC biology. Single-cell RNA sequencing analysis of developing mouse and human retinas showed that Pou2f2 is enriched in RGC clusters and suppressed by an RGC fate suppressor in the mouse retinal progenitor cell culture. Pou2f2 protein was detected in mouse RGCs and optic nerves, where its expression decreased following optic nerve crush (ONC). In primary RGC cultures, AAV2-mediated Pou2f2 overexpression enhanced neurite outgrowth, whereas Pou2f2 knockdown reduced neurite length. In vivo, intravitreal injection of Pou2f2 overexpression AAV2s increased axon regeneration, improved RGC survival, and partially preserved RGC function after ONC. Bulk RNA sequencing data revealed early activation of cytoskeletal growth pathways and later upregulation of DNA repair-associated genes, whereas immunostaining and in vitro analyses suggested activation of AKT/mTOR signaling following Pou2f2 overexpression. Together, these findings identify Pou2f2 as a promising molecular target for gene-based therapies for RGC degenerative diseases, including glaucoma and other optic neuropathies.
authors: D. N. Stavropoulos; Chia-Chun Liu; Shining Wang; Chi-Yu Chen; Mishal Rao; Laman Mirzaliyeva; Hui-Chun Cheng; Ya-Ling Lin; Andrew M. Williams; Yuan Pan; Takaaki Kuwajima; Jeffrey Louis Goldberg; José‐Alain Sahel; Kun‐Che Chang

title: Presumed acquired traction diverticula of the small bowel causing occult bleeding in a child after congenital diaphragmatic hernia repair: a case report
abstract: Small bowel diverticula other than Meckel's diverticulum are rare in children, and acquired traction diverticula caused by adhesions have rarely been described.An 11-yearold boy with a history of neonatal congenital diaphragmatic hernia repair presented with refractory iron deficiency anemia and persistently positive fecal occult blood tests.Endoscopy, pertechnetate scintigraphy, computed tomography, and magnetic resonance enterography found no source of bleeding.Capsule endoscopy identified multiple ulcerated jejunoileal diverticula, and the capsule was retained.Laparotomy revealed diffuse adhesions involving nearly the entire small bowel, and histopathological examination confirmed true diverticula in the resected segment.During 2 months of postoperative follow-up, the patient remained free of overt bleeding and abdominal symptoms without iron supplementation.Traction diverticula may be considered as a possible cause of occult small bowel bleeding in children with a history of abdominal surgery.
authors: Young Hoi Kwon; Yiyoung Kwon; Tae Jong Jeong; Yon Ho Choe; Seok Hyung Kim; Mi Jin Kim; Yoon Zi Kim

title: Prevalence of Pathological Lesions and Normal Variations in the Oral Mucosa among Geriatric Patients at the University Veracruzana
abstract: Objective: To determine the prevalence of pathological lesions and variants of normalcy in the oral mucosa among geriatric patients who visited the University of Veracruz. Materials and Methods: A descriptive study was conducted by analyzing clinical records of 34 patients treated in two groups of the Geriatric Dentistry Educational Experience during the period from August to December 2024; To evaluate the association between variables (age, presence of chronic degenerative diseases, and sex), Fisher's exact test was used, with a statistical significance level of p < 0.05. Results: 32.4% had at least one pathological lesion, and 85.3% had at least one variant of normal. No statistically significant association was identified between the variables and the presence of lesions and/or variants. Conclusions: The study characterized the oral lesions present in the geriatric population. The findings highlight the importance of a systematic intraoral examination in geriatric dentistry.
authors: Claudia Citlalli Yanez Cedillo; Claudia Olguín Yobal; Mercedes Soledad Briceno Ancona; Jacinto Izquierdo Jacome
venue: International Journal of Science and Research (IJSR)

title: Programable Acoustic Single‐Cell Manipulation With Model‐Free Machine Learning
abstract: Precise, noninvasive manipulation of individual living cells remains a central challenge in biomedical science, with far‐reaching implications for single‐cell analysis, tissue engineering, and the study of cell–cell interactions. Here, we report the first demonstration of single‐cell control using bulk acoustic standing‐wave acoustofluidics with closed‐loop feedback. We introduce VeLO (Vector‐based Local Optimization), a model‐free, reinforcement learning–inspired algorithm that enables programable two‐dimensional manipulation of individual cells using a single piezoelectric transducer. Without prior calibration or physical modeling, VeLO learns system dynamics online from acoustically induced cell displacements and automatically adapts to nonlinear, time‐varying conditions. We achieve robust control across multiple cell types (DU‐145, Jurkat, K‐562) and independent manipulation of multiple cells, including controlled cell–cell contact. By combining simplicity of hardware with autonomous, adaptive control, this approach establishes multimodal acoustofluidics as a versatile tool for label‐free, high‐precision single‐cell manipulation.
authors: Alexander Edthofer; Guilherme Perticarari; Selma Hevelius Bounja; Thierry Baasch

title: Pulsatile Red Reflex: Identification and Quantitative Characterization of a Previously Unreported Phenomenon
abstract: Purpose To describe and quantitatively characterize a previously unreported pulsatile component of the red reflex, which we term the pulsatile red reflex (PRR). Methods Thirty-one phakic participants underwent red-reflex video recording using a slit lamp and smartphone adapter after pharmacological mydriasis. A multichannel imaging photoplethysmography pipeline extracted pulse-related intensity changes. Relative signal amplitude and recording quality were characterized, and PRR-derived pulse rates were compared with contemporaneous fingertip pulse oximetry using Bland–Altman analysis. Results Twenty-one participants provided valid recordings (67.7%); three acquisitions failed because of dense posterior subcapsular cataract and seven did not meet the 10-s duration criterion. Green-channel root mean square alternating-to-direct-current (AC/DC) ratios ranged from 0.19% to 0.52% (median 0.28%). Reference pulse rates ranged from 55 to 90 beats per minute (bpm). Mean difference was + 0.03 bpm (SD 1.34), with 95% limits of agreement of − 2.60 to + 2.66 bpm. Mean absolute error was 1.04 bpm and root mean square error 1.31 bpm. Signed differences increased with the paired mean (slope 0.11 bpm/bpm; 95% confidence interval 0.07–0.15). Conclusion The familiar red reflex contains a measurable pulsatile intensity component at a frequency consistent with the peripheral pulse. These findings identify and quantitatively characterize PRR, with pulse rate agreement providing evidence of its pulse-related nature. PRR introduces a dynamic dimension to red-reflex assessment and a basis for further investigation of ocular pulsatile signals.

title: Quality Assessment and Model Training Impact of Synthetic Images in Medical Diagnostic Imaging: Systematic Review
abstract: Background AI has increasingly been used to generate synthetic images to overcome the scarcity of large, regulatory-compliant medical image datasets. However, their quality and actual utility for algorithm development across deep learning architectures, medical settings, and image types have been poorly assessed. Objective This study aimed to review the use of synthetic images for algorithm development and to assess their quality and effects on downstream algorithms trained on these images, according to AI architecture, medical setting, and image type. Methods The authors conducted a systematic review of studies published between January 2020 and September 2025. PubMed, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and Embase were searched for peer-reviewed studies evaluating synthetic images generated from human medical imaging data. Data were extracted for imaging modalities, generative architectures, image-quality assessment methods, downstream model performance, explainability approaches, reproducibility practices, and risk of bias. Given substantial heterogeneity and incomplete statistical reporting, findings were synthesized descriptively. Results A total of 160 studies were included. Generative adversarial network–based architectures dominated image generation (119 studies, 74.4%), although hybrid and diffusion-based approaches became increasingly represented in recent years. Image-quality evaluation was highly heterogeneous: 50 studies included human-reader evidence, and 101 reported an automated image-quality assessment. Synthetic-only training generally underperformed real-data training, including a median Dice similarity coefficient change of –10.2% for segmentation. Adding synthetic data to real training sets was associated with median improvements in classification precision (+7.8%), recall (+5.3%), F 1 -score (+5.5%), accuracy (+4.3%), and area under the curve (+4.0%), while the median Dice coefficient improvement was +1.2%. Explainability evidence was reported in 68 (42.5%) studies and was rarely validated against expert annotations. Reproducibility reporting was inconsistent, and only 38% (60/160) of studies were judged to have low overall risk of bias. Conclusions Unlike previous reviews restricted to particular diseases, imaging modalities, or generative architectures, this review provides a cross-domain quantitative synthesis of both synthetic-image quality assessment and downstream model performance. Synthetic images currently appear more valuable as a complement to real training data than as a replacement, with modest improvements in classification performance, smaller gains in segmentation, and generally poorer performance with synthetic-only training. For researchers, developers, and regulators, these findings highlight the need for standardized multimethod image-quality evaluation, complete reporting, and rigorous external validation before synthetic-image pipelines are translated into clinical AI applications.

title: Quicklime Slaking‐Mediated Exothermic Reactions in Polidocanol‐Integrated Ablators with Inhibited Heat Diffusion Enable Cancer Thermal Ablation
abstract: Despite showing a wide application in tumor therapy, the clinically‐used exogenous thermal ablation still suffers from uncontrollable temperature field with rapid heat diffusion. Here an endogenous trigger‐encouraged thermal ablation, namely exothermic reaction‐based thermal ablation (ERTA) based on quicklime slaking and acid‐base neutralization reactions, has been established, wherein CaO nanoparticles were encapsulated with Ag nanoparticles by liposomes to construct ERTA ablators. CaO consumes H 2 O and H + after exothermic reactions to give birth to Ca 2+ and heat. Liposome shell prolongs ERTA via limiting the exothermic reaction rate, and intracellular Ca 2+ overload unites with Ag nanoparticles to produce antitumor ROS to boost cancer ERTA. Importantly, polidocanol‐based foam sclerosing agent (PFSA) with low heat conductivity was integrated to inhibit heat diffusion and confine heat in tumor to elevate temperature and enhance ERTA efficiency. Additionally, PFSA as a routine clinical embolism agent destroys intratumoral blood vessels to occlude blood vessels and establish starvation therapy, which further improves PFSA‐enhanced ERTA efficiency. Consequently, such ERTA‐based ablators and PFSA‐integrated ones outperform the scale‐matched microwave ablation and laboratory‐in photothermal ablation in repressing subcutaneous and orthotopic hepatocellular carcinoma, and orthotopic pancreatic cancer. This endogenous trigger‐activated thermal ablation method provides distinctive insights into thermal ablation, presenting a new thermal ablation protocol.

title: Radiographic manifestations of pneumatosis intestinalis and construction of an AI-assisted diagnostic system
abstract: Pneumatosis intestinalis (PI) has a wide range of etiologies, and the imaging differentiation between benign and ischemic PI is difficult, leading to a high risk of missed diagnosis. This study systematically summarizes the CT (Computed Tomography) imaging manifestations of PI and constructs an AI (Artificial Intelligence)-assisted diagnostic model that integrates multidimensional features. This study retrospectively collected CT and x-ray data from 612 patients with PI (398 benign and 214 ischemic cases) from three tertiary hospitals, and included an external validation set of 106 cases. Imaging analysis established a five-level PI-CT severity scoring system based on gas morphology, distribution, portal venous gas (PVG), intestinal wall enhancement, mesenteric edema, and ascites. The AI system adopted a two-level architecture: The first level used EfficientNet-B3 for rapid screening on x-ray films; the second level used 3D nnU-Net (No-new-Net) to segment intestinal wall gas, and then fused the data through a three-branch network (gas morphology, accompanying signs, and clinical metadata) via cross-attention to output the probability of ischemic PI. In the internal test set, the model achieved an AUC (Area Under the Curve) of 0.947 for ischemic PI (sensitivity 91.3%, specificity 93.6%), significantly outperforming senior radiologists (AUC = 0.876); the AUC on the external validation set was 0.931. SHapley Additive exPlanations analysis showed that PVG and blood lactate were the most important predictors. This two-tiered AI system can significantly improve the early identification of the causes of critical PI, providing a reliable method for intelligent diagnosis of emergency imaging.

title: Real-time instance segmentation of spine endoscopy images using a YOLO-V11 deep convolutional neural network
abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Spine endoscopic surgery requires precise anatomical recognition and real-time bleeding detection to enhance surgical safety and efficiency. However, most existing computer vision studies do not offer real-time multi-class segmentation of the entire scene. This study aims to develop a real-time instance segmentation model based on YOLO-V11, capable of automatically identifying surgical instruments, critical anatomical structures, and bleeding sites in spine endoscopy. METHODS: The model was trained and evaluated using 2,181 annotated frames (training 1,741 / validation 216 / held-out test 224) from spine endoscopy images, covering nine key categories: instruments, bone, ligamentum flavum, dura, soft tissue, vessels, fat, the radiofrequency ablation wand, and bleeding focus. The segmentation model's performance was evaluated across various YOLO-V11 variants. RESULTS: Across five random seeds per variant on the same NVIDIA A100 GPU, YOLO-V11 l achieved the highest mask mAP50, defined as mean average precision at an intersection-over-union threshold of 0.50, with a value of 0.7735 ± 0.0030 (mean ± SD, n = 5). It also maintained real-time inference, reaching 270 ± 35 frames per second (FPS) with a per-frame latency of 3.75 ± 0.51 ms. All five variants exceeded 30 FPS, the widely accepted real-time threshold for surgical imaging. The model demonstrated high precision in segmenting vital structures such as the dura and ligamentum flavum and accurately identified bleeding regions. CONCLUSION: This research contributes to AI-driven surgical guidance systems, with potential applications in robotic-assisted spine surgery. The developed model enables real-time navigation, improving intraoperative decision-making and enhancing surgical outcomes. In particular, our YOLO-V11-based framework extends prior single-structure or lower-frame-rate multi-element approaches by delivering real-time multi-class instance segmentation of instruments, anatomical structures, and bleeding sites in spine endoscopy, with explicitly quantified inference latency.
