title: Serial fecal calprotectin as a screening tool for subclinical ileitis in patients with idiopathic uveitis or scleritis: a prospective cohort study.
abstract: Idiopathic uveitis accounts for 27%-51% of uveitis cases in Europe and the United States. Subclinical inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) may remain undiagnosed in patients with idiopathic uveitis or scleritis despite shared immunopathogenic mechanisms and the absence of digestive symptoms. Early identification may enable intervention within the inflammatory window of opportunity, yet subclinical ileitis has not been systematically explored in this population. We evaluated the diagnostic performance of serial fecal calprotectin for identifying subclinical inflammatory bowel disease in a prospective cohort of 69 patients with idiopathic uveitis or scleritis, using a baseline measurement repeated at 6-12 months if negative or at three months if positive, defining four longitudinal patterns (A-D). Subclinical ileitis was confirmed by capsule endoscopy and/or colonoscopy in 5 of the 62 patients with an evaluable outcome (8.1%). Baseline fecal calprotectin was significantly higher in patients with confirmed ileitis (p = 0.024), a difference that became more pronounced at the second determination (p = 0.002). The pattern of persistent elevation (subgroup D) showed the best diagnostic balance: sensitivity 100% (exact 95% CI: 47.8-100.0), specificity 82.5% (95% CI: 70.1-91.3), negative predictive value 100% (95% CI: 92.5-100.0), and positive likelihood ratio 5.7 (95% CI: 3.25-10.01). ROC curve analysis showed a numerically higher discriminative capacity for the second calprotectin determination (AUC: 0.932; 95% CI: 0.850-1.000) than for the baseline measurement (AUC: 0.809; 95% CI: 0.652-0.966), although a formal DeLong comparison between both c-statistics found no statistically significant difference (p = 0.242). This exploratory, hypothesis-generating cohort suggests that a persistently elevated fecal calprotectin trajectory identifies a subgroup of patients with idiopathic uveitis or scleritis who may warrant digestive evaluation; because subgroups A and C were not endoscopically verified, the reported sensitivity and negative predictive value are estimates conditioned on this verification scheme and on only five events, not validated evidence that a negative trajectory excludes subclinical ileitis. Confirmation in larger, prospectively verified, multicenter cohorts is required before any screening recommendation can be made.
authors: Lavilla Olleros C, Menchén L, Ramos-Ferreira J, Merino Rodríguez B, de Miguel-Yanes JM, Gutierrez Bonet R, Torresano Rodríguez J, Ausín García C, Puertas López C, Alvarez-Sala Walther L, Ibares-Frías L.

title: Sign Primal-Dual Gradient Dynamics for Supply-Demand Coordination under Binary Human Feedback
abstract: This paper addresses supply-demand coordination, in which a supplier sets prices to balance the demands of multiple buyers against limited resources. Existing studies typically solve the supply-demand coordination problem with a distributed algorithm called primal-dual gradient dynamics (PDGD), assuming that each buyer discloses the value of its own utility or marginal utility function. In contrast, we assume that each buyer discloses only binary information, namely whether it wants more or less of the current amount, and propose Sign PDGD. Sign PDGD is a PDGD algorithm in which the buyers' update depends only on the sign information. We analyze the convergence of Sign PDGD by interpreting it as a sliding mode control (SMC). For a quadratic cost and linear constraints, we show that under a gain condition, the primal and dual variables converge to the optimal solution. Numerical simulations on a toy resource-sharing problem confirm the two-phase behavior of SMC and show that the primal and dual variables approach the optimal solution.
authors: Yuya Miyaoka; Kengo Urata; Masaki Inoue

title: Simulating Vein Compressibility for Ultrasound-Guided Femoral Access: Speed, Accuracy, and Phantom Validation
abstract: In ultrasound-guided femoral access, probe pressure deforms the tissue and changes the vascular anatomy a robot observes. A simulator must reproduce these mechanics fast enough for robotic interaction, yet the computational effort needed for a clinically meaningful signal like vein collapse before artery is unclear. We test the feasibility of a physics-based simulation in NVIDIA's Isaac Sim for Healthcare, with Stable Neo-Hookean tissue solved by Vertex Block Descent on one GPU. A simulation of a low-fidelity cylindrical benchtop phantom with known geometry and mechanical properties, pressed by a robot, predicted its artery within 5 percentage points at every depth. It matched the vein within 3 points through 11 mm of a 25.4 mm press and followed the collapse behavior of the low-fidelity physical phantom. Across element size, time step, and solver iterations, wall clock time per frame scaled linearly with solver work, but accuracy did not improve with more work. The chosen setting reduced solver time per frame by a factor of 976, from 29,700 ms to 30.4 ms, while remaining within 1.03 points of the finest reference setting. The physics solver alone took 30.4 ms per frame, while the full stack, including ultrasound and graphics rendering, took 56.4 ms per frame. Finally, when seeded with realistic literature-based mechanical properties, the digital leg model compressed the vein far more than the artery at every setting, reproducing the expected clinical signal of vein collapse before artery, which is used to distinguish them. In total, these results suggest that the NVIDIA Isaac Sim platform may be suitable for augmenting reinforcement learning training or online simulation for autonomous femoral access with ultrasound.
authors: Amit Manicka; Laurent Coulon; Darwin Ang; Michael Loushin; Timothy M. Kowalewski

title: Single-View RGB-D Force--Deformation Estimation for Robotic Manipulation of Elasto-Plastic Materials
abstract: Persistent deformation complicates elasto-plastic manipulation by coupling physical interaction with spatially distributed shape changes. We investigate the force--deformation relationship using a standard robot, a single eye-in-hand RGB-D camera, and intrinsic force estimates. A 7-DoF Franka Emika FR3 performs normal indentations while an Intel RealSense L515 captures pre- and post-contact surfaces. Point-cloud processing localizes deformation and estimates displaced volume. Force--volume characterization includes 27 measurements over nine force levels. A compact multilayer perceptron (MLP), trained on 52 force--volume pairs at four levels, achieves a held-out RMSE of 1.857 N and $R^2=0.440$. A separate comparison shows lower error for a quadratic model at 16 N and for the MLP at 19 and 23.5 N. An eight-step experiment at 4 N per interaction demonstrates cumulative deformation localization from the second indentation onward. These results establish a practical measurement basis for deformation-aware manipulation using intrinsic force estimates and single-view geometry.
authors: Dezhi Sun; Marijn Van Hilten; Kenan Niu

title: Small Bowel Volvulus Diagnosed and Treated Using Intraoperative Angiography in a Hybrid Operating Room: A Case Report.
abstract:
Introduction

Small bowel volvulus is a surgical emergency that may cause mesenteric ischemia; however, diagnosis may be difficult when bowel perfusion appears preserved.

Case presentation

An 84-year-old man presented with recurrent postprandial abdominal pain and melena 6 months after a total pharyngolaryngectomy with a jejunal free flap reconstruction. Extensive endoscopic evaluations, including capsule endoscopy, revealed no bleeding source. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed the whirl sign at the root of the small-bowel mesentery with the narrowing of the superior mesenteric artery (SMA), while bowel wall enhancement was preserved. Because the symptoms recurred after resuming oral intake, a hybrid surgery combined with angiography was planned for both diagnostic and therapeutic purposes. The SMA angiography demonstrated significant stenosis without apparent bowel hypoperfusion. After the intra-arterial administration of alprostadil, distal mesenteric perfusion deteriorated on the angiography, and laparoscopic exploration revealed ischemic changes consistent with small bowel volvulus. Because laparoscopic reduction was difficult, an open reduction was performed. Repeat angiography confirmed the resolution of the SMA narrowing and the restoration of distal flow. The patient's symptoms resolved completely.

Conclusions

The hybrid surgery enabled a functional assessment of mesenteric hemodynamics and immediate surgical treatment during a single procedure. It may be useful in selected patients with small bowel volvulus who have preserved bowel perfusion at rest but recurrent symptoms suggestive of intermittent mesenteric ischemia, and in whom the indication for surgical detorsion remains uncertain.
authors: Gambo H, Maki H, Tanaka M, Momiyama M, Nakajima K, Nagao A, Osawa M, Satou S.

title: SmartPhone iOralForens App for Forensic Luminosity and Colour Identification of Tooth Surfaces Using WiFi Wireless Intra-Oral Cameras
abstract: This article introduces the SmartPhone iOralForens App, an image-analysis application developed to support comparative forensic assessment of tooth-surface luminosity and colour using images acquired from WiFi-enabled or manually transferred intra-oral cameras. The application is intended as an adjunctive tool for dentists, forensic odontologists, forensic scientists, and appropriately trained researchers examining corresponding ante-mortem (AM) and post-mortem (PM) dental images. The iOralForens workflow incorporates Origin, LuminosityID%, and ColourID% image-processing functions, generating processed red and green representations and corresponding quantitative measurements from selected dental-image regions. For the present methodological evaluation, a simulated dataset comprising 132 dental-image observations distributed across 11 groups was analysed to demonstrate the proposed comparative statistical framework. Microsoft Excel was used to calculate mean values, standard deviations (SD), and percentage discrepancies between corresponding AM and PM measurements. The overall mean AM and PM values were 76.2% and 74.5% for LuminosityID%, respectively, and 78.5% and 76.7% for ColourID%, respectively. The mean group-level discrepancy was 2.42% for LuminosityID% and 2.46% for ColourID%, with observed discrepancies ranging from 0.65–4.55% and 0.64–4.70%, respectively. Under the proposed application-specific framework, the overall results were classified as moderate numerical similarity. These findings demonstrate the intended use of iOralForens for structured quantitative comparison but do not constitute independent forensic validation, because the dataset was simulated. The application emphasizes standardized acquisition, preferably using the same intra-oral camera model and comparable imaging conditions, because camera-specific optical characteristics may affect quantitative measurements. The proposed 0%, approximately 1%, 1–5%, and >5% discrepancy categories are exploratory and should not be interpreted as validated forensic identification thresholds. Further independent studies using real and controlled forensic dental datasets are required to establish repeatability, reproducibility, diagnostic performance, and evidentiary validity. iOralForens is therefore proposed as an adjunctive forensic dental image-analysis tool, with final identification decisions remaining the responsibility of appropriately qualified forensic professionals.
authors: F Shakibaie
venue: International Digitized Journal of Tele-Optic Services

title: SonoAtlasWorld: Anatomy-Grounded Ultrasound World Models for Wide-Range Scanning
abstract: Learning robotic ultrasound policies requires interactive environments for scalable data generation and repeatable evaluation, while exploration on real patients is limited by acquisition costs and safety constraints. Generative world models offer an alternative, but image history and probe actions alone do not ensure anatomical consistency across wide-range scans and changing acoustic windows. We introduce SonoAtlasWorld, an ultrasound world model built on anatomy as state. A persistent 3D anatomical asset extracted from computed tomography (CT) anchors each scan to a specific anatomy. Probe actions determine anatomical and acoustic visibility conditions for a causal ultrasound generator trained on clinical videos. Our three-stage pipeline combines anatomy-conditioned pretraining, causal conversion and long-rollout alignment. Inference optimizations achieve pose-to-ultrasound throughput of 81.2 FPS. To evaluate anatomical control beyond image similarity, we introduce the Action-Following Index (AFI), which measures normalized reconstruction gain over a static-prefix baseline. On 40 held-out 3D volumes, SonoAtlasWorld achieves liver and macro-organ AFI of 0.428 and 0.262, compared with at most 0.117 and 0.038 for the tested action- and geometry-conditioned methods. Long-rollout alignment reduces brightness drift by 3.46x at the end of 40 repeated scan cycles. SonoAtlasWorld also generates offline policy-training demonstrations and supports anatomically grounded closed-loop evaluation. Scaling the generated training data improves key-plane acquisition success from 48.2% to 81.2% on unseen anatomies in simulation, demonstrating its utility for robotic ultrasound policy learning.
authors: Zheyuan Zhang; Boris Mailhe; Hang Yu; Yikang Liu; Xiao Chen; Ankush Mukherjee; Terrence Chen; Shanhui Sun

title: SonoWorld: Towards Interactive Pose-Controllable Ultrasound World Models
abstract: Robotic ultrasound can standardize image acquisition and reduce operator workload and variability, but policy learning remains limited by the lack of realistic, controllable simulation environments. While controllable world models have advanced rapidly in natural-image domains, ultrasound world modeling remains challenging because each frame captures only a cross-section of unobserved 3D anatomy, causing small probe motions to induce large appearance changes. Existing approaches rely on robot-tracked poses and latent-space prediction, but do not directly generate the observations required for interactive control. We propose SonoWorld, a causal ultrasound world model that learns video dynamics from unlabeled clinical videos and grounds them to 6-DoF control using a small set of freehand clinical scans tracked with an EM sensor. SonoWorld is trained in three stages: pretraining a latent-action-conditioned video diffusion model on around 6.9 million unlabeled multi-organ ultrasound frames; grounding the learned video dynamics to metric probe poses with a small EM-tracked thyroid dataset; and applying distribution matching distillation to enable causal, long-horizon autoregressive generation with selectively caching eviction tokens at inference time. We evaluate controllability through pose-following fidelity, round-trip consistency, and axis-specific control under synthetic actions on held-out tracked scans, and further validate it with a user study. In model-based action discrimination, SonoWorld correctly ranks the target-directed probe motion over an equal-magnitude opposite motion in up to 74.8% of trials. To our knowledge, SonoWorld is the first causal, pose-controllable ultrasound world model learned primarily from freehand clinical videos, providing a data-driven interactive environment for robotic ultrasound data acquisition and policy evaluation.
authors: Zefan Yang; Zheyuan Zhang; Boris Maihe; Yikang Liu; Hang Yu; Ankush Mukherjee; Xiao Chen; Pingkun Yan; Terrence Chen; Shanhui Sun

title: Spatiotemporal multiplexing on subretinal prosthesis increases selectivity of the network-mediated stimulation
abstract: Subretinal photovoltaic implants (PRIMA) provide form vision in patients blinded by age-related macular degeneration. The success of this approach is attributed in part to the network-mediated stimulation, which preserves many features of the natural retinal signal encoding. For efficient stimulation of bipolar cells (BC) with smaller pixels, electric field confinement should be relaxed, yet direct activation of the retinal ganglion cells (RGC) should be avoided. Here we present a new method for selective stimulation of bipolar cells using image multiplexing – sequential presentation of the image’s components in several subframes. With sizes of the subframe islands optimized by computational modelling, the selectivity of network (BC) mediated retinal stimulation increased over 5 times in rats. Using this approach, electric field confinement can be relaxed, allowing pixels as small as 20 µm to efficiently stimulate bipolar cells, while avoiding direct stimulation of RGCs and preserving high contrast of the pattern. This software-based improvement enables higher visual acuity of prosthetic vision without a change in implanted hardware.
authors: NATHAN KENNETH JENSEN; Keith Ly; Davis Pham-Howard; Mohajeet B. Bhuckory; Daniel Palanker

title: Standardising ocular surface photography for artificial intelligence: current limitations and a proposed roadmap
abstract: Slit-lamp colour photography remains a cornerstone of anterior segment documentation and longitudinal monitoring. However, conventional slit-lamp photography has seen relatively limited technological advancement compared with the rapid development of quantitative anterior-segment modalities such as AS-OCT, Scheimpflug tomography and confocal microscopy. Despite the wide diffusion of digital cameras, smartphones, and high-end slit-lamp systems, ocular surface photography (OSP) remains hampered by the absence of standardised acquisition and processing protocols. The convex, aspheric geometry of the ocular surface, off-axis illumination, peripheral defocus, automatic colour correction, and pupil-driven exposure variation in retroillumination limit reproducibility, inter-device comparability, and clinical utility. In this review we critically appraise current OSP applications across major ocular surface conditions (dry eye disease, conjunctival hyperaemia, infectious keratitis, ocular surface burns, and ocular surface neoplasia), mapping the hardware, software, and reproducibility limitations that constrain clinical practice. We then examine how these limitations propagate into artificial intelligence (AI) development, where the absence of large, well-annotated, demographically diverse OSP datasets, together with the lack of reproducible quantitative phenotypes and reliable labels, is now the principal bottleneck to clinically deployable models; we discuss patient-level data partitioning and external validation, and outline how deep learning, federated learning and foundation models can both utilise and improve OSP. Finally, we propose a minimum acquisition and dataset specification, tiered by clinical setting from research to community screening, and a staged roadmap that combines hardware standardisation (focus-stacked, illumination-controlled, colour-calibrated acquisition), interoperable metadata-rich storage (DICOM where infrastructure permits), quantitative phenotype definition, and diverse international dataset collaborations, so that the ocular surface can benefit from quantitative imaging and AI as other areas of ophthalmology have begun to.
authors: Vito Romano; Bernhard Steger; Matteo Airaldi; Ferdinando Giuliano; Mariantonia Ferrara; Davide Romano; Mario Rosario Romano; Yalin Zheng; Darren Shu Jeng Ting
venue: Progress in Retinal and Eye Research

title: Static, Dynamic and Robotic CAIS in Healed Partially Edentulous Sites: Accuracy and Chair‐Side Time
abstract: AIM: To evaluate the accuracy and chair-side efficiency of static (s-CAIS), dynamic (d-CAIS), and autonomous robotic (r-CAIS) computer-assisted implant surgery in healed partially edentulous sites. MATERIALS AND METHODS: In this retrospective comparative study, 73 patients with 92 implants, treated from September 2022 to October 2024, were included (s-CAIS: 21 patients/33 implants; d-CAIS: 29 patients/32 implants; r-CAIS: 23 patients/27 implants). Pre- and postoperative CBCT scans were used to assess linear and angular deviations. The duration of chair-side preparation and drilling/implant placement was recorded for d-CAIS and r-CAIS. RESULTS: At implant level, mean platform deviations were 0.85 ± 0.38 mm (s-CAIS), 1.37 ± 0.71 mm (d-CAIS), and 0.59 ± 0.32 mm (r-CAIS; median [IQR]: 0.54 [0.30] mm); apex deviations were 1.36 ± 0.51, 1.48 ± 0.66, and 0.64 ± 0.52 mm (r-CAIS; median [IQR]: 0.53 [0.30] mm); angular deviations were 4.34° ± 2.13°, 2.53° ± 0.99°, and 1.54° ± 1.50° (r-CAIS; median [IQR]: 1.28° [1.40°]). At patient level, platform deviations were 0.88 ± 0.35, 1.37 ± 0.69, and 0.57 ± 0.29 mm; apex deviations 1.38 ± 0.44, 1.48 ± 0.65, and 0.58 ± 0.43 mm; angular deviations 4.48° ± 1.81°, 2.52° ± 0.97°, and 1.45° ± 1.30°. r-CAIS showed significantly superior accuracy compared with s-CAIS and d-CAIS (p < 0.05). Because r-CAIS data were not normally distributed, medians [IQR] were additionally calculated and are reported parenthetically. Drilling and placement time was longer for d-CAIS than r-CAIS (18.06 ± 5.54 vs. 10.81 ± 3.55 min, p < 0.05), while chair-side preparatory time did not differ (10.78 ± 2.53 vs. 9.61 ± 2.72 min, p > 0.05). CONCLUSIONS: Among the three systems, r-CAIS provided the highest accuracy and was more time-efficient during the intra-operative (chair-side) phase than d-CAIS in partially edentulous patients. CLINICAL RELEVANCE: In patients with partial edentulism, r-CAIS demonstrated superior accuracy compared with both s-CAIS and d-CAIS approaches. Furthermore, r-CAIS offered greater chair-side efficiency during the intra-operative phase than d-CAIS. This cutting-edge technology holds great promise for enhancing the precision of dental implant procedures, offering substantial benefits to both surgeons and patients.
authors: 赵旭; MiaoZhen Wang; Tao Yu; Feifei Ma; Xiaohui Rausch‐Fan; Feng Liu
venue: Clinical Implant Dentistry and Related Research

title: Stretchable high-fill-factor silicon-liquid metal platform for multilevel visual acquisition and depth sensing.
abstract: High-density stretchable pixelated electronics that conform to complex, non-developable surfaces are key enablers of next-generation robotic vision systems, skin-mountable sensors and wearable electronics. Existing strategies for stretchable pixelated device arrays-such as buckling mechanics, pop-up structures, serpentine interconnects and kirigami designs-have offered partial solutions. However, a strategy that simultaneously achieves high device performance, stretchability, fill factor and integration density has remained elusive. Here we present a next-generation platform for stretchable pixelated electronics that integrates high-performance single-crystalline silicon pixels with finely patterned liquid metal interconnects on ultrathin elastomeric substrates. We developed a monolithic microfabrication strategy that enables customizable, densely packed and mechanically compliant pixelated device arrays. Using this platform, we demonstrate shape-reconfigurable imaging devices that achieve superb fill factors of up to 81% and a biaxial stretchability of 100%. We also present a human-eye-inspired robotic vision system with tunable focus and a skin-mountable lens-free imaging system. The complementary operation of retinal and epidermal imaging systems enables multiscale visual acquisition and depth sensing.
authors: Chansul Park; Do Hyeon Kim; Woosang You; Jinyoung Jang; Hyeonseung Choi; Sehui Chang; Donggook Joo; Ji Su Kim; Jisang Ha; Dongyun Lee; Ji Hoon Kim; Mincheol Lee; Young Min Song; Dae-Hyeong Kim

title: Superior Ophthalmic Vein Thrombosis Presenting as Isolated Headache: A Case Report
abstract: Introduction: Superior ophthalmic vein thrombosis (SOVT) is a rare condition that can present with varied symptoms, including headache and orbital pain. Its diagnosis requires advanced imaging techniques, including CT angiography and MRI. This case report describes a patient presenting with headache and orbital pain attributed to superior ophthalmic vein dilation and thrombosis. Case Presentation: An 81-year-old female patient presented with headache, orbital pain, periorbital edema, and mild palpebral ptosis. Initial investigations included a brain CT scan and CT angiography, which revealed tortuous and dilated superior ophthalmic veins with massive thrombosis of the left superior ophthalmic vein. Brain MRI and MR angiography were also performed. Other examinations included ophthalmological evaluation, fluorescein angiography, and blood tests. The patient's symptoms, including headache and orbital pain, were attributed to the confirmed dilation and massive thrombosis of the left superior ophthalmic vein. CT angiography initially suggested a carotid-cavernous fistula, which was subsequently excluded by brain MRI and MR angiography. Fluorescein angiography revealed severe myopic chorioretinopathy with peripapillary atrophy and disc hyperfluorescence consistent with venous congestion in the left eye. Thrombophilia screening identified elevated anticardiolipin IgM antibodies, raising suspicion for antiphospholipid syndrome (APS). Anticoagulant therapy was initiated with enoxaparin and subsequently transitioned to warfarin, in accordance with current guidelines that favor vitamin K antagonists over direct oral anticoagulants for APS-associated thrombosis. Conclusion: This case highlights the importance of considering SOVT in the differential diagnosis of headache accompanied by orbital symptoms.
authors: Vincenzo Laterza; Alfredo De Liso; Franscesco Macchione; Alessandra Bavaro; Marco Rossi; Giuseppe Rinaldi

title: Supplemental Material for: Complementary Roles of Intestinal Ultrasound and Capsule Endoscopy in Crohn’s Disease: A Prospective Blinded Comparative Study
abstract: Background and Aims: Precise and longitudinal assessment of small-bowel inflammatory activity is essential in Crohn’s disease (CD). Capsule endoscopy (CE) provides comprehensive mucosal evaluation but is limited for routine use by cost and availability. Intestinal ultrasound (IUS) has emerged as a non-invasive, accessible, and complementary imaging modality. This study compared the diagnostic performance of IUS with CE for detecting terminal ileum inflammation.Methods: In this prospective blinded study, adult patients with suspected or established CD referred for CE underwent same-day IUS. Inflammatory activity was quantified by the International Bowel Ultrasound Segmental Activity Score (IBUS-SAS) for IUS and the Lewis score for CE.Results: Ninety-eight patients were included with a mean age of 42±14 years, 42% male. IBUS-SAS showed a significant association with the 3rd tertile Lewis score (ρ=0.515, p<0.001). This association differed according to inflammatory burden, as among patients with a Lewis score <350, the correlation was weak and non-significant (ρ=0.149, p=0.198), whereas a stronger correlation was observed in those with a Lewis score ≥350. IBUS-SAS demonstrated excellent discrimination for a Lewis Score ≥350 (AUROC 0.889; 95% CI 0.807–0.972), and an IBUS-SAS cut-off of ≥13.7 yielded 90.5% sensitivity, 76.3% specificity, and 96.7% negative predictive value. Discriminative performance remained high across suspected and established CD. IBUS-SAS was the only predictor of capsule-derived inflammation, when adjusted for clinical and laboratorial biomarkers (OR 1.149 per point increase; 95% CI, 1.070–1.234; p<0.001).Conclusions: IUS accurately detects clinically significant ileal inflammation (Lewis score ≥350) and performs best in patients with higher inflammatory burden. In contrast, its performance was lower in patients with absent or low-grade inflammation, in whom the correlation between IBUS-SAS and Lewis score was weak. These findings support a complementary approach, with CE remaining the reference standard for detailed mucosal assessment and IUS serving as a practical, non-invasive tool for the assessment of clinically significant ileal inflammation.
authors: figshare admin karger; João Carlos Gonçalves; Francisca Dias-Castro; Leite Sílvia; Joana Magalhães; Bruno Rosa; José Cotter

title: System-level design and integration of next generation wireless implantable medical devices: A review and future research directions
abstract: Next-generation wirelessly enabled implantable electronic medical devices demand simultaneous improvements in wireless communication, power autonomy, biocompatibility, and long-term reliability, yet current literature addresses these aspects in isolation, creating critical gaps in cross-disciplinary integration. This review systematically analyzes recent advances in implantable medical device (IMD) antennas, sensors, wireless power transfer (WPT) schemes, and biocompatible materials to clarify how these components interact under realistic in-body environments. Using a comparative and mechanism-oriented evaluation framework, the paper identifies unresolved challenges including limited miniaturization without performance degradation, unstable in-tissue communication links, material–tissue mismatch effects, and insufficient guidelines for co-optimizing power efficiency, safety, and data rate. The review uniquely consolidates therapeutic, diagnostic, and continuous-monitoring perspectives to map how device geometry, electromagnetic behavior, material properties, and energy delivery constraints jointly influence IMD performance. By synthesizing design rules, benchmarking emerging bioresorbable and soft-tissue-compatible materials, and evaluating system-level trade-offs, this work provides a unified understanding of where current technologies fall short and outlines concrete research directions for highly reliable, wirelessly powered IMDs in future healthcare systems.
authors: Muhammad Ikram; Altaf Ahmed Mugheri; Anwer S. Abdelhamid; Yara A. Kamel; Abdulrahman S. M. Alqadami; Zubair Akhter; Niamat Hussain; Syed Shahan Jehangir; Kamel Sultan

title: Systematic Review of Artificial Intelligence in Pre-Implant Radiographic Imaging: A Structured Qualitative Synthesis of Performance Across Imaging Modalities and AI Architectures.
abstract:
Purpose

To evaluate contemporary evidence on artificial intelligence (AI) applied to radiographic imaging for pre-implant dental assessment and treatment planning, with emphasis on the distinction between technical algorithmic performance and clinically oriented planning outcomes.

Materials and methods

Peer-reviewed original studies published from January 2021 through December 2025 were identified through PubMed/MEDLINE, the Cochrane Library, ScienceDirect, JSTOR, and supplementary searches. Eligible studies used radiographic imaging as an integral input to AI for pre-implant assessment, planning, decision support, virtual positioning, or outcome prediction. Reporting completeness was assessed with CLAIM 2024. Risk of bias was assessed with QUADAS-3 for eligible diagnostic/test-accuracy studies, PROBAST+AI for the prognostic prediction-model study, and RoB 2 for the randomized clinical study. Owing to heterogeneity, findings were synthesized qualitatively.

Results

Thirty-six studies were included. CBCT was the predominant modality. Applications included anatomical detection and segmentation, bone assessment, decision support, implant-position prediction, automated virtual placement, workflow integration, and preoperative outcome prediction. Segmentation and anatomical-analysis studies generally reported high task-specific performance, while clinically oriented positional accuracy and planning outcomes were more variable. AI frequently reduced workflow time. QUADAS-3 was applicable to five studies; four had high overall risk of bias and one unclear risk. The prognostic prediction-model and randomized clinical studies also had high risk of bias under their respective tools.

Conclusions

AI shows greatest current support for anatomical analysis and selected workflow tasks. Evidence for autonomous implant positioning and outcome prediction remains limited and heterogeneous. Current findings support clinician-supervised integration, with further multicenter external testing, standardized clinically meaningful outcomes, reproducibility, and prospective evaluation required before broader routine implementation.
authors: Jeevitha M, Balaji P, Kavya BT, Rajesh KS, Keerthana GS.

title: Tasty and Healthy Diet Reduces Fecal Calprotectin in High-Risk First-Degree Relatives of Patients With Crohn's Disease: Preventing IBD ONset in Individuals at Risk (PIONIR) Randomized Crossover Trial.
abstract:
Background & aims

With the rising prevalence of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), preventing new-onset disease becomes a priority. The PIONIR (Preventing IBD ONset in Individuals at Risk) randomized controlled trial explored whether the Tasty&Healthy (T&H) diet reduces inflammatory markers in high-risk first-degree relatives (FDRs) of patients with Crohn's disease (CD).

Methods

FDRs with persistently elevated fecal calprotectin (FC, >70 μg/g) and, at most, nonspecific mucosal abnormalities (edema or ≤10 aphthous ulcers) on video-capsule endoscopy or ileocolonoscopy were randomized to T&H or habitual diet for 8 weeks, followed by crossover for additional 8 weeks. Treatment effect on the primary outcome, FC response, was analyzed using generalized estimating equations for the 2-period, 2-sequence crossover design, following the intention-to-treat principle.

Results

The study randomized 29 FDRs: 14 to T&H-first and 15 to habitual diet-first groups. At week 8, median FC was lower with T&H (64 μg/g; interquartile range [IQR], 44-127 μg/g) vs habitual diet (112 μg/g; IQR, 74-227 μg/g; P = .022). FC decreased by ≥50% in 71% on T&H vs 27% on habitual diet (relative risk, 2.68; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.09-6.60; P = .016). Across both crossover periods, estimated marginal mean FC declined by 61%, from 185 μg/g (95% CI, 144-237 μg/g) to 72 μg/g (95% CI, 57-91 μg/g) with T&H vs by 38% to 114 μg/g (95% CI, 93-140 μg/g) with habitual diet (FC ratio 0.63; 95% CI, 0.51-0.80), translating to 37% overall decrease with T&H (P < .001). Six microbial species differed between diets after false discovery rate correction. By week 8, 79% rated T&H acceptable, and 83% had good or complete adherence.

Conclusions

These findings demonstrate the modifiability of low-grade intestinal inflammation in healthy high-risk FDRs with persistent FC elevation but without diagnostic endoscopic evidence of CD, supporting long-term dietary prevention trials (ClinicalTrials.gov no. NCT05211518).
authors: Turner D, Kenigsberg S, Plotkin L, Aharoni-Frutkoff Y, Sokolik M, Focht G, Gasasa S, Turpin W, Waslyk AM, Ledder O, Griffiths AM, Martincevic I, Huynh HQ, Godny L, Avni-Biron I, Torres J, Panaccione R, Jacobson K, Otley A, Sharar-Fischler T, Li Q, Azulay A, Sigall-Boneh R, Lee SH, Croitoru K.

title: Technology Anxiety and Acceptance of Health Education Robots Among Patients After Abdominal Surgery: A Cross-Sectional Study
abstract: Background: Patients differ in their willingness to accept health education robots. This study examined the association between technology anxiety and robot acceptance among patients recovering from abdominal surgery and estimated indirect associations through negative attitudes toward robots and human-robot trust. Methods: This cross-sectional study included 303 adults recovering from elective or emergency abdominal surgery at a tertiary hospital in Zhejiang Province, China (May-June 2026), all of whom had received at least one robot-delivered health education session. Patients with cognitive impairment, postoperative complications, or psychiatric illness were excluded. Participants completed the Robot Acceptance Questionnaire, Technophobia Scale, Negative Attitudes Toward Robots Scale, and Trust Between People and Automation Scale. PROCESS Model 6 (5,000 bias-corrected bootstrap resamples) estimated indirect associations, specifying negative attitudes before trust a priori and adjusting for age, education, employment, income, residence, and prior robot experience. Sensitivity analyses examined the reversed ordering, HC3 standard errors, Tobit regression, and an unadjusted model. Results: = -0.511, p < 0.001). The standardized direct association was -0.204 (95% CI, -0.327 to -0.081). Indirect associations were -0.077 (95% CI, -0.145 to -0.012) through negative attitudes, -0.059 (95% CI, -0.111 to -0.017) through trust, and -0.014 (95% CI, -0.035 to -0.004) for the theory-ordered serial sequence. The reversed serial sequence, with trust preceding negative attitudes, was also statistically detectable (-0.012; 95% CI, -0.031 to -0.002); therefore, their ordering could not be distinguished. Conclusion: Higher technology anxiety was associated with lower robot acceptance, and part of this association was statistically linked to negative attitudes and trust. Because both orderings were compatible with the cross-sectional data, these findings do not establish temporal sequence, causal mediation, or intervention effects.
authors: Jingya Meng; Yunyun Feng; Liping Peng; Lijuan Zhong; Qingqing Pang; Xia Feng; Jiayun Zhong

title: Teledentistry: Bringing Dental Care Closer to Every Home
abstract: Abstract Teledentistry represents a transformative integration of telecommunication technologies into dental practice, enabling the remote exchange of clinical data, high-resolution images, patient histories, and expert consultations for diagnosis, treatment planning, and longitudinal care management. This modality significantly enhances accessibility to oral health services, particularly in geographically isolated or underserved populations, while optimizing operational efficiency, reducing healthcare expenditures, and minimizing patient travel burdens. It effectively mitigates urban-rural disparities, facilitates interdisciplinary collaboration, and supports continuous professional education. This expanded review delves deeply into teledentistry's historical evolution, multifaceted operational frameworks, underlying technical infrastructures, diverse clinical applications across dental specialties, robust evidentiary base from global studies, and critical ethical, legal, regulatory, and economic dimensions. Furthermore, it incorporates contemporary advancements—such as artificial intelligence (AI)-augmented diagnostics, 5G-enabled real-time interactions, and blockchain-secured data transmission—and prognosticates future trajectories, including integration with robotic systems and wearable sensors, to underscore its pivotal role in reshaping equitable, sustainable oral healthcare delivery in the digital era.
authors: Avantika Tuli
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Telemedicine in Retinopathy of Prematurity: A Review of Current Evidence and Clinical Outcomes
abstract: Background/Objectives: Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) is a leading cause of preventable childhood visual impairment, particularly in settings where access to specialized ophthalmologic care is limited. Telemedicine offers an alternative approach to ROP screening and monitoring through remote retinal imaging and expert interpretation. This narrative review aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance, clinical benefits, implementation challenges, and future perspectives of telemedicine in ROP screening and management. Methods: A narrative literature review was conducted with consideration of the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles (SANRA) criteria. PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar were searched in August and August 2026 for relevant publications from January 2000 to the search date. Two authors independently screened titles and abstracts, followed by full-text assessment according to predefined eligibility criteria. A total of 143 scientific articles and other high-quality sources were included in the final narrative synthesis. Evidence was evaluated qualitatively, without a formal risk-of-bias assessment. Findings: The reviewed literature indicates that telemedicine can expand access to ROP screening, facilitate remote specialist consultation, support longitudinal disease monitoring, and improve the triage of infants requiring urgent assessment. In selected settings, remote retinal image interpretation has demonstrated diagnostic performance comparable to conventional examinations for clinically significant and vision-threatening ROP. Artificial intelligence-based assessment and smartphone-based retinal imaging represent promising approaches to improving screening accessibility and workflow efficiency, particularly in resource-limited settings. However, implementation remains constrained by equipment costs, infrastructure limitations, image quality, workforce training requirements, and ethical and legal considerations. Conclusions: Telemedicine represents a promising complementary strategy for ROP screening and management, with the potential to improve access to timely specialist assessment and help prevent ROP-related visual impairment. Its successful integration into clinical practice requires sustainable infrastructure, standardized protocols, trained personnel, and reliable referral pathways that ensure timely in-person examination and treatment when indicated. Further research is needed to establish the effectiveness, cost-efficiency, and long-term sustainability of different telemedicine-based approaches across diverse healthcare settings.
authors: Ilinca-Medeea Iftime; Andreea Ramona Treteanu; Andreea Pușcașu; Mihai Craiu; Octaviana Cristea; Alina Angelica Ciolpan

title: The Ethics of Autonomous Clinical AI: Shifting From Model Accuracy to Model Impact
abstract: The ethics of autonomous clinical AI are controversial. Traditional ethics assessments have focused on AI model performance rather than health system outcomes. Nichol and colleagues translate established research ethics principles into 9 practical recommendations for trials of autonomous clinical AI. Their findings support an evolution in clinical trial design. The accuracy and performance of the model is important, but the ethical unit of evaluation should be the complete care pathway, with prespecified obligations for subgroup performance, follow-up care, system failures, and model change.
authors: Clair M. Sullivan

title: The Future of Clinical Assessment in US Dental Education: Competency‐Based or Entrustable Professional Activities?
abstract: In the late 1990s, US dental education embraced competency-based education (CBE), replacing time- and procedure-based requirements with an outcomes-oriented approach centered on demonstrated abilities and readiness for independent practice. Nearly three decades later, entrustable professional activities (EPAs) is emerging as an assessment framework. Do EPAs represent a new paradigm for dentistry, or are they an extension of assessment principles already embedded in competency-based dental education (CBDE)? This paper examines the similarities and differences between CBDE and entrustable professional activities-based education (EPABE), with particular attention to terminology, assessment methods, decision-making, and the evidence required to demonstrate compliance with US predoctoral dental education standards. CBDE commonly assesses competencies, defined as knowledge, skills, and professional behaviors, through discrete examinations, simulations, structured clinical assessments, or patient-based competency examinations. These methods can establish whether a learner performs a defined task at an acceptable level, but assessments conducted at a single point in time may provide limited evidence of consistency, adaptability, judgment, or sustained performance across clinical contexts. EPABE assesses authentic, integrated professional activities through repeated observation in the clinical workplace. Entrustment decisions address the level of supervision a learner requires and are informed by longitudinal evidence of reliable performance, including technical skill, clinical judgment, efficiency, communication, and professionalism. Unlike many competency assessments, entrustment is dynamic: It may be maintained, withdrawn, or re-established as performance changes. EPABE therefore requires assessment systems capable of aggregating and displaying sequential performance data to support defensible decisions about readiness for independent practice. We argue that EPAs offer a clinically grounded evolution of competency assessment but should not be viewed as a universally sufficient method. Infrequent, unpredictable, or high-risk activities may be better assessed through simulation, case-based methods, or other summative approaches. Hybrid assessment models that combine longitudinal workplace-based observations with targeted high-stakes assessments may provide the most valid, feasible, and CODA-aligned evidence of predoctoral dental graduates' readiness for practice.
authors: Cecile A. Feldman; Emily H. Sabato; Janine Fredericks-Younger; Kenneth J. Markowitz; Kim E. Fenesy

title: The Nano-Dental Complex: Clinical Breakthroughs, Structural Advancements and Global Horizons in Nanodentistry
abstract: Background: Nanobiotechnology is rapidly transforming modern healthcare, with its integration into dentistry opening novel pathways for advanced clinical outcomes.This review provides a comprehensive overview of the practical applications of the nano-dental complex (nanodentistry) and explores how recent innovations are revolutionizing oral healthcare.Methods: A systematic literature search was conducted across major electronic databases, including PubMed, Google Scholar, and Scopus, alongside official health repositories such as the World Health Organization (WHO), to synthesize recent data on nanotechnology in dental science.Results: Nanodentistry leverages nanomaterials, nanorobotics, and molecular engineering to optimize the diagnosis, management, and prevention of oral pathologies.The descriptive analysis categorizes these advancements across diverse dental specialties, including orthodontics, preventive dentistry, prosthodontics, restorative dentistry, periodontics, and oral surgery.Additionally, the evolution of dental restoration technologies through nanomaterial integration is detailed.Conclusion: While nanodentistry holds immense potential to enhance treatment planning, patient care, and regulatory frameworks in healthcare, widespread adoption faces significant hurdles.High production costs and limited accessibility remain primary barriers, particularly in resource-constrained regions.This review maps the historical trajectory, current clinical landscape, and future horizons of nanotechnology to guide subsequent research and development in oral healthcare.
venue: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology

title: The Role of Micro-Ultrasound in Prostate Cancer Detection
abstract: PURPOSE OF REVIEW: To synthesize current evidence on the role of 29-MHz micro-ultrasound (microUS) in prostate cancer (PCa) detection and to define its position relative to multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) across the diagnostic pathway. We conducted a narrative review of prospective, comparative, and randomized studies, with clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa) detection as the primary endpoint. RECENT FINDINGS: MicroUS provides ~ 70-µm axial resolution and enables real-time PRI-MUS-based risk stratification. Across head-to-head studies, microUS achieves diagnostic performance comparable to mpMRI. Evidence supports utility in biopsy-naïve patients, selected MRI-negative men with persistent clinical suspicion, repeat-biopsy settings, active surveillance, and local tumor staging, while combined mpMRI-microUS approaches have been shown to maximize yield of csPCa detection. Key limitations include operator dependence, interobserver variability, lack of validated biopsy-avoidance thresholds, and reduced sensitivity in anterior lesions. MicroUS is a practical, high-resolution platform that complements mpMRI and may enhance accessibility, efficiency, and precision in prostate cancer care.
authors: Navid Jabalameli; Feres Camargo Maluf; Fatema Bhinderwala; Thomas James Polascik; Soroush Rais‐Bahrami

title: The Role of Top‐Down Proteomics in Mass Spectrometry Imaging
abstract: In this Top-Down Proteomics special issue article, we focus on the integration of top-down proteomics in mass spectrometry imaging (MSI). MSI enables the label-free, untargeted, visualization of biomolecules in thin tissue sections. MSI has been widely applied for determining the spatial distributions of small molecules (e.g., metabolites, lipids) and proteins. In the case of proteins, imaging workflows that exploit on-tissue digestion and subsequent analysis of proteolytic peptides (i.e., bottom-up proteomics) are well-established, whereas those that involve analysis of intact proteins are less common. Often, imaging of intact proteins is accompanied by separate bottom-up analysis to identify the protein(s). Rarer still are workflows which combine MSI and top-down proteomics. Top-down proteomics-the analysis of intact proteins by mass spectrometry-allows the identification of unknown proteins and provides information on sequence variants, protein isoforms and posttranslational modifications. It may be conducted under denaturing conditions, where the proteins are intact but unfolded, or under native-like conditions, where solution-phase noncovalent interactions are retained in the gas-phase and proteins remain folded. The latter can provide information on tertiary and quaternary structure, and ligand binding. Top-down proteomics therefore has the potential to provide a comprehensive overview of the proteoform landscape and a more complete picture of the underlying biology. In this article, we provide a brief history of protein MSI together with a more detailed examination of techniques with capabilities for intact protein MSI and associated top-down proteomics, including matrix assisted laser desorption/ionization (MALDI), desorption electrospray ionization (DESI), matrix assisted laser desorption electrospray ionization (MALDESI), laser ablation electrospray ionization (LAESI), liquid extraction surface analysis (LESA), continuous-flow solvent sampling (Flowprobe) and nanospray desorption electrospray ionization (nano-DESI). We discuss the relative merits of the various techniques and provide examples of their application to biological questions.
authors: Sarah R. W. Vickers; Cameron Baines; Helen J. Cooper

title: The Smart Root Canal Era: A Review of Artificial Intelligence in Endodontics
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) technologies, especially machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) algorithms, are being used more and more to interpret radiographs, identify root canal morphology, detect periapical lesions, and accurately forecast treatment outcomes.By improving clinical efficiency, treatment planning, and diagnostic accuracy, AI is quickly revolutionizing the area of endodontics.By lowering human error, these tools help clinicians make quicker, more evidence-based judgements.Cone beam computed tomography (CBCT) analysis, automated working length (WL) determination, and retreatment requirements evaluation are all supported by AI in endodontic practice.Additionally, smart tools and robotic systems powered by AI have the potential to increase procedural accuracy during root canal therapy.Notwithstanding its benefits, issues including algorithm bias, data privacy, expense, and the requirement for physician training continue to be major obstacles.However, the use of AI in endodontics is a potential step toward more individualized, effective, and minimally intrusive patient care.To maximize its potential possibilities, dental professionals and technology developers must continue to collaborate and conduct research.This abstract gives an overview of AI in endodontics.
authors: Ragavi P Pillai; Jayanthi Govindarajan; Susila V Anand; Ottilingam Kamalakannan Preethi; Aravind Kumar Duraivel

title: The future of robotic artificial intelligence in acute care surgery: an early proving ground and a final frontier for autonomous surgical robotics
abstract: Acute care surgery (ACS), spanning emergency general surgery, trauma surgery, and surgical critical care, demands high-stakes decisions in settings characterized by hemodynamic instability, distorted anatomy, contamination, and time pressure. Artificial intelligence (AI) is proposed as a means to reduce cognitive burden, standardize technically sensitive tasks, and extend surgical capability in resource-constrained environments. This review examines the autonomy continuum in surgical AI, with ACS as the primary lens. We argue that ACS occupies a paradoxical position: it has produced the earliest preclinical demonstrations of autonomous surgical robotics, yet the very conditions that motivate autonomy in this specialty make it among the most challenging environments in which to deploy these systems safely in human patients. For ACS, the central question is less whether AI can perform surgical tasks than how autonomy should be sequenced and bounded for emergency surgery. We synthesize the literature across four domains: (1) how autonomy is defined and operationalized in surgical AI and robotics; (2) the current and emerging spectrum of automation in operative environments; (3) the technical feasibility of automation for ACS-relevant tasks; and (4) the ethical boundaries of autonomy in high-risk, time-critical cases. We argue that the safest course is incremental: deploying supervised task autonomy where safety properties are demonstrable and reserving higher autonomy for rigorously evaluated, tightly bounded domains. Realizing this course will require evaluation strategies that align autonomy level to clinical risk, preserve meaningful human oversight, support post-market monitoring, and address liability, patient trust, and equitable access.
authors: Joel Grunhut; Ruhika Iyer; Jesse Haworth; Gabriel A. Brat; Axel Krieger; Jeffrey K. Jopling

title: The rise of agentic AI in drug discovery from static tools to autonomous virtual scientists
abstract: Driven by large language models, AI agents are transforming drug discovery, enabling AI to break free from task-specific tools and advance toward the vision of autonomous virtual scientists. This perspective reviews applications across the R&D lifecycle. To evaluate system maturity, we introduce a 6-level "Spectrum of Agentic Autonomy." We advocate for novel evaluation paradigms centered on full-chain traceability and outline adoption barriers, positioning AI agents as pragmatic scientist-in-the-loop co-pilots.
authors: Donghai Zhao; Meijing Fang; Lexiao Mao; Yuchen Zhu; Qun Su; Hui Shi; Hongxia Xu; Lanqing Li; Tingjun Hou; Chang-Yu Hsieh

title: The use of artificial intelligence in the diagnosis and monitoring of retinal diseases: analysis of clinical effectiveness and prospects for implementation into domestic protocols (a review)
abstract: Age-related macular degeneration and diabetic retinopathy remain the leading causes of preventable vision loss worldwide. In Russia, the availability of ophthalmologists is 18 specialists per 100,000 population, which is substantially below the World Health Organization recommendation of 55 per 100,000 population. Given the rising prevalence of diabetes mellitus, this circumstance requires the introduction of automated screening systems. Results of meta-analyses indicate high diagnostic accuracy of artificial intelligence models: sensitivity for detecting diabetic retinopathy ranges from 87% to 95%, specificity from 87% to 94%, and the area under the ROC curve reaches 0.98. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved autonomous systems for diabetic retinopathy screening (IDx-DR, EyeArt, AEYE-DS), as well as platforms for remote monitoring of age-related macular degeneration based on home optical coherence tomography—SCANLY Home OCT. The use of AI enables the selection of only 10%–15% of images for manual assessment by specialists, thereby significantly saving specialists’ working time. The application of home optical coherence tomography for remote monitoring of patients with age-related macular degeneration increases the interval between injections from 8.0 to 15.3 weeks (p = 0.004). The main barriers to the implementation of artificial intelligence into clinical practice include insufficient personnel training (20.5%), high implementation costs (16.5%), and the risk of algorithmic bias (44.2%). Successful integration of these technologies into domestic clinical protocols requires the development of educational programs for physicians, validation of artificial intelligence systems on Russian population-based data, the formation of a regulatory framework, the creation of insurance reimbursement mechanisms, as well as the inclusion of issues of AI application in the curricula of medical universities.
authors: Anastasia N. Koltakova; Anna A. Raminskaya; A. I. Grebenyuk; Zaira R. Bagomedova; Anastasia I. Plotko; Giuler Ch. Gubadova; Maria V. Gnezdilova; Ekaterina V. Gartvikh; Aza A. Kikova; Amina R. Klycheva; Larisa A. Uzdenova; Ivan V. Mukha

title: Three-dimensional reconstruction of ultrasound imaging in dentistry: a systematic review.
abstract:
Background

Three-dimensional ultrasound (3D-US) reconstruction has emerged as a potential solution to the limited field of view and operator dependence of two-dimensional intraoral ultrasonography. Multiple acquisition, tracking, and reconstruction strategies have been proposed, yet no prior systematic review has synthesized the methods used specifically within dentistry.

Objective

To identify and compare 3D-US reconstruction techniques applied in dentistry and evaluate how acquisition strategy, spatial tracking, and reconstruction methodology influence accuracy, reproducibility, feasibility, and clinical applicability.

Methods

A systematic search of 5 databases was performed. Studies were included in the review if they used ultrasound imaging with any 3D-US reconstruction method for a defined dental application. Risk of bias was assessed using a customized hybrid QUADAS-2/QUIN/STARD framework.

Results

Thirteen studies (2010-2025) met the inclusion criteria; 10 were in vitro and 3 in vivo. Acquisition methods included mechanized linear-stage scanning (n = 6), robotic arm control (n = 2), tracked freehand (n = 2), untracked freehand (n = 1), and custom intraoral jigs (n = 2). Accuracy ranged from 12 to 50 μm for digital impressions to sub-millimeter deviations for periodontal and ridge assessments, with most error rates below 10%. Reproducibility and clinical feasibility were both inversely related to hardware complexity: mechanized and robotic systems achieved the highest precision and enabled precise positioning for repeated evaluations; however, they had the lowest clinical usability. Conversely, freehand approaches demonstrated the strongest clinical potential but at the expense of reproducible positioning and highly precise measurements. Risk of bias was high or unclear in all studies due to heterogeneity, small sample sizes, and limited in vivo validation.

Conclusions

Over 15 years, 3D-US reconstruction in dentistry has advanced substantially, demonstrating promising accuracy for digital impressions, periodontal assessment, ridge measurement, and implant planning. However, most studies remain feasibility-based and in vitro, and methodological variation limits comparability. Future progress will depend on standardization of validation frameworks, increased in vivo accuracy studies, and development of compact, automated acquisition workflows. With continued refinement, 3D-US has the potential to become a clinically practical, radiation-free imaging modality for diagnostic and procedural applications in dentistry.
authors: Nalley A, Torres REG, Hung KF, Tanaka R, Hayashi T, Tarce M.

title: Toward Autonomous Ophthalmic Surgery
abstract: Ophthalmic microsurgery is one of the most technically demanding fields in medicine, constrained by the physiological limits of human vision, motor control, and tactile perception. This chapter explores the shift from manual intervention to autonomous, and intelligent surgical systems enabled by the convergence of artificial intelligence (AI), robotics, and advanced imaging. It traces the evolution of ophthalmic surgery from conventional microsurgical and minimally invasive techniques to robot-assisted platforms capable of tremor cancellation and motion scaling. Central to this transformation is the integration of real-time data processing, in which deep learning algorithms support precise tissue segmentation, surgical phase recognition, and intraoperative guidance through modalities such as intraoperative optical coherence tomography (iOCT). The chapter also outlines pathways toward surgical autonomy, emphasizing the role of imitation learning, reinforcement learning, and model predictive control in performing complex tasks like subretinal injection with sub-millimeter precision. In addition, it critically examines the multidimensional barriers to full autonomy, including technical, translational, regulatory, and ethical challenges. By synthesizing current technological advances with the obstacles to clinical implementation, this chapter proposes a roadmap for the next generation of intelligent intervention systems aimed at improving surgical safety, standardizing outcomes, and expanding the therapeutic possibilities of ophthalmic care.
authors: Niyi Ezekiel Olukayode; Temitope Emmanuel Komolafe; Asad Saleem; Blessing Funmi Komolafe; Liang Zhou

title: Towards Automated Initial Probe Placement in Transthoracic Teleultrasound Using Human Mesh and Skeleton Recovery
abstract: Cardiac and lung ultrasound require operators to locate patient-specific intercostal acoustic windows and adjust probe position, rotation, and force to acquire standard views. In teleultrasound, experts may navigate using ultrasound images after approximate placement, but limited 3D perception makes remote guidance of initial placement difficult. We present tUS-PIPG, a framework for teleultrasound Patient registration and anatomy-informed Initial Probe placement Guidance. A novice captures calibrated RGB and depth images using a mixed reality headset. An edge server reconstructs the patient’s body surface and estimates skeletal landmarks from multiview RGB images and an accumulated depth point cloud. The method leverages spatial and temporal consistency across observations to achieve robust, training-free human registration. Skeletal landmarks guide estimation of intercostal regions, and the headset overlays virtual probe placement on the reconstructed body surface. We evaluated registration and placement guidance in a healthcare setting across multiple transthoracic cardiac and lung scan planes in situ. In a pilot study with five healthy volunteers, mean surface error was 15 mm, and mean error relative to palpated anatomical landmarks was 41.0 mm. These results suggest that the framework can effectively provide novice operators with a warm start in positioning the probe for remote expert adjustment.
authors: Yu Chung Lee; David Black; Ryan Yeung; Septimiu E. Salcudean

title: Towards Vacuum-Assisted Robotic Needle Interventions: From Fluid Aspiration to Tissue Biopsy
abstract: Robotic ultrasound-guided needle interventions have primarily focused on target localization and accurate needle placement, while the subsequent acquisition of diagnostic material remains comparatively underexplored. Moreover, pleural fluid aspiration and tissue biopsy are typically addressed as separate procedures, despite sharing common requirements for ultrasound guidance, safe access, and sample transport. This work presents a unified robotic framework for ultrasound-guided fluid and tissue extraction using a single vacuum-assisted end effector. The proposed system combines force controlled ultrasound scanning, semantic target identification, automated needle deployment, and procedure specific material acquisition. A coaxial needle assembly and shared pump assisted pathway enable direct pleural fluid aspiration, while controlled cannula actuation provides the additional cutting action required for solid-tissue acquisition. End-to-end evaluation using a Franka Emika Panda robot over 50 phantom trials achieved successful extraction in 23/25 pleural fluid aspiration trials (92\%) and 22/25 tissue acquisition trials (88\%). Following successful tissue-target access, acquisition and transport were completed in all 22 trials.
authors: S. Shabana; Laxmi Nag Laxminarayan Nagesh; Marta Vallejo; Karen Donaldson; Maria Koskinopoulou

title: TransGHOST: Real-Time, Synthesis-Free Reconstruction of Instrument-Occluded Regions in Ophthalmic Microsurgery
abstract: Intraoperative scene perception in ophthalmic microsurgery is limited by instrument occlusion: when a tool enters the high-magnification field, it conceals tissue from both the surgeon and the perception components of robot-assisted systems that process the video. Generative inpainting can remove the occluder but replaces the missing image content with synthesis, which is unsuitable when visual provenance matters. Many video inpainters also depend on future frames and cannot operate online. We present TransGHOST, a causal reference-guided reconstruction pipeline whose non-generative safe mode operates in real time. Every restored value is obtained by resampling a recorded frame using geometric transforms fitted only to visible regions. The system provides per-pixel confidence and provenance and marks unsupported pixels as abstentions. We evaluate TransGHOST on a new veterinary clinical corpus of canine cataract surgery with pixel-level instrument and anatomy labels. Only the occluded region is scored, and each scoring target is verified to differ from the reference supplied to the system. Safe mode reaches 31.89 dB masked PSNR and 0.915 masked SSIM at 51.7 ms median and 85.5 ms 95th-percentile latency. On a pre-declared held-out cohort using instrument cutouts excluded from segmentation training, it reaches 29.83 dB masked PSNR, while matched-mask evaluation on validation shows a 3.45 dB advantage over LaMa. Region-aware reference selection improves masked PSNR by 3.60 dB over recency when candidate references can themselves be occluded. Reference-age analysis further defines the operating interval for the brief, repeated occlusions targeted by TransGHOST.
authors: Niran Nataraj; Maina Sogabe; Norihiko Ito; Kenji Kawashima

title: Translating Super Intelligence to Clinical Practice: Methodological Challenges and Safety Limits in Autonomous Healthcare
abstract: Background: Public and professional discourse increasingly describes medical artificial intelligence (AI) in the vocabulary of “superintelligence”, implying that clinical autonomy is a matter of engineering time rather than of evidence. This framing is rarely tested against the methodological quality of the studies on which it rests. Objective: To appraise, in a deliberately sceptical manner, the methodological obstacles and the safety limits that separate benchmark-level machine performance from accountable, autonomous clinical care. Methods: A structured narrative synthesis was conducted, reported in line with the principles of PRISMA 2020 and its scoping-review extension (PRISMA-ScR). Two evidence streams were combined: a supplied bibliographic corpus of 117 records, which was screened to 41 topically eligible items, and 47 purposively selected external sources comprising systematic reviews, trials, reporting standards, regulatory instruments and safety-science literature. Findings were organised into evidence quality, validity, human-factor, equity, governance and liability domains. Results: Across the benchmark literature, headline accuracy was repeatedly accompanied by retrospective designs, limited external validation, high risk of bias, scarce prospective evaluation and weak reporting. Documented deployments revealed failures that laboratory metrics did not predict, including poor sensitivity of a widely implemented sepsis alert, proxy-driven racial bias in a population-health algorithm and workflow friction in a field-deployed retinal screening tool. Human oversight was found to be a fragile safeguard because of automation bias and alert fatigue. Only a narrow class of tightly bounded tasks currently has trial-grade evidence supporting autonomous operation. Conclusions: Autonomy in healthcare should be earned incrementally, task by task, through prospective, externally validated, equity-audited and legally accountable evaluation. A five-level Clinical Autonomy Ladder and an evidence-gated promotion protocol are proposed. Claims of superintelligent medicine are, at present, aspirations about the future and not findings about the present.
authors: Parhlad Singh Ahluwalia

title: Translational Applications of Retinal Biomarkers in Chronic Cardiovascular, Neurological, Metabolic, and Renal Diseases
abstract: Imaging the retina is a powerful non-invasive probe of systemic vascular, neurological, metabolic, and renal disease, making it a cornerstone of the new field of systemic oculomics. Advanced retinal imaging techniques like optical coherence tomography (OCT) and optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA) provide detailed imaging of structural and microvascular changes potentially associated with systemic disease. Derived from fundus photography, structural imaging, vascular imaging, and artificial intelligence-based image analysis, retinal biomarkers have been associated with cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disease, neurodegenerative disorders, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, and related clinical outcomes. However, the translational maturity of these biomarkers is variable depending on imaging modality, target disease, intended clinical use, and level of validation. Longitudinally, retinal vascular characteristics have been associated with cardiovascular as well as cerebrovascular outcomes. In addition, optical coherence tomography has provided reproducible measures of neuroaxonal injury in selected neurological conditions. This is especially true for multiple sclerosis. The majority of retinal biomarkers in Alzheimer disease, Parkinson disease, chronic kidney disease, and systemic risk prediction remain experimental because of heterogeneous methodologies, insufficient external validation, and insufficient evidence for incremental clinical utility. Diabetes is the most developed translational model with established retinal screening pathways and validated ocular applications of imaging and artificial intelligence, although these cannot be directly extrapolated to systemic diagnosis or treatment guidance. This narrative review assesses retinal biomarkers for cardiovascular, neurological, metabolic, and renal disease with a focus on analytical validity, clinical validity, incremental value, clinical utility, and implementation. The retina is increasingly accepted as a site for discovery of systemic biomarkers and adjunctive risk assessment, although most applications to systemic disease remain to be standardized, validated independently, and studied prospectively before being suitable for routine clinical use.
authors: Matteo Capobianco; Marco Zeppieri; Simonetta Gaia Nicolosi; N Castellino; F. Cappellani; Irene Gattazzo; Caterina Gagliano

title: Transoral robotic surgery in otorhinolaryngology: patient perspectives and determinants of outcomes
abstract: Operating through the mouth with the help of a robot: this is transoral robotic surgery (TORS). The surgeon controls the robot, allowing precise surgery in hard-to-reach areas of the throat and at the back of the tongue. This means that invasive operations, which previously involved splitting the lower jaw, can now be avoided. This thesis investigates which patients may benefit from TORS and what the treatment means for their symptoms and quality of life. In patients with metastases in the neck whose original tumour was unknown, TORS enabled the tumour to be found in 40% of cases. TORS can also be used to remove throat tumours. Research into Dutch care for patients with an unknown primary tumour revealed considerable differences between hospitals. More consistent agreements could help improve care and allow better comparison of outcomes. TORS also showed promising results in selected patients with sleep apnoea, a condition in which breathing repeatedly stops during sleep. Patients reported improvements in sleep, swallowing difficulties and quality of life. In patients with chronic inflammation of the tonsil tissue at the back of the tongue, symptoms decreased and swallowing-related quality of life improved. Pain after surgery remains an important concern. Some patients experience considerable pain for several days. Effective pain management and patient education are therefore essential. TORS offers opportunities, but is not suitable for everyone. Careful patient selection, well-trained surgeons and further research are needed to determine who benefits most from this treatment.
authors: Alexandra G. L. Toppenberg

title: Trust me, I’m a robot: relational determinants of social robot acceptance among university students
abstract: Purpose Although social robots are increasingly being used in higher education‚ the relational antecedents of students’ acceptance of these robots remain unexplored. This study re-conceptualises the technology acceptance model (TAM) for social robots by shifting the theoretical focus from utilitarian beliefs toward the relational quality of the human–robot interaction (HRI), positioning trust‚ satisfaction and rapport as main relational antecedents of students’ attitudes and behavioural intentions toward social robots. The study also examines the moderating effects of user motivation‚ empathy‚ risk aversion and technology readiness on the attitude–behavioural intention relationship. Design/methodology/approach Cluster sampling was used to define the sample‚ which comprised 900 university students from six public universities in Greece. Structural equation modelling (SEM) was conducted with AMOS 29 to test the proposed model. Findings Trust‚ satisfaction and rapport are strong positive predictors of student attitude toward social robots‚ which in turn positively influences students’ behavioural intention to use social robots. User motivation‚ empathy and technology readiness motivators (optimism and innovativeness) strengthen the relationship between attitude and behavioural intention towards social robots‚ while risk aversion and technology readiness inhibitors (discomfort and insecurity) attenuate this relationship. Research limitations/implications Despite the contributions achieved here‚ there are some limitations that deserve to be mentioned and suggest promising paths for future research. Because this research used a cross-sectional design‚ it does not allow for causality and the possibility to observe how attitudes and intentions towards social robots develop over time. Future studies with longitudinal designs are needed to test whether the identified antecedents for establishing a relationship with social robots (i.e. trust‚ satisfaction‚ rapport) can increase or decrease with repeated social robot interactions (Donnermann et al.‚ 2022). Practical implications Given the tight connection of trust‚ satisfaction and rapport with students’ perceptions‚ it is important that institutions also consider the quality of the HRI when deciding whether or not to use social robots as teaching assistants. This includes the robots’ ability to build trust through reliable behaviour‚ provide satisfaction through responsive interaction and achieve rapport through attentive‚ empathic and positive communication (Buhmann et al., 2026; Lemon and Dhanesh, 2026). Originality/value This study adds to the literature by being one of the first to conceptualise social robot acceptance as a relational phenomenon‚ positioning trust‚ satisfaction and rapport as core antecedents of attitude and behavioural intention‚ a theoretical move entirely absent from existing social robot acceptance and educational HRI research. Beyond the direct effects‚ this study introduces two theoretically grounded categories of individual-level moderators: psychological-relational moderators (motivation‚ empathy and risk aversion) and technology-related moderators (technology readiness)‚ which collectively provide a coherent and empirically novel account of the boundary conditions governing social robot acceptance among university students.
authors: Δήμητρα Παπαβασιλείου; Kleopatra Κonstantoulaki; Ioannis Kostopoulos; Ioannis Rizomyliotis

title: US-VLA: An Ultrasound Vision-Language-Action Model for Embodied Abdominal Scanning
abstract: Artificial intelligence–assisted ultrasound scanning enhances diagnostic reliability and efficiency by providing real-time guidance for standardized image acquisition and reducing operator dependence. However, existing reinforcement learning and learning-assisted ultrasound scanning methods typically rely on carefully designed reward functions or extensive interaction data, which limits their generalization ability and stability across different devices, patient populations, and complex clinical scenarios. To address these challenges, we propose an ultrasound vision-language-action model (US-VLA) for automated ultrasound scanning that explicitly encodes clinical semantic goals and generates sequential probe manipulation actions under real-time ultrasound feedback. In particular, we first design an ultrasound-aware expert fusion module to jointly integrate ultrasound observations with auxiliary contextual information, enabling semantic ultrasound feedback to effectively guide the scanning process. Then, we construct US-VLA-Data, a real-world dataset covering liver and kidney examinations, which includes five clinically defined standard planes and comprises 320 expert scanning trajectories with approximately 80,000 synchronized timesteps. Extensive experiments demonstrate that US-VLA achieves competitive performance in ultrasound probe manipulation tasks, indicating its effectiveness and promising generalization within the evaluated abdominal ultrasound setting. The source code is available at https://github.com/VMVLab/US-VLA.
authors: Cheng Zhang; Xingzheng Wu; Gu Yan; Xifeng Hu; Zhi Liu; Mei Wu; Qing Cai
