title: Adult Child Sexual Abuse Survivors
abstract: An overview of the prevalence of adults with a history of child sexual abuse and their presentation as clients in counseling. This practice brief covers the definitions, important clinical considerations in assessment, case conceptualization, interventions, and best practices for treatment. Cultural and social identity implications are important modifiers, as are the concepts of resilience and posttraumatic growth.
authors: Devika Dibya Choudhuri

title: Advanced piezoelectric nanogenerators for next-generation self-powered nano-bio sensors
abstract: Two-dimensional (2D) material-based piezoelectric nanogenerators (PENGs) are emerging as efficient energy-harvesting devices that convert mechanical stimuli into electrical energy. Owing to their tunable electronic, mechanical, and structural characteristics, 2D materials, including TMDs, MXenes, h-BN, etc, offer significant advantages in flexibility, durability, and low-power operation, making them highly suitable for next-generation self-powered systems. This review systematically highlights recent advances in 2D material-based PENGs, emphasizing fabrication strategies, performance optimization, electromechanical coupling enhancement, and their applications in self-powered nano-biosensors. The interdependence between material properties, device architecture, and measurement conditions is comprehensively analyzed to establish robust structure-performance relationships. Furthermore, critical challenges, including low output power, signal instability, integration complexity, and the lack of standardized evaluation protocols, are systematically analyzed. Emerging strategies to enhance energy-harvesting efficiency, signal reliability, and device scalability are also highlighted. Overall, this review establishes a unified framework for the rational design and advancement of high-performance 2D PENGs, providing key insights for their practical implementation in portable, wearable, and autonomous self-powered systems.
authors: Abhay Singh; Manish Sharma; Rajesh K. Gangwar; Ajeet Kumar Kaushik; Sanjeev Kumar K. Sharma

title: Advancement in deep learning for skin lesion identification and classification: A comprehensive survey
abstract: Cancer remains a life-threatening disease with an increasing number of hereditary and metabolic disorders contributing to its onset. Carcinogenic cells can proliferate into any tissue or organ of the human body, thus often leading to fatal consequences. Malignant skin lesions are among the most dominant cancer types worldwide and are classified into three major types: 1) 'melanoma,' which is highly aggressive and accounts for a major proportion of deaths caused by skin cancers; 2) ‘squamous cell carcinoma'; and 3) ‘basal cell carcinoma.' The ahead-of-time and accurate detection is crucial and extremely imperative due to the intensifying prevalence of skin cancer. Of late, deep learning-based intelligent models are being significantly developed for skin cancer classification, yielding promising results. However, only a limited number of comprehensive reviews address the key challenges in this domain. This study presents an exhaustive survey of the contemporary deep learning-derived studies conducted for skin cancer detection and classification tasks and their systems. This study begins by introducing three primary types of dermatological images and providing an overview of openly available standard datasets for skin lesions. Subsequently, we attempted to explore the prominent applications of deep learning in skin cancer classification. The study further focuses on discussing critical challenges encountered while implementing deep learning-based models, including limited data availability, data imbalance, domain adaptation, computational efficiency, and model robustness. Additionally, we have the current headway in deep learning algorithms designed to deal with the said issues and improve decision-making accuracy. In the end, we discuss the future of skin cancer classification systems, including multimodal algorithms and large data source requirements for enhancing diagnostic accuracy.
authors: Ramneek Kaur Brar; Manoj Sharma

title: Advancements in optical fiber coatings and functionalization for chemical and biological sensing applications
abstract: Recent advances in optical fiber engineering have enabled the transformation of conventional fibers into sophisticated platforms for chemical and biological sensing. Innovations in coating technologies-incorporating polymers, metals, nanoparticles, and hybrid nanocomposites, have significantly enhanced light-matter interactions at the fiber interface, thereby improving analytical sensitivity and performance. Polymeric coatings provide chemical tunability and mechanical flexibility, while metallic films enable plasmonic-based refractive index sensing with high responsiveness. In parallel, the integration of nanoparticles and nanocomposite materials introduces tailored optical properties and multifunctional behavior, expanding the capabilities of fiber-based sensing systems. Complementary surface functionalization strategies, including self-assembled monolayers and molecular imprinting have further advanced the field by enabling the controlled immobilization of biorecognition elements such as enzymes, antibodies, and aptamers. These approaches confer high selectivity and stability, facilitating the development of next-generation optical fiber sensors for the detection of gases, volatile organic compounds, biomarkers, pathogens and genetic targets. This review summarizes recent progress in coating materials, surface functionalization methods, and optical transduction mechanisms for fiber-optic chemical and biological sensors. Particular emphasis is placed on the relationship between coating morphology, sensing performance, and practical challenges, including coating instability, signal drift, reproducibility, and operation in complex sample environments. Emerging trends in distributed sensing and artificial intelligence-assisted signal processing are also discussed as promising directions for next-generation intelligent optical fiber sensing systems.
authors: Maxwell Ogochukwu Ojukwu; Jonas H. Osório; Júlio César Ugucioni; Fabiana S. Felix

title: Advances in the management of mitral valve disease: contemporary review for clinicians
abstract: Mitral valve disease is a major global contributor to cardiovascular morbidity and mortality, with its epidemiology shaped by regional characteristics and changing causes. In high income countries, degenerative mitral regurgitation predominates, resulting from ageing populations, although functional mitral regurgitation is increasingly recognised and constitutes an increasing proportion of the burden of mitral regurgitation. In contrast, rheumatic mitral stenosis and regurgitation affect younger patients in low and middle income areas. Advances in multimodality cardiac imaging have enhanced the precision of diagnostic and prognostic evaluation, and periprocedural planning and guidance. Management strategies are evolving, with surgical repair or replacement remaining the standard for eligible patients, supported by minimally invasive approaches and optimal timing and indications. Transcatheter edge-to-edge repair and transcatheter mitral valve replacement are new treatment options for patients at high risk or previously considered to be inoperable. This review summarises the contemporary perspectives of the epidemiology of mitral valve disease, the pathophysiology, diagnostic imaging modalities, and treatments for mitral regurgitation and stenosis, and outlines future directions.
authors: Susan Keen; Tom Kai Ming Wang; Brian P. Griffin

title: An analytical approach to privacy and performance trade-offs in healthcare data sharing
abstract: The secondary use of healthcare data is essential for research and clinical innovation, motivating data owners, such as healthcare providers, to share data with researchers as data receivers. Regulatory frameworks, including the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), define requirements for such data sharing. However, prior studies show that healthcare data meeting regulatory standards may still be vulnerable to privacy attacks, motivating the use of additional anonymization techniques. While further anonymization can enhance privacy protection, it may also introduce information loss and degrade downstream tasks such as machine learning (ML) performance. This study investigates how to balance privacy preservation and data utility in healthcare data sharing from both data owner and data receiver perspectives. Using healthcare data from adult patients hospitalized in the United States between 2013 and 2015, originally collected for sepsis prediction, we examine how different data-sharing strategies, including the inclusion or exclusion of individuals vulnerable to privacy attacks, affect privacy protection and ML performance within a HIPAA-compliant setting. We identify subpopulations, including older adults, frequently hospitalized patients, and racial minorities, that are particularly vulnerable to privacy attacks due to distinctive demographic and utilization patterns. Excluding these groups leads to notable reductions in ML performance. We further evaluate three anonymization methods, k -anonymity (Domingo-Ferrer and Torra, 2005), the model by Zheng et al. (2019), and the MO-OBAM model (Wei et al., 2025), with respect to re-identification risk and ML utility. Results show that k -anonymity offers limited protection. The methods of Zheng et al. (2019) and MO-OBAM provide stronger privacy safeguards, with MO-OBAM yielding the best utility outcomes: only a 2% change in precision and recall compared to the original dataset. These findings provide actionable guidance for data owners, demonstrating that advanced anonymization can enable privacy-preserving data sharing without substantially compromising ML performance.

title: Artificial Intelligence Models for Early Disease Detection Using Clinical Data
abstract: In a variety of chronic and acute diseases, earlier detection of disease is a major determinant of better patient outcomes, better treatment costs savings and reduced mortality.The current diagnostic process, mostly manual, manual interpretation of clinical data, is limited by the capacity of the human mind, by inter-observer variability and by the amount of data produced by modern healthcare systems.Artificial Intelligence (AI) that leverages machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) capabilities has become a rapidly evolving technology that can help uncover patterns within very large, heterogeneous and high-dimensional clinical datasets, well in advance of what traditional methods could accomplish.In this research paper, a thorough investigation of AI models for early disease detection from medical data, such as laboratory results, electronic health records (EHR), vital signs, and medical image metadata is conducted.We examine the theoretical underpinnings of important classifiers like Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machines, Random Forests, Gradient Boosting methods, Artificial Neural Networks, Convolutional Neural Networks and Long Short-Term Memory networks and compare their performances using the metrics: accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC).A systematic procedure of data acquisition, data preprocessing, feature engineering, model training, model validation and interpretability is suggested and illustrated using simulated experiments.The results show that ensemble and deep learning algorithms (especially XGBoost and CNN) are more accurate at forecasting than traditional statistical models, but they are less interpretable and more demanding in terms of resources.The paper also highlights these issues of data privacy, class imbalance, explainability of AI models, and clinical integration, and proposes directions for future research such as federated learning, explainable AI, multimodal data fusion for early disease detection, among others.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Intensive Care: From Clinical Applications to Ethical and Medico-Legal Challenges
abstract: From a medico-legal perspective, AI functions as a clinical decision support tool without legal autonomy. Responsibility for AI-assisted clinical decisions remains subject to the applicable legal and regulatory framework and depends on the degree of human oversight. The use of artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming intensive care medicine, offering advanced tools for data processing, prediction, and clinical decision support. This narrative review explores current applications of AI in the intensive care unit (ICU), along with associated ethical, medico-legal, and regulatory challenges. AI systems, particularly those based on machine learning and deep learning, have demonstrated promising predictive performance across several intensive care applications. Systematic reviews of machine learning models for ICU prediction tasks have reported AUROC values generally ranging from approximately 0.80 to over 0.90 for early sepsis prediction and ARDS risk stratification, although performance decreases in external validation cohorts. AI has also shown encouraging performance in predicting weaning success and supporting mechanical ventilation management, while evidence of improved patient-centered clinical outcomes remains limited A narrative literature search was conducted in PubMed and Scopus for studies published between January 2015 and December 2025. Additionally, AI contributes to continuous patient monitoring, reduction in false alarms, and improved workflow efficiency. Despite these advances, most models are derived from retrospective and single-center datasets, limiting generalizability and real-world applicability. Moreover, only a limited number of AI systems have undergone prospective clinical evaluation or demonstrated improvements in patient-centered outcomes following real-world implementation. A key limitation of current AI systems is the "black box" nature of many algorithms, which reduces interpretability and may undermine clinician trust. Furthermore, algorithmic bias, data quality issues, and limited external validation raise concerns regarding safety, equity, and reliability. Importantly, improved predictive accuracy does not necessarily translate into better clinical outcomes, highlighting the need for prospective validation studies. From a medico-legal perspective, AI functions as a clinical decision support tool without legal autonomy. Responsibility for AI-assisted clinical decisions remains subject to the applicable legal and regulatory framework and depends on the degree of human oversight, the intended use of the AI system, and the relevant jurisdiction. The emergence of regulatory frameworks, such as the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act and the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), reflects the increasing regulation of healthcare AI according to the intended purpose, level of autonomy, and potential impact of each system, emphasizing requirements for transparency, human oversight, and data protection.
authors: Francesco De Lazzaro; Giovanna Barletta; Eugenia Magnanimi; Bruno Cirillo; Paola Frati; Enrico Marinelli; Francesco Rocco Pugliese; Lina De Paola; Giovanni G. Giordano

title: Artificial Intelligence in Pediatric Orthopedics: From Technical Performance to Clinical Utility - A Narrative Review
abstract: Background Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly applied in pediatric orthopedics, where serial imaging, quantitative measurements, growth-related anatomical change, and uneven access to subspecialty expertise create opportunities for computational support. Objective This narrative review aims to evaluate how pediatric orthopedic AI has progressed from technical performance toward clinically useful deployment, emphasizing validation, human-AI interaction, and downstream clinical value. Methods We conducted a narrative review with structured searches of PubMed, Scopus, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and Web of Science from inception through July 2026. Evidence was organized by clinical task and interpreted according to target reproducibility, validation depth, human-reader or workflow effects, reviewable uncertainty, and pathway- or patient-level benefit. Study selection was documented in a flow diagram, and methodological quality was assessed across 115 primary studies. Results The corpus comprised 147 cited records, including 127 domain-specific evidence records and 20 general or contextual records. The evidence map included 115 pediatric or mixed-age primary studies and one adult primary comparator across spine, upper limb, lower limb, hip/pelvis, cerebral palsy/gait, foot/ankle, and trauma. Sixteen records evaluated large language models or generative AI. Evidence was most developed for bounded tasks such as landmark localization, deformity and alignment measurement, fracture detection, and selected developmental dysplasia of the hip screening. External validation and patient-centered outcomes remained uncommon, and evidence was less consistent for multiclass classification, prognosis, treatment selection, and individual-response prediction. Among the 115 primary studies, 23 (20.0%) reported independent external validation and six (5.2%) assessed patient outcomes; 59 (51.3%) were classified as high risk of bias. Conclusions Pediatric orthopedic AI is currently best supported as human-supervised augmentation. Clinical adoption should prioritize multicenter validation, growth-aware and equitable modeling, explicit uncertainty, human-factors evaluation, and prospective assessment of clinically meaningful outcomes.
authors: Maria Cesarina May; Qingshuang Zhang; Haytham Alhourani; Ji Lin; Lucia Baio; Ruiping Wang; Michele Bonomo; Wenxuan Zheng; Federico Canavese; ShunYou Chen

title: Artificial Intelligence in Spinal Diagnostics: Advances, Challenges and Future Directions
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in spinal diagnostics, particularly through machine learning and deep learning applied to medical imaging and clinical data. These technologies may improve the detection and classification of spinal disorders, automate image interpretation and support clinical decision-making. This narrative review summarizes current applications of AI in spinal diagnostics, focusing on methods for detecting spinal cord injuries, spinal tumors, degenerative spine diseases and vertebral fractures, as well as predicting treatment outcomes and postoperative complications. It also examines convolutional and recurrent neural networks, automated image segmentation and other machine learning approaches for analyzing spinal images and clinical information. Available evidence suggests that AI models can perform comparably to conventional methods and expert assessments and may exceed them in some settings. However, implementation remains limited by challenges related to dataset quality and diversity, model generalizability and interpretability, data privacy and regulatory and ethical considerations. This review highlights both the clinical potential of AI and the major barriers to its integration into routine spinal diagnostic practice. Further prospective validation, external testing across diverse patient populations and interdisciplinary collaboration will be essential to establish the clinical utility and ensure the safe implementation of AI-based spinal diagnostic tools.

title: Association between alpha-fetoprotein elevation and recurrence in patients who achieved normalized alpha-fetoprotein after curative resection for hepatocellular carcinoma: A retrospective cohort study.
abstract: Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is a cornerstone biomarker for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) surveillance following curative resection. Although AFP normalization generally indicates effective tumor control, subsequent AFP elevation poses a diagnostic dilemma due to its potential association with both tumor recurrence and nonneoplastic liver conditions. This study aimed to determine the factors influencing AFP elevation and to assess the role of serial AFP testing for the early detection of recurrent HCC, thereby addressing an unmet need in refining postoperative surveillance strategies. In this retrospective cohort study, 705 patients who underwent curative resection for HCC between January 2018 and March 2020 and achieved AFP normalization were analyzed. Postoperative surveillance included AFP and imaging exams, with AFP elevation defined as ≥ 20 ng/mL and normalization as AFP < 20 ng/mL post-surgery. Multivariable analysis identified factors associated with AFP elevation. Recurrence occurred in 34.6%. Independent factors associated with AFP elevation included recurrence (odds ratio [OR] = 21.9; 95% confidence interval [CI] = 7.5-64.2), preoperative AFP elevation (OR = 3.6; 95% CI = 1.7-7.6), logAFP at normalization (OR = 12.7; 95% CI = 3.5-45.7), and cirrhosis (OR = 2.2; 95% CI = 1.0-4.5). In patients without recurrence, logAFP at normalization (OR = 12.6; 95% CI = 3.7-43.4) and cirrhosis (OR = 2.2; 95% CI = 1.1-4.5) were independently associated with false positive elevation. Intrahepatic recurrence accounted for 69.2%, with lesions of ≤ 1 cm composing 88.9%. Following a preceding AFP elevation, recurrence was detected after a median of 4.8 months and within 12 months in all cases. AFP elevation during postoperative surveillance is a strong indicator of HCC recurrence. In cases where AFP elevation occurs without clear radiologic evidence of recurrence, early and frequent liver MRI (at intervals of ≤ 3 months for at least 12 months) is recommended to facilitate prompt detection of intrahepatic lesions. Moreover, clinicians should be mindful that elevated normalized AFP levels and underlying cirrhosis increase the risk of false positive elevations. These findings underscore the need for a tailored surveillance strategy to optimize the early diagnosis and management of recurrent HCC.
authors: Jeong Ah Hwang; Jisun Lee; Kyung Sik Yi; Chi-Hoon Choi; Kil Sun Park; Ji Hye Min

title: Association of Preexamination AI Virtual-Patient Trainer Scores With Scores on a Local Single-Station History-Taking Objective Structured Clinical Examination: Observational Cohort Study
abstract: Background Large language model–based virtual-patient systems score history-taking practice, but whether scores correspond to independently scored examination performance remains untested. Existing evaluations emphasize internal platform metrics or simulated-patient fidelity, leaving criterion-related evidence limited. Objective This study tests whether mean preexamination AI-trainer practice scores were associated with performance on 1 local objective structured clinical examination (OSCE) history-taking station, whether the association depended on the complaint-matched training case, and whether a model including the trainer score retained predictive performance in held-out students. Methods At 1 medical school, second-year students received a required 6-case assignment on the AI-Powered Medical History-Taking Training and Evaluation System (AMTES) and completed an end-of-course OSCE. Each student completed 1 station rated by 1 examiner; interrater and cross-station reliability could not be estimated. The 4 OSCE diagnoses differed from the training diagnoses: 3 shared a presenting-complaint category with an AMTES case, whereas 1 OSCE case had no presenting-complaint match. Platform-to-OSCE record linkage was 474 out of 480 (98.8%); 473 students with analyzable preexamination practice formed the analytic sample. The primary predictor was the mean of normalized scores across practice records time-stamped before each student’s examination-day cut-off. Analyses used Spearman correlations, OSCE-case fixed-effects regression, and repeated 5-fold cross-validation. Results OSCE scores (mean 81.5, SD 6.7) were associated with platform practice scores (Spearman ρ=0.388; P<.001). With OSCE-case fixed effects, each 1SD increase in the platform score corresponded to a 2.83-point increase in the OSCE score (95% CI 2.26-3.39). The association was observed in the AMTES-unmatched low back/flank pain stratum (Spearman ρ=0.370; n=108) and with a leave-matched-case-out score (Spearman ρ=0.398 vs 0.370 for the full mean among the same 339 students). Under a single cohort-wide cut-off at the first examination day, the association attenuated but persisted among the same 469 students (Spearman ρ decreased from 0.385 to 0.346; paired difference −0.040, 95% CI −0.065 to −0.018; regression coefficient decreased from 2.83 to 2.68 points per SD). In repeated 5-fold cross-validation (n=471), the platform-only model achieved Spearman ρ=0.374 and R2=0.176. Adding the platform score to the 2 prior physical-examination course scores increased cross-validated R2 from 0.141 to 0.236 (ΔR2=0.096; 95% CI 0.053-0.142). Adding practice volume and case breadth did not improve performance (ΔR2=−0.002). Conclusions By linking required curricular practice scores to the score on 1 independently scored local OSCE history-taking station, this observational study provides criterion-related evidence for interpreting AMTES scores. The association did not depend on including the complaint-matched training-case score. The scores also added predictive information beyond the 2 prior physical-examination course scores in internal cross-validation. These findings establish neither causal effects of practice nor within-student transfer, and residual confounding by prior ability cannot be excluded. They support further evaluation of AMTES analytics as a candidate low-stakes formative signal, with independent external validation required before operational use.
authors: Weishan Zhang; Yang Liu; Yiying Zhu; Xian Lu; Liping Wu; Minghui Yue; Xiaolin Hong; Oudong Xia; Chujun Shi

title: Association of alkaline phosphatase and segmented neutrophils count with low appendicular lean mass in middle-aged women: Evidence from an American cross-sectional survey
abstract: OBJECTIVES: Sarcopenia is associated with an increased risk of frailty, falls, and mortality. Women exhibit distinct characteristics in appendicular lean mass and metabolism compared with men, and hormonal changes may further accelerate appendicular lean mass. This study aimed to identify key blood biomarkers associated with appendicular lean muscle mass index adjusted by body mass index (ALMBMI) in women and to explore their potential relationship with chronic inflammation. METHODS: Based on NHANES 2015-2018 data from middle-aged women, the ALMBMI was calculated. A multimodal machine learning framework was constructed using elastic net logistic regression and generalized linear models (GLMs) to screen core variables affecting ALMBMI. Weighted quantile sum (WQS) regression and Bayesian kernel machine regression (BKMR) jointly determined variable weights and effect directions, and restricted cubic spline (RCS) models characterized dose-response curves to identify key blood indicators and their magnitudes of change associated with low appendicular lean mass risk. RESULTS: A total of 1,082 participants were included in this study. Following variable screening, 12 variables were identified as significantly associated with ALMBMI. WQS regression indicated that segmented neutrophil count (weight: 0.25) and alkaline phosphatase (ALP) (weight: 0.22) were the predominant factors associated with low ALMBMI. BKMR analysis, which assesses all variables jointly, identified segmented neutrophil count (36.0%), and ALP (27.6%) as the core variables. RCS analysis revealed that segmented neutrophil count and alkaline phosphatase showed an L-shaped trend with ALMBMI, with inflection points at 4.00 (1000 cells/μL) and 76.00 IU/L, respectively. In each case, the curves plateaued to the right of the inflection point. Relative to participants classified as having low ALMBMI according to FNIH criteria, those with normal ALMBMI exhibited reductions of 16.01% in ALP and 11.17% in segmented neutrophil count, respectively. CONCLUSION: Among middle-aged women, higher segmented neutrophil count and ALP levels were identified as positive correlates of low ALMBMI, with both biomarkers demonstrating threshold phenomena. Such hematological alterations are consistent with chronic low-grade inflammation, underscoring their potential utility in early sarcopenia screening and prevention.
authors: Shanlan Yang; Jiaofeng Wang; Dayoung Kim; Han Xu; Sheng Zhou; Fan Yang; Zhijun Bao

title: BAARC: Uncertainty-Driven Adaptive Partial Spectral Measurement to Full Reconstruction for Material Classification
abstract: Spectroscopic instruments with limited wavenumber coverage require accurate scan positioning or multiple measurements to complete the material analysis. This often requires prerequisite knowledge about the material under diagnosis to measure the spectral regions with distinguishing peaks. In our study, we simulate a Bayesian Adaptive Acquisition with Reconstruction-driven Classification (BAARC) framework for Raman spectral measurements, using masked training to learn spectral features that dynamically drive laser channel selection until the material is identified. We present a jointly trained two-level framework that takes progressive partial measurements of small wavenumber patches across the complete spectral range and, at each step, first attempts to reconstruct the full spectra until the model uncertainty is low. Secondly, material classification is performed at each reconstruction step until stoppage. Uncertainty quantification during reconstruction steps helps determine the measurement position of our next patch, while combining it with classification uncertainty determines measurement termination. By closing the loop between hardware acquisition and deep probabilistic modeling, the proposed system minimizes physical measurement steps while maintaining both spectral fidelity and diagnostic accuracy. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that our framework achieves high-accuracy sample identification using only a fraction of full-spectrum channels, offering a scalable solution for real-time, high-throughput spectroscopic instruments.
authors: Adithya Ashok Chalain Valapil; Aishwarya Venkataramanan; Joachim Denzler

title: Biomaterial-driven remove–remodel–repair (3R) strategy for full-cycle gastric cancer management: bibliometric mapping, preclinical evidence, and a translational roadmap
abstract: Gastric cancer (GC) remains a leading cause of cancer mortality worldwide and is characterized by prolonged precancerous progression, dynamic tumor-immune-microbiota interactions, and treatment-associated toxicity that can compromise host defense and tissue recovery. These features create a clinical need for full-cycle management spanning prevention, early eradication, advanced therapy, and postoperative rehabilitation. Here, we propose a biomaterial-driven 3R framework for GC management across the disease continuum, comprising remove for lesion clearance, remodel for immune microenvironment regulation, and repair for tissue restoration. A bibliometric analysis of 1559 publications maps the evolution of biomaterial-enabled GC research and provides an evidence landscape for this framework. Representative nanomaterials, biomimetic hydrogels, engineered microbial carriers, and regenerative matrices are mapped to clinical needs across prevention, endoscopic and perioperative intervention, systemic therapy, and rehabilitation. The 3R occupy distinct translational tiers: remove- and remodel-oriented platforms are predominantly supported by mechanistic preclinical studies, whereas selected repair-oriented materials, including endoscopic hemostatic, sealing, and submucosal-support platforms, already have human clinical evidence. Overall, the 3R framework links therapeutic objectives, material functions, disease stages, and clinically relevant endpoints into a translational roadmap for integrated GC management.
authors: Yijie Xie; Yuankai Gu; Qiwen Jiang; Markus Gerhard; Jun Zhang; Jinxin Zhao; Jiulong Zhao; Jie Gao

title: Biomedical Self-Supervised Learning using Sequential and Action-Conditioned Prediction: A Proof of Concept in Histopathology
abstract: Self-supervised foundation models for biomedical imaging are typically trained with non-sequential objectives that encourage invariance between augmented crops or predict missing content within a limited spatial resolution or range. This paradigm can be limiting for biomedical images, where diagnostically relevant structure often depends on relationships across widely different spatial extents and resolutions. We investigate sequential, action-conditioned prediction as an alternative self-supervised pretraining objective for biomedical imaging. As a proof of concept, we adapt seq-JEPA, originally developed for natural images, to 256 × 256 px histopathology images by extending its action space with zoom, and introduce seq-JEPA-dense, which predicts the next representation for every step in the sequence. Under the same per-crop augmentation distribution and with one run per method, seq-JEPA-dense improved tissue classification accuracy in the aggregated linear-probe evaluation from 88.3% to 91.9%, narrowing the gap to SimCLR, which achieved 93.3%. Both sequential variants recover a held-out crop from the preceding crops and the relative action leading to it at roughly twice the chance rate within the same image, indicating that the prediction depends on the action; whether position, zoom, or both drive this remains to be isolated. These results provide proof-of-concept evidence that sequential, action-conditioned self-supervision can be adapted to histopathology by extending its action space with zoom, yielding representations that approach a contrastive baseline, a first step toward its investigation as a self-supervised approach for extended biomedical images such as whole-slide images.
authors: Linus Schilpp; Angelo Jovin Yamachui Sitcheu; Thomas Lautenschlager; Leonard Saur; Nils Friederich; Ralf Mikut; Stephan Allgeier

title: Cardiolipin-Based Electrochemical Biosensor for Non-treponemal Antibody Detection Using Screen-Printed Electrodes: A Proof-of-Concept Study
abstract: Syphilis remains a major public health concern. Although non-treponemal tests are widely used for screening and treatment monitoring, their interpretation relies on visual assessment of flocculation. Here, an amperometric biosensor using isolated cardiolipin (0.03–0.12%) as the sole biorecognition element was developed on carbon/graphene screen-printed electrodes. The 0.06% concentration was selected for subsequent experiments, and the biosensor discriminated positive and negative control materials across two electrode batches. Progressive positive-control dilution produced a systematic electrochemical response (R2 = 0.921). Electrode functionalization significantly affected the response (p < 0.001), supporting the contribution of immobilized cardiolipin. Discrimination was maintained under physiological and pathological glucose conditions (adjusted p < 0.001). These findings provide a preliminary proof-of-concept for cardiolipin-based electrochemical assessment of non-treponemal antibody reactivity. Further studies using clinical samples are required to establish analytical and clinical performance and investigate semiquantitative evaluation by correlating electrochemical responses with defined serological titers.
authors: Duane da Silva Moraes; Bruna Ferri Serafini; Felipe Longaray Kadel; Gabriela Victória de Mello Jantzch; Milleny Germann Souza; Willyan Hasenkamp; Antônio Shigueaki Takimi; Júlia Konzen Moreira
