title: Robot-assisted laparoscopic resection of renal arteriovenous malformation: a case report
abstract: Objective This study aimed to describe the experience of performing robot-assisted laparoscopic resection of renal arteriovenous malformation of one case. Case summary A 44-year-old female patient reported with a five-day history of dull right flank pain. Abdominal enhanced computed tomography showed a well-demarcated lesion measuring 4.2 cm × 5.3 cm × 6.1 cm. The renal angiography showed a renal arteriovenous malformation. The patient underwent successful robot-assisted laparoscopic resection of the renal arteriovenous malformation, and recovered completely. Results The medical records of this patient in our hospital were assessed. The body mass index was 20.4 kg/m 2 , the operative time was 126 min, the estimated blood loss was 30 mL, and the postoperative drainage volume was 80 mL. There was no severe complication after the surgery. At one-month follow-up, contrast-enhanced CT revealed that the rAVM had been completely resected and that hydronephrosis had significantly improved. Renal function was well preserved, except for a small renal infarction. Conclusion Robot-assisted laparoscopic resection of renal arteriovenous malformation is a feasible treatment for selected cases; however, more cases are required to further define its utility.
authors: Xiaofeng Guan; Xiang Wang; 韩泽平; Deng Yaoliang

title: Robotic search and rescue in earthquake-collapsed buildings: capabilities, evidence gaps, and a roadmap for human-multi-robot rescue
abstract: Following an earthquake, rescue robots must search for and assist trapped individuals in complex environments characterized by unstable rubble, narrow cavities, darkness, dust, and unreliable communications. This paper reviews the technical evidence for seven categories of robots within the seven-stage mission chain of search and rescue (SAR) in building collapse scenarios, covering unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs); tracked, wheeled, and reconfigurable robots; quadrupedal robots; snake-like and continuum robots; humanoid and hybrid robots; heavy-duty engineering robots; and casualty evacuation and medical transport robots. This paper evaluates representative “platform-sensor-mission” capabilities across two independent dimensions: validation maturity (E0–E4) and relevance to collapse rescue scenarios (S0–S4). The study clearly distinguishes between signals indicating the possible presence of trapped individuals, 3D positioning information usable to guide excavation operations, and the actual execution of subsequent rescue operations. Currently, evidence of field applications is primarily concentrated on tasks such as site entry, reconnaissance, mapping, visual search, and the detection of vital signs through rubble. In contrast, evidence regarding sustained communication, supply delivery, close-range manipulation of casualties, casualty management, evacuation, and mission handoffs is significantly lacking. This leads to the identification of three major gaps: the transition from search and detection to rescue operations; the coordinated transition between different platforms; and the assurance of safe deployment. The roadmap proposed in this paper emphasizes that human-supervised robot teams should share rescue information while preserving its uncertainty; maintain communication links where feasible; hand off tasks to appropriately equipped robots; and obtain authorization before performing critical operations involving safety. End-to-end evaluations should quantify information loss during task handoffs, positioning uncertainty, resilience following team failures, and the level of protection provided to trapped individuals.
authors: Defeng Xu; Feifei Sun; Songhang He; Xiangdian Chen; Yuqing Gao; Haiying Wang; Zhen Wang

title: Role of microthrombosis in coronary microvascular dysfunction
abstract: Coronary microvascular dysfunction is a common and prognostically important event of ischemic heart disease, yet effective therapeutic strategies remain limited. Microthrombosis is a pivotal driver of microvascular obstruction and no-reflow. This review focuses on the self-amplifying loop between inflammation and platelet activation that sustains microvascular occlusion. Within this loop, myocardial inflammatory signaling suppresses protective autophagy, predominantly in cardiomyocytes, and promotes endothelial dysfunction. The resulting prothrombotic endothelial surface supports activated platelet adhesion, inflammatory mediator release, and platelet-leukocyte aggregation. Neutrophil-derived web-like structures, known as neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs), further enhance platelet aggregation and fibrin deposition. These thromboinflammatory processes lead to microinfarcts, contractile dysfunction, and elevated cardiac troponin, and extend to multiple organs, particularly in patients with common cardiometabolic risk factors such as hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia, and hyperhomocysteinemia. Platelet-derived microparticles, platelet-monocyte aggregates, and soluble activation markers show promise as diagnostic biomarkers, but further clinical validation is required. Current antiplatelet, anti-inflammatory strategies, or ischemic conditioning are limited by bleeding risk, narrow therapeutic windows, or inconsistent efficacy. We outline future directions, including developing validated biomarker panels, multi-target therapies that block key inflammatory pathways or NET formation, and human-relevant microphysiological models. Understanding the positive feedback cycle between inflammation and platelets is essential for developing novel diagnostic and therapeutic approaches to mitigate microvascular damage in coronary artery disease as well as other thromboinflammatory disorders.
authors: Junjie Bei; 胡厚源

title: Second‐line MRI after expert transvaginal ultrasound in selected patients with suspected complex deep endometriosis: A prospective cohort study
abstract: INTRODUCTION: The objective of this study was to evaluate the added diagnostic yield of second-line magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) after expert transvaginal ultrasound (TVS) for preoperative mapping of deep endometriosis (DE). MATERIAL AND METHODS: In this prospective observational cohort study, women with suspected DE scheduled for surgery after expert ultrasound were included. TVS was performed according to the International Deep Endometriosis Analysis (IDEA) protocol. MRI was selectively performed as a second-line investigation in patients with suspected advanced disease, inconclusive TVS, or advanced symptoms despite negative TVS findings. Surgical visualization served as the primary reference standard, with histopathology used as a secondary reference standard when available. Diagnostic performance (sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, likelihood ratios, and Cohen's κ) was assessed for TVS, MRI, and their combination, and stratified by prior surgical status. For the combined approach, a positive result was defined as a positive finding on either modality (TVS or MRI), representing a rule-out strategy. RESULTS: Among 221 women with suspected deep endometriosis, 189 underwent surgery, of whom 112 had both TVS and MRI; 55 had previous abdominal surgery. Combined imaging improved sensitivity for rectosigmoid DE (+10.3%; +6 true positives (TP), +3 false positives (FP)) and uterosacral ligament involvement (+29.2%; +14 TP, +12 FP) but reduced specificity for endometriomas (-19.0%; true negatives (TN) 18 to 14), obliteration of the pouch of Douglas (-13.3%; TN 14 to 8), and uterosacral ligaments (-20.3%; TN 35 to 23). Most lesions missed by TVS were in the mid or upper rectum. Accuracy for the urinary bladder and ureters decreased with the addition of MRI (82.2% to 75.7%). Sensitivity for rectosigmoid lesions was higher with the combined method (TVS + MRI) in women with prior surgery. CONCLUSIONS: Among selected complex patients undergoing second-line MRI after expert TVS, combined imaging increased detection of rectosigmoid and uterosacral ligament lesions, but at the cost of reduced specificity. The sensitivity for rectosigmoid disease was greatest among patients with prior abdominal surgery, although this subgroup finding should be considered exploratory. These findings are consistent with a selective rather than routine role for MRI after expert TVS.
authors: Mira Rehal; Malin Brunes; Takayuki Suzuki; E. Epstein

title: Sensor-integrated PMMA bone cement enables multimodal data acquisition in a load-bearing orthopedic knee spacer implants.
abstract:
Introduction

Periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) is a severe complication of total knee arthroplasty, is a leading cause of revision surgery, and is associated with significant morbidity. Two-stage exchange using antibiotic-loaded polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) spacers remains the clinical gold standard, yet the decision to reimplant relies largely on indirect markers and clinical judgment, as no method allows continuous in situ assessment of infection resolution. Here, we report the development of a sensorized knee spacer that transforms medical-grade PMMA bone cement from a passive structural material into an implantable multimodal sensing platform by embedding fully functional sensing and communication systems.

Methods

We developed an integration strategy addressing previously limiting factors, including exothermic polymerization, mechanical load transfer, and spatial constraints, while retaining the conventional PMMA molding principle during final spacer fabrication. A miniaturized multimodal sensor unit was integrated within PMMA cement, and the functionality of the embedded camera, spectrometer, positioning, and temperature sensors following cement integration was evaluated. The mechanical behavior of the sensor-integrated spacer was assessed under adapted dynamic biomechanical loading conditions based on ISO 14879-1:2020. In vivo functionality and longitudinal multimodal data acquisition were evaluated in a porcine pilot experiment using human knee spacer dimensions.

Results

Stable integration of the miniaturized multimodal sensor unit within PMMA cement was achieved while maintaining sensor functionality and wireless data transmission despite the thermal, mechanical, and geometric constraints of bone cement integration. The functionality of the embedded camera, spectrometer, positioning, and temperature sensors was maintained following cement integration. In vivo functionality and longitudinal multimodal data acquisition were demonstrated over 148 h in the porcine pilot experiment.

Discussion

These findings demonstrate the technical feasibility of integrating active sensing systems into load-bearing bone-cement implants under the investigated experimental conditions. The SmartSpacer provides a platform for longitudinal multimodal data acquisition during the spacer interval, establishing a technical basis for future studies investigating infection-associated biomarkers.
authors: Tran NB, Capogrosso L, Dillitzer C, Morandell P, Lallinger V, Micheler C, Werner J, Reiser J, Baumgartner C, Burgkart R, Lazic I, Hayden O.

title: SepsisFlow: an event-stream foundation model for continuous risk warning and trajectory modelling in ICU sepsis
abstract: Sepsis is a leading cause of ICU death with heterogeneous onset and course, yet most warning models predict only whether sepsis will occur, leaving clinicians uncertain of its onset context and early trajectory once an alarm sounds. To answer these questions on one hourly clock from ICU admission, we built SepsisFlow: before onset, it combines a Mamba model pretrained on 2.57 million EHRs with about 1,700 hourly features in gradient-boosted trees to predict 6/12/24-h risk; at onset, it fuses Mamba and tabular encoders via a gated network into continuous patient states defining onset contexts; after onset, it encodes 72-h organ-support and physiological trajectories via an attention bidirectional recurrent network into early courses. For pre-onset warning in MIMIC-IV, SepsisFlow detected more cases than NEWS2, qSOFA, and SIRS at equal alarms, gaining about 8 cases per 100 from hourly updating, while outperforming 16 retrained algorithms and maintaining risk ranking in eICU. At onset, its contexts separated 2% cardiovascular-ICU from 15%-17% other 28-day mortality, and within each context after onset, persistent support carried fivefold higher mortality than de-escalation. SepsisFlow establishes a foundation-model paradigm for continuous risk and trajectory stratification in critical care.
authors: Yawen Zhang; Wanzhe Xu; Zhenhua Zhang; Jinyu Wu; Yizhou Zhuang; Yitao Yang; Kenta Nakai

title: Silver Thickness Optimization for Sensitivity Enhancement in a Surface Plasmon Resonance Biosensor for Multi-Cancer Detection
abstract: This work proposes a highly sensitive Surface Plasmon Resonance (SPR) biosensor for label-free refractive index (RI) and biological sensing applications based on a BK7 prism-coupled bimetal (Ag/Au) and Tantalum Diselenide (TaSe2) hybrid structure. The transfer matrix method (TMM) is used to examine the sensing performance of the suggested structure while accounting for the effects of various biological sensing media (SM) and plasmonic layer thickness. To attain optimal plasmonic coupling, the impact of Ag layer thickness on sensitivity and minimum reflectance (Rmin) is methodically examined. For the long RI range of 1.35–1.40, the maximum sensitivity is 206.32°/RIU at the Rmin value. Depending on the sensing layer, the Ag thickness ranges from 39 to 42 nm, offering better resonance properties for various cancer detection. Basal, HeLa, Jurkat, PC12, MM-231 and MCF-7 have remarkable Rmin values and the highest sensitivity of 260.49°/RIU, 280.13°/RIU, 290.24°/RIU 260.49°/RIU, 280.13°/RIU and 290.24°/RIU with an optimized Ag thickness of 42–39 nm among the biological layers under investigation, respectively. Moreover, the penetration depth (PD) of 192.94 nm and 181.5 nm is attained at RIs of SM 1.35 and 1.40. The suggested SPR biosensor is a promising platform for biosensing, disease diagnosis, and real-time monitoring applications because of its exceptional sensitivity, low resonance reflectance, and improved detection capability.
authors: Rajeev Kumar; Biswajit Brahma; Jitendra Singh Tamang; Paolo Barsocchi; Akash Kumar Bhoi

title: Single Center, Single-Group Trial to Evaluate the Safety and Feasibility of 50 Hz Stimulation to Enhance Stroke Recovery of Upper Limb Function: The Motor Recovery Through Plasticity-Inducing Cortical Stimulation Open-Loop Protocol
abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: trial) of epidural cortical stimulation showed improved rehabilitation outcomes in a subset of those with poststroke related disability as long as (1) the individual had a degree of surviving corticospinal tracts and (2) an electrode that when delivering stimulation could evoke a motor response. The goal of this study is to examine the safety and feasibility of new sense-and-stim capable implantable devices with configurable electrode arrays, using subdural stimulation, to improve stroke rehabilitation and associated motor functional outcomes. METHODS: We will implant 4 patients who have chronic upper limb impairment after stroke to (1) demonstrate the safe usage of a cortical sensing-enabled stimulation system in a stroke rehabilitation protocol and (2) evaluate the system's capability to deliver activity-triggered stimulation for future clinical studies using neuroplasticity-inducing stimulation to enhance stroke rehabilitation outcomes. Each participant will receive 50 Hz stimulation delivered through the cortical, subdural, electrodes during clinical rehabilitation visits for 2 hours a day, 5 days a week, for 6 weeks. Devices are explanted approximately 9 months after implant. EXPECTED OUTCOMES: We anticipate that the surgical implantation of the cortical stimulation device and use of the device to deliver stimulation to enhance rehabilitation outcomes will succeed without identifying unanticipated safety concerns or encountering unexpected adverse events. DISCUSSION: Although the generalizability of the results will be limited based on the small number of study participants, it is nonetheless a crucial research milestone for reestablishing cortical stimulation as a potential method for enhancing poststroke rehabilitation.

title: Single-incision laparoscopic surgery for blunt abdominal trauma: A single-institution experience at a level I trauma centre
abstract: BACKGROUND Laparoscopic surgery remains a safe and feasible option for managing traumatic intra-abdominal organ injuries, offering advantages over laparotomy in terms of pain, cosmesis, and postoperative recovery. Single-incision laparoscopic surgery (SILS) is an evolving technique that aims to further reduce the invasiveness of laparoscopy. The authors report seven cases of small bowel injury from blunt trauma treated with SILS. AIM To evaluate the feasibility and safety of SILS in hemodynamically stable patients with blunt abdominal trauma. METHODS Adult patients with blunt abdominal trauma who presented to a level 1 trauma centre and were diagnosed with small bowel injury were retrospectively reviewed. Patients who had undergone SILS were identified. Clinical data, operative details, and postoperative outcomes were analyzed. RESULTS Seven patients were included in this study. Four patients were male, with a median age of 68 years. The most common mechanism of injury was in-car traffic accidents (5 cases). All patients presented with hemodynamic stability and an alert mental status upon arrival. Injured sites included the ileum (3 cases), mesentery (3 cases), and jejunum (2 cases), with no associated solid organ injuries. Surgical procedures consisted of primary repair in 5 cases and resection with anastomosis in 2 cases. No injuries were missed. Postoperative complications included ileus in 2 cases, with no other complications reported. No mortality was observed during the study period. CONCLUSION SILS appears feasible and safe in carefully selected hemodynamically stable patients with blunt abdominal trauma, although larger studies are required to confirm its clinical role.
authors: Hancheol Jo; Dong Hun Kim; Jung Wook Suh

title: Six in One: 6S‐NP Supramolecular Nanoparticles for Super‐Lubrication, Inflammation Suppression, and Senescence Reversal in Mechanically Aggravated Joint Disorders
abstract: Mechanical overload and oxidative inflammation jointly drive the progression of friction-induced, age-related joint degeneration. Current clinically employed viscosupplementation strategies, such as hyaluronic acid, only offer transient lubrication, and under high-shear conditions, it undergoes rapid viscoelasticity deterioration, greatly limiting lubrication property. Here, we reported a multifunctional nanoplatform system (6S-NP), which integrated stimuli-responsive, self-renewable, supramolecular-synergistic, super-lubricating, sustained-retaining, and senescence-reversible features for achieving adaptive treatment in mechanically aggravated age-related joint disorders. Under shear, the host-guest bonds partially dissociated, which released and redistributed hydrated zwitterionic chains to rebuild a highly lubricated layer and minimize friction. When shear was removed, the bonds spontaneously reformed, the nanocrown assembled back, and the lubricating components were retained for the next cycle. This mechanically programmed dissociation-reassembly cycle maintained ultralow friction over repeated loading, achieving a >90% lower coefficient of friction than commercial hyaluronic acid. The reactive oxygen species-cleavable linkers enabled targeted drug release in inflammatory joints, effectively reducing IL-6/IL-1β, protecting extracellular matrix integrity, and reversing chondrocyte senescence. In load-driven knee osteoarthritis and frequency-driven temporomandibular joint osteoarthritis model, 6S-NP preserved cartilage, suppressed inflammation, and improved joint morphology. The adaptable design principles of 6S-NP could also be extended to other mechanically and oxidatively stressed degenerative conditions, providing a broadly applicable therapeutic strategy.
authors: Yinuo Yang; Gengtian Sun; Jinna Ren; Yuguang Wang; Hongyu Zhang

title: Smart hip implants: listening to the joint: evaluating biochemical sensors for early detection of peri-prosthetic infection and inflammation
abstract: Total hip implants are being placed in more patients than ever before, with numbers increasing yearly. As implants are increasingly given to younger, more active patients with longer life expectancy, the risk of failure increases. Infection and aseptic loosening are the main causes of hip implant failure and are difficult to detect at an early stage. Current diagnostic methods are often initiated after symptoms appear, delaying treatment and often complicating revision surgery. This thesis explores smart hip implants, implants equipped with integrated sensors, to facilitate earlier detection of hip implant failure. A review of 49 biomedical sensors and a stakeholder analysis identified several types of sensors capable of continuously measuring indicators of failure. Among these, acidity (pH) and reactive oxygen species (ROS) sensors emerged as promising and underdeveloped options. To evaluate their potential, the two types of sensors were tested in controlled laboratory environments designed to represent conditions surrounding a hip implant. Both demonstrated potential for detecting biochemical changes associated with infection and the underlying cause of aseptic loosening: inflammation. The tests also revealed challenges related to sensor performance in the complex hip environment. Together, the findings support the potential of integrating biochemical sensors into the hip implant. While technical, biological, and data safety related challenges remain, this work demonstrates that biochemical sensing in hip implants is both feasible and clinically meaningful. It outlines a pathway toward smart hip implants capable of continuously monitoring, enabling earlier failure detection and targeted clinical intervention, transforming long term patient outcomes.
authors: Helene Noordhuis

title: Smooth total variation regularization for interference detection and elimination (STRIDE) for MRI
abstract: Objective. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is increasingly required to operate near electronic devices that emit dynamic electromagnetic interference (EMI). Existing reference-channel EMI removal methods estimate a transfer function between EMI sensors and imaging coils from the measured data alone, and do not use prior knowledge about the structure of MR images. We develop and validate an EMI removal method that uses the inherent spatial smoothness of MR images as an additional prior, demonstrated on a head-only 0.5 T scanner. Approach. Smooth total variation regularization for interference detection and elimination (STRIDE) operates in the image domain. For each image column, EMI sensor data are combined and subtracted from the imaging coil data such that the L 2 norm of the total variation (TV) along the readout direction is minimized. This exploits the smoothness of MR images, a property well-known in compressed sensing but not previously used in EMI removal. STRIDE was evaluated on phantom and in-vivo brain datasets under EMI scenarios replicating sources encountered at our affiliated hospitals, and compared against two implementations of External Dynamic Interference Estimation and Removal (EDITER). Main results. STRIDE produced visually better EMI removal and generally higher temporal signal-to-noise ratio than both EDITER implementations, with comparable EMI removal percentage. STRIDE also resulted in lower or equal root-mean-square error than both EDITER implementations in all 8 phantom EMI conditions tested. These results held across both phantom and in-vivo datasets. Significance. STRIDE shows that incorporating known properties of MR images into the EMI removal problem provides meaningful improvements over methods that rely on measured data alone. The approach is deterministic, training-free, sequence-independent, and compatible with existing EMI sensor hardware. STRIDE therefore extends reference-channel EMI removal to scenarios where existing methods fail, particularly point-of-care and interventional MRI outside fully shielded environments, providing a deterministic, training-free alternative to machine-learning approaches.
authors: Alexander Mertens; Diego F. Martinez; Amgad Louka; Ying Yang; Chad Harris; Ian R. O. Connell

title: Staphylococcus epidermidis-associated brain abscess following endovascular treatment of a ruptured intracranial aneurysm: potential immune-inflammatory mechanisms—a case report and literature review
abstract: Background Endovascular treatment(EVT) is a key therapeutic approach for ruptured intracranial Aneurysms; however, postoperative brain abscesses are extremely rare, and their pathogenesis and optimal treatment strategies remain unclear. This article reports a case of a Staphylococcus epidermidis -associated brain abscess that developed following stent-assisted coil embolization for subarachnoid hemorrhage caused by a ruptured anterior communicating artery aneurysm and discusses the underlying immune and inflammatory mechanisms as well as treatment strategies. Case presentation A 49-year-old man underwent stent-assisted coil embolization for subarachnoid Hemorrhage(SAH) from a ruptured anterior communicating artery aneurysm. Recovered well from operation and discharged. He, however, presented on the 34th postoperative day with a high-grade fever, headache, nausea, and vomiting. Brain imaging showed a brain abscess in the left frontal lobe, approximately 42 mm × 27 mm. However, there were no clear signs of severe neurological deterioration or a critical phase of cerebral herniation. Laboratory tests revealed high white blood cell and neutrophil counts, low lymphocyte counts, and variable reductions in CD3+, CD4+, and CD8+ T cells, CD19+ and CD20+ B cells, and Natural Killer cells(NK cells). Meanwhile, IL-1β, IL-6, TNF- α, and IL-10 levels increased, indicating deep immunological and inflammatory changes during infection. Inflammatory and immune markers improved slightly after antimicrobial therapy, but clinical symptoms persisted, and robot-assisted stereotactic abscess drainage was performed. A culture of pus grew methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus epidermidis (MRSE). Whole-genome sequencing confirmed the species and ST2 subtype and genetic features associated with β-lactam resistance. Initially, based on the consultation findings, meropenem and metronidazole were empirically administered as broad-spectrum antibiotics; after MRSE was confirmed, treatment was switched to vancomycin, and the patient’s clinical symptoms and laboratory parameters gradually improved. Postoperative imaging showed no recurrence of abscess, and the patient was in satisfactory general condition and no aftereffects whatsoever at six months’ follow-up. Conclusion We present a case report of an isolated brain abscess due to Staphylococcus epidermidis that developed after EVT of a ruptured intracranial aneurysm, which is a novel and clinically rare case. It also provides new clinical evidence for understanding this type of rare complication and optimizing treatment strategies.
authors: Xufeng Sun; Qile Sun; Shenao Li; Jiahao Zhang; Xiaolin Xu; Yueyang Peng; 温志峰

title: Stop Early, Stay Simple: Evidence Acquisition for Power System Fault and Attack Diagnosis
abstract: Diagnostic models for cyber-physical power systems usually inspect every telemetry source for every event, although some events are clear from one source and others need several. We ask when a learned policy for choosing that evidence is worth its added complexity. To answer this, we present ActiGrid, a benchmark framework for active evidence acquisition that pairs a classifier trained to tolerate missing modalities with a Double Deep Q-Network (DQN), which either requests another source or stops and diagnoses but never operates grid actuators. On the public TU Delft digital substation and MSU/ORNL power system attack benchmarks, we compare the DQN with fixed subsets and orders, calibrated entropy stopping, a greedy value of information rule, and tree ensembles trained per subset. The learned policy does adapt to what it observes, yet it is statistically indistinguishable from entropy stopping on TU Delft and Pareto dominated by simple controls on MSU/ORNL, while compact subset classifiers outperform it while reading fewer sources on both benchmarks. Entropy stopping run over those subset classifiers reaches the highest mean Macro-F1 on TU Delft (0.928 while reading 57% of the sources) but brings no saving over a static three source subset on MSU/ORNL, where no method exceeds 0.45 Macro-F1. Selective acquisition can pay off, but on these benchmarks it does not need a learned policy.
authors: S M Zia Ur Rashid; Sazidul Islam Hira; Rupesh Sah; Suman Rath

title: Strangulated Obturator Hernia with Intestinal Perforation in a Nonagenarian: A Case Report and Management Challenge
abstract: Introduction: Obturator hernia is a rare type of pelvic hernia, representing less than 1% of all abdominal hernias. It predominantly affects frail, elderly, multiparous women, leading to high morbidity and mortality rates due to diagnostic delays and the frequency of strangulation. Case Presentation: We report the case of a 95-year-old woman. She presented with a four-day history of obstructive syndrome Associated with pain on the inner thigh. Vital signs were normal except for a heart rate of 95 beats per minute. Clinical examination revealed a distended, tympanic abdomen and free hernia orifices and a positive Howship-Romberg sign. Laboratory tests showed leukocytosis (14,000/mm³) and elevated C-reactive protein (100 mg/L) in front of this clinical presentation an obturator hernia was suspected and an abdominal computed tomography (CT) scan confirmed a small bowel obstruction caused by a left obturator hernia, with no signs of bowel compromise. Management and Outcome: The patient was emergently transferred to the operating room. A sub-umbilical midline laparotomy was performed. Exploration revealed a dilated small bowel proximal to an incarceration in the left obturator foramen. The incarcerated loop was carefully isolated with a tissue tape to protect the surgical field. Upon gentle extraction using a dissector, an 8-cm segment of non-viable small bowel with a 1-cm perforation was identified. A manual small bowel anastomosis was performed after small bowel resection. The hernia defect was repaired by closing the peritoneum with a single buried suture and reinforcing the area with a plasty using the adjacent round ligament. The postoperative period was good with transit resumption at day 4, we however noticed a fixed evisceration successfully treated with Vaseline gauze dressings and cutaneous approximation sutures. title: Study of an Assisted Diagnosis System of Traditional Chinese Medicine Based on RAG
abstract: This study developed an information system designed to support traditional Chinese medicine knowledge applications. Although large language models offer strong generative capabilities, their reliability in specialized medical domains is limited by domain-specific hallucinations. To address this issue, a retrieval-augmented generation-based traditional Chinese medicine information system was developed by integrating authoritative domain data into a structured knowledge base. The system emphasized information system modeling and design, combining semantic representation, retrieval, and generation processes to improve the consistency and interpretability of system outputs. Experimental results showed that the proposed system effectively supported semantic search and knowledge-based information services. This work demonstrated the applicability of information system design methods in knowledge-intensive medical contexts and provides a reusable framework for integrating large language models with structured information systems.
authors: Yang Wenhao; Yan Wang; Yang Peng
venue: International Journal of Information System Modeling and Design

title: Surgical Approaches and Prognostic Factors in Superior Sulcus Tumors
abstract: Objective: To evaluate surgical approaches, clinical characteristics, and prognostic factors in patients with superior sulcus tumors (SSTs) and to assess survival outcomes according to resection type.Materials and Methods: This study included 20 patients with histopathologically confirmed SSTs who underwent surgical treatment between 1997 and 2004. Eight patients were evaluated retrospectively and twelve prospectively. Demographic, clinical, radiological, histopathological, and treatment-related data were analyzed. Survival outcomes were assessed using the Kaplan–Meier method, and comparisons between groups were performed using the log-rank test.Results: All patients were male, with a mean age of 53 years. Pain was the most common presenting symptom (100%). Tumors were predominantly located in the right hemithorax (75%). Lobectomy was performed in 85% of patients, while 15% underwent wedge resection due to limited pulmonary reserve. Postoperative complications occurred in 45% of patients, with atelectasis being the most frequent. Squamous cell carcinoma was the most common histopathological subtype. Median survival was longer in the lobectomy group compared with the wedge resection group (38 vs. 14 months), although the difference did not reach statistical significance (p=0.075). Patients with nodal involvement and vertebral invasion had poorer survival.Conclusion: Extent of resection, nodal status, and local invasion remain key determinants of prognosis in SST. Lobectomy was associated with more favorable survival outcomes than limited resection, although these findings should be interpreted cautiously. Despite advances in multimodality treatment, prognostic factors continue to guide clinical decision-making in this complex disease.
authors: Hüseyin Eren; Tamer Altınok; Abdullah İrfan Taştepe

title: Surgical management of endometrial cancer: evidence-based principles and recommendations: Number 15 – 2026
abstract: Key Points• Endometrial cancer (EC) is the most prevalent gynecologic malignancy in high-income nations, with incidence rates rising due to aging and obesity.• Surgery is the primary therapeutic modality, providing essential data for staging, risk stratification, and adjuvant planning.• Minimally invasive surgery (MIS) provides equivalent oncologic outcomes to open surgery while significantly reducing perioperative morbidity and recovery time.• Sentinel lymph node (SLN) mapping offers high diagnostic accuracy and has replaced systematic lymphadenectomy as the preferred method for nodal assessment. Recommendations• Patients with suspected or confirmed endometrial cancer should undergo systematic initial assessment including: comprehensive clinical assessment, histopathologic confirmation, and appropriate imaging based on clinical and pathologic risk.• Preoperative risk stratification should integrate clinical characteristics, imaging findings, histopathologic features, and molecular classification whenever available.• Minimally invasive total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (TH/BSO) should be offered as the standard surgical approach for eligible patients with apparent early-stage disease.• Sentinel lymph node mapping should be the preferred method for lymph node assessment.Systematic lymphadenectomy should be performed in suspected lymph node metastases, but not in uterine-confined disease.• Molecular tumor classification, including assessment of mismatch repair genes status, should be performed in all patients to inform prognosis, hereditary risk, and adjuvant treatment decisions.• Fertility-sparing treatment should be restricted to highly selected patients with strictly low-risk disease and managed in specialized centers with strict surveillance.• Patients who are not candidates for surgery should be managed with radiotherapy, systemic therapy, hormonal treatment, or combined approaches according to disease extent and tumor biology.• Surgical treatment of advanced or recurrent endometrial cancer should be reserved for carefully selected patients in whom complete cytoreduction or meaningful palliation is achievable.• Multidisciplinary decision-making is essential at all stages of endometrial cancer management to optimize oncologic outcomes and preserve quality of life.
authors: Agnaldo Lopes da Silva Filho; Eduardo Batista Cândido; Jesus Paula Carvalho; Caetano Da Silva Cardial; Matheus Eduardo Soares Pinhati; Mariana Seabra Leite Praça

title: Syndrome-oriented CNS infectious complications after haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation and CAR T-cell therapy, part 2—focal brain infections and meningitis of bacterial, fungal, and parasitic origin: recommendations from the EBMT Practice and Harmonization Committee
abstract: Central nervous system (CNS) infections in patients after haematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) and CAR T-cell therapy are caused by a broad range of pathogens and associated with high morbidity and mortality. Lack of standardised definitions and uniform diagnostic approach contributes to underdiagnosis and heterogeneity in reporting. This EBMT Practice Harmonization and Guidelines Committee consensus document provides harmonised definition and recommendations on diagnostics, treatment, and response assessment for focal CNS infections and meningitis of bacterial, fungal and parasitic origin in cellular therapy recipients. Focal brain infections are predominantly caused by Aspergillus spp, Toxoplasma gondii , and Nocardia spp, whereas common bacteria are rare. Bacterial or fungal meningitis is rare and typically occurs late post-HSCT. Rapid diagnosis and treatment are crucial to improving outcomes. Benefits of corticosteroids in bacterial meningitis have not been evaluated in this population. Standardised definitions and outcome reporting should be adopted in registries and studies to improve comparability and strengthen the evidence base for management.
authors: Małgorzata Mikulska; Dina Averbuch; Dionysios Neofytos; Francesco Baccelli; José Luis Piñana; Martin Schmidt‐Hieber; Rafael de la Cámara; Simone Cesaro; David Navarro; Francesco Onida; Annalisa Ruggeri; Per T Ljungman; Isabel Sánchez‐Ortega; Ibrahim Yakoub Agha; Jan Styczyński

title: Synergistic Li + -functionalized Mo 2 CT X MXene and polyaniline composite for rapid and stable moisture sensing in wearable wound monitoring application
abstract: Managing optimal moisture balance is essential for chronic wound healing, yet current clinical assessments are often subjective and intermittent. This study reports the development of a high-performance, flexible resistive moisture sensor designed for real-time, quantitative wound monitoring. The active sensing layer consists of a lithium-ion (Li + ) functionalized Mo 2 CT X MXene and polyaniline (PANI) composite. Li + intercalation was utilized to expand the MXene interlayer spacing, enhancing water adsorption and ion transport. Simultaneously, in situ polymerized PANI was introduced to provide stable proton-conductive pathways. Current–voltage characterization verified that the Li + –Mo 2 CT X /PANI composite forms robust Ohmic contacts with the electrodes, exhibiting over a 40-fold enhancement in baseline electrical conductance compared to pristine Mo 2 CT X . The composite was integrated onto screen-printed circular interdigitated electrodes on a flexible PET substrate and encapsulated with poly(diallyldimethylammonium chloride) (PDAC). This protective PDAC layer acts as a semi-permeable moisture-diffusion barrier that regulates water molecule transport, prevents surface fouling and uncontrolled hydration saturation, and ensures environmental stability without compromising response speed. The sensor demonstrates a linear response across a wide relative humidity (RH) range of 20%–80%, featuring sensitivity of approximately 2.0 Δ R /%ΔRH, with a rapid response time of ∼1 s and a recovery time of ∼11 s. The device demonstrates high mechanical flexibility, and stable operation over a 15 d period. Real-time assessments using finger-touch tests and PVA-hydrogel wound models successfully distinguished between dry, normal, and wet clinical states. The superior performance is attributed to the synergistic effects of Li + -assisted interlayer hydration, Grotthuss-type proton hopping, and moisture-induced PANI protonation. These findings position the Li + –Mo 2 CT X /PANI composite as a promising candidate for next-generation smart dressings in digital wound management.
authors: Syahirah Umairah Mahadi; Siti Nabila Aidit; Norazriena Yusoff; Sharifah Fatmadiana Wan Muhamad Hatta; Yasmin Abdul Wahab; Fazliyatul Azwa Md Rezali

title: Synthetic Bioactive Peptides for Skin Diseases: From Rational Design to Therapeutic Applications
abstract: Synthetic bioactive peptides (SBPs) are a class of versatile therapeutic drugs for skin diseases, demonstrating unique molecular advantages in terms of sequence programmability, multi-functional integration, and responsiveness to microenvironmental signals. From the perspective of integrating molecular engineering with application requirements, this review systematically elaborates on the design principles of SBPs, with a focus on summarizing three core design strategies: functional design, stability design, and responsiveness design. Functional design endows SBPs with specific biological functions; stability design protects SBPs from degradation in the protein-rich skin environment; responsiveness design allows for their spatiotemporal activation and release at the lesion site, ultimately minimizing off-target effects. Furthermore, this review provides a comprehensive overview of the therapeutic applications of SBPs across a diverse range of skin pathologies, highlighting their progress in managing infected and immune-mediated inflammatory skin diseases, cutaneous malignancies, alongside other aesthetic and pathological conditions ( e.g. , photoaging, pathological scarring, and alopecia). Finally, we discuss the main challenges currently faced in the clinical translation of SBPs, including insufficient stability, immunogenicity risks, delivery barriers, and high manufacturing costs, and envision the integration of artificial intelligence-driven rational design, intelligent responsive systems, and personalized peptide therapies based on spatial omics data.
authors: Kehan Du; Zhuo-Ran Yang; 甘庭宇; Ting Li; Hao Jiang; Jintao Zhu

title: Tailored Co-Ni bimetallic MOF interfaces for selective recognition and electrochemical quantification of ornidazole
abstract: Ornidazole (ODZ) is a nitroimidazole antibiotic widely used in clinical and veterinary treatments. However, the presence of trace-level ODZ residues in environmental and biological systems causes potential risks to human health. In this work, a novel electrochemical sensor was fabricated using a Co-Ni bimetallic metal-organic framework (MOF) with 2,3-pyrazine dicarboxylic acid as an electrode modifier for ODZ detection. The electroactive nitro group of ODZ undergoes electrochemical reduction, providing the basis for electrochemical sensing. The synergistic interaction between Co and Ni metal centers enhances redox activity, while the porous framework and π-conjugated linker facilitate effective adsorption and preconcentration of ODZ molecules. The nitroimidazole moiety of ODZ interacts with unsaturated metal sites through coordination and electrostatic interactions, thereby enhancing electron transfer. The fabricated Co-Ni MOF/GCE sensor shows a wide linear range of 0.04–1236.54 μ M with a low detection limit of 0.008 μ M . Density Functional Theory (DFT) calculations were performed to investigate the electronic properties of ODZ. The sensor shows good selectivity, stability, and recoveries of 97%–102.2% in river water, tap water, milk, and ODZ tablets, highlighting its potential for practical antibiotic monitoring.
authors: Chettipalayam Arunasalam Dhayanithi; Sundaram Ganesh Babu

title: Tapering to Enhance the Performance of Nanowire-Based Fluorescent Biosensors
abstract: High-refractive-index nanowires are of interest for signal enhancement in fluorescence-based biosensing. Here, through electromagnetic modelling, we demonstrate substantial fluorescence signal enhancement by incorporating a tapered section into a cylindrical nanowire and investigate two complementary tapering configurations to address practical implementation challenges. Under near-normal excitation, the excitation enhancement increases approximately linearly with taper length, reaching more than three times that of the corresponding non-tapered nanowire at a taper length of 8000 nm. In a non-imaging signal detection scheme using a low numerical aperture (NA), the proposed tapered nanowire achieves more than three orders of magnitude enhancement in fluorescence signal compared with a planar biosensor. Thus, the tapered nanowire should enable efficient fluorescence detection using compact, low-NA optical configuration. In imaging mode, similarly as for non-tapered nanowires, imaging sharpness beyond conventional microscopy limitations is obtained when imaging from the non-tapered nanowire end, while strongly increased excitation enhancement is simultaneously obtained when exciting from the opposite, tapered end.
authors: Farhana Akter Mou; Nicklas Anttu

title: Temporal signatures of prediction error reveal external forces on an embodied robot
abstract: Embodied robots must distinguish self-generated sensory consequences from externally caused perturbations. In predictive processing, such deviation is accounted for as prediction error, but it is commonly treated primarily as a signal to be minimised. Here, we test whether the temporal profile of load-related prediction error provides diagnostic information about the type of physical interaction a robot experiences. We trained and evaluated windowed multilayer perceptrons to predict servo current, used as a proxy for joint load, from proprioceptive, inertial, and servo current history. The training data were recorded during random movements of tilt and pan servo motors of a robotic head. The best model was deployed in the robot in real time and evaluated across free movements and external perturbations, including brief pushes, sustained forces, and obstacle interactions. Prediction error and raw current time series were summarised using features capturing magnitude statistics, temporal structure, and signal shape. A random forest classifier was then used to classify the conditions based on the features. Different interaction conditions produced distinct profiles that supported robust perturbation classification with high cross-validated accuracy. Classification performance for prediction error was equal to the classification of raw current. The results suggest that load-related prediction error is not only a residual of imperfect prediction. Its temporal structure can act as an embodied self-monitoring signal for classifying physical interactions.
authors: Pierre Klintefors; Birger Johansson; Christian Balkenius

title: Testicular Necrosis Following Inguinal Herniorrhaphy: A Case Report
abstract: Testicular necrosis is a rare complication associated with inguinal herniorrhaphy. The main blood supply to the testicles comes from the testicular artery (internal spermatic artery), which branches off from the abdominal aorta; the external spermatic artery, which branches off from the inferior epigastric artery; and the arteries supplying the vas deferens. The testicles are extremely resistant to necrosis. Although early surgical intervention may reverse testicular ischemia, delayed diagnosis can necessitate orchiectomy. We report a case of testicular necrosis shortly after radical inguinal herniorrhaphy requiring orchiectomy following emergency exploration. A 73-year-old man presented to our hospital 18 months after undergoing robot-assisted radical prostatectomy. He developed a left inguinal hernia following radical prostatectomy and subsequently underwent inguinal herniorrhaphy. On the fifth postoperative day, the patient presented to the hospital complaining of pain and swelling in the left testicle. Physical examination revealed swelling of the left scrotum, and scrotal ultrasonography showed no blood flow in the left testicle. Emergency scrotal exploration for suspected testicular necrosis revealed scrotal skin thickening and black discoloration of the testis and epididymis without evidence of strangulation. Owing to absent testicular blood flow on intraoperative ultrasonography, left orchiectomy was performed. Histopathological examination revealed hemorrhage and ischemic necrosis. When scrotal pain, erythema, or swelling develops after inguinal surgery, prompt evaluation with scrotal ultrasonography is warranted, and the potential need for emergency surgical exploration should be considered.
authors: Takuya Yashima; Yoshihiro Nakagami; Kazuhiko Oshinomi; Masakazu Nagata; Takashi Fukagai

title: The Japanese Hernia Society (JHS) Guidelines for Adult Groin Hernia Management 2024
abstract: Groin hernia is a common surgical condition. The Japanese Hernia Society (JHS) Guidelines for Groin Hernia Management 2024 were developed to reflect both international evidence and the realities of clinical practice in Japan. This article is an authorized English translation of a summary of the adult section of the JHS Guidelines for Groin Hernia Management 2024, presenting key clinical questions, recommendations, and concise explanations for an international readership. It covers diagnosis, classification, surgical indications, operative approaches, mesh and fixation, anesthesia, chronic postoperative inguinal pain, recurrent and emergency hernia, training, cost-effectiveness, and registry-based outcome assessment; relevant differences from the international HerniaSurge guidelines are discussed. Laparoscopic repair is favored in selected patients when performed by experienced surgeons, particularly for pain reduction and early recovery, whereas open anterior mesh repair remains appropriate when general anesthesia or laparoscopy is unsuitable. For femoral hernia, chronic pain management, recurrent hernia, and incarcerated or strangulated hernia, evidence remains limited, leading to cautious or conditional recommendations.
authors: Hitoshi Idani; Gen Shimada; Katsuhito Suwa; Yoshiko Honda; Yuji Konishi; Itsuro Nagae; Kenta Saito; Takafumi Tamura; Satoshi Nagayama; Chie Tanaka; Seiko Hirono

title: The Lived Experience of Chinese Patients With Somatic Symptom Disorder: An Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis
abstract: Aim To deeply explore the subjective illness experience of patients with Somatic Symptom Disorder (SSD) throughout the entire course from the initial onset of symptoms and repeated medical consultations to receiving psychological interventions. Methods Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis (IPA) was adopted. Purposive sampling was used to recruit 8 patients meeting the diagnostic criteria for somatic symptom disorder in DSM-5 from the clinical psychology department of a tertiary general hospital between June 2025 and December 2025. Semi-structured in-depth interviews were conducted with these patients. After verbatim transcription of interview recordings, data analysis was carried out in accordance with the six-step coding procedure of IPA. Results Four main superordinate themes emerged from data analysis: (a) Embodied processing of distress and enduring somatic imprinting; (b) An unsafe living world co-existing with Symptoms; (c) Tracing symptom origins and the journey of help‑seeking; (d) Self‑growth within the lived experience of symptom co‑existence Conclusion The underlying driving force for patients with SSD is fear of death. These individuals frequently endure intense feelings of helplessness and insecurity, yet they consistently attribute their symptoms to physical pathology. Healthcare providers may obtain medical histories from patients with SSD to assess their emotional difficulties, family-related factors, personality traits, and illness-related beliefs. Furthermore, clinicians ought to provide feedback on physical-examination findings, refrain from redundant investigations, and validate patients’ distress through empathic responding. It is essential to reframe the meaning of symptoms: draw connections between symptoms and stress- or lifestyle-related triggers; illustrate the anxiety-to-illness transition pathway, alongside the vicious cycle that sustains somatic symptom responses.
authors: Xue Y, Chen F.

title: The Role of Laparoscopic Surgery in Abdominal Trauma: A Case Report and Review
abstract: Background: Abdominal trauma accounts for approximately 15 % of trauma admissions and remains a leading cause of preventable mortality.Traditionally managed by exploratory laparotomy of which up to 40 % are non-therapeutic the paradigm has shifted toward minimally invasive approaches.Laparoscopy now demonstrates diagnostic accuracy rates of 96-98 % and enables therapeutic repair in hemodynamically stable patients, resulting in reduced morbidity, infection rates, and length of stay.Case Presentation: A 23-year-old male sustained blunt abdominal trauma following a motorbike accident.He was hemodynamically stable with a positive FAST scan and CT evidence of hemoperitoneum and mesenteric contusion without solid-organ injury.Diagnostic laparoscopy revealed 6.3 L of hemoperitoneum and a through-and-through mesenteric tear 20 cm proximal to the ileocecal junction.Hemostasis was achieved using V-Loc 2.0 sutures with peritoneal lavage and drain placement.One unit of PRBC was transfused.Postoperatively, hemoglobin rose from 7.6 to 12.0 g/dL and CRP fell from 64 to 21 mg/L.The patient tolerated oral intake within 24 h and was discharged on day 4 without complications.Discussion/Review: Nontherapeutic laparotomies decreased by 58%, postoperative complication rates decreased by four times, and hospital stays decreased from 10.8 to 3.9 days, according to a targeted literature review (2020-2025; 24 studies).Conclusion: Laparoscopy should be a mainstay of contemporary trauma therapy since it provides therapeutic benefit and diagnostic accuracy in stable trauma patients, lowering hospitalization and morbidity.
venue: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology

title: The application of machine learning for the diagnosis and assessment of adolescent idiopathic scoliosis: a systematic review
abstract: Aim: This systematic review evaluated the applications, methodologies, and reporting quality of artificial intelligence (AI) models for the diagnosis and assessment of adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS). Methods: PubMed, Embase, and IEEE Xplore were searched for studies published from January 2015 to May 2026, with additional searches of Medical Image Computing and Computer Assisted Intervention (MICCAI), IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR), and International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML) proceedings (2020-2026). Studies applying AI or machine learning (ML) for AIS diagnosis or assessment were included. Methodological quality was assessed using a 12-dimensional framework based on the 2024 Checklist for Artificial Intelligence in Medical Imaging (CLAIM). Results: Of the 8,579 records initially identified, 45 studies were included. Automated Cobb angle measurement was the most common application, reported in 32 studies. The mean absolute error for Cobb angle measurement ranged from 1.07° to 5.31°. Other applications included binary scoliosis classification (8 studies), curve classification and severity grading (12 studies), vertebral rotation assessment (2 studies), and skeletal maturity assessment (2 studies). Eleven studies (24.4%) used non-radiographic inputs encompassing six modalities. Quality assessment showed that data partitioning (93.3%) and comparisons with competing models (93.3%) were well reported, whereas external validation (26.7%), code availability (13.3%), and explainable AI (35.6%) remained uncommon. Conclusion: AI demonstrates technical accuracy in Cobb angle estimation comparable to manual measurement variability. However, limited external validation, prospective evaluation, and transparent reporting remain barriers to clinical translation. Future studies should emphasize characterization of clinical practice variation, prospective validation, and standardized reporting to facilitate clinical implementation.
authors: Jingxi Su; Chang Liu; Guilin Chen; Terry Jianguo Zhang; Nan Wu

title: The dual future of OPM-MEG: Clinical translation and naturalistic neuroscience
abstract: Optically pumped magnetometer magnetoencephalography (OPM-MEG) has moved beyond proof of principle. The decisive question is no longer whether cryogen-free sensors can detect neuromagnetic fields from the human brain with sufficient sensitivity, but whether complete systems can deliver clinical decision value and interpretable recordings during more naturalistic behaviour. Here we argue that OPM-MEG is developing along two partly overlapping trajectories. One is clinical translation, where usefulness depends more on reliable workflows, calibrated source localisation, auditable quality control, and empirical evidence for improved diagnostic or treatment decisions. The other is naturalistic neuroscience, where wearable measurement can connect neural dynamics to movement, action, and social behaviour without conflating neural activity with movement-related artefacts. Both trajectories depend on a shared engineering stack including magnetic field control, dense spatial sampling, accurate calibration, integrated electronics, artefact suppression, participant comfort, and synchronised behavioural measurement. The next stage of OPM-MEG should be evaluated by clinical utility in specific patient groups, statistically identifiable neural dynamics in behaviourally rich settings, and sufficient system detail for replication across systems and sites.
authors: Lang Qin; Miao Cao; Zhen Yuan; Bingjiang Lyu; Jia-Hong Gao

title: The effects of the arts and arts therapies on mental health outcomes of children and young people: a systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: Background There is growing evidence on the positive effects of the arts and arts therapies for mental health (MH) outcomes. This review aims to fill a research gap by establishing the evidence on the effects of arts-based interventions on selected MH outcomes for children and young people (CYP). Methods Our systematic review and meta-analysis included randomised controlled trials with CYP aged 5–24 years receiving any type of arts-based intervention. Five databases (CINAHL, Embase.com, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, and Web of Science) were searched for studies published between 1/1/2005 and 18/5/2025. Two reviewers independently screened all records and assessed risk-of-bias using Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB2) and certainty using Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE). Data were initially extracted using the AI-assisted review tool Elicit and independently verified by two reviewers. All data were pooled using random-effects meta-analysis, and effect estimates for MH outcomes are summarised as Standardised Mean Differences (SMD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Heterogeneity was assessed using the I 2 statistic, with pre-specified subgroup and sensitivity analyses conducted to explore possible sources of inconsistency. This study is registered with PROSPERO (CRD420251015352). Findings One hundred trials across 29 countries involving CYP aged 5–24 years with a range of health conditions, alongside healthy populations, were included in this review. Based on studies with some concerns or high risk-of-bias, arts-based interventions were found to reduce individuals' depression (1.06 SMD lower [95% CI 0.45–1.67, n=1655, I 2 = 97%]), anxiety (0.75 SMD lower [95% CI 0.57–0.94, n=3898, I 2 = 87%]), and increase individuals' wellbeing (0.53 SMD higher [95% CI 0.26–0.80, n=538, I 2 = 49%]) and quality of life (0.54 SMD higher [95% CI 0.25–0.83, n=441, I 2 = 53%]) on average post-intervention. Certainty of results relating to wellbeing and quality of life was low due to imprecision and concerns about risk of bias, and very low for depression and anxiety due to additional inconsistency associated with high heterogeneity. Findings relating to anxiety were further supported by biomarker data (blood pressure and heart rate) with moderate certainty. Interpretation This systematic review provides a comprehensive synthesis of evidence from randomised controlled trials assessing the effects of a wide variety arts-based interventions on the mental health of CYP. Although the strength of any conclusions is limited by heterogeneity, imprecision and bias of the studies assessed, average effects were similar to those typically reported for established non-arts-based psychosocial interventions, including talking therapies. These findings advance our understanding of arts-based therapeutic strategies for CYP's MH. Further high-quality trials, with larger sample sizes and standardised outcome measures and timepoints, are needed to improve the certainty of evidence in this area. Funding UKRI.
authors: Pui Sze Cheung; Sarah Rhodes; Elisabeth Bahr; Wilfried Lakena; Nisha L. Sajnani; Nils Fietje; Vicky Karkou

title: Toward Sustainable Chemical Sensing: Integrating Interfacial Chemistry, Energy Efficiency and Life-Cycle Design
abstract: Chemical sensing must reconcile analytical performance with energy efficiency and environmental sustainability. Conventional thermally activated metal-oxide sensors enable effective detection but often require substantial operating energy. Although existing reviews address room-temperature sensors, polymer- and carbon-based materials, and non-faradaic transduction, an integrated framework connecting sensing mechanisms with energy demand, material sustainability, and life-cycle impacts remains essential. This Perspective proposes a design framework linking four dimensions: interfacial chemical recognition and signal transduction, operational energy efficiency, sustainable materials and manufacturing, and life-cycle assessment and circularity. Using ammonia (NH3) sensing as a representative model, we discuss how hydrogen bonding, acid–base interactions, charge redistribution, and, where applicable, proton transport enable sensing responses under ambient conditions. We examine bio-derived polymers, functionalized carbon materials, biomolecular systems, and waste-derived materials, highlighting opportunities and limitations in selectivity, humidity tolerance, stability, reproducibility, and scalability. By connecting analytical performance with energy and environmental criteria, this Perspective establishes a basis for evaluating sustainable chemical sensors beyond sensitivity alone, emphasising that sustainability requires quantitative validation across the device life cycle rather than assumptions based on room-temperature operation or material origin.
authors: Abdullah; Hafiza Fatima
venue: Journal of Engineering Science and Technological Trends

title: Toward agentic AI co-practitioners in dermatology.
abstract: Multimodal foundation models have given dermatological artificial intelligence a strong perceptual baseline, although performance on darker skin, rare conditions, and real-world images remains uneven. The next challenge is clinical agency. Here we propose a conceptual framework for agentic co-practitioners: systems in which a reasoning engine orchestrates active sensing, specialized tools, and longitudinal memory to take part in the clinical encounter from referral to management plan. No such system has yet been validated end to end in dermatology. We argue that sustained clinical value requires these systems to co-evolve with their physician users through structured feedback that captures local expertise without retraining. Because the value of a co-practitioner lies in its reasoning process and its effect on clinicians, retrospective benchmarks are insufficient; evaluation must assess complete clinical episodes, including patient-centered and health-system outcomes. We also set out the workforce, cost, liability, and regulatory questions that the framework does not yet resolve.
authors: Siyuan Yan; Victoria Mar; Harald Kittler; Zongyuan Ge

title: Towards clinical communication training with LLM-based conversational virtual patients and automatic evaluation systems
abstract: Clinical communication is a fundamental skill that impacts patient satisfaction, treatment adherence, and clinical outcomes. Traditional training methods, such as standardized patients (SPs) or virtual standardized patients (VSPs), face barriers including high costs, logistical complexity, and lack of spontaneous interaction. This study addresses these challenges by developing a scalable alternative based on Large Language Models (LLMs) to train medical students in the anamnesis phase. We developed an interactive Conversational Virtual Patient (CVP) system, understood here as a text- and voice-based simulated patient without graphical embodiment. The conversational logic is orchestrated as an explicit state machine over the interview, implemented with LangGraph, a graph-based framework in which each node performs one processing stage and a shared state persists across turns. Clinical consistency across the interview is maintained by a semantic memory layer implemented with LangMem, a library that stores clinical facts as vector embeddings and retrieves them by similarity. Performance is measured by an automatic evaluation module assessing 24 communication criteria derived from validated instruments such as the Communication Assessment Tool (CAT) and the Communication Skills Scale (CSS). The platform was validated with 21 participants, comprising 9 eighth-semester medical students, 11 practising physicians, and 1 expert in healthcare technology. All sessions were conducted in Spanish. Considering the student cohort, which addresses the educational utility of the tool, the system obtained a Chatbot Usability Questionnaire (CUQ) score of 82.3/100 and an average acceptance of the automated feedback of 4.50/5. The physician and expert cohort, which provides expert clinical validation, obtained 96.5/100 and 4.21/5 respectively, yielding a pooled usability score of 90.4/100 and a pooled feedback acceptance of 4.33/5. In an exploratory comparison against eleven physician ratings of the same interviews, rank agreement was highest for “Interest” ( $$\rho = 0.64$$ ) and lowest for “Completeness” ( $$\rho = 0.09$$ ), and the automated scores fell below the physician scores in every dimension. No dimension attained significance after correction for six comparisons, and the confidence intervals were wide, so these coefficients describe the observed sample rather than the agreement attainable in general. The results support the feasibility of the system as a complement to traditional medical training, providing immediate and standardized feedback. Given the sample size and the single-institution design, these findings should be read as an initial validation of feasibility and acceptability rather than as evidence of pedagogical efficacy.
authors: Andrea Bayona; Rubén Manrique; Christian Grévisse

title: Training the Next Generation of Future Surgical Residents: A Scoping Review and Proposal for an Undergraduate Curriculum From the Italian Polispecialistic Society of Young Surgeons
abstract: AIM: The transition from medical school to surgical residency is marked by a persistent gap between theoretical instruction and clinical readiness. In Italy, variability in training programs across centers creates persistent gaps in residents' medical education. Scientific societies are asked to identify current training gaps and define the core competencies required for effective surgical training. We propose an undergraduate curriculum to support last-year medical students in Italy. METHODS: A scoping review of the literature focusing on structured surgical curricula for undergraduate medical students was conducted. A suggested "curriculum" was introduced at the 2025 Congress of the Italian Polispecialistic Society of Young Surgeons (SPIGC) in Bari, Italy. RESULTS: The SPIGC curriculum includes seven domains: (1) soft skills: communication, informed consent, and interdisciplinary collaboration; (2) clinical and diagnostic skills: outpatient clinic management and perioperative care; (3) hygiene, prevention, healthcare systems; (4) technical skills; (5) emergency and trauma surgery; (6) perioperative management, integrating Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) protocols, nutritional assessment, and infections; (7) evidence-based medicine and recommendations. The SPIGC curriculum highlights the importance of simulation labs, hands-on workshops, and online learning, while providing clear pathways for fellowships or masters. It also introduces artificial intelligence (AI) systems as a modern learning tool, while highlighting the importance of their safe and responsible use. CONCLUSIONS: The SPIGC curriculum may provide a structured plan to improve surgical education for medical students in Italy and to align it with international standards. Its acceptability and impact on training quality and patient outcomes remain to be evaluated through future consensus and prospective studies.
