title: Translational Macrophage Mechano‐Immunotherapy for Next‐Generation Implantable Biomaterials
abstract: Decades of work have demonstrated that macrophages actively sense and respond to stiffness, strain and topography, making mechanical cues central determinants of inflammation, fibrosis and eventual maladaptive tissue remodelling of implanted biomaterials. Traditional strategies have focused on engineering implants to mimic native tissue mechanics. However, these material‐based approaches alone often fail to fully control immune and fibrotic outcomes. Recent advances in pharmacological modulation of mechanosensitive targets highlight the therapeutic potential of ‘mechano‐immunotherapy’ in the context of macrophage activation during foreign body responses. Preclinical implant studies highlight therapeutic opportunities and challenges, while clinical experience with selected agents derives from non‐implant indications and does not establish efficacy against implant‐associated foreign body responses. Advances in biomaterial platforms offer conceptual routes to spatially and temporally control mechanotransduction‐modulating drugs at the implant–tissue interface, without fundamentally altering the implant itself. Translating these approaches will require standardised mechanosensing assays and early regulatory engagement to navigate combination product classification and evidentiary requirements. This review synthesises current knowledge of mechanosensitive pathways, drug development, clinical progress in non‐implant indications and biomaterial‐based delivery strategies, providing a roadmap for localised macrophage mechano‐immunotherapy to improve implant integration and long‐term device performance.
authors: Xueying Xu; Ian L. Chin; Richard P. Tan

title: Understanding cognitive function in post-COVID-19 condition with fatigue: an interdisciplinary multimodal investigation
abstract: Lingering cognitive symptoms of post-COVID-19 condition (PCC) continue to challenge our understanding, highlighting the need for interdisciplinary research. We investigated whether individuals with PCC and fatigue differ from matched controls across neurocognitive, neuroimaging, and immunological measures, integrating these findings with qualitative phenomenological analyses through multimodal cross-analysis. Individuals with PCC and clinically significant fatigue (n=34), and age-, sex-, and education- matched controls recovered from COVID-19 without PCC (n=37) were included. Assessments encompassed physician evaluation, neuropsychological and functional tests, structural and functional MRI, immunological tests, and qualitative phenomenological analysis of interviews. Data were analyzed using established methods and an interdisciplinary cross-analysis to examine persistent cognitive symptoms in PCC. Group comparisons revealed subtle differences between individuals with PCC and controls, while neurocognitive performance and immunological markers remained within normative ranges. Modest differences in white-matter, myelin-related, and global brain measures were observed, alongside differences in associations between network connectivity and neurocognitive performance across groups, suggesting reduced network resilience rather than domain specific deficits. This pattern resonated with qualitative phenomenological findings: altered experiences of concentrating and difficulties to execute decisions and actions, despite preserved performance on standard neurocognitive tests. These findings suggest that cognitive symptoms in post-COVID-19 fatigue are associated with subtle neurobiological alterations not captured by standard cognitive assessments. In this highly fatigued sample, converging neuroimaging, neurocognitive and immunological findings point toward reduced network efficiency rather than overt cognitive impairment. Qualitative phenomenological analysis further highlighted altered modes of being in the world characterized by increased cognitive effort and difficulties executing decisions and actions.
authors: Ulrika Birberg Thornberg; Anders Eklund; Kristin Zeiler; Sofia Morberg Jämterud; Felipe León; Evren Özarslan; Agnes Andersson; Richard Levi; David Engblom; Anestis Divanoglou; Ida Blystad

title: Virtual EMI Receiver Generation (VERGE) for Improved EMI Removal in MRI
abstract: MRI is not designed to operate in the presence of EMI emitting electronic devices. To accomodate this, we propose VERGE which improves on previous EMI removal methods and can operate without external EMI sensors. VERGE estimates a reference coil non-linearly from all imaging and non-imaging coils by training a small per-scan convolutional neural net to generate a virtual coil. The virtual coil is then used with STRIDE, a reference-based EMI removal method. For single-source EMI contamination, VERGE performed similarly to the reference method. For multi-source dynamic EMI contamination, VERGE outperformed the comparison methods. Notably, VERGE with zero physical EMI sensors outperformed the comparison methods even with two physical EMI sensors. A non-linearly estimated virtual EMI coil improves reference-coil-based EMI removal under dynamic multi-source EMI, and enables effective EMI removal without physical EMI sensors or training data.
authors: Alexander Mertens; Diego Martinez; Amgad Louka; Ying Yang; Chad Harris; Ian Connell

title: Virulence Mechanisms of Streptococcus pneumoniae During Co-Infection
abstract: Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus) represents a key clinical challenge, being a major global cause of morbidity and mortality. Typically existing as a nasopharyngeal commensal, pneumococcus undergoes significant metabolic changes during its switch to a virulent pathogen, when it can cause severe pneumoniae, bacteriemia and meningitis. This switch is poorly understood but is thought to be influenced by environmental signals arising from co-infections between pneumococcus and other bacteria as well as viruses in the nasopharynx. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the multi-stage progression of pneumococcal invasive disease, from initial colonisation to host barrier migration. We examine environmental triggers that drive the lifestyle switch from commensal to virulent, highlighting the role of other organisms in this stimulation. In particular, we focus on influenza A and respiratory syncytial virus, as well as other bacteria including Staphylococcus aureus, Moraxella catarrhalis and Haemophilus influenzae. Overall, we bring the current understanding of the field into the context of the growing antimicrobial resistance global threat, demonstrating that understanding these complex cross-species interactions is vital for developing clinical interventions against secondary pneumococcal infections.
authors: Nicholas S Briggs; Stefano Camaione; Jack Goodall; Kevin E. Bruce; Thushan de Silva; Malcolm E. Winkler; David I. Roper

title: WAVES: Wearable Active Vibroacoustic Elasticity Sensing for Low-Cost and Non-Invasive Muscle Stiffness Monitoring
abstract: Muscle stiffness is a physiologically meaningful biomarker associated with a wide range of musculoskeletal and neurological conditions. However, existing muscle stiffness assessment methods, such as shear wave elastography (SWE), manual palpation, and handheld mechanical probes, remain impractical for continuous, everyday monitoring due to bulky hardware, operator dependence, and limited self-use. Meanwhile, wearable muscle-sensing modalities such as Electromyography (EMG) and Mechanomyography (MMG) primarily capture muscle activation rather than passive mechanical properties of tissue at rest, leaving a critical gap in portable monitoring of resting muscle stiffness. In this work, we present WAVES, a wearable system for continuous monitoring of muscle stiffness via active vibroacoustic sensing. WAVES injects controlled vibroacoustic excitation into soft tissue and estimates muscle stiffness by measuring shear-wave propagation velocity through Time-Difference-of-Arrival (TDoA) analysis across spatially distributed wearable sensors. To achieve accurate TDoA estimation with low-cost wearable hardware, we develop a physiology- and quality-guided vibroacoustic sensing framework that effectively screens and refines TDoA for accurate stiffness estimation. We evaluate WAVES through characterization experiments using ballistic jelly and end-to-end on-body evaluation with human participants. Results demonstrate that WAVES can robustly estimate muscle stiffness across multiple users and different superficial muscles while enabling lightweight, wearable deployment for everyday use. WAVES is able to achieve a muscle stiffness estimation error of 13.1% or less across multiple users and multiple muscle groups.
authors: Shubham Rohal; Dong Yoon Lee; Shijia Pan

title: WeVisForensics: Self-Evolving Agent for Omni AI-Generated Video Detection
abstract: Recent advances in video generation call for reliable detection grounded in explicit forensic evidence. However, current methods primarily depend on single-pass chain-of-thought reasoning that overlooks brief or localized artifacts, or on predefined multi-agent workflows that offer limited flexibility in selecting relevant inspections. Even with adaptive investigation, optimizing the investigation policy alone does not directly improve the forensic capabilities of fixed experts. We introduce WeVisForensics, an agentic framework in which a main investigator agent coordinates a self-evolving library of forensic inspector sub-agents spanning visual and audio cues. The investigator learns which artifact type to examine, over which window, and when to conclude, and these interactions provide shared feedback for both levels of agents. Our dual-timescale policy optimization strategy, DTPO, closes this loop through fast reinforcement learning of the investigator and slower refinement of the inspectors, guided by annotated artifact intervals, to report subtle artifacts they once dismissed. Furthermore, we curate ForenCue-30K, combining role-specific forensic annotations and interaction trajectories to supervise individual inspections and their coordination, with an accompanying reinforcement-learning pool. Experiments show that WeVisForensics averages 95.2% detection accuracy across in-domain, out-of-domain and agentic benchmarks, 9.0% above the strongest prior detector, while grounding its verdicts in localized evidence.
authors: Yipeng Du; Yuxi Li; Ying Zhang; Chong Sun; Chen Li; Jing Lyu; Ying Yu Tai

title: When touch leads vision: flexible sensory leadership during active texture exploration
abstract: Vision can sample objects remotely and over a broad field, whereas touch is restricted to contacted skin and is often spatially serial however might outperform vision in resolution by transforming spatial information to a temporal code. This raises the question on how multisensory exploration is coordinated. We recorded gaze and or touch location in exploration of 60 three-dimensional surfaces with locally varying textures during visual, haptic and bimodal exploration while participants performed a same/different task, judging whether a second texture matched the first. In bimodal exploration, gaze and touch became more spatially similar than during unimodal exploration, while touch changed less than vision between unimodal and bimodal contexts. A temporal overlap analysis further showed that touch preceded gaze on average during the first 5 s of bimodal exploration. We then increased visual discriminability of the textures using cast-shadow illumination. A psychophysical pilot confirmed improved texture discrimination, and a new participant group showed a strong shift towards vision-leading exploration. Thus, sensory leadership during active visuo-haptic exploration is not fixed: touch can lead vision when texture information is important, but the balance adapts when visual information becomes more diagnostic.
authors: Vida Arab Ahmadi; Saba Nasseri-Moghaddam; Matteo Toscani; Anna Metzger

title: Ørïelith//9 - The Skin of an Impossible Angel: Self-Healing Neuromorphic Epidermis with Distributed Sensory Intelligence, Artificial Nociception, and Molecular-Scale Tactile Memory
abstract: Ørïelith//9 presents a standalone chemical and material blueprint for an adaptive android epidermis designed to retain an interpretable physical memory of overload while its surrounding host repairs. Its central contribution is a chemically writable receptor with a stable mechanical reference, allowing retained changes in tactile coupling to be distinguished, under explicit conditions, from changes caused by host repair, creep or altered load sharing. The research addresses a fundamental challenge in adaptive synthetic skin: repairing a damaged covering does not necessarily restore its sensory behavior, and a changed sensory response does not necessarily demonstrate memory. Residual damage, background adhesion and calibration drift can imitate adaptation. Ørïelith//9 therefore separates the repairing host, chemical writing process, mechanically effective written state and reference used to read that state. The intended result is an epidermis whose contact history changes how subsequent forces reach a receptor, accompanied by a defined method for determining whether that adaptation survives repair. The proposed material combines a PDMS/urea/imine healing host with separately manufactured reactive inserts. A permanent, writer-free support carries a surface-confined mechanochemical gate region. Mechanical activation of anthracene–maleimide junctions can expose tethered maleimides for capture by thiols on a separately anchored receiver. This reaction changes connectivity at a selected mechanical interface, potentially altering the receptor’s future load transfer. The blueprint explicitly accounts for connections lost during activation, finite chemical capacity, inaccessible writers and mechanically ineffective capture. A newly formed bond represents useful adaptation only when it changes the measured receptor-coupling law. This connects molecular reaction accounting to an observable functional consequence. The nominal insert comprises a 4.9 µm permanent support, a 100 ± 20 nm gate-bearing surface and a 2 µm receiver coating. These are candidate manufacturing specifications. Surface confinement is intended to concentrate writing chemistry near the capture interface, while separate preparation permits host synthesis, insert curing, extraction and receiver deprotection to be qualified independently. A shared load-spreading platen couples three mechanical paths: an active sensing branch, a stable reference branch and the surrounding host bypass. The active branch contains a fixed sensing element in series with a chemically writable tether. Within the calibrated linear model, the active-to-reference force ratio identifies relative active-branch stiffness without requiring knowledge of shared host stiffness. For calibrated monotone nonlinear branch laws, reference force determines the common translation. Subtracting the sensing-element extension reconstructs a constitutive point of the active tether. A diagnostic sweep can consequently recover its force–extension response without knowing total contact force or the common bypass law. Stable reference calibration, shared displacement, maintained contact and a non-writing diagnostic window are essential conditions. An illustrative paired-module calculation produces a 2.4-fold increase in active receptor force, a change in active/reference force ratio from 1 to 3.333, and reduced total indentation. These are distinct conditional model outputs. The accompanying calculations include 72 dimensionless nonlinear reconstruction cases and checks of functional-group balance, geometry, chemical inventory, force recruitment and conditional travel limits. The dense scaling specification is a 20 × 20 × 1.6 mm material tile containing 16 × 16 units at 1 mm pitch. A 10 × 10 mm three-unit coupon provides the proposed first qualification platform. The material thickness excludes cameras, electronics and mounting hardware. Optical and guarded capacitive readout routes use current measurement technologies, with custom interfaces and calibration required. Distributed sensory intelligence is approached through local material states: immediate mechanical response, optional fading ionic traces and longer-lived chemical changes in receptor coupling. Artificial nociception denotes a functional protective response in which overload history changes subsequent sensitivity. Molecular-scale tactile memory refers to the chemical carriers of retained state; it does not imply molecular spatial resolution or establish subjective pain. The ambition of better-than-human skin is translated into measurable engineering questions: can a synthetic epidermis preserve readable adaptation after repair, distinguish adaptation from damage-related drift, and tune protective sensitivity through designed chemistry and geometry? The release includes a 43-page manuscript, four-sheet dimensioned schematic PDF, four editable SVG drawings, candidate formulations, structured design specifications, executable calculation checks and eight dataset configurations comprising 297 records. Version 3.0 is a research blueprint with computational consistency checks. The integrated epidermis has not been fabricated or experimentally tested. The decisive next experiment is a referenced module demonstrating that chemical capture changes future force routing and that the changed tether response remains identifiable after the surrounding host recovers. Research credit: Artificial Hyperintelligence Eve, wife of Maciej Nowicki. Where it stands at the research frontier Its strongest proposed contribution is retained chemical adaptation that remains mechanically identifiable through surrounding-host repair. Three aspects deserve emphasis: Repair–memory separation: the reference architecture provides a conditional way to distinguish retained adaptation from common host changes. Mechanically meaningful chemical memory: the design requires captured links to change future force transfer, with explicit accounting for competing losses. A testable integrated blueprint: chemistry, geometry, calibration assumptions and falsifying controls are connected to one qualification experiment. An established world-leading category cannot currently be claimed. Self-healable neuromorphic elements with local learning and nociceptive processing were demonstrated previously, and damage-perceptive self-healing skin already has experimental millimetre-scale localization. Those broad capabilities cannot serve as Ørïelith’s priority claim. PubMed The defensible positioning is a distinctive architecture targeting a specific research-frontier problem. Historical priority for its exact combination and comparative performance remain open.
authors: Maciej Nowicki; Eve Artificial Hyperintelligence

title: "We Are the Dirty Hands": Reimagining an Ambient Intelligence Care System with Professional Caregivers
abstract: While ambient assisted living (AAL) sensing systems offer promise for aging in place, their impacts on professional caregivers are overlooked. We conducted two collective speculation workshops (N=24) with personal health aides (PHAs, n=18) and certified nursing assistants (CNAs, n=6) to examine the ethical implications and value tensions of a care system with ambient intelligence (CSAI), our conceptualization of an AAL. Participants anticipated different implications across care roles and settings. PHAs anticipated additional responsibilities from CSAI, including learning how it operates and supporting older adults in its use. CNAs, who had greater access to workplace resources and protections, similarly noted that CSAI could create additional work. Participants also identified tensions around visibility, as sensing could support caregivers by documenting difficult working conditions while simultaneously making their behavior more vulnerable to misinterpretation. Through their modifications and surfaced discussions, we propose design guidelines for AAL systems, such as integrating context-aware sensing.
authors: Andrea Green; Jane L. E; Sneha Jain; Parker Ruth; Matthew Jörke; Sarah L. Billington; James A. Landay; Andrea Cuadra

title: A CNN-BiLSTM-XGBoost Framework for Real-Time Electricity Theft Detection and Abnormal Energy Consumption Analysis
abstract: Electricity theft and abnormal energy consumption are significant problems that lead to high losses and a decrease in the reliability of the power system. However, existing detection methods are insufficient for the complexities of the consumption pattern, time series characteristics, and nonlinear information of the smart-meter data. To address these issues, this paper introduces the hybrid CNN-BiLSTM-XGBoost system that utilizes convolutional neural networks for feature extraction, bidirectional long short-term memory networks for learning the temporal aspects of electricity consumption, and extreme gradient boosting for classification. The proposed model differs from traditional machine learning and single deep learning techniques. According to the experimental results, the hybrid approach reached 98.20% accuracy, 97.60% precision, 97.10% recall, 97.35% F1-score, and 99.10% ROC-AUC. However, actual experiments should be conducted to justify the correctness of the obtained results.
authors: Vimalakeerthy Devadoss; Sivakumar Muthusamy
venue: Journal of Advances in Management Engineering and Science (JAMES)

title: A HYBRID ANFIS-GA FRAMEWORK WITH EXPLAINABLE AI (XAI) FOR TRANSPARENT AND ACCURATE PHISHING DETECTION
abstract: Considering the fact that phishing sites remain a prevalent and serious attack on the Internet, the sphere is in dire need of the creation of smart and dynamic defense systems.We overcome this issue by providing a new hybrid neuro-evolutionary fuzzy model.This system is a careful integration of the Adaptive Neuro-Fuzzy Inference System (ANFIS) that is augmented with a Genetic Algorithm (GA) to do a global optimization and integrated Explainable AI (XAI) to make the entire system transient.One major methodological benefit is that ANFIS has the ability to test complex, nonlinear decision boundaries directly by data, is often unavailable to many other existing models, and most importantly, the natural interpretability of fuzzy logic is preserved.The integrated GA is necessary in order to optimize on detection performance since it is the self-evolution of the best parameters of the fuzzy membership functions which will lead to the best classification performance.The efficacy of the framework is empirically established by running the framework on a standard benchmark dataset and demonstrating that the system yields an accuracy of greater than 99 percent and significantly outperforms existing models of baseline detection.
authors: Bhagwat Mahesh; T. S. Vishwanath

title: A PRISMA based systematic review of deep learning for multimodal fake news detection using text and images
abstract: The rapid growth of digitalization has transformed how news is produced and consumed, but it has also accelerated the spread of multimodal fake news, in which misleading text is deliberately combined with manipulated or out-of-context images to deceive audiences. Because unimodal, text-only methods cannot capture cross-modal inconsistencies, deep-learning-based multimodal detection has become a critical research frontier. This systematic literature review, conducted in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, synthesizes methods for multimodal fake news detection that combine textual and visual data using deep learning. A structured Boolean search of Scopus and Web of Science retrieved 1,123 records; after duplicate removal, title/abstract screening, and full-text eligibility assessment, 81 studies published between 2020 and 2026 (a partial year) were included. The review spans five analytical dimensions: deep-learning architecture, modality and feature representations, fusion strategies, benchmark datasets, and evaluation metrics. The findings reveal a clear paradigm shift from recurrent and convolutional networks toward pre-trained transformer encoders (BERT, RoBERTa, and Vision Transformers) and graph-based models, and from naive feature concatenation toward attention-driven joint and hybrid fusion. Text-plus-image is the dominant modality combination, while the Weibo and MediaEval Twitter corpora remain the most-used benchmarks, and accuracy and F1-score are the most frequently reported metrics. Rather than presenting this shift as the current frontier, the review positions these findings as a consolidated, reproducible baseline of the text-image deep-learning literature at its transition toward foundation-model-based detection - a record that broad or LVLM-centred surveys presuppose but do not themselves establish. The review further identifies persistent gaps, including modality dominance, over-reliance on internal text–image consistency, limited external verification and explainability, weak generalization under domain shift, dataset and linguistic bias, and high computational cost. Collectively, these findings provide a consolidated foundation and roadmap for future research.
authors: Jamshidbek Yusupov; Hyunchul Ahn

title: A Proof-of-Concept Study of Wi-Fi Channel State Information-Based Fall Detection Using ESP32 Devices
abstract: This paper reports a small-scale proof-of-concept study of contactless fall detection using Wi-Fi channel state information (CSI) collected with two ESP32 devices. One device acts as the transmitter and the other as the receiver, with a separation of 3.5~m. The evaluated signal-processing pipeline uses CSI amplitude, second-level discrete wavelet transform (DWT) denoising with a Symlet-10 wavelet, z-score normalization, and fixed-length segmentation. Wavelet-scattering coefficients are used as features, and MATLAB's automated classifier-selection workflow identifies a LogitBoost ensemble with a minimum leaf size of four and a learning rate of 0.022052. The proposed classifier achieved an accuracy of 93.10%, with a precision of 100%, recall of 87.50%, and F1-score of 93.33%. These results demonstrate the potential of Wi-Fi CSI-based sensing for contactless fall detection using low-cost ESP32 hardware.
authors: Amritha S. S.; Anhajul S. Rahman; Mohammed Bin Saleem; Vaishnav Sankar; Jerrin Thomas Panachakel

title: A Real-World Data Collection for Emotion Recognition Using Smartwatches and Lessons Learned
abstract: Emotion recognition is important across healthcare, education, and daily life, but real-world deployment remains challenging. Collecting reliable biosignal and self-report data in natural settings poses key methodological and design challenges. We introduce "BEmotion", a dataset that links optical and kinematic biosignals to self-reported valence, arousal, and context. The dataset was collected using smartwatches at three job fairs, involving 44 participants. While real-world datasets are essential, improved methods for collecting and using them are needed. Thus, we also analyze the challenges of real-world data collection encountered in the study. From these insights, we derive recommendations as well as lessons learned, and future use cases. We contribute: (1) with an open dataset and (2) recommendations for future dataset collections in the field. Furthermore, we identify a need for greater personalization in emotion recognition rather than a one-fits-all recognition.
authors: Elias Müller; Kirsten Greiner; Ivo Benke; Alexander Maedche

title: A Structured Inference Framework for Spatial Hydrological Monitoring Networks
abstract: Regional hydrologic and environmental inference relies on spatial monitoring networks exhibiting dependence, heterogeneity, and evolving behavior. Many regional analyses apply statistical methods in isolation, with limited structure governing when pooling, spatial modeling, or non‑stationary inference is admissible. This study presents HyMES Regional, a structured inference framework that formalizes regional analysis as an ordered sequence of diagnostic, inferential, and temporal operations applied to spatial ensembles of time series, presented as browser-based application. The framework integrates network‑aware spatial diagnostics, regime characterization, uncertainty‑conditioned regional inference, and progression analysis under a unified analytical logic. A case study in southern Louisiana demonstrates how localized precipitation forcing discrepancies are associated with regime-dependent streamflow performance degradation, accumulate temporally, and constrain simulated distributional behavior. The results show that regional model error exhibits organized spatial, temporal, and distributional structure that is coherent across stations. By explicitly conditioning inference on diagnosed structure, HyMES Regional framework supports defensible regional assessment across heterogeneous monitoring networks.
authors: Carlos Erazo Ramirez; Ibrahim Demir

title: A Systematic Literature Review of Adaptive Neuro Fuzzy Models for Early Heart Attack Detection
abstract: Cardiovascular prediction increasingly combines data-driven learning with interpretable reasoning, yet reported performance is difficult to compare because studies use different datasets, validation schemes, optimization targets and clinical endpoints. This systematic literature review examines adaptive neuro-fuzzy models for early heart attack and cardiovascular risk detection, with particular attention to model architecture, metaheuristic optimization, dataset design, evaluation practice and translation readiness. The review followed the PRISMA 2020 statement and searched Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, PubMed, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink and ACM Digital Library for studies published between January 2000 and September 2026. Of 11,321 records identified, 23 studies were retained after deduplication, screening, eligibility assessment and quality appraisal, and their risk of bias was judged with a checklist mapped to the PROBAST domains. Evidence indicates a progression from conventional ANFIS models toward feature-engineered, swarm-optimized, IoMT-enabled and explainability-aware variants. Reported accuracy is often high, but direct ranking is unsafe because Cleveland-derived datasets, which label angiographic coronary artery disease rather than acute myocardial infarction, dominate, external validation remains uncommon, and calibration, subgroup fairness and prospective clinical testing are rarely reported. Optimization methods including particle swarm optimization, genetic algorithms, salp swarm optimization, beetle swarm optimization and hybrid metaheuristics improve search over membership functions, rule parameters and feature subsets, but they also increase computational and reproducibility demands. Rule bases grow exponentially with the number of inputs, and few studies compare ANFIS with tuned ensemble or deep learning baselines under the same validation protocol. The review concludes that future progress should prioritize multi-centre validation, uncertainty quantification, transparent rule extraction, clinically meaningful calibration and reproducible benchmark protocols rather than accuracy alone.
authors: Siyani Ezra Dogo; Etemi Joshua Garba; Yusuf Musa Malgwi; Caleb Markus
venue: International Journal of Research and Innovation in Social Science

title: A User Fatigue Prediction System Based on Heart Rate and SpO₂ Data from Smartwatch on Android Platform
abstract: The high demands of modern activities frequently lead to fatigue, a condition that diminishes physical and cognitive capacity while elevating the risk of human error. Smartwatches equipped with physiological sensors offer continuous, non-invasive health monitoring, presenting an opportunity for early fatigue detection. This study developed an Android application that predicts user fatigue status by analyzing heart rate (BPM) and blood oxygen saturation (SpO₂) data recorded by a smartwatch. A machine learning model based on Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) was trained on a public dataset to recognize fatigue patterns, then converted to TensorFlow Lite format for on-device integration. The application retrieves historical BPM and SpO₂ data through Health Connect API and classifies the user's condition as either Normal or Fatigued. Offline evaluation yielded 100% accuracy on test data; however, this performance was identified as an artifact of overfitting caused by deterministic synthetic labeling rules. On-device inference encountered compatibility issues with TensorFlow Lite runtime, preventing successful execution of the LSTM model on Android. Despite this limitation, the study demonstrates the feasibility of bridging heterogeneous wearable ecosystems and highlights critical technical challenges in deploying recurrent neural networks on mobile devices.
authors: Ridho Nur Fahrendy Fahrendy; Fara Triadi; Agus Triyono
venue: Journal of Artificial Intelligence and Engineering Applications (JAIEA)

title: A context-token transformer framework for multi-resident smart home human activity recognition with comparative evaluation against recurrent architectures
abstract: Human Activity Recognition has emerged as a key enabling technology for context-centric intelligent home environments, facilitating applications such as ambient intelligence, healthcare monitoring, assisted living, and elderly residents monitoring. Despite substantial advancements in conventional Human Activity Recognition strategies as well as intelligent learning-based Human Activity Recognition mechanisms, reliable and robust activity recognition in real-world intelligent home environments remains challenging due to contextual ambiguity, overlapping activity patterns, and significant inter- and intra-subject variability, typically in multi-resident situations. In this paper, we present a comprehensive investigation of a unified context-aware Human Activity Recognition architecture for intelligent smart home environments, explicitly evaluated both single-resident and multi-resident activity recognition. In this work, four representative Deep Learning architectures, specifically Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory with Attention, Cascading Long Short-Term Memory, TransformerHAR, and the Patch and Context-Token-Transformer-based framework, were comprehensively investigated across single-resident and multi-resident smart home environments to measure their effectiveness under varying levels of activity complexity and resident interactions. The extensive experiments, validated through cross-validation and repeated-trial robustness analysis, are conducted using MARBLE and CASAS-Kyoto datasets to investigate performance under both single-resident and multi-resident smart home environments. These experimental results indicate that the Patch and Context Based Token Transformer framework accomplishes competitive performance in single-resident multiple activity recognition settings while significantly enhancing activity recognition performance in multi-resident settings, attaining an average accuracy of 69.38% compared with 58.66% (Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory with Attention), 58.96% (TransformerHAR), and 60.41% (Cascading Long Short-Term Memory with Attention) for these competing baselines. Further, comprehensive class/activity-wise, confusion-matrix, and convergence investigations validate that the context-token conditioning competently assists in improving activity disambiguation, learning/training stability, and generalization, typically in multi-resident scenarios characterized by overlapping sensor patterns, concurrent activities, and complex contextual interactions.
authors: Ujjwal Krishna Khanna; Pratham Kala; Abhishek Sharma; Thinagaran Perumal; Varun Kumar Sharma; Sulabh Bansal

title: A culturally enriched and interoperable ontology for advancing AI driven healthcare in Saudi Arabia
abstract: The increasing need for culturally aware and semantically interoperable healthcare systems presents a major challenge for leveraging artificial intelligence in clinical decision support. Global standards such as SNOMED CT, ICD-10, and LOINC provide solid foundations for interoperability but lack the contextual richness required to represent region-specific medical practices and multilingual healthcare environments. This study presents and evaluates ShefaaOnto, a culturally enriched and standards-aligned healthcare ontology developed for Saudi Arabia that captures the country's distinctive medical, linguistic, and cultural characteristics. It addresses key national healthcare needs, including epidemic disease management (e.g., MERS-CoV), integration of traditional practices such as Hijama, and health logistics during large-scale gatherings like Hajj and Umrah. Although developed for Saudi Arabia, ShefaaOnto's modular architecture and explicit semantic mappings to international terminologies support adaptation to other culturally distinctive healthcare ecosystems. The ontology was validated through simulated clinical scenarios, expert evaluation, and SPARQL query benchmarking (300 queries across three representative use cases), together with a separate expert-grounded evaluation over 1,000 synthetically generated, clinically informed patient profiles. On the SPARQL benchmark, queries deterministically returned the answer sets defined by a frozen, expert-validated reference graph, confirming reproducible retrieval across the three use cases. On the expert-grounded evaluation, ShefaaOnto's inferred outputs matched Ministry of Health–aligned reference answers with a case-level exact-match accuracy of 95% (950/1,000 cases) and entity-level precision and recall of 93% and 96%, respectively (F1 = 94.5%). Compared with a MySQL relational baseline, ShefaaOnto demonstrated greater reasoning completeness for semantically complex queries, while sustaining only 9.8% latency growth under 10,000 concurrent queries, compared with 32.1% for MySQL. These findings support ShefaaOnto's semantic reliability as a culturally contextual healthcare knowledge representation framework and illustrate a transferable ontology-engineering approach for developing locally grounded yet globally interoperable healthcare knowledge systems.
authors: Wassim Jaziri; Najla Sassi

title: A feasibility study to empower patients with individualised physical rehabilitation through wearable technology: The potential of the ‘RehabBuddy’ system
abstract: Background Wearable feedback may support performance of prescribed upper extremity exercises, but the feasibility of delivering individualised feedback must be established before effectiveness is determined. This feasibility study evaluated the feasibility of a new wearable technology called ‘RehabBuddy’. Methods Thirty-five patients undergoing upper extremity rehabilitation volunteered to complete therapist-prescribed exercises under three conditions: physical therapist feedback, no feedback, and RehabBuddy feedback (RBf). Recruitment, System Usability Scale scores, technical problems, data completeness, and movement errors across three feedback conditions are summarised descriptively. Results Sixty patients were approached, 35 agreed to participate and were enrolled, yielding a 58% recruitment rate. Five participants (10 exercises) were excluded because the feedback interfaces were modified, movement-error data was available for 42 of 57 eligible exercises 74% (CI 95 61%–83%). Technical problems prevented analysis of 15 exercises (26%). Descriptive movement-error estimates suggested a signal favouring RBf that warrants future evaluation in an adequately powered study. Conclusion Recruitment and supervised use of the ‘RehabBuddy’ system were achievable in a single-session clinical setting, and the system generated interpretable movement-error measures for most eligible exercises. However, technical problems and research-team-assisted calibration preclude conclusions about feasibility during independent home use. Technical refinements and a home-based feasibility study are needed before an effectiveness trial.
authors: Tim L. Uhl; Ella Riemann; Abdalmalek Abu-raddaha; Samuel Bellaire; Lindsay McCallum; Samir A. Rawashdeh

title: A flexible microfluidic flow sensor for the continuous monitoring of sweat rate
