title: A four-domain framework for AI-enabled mobile health: from sensing to equitable governance
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is widely expected to strengthen mobile health (mHealth) responses to the dual burden of non-communicable and infectious disease, yet translation into demonstrable population health benefit remains limited. This narrative review conceptualizes AI-mHealth as the mobile and wearable layer of an Internet of Things (IoT)-enabled connected health ecosystem. Because the literature has largely examined sensing, modeling, and implementation as discrete problems, the dependencies that govern system-level utility remain poorly characterized. We therefore appraise the evidence across four linked domains: Sensing, Inference, Intervention, and Governance. We searched PubMed/MEDLINE and the Web of Science Core Collection from October 2015 to September 2026. Sensing performance depended on device and measurement context. Wrist-worn photoplethysmography showed no consistent skin-tone-related error at rest, whereas error in darker skin tones exceeded that in lighter skin tones more than fourfold at higher exercise intensities. Inference models improved risk stratification but lacked the interpretability required to support clinical accountability, and model compression for on-device deployment degraded subgroup performance unevenly. Just-in-time adaptive interventions improved proximal response, although effect durability varied across microrandomized trials, and remote heart failure management has not yet demonstrated a consistent effect on readmission. Algorithmic bias, the digital divide, deficiencies in data stewardship and cybersecurity, limited human oversight, and regulatory latency form a mutually reinforcing system of risk across the AI-mHealth lifecycle. Our principal finding is an asymmetry: upstream limitations propagate downstream automatically, whereas their correction requires deliberate institutional design. We propose an operational roadmap of four implementation phases, from technical readiness to accountability at scale. Each phase is mapped to the framework domains it engages and to the specific Sustainable Development Goal 3 targets it serves, spanning communicable disease screening, chronic disease management, workforce capacity, and universal coverage. Aggregate accuracy concealed reliability loss in the subgroups most in need of intervention, and the roadmap therefore makes subgroup-level equity auditing a condition of deployment.
authors: Chen Zhang; Wenhui Jiang; Qiming Zhao; Minglian Ouyang; Nan Wu; You Guo

title: A framework for talk-to-me detection and human action recognition on smart eyewear
abstract: Understanding who is talking to me and what actions are being performed represents an important aspect of human perception on embedded edge devices, such as smart eyewear and mobile robots. While Talk-To-Me (TTM) detection and skeleton-based Human Action Recognition (HAR) have typically been studied as separate tasks, in real-world scenarios, these tasks contribute complementary information toward understanding what is happening around the user. The outputs of these tasks are complementary: TTM indicates whether an interaction is directed toward the user, while HAR describes the ongoing physical actions of surrounding people. Exploiting them jointly is therefore beneficial for robust real-world interaction understanding. However, most existing TTM and HAR models are computationally demanding and poorly suited for deployment on resource-constrained edge devices. We propose the ExoAction, an edge-AI-compatible framework that jointly addresses TTM detection and HAR. For TTM detection, we develop EAIC-TTM, a lightweight RGB-only model specifically designed for edge-AI hardware. Despite using only visual input, EAIC-TTM achieves mAP comparable to the RGB+Audio Ego4D baseline while improving overall accuracy and requiring only RGB input, demonstrating an efficient solution for edge deployment. For HAR, we build upon HT-ConvNet, a compact convolutional model originally designed for efficient skeleton-sequence human action analysis. We enhance it with a new online recognition pipeline that processes incoming skeleton frames without needing the full action sequence. Our approach is evaluated on the POLIMI-ITW-S and NTU benchmarks. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that our framework achieves competitive accuracy while maintaining high computational efficiency. Furthermore, deployment on a smart eyewear prototype equipped with an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano validated the framework’s real-world feasibility, achieving promising performance for pose estimation and HAR, and demonstrating strong potential for fully on-device egocentric perception in edge-AI applications.
authors: Hao Quan; Greta Corti; Sara Pidò; Pietro Bartoli; Chiara Plizzari; Andrea Giudici; Francesca Palermo; Matteo Matteucci; Simone Mentasti

title: A graphical interface for consolidating data from multiple wearable devices: concordance and the effect of sensor positioning relative to the smartwatch
abstract: Currently, smartwatches are widely used to record heart rate (HR) and heart rate variability (HRV), but two obstacles limit their use: closed ecosystems and signal degradation during daily activities. Consolidating data from multiple devices requires asynchronous export, making beat-for-beat comparison impractical. To solve this, we developed a centralized graphical interface that ingests, chronologically orders, and displays raw streams from three Samsung Galaxy Watch 4s simultaneously, recording independent columns with timestamps, signaling anomalies in real time, and exporting a consolidated table. The platform demonstrated high stability (50 Hz sampling, 19.1 ± 18.5 ms latency, 99.8% integrity, zero connection loss, and 1.2% false alarms). We used the system to examine the consistency of heart rate intervals in volunteers instrumented at the right wrist (S1), left wrist (S2), and left ankle (S3) during 19-minute sessions (treadmill walking at 1.5 km/h with supine or seated resting postures). Wrist data showed a normal distribution, while ankle data deviated (Shapiro-Wilk, p = 0.028), justifying the use of the Friedman test. Monitoring identified distinct sources of artifacts, such as attenuation at the ankle and flow occlusion at the left wrist by a sphygmomanometer. RR intervals were processed in Python (PyBios) to obtain the RMSSD. The main contribution is not a smoothing method, but an acquisition layer that makes multi-site wearable data recording auditable at the time of capture, converting fragmented exports into a single synchronized and traceable record.
authors: Alexandre Messias da Silva; Daniel Gustavo Goroso

title: A high-precision measurement method for ruby balls based on multi-scale adaptive edge detection
abstract: A high-precision, non-contact measurement method for ruby balls is proposed by integrating annular dark-field imaging with multi-scale adaptive edge detection. Multi-scale gradient-response fusion and entropy-guided local thresholding are used to improve outer-contour extraction under non-uniform contrast and noise. Cubic-spline interpolation provides sub-pixel edge localization, while RANSAC screening and geometric-distance circle fitting reduce the influence of outliers. For a 5 mm ruby-ball sample, the method achieved a mean absolute error of 1.6 μm and a standard deviation of 0.7 μm. At an SNR of 20 dB, the measurement error remained at 2.4 μm, compared with 6.5 μm for the Hessian-matrix method and 11.8 μm for the conventional pixel-level regionprops method. Experiments on ruby, ceramic, and cemented-carbide balls with diameters of 3–12 mm further demonstrated stable performance across different materials, sizes, and imaging conditions. The proposed framework therefore provides a robust approach for the non-contact dimensional inspection of precision spherical components.
authors: Wen Sun

title: A multi-objective quantum rotation-based algorithm enhanced for overlapping communities detection in social networks
abstract: One of the critical operations in the analysis of social networks is community detection. Society is also a set of coherent vertices, where the internal communication of the society is more than the communication outside the society and in many real-world networks, communities can overlap. This paper employs an overlapping community detection using a multi-objective optimization approach based on learning automata that have been used to hybridize and avoid computational load intelligently. Artificial Gorilla Troops Optimizer (GTO), Fruit Fly Optimization (FFO) algorithms, and Quantum Rotary Gate (QRG) are used for this purpose and then integrated with the Pareto dominance technique. Also, fuzzy clustering and initialization strategies have been used for overlapping community detection. The tests conducted in this paper are based on 16 real-world data sets and synthetic data sets. The proposed model's findings were compared to existing optimization techniques, demonstrating that it outperforms the examined approaches.
authors: Ahmad Heydariyan; Farhad Soleimanian Gharehchopogh; Mohammad Reza Ebrahimi Dishabi

title: A review of machine learning and the internet of things for remote patient monitoring covering advances challenges and opportunities
abstract: As Machine Learning (ML) and the Internet of Things (IoT) have matured, their convergence has placed Remote Patient Monitoring (RPM) at the centre of personalized, cost-effective care. The present work reviews progress in ML and IoT based RPM, covering how ML is applied within RPM, the principal ML models employed, the IoT infrastructures that underpin it, the use of RPM across different patient populations, the challenges that arise, and the directions the field may take. After a PRISMA-guided screening of work indexed in Springer, IEEE, MDPI, ACM, and Elsevier, 101 peer-reviewed studies published from 2020 onward were retained for a qualitative (narrative) synthesis structured around five research questions. The review is narrative in form yet is carried out under a structured and transparent protocol. Within the studies examined, RPM was reported to enable real-time monitoring, cut the number of in-person hospital visits, and reduce the cost of patient-centred care, while IoT- and ML-based designs that built in privacy-preserving techniques strengthened data security; across these studies, deep learning and hybrid ML models often reported higher predictive accuracy than conventional approaches, though typically on particular datasets and at greater computational cost. Across the ten systems compared here, the eight that reported a single determinate figure gave accuracies with a median of 94.5% (range 92% to 98%) and latencies with a median of 265 ms (range 120 ms to 350 ms), and not one of them was evaluated at a site other than the one where it was developed, so these numbers describe individual study conditions rather than performance at population level. Among the obstacles that surface repeatedly are patient adherence, interoperability, scalability, and the protection of data. On balance, the body of evidence gathered here suggests that RPM built on ML and IoT can make monitoring safer, more flexible, and more anticipatory; reaching that level across whole populations, however, will call for sturdier systems, broader patient participation, and thorough clinical validation.
authors: Sumitra Singar; Raghuveer Singh Dhaka; Manmohan Sharma

title: A review of older adults’ acceptance of health monitoring tools: application status, theoretical acceptance models, and user-related and context-level influencing factors
abstract: Health monitoring tools enable real-time, accurate monitoring of physiological data in older adults, offering timely alerts and feedback that facilitate early detection of health problems and prompt intervention. However, adoption and use of these tools among older adults remains limited, significantly constraining their practical effectiveness. This narrative review examines the factors influencing older adults' acceptance of health monitoring tools by synthesizing 49 studies, comprising 40 studies classified as core evidence and 9 as supplementary contextual evidence. Relevant literature was identified through a snowballing approach, beginning with key articles and tracing their reference lists and citing articles. Findings were synthesized through a thematic approach. Among the theoretical models identified in this review, the Technology Acceptance Model and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology are the most frequently applied, whereas the Senior Technology Acceptance Model, despite its specific relevance, has not been applied to health monitoring tool acceptance in any study included in this review. Key influencing factors can be grouped into two categories: user-related factors, such as demographic, health-related, and psychological characteristics; and tool- and context-level factors, such as privacy and security of monitoring data, interaction experience and ease of use, device appearance and invasiveness, and economic costs associated with pricing and technology access. Enhancing acceptance may require a comprehensive approach encompassing targeted health education and digital skills training, optimized user interfaces and privacy safeguards, multi-tiered financial subsidies, and the development of innovative theoretical models tailored to the older adult population.
authors: Qi Zhang; Zhang Yongqin

title: A scoping review of the application of intelligent technology in medication adherence among older adults with chronic diseases.
abstract: BACKGROUND: The accelerating pace of population aging has led to the increasing prevalence of multimorbidity among older adults. Poor medication adherence has become a key risk factor for adverse health outcomes. While the development of smart technologies offers new pathways for optimizing medication management, their application effectiveness and dissemination models require systematic review. This scoping review aims to systematically analyze the application forms, empirical effectiveness, and implementation challenges of smart technologies in improving medication adherence among older adults with chronic diseases, providing evidence for developing localized, age-friendly smart medication management strategies. METHODS: Following the Joanna Briggs Institute scoping review framework and guided by the PRISMA-ScR guidelines, we systematically searched 6 major databases (China National Knowledge Infrastructure, Wanfang, SinoMed, PubMed, Web of Science, and Embase) for literature published between January 1, 2014, and December 31, 2024. Using the Population, Concept, and Context framework, we defined our scope as follows: Population: Adults aged 60 years or older with chronic diseases; Concept: smart technology interventions targeting medication adherence; and Context: community-dwelling settings. Only original empirical studies were included. The literature screening and data extraction processes were conducted independently by 2 researchers. Consistent with standard scoping review methodology, a formal risk-of-bias assessment was not performed. RESULTS: Eight studies were included, comprising 4 quasi-experimental studies, 1 randomized controlled trial, 1 prospective observational study, 1 cross-sectional study, and one usability-testing study. Smart technology applications primarily consisted of smartphone apps, smart pillboxes, and remote platforms, forming a "reminder-monitoring-feedback" system. Results indicated that the included studies generally reported improvements in medication adherence and clinical indicators. Key challenges included urban-rural digital literacy gaps and low long-term retention. CONCLUSION: Smart technologies demonstrate preliminary benefits and show promise for enhancing medication adherence in this population. While these early signals are encouraging, limitations such as short intervention durations and small samples necessitate cautious interpretation. Practical implementation should prioritize age-friendly design and family-community collaborative models to advance "digital healthy aging."
authors: Sisi Cai; Jiekun Zhao; Xi Xu; Mengyi Li

title: A single-plane electrical impedance tomography framework for integrated liver and kidney assessment
abstract: Chronic liver and kidney diseases frequently coexist, but their assessment typically requires separate clinical workflows involving serum-based estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) testing and liver elastography-based controlled attenuation parameter (CAP). Electrical impedance tomography (EIT) has recently shown promise for providing portable, non-invasive proxies for both reference measurements. However, existing multi-organ EIT assessment still requires different acquisition protocols for each organ. To simplify this procedure, we assessed the feasibility of a single-plane EIT framework for reconstructing organ-specific images and estimating liver and kidney health from one abdominal belt placement. Across diverse abdominal belt locations, opposite-plane deviation was significantly greater for eGFR EIT estimates (2.92%; IQR, 0.46-12.53%) than for CAP EIT estimates (0.94%; IQR, 0.66-1.70%) (p < 0.01). For both organs, compared to images acquired at the conventional organ-specific planes, image correlation significantly decreased (both, p < 0.05) and normalized root mean squared error significantly increased (both, p < 0.05) at the furthest imaging plane, with these differences being numerically larger for the kidney. Together, these results supported the kidney plane as the preferred location for multi-organ assessment. Test-retest evaluation after belt removal and reapplication demonstrated that the correlation between two repeated CAP EIT estimates was just as strong at the kidney plane (R 2 = 0.98, p < 0.001) as it was at the conventional liver plane (R 2 = 0.97, p < 0.001). Finally, in an independent clinical cohort, kidney-plane CAP EIT estimates were significantly higher in participants with a high metabolic liver-risk profile (i.e. diabetes and high blood pressure) (p < 0.005). CAP EIT estimates also distinguished high and low metabolic risk groups with an AUC of 0.756. Together, these findings support the feasibility of a portable multi-organ EIT imaging framework capable of extracting complementary liver and kidney information from a single belt placement.
authors: Aywin Wu; Jen-Chien Lai; Mo Kwan Ho; Justin Q. J. Ge; Nan‐Jie Gong; Iris Yuwen Zhou; Monica Wong; Bradley Jay Edelman; Russell W. Chan

title: A systematic review of non-contact medical IoT systems for physiological biomarker monitoring
abstract: Introduction: Non-contact medical Internet of Things systems measure physiological biomarkers such as heart rate (HR), respiration rate (RR), temperature, oxygen saturation (SpO₂), and blood pressure (BP) without physical contact with the patient. These systems combine sensing modalities including cameras, radar, Wi-Fi, acoustic, and infrared sensors with signal processing and learning algorithms to deliver comfortable, non-invasive monitoring. Prior reviews have largely examined individual sensing modalities or signal processing techniques in isolation, leaving cross-modality system architecture and privacy-preserving design underexamined. Methods: We conducted a systematic review following PRISMA guidelines and analyzed 88 recent studies of non-contact monitoring systems. Studies were characterized by sensing modality, system architecture, target physiological parameter, validation setting, and reported performance. We additionally assessed each study for methodological quality and examined the extent to which privacy-preserving mechanisms were incorporated into system design. Results: Radar and vision-based systems dominate the corpus, together accounting for approximately three-quarters of included studies, while sound, Wi-Fi, embedded sensor, and mixed-modality designs remain at an earlier stage of validation. Research effort is heavily concentrated on two parameters: RR appears in 83% of studies and HR in 67%, while no other parameter exceeds 11%. BP, SpO₂, and temperature therefore remain largely unaddressed by contactless methods. Heterogeneous reporting metrics across studies prevent direct statistical comparison of performance between modalities. Discussion: The findings indicate that modality selection should be driven by deployment context rather than headline accuracy. Radar suits wards and intensive care units where patients are covered or moving, vision and sound suit structured clinical spaces with stable conditions, embedded sensor designs suit eldercare beds and chairs, and mixed radar and vision systems suit precision-critical settings such as neonatal and postoperative monitoring. Persistent challenges include signal reliability in uncontrolled environments, limited benchmarking due to the absence of standardized datasets, privacy and ethical concerns, and poor integration with existing healthcare infrastructure. Building on these insights, we propose a conceptual federated, edge-based learning framework, presented as a design proposal for future implementation rather than a validated system, and outline research directions to accelerate clinical translation.
authors: Bithi Banik; Saptanil Ghose; Ahnaf Hasnain Nahiun; Yuan Lin; Andrii Shalaginov; Debasish Ghose

title: A translational bioethical & implementation framework for the use of artificial intelligence in cardiovascular medicine
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) in cardiology is rapidly expanding, but enthusiasm for anticipated benefits should be balanced by a more critical inspection of ethical concerns. In this state-of-the-art review, we discuss the four pillars of bioethics and their overlap with AI regulatory requirements to identify the potential gain and challenges, for both cardiologists and cardiac patients alike, in integrating AI-based clinical tools within various aspects and settings of care. By investigating the current gaps in regulatory oversight and illustrating hypothetical case scenarios, we aim to locate points of weakness along the course of implementation, from algorithm design to tool misuse, which endanger autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, and justice if AI production proceeds without further attention into safeguard development. Finally, we propose governance principles and priorities for AI in cardiovascular medicine to highlight areas where a bioethical-regulatory framework needs to be adapted in order to ensure responsible use of AI in patient care.
authors: Camryn J. Kimura; Keshav R. Nayak; Sam Whitman McGrath; Leeda Rashid; Sanjeev P. Bhavnani

title: AI-Assisted Wearable Devices for Women's Safety with Real-Time Threat and Anomaly Identification
abstract: Recently, harassment, assault, stalking, and other forms of violence in both public and private settings have become a social and technological issue of great concern to women's safety.Traditional safety measures like location-tracking, panic buttons and emergency mobile applications are typically reactive and only respond to a threat after it has happened.The latest innovations in the field of wearable technology, artificial intelligence, machine learning, computer vision and sensor integration have presented new possibilities for the creation of proactive safety systems which can detect dangers before they become a dangerous situation.The current research suggests the idea of smart sunglasses that will be equipped with a wearable device to be used and operated by women for monitoring, detecting threats and identifying anomalies in real time.The system proposed for this work incorporates a number of sensing technologies such as GPS, GSM, physiological sensors, accelerometers, cameras, and environmental monitoring modules.The data collected is analysed with the help of deep learning and machine learning algorithms to detect suspicious and unusual activities, patterns of behaviour, environmental hazards, and emergencies.The wearable device uses the You Only Look Once version 8 (YOLOv8) object detection framework to detect potentially dangerous objects and people around the wearer in real time.At the same time, behavioural analysis models analyse the user's movement patterns, physiological responses and contextual environmental data to detect anomalies that could signal distress or danger.If a potential threat is identified the system automatically alerts and provides location data to pre-programmed emergency contacts and authorities.A series of simulated urban environments and controlled testing scenarios that incorporated multiple threat categories were employed to test a prototype evaluation.The results of the experiment showed that the object detection rate was 96.8%, anomaly detection rate was 94.2%, and the emergency response notification success rate was 98.5%.The findings suggest that AI-driven wearable devices have the potential to be a powerful tool for improving personal safety by enabling proactive monitoring and intelligent threat assessment.The study advances wearable safety technologies and provides the basis for future research on the intelligent protective systems for vulnerable people.
venue: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology

title: AI-Based Elderly Care and Fall Detection: A Review of Weara-ble Sensors, Machine Learning, IoT, and Edge AI Approaches
abstract: The growing number of older adults has increased the need for monitoring tools that can support safety and help caregivers respond quickly. Age-related changes in balance, strength, and movement may make falls more likely, while a person who lives alone may not be able to call for help immediately. This review looks at three studies that use different ways to identify falls. Care Fall analyses smartwatch accelerometer and gyroscope signals with threshold rules and machine-learning methods. A second system combines motion and basic health sensors with a microcontroller and GSM/Wi-Fi alerts. The third approach uses a camera, the YOLOv5s model, and an edge-computing device for visual detection. Together, the studies show that wearable sensors, embedded systems, and camera-based AI can all support fall monitoring, but they differ in cost, privacy, response time, and practical use. Common concerns include false alarms, changes in fall patterns, environmental limitations, battery life, and data protection. The review compares the systems and outlines areas that need further testing before these approaches can be relied on in everyday care.
authors: Sawant Pranjal Parshuram; Khatri A.A.; S. B. Bhosale; Banger A.P
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: AI-Based Shrimp Detection and Size Estimation Using Smartphone Sensors
abstract: Shrimp aquaculture is a major contributor to global seafood production, where accurate monitoring of shrimp size and weight is essential for feeding management, growth evaluation, and harvest planning. In modern farming conditions, shrimp size is commonly assessed through manual sampling, which requires physical handling of individual shrimps. This process is labor-intensive and time-consuming, and repeated handling may also induce stress that negatively affects shrimp growth and survival. This paper presents a smartphone-based system for whiteleg shrimp ( Litopenaeus vannamei ) detection, length estimation, and average weight prediction using computer vision methods. The proposed system employs a YOLOv8 object detection model to identify shrimps in images captured by standard smartphone cameras under actual aquaculture conditions. Shrimp length is estimated by converting pixel measurements obtained from detected bounding boxes into real-world dimensions through reference calibration using an object of a known size. Image-level features extracted from the detected shrimp regions are then used by a Support Vector Regression model to predict average shrimp weight. The detection model was trained using 6,350 images and tested using a separate set of 280 images. Length estimation was evaluated using 29 separate images, while weight prediction was evaluated using another 26 images. The detection model achieved a precision of 0.988, a recall of 0.927, an mAP@0.5 of 0.982, and an mAP@0.5:0.95 of 0.877. Length estimation achieved an MAE of 1.54 cm, an RMSE of 1.63 cm, and a MAPE of 14.6%. Average weight prediction achieved an MAE of 1.05 g, an RMSE of 1.78 g, and a MAPE of 7.5%. The results demonstrate the feasibility of combining shrimp detection, reference calibration, length estimation, and average weight prediction in one smartphone workflow under the tested outdoor farm conditions.
authors: Yuyu Chen; Eka Sari Oktarina; Valentinus Roby Hananto; Victor V. Kryssanov
venue: Atlantis Highlights in Computer Sciences/Atlantis highlights in computer sciences

title: AI-Based WiFi Imaging
abstract: This paper presents a literature-based study of AI-Based WiFi Imaging, a camera-free sensing approach that uses wireless signal measurements to reconstruct representations of indoor environments. It reviews 15 research studies involving Channel State Information (CSI), Received Signal Strength Indicator (RSSI), Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces (RIS), beamforming, low-rank optimization, deep learning, and generative AI. Special emphasis is placed on high-resolution WiFi imaging using RIS-assisted beamforming and super-resolution reconstruction. The paper examines system architectures, methodologies, algorithms, performance evaluation metrics, advantages, limitations, and future research opportunities. It highlights potential applications in smart environments, contactless sensing, and indoor monitoring. The study is based on previously published research and does not claim new experimental results.
authors: GNANA SESHA SAI TIRUPATI
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: AI-Driven Panic Detection system using efficient learning model
abstract: Wearable devices such as smartwatches are becoming useful tools for monitoring different aspects of human health. In this study, an AI-based approach is developed to identify panic events using physiological and activity-related data obtained from commercial smartwatches. The study uses six features: gender, age, weight, heart rate, step count, and physical activity type. A dataset of 16,200 observations collected from 27 participants was used, with separate training and testing sets already provided. Before training the models, duplicate records were removed, categorical data was converted into numerical form, and MinMax normalization was applied. Different machine learning algorithms, along with three deep learning models, were tested and compared using Accuracy, Precision , Recall, F1-score, ROC-AUC, Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC), and Cohen’s Kappa. The results revealed that machine learning models performed better than deep learning models for the selected features. K-Nearest Neighbours (KNN) achieved the best accuracy of 96.05%, while Random Forest and Decision 1 Tree also produced good results. This work shows that basic information available through smartwatches can be explored for panic event detection and may help in developing wearable-based systems for continuous mental health monitoring.
authors: Balaram Pal; Munshi Mostafijur Rahaman; Sakshi Verma; Soumyajit Paul

title: AI-Enabled Intelligent Traffic Control with Emergency Vehicle Detection: A Design-Stage Framework
abstract: Fixed-time traffic signals cannot respond to changing vehicle demand or to the urgent movement of emergency vehicles, and ambulances in particular can lose critical minutes at congested intersections. This paper proposes an AI-enabled Intelligent Traffic Control with Emergency Vehicle Detection framework that uses YOLOv8 to detect ambulances, fire trucks, and police vehicles from camera video, estimates lane-wise traffic demand, and requests priority for the emergency vehicle’s lane through a controlled signal transition. Detection results travel through an ESP32 communication unit to an STM32 controller that runs a finite-state signal machine. At the same time, a MERN-stack dashboard shows live counts, signal states, alerts, and detection history. We review an earlier IoT-based base paper and related studies, define the design problem, and describe the architecture, decision logic, message format, safety rules, and fallback behaviour. The work is at the design stage, so no measured results are claimed. Instead, we set out an evaluation plan covering detection quality, response latency, waiting time, communication reliability, and signal safety. The framework is a starting point for an LED-signal prototype, not for use on public roads
authors: Deepaly Thorat; Dipti Bhawar; Ragini Dighe; Anushka Kakade; Sudhanshu Badgujar
venue: International Journal for Research in Applied Science and Engineering Technology

title: AI-Powered Sound-Based Wildlife Monitoring System for Real-Time Detection and IoT Alerting
abstract: This paper presents an AI-powered wildlife monitoring system designed for early detection of wildlife activity using acoustic sensing, convolutional neural network (CNN)-based intelligence, GPS localization, and Internet of Things (IoT) communication. A high-sensitivity LM393-based sound sensor connected to a NodeMCU ESP8266 monitors ambient events and provides the trigger for intelligent analysis. The project architecture also documents a camera-to-PC CNN inference path, allowing visual verification and emergency assessment in addition to the sound-based detection concept. When a positive wildlife event is obtained, the system acquires geographic coordinates using a GPS module, displays status locally through a 16x2 LCD and I2C interface, transmits event information to an IoT platform such as Blynk or ThingSpeak, and sends an SMS alert to the forest department. Reported experiments achieved more than 92% classification accuracy in a controlled environment and approximately 85% in semi-outdoor conditions. GPS localization was reported within 5-10 m, while alerts were received within 5-10 s of detection. The system operated for several hours of continuous testing and across multiple days of field simulation, although weak Wi-Fi caused occasional cloud transmission failures. The results indicate that a low-cost, non-invasive, and automated sensing architecture can support proactive wildlife monitoring while highlighting the need for larger real-world datasets, robust noise handling, and alternative communication paths for deployment in connectivity-constrained regions.
authors: Shantha Kumar S Kamaleshware P; P Rohini Dr. S Mohana
venue: International Journal of Advanced Research in Science Communication and Technology

title: Abstract 16870: Complete Heart Block Detected by Smartwatch: A Diagnostic Challenge Between Lyme Carditis and Sarcoidosis
abstract: Consumer wearable devices are increasingly identifying clinically significant arrhythmias. Complete heart block (CHB) in younger patients warrants evaluation for reversible and infiltrative etiologies. We present a case in which positive Lyme serologies initially suggested Lyme carditis, but subsequent findings supported cardiac sarcoidosis. A 36-year-old man with non-insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus, obesity, hyperlipidemia, and hypertension presented in early spring after receiving an Apple Watch notification of heart rates in the 40s. He reported months of chest discomfort, palpitations, dizziness, dyspnea, and reduced exercise tolerance. On presentation, he was bradycardic but hemodynamically stable. Electrocardiography demonstrated complete heart block with atrioventricular dissociation. Chest radiography revealed hilar fullness. Transthoracic echocardiography showed mild left ventricular dilation with preserved systolic function and normal wall thickness. Initial laboratory evaluation, including thyroid function and troponin levels, was unremarkable. Lyme IgG and IgM antibodies were positive despite symptom onset during winter and absence of typical infectious manifestations. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated pulmonary nodules and diffuse mediastinal, hilar, and abdominal lymphadenopathy. Lymph node biopsy confirmed noncaseating granulomas. Angiotensin-converting enzyme levels were mildly elevated. Cardiac PET imaging demonstrated focal FDG uptake within the interatrial septum, supporting cardiac sarcoidosis. Empiric intravenous antibiotic therapy was initiated for presumed Lyme carditis while the diagnostic evaluation continued. Complete heart block persisted despite two weeks of antibiotic therapy, arguing against a reversible Lyme-mediated process. A dual-chamber ICD was implanted for pacing support and primary prevention of sudden cardiac death. Both Lyme disease and sarcoidosis may present with high-grade atrioventricular block, creating significant diagnostic overlap. This case highlights the importance of integrating clinical context, disease prevalence, seasonality, and response to therapy when interpreting positive test results. Although Lyme carditis is an important reversible cause of CHB, indiscriminate testing may identify misleading results and delay recognition of alternative diagnoses. Wearable technology served as the initial trigger for evaluation, ultimately leading to diagnosis of cardiac sarcoidosis and appropriate device therapy.
authors: Christopher Rudmann; Yashvardhan Batta; Edmond Cronin

title: Abstract 18322: Nocturnal Respiratory Rate Baseline and Variability Predict Long-Term Mortality in a Clinically Stable Outpatient Population
abstract: Background: Respiratory rate is a powerful but underused vital sign. Measured while awake, it is confounded by activity and stress, limiting its value as a long-term biomarker. Nocturnal respiratory rate (NRR), recorded during sleep, may offer a more stable signal. Whether its baseline and its variability independently predict mortality is unknown. Hypothesis: We hypothesized that both baseline NRR (median) and NRR variability (standard deviation, SD) are independent predictors of all-cause and cardiovascular (CV) mortality. Methods: We analyzed chest-belt respiratory waveforms from overnight polysomnography in 5,679 adults in the Sleep Heart Health Study (mean age 63±11 years; 52% women). Median and SD of NRR were derived via sliding-window breath detection. Using fifth-quintile thresholds (median 17 breaths/min; SD 1.35 breaths/min), participants were stratified into low-risk (low median + low SD), high-risk (high median + high SD), and mid-risk (all others). Kaplan-Meier and Cox proportional-hazards models assessed 3-year mortality, adjusting for age, sex, obesity, heart failure, atrial fibrillation, diabetes, hypertension, COPD, asthma, smoking, and severe sleep apnea (AHI>30). Results: Median NRR showed a dose-dependent relationship with all-cause and CV mortality; higher SD of NRR was likewise associated with reduced survival. Combining both metrics improved stratification. The high-risk group (n=412) had a near five-fold higher 3-year all-cause mortality incidence than the low-risk group (n=3,828). High-risk status independently predicted 3-year all-cause mortality (univariate hazard ratio 2.61, 95% CI 1.65-4.14, p<0.001; multivariate hazard ratio 2.15, 95% CI 1.30-3.55, p=0.003), whereas mid-risk status did not (multivariate hazard ratio 1.24, 95% CI 0.83-1.85, p=0.305). Conclusions: Median NRR and its variability are independent predictors of long-term all-cause and CV mortality and enable risk stratification in clinically stable outpatients. As consumer and contactless devices increasingly capture NRR, these passively measured biomarkers may support scalable long-term risk monitoring.
authors: Raimon Padrós-Valls; Nicholas W Harrington; Justin Yu; Robert Owens; David Torres Barba; Keshav Gupta; Jeremy E. Orr; Kevin R. King

title: Adaptive Glucose Management in Critically Ill Adults: Glycemic Effectiveness, Safety, and Clinical Outcomes in a Systematic Review
abstract: Dysglycemia is common during critical illness; however, optimal approaches to glucose monitoring, target selection, and insulin delivery remain uncertain. This systematic review evaluated whether adaptive glucose-management strategies, including individualized glucose targets, algorithm-guided insulin therapy, continuous glucose monitoring, and closed-loop systems, improve mortality, glycemic control, and safety compared with conventional or alternative glucose-control strategies in critically ill adults. PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials were searched for randomized controlled trials published between January 1, 2020, and August 25, 2026. Two reviewers independently performed study selection, data extraction, and risk-of-bias assessment using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool. Six randomized trials involving 11,674 participants were included. Because of substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity, the findings were synthesized narratively. Adaptive strategies generally achieved their intended technical objectives, including clearer separation between assigned glucose targets, improved protocol adherence, increased detection of dysglycemia, and more consistent maintenance of glucose concentrations within target ranges. However, these improvements did not consistently reduce mortality, length of stay in the intensive care unit or hospital, or other patient-centered outcomes. Continuous glucose monitoring had mixed effects on time in range and other glycemic measures, whereas closed-loop and algorithm-guided systems demonstrated that tighter glycemic control could be achieved with relatively low rates of severe hypoglycemia in selected settings. Individualized targets based on glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) did not improve overall survival. A post hoc signal of increased mortality among patients without diabetes warrants further investigation but should not be interpreted as definitive. One trial was judged to have a low risk of bias, four raised some concerns, and one had a high risk of bias. Current evidence supports the technical feasibility of adaptive glucose management but does not establish that more intensive monitoring, tighter targets, or individualization according to preadmission glycemia reliably improves survival or recovery. Future trials should integrate glucose sensing, treatment algorithms, and target selection while accounting for diabetes status, baseline glycemia, insulin exposure, treatment burden, and clinically meaningful outcomes.
authors: Abdullah Farooq; Subhan Idrees Shah; Hashir Habib; Asma Gulshan; Mozam Ali F Rathor; Ahsan Javed; Simran Kumari; Ashish Amatya; Saad Rafiq; Mehwish Jabeen

title: Advances in Deep Learning and Image Processing for Brain Tumor Detection and Classification: A Comprehensive Review
abstract: Brain tumor identification and classification by the application of deep learning and sophisticated image-processing techniques have been receiving a lot of attention in the medical field. Accurate diagnosis, treatment planning, and patient outcome rely on the accurate identification and differentiation of brain tumors, such as gliomas, meningiomas, and metastases. The most recent developments in deep learning-based techniques for brain tumor identification and categorization by applying medical imaging data, including Computed Tomography (CT). This study looks at CT and Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI). The main topic of this study is the general theory and developments in deep learning methods for the identification and classification of brain tumors. It investigates how the precision and efficacy of tumor detection can be increased through a variety of models, including Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). The paper emphasizes the Significance of applying novel deep-learning techniques for facilitating precise and automated brain tumor identification for individualized treatment, with an emphasis on important achievements, challenges, and opportunities in the area.
authors: V. Chanemougavel; Jayanthi Dr. K

title: Advances in Mobile Health Strategies for Atrial Fibrillation Detection and Patient Care
abstract: Atrial fibrillation (AF), a prevalent cardiac arrhythmia, poses significant risks for stroke and other severe complications. Traditional approaches frequently lack accessibility, accuracy, and patient engagement despite advancements in detection and management. The revolutionary effects of mobile health (mHealth) technologies on the treatment of AF are reviewed in this paper. These innovations, which make use of wearable technology, smartphone apps, and sophisticated algorithms, improve patient adherence, increase early detection, and lower healthcare costs. Better results are produced when real-time monitoring and patient-centered tools are incorporated into daily life because they empower people and allow for prompt interventions. However, issues like device restrictions, possible user anxiety, and fair access still exist. This study recognizes areas for additional research and development while highlighting the potential of mHealth to transform the management of AF.

title: Advances in Noise and Vibrations for Machines
abstract: Vibration analysis and monitoring are currently required in various industrial fields, such as in the automotive and aeronautics sectors, and in manufacturing, quality control, machining and maintenance, and civil engineering.Machine vibration is a normal and typically unavoidable result of moving and rotating parts or of ground motion transfer on an object. To mitigate its negative effects, in many cases, vibration needs to be assessed and monitored. Vibrations, as well as noise measurements, are also a good indication of systems' behaviour or the degrading quality of a product in the case of manufacturing. Vibration, especially the modal analysis of structures and machines, is also a good way in which to validate a finite element model.The current industrial trends focus on noise and vibration mitigations but also on the use of contact and non-contact novel-sensing technologies for measurements.
authors: Łukasz Ścisło; Davide Astolfi; Francesco Castellani

title: Advances in digital phenotyping for relapse risk monitoring and community-based treatment and rehabilitation in methamphetamine use disorder
abstract: Methamphetamine use disorder (MUD) lacks widely approved pharmacological treatments with consistent efficacy, and community-based care relies largely on psychosocial interventions. Earlier identification of relapse risk in daily life is therefore a practical priority. Digital phenotyping uses smartphones, wearable devices, ecological momentary assessment (EMA), and passive sensing to collect repeated information on behavior, activity rhythms, subjective states, and environmental exposure in naturalistic settings. This narrative review maps evidence on digital and contextual signals for dynamic relapse-risk monitoring in MUD and examines how these signals may support human-reviewed community responses. It focuses on EMA, passive sensing, wearable devices, multimodal dynamic risk-state modeling, explainable risk prompts, just-in-time adaptive intervention (JITAI), and human-in-the-loop workflows. Direct MUD evidence primarily supports feasibility and concurrent or post-use correlates, while broader digital-intervention studies suggest potential benefits for treatment engagement and self-monitoring. These findings may support contextual understanding, but they do not establish prospectively validated relapse warning or demonstrated benefit from monitoring-triggered support. Long-term relapse outcomes, external validation, data standards, ethical governance, and real-world implementation remain limited. Digital phenotyping should therefore be viewed not as a mature automated relapse prediction system, but as a supportive framework for dynamic risk monitoring and stratified community response. Future work should prioritize multicenter validation and comparative evaluation of population-level, individualized, and hybrid risk models, including cold-start performance and recalibration, alongside transparent and explainable modeling, privacy-preserving data governance, and integration with existing community service workflows.
authors: Zhiwen Wang; Genmeng Yang; Ziyan Zhu; Ruike Xu; Yanxia Peng

title: Aerial Magnetic Anomaly Target Detection Method Based on Multi-Scale Orthonormal Basis Function Convolution and Convolution-Augmented Gated Attention
abstract: Magnetic anomaly detection from aerial platforms enables passive, non-contact detection of underwater ferromagnetic targets. To address the issues of traditional Orthonormal Basis Function (OBF) detection relying on prior knowledge of the closest contact distance and susceptibility to mismatch with single-scale templates, this paper proposes an aerial magnetic anomaly target detection method that integrates multi-scale OBF with a convolution-augmented gated attention unit (CGAU). Six sets of fixed OBF convolution kernels each output three matching responses, which are concatenated with the original sequence to form 19-channel features. Four layers of one-dimensional (1-D) convolution and two stages of CGAU extract local waveform features and capture long-range dependencies. The precision (PC), detection rate (DR), and F1-score of the proposed network on the simulated test set are 94.70%, 95.11%, and 94.90%, respectively (best-performing seed = 42). On the measured dataset, it detected 11 of 12 overpass events, achieving an event detection rate of 91.67%. The proposed network has approximately 0.43 M trainable parameters and achieves a higher mean F1 across three random seeds than the seven selected baselines, demonstrating its potential for aerial magnetic anomaly target detection.
authors: Haozhe Chen; Ke Zhang; Wanhua Zhu

title: AlertSafeNet a multichannel deep learning framework for real time anomaly detection using wearable device data
abstract: This research investigates the integration of wearable device data analysis to enable proactive safety monitoring within intelligent systems. The objective is to develop a deep learning framework capable of automatically detecting anomalous gait patterns from the wearable device data and generating alerts in real-time. Smartwatches and fitness trackers, through their built-in sensors, continuously record physiological and contextual signals including heart rate, SpO₂, ECG, location, and more. Analyzing this multichannel time-series data lets the proposed framework flag abnormal behavioral patterns that could signal a safety risk. The proposed framework enables the identification of abnormal behavioral patterns that may reflect potential safety risk scenarios. In high-risk scenarios, such systems can activate real-time alerts to trusted contacts or concerned authorities. In this work, we propose AlertSafeNet, a multichannel 1D convolutional neural network with residual connections, designed to learn temporal dependencies and detect anomalies from wearable sensor data. The dataset is created using smart watch-derived physiological signals combined with contextual information from smartphones. Once trained, the model runs in a cloud-based environment, supporting real-time inference and continuous monitoring. The results demonstrate promising performance: the model reaches 97.9% classification accuracy, with strong precision, recall, and F1-score — a good indicator of its usefulness for real-time anomaly detection in safety-critical settings.
authors: Bharati Ainapure; Reshma Nitin Pise; Nishu Gupta; Mohammad Omar Derawi

title: All-optical sensing of dermal activity enables an AI-powered wearable ring for continuous stress monitoring
abstract: Electrodermal activity (EDA), a primary stress-sensing signal in today's wearables, requires skin-electrode contact that drifts and degrades over time, limiting long-term use. Here, we present an artificial intelligence (AI)-powered ring for all-optical sensing of dermal activity (ODA), using light rather than electrodes to track sweat gland activation, thereby enhancing durability and comfort. An optimized dual-wavelength design (960 and 1250 nanometers) captures perspiration dynamics while concurrently recording photoplethysmography. The ODA ring integrates temperature and motion sensors for multimodal monitoring with on-device inference. In correlation studies, ODA and EDA signals showed 86% agreement. In classification tasks, the ODA ring achieved 92.3% binary accuracy versus 77.95% for EDA. In multiclass tasks, ODA outperforms EDA by 100 to 74.58% (short term) and 89.72 to 43.20% (long term). On-device one-dimensional convolutional neural network inference enabled 87.53% autonomous accuracy. This electrode-free modality establishes a scalable, all-optical platform for rings, watches, and patches for accurate, robust, and long-term stress monitoring.

title: An Artificial Intelligence-Based Personalized Sports Recommendation Framework for Children with Disabilities: A Narrative Review and Cross-Disability Conceptual Model
abstract: Background: Children with disabilities are less physically active than their peers and face personal, social and environmental barriers to sport. Their needs differ across and within diagnostic groups, so uniform activity programs often fit poorly. Artificial intelligence (AI) and the Internet of Things (IoT) could support individualized activity recommendations, but their readiness for this purpose is uncertain. Objective: To synthesize evidence on physical activity (PA) and AI- and IoT-enabled technologies across disability groups and to propose a cross-disability framework for personalized sports recommendation. Methods: This narrative review combined a previously completed thematic synthesis of 49 studies (2015–2025) with a targeted PubMed/MEDLINE search (January 2000 to November 2026) using predefined terms and inclusion criteria, plus checks of IEEE Xplore and publisher records. Results: PA interventions show small-to-moderate benefits that vary by disability and outcome; for example, aerobic exercise improved attention in attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD; standardized mean difference = 0.84), whereas exercise trials in cerebral palsy were at high risk of bias. Technologies follow disability-specific patterns: gesture sensing in autism, activity monitoring in ADHD, gait sensing in cerebral palsy, seizure-detection wearables in epilepsy and sign-language recognition in hearing impairment. Small samples, laboratory validation and weak privacy reporting are common. The proposed framework links six modules: individual profiling, a structured activity catalog, hard safety filtering, transparent ranking, feedback and human governance. Conclusion: AI-supported recommendation may help organize accessible choices, but no health benefit has yet been shown. Staged evaluation is required.
authors: Mossammat Ruksana Rashid

title: An Enhancing Lung Disease Detection with Scalable UNet-Mamba Segmentation
abstract: Lung diseases are conditions that damage the lung tissues, airways or blood vessels of the lungs, causing breathing difficulties and decreased oxygen supply to the body. Computed Tomography (CT) plays a crucial role in lung disease prediction because it provides detailed cross-sectional images for detecting tumors at initial stages. However, CT scans have drawbacks such as radiation exposure, high cost, large data size, and the possibility of false positives. Recently, many Deep Learning (DL) techniques have been used to automatically analyze CT images for early and accurate detection of lung diseases, improving diagnostic efficiency. However, existing models may struggle to capture fine spatial details, leading to inaccurate boundary delineation and poor segmentation of small or low-contrast regions. Some models are also sensitive to imaging artifacts, which can reduce performance in real-world conditions. In this paper, a lung disease prediction model is developed using ResNet and Mamba Network (LRMNet) to solve the aforementioned issues for lung disease prediction. The first step is improving the model's ability to conduct pre-processing and enrich the data using a Deep Convolutional Generative Adversarial Network (DCGAN). Then, the Scalable Vision UNet-Mamba (SVU-M) model is developed to efficiently capture fine spatial details along with long-range contextual information. SVU-M leverages Scalable Vision State Space (SVSS) blocks to efficiently model the global dependencies while maintaining linear computational complexity. The integration of SVSS within a U-shaped framework enhances the boundary delineation and improves segmentation of small or low-contrast regions, which increases the efficiency against imaging artifacts for more reliable performance. The decoder feature maps of SVU-M are further processed using Global Average Pooling (GAP) to determine image-level feature representations for classification. Simultaneously, the input image is directly fed into ResNet-50 for capturing the whole image's semantic features. A Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) classifier is trained with the extracted features to forecast lung diseases. A total accuracy of 94.15% on the customized dataset and 93.29% on the SARS-CoV-2 CT dataset was achieved by the suggested model, according to the experimental results, exceeding the performance of other models.
authors: Sivasakthi S; Radha V
venue: International Journal of Engineering Trends and Technology

title: An Explainable Software-Based Framework for Pre-Symptomatic Grape Disease Risk Assessment Using MobileNetV2, Grad-CAM, and Weather Data
abstract: Viticulture faces severe yield losses from major fungal diseases such as Downy Mildew, Powdery Mildew, and Black Rot. Existing deep learning classification models predominantly rely on visible symptomatic lesions on leaves or fruit clusters. However, waiting for visual symptoms to manifest often delays chemical mitigation beyond the optimal therapeutic window, resulting in irreversible crop degradation. This paper proposes a software-based, explainable framework for pre-symptomatic grape disease risk assessment. The architecture combines finegrained leaf image feature extraction using MobileNetV2 with micro-climate weather telemetry (temperature, relative humidity, leaf wetness duration, and rainfall forecast). To ensure clinical transparency for agronomists and farmers, Explainable AI (XAI) is integrated via Gradientweighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM), generating visual saliency heatmaps that highlight sub-visual cellular stress indicators and necrotic margins. A dynamic Epidemiological Micro-Climate Risk Index (EMRI) fuses deep learning probabilities with real-time weather analytics. Evaluated on multi-source datasets including PlantVillage and field-captured vineyard imagery, MobileNetV2 achieves a classification accuracy of 97.84%. Based on a comprehensive literature review, a critical research gap is identified: current agricultural systems treat image classification and micro-climate forecasting as disjoint workflows without explainable decision support. The proposed framework fills this gap through an integrated web and mobile platform featuring automated risk alerts and actionable advisory generation

title: An Overview on Biological Security for Smart IoT Devices: B-Cell Approach to IoT Threats
abstract: The rapid proliferation of Internet‑of‑Things (IoT) devices has transformed everyday environments into richly interconnected ecosystems, yet it has also created a sprawling attack surface that traditional perimeter‑based defenses struggle to contain. Inspired by the adaptive humoral immunity of vertebrates, this paper introduces a B‑Cell‑based security framework (KVS approach) for IoT networks—a biologically‑motivated, self‑organizing approach that continuously learns to recognize and neutralise anomalous behaviour. Each “B‑cell” is a lightweight, autonomous agent embedded on a device or edge node; it monitors local telemetry, extracts feature‑vectors, and generates “antibodies” (signature models) through an incremental clustering‑and‑affinity‑maturation process. When a new pattern deviates beyond a dynamically‑adjusted affinity threshold, the corresponding B‑cell flags the event, propagates a concise alert to neighbouring cells, and collaboratively refines its detection model. We implement the framework on a heterogeneous test‑bed comprising smart‑home appliances, industrial sensors, and wearables, and evaluate it against a suite of realistic threat scenarios (botnet recruitment, firmware tampering, side‑channel data exfiltration, and zero‑day exploits). Empirical results demonstrate up to 96.8 % detection accuracy with less than 2 % false‑positive rate, while maintaining an average CPU overhead of 1.8 % and memory footprint of 45 KB per B‑cell—well within the constraints of typical IoT microcontrollers. Moreover, the distributed nature of the B‑cell population enables rapid containment of compromised nodes, reducing lateral‑movement windows by 71 % compared with conventional centralized intrusion‑detection systems. The contributions of this work are three‑fold: (1) a novel, biologically‑inspired paradigm that maps B‑cell maturation to adaptive signature generation in resource‑constrained devices; (2) a concrete, low‑cost implementation that integrates seamlessly with existing IoT middleware; and (3) a comprehensive experimental validation that quantifies security gains, performance trade‑offs, and scalability across diverse deployment topologies. By fusing immunology with cyber‑defence, the B‑Cell approach called as KVS (Kutubuddin Vahida Sultana) Approach opens a promising pathway toward self‑healing, resilient IoT infrastructures.
authors: IR. Dr. Kazi Kutubuddin Sayyad Liyakat Saheb

title: An fNIRS dataset on prefrontal cortical activation and behavioral performance during Stroop task before and after acute VR-integrated cycling in healthy young adults
abstract: Inhibitory control, a core component of executive function, is sensitive to acute physical exercise and may also be influenced by immersive virtual reality (VR) environments. However, openly available multimodal datasets that combine behavioral performance, physiological responses, and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) recordings before and after VR-integrated exercise remain limited. Here, we present an open dataset including trial-level behavioral responses during a color-word Stroop task, heart-rate recordings, and prefrontal fNIRS data from 42 healthy young adults assigned to a VR cycling group, a traditional cycling group, or a no-intervention control group. Data were collected using a randomized between-subjects pre-test/post-test design. The dataset includes raw and processed behavioral files, raw and preprocessed fNIRS recordings, event markers, channel information, demographic variables, physiological monitoring data, and derived statistical outputs. Experimental materials, metadata, analysis scripts, and documentation are publicly available through the Open Science Framework. This dataset is intended to support secondary analyses, methodological benchmarking, fNIRS preprocessing comparisons, and exploratory investigations of behavioral and prefrontal hemodynamic responses associated with acute VR-integrated cycling.
authors: Jingjing Li; Yang Yang

title: Antecedents of Adoption Intention for AI-Driven Wearable Technology in Malaysian Healthcare: A Pilot Study Using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling
abstract: This study reports the pilot phase of a larger doctoral investigation into the adoption of AI-driven wearable technology in Malaysian healthcare. Guided by an integration of Diffusion of Innovations theory and the Technology Acceptance Model, the pilot tested seven direct effect hypotheses linking compatibility, relative advantage, trialability, complexity, observability, perceived ease of use, and perceived usefulness to adoption intention. Data were collected from healthcare sector respondents at a professional conference in Kuala Lumpur in August 2026 (N = 93, after removing two duplicates from 95 raw responses). Partial least squares structural equation modeling was used for its suitability to prediction oriented research. The structural model explained 60.0 percent of the variance in adoption intention. Perceived usefulness (beta = 0.261), perceived ease of use (beta = 0.201), observability (beta = 0.174), compatibility (beta = 0.162), and complexity (beta = -0.152) significantly predicted adoption intention (all p < .05); relative advantage and trialability did not. Composite reliability exceeded 0.78 for all nine constructs, and heterotrait monotrait ratios for all 36 construct pairs fell below the conservative 0.85 threshold as point estimates, but bootstrap confidence intervals crossed 0.85 for six of the eight adoption intention pairs, so discriminant validity for that construct remains provisional. Perceived regulatory support was retained for reliability assessment but not tested as a moderator here, a test reserved for the full study. Findings offer preliminary support for the framework and considerations for the full scale study.
authors: Syeda Hafsa Rizwan; Anusuyah Subbarao; Shereen Khan
venue: The Journal of Applied Technology and Innovation

title: Architecture-Level Evaluation of Standalone Wearable Systems for Real- Time Non-Invasive Blood Glucose Inference
abstract: Non-invasive glucose monitoring is shifting from analyte-centric optical sensing toward system-level physiological inference based on autonomic and metabolic state variables. Building on a systems physiology framework in which glycemic dynamics are inferred from multiparametric signals such as heart rate variability, tissue oxygenation, physical activity, and circadian rhythm, this study compares two hardware deployment architectures: smartphone-dependent wearable systems and standalone display-integrated wearable devices. The comparison is conducted across latency, power consumption, data-processing hierarchy, privacy, human–machine interaction, and long-term clinical adherence. The analysis shows that standalone devices combining local edge computation on low-power microcontrollers with integrated OLED feedback can reduce dependence on continuous Bluetooth Low Energy transmission, shorten the real-time inference pathway, and provide low-friction visual feedback directly on the wearable node. Although integrated displays introduce additional power demand, dark-mode OLED rendering, event-driven screen activation, adaptive sampling, and microcontroller-level power management can mitigate this burden. Compared with smartphone-dependent systems, the standalone architecture provides a more robust deployment pathway for real-time non-invasive glucose inference by improving immediacy, autonomy, privacy, and user engagement. These findings suggest that edge-enabled standalone wearables may provide a suitable architecture for future continuous physiological monitoring and proactive metabolic self-management.
authors: Mingyang Huang

title: Artificial Intelligence in Biosensing and Wearable Health Monitoring
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) can facilitate the interpretation of data obtained from biosensors and wearable devices. However, the full utility of AI in the measurement and clinical follow-up process is not yet fully realized. This narrative review will explore the applications of machine learning in conjunction with personalized monitoring and multimodal sensing in healthcare. It will cover already published studies in this field and provide examples of signal classification, detection and other opportunities while addressing blind spots in data and coverages, referencing testing and population representation. The review will cover diagnostic accuracy and the need for evidence of improved patient outcomes. The review will also cover a hypothetical example of a screening test to illustrate that in cases of sensitivity and specificity being close to 100%, large numbers of false alerts can still occur. The review aims to communicate that, for clinical utility of such systems, the follow-up and control of model updates will be necessary.
authors: Jinxin Gao

title: Artificial Intelligence in Cardiovascular Medicine
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming cardiovascular medicine, offering new opportunities to improve the prevention, diagnosis, and management of cardiovascular disease.Advances in computational power, the availability of large-scale clinical datasets, and the development of complex computational algorithms have enabled AI to identify complex patterns in medical images, physiological signals, and electronic health records that may not be readily apparent through conventional approaches.From automated interpretation of cardiovascular imaging and electrocardiograms to personalized risk prediction and clinical decision support, AI has the potential to improve diagnostic accuracy, enhance clinical efficiency, and enable more individualized patient care.1,2 Yet, despite remarkable technological progress, important questions remain regarding the generalizability, interpretability, clinical integration, and real-world impact of these emerging tools.Ultimately, the value of AI will be determined not simply by its predictive performance, but by its ability to meaningfully improve clinical decisions and patient outcomes.3 In this issue of the Methodist DeBakey Cardiovascular Journal, we explore the evolving role of AI and digital health across the spectrum of cardiovascular medicine through articles authored by experts in their respective fields.These reviews examine applications in preventive cardiology, coronary artery disease, valvular heart disease, heart failure, aortic and peripheral vascular disease, and congenital heart disease as well as the growing role of consumer wearable devices in detecting and managing arrhythmia.Together, they provide an overview of the current state of the field, highlighting both the promise of AI-driven innovations and the challenges that must be addressed before their widespread adoption into routine clinical practice.We start with a review titled "Artificial Intelligence in Valvular Heart Disease: Imaging, Quantification, and Clinical Decision Support," in which Drs. Yeva Fakikh and Maan Malahfji explore the expanding role of AI in the detection, evaluation, and management of valvular heart disease.The authors highlight how AI-enabled electrocardiography and point-of-care ultrasound may improve early detection while advances in echocardiography, cardiac computed tomography, and magnetic resonance imaging enable more accurate and reproducible assessment of disease severity.They also discuss the potential of machine learning to identify distinct patient phenotypes, improve procedural planning, and inform the optimal timing of intervention.These applications offer opportunities to address longstanding challenges in valvular heart disease, particularly
authors: Sadeer G Al-Kindi; Khurram Nasir; Ashutosh Sabharwal

title: Artificial Intelligence in Congenital Heart Disease: A Roadmap
abstract: Congenital heart disease (CHD) is a lifelong condition that requires ongoing monitoring due to its heterogeneous anatomy, physiology, and clinical course. Despite major advances in diagnosis and treatment, challenges remain in early detection, risk stratification, and long-term management. Artificial intelligence (AI) has the potential to enhance CHD care by extracting actionable insights from complex clinical data. This review examines current and emerging applications of AI in three key domains: cardiovascular imaging, wearable technologies, and clinical registries. We highlight opportunities to improve diagnosis, monitoring, and outcome prediction, while discussing important challenges related to data quality, validation, interpretability, and clinical implementation. Together, these areas illustrate both the promise and the barriers to integrating AI into CHD care.
authors: Rajkumar Dhar; Darpit Dave; Jacob Heiss; Kristopher Kormos; Animesh A Tandon

title: Artificial Intelligence in Heart Failure: Early Detection, Phenotyping, and Prognostic Modeling
abstract: This review examines the role of artificial intelligence (AI) across the heart failure (HF) continuum, with particular emphasis on patient identification and early recognition, AI-enabled electrocardiography and echocardiography, etiologic and phenotypic classification, electronic health record-based staging and risk prediction, advanced HF identification, continuous monitoring, treatment optimization, and emerging applications of agentic AI.
authors: Sanmit Jindal; Ankitha Lavi; Ashrith Guha

title: Artificial Intelligence in Heart Failure: From Earlier Disease Detection to Integrated Care Delivery
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly positioned to improve heart failure (HF) care by predicting risk, enabling earlier disease identification, and supporting more reliable delivery of evidence-based management. Current applications span opportunistic detection for low ejection fraction, HF with preserved ejection fraction, and structural heart disease using tools such as AI-enabled electrocardiography, imaging- and electronic health record‒based risk stratification, clinician-facing decision support, remote medication titration, and wearable monitoring platforms. The strongest evidence suggests that AI is most effective when embedded into active clinical workflows that guide targeted testing, treatment optimization, and longitudinal follow-up, rather than functioning as passive alerts alone. This review examines the emerging landscape of AI-enabled HF care delivery from early detection through chronic management, with emphasis on implementation, workflow integration, and the capacity of these tools to improve diagnostic yield and ultimately scalability.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Neurology: A Critical Narrative Review of Clinical Evidence, Translation, and Responsible Implementation
abstract: PURPOSE: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly applied to neuroimaging, electrophysiology, clinical text, and digitally measured behavior, but reported performance often exceeds the maturity of clinical evidence. METHOD: We conducted a structured narrative review, informed by SANRA principles, of English-language human studies, reviews, and regulatory sources identified in PubMed/MEDLINE and IEEE Xplore from January 2022 through July 2026; older landmark studies were retained when necessary for historical or methodological context. We applied a common translational-evidence framework across six prespecified neurological domains to distinguish technical performance from external validation, prospective clinical evaluation, implementation, and demonstrated patient benefit. Evidence was appraised according to cohort representativeness, patient-level data separation, external and prospective validation, calibration, clinical comparators, regulatory status, workflow integration, and patient-level benefit. FINDING: Across stroke, dementia, Parkinson disease, epilepsy, multiple sclerosis, and neuro-oncology, the strongest evidence concerns narrowly defined imaging and signal-processing tasks. A cluster-randomized stroke study demonstrated shorter thrombectomy workflow time, and several externally validated models show improved portability. In contrast, many high-accuracy classification and segmentation studies remain retrospective, single-dataset, internally validated, and uncalibrated. Multimodal learning, foundation models, federated learning, and large language models broaden capability but introduce additional risks related to dataset shift, bias, opacity, privacy, and automation. CONCLUSION: Neuro-AI should be judged by its intended clinical task and evidence maturity rather than headline accuracy. Multicenter external validation, prospective workflow evaluation, calibration, subgroup reporting, human-factors testing, and post-deployment surveillance are prerequisites for safe and equitable clinical use.
