title: Artificial Intelligence in Preventive Cardiology: Risk Prediction, Exposomics, and Personalized Interventions
abstract: Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide. Prevention has shifted from a narrow focus on atherosclerosis to the cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) framework, which requires integrating data across organ systems, specialties, and care settings. Artificial intelligence (AI) can work with the high-dimensional, weakly structured data this integration produces, and its use in prevention is now endorsed by major cardiovascular societies. This review covers two applications. The first encompasses risk prediction, spanning electrocardiogram-based models that reframe routine tracings as general biomarkers of cardiovascular health, AI-enhanced cardiac imaging that extracts biological signals invisible to standard reads, opportunistic analysis of scans acquired for unrelated indications, and emerging efforts to quantify environmental and neighborhood-level exposomic risk. The second is the management of modifiable risk factors across early CKM stages: lifestyle behavior, obesity phenotyping, hypertension monitoring, dyslipidemia detection, glycemic management, and chronic kidney disease risk stratification. In both domains, retrospective discriminative performance is frequently excellent, while prospective evidence that AI-guided intervention improves patient-relevant outcomes remains limited.
authors: Corrado Magnino; Matthew A Coker; Eleonora Avenatti

title: Artificial intelligence in influenza prevention and control: translational pathways, supporting evidence, and system-level challenges
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly applied to influenza prevention and control. AI encompasses conventional machine learning, deep learning, and protein language models. Large language models (LLMs) are an emerging subset of AI. Current evidence remains weakly linked to real-world workflows and population health outcomes. This structured narrative review proposes a three-stage translational maturity framework. Phase I is technical efficacy assessment. Phase II is implementation effectiveness verification. Phase III is population impact and sustainability. We synthesized evidence in three domains: viral evolution prediction and vaccine design; epidemic surveillance and early warning; and individual-level infection risk detection and clinical monitoring. We used a three-level evidence hierarchy. Level A is influenza-specific evidence. Level B is transferable evidence from other infectious diseases. Level C is general biomedical or methodological evidence. Only two Phase II studies were identified, both in epidemic surveillance and early warning; no Phase II studies were identified in virus evolution and vaccine design or in individual-level infection risk detection. No study met the prespecified Phase III criteria. Phase III requires demonstrated downstream population health benefit. Prospective deployment or improved forecasting alone is not sufficient. Across domains, bottlenecks have shifted from model accuracy to governance, interpretability, accountability, interoperability, workflow integration, equity, and sustainable monitoring. LLMs attract major attention, but their influenza-specific evidence remains limited. Their greatest value may lie in augmenting, not replacing, specialized models and human expertise. We propose phase-specific evidence thresholds, implementation-oriented evaluation metrics, an implementation readiness checklist, and priority evidence gaps for translating AI-enabled influenza tools into implementation-ready public health applications.
authors: Xingting Li; Qiaozi Lin; Xin Guo; Qiaoyan Li; 宫金伶; Peiqun Li; Jiaxun Li; Wenpeng Pang; Yuchen Gu; Xue Liu; Qiuyue Ning; 张增峰; Lingxi Gao; Liping Guo

title: Artificial intelligence in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease: A short narrative review of diagnostic and therapeutic implications
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease is the most prevalent chronic liver disease worldwide and may progress from steatosis to metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis, fibrosis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma. Insulin resistance, obesity, mitochondrial dysfunction, inflammation, and impaired autophagy contribute to its pathogenesis. Early diagnosis, monitoring of disease progression, and assessment of therapeutic response remain important clinical challenges. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning may improve disease prediction by integrating laboratory, metabolic, imaging, histological, and molecular data. Natural language processing and deep-learning approaches applied to radiological imaging and digital histopathology may support automated quantification of steatosis, inflammation, and fibrosis, while AI-assisted multi-omics analysis may identify molecular signatures relevant to disease stratification. Current evidence is strongest for retrospective case identification, imaging-based classification, and quantitative digital pathology; therapeutic selection and monitoring remain largely investigational. AI should therefore be viewed as a decision-support technology rather than a replacement for clinical judgment.
authors: Mona Mohamed Ibrahim Abdalla; Fabian Amalraj Davamani; Nabil A. S. Eid

title: Attitudinal and behavioral factors affecting willingness to engage in Alzheimer's disease biomarker testing
abstract: INTRODUCTION Ethnoracialized individuals, for example, Black/African American (AA), American Indian/Alaska Native (AI/AN), and Hispanic/Latinx (H/L), are underrepresented in Alzheimer's disease (AD) biomarker studies. We investigated whether and how ethnoracialized groups differ in their willingness to engage in preclinical AD biomarker studies. METHODS We administered an online questionnaire to 1825 adults (725 non‐Hispanic White, 599 AA, 352 AI/AN, and 149 H/L). We examined factors hypothesized to be associated with AD biomarker testing willingness: gender, family history of dementia, education level, attitudes toward research, attitudes toward genetic testing, and preventive and proactive health behavior engagement using structural equation modeling. RESULTS The unconstrained (configural) model demonstrated good overall fit to the data. However, the constrained model and nested chi‐square difference test indicated a lack of structural invariance, that is, relationships between the variables and testing willingness differed by group. DISCUSSION The findings provide impetus for tailoring engagement strategies based on contextual factors such as ethnoracialized group membership.
authors: Diane Carol Gooding; Emre Umucu; Gilda E. Ennis; Carol Ann Van Hulle; Fabu P. Carter; Jordan Lewis; Maria C. Mora-Pinzon; Lauren W. Y. McLester‐Davis; Megan L. Zuelsdorff; Taryn T. James; Carey Elizabeth Gleason

title: Bench Testing of an 8 N Slip-Resistance Specification for the Handle–Shaft Locking Interface of an Articulated Laparoscopic Instrument
abstract: Background Articulated laparoscopic instruments require a reliable mechanical connection between the handle and shaft to maintain the intended instrument configuration during surgical manipulation. The handle–shaft locking interface should resist unintended relative displacement under external loading. However, the appropriateness of a specific slip-resistance threshold must be evaluated in relation to the instrument design and intended conditions of use. Objective To evaluate the mechanical performance associated with an 8 N slip-resistance specification for the locked handle–shaft interface of an articulated laparoscopic instrument using a controlled bench model. Methods A bench-based mechanical evaluation method was designed using the instrument under test, mechanical fixtures, a calibrated force-measurement device, and displacement-measurement equipment. After engagement of the handle–shaft locking mechanism, external forces were applied to evaluate resistance to relative displacement. Testing included axial loading, loading in relevant transverse directions, and repeated locking–unlocking cycles. The primary outcome was the force corresponding to the onset of relative slippage at the locked interface. Secondary outcomes included displacement under load, complete locking failure, and changes in mechanical performance after repeated operation. Acceptance criteria should be established before confirmatory testing. Results All 30 instruments from three production batches met the 8 N axial requirement (30/30). The axial slip-onset force was 12.40 ± 0.97 N (range, 10.80–14.00 N). Under a sustained load of 8 N for 60 s, mean relative displacement increased from 0.06 mm to 0.10 mm, and mean residual displacement was 0.02 mm. After 1,000 cycles, the axial slip-onset force was 12.00 ± 0.97 N (range, 10.40–13.60 N). Conclusions This study provides a bench-testing framework for evaluating an 8 N slip-resistance specification for the handle–shaft locking interface of an articulated laparoscopic instrument. Whether this specification provides adequate mechanical stability can be determined only by comparing the measured performance with engineering acceptance criteria established in advance on the basis of the instrument’s intended use and foreseeable loading conditions.
authors: Hongchang Ma

title: Benchmarking Wearable Bioelectronics: A Multimodal Evaluation Framework Integrating Parametric Regression, Machine Learning, and Fuzzy Logic Across Domain Applications
abstract: This paper examines how a range of factors, including hardware architecture, sensor accuracy, battery lifetime, and user satisfaction, influence the performance and applicability of wearable technology. Through a study of 29 hardware and more than 2,300 hardware-enabled outcomes, we present a comprehensive analytical model, which includes ordinary least squares regression, nonlinear Random Forest feature extraction, and Takagi–Sugeno fuzzy logic inference. The models indicate that the four main performance indicators are heart rate accuracy, sleep tracking accuracy, battery life, and consumer satisfaction. Sensitivity analysis reveals that the hardware form factor is a unique technological architecture that no other hardware form factor can substitute for. People believe that denser hardware improves electronic quality; however, our analysis revealed that the more sensors a piece of hardware has, the lower its performance is (𝛽 = −0.542, p < .001). To facilitate the practical application of the study, we have created an application suitability matrix and rules for the decision-making process across four realms of study: clinical remote patient monitoring, longitudinal sleep research, military activities, and consumer wellness. While smart rings maximize sleep compliance through lower sensor density and longer battery life, smartwatches aim to deliver higher diagnostic output with more sophisticated systems. These results show that the effectiveness of wearables depends more on application-specific sensors than on high feature versatility, which guides the design of wearable bioelectronics. title: Between algorithmic alerts and bodily sensations: a qualitative study of post-PCI patients' experiences with wrist-worn heart health information
abstract: Background: Smart wrist-worn devices are increasingly used by patients after percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) to monitor heart rate, rhythm-related alerts, sleep, activity, and other health-related data. However, limited qualitative evidence exists on how post-PCI patients interpret and respond to such information in daily life. Objective: This study aimed to explore how patients with coronary heart disease after PCI understand, evaluate, and respond to heart rate, heart rhythm, and health-related information generated by smart wrist-worn devices. Methods: A qualitative descriptive design was adopted. From January to May 2026, purposive sampling was used to recruit 23 post-PCI patients who had used smartwatches or smart bands in daily life. Semi-structured interviews were conducted, audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and analyzed using thematic analysis. Data collection and analysis were conducted concurrently until data saturation was achieved. Results: Four themes were developed: (1) cardiac status became continuously datafied; (2) calibrating risk between alerts and sensations; (3) device information awaited medical interpretation; and (4) from self-management to disease burden. Patients did not simply accept or reject device-generated data. Instead, they interpreted alerts by comparing them with bodily sensations, previous cardiac events, stent implantation experiences, follow-up results, and healthcare professionals' explanations. Device information could enhance awareness of medication use, follow-up, and lifestyle management. However, when alerts lacked medical interpretation or follow-up response, they also increased uncertainty, worry, repeated self-monitoring, and perceived disease burden. Conclusions: Smart wrist-worn devices may support daily observation and clinician-patient communication in post-PCI management, but they should not be regarded as substitutes for clinical examinations or professional judgment. Clearer interpretive boundaries, stratified guidance, and follow-up response pathways are needed to help patients appropriately understand and act on device-generated information.
authors: Angang Tong; Ruiqi Luo; Pan Jin; Cuihuan Wu

title: Beyond Atrial Fibrillation: Emerging Clinical Applications of Photoplethysmography in Consumer Wearables
abstract: Introduction: Photoplethysmography (PPG) is an optical sensing technology embedded in many current consumer smartwatches and smart rings. Long used for heart-rate monitoring and pulse oximetry, PPG has more recently become the foundation for population-scale screening for atrial fibrillation. The clinical applications of PPG now extend well beyond rhythm monitoring. Method: A narrative literature review of English-language publications indexed in PubMed, Europe PMC, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar between January 2020 and May 2026 was conducted, using combinations of the search term photoplethysmography with application-specific search terms. Earlier foundational publications were included selectively where necessary. Discussion: Current evidence most strongly supports consumer-wearable PPG for resting heart-rate estimation and for atrial-fibrillation notification pathways with adjudicated electrocardiographic confirmation. SpO2 trending is conditionally supported in healthy, normoxaemic adults but is insufficient for clinical decision-making during desaturation, motion, low perfusion, or in populations under-represented in validation datasets. Cuffless blood-pressure estimation, heart-rate variability, sleep staging, and obstructive sleep apnoea screening show device-, context-, and reference-standard-dependent reliability. Non-invasive blood-glucose monitoring through smartwatches or smart rings should not be used for diabetes management and is the subject of an explicit FDA safety communication. Conclusion: Consumer-wearable PPG is a multifunctional clinical sensing platform whose evidence maturity differs sharply by application. Responsible deployment requires awareness of signal quality, motion artefact, skin-tone bias, regulatory authorisation status, and local validation, particularly in the Indonesian primary-care context.
authors: Muhammad Rifqi Haikal

title: Bioinspired Selective Perception Through On‐Chip Te/Ag Integration and Interface Interference
abstract: Infrared sensing in the 1–4 µm band is of great significance in fields such as thermal detection and flame identification. However, in practical applications, this band is often disturbed by strong visible solar background radiation, leading to a reduction in signal‐to‐noise ratio. Here, inspired by jewel beetles, which use specialized thoracic pit organs to block visible light and transmit infrared radiation for forest fire detection, we present an on‐chip recognition strategy based on tellurium/silver hybrid films. The optimized films exhibit high infrared transmittance (91.5% at 2400 nm) while strongly suppressing visible light (20.6% at 400 nm) based on the interface interference effect. Leveraging this bio‐inspired spectral selectivity, we demonstrate a highly compact sensing platform integrated with a low‐cost integrated microcontroller unit running a lightweight multilayer perceptron network (0.6 kB, 149 parameters) for real‐time gesture recognition. Under the interference of visible light at 405 nm, this device achieves an on‐chip recognition accuracy up to 98.8%, significantly outperforming the pristine device (50.9%). This low‐cost and transferable bio‐inspired integration provides a practical pathway toward robust non‐contact sensing for human‐machine interaction applications.
authors: Tao Zheng; Junyi Li; Guangjie Zhou; Jie Zhang; Xiang Lin; Yupeng Guo; Xinyue Niu; Chengyi Zhu; Wenxiao Wang; Jiewei Chen

title: Biometric Data Acquisition and Monitoring via Light Signal Processing Technologies
abstract: Wearable devices enable continuous monitoring of physiological parameters through non-invasive sensors. This paper presents a biometric data acquisition and monitoring system implemented on the open-source PineTime smartwatch. The system is designed for heart-rate estimation and stress assessment based on photoplethysmography (PPG) signal processing.The proposed system consists of two applications, HRX and Zenify. HRX provides real-time heart-rate monitoring by displaying the photoplethysmographic waveform, the current heart-rate estimate, and the minimum recorded heart rate. Zenify assesses stress through heart-rate variability (HRV) analysis and classifies stress levels as low, moderate, or high.The system architecture relies on the PineTime smartwatch’s built-in optical heart-rate sensor and accelerometer, which are combined with light-signal processing algorithms. The original InfiniTime firmware was replaced with Wasp-OS, an open-source MicroPython-based watch operating system that supports rapid development and testing of biometric applications.The proposed system may be applied in preventive medicine to support early detection of physiological abnormalities, stress monitoring, and personalized health management.
authors: Anna Hovakimyan; Areg Oseyan; Siranush A. Sargsyan
venue: International Journal of Data Processing & Networking

title: Braive: IoT Enabled Smart Braille Learning Glove for Assistive Education
abstract: Learning Braille is essential for visually impaired children, yet trained teachers and affordable tactile learning tools are scarce.This paper presents Braive, an IoT-based Braille learning system that pairs a wearable glove with an Android application over Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE).An ESP32 in the glove drives six vibration motors arranged as the dots of a Braille cell and reads six tactile switches for input.The Kotlin application offers a Learning Mode, a fivelevel gamified Practice Mode with an adaptive question generator, and a word-spelling Test Mode, while speech recognition, text-to-speech feedback and an on-device Room database allow fully offline operation.BLE latency, recognition accuracy and learning outcomes were not measured, and no study with visually impaired learners has yet been carried out.The two-part architecture keeps lesson logic on the phone and real-time actuation on the glove, providing a modular, low-cost approach to Braille education built from commodity components.
authors: Swathi S; Thanmayi Rai A; Thashvi Rai K; Vibha H D; Deepthi M B

title: Can a Sustained Fall in Daily Steps From a Person's Own Baseline Flag Incident Heart Failure? A Preregistered Validation in the All of Us Research Program (Stage 1, CDR v9) With an Unchanged Rerun in the Next Data Release (Stage 2)
abstract: Heart failure (HF) is often diagnosed late. In an earlier preregistered matched case-control study in the All of Us Research Program (registered October 27, 2026), Fitbit wearers walked about 1,000 fewer steps a day before HF diagnosis than matched controls, and the deficit was present before the first symptom visit, but average step features did not improve discrimination. This registration tests a different, clinically usable question in the full wearer cohort: whether a sustained fall in daily steps from a person's own year-earlier level (3 consecutive months, each at least 20% and 1,000 steps a day below the same month a year earlier) flags incident HF in the following 12 months, in adults aged 50 or older. We estimate the HF rate ratio after an alert, the rate ratio per 10% sustained decline, the positive predictive value, sensitivity and alert rate, overall and in a higher-risk group, with comparator outcomes to test specificity. Stage 1 uses CDR v9. Stage 2 reruns the same code unchanged on the next All of Us release, restricted to person-time after the v9 cutoff, as the confirmatory test.
authors: Samir Bipin Pancholy

title: Cardiac autonomic and behavioral signatures of clinically meaningful weight loss: a 12-week wearable study of 31,126 adults
abstract: Achieving ≥5% body weight loss is clinically meaningful for reducing cardiometabolic risk, yet most evidence on the physiological and behavioral correlates of early weight loss comes from small, supervised interventions. Whether these adaptations replicate using consumer wearable data in free-living adults is unclear. We analyzed 12 weeks of near-continuous wearable data from 31,126 adults (37.4 ± 10.4 years, 79% male, BMI 29.7 ± 4.2 kg/m 2 ) who initiated a weight-loss goal within a consumer health platform (WHOOP). Participants achieving ≥5% weight loss ( n = 4,465; 14.3%) were 1:1 propensity-matched to participants who did not (3,912 pairs; N = 7,824). We compared trajectories of cardiac autonomic function (heart rate variability [HRV], resting heart rate [RHR]), physical activity (Strain), sleep, application engagement, and artificial intelligence (AI) Coach interactions. The weight loss group lost 7.5% of body weight versus 0.9% in the matched group, with greater improvements in HRV (+2.78 ms, 95% CI [1.71, 3.85]) and RHR (−1.75 bpm [−2.10, −1.40]) by Week 12, with between-group differences emerging at Week 4. Physical activity was the strongest behavioral predictor of clinically meaningful weight loss ( β = −0.72 [−0.77, −0.67]; OR = 1.22 per Strain unit, 95% CI [1.19, 1.24]). Application engagement and AI Coach interactions, particularly motivation and exercise discussions, were independently associated with ≥5% weight loss and percent weight change. Consumer wearables can capture physiological and behavioral signatures of clinically meaningful early weight loss in free-living adults.
authors: Jenna G. Cohen; Christian P. Cheung; William von Hippel; Dylan J. Curran; Finnbarr Fielding; Lauren R. Parola; Christopher J Chapman; Kristen Erika Holmes; Gregory J. Grosicki

title: Cardiopulmonary Exercise Testing in Preoperative Assessment: From Exercise Physiology to Personalized Perioperative Care
abstract: Major surgery imposes physiological stress requiring coordinated adaptation of the cardiovascular, respiratory, hematological, and musculoskeletal systems. Conventional preoperative assessment remains essential but may underestimate heterogeneity in physiological reserve because resting measurements incompletely capture the response to increasing metabolic demand. Cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) provides an integrated assessment of oxygen transport and utilization, linking pulmonary ventilation and gas exchange to cardiovascular performance and peripheral oxygen extraction. This narrative review examines the role of CPET in preoperative assessment, from prognostic testing to physiological phenotyping and personalized perioperative care. We summarize the physiological basis of key variables, including peak oxygen uptake, anaerobic threshold, oxygen pulse, ventilatory efficiency, end-tidal carbon dioxide, breathing reserve, and exercise kinetics, and discuss how integrated interpretation can identify patterns suggestive of haemodynamic, ventilatory, pulmonary vascular, or peripheral limitations. Evidence across major surgical populations is critically appraised, with attention to isolated thresholds and the distinction between prognostic association and clinical effectiveness. The current data support selective rather than universal use of CPET, particularly when functional capacity is uncertain or physiological information may alter management. We propose a phenotype-oriented framework in which CPET findings identify potentially modifiable impairments and inform cardiovascular optimization, respiratory treatment, nutritional support, exercise training, and prehabilitation. Emerging approaches combining complex CPET, non-invasive haemodynamic assessment, wearable technologies, and artificial intelligence may enable personalized profiling, although prospective validation remains necessary. CPET should therefore be considered not simply a risk-prediction tool, but an in vivo interrogation of physiological reserve that can contribute to mechanism-oriented perioperative assessment.
authors: Carlo Vignati; Piergiuseppe Agostoni; Beatrice Pezzuto
venue: Journal of Cardiovascular Development and Disease

title: Caregiver engagement with notifications based on resident-monitoring parameters in dementia care
abstract: In person-centred dementia care, early detection of behavioural changes prevents escalating situations. However, sensor-derived notifications frequently lack supporting situational context. Integrating caregiver feedback via active learning addresses this deficit, yet operational workload restricts technology interaction. This study analyses caregiver-technology interactions and feedback on resident-status notifications to initialize active learning in dementia care. We retrospectively compare context-aware event selection to a static threshold method to evaluate its effect on engagement. A 7-week pilot study in a Dutch nursing home monitored two residents using smartwatches and ambient sensors. Following a 25-day baseline, caregivers received high heart-rate notifications (n = 96) via shared departmental smartphones on which they provided free-text responses. Engagement evaluation included response frequency, latency, and shift-level temporal patterns. Caregivers responded to 65% of notifications. Response likelihood increased and stabilized over time, indicating a required adaptation period. Baseline data was used to train resident-specific models to forecast physiological states. A retrospective comparison demonstrated that applying predictive-error thresholds selected partially different physiological events compared to static thresholds. Although both models yielded similar response rates and feedback content, the context-aware approach theoretically optimizes active learning by filtering predictable variance. To establish viable initialization strategies in dementia care, future context-aware models must integrate spatial-temporal reasoning, Cyber-Physical-Human System ontology grounding, and structured feedback elicitation.
authors: Jan Kleine Deters; Burcu Güvenatam; Jair Adriano Lima Silva; Sarah I. M. Janus; H. J. Wörtche

title: Chapter 9: IoT-Integrated Digital Twins and Artificial Intelligence for Smart Automotive and Mechanical System Management
abstract: The increasing operational complexity, electrification, and structural integration of intelligent automotive and mechanical systems demand continuous, high-fidelity monitoring of internal physical states that cannot be directly measured by onboard physical sensors. Critical electro-thermal and mechanical states—such as internal lithium-ion battery core temperatures, permanent magnet rotor thermal demagnetization flux, dynamic bearing lubricant film thickness, and structural micro-strain concentrations—remain hidden behind solid metal casings or within high-voltage environments. Relying exclusively on surface-mounted physical sensors introduces severe measurement time lags and spatial errors that degrade control performance and compromise safety margins.
authors: M. Saravanakumar M; J. Manoj Prabhakar J

title: Clinical Implementation of Continuous Glucose Monitoring for Hospitalized Patients: A Position Statement of the Korean Diabetes Association Digital Health Committee
abstract: Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) has emerged as a promising approach to improving glycemic management in hospitalized individuals. Evidence from inpatient studies supports the benefits of CGM in monitoring glucose trends and improving the detection of otherwise unrecognized hypoglycemic and hyperglycemic episodes. Improvements in glycemic control have also been reported with CGM-integrated management, although these benefits may depend on structured insulin titration protocols, confirmatory point-of-care testing, dedicated glycemic management teams, and institutional workflows. However, the inpatient setting presents unique challenges, including hemodynamic instability, surgical interventions, radiologic procedures, and potential drug interference, which may affect CGM accuracy and safety. Systematic guidelines for implementing CGM in inpatient care remain scarce internationally, highlighting the need for structured evidence synthesis and practical recommendations. In this position statement, the Korean Diabetes Association Digital Health Committee reviews current evidence on the efficacy and accuracy of CGM in inpatient settings and highlights key considerations for its safe implementation, including target populations, hybrid monitoring strategies, and procedural safety. We propose an operational framework for inpatient CGM use, aiming to establish a foundation for its systematic adoption and to inform future institutional and regulatory frameworks.
authors: Jee Hee Yoo; Sun Joon Moon; Won‐Young Lee; So Yoon Kwon; Kyuho Kim; Joonyub Lee; Yunjung Cho; Sungrae Kim; Jae‐Seung Yun

title: Clinical performance and applicability of prediction models using wearable‐derived physiologic signals to anticipate migraine or headache attacks: A systematic review
abstract: OBJECTIVE: This study evaluated the performance, risk of bias, and clinical applicability of prediction models using wearable-derived or ambulatory physiologic signals to anticipate short-term migraine or headache outcomes in adults. BACKGROUND: A migraine or headache forecast can support self-management only when it is accurate, calibrated, actionable, and associated with an acceptable false-alarm burden. Wearable devices estimate autonomic, activity, and sleep-related features from surrogate signals, but their clinical readiness has not been systematically evaluated. METHODS: We reviewed prediction-model studies using objective wearable or ambulatory physiologic signals to anticipate migraine or headache outcomes in adults. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science Core Collection were searched from inception to May 18, 2026. Reporting was structured according to Transparent Reporting of a Multivariable Prediction Model for Individual Prognosis or Diagnosis-Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses, with Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses 2020 used for study selection. We used Prediction Model Risk of Bias Assessment Tool/Prediction Model Risk of Bias Assessment Tool +artificial intelligence-compatible criteria and a task-specific narrative synthesis. RESULTS: Eight studies were included. Tasks were near-onset detection (20-40 min), night-to-next-day forecasting, and multi-day forecasting. Among comparable models, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve ranged from 0.62 to 0.84. In the largest study (146 adults; 21,550 prediction days), area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was 0.84 (95% confidence interval, 0.82-0.85) for next-day moderate-to-severe headache and 0.76 (95% confidence interval, 0.74-0.77) for a 3-day horizon. Five studies had high analysis-domain risk of bias and three had some concerns. No study reported external validation; calibration was reported once. CONCLUSION: Wearable-based prediction models remain early proof-of-concept studies, not clinically validated alert systems. Their reported discrimination may partly reflect between-person differences in headache frequency rather than within-person forecasting. External validation, calibration, threshold-specific alert burden, and evidence that acting on forecasts improves outcomes are needed before clinical use.

title: Compass: Continuously Aligning Social Media Feeds via In-Situ Reflections
abstract: Social media recommendation feeds often optimize for users’ immediate impulses rather than preferences they would hold after deeper reflection. Some systems address this misalignment by incorporating users’ explicit preferences via a configuration page or in-feed controls instead of just behavioral signals. However, users typically have evolving preferences, and their stated preferences and behavior naturally diverge, necessitating continuous reflection and feed realignment. But existing strategies require the user to take initiative and are often effortful; as a result, in practice they are rarely invoked. We present Compass, a system that aligns a user’s feed with their reflective preferences by helping users reflect on and articulate their preferences given their behavior. To enable continuous reflection during everyday browsing, Compass surfaces in-situ reflections via lightweight notifications, while feed alignment is achieved by periodically simulating behavioral signals and directly manipulating feed content. We embedded Compass within YouTube Shorts and compared it against a baseline without continuous support through a 10-day field study (N = 15). We found that Compass promoted more reflective and purposeful feed consumption, iterative preference adjustment, and stronger feed alignment, without sacrificing the casual nature of feed browsing.
authors: Aadit Barua; Leijie Wang; Amy X. Zhang
venue: ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)

title: Compassion-Focused Implementation of Smartwatches in Acute Mental Health Care: Mixed Method Replicated Single-Case Study
abstract: Background: Smartwatches can support mental health care by providing insights into activity and sleep, which are closely linked to mental health and daily functioning. However, their implementation in mental health care practice remains limited. Professionals can feel resistance toward digital mental health interventions if they feel their use is not aligned with therapeutic values, and report a need for guidance on how to use technologies in ways that do align with such values. Compassion, a core value in mental health care, may offer a meaningful frame for implementation. Therefore, we previously co-designed compassion-focused implementation materials: a card set offering practical suggestions of how smartwatch data can support group treatments in ways that counter the self-optimization logic of commercial devices and instead align with compassion. Objective: The current study evaluated the compassion-focused card set in practice, to explore whether the introduction of the card set influenced the use of smartwatches in treatment sessions, and mental health professionals' experienced compassion when working with smartwatches, the therapeutic alliance, and acceptance of smartwatches. Methods: The card set was evaluated in a mixed methods replicated single-case design with 5 social psychiatric nurses from an acute mental health care team. Data collection included pre- and post-questionnaires, repeated measures, a focus group, and interviews. Results: =.02). This participant reported that the card set helped to make the use of smartwatches more concrete and insightful. For therapeutic alliance and acceptance of the smartwatches, no intervention effects were found. These scores were rather stable over time for most participants. The card set was experienced as flexible and easy to use, supporting session structure and enabling more in-depth, compassionate conversations. At the same time, barriers to sustained smartwatch integration included low patient uptake, challenges in mixed groups in which only some patients wore the smartwatch, and varying digital affinity among professionals. Conclusions: These findings suggest that compassion-focused materials may trigger initial adoption and help reframe smartwatch use in line with therapeutic values. Broader implementation strategies, including further training and tailoring to patient readiness, are required for sustainable integration.
authors: Charlotte M. van Lotringen; Tessa Dekkers; Saskia M. Kelders; Gerben J. Westerhof; Matthijs Leendert Noordzij

title: Contactless Oxygen Desaturation Prediction and Oxygen Desaturation Index (ODI) Estimation from Nocturnal Breathing Sounds via Deep Learning
abstract: STUDY OBJECTIVES: Intermittent hypoxemia is increasingly recognized as a stronger predictor of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality in obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) than the apnea-hypopnea index (AHI). We developed a sound-based AI model to detect oxygen desaturation events and estimate the oxygen desaturation index (ODI) from nocturnal breathing sounds in a fully contactless manner. METHODS: The model was trained using 2,973 nights of synchronized polysomnography (PSG) and audio recordings obtained from hospital- and home-based settings. Validation and independent testing were performed on 664 and 802 nights, respectively. Audio signals were converted into Mel spectrograms and processed using a Vision Transformer-based architecture. Performance was evaluated at the 30-second epoch level using sensitivity, specificity, precision, F1 score, accuracy, and Cohen's κ. ODI estimation was assessed using Pearson correlation, Bland-Altman analysis, mean absolute error (MAE), and root mean square error (RMSE). RESULTS: For epoch-by-epoch desaturation detection, the model achieved a sensitivity of 0.79, specificity of 0.95, precision of 0.78, F1 score of 0.79, overall accuracy of 0.92, and κ of 0.74. Estimated ODI showed agreement with PSG-derived ODI (r = 0.93, R² = 0.87, p < 0.001). Bland-Altman analysis demonstrated a mean bias of -0.29 events/h with 95% limits of agreement from -14.73 to 14.14 events/h. CONCLUSIONS: Breathing sound-based deep learning enables contactless detection of oxygen desaturation events and reliable ODI estimation. This approach may provide a scalable, non-contact method for sleep-disordered breathing assessment in real-world settings.
authors: Hayun Choi; Eunsung Cho; Seunghun Kim; Sungjin Heo; Sungeun Moon; Joonki Hong; Dongheon Lee; Sujin Lee; Jeong-Whun Kim; In-Young Yoon

title: Cybersecurity-driven communication framework for edge-assisted satellite internet of things environmental monitoring
abstract: Satellite-enabled Internet of Things (IoT) networks collect environmental observations where terrestrial backhaul is absent, but an authenticated packet can still carry stale, replayed, fabricated, or implausible telemetry. This article presents SAFE, a Secure Adaptive Framework for Edge-Assisted Satellite-Enabled IoT, in which the edge gateway admits telemetry to a low-Earth-orbit pass only after five calibrated trust anchors pass a non-compensatory lattice test. A corroborated-event rule retains spatially consistent extreme observations. Pass-bounded micro-sessions derive ratcheted epoch keys, attach gateway and end-to-end tags to every capsule, and resynchronise after lost receipts, missed passes, or gateway restarts. Theorems bound forgery, replay, rollback, and key-compromise exposure. SAFE was evaluated by replaying U.S. Climate Reference Network and U.S. Geological Survey observations for wildfire, snowpack, groundwater, and flood deployments, propagating a 12-satellite constellation with SGP4, and comparing SAFE against six baseline implementations with stated approximations. Across 120 paired runs, SAFE contained 99.1% of attack attempts (best baseline: 50.8%), delivered trusted alerts with a median in-contact latency of 13.6 s, and consumed 0.787 J per trusted capsule.
authors: Muhammad Qasim; Kamran Ahmad Awan; Meshari Huwaytim Alanazi; Anand Nayyar; Sumendra Yogarayan; Mueen Uddin

title: Deep Learning Object Detection for Maritime Security: A Critical Review of Task Evidence, Benchmark Comparability and Deployment Constraints
abstract: Deep learning has been used successfully for object detection in optical, infrared,SAR, and multispectral images of maritime environments. Nevertheless, itsdeployment in maritime security systems remains challenging. This review anal-yses major object detection architectures, sensing methods, application domains,and deployment constraints in this domain. The most frequently representeddetection architectures in the reviewed papers include You Only Look Once(YOLO) detectors (199 papers) and attention-based and transformer models(123 papers). Tracking, multimodal fusion, threat reasoning, and detector secu-rity are much less represented. There are also major deficiencies in evaluationpractices. For example, 121 out of 299 papers reporting detection metrics donot provide an intersection-over-union threshold value. Inference latency, energyconsumption, and target hardware are also insufficiently reported in many stud-ies. Besides detection accuracy, we discuss how security-task evidence affectsbenchmark selection and detector deployment in communication-aware settings.The review provides a reporting checklist and a roadmap for future research.Future work should concentrate on multimodal benchmarks, small-object detec-tion, cross-sensor generalisation, trustworthy sensor fusion, edge intelligence, andrealistic evaluation of detectors.
authors: Syed Muhammad Waqas; Muhammad Ahsan; Fahad Ur Rehman; Muhammad Bilal Jeeva; Mazliham Mohd Suud; Romeis Riaz; Muhammad Usman Khan; Mansoor Alam

title: Defect-Engineered ZIF-8-Derived Nanoporous Carbon for Ultra-Stable Flexible Cryogenic Thermistors and Ultra-Miniature Physiological Sensors.
abstract: In cryogenic electronics and biomedicine, there is a growing need for flexible temperature sensors operating reliably down to liquid-nitrogen temperatures while conforming to complex, moving surfaces. However, state-of-the-art metal or ceramic thermistors are rigid and bulky, whereas polymer and hydrogel sensors lose conductivity or drift severely below -150°C, making robust cryogenic sensing extremely challenging. Herein, we design a ZIF-8-derived nanoporous carbon as a cryogenic thermistor material by rational defect engineering. By tuning the carbonization temperature, the heteroatom/vacancy defect landscape (N, O, Zn, and carbon vacancies) is programmed to balance percolated graphitic pathways and dense ionized impurity centers, leading to ionized-impurity-scattering-dominated transport at deep cryogenic temperatures. The printed carbon thermistors exhibit a wide operating window from 150 to -190°C, a high cryogenic temperature coefficient of resistance (TCR) up to -4.7%/°C, a temperature resolution of 0.05°C, and a response time of 0.58 s. After 100 days of immersion in liquid nitrogen, the TCR drift remains within ±0.2%, evidencing outstanding long-term cryogenic stability. Benefiting from the printable nature, 0.3 × 0.3 mm2 micro-thermistors are integrated into cryopreservation needles and oxygen tubes for real-time in vivo freeze-thaw monitoring and contactless sensing, demonstrating the promise of defect-engineered MOF-derived carbons for next-generation flexible cryogenics.
authors: Qingqing Hu; Xuemin Chen; Yubo Huang; Yunfeng Zhan; Guanting Chen; Haolong Wu; Zixuan Liang; Hao Zhang; Lu Yao; Zixuan Wu; Xiufeng Tang; Jianyi Luo

title: Defining the clinical benefits of disease-modifying therapy in people living with spinal muscular atrophy who require permanent ventilation: a UK-based modified Delphi consensus process
abstract: Background: Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is a rare inherited neuromuscular disorder that may require permanent ventilation (PV) in severe cases. Although disease-modifying therapies (DMTs) have transformed outcomes for many, prior to this research, access in the UK was restricted for patients receiving PV (SMA-PV). This study aimed to develop consensus recommendations on DMT use and to define clinical benefit in SMA-PV. Methods: A multidisciplinary UK-based expert panel conducted a modified Delphi consensus process between 08 April and 09 June 2025. Draft statements informed by published evidence and expert insights were anonymously voted on for up to three rounds, with consensus defined as ≥75% agreement. Statements not achieving consensus were revised and re-evaluated. Input from a non-voting patient advisory panel (PAP) was also considered. The study was not prospectively registered. Findings: Excluding the Chair, 18 participants evaluated 22 statements across seven thematic areas specific to SMA-PV: DMT access; treatment initiation; treatment monitoring; defining clinical benefit; functional outcomes; quality of life (QoL); and future research priorities. All 22 statements achieved consensus after two voting rounds (100% participation; agreement range 89-100%). Two statements were revised and re-voted in round 2: one after narrowly missing consensus (72% agreement) and the other to incorporate PAP feedback despite achieving 100% agreement in round 1. The panel agreed that PV alone should not preclude access to DMTs and that trial access with personalised treatment goals may be appropriate. The panel also emphasised broader definitions of clinical benefit, including subtle changes in function and QoL, alongside sensitive assessment approaches and harmonised outcome measurement. Interpretation: These consensus-based recommendations support careful reconsideration of treatment exclusions for patients with SMA-PV and more inclusive, patient-centred approaches to evaluating treatment benefit. Funding: Roche Products Ltd.
