title: Demo: Surface Material and Roughness Sensing via mmWave Vibrometry
abstract: mmWave sensing has emerged as a promising contactless solution for object detection and material sensing. While existing material-sensing approaches exploit differences in mmWave signal reflectivity, their performance in understanding fine-grained surface characteristics, such as texture and roughness, is limited by sensing wavelength and spatial resolution. We propose mmTexora, a novel system that extends mmWave material sensing to surface roughness sensing for robotic grasping and manipulation. mmTexora adapts vibrometry principles to mmWave radar by leveraging ambient vibrations from sources such as air conditioning or machinery, which subtly modulate surface scattering and embed roughness-related information in the received radar signals. By extracting these vibration-induced features, mm-Texora enables texture and roughness sensing in quasi-static scenes. In this demonstration, we show that a simplified mmTexora prototype using a single TI AWR1843 mmWave radar can identify surfaces made of different materials and distinguish surfaces with different textures and roughness levels, even when they are made of the same material.
authors: Y. F. Liu; Swarun Kumar
venue: ACM Annual International Conference on Mobile Computing and Networking (MobiCom)

title: Design and Development of Smart Obstacle Detection Glasses for Visually Impaired Persons
abstract: This paper presents the design and development of smart obstacle detection glasses intended to assist visually impaired persons in identifying obstacles in front of them. The prototype is built around an Arduino Nano microcontroller and an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor mounted on a spectacle frame. The sensor measures the distance to an object by transmitting ultrasonic waves and receiving the reflected echo. The Arduino Nano processes the sensor output and activates an audible alert through a 5 V active buzzer when an obstacle is detected. A green light-emitting diode (LED) is also included as a visual status indicator. The system is powered by a rechargeable 3.7 V lithium-ion battery using a TP4056 charging module and a 5 V boost converter. The developed prototype is reported to be operational and provides a compact, wearable approach to front-side obstacle warning. The design focuses on affordability, portability, and simple operation. The present version uses one ultrasonic sensor and therefore provides front-direction detection only. Multi-direction sensing, voice guidance, and improved outdoor performance are identified as possible future enhancements.
authors: Priya Chaughule; Ujwal Ankush Karle

title: Design and Evaluation of a Low-Cost IoT Indoor Air Quality Monitoring Prototype for Early Hazard Detection and Alerting
abstract: Affordable indoor environmental monitors provide practical potential for continuous exposure tracking and timely hazard notification in resource-constrained environments such as schools, offices, and households. However, deploying low-cost prototypes for early hazard alerting requires distinguishing functional system actuation from calibrated analytical measurement. This study evaluates the design, sensor acquisition behavior, and threshold-driven notification logic of an Internet of Things (IoT) indoor air quality monitoring prototype. The hardware architecture integrates an Arduino UNO and ESP32 microcontroller paired with a DHT22 temperature and humidity sensor, an MQ135 metal-oxide semiconductor gas sensor for volatile chemical vapors, and a GP2Y1010AU0F optical dust sensor for airborne particulates. The prototype was tested across baseline conditions and six simulated indoor exposure scenarios: elevated heat, high moisture, medicated oil vapor, incense combustion, adhesive solvent vapor, and smoke particulates. Baseline readings were 32.3 °C, 62.3% relative humidity, 1.20 for the gas response indicator, and 9.1 for the dust response indicator. Thermal and moisture stimuli drove temperature and relative humidity to 37.2 °C and 85.9%, respectively. Gas response indicators increased to 3.13, 6.59, and 4.15 under medicated oil, incense, and glue exposures, while smoke exposure elevated the dust response indicator to 35.5. Across all six exposure cases, the automated relay reliably engaged ventilation fans, and four scenarios exceeding upper setpoints initiated local auditory alarms and remote cloud-based mobile alerts. While low-cost sensors exhibit non-linearities, uncalibrated scaling, and cross-sensitivities that preclude direct clinical exposure grading, the prototype demonstrates reliable threshold-driven functional execution. These findings support the viability of accessible IoT systems as early-warning risk communication tools, provided they are supported by secondary reference calibration and qualitative risk framing.
authors: Anis Niza Ramani; Kiang Zheng Yu; Kyairul Azmi Baharin; Aine Izzati Tarmizi
venue: International journal of research and scientific innovation

title: Design and evaluation of a behaviorally adaptive, multi-channel phishing simulation and training platform
abstract: Phishing attacks have expanded beyond email to SMS and social media, yet most awareness-training platforms remain email-centric, provide no real-time behavioral measurement, and deliver generic feedback long after a simulated failure. This paper presents the design, implementation, and empirical evaluation of a Behaviorally Adaptive, Multi-Channel Phishing Simulation and Training Platform (PhishSim) built on Python Flask, React.js, and PostgreSQL. The system delivers browser-rendered phishing stimuli across email, SMS, and mock social-media channels with no third-party messaging dependencies, computes a Behavioral Risk Score (BRS) from click-through rate, normalized click latency, a channel vulnerability multiplier, and a failure-frequency modifier, and routes participants to channel-specific micro-training the moment a simulation is failed. A two-group, pre-test/post-test randomized controlled pilot study was conducted with 10 undergraduate volunteers at the Air Force Institute of Technology (AFIT), Kaduna, Nigeria, across three simulation cycles; because the pilot fell short of its planned 40-participant, adequately powered design, all findings reported here are preliminary and directional rather than confirmatory. Results show that the BRS engine computes mathematically accurate and well-differentiated risk scores (range 0–68 in Cycle 1) and that the adaptive-training router correctly triggers channel-specific interventions. A paired-samples analysis of the available longitudinal data (n = 5 participants who completed more than one cycle) found no statistically significant change in BRS (t(4) = −0.59, p = 0.587; Wilcoxon W = 1.0, p = 1.00; Cohen's d = −0.26), which is consistent with a pilot too small and too incomplete to detect an effect rather than with an absence of one. This work extends the multi-channel simulation framework of Alsaqer et al. [12], which was validated only on simulated data, through a real-user evaluation, and it contributes two mechanisms absent from the baseline model: a failure-frequency escalation modifier and a channel-vulnerability offset term, together with an explicit weight-sensitivity analysis of the scoring formula.
authors: Abdurraheem Adedamola Abdulfattah; Bello Musa Yakubu; Samson Adeyinka
venue: Journal of Statistical Sciences and Computational Intelligence

title: Developing JEEVHITAA: Designing and Evaluating a Human-Centered AI Ecosystem for Collective Care
abstract: Health management is often a collective activity, involving family members and close relations in monitoring, interpreting, and coordinating care. Yet, most digital health technologies remain individual-centric, offering limited support for the distributed responsibilities and negotiated information sharing that characterize collective care. We present JEEVHITAA, a human-centered AI ecosystem designed to address this gap. Drawing on existing literature on collective health practices, we identify key requirements and translate them into a canonical ontology and a versioned data schema that underpin a mobile ecosystem integrating wearable data, role-aware sharing, granular access controls, auditable histories, and AI-assisted health summarization and verification. We first evaluated core system primitives using 1,000 ontology-driven synthetic care circles to test data visibility and information-processing workflows. We then conducted a controlled lab study with 13 subject--care-actor dyads (26 participants), combining task-based interactions, semi-structured interviews, the System Usability Scale, and component-level usability assessments. Findings indicate positive perceptions of usability and highlight the value of granular sharing and transparent information provenance. They also expose tensions between reciprocal transparency and surveillance, and between AI-mediated assistance and potentially intrusive notifications. We discuss implications for designing accountable, context-sensitive technologies that support collective care.
authors: Shyama Sastha Krishnamoorthy Srinivasan; Harsh Pala; Shahnawaz; Mohan Kumar; Pushpendra Singh

title: Development of a Lyapunov-based online RPM-task offloading method with migration control
abstract: The object of research is the processes of dynamic allocation of computational tasks in heterogeneous Edge-Fog infrastructures of remote patient monitoring systems. The problem of dynamic distribution of computational tasks in remote health monitoring systems was addressed. In particular, ensuring a balance between medical data processing latency, energy consumption of wearable devices and compliance with deadlines. Additionally, user mobility, changes in the quality of wireless communication and the cost of transferring tasks between Edge and Fog nodes were taken into account. Data confidentiality was ensured using secure communication channels, remote attestation and a trusted environment for execution. A system model of dynamic distribution of RPM tasks in a multi-level Cloud-Fog-Edge-IoT infrastructure was developed. The model covers ECG classification (Electrocardiogram, ECG), arrhythmia detection, temperature analysis and user activity recognition. An online offloading algorithm based on Lyapunov theory (Migration-Gated Lyapunov Offloading, MGLO) is proposed. The algorithm accounts for energy consumption, delay, deadlines and the costs of changing the execution node. To protect medical data, the use of TEE (Trusted Execution Environment), secure communication channels and remote attestation of Fog nodes is provided. To validate the solutions, a series of simulations were conducted in the YAFS (Yet Another Fog Simulator) environment with a comparison of the Edge only, LP and Horizon MILP scenarios in modes with and without handover support. It was experimentally established that the proposed MGLO algorithm provides effective distribution of RPM tasks in a mobile Edge-Fog environment. In the mode without handover support, the total energy consumption of wearable devices decreased by more than 2 times compared to the Edge only scenario (from 1,354.74 mWh to 630.15 mWh). In the handover mode, the energy consumption decreased by more than 5 times (from 1,354.74 mWh to 259.39 mWh). The proportion of deadline violations was 0.14% and 0.12%, respectively. The average decision time was 1.9 ms (54–85 times faster compared to the Horizon MILP scenario). Overall, the results confirmed the feasibility of using MGLO for online offloading management in remote health monitoring systems.
authors: I.O. Shevtsov; Tetiana Fesenko

title: Diagnostic accuracy of wearable technologies for atrial fibrillation detection: a systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia and a major cause of ischemic stroke. Because AF is frequently paroxysmal and asymptomatic, conventional short-term monitoring often fails to detect it. Wearable technologies have emerged as promising tools for AF screening, but their diagnostic performance requires comprehensive evaluation. We conducted a systematic review and diagnostic test accuracy meta-analysis following PRISMA-DTA guidelines. PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception to 25 February 2026 for prospective and retrospective studies using electrocardiographic reference standards. Bivariate random-effects and Bayesian hierarchical models were used to pool diagnostic accuracy estimates. Fifty-one studies involving 33,374 participants from 15 countries were included. PPG-based smartwatches demonstrated the highest sensitivity (96.3%) with specificity of 93.6%. ECG-based smartwatches achieved sensitivity of 89.0% and specificity of 92.8% (DOR 103.9). Smartphone-based ECG devices showed the strongest overall diagnostic performance, with sensitivity of 94.5%, specificity of 95.8%, DOR of 396.4, LR+ of 22.6, and LR− of 0.057. Smartphone-based PPG applications achieved sensitivity of 92.0% and specificity of 91.9%. Apple Watch demonstrated sensitivity of 94.1% and specificity of 94.6%. Meta-regression revealed no statistically significant differences in diagnostic accuracy between device categories despite slightly higher point estimates for PPG-based smartwatches. No significant publication bias was detected (Deeks' test, p=0.18). Wearable devices demonstrate excellent diagnostic accuracy for AF detection, particularly smartphone-based ECG applications. These technologies support scalable AF screening and monitoring, although heterogeneity in study populations and diagnostic thresholds should be considered when applying these findings to routine clinical practice.
authors: Alina Abbas; Gauhar Hamid; Beesham Kumar; Sajida Moiz Hussain Qamari; Hira Riaz

title: Digital Phenotypes of Obstructive Sleep Apnea in the Natural Home Environment: A Scoping Review
abstract: This scoping review maps the digital indicators and digital phenotypes used to characterize obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) in adult natural home settings. OSA is commonly assessed by in-hospital polysomnography (PSG), which is costly and provides only a short-time-point measurement; core metrics such as the apnea–hypopnea index (AHI) show substantial night-to-night variability, and a single-night recording may overestimate or underestimate a patient's true disease status. Wearable and contactless sensing technologies enable home-based OSA screening and monitoring, but existing studies vary widely in features, preprocessing, validation paradigms, and time scales, and "digital phenotype" has no established operational definition in the OSA field. Following JBI scoping review guidance and reported in accordance with the PRISMA-ScR checklist, this review identifies the set of digital metrics used to characterize OSA-related physiological, sleep, and behavioral states in real home settings, and maps the health dimensions, time scales, stability evidence, and clinical validation approaches associated with these metrics. Eligible studies include adults (≥18 years) with identifiable home-collected OSA-related digital data; conference papers, abstracts, standards, book chapters, theses/dissertations, grey literature, reviews, commentaries, and case reports are excluded. Three databases (Web of Science Core Collection, PubMed, IEEE Xplore) are searched, supplemented by citation snowballing of eligible seed studies. The review does not assess evidence quality or pool effect sizes. Review question: In adult natural home settings, what reproducible digital metrics have been used to characterize or assess OSA-related physiological, sleep, and behavioral states? What health dimensions do these metrics reflect, at what time scale are they collected and analyzed, and what evidence is available for their clinical validity, measurement reliability, and within- and between-individual variability?
authors: Yao Chao; Qi Xia; Shilu Zhong

title: Digital transformation of clinical trials with remote patient monitoring solutions
abstract: Remote patient monitoring (RPM) is becoming increasingly feasible to implement in clinical trials. A framework is presented for developing RPM digital solutions incorporating the needs and perspectives of patients and healthcare professionals, and regulatory requirements/guidance. This framework is illustrated with recent examples of RPM deployments in the context of skin toxicities and stomatitis. Strategies to overcome challenges in the adoption of RPM solutions in clinical trials are discussed.
authors: Elisabeth Piault; Ramya Sita Palacholla; SIMON PULMAN‐JONES; Emmett Alton Sartor; Sergio Simön; Jill Bell

title: Disease progression shapes circadian and locomotor disruption in a model of multiple sclerosis
abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an autoimmune demyelinating disease of the central nervous system featuring a wide range of debilitating symptoms. Wearable activity recording devices have recently been adopted to improve symptom monitoring in MS, capturing symptoms related to sleep/wake cycles, circadian disruption, and fatigue. However, comparable measures of activity have yet been established in pre-clinical models of MS, the most widely used being experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE). We therefore sought to characterize changes in continual home-cage activity over the course of EAE, and establish whether home-cage monitoring can be used as an observer-independent measure of disease progression. Our results showed that locomotor activity in the mid-active/dark phase was most severely affected by EAE. Disrupted circadian (24-hour) activity was observed during the peak and onset stages of disease. Bout activity analysis revealed >40-minute long activity bouts as a sensitive indicator of non-motor symptoms independent of clinical score-based motor deficits. Current assessment of disease progression in EAE relies on clinical scores, which primarily assess motor deficits through visual observation prone to observer bias. Various computed activity parameters were found to be altered during key disease stages, suggesting that a combination of activity measures can serve as objective indicators of disease progression. Overall, our results show that home-cage activity effectively captures signs of non-motor symptoms in the EAE model of MS and can serve as an observer-independent measure of EAE disease progression.
authors: Vina Wenyu Li; Julia P. Segal; Nader Ghasemlou

title: Do We Still Need Conventional Holter ECGs in the Era of Smart Devices?
abstract: Wearable devices for rhythm monitoring are increasingly available and are being used by patients across a broad spectrum of technologies, including smartwatches with electrocardiogram (ECG)-recording functions and ECG patch systems. Early development of automated rhythm classification algorithms using artificial intelligence primarily focused on atrial fibrillation (AF), although indications and validated use cases differ substantially between device types and continue to evolve. This review aims to provide an overview of contemporary smart devices, their capabilities in arrhythmia care, and future perspectives. Currently, two main technologies are used for rhythm assessment: photoplethysmography (PPG) and single- or multi-lead electrocardiography. PPG enables continuous monitoring of heart rate and pulse regularity, whereas ECG acquisition is typically user-initiated. The use of a 30-second single-lead ECG (SL-ECG) strip with physician confirmation for the diagnosis of AF is supported by current ESC AF guidelines. Systematic screening approaches using wearables have demonstrated higher AF detection rates compared with standard diagnostic pathways; however, whether this translates into improved stroke prevention remains to be proven. Beyond AF, wearables may be particularly useful for infrequent symptomatic arrhythmias, such as supraventricular tachycardias, by enabling SL-ECG recording during symptoms and thereby supporting diagnosis and management. Additional applications include monitoring of QT prolongation, conduction disturbances, and rhythm surveillance following interventions. As an established alternative to user-dependent ECG acquisition, ECG patches provide continuous rhythm recording for up to 30 days and are generally more user-friendly than conventional Holter monitoring. A key challenge remains automated rhythm detection for non-AF arrhythmias, as well as a relevant proportion of inconclusive tracings in real-world populations, for example in the presence of conduction abnormalities or frequent premature atrial or ventricular complexes. From a physician's perspective, clear workflows and dedicated technical solutions are essential to manage the growing volume of data, and reimbursement mechanisms for analysis of these recordings must be established. Ultimately, the future of wearable-based rhythm monitoring lies in its structured integration into clinical workflows, enabling more individualized and optimized arrhythmia care. In parallel, combining rhythm information with additional health metrics may facilitate a more holistic approach to prevention and management of cardiovascular disease. Despite all technical advances, traditional Holter ECG still has irreplaceable value in patients with frequent arrhythmia symptoms or when coronary vasospasms or Brugada syndrome are suspected.
authors: Reto Stump; Jonas Brügger; Patrick Badertscher

title: Documented patient consent for ambient video monitoring technologies in an academic hospital: a cross-sectional analysis of consent outcomes and demographic differences
abstract: Objective To quantify the documented consent outcomes for ambient monitoring technologies in an academic hospital and evaluate whether documented consent acceptance differed by age, gender, and race. Patients and methods We performed a retrospective cross-sectional study of 9,522 consecutive patients approached for ambient monitoring consent during routine hospital care from 1/1/2025 to 2/12/2026. Consent status was categorized as received, refused, or missing/unable. The primary multivariable analysis used a binary outcome of documented acceptance (received vs. refused or missing/unable) modeled with age, gender, and race. Secondary models used age categories. Results Overall, 9,125 patients (95.8%) consented, 184 (1.9%) refused, and 213 (2.2%) had missing or unobtainable consent. Acceptance did not differ by gender (95.6% among female patients vs. 96.1% among male patients; adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 1.11, 95% CI 0.91–1.36; p = 0.30). Compared with White patients, lower adjusted odds of acceptance were observed among Black or African American patients (aOR 0.66, 95% CI 0.49–0.88; p = 0.005) and patients categorized as Unknown/Declined/Other (aOR 0.56, 95% CI 0.37–0.83; p = 0.004). Acceptance was highest among Asian patients, but the adjusted difference was not significant (aOR 2.44, 95% CI 0.90–6.59; p = 0.079). Acceptance exceeded 95% across all age groups and was highest among patients aged 65–74 years (96.7%). Younger patients more often refused, whereas older patients more often had missing or unobtainable consent. Conclusion Documented consent acceptance was high in this single academic hospital. Acceptance did not vary by gender, but modest differences were observed by race and age-related patterns. Consent status alone does not establish patient comprehension, voluntariness, motivation, or durable endorsement. These findings demonstrate operational feasibility while underscoring the need for transparent consent, subgroup monitoring, and prospective evaluation of patient experiences.
authors: Emily L. Godsey; Taylor M. Galloway; Jennifer S. Crews; Scott A. Helgeson

title: Domestic sensor-based monitoring for supporting independent-living older adults: A scoping review
abstract: Population ageing is accelerating globally, placing increasing pressure on local health and social care systems. Older people who remain living independently generally have better health outcomes and use fewer care resources. Moreover, many older people express a preference for living independently. Therefore, supporting independent living represents a cost-effective objective for health and care systems. One potential means for supporting such ageing in place is domestic sensor-based activity monitoring technologies; however, to date evidence on their effectiveness, usability, and real-world implementation has been inconclusive. A scoping review has been undertaken following PRISMA-ScR guidance to map the latest evidence on domestic passive sensor-based monitoring for older adults. Twenty-nine studies met the inclusion criteria; the evidence they provide suggests domestic sensors can support monitoring of activities of daily living, detect early functional or cognitive decline, and are generally acceptable to users. However, robust evidence for improved clinical outcomes, cost-effectiveness, and effective integration into health systems remains limited.
authors: Afia Murshida; Stephen Potter; Mark Hawley
venue: Journal of Ambient Intelligence and Smart Environments

title: Dyadic technology-based interventions for community-dwelling people with dementia and their informal caregivers in low- and middle-income countries: a scoping review
abstract: OBJECTIVES: Over 60% of people living with dementia reside in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), where limited awareness and scarce supportive services can intensify caregiver burden. Although dyadic technology-based interventions (DTIs) show promise in high-income countries, their scope in LMICs remains unclear. This scoping review aimed to identify the types of DTIs used for dementia dyads in LMICs and to map reported outcomes, with particular attention to caregiver burden. METHODS: This review followed JBI methodology for scoping reviews and was reported according to PRISMA-ScR. MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, CINAHL, Scopus, and Cochrane Library were searched without date restrictions. RESULTS: Twelve studies from six middle-income countries were included. Five technological platforms were identified: videoconferencing-based interventions, mobile applications, computer software, robotics, and ambient intelligence. Most DTIs were multifunctional, commonly supporting telemedicine or telerehabilitation and targeted health information or therapeutic content. Outcomes were heterogeneous and primarily focused on feasibility, acceptability, usability, and implementation rather than health-related outcomes. Most studies did not report caregiver burden directly, though two case studies suggested that ambient intelligence may reduce caregiver burden. CONCLUSION: Evidence on DTIs in LMICs is limited, fragmented, and largely excludes low-income countries. Further rigorous, context-sensitive studies on DTIs are needed to explore feasibility and effectiveness.
authors: Chi Linh Bui; Susan Rampling; Linh Kim Le Nguyen; Maayken van den Berg

title: EEG-Based Acute Stress Detection for Post-Trauma Rehabilitation and Biofeedback: Limits of Cross-Dataset Generalisation
abstract: Objective. EEG stress classifiers are usually trained and tested on a single dataset, and accuracies above 90% are common in the literature. We asked how much of this performance holds for participants the model has never seen, and for a dataset recorded with other hardware and another stress protocol.Approach. Two open datasets were processed with one pipeline: SAM40 (40 participants; Stroop, arithmetic and mirror-image tasks versus relaxation; 32-channel Emotiv, 128 Hz) and EEGMAT (36 participants; serial subtraction versus rest; 19-channel clinical system, 500 Hz). Four compact classifiers(logistic regression, random forest and RBF-SVM on band power, and a Riemannian tangent-space classifier) were evaluated with leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) validation, with cross-corpus transfer in both directions on ten shared electrodes, and with two unsupervised alignment methods, Riemannian re-centring and CORAL. Main results. Within SAM40, the best LOSO macro-F1 for one stressor against relaxation was 70.3% (best AUROC 0.804). Cross-corpus transfer lowered macro-F1 significantly in 22 of 24 model–direction–stressor settings (pairedWilcoxon test, ???? < 0.01), by up to 37.6 percentage points. Transfer was asymmetric: classifiers trained on EEGMAT reached an AUROC below 0.5 on SAM40 in 9 of 12 settings, so the learned decision direction was reversed. Re-centring improved within-corpus performance (EEGMAT macro-F1 from 0.690 to 0.728) but not transfer, whereas CORAL raised the EEGMAT→SAM40 AUROC of band-power models by 0.04–0.19. Removing ocular components withICA reduced band-power macro-F1 by only 1.1–3.0 points. Significance. Stress labels defined by the task carry protocol-specific information that does not survive a change of dataset. Cross-corpus testing should come before any claim that an EEG stress detector is ready for everyday or biofeedback use.
authors: Anar Mengdigali; Medet Mukushev; Beibit Abdikenov; Almira Kustubayeva; Altyngul T. Kamzanova; Manzura Zholdassova

title: EETANet: A Human-Centered Intelligent Framework for Exercise Posture Quality Assessment.
abstract: As physical rehabilitation and fitness monitoring increasingly shift toward autonomous and home-based healthcare, accurate and intelligent posture assessment systems have become essential for supporting personalized rehabilitation and clinical decision making. This study proposes the Edge-Enhanced Temporal Attention Network (EETANet), a human-centered ambient intelligence framework for automated exercise posture assessment and quality evaluation. The proposed framework is designed as an end-to-end computational pipeline that transforms raw multivariate motion signals into posture quality predictions using a compact set of core biomechanical posture features. The pipeline integrates data preprocessing, signal enhancement, multi-domain feature representation, and deep neural classification to capture the relevant spatial and temporal characteristics of human movement. Signal preprocessing incorporates data cleaning, z-score normalization, and Savitzky-Golay smoothing to improve signal quality while preserving temporal dynamics. Subsequently, informative posture representations are extracted through complementary temporal, spectral, and morphological descriptors, enabling the model to characterize motion variations associated with posture quality. These representations are learned using a Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) classifier within the proposed EETANet framework to model nonlinear relationships between posture features and quality levels. Experimental evaluation demonstrates that the compact five-feature configuration achieves an accuracy of 90.83%, precision of 90.99%, recall of 90.83%, and F1-score of 90.84%. Notably, this compact configuration outperforms the corresponding 24-feature MLP configuration, which achieves 88.83% accuracy, indicating that a reduced set of core posture features can provide effective discriminative information while avoiding unnecessary feature redundancy. These findings demonstrate the potential of EETANet as an efficient framework for automated posture quality assessment in rehabilitation, fitness monitoring, and ambient healthcare applications.
authors: Esraa Hassan; Amira Samy Talaat; Aliya Aleryani; Rana Albelaihi; M A Elsabagh

title: EITWatch: Smartwatch-Integrated Planar Electrical Impedance Tomography for Hand Gesture Recognition
abstract: Wrist Electrical Impedance Tomography (EIT) senses hand gestures from muscle- and tendon-driven impedance changes, but prior wrist-EIT systems require electrode coverage beyond the watch-back contact patch and separate analog front ends. We present EITWatch, the first wrist-EIT system built around smartwatch case-back geometry, asking whether this contact patch alone can support gesture recognition: eight planar electrodes in a 31 mm ring acquire 35 impedance measurements at 48 Hz. Because a planar array cannot encircle the wrist, EITWatch uses multi-depth scanning to sample multiple source-sink distances and current paths; it beat matched adjacent injection by 15.1/10.4 percentage points (macro/micro) across all 12 participants. In a prompted study, within-session leave-one-round-out accuracy reached 91.4%/92.5% (window/trial) for six macro-gestures, and 90.1%/91.5% (window/segment) for five micro-gestures plus relax; window-level cross-session and leave-one-user-out transfer reached 73.2%/70.4% and 63.1%/55.3% (macro/micro).
authors: Xuanyou Liu; Novel Alam; Karan Ahuja
venue: ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)

title: ENERGY-Matched Heart-Rate Sensing Schedules for Pre-Symptomatic Infection Detection on Low-Cost Wearables
abstract: Most wearable infection-detection studies have assumed that more sensing is better, and focused on deviations in resting heart rate preceding self-reported symptoms; however, not much consideration has been given to when sensing is needed when there is a limited budget for the amount of energy the device can expend. This study asks: Is there a difference in pre-symptomatic warning performance when the timing of the heart-rate acquisition is considered in addition to the amount of sensing? Two publicly released data sets (Stanford Phase 1 and Stanford Phase 2) were re-analyzed using a preregistered causal pipeline. The final frozen base cohort included 38 participants; 30 contributed to the primary paired comparison after arm-specific calibration requirements. On the primary, modelled-energy budget (E3), sparse schedules were employed with 7 acquisition bursts per day of 10 minutes each. The confirmatory comparison tested nocturnally sensing (S3) against uniform block (S2) through the personalized time-of-day-normalized resting-heart-rate detector, with an identical alert burden (no more than two alert-days/person-month) and with a hierarchical paired endpoint of detection and warning time. S3 did not outperform S2: W/L/T = 8/12/10, θ = 0.433 (95% BCa CI 0.300-0.583), exact two-sided p = 0.5034. Detection rate was 63.3% for S3 and 66.7% for S2 and median warning time was 13 and 14 days respectively for the detected cases. Due to H1 failure, the fixed-sequence gate was closed and the remaining schedule comparisons were estimation-only. For all sensitivity analyses reported in H1, θ was kept at or below 0.5. These results do not demonstrate equality, but they do not offer any evidence that heart-rate acquisition focused at night is superior to an energy-matched uniform heart-rate acquisition schedule in warning about infection prior to symptoms onset in this sample. The study presents a framework for evaluation of sensing placement, alert burden, missingness and modeled device energy that is reproducible and suggests the need for larger prospective validation and measured hardware-energy experiments.

title: Early Detection of Apple Scab in Orchards and Mildew in Vineyards Using A Novel Deep Learning Model and Multispectral Imagery
abstract: Agricultural diseases are a significant problem for growers as they cause substantial damage to fruits and leaves, leading to yield losses. Therefore, developing systems for early detection of plant diseases is a crucial issue. In this study, a new deep learning-based hybrid model is presented for the detection and segmentation of plant diseases, specifically apple scab disease in apple orchards and mildew disease in vineyards. Multispectral imagery data collected in agricultural areas of Tekirdag province in Turkey via drones between May 2023 and December 2024 were used in developing the early disease detection system. The datasets contain 3625 images of apple orchards and 5625 images of vineyards. DJI Phantom 4 Multispectral drone, equipped with five spectral bands (Blue, Green, Red, Red Edge, and Near Infrared), was utilized to capture both spectral richness and temporal progression. This study introduces a novel deep learning architecture developed specifically for time series-based disease detection and segmentation using multispectral drone imagery. Changes in plants over time provide important information about the occurrence of plant diseases. For this reason, time series were used in this study to extract features from the changes in plants over time. The proposed model architecture was specifically designed to leverage time series information, enabling robust tracking of crop health changes over time. The model trained with the dataset collected for apple diseases achieved an average Intersection Over Unit (IoU) value of 82.05%, while the model trained with the dataset collected for vineyard diseases reached an IoU value of 79.67%. The findings highlight the effectiveness of integrating drone-acquired multispectral time-series data with advanced deep learning models for scalable, accurate, and timely plant disease detection in precision agriculture.
authors: Batuhan Aşıroğlu; Aydın Kağan Turkoglu; Fatih Sinan Bir; Sibel Senan

title: Editorial: Revolutionizing obstetric and pediatric pharmacology through artificial intelligence and digital health innovations
abstract: Zhang et al. (https://doi.org/10.3389/fphar.2026.1817282) combined a population pharmacokinetic model of linezolid with machine learning in critically ill children, using SHAP to trace predictions back to clearance, dose, weight, and renal function. Notably, the authors flag their own strong validation metrics as optimistic, since the pharmacokinetic parameters used as model inputs were derived from the same concentration data being predicted, a transparency that usefully clarifies what leakage-free, prospective validation will need to look like before such hybrid models reach the bedside. Westvik et al. (https://doi.org/10.3389/fped.2026.1881474) took a related approach in very preterm infants, estimating serum phosphate levels from routinely collected blood gas, anthropometric, and nutritional data, with small-for-gestational-age status emerging as the dominant risk factor for early hypophosphatemia. Both studies point to the same opportunity that has long motivated modelinformed dosing: extracting more clinical value from data already being collected, rather than adding burden to already vulnerable patients. Recent physiologically based pharmacokinetic modeling of pediatric antibiotic dosing offers a complementary, developmentally grounded route to the same goal (Tanaka et al., 2025).A second cluster of studies extends prediction into real-time obstetric care. Li et al. (https://doi.org/10.3389/fmed.2025.1686637) evaluated a consumer smartwatch for detecting spinal anesthesia-induced hypotension during cesarean delivery, finding moderate accuracy at a clinically relevant threshold (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUC] 0.87, sensitivity 79.2%, specificity 82.0%) but reduced sensitivity at a milder one, appropriately positioning the device as a screening aid rather than a diagnostic replacement. Wang and He (https://doi.org/10.3389/fmed.2026.1794753) developed logistic regression, Naive Bayes, random forest, support vector machine, and XGBoost models to predict intrapartum labor analgesia efficacy from preoperative demographic, clinical, ultrasound, and psychological indicators in 137 parturients; their XGBoost model showed strong discrimination in training (AUC 0.875) that declined in validation (AUC 0.759), an instructive reminder that external testing must precede clinical use. He et al. (https://doi.org/10.3389/fmed.2026.1908970) studied nalbuphine-ropivacaine infiltration along the epidural puncture tract in a prospective cohort of 473 women undergoing cesarean delivery, reporting lower rates of post-neuraxial puncture-site pain alongside an interpretable XGBoost risk model (AUC 0.912); as the authors themselves note, SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) values describe statistical association within the model, not causal mechanism, so the treatment comparison still needs confirmation in an appropriately controlled trial.None of the above is clinically useful without infrastructure that turns knowledge into action at the point of prescribing, the kind of routinely collected, real-world clinical data that increasingly underpins broader evaluations of drug safety and effectiveness (Corrigan-Curay et al., 2018). Wu et al. (https://doi.org/10.3389/fped.2026.1736268) describe the construction of China's first Pediatric Rational Medication Intelligent Decision System, a database of more than 400,000 entries across 1,030 medications covering dosing, interactions, infusion parameters, pharmacogenomics, and compatibility with traditional Chinese medicines. Embedded into the hospital information system with real-time access to patient biochemical and disease data, the system was associated with a significant reduction in higher-severity prescription alerts. This contribution is a reminder that predictive algorithms and curated, governed knowledge bases are not competing approaches but necessary complements; sophisticated models still depend on structured, pediatric-specific, continuously maintained medication data to reach the bedside. It also highlights the adoption, implementation, and governance of the underlying systems that support this application, with the intention of improving patient outcomes.These six contributions sit within a much broader shift already reshaping drug discovery and clinical trial design (Paul et al., 2021) and raising ethical and regulatory questions across the clinical pharmacology discipline (Petkovic et al., 2024); obstetric and pediatric applications carry that broader shift into two of medicine's least evidence-rich populations. Across the six studies specifically, common priorities emerge: external validation across institutions, developmental stages, and healthcare systems; evaluation that extends beyond discrimination to calibration, transportability, workflow burden, and effect on patient outcomes; and transparent, explainable models with human clinical oversight retained wherever predictions influence dosing, monitoring, or intervention. These considerations carry strong emphasis when the populations affected are pregnant women, neonates, and children. The next challenge is translating these advances into routine pediatric and obstetric practice beyond specialist centers (Thompson et al., 2024).The contributions to this Research Topic show that AI and digital health can strengthen obstetric and pediatric pharmacology. The next phase of this work should shift from retrospective prediction and single-center feasibility to prospective evaluation and interoperable implementation. Ultimately, the success of artificial intelligence in obstetric and pediatric pharmacology will not be measured solely by algorithmic performance, but by its ability to support safer, more effective, and more individualized pharmacotherapy for mothers and children. As confidence in these approaches increases, we can hopefully expect more routine deployment, with vigilance in place to ensure they continue to perform as expected as our knowledge and experience improve.Artificial intelligence tools were used to assist in creating the figure; Claude (Anthropic) was used for schematic layout generation. The authors reviewed, edited, and verified the accuracy of all AI-generated visual content. AI tools were not used for reference selection, data interpretation, or the generation of scientific conclusions. The authors assume full responsibility for all content in this publication. authors: Jeffrey S. Barrett; Catherine M.T. Sherwin; Samuel L. SewardJr

title: Emerging Antibiotherapeutic Strategies for Neonatal Sepsis: Trends and Challenges
abstract: Neonatal sepsis remains a leading cause of mortality in Nigeria, accounting for 23-30% of neonatal deaths, with antimicrobial resistance (AMR) complicating treatment efficacy. The dominance of Multidrug resistant (MDR) pathogens particularly K. pneumoniae and E. coli has rendered the first line drugs such as ampicillin and gentamicin ineffective. This comprehensive review examines emerging antibiotic strategies, current trends, and persistent challenges in managing neonatal sepsis in Nigeria. The current review synthesizes findings from more than fifty (50) studies from 2016 to 2026 on pathogen profiles, resistance patterns, diagnostic advancements, and novel therapeutic approaches. Key challenges include limited healthcare infrastructure because only about 42% of hospitals perform blood cultures due to cost, antibiotic misuse mostly from antibiotics dispensed without prescriptions, and sustainability of interventions. Integrated solutions including antimicrobial stewardship, capacity building, and policy reforms should be adopted to mitigate AMR and improve neonatal sepsis treatment outcomes
authors: Samaila Abdullahi; Bindawa Almustapha

title: Emerging Neurobiomarkers in Neurodegenerative Disorders: From Molecular Mechanisms to Clinical Translation
abstract: Neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer’s Disease (AD) and Parkinson’s Disease (PD) are characterized by a progressive loss of neurons, correlating with loss of motor and cognitive function that has an impact on global health. Diagnosis of these diseases in clinical settings is generally delayed due to reliance on clinical features and diagnostic criteria that focus on symptomatic stages of the neurodegenerative disorder. Growing evidence suggests that pathological activity at a molecular level can occur years before the onset of symptoms. This narrative review focuses on recent progress in fluid, imaging, genetic, and multi-omics as well as digital biomarkers, with an emphasis on their diagnostic implementation, feasibility, value, and translation into clinical settings. In AD, cerebrospinal fluid and plasma biomarkers such as Glial Fibrillary Acid Protein (GFAP), Aβ1–42/Aβ1–40 ratios, and phosphorylated tau isomers (p-tau181, p-tau217) have been shown to have promising diagnostic relevance and utility. Protein Misfolding Cyclic Amplification (PMCA) and Real-Time Quaking-Induced Conversion (RT-QuIC) have shown high diagnostic specificity for detecting α-synuclein seeding activity, accurately distinguishing synucleinopathies, which are of particular interest in PD. Corresponding imaging biomarkers, including structural and functional MRI, Positron Emission Tomography (PET), and multimodal imaging, provide complementary insight into the relevance of disease-stage categorization. Multi-omics profiling and digital biomarkers, including wearable sensors, speech and gait analysis, and electroencephalography combined with artificial intelligence-driven pattern recognition, further broaden the biomarker terrain toward continuous, precision-based monitoring of neurodegeneration. Despite significant progress, limitations remain in standardization, biological heterogeneity, and validation of relevant findings. Ethical considerations related to preclinical diagnosis also require considerable premeditation. The change toward the implementation of a multimodal framework has the potential to shift neurodegenerative disease diagnosis from symptomatic late-stage diagnosis to early, molecularly mechanistic-driven medical aftermath.
authors: Maryam; Ahmed Hasan Mohiuddin

title: Empowering the anesthesiologist: Navigating the future of AI-driven visualization and wearable technology in regional anesthesia
abstract: In current regional anesthesia practice, “visualization” typically refers to the real-time imaging and display of subcutaneous anatomical structures with ultrasound imaging, and “wearable technology” refers to hands-free, optical head-mounted displays (e.g., smart glasses) that can project digital information directly into the clinician’s field of view. The paradigm shift in the history of regional anesthesia from anatomical landmark techniques to ultrasound guidance has revolutionized the art of regional anesthesia and transformed a blind procedural technique into a visually guided intervention.
authors: Qi Chen; Yaohui Huang; Daqiang Zhao

title: Enabling Versatile Human Sensing through Wi-Fi Beamforming Feedback
abstract: Wi-Fi sensing enables contactless human sensing, while most existing systems rely on Channel State Information, which is accessible only on a limited range of Wi-Fi chipsets. In contrast, Beamforming Feedback Information (BFI) is standardized in modern Wi-Fi and readily accessible on a wide range of commodity devices, offering new opportunities for human sensing. In this paper, we present BeamLens, a Wi-Fi sensing system that extracts fine-grained spatial information from BFI to enable versatile human sensing. Specifically, we jointly estimate the angle of departure and relative time of flight from BFI to extract fine-grained spatial information and leverage two AP-STA links to capture complementary azimuth and elevation views. We further design a sparse physical antenna array and construct a uniform virtual antenna array to enhance spatial resolution. Moreover, we fuse complementary views through self-supervised learning, combining temporally aware cross-view contrastive learning and temporal masked reconstruction to learn a versatile backbone for diverse human sensing tasks. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that BeamLens achieves 90.16\% accuracy in human activity recognition, a mean per-joint position error of 8.64\,cm in 3D human pose estimation, and 70.64\% intersection over union in human silhouette estimation, while exhibiting strong generalization to unseen environments and subjects.
authors: Jingzhe Zhang; Peiliang Wang; Yitong Shen; Ning Wang; Mingzhe Chen; Yili Ren

title: Energy-Efficient Smart Agriculture Management Framework Using IoT and Ensemble Machine Learning for Intelligent Crop Health Monitoring and Resource Optimization
abstract: Context: Smart agriculture plays an important role in addressing the challenges of food security, environmental sustainability, and sustainable farming through IoT.Farmers are facing many issues in traditional farming, such as inefficient monitoring and poor crop health detection.Traditional farming has a negative impact on crop production and sustainability.In this regard, the development of intelligent and energy-efficient agricultural monitoring systems has become crucial for contemporary precision farming applications.Objective: This study aims to monitor crop health and optimize resource use using machine learning techniques.Our proposed system intends to monitor crop conditions in real time, enhance agricultural management, and minimize unnecessary sensor utilization and communication overhead.Material/methods: In this paper, we used five machine learning classifiers to monitor crop health using sensor data.The agricultural sensor data (soil moisture, soil temperature, soil pH, humidity, air temperature, solar radiation, wind speed, NDVI index, and 5G latency) were used for crop health monitoring.The models, such as RF, XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost, and soft voting were used for crop health classification into the Healthy, High_Stress, and Moderate_Stress categories.The experimental observation revealed that soft voting achieved the highest accuracy of 94.5%, macro-F1 score of 0.945, weighted F1 score of 0.945, and AUC-ROC score of 0.988 compared to the other models.The cross-validation results further validated the robustness and stability of the proposed framework.The IoTenabled intelligent agriculture management system offers an efficient, scalable solution for real-time crop health monitoring, energy-efficient resource optimization, and sustainable smart farming.
venue: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology

title: Engagement-Supportive Mechanisms in Stress-Focused Digital Mental Health Interventions With Adaptive, Conversational, and Context-Aware Systems: Narrative Review
abstract: Background: Stress is a widespread public health concern associated with cardiovascular disease, depression, anxiety, and reduced quality of life. Digital mental health interventions (DMHIs), delivered through smartphones, web platforms, and wearables, offer scalable support for stress management but often struggle to sustain user engagement. Evidence describing how adaptive, conversational, and context-aware mechanisms function together within stress-focused DMHIs remains fragmented. Objective: This review aims to synthesize evidence on engagement-supportive mechanisms in stress-focused DMHIs, with attention to personalization; biometric feedback; just-in-time adaptive interventions (JITAIs); gamification; AI, including large language models (LLMs); and methodological approaches to studying engagement. It also examines methodological, motivational, and experiential dimensions of engagement. Methods: This narrative review was informed by a structured search of PubMed, IEEE Xplore, and Scopus for peer-reviewed studies published between January 2018 and April 2025, followed by an evidence update through August 2026. Eligible studies described stress-focused DMHIs or related affective support interventions reporting at least 1 engagement-supportive mechanism. Randomized controlled trials, qualitative investigations, simulation or modeling studies, and implementation studies were included. Data were extracted using a structured form capturing study characteristics, engagement mechanisms, outcomes, and alignment with the review domains. Descriptive mapping summarized study types and mechanism frequencies, while a narrative synthesis integrated behavioral, experiential, methodological, and theory-informed findings. Results: Thirty-two studies met the inclusion criteria. Randomized or microrandomized controlled trials were the most common design (n=17), followed by qualitative investigations (n=6), design or implementation studies (n=3), mixed methods studies (n=3), simulation or modeling studies (n=2), and a quasi-experimental study (n=1). Dynamic adaptation was identified in 14 studies, conversational support in 10, static tailoring in 9, social or co-design mechanisms in 9, context-aware prompting in 7, gamified reinforcement in 5, biometric-responsive adaptation in 4, and narrative immersion in 2. These mechanisms frequently overlapped within layered adaptive architectures rather than functioning as isolated engagement features. AI-enabled systems included conversational agents, LLM-supported systems, recommender systems, reinforcement learning, and computational modeling approaches. Outcomes included behavioral indicators such as adherence, retention, and prompt receptivity, alongside experiential indicators such as perceived relevance, trust, emotional support, and immersion. Evidence strength varied substantially; many AI-enabled systems contributed feasibility, acceptability, or optimization-oriented evidence rather than definitive comparative effectiveness evidence. Conclusions: Stress-focused DMHIs are increasingly adopting adaptive, conversational, and context-aware engagement-supportive mechanisms, but the evidence base remains heterogeneous and methodologically uneven. Dynamic adaptation, conversational support, and static tailoring were most frequently represented, whereas biometric-responsive adaptation, narrative immersion, and deeply integrated gamified systems were less common. AI-enabled systems may support contextual responsiveness and personalized interaction but require transparent adaptive logic, privacy safeguards, and human-centered evaluation. Future work should prioritize longitudinal, mixed methods research capable of distinguishing behavioral engagement, experiential engagement, feasibility, acceptability, and sustained stress-related outcomes.
authors: Munesu Maminimini; Sofia Asteria Piffer; Silvia Gabrielli

title: Enhancement of Measurement Distance in Vision Sensor-Based System Using Super-Resolution for Dynamic Response Measurement Under Low-Illumination Conditions
abstract: Displacement is a key response index for evaluating the serviceability and safety of civil infrastructure. Although vision sensors have emerged as non-contact and cost-effective alternatives to conventional sensing systems, their performance deteriorates under low-illumination and long-distance conditions because reduced spatial resolution and weakened local intensity information make feature extraction and tracking unreliable. To address this limitation, this study investigates the feasibility of integrating a real-world super-resolution (SR) framework into a vision-sensor-based system for dynamic displacement measurement under low-light conditions. A GAN-based RealSR model was employed to restore low-resolution image sequences, and the restored images were processed using a KAZE-based feature tracking approach. The proposed framework was validated through shaking table tests of a three-story frame structure under a low-illumination condition of 120 lux at measurement distances ranging from 10 to 40 m. Dynamic displacement responses induced by a harmonic excitation of 9.0 Hz were estimated and compared with reference measurements obtained from a linear variable differential transformer (LVDT). The results show that the SR-restored images provided more stable feature extraction and more reliable displacement tracking than bicubic upsampling, particularly for natural targets under low-light and long-range conditions. Furthermore, the application of SR improved the measurability of targets at extended distances, demonstrating that real-world SR is an effective preprocessing strategy for robust vision-based displacement measurement under low illumination.
authors: Junho Gong; Kyuwan Lee; Dooyong Cho

title: Enhancing Performance and User Engagement in Everyday Stress Monitoring: A Context-Aware Active Reinforcement Learning Approach
abstract: Accurate stress monitoring in everyday settings requires informative labels without excessive user burden. Ecological Momentary Assessments (EMAs) provide self-reported labels, but poorly timed or frequent prompts can reduce their utility. This article presents a context-aware active reinforcement learning algorithm for stress detection using photoplethysmography (PPG) from smartwatches and contextual data from smartphones. The algorithm uses the user’s current context and response history to decide when to trigger an EMA. We first evaluate context-aware label selection in an offline study and then deploy the approach for real-time EMA triggering in a separate online cohort. Under the reported evaluation, Random Forest F1 increased from 0.21 for the offline cohort to 0.32 for the online cohort; adding contextual features increased it to 0.36. Personalization increased AUC by up to 0.10 across Random Forest, XGBoost, and SVM classifiers. These results support context-aware EMA scheduling and personalized modeling for real-world stress monitoring, while differences between the study cohorts limit causal attribution of the observed performance gains.
authors: Seyed Amir Hossein Aqajari; Ziyu Wang; Ali Tazarv; Sina Labbaf; Salar Jafarlou; Brenda Nguyen; Nikil D. Dutt; Marco Levorato; Amir M. Rahmani
venue: ACM Transactions on Computing for Healthcare

title: Epidural Spinal Cord Stimulation Reduces Intrinsic Gait Abnormalities in Spinal Muscular Atrophy
abstract: Introduction/Aims Epidural spinal cord stimulation (SCS) has recently been explored in ambulatory individuals with spinal muscular atrophy (SMA), where an increase in muscle strength and endurance with concomitant reduced fatigability was observed. However, the underlying kinematic changes associated with these improvements remain poorly understood. This study aimed to examine whether previously documented improvements following SCS were associated with changes in joint kinematics and movement strategies. Methods A secondary kinematic analysis of previously collected 6‐min walk test (6MWT) data using a 3D motion‐capture system and subsequent principal component analysis (PCA) was completed on two ambulatory individuals with SMA. Speed as well as spatio‐temporal gait variables and sagittal‐plane joint kinematics were defined and compared before and after SCS intervention. Results After 4 weeks of SCS, participants walked farther and showed faster, more consistent speeds during the 6MWT. PCA revealed that these improvements were associated with changes in proximal joint velocity (SMA02 mean(L 2 ) = 0.45, SMA03 mean(L 2 ) = 0.54) and proximal joint mobility (SMA 02 mean(L 2 ) = 0.51, SMA03 mean(L 2 ) = 0.40) in both SMA participants. Consistent with these findings, hip range of motion, velocity, and acceleration increased by up to 48%, 44% and 28%, respectively, without evidence of exacerbated compensatory strategies. Discussion SCS may restore access to motor pathways selectively impaired in individuals with SMA. While confirmatory, larger cohort studies are needed, SCS has the potential to reduce intrinsic movement abnormalities and enhance treatment opportunities for SMA.
authors: Serena Donadio; Carly Magun; Cara H. Kanner; Rafael S. Rodriguez-Torres; Genís Prat-Ortega; George Z. Mentis; Marco Capogrosso; Jacqueline Montes

title: Ergo Analyzer: Ergonomic Risk Assessment System Using Computer Vision & REBA
abstract: Work-related musculoskeletal disorders remain a leading cause of injury and lost workdays in manufacturing, yet ergonomic assessment on the shopfloor is still largely periodic, manual and subjective. This paper presents Ergo Analyzer, a contactless, camera-based system that converts ordinary video into real-time, actionable ergonomic insight. The framework detects workers in the video stream, estimates seventeen body keypoints using a real-time pose estimation model, computes joint angles and body alignment, and compares them against ergonomic thresholds. A machine learning classifier then assigns a color-coded risk level and a numerical score from zero to one hundred, together with body region sub-scores for the back, shoulders, wrists and legs. A recommendation engine converts the result into task-specific corrective feedback such as adjusting posture, raising the work surface or taking micro-breaks. A prototype built with Python and OpenCV and exercised in simulated shopfloor conditions assigned distinct risk levels to good posture, improper lifting and excessive bending, and, in a live qualitative demonstration, the risk score fell from 72 to 32 after the recommended posture was adopted. We describe the architecture, scoring method, implementation and limitations, and outline a validation plan and roadmap toward alerts, mobile applications and wearable integration
authors: Riddhi Gole Khushi Kaduskar; Vaishnavi Mane Sakshi Khade
venue: International Journal of Advanced Research in Science Communication and Technology

title: Establishment of Standardized Normative Reference Values for Pressure-Based Gait Analysis in the Healthy Korean Population: A Nationwide Multi-Center Registry Study
abstract: Objective: Normative gait data for Asian populations remain scarce, and Western reference values may not apply to Koreans. We aimed to establish nationwide reference values for pressure-based gait analysis in healthy Korean adults. Methods: Healthy community-dwelling adults (N = 612, aged 20 to 80s) were enrolled at 11 randomly selected centers using quota-based recruitment across 18 sex- and age-stratified cohorts. Spatiotemporal gait parameters, classified into five domains, were recorded on a pressure-based electronic walkway. Gait speed cutoffs were defined at -1.0 and -1.5 standard deviations (SD) below age- and sex-specific means. Age-group differences were evaluated using ANOVA and linear mixed-effects models adjusted for height and study site. Results: Gait velocity followed a normal distribution in all strata. In both sexes, older age groups showed lower Pace domain values and higher step length variability, which remained significant after adjustment for height and study site. In contrast, Rhythm domain parameters and asymmetry indices were preserved across age groups. Cutoffs were provided at -1.5 SD for normally distributed parameters and the 7th percentile for non-normally distributed parameters. Conclusions: This is the first nationwide multicenter reference dataset for spatiotemporal gait parameters in healthy Korean adults across the full adult age range. These population-specific values provide a practical baseline for interpreting pressure-based gait analysis and for applying gait-based clinical criteria in Korea.
authors: Jinse Park; Phil Hyu Lee; Seong‐Beom Koh; Jinyoung Youn; Do‐Young Kwon; Kyum‐Yil Kwon; Jeongho Park; Min Seung Kim; Suk Yun Kang; Kyoungwon Baik; Jung Hwan Shin; Min Seok Baek; Sang‐Myung Cheon

title: Evaluating Smart Home Device Users’ Responses to their (Un)Confirmed Privacy Expectations
abstract: Users of smart home devices are often unaware of how their devices handle personal data. We examine how revealing these data practices influences users’ trust, satisfaction, and coping behaviors, including decisions to block device communications. Using Expectation-Confirmation Theory, we conducted two complementary studies to balance ecological validity with experimental control. An exploratory in-situ field study ( N = 35) used network monitoring to reveal actual device traffic, and an online experiment ( N = 132) presented simulated reports with manipulated levels of advertising-related communications. Across both studies, when data practices aligned with users’ expectations, satisfaction with the device’s data practices increased, strengthening intentions to continue using the device. Defensive responses, however, followed different pathways: satisfaction predicted willingness to block in the in-situ field study, whereas collection concerns were the primary predictor of blocking in the experiment. Together, these findings suggest how transparency reshapes attitudes and behaviors among existing smart-home users, underscoring the role of expectation confirmation in real-world, continued-use contexts.
authors: Tania Khatun; Mahdieh Sheikh Rezaei; Danny Yuxing Huang; Oded Nov; Reza Ghaiumy Anaraky

title: Everyday Instagram behavior maps distinct facets of loneliness in young adults
abstract: Loneliness is a major health risk and is often hard to detect. It is multidimensional and can involve social, emotional, and structural facets with different causes and behavioral consequences. An open question is whether these facets can be differentiated in everyday Instagram behavior. We analyzed consented Instagram data exports from 415 US college students and modeled five validated measures related to loneliness using activity patterns, language, and images. Multimodal traces distinguished subjective loneliness but were less informative for structural isolation. Model explanation analyses revealed dissociable signatures: social loneliness was linked to low interpersonal engagement (fewer likes and comments), whereas emotional loneliness was linked to negative affect (negative language and sad/angry facial expressions) and late-night activity. Together, these results provide a cross-measure behavioral “construct map” of loneliness, suggesting that multimodal digital traces can separate markers of dissatisfaction with social connections from markers of emotional isolation, moving beyond generic prediction toward construct-sensitive characterization. Because the sample was of college age, predominantly female, and largely Asian or White, an important next step is to test whether these signatures generalize to more diverse populations.
authors: Yueyi Jiang; Kevin Lewis; Barton W. Palmer; Fei Dai; Piotr Winkielman

title: Evidence-Consistent Generative Detection under Scenario-Level Distribution Shift
abstract: Conventional in-distribution evaluation can overestimate robustness when training and test data share recurring task-specific patterns or surface cues. This risk is especially relevant in social-engineering fraud detection, where attackers can preserve malicious intent while changing the scenario, impersonated entity, or wording. We study this problem as scenario-level out-of-distribution (SL-OOD) detection for SMS and voice phishing, where entire attack scenarios are held out from training while the label space remains fixed. This setting tests whether models can generalize to unseen attack scenarios using decision-relevant evidence rather than familiar scenario-specific cues. Using this SL-OOD evaluation, we find that high in-distribution performance does not reliably predict held-out robustness across feature-, encoder-, and decoder-based baselines. We interpret this gap as scenario memorization: reliance on recurring scenario-specific lexical or entity cues rather than decision-relevant evidence. We propose ECoG, an evidence-consistent generative framework that combines evidence-span supervision with a rationale-label consistency objective during training. On the 0.5B decoder, relative to the same backbone trained without consistency regularization, ECoG raises Macro-F1 on OOD challenging instances by 3.22 points, reduces the share of predictions whose generated rationale supports the opposite label by 4.22 points, and increases token-level overlap with reference evidence spans by 8.38 points; the reduction in prediction-rationale inconsistency is consistent across four decoder backbones. These results suggest that compact generative detectors can benefit from evidence supervision and rationale-label consistency under social-engineering shift.
authors: San Kim; JinYeong Bak
venue: ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM)

title: Exercise-based interventions for internet gaming disorder: current evidence, mechanistic rationale, and the augmenting role of serious games and digital therapeutics
abstract: Background Internet gaming disorder (IGD) is an emerging public health concern among adolescents and young adults and is associated with adverse mental health, cognitive, academic and social outcomes. Exercise-based interventions may reduce IGD symptoms, but long-term adherence remains challenging. Emerging digital health technologies, including serious games, digital therapeutics, wearable devices, artificial intelligence (AI) and neuromodulation, may improve engagement, personalisation and behavioral change. Objective This narrative review synthesises current evidence on exercise-based interventions for IGD and examines the complementary roles of serious games, digital therapeutics, wearable technologies, AI-assisted personalisation and neuromodulation in treatment engagement, adherence, assessment and monitoring. It also identifies evidence gaps and priorities for future research. Methods A narrative review was performed based on literature identified through PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science up to March 2026, with relevant later publications also considered. We synthesised evidence regarding exercise interventions and emerging digital health technologies for the prevention and management of IGD. Results Exercise-based interventions may reduce IGD symptoms and improve executive function and emotional regulation, although findings vary across modalities and protocols. Serious games and exergaming may enhance motivation and adherence, while digital therapeutics such as virtual reality-based interventions remain supported by limited clinical evidence. Neuromodulation, particularly transcranial direct current stimulation, may improve inhibitory control, although effects on craving are inconsistent and no trial has combined tDCS with exercise in IGD. Wearable and AI-assisted approaches have mainly been studied for IGD assessment, classification and behavioral monitoring, with no direct evidence of clinical outcome benefits. Adaptive intervention delivery has been demonstrated mainly in non-IGD digital health settings. Safety data are limited because adverse events were not consistently assessed or reported. Overall, evidence remains constrained by heterogeneous designs, small samples, inconsistent outcomes and limited long-term follow-up. Conclusion Combining exercise with digital health technologies is a conceptually promising but not yet empirically validated approach to improve IGD management. Future research should prioritise high-quality multicentre randomised controlled trials, standardised outcomes, long-term follow-up, mechanistic validation, real-world implementation and ethical considerations for AI-enabled interventions in adolescents.
authors: Wentao Liu; Kangle Wang; Minling Yu; Fenghua Sun

title: Exploring On-Skin Interfaces as Interactive Intelligent Technologies for Health Diagnostics: Systematic Review of Current Practices and Future Directions
abstract: On-skin interfaces are emerging as intelligent, non-invasive technologies that enable continuous physiological monitoring and health diagnostics. This systematic review explores the current landscape, design practices, effectiveness, and ethical implications of on-skin interfaces in healthcare. A total of 174 peer-reviewed studies published between 2015 and 2025 were identified across six major databases and analyzed to synthesize trends in sensor application, body placement, user interaction, and diagnostic focus. Findings reveal that most systems are concentrated on physical health (e.g., cardiac, respiratory, hydration), with limited but growing attention to mental and behavioral health contexts. Despite promising technical performance, the widespread clinical adoption of these technologies is hindered by challenges in real-world validation, signal robustness, long-term wearability, and a lack of personalized feedback, and only 21 studies (12.1%) evaluated the technology from the perspective of its users. Five core design recommendations emerged: enhancing clinical feasibility, ensuring user comfort, improving signal generalizability, incorporating intervention-driven interfaces, and embedding ethical safeguards. This review highlights a growing need for user-centered and ethically responsible design strategies that extend beyond monitoring to actionable interventions. The findings offer a roadmap for advancing on-skin interfaces into intelligent, interactive health companions capable of supporting both short- and long-term care. Bridging research innovations with clinical application will be essential to realizing the full potential of these technologies in personalized and preventive healthcare.

title: Extended Wearable ECG Monitoring Detects Unrecognised Arrhythmias After COPD Exacerbation: The PRECURSOR Pilot Study
abstract: BACKGROUND: The period after hospitalisation for an acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is associated with cardiovascular vulnerability. Clinically important rhythm disturbances may be intermittent or asymptomatic and escape routine postdischarge assessment; however, the diagnostic yield of prolonged monitoring is intrinsically influenced by monitoring duration. METHODS: In this prospective, single-centre observational pilot, 18 adults recently hospitalised for COPD exacerbation underwent continuous remote monitoring for 21 days between September 2019 and February 2020. The three-lead ZENSOR wearable recorded electrocardiographic rhythm, heart rate and respiratory rate and transmitted full-disclosure data and predefined alerts for clinician review. The primary outcome was participant-level detection of previously unrecognised, cardiologist-confirmed arrhythmias warranting therapeutic evaluation or intervention. Outcomes were analysed descriptively with exact 95% binomial confidence intervals. RESULTS: Participants were predominantly male (15/18; 83.3%), with a mean age of 73 ± 6 years. Seven had GOLD grade 3-4 airflow limitation, seven received long-term oxygen therapy, five had coronary artery disease and four had chronic atrial fibrillation. During the planned 21-day monitoring period, previously unrecognized clinically actionable arrhythmias were detected in 9/18 participants (50.0%; 95% CI: 26.0-74.0). Nonmutually exclusive findings included trigeminy (2/18), third-degree atrioventricular block (2/18), bradycardia (5/18), newly detected atrial fibrillation (1/18), supraventricular tachycardia (2/18) and nocturnal atrial or ventricular ectopy (8/18). Sixteen participants (88.9%; 95% CI: 65.3-98.6) reported satisfaction with monitoring. CONCLUSIONS: Extended wearable electrocardiographic monitoring produced a high participant-level detection yield of previously unrecognised arrhythmias during early recovery from hospitalised COPD exacerbation. This finding supports targeted postdischarge rhythm surveillance but does not distinguish biological post-exacerbation vulnerability from the greater ascertainment achieved by prolonged monitoring. Confirmation requires larger controlled studies with comprehensive cardiopulmonary phenotyping, standardised monitoring-performance metrics and comparative clinical outcomes.
