title: Facilitators and Barriers to Home Use of Wearable Devices Among Older Adults With Ischemic Stroke: An Exploratory Qualitative Study
abstract: Background Long-term management of modifiable risk factors is essential for secondary stroke prevention, yet home-based health management among older adults with ischemic stroke remains suboptimal. Wearable devices may support continuous monitoring and personalized health feedback; however, little is known about how this population perceives their use at home or the factors shaping their adoption and continued engagement. This study aimed to explore older adults’ perceptions and experiences regarding the use of wearable devices for home-based health management after ischemic stroke and to identify perceived facilitators and barriers to their adoption and continued use. Methods The Health Belief Model and the Technology Acceptance Model were integrated to guide the conceptual framework of this study. Using purposive sampling, 26 older adults with ischemic stroke who had prior knowledge of or experience with wearable devices were recruited from the neurology department of a Grade A tertiary hospital and a community health service center in Xuzhou, China, between November 2025 and January 2026. Data were collected through focus groups and individual semistructured interviews and analyzed using qualitative content analysis that incorporated both deductive and inductive approaches. Results The analysis identified 6 themes: (1) practical challenges in home health management; (2) perceived technological value and health benefits; (3) barriers to technology use and challenges concerning trust; (4) multilevel social support and empowerment through technology; (5) preferences for age-friendly design; and (6) needs for functions specific to stroke and expectations for health care integration. Continuous health monitoring, real-time feedback, behavioral reminders, and support from family members, peers, communities, and healthcare professionals emerged as key facilitators of wearable device adoption. Major barriers included limited digital literacy, complex operation, concerns regarding monitoring data accuracy, privacy and data security, and affordability. Participants also emphasized the need for personalized monitoring, timely risk alerts, and integration with primary healthcare services. Conclusions Wearable devices have potential to support home-based health management among older adults with ischemic stroke, but successful adoption requires attention to patients’ perceptions, technology-related challenges, social support, and stroke-specific needs. Future interventions should incorporate user-centered and age-friendly design principles, strengthen support from families, communities, and healthcare professionals, and integrate wearable technologies into stroke self-management and preventive care pathways. These findings highlight the importance of developing patient-centered approaches to support sustainable use of wearable technologies in post-stroke home health management.

title: FactNudger: An AI-Powered Wearable Fact-Checker for Everyday Conversations
abstract: Misinformation is often encountered through speech, where claims are fleeting and verification requires leaving the interaction. We present FactNudger, a wearable system that fact-checks everyday speech and selectively alerts users through a smartwatch. FactNudger transcribes conversation, interprets claims in context, retrieves web evidence, and decides whether to wait for more speech, remain silent, or deliver a haptic nudge. The watch presents a concise rationale, while a companion phone provides supporting sources. FactNudger achieved 77% binary verdict accuracy on 125 sampled AVeriTeC claims and selected the intended action for 40 of 50 conversational edge cases. The demonstration lets attendees experience and inspect real-time fact-checking across false claims, incomplete statements, corrections, repetitions, and context-dependent speech.

title: Factors influencing the intention to use smart wristbands among patients with COPD: an extended UTAUT model
abstract: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) imposes a substantial global health burden. Despite the considerable potential of wearable devices for early detection and disease management, suboptimal engagement limits their clinical utility. This study aims to identify factors associated with the intention to use smart wristbands among patients with COPD. The study extends the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) by incorporating health risk perception and interface presentation. A sequential mixed-methods design was employed, commencing with semi-structured interviews ( n = 28), followed by a questionnaire survey ( n = 233). Structural equation modeling was used to validate the measurement model and examine the hypothesized relationships. All six constructs demonstrated statistically significant positive associations with intention to use ( P < 0.05). Health risk perception (β = 0.272, P < 0.001) and social influence (β = 0.271, P < 0.001) were the primary correlates of intention to use. This study extends UTAUT by identifying factors correlated with COPD patients’ intention to use smart wristbands. The findings offer practical insights for user-oriented device design and intervention strategies, thereby supporting the promotion of digital health monitoring among COPD patients.
authors: Jingyi Ye; Jianhua Chen; Mi Yao; Guanning Jing; Wenping Li; Yujing Su; Hongjing Pei; Jiapei Xu; Chunhua Chi

title: Fake Review Detection from Classical to Transformers: Gains and Limits
abstract: Reported fake review detection performance is hard to interpret when model families are evaluated under different data splits and development procedures. This study compares six traditional machine learning systems, five deep learning models, seven pretrained Transformer encoders, and seven sentiment‐augmented Transformer variants on the Amazon‐based fake reviews dataset (FRD) under one leakage‐controlled protocol: a duplicate‐safe 70/10/20 partition; validation‐only selection of checkpoints, thresholds, models, and ensembles; and a test set reserved for final evaluation and paired inference. Accuracy rises from 94.32% (TF‐IDF + SVM) and 95.00% (Word2Vec + LSTM) to 98.23% with the validation‐selected plain Transformer (ModernBERT), the largest stage‐level gain. A validation‐selected soft‐voting ensemble adds a small but significant improvement, to 98.75% (ROC‐AUC 0.9991). Sentiment augmentation, an explicit sentiment profile added through a dedicated fusion head, did not improve accuracy consistently: Over five training runs per backbone, its effect changed sign for all seven encoders, including the three with a significant first‐run effect. Zero‐shot evaluation on AiGen‐FoodReview, which replaces Amazon/GPT‐2 with Yelp/GPT‐4‐Turbo reviews, shows that the in‐domain operating performance does not carry over: Every transferred Transformer‐based system labels nearly all machine‐generated reviews as authentic, and the final ensemble ranks the two classes in reverse (ROC‐AUC 0.4357). No configuration ranks generated reviews above authentic ones in all five runs; plain BERT reaches a ROC‐AUC of 0.9055 in one run but only 0.30–0.77 in the others. Controlled in‐domain gains and external validity must be established separately.
authors: Arzu Karataş; Gülsüm KAYABAŞI KORU

title: Faradaically Resilient Triphase Wedge‐Shaped Nanowire Arrays for Robust Bioanalysis
abstract: Gas‐containing triphase interfaces are attractive for oxygen‐mediated electrochemical systems, yet faradaic stress‐induced electrowetting remains unresolved in triphase biointerfaces. This work presents faradaically resilient wedge‐shaped copper nanowire arrays (W‐CuNWAs) that stabilize oxygen‐enriched triphase interfaces during sustained and repeated electrochemical operations. In contrast with conventional passive liquid‐repellent nanostructures, W‐CuNWAs employ co‐programmed structural–wettability anisotropy to reconcile wettable charge‐transfer regions with gas‐retaining regions within a single nanoarchitecture. Compared to cylindrical CuNWAs, W‐CuNWAs introduce shape‐encoded wetting barriers that increase capillary breakthrough pressure by 2.85‐fold and pin the contact line at the upper edge. Across 3 h of continuous bias, 500 potential cycles, repeated impedance perturbations, and cathodic electrodeposition of a high‐surface‐energy co‐catalyst, W‐CuNWAs retain stable wettability and electrochemical responses with only 0.88 kΩ mass‐transport‐resistance drift, whereas cylindrical counterparts undergo electrolyte infiltration and structural failure. The retained atmosphere‐connected gas phase enables Pt/W‐CuNWAs to achieve 1.65‐fold higher oxygen‐reduction current, 8.96‐fold lower oxygen mass‐transfer resistance, and 2.96‐fold faster current stabilization than cylindrical counterparts. Integration with an FeOOH/BiVO 4 photoanode enables near‐drift‐free, unbiased photoelectrochemical operation over 8.42 h of repeated cathodic cycling, and reliable detection of Alzheimer's neurofilament light chain in clinical plasma. This work establishes shape‐encoded faradaic electrowetting resistance as a design principle for operationally stable, oxygen‐mediated triphase nanoarchitectures in bioanalysis.
authors: Hayeon Kim; Hyeok Lim; Sung Hyun Park; Jaejin Kim; Joonseok Lee; Kayoung Kim

title: Fault identification for intelligent real-time monitoring via mobile accessible networks: a critical review of MEMS microphone-based sensing for bearing diagnostics
abstract: The main objective of Condition Monitoring (CM) is to prevent unexpected downtime by monitoring machine conditions and reducing maintenance costs. To prevent failure, particularly in rotating machinery, CM is performed utilizing sensing devices, which have been the focus of extensive research in recent decades. This paper presents a critical review and provides comprehensive coverage of recent advances in CM for rotating machinery that utilize MEMS microphone-based sensing, with particular emphasis on bearing fault diagnosis relevant to the Fault Identification for Intelligent Real-time Monitoring via Mobile Accessible Network research programme. It synthesises recent journal articles focusing on MEMS (Micro-Electro-Mechanical Systems) microphone technologies, signal processing and machine learning techniques, methodological study design and experimental framework, and reported comparative analysis, advantages, limitations, and future research directions. Furthermore, the study reveals a dominant trend toward the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) techniques, resulting in significant advances in CM and an emerging on non-contact-based sensing via mobile accessible system and self-powered sensing. Key gaps identified include the under-representation of MEMS microphone-based sensing, noise robustness and high sensitivity sensors, insufficient edge-deployment validation, the barriers of large datasets processing to achieve effectiveness, and the absence of multi-domain adaptive diagnostic frameworks. As a final point, options for scalable, low-cost, acoustic-based sensing and edge-intelligent computing are proposed, to deliver real-time monitoring across multiple domains.
authors: Firmansyah; Muhammad Khan; Isidro Durazo Cardenas

title: Feasibility and Acceptability of a Prospective Remote Pilot Study for Assessment of Airborne Environmental Exposures and Male Fertility
abstract: Objective: To evaluate the feasibility and acceptability of serial biosampling and environmental exposure assessment in reproductive-aged men and compare participant experiences with in-person versus remote sample collection. Design: Prospective cohort pilot study. Subjects: Eighteen healthy men aged 21-44 years with no history of infertility, medical conditions or medications known to cause infertility, or prior scrotal or testicular surgery. Exposure: Indoor and personal environmental exposure monitoring using PurpleAir monitors and Fresh Air wristbands, respectively. Main Outcome Measures: Feasibility of repeated remote semen and blood collection, evaluated by participant retention and number of samples returned, and participant-reported acceptability, ease of use, discomfort, preference for at-home versus in-clinic sampling, and willingness to participate in longitudinal studies. Results: 18 participants completed the initial in-person and scheduled at-home sampling, and 16 (89%) completed subsequent remote sampling. Participants successfully collected and shipped serial capillary blood samples using homeRNA and semen samples using the Fellow Semen Analysis Kit. Participants rated both collection methods as easy to use and reported minimal discomfort with blood collection. At-home participation was preferred over in-clinic sampling, particularly for semen collection. All 16 participants completing the final survey reported willingness to participate in a similar study again. Participants were willing to provide a median of 18 semen samples (range, 2-40) and 18 blood samples (range, 5-40) over a future hypothetical study. Both home-based environmental monitoring approaches were well accepted. Conclusion: Serial remote semen and blood collection paired with environmental exposure monitoring was feasible and acceptable among reproductive-aged men. High retention, preference for at-home sampling, and willingness to provide repeated samples support this approach for larger longitudinal studies investigating environmental exposures and male reproductive health.

title: Feasibility and Preliminary Outcomes of Smartphone-Based Remote Patient Monitoring in Patients With Solid Tumors: Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial.
abstract:
Background

Remote patient monitoring (RPM) using mobile apps and wearable devices may support symptom reporting and communication between patients with cancer and health care professionals. However, evidence regarding sustained engagement, wearable-data completeness, and preliminary clinical outcomes in routine oncology practice remains limited.

Objective

This pilot randomized controlled trial aimed to assess the feasibility of implementing a smartphone-based RPM system integrated with a wearable device among patients with solid tumors and to generate preliminary estimates of between-group differences in quality of life, emergency department (ED) use, and side-effect literacy over 6 months.

Methods

Thirty patients from a single outpatient oncology clinic were randomized 1:1 to receive either the WellHealth RPM intervention plus standard care or standard care alone. The intervention included smartphone-based symptom reporting, medication recording, wearable-device monitoring, and provider-facing alerts. Feasibility outcomes included participant retention, symptom-reporting engagement, wearable-data completeness, and alert generation. The principal exploratory clinical outcome was quality of life measured using the Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy-General (FACT-G) at baseline and at 1, 3, and 6 months. Secondary exploratory outcomes included cancer- or treatment-related ED visits and side-effect literacy.

Results

Twenty-six of 30 participants (86.7%) completed the 6-month follow-up. All 15 intervention participants generated symptom-monitoring data, although only 6 (40%) continued symptom recording at week 26. Wearable-device integration was substantially less complete: 8 of 15 intervention participants had any successfully synchronized wearable data, 7 never successfully synchronized their device, and wearable data were available for only 27.2% (n=2715) of expected participant-days. The provider system generated 56 alerts. At 6 months, the mean total FACT-G score was numerically higher in the intervention group than in the control group (84.23, SD 12.13 vs 77.15, SD 14.00; Hodges-Lehmann estimate 6.50, 95% CI -0.83 to 16.50; P=.07), but no FACT-G total or subscale comparison remained statistically significant after Holm adjustment for multiple comparisons. Cancer- or treatment-related ED visits occurred in 0 of 13 intervention participants and 3 of 13 control participants (P=.22). Side-effect literacy did not differ significantly between groups at 3 months (P=.46).

Conclusions

This pilot study supports the feasibility of initial smartphone-based symptom reporting among patients with solid tumors but provides less support for sustained engagement and reliable wearable-device integration. Exploratory clinical outcomes did not provide confirmatory evidence of effectiveness. Future studies should improve wearable synchronization, incorporate strategies to sustain patient engagement, standardize clinical alert-response pathways, and evaluate the intervention in a larger, adequately powered multicenter randomized trial.
authors: Sainamthip P, Supamontri K, Kudtiyakarn S, Sakunma P, Suthanaseriporn S, Limtrakun N.

title: Feasibility of Using a Wearable Device to Identify Loneliness Among Older Adults Living Alone: Mixed Methods Study
abstract: Background: Addressing loneliness is a public health priority, with increasing interest in technological solutions for older adults. However, evidence on real-world feasibility and acceptability of such technologies remains limited. Objective: This study evaluated the feasibility and acceptability of the Conversation as Therapy (CaT) Pin, a wearable device designed to capture time spent in conversation among older adults living alone, following prototype refinement. Specifically, the study assessed whether a sufficient amount of synchronized, device-derived conversation data and self-reported loneliness data could be generated to explore the relationship between conversation time and loneliness. Methods: A 2-phase, mixed methods feasibility study was conducted. In phase 1, a Consumer Advisory Group (CAG) participated in a 1-hour discussion to inform study processes and device design, followed by a 1-week prototype test with older adults (n=3). Prototype usability, device design, and study procedures were explored through interviews and informed iterative refinement. In phase 2, community-dwelling adults aged 65 years or older living alone trialed the device for 2 weeks. Participants completed activity logs capturing loneliness, activity engagement, device wear, and conversations at 6-hour intervals. Device-captured conversation time was compared with self-reported data where available. Qualitative interviews were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis to understand participant experiences of device acceptability and feasibility. Results: In phase 1, 6 CAG participants, including 3 prototype testers, identified usability and design issues that led to modifications before phase 2. Phase 2 involved 23 participants (15 women; mean age 79.4 y, SD 6.7 y), with 7 classified as lonely using the UCLA-3 scale. However, only 8 (34.8%) participants generated sufficient concurrent device and activity log data, preventing meaningful assessment of the relationship between conversation time and loneliness. Feasibility challenges were driven by device acceptability, namely usability, comfort, aesthetics, and integration into daily life, which limited sustained wear and data synchronization. Qualitative findings indicated that participants prioritized quality rather than quantity of social interaction, and many did not perceive personal benefit from device use, citing lack of perceived need or concerns related to functionality and design. Together, methodological and conceptual challenges were identified in using conversation time as a potential indicator of loneliness. Conclusions: This study demonstrated that, in its current form, using a wearable device to capture time spent in conversation and align these data with self-reported loneliness was not feasible among older adults living alone. Feasibility was constrained by device acceptability related to usability, participant adherence, and data synchronization challenges. Findings also suggest that conversation time alone may be insufficient as an indicator of loneliness, given participants' emphasis on the quality and personal meaning of social interaction. These results provide practical lessons for future digital health research with older adults, including the need for early co-design, monitorable data-capture systems, and more nuanced approaches to measuring loneliness.
authors: Rajna Ogrin; Georgina Johnstone; Bradley Crammond; Judy A. Lowthian

title: Feasibility of home sleep apnea testing with NightOwl and SleepImage in patients with type 2 diabetes: an external pilot study
abstract: Background Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is more prevalent and substantially underdiagnosed in patients with type 2 diabetes (T2DM), whose regular follow-up offers an opportunity for OSA screening. The current diagnostic approach requires resources not available in that setting, whereas the less complex and less obtrusive wearables NightOwl and SleepImage are promising alternatives. Their diagnostic accuracy must be established in patients with T2DM, in whom cardiac autonomic neuropathy may affect the signals acquired by both devices. This external pilot feasibility study aimed to assess device and study feasibility prior to a diagnostic accuracy study. Methods Adults with T2DM in Denmark were recruited through a tertiary diabetes outpatient clinic, general practice, and Facebook. In this single-arm, non-randomized study, participants underwent home sleep apnea testing on three consecutive nights with the two wearables NightOwl and SleepImage, with the cardio-respiratory monitor Nox T3 added on the third night as a comparator. Failed test nights were repeated. Device feasibility comprised the proportion of analyzable recordings per device and participants' experience with the two wearables, assessed by a questionnaire using visual analog scale (VAS) ranging from 0 to 100 and categorical items. Study feasibility comprised the inclusion rate, recruitment source, and measures of completion. All outcomes were analyzed descriptively. Results Forty-three adults were included. Median age was 61 years, and 51% were male. Most were recruited through Facebook (79%), and the inclusion rate was 3.9 participants per month. Median VAS scores were 83 for NightOwl and 92 for SleepImage. Analyzable recordings were obtained on 75% to 85% of intended test nights across all three devices. Sixty-seven percent completed all planned test nights after a median of three attempted nights, whereas non-completers attempted a median of six nights. Moderate-to-severe OSA was found in 56% of participants with an analyzable Nox T3 recording. Conclusions Participants reported a favorable experience with both NightOwl and SleepImage, and the main diagnostic accuracy study will proceed with active recruitment added. Its design should account for a technical success rate of roughly three in four recordings and a completion rate of two in three. Trial registrations Registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT07778121) on 14 January 2026. Retrospectively registered during recruitment.
authors: Mathilde Hvidtfelt Kjeldsen; Line Troest Dolleris; Asbjørn Kørvel-Hanquist; Gitte Bjørn Hvilsom; Mads Mose Jensen; Troels Wienecke; Preben Homøe

title: Fine-Grained Human Activity Recognition in Domestic Settings Using Ultra-Wideband Radar: A Comparative Study of Deep Learning Models
abstract: Human activity recognition with ultra-wideband (UWB) radar offers contactless, privacy-preserving monitoring of daily living, but distinguishing fine-grained activities performed in the same posture remains difficult. We recorded nine daily activities from 30 participants with a single PulsON 410 radar (3.1-5.3 GHz); seven are performed seated in the same chair and differ only by subtle hand and arm motions. Each 15 s recording is a 120×1440 channel-impulse-response matrix, preprocessed by background subtraction, two-dimensional wavelet denoising and standardization. Six deep learning models (Transformer, CNN-LSTM, 1D-CNN, LSTM, GRU and MLP) and a soft-voting ensemble were compared with participant-independent splits (22 training, 3 validation and 5 test participants) and five-fold cross-validation. The Transformer reached the highest cross-validation accuracy (97.74±0.30%). On the held-out participants, the Transformer (97.16%), 1D-CNN (96.93%) and GRU (96.45%) performed similarly, ahead of the CNN-LSTM, LSTM and MLP (87.47%), and a three-model ensemble reached 98.35%. Two additional participant splits and a retrained re-run confirmed that the MLP is clearly the weakest model, but the order of the other models changed by several points between runs; in the re-run, an ensemble of all six models did not exceed the Transformer (97.74%), and a range-Doppler baseline reached only 50.63%. Eating versus drinking tea and mobile phone use versus reading or sitting idle were the most confused pairs. Given the small test cohort and the controlled setting, the results are indicative rather than definitive.
authors: Muhammad Amjad Raza; Nasir Mehmood; Hafeez Ur Rehman Siddiqui; Adil Ali Saleem; Lázaro Javier Hernández Rodríguez; Pablo Herrero García; Isabel de la Torre Díez

title: Fostering professional vision in clinical ward rounds through digital simulation-based learning with eye-movement modelling examples and personalised feedback: study protocol for four experimental studies
abstract: Introduction Clinical ward round communication is a core competency in medicine. Advanced professional vision (aPV)—comprising visual noticing and knowledge-based reasoning—is foundational to effective ward round performance. Eye movement modelling examples (EMMEs) represent a promising simulation-based approach to training aPV in medical students. This protocol describes four randomised experiments embedded within the EMMA learning environment examining design features of EMME-based training. Methods and analysis Four pre-registered randomised controlled experiments with pre-test/intervention/post-test design. Studies 2a and 2b (October 2026–January 2027): parallel screening experiments; Study 2a: EMME-based learning with raw fixation visualisation versus attention map visualisation versus minimal control (same ward round videos without gaze visualisation) (pre-post design). Study 2b: video-based learning without EMME gaze visualisation, with textual versus graphical versus combined large language model (LLM)-generated feedback versus minimal control (pre-post design). Study 3 (Q2–Q3 2027): confirmatory 2×2 factorial (4 cells, n≈55 per cell) crossing the best visualisation (Study 2a) with the best LLM feedback (Study 2b). Study 4 (Q1-Q2 2028): EMME-based simulation with embedded prompts versus a priori prompts versus no prompts. Participants are randomly assigned via computerised allocation and are medical students in the clinical phase of their studies (third year onwards) at the Technical University of Munich (TUM) with no prior clinical ward round leadership experience. Study 2a: n=96; Study 2b: n=88; Study 3: n=220; Study 4: n=190 (all studies f=0.25, α=0.05, power=0.80, mixed split-plot Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)). Ethics and dissemination Ethical approval was obtained from the Munich Technical University ethics committee (03/2026; grant code 2025-702 S-CT). Dissemination is planned in peer-reviewed journals in the areas of education psychology and medical education. Data of studies 2–4 will be made available following the findability, accessibility, interoperability, and reusability (FAIR) principles () in the TUM Open Data Repository or OSF including metadata and persistent identifier (PID)/digital object identifier (DOI) assignment. Trial registration number The four studies will be pre-registered separately prior to participant enrolment at the Open Science Foundation (OSF) Registries (https://osf.io/registries). Registration numbers and dates will be inserted here upon receipt. Each study will be registered as a separate pre-registration entry, given their distinct hypotheses and designs.

title: From Burden to Breakthrough: A Roadmap to Disentangle Fatigue in Spinal Muscular Atrophy
abstract: Despite observed benefits of current treatments, several burdensome symptoms persist in people living with spinal muscular atrophy (SMA). Fatigue is consistently indicated as a top unmet need by the SMA community. Historically ascribed as an inevitable consequence of underlying muscle weakness, fatigue is now recognized as central to the lived SMA experience, and several efforts have been made to better characterize it. As in other disorders, the study of fatigue in SMA is complicated by inconsistencies in terminology and nomenclature, a challenge compounded by the heterogeneous language patients use to describe their experiences. Without shared language and conceptual frameworks, progress toward an improved understanding of fatigue has been impeded. Critical to this aim is distinguishing between related but distinct constructs: perceived fatigue, a subjective multidimensional experience, and fatigability, a measurable decline in motor output or sustained activity. Both are prominent in SMA, but their biological causes remain unclear. Here, we draw on available evidence and the perspectives of experts, community stakeholders, caregivers, and patients to propose a uniform, collaboratively developed methodology that aims to advance SMA fatigue research and clinical management. This review outlines a roadmap to enhance identification of biological mechanisms and harmonize assessment tools, ultimately leading to a breakthrough in the treatment of fatigue. This iterative process is likely to extend beyond SMA and yield similar benefits in related neuromuscular conditions.
