title: From Data to Awareness: Are Smartwatches Driving Awareness and Healthy Lifestyle Changes?
abstract: The development of wearable technology allows individuals to monitor their health conditions in real-time. The high rate of technology adoption among adolescents to adults allows smartwatches to potentially become an effective intervention tool in shaping healthy lifestyle behaviors. This study aims to analyze whether smartwatch use can encourage increased health awareness and healthy lifestyle changes in adolescents. A quantitative approach was used in this study with a cross-sectional design involving 121 adolescent respondents aged 17–58 years who had used a smartwatch for at least three months. Data were collected through a Likert-scale-based questionnaire that measured smartwatch use, health awareness, and healthy lifestyle changes. Data analysis was performed using Structural Equation Modeling (SEM). The results showed that smartwatch use had an effect on health awareness of β_xy = 0.684, with a p-value of 0.000. In addition, health awareness also had an effect on a healthy lifestyle of β_yz = 0.831, with a p-value of 0.000. The model’s goodness-of-fit test used SRMR with a value of 0.086, which is less than 0.1, so the model is considered fit. These findings are expected to contribute to the development of digital technology-based health interventions and serve as a basis for the use of wearable devices in promoting adolescent health in Indonesia.
authors: Nia Murniati; Fia Fridayanti Adam; Debrina Vita Ferezagia
venue: Advances in Social Science, Education and Humanities Research/Advances in social science, education and humanities research

title: From Prediction to Prevention: A Systematic Review of AI-Driven Predictive Analytics In Healthcare
abstract: Purpose: This study examined how Artificial Intelligence (AI)-enabled predictive analytics moves from technical prediction towards actionable preventive healthcare and identified the conditions that enable or constrain this translation. Design/methodology/approach: A systematic literature review of 12 peer-reviewed studies published between 2021 and 2026 was conducted using Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA)-guided screening, Critical Appraisal Skills Programme (CASP) quality assessment, and open, axial, and selective coding with frequency analysis. Findings: Three themes emerged: predictive performance does not equal preventive value, timeliness and actionability shape preventive utility, and implementation conditions shape translation into practice. The findings show that preventive value depends on the alignment of predictive validity, timely action, workflow integration, decision ownership, and governance. Originality/value: The study introduces the prediction-to-prevention translation gap and develops a decision-oriented framework for evaluating AI beyond model performance.
authors: Soon Eu Hui; Marcus Teunissen; Yash Bafna; Nishu Ayedee
venue: Asia Pacific Journal of Health Management

title: From White Canes to Edge AI: A Survey of Assistive Navigation Technologies for Blind and Low-Vision Individuals
abstract: Independent mobility is a foundational requirement for the autonomy of blind and low-vision (BLV) individuals, yet the assistive technologies that support it have historically evolved slowly. This survey systematically reviews 108 peer-reviewed studies published between 2008 and 2026, organizing the field into four technological eras: (i) a foundational era of passive mechanical aids, namely the white cane and the guide dog; (ii) a hardware era of electronic travel aids built on ultrasonic, infrared, and satellite positioning sensors that alert users to proximity but lack semantic understanding; (iii) a deep learning era in which convolutional and transformer-based detectors introduced context-aware scene understanding, initially tethered to cloud infrastructure; and (iv) a contemporary edge-native era defined by model compression, quantization, hardware acceleration, and multi-sensor fusion that relocate intelligence onto resource-constrained wearable and mobile devices. For each era we analyze representative systems, sensing modalities, computational architectures, and reported performance, and we consolidate the field's model-optimization techniques into a single technical reference spanning four detector families and twelve compression strategies. Across the corpus, we find a persistent mismatch between rapid algorithmic progress and slow real-world adoption, driven by cognitive overload in user interfaces, fragmented evaluation protocols, and the scarcity of studies involving BLV participants. We conclude with open challenges, including seamless indoor-outdoor transition, standardized benchmarks, privacy-preserving perception, and the emerging role of multimodal foundation models, and outline a roadmap for socially acceptable, user-centered assistive navigation.
authors: Abtin Zandi; ARIAN ASHRAFI; Sarvin Nami; Seyed Sina Negahban; Amirabbas Entezari; Parsa Abbasian; Ariyan Azami; Parisa Taherzadeh; Bardia SabaghKermani; Roza Ganjipour; Hamed Farbeh

title: From affect to rules: A conceptual model of compensation in prodromal behavioral frontotemporal degeneration
abstract: Behavioral-variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD) is typically described in terms of progressive loss of social and behavioral control. However, the earliest stages of the disease may also involve active, developed forms of compensation that remain largely invisible to standard assessment. These strategies are rarely characterized, yet they may offer a unique entry point into the mechanisms by which social functioning is temporarily preserved despite emerging degeneration. Here, I report a longitudinal single-case study of a young C9orf72 repeat-expansion carrier followed from the prodromal stage to established moderate bvFTD. Based on more than a dozen hours of semi-structured interviews initiated at symptom emergence, thematic analysis identified five compensatory subthemes. Together, these strategies suggested a coherent shift in the architecture of behavioral control that remain largely invisible to standard medical or neuropsychological assessment. As implicit, flexible, and internally sustained regulation became less reliable, functioning appeared to rely on control processes that were more explicit, environmentally distributed, routine-based, and effortful. These observations can be organized around three broader principles: explicitation, externalization, and stabilization. The case suggests that early preservation in bvFTD may reflect not only residual capacities, but also an active and fragile reorganization of social and behavioral control. By foregrounding the patient's own compensatory work, this study provides a hypothesis-generating conceptual framework for understanding how everyday functioning may be maintained during the prodromal-to-dementia transition, and highlights qualitative longitudinal single-case designs and participatory research as a powerful tool for identifying hidden forms of adaptation in neurodegenerative disease and refine theoretical models of social behavior.
authors: Maxime Bertoux

title: From continuous signals to accountable care: a trajectory-based framework for wearable monitoring in older adults.
abstract: Wearable technologies can continuously measure cardiovascular, physiological, and behavioral signals outside clinical settings, but more measurement does not necessarily produce better care. This limitation is particularly important in older adults, in whom frailty, multimorbidity, polypharmacy, cognitive impairment, altered vascular physiology, and caregiver dependence modify both signal reliability and clinical meaning. We argue that wearable monitoring in later life should move from population thresholds toward individualized physiological trajectories and from automated alerts toward accountable clinical action. We propose a trajectory-to-action framework based on five elements: individual baseline, within-person deviation, multimodal concordance, geriatric contextualization, and predefined clinical response. The framework is conceptual and has not been prospectively validated; its clinical utility, safety, implementation feasibility, and impact on outcomes require prospective testing. In this model, an alert is not a diagnosis but a request for attention whose recipient, response time, confirmatory pathway, and escalation rules are established in advance. Evaluation should therefore extend beyond sensor accuracy to include actionability, alert burden, clinical utility, equity, and net benefit. We propose that wearable monitoring in older adults should be evaluated by whether continuous signals can be translated into proportionate, context-aware, and accountable care.
authors: Jose E Krieger

title: From digital phenotype to closed-loop therapy: artificial intelligence–enabled wearable and connected technology for allergic diseases
abstract: Background The prevalence of allergic diseases continues to rise, yet episodic outpatient care remains constrained by delayed symptom recognition, the "black box" of medication adherence, and fragmented management. Wearables, the Internet of Things (IoT), and artificial intelligence (AI) now converge in "digital phenotyping." From a pharmaceutical perspective, this review appraises these AI-enabled technologies for allergic diseases along the thread of "from digital phenotype to closed-loop therapy." Methods A narrative review synthesizing recent literature on the technical framework, real-time monitoring, risk early warning, long-term management, therapeutic wearables, psychological digital phenotypes, and equity and safety. Results These technologies span the "sensing–warning–management–treatment" chain. Adaptive baseline learning, time-aware modeling, and multimodal fusion enable individualized early warning from noisy physiological and environmental signals. The strongest evidence concerns long-term management: digital inhalers and smartwatches, validated in randomized controlled trials and meta-analyses, improve adherence and asthma control and reduce exacerbations, with economic value in averting biologic escalation; devices are extending from passive sensing to active interventions—nasal acoustic therapy, "feedback as therapy," and conceptual closed-loop epinephrine injection. However, most applications remain at small-sample, single-center validation; portable quantitative pollen detection is an empty niche; and drug confounding of digital phenotypes (β 2 -agonist contamination of heart rate variability) and closed-loop amplification of skin-tone–related bias challenge clinical translation. Conclusions AI-enabled wearables are shifting allergy care from intermittent, subjective consultation toward continuous, closed-loop management, with evidence most mature for digital inhalers. Future work should develop multimodal digital phenotypes and allergy-specific foundation models and strengthen medication-covariate modeling, hard-endpoint validation, and whole-lifecycle equity governance.
authors: Yuxiang Pei; Yongxia Wu; Ruoyu Hou; Kun Wan

title: From the Home to the Tertiary Center: A Personal Health Care Model in Oncology
abstract: Background:Tertiary cancer centers were built for depth and nuance rather than speed, yet patients increasingly judge access by how quickly and with how little friction they can reach a clinician. This mismatch is widening as cancer demand rises and the workforce fails to scale, and added physical capacity alone cannot close it. Durable gains in access, quality, and cost instead require safe, evidence-based capabilities beginning in the patient’s home. Summary:This review outlines a personal health care (PHC) model in oncology that relocates the early work of evaluation from the clinic into the home and examines where the model holds and where it does not. Key Messages:The model is organized as five capability layers: sensing, deciding and acting, monitoring with governance and safety, escalation, and external integration. Patient-owned sensing at home, such as validated at-home urine testing and wearable smart devices, feeds clinician-supervised decision support, while the first in-person visit is preserved for treatment initiation. The clinician remains in the loop across all five layers, as a clinically trained reviewer can draw more decision-relevant information from a brief virtual encounter than an untrained intermediary following a fixed algorithm. For at-home diagnostics and artificial intelligence (AI) tools, the appropriate comparator is not the leading specialists but the large share of patients who currently reach no specialist at all. As the cost of cancer care is driven by the workforce rather than by buildings or equipment, relocating an encounter to the home does not by itself reduce cost, and only a lower-cost workforce meaningfully changes that trajectory.
authors: Jesse T. R. Spooner; Neema Navai

title: Fundamentals of mHealth Technologies and Architectures
abstract: Chapter 1 motivates the need for mHealth in healthcare amid aging populations, chronic disease, access inequities, and workforce pressures. It defines mHealth as a socio-technical system spanning capture, connectivity, computation, interoperability, experience, and governance. We trace historical waves from SMS to learning health systems; survey key technologies (wearables, telemedicine, healthcare IoT, and edge–cloud); and introduce a vendor-neutral reference architecture covering components, network structures, data flows, and stakeholders. Benefits include access, timeliness, personalization, closed-loop workflows, efficiency, equity, and research enablement. We close by mapping cybersecurity risks to each layer and foreshadowing threat models and safeguards developed in the following chapters.
authors: Honggang Wang; Hua Fang; Ye Liu; Ashikur Nobel

title: Future Directions in Tiny Machine Learning
abstract: Tiny machine learning (TinyML) represents a transformative frontier in the evolution of artificial intelligence (AI), merging machine learning capabilities with ultra-low-power embedded systems to enable real-time inference at the edge. As data generation accelerates across billions of Internet of Things (IoT) devices, the need for intelligent edge computing that operates efficiently without relying on cloud infrastructure has become critical. TinyML addresses this demand by enabling localized AI processing on constrained devices with limited memory, computation, and energy resources. This chapter provides a comprehensive exploration of the cutting-edge advancements and research trends shaping the present and future landscape of TinyML. We begin by analyzing the core technological enablers of TinyML, including the rise of energy-efficient microcontrollers, specialized AI hardware accelerators, and neuromorphic computing platforms that emulate human brain-like functionality. Innovations in model compression techniques—such as pruning, quantization, and knowledge distillation—play a central role in shrinking complex deep learning models into formats suitable for resource-constrained environments. Additionally, adopting federated learning architectures allows distributed training and data privacy preservation directly on edge nodes, enabling collaborative intelligence without centralized data aggregation. The chapter also highlights the emergence of event-driven AI, which processes sensory inputs based on relevance or change detection rather than continuous sampling, thus reducing power consumption and latency. These techniques are further enhanced by software frameworks tailored for TinyML deployment, including TensorFlow Lite Micro, Edge Impulse, and TVM. Their integration enables scalable development across various application domains. Real-world implementations of TinyML are explored in depth, with practical use cases spanning healthcare, industrial IoT, agriculture, and smart cities. In healthcare, wearable biosensors powered by TinyML enable continuous physiological monitoring, early disease detection, and personalized health feedback. In industrial environments, TinyML enables predictive maintenance systems that detect anomalies in machinery before catastrophic failures occur. Additionally, autonomous drones and surveillance systems powered by on-device AI offer scalable solutions for crowd analytics, traffic monitoring, and environmental sensing in urban settings. Despite its growing potential, TinyML faces significant challenges, particularly concerning energy constraints, data privacy, and security. To address these issues, emerging solutions such as homomorphic encryption for secure inference, blockchain-based identity management for trusted edge collaboration, and hardware-rooted trust anchors for secure boot processes are examined. Furthermore, the ethical dimensions of deploying AI at the edge—such as algorithmic bias, data ownership, and transparency—are critically assessed. Looking forward, the chapter investigates future research directions and anticipated breakthroughs. The integration of TinyML with 6G-enabled IoT ecosystems is poised to enable intelligent, real-time, and ultra-reliable machine-type communication. Biomedical AI applications powered by TinyML are expected to revolutionize early diagnostics and personalized treatment using implantable or ingestible AI chips. Additionally, advances in cognitive computing and neuromorphic architectures hold promise for self-learning edge devices that adapt dynamically to contextual changes in their environments.
authors: P. Lokeshkiran; C. Mathankumar

title: Fuzzy Fault Detection and Band-Conditioned Data Quality Assessment for Sensor Streams: A Continuous Glucose Monitoring Case Study
abstract: Sensor faults can propagate beyond raw measurements and distort the aggregates used to interpret a monitored phenomenon. We propose a domain-agnostic, five-layer fuzzy pipeline that characterizes the reliability of a sensor stream jointly over time and value bands and carries it through to every derived aggregate: (L1) fault tagging of each sample against five fuzzy failure primitives; (L2) fuzzy windowing; (L3) band reliability; (L4) routed repair with propagated reconstruction uncertainty; and (L5) veracity aggregation with linguistic protoforms. An end-to-end acquisition architecture is also specified. The pipeline was instantiated for continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) with clinical knowledge of glucose dynamics and applied to a 14-month recording of an adult with type 1 diabetes (FreeStyle Libre 3, 5-min cadence), of which 294 days contained at least 120 readings. Clean reference days remained essentially unchanged (mean sample quality 0.98-0.99). On the most corrupted day, the estimated time below range fell from 16% to 3%, with a veracity of only 0.14. Over the recording, 38% of the days were too unreliable to phenotype and 5% changed phenotype. Joint time- and band-conditioned reliability assessment thus prevents corrupted sensor data from producing falsely precise clinical conclusions.
authors: Juan Guerrero; Carmen Martínez-Cruz; Macarena Espinilla; José Luis López Ruiz

title: Gaze in the Machine: How Mechanical and AI-Based Eye Contact Correction Shape Communication Experience and Gaze Behaviour in Video Calls
abstract: Video calls prevent mutual eye contact because the camera and the partner’s image on screen are spatially separated. Teleprompters and AI-based gaze correction promise to restore it, but their effect on users is largely unknown. In a within-subjects study (N = 32), participants played a conversational guessing game with a partner in four conditions: face-to-face, a standard video call, a video call in which the partner used a teleprompter, and a video call with AI-based gaze correction of the partner’s video. We measured social presence , gaze-specific experience and camera awareness by questionnaire, and gaze behaviour by mobile eye tracking. All video conditions showed a large and robust loss of co-presence compared with face-to-face conversation (Cohen’s d z ≈ −1.5 to −1.8), together with heightened camera awareness. Neither intervention narrowed this gap; equivalence tests confirmed comparable co-presence and camera awareness across video conditions. AI-based correction made eye contact feel less natural than the standard video call (d z = −0.54), yet participants’ gaze behaviour remained equivalent. Gaze differences in the teleprompter condition 1 coincided with a smaller on-screen face and are attributable to framing. Restoring the appearance of eye contact thus does not restore what video calls lack. We discuss implications for evaluating and designing gaze technologies.
authors: Leonie Wichers; Leon Schreiber; Sebastian Möller; Robert P. Spang

title: Generation of 12-Lead Electrocardiogram Using Smartwatches in Patients With Cardiac Conditions: Clinical Validation Study
abstract: Background: Smartwatches have significantly expanded personal health monitoring capabilities; however, their application in comprehensive cardiac assessment remains limited by single-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) acquisition. The inability to directly obtain augmented limb leads represents a major limitation for the evaluation of ischemic and arrhythmogenic conditions. Objective: This study aimed to present and preliminarily evaluate a methodology for generating augmented limb leads (augmented voltage right [aVR], augmented voltage left [aVL], and augmented voltage foot [aVF]) from sequential smartwatch recordings through signal synchronization and RR interval alignment, and to combine this approach with precordial smartwatch recordings to reconstruct a full 12-lead ECG in a proof-of-concept setting. Methods: A signal-processing framework was developed to preserve ECG morphology across sequential smartwatch lead recordings. The method is based on RR interval-guided temporal resampling, enabling interlead synchronization and analytical reconstruction of augmented limb leads. A prospective proof-of-concept clinical validation was conducted in 20 cases with diverse cardiac pathologies, including 1 healthy control. Smartwatch-derived ECGs were compared with standard 12-lead ECGs. Evaluation included expert-based clinical interpretation by 85 health care professionals and objective quantitative analysis of key electrocardiographic parameters, including heart rate, PR interval, QRS duration, QT interval, QTc, RR interval, P-wave duration, and PP interval. Mean values, SDs, and intermethod differences were calculated to assess agreement and variability. Results: Reconstruction of a 12-lead ECG from smartwatch-acquired signals was successfully achieved in all cases. Visual correlation scores between smartwatch-derived and conventional ECGs ranged from 78.1% to 91.3% across specialty-level means (mean 81.1, SD 22.7), indicating high perceived concordance; individual case-level scores ranged more widely, from 47.0% to 96.3%. Evaluator-perceived axis agreement reached 95.4% across all cases, while the investigators' direct axis measurements showed complete concordance in all cases. Quantitative analysis demonstrated small mean differences between modalities, with particularly high agreement observed in structurally stable parameters such as heart rate (mean 77.2, SD 22.3 vs mean 75.9, SD 23.1 bpm; Δ=1.3 bpm) and PR interval (mean 176.2, SD 29.1 vs mean 180.8, SD 19.8 ms; Δ=-4.6 ms). Greater variability was observed in atrial activation parameters such as P-wave duration (Δ=-13.3 ms) and time-dependent parameters such as QT (Δ=-19.2 ms) and QTc (Δ=-12.7 ms). Conclusions: This proof-of-concept study demonstrates the feasibility of reconstructing a full 12-lead ECG from smartwatch-derived signals using a synchronization-based approach. The results demonstrated generally small mean differences between conventional and smartwatch-derived ECG measurements, although larger interval differences were observed in some individual cases. Importantly, due to the sequential nature of signal acquisition, the proposed methodology does not aim to achieve direct waveform equivalence but rather clinically meaningful agreement in electrocardiographic parameters. These findings support the potential of smartwatches as accessible tools for advanced cardiac monitoring and broaden their applicability beyond single-lead screening.
authors: Mauro Luis Buelga Suárez; Carmen Plaza–Seco; Roberto Matía; Gonzalo Luis Alonso Salinas; Manuel Blanco–Velasco

title: Generative-AI Rewriting and the Robustness of Health Misinformation Detection: A Cross-Dataset Evaluation of Failure Mechanisms and Mitigation
abstract: Background: Generative AI can alter the surface form, fluency, rhetorical organisation, and evidential register of a health claim without necessarily changing its underlying proposition. High original-text accuracy therefore does not establish model robustness to claim-preserving rewriting, introducing a critical vulnerability into automated public health infrastructure and personalised digital health tools. Objective: To quantify how ChatGPT-based neutral, ELM central-route, and ELM peripheral-route transformations alter health-misinformation detector performance, computational persuasion features, and detector failure mechanisms, and to evaluate whether transformation-aware training mitigates detector failures and improves the reliability of automated health-information assessment. Methods: COVID-19 FNIR and Monkeypox corpora were evaluated under a paired C0–C3 design using four classical and five CNN/recurrent detectors. A balanced 200-root intervention cohort was generated with one C1–C3 descendant per condition. For mitigation, each dataset's intervention roots were divided into 50 augmentation roots and 50 untouched mitigation-test roots; C0-only augmentation was compared with C0+C1–C3 transformation-aware augmentation. Results: Across the initial intervention panel, macro-F1 fell from 0.987 to 0.428–0.479 on FNIR and from 0.922 to 0.731–0.781 on Monkeypox. Failure modes differed sharply, revealing distinct information-quality risks relevant to digital health safeguards. FNIR failure was dominated by false-positive inflation, indicating a risk of incorrectly flagging reliable health information, whereas mpox showed substantial increases in misinformation false negatives, indicating a risk of failing to identify rewritten misleading claims. Transformation-aware training increased mean C1–C3 macro-F1 on unseen Monkeypox roots by 0.148 across nine models (9/9 improved; Wilcoxon p=0.0039) while preserving panel-level C0 performance (+0.004). FNIR mitigation was smaller and heterogeneous (+0.035; 7/9 models improved; p=0.164), and cross-dataset transfer was inconsistent. Conclusions: Generative-AI rewriting produced substantial, dataset-dependent deterioration in health-misinformation detector performance, even under transformation instructions intended to preserve the underlying claims. Transformation-aware augmentation improved in-domain robustness, particularly for mpox, but did not consistently generalise across datasets. These findings support the inclusion of transformation-based stress testing and class-specific error analysis when evaluating potential automated health-information safeguards. Independent semantic-fidelity validation and application-specific evaluation remain necessary before clinical deployment implications can be established.
authors: Mkululi Sikosana

title: Geography-Aware Energy-Adaptive IoT-WSN Monitoring for Sustainable Smart Irrigation in Precision Agriculture.
abstract: IoT-based wireless sensor networks are increasingly used in smart irrigation, allowing continuous monitoring of soil, weather and crop-water conditions. However, the deployment of sensors knowing only the geographical location cannot ensure sustainable monitoring as the operational constraints such as communication distance, residual energy, packet delivery, dynamic irrigation risk, and node lifetime are still critical. This paper presents a sustainable smart irrigation monitoring framework using a geography-aware energy-adaptive IoT-WSN. The framework encompasses optimized sensor deployment, radio-energy modeling, sink placement analysis, event-driven and adaptive communication, solar energy harvesting, and machine learning-based next-round irrigation risk prediction. Simulations were performed with an irrigation monitoring dataset consisting of multiple measurements of soil moisture, soil nutrient status, temperature, humidity, precipitation, solar radiation, evapotranspiration, spatial coordinates, and critical-event labels. Results show that direct transmission provides complete packet delivery but short lifetime, and event-driven communication reduces transmissions over 94% but weakens the monitoring continuity. ML-assisted adaptive monitoring reduces the transmissions between 56.57%–61.94% while adaptive harvesting achieves the strongest composite sustainability ranking of 0.8317 packet delivery ratio and 1000-round lifetime. This work provides an integrated framework for the joint assessment of energy efficiency, reliability, prediction and sustainability under field constraints for precision agriculture.
authors: Giriraja C. V; T. K. Ramesh

title: Harnessing AI for Hypothyroidism Monitoring Using Wearable-Derived Heart Rate Data: Retrospective Cohort Study
abstract: Background: Hypothyroidism is a prevalent endocrine disorder characterized by an insidious onset and nonspecific symptoms, often leading to significant diagnostic delays. While biochemical thyroid function tests (TFTs) are the gold standard, their invasive nature and cost make them impractical for continuous, proactive screening of at-risk populations. Thyroid hormones exert direct chronotropic effects on the cardiovascular system, and their levels are closely correlated with heart rate (HR). Wearable devices capable of continuous HR monitoring offer a novel opportunity for noninvasive, digital phenotype-based detection. Objective: This study aimed to develop and validate an AI-assisted system that uses wearable-derived sleep HR data as a digital monitoring tool for individuals at risk of hypothyroidism, helping identify those who warrant further confirmatory thyroid testing. Methods: This retrospective cohort study used 1677 paired observations consisting of sleep HR data and serum TFT results, including free thyroxine (T4) and thyroid-stimulating hormone levels, from 413 participants (mean age 43.1, SD 9.7 y; women: n=314, 76%). Participants wore consumer-grade wearables (Fitbit) that recorded HR and sleep data. Each TFT result was paired with sleep HR data extracted from the 15 consecutive nights preceding the blood test. An AI system was developed using a gradient boosting algorithm (LightGBM) to classify thyroid status by integrating baseline TFT results with statistical and temporal HR features. The model's performance was evaluated using patient-level leave-one-out cross-validation. To examine the benefit of longitudinal data, performance was compared using 1, 2, or 3 prior paired observations as reference points. Results: To ensure clinical relevance and avoid performance inflation from hyperthyroid cases, we prioritized the analysis of a subset containing only euthyroid and hypothyroid data (n=744 paired observations). In this clinically challenging subset, the system achieved an accuracy of 74.6%, with a sensitivity of 82% and a specificity of 73.5% using a single-reference data pair. Incorporating longitudinal HR patterns further enhanced performance; using 3 reference pairs improved accuracy to 78.1% (sensitivity 81.8% and specificity 77.7%). In the overall dataset (n=1677 paired observations), the system demonstrated an accuracy of 80.8%, with a sensitivity of 82% and a specificity of 80.8% using a single-reference pair. Notably, the system achieved high clinical safety by detecting 96.3% of severe overt hypothyroidism cases (free T4 <0.5 ng/dL). Conclusions: This AI-assisted system demonstrates the feasibility of a sensitive, noninvasive longitudinal monitoring tool for hypothyroidism, robustly identifying a high proportion of hypothyroid cases-particularly severe ones-to prioritize at-risk individuals for confirmatory blood tests. Given the predominantly female iatrogenic-withdrawal cohort, prospective sex-balanced validation in primary hypothyroidism is warranted.
authors: Kyubo Shin; Yewon Jung; Won Sang Yoo; Min Joo Kim; Tae Jung Oh; Joon Ho Moon; Sung Hye Kong; Won Woo Lee; Jae Hoon Moon

title: HeadRoom: Lightweight, Edge-deployable Pipeline for Adaptive Notification Routing
abstract: Emerging wearables, such as smart glasses, can deliver notifications through multiple sensory channels, but there is still a limited understanding of how to choose the right channel at the right moment. We propose HeadRoom, a lightweight, edge-deployable pipeline that estimates the availability of visual and auditory channels in real time from egocentric video and audio. Our controlled user study (N = 25) shows that, under high perceptual load, routing notifications to the more available channel reduces response time relative to routing them to the less available channel. This work opens up a new possibility for adaptive routing of notifications in wearable and immersive systems.
authors: Dinithi Dissanayake; Prasanth Sasikumar; Suranga Chandima Nanayakkara
venue: ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)

title: Health Care Utilization Among Patients With Coronary Artery Disease Using mHealth Wearable Devices: Feasibility Observational Study
abstract: Background: Although prior research has explored patient engagement with health care providers through software applications such as patient portals, the impact of patient engagement with mobile health (mHealth) technologies on subsequent utilization of health care resources remains poorly understood. Specifically, it remains unclear whether physiological data collected from wearable devices can be linked to future health care encounters across different modes of care utilization. Objective: This pilot study was aimed at evaluating the feasibility of an mHealth prototype for analyzing cardiovascular disease outcomes and health care utilization among patients using digital health interventions. Specifically, we examined the feasibility of integrating physiological data from wearable devices to examine associations with future care utilization, offering early evidence for the effectiveness of patient engagement with mHealth platforms. Methods: Patients with a history of coronary artery disease were recruited from the cardiology clinic of a large academic medical center. Before data collection, the study coordinator trained 20 patients on the use of Garmin devices, of whom 19 were included in the analyses. Data collected from the use of wearable devices were analyzed together with electronic health record data. Patient health outcomes were tracked from June 2019 to May 2021, including approximately 1500 health care encounters that encompassed hospital and outpatient visits, telehealth visits, and other encounters. Beyond establishing the feasibility of the mHealth platform, this work provided preliminary evidence of associations between (1) mHealth device use and future health care utilization and (2) physiological data and the frequency of future health care encounters. Results: This study demonstrated the feasibility of an mHealth prototype for collecting and analyzing data to measure care utilization among patients with cardiovascular disease. Participants' use of the wearable mHealth device was associated with a statistically significant lower frequency of subsequent hospital and outpatient visits but greater utilization of other health care services, such as procedures, infusions, and medication refills, during the study period. However, none of these associations were statistically significant when the pretreatment period was restricted to the COVID-19 era. Minimum heart rate was associated with a higher frequency of future hospital and outpatient utilization, whereas activity time was associated with a higher frequency of procedural and refill visits. Conclusions: This pilot study provides preliminary evidence that mHealth device use is associated with a reduction in future inpatient and outpatient visits and an increase in the number of visits for other health care services. It also indicates that patients' physiological data, such as minimum heart rate and activity time, are associated with the frequency of future health care encounters. These findings should be interpreted as exploratory signals rather than statistically definitive conclusions. This study provides proof of concept that an integrated mHealth platform can generate physiologically meaningful measures associated with subsequent care utilization, supporting its potential as a scalable tool for patient engagement and care coordination.
authors: Indranil R. Bardhan; Gari D. Clifford; Mujeeb A. Basit; DuWayne L. Willett; Tianjian Guo; Herman A. Taylor

title: Healthsync-AI: Health Monitoring and AI-Driven Emergency System
abstract: HealthSync AI (HSAI) is an intelligent health monitoring system designed to make personal healthcare more accessible, convenient, and proactive through the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI), the Internet of Things (IoT), and software technology. In today's busy lifestyle, people may overlook changes in their health until they become serious, highlighting the need for continuous monitoring and timely awareness. HealthSync AI addresses this need by providing a desktop application where users can manage their health profiles, monitor vital signs and physical activity through compatible Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) devices, and store their health information securely in a user-specific database. The system uses AI-based analysis to examine available health readings, identify unusual patterns, and provide personalized health insights and general wellness recommendations. It also incorporates features such as nearby hospital discovery, emergency contact support, and outbreak-related information to help users make more informed decisions. By combining wearable sensor data, intelligent analysis, and an easy-to-use interface, HealthSync AI aims to encourage healthier habits and support early awareness of potential health concerns. The system is intended to complement, rather than replace, professional medical advice and diagnosis. Right now, our healthcare system is fundamentally reactive, meaning people usually only end up in a hospital after their symptoms have already become severe. Most healthcare apps available today are pretty limited, functioning mostly as digital filing cabinets for storing medical records or simple tools for booking appointments. On a broader scale, public health authorities are constantly fighting an uphill battle. Because medical data is scattered across different systems and reporting is often delayed, officials struggle to spot disease outbreaks at an early stage when intervention could actually save lives. To move far beyond the single-metric limitations of typical open-source projects, HealthSync AI is designed to ingest and process eleven distinct telemetry streams simultaneously, offering a complete and continuous window into a user's physiological state. This multi-parameter data doesn't just sit in a silo; it is securely managed through local SQLite persistence and channeled into an intelligent backend framework that processes structured health observations rather than relying on superficial, generic API wrapper chatbots. The platform also tackles the broader systemic issues of delayed reporting and fragmented medical data by introducing integrated outbreak analysis. While traditional systems leave public health authorities struggling to spot community-level risks in time, HealthSync AI bridges individual continuous monitoring with aggregated insights to help track potential health threats at an early stage. Combined with built-in emergency response features and a clean separation of responsibilities across its BLE, database, and UI layers, HealthSync AI transforms personal wellness tracking and community health intelligence into a single, cohesive, and future-ready solution.
authors: Ayush Nanekar; Anant Kumbhar; Shubham Mutkule; Sarthak Wagh; Soni Ragho

title: Higher explanation-necessity scores are associated with longer written explanations of autonomous driving scenes
abstract: Explanations of automated-vehicle behavior may help occupants understand what prompted a maneuver, but how much an explanation should say remains an open design question. Retrospective annotation of recorded driving scenes can supply candidate content. We analyzed 1,103 training and test records from the release, matching the source-described corpus size; each paired human-written text with an aggregate perceived explanation-necessity score. Explanations contained 9,541 whitespace-delimited tokens (mean 8.65; range 2–20) before lexical preprocessing. Higher scores were associated with longer explanations (Pearson’s \(r=0.374\) ; template-cluster bootstrap 95% interval [0.266, 0.448]), including after score-1.0 observations were excluded. We call this corpus-level length association progressive elaboration . Bounded-model comparisons did not identify a unique latent-category count. For groupwise summaries, we used four descriptive partitions: three below-ceiling regions and 59 records scored 1.0. Record-weighted and unique-template analyses showed higher within-partition lexical distinctiveness in upper than in lower partitions. In template-grouped cross-validation of these exploratory partitions, the unweighted text model exceeded token-count and stratified-dummy baselines in balanced accuracy (0.382 versus 0.327 and 0.247). The 1,280-record rerun preserved the score—length, lexical, and predictive findings and left the latent-category count unresolved. These results motivate prospective studies of how annotation-derived content should be selected, compressed, and delivered in real time.
authors: Gwangbin Kim; Dohyeon Yeo; Yumin Kang; Minwoo Oh; SeungJun Kim

title: Historical Perspectives on Spinocerebellar Ataxia Type 2: The Cuban Contribution
abstract: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 2 (SCA2) is one of the most extensively investigated hereditary ataxias worldwide. Although the first clinical description of the disorder was reported in India in 1971 by Wadia and Swami, the province of Holguín, Cuba subsequently became recognized as a major geographical focus of SCA2, with a particularly high concentration of affected families and individuals, where it became internationally recognized as Cuban ataxia. Since the late 1970s, Cuban investigators have played a pivotal role in the clinical, epidemiological, neuropathological, and genetic characterization of the disorder. This article presents a historical review of the scientific development of Cuban ataxia based on a comprehensive bibliographic and documentary analysis, complemented by interviews with key neurologists involved in its early investigation. Particular emphasis is placed on the pioneering contributions of José Rafael Estrada González, Lionel Valles Calaña, Guillermo Orozco Díaz, and Luis Velázquez Pérez, whose work established the foundations for the current understanding of SCA2. Their investigations culminated in the identification of one of the world's largest SCA2 clusters and substantially advanced knowledge of the disease's clinical spectrum, epidemiology, and molecular genetics. The Cuban experience illustrates how sustained clinical observation, multidisciplinary collaboration, and international partnerships transformed a regional neurological disorder into one of the best-characterized hereditary ataxias worldwide. © 2026 International Parkinson and Movement Disorder Society.
authors: Otto Jesús Hernández Fustes; Carlos Arteaga Rodríguez; Hélio Afonso Ghizoni Teive

title: HomeLoop: A Simulation Framework and Benchmark for Robot-IoT Coordination in Everyday Domestic Assistance and Safety
abstract: Recent progress in embodied robotics is bringing robots closer to deployment in homes, as vision-language models (VLMs) are demonstrating significant advances in reasoning, making VLM-driven robots promising home assistant agents. These agents will often be introduced into homes that already have cameras, Internet of Things (IoT) devices, and residents with wearables. To fulfill their potential, they need to integrate with existing smart infrastructure and reason through ambiguous scenarios: a smoke alarm may come from a pan about to ignite, a pan already on fire, a resident cooking or a faulty sensor, and each calls for a different response. To that end, we introduce HomeLoop, a simulation framework and benchmark built on Isaac Sim that combines robot bodies, networked devices and wearables, simulated residents and visitors, faulty sensors, and hazards that evolve over time. Our benchmark is composed of 20 tasks across five families grounded in real-world household hazards and needs, and designed so that the same alert can have different causes. A runtime monitor scores each episode with temporal-logic checks on the final outcome and the actions along the way, and every action carries a predefined cost. We evaluate six open-weight and proprietary VLMs. The best achieves a family-balanced score of 61.9%, and across models we see a pattern of over-reaction: failed episodes involving prohibited interventions outnumber those involving missed required interventions by more than two to one, with models often shutting off the stove before investigating the alarm's cause. HomeLoop is an extensible foundation intended for use in research on robot-IoT coordination, long-term memory, proactive assistance, and privacy-safety trade-offs. HomeLoop will be released with 2,100 home layouts that can be automatically furnished in diverse configurations, five robot bodies and 20 networked device types.
authors: Ramy ElMallah; Marc Bishara; Hyegang Kim; Yuxi Zhang; Chongyu Zhu; Chi-Guhn Lee

title: HomeNarrator: Natural-Language Activity Descriptions From Binary Ambient Sensors
abstract: Smart homes with ambient sensors record daily life continuously and privately, underpinning aging-in-place monitoring and ambient intelligence. Yet for two decades such systems have produced only discrete activity labels, which cannot express concurrent, ambiguous, or transitional behaviour; roughly half of all recorded data collapses into an uninformative “Other” class. We present HomeNarrator, to our knowledge the first system to generate free-text descriptions of resident activity from binary PIR and door sensors. It converts raw CASAS events into structured elapsed-time segments, which a large language model (LLM) narrates under evidence-bounded rules that limit hallucination. Lacking reference descriptions, we evaluate reference-free: a three-model LLM jury, cross-validated against human annotators, scores each description on an evidence-grounded rubric. In the stratified annotation subset, raters judged 78 % of windows high quality (mean nine or above), and the jury tracked that mean within one point (MAE 0.76 / 0.84). These results establish descriptive human activity recognition (HAR) as feasible on sparse ambient sensors in single-resident homes.
authors: Sebastian Pilatus; Nika Strem; Reiner Wichert

title: Host–Virus Immune Interactions in Andes Virus Infection: Implications for Human-to-Human Transmission, Pathogenesis, and Public Health
abstract: , andesense) is unique among hantaviruses in that it may transfer from person to person and cause severe vascular damage. The evidence on host-virus immunological interactions and their importance in disease progression, transmission, and public health is compiled in this narrative review. ANDV mostly affects pulmonary endothelial cells and does not result in widespread cell loss. Rather, the loss of vascular barrier integrity is caused by vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) signaling, Ras homolog family member A (RhoA) activation, breakdown of vascular endothelial (VE)-cadherin, hypoxia-related pathways, and mediators produced from infected pericytes. Additionally, the virus interferes with early antiviral defenses involving protein kinase R (PKR), TANK-binding kinase 1 (TBK1)-interferon regulatory factor 3 (IRF3), mitochondrial antiviral-signaling protein (MAVS), and retinoic acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I)/melanoma differentiation-associated protein 5 (MDA5). The intensity or outcome of the disease has been associated with increased interleukin-6 (IL-6), altered complement activity, thrombocytopenia, neutralizing-antibody reactions, and specific host genetic variations; nevertheless, significant T-cell activation does not necessarily correspond with viral clearance. Blood and a number of mucosal and secretory samples have been found to contain ANDV ribonucleic acid (RNA), albeit RNA discovery by itself does not prove the presence of an infectious virus. Epidemiological evidence indicates that Secondary transmission is rare and mostly linked to extended close or intimate contact. Genomic sequencing, when paired with epidemiological evidence, can shed light on transmission chains. Recent outbreaks linked to travel further emphasize the significance of worldwide surveillance and coordinated contact tracing. Prospective studies integrating genomic analysis, serial virological sampling, and standardized exposure evaluation are required to more effectively define the infectious phase and transmission patterns.
authors: Awadh Alanazi; Mohamed Nabil Fathy Ibrahim; MaramAwied Alenezi; Rahaf Ziyad I. Alabdullah

title: Human Centered Design Perspectives on Edge Intelligent Wearable Devices for Continuous Physiological Monitoring
abstract: The advancement of biomedical technology through wearable devices enables continuous physiological monitoring; however, challenges remain regarding user comfort, acceptance, and data processing efficiency. This study aims to analyze the application of Human-Centered Design in edge intelligent wearable devices for continuous physiological monitoring. The research was conducted in one manufacturing industry in Surabaya City, East Java Province, using a mixed-method approach. Data were collected through interviews with 15 informants and prototype evaluations involving 40 respondents through usability assessments and physiological parameter measurements. Data were analyzed using thematic analysis and system performance evaluation. The results indicate that a human-centered approach improves user comfort and acceptance, while edge intelligence supports more responsive real-time physiological monitoring. This study contributes to the development of adaptive and user-oriented wearable biomedical systems.
authors: Lamidi Lamidi; Abd Kholiq; Sumber Sumber; Bedjo Utomo

title: Hybrid intelligent modeling for enhanced surface integrity, process dynamics, and sustainable performance in finish ultra-precision hard turning of AISI D2 under dry conditions
abstract: This study presents a hybrid intelligent modeling framework for improving surface quality, process dynamics, and sustainable performance in ultra-precision hard turning of AISI D2 steel of 62 HRC under dry conditions. To address gaps in material-specific modeling and the omission of dynamic process variables in sustainable machining, tool vibration ( V rms ) was integrated with cutting speed, feed, and depth of cut using a full factorial experimental design. ANOVA and Sobol sensitivity analyses identified feed as the most influential factor affecting surface roughness ( R a ) and resultant cutting force ( F R ), while tool vibration exhibited significant interaction effects. Three machine-learning models, Bayesian regularization neural network (BRNN), GA-BRNN, and PSO-BRNN, were developed and compared. BRNN demonstrated the best overall performance based on predictive accuracy and computational efficiency. External validation showed highly accurate prediction of F R with an R 2 of 80.35% and a MAPE of 9.30%. For R a , BRNN achieved an R 2 of 70.43% and a MAPE of 38.41%, corresponding to satisfactory predictive performance according to the adopted MAPE criteria. The comparatively lower R a accuracy reflects the greater complexity and variability of surface generation compared with cutting force formation. The BRNN model was analytically formulated and integrated with a multi-objective particle swarm optimization algorithm to determine Pareto-optimal machining parameters. The optimal conditions ( v c = 75 m/min, f = 0.025 mm/rev, a p = 0.06 mm) yielded predicted F R and R a values of 119.87 N and 0.58 µm, respectively. Confirmation experiments produced an average minimum error of 6%, supporting the framework''s applicability for sustainable machining optimization and intelligent decision support in smart manufacturing.
authors: Ugonna Loveday Adizue; Vahid Pourmostaghimi

title: IOT-Connected Parental Safety System
abstract: This paper shows a parental safety device that uses the Internet of Things. The device is built around an ESP32 microcontroller. The device uses a NEO-6M GPS module to get location information. A MAX30102 sensor measures heart rate. Estimates SpO₂ levels. An MPU6050 sensor checks for movement. A MAX4466 module measures sound levels around the device. The ESP32 uses Wi-Fi to send data to a monitoring interface. A passive buzzer and LED lights give alerts directly on the device.The paper describes how the parts work together. It also summarizes the tests done in the project report. The report does not have data to say anything about accuracy or how fast the system works. The system is meant to help parents stay aware. It is not a replacement for a grown-up watching over a child or for equipment.
authors: Pradeep Gowda; Ushashree B N; Anjan Kumar S.; Mohammadtouz Inamadar; Prajwal A; Sufiyan Aslam Goundi
