title: IOT-enabled wearable device and cloud framework for chronic disease identification and health monitoring using LST-BCLNM
abstract: The continuous monitoring of healthcare data addresses health anomalies and the timely reduction of the chronic disease risk. None of the existing works considered in mitigating the interference of Internet of Things (IoT) healthcare data meant for actual disease identification, besides monitoring. Therefore, this paper presents the mitigation of IoT data interference and healthcare data analysis. Initially, the data from IoT-based wearable devices, healthcare apps, and patient symptoms data are collected. Then, the interference between the IoT data is mitigated using the Sparsity-inducing Reinforcement Learning Regularized Least Mean Square (S-2(RL)MS) technique. Next, the data is secured using the Hyperbolic Tangent Elliptic Logistic Curve Cryptography (HTELCC). Also, the data is transmitted to the edge node based on Ontology Weighted Fair Queuing (OWFQ). In the edge node, data is filtered and aggregated. Then, the features are extracted, and by utilizing Long Short-Term Batch-Centric Layer Normalization Memory (LST-BCLNM), the anomaly is detected. For the presence of disease (anomaly), information is secured and sent to the cloud server. Apache Kafka processes big data, while LST-BCLNM extracts features and classifies chronic diseases accurately. Finally, to access the healthcare data, the doctor/healthcare provider registers and logs into the cloud server. Experimental evaluation demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed IoT-cloud healthcare framework. The LST-BCLNM model achieved 97.58% classification accuracy, 96.56% precision, 97.24% recall, and 98.95% F-measure, while HTELCC attained 98.82% security and S-2(RL)MS achieved a 98.51% convergence rate. These results confirm improved healthcare data reliability, security, and chronic disease monitoring performance.
authors: J. Poongodi; K. Kavitha; Lakshmana Kumar R; Punitha P

title: Identifying Burnout in Pediatric Clinicians Using Wearable Biometric Data: Development and Feasibility Study
abstract: Background: Addressing the burnout epidemic among health care providers remains one of the foremost challenges of modern health care systems. Past researchers have turned to passively gathered biometric data from wearable devices to identify key variables that predict burnout. However, this has resulted in limited success. Objective: This pilot and feasibility study aimed to test the feasibility and accuracy of developing an Extreme Gradient Boosting machine learning model to classify health care providers as being at higher or lower risk of burnout based on their biometric data. Methods: We conducted a 3-month pilot and feasibility study where health care providers self-reported burnout every 6 weeks and wore a Garmin Venu 3 smartwatch to collect continuous biometric data. Participants were recruited from 3 pediatric urgent care sites and an inpatient hospitalist division of a pediatric health care system. We had a final sample of 41 participants who met our inclusion criteria requiring completion of burnout measurements at 2 of the 3 time points and having worn the watch for at least 70% of the study period. Participants were asked to wear the Garmin watch continuously over the course of the study. Burnout self-report surveys were delivered via email. Our main outcome was burnout as measured using the Maslach Burnout Inventory-Human Services Survey. The measure consists of 3 subscales that together constitute burnout: emotional exhaustion, depersonalization, and reduced personal efficacy. Results: First, we found evidence of feasibility for wearable watches to be used in situ for health care providers to gather data passively for the purposes of classifying burnout. A total of 82% (51/62) of participants met our criteria of wearing the watch 70% of the time, with 66% (41/62) having corresponding burnout scores to be included in analyses. Second, our machine learning model achieved strong overall performance in identifying risk of burnout, with strong sensitivity and specificity, demonstrating that biometric data collected using wearable devices can accurately predict burnout. Conclusions: Our evidence of feasibility offers promising results for a passive method of data collection to be used for classifying burnout risk in other health care settings. Furthermore, the strong performance of our machine learning model provides a foundational step toward improving an organization's ability to respond and mitigate burnout through thoughtful intervention strategies.
authors: Thomas B. Ayres; George E. Quaye; Harpreet Singh Gill; Addison Leabo; Catherine Koertje; James Steven Leeder; Brooke L. Fridley; Tiffany Addington

title: Innovative contactless dual-coupled microwave sensor for non-invasive blood glucose monitoring
abstract: In this paper, a novel non-invasive blood glucose monitoring system based on microwave sensing using a compact, contactless and sensitive dual-coupled sensor configuration is proposed. The proposed sensor consists of two electromagnetically coupled resonators, configured as a bandpass filter centered around 2.2 GHz. The sensor is fabricated on a 40 × 40 mm 2 Rogers RO3003C substrate with a 20 mm gap between the resonators to accommodate different finger sizes and incorporates a dedicated mechanical isolation structure to minimize measurement variability caused by direct contact, applied pressure, and positioning uncertainty. The operation of the sensor is based on near-field electromagnetic coupling between the resonators and biological tissue, enabling detection of glucose-correlated variations in dielectric properties without direct skin contact. The experimental trials for glucose concentrations from 76 to 201 mg/dL showed a monotonic decrease in the transmission coefficient with increasing glucose concentration with a sensitivity of 0.031 dB/mg/dL and frequency shift sensitivity of 0.41 MHz/mg/dL. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed sensor and indicate the feasibility of sensitive contactless glucose monitoring using a microwave-based sensor.
authors: R. A. Elgeddawy; A. S. Abd El-Hameed; A. R. Eldamak; H. M. Elhenawy

title: Integrated Taguchi and Grey Relational Optimization of Drilling Process Parameters
abstract: The appropriate selection of machining parameters plays a vital role in enhancing productivity, improving surface finish, and reducing machining costs in drilling operations. The present study focuses on optimizing spindle speed, feed rate, depth of cut, and drill diameter to improve Material Removal Rate (MRR) and minimize surface roughness. Experimental investigations were conducted on EN 36 steel using a CNC drilling machine equipped with carbide-coated HSS twist drills, following an L16 orthogonal array based on the Taguchi design. Signal-to-Noise (S/N) ratio analysis was employed to identify the optimal parameter settings for the individual performance characteristics. Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) was subsequently performed to assess the statistical significance and relative contributions of the selected machining parameters. To achieve simultaneous optimization of MRR and surface roughness, Grey Relational Analysis (GRA) was implemented to convert the multiple-response problem into a single Grey Relational Grade (GRG). Based on the GRG analysis, the optimal machining conditions were determined as a spindle speed of 2500 rpm, a feed rate of 100 mm/min, a depth of cut of 15 mm, and a drill diameter of 18 mm. The ANOVA findings indicated that depth of cut was the most significant factor influencing the overall drilling performance, followed by drill diameter, spindle speed, and feed rate. The results demonstrate the applicability of integrating Taguchi methodology, ANOVA, and GRA for optimizing multiple performance characteristics in the drilling of EN 36 steel.
authors: Naveen Gandhi M; P Rajeswari

title: Interpersonal physiological synchrony in piano ensemble performance: an interdisciplinary study of music psychology and psychophysiology
abstract: Introduction: Whether autonomic nervous system (ANS)-level physiological synchrony exists between ensemble performers, and whether such coupling predicts the quality of collaborative musical performance, has not been directly examined. Methods: = 60) performed four pieces corresponding to a four-quadrant emotional design-high arousal/positive valence (HA/PV), high arousal/negative valence (HA/NV), low arousal/positive valence (LA/PV), and low arousal/negative valence (LA/NV)-based on the valence-arousal circumplex model, in a within-participants repeated-measures design. Heart rate (HR) and electrodermal activity (EDA) were recorded continuously; dyadic synchrony indices were computed via cross-correlation functions (CCF) with cross-pair surrogate permutation control. Multilevel linear models examined whether synchrony predicted expert-rated expressiveness, ensemble cohesion, and overall quality. Results: Both HR-CCF and EDA-CCF significantly exceeded surrogate baselines across all conditions, with peak synchrony under HA/PV. Negative-valence conditions significantly suppressed rated expressiveness, and HR-CCF uniquely predicted ensemble cohesion, whereas EDA-CCF did not significantly predict expressiveness. Neither collaboration duration nor trait empathy reached significance, and no systematic unidirectional leader-follower structure was identified. Discussion: These findings provide the first objective physiological evidence for ANS-level interpersonal physiological synchrony between co-performing musicians and offer partial support for functional differentiation between HR and EDA synchrony channels.
authors: Chang Li

title: Investigating Patient and Public Acceptability of Wearable Technology used during Surgery: An Exploratory Sequential Mixed Methods Survey.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Wearable technologies are increasingly being developed for surgeons to wear intraoperatively, to support decision-making, monitor surgeon performance, and aid training; yet there remains a lack of research into patient's perspectives on them. This study aims to explore patient and public understanding and acceptability of surgeon-worn intraoperative wearables. METHODS: A two-stage, mixed-methods, cross-sectional study was conducted. In Stage 1, neurosurgical inpatients at a UK academic centre participated in semi-structured interviews, supported by an explanatory video; responses were thematically analysed to inform the development of a quantitative survey. In Stage 2, a survey disseminated via social media and patient groups presented six wearable vignettes, which participants rated for appropriateness and comfort. RESULTS: In Stage 1 (n=30), most participants (25/30) had never heard of wearables, yet after the video most (23/30) identified specific benefits, including improved safety and precision. Thirteen expressed no concerns, nine were unconcerned provided devices were tested, regulated, and used by well-trained surgeons, and eight raised specific concerns. In Stage 2 (n=123), 80-95% of participants rated each scenario appropriate, and 87-99% were not uncomfortable with it. Comfort differed significantly by device type (p<0.001), from body-worn (98%) through head-worn (92%) to robotic (87%) wearables. After correction for multiple comparisons, no demographic or familiarity variable, including self-reported understanding, predicted appropriateness or comfort. CONCLUSION: Patients and the public appear highly accepting of surgeon-worn intraoperative wearables, although acceptance varied by device type and, for some, was conditional on safeguards. Device-specific patient education and transparent communication of risks and benefits should accompany their introduction.
authors: Sanchit Aapan; James Booker; Honglin Zhu; Udhay Singh Cheema; Simon C. Williams; Chan Hee Koh; Hani Joseph Marcus

title: Invisible Labour and Silent Burnout: Validating the LIS Identity Strain Scale (LISIS) as an Indicator of Occupational Mental Health among Nigerian Academic Librarians
abstract: Invisible labour and silent burnout remain persistent but poorly measured sources of psychological strain in academic librarianship, particularly in under-resourced institutions. This study develops and validates the Library and Information Science Identity Strain Scale (LISIS), a twelve-item instrument designed to measure identity-based occupational strain among academic librarians. A mixed-methods design was used, with survey data from fifty early-career librarians in three Nigerian universities and semi-structured interviews with ten of them. Occupational mental health is indexed throughout by two established measures, emotional exhaustion on the Maslach Burnout Inventory and satisfaction on the Job Satisfaction Survey. No clinical construct is measured or implied. The LISIS returned an overall internal consistency of .825, with subscale values between .79 and .86, and exploratory factor analysis returned the four dimensions on which it was built, although on a sample of fifty that solution is better read as provisional. Identity strain, and in particular role invisibility and recognition deficit, were strongly associated with emotional exhaustion (r = .62, p < .01) and inversely associated with job satisfaction (r = -.55, p < .01), with the four dimensions together accounting for 51 per cent of the variance in emotional exhaustion. All five null hypotheses were rejected. The evidence reported here is preliminary and awaits confirmatory testing, but it establishes the LISIS as a workable diagnostic instrument for a professional group that has remained largely absent from occupational health scholarship.
authors: Aderinola Ololade Dunmade; Adeyinka Tella

title: IoT Based Smart Safety Wristband Using BLE Zone Sensing and LoRa Long-Range Alerting for High-Density Public Gatherings
abstract: Large religious and public gatherings, such as the Kumbh Mela, bring together millions of people in a small area for a short period. In these conditions mobile networks become congested, and an individual in distress often cannot be identified or reached in time. This paper presents the design of an IoT Based Smart Safety Wristband that combines two complementary low-power radio technologies. Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) is used for short-range zone sensing and active geofencing: fixed beacons advertise their zone identity, and the wristband classifies the zone it is in. LoRa is used for long-range, infrastructure-independent delivery of compact alert packets to a gateway, from where a web dashboard shows the zone and status of every wristband. The wristband is built around an ESP32 microcontroller with an SOS button, an OLED display, a vibration motor, a buzzer and status LEDs, and is powered by a rechargeable Li-ion cell. We review thirteen published studies on LoRa range and reliability, BLE zone detection and crowd safety, and use their findings to justify key design choices: a very short payload, a sliding-window RSSI filter with hysteresis, and local alerting that works even when the backhaul is unavailable. The paper reports the system design, the alert protocol, an analytical time-on-air estimate and a structured evaluation plan. Field measurements are deliberately not reported, because the prototype tests are still in progress; the evaluation tables are provided so that measured values can be entered once available
authors: Aditi Adke, Aditya Bhor, Aditi Tarle; Sachin Suryawanshi Rohit Uphade
venue: International Journal of Advanced Research in Science Communication and Technology

title: Iot-Enabled Wearable Device For Monitoring Adolescent Physical Activity and Cardiometabolic Health
abstract: The increasing prevalence of physical inactivity and sedentary behavior among adolescents has created a need for continuous and objective approaches for monitoring physical activity and associated cardiometabolic health indicators. This study developed an IoT-enabled wearable monitoring framework integrating multimodal movement, physiological, behavioral, and anthropometric information for automated physical-activity recognition and cardiometabolic-risk screening. The proposed wearable system incorporated a three-axis accelerometer, gyroscope, optical heart-rate sensor, oxygen-saturation sensor, and skin-temperature sensor. Sensor measurements were synchronized, preprocessed, segmented, and transformed into relevant movement and physiological features. Physical activities including sitting, standing, walking, running, and stair climbing were analyzed using a dataset comprising 893 samples with balanced representation across activity categories. Random Forest and Support Vector Machine models were employed for activity classification and cardiometabolic-risk screening. The results demonstrated clear increases in movement intensity and physiological response with increasing activity level. Accelerometer magnitude increased from 0.50 during sitting to 2.25 during running, while average heart rate increased from 85.2 BPM to 154.8 BPM. The seven-day monitoring analysis recorded an average sedentary duration of 422.4 minutes and total active duration of 228.6 minutes per day. Random Forest achieved superior activity-classification performance, with 98.3% accuracy, 98.4% precision, 98.3% recall, and a 98.3% F1-score. For cardiometabolic-risk screening, Random Forest achieved 96.8% accuracy, 96.2% sensitivity, 97.1% specificity, and an AUC of 0.982. The proposed framework demonstrated the potential of integrating wearable sensing, IoT connectivity, and machine learning for continuous adolescent activity monitoring and data-driven cardiometabolic-risk screening, providing a foundation for personalized health monitoring and preventive intervention.
authors: Priyanka SinhaS; Siddharth GautamS; Medapati Prema KumarS; U. SivajiS; H. VidyalakshmiS; Shriram N. KargaonkarS

title: LLM-Driven Automatic Reward Optimization for Ambient Intelligence Robots with Curriculum Interference Auto-Correction
abstract: Service robots in ambient intelligence (AmI) scenarios such as smart factories and home services must rapidly adapt to diverse manipulation tasks, yet traditional reinforcement learning (RL) reward design heavily relies on domain expertise, requiring days to weeks of manual tuning. Existing LLM-assisted reward design methods assume that generated rewards can be directly applied to training environments, overlooking potential incompatibility with built-in training mechanisms such as curriculum learning. To our knowledge, this is the first study to quantify the signal interference phenomenon between LLM-generated rewards and curriculum dynamic weight adjustments---experiments reveal that curriculum modules amplify penalty weights from an initial $-1\times10^{-4}$ to $-0.1$ (a factor of 1000$\times$), overwhelming the positive reward signals---and it proposes an automatic detection and correction mechanism based on feedback ratio anomaly detection. A unified dual-paradigm framework adapting to both ManagerBasedRL and DirectRL paradigms on the IsaacLab platform, along with a humanized interaction paradigm for non-expert users, are also developed. Systematic experiments on five robot tasks of varying difficulty, including ablation studies, 8-sample random search baselines, and multi-seed statistical tests, demonstrate: on Franka Lift the success rate increases from 0\% to 84\%$\pm$2\% and the mean reward from 0.90 to 84.41$\pm$5.50, where simply disabling the curriculum yields a roughly 5$\times$ increase in mean reward (0.90$\rightarrow$4.47)---a necessary prerequisite for LLM reward optimization to take effect---and combining it with the LLM-designed multi-stage reward structure multiplies the improvement by a further 18.9$\times$; under an equal-compute random-search comparison, LLM weight optimization achieves a 47\% improvement over the best random configuration. Mean-reward ratios depend on the reward definition and should be read together with the scale-invariant success rate. The method reduces reward design time from expert-days to hours, validated on the commercial LLM DeepSeek-V4-Pro.
authors: Bi P, Ren R, Zhang Z, He Y.

title: LLMs as Narrators of Lived Experience: A Study of Generative Hermeneutical Epistemic Injustice in ADHD Sense-Making
abstract: Large language models (LLMs), as non-human actors, do not have access to first-hand experiences. Yet they are increasingly consulted in processes of making sense of them, from mental health chatbots to reflexive journals. As a result, complex lived realities risk being distorted or flattened through second-order representations. In this paper, we expand on conceptual work to empirically examine narrative mechanisms through which LLMs as narrators give rise to hermeneutical epistemic injustice. We foreground narration as a key interpretive process through which experience is made intelligible. Focusing on ADHD as a motivating case, we compare first-person narratives from online ADHD communities with narratives generated by LLMs. Using an interpretive, reflexive analysis, we examine how these forms of narration construct lived experience. We find that generated narratives organise ADHD experience through recurring modes that individualise, standardise, and stabilise interpretation, reducing messiness, complexity and ambiguity present in community narration. More situated and unresolved accounts remained possible when foregrounded through prompting. We argue that the epistemic concern lies not only in what models can represent, but in which interpretations they make readily available and which require prior conceptual and prompting work.
authors: Anne Arzberger; Dongying Zhang
venue: Proceedings of the AAAI/ACM Conference on AI Ethics and Society

title: Low-Terahertz Channel Performance in Falling Wheat for Moisture Sensing
abstract: Terahertz (THz) waves are highly sensitive to water and therefore offer a promising noncontact approach to wheat moisture sensing, but existing THz studies have been limited to static samples. This article investigates moisture sensing based on the performance of a THz channel in falling wheat, as encountered at grain intake. The channel power loss is measured at six frequencies from 120 to 320 GHz for three moisture contents and interpreted with a physics-based model that couples the double-Debye permittivity of water, Landau-Lifshitz-Looyenga mixing, and Lorenz-Mie extinction. The model reproduces the measured loss. Above the extinction maximum, the dielectric moisture response peaks where the wavelength approaches the kernel diameter, and that a two-frequency loss ratio removes the loading dependence. A channel-level analysis of QPSK and 16-QAM links shows that a 1 dB moisture-induced loss change alters the bit error rate (BER) by a factor of 3 to 30. THz communication channels at grain intake could therefore sense moisture as a byproduct of data transmission.
authors: Xiaoxiang Li; Hanchen Liu; Kefeng Huang; Jiabiao Zhao; Mingxia Zhang; Jie Yang; Yuheng Song; Wenbo Liu; Peian Li; Chunhua Zhu; Jianjun Ma

title: MEM-STRESS: Longitudinal Field Study of a Wearable-Informed AI Chatbot for Stress Management
abstract: Stress is an increasingly prevalent concern, creating a need for accessible and personalized support. Stress-management chatbots primarily rely on what users report, which may not capture their physiological changes. Wearables capture these changes, but chatbots rarely use them as memory across conversations. We therefore present MEM-STRESS, a stress-support chatbot that turns a wearable ring's physiological data into a layered memory of daily records, baseline deviations, LLM-generated summaries, and uses it to drive multi-session conversations grounded in Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT). In a four-week, non-randomized study with 60 adults, we compared MEM-STRESS (Treatment) with a chatbot remembering only past conversations (Control). Memory shaped the conversations: The Treatment chatbot referenced participants' physiological features (e.g., activity in 71.8% of sessions) and suggested more body-related DBT skills than Control (14.5% vs. 5.7%), with Treatment participants also using slightly more body-related words (1.76% vs. 1.45%). Treatment participants praised personalization three times as often (44.4% vs. 14.3%), more frequently reported reflecting differently on stress (69.0% vs. 46.4%, not significant), and described gaining insight into their stress signals. Their perceived stress fell 14.2% from baseline versus 3.6% for Control, though the group difference was not significant. Grounding stress-support chatbots in layered physiological memory is thus feasible and may improve perceived personalization, motivating larger randomized studies.
authors: Soorya Ram Shimgekar; Pragya Singh; Shivam Sharma; Chandrayee Roy; Koustuv Saha; Antti Oulasvirta; Talayeh Aledavood

title: MSF-PSD: multi-scale features based panoptic segmentation and detection framework for lung disease classification
abstract: Complex anatomical variations and heterogeneous pathological patterns make it difficult to accurately segment lung images from Computed Tomography (CT) scans, especially in lungs affected by COVID-19. Conventional segmentation techniques often struggle to capture Panoptic Segmentation information and fine-grained structures across diverse clinical datasets. This study suggests a novel Multi-Scale Feature-based Panoptic Segmentation and Detection (MSF-PSD) framework for simultaneous lesion boundary detection and lung disease classification. To improve multi-scale feature representation, the suggested framework incorporates an Efficient Channel Attention (ECA) and uses EfficientNet-B7 as its foundation. For hierarchical feature fusion, a Region Proposal Network (RPN) and Region of Interest (RoI) refinement with Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS) are used after a Feature Pyramid Network (FPN). An end-to-end panoptic detection pipeline is made possible by three parallel prediction heads that carry out category classification, bounding box regression, and mask segmentation. The COVIDx-CT and SARS-CoV-2 datasets are preprocessed using Gaussian filtering and CLAHE to increase structural visibility. Supercomputing resources are utilised to guarantee scalable training and effective inference because multi-head learning and parallel feature extraction have high computational demands. Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) localises discriminative pathological regions and improves model interpretability. MSF-PSD achieves 98.4% accuracy, 97.12% precision, 94.2% recall and 93.33% F1-score, demonstrating its efficacy and clinical potential for dependable automated COVID-19 screening and lung disease assessment.

title: MVGSig: Multi-View Graph Fusion for Out-of-Distribution Detection in FMCW Radar-Based Person Identification
abstract: Radar-based person identification using FMCW sensors enables privacy-preserving authentication but risks overconfident predictions for out-of-distribution (OOD) individuals. We propose MVGSig, a multi-view graph fusion framework for open-set identification. Six complementary signal representations (spectral, temporal, time-frequency, wavelet, cepstral, and higher-order statistical) are extracted from a single FMCW radar sensor and fused through graph attention networks with learnable edge biases and quality-weighted pooling. View-Aware Collaborative Calibration (VACC) transfers knowledge from high-quality to low-quality views during training. A learned meta-detector combines node, edge, graph, and reconstruction anomaly scores. Under leave-one-subject-out cross-validation on a public ten-participant dataset, MVGSig reduces the false accept rate at 95% true positive rate from 0.697 to 0.375 ± 0.103, a 46.2% reduction relative to the raw signal baseline, and increases mean AUROC from 0.846 to 0.896 ± 0.031. FPR@95 is the primary metric because admitting unknown individuals is the security-critical failure. Closed-set accuracy reaches \(66.5 \pm 10.1\% \) on data collected for vital-sign estimation, a deliberately low-discriminability regime where overconfident predictions are particularly concerning. Ablation under matched scoring conditions attributes + 0.025 AUROC to multi-view fusion and another + 0.025 to collaborative view learning, which eliminates more remaining false accepts (32.1% versus 20.8%).

title: Machine Learning Algorithms for Predicting Psychostimulant Intoxication in Emergency Department Patients: A Multicenter Study
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Psychostimulant detection rates among emergency department (ED) patients presenting with suspected substance intoxication are low and are influenced by limited access to confirmatory testing, insufficient clinical information, and variability in physician experience. These challenges often result in high false-positive rates and unnecessary resource use. We hypothesized that machine learning (ML) algorithms could maintain reliable diagnostic performance across a temporal validation cohort and perform comparably to physicians with varying experience levels. METHODS: This multicenter study prospectively enrolled ED patients with suspected substance intoxication between March 2019 and January 2020. We chronologically partitioned data into a training set (March-October 2019) and a temporal validation cohort (November 2019-January 2020) to assess model generalizability. After determining psychostimulant intoxication via liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry from urine samples, we trained the ML algorithms using the confirmed positive cases. The primary outcome was the diagnostic discrimination of the models, measured by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) in the temporal validation cohort. Secondary outcomes included model accuracy, the Youden index, and a comparative assessment of sensitivity and specificity relative to five physicians of varying experience levels. RESULTS: Among 1,382 patients (mean age 43.8 [standard deviation 19.2] years; 55.3% male), 302 patients (21.9%) had confirmed psychostimulant intoxication, primarily involving (meth)amphetamines (134 [44.4%]), cathinones (107 [35.4%]), and ketamine (97 [32.1%]). In the temporal validation cohort (n = 382), the ML models demonstrated consistent performance, with AUCs ranging from 0.786 to 0.836. The primary outcome was met by the top-performing extreme gradient boosting (XGB) model (AUC, 0.836, 95% CI, 0.785-0.882; accuracy, 0.866 (95% CI, 0.838-0.895); and Youden index, 0.590 (95% CI, 0.480-0.694). To evaluate secondary outcomes, the XGB model's predictive accuracy was evaluated against 5 emergency physicians. The model surpassed the junior emergency physicians in both specificity (0.910 vs 0.633-0.867) and sensitivity (0.681 vs 0.500-0.633); its specificity was comparable to that of the senior emergency physicians (0.900-0.933). CONCLUSION: Machine learning models provide reliable diagnostic utility for identifying psychostimulant intoxication, achieving performance comparable to senior emergency physicians. While moderate sensitivity (0.389-0.708) limits their role as standalone rule-out tools, their high specificity provides a standardized tool to assist clinical decision-making and reduce diagnostic uncertainty in the fast-paced ED setting.

title: Machine Learning Improves Questionnaire‐Based Sleep Apnea Screening: A Multi‐Cohort Multi‐Visit Validation Study
abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) affects a large portion of the global population but remains substantially underdiagnosed due to limited access to polysomnography. While machine learning has shown promise for scalable OSA screening, many recent models rely on overnight physiological monitoring and are not validated across heterogeneous cohorts. This study develops and evaluates questionnaire‐based CatBoost models for OSA detection using two large, multi‐cohort datasets (SHHS and WSC). The models use 42 easily obtainable features that require no specialized equipment, which could potentially enable highly accessible screening. We assessed performance through comprehensive internal and external validation, including within‐cohort external testing (SHHS1 SHHS2) and cross‐cohort generalization (SHHS1 WSC1), across three clinically relevant AHI cutoffs ( 5, 15, 30 events/h). In internal validation, models achieved consistently balanced performance with AUC 0.74–0.76, sensitivity 67%–73%, and specificity 62%–70% across all cutoffs. Performance remained stable during within‐cohort external testing at cutoff 15 (AUC 0.75, sensitivity 71%, specificity 65%). However, cross‐cohort validation revealed noticeable performance degradation due to population distribution shifts, most pronounced at 5 where specificity dropped substantially (48.5% 4.7%) when models trained on the older SHHS cohort were applied to the younger WSC population. SHAP analysis confirmed that predictions relied primarily on established clinical risk factors including neck circumference, age, BMI, and symptom history. These results demonstrate that questionnaire‐based machine learning can achieve more balanced sensitivity‐specificity trade‐offs than traditional scoring rules, and highlight the importance of multi‐cohort external testing.

title: Machine Learning–Powered Wearable Sensors for Gait Analysis: A Technical Validation in Healthy Subjects Toward Parkinson’s Disease Monitoring
abstract: Parkinson's disease is characterized by progressive motor impairments that require continuous and objective monitoring beyond episodic clinical assessments. This study presents the design and technical validation of an Internet of Things-based wearable system for inertial gait monitoring, integrating a smartwatch sensing node, a mobile gateway, cloud analytics, and a web-based dashboard. We conducted a standardized experimental protocol with 40 apparently healthy adults performing three walking conditions (slow, normal, and fast), yielding 120 gait segments acquired in fixed 10-second windows. We conducted this study under controlled conditions to establish a baseline for future clinical validation in Parkinson’s disease populations. We extracted temporal, spectral, and step-related features from triaxial accelerometer signals and used them to train a supervised gait classification model based on a Random Forest algorithm, evaluated using stratified five-fold cross-validation. The proposed classifier achieved consistent discrimination performance under inter-subject variability. Although this work is limited to healthy participants, the results demonstrate the technical feasibility and reliability of the proposed system. The platform provides a technically validated foundation for future deployment in Parkinson's disease populations, supporting the development of monitoring applications and digital motor biomarkers.

title: Machine-knitted magnetoactive textiles for wireless charging, biomechanical sensing, and haptic feedback
abstract: A central goal of wearable computing is to understand and augment human physical interactions. This requires equipping wearable devices with functionalities such as wireless charging, biomechanical sensing, and haptic feedback. Most wearable devices integrate each of these functions separately with specialized components, which limits the device’s overall flexibility, comfort, and scalability. Here we present machine-knitted magnetoactive textiles that unify the physical mechanisms of wireless power transfer, biomechanical sensing, and haptic feedback in a single soft architecture. By coupling extruded magnetic fibers with digitally machine-knitted electromagnets, we enable functional textile transducers that can stably charge a 7.4 V battery, sense body movements up to 3000 Hz, and provide perceivable haptic forces up to 4.2 mN. We demonstrate how these transducers can seamlessly integrate into garments for applications like smart home control, motor rehabilitation, and skill acquisition, establishing a foundation for multifunctional wearable interfaces that are intrinsically compatible with everyday clothing.

title: Management Strategies of Atrial Fibrillation Detected by Consumer Wearable Devices: A Systematic Review of Clinical Practice and Decision-Making
abstract: Consumer-grade wearable devices using photoplethysmography (PPG) and single-lead electrocardiography (ECG) are increasingly used to detect irregular rhythms suggestive of atrial fibrillation (AF) in ambulatory, asymptomatic populations. While these technologies have expanded opportunities for early AF detection, their rapid adoption has outpaced the development of standardized management pathways, and it remains unclear how a PPG-based notification, a patient triggered single-lead ECG tracing, and a continuously recorded ambulatory ECG patch should be evaluated in practice. A systematic search of MEDLINE, the Cochrane Library, and Google Scholar identified literature published from January 2015 through December 2025. Ten studies met eligibility criteria: one randomized clinical trial, five prospective or retrospective observational studies and single-arm studies, and four clinician surveys. Patient-level studies demonstrated high actionability of wearable alerts, with 57% to 83.5% of alert recipients seeking medical follow-up. Among patients whose alerts were subsequently confirmed as AF, direct oral anticoagulation initiation varied widely from 12% to 90%, reflecting differences in population risk, confirmation method, and reporting denominators rather than a single consistent practice. Survey data revealed a parallel lack of consensus: 99.5% of physicians required traditional diagnostic confirmation before treatment, yet thresholds for the AF duration warranting anticoagulation ranged from 5 to 6 minutes (15% of clinicians) to more than 24 hours (34%). Management also varied by specialty, with emergency medicine physicians more than twice as likely as primary care physicians to refer to a specialist. Building on these patterns, we propose a conceptual clinical pathway requiring prospective validation that integrates confirmatory diagnostic testing with risk-stratified management to help close this guideline-practice gap.

title: Mechanisms Matter: A Demonstration of the Importance of Mechanistic Analysis for Evidence Synthesis Using Two Case Studies
abstract: RATIONALE: Despite a growing recognition of the importance of mechanisms, driven largely by the EBM+ movement, there appears to be little understanding of how to include mechanistic analysis in evidence synthesis. AIMS AND OBJECTIVES: To demonstrate the importance of mechanistic analysis for the appraisal of study quality and evidence review. METHOD: Two case studies - masking to prevent the spread of respiratory illnesses and talking therapy for treatment resistant depression - are used to illustrate the issues arising from appraising outcome research without considering mechanisms. RESULTS: Mechanistic analysis is important for: designing high-quality RCTs, appraising their quality (with Risk of Bias tools, GRADE analyses and more broadly) as well as other areas of evidence synthesis.

title: Metaheuristic and Nonlinear Optimization for Intelligent Energy and Environmental Systems: A Review of Renewable Generation, Smart Metering, Networks and Environmental Monitoring
abstract: Energy and environmental systems are full of decisions that must be tuned under uncertainty: how much power to draw from a solar panel, how to bill and balance consumption on a smart grid, how to share spectrum in a wireless network and how to read a biosensor in the field. Computing itself is part of the problem, since data centres, web services and smartphones draw a growing share of electricity. Many of these decisions have no closed-form solution because the underlying models are nonlinear, noisy or only partly known. Metaheuristic search, fuzzy reasoning, nonlinear analysis and data-driven forecasting are now used to find good settings, but studies are spread across power engineering, networking and environmental science. This chapter reviews optimization and learning methods for five groups of problems: renewable generation and grid interfacing, smart metering and energy forecasting, resource allocation and energy-aware computing in communication and IoT systems, environmental and agricultural monitoring, and the approximation of nonlinear physical models. The review finds that hybrid metaheuristics, such as grey wolf optimization with opposition-based learning, improve tracking and control in renewable systems, that tree ensembles and regression models are standard for consumption forecasting, that fuzzy optimization handles uncertainty in network resource allocation, that signal-aware transfer scheduling and green design guidelines reduce the energy used by smartphones and web services, and that neural approximation can stand in for expensive solvers of nonlinear equations. Few studies, however, compare methods on shared benchmarks or report computation cost. Future work should use common test systems, report run time next to solution quality and link optimization with forecasting in one loop.

title: Minute-Scale Sleep-Onset HRV as a Candidate Risk-Stratification Biomarker for Diabetic Retinopathy: An Exploratory Pilot Study
abstract: Background: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is the most common microvascular complication of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), yet DR screening coverage remains inadequate worldwide. Diabetic autonomic neuropathy typically precedes DR, and heart rate variability (HRV) provides a non-invasive autonomic measure; however, whether HRV can screen for DR remains unexplored. Methods: This pilot study investigated whether sleep-onset minute-scale HRV indices—SDANN1 (standard deviation of 1-min segment means of normal-to-normal intervals) and SDANN2 (2-min segments)—serve as candidate screening biomarkers. Using a public 24-h Holter ECG dataset of T2DM inpatients (N = 39; 11 DR-positive, 28 DR-negative), sleep-onset time-points from cardiopulmonary coupling analysis were used to extract 30 min of post-onset ECG. Results: SDANN1 was significantly lower in the DR group (median 23.6 vs. 44.8 ms, p = 0.028, d = 0.74), with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.731 (95% CI: 0.530–0.901). At the optimal threshold of ≤ 25 ms, the odds ratio was 8.1 (95% CI: 1.7–38.4), with DR prevalence of 58% in the high-risk versus 12.5% in the low-risk group. Among 12 candidates, only the SDANN family reached significance. Conclusions: sleep-onset minute-scale HRV shows promise as a candidate risk-stratification biomarker for DR; prospective longitudinal validation in larger, sex-balanced cohorts is required before any screening application.
authors: Yi-Ting Cheng; Yu-Cheng Lin; Yu‐Ting Ho; Terry B. J. Kuo; Cheryl C.H. Yang

title: Mobility Enhancement of Patients Body Monitoring based on WBAN with Multipath Routing
abstract: One of the promising applications of wireless sensor networks (WSNs) is monitoring of the human body for health concerns. For this purpose, a large number of small sensors are implanted in the human body. These sensors altogether provide a network of wireless sensors (WBANs) and monitor the vital signs and signals of the human body; these sensors will then send this information to the doctor. The most important application of the WBAN is the implementation of the monitoring network for patient safety in the hospital environment. In this case, supporting patients’ mobility is one of the basic needs, which has been underestimated in recent studies. The problem that involves providing the required energy for the units used in this type of network is challenging; for this reason, sent/ received units with very low power consumption and with a very small radius are used in order to save energy. The resulting small sending range, leads to the lack of support for patients' mobility. In this paper, the AD HOC mode is suggested for use to establish a network and a multi-path routing algorithm, for the purpose of importing patients’ mobility in hospital setting. The results of the simulation show that in addition to supporting patients' mobility, the use of the proposed idea instead of previously presented protocols, reduces delays in data transmission and energy consumption; and it also increases the delivery rate depending on the destination and the lifetime of the network, while on the other hand, it increases routing overhead.

title: Multimodal deep learning with particle swarm guided feature refinement for automated pain detection
abstract: Pain assessment remains a significant challenge in clinical practice because conventional self-reporting methods are subjective and unreliable for non-verbal, cognitively impaired, and critically ill patients. Existing automated pain detection approaches primarily rely on single-modality data or limited multimodal integration, resulting in inadequate feature representation, feature redundancy, and reduced classification performance. To address these limitations, this study proposes a multimodal deep learning framework that integrates physiological signals, facial images, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and clinical text for objective pain detection. The physiological branch employs a hybrid architecture comprising a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network, Bidirectional Gated Recurrent Unit (BiGRU), and Deep Neural Network (DNN) to learn hierarchical spatial-temporal representations. The facial branch combines EfficientNet and Residual Network (ResNet) to extract discriminative facial features, while a CNN-based architecture processes MRI images. Clinical narratives are encoded using Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) and BioBERT to capture contextual semantic information. An Adaptive Feature Refinement Layer (AFRL) enhances modality-specific feature learning, followed by Particle Swarm Optimisation (PSO) for feature selection and a novel PSO-Guided Feature Refinement Layer (PFRL) for adaptive feature weighting prior to multimodal fusion. We implement the framework in TensorFlow and PyTorch and evaluate it on the BioVid, UNBC-McMaster, and Trigeminal Neuralgia MRI datasets. Experimental results achieve 96.2% accuracy, outperforming Support Vector Machine (82.4%), K-Nearest Neighbors (79.6%), Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (88.9%), and AdaBoost (90.7%). The proposed framework provides a robust, scalable, and clinically applicable solution for automated multimodal pain detection and improved clinical decision support.

title: Navigating human-robot interaction challenges in private and residential aged care homes
abstract: This chapter explores how robotic systems and ambient intelligence can enhance care for older adults in residential aged care (RAC) homes and private homes. Although these settings differ, we frame both as extreme and challenging environments for human-robot interaction (HRI), characterised by cluttered and dynamic layouts, diverse resident needs, and limited on-site technical support. We review embodied and non-embodied systems that assist with daily living, safety monitoring, and social engagement, highlighting hybrid deployments where robots complement fixed and wearable sensors. To ensure these technologies are usable and effective, design considerations consider the cognitive, physical, and social needs of older adults. Interaction design prioritises accessibility for older adults with low digital literacy, using robust but simple voice interfaces, small sets of non-verbal cues, accessible screen-based companions, and safe object handovers. Privacy, trust, and acceptability are addressed via practical strategies such as on-device inference, data minimisation, visible consent controls, and transparent data handling aligned with emerging artificial intelligence (AI) and privacy regulation. Evaluation emphasises real-world metrics including false alarms per day, time to recover from faults, staff workload, and long-term system reliability. We close by outlining open research challenges and future directions for scalable, regulation-ready deployments that support aging with dignity, safety, and independence.

title: New Oxygen Sensor with Polyaniline Spin Probe and Low Frequency EPR (L-Band) Detection System
abstract: Our research demonstrates the potential of certain PANI samples to serve as sensitive and reliable spin probes for oxygen detection, while also highlighting the advantages of the lowfrequency EPR technique. Compared to other methods of measuring oxygen concentration, the new sensor—based on a PANI spin probe and a low-frequency EPR detector—offers unique benefits: it ensures high sensitivity to changes in oxygen concentration and does not require direct contact between the EPR detector and the sensor itself (the polyaniline probe). This sensor can be placed in isolated environments, including biological samples (tissues), and - thanks to the use of nanodispersed polyaniline - even inside living cells.

title: Newborn Screening for Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy: Contemporary Considerations for Implementation of an Early Diagnostic Paradigm
abstract: PURPOSE OF REVIEW: variants in NBS algorithms. In an evolving model of care, the challenges and potential factors that may strengthen the practice of family-centered care are considered. RECENT FINDINGS: Contemporary DMD NBS programs have adopted measurement of the muscle isoform of creatine kinase (CK-MM), after US Food and Drug Administration approval of high-throughput assays in 2020. Since then, 7 pilot studies from China, Taiwan, and the United States have reported outcomes using varied screening algorithms. Those incorporating repeat dried blood spot (DBS) testing after an initially elevated CK-MM level increased the positive predictive value compared with single-sample screening. Incorporating molecular genomic analysis of DMD in infants with persistently elevated CK-MM levels further increased the positive predictive value to 100%; however, this multistep approach also highlighted the practical challenges of DBS recollection, with a 17.1% (108/632) attrition rate before confirmatory testing. The choice of screening algorithm also determined the scope of conditions identified. The optimal timing for initiation of disease-modifying therapies is uncertain, and this represents a key priority for future research. The recommended model of care for DMD in early life incorporates genetics; psychosocial support; proactive monitoring and individualized support for cognitive, behavioral, and emotional difficulties; access to educational resources and support networks; and clinical trial readiness. SUMMARY: Health system preparedness, collaboration across countries, and coordination mechanisms within a multidisciplinary team are important for building effective health care in the context of early diagnosis of DMD through NBS. There is an ongoing need to evaluate screening algorithms using large systematic data sets, assess their cost-effectiveness, explore the potential for earlier initiation of disease-modifying treatments with validated outcome measurement tools, and establish a comprehensive evidence-based model of care to support global implementation of DMD within NBS programs.
authors: Uen Tsun Eugenia Yau; Michelle Lorentzos; Didu S. T. Kariyawasam; Michelle Anne Farrar

title: Next-Generation Brain Health Monitoring Enabled by Integrated Wearable AI Infrastructure.
abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases are difficult to detect during their pre-symptomatic stages, when intervention is most effective. Advances in wearable biosensors, artificial intelligence (AI), and neuroscience now enable continuous monitoring of brain-related physiological signals in real-world settings. However, progress in sensing technologies, signal analytics, and machine learning remains fragmented, limiting the biological specificity, robustness, and clinical translation of many digital biomarkers. This review presents an integrated framework that links molecular pathology and neural circuit dysfunction to sensor-detectable digital phenotypes across sleep, autonomic regulation, gait, speech, and ocular dynamics. We evaluate emerging wearable platforms, including bioelectric, optical, and neuromotor sensors, and discuss critical design considerations such as signal quality, user-centered form factors, and ultra-low-power edge AI systems. We further examine how self-supervised learning, federated AI, mechanistic modeling, and fairness-aware validation can improve biomarker reliability, interpretability, and generalizability. To facilitate clinical deployment, we introduce the Personalized Brain-Health Operating System (pBH-OS), a privacy-preserving reference architecture for scalable digital phenotyping. The framework maps conceptual layers to existing technologies while identifying key validation gaps. We also address practical challenges, including adherence, device dropout, informative missingness, regulatory compliance, and accountability. Together, these advances provide a pathway toward biologically grounded and regulation-ready systems capable of identifying neurodegenerative risk years before clinical symptom onset.

title: OAK-Mind: Zero-Training Mental Health Change Inference from Passive Sensing via Knowledge-Grounded Multi-Agent LLMs
abstract: Wearable and smartphone sensors capture behavioral signals associated with mental health, yet inferring mental health outcomes from these signals has traditionally relied on supervised models requiring labeled data and offering limited insight into their predictions. Large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities to reason over behavioral evidence, but existing LLM-based approaches to passive sensing have largely continued to rely on task-specific fine-tuning or sensor-specific pretraining. In this paper, we introduce OAK-Mind, a zerO-training, multi-Agent, Knowledge-grounded LLM pipeline for inferring mental health changes from passive sensing data. The pipeline organizes sensing data into behavioral dimensions including sleep, physical activity, location mobility, and smartphone use, and orchestrates specialized agents grounded in mental health literature to interpret longitudinal behavioral changes. It synthesizes their assessments and applies questionnaire-based symptom rating to infer changes relative to an individual's baseline assessment with human-readable rationale grounded in observed behavioral patterns and domain knowledge. Across datasets and prediction tasks, while without task-specific training, OAK-Mind achieves comparable or better performance than the most predictive supervised baselines trained on additional labeled samples. It also demonstrate consistent improvement upon direct prompting across four tested LLM backbones. Ablation analyses support the benefits of combining behavioral interpretation with symptom rating, distributing analysis across domain-specific agents, and incorporating domain knowledge. Our findings highlight the potential of knowledge-grounded, multi-agent LLMs for training-free inference of mental health changes from passive sensing data.
authors: Yishu Ji; Zhihan Jiang; Will Ke Wang; Yuang Fan; Anind K. Dey; Xuhai "Orson" Xu

title: Obstructive Sleep Apnea and Oral Cancer: A Pneumology Perspective on Hypoxia, Airway Dysfunction, Quality of Life and Survivorship
abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) and oral cancer intersect through shared upper-airway anatomy, treatment-related structural changes, intermittent hypoxia, systemic inflammation, and long-term survivorship burden. Oral and oropharyngeal tumors may compromise airway patency directly, while surgery, reconstruction, radiotherapy, edema, fibrosis, and neuromuscular dysfunction may precipitate or worsen sleep-disordered breathing. OSA-related intermittent hypoxia and sleep fragmentation also provide biologically plausible mechanisms involving oxidative stress, inflammatory signaling, angiogenesis, metabolic adaptation, and immune alteration. However, current evidence does not establish a causal relationship between OSA and oral cancer progression or survival. Diagnosis is challenging because fatigue, insomnia, pain, dysphagia, xerostomia, psychological distress, and daytime dysfunction may arise from either OSA or cancer treatment. Screening questionnaires can support risk stratification but should not replace objective testing. Polysomnography remains the reference standard, whereas technically adequate home sleep apnea testing may be appropriate in selected patients. Management requires multidisciplinary collaboration among pulmonologists, sleep physicians, oral and maxillofacial surgeons, otolaryngologists, oncologists, dentists, and rehabilitation specialists. Positive airway pressure therapy remains the standard treatment, although adherence may be limited by altered anatomy, pain, mucositis, xerostomia, and treatment-related functional impairment. These challenges are amplified in low- and middle-income countries, where access to diagnostic testing, specialist care, and long-term treatment is often restricted. Overall, OSA should be regarded as a clinically relevant and potentially modifiable comorbidity in oral cancer. Systematic screening, objective diagnosis, individualized treatment, and longitudinal reassessment should be integrated into perioperative and survivorship care.
authors: Ramona Cioboată

title: Oculomics using artificial intelligence derived retinal biomarkers for cardiovascular health
abstract: This narrative review synthesizes evidence from retinal vascular morphology, structural and perfusion imaging, retinal aging, metabolomics, and artificial intelligence models linking retinal biomarkers with cardiovascular risk factors, subclinical disease, clinical events, and cardiorenal and metabolic outcomes. These biomarkers may complement conventional risk assessment, but clinical utility is unproven and integration into cardiovascular digital twins remains conceptual. Prospective validation, standardized acquisition, interoperability, interpretability, and equitable evaluation are required before implementation.

title: Optimization of Wear Behavior Analysis in MWCNT-Reinforced GFRP Composites Using RSM and ETLBO
abstract: This study aims to optimize the fabrication process of Multi-walled Carbon Nanotube (MWCNT)-filled Glass Fiber-reinforced Polymer (GFRP) composites to enhance their tribological performance during the hand layup process. A structured experimental approach based on the Box–Behnken design within the Response Surface Methodology (RSM) framework was used to evaluate the influence of wt.% MWCNT loading, applied load, and sliding velocity. The fabrication was performed, ensuring a uniform MWCNT dispersion via mechanical stirring and probe sonication. The performance of the composites was assessed in terms of their Specific Wear Rate (SWR) and Wear Coefficients (WCs). Statistical analysis, including ANOVA and Pareto charts, revealed that the load and sliding velocity significantly affected both the SWR and WC, whereas interactions such as the MWCNT content and sliding velocity also played a crucial role. Mathematical models were developed for SWR and WC and optimized using Elitist Teaching-learning-based Optimization (ETLBO). The optimal fabrication settings were found to be 1 wt.% MWCNT loading, 30 N load, and 2 m/s sliding velocity, yielding improved wear characteristics. Confirmatory tests validated the model predictions and showed minimal errors. Scanning electron microscopy further confirmed that optimal nanotube dispersion led to a more uniform and durable composite structure, supporting its potential for high-performance engineering applications. The proposed integrated approach demonstrates the effectiveness of combining RSM and ETLBO to develop high-performance MWCNT–GFRP composites with superior wear resistance. The findings of this study provide practical guidelines for fabricating durable, wear-resistant composite structures for automotive brake systems, aerospace joints, and industrial machinery parts, where reliability under continuous sliding conditions is essential.
authors: Ch. Rajeswari; Namala Kiran Kumar; P. Saritha

title: PHISHREV+: An ASP-Based Post-Hoc Defeasible Machine Learning Framework for Phishing Detection
abstract: Phishing website detection remains a critical cybersecurity challenge. Although machine learning classifiers achieve high accuracy on benchmark datasets, they suffer from a fundamental limitation: once trained, their decision boundaries are fixed and cannot incorporate new contextual evidence without retraining the model. This work presents \textbf{PHISHREV+}, a hybrid framework that instantiates the notion of \textit{post-hoc defeasible machine learning}. This framework does not replace the classifier. It treats the initial classifier predictions as defeasible beliefs and revises them through an Answer Set Programming based non-monotonic reasoning(NMR) layer. The framework operates in two phases. In the machine learning phase, four classifiers (SVM, KNN, DT and RF) are trained on the 87 feature benchmark dataset. In the post-hoc NMR phase, four defeasible rules derived from exploratory data analysis of the training set, and validated through Chi-square and Mann-Whitney U tests, formally revise initial predictions. The proposed framework achieves consistent false positive reduction across all our classifiers SVM (41$\rightarrow$39), KNN (47$\rightarrow$46), DT (62$\rightarrow$61), and RF (52$\rightarrow$51) while maintaining complete false negative parity with zero increase overhead. A comprehensive ablation studies across seven rule configurations confirms that the hierarchical combination of all four defeasible rules is necessary to achieve this optimal balance. Instance level explainability is provided through eXplainable ASP (XASP), which generates formal derivation graphs showing which defeasible rules fired and why the initial belief was retracted, a capability absent from all existing phishing detection approaches.
authors: Mainak Sen; Kumar Sanka Ray; Amlan Chakrabarti

title: Passive and continuous assessment of subjective sleep quality using smartwatches
abstract: Sleep is a fundamental physiological process that directly impacts nearly every aspect of human health. Poor sleep quality has been linked to cardiovascular disease, stress, anxiety, depression, inflammation, impaired cognitive performance, and even increased mortality. When assessing sleep quality, it is important to capture two fundamentally different yet complementary dimensions: objective sleep quality and subjective sleep quality, which are both independent predictors of adverse outcomes. While advances in wearable technology now allow continuous monitoring of objective physiological characteristics of sleep, subjective sleep quality still relies exclusively on self-reported questionnaires, which inherently require active user participation and are limited to specific points in time. In this study, we present a machine learning framework for the passive and continuous assessment of subjective sleep quality, leveraging physiological signals collected from commercial smartwatches, such as sleep data, physical activity, heart rate, and stress inferred from heart rate variability, alongside individual characteristics, including sociodemographic factors, personality traits, and health-related attributes. Our machine learning model was trained using data from the PerMed prospective observational study, which includes 4,794 participants, 759,116 self-reported daily questionnaires and 1,765,264 days of smartwatch recordings collected over a three-year period. We show that the model achieves an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.88 in distinguishing between extreme subjective sleep quality ratings. Our passive and continuous approach to assessing subjective sleep quality represents a conceptual shift in how subjective sleep quality is measured, with the potential to enable timely, personalized interventions that support not only sleep-related conditions but also broader aspects of overall health and well-being.
authors: Omer Hausner; Eva Mishor; Maya Reiner; Erez Shmueli

title: Patient‐Reported Outcome Measures in Musculoskeletal Oncology: Current Concepts, Barriers, and the Future
abstract: Patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) remain underutilized in musculoskeletal oncology, with only 4.9% of tumor-focused articles incorporating them. This review synthesizes current PROM instruments-including Toronto Extremity Salvage Score, PROMIS, and emerging tools such as the Sarcoma Assessment Measure-and identifies barriers unique to this population, including psychological distress, workflow complexity, and disease heterogeneity. Future directions include flexible baseline collection, EHR-integrated dashboards, national registry linkage, wearable technology, and AI-driven processing to increase PROMs utilization.
authors: Shujaa T Khan; Rowan J Barker-Clarke; Brian Benyamini; Zachary D. C. Burke; Nathan W. Mesko; Lukas M. Nystrom

title: Perceived Acceptability, Design Preferences, and User Requirements for a Proposed Ear-Worn Device for Heart-Rate and Ear-Temperature Monitoring with Localized Neck Cooling: A Pre-Prototype Mixed-Methods Study in People with Multiple Sclerosis.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Heat sensitivity in multiple sclerosis (MS) can worsen neurological symptoms and impair daily functioning and quality of life. As current cooling strategies are largely reactive, wearable technology may offer a proactive approach, provided it is acceptable to users. This pre-prototype study evaluated the perceived acceptability of a proposed ear-worn device, not yet fabricated, that would measure ear-site temperature and heart rate, alert the user, and direct localized airflow at the neck, and identified the user priorities that should guide its development. No technical feasibility or device-performance testing was performed. Methods: Adults with MS completed an electronic questionnaire on design preferences, functional features, and overall acceptability; a subset took part in semi-structured interviews analyzed thematically. Results: Forty-seven participants completed the survey. Comfort during prolonged use (72.3%) and compatibility with prescription glasses (66.0%) were the design features most often rated important; health reports (93.6%), communication with healthcare providers (91.5%), symptom monitoring (89.4%), emergency contact (85.1%), and automatic cooling activation (83.0%) were each rated important by more than 80% of participants, with overlapping confidence intervals that do not permit these functions to be ranked. Anticipated acceptability of the concept was uncertain: 46.8% (95% confidence interval [CI] 33.3-60.8) expressed some degree of acceptability (34.0% when only 'acceptable' or 'very acceptable' responses were counted), 36.2% were neutral, and 17.0% found it not acceptable. Six interviews generated four themes: uncertainty, the impact of heat on daily life, independence through self-management, and practical considerations for implementation. Conclusions: These findings reflect anticipated, concept-level acceptability rather than acceptability after use of a physical device. Because the proposed device would measure ear-site temperature and heart rate rather than neurological symptoms, the priority given to symptom monitoring is addressed through physiological early warning combined with user-reported symptoms. The identified priorities are translated into measurable specifications and verification tests for the next prototype; the technical performance of the device, including its cooling capacity, remains to be demonstrated.
authors: Almuwais A, Alotaibi M, Binshaye D, Alhumaid D, Almohsen F, Alsubaie S, Alshareef R, Alkhushayban N.

title: Personalized AI-Supported Sport and Physical Activity for Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder: A Narrative Review and Conceptual Framework
abstract: Background: Children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) show frequent motor difficulties, lower physical activity (PA) and fewer opportunities for sport participation than their peers. Individualized programs are therefore needed. Artificial intelligence (AI), wearable sensors and the Internet of Things (IoT) could support such personalization, but the evidence base has not been examined from a sport-science perspective. Objective: To synthesize evidence on PA interventions and AI- and IoT-enabled technologies relevant to children with ASD and to propose a framework for personalized, AI-supported sport and PA programs. Methods: A narrative review, guided by the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles (SANRA), combined a previously completed thematic synthesis of 49 studies of AI- and IoT-enabled assistive systems for children with disabilities (16 ASD-related) with targeted searches of PubMed/MEDLINE and publisher databases up to November 2026. Results: Meta-analyses indicate moderate benefits of PA interventions for motor skills, skill-related fitness and social functioning (e.g., Hedges' g = 0.62), although study quality is generally low. ASD-focused AI research mainly addresses gesture recognition, emotion analysis and socially assistive robotics in small samples (about 10–24 children), and none has tested fitness outcomes. The proposed artificial intelligence of things (AIoT)-CARE framework (Capability, Applicability, Robustness, and Ethics and Safety) links five stages: co-designed profiling, an accessible activity catalog, consent-based sensing, explainable recommendations with human override, and family-involved review. Conclusion: AI-supported personalization is a promising design direction, not a proven intervention. Phased evaluation using participant-level validation, real-world testing and AI-specific reporting guidelines is required.
authors: Mossammat Ruksana Rashid

title: Perspectives and experiences of youth and caregivers on screening and monitoring islet autoimmunity
abstract: Aims: Screening and monitoring programs for islet autoantibodies, which signal risk of clinical type 1 diabetes, are being implemented globally. No studies have qualitatively explored youths' perspectives on islet autoimmunity screening and monitoring, nor integrated their views with those of caregivers. Methods: = 18 girls) with one or more islet autoantibodies and 49 caregivers of affected youth. Youth had been monitored for approximately 9 years (median). All families, except one, had a relative with type 1 diabetes. Twenty-one (42.86%) caregivers lived with clinical type 1 diabetes. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Results: Seven themes reflected our findings. Youth had limited understanding of the advantages of monitoring outside of research. They were predominantly focused on testing experiences rather than clinical risk. Caregivers generally displayed strong psychological responses, as did older adolescents. Family experience of diabetes shaped psychological responses in multifaceted ways. Caregivers further emphasised flexible service delivery and specific logistical considerations for screening and monitoring. Conclusions: Youths' focus on the practicalities of testing, rather than health risk, is reassuring in the context of planning international screening and monitoring programs. However, it highlights the need to prioritise procedural experiences. Youth should also be educated on the real-world benefits of monitoring. Psychosocial support is needed, particularly for caregivers and older adolescents, with healthcare individualised to the unique influence of family history of clinical diabetes. Caregivers further need reliable, structured monitoring pathways to manage distress, with equity and accessibility prioritised for sustained engagement.
authors: Mia Majstorovic; Kelly J. McGorm; John M. Wentworth; Tony Huynh; Fergus Cameron; Maria E. Craig; Elizabeth Ann Davis; Kirstine J. Bell; Georgia Soldatos; Megan A. S. Penno; Alyssa C. P. Sawyer; Melissa Oxlad; Jennifer Couper

title: PhishShield: A Multi-Modal AI-Based Anti-Phishing Detection Platform
abstract: Phishing is a trick in which a fake website pretends to be a real one, such as a bank, to steal a person’s password or money. Many existing tools check only one thing, such as whether a link appears on a blacklist. A new fake site that is not yet listed can pass such a check. This paper proposes PhishShield, a platform that studies a website through five separate channels: the URL text, the HTML code of the page, the SSL certificate, the domain registration record (WHOIS), and a screenshot of the page. Each channel gives its own risk score between 0 and 1. A weighted sum then combines these scores into one final score. If the final score crosses a set limit, the user sees a warning and the event is saved in a log. The system is built as small separate services using FastAPI, so that each part can be changed without touching the others. This is a design paper. Testing is planned and is described in the Future Work section.
