title: Physical AI for Aged Care: Robotics, Digital Twins, and Intelligent Care Ecosystems
abstract: Population aging is one of the defining global healthcare challenges of the twenty-first century. Increasing longevity, declining workforce availability, rising chronic disease burden, and escalating care costs are placing unprecedented pressure on aged care systems worldwide. Physical AI—the integration of artificial intelligence, robotics, digital twins, sensing systems, and embodied intelligence—has emerged as a transformative paradigm capable of reshaping aged care delivery. Unlike conventional healthcare AI focused primarily on data analytics and decision support, Physical AI enables intelligent systems to perceive, reason, and act within real-world care environments. This chapter explores the emerging role of Physical AI in aged care, with emphasis on robotics, ambient intelligence, digital twins, multimodal sensing, simulation environments, and NVIDIA Isaac for Healthcare. The chapter examines how Physical AI can support independent living, mobility assistance, rehabilitation, cognitive support, social engagement, remote monitoring, and workforce augmentation. Key technological foundations including embodied AI, sensor fusion, reinforcement learning, synthetic data generation, and edge AI are discussed alongside ethical, regulatory, and socio-technical considerations. The chapter concludes by presenting future research directions and a vision for intelligent aged care ecosystems integrating humans, robotics, and adaptive AI systems.
authors: Nilmini Wickramasinghe

title: Physical Activity and Exercise, Novel Therapies and Technologies in Adolescents with Type 1 Diabetes
abstract: Regular physical activity provides well-established benefits for individuals with type 1 diabetes (T1D), including improved insulin sensitivity, cardiovascular health, and psychological wellbeing. However, exercise is also associated with rapid glycaemic fluctuations and an increased risk of dysglycaemia. This risk is particularly pronounced in adolescents, as pubertal physiology and irregular activity patterns complicate glycaemic management. Accordingly, this cumulative dissertation aims to advance the understanding of exercise in adolescents with T1D, with a focus on safety, efficacy, and the role of diabetes technologies in supporting glycaemic control. The first study, a randomized controlled trial (ChilDFiT1), evaluated a 4-week structured track and field training intervention combined with intensive glycaemic management in adolescents with T1D. Compared with intensive glycaemic management alone, the intervention resulted in significant improvements in key glycaemic outcomes, demonstrating the safety and feasibility of structured exercise in this population. The second study assessed the performance of real-time continuous glucose monitoring (rtCGM) before, during, and after exercise sessions. While overall accuracy was acceptable, sensor reliability declined during rapid glucose changes, particularly during hypoglycaemia, underscoring the need for cautious, context-aware interpretation of CGM data around physical activity. The third study synthesized current evidence on automated insulin delivery (AID) systems in the context of exercise. While AID systems effectively improve glycaemic outcomes when physical activity is announced, unannounced exercise remains a significant limitation, highlighting the need for further technological adaptation. Taken together, these studies provide an integrative perspective on the interplay between exercise physiology, glucose monitoring, and diabetes technology in adolescent T1D. By combining clinical evidence, methodological evaluation, and technological analysis, this dissertation establishes a comprehensive framework to support safe exercise participation among this vulnerable population. The findings demonstrate that structured exercise can safely and effectively improve glycaemic outcomes in adolescents, with direct implications for clinical exercise counselling to support informed, confident, and individualized care. Overall, the work provides a coherent foundation for future research and for integrating exercise therapy and diabetes technology into paediatric T1D management.
authors: Rebecca Tanja Zimmer

title: Physical activity in preclinical Alzheimer disease: current evidence and implications for multimodal longitudinal research
abstract: Alzheimer disease (AD) pathology may be detectable years before cognitive symptoms, but biomarker testing of cognitively unimpaired people is not recommended for routine clinical use. Objective physical activity (PA), gait, and rest-activity measures are attractive research signals because they are repeatable and relatively inexpensive; however, none are specific to AD. This narrative review examined evidence linking PA, gait, and rest-activity measures to AD-related outcomes and considered their role in multimodal longitudinal research within biomarker-characterized cohorts. Targeted searches of PubMed, Scopus, and IEEE Xplore were conducted from inception through 25 August 2026, and reference lists of pivotal studies and guidance documents were hand-searched. Priority was given to guidelines, longitudinal cohorts, randomized trials, studies using objective behavior measures and AD biomarkers, and externally evaluated prediction models. Observational evidence links higher activity with lower dementia risk, but reverse causation remains plausible. In biomarker-characterized cohorts, greater baseline step count has been associated with slower amyloid-related tau accumulation and slower cognitive and functional decline, not with lower amyloid burden. Rest-activity fragmentation has shown cross-sectional and prospective associations with amyloid-related measures, whereas a 1-year aerobic-exercise trial did not reduce amyloid accumulation. Recent multimodal AI studies demonstrate that non-PET (positron emission tomography) data can estimate amyloid and tau status. Yet, they do not establish the incremental value of free-living PA in cognitively unimpaired community samples. We therefore outline a framework for longitudinal behavioral research in cohorts whose biomarker status has been characterized independently of PA-based selection. Its primary purpose is to examine associations between behavioral measures and subsequent cognitive, functional, and tau trajectories. Whether PA improves individual prediction beyond clinical information and baseline biomarkers remains a separate, unresolved question. PA is considered a contextual behavioral measure, and the framework does not propose using it to determine eligibility for biomarker testing or research recruitment.
authors: Liang Wang; Wei Lai; Tianqi Wei; Yunbang Zhang; Youliang Wen

title: Physiological Correlates of Passenger-Facing HMI Communication in Automated Driving
abstract: Passenger-facing vehicle interfaces must inform without disrupting non-driving activities. This study related HMI communication during fully automated driving to passenger physiology and interaction quality during concurrent reading. Twenty-six participants completed a no-communication Baseline drive and one HMI drive with abstract auditory-tactile cues (Simple) or synthesised speech (Extended); 24 contributed physiological data. Electrodermal activity (EDA) was the primary measure, with User Experience Questionnaire ratings. Because HMI variant was assigned between participants, participant-level analyses provided primary condition inference. Mean EDA was lower in both HMI conditions than Baseline, but no contrast was statistically supported (Simple–Baseline −73.1, 95% CI [−160.3, 14.0], p = 0.092; Extended–Baseline −44.7, p = 0.296; Extended–Simple 28.4, p = 0.614). No UEQ scale survived multiplicity correction. Segment-level mixed-effects models (803 segments) reproduced this ordering with narrower intervals reflecting repeated observations, not independent assignments. Participant-level contrasts matched the unit of assignment; segment-level models characterised temporal physiological variation.
authors: Gregor Strle; Kristina Stojmenova; Jaka Sodnik

title: Physiological micro-movement tracking via FMCW radars: An actuator-driven phantom setup with machine learning and image processing
abstract: Continuous, contactless vital sign monitoring is constrained by two persistent gaps: evaluation scenarios tied to limited cohorts of live subjects, and signal-processing pipelines that prioritize tissue velocity over the clinically valuable absolute displacement measurement. This study addresses both gaps by building an actuator-driven oil-in-gelatin phantom testbench that mimics chest-wall/skin-surface movements, and using it to test the micro-motion tracking capabilities of two Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) radar platforms working at 24 GHz and 77 GHz. A 1 cm-thick oil-in-gelatin phantom, mounted on a servo-actuation mechanism, was driven through 20 synthetic periodic motion profiles spanning 36–272 bpm equivalents while both radars, suspended 60 cm above the target, logged raw range profiles. Regressive modeling yielded promising relative tracking performance. However, direct frequency analysis of raw range bin amplitude fluctuations proved more robust for transient periodicity tracking, resolving 16 of 20 profiles, whereas the regression model, optimized on quasi-static signals, reduced the number of resolved profiles by 5. Furthermore, by conceptualizing the radar data matrix as a two-dimensional digital image, a computationally efficient pixel-wise tracking method was implemented to extract one-dimensional relative time series that faithfully preserve the temporal and morphological characteristics of the underlying signals. These outcomes validate the phantom–actuator framework as a reproducible test platform and demonstrate the feasibility of applying image processing to range-FFT matrices for advancing non-contact, high-precision clinical monitoring.
authors: Nurhan Güneş

title: Point-of-Care Electroanalytical Technologies for Lithium Carbonate Monitoring in Bipolar Affective Disorders
abstract: Lithium (Li), administered as lithium salts such as lithium carbonate (Li2CO3), remains a gold-standard maintenance treatment for bipolar affective disorder (bipolar disorder), but its narrow therapeutic index requires regular monitoring of lithium−ion (Li+) concentrations. This review critically examines electroanalytical strategies for decentralized Li measurement, including conventional electrodes, screen-printed electrodes, wearable platforms, and minimally invasive sampling. Attention is given to ion-selective recognition, manganese (Mn)-spinel intercalation materials, matrix effects, and the evidence supporting saliva, sweat, interstitial fluid, and capillary blood. The available literature supports these matrices as promising adjuncts but not as universal replacements for standardized venous testing. Their clinical use still requires paired matrix validation, control of sampling time and environmental effects, long-term sensor stability studies, and explicit confirmatory testing rules for suspected toxicity. Laser-induced graphene and fused deposition modeling are therefore discussed only as enabling fabrication concepts rather than as established Li-sensing technologies. Finally, the review outlines regulatory, human factor, connectivity, and healthcare integration requirements that must be addressed before wearable or home-use Li devices can support routine care.
authors: Christiane T. de Oliveira; Raphael Menechini Neto; Gideã Taques Tractz; Evandro Bona; Eduardo Giometti Bertogna; Leda Leme Talib; Oretes V. Forlenza; Ana Paula Peron; Osvaldo Valarini

title: Predicted vs. Proven: A Validated Machine Learning and Desirability Based Framework for Multi Response Optimization of EN31 Bearing Steel Turning Parameters
abstract: Turning of EN31 alloy steel (equivalent to AISI 52100) a high-carbon, high-chromium bearing-grade alloy prized for its hardenability, wear resistance, and dimensional stability remains a challenging machining operation because of the steel's high hardness and abrasiveness. A growing body of literature has applied machine learning (ML) and desirability-function-based optimization to hardened-steel and AISI 52100/EN31 turning, typically reporting a single “optimal” parameter combination without checking whether that combination lies within the region actually sampled by the underlying experimental design. This paper addresses that gap directly. Using a 200-observation EN31 turning dataset (cutting speed, feed, depth of cut, coolant condition, and tool material as inputs; surface roughness, tool wear, cutting force, temperature, material removal rate, power, and chip reduction coefficient as responses), five regression algorithms linear regression, random forest, gradient boosting, support vector regression, and an artificial neural network were trained and compared via 5-fold cross-validation, achieving cross-validated R² up to 0.998 for the best model per response. A desirability-function-based multi-objective optimization over a continuous parameter grid identified a model-predicted optimum (cutting speed ≈ 389 rpm, feed ≈ 0.127 mm/rev, depth of cut = 0.25 mm, MQL cooling, carbide tool; desirability D = 0.520). Cross-checking this recommendation against the raw experimental design revealed that the tested cutting speeds were confined to six discrete levels with a 304 rpm gap (196–500 rpm) containing no trials, so the model-predicted speed of 389 rpm falls inside an unsampled region and is, strictly, an unvalidated interpolation. Repeating the same desirability analysis using only the 200 physically measured rows identified a data-validated optimum of 500 rpm cutting speed, 0.168 mm/rev feed, 0.35 mm depth of cut, MQL cooling, and a carbide tool (D = 0.497), which trades a modest surface-finish/tool-wear penalty for substantially higher measured MRR (23.5 vs. 12.7 mm³/s) than the unvalidated prediction. To the best of our knowledge, the finding that a continuous ML-based optimizer can recommend an operationally untested parameter combination even when its underlying response models are locally accurate has not been reported in prior EN31/AISI 52100 ML-optimization studies, and constitutes the principal methodological contribution of this work. The findings corroborate and extend prior EN31-specific and hardened-steel machining literature and offer a validation protocol directly transferable to other ML-based machining-optimization studies. A confirmatory turning-trial protocol, a discussion of how tree-based models behave across unsampled gaps, and constraint-aware (convex-hull and density-based) strategies for automated optimization workflows are also presented.

title: Preliminary laboratory analytical comparison of quantitative at-home urinary hormone monitoring systems using artificial urine
abstract: Background: Quantitative at-home urinary hormone monitoring systems are increasingly used for reproductive health tracking, but their analytical behaviour requires systematic characterization. This preliminary laboratory comparison aimed to provide an analytical framework to compare multiple commercially available at-home urine hormone monitoring devices across key performance metrics under controlled artificial urine conditions. Methods: Laboratory experiments were informed by Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute's (CLSI) validation principles. Four urine hormone monitoring devices were evaluated using a pre-registered analytical framework for luteinizing hormone (LH), follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), estrone-3-glucuronide (E3G), and pregnanediol glucuronide (PDG). Metrics included coefficients of variation (CV, for precision), relative deviation (RD, for accuracy), linearity, limit of blank (LoB), limit of detection (LoD) for each device, using artificial urine samples with standard hormone concentrations. Cross-reactivity was tested with other hormones including human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), cortisol, thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) and progesterone subtypes. Device-specific evaluations, including the impact of ambient light and various camera systems, were also conducted for relevant devices. Results: There were device- and analyte-specific differences in precision, accuracy, linearity and detection limits. Precision and accuracy ranged from CV/RD values near the 15% acceptability threshold to levels exceeding 50% at some concentrations. External lighting conditions affected camera-based strips at low hormone concentrations. False positive results for LH can occur in the presence of 100 mIU/mL hCG, which could lead to misinterpretation in the context of pregnancy. One device that measures the LH-beta subunit avoided this cross-reactivity. Conclusions: A preliminary analytical framework was applied to evaluate the performance of quantitative urinary hormone devices for at-home use. This framework can be used in future research and development of menstrual health monitoring technologies. Longitudinal clinical studies using human urine samples and appropriate ovulation reference standards are required before conclusions can be drawn regarding ovulation detection, fertile-window estimation or menstrual-phase classification.
authors: Thomas Paul Bouchard; Paul J. Yong; Patricia K. Doyle–Baker

title: Preparation and performance study of non-metallic core piezoelectric optical fiber
abstract: In response to the problem of insufficient toughness and limited piezoelectric performance of traditional metal core piezoelectric fibers (MPF) under complex loads, this study proposes the use of dual thermal shrinkage method to prepare Kevlar core piezoelectric fibers, replacing the metal core with lightweight and high toughness Kevlar fibers to construct a new non-metallic core piezoelectric fiber system. The stress-strain curve test shows that the toughness and tensile strength of Kevlar core are significantly improved compared to metal core, with toughness being 2.22 times that of metal core and tensile strength being 7.8 times that of metal core, effectively solving the problem of interface stress concentration caused by rigid support in traditional metal core. During the preparation process, the synergistic thermal shrinkage effect of thermoplastic [polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF)] tube and silicone tube was utilized to achieve tight bonding and uniform coaxiality of the core-shell structure. Performance testing shows that the prepared Kevlar core piezoelectric fibers have excellent global dynamic sensing capabilities, with a deviation of less than 5.21% between the average voltage at each point and the total average voltage; The piezoelectric performance test shows that under the same load and impact rate conditions, its peak voltage can be increased by up to 25.41% compared to traditional metal core fibers. This method combines the advantages of simple process, low equipment cost, and efficient production, providing a lightweight and high-performance piezoelectric material solution for the fields of flexible sensing, wearable devices, and structural health monitoring.
authors: Dafei Hou; Xiangdong Kong; Keliang Feng
venue: Journal of King Saud University - Science

title: Probing and Sensing Layer-Dependent van der Waals Interaction via Induced Anisotropy
abstract: Van der Waals (vdW) interaction, a fundamental force, plays an important role in two-dimensional (2D) systems by enabling atomically sharp assemblies and giving rise to many emergent phenomena. However, experimentally probing and sensing the evolution of vdW interaction between 2D layers remains challenging due to its extreme weakness, very short range, and the difficulty of keeping two atomic layers perfectly parallel while finely adjusting the interaction. Here, we demonstrate an optical strategy to indirectly probe vdW interactions by exploiting induced anisotropy in MoS2/NbIrTe4 heterostructures. We construct heterostructures using isotropic MoS2 and anisotropic NbIrTe4 to ensure perfect parallelism. We modulate and probe the vdW interaction by varying the NbIrTe4 thickness and monitor the vdW-interaction-induced anisotropy in MoS2. We find such induced anisotropy to strongly depend on the NbIrTe4 thickness and clearly observe its fast-decaying nature. This work provides a simple, noncontact approach for indirectly probing interlayer vdW interactions.
authors: Ting Wen; Shuang Cai; Ziluo Su; Yalan Wang; Jiaqi Wu; Jiaze Qin; Chenyin Jiao; Zenghui Wang; Zejuan Zhang; Shenghai Pei

title: Prototyping an inductive conductivity sensor with wide amplitude and frequency range using low cost components
abstract: Quick and cheap water quality monitoring is an increasingly important tool to make the best use of an increasingly valuable resource. Fluid conductivity is an important parameter and can be measured contactless using inductive or capacitive coupling while maintaining low cost. Only the inductively coupled sensors are completely free of electrode polarization effects due to the absence of electrodes. In this work, a sensor based on a newly developed tubular inductor (patented) is presented. It has a high dynamic range and excellent high frequency properties as it does not have multiple (toroid) windings. An analytical derivation of the generated electromotive force based on the Maxwell equations is presented which provides insight for dimensioning the sensor parameters. The use of ferrites will also be discussed, as they play an important role in magnetics, especially for high frequency applications. The novel drive electronics combine low cost with more than three decades of dynamic (amplitude) range at frequencies from 50 kHz to 100 MHz. Key components are a NanoVNA Vector Network Analyzer and high frequency op-amps. A fluid circuit is constructed with simple silicone tubing to form a closed loop with separated drive and detect tubes to exclude crosstalk. Test results are presented measuring five different salt solutions in four decades of concentration, demonstrating a proof of principle and opening a wide field of potential applications.
authors: F. B. Segerink; Herman Leonard Offerhaus

title: Pulse waveform morphology encodes haemodynamic signatures of impending stroke
abstract: Stroke is a disorder of the circulation, yet the haemodynamic state that immediately precedes it has rarely been observed, because continuous physiological recordings before a stroke are seldom available. Photoplethysmography (PPG), recorded by every pulse oximeter and by hundreds of millions of wearable devices, captures the peripheral pulse beat by beat, but its morphology is largely discarded. Here we ask whether pulse waveform morphology encodes haemodynamic signatures of impending stroke. Using in-hospital stroke as a natural experiment that provides continuous PPG before physician-adjudicated stroke recognition, we studied intensive-care (MIMIC-III, $n=176$) and emergency-department (MC-MED, $n=154$) cohorts and described each beat with interpretable descriptors of pulse timing, amplitude, contour and variability. At a nominal 360-min horizon, morphology separated pre-recognition from stable windows with $F_1$ scores of 0.941 and 0.989 (sensitivity 0.998 and 0.980), with models transferred unchanged to the second cohort, and outperformed heart rate alone on identical windows. The signature was dominated by systolic crest time and its change from each patient's own baseline, feature attribution was concordant across cohorts (Spearman $ρ=0.865$), and morphology recorded in the first two hours of care stratified the subsequent clinical course ($F_1$ 0.714 and 0.691). In high-risk patients without stroke, 29% and 14% of windows were positive, but five-window persistence rules limited alerts to 17% and 2% of patients. The results demonstrate that the routinely recorded pulse thus carries haemodynamic imprint of the period preceding stroke, positioning pulse morphology as a candidate continuous cerebrovascular biomarker.
authors: Cheng Ding; Jiaming Liu; Jian Wu; Hongxia Xu; Daoqiang Zhang

title: Pushing Bistatic Wireless Sensing toward High Accuracy at the Sub-Wavelength Scale
abstract: Contactless sensing using wireless communication signals has garnered significant attention due to its non-intrusive nature and ubiquitous infrastructure. Despite the promise, the inherent bistatic deployment of wireless communication introduces clock asynchronism, which leads to unknown phase offsets in channel response and hinders fine-grained sensing. State-of-the-art systems widely adopt the cross-antenna channel response ratio to cancel these detrimental phase offsets. However, the channel response ratio preserves sensing feature accuracy only at integer-wavelength target displacements, losing sub-wavelength fidelity. To overcome this limitation, we derive the first quantitative mapping between the distorted ratio feature and the ideal-channel sensing feature. Building on this foundation, we develop a robust framework that leverages raw channel response amplitude to recover the ideal sensing feature from the distorted ratio. Real-world experiments across Wi-Fi and LoRa signals demonstrate that our method can effectively reconstruct sub-wavelength displacement details, achieving nearly an order-of-magnitude improvement in accuracy.
authors: Wenwei Li; Jiarun Zhou; Qinxiao Quan; Fusang Zhang; Daqing Zhang
venue: ACM International Symposium on Theory, Algorithmic Foundations, and Protocol Design for Mobile Networks and Mobile Computing (MobiHoc)

title: Quo Vadis (Where to), Illicit Drug Testing? Status, Developments, and Perspectives
abstract: Drug testing is a critical tool used in many settings that span clinical care, employers, forensics, and law enforcement. It strives to accurately identify and quantify drugs with high addiction potential by utilizing the available analytical methods and sensors. This editorial offers an insight into the evolution of drug testing into its current set of methods and looks at the current trends that aim to transform the current practice, with a particular focus on the role of sensors and sensor-based devices. Unmet needs for different use cases are discussed, particularly the need for sensors capable of faster, lower-cost, and more specific detection at the point of need. An overview of the efforts in the state-of-the-art technologies that are developed while aiming to address these needs is presented. The paper aims to encourage further work on devices and sensors in the area and highlights the interests of NIDA.

title: RailGuard: Vision-Based Railway Track Inspection and Fault Detection Using a Pole-Mounted Camera
abstract: Railway tracks require frequent and reliable inspection because geometric irregularities, rail-surface defects, fastener failures, ballast deterioration, and objects on or near the track can affect safety, ride quality, and maintenance planning. Conventional manual patrols and specialized track-recording vehicles provide valuable measurements, but they can be labour-intensive, costly, and difficult to scale for frequent monitoring. This paper reviews contactless railway monitoring approaches based on computer vision, LiDAR, GNSS/RTK, inertial sensing, machine learning, ground-penetrating radar (GPR), and InSAR, and uses the findings to motivate an indigenous Integrated Track Monitoring System (ITMS). The proposed direction combines stereo or line-scan cameras, LiDAR, GNSS/RTK, IMU, an encoder, onboard edge computing, SSD storage, and real-time alerts. A practical system should not only detect a defect but also estimate its severity, associate it with a reliable track position, retain evidence, and communicate an actionable maintenance alert. The review highlights calibration, weather and lighting variation, vibration, limited labelled data, computing constraints, and the integration of detection with localization as key engineering challenges.
authors: P. Anlet Pamila Suhi; Harsha K; Nithyashree T S; Rakshitha Reddy V
venue: International Explore Journal of Computer Science and Applications

title: Real-Time Monitoring and Predictive Analytics for Preventing and Reducing Restrictive Practices in Health and Social Care: Protocol for a Scoping Review
abstract: Background: Restrictive practices, including restraint and seclusion, are used across aged care, mental health, and disability support settings to manage behaviors of concern. These practices are associated with substantial ethical, psychological, and physical harms. Digital health technologies, including real-time monitoring systems and AI-enabled predictive analytics, are increasingly used to detect early behavioral escalation. However, detection or prediction alone does not reduce restrictive practices. It remains unclear how these technologies are translated into care actions, decision-making, and measurable outcomes in real-world settings. Objective: This scoping review aims to identify and map evidence on real-time monitoring, predictive analytics, and related digital technologies used to prevent or reduce restrictive practices in health and social care. The review will examine the technologies and contexts studied; how technology outputs are translated into care responses and workflows; and the implementation, outcomes, governance, and ethical considerations reported. Methods: The review will be conducted in accordance with Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and will be reported using the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews). Librarian-assisted searches were conducted in MEDLINE, CINAHL Ultimate, PsycINFO, Scopus, and IEEE Xplore on March 11, 2026. The executed database search strategies were not modified after Open Science Framework registration. Reference lists of included studies and relevant reviews will be screened using citation chasing. Eligible English-language sources will be those that examine digital technologies linked to care responses intended to reduce restrictive practices or to reported restrictive-practice outcomes. Two reviewers will independently screen records and chart all included sources. Standard scoping-review mapping categories will be used to describe the evidence landscape. The Implementation Research Logic Model will inform analysis of explicitly reported implementation determinants, strategies, mechanisms, and outcomes. Results: Electronic database searches were completed on March 11, 2026. Protocol version 5.0 was registered with the Open Science Framework on March 22, 2026. Title and abstract screening had not commenced at the time of registration. The review is expected to be completed by July 2027. Conclusions: By clarifying how digital detection and prediction technologies are translated into care actions, and the conditions under which restrictive practice-related outcomes are reported, this review will support safer, more ethical, and more implementable digital health approaches.
authors: Angela Rong Yang Zhang; June Alexander; Lijun Zhao; Jennifer Tieman; Priyanka Vandersman; Donald Dong Zhang; Russell S. A. Brinkworth; Niranjan P. Bidargaddi; Shengjian Jammy Chen

title: Rehabilitation Wearable Boots and Offloading Methods for Diabetic Foot Ulcer Treatment: A Systematic Review
abstract: Diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs) are a serious and common complication of diabetes, primarily affecting the plantar surface and toes. They are associated with high rates of recurrence, amputation and mortality, making effective treatment strategies essential. This review explores the current landscape of offloading methods and rehabilitation wearable boots used in DFU management, with an emphasis on clinical efficacy, patient adherence and the integration of emerging technologies. Total contact casts (TCCs), the gold standard, achieve healing rates exceeding 80%-90% but face limited adoption due to discomfort, stigma, and lifestyle disruption. Meta-analyses indicate that custom orthotics may reduce ulcer recurrence by up to 50% compared with standard footwear, although the magnitude of benefit varies across studies. In contrast, recent advances in smart wearable devices, multimodal sensors, custom orthotics and AI-driven adaptive systems demonstrate potential to enhance patient compliance and therapeutic outcomes. Despite the availability of evidence-based guidelines, a significant gap persists in their consistent application in clinical settings. Bridging this gap requires the development of patient-centric solutions that integrate technological innovation with usability, comfort and accessibility. This review highlights the need and future for innovative approaches that integrate technology and design to support healing, rehabilitation, adherence and quality of life providing pathways for more effective and sustainable DFU management.
authors: Yaser Sabzehmeidani; Andrei-Alexandru Popa

title: Reliability-Guided Video Token Learning for Contactless Vital Sign Estimation
abstract: Contactless vital-sign estimation from video remains difficult because physiological cues are weak, spatially localized, and easily corrupted by illumination changes, motion artifacts, pose variation, and sensor noise. Existing methods typically learn deterministic mappings from video to physiological waveforms or rates, but they rarely model which visual evidence is reliable or when a prediction should be trusted. We propose a reliability-guided video token learning framework for uncertainty-aware physiological signal estimation. The framework learns to mine informative spatiotemporal tokens, suppress unreliable visual evidence, and infer structured physiological dynamics through masked video-token modeling, signal-guided alignment, and supervised vital-sign estimation. In addition to predicting physiological waveforms and rates, the model outputs an uncertainty score that reflects visual ambiguity and prediction reliability. We evaluate the framework across heterogeneous contactless sensing settings, including respiratory and rPPG benchmarks. In addition to standard accuracy metrics, we assess reliability using uncertainty separation, high-error detection, and risk--coverage analysis. Results show that explicit visual-evidence reliability modeling improves robustness across datasets and provides a practical confidence measure for contactless physiological monitoring.
authors: Shadman Sakib; Haley Patel; Nirmalya Roy
venue: ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM)

title: Remote activity and rhythm monitoring using patient-owned consumer devices after first-time pulmonary vein isolation
abstract: BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Passively collected physical activity data from consumer devices could provide a scalable, objective measure of functional status in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF). This study assessed the feasibility of remotely collecting activity and rhythm data from patients undergoing index pulmonary vein isolation (PVI). METHODS: AF patients enrolled in the prospective TRUST registry who underwent index PVI and reported owning an eligible smartphone were re-contacted to provide informed consent and share their smartphone- and smartwatch-generated data. Pre-specified feasibility criteria were participation rate, technical success, and temporal data coverage. The primary functional outcome was the mean daily step-count change between the one-year pre-PVI and two-year post-PVI windows. Exploratory analyses examined associations of daily activity with AF recurrence and AF burden. RESULTS: Of 280 eligible patients, 172 (61%) attempted and 154/172 (90%) completed data transfer, of whom 123 met pre-specified completeness criteria. Median monitoring duration was 6.0 [3.6, 6.6] years, with 98% [77, 100] coverage. Mean daily step count increased from 5731±2808 to 6220±2816 steps/day after PVI (+488 steps/day [187, 789]; p=0.002). In 35 smartwatch users, AF burden decreased from 3.6% [1.6, 10.8] to 0.0% [0.0, 0.3] after PVI (p<0.001). Baseline AF burden was inversely correlated with daily step count (ρ=-0.36, p=0.035). CONCLUSION: Remote collection of activity and rhythm data from consumer smartphones and smartwatches is feasible, yielding high-coverage, multi-year research data. This enables scalable, objective quantification of longitudinal functional outcomes. Daily step count increased after PVI in this exploratory cohort and was inversely related to baseline AF burden.
authors: Kyra Lachmann; Sandro Jaeckle; Christoph Al-Taie; Jan Leon Rieß; Marc Daniel Lemoine; Niklas Schenker; Moritz Nies; Silke van Elferen; Jan Baumbach; Milaim Kas; Bruno Reißmann; Feifan O. Ouyang; Larissa Fabritz; Stefan Blankenberg; Andreas Rillig; Andreas Metzner; Paulus F. Kirchhof; Julius Obergassel

title: Research Progress and Development Trends in Smart Hospital Operations Management under Digital Transformation
abstract: Digital transformation is changing hospital management from fragmented information processing toward integrated, data-driven, and increasingly intelligent operations. Smart hospitals combine electronic health records (EHRs), interoperable data platforms, artificial intelligence (AI), the Internet of Medical Things (IoMT), cloud computing, automation, real-time dashboards, and emerging digital twin technologies to support clinical services and organizational management. This narrative review synthesizes recent research on the progress, management value, implementation barriers, and development trends of smart hospital operations. Current applications are concentrated in patient flow and bed management, operating-room scheduling, workforce and equipment allocation, medication and supply-chain management, quality and safety monitoring, and administrative automation. Evidence suggests that digital technologies can improve information visibility, forecasting, coordination, and process standardization; however, technology deployment alone does not guarantee better outcomes. Benefits depend heavily on interoperability, data quality, workflow redesign, organizational leadership, user acceptance, cybersecurity, governance, and continuous performance evaluation. In particular, poorly designed EHR workflows may increase documentation burden, while AI systems introduce risks related to bias, transparency, accountability, and lifecycle monitoring. Future smart hospitals are likely to evolve toward integrated command platforms, multimodal AI, ambient intelligence, predictive and prescriptive analytics, and digital twins capable of simulating operational scenarios before real-world implementation. From a medical management perspective, the central task is therefore to shift from technology-centered construction to value-oriented digital governance. Hospitals should align digital investment with measurable operational objectives, establish multidisciplinary governance mechanisms, and evaluate efficiency, quality, safety, workforce experience, equity, and return on investment simultaneously.
authors: Zhijuan Geng; Xiaotian Hu; Haiying Bao; Xiaokang Yao

title: Research on Aircraft Ground Ice Detection Method Based on Polarization Characteristics under Visible Light
abstract: To address the problem of detecting aircraft ground icing under static conditions, this study proposes a non-contact aircraft ground icing detection method based on polarization characteristics in visible light. First, based on the Fresnel equations and the microfacet polarization bidirectional reflectance distribution function (pBRDF) model, the polarization properties of light at the interface of dielectric media were theoretically analyzed. The relationship between the degree of polarization (DoP), the complex refractive index of materials, and the observation geometry was derived, and a polarization optical model was established. The complex refractive indices of five typical aircraft skin coatings were experimentally measured in the visible spectrum, and the corresponding full-angle transmission curves of the degree of polarization (DoP)and angle of polarization(AoP) were obtained. On this basis, an icing detection system was developed using the Brewster angle of ice (52.7°) as the observation angle. Polarization images under both strong and weak illumination conditions were captured, and the differences in degree of polarization and angle of polarization (ΔDOP and ΔAOP) were calculated as key parameters for icing detection. A K-means grayscale clustering segmentation algorithm was employed to identify icing regions. Furthermore, a hierarchical decision model for determining icing location and type was established according to the ΔDOP and ΔAOP characteristic values of aircraft skin and different ice types (glaze ice, rime ice, and mixed ice). The results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves an ice type recognition accuracy of 98.6%. Compared with improved polarization reflection symmetric decomposition detection, polarization detection based on the Otsu algorithm, polarization scattering detection, and polarization-based transparent object segmentation, the proposed method shows significant advantages in ice type recognition accuracy and is more suitable for aircraft ground icing detection tasks.
authors: Jingchang Zhuge; Rongnian Tang; Zhiwei Xing
venue: SAE technical papers on CD-ROM/SAE technical paper series

title: Research on Smart Helmet for Coal Miners with Locking System
abstract: The Smart Helmet for Coal Miners with Locking System represents a practical and effective approach to improving worker safety in underground mining environments. The system combines helmet-lock detection, hazardous gas monitoring, automatic work-time recording, and real-time communication into a single wearable device, making it more than just a conventional safety helmet. The paper contributes to creating a safer and more organized working environment while encouraging better compliance with workplace safety practices. The proposed smart helmet demonstrates how affordable IoT technology can be integrated with personal protective equipment to improve workplace safety, reduce operational risks, and support better monitoring in hazardous environments. It offers a reliable foundation for smarter mining practices and highlights the importance of combining technology with safety to protect workers in challenging underground conditions.
authors: Parth Mehare; Sagar Nikode; Vedant Dange; Yogesh Yadav
venue: International Journal of Creative and Open Research in Engineering and Management

title: Research on perioperative delirium prediction using evolutionary spiking neural networks
abstract: Background Postoperative delirium is a serious complication after surgery. This study evaluates prediction from preoperative hospital records and a separate exploratory ICU classification task. Objective To evaluate a shared evolutionary plus surrogate-gradient spiking neural network (E-SNN) for predicting physician-diagnosed delirium within the first postoperative week after orthopedic surgery, with MIMIC-III retained as a distinct exploratory ICU analysis. Methods The hospital cohort included 577 orthopedic surgery patients, including 84 with physician-documented delirium, evaluated across three stratified splits. MIMIC-III was analyzed separately as an exploratory ICU classification dataset. Both datasets used training-only preprocessing, LASSO feature selection, minority oversampling, and the same E-SNN and baseline pipeline. Results Across three hospital splits, the E-SNN achieved mean AUROC 0.629 (SD 0.075) and average precision 0.278 (SD 0.140); mean positive-class F1 at the common threshold of 0.50 was 0.279 (SD 0.167). Histogram gradient boosting performed better on AUROC and average precision. MIMIC-III findings were exploratory and do not constitute external validation for postoperative delirium prediction. Conclusion The E-SNN showed modest, dataset-specific performance and did not outperform histogram gradient boosting on the main discrimination measures. The MIMIC-III analysis should be interpreted as exploratory ICU classification, not external validation of postoperative delirium prediction.
authors: Haohan Zhang; Jianyu Hao; Xutao Bian; Ke Cui; Yong Yang; Lei Zhao

title: Retrieval-augmented LLM decision support for river water quality monitoring: a Manchester case study
abstract: River water quality monitoring generates large, heterogeneous datasets that can be difficult to translate into actionable insights. This study proposes a multi-agent Retrieval-Augmented Generation Large Language Model (RAG-LLM) decision-support framework that integrates specialised agents for query understanding, retrieval, data analysis, visualisation, and grounded response generation. The framework enables users to analyse environmental monitoring data through natural language (NL) interaction and supports evidence-based assessment of water quality trends, pollution hotspots, monitoring coverage, and station status. The framework was evaluated using UK Environment Agency water quality data from Greater Manchester, comprising 291 river monitoring stations and 45,342 observations recorded during 2024–2026, with data for 2026 covering only part of the year. Evaluation using 50 representative NL queries achieved 88.6% accuracy, 86.9% completeness, and 89.1% groundedness. The proposed framework also achieved a 10.9% hallucination rate compared with 17.0% for a standard text-only RAG baseline, representing a 6.1 percentage-point reduction in unsupported claims. These results demonstrate the framework’s ability to generate grounded and interpretable analytical responses. By integrating retrieval, structured environmental analysis, automated visualisation, and NL interaction, the framework provides an accessible and evidence-grounded approach to environmental monitoring and decision support.
authors: Muhammad Arslan; Saba Munawar

title: Role of Chatbots and Virtual Assistants in the Management of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
abstract: The rising prevalence of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM) calls for new digital tools and chatbots and virtual assistants are emerging as important enablers of patient care. In this article, we review their core technologies, including rule-based designs and advanced AI models using natural language processing, machine learning, and dialogue systems, and their roles in T2DM support, such as education, medication compliance, blood glucose tracking with tailored insights, dietary and physical activity changes, and connections with wearable devices and electronic health records. Clinical data from meta-analyses, randomised trials and implementation studies show significant impacts, including HbA1c reductions of 0.5–1.2%, increased patient engagement, and economic benefits. But there are still challenges, including technological limitations (such as accuracy issues), privacy concerns, moral questions (such as bias and access inequality), and issues with broad adoption by diverse groups. Future directions include next-generation AI with multi-sensory capabilities, harmonised regulations, and embedding into pharmacy-led clinical workflows to enable inclusive and effective T2DM management.
authors: Manish Kumar; Pranav Bhati; Ritu Mishra; Rajiv Yadav; Sushma Chaturvedi
venue: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology

title: Routine longitudinal sleep assessments in psychiatry: a narrative review and a proposed triangulated framework
abstract: Sleep disturbance and mental illness are strongly associated. Focused interventions that take into account or target sleep disturbances could therefore provide substantial therapeutic benefits. This narrative review article explores the limitations of current psychiatric practice for monitoring and understanding sleep, the advances made in practical digital wearable devices, and newer methods that go beyond routine insomnia assessment and management by leveraging readily available data. In turn, we propose a triangulated approach that combines patient-reported experiences, passive sensing, and selectively indicated specialist investigation. We argue for a measurement-based, ecological routine assessment of sleep to deepen our understanding of sleep and circadian disturbances and guide actionable interventions to improve patient outcomes. We present this as a six-step clinical pathway that outlines when to initiate prospective monitoring, how to approach formulation, and what clinical considerations to weigh for management. The pathway incorporates a 14-day paired diary and wearable protocol that tracks seven core metrics and includes a proposed heuristic for interpreting persistent subjective-objective discordance. Lastly, we outline implementation challenges and research priorities that aim to address how digital health workflows can facilitate an integrated framework, shifting care from unstructured, cross-sectional models to longitudinal and personalised approaches.
authors: Lily Farakish; Sahil Bhandari; Robert Hickman; Sajitha Nair; Dan W. Joyce

title: SMART-Glasses: Low-Power Smoking Monitoring via Acoustic Sensing on Eyewear
abstract: The global tobacco epidemic affects the well-being, health, and development of millions of people. While recent advances have greatly improved smoking behaviors monitoring, there remains a lack of widely acceptable, low-power, unobtrusive smoking behaviors monitoring way in real-world scenarios. In this paper, we present SMART ( S moking M onitoring with A coustic Sensing and Sequence R ecognition T echnology)-Glasses, a low-power and minimally obtrusive system that leverages both active and passive acoustic modalities on smart glasses to monitor smoking behavior or recognize the action of lighting a cigarette which enables timely detection, adapting to different user needs. SMART-Glasses innovatively utilizes two speakers and one microphone mounted on the lower rim of the eyeglass frame to emit ultrasonic signals and capture the resulting echoes and passive sounds, thereby extracting features related to smoking behaviors. Furthermore, we introduce a gated sensing enhancement model that amplifies smoking-related features across various noisy conditions. Finally, a smoking action sequence recognition model captures temporal dependencies, allowing the system to distinguish smoking behavior sequences from irrelevant actions. SMART-Glasses is designed for ordinary users who wish to quit smoking and is intended for use in naturalistic environments such as homes, offices, and outdoor areas. Evaluation in both lab and semi-wild settings demonstrates high performance in recognizing lighting and smoking behaviors, showing strong potential for real-world deployment.
authors: Tianyu Wu; Lei Yan; Kaiyi Guo; Changfei Dong; Qian Zhang; Dong Wang
venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction

title: SNR-Robust Active Frame Detection for Dual-Radar Fall Monitoring via Maximum Ratio Combining
abstract: In a practical setting of radar-based fall detection system, radar data arrives as a continuous, stream rather than packaged events. Before the system can recognise a fall, it must first constantly scan this incoming stream to isolate the exact moments of genuine movement from empty background recordings. The conventional approach of using a fixed energy threshold to make this approach vulnerable to failure because it cannot adapt to its unexpected background noise. This situation can easily trigger false alarms, and on the other hand, weak signals from a distant fall might go completely undetected. Furthermore, a threshold perfectly tuned for one room often fails in another, making constant manual recalibration impractical for real-world deployment to address this, we propose a noise-adaptive diversity-combining approach. Based on the principle of maximum-ratio combining, this method weights horizontal and vertical radar energies according to their respective noise levels. We evaluated our approach on a dual-radar dataset against independent time-domain ground truth, testing across simulated signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs) from +20 to −10 dB. As expected, uncalibrated fixed-thresholds performed poorly (mean F1-score: 0.095). However, our proposed method (F1-score: 0.75–0.86) also significantly outperformed calibrated single- and dual-radar constant false-alarm-rate (CFAR) baselines (F1-score: 0.74–0.77) at every SNR level (p < 0.001). These results demonstrate that threshold calibration alone is insufficient for robust frame detection, and that our noise-adaptive approach provides consistent improvements regardless of environmental noise
authors: Nur Iman Syahirah; Nur Emileen Abdul Rashid; M. M. Awang Kechik; Khairul Khaizi Mohd Shariff
venue: Journal of Electrical & Electronic Systems Research

title: SUSPENSE: The Smart Exploration Rover
abstract: Exploration of unknown, inaccessible and potentially hazardous environments presents significant challenges to human safety. Underground tunnels, mines, caves, disaster-affected areas and remote locations may contain obstacles, hazardous gases and unpredictable environmental conditions. Direct human inspection in such environments can expose personnel to considerable risks. This paper proposes SUSPENSE (Smart Unmanned Surface Patrol for Exploration, Navigation, Safety and Environmental Monitoring), a low-cost, four-wheeled autonomous exploration rover designed to support preliminary inspection and environmental monitoring. The proposed system uses a Raspberry Pi as its main processing unit, ultrasonic or time-of-flight distance sensors for obstacle detection, a camera for visual monitoring, a BME280 sensor for temperature, humidity and atmospheric pressure measurement, and a separate gas sensor for detecting selected hazardous gases. The rover is designed to perform autonomous movement and basic obstacle avoidance while transmitting live video, environmental readings, alerts and system information to a laptop through Wi-Fi. Additional functionalities include event-based video recording, battery monitoring and a proposed low-battery return-to-station procedure. When an important event occurs, such as obstacle detection or a gas-level threshold being exceeded, the system is intended to generate an alert and save a corresponding video clip. The laptop acts as a monitoring and supervisory station rather than a continuous manual driving controller. SUSPENSE is intended to support preliminary inspection in disaster-related environments, underground locations, industrial sites and terrestrial research related to planetary exploration. This paper presents the proposed architecture, hardware requirements, software design, methodology, expected functionality and future evaluation plan. The system is currently at the design stage and requires hardware implementation and experimental validation. Keywords— Autonomous Rover, Environmental Monitoring, Disaster Inspection, Obstacle Avoidance, Raspberry Pi, Wireless Communication, Event-Based Recording, Battery Management

title: Scentronic: An artificial intelligence–assisted olfactory interface for remote odor sharing and transmission
abstract: Recent years have witnessed the surge of human-machine interfaces (HMIs) for various applications. Olfaction is a fundamental chemical sense crucial to perception, memory, and emotion. Current limitations arise from the difficulty of accurately capturing, transmitting, and reproducing odor signals, and the lack of standardized, network-enabled platforms. This work presents an internet of things (IoT)-enabled olfactory interface for remote odor sensing and stimulation. The system integrates an artificial intelligence-assisted odor sensing platform with a wearable piezoelectric olfactory actuation system. We demonstrate the design, characterization, and application of this framework, which integrates devices, circuit architecture, and software algorithms. Applications in medical contexts include psychophysical testing to study olfactory pathways and evaluate sensory loss. We further showcase multisensory stimulation through integrated olfactory and gustatory interfaces for enhanced immersion. This study establishes a scalable framework for IoT-based olfactory interaction, advancing HMIs toward a future that includes the long-overlooked chemical senses.
authors: Chunyu Yang; Qi Wang; Chen Wang; Antonia Akoto-Yeboah; Shaoru Cheng; Billings Amoah; Yizhen Jia; Shulin Chen; Akhil Canumalla; Kai Zhao; Christopher T. Simons; Jinghua Li

title: Scoping review of wearable device data evaluated in clinical studies
abstract: Background Wearable device data are increasingly used to provide physiological and behavioural measures in clinical studies. Aims This scoping review maps out the data collected by wearable devices from participants in clinical studies, including the approaches used to interpret this data. Methods Scopus, Web of Science, the Cochrane Library and PubMed, along with ClinicalTrials.gov, were searched using relevant keywords. Clinical studies published or registered from January 2020 to July 2026 inclusive, in which wearable devices were used to monitor participants, were sought. Data on disease demographics, sample size, gender, ethnicity, study design, wearable type, application and data interpretation approaches were extracted using a data extraction form within Covidence software and then exported and compiled for analysis. Results Out of 13 744 identified records, 147 original articles were included. Cardiovascular diseases, followed closely by neurological diseases, were the most frequently studied clinical indications. The median sample size was 85 (range 1–455 699). Overall, the most measured wearable data were physical activity (106 (72%)), heart rate (48 (33%)) and sleep (34 (22%)). 98 studies used wearable data to measure outcomes (52 primary and 46 secondary), and 49 studies used wearable data for disease monitoring. 27 studies applied advanced computational or machine learning methods, with 9 studies integrating multiple wearable-derived variables to develop composite or disease-specific digital biomarkers. Conclusions The studies included in this review report the use of wearables to provide continuous, real-world data on patients’ physiological and behavioural metrics to assess health outcomes and disease progression outside traditional clinical settings. Advanced computational approaches remain a minority, with most studies relying on device-derived measures and conventional analytical methods.
authors: Emer Gunne; Saber Azami Aghdash; Sinéad Holden; Peter Doran

title: Seizure quantification using wearable devices
abstract: Accurate assessment of seizure occurrence is central to treatment optimization, risk stratification, and management of epilepsy, yet remains largely dependent on patient-reported seizure diaries, which are frequently incomplete and unreliable. Wearable technologies have emerged as promising tools to enable objective and continuous seizure monitoring by capturing seizure-induced physiological signals. Over the past decade, substantial progress has been made in the development and clinical validation of wearable seizure detection systems, particularly for generalized convulsive seizures, where high sensitivity can be achieved, whereas detection of nonconvulsive seizures remains more limited. However, translating detection into clinically meaningful seizure quantification presents important challenges, including variability in performance across seizure types, patient populations, and individual physiological responses, as well as differences between controlled and real-world settings. This narrative review critically examines wearable technologies for seizure quantification, integrating recent clinical evidence and expert perspectives. We discuss key sensor modalities, including accelerometry, electrocardiography-derived features such as heart rate variability, multimodal biosignal integration, and emerging ultra-long-term wearable and subcutaneous electroencephalographic systems. Each modality offers specific advantages and limitations depending on seizure type and clinical context. Attention is also given to the importance of user trust, adherence, and data quality as key determinants of clinical utility. We further examine the role of wearable seizure quantification in clinical practice, including treatment monitoring, tele-epileptology, and clinical trials, as well as potential future contributions to sudden unexpected death in epilepsy risk assessment. With continued technological advances and robust real-world clinical validation, wearable systems have the potential to transform seizure monitoring and support more precise, data-driven epilepsy care.
authors: Jesper Jeppesen; Tobias Loddenkemper; Roland D. Thijs; Guido Rubboli; Philippe Ryvlin

title: Self supervised multi scale learning for WiFi CSI contactless human activity recognition with potential applications in health monitoring
abstract: WiFi Channel State Information (CSI) provides a privacy-preserving and contactless sensing modality for human activity recognition, but practical CSI recognition remains challenged by limited labeled data, heterogeneous motion dynamics, and signal perturbations. This study proposes CSI-MSRNet, a self supervised representation-learning framework that combines CSI-aware contrastive augmentation with a lightweight temporal and subcarrier multi scale encoder. The encoder models motion evolution at multiple temporal receptive fields and complementary frequency-selective responses across OFDM subcarriers, while Efficient Multi-Scale Attention is used only as a lightweight feature-refinement component rather than as the primary methodological novelty. Self supervised pretraining is restricted to the training partition, after which the encoder is fine tuned with different proportions of labeled samples. Experiments were conducted on the public UT-HAR and NTU-Fi HAR benchmarks using the SenseFi data partitions. Main recognition and low-label experiments were repeated five times with random seeds 42–46, and low-label subsets were independently sampled by stratified class sampling in each run. CSI-MSRNet achieved 98.76 ± 0.18% accuracy on UT-HAR and 99.85 ± 0.21% on NTU-Fi HAR. With only 1% labeled data, the corresponding accuracies were 73.6 ± 2.4% and 77.8 ± 2.8%, respectively. Controlled synthetic tests further indicated improved tolerance to amplitude noise and random subcarrier loss. These results should be interpreted as benchmark-level behavioral recognition rather than evidence of subject-independent generalization, clinical monitoring effectiveness, or embedded-device deployment. The framework therefore provides a computationally lightweight approach with potential applications in smart-home and health-related behavioral sensing.
authors: Hui Xu; Dengju Yao; Wei-dong Liu; Lu Li; Lin Ma; Chao Jiang

title: Sensing the Invisible: How AI Learns to Read Human State, from Virtual Reality Therapy to Real-World Customer Systems
abstract: Until now each and every discussion you've had has happened on 2 channels. One carries words. The other has all other kinds in it – the rising of the shoulder when the subject get awkward, the quickening of the pulse under the collar, the pause before an answer even when he wants to; and the catch in his voice. According to people, it's a channel they are reading ALL the time and usually without their knowledge. We refer to this as intuition, ‘rapport' or a ‘bedside manner'.Most of the time, in computer history, computing machines were only listening to the first channel. Helplessness was not recorded on a keyboard, nor were any multiplications or subtractions. A form is a thing that captures answers, not frustration from the one that's filling it out. That's been speedily altered. The 2nd channel is now available as a result of cameras, microphones, wearables, headsets and the barrage of digital communication. Machine learning provides the software with a method to make an educated guess about the 2nd channel.It is this guess that this book is about – how it is made, where it works, where it doesn't, and what it should and should not be used for.So why first with virtual reality?Few things capture the application of technology under the most controlled and most humane conditions than the therapy setting inside a therapy room, hence its use as the setting for the beginning of the story. When a person is using a VR system for clinical purposes, they have consented to the sensing, the intent is their personal healing, and the virtual reality environment is completely known a priori by the virtual reality system. Human reading is relatively easy pretty much everywhere, so it should be easy there.From there the book unfolds, trastornado, traversing increasingly commercial and less consensual environments—the car, the contact center, the shop floor, the smartwatch worn by millions of wrists. As you go out beyond the steps, you are going out beyond what was effective in the therapy room. The best way to understand this field is to see which condition is missing in the person and what doesn't work as a consequence of that missing condition.The intended audience of the book.The book is addressed to four types of reader. This book will provide product leaders and designers with a common beneficial language for the capabilities and limitations of these systems and design patterns for constructing them in a responsible way. A map of signals, models and evaluation pitfalls will be found by engineers and data scientists – one that extends across disciplines traditionally taught separately. Therapeutic work is also included alongside its commercial cousins, making it easy for both clinicians and researchers to comprehend how there could be a public trust relationship between the two. Since will ensure that policymakers and general readers can make assessments on science claims made by vendors and critics alike.Only the occasional ratio is used and no other mathematics is needed. When there is a technical suggestion involved, it is described in words before.This book presents the argument thatThere are three themes throughout the chapters. They are given once here and each of the others follows along the same line, but does not repeat them.Emotion is not recognized by machines, it is a state that is inferred from signals detected by the machine. A camera captures motion of the muscle, not anger. The sweat-gland activity measured by a wristband does not indicate fear. The leap from signal to state is an inferential process under conditions of uncertainty, and it is in this area that a lot of the trouble arises when these implications of uncertainty are forgotten.2) There's insight and there's noise and context is the difference. The concept that works on racing on a bike is not the same on a treadmill, or during the job interview or in a VR experience of an otherwise frightening height. Systems, that know the context, do much better than systems that don't; virtual reality is the extreme paradigm, in which a system constructs the context.There is no question about whether a machine can read the human state or whether it should, but who and under what circumstances? The same ‘pipeline’ that can help a veteran of a horrendous or traumatic event pace themselves to revisit the memory at a manageable moment could be used to measure a customer's mood at a call centre or to time a sales pitch when they are in a weak moment. The technology is virtually the same. The ethics are not.How to read itThe 14 chapters can be divided into four parts. Part I (Chapters 1-4) focuses on laying the groundwork – defining human state, identifying signals of it, and how machine learning is used to convert signals to estimates. Part II (Chapter 5-7) explores Adaptive VR therapy, which gets under the hood of VR headsets. Part III (Chapters 8-10) takes the technology into cars, customers systems and consumer wearables. Part IV (Chapters 11–14) provides information on the limits of scientific possibility, law and ethics, a practical design process and the future.While chapters may be read stand alone, each one is completely described once and hardily referenced again in another chapter, so it is easiest to read the chapters in order. In fact, there are three varieties of shaded boxes throughout:In neither of these boxes are they using a lot of jargon. Those who have already read about the idea, can skip them!Case study boxes: features real deployments, trials or enforcement actions of which measurable results are published. All are noted in "References" at the end of the book.Worked examples of design decisions, particularly on issues of privacy, consent and bias are provided in practice boxes.The notion of the recurring characters of Meera, the patient, and Arjun, the bank customer, are passed through the book with very short scenarios. They are composites (labels and descriptions) created with the aim of demonstrating how systems behave and are not descriptions of real people.ConventionsThe figures and tables are numbered chapterwise (Fig. 2.3 is the third figure in Chapter 2). Citations are prepared in the Vancouver Style - that is, given a number in the text, numbered in the sequence in which the source is first cited, and then a complete reference list at the end of the book. Each chapter ends with a brief list of main points instead of a written summary of the chapter.It was a completed edition in October of 2026. The regulatory cut-off and the products in same evolves rapidly. The legal/commercial information contained in the text has been verified as of October 2026 but in the event of the fact changing the reader should consult up to date sources before taking any action on the basis of the specific information.

title: Seroprevalence of contagious caprine pleuropneumonia (CCPP) in goats and sheep from Karamoja region, North-eastern Uganda
abstract: Contagious caprine pleuropneumonia (CCPP) is a notifiable respiratory tract disease of goats and sheep caused by Mycoplasma capricolum subspecies capripneumoniae (Mccp). CCPP is associated with high economic losses due to reduced growth rates, high morbidity, mortality, restrictions to movement of livestock, products, and market access. Endemic countries need to generate regional Mccp seroprevalence data and use these data to inform the design of CCPP control and surveillance programs. A total of 2,296 serum samples were collected; sheep (n = 1,066) and goats (n = 1,230) from 38 randomly selected small ruminant village flocks. These flocks were drawn from three randomly selected districts (Amudat, Kaabong, and Karenga) out of nine districts in the Karamoja region, north-eastern Uganda. The serum samples were screened for anti-Mccp IgG antibodies using the IDEXX CCPP competitive ELISA kits. A mixed-effects Poisson regression model with log link and village as a random effect was then fitted to identify risk factors influencing the observed Mccp seropositivity, and to account for village-level clustering. Goats were 3.39 times more likely to be Mccp seropositive than sheep (aPR: 3.39, 95% CI: 2.91 – 3.96). Female goats and sheep were 1.20 times more likely to be Mccp seropositive than males (aPR: 1.20, 95%CI: 1.01 – 1.43). Statistically significant (p<0.05) predictors of Mccp seropositivity in goat and sheep included: age category, being female and species (goat or sheep). We report a high Mccp seroprevalence across the study area, suggesting increased natural exposure to Mccp since the sampled flocks had no history of CCPP vaccination. Risk-based CCPP control programs should target these predictors of Mccp seropositivity. The observation that every village had at least one seropositive small ruminant [goat or sheep] indicates that goats and sheep potentially contribute to the epidemiology of CPPP alike and should therefore be targeted in CCPP vaccination programs. CCPP control programs in Uganda should prioritize small ruminant flocks from districts near the South Sudan and Kenya international borders especially if sufficient resources to conduct mass vaccination are unavailable.

title: Seroprevalence, Risk Factors, and Farmer’s Knowledge and Practices on Contagious Bovine Pleuropneumonia in Morogoro Rural District, Tanzania
abstract: Background: Contagious Bovine Pleuropneumonia (CBPP), a highly contagious disease of cattle, is a major constraint to cattle production in Tanzania. Purpose: This study aimed to determine the seroprevalence of CBPP, identify animal and herd level risk factors of the disease, and assess the knowledge and practices (KP) of cattle farmers regarding CBPP. Method: Data were collected from August to November 2025 through a cross sectional study involving three cattle production systems; pastoral, agropastoral, and ranching. Overall, 409 cattle with no history of vaccination against CBPP were randomly selected, and blood samples were collected for the cELISA test. Results: Most respondents practiced pastoralism (61.8%), followed by agro pastoralism (35.9%) and ranching (2.3 %). Majority reared indigenous cattle (71.0%), with cattle herd sizes ranging from fewer than 100 to over 200 animals. Risk related management practices were common among the respondents, with all reporting the use of communal grazing and watering points, followed by seasonal movement of cattle beyond village boundaries for grazing (64.9%) and herd mixing (61.8%). Overall animal and herd level seroprevalence of CBPP were 3.4% and 16.1%, respectively. Seroprevalence was higher among young cattle (3.8%) than adults (3.1%), females (4.0%) than males (1.2%), and crossbred cattle (5.5%) compared with indigenous breeds (2.7%). Moreover, cattle reared under the ranching production system exhibited the highest seroprevalence (4.6%), followed by agro pastoral (1.8%) and pastoral (1.7%) systems. Conclusion: This study detected CBPP exposure across pastoral, agro pastoral, and ranching cattle systems, with the highest seroprevalence in ranching cattle at Morogoro Rural District.

title: Should I “stay” or should I “go”? Influence of an anticipated stop on cortical correlates of overground walking
abstract: Real-world walking frequently requires pedestrians to maintain proactive inhibition to safely navigate unpredictable environments. While cortical modulations occurring during locomotion under environmental uncertainty are well-established, the specific proactive mechanisms underlying this state of inhibitory anticipation remain unexplored. This study aimed to investigate the behavioral and cortical shifts associated with anticipating a stop during overground walking. Fourteen healthy young adults performed fluent and cautious walking tasks with an expected stop. Cortical activity and trunk acceleration were recorded using a 32-channel mobile electroencephalography and an integrated accelerometer. Step-1 latency and step-interval variability were calculated via heel strike detection. Gait-phase-related power modulations were computed, and spectral principal component analysis was applied to attenuate artifacts. The results revealed that cautious walking significantly increased step-interval variability, whereas step-1 latency remained unaffected. At the cortical level, left frontotemporal areas exhibited an attenuated and delayed theta desynchronization during the swing phase. Furthermore, centroparietal regions demonstrated an altered temporal profile of alpha and beta synchronization, characterized by enhanced late-stance synchronization and reduced swing-phase synchronization. The present findings suggest that anticipating a potential stop may alter the rhythmic consistency of gait and reorganize phase-specific cortical dynamics. Being prepared to stop may shift the neural control of automated locomotion toward active monitoring, highlighting the relevance of proactive inhibition during everyday mobility.
authors: Daghan Piskin; Saskia Kurtzhals; Jochen Baumeister

title: Smart AI-Based Public Washroom System for Automated Hygiene Monitoring and Self-Cleaning
abstract: Public washrooms require continuous monitoring and timely maintenance to maintain hygiene and improve user experience. Conventional systems depend largely on periodic manual inspection, which may result in delayed cleaning, overflowing waste bins, unpleasant odor, unnecessary water consumption, and inconsistent maintenance. This paper presents a Smart AI-Based Public Washroom System that combines Internet of Things (IoT) sensing, embedded control, automation, and privacy-aware design. The proposed prototype uses a microcontroller such as ESP8266/ESP32 together with sensors for user presence, waste-bin level, and environmental or odor-related conditions. Sensor information is processed locally to trigger appropriate actuators, including automatic flushing, cleaning, odor-control, and maintenance alerts. A cloud or mobile monitoring layer can provide remote status information to maintenance personnel. A key design principle is that no camera is required inside the washroom; non-visual sensors are used for automation and monitoring to reduce privacy concerns. The proposed system provides a foundation for intelligent sanitation infrastructure and can be extended with historical data analytics and machine-learning models for predictive cleaning and maintenance.
authors: Dnyaneshwari Bhosale
venue: International Journal of Innovative Research in Technology

title: Smart Biosensing Platforms and Internet-of-Things-Enabled Microbial Monitoring: Transforming Real-Time Microbiology
abstract: Rapid microbial information is essential for clinical care, food safety, water quality, agriculture, industry and environmental surveillance. Conventional culture remains vital for recovering viable organisms and confirmatory testing, but its time demands limit continuous monitoring. This chapter examines smart biosensing platforms that combine biological recognition, transducers, connectivity and automated analytics within Internet-of-Things systems. It compares electrochemical, optical, paper-based, wearable and microfluidic sensors, alongside antibodies, nucleic-acid probes, aptamers, CRISPR, enzymes and bacteriophages. It also addresses sample preparation, matrix effects, viability, calibration, uncertainty, false alerts, cybersecurity, interoperability, regulation and ethical governance. Applications include healthcare, food chains, drinking water, wastewater, agriculture, pharmaceuticals and environmental monitoring. The chapter argues that smart microbial monitoring should be developed as a validated and quality-assured socio-technical system rather than a stand-alone sensor.
authors: Ebinyo Rebecca Aseibai; Kingsley Excel Dunga; Vivian Ibienebakabobo Promise; Nsikak Godwin Etim; Godgift Nabebe
