title: Smart Classroom Monitoring System Using IoT for Intelligent Educational Infrastructure
abstract: The rapid advancement of Internet of Things (IoT) technology has significantly transformed traditional educational environments into intelligent learning spaces capable of enhancing teaching efficiency, student safety, and resource management. Conventional classroom management methods often depend on manual monitoring, resulting in inefficient utilization of classroom resources, delayed environmental control, and increased energy consumption. This paper presents an IoT-based Smart Classroom Monitoring System that continuously monitors critical environmental and occupancy parameters, including temperature, humidity, air quality, illumination, sound level, and human presence. The proposed system integrates multiple sensors with an ESP32 microcontroller to collect real-time data and transmit it to a cloud platform via Wi-Fi for remote monitoring and analysis. The collected data are visualized through an IoT dashboard, enabling administrators and faculty members to observe classroom conditions from any location. Automated control mechanisms are incorporated to regulate electrical appliances such as lighting and ventilation based on predefined threshold values, thereby improving occupant comfort while minimizing unnecessary energy usage. The proposed architecture supports scalable deployment across multiple classrooms and provides historical data for predictive maintenance and infrastructure optimization.

title: Smart Shoe for Women Safety Device
abstract: This paper presents a smart safety sandal designed to enhance the personal security of women using GSM and GPS technology. When the wearer presses a panic switch, the system sends a real-time location alert to pre-defined emergency contacts. The sandal also includes a non-lethal electric shock mechanism that serves as a self-defence measure. The device is compact, wearable and designed for quick response in emergency situations.
authors: S Soni, Zaveria M Sheikh, Drakshayani V; Hanumantha Rao A Priyanka VJ

title: Smart Technologies in the Management of Metabolic Syndrome and Oral Health: A Narrative Review
abstract: Background/Objectives: Metabolic syndrome (MetS) and periodontitis are two of the most common chronic conditions sharing an underlying mechanism represented by systemic inflammation. Smart technologies, including machine learning (ML), wearable and Internet of Things (IoT) devices, telemedicine and intraoral sensors, are increasingly used in both fields. This narrative review examined how these technologies are used to predict, monitor and manage MetS and oral diseases and what evidence supports combining oral and metabolic data. Methods: Following the SANRA framework, PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science were searched for English-language articles published between January 2021 and May 2026. Of the 6922 records identified (3520 after de-duplication), 1852 were screened by title and abstract, and studies were selected by relevance to three research questions. Applications were classified by their current level of evidence. Results: ML models for MetS prediction often reported high discrimination (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUC] up to 0.99), but most were validated only internally, and several used the diagnostic components of MetS as predictors. Wearable, telemedicine and mobile interventions, usually combined with lifestyle programs, were associated with improvements in body weight, blood pressure and glycemic markers; artificial intelligence tools for dental imaging showed accuracy comparable to clinicians in mostly retrospective studies, with limited evidence on patient outcomes. Few studies combined oral and metabolic data: cross-sectional ML studies identified periodontal severity as a predictor of MetS and metabolic conditions as predictors of periodontitis, and salivary glucose correlated with blood glucose mainly in people living with diabetes, which does not establish diagnostic accuracy. No prospective study has tested an integrated dental–medical pathway. Conclusions: Integrating oral and metabolic data through smart technologies is biologically plausible and appears technically feasible, but its added diagnostic value, clinical effectiveness and cost effectiveness have not been established. Externally validated models, prospective cohorts and trials of integrated care pathways are required before routine use.
authors: Anna-Maria-Clara Gherbon; Deiana Roman; Romulus Zorin Timar; Oana Albai

title: Smart Tourist Safety Monitoring and Incident Response System Using AI
abstract: Tourists travelling through remote, forested, hilly, wildlife, and adventure destinations may encounter disorientation, restricted areas, accidents, health emergencies, crime, or communication failure. Conventional mechanisms often separate location tracking, emergency reporting, identity verification, and authority coordination, which can delay intervention when a tourist cannot communicate or when a location signal lacks behavioural context. This paper proposes a unified Smart Tourist Safety Monitoring and Incident Response System that combines a mobile application, GPS tracking, geo-fencing, artificial-intelligence and machine-learning analytics, blockchain-based digital tourist identity, authority monitoring, and optional IoT wearable devices. After registration, a tourist receives a Digital Tourist ID associated with the mobile application or wearable. Location, movement, activity, and optional health signals are processed to identify unsafe-zone entry, route deviation, prolonged inactivity, fall-like events, and explicit SOS requests. Alerts are delivered to an authority dashboard for verification, prioritisation, escalation, and response recording. The paper presents the research foundation, system architecture, operational methodology, implementation plan, and evaluation framework. It does not claim completed experimental results; accuracy, latency, scalability, privacy, and field effectiveness remain evaluation objectives.
authors: V. Janani; Aditya; Niharika Jena; Rushikesh S

title: SmartSign: Real-Time Hand Gesture Recognition and Speech Generation Platform
abstract: Sign language is an essential means of communication for individuals with hearing and speech impairments. However, communication barriers often arise between sign language users and people who are unfamiliar with sign language. To address this challenge, this paper presents a SmartSign: Real-Time Hand Gesture Recognition and Speech Generation Platform that uses computer vision and deep learning techniques to recognize hand gestures and convert them into understandable text. The proposed system is developed using Python, Flask, OpenCV, MediaPipe, and a trained machine learning model. It provides multiple detection methods, including image-based detection, video-based detection, multi-image processing, and real-time webcam recognition. The system also incorporates interactive learning features such as sign language practice, tutorials, a chatbot, progress tracking, history, and analytics to support continuous learning. Additionally, an administrative panel enables administrators to manage users, tutorials, detection history, and application settings. The system processes hand landmarks and extracts relevant features to identify corresponding signs and display the predicted results through a user-friendly web interface. By integrating sign recognition with learning and progress-monitoring facilities, the proposed application aims to improve accessibility, support sign language education, and reduce communication barriers. The system demonstrates the potential of combining computer vision, deep learning, and web technologies to develop an interactive and accessible sign language recognition platform

title: Speckle Vibrometry:Towards a Clinical Implementation of Contactless Vital Signs Monitoring
abstract: Monitoring vital signs is crucial in a hospital setting. For example, in the general ward, but also in other disciplines, such as critical care or sleep, to make a proper diagnosis. The monitoring of such vital signs (e.g., heart rate, respiration rate) is done with wired sensors. However, this is obtrusive and may interfere with the results. Therefore, the purpose of our work is to develop a contactless sensing technology, Speckle Vibrometry (SV), for the continuous monitoring of heart rate and respiration rate in a clinical setting. Our work also serves as the first to present human clinical studies for SV.SV is a contactless sensing technology that exploits the secondary laser speckle effect. A typical SV setup consists of a laser source and a camera that is defocused at the laser spot. Using imaging processing techniques, SV tracks the overall movement of individual speckles to measure minute cardiac motions even through layers of textiles. It differs from laser speckle contrast imaging (SCI) and laser speckle plethysmography (SPG), which both require visible skin and a focused camera. SCI uses the overall blurring of the speckle pattern formed on biological tissue to measure blood flow, whereas SPG uses the mean intensity of the laser speckle pattern formed on the human finger to measure cardiac pulses. By comparison, SV is an attractive option among the existing contactless technologies (e.g., camera photoplethysmography) because it is highly sensitive to minute motions and does not require visible skin (i.e., it works on multiple layers of blankets). In this work, we investigate the use of SV for heart rate and respiration rate monitoring in an intensive care unit to lay a solid foundation for future work delving into the practical large-scale implementation of SV in hospitals, as well as the feasibility study of pulse transit time monitoring. Pulse transit time is another potentially valuable cardiorespiratory parameter for clinical diagnosis. It has been shown to indicate blood pressure changes, respiratory effort, and is linked to obstructive sleep apnea. Pulse transit time is conventionally measured as the time it takes for the pulse wave to travel from the aortic valve to a peripheral site (e.g., the fingertip). Research has also utilized two arterial sites (e.g., between the carotid and femoral pulses). Existing techniques to compute pulse transit time are based on accurate cardiac measurements, i.e., clear and visible cardiac peaks. Following the same assumption, in this work, we focused on extracting high-quality cardiac measurements from SV in an intensive care unit as a step toward future investigations into pulse transit time. Specifically, we propose solutions that tackle two challenges: the device setup of SV and the successful extraction of cardiac and respiratory motions, heart rate, and respiration rate through algorithm development. Our solutions were conditioned under two scenarios: a sleep scenario in a laboratory-controlled environment and a sedated/sleep scenario in an intensive care unit. Innovative algorithms have been proposed to take into account the practical challenges present in such a real clinical setting, which is a crucial step in transitioning SV from the lab to the real clinical world. Although our current results cannot provide a conclusive answer to whether or not SV can be used to measure pulse transit time in a stand-alone manner, this thesis work shows that SV is able to measure instantaneous heart rate, serving as a solid first step. To comprehensively present the scientific contributions of this thesis, we organize our work into six chapters, each summarized below. In Chapter 2, we review current gold-standard measurements of heart rate, respiration rate, and pulse transit time. In addition, we present contact-based alternatives that measure these vital signs in a wireless manner. We then introduce existing contactless vital sign sensing modalities, such as camera-based, radar-based, thermographic, and SV systems in existing works. To highlight the novelty of the SV system developed in this work, we describe its experimental setup in detail and compare it with both prior SV implementations and other contactless sensing modalities discussed. In Chapter 3, we present a proof of concept to assess the viability of employing SV for monitoring average heart rate in situations where the human subject remains at rest in bed. We developed an image processing pipeline to extract average heart rates from SV video recordings and compared them with ECG. The first step was extracting the displacements between consecutive SV video frames based on a sub-pixel image registration method from existing literature. We then proposed an algorithm to merge displacements along the x-axis and y-axis of the image plane, to derive a single-channel SV measurement as well as to remove the impact of camera-to-surface orientation. For peak detection, we implemented a simplified Hilbert-based method that was designed to extract the aortic valve opening (AO) peaks from Seismocardiogram signals. Results show that our methods can be used to extract average heart rate from 1-minute windows from the human subject's thoracic area under different textile coverage scenarios, including bedsheet covers (8, 32, and 64~mm of thickness), furry blankets (8, 32, and 64~mm of thickness), and comforters (32, and 64~mm of thickness). From this chapter, we conclude that our SV setup works and SV can detect minute cardiac motions without skin visibility. This result opened the possibility of moving SV one step further towards a longer measurement duration and different anatomical locations that have weaker cardiac pulses than the thoracic area. In Chapter 4, we proceeded with SV from average heart rate measurement to instantaneous heart rate monitoring. In contrast to the previous study mentioned in Chapter 3, we increased the duration of each unique measurement from 1 minute to 5 minutes. Most importantly, new anatomical locations were included to tackle different resting positions. Our experimental protocol included three resting positions. For the supine position, one laser source was illuminated on the sternum. For the lateral and prone positions, the anatomical locations were the upper left arm and upper left scapular, respectively. For instantaneous heart rate comparison, we improved the Hilbert-based method by incorporating an adaptive thresholding scheme and proposed a peak alignment algorithm to match each AO-peak from SV measurement to their corresponding R-peak from ECG. In a laboratory-controlled environment, our results demonstrated SV's capability of extracting instantaneous heart rates from various anatomical locations with different resting positions regardless of the textile coverage scenarios tested. In Chapter 5, we moved SV from a laboratory-controlled environment to an intensive care unit, i.e., from healthy volunteers to real patients. Apart from the thoracic area, we included the neck as the additional measurement location because it is a challenging spot and thus can be used as a technical study of SV. More importantly, the carotid on the neck is an arterial site for future investigations into using SV for two arterial site-based pulse transit time monitoring. The practical challenges present in an intensive care unit were addressed, including variant ambient lighting conditions and diverse cardiorespiratory waveforms of the patients. For the first challenge, We proposed a new motion extraction algorithm that is based on multiple regions of interest (multi-ROI). We defined two signal quality index values to select the best 4 ROIs out of 16 and performed principal component analysis to derive one single motion measurement at run-time (i.e., over each 10-second sliding window). This multi-ROI method proved to be robust against the sensor noise and outperformed the method that is based on one region of interest, i.e., the full video frame. Given a sensor-noise-free cardiac motion measurement, we then utilized the discrete first-integral to successfully extract the modulated respiratory motion signal. For the second challenge, we proposed a semi-automated peak detection algorithm that was based on waveform matching. The only manual part was the construction of the waveform template for each patient. This new peak detection algorithm enabled more precise labeling of the AO peaks compared with the Hilbert-based method, which provided a good foundation for future endeavors into pulse transit time calculation. Finally, in Chapter 6, we provide a general discussion of the scientific contributions, strengths, limitations, and future directions of this thesis. First, we conclude the advancement achieved by this thesis in terms of using SV to successfully measure both cardiac and respiratory motions, and subsequently the extraction of instantaneous heart rate and respiration rate in a clinical setting. Second, we examine current limitations, including sensitivity to body motion and the need for precise optical alignment. Subsequently, we outline potential solutions through sensor fusion and algorithmic enhancement. Future research directions emphasize extending SV to long-term and ambulatory monitoring, exploring its integration with other modalities for pulse transit time estimation, and investigating its potential application in MRI cardiac gating. Overall, this chapter delineates the remaining steps required for SV to evolve into a robust, stand-alone tool for multi-vital-sign monitoring.
authors: Shuhao Que

title: Stable and Interpretable Cognitive Status Screening Using Longitudinal Wearable Data
abstract: Wearable devices repeatedly measure activity, sleep, and nocturnal physiology, but their value for three-class cognitive screening remains uncertain. We developed an interpretable hierarchical framework to distinguish cognitively normal (CN), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and dementia (DEM) without the Mini-Mental State Examination or device-generated composite scores. Data from 174 adults aged 55 years or older were represented by seven-day windows encoding level, variability, trend, transitions, bouts, and complexity. Stage 1 separated DEM from non-DEM using the top-3 mean of window probabilities; Stage 2 separated CN from MCI using participant-median slope-and-change features. Participant-level cross-validation and repeated 3- to 6-fold sensitivity analyses preceded evaluation on an internal holdout of 38 participants. Accuracy was 0.711, balanced accuracy was 0.738, and macro F1 was 0.692; recall was 0.682, 0.700, and 0.833 for CN, MCI, and DEM, respectively. TreeSHAP and correlation grouping yielded four preliminary DEM patterns---activity complexity, device-state organization, rest, and light-sleep structure---and three exploratory MCI domains spanning activity persistence, sleep-wake timing, and nocturnal physiology. These findings support risk screening and hypothesis generation rather than diagnosis or validated biomarker claims; external multicenter validation is needed.
authors: HaEun Kim; Taewan Cho; Andrew Jaeyong Choi; Seon-Heui Lee

title: Stow-able passive supernumerary dorsal grasping
abstract: For people who have experienced the loss of hand function due to cervical Spinal Cord Injury (SCI) or disease, the inability to grasp and manipulate objects during their activities of daily living (ADL) can severely hinder their ability to complete tasks independently. This work presents the design and initial evaluation of the passive Dorsal Grasper, a hand orthosis comprising two deployable supernumerary fingers above the dorsal face of the hand opposing wrist extension to permit grasping. The pull-out grip force for a range of object sizes is presented in addition to the graspability and manipulation (supination and pronation) of 15 different objects with varying shapes and sizes that one may encounter in ADLs. The device was evaluated by two participants, one without SCI and one with cervical SCI, both authors of this study. Preliminary results demonstrated grasping and manipulation of various objects, including selected tasks during an in-home demonstration. Performance depended on object characteristics and available space, with difficulties grasping objects in clustered environments. These findings suggest potential benefits for users with cervical SCI and sufficient wrist extension strength. However, the small sample and participants' dual role limit generalizability and introduce potential bias, requiring further validation with independent participants.
authors: Jungpyo Lee; Andrew I. W. McPherson; Derrick Ma; Hannah S. Stuart

title: Studies on mechanical tribological corrosion fracture surface and prediction of waterjet machining parameters for Al7075/n-ZrO2 composites using taguchi and machine learning algorithms
abstract: The mechanical and tribological properties of aluminum metal matrix composites (MMCs) are remarkable. This study assesses the effects of 0-2 weight percent nanoscale zirconium dioxide (ZrO 2 ) on the corrosion resistance, wear behavior, and mechanical strength of stir-cast Al7075 composites. Additionally, the impacts of water pressure, traverse speed, and standoff distance during abrasive water jet machining (AWJM) were comprehensively analyzed using a Taguchi L27 orthogonal array. The 1.5 weight percent Al7075 composite produced the best results, and SEM confirmed the uniform dispersion of n-ZrO 2 . The nano-composite's hardness (29.54%), tensile strength (16.98%), wear resistance (38.88%), and corrosion resistance (37.90%) all showed notable improvements. ANOVA revealed that the primary factor affecting machining is water pressure, which drives 64.68% of material removal rate (MRR) and 41.99% of surface roughness (Ra). Confirmation tests verified that error margins were within allowable limits, even though machine learning models successfully demonstrated parameter evaluation and process optimization.
authors: S M Pradeepa; Hanumanthe Gowda; K Arun Kumar; A Anusha; K Nisha; Sushma; C. Durga Prasad; S. Harish; C M Manasa
