title: Survey on intelligent video surveillance
abstract: Video surveillance systems have witnessed rapid advancements over the past two decades, fueled by progress in computer vision, artificial intelligence, and edge computing. However, despite extensive research, there remains a need for a review that synthesizes the architectures, methodologies, and evolving trends of intelligent video surveillance systems from a system-level perspective. Most existing literature reviews focus narrowly on individual tasks such as object detection, motion tracking, or anomaly recognition, without addressing how these components integrate within a complete system. This paper addresses this gap by conducting a systematic review of research published between January 2000 and July 2025, drawing from major digital repositories. The main contributions of this work are threefold: (1) it proposes a structured taxonomy of intelligent surveillance systems based on key functionalities, including object detection, motion tracking, abnormal event detection, vehicle and traffic monitoring, object counting, and multi-camera coordination; (2) it provides a comparative analysis of methodologies, datasets, and platforms used across studies; and (3) it explores the interconnections among these core tasks while identifying critical challenges such as real-time processing, privacy preservation, data scalability, and system interoperability. Key outcomes of this review include the identification of underexplored research areas—such as federated learning and cross-camera integration—and practical guidelines for designing next-generation surveillance systems. The literature analyzed was sourced from major digital repositories including IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, Google Scholar, arXiv, Springer, and the ACM Digital Library.
authors: Mahmoud Elnady; Hossam E. Abdelmunim; Diaa Abidou; Islam Elmadah

title: Synovial Fluid Alpha-Defensin Levels and Serum Fibrinogen Levels for Optimization of the Differential Diagnosis of Complications of Joint Arthroplasties
abstract: Background Differential diagnosis of periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) remains a major clinical challenge despite advances in diagnostic criteria and laboratory methods. Although modern definitions such as the EBJIS criteria have improved diagnostic accuracy, uncertainty persists in selected cases, particularly when microbiological findings are negative or inconclusive. Methods At our institution, we focused on two complementary biomarkers for the differential diagnosis of complications of joint arthroplasties: synovial fluid alpha-defensin (HNP 1–3) concentrations measured by high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) and serum fibrinogen levels. A total of 141 patients with painful joint arthroplasties underwent diagnostic aspiration between 2021 and 2024. Synovial fluid samples were analyzed microbiologically (culture with prolonged incubation and PCR testing) and by HPLC for precise HNP 1–3 concentrations. C-reactive protein (CRP), leukocyte count, D-dimers, and fibrinogen were measured in venous blood samples. Results Statistical analysis demonstrated that comparison of synovial HNP 1–3 concentrations with serum fibrinogen levels improves differentiation between infectious and aseptic complications. Simultaneous elevation of both HNP 1–3 and fibrinogen was strongly associated with infectious etiology, reflecting a systemic inflammatory response. In contrast, isolated elevation of HNP 1–3 with normal fibrinogen levels was predominantly associated with aseptic loosening, especially in case of metal wear, suggesting localized inflammation without systemic activation, or in patients with rheumatologic conditions. Conclusions These findings indicate that the combined assessment of HNP 1–3 and serum fibrinogen represents a clinically meaningful and readily available non-microbiological diagnostic approach for optimizing the differential diagnosis of joint arthroplasty complications.
authors: Pavel Melicherčík; David Jahoda; Tomáš Judl; René Kizek; Mária Mellová; Valerij Semjonov; Vladimír Barták; Petr Fulín; Eva Klapková

title: System Trust or Self-Efficacy? Behavioral Intention Toward Wearable Devices in Immersive Embodied VR for Upper-Limb Training: An Integrated Cognitive-Affective Perspective
abstract: Although virtual reality (VR) and motion capture technologies are increasingly being applied in rehabilitation training, existing research has largely focused on analyzing users’ experience. The underlying mechanisms of cognitive-emotional trust resulting from the synergistic effects of technological features and in-depth gamification design remain unclear. This study aimed to examine the determinants that influenced behavior in immersive VR upper-limb training by integrating the stimulus-biological-response and cognitive-emotional-behavioral models. Furthermore, we combined technical features, the situational learning theory, and two-dimensional trust (based on the trust and self-efficacy theories) from an attribution perspective. We developed an immersive VR training system and obtained experimental data from 280 users. Analysis employed Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM), Necessary Configuration Analysis (NConfA), and Artificial Neural Networks (ANN). Results revealed that Environmental Embeddedness had a significantly greater effect on the situational cognition dimension than Embodied Interactivity. However, Perceived Incentives had no significant effect on Affective Trust in Technology. NConfA results identified four necessary configurations that promoted high levels of behavioral intention. Furthermore, ANN findings illustrated strong non-linear relationships between Immersion, learning motivation, and task-specific self-efficacy, demonstrating Immersion’s crucial role in the overall formation mechanism. Based on a cognitive-affective trust perspective, this study provides guidance for all relevant stakeholders: Immersion and interactive experiences should be strengthened to promote self-efficacy, thereby fostering behavioral intentions.
authors: Yujun Chen; Zheng Xu; Tao Yang

title: Systematic Review of Smart Home Assistive Technology Devices for Supporting People With Dementia Living in Their Homes
abstract: OBJECTIVES: Most people with dementia prefer remaining in their own homes as long as possible. Smart home assistive technologies are being developed to enhance safety and autonomy of people with dementia and to support their caregivers. However, evidence for their efficacy and effectiveness in community-based dementia care remains uncertain. Hence, we aim to systematically review the available evidence on the efficacy of smart home assistive technology devices for supporting people with dementia living in their homes. METHODS: We conducted a systematic review following PRISMA-2020 guidelines (PROSPERO ID:CRD420251051358). We comprehensively searched four databases. Eligible studies examined smart home or wearable devices used by people with dementia in home or supported accommodation settings. We systematically performed quality assessment, data extraction, and the GRADE assessment. Meta-analyses were conducted when three or more studies investigated similar outcomes. RESULTS: We screened 3176 abstracts and identified 18 eligible studies that investigated 17 devices. There is level-2 evidence supporting the use of companion robots, electric calendar, a night-time home monitoring system and the People Power Caregiver system. Our meta-analysis did not find evidence supporting the use of the investigated devices for reducing caregiver burden (p = 0.68; Hedges's g = 0.01; 95% CI -0.14 to 0.17). CONCLUSIONS: Smart home technologies for dementia care are acceptable and feasible. However, current evidence for their efficacy remains limited. Larger clinical trials are required to strengthen their evidence base and justify their routine use in supporting people with dementia and caregivers.
authors: Oscar Han; Reagan Lee; Anne Lee; Naomi Thorpe; Hui Zhi Tan; Changmin Doh; Anto Praveen Rajkumar

title: Terahertz Wireless Human-Like Sensing in the Microscopic Molecular Level
abstract: Perceptual intelligence is a fundamental research area in artificial intelligence, and human-like full-information perception represents a frontier direction in this field. Among the major challenges in this field, contactless human-like perception remains an open problem worldwide, and wireless sensing has emerged as a promising new technological pathway toward its realization. Previous studies have shown that the excitation of molecules by terahertz signals produces absorption spectra that encode molecular properties, thereby enabling microscopic, molecule-level sensing. In addition, the interactions between terahertz signals and objects can be exploited to identify material properties and surface geometries. This paper presents our exploration of terahertz wireless sensing for microscopic, molecule-level human-like sensing. We introduce the concept of a digital perceptual membrane that integrates terahertz signals with deep neural networks and develop a series of terahertz human-like sensing methods at the molecular level, including contactless taste, olfactory, and tactile sensing. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods, providing a novel solution for realizing contactless human-like sensing. Finally, we discuss future research directions in terahertz wireless human-like sensing and highlight its potential applications in embodied intelligence, healthcare, food safety, and other fields.
authors: Huadóng Ma; D. W. Song; Zhan Zhang; Rui Lyu
venue: ACM Transactions on Internet of Things

title: The Barriers and Facilitators for People With Bipolar Disorder Deciding to Attend and/or Complete Cancer Screening of the Cervix, Breast and Bowel: A Qualitative Study Using Normalisation Process Theory
abstract: BACKGROUND: Bipolar disorder affects 1.3 million people in the United Kingdom. People with bipolar disorder are less likely, than the general population to attend and/or complete cancer screening. AIMS: To explore the barriers and facilitators towards thinking about, and/or completing cervical, breast and colorectal screening by people with bipolar disorder. METHODS: Semi-structured interviews with 27 people living with bipolar disorder in the North-East and Cumbria (January 2023 to June 2023). Deductive thematic analysis was completed using the constructs of Normalisation Process Theory (NPT). NPT was used to ensure recommendations from the study were developed through an implementation lens. RESULTS: Participants with bipolar disorder highlighted how their mental health influenced their decision to complete cancer screening, or not. Most participants understand what screening was and why it was important to complete screening. However, they described barriers such as anxiety, forgetfulness and fear in completing screening. As well as systemic barriers such as appointments not being at a good time, unfamiliar screening locations and discomfort in waiting rooms were also specifically highlighted for cervical and breast screening. Whilst for colorectal screening, home testing kits were seen as useful, participants felt unsupported in completing the kit, and feared completing the kit wrongly. CONCLUSIONS: The identification of barriers and facilitators to cancer screening has highlighted a clear need to increase awareness and providing tailored support for people with bipolar disorder. Offering multiple screening options could further improve screening participation among the group.
authors: Kate Sykes; Jill Barker; Emma L. Giles; Jula Sill; Emma Tuschick

title: The Electrocardiogram as a Preventive Biomarker: From Conventional Risk Markers to Actionable Artificial Intelligence - A Narrative Review
abstract: The electrocardiogram (ECG) is an established tool in cardiovascular prevention, identifying silent arrhythmias, hypertrophy, prior myocardial infarction, conduction disease, and inherited electrical disorders. However, conventional interpretation captures only a fraction of the information embedded in the cardiac electrical signal. Because the ECG is inexpensive, non-invasive, standardized, and already acquired at scale, it provides an attractive substrate for artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled screening and risk stratification. Deep-learning models can identify latent signatures of ventricular dysfunction, structural heart disease, atrial fibrillation, cardiomyopathy, heart failure, and mortality risk. Importantly, evidence is beginning to extend beyond retrospective validation: prospective implementation studies have increased disease detection, while randomized data suggest that AI-ECG-guided clinical alerts may improve outcomes in selected high-risk populations. Whether such benefits extend to preventive populations remains uncertain. This review examines the preventive role of conventional, ambulatory, and wearable ECGs and distinguishes AI applications for detection, prediction, prognostication, treatment selection, and longitudinal monitoring. We argue that performance metrics alone are insufficient. Preventive value requires a defined target population, calibrated and externally validated predictions, an appropriate confirmatory test, a feasible clinical workflow, and an intervention proven to improve outcomes. The most credible near-term applications are those that triage patients to established diagnostic pathways, such as echocardiography or prolonged rhythm monitoring. The central challenge is therefore to transform accurate AI-ECG predictions into actionable, affordable, scalable, safe, and equitable prevention.
authors: Rodrigue Garcia; Aymeric Menet; Josselin Duchâteau; Laurent Fiorina; Abderrazzaq Moufidi; Jérôme Taieb; Benoît Lequeux; Olivier Piot

title: The Growing Role of Technology in Healthcare: A Systematic Literature Review and Analytical Assessment of Evidence, Equity and Governance
abstract: Background: Health systems face ageing populations, rising chronic disease, workforce shortages and escalating costs. Meanwhile, electronic health records (EHRs), telemedicine, artificial intelligence (AI), wearables and connected devices are being adopted at unprecedented speed. The evidence on what these technologies deliver, for whom, and at what risk remains fragmented. Objective: To synthesise and critically appraise evidence on the clinical, operational, economic, equity and governance consequences of technology in healthcare. Methods: A protocol-driven systematic literature review (SLR), guided by PRISMA 2020 reporting principles, covered peer-reviewed primary studies, systematic reviews, meta-analyses and authoritative policy documents. Findings were extracted into structured tables and synthesised through narrative and thematic analysis. An analytical research stage followed. It applied an ordinal Translational Readiness and Equity Exposure appraisal, a multi-stakeholder analysis and the derivation of analytical propositions. Results: Evidence is most mature for EHR-enabled safety gains and for telemedicine in selected chronic conditions. Hospital adoption of at least a basic EHR rose from 9.4% to 83.8% in the United States between 2008 and 2015. Telehealth use stabilised at roughly 38 times its pre-pandemic level. Deep-learning diagnostic systems achieved pooled sensitivity of 87.0% against 86.4% for clinicians, but only a small minority of comparative studies were prospective. Documentation burden, algorithmic bias, weak external validation and the digital divide emerged as the principal threats to value. Conclusions: Technology creates value only when evidence, equity and embedding in workflows advance together. We propose an Evidence–Equity–Embedding (3E) framework and a set of actor-specific recommendations for clinicians, managers, regulators and researchers.
authors: Parhlad Singh Ahluwalia

title: The Temporal Investigation of Multimodal Elements (TIME) Study: protocol for an observational, longitudinal study to characterize the dynamic structure of molecular and digital data in older adults in stable health
abstract: Background: Biological systems exhibit dynamic patterns over multiple temporal scales-from minutes to months-that are poorly captured by conventional cross-sectional or low-frequency longitudinal studies. These patterns, including diurnal variations and underlying continuous rhythms, may be critical determinants of health, resilience, and disease risk in aging. Existing longitudinal studies in older adults lack high-frequency, multimodal measurements that integrate molecular, physiological, and digital health data streams. Objectives: The TIME Study aims to: (i) Characterize temporal patterns in molecular, physiological, and digital health measures in healthy older adults; (ii) determine how these patterns vary across biological domains and relate to each other; and (iii) assess how physiological systems respond to defined perturbations (oral glucose tolerance and maximal exercise). Methods: TIME is a single-site, observational, longitudinal study enrolling up to 150 adults aged ≥55 years. Over an 11-week main phase, participants complete seven weekly low-frequency visits, two perturbation challenge visits, and two, two-day high-frequency sampling epochs. Biospecimens, clinical measures, cognitive and physical performance tests, and continuous digital health data are collected. Follow-up visits occur at 6 and 12 months. Expected impact: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07107386, identifier NCT07107386.
authors: James T. Yurkovich; Emma Glass; Audrey N. Nash; Noah Levine; Sophia Lee; Katheryn Ehlen; Eduardo Hernandez; Prabin Gharti; Chatura Senadheera; Ashen Fernando; Drew Witherington; Lance T. Pflieger; Jyotika Erram; Noa Rappaport; Alison Le; John C. Newman; Brianna J. Stubbs

title: The association between wearable device use and exercise adherence: a chain mediation model of exercise self-efficacy and positive experiences
abstract: Objective To examine the association between wearable device use and exercise adherence and to investigate the chain-mediated roles of exercise self-efficacy and positive experiences in this relationship. Methods A questionnaire survey was administered to individuals who used fitness apps or smart wearable devices ( N = 367). Structural equation modeling (SEM) was conducted to examine the hypothesized associations and mediation pathways. The Bootstrap method with 5,000 resamples was applied to assess indirect effects. Results Wearable device use showed a statistically significant total association with exercise adherence ( β = 0.430, p < 0.001); after the two proposed mediators were included, the direct association was β = 0.197 ( p < 0.001). Exercise self-efficacy and positive experiences each showed significant independent indirect associations, and the sequential (chain) indirect pathway involving both variables was also statistically significant (indirect association = 0.059, 95% CI [0.035, 0.086]). The indirect associations statistically accounted for 54.0% of the total association. Conclusion Among physically active users of digital fitness technologies, wearable device use was positively associated with exercise adherence, and this association was partially accounted for by a chain mediation pathway involving exercise self-efficacy and positive experiences. The findings are consistent with, but do not confirm, the proposed directional model; they identify psychological factors associated with exercise adherence among wearable device users and may inform future research on technology-assisted approaches for supporting sustained exercise behaviour.
authors: Ziqi Qin; Ying Guo; Xinlong Liu

title: Theorizing future phenomena: Metaverse, wearables, and humanoids
abstract: Research Summary We propose that entrepreneurship and strategy research can develop theory about phenomena of the future rather than only explain those of the past. Research has potential for practical relevance when researchers make claims towards applications to decisions practitioners have yet to make. Theory grounded in a world that may differ from the observed world can be built through a process of extrapolation from technological trends, a practice utilized by entrepreneurs and science fiction authors alike. Assuming advances in artificial intelligence, we apply this process to three emerging phenomena: governing scarcity in metaverse virtual worlds, redesigning organizations around pervasive monitoring via wearable devices, and allocating the intellectual property rights of humanoid robots. We argue that embracing theory that speaks to the future can enhance the practical and educational relevance of management research. Managerial Summary Assuming artificial intelligence continues to improve, we highlight three impending phenomena poised to transform conventional approaches to entrepreneurship and strategy. First, in metaverse virtual worlds, managers must manage resources governed by artificial scarcity. Second, with wearable devices allowing continuous monitoring, managers must consider alternative structures for vertical hierarchy and horizontal collaboration. Third, deployment of humanoid robots will complicate intellectual property rights and asset ownership. We propose that scholarship towards developing theoretical frameworks addressing these and other phenomena of the future will be relevant to both managers and students.
authors: Andy Wu; Ronald Wang

title: Titanium degradation and peri-implant tissue health: A review
abstract: Titanium and its alloys are widely used in dental implants because of their strength, corrosion resistance and predictable osseointegration. However, corrosion, mechanical wear and tribocorrosion can release titanium particles and ions into peri-implant tissues, potentially contributing to inflammation and marginal bone loss. Therefore, it is of interest to examine the titanium degradation mechanisms, particle distribution and biological pathways involving macrophage activation, cytokine release, osteolysis and inflammasome signalling. Diagnostic challenges include the absence of validated biomarkers and limited evidence establishing a direct causal relationship between titanium degradation and peri-implantitis. Thus, improved diagnostic methods, surface modifications, antimicrobial coatings and alternative implant materials may help reduce degradation-associated tissue damage and improve long-term peri-implant health.
authors: H.D Yatheesh

title: Translational maturity of artificial intelligence-enabled electrocardiography varies across cardiovascular diseases
abstract: Electrocardiography is a widely available and low-cost cardiovascular test, and artificial intelligence-enabled electrocardiography (AI-ECG) can identify latent electrical phenotypes beyond conventional interpretation. However, high retrospective discrimination does not necessarily translate into clinically reliable or actionable benefit. This critical narrative review evaluates the translational maturity of AI-ECG across arrhythmias, acute myocardial infarction, heart failure, valvular heart disease, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and cardiac amyloidosis. PubMed, IEEE Xplore, and Web of Science were searched from January 1, 2022, through July 10, 2026, with earlier landmark studies added by backward citation tracking. Seventy-seven publications informed the review. Evidence was appraised using five clinically oriented criteria: intended use, reference-standard reliability, external validation and transportability, clinical actionability, and effects on workflow or patient outcomes. AI-ECG has progressed furthest in ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction triage and reduced-left-ventricular-ejection-fraction screening, where prospective or randomized studies have demonstrated workflow or diagnostic-yield benefits, whereas acute myocardial infarction rule-out has reached prospective multicenter diagnostic validation. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy screening has also advanced through international validation and prospective implementation. By contrast, occlusion myocardial infarction detection, prediction of occult or future atrial fibrillation, valvular heart disease, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, long-term heart-failure prediction, and cardiac amyloidosis remain primarily validation-stage or risk-enrichment applications. Across domains, broader adoption is constrained by label quality, calibration, transportability, operating-threshold selection, and limited patient-outcome evidence. AI-ECG is therefore best positioned as clinician-supervised decision support linked to explicit downstream testing and care pathways.
authors: Huanhuan Chen; Jingjuan Huang; Xumin Hou

title: Transmission‐Based Precautions
authors: Tammy Hanks

title: Triboelectric Nanogenerators for Human‐Robot Motion Energy Harvesting and Sensing: Structures, Embodied Artificial Intelligence, and Self‐Powered Applications
abstract: The rapid development of humanoid robots and embodied artificial intelligence (EAI) is accelerating the transformation of elderly care and rehabilitation toward interactive, adaptive, and personalized human-robot collaboration. In this context, motion sensing technology is of critical importance. Triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs), which convert biomechanical motions into electrical signals, offer a promising route toward self-powered motion perception in embodied healthcare. This review summarizes recent advances in TENG-based multimodal motion sensing for human-robot interaction, covering inertial vibration sensing, tactile sensing, non-contact sensing, continuous trajectory sensing, and joint rotation sensing. The influences of structural configuration, motion mode, sensing direction, detection range, sensitivity, resolution, electrical output, and channel number on sensing performance under specific application scenarios are analyzed. Particular attention is paid to how TENG design strategies influence sensing universality, signal effectiveness, and the reliability of health monitoring and rehabilitation evaluation. Furthermore, the integration of TENGs with artificial intelligence (AI) technologies, including multimodal fusion, network architectures, edge computing, transfer learning, and large language models, is reviewed. Finally, applications in adaptive rehabilitation sensing, self-powered electrical stimulation, fully self-powered systems, and human‑robot interfaces are highlighted, offering perspectives on closed-loop "sensing-evaluation-regulation" frameworks for green, low-carbon EAI healthcare.
authors: Jian Li; Gefan Yin; Zhen Sun; Chenhao Li; Yadong Mo; Cong Gu; Xiangyan Zhang; Sikai Wang; Xiangjie Xu; Runxiao Liu; Jiahe Wang; Pengyu Chen; Ziyang Li; Shimin Wei

title: Trustworthy Phishing URL Detection Using Machine Learning: Performance Analysis and Future Directions
abstract: Over the years, Uniform Resource Locator (URL) Phishing has been a threat to online security because their scams exploit trust in a misleading URL to trick unsuspecting users into disclosing their username or passwords and other personal information. Not only that, but it is also crucial to identify these malicious URLs and ensure online platforms and users are protected. The ISCXURL2016 data was utilized for the purpose of analyzing the performance of different Machine Learning (ML) models in differentiating phishing and legitimate URLs in this paper. A wide range of classifiers were explored including the classic classifiers as well as more advanced ensemble classifiers. The results of the experiments indicate that ensemble-based boosting models can be more beneficial for URL phishing detection. HistGradientBoost achieved the highest accuracy of 98.47%, followed closely by LightGBM and XGBoost that both outperformed the accuracy of 98%. The other classifiers, RandomForest and ExtraTrees, also performed well with accuracy above 97% and traditional classifiers such as Quadratic Discriminant Analysis (QDA) showed the poorest performance with an accuracy of 67.75%. The results show that the boosting-based ensembles provide a suitable negation of the complex and non-linear structure of phishing URLs. Along with empirical evaluation, it offers a Properties & Positioning viewpoint as well as the importance of the ML-based phishing detection in the broader context of cybersecurity issues. Moreover, it discusses the future directions, with Federated Learning (FL) in the context of decentralized and privacy-preserving collaboration and Large Language Models (LLM) in the context of semantic reasoning and flexibility. These insights together will provide the building blocks for more intelligent, adaptive and trustworthy phishing organizations.
authors: Omer ِAlmomani; Ahmad Shalaldeh; Mohammed Almaayah; Ahmad Saleh Shatat; Mohammed Madi; Mutasem K. Alsmadi; Ibrahim Mohammed Dweib
venue: International Journal of Advances in Soft Computing and its Applications

title: Trustworthy multimodal biosensing in cardiovascular health: integrating uncertainty, causality, and signal integrity for clinical reliability
abstract: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) monitoring increasingly relies on multimodal biosensors, including electrocardiography (ECG), photoplethysmography (PPG), and advanced imaging systems. While deep learning has enhanced the analytical capacity of these biosensors, the translation of multimodal sensing data into clinical practice is hindered by a trustworthiness gap. Current biosensing architectures often lack robustness to sensor noise, produce poorly calibrated confidence estimates, ignore physiological causality, and fail to align with clinician workflows. Employing a systematic narrative review methodology across PubMed, IEEE Xplore, Scopus, and arXiv (2018–2026), this paper synthesizes the literature around six interconnected challenge areas in biosensor data integration: uncertainty quantification and conflict resolution; handling missing and misaligned modalities; knowledge-guided representation and fusion; causal and evidential reasoning; robust clinical evaluation; and human-centered integration. We propose a taxonomy of fusion strategies based on their trustworthiness properties and identify critical limitations in current methodologies, such as the tendency of black-box transformers to exploit spurious correlations in sensor data and the brittleness of early fusion under distribution shift. Furthermore, we outline a comprehensive research roadmap emphasizing causal disentanglement, federated multimodal learning, and interactive clinician-AI loops. By bridging algorithmic innovation with biosensor reliability, this review provides a blueprint for developing reliable, interpretable, and equitable multimodal biosensing systems. However, we emphasize that while these technical directions are promising, prospective clinical validation, standardized regulatory benchmarks, and equitable dataset curation remain essential prerequisites before these systems can be considered clinically validated solutions capable of transforming cardiovascular care.
authors: Adeel Akram; Wasim Ullah Khan; Qaisar Khan; Derrick Boateng; Lanfang Lei; Chen Zhong; Muhammad Shehzad Khan

title: USE OF MODERN SMARTWATCHES IN EARLY DETECTION OF HEART RHYTHM DISTURBANCES AND PREVENTION OF CARDIOVASCULAR COMPLICATIONS: A NARRATIVE REVIEW
abstract: Atrial fibrillation (AF) and other cardiac rhythm disturbances represent a major and growing global health burden, contributing substantially to stroke, heart failure, and cardiovascular mortality worldwide. Because AF is frequently asymptomatic or paroxysmal, timely diagnosis remains a persistent clinical challenge. This narrative review aims to synthesize current evidence on the technological principles, diagnostic performance, clinical utility, and limitations of consumer smartwatches equipped with photoplethysmography (PPG) and single-lead electrocardiography (ECG) for the detection and prevention of heart rhythm disturbances. Large prospective cohorts, including the Apple Heart Study and the Fitbit Heart Study, together with multiple systematic reviews and meta-analyses, demonstrate that smartwatch-based PPG and ECG algorithms achieve high sensitivity and specificity for AF detection. This enables opportunistic screening and supports targeted secondary prevention of thromboembolic events, particularly ischemic stroke. However, real-world implementation raises concerns regarding false-positive alerts, overdiagnosis, patient anxiety, and the necessity of physician-confirmed diagnosis. Smartwatch-based rhythm monitoring constitutes a clinically meaningful, evidence-supported adjunct to conventional arrhythmia detection, but its integration into routine cardiological practice requires structured confirmatory pathways, clinician education, and further research addressing diverse populations and long-term outcomes.
authors: Michal Balenkowski; Mateusz Antonow; Agnieszka Górska; Anna Kozieł; Amelia Sztangierska; Konrad Kowalski; Michał Kardela; Katarzyna Gołąbek; Mariusz Siemiński
venue: International Journal of Innovative Technologies in Social Science

title: Understanding Smart Glasses: Technology, Risks, and Opportunities in the Postplagiarism Era
abstract: Smart glasses are not new, but the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) has changed what they can do and where people wear them. Current consumer models combine cameras, microphones, and, in some cases, in-lens displays with large language models (LLMs) and computer vision. Many are difficult to distinguish from conventional eyewear. In this report, we provide educators, educational developers, academic integrity practitioners, and institutional leaders with a working knowledge of smart glasses with AI capabilities. We review terminology, the evolution of the technology, applications, social acceptance, and privacy concerns. We also analyze responses from governments, testing bodies, and universities through November 2026. Reported cases of examination cheating in South Korea, Taiwan, and Japan indicate a real risk to assessment security. Nevertheless, we argue that prohibition and inspection cannot resolve that risk. Detecting a device cannot establish whether, when, or how a student used it. Enforcement based on appearance moves scrutiny from student work to student bodies. That shift places the heaviest burden on students with disabilities, students with limited finances, multilingual learners, and racialized students. Smart glasses also serve as assistive technology, and many students who rely on them never register for formal accommodations. Drawing on the tenets of postplagiarism, we contend that historical definitions of cheating may not hold once the moment of unauthorized help becomes impossible to identify. We recommend that institutions separate possession from misconduct, write rules based on what devices do, redesign assessment around process and reasoning, and track enforcement for inequitable outcomes. Keywords: smart glasses, AI glasses, wearable AI, wearable technology, academic integrity, academic misconduct, academic dishonestly, academic cheating, cheating, examinations, postplagiarism, assessment, accessibility, privacy, higher education
authors: Fuat Ramazanov; Sarah Elaine Eaton
venue: Libraries and Cultural Resources (University of Calgary)

title: Understanding irritable bowel syndrome care: Co-create with patients and providers for diagnostic and management innovations
abstract: BACKGROUND A non-invasive, biomarker-based, breath analysis device is currently being developed to support the diagnosis and management of irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). Understanding existing IBS diagnostic and management processes is essential to ensure its alignment with end users’ needs and existing IBS care. AIM To understand IBS diagnosis and management processes and explore how a breath analysis device might integrate with care processes. METHODS This qualitative, explorative study comprised two research activities: (1) Desk research; and (2) Semi-structured interviews with stakeholders. Desk research sources included (grey) literature such as Dutch College of General Practitioners guidelines and the patient association website. Nineteen semi-structured interviews were performed: 11 with patients and eight with health care professionals. RESULTS Despite the complexity of diagnosing and managing IBS, our results provide comprehensive insight into current IBS care processes. Although health care professionals felt that they provided sufficient information and fully discussed treatment options, patients nevertheless experienced a lack of guidance, often turning to complementary medicine. Additionally, while many participants were receptive towards the idea of a breath analysis tool to support the diagnosis and management of IBS, skepticism was expressed regarding its likely diagnostic accuracy, and the risk of misdiagnosis and underdiagnosis of other gastrointestinal diseases was also mentioned. CONCLUSION Stakeholders expressed a need for more definitive diagnostic testing for IBS. Co-creating digital health tools based on lived experiences may improve patient outcomes and strengthen patient–provider relationships.
authors: Atena Mahboubian; Welmoed Jonker; Elise Hogewoning; Gertrude van den Brink; Jiska J Aardoom; Marise Jeannine Kasteleyn

title: Utilising wearable technology to enhance neurosurgical training: a systematic scoping review
abstract: PURPOSE: Contemporary neurosurgical training faces challenges due to reduced operative exposure and the limited, inconsistent feedback provided to trainees. Wearable technologies may help address these issues by offering objective data and real-time support. This scoping review systematically evaluates the evidence of wearable technology in surgical training, analysing device types, their applications, and the supporting evidence for their effectiveness. MATERIALS AND METHODS: A systematic literature search was conducted in 10 pre-clinical and clinical databases from inception to May 2024, searching for keywords "wearable technology" AND "surgery" AND "training". The search yielded 25,806 results. After removing duplicates, papers were screened by title and abstract (n = 12,306), followed by full-text screening (n = 482). RESULTS: Forty-one studies, including 985 participants, were included in the review. Head-mounted displays were predominantly used for augmented and mixed reality applications, while smart glasses facilitated telementoring and procedure recording. Other wearables enabled biomechanical analysis and ergonomic assessments. Reported outcomes varied widely, with clinician-centred metrics, such as procedural accuracy, error rates, completion times, and satisfaction, being the most frequently assessed. Devices including HTC VIVE and HoloLens were associated with improved surgical performance. Clinicians often reported enhanced visualisation and anatomical orientation, though barriers such as learning curves, technical issues, and discomfort were noted. CONCLUSIONS: This review provides a comprehensive evaluation of wearable technologies in surgical training, highlighting their potential to improve performance metrics and support a range of educational uses for neurosurgical trainees. However, key challenges must be addressed to enable broader adoption and integration into surgical education.
authors: Honglin Zhu; James Booker; Sanchit Aapan; Udhay Cheema; Joachim Starup‐Hansen; Chan Hee Koh; Evangelos B. Mazomenos; Manish Kumar Tiwari; Hani Joseph Marcus

title: VERITAS AI: FAKE NEWS DETECTION USING NLP
abstract: Online misinformation is difficult to assess at scale because a label produced by a text classifier does not, by itself, explain why a claim should be trusted or rejected. This paper presents VERITAS AI, a capstone prototype designed around an evidence-centred workflow for claim analysis. The system accepts article text, a URL, or a directly entered claim; normalizes text; identifies and decomposes checkable claims; generates both supportive and skeptical search queries; retrieves candidate news, web, and fact-check results; and presents source metadata and uncertainty in a web interface. Inspection of the supplied Phase 1 code indicates that claim detection/decomposition, query generation, evidence normalization and deduplication, provider abstractions, API endpoints, and a React-based interface are implemented. The repository also explicitly reports demo mode by default and marks the machine-learning classifier as not configured. Consequently, this paper reports an implementation review and test-design evidence, not a completed accuracy comparison between TF-IDF and DistilBERT. The contribution is a transparent workflow that separates claim extraction and evidence retrieval from the final judgement, labels demo data, preserves partialfailure states, and avoids presenting unavailable model predictions as fact. Future work includes configuring live providers securely, completing evidence entailment assessment, training and evaluating the proposed classifiers, and conducting multilingual and user-centred validation.
authors: Mithilesh Meshram; Gyaneshwar Tiwari; Vishwajeet Sutar; Aditya Raut; Archana Bhosale
venue: International Journal of Engineering Applied Sciences and Technology

title: VeV: Video-Enhanced Vibration Data Augmentation For Structural Difference
abstract: Surface-mounted vibration sensing provides non-invasive structural monitoring with high temporal fidelity across diverse ubiquitous computing scenarios such as smart farms, yet structure-borne wave models remain fragile to physical relocation and structural shifts. However, addressing this spatial data discontinuity remains limited by costly manual recalibration, insufficient physical grounding in data-driven synthesis, and substantial sim-to-real gaps in numerical digital twins. To resolve this spatial bottleneck without labor-intensive data recollection, we propose VeV, a physics-consistent spatial augmentation framework that synthesizes vibration responses at unmeasured target coordinates from sparse reference observations by coupling a monocular Vision-Derived Propagation Possibility Map for structural wave-guiding paths with a Visual Feature Map for transient source kinetics and implicit material dynamics. Evaluated on a 1,237 sensor-hour sow pig and piglet farm across disparate structures, VeV reduces waveform reconstruction MSE by over 57.5% compared to data-driven baselines and achieves up to 81.69% zero-shot classification accuracy, while reaching peak performance within just 30-50 calibration chunks to effectively eliminate cold-start retraining overhead and establish a scalable foundation extending to human-centric floor vibration sensing and ambient intelligence.
authors: Joonhee Lee; Jiale Zhang; Sungmin Lee; Ruiqing Wang; Jeffrey D Shulkin; Yiwen Dong; Pei Zhang; Ko JeongGil

title: ViMG: a contactless deep learning framework for estimating sEMG amplitude envelopes from facial videos.
abstract: Traditional surface electromyography relies on contact electrodes that can restrict natural facial movements and cause discomfort. These limitations are particularly critical in cognitive and developmental research, where sensor placement can alter the very behavior being observed, especially in longitudinal monitoring. We present Video Myography (ViMG), an approach for the contactless estimation of window-averaged zygomaticus major sEMG envelope amplitude from facial video data. Rather than reconstructing the raw sEMG waveform, ViMG predicts a single scalar per 0.7-s video window, corresponding to the mean amplitude of the processed root-mean-square sEMG envelope over that window. Our method employs a hybrid 3D U-Net architecture integrated with a Long Short-Term Memory network intended to capture spatiotemporal dynamics of perioral facial movements. On a dataset of 23 subjects recorded in a controlled laboratory setting, we estimate window-averaged sEMG envelope amplitude over short temporal windows, achieving a mean Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.661 (range across the five folds: 0.536-0.872). A landmark-based baseline achieved comparable performance ( r = 0.670 ) , indicating that the recoverable signal is largely explained by coarse perioral kinematics and can be captured by substantially simpler models. Gradient-based saliency maps indicate that the model's predictions are informed by anatomically plausible perioral regions. While currently limited to controlled environments, this work establishes a proof-of-concept for contactless physiological assessment and a starting point for future contactless monitoring systems.
authors: Faraz A Nizamani; Mayur J Bhamborae; Sophie Bonnaire; Farah I Corona-Strauss; Daniel J Strauss

title: Vibe Interventions: Can Users Personalize and Iterate Their Way to Behavior Change?
abstract: Recent advances in large language models allow a working application to be generated from natural-language description, and is referred to as generative user interfaces. Their application to behavior change is unexplored, and we provide one of the first controlled investigations of it. We distinguish two components of authorship: iteration, the revision of a generated artifact in natural language, and personalization, the conditioning of generation on stated context. In a pre-registered between-subjects experiment (N = 300, 60 per condition), we crossed these two factors and added a static intervention as a control, yielding five conditions; participants stated a goal and received a generated intervention. The personalized generative condition ranked highest on every self-report outcome, including ownership, satisfaction, and intended adoption. Randomized iteration had no detectable effect, and higher revision counts were negatively associated with evaluative ratings. This work establishes which component of authorship carries motivational value in generative behavior change tools.
authors: Sally Ahmed; Ayse Alomar; Tawab Safi; Pattie Maes; Pat Pataranutaporn

title: WatchGuardian: Enabling User-Defined Personalized Just-in-Time Intervention on Smartwatch
abstract: While just-in-time interventions (JITIs) have effectively targeted common health behaviors, individuals often have unique needs to intervene in personal undesirable actions that can negatively affect physical, mental, and social well-being. We present WatchGuardian, a smartwatch-based JITI system that empowers users to define custom interventions for personal actions with few samples. To detect new actions from limited data, we developed a few-shot learning pipeline that fine-tuned a pre-trained inertial measurement unit (IMU) model on public hand-gesture datasets. We then designed a data augmentation and synthesis process to train additional classification layers for customization. Our offline evaluation with 26 participants showed that with three, five, and ten examples, our approach achieved an accuracy of 76.8%, 84.7%, and 87.7%, and an F1 score of 74.8%, 84.2%, and 87.3%. We then conducted a 4-hour intervention study to compare WatchGuardian against a rule-based intervention. Our results demonstrated that our system led to a significant reduction by 64.0 ± 22.6% in undesirable actions, substantially outperforming the baseline by 29.0%. Our findings underscore the effectiveness of a customizable, AI-driven JITI system for individuals in need of behavioral intervention in personal undesirable actions. We envision that our work can inspire broader applications of user-defined personalized intervention with advanced AI solutions.
authors: Ying Lei; Yancheng Cao; Will Ke Wang; Yuanzhe Dong; Changchang Yin; Weidan Cao; Ping Zhang; Jingzhe Yang; Bingsheng Yao; Yifan Peng; Chunhua Weng; Randy Patrick Auerbach; Lena Mamykina; Dakuo Wang; Yuntao Wang; Xuhai Xu
venue: ACM Transactions on Computing for Healthcare

title: Wearable Arrhythmia Detection: Moving from your Watch to your Shirt?
abstract: PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Digital devices play an increasingly important role in the detection and screening of cardiac arrhythmias. Atrial fibrillation (AF), the most common arrhythmia, is associated with an increased risk of stroke, heart failure, and mortality. This review summarises the current evidence on wearable devices for screening and diagnosing atrial fibrillation. RECENT FINDINGS: Numerous studies have demonstrated the value of wearables for AF detection and diagnosis. In addition, artificial intelligence enhances automated rhythm analysis and signal processing, supporting the increasing clinical implementation of digital technologies in outpatient care. Single-lead ECG devices provide the strongest evidence for AF detection, with smartwatches representing one of the most extensively investigated wearable technology. Limitations include motion artefacts and predominantly semi-continuous monitoring. Future research should focus on integrating artificial intelligence to improve signal analysis and artefact reduction, and on evaluating the impact of wearable-based strategies on clinically relevant outcomes, including stroke and heart failure.
authors: Janna-Luisa Beermann; David Duncker

title: Wearable Biosensors and Remote Patient Monitoring
abstract: The rapid advancement of wearable technologies and digital healthcare systems is transforming the delivery of modern medical care. Wearable Biosensors and Remote Patient Monitoring presents a comprehensive overview of emerging technologies, scientific principles, clinical applications, and future perspectives in continuous health monitoring. This edited book aims to bridge the gap between technological innovation and clinical practice by highlighting the growing importance of wearable biosensors in early disease detection, personalized healthcare, and remote patient management. The book brings together diverse topics, including wearable ECG and cardiac monitoring, continuous glucose monitoring, respiratory health assessment, neurological monitoring, flexible and skin-integrated sensors, and smart wearable devices. It also explores the role of artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning, the Internet of Medical Things (IoMT), and connected healthcare platforms in transforming physiological data into meaningful clinical insights. Particular attention is given to the applications of remote patient monitoring in cardiovascular diseases, diabetes, chronic respiratory conditions, geriatric care, and postoperative rehabilitation. Beyond technological developments, this volume critically examines important challenges associated with sensor accuracy, clinical validation, data security, patient privacy, regulatory requirements, and interoperability. By discussing current research gaps and emerging opportunities, the book encourages a deeper understanding of the scientific and practical considerations necessary for the successful integration of wearable technologies into healthcare systems. This edited volume is intended for healthcare professionals, researchers, academicians, students, biomedical engineers, and technology developers interested in digital health and biomedical innovation. It seeks to promote interdisciplinary collaboration and inspire further research into reliable, accessible, and patient-centred monitoring solutions. Ultimately, this book envisions a future in which continuous monitoring, intelligent data analysis, and timely clinical intervention contribute to more preventive, personalized, and efficient healthcare. We hope this volume serves as a valuable academic resource and encourages innovation toward a smarter and more connected healthcare environment.
authors: Syed Nazar Raza; Md Rehan Akhtar; Insha Khan

title: Wearable Device Feedback in Physical Education: A Narrative Review of Movement Load Monitoring, Motor Skill Learning and Student Engagement
abstract: Wearable devices are increasingly used in physical education (PE) to provide real-time feedback on movement load, but their role in supporting motor skill learning and student engagement remains insufficiently synthesized. This narrative review examines current evidence on wearable-device feedback in PE settings, focusing on three themes: movement load monitoring, motor skill learning, and student engagement. Studies published in recent years were identified through major databases and analysed thematically. The findings indicate that wearable-device feedback helps teachers quantify lesson intensity and adjust teaching loads, provides learners with immediate, task-relevant information that supports skill acquisition, and enhances engagement through goal setting, self-monitoring and gamified elements. However, the evidence base is limited by small samples, short intervention periods and inconsistent outcome measures, and effective use depends on teacher data literacy and alignment with pedagogical goals. The review concludes that wearable-device feedback is a promising but not self-executing tool: its value in PE depends on how feedback is designed, interpreted and integrated into instruction. Implications for teaching practice and directions for future research, including school-based intervention studies, are discussed.
authors: Xiaoqing Huang; Jun Lang

title: Wearable IoT Patient Monitoring with On-Device Fall Detection: A Review of Edge-AI Methods, Embedded Deployment, and Open Challenges
abstract: Falls are a leading cause of injury in older adults and in patients recovering from illness or surgery, and wearable monitors that recognize a fall at the point of sensing are an active research area. This review examines wearable Internet of Things (IoT) patient monitors that combine physiological sensing with on-device fall detection, using 40 peer-reviewed and preprint studies published between 2024 and 2026. The literature is organized around the architecture of edge-AI wearables, fall-detection and activity-recognition algorithms, embedded deployment via tiny machine learning (TinyML), physiological sensing, and the connectivity, privacy, and evaluation practices that surround them. Threshold, classical machine-learning, and deep-learning detectors report high offline accuracy, often above 95%, yet performance degrades in real-time use, under integer quantization, and during subject-independent validation. A smartwatch CNN-LSTM, for example, dropped from an F1-score of 87.6% offline to 70.2% in live tests. Few studies report latency, memory, energy, and false alarms per hour together, and most live validation involves young volunteers performing simulated falls. Low-cost optical sensors estimate pulse rate and oxygen saturation with small errors in controlled tests, although motion, skin tone, and sensor placement remain unresolved, and privacy-preserving designs such as lightweight encryption and federated learning are rarely tested on microcontrollers. The evidence is summarised in seven tables and seven figures, six research gaps are identified, and a five-level validation roadmap is proposed that moves from public datasets to long-term daily wear. The review provides a structured basis for researchers designing low-power, privacy-aware wearable monitors and for clinicians evaluating them.
authors: Salunkhe Anita Tanaji; S M. Kulkarni
venue: INTERANTIONAL JOURNAL OF SCIENTIFIC RESEARCH IN ENGINEERING AND MANAGEMENT

title: Wearable Technologies to Improve Physical Activity, Sedentary Breaks, Training, Sleep, and Safety: The ECSS‐Wearable Technologies Special Interest Group Calls for Interdisciplinary Collaboration
abstract: Wearable technologies ("wearables") are lightweight sensor-based devices that detect, analyze, and transmit physiological, biomechanical or environmental data, and are increasingly used across physical activity, sedentary behavior, athletic training, safety and sleep research. Applications include for example large-scale physical activity surveillance, ambulatory assessment, and real-time feedback during athletic training. Despite promising use cases such as heart rate variability-informed endurance training or gait retraining via biomechanical feedback, critical challenges remain. These include insufficient data quality, inadequately evaluated and inaccessible algorithms, limited interoperability between systems, difficulties translating sensor data into actionable insights, and insufficient wearable technology literacy among users. The Wearable Technologies Special Interest Group of the European College of Sport Science (ECSS-WT-SIG) identifies the need for interdisciplinary collaboration to address these challenges. Key priorities include developing regulatory frameworks, promoting standardized and open data infrastructure, improving wearable literacy of users, and conducting rigorous intervention studies under real-world conditions. The ECSS-WT-SIG calls on researchers, industry partners, NGOs, and other stakeholders to collectively advance the scientific and practical application of wearables in physical activity, sedentary behavior, training, sleep, and safety research.
authors: Peter Düking; Marco Giurgiu; Shona Leigh Halson; René Schilling; Billy Sperlich; Martina K. Kanning; Birte von Haaren‐Mack; Alexander Ferrauti; Tomáš Větrovský; Markus Reichert

title: Wearable activity-sequence measures and subsequent handgrip strength in adults aged 65 years and older: measurement characteristics and longitudinal associations
abstract: Background Temporal organization of everyday activity may provide information complementary to conventional movement-volume summaries. We examined the measurement properties of activity-state sequence descriptors and their longitudinal associations with handgrip strength. Methods We analyzed SHARE Wave 8 three-day thigh accelerometry and Wave 9 handgrip data. There were 490 participants aged at least 65 years with eligible sequences; follow-up grip was available for 410 and the negative-code-corrected, fully adjusted model included 391. Five activity states were coded in 5-second epochs. The original research workflow prioritized run-collapsed LZ76, while the H1–H3 conditional-entropy analysis was an exploratory evaluation whose final screening took place after initial outcome analyses. Daily-average ICC and correlation-based redundancy were distinguished from a new post hoc two-window evaluation of the identical nonlinear 72-hour scores among 407 participants with six valid days in the same wear episode; inference was limited to within-wear agreement. Participant-level analyses were replayed locally from the three licensed SHARE source archives. Results In corrected complete cases, the adjusted 72-hour H1–H3 coefficient was β = 0.535 kg/SD (95% CI -0.335 to 1.404; P = 0.228), with ΔR²=0.00067. The original historically prioritized run-collapsed LZ76 measure gave β = 0.906 kg/SD (95% CI 0.171 to 1.641; P = 0.016), ΔR²=0.00301; this age-restricted contrast is not an independent preregistered confirmatory test. Fifty repeated, strictly foldwise 10-fold validation analyses yielded mean ΔR²=-0.000341 and mean ΔRMSE = 0.0038 kg on adding H1–H3. Twenty-draw predictive-mean-matching sensitivity gave β = 0.471 kg/SD (95% CI -0.380 to 1.322; P = 0.278). In a post hoc within-wear paired-window analysis ( n = 407), the complete-72-hour H1–H3 had ICC(A,1) = 0.775 (participant-bootstrap 95% interval 0.723–0.822), and run-collapsed LZ76 had ICC(A,1) = 0.876 (0.848–0.898). Conclusions Activity-sequence descriptors differed in their relationships with conventional movement measures and later handgrip strength. Among participants with two complete 72-hour windows within one wear episode, H1–H3 and run-collapsed LZ76 showed absolute-agreement ICCs of 0.775 and 0.876, respectively. H1–H3 showed an imprecise handgrip association and no mean gain in repeated cross-validated prediction. These findings highlight the value of assessing temporal activity organization and its measurement properties alongside conventional activity summaries. Clinical trial registration Not applicable.
authors: Yifu Zhu

title: Wearable ear-EEG can record brain activity during auditory tasks in hyperacusis
abstract: Hyperacusis, characterized by physical discomfort from everyday sounds, lacks an objective measure, so clinicians rely on questionnaires and loudness discomfort levels, which give inconsistent diagnoses. Ear electroencephalography (ear-EEG) could fill this gap but, to our knowledge, is untested in hyperacusis. We recorded cEEGrid ear-EEG in 21 adults with hyperacusis and 13 controls during loudness, speech-in-noise, aversive-sound and visual fixation tasks. All participants completed the tasks, data quality was similar between groups, and most showed alpha peaks and stimulus-locked phase coherence. Onset power during speech in noise, the primary outcome, was higher in hyperacusis in every planned sensitivity analysis (Hedges’ $$g = 0.86$$ ) and absent in the visual task. Further analyses found no relation to hearing thresholds, but its source is not yet identified, because it spanned $$\theta $$ to , appeared before the sound and shrank when single epochs were down-weighted. Between-ear $$\delta $$ synchronization in this task was lower in hyperacusis and passed correction at ages 18–40 without hearing loss, although at this sample size none of 29 hypotheses from an exploratory analysis survived study-wide correction. Ear-EEG during auditory tasks is therefore feasible, and both effects are candidates for confirmatory testing, which for onset power needs 47–104 per group.
authors: Anarghya Das; Elizabeth Rivera Rosario; Yuanshan Zhong; Wei Bo; Alexander Gherardi; Wei Sun; Wenyao Xu

title: Wearable-based sleep and activity tracking detects Parkinson's disease and associated pathological hallmarks
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is associated with sleep and motor function impairment, even in the early stages. Here, we investigated whether passive wearable-based sleep and activity tracking can detect PD and its associated pathological hallmarks, dopaminergic deficit and α-synuclein pathology. Sleep and activity metrics (SAM) were derived from free-living wrist accelerometry data of a U.S. cohort and used to train a machine learning model (SAM-PD) to distinguish persons with PD (n = 133) from healthy controls (n = 26). The model achieved an AUROC of 0.93 and an AUPRC of 0.98, demonstrated excellent test-retest reliability, and generalized without retraining to an independent European cohort (n = 40; 50% PwPD) monitored with a different device (AUROC, 0.95; AUPRC, 0.95). REM sleep duration, walking cadence, and low-level acceleration features were most predictive. Applied to a U.S. at-risk cohort, SAM-PD performed comparably to the resource-intensive Movement Disorder Society (MDS) prodromal PD risk score in detecting dopaminergic deficit (AUROC, 0.86 vs. 0.80; AUPRC, 0.45 vs. 0.46; n = 121; 12.4% prevalence) and α-synuclein pathology (AUROC, 0.76 for both; AUPRC 0.50 vs. 0.42; n = 114; 16.7% prevalence). A combination with the MDS score modestly improved detection. Findings support further evaluation of wearable monitoring for PD screening and biomarker enrichment in larger populations.
authors: Apostolos Moustaklis; Ioannis Gerasimou; Charalampos Sotirakis; Paraskevi Chairta; Monica M. Kurtis; Natália do Campo; Tim Feige; Nils Schnalke; Maria-Luisa Almarcha Menargues; Kyriaki Michailidou; Kyproula Christodoulou; Margherita Fabbri; Björn H. Falkenburger; Leontios Hadjileontiadis; Stelios Hadjidimitriou

title: Wearable-derived sleep and circadian features associated with electronic health record-documented persistent postsurgical pain
abstract: A substantial percentage of surgical patients develop persistent postsurgical pain, and sleep disruption is an established, modifiable contributor. We examined temporal dynamics linking sleep and circadian rhythms to persistent postsurgical pain, using longitudinal Fitbit and electronic health record (EHR) data from the NIH All of Us Research Program to track sleep and circadian changes preceding EHR documentation of pain beyond expected surgical recovery. Patients later documented with persistent pain showed systematic shifts in wake timing and in heart rate circadian rhythms (elevated amplitude and mesor), with wake timing decoupled from heart rate circadian timing. These changes were absent in a comparison cohort without persistent pain documentation, indicating specificity to persistent postsurgical pain rather than a postoperative or clinical-encounter effect. Findings align with evidence linking altered sleep to pain outcomes and identify cardiac circadian disruption as a distinct marker, suggesting wearable-derived features could capture physiological changes before documentation and inform intervention.
authors: Ruby Kim; Julia M. Evanski; Tristin Smith; Daniel B. Forger; Chelsea M. Kaplan; Daniel Joseph Clauw; Daniel Whibley

title: When is travel-health AI inference transportable? Mobility-conditioned admissibility for cross-border disease risk and decision support
abstract: BACKGROUND: Artificial intelligence is increasingly used for infectious disease surveillance, traveller risk assessment, outbreak forecasting and decision support. Travel creates a distinctive transportability problem because people move between epidemiological, geographic, climatic and healthcare contexts in which the conditions supporting an inference may change rapidly. METHODS: This conceptual/theoretical methodological-development study was informed by a targeted narrative review of travel medicine, infectious disease surveillance, human mobility, border health, mass gatherings, antimicrobial resistance and health-AI validation literature. RESULTS: We develop a mobility-conditioned admissibility framework that treats travel as movement across origin, transit, destination and return regimes. Interpretation is conditioned on mobility state, epidemiological regime, exposure history, time-dependent constraints and clinical or biological constraints. Five proposed operational states are retained: supported inference, conditionally transportable inference, active monitoring, restricted interpretation and withholding. The framework also distinguishes low probability from infeasibility and requires preservation of rare but epidemiologically feasible events. CONCLUSIONS: Model availability and conventional predictive validity do not establish inferential transportability across changing travel contexts. Mobility-conditioned admissibility provides a complementary use-boundary layer for travel health AI by making cross-regime support explicit before outputs are interpreted or released. Its incremental value requires prospective evaluation against calibrated uncertainty, external validation and dataset-shift monitoring.
authors: Adegoke Olusegun Adefolalu

title: Wire-Level Interrupt-to-Decision Latency of On-Sensor MLC Versus Host Inference on the NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano: A Preregistered Measurement Study
abstract: The Machine Learning Core (MLC) embedded in the STMicroelectronics LSM6DSOX IMU is widely cited as a low-latency alternative to host-side inference, yet wire-level decision-delivery latency is rarely measured. Using a Saleae Logic Pro 8 logic analyzer on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano, we measured interrupt-to-decision latency (sensor INT1 edge to host decision GPIO) for three pipelines (a host-side decision-tree classifier, the standard MLC bank-switch read protocol, and an MLC binary-fast variant) under idle, I2C bus contention, and CPU stress. The protocol was pre-registered with 13 externally-timestamped Zenodo amendments before confirmatory data collection (4,770 of 4,860 trials included, 98.15%, across nine cells). The host pipeline exhibits lower median latency than the MLC pipeline under all conditions: 321.7 vs 681.5 us at idle (2.1x faster) and 574.5 vs 1,325.4 us under I2C contention (2.3x faster). The three-transaction I2C read protocol, not the silicon's classification, is the dominant latency contributor. We additionally characterize a reproducible 706.5 ms MLC decision cadence that bounds full stimulus-to-decision latency. Code, data, and pre-registration: github.com/akulswami/sensor-mlc-latency.
authors: Akul Swami; Dnyaneshwar Sonawane

title: Yearning to Be Our Younger Self: The Relationship Between Grief and Yearning to Internalized Ageism and Ableism
abstract: Internalized ageist and ableist beliefs significantly influence health outcomes, happiness, and longevity. Idealization of youth and pervasive ageist and ableist narratives devalue aging, contributing to perceptions of later life and potentially fostering grief over lost opportunities. To develop evidence-based interventions, it is essential to examine the potential relationship between grief, yearning, and fears about aging. A cross-sectional survey was conducted using ResearchMatch, and 384 individuals responded to questions regarding ageism, ableism, and experiences with grief. Yearning was significantly associated with internalized ageism, excessive fear of aging, and loss of physical health. Grief was significantly associated with age, internalized ageism, and excessive fear of aging. Interventions to address feelings of loss as we age, both experienced and anticipated, can be developed to address and improve personal attitudes toward growing older.
authors: Tracey L. Gendron; Kris Geerken

title: mmVibFlow: Gauging the Airflow of Air Conditioning Using mmWave Signal
abstract: Effective heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC) systems are increasingly vital for public health, safeguarding indoor air quality and occupant safety across residential, occupational, and educational settings. Accurate, real-time monitoring of airflow speed is essential for optimizing HVAC performance and ensuring healthy environments. However, existing solutions face significant limitations: traditional anemometers are intrusive and incur high deployment costs, acoustic methods raise severe privacy concerns and are highly susceptible to environmental noise, and contact-based vibration sensors struggle to isolate blade micro-vibrations from overwhelming chassis noise. Millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar emerges as a compelling alternative, offering non-contact, privacy-preserving, and noise-robust sensing. Furthermore, it significantly reduces the Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) by multiplexing existing smart building sensors for a zero-marginal-cost deployment. Yet, the core challenge of reliably distinguishing and extracting fan blade micro-vibrations from dominant structural vibrations using commodity mmWave radar in noisy HVAC environments remains largely unaddressed. Motivated by this gap and the potential of mmWave sensing, we propose mmVibFlow, a mmWave radar-based method for airflow speed estimation by capturing the micro-vibrations of fan blades. mmVibFlow identifies the operating gear (speed level) of an air conditioner and predicts real-time airflow speed from the machine’s vibrations. To effectively distinguish mechanical chassis vibrations from the target fan blade micro-vibrations, we develop an interference-resistant vibration sensing framework. This framework first utilizes beamforming to decorrelate vibrations from the blade region and the chassis, then employs phase-based subtraction to isolate the fan blade vibrations. To extract informative features for airflow speed estimation from RF signals, we develop a signal representation method that captures multi-domain frequency features at different airflow speeds. We validate mmVibFlow, achieving 99% accuracy in gear classification and a mean squared error (MSE) of 0.05 in airflow speed estimation when the radar is placed within 1.5 meters of the air conditioner outlet. Experimental results demonstrate that mmVibFlow accurately measures airflow speed in real-world environments.
