title: 3D Printing as a New Solution for Paper-Based Device Manufacturing: On-Demand Wax 3D Printing for Integrated Microfluidic Reagent Delivery, Sample Treatment, and Biosensing.
abstract: Since George Whitesides introduced the first paper-based device in the early 2000s, many scientists have faced challenges because wax printers are no longer produced. Although diverse strategies have been developed, there is still a need for cheap, scalable, and easy-to-use alternatives. Here, we introduce 3D printing of wax-based filaments as a direct, programmable strategy for fabricating microfluidic paper-based architectures and devices. Commercial wax filaments originally developed for investment casting and jewelry manufacturing were exploited owing to their low melting temperature, ultralow melt viscosity, and intrinsic hydrophobicity. Similarly to wax printing, here the wax filament is 3D-printed into the cellulose network, producing continuous through-thickness hydrophobic barriers and reliable fluid confinement. Using a low-cost commercial 3D printer, we established a library of customizable two- and three-dimensional architectures, including single-channel devices, multichannel configurations for fluid splitting and mixing, reaction networks, and miniaturized enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA)-like well arrays. The structures were evaluated for dimensional fidelity, barrier integrity, fluid transport, flow time, reproducibility, batch consistency, dimensional retention, scalability, and nozzle-dependent spatial resolution. As a proof of concept, an integrated multistep paper-based electrochemical biosensor was fabricated incorporating dry-stored duplex-specific nuclease, a methylene blue-labeled DNA probe, sequential reagent reconstitution, and downstream electrochemical detection for microRNA analysis. Control and interference experiments further supported the analytical response under the investigated conditions. This work demonstrates how digital additive manufacturing can extend microfluidic paper-based analytical devices (μPADs) beyond conventional patterning, providing a rapid, customizable, accessible, and scalable route toward multifunctional analytical devices for decentralized and point-of-care applications.
authors: Panagiota M Kalligosfyri; Luca Cimmino; Enrico Gallo; Yemin Guo; Ibrahim A Darwish; Sarah Alrubia; Stefano Cinti

title: 3D biomanufacturing in tissue engineering: From structural biomimicry to functional integration
abstract: Objectives Three-dimensional (3D) biomanufacturing has emerged as a cornerstone of tissue engineering by recreating physiologically relevant microenvironments. This review aims to integrate scaffold-free self-organization, scaffold-based biomimetic construction, and dynamic bioreactor culture into a unified framework and to chart the transition from structural biomimicry to functional integration. Methods An integrative literature review was performed across tissue engineering, biomaterials, bioengineering, and regenerative medicine. Representative studies were synthesized to compare scaffold-free, scaffold-based, and hybrid strategies; to clarify the distinction between multicellular spheroids and organoids; and to evaluate material-cell crosstalk, dynamic culture systems, and translational barriers. The reviewed technologies include spheroid and organoid models, natural, synthetic, and composite biomaterials, bioreactors, 4D printing, electroactive scaffolds, and organ-on-a-chip platforms. Results Scaffold-free systems preserve native cell-cell interactions but are limited by diffusion and scalability, whereas scaffold-based systems provide tunable mechanical and topographical cues through natural, synthetic, and composite biomaterials. Material properties regulate stem cell fate via YAP/TAZ mechanotransduction, and functional biomimicry is advanced by 4D printing, electroactive scaffolds, and stimuli-responsive materials. Integration with 3D bioprinting, microfluidics, and organ-on-a-chip platforms improves vascularization and intertissue communication. Bioreactors further enable scalable, physiologically relevant culture. Hybrid approaches that pair spheroids with scaffolds or bioreactors mitigate individual limitations and support macroscale tissue assembly. Key translational barriers remain vascularization, immune compatibility, GMP-compliant manufacturing, and standardization. Conclusions Hybrid systems that combine cellular self-organization with structural and dynamic cues offer the most promising route to functional tissue regeneration. A 5 to 10 year roadmap emphasizing vascularization, quality standardization, AI-driven process optimization, digital twins, and regulatory harmonization is proposed to accelerate clinical translation and personalized medicine.
authors: Jiameng Li; Yuxiang Wang; Xiaoru Weng; Yongjun Zheng; Shichu Xiao; Zhaofan Xia

title: 3D bioprinting as an in vitro tool to model the tumor microenvironment
abstract: Three‑dimensional (3D) bioprinting has rapidly emerged as a powerful strategy for engineering physiologically relevant tumor microenvironment (TME) models that overcome the limitations of traditional 2D cultures and animal systems. The TME is a highly dynamic and heterogeneous ecosystem composed of malignant, stromal, immune, and vascular cells embedded within a biochemically and mechanically complex extracellular matrix (ECM). These components collectively regulate tumor progression, immune evasion, metastasis, and therapeutic resistance. Conventional preclinical models fail to capture this complexity, contributing to poor clinical translation of oncology therapeutics. Advances in extrusion‑based, inkjet, laser‑assisted, and stereolithographic bioprinting now enable spatially organized, multicellular constructs with tunable biochemical and biophysical cues that more accurately recapitulate TME architecture and function. Complementary innovations in biomaterials, microfluidics, and computational modeling further expand the capabilities of bioprinted systems for drug screening, mechanistic studies, and personalized medicine. This review summarizes the cellular and acellular components of the TME, outlines major bioprinting technologies and biomaterial strategies, and highlights emerging applications in cancer modeling. We also identify key research gaps and opportunities that must be addressed to advance bioprinted TME platforms toward robust, standardized, and clinically meaningful tools for precision oncology.
authors: Zahra Mantaka; Ekaterina Shteinberg; Matthew Le Roux; Bahram Mirani; Stephanie Michelle Willerth

title: 3D-printed reconfigurable magnetic soft millirobots for intelligent digital microfluidics
abstract: Magnetic digital microfluidics (MDM) offers an attractive approach to miniaturised in vitro diagnostics, but most conventional platforms remain limited to predefined, planar droplet handling without the ability to rectify operation failures. Here, we present an intelligent MDM platform in which magnetic soft millirobots (MSMRs) function as reconfigurable robotic end-effectors for 3D droplet manipulation under closed-loop control based on 2D visual detection and height-dependent perspective correction. A magnetic pick-and-place mechanism exchanges a 3D-printed MSMR gripper and pipettor on demand. These MSMRs transport, merge, dispense, and split droplets, as well as collect and resuspend bacterial colonies in an oil-immersed workspace. The MSMR gripper captured 10–30 μL droplets with a success rate above 95%, and the MSMR pipettor dispensed 5.19 μL droplets with a coefficient of variation of 2.1%. Both tools retained their droplet-handling function after 10 000 reversible actuation cycles. The computer vision module enables real-time recognition and tracking, spatial calibration, operation verification, failure rectification, and result interpretation. With samples, reagents, and protocols preloaded, the platform autonomously completed the Carba NP assay for detecting carbapenemase-producing Enterobacteriaceae. These results establish MSMRs as a promising strategy for adaptive, failure-aware MDM platforms for diagnostic automation.
authors: Aiwu Zhou; Yuxuan Tang; Zhengnan Sun; Liang Zhou; Hanyu Yang; Qian Wang; Kang Li; Ciprian Iliescu; Xiaosheng Zhang; Yi Zhang

title: A Highly Efficient DLD Microfluidic Chip With Two‐Stage Inclined Elliptical Pillars for Particle Separation and Purification
abstract: Deterministic lateral displacement (DLD), a hydrodynamic particle manipulation technology, has been extensively studied for the development of fast and efficient microfluidic chips for particle manipulation and detection. However, particles are prone to clogging in DLD chips with closely spaced pillars, which can reduce sorting efficiency. Previous studies have shown that elliptical pillars provide better separation performance than equilateral triangular pillars. In elliptical-pillar DLD, a negative angle of inclination (Aoi) reduces the particle period and facilitates efficient isolation of large particles, whereas a positive Aoi decreases the critical diameter, thereby improving the sorting of smaller particles. On the basis of these findings, we designed a two-stage DLD microfluidic chip with inclined elliptical-pillar arrays, using an Aoi of -45° in the first stage and 45° in the second stage. The combination of negative and positive Aoi values enhanced the isolation of large particles, improved the purification of medium- and small-sized particles, and reduced the risk of clogging. This design provides a practical approach for improving the separation and purification performance of DLD devices and offers potential for efficient multi-size particle separation.
authors: Di Jiang; Yujiang Li; Jiawen Guo; Pengcheng Zhao; Bin Wu

title: A Modular Micro‐Chemostat System for High‐Throughput Continuous Cultivations
abstract: Improving the fidelity of computational eukaryotic models will require an enormous amount of high quality and reproducible data from biological experiments. In this study we present and demonstrate a modular 12‐channel micro‐chemostat system. This micro‐chemostat is designed for use by Genesis, a Robot Scientist developed to automate scientific research in yeast systems biology. We performed bioreactor characterization experiments to evaluate the performance of the micro‐chemostat system. We also cultivated the Saccharomyces cerevisiae reference strain, BY4741, at three different dilution rates (0.1, 0.2, and 0.3 h −1 ) and under two aeration conditions (microaerobic and aerobic), resulting in six different conditions. The bioreactor performance fulfilled our requirements, and enabled substrate‐limited continuous cultivation of yeast. Furthermore, the empirical results from the biological experiments were consistent with the literature, suggesting that results obtained from our system are comparable to those reported for other platforms in the field. Based on the evidence presented in this study, we conclude that the 12‐channel micro‐chemostat system is a suitable platform for yeast systems biology research. The modular design of the micro‐chemostat system enables future scaling to hundreds or thousands of concurrent chemostats and facilitates integration with autonomous agents for automated optimization and improvement of eukaryotic model systems.
authors: Erik Y. Bjurström; Filip Kronström; Ronald S. Reiserer; David K. Schaffer; Dmitry A. Markov; John P. Wikswo; Ross D. King; Ievgeniia Tiukova

title: A Portable Microfluidic Platform with Integrated Flexible Temperature Control and Real-Time Visualization
abstract: Many biochemical reactions performed in microfluidic systems, such as nucleic acid amplification and enzymatic assays, require precise, compact, portable, and programmable temperature control. However, existing platforms are often limited by high cost, bulkiness, and poor integration with real-time visualization. Here, we present a portable microfluidic platform that integrates a high-precision thermal regulation module with a smartphone-based imaging interface, enabling real-time sample monitoring under programmable temperature protocols. An STM32 microcontroller with a positional PID algorithm achieves a steady-state temperature accuracy of ±1.5 °C and adjustable heating and cooling rates of 0.1–5 °C/s, supporting both constant-temperature and thermal-cycling modes. As a representative application, we use this platform to evaluate the thermal stability of water-in-oil single-emulsion droplets under programmable heating. In this system, the oil phase was a mixture of silicone oil and RSN-749, and the mass ratio of the two components was varied to examine its effect on droplet stability. Our results suggest that, under the tested conditions, droplet coalescence tended to be more pronounced during temperature ramping than during isothermal holding. For this oil–surfactant formulation, the coalescence ratio remained below 4% across 20–95 °C. Therefore, this low-cost, user-friendly platform offers a practical analytical tool for temperature-controlled microfluidic reactions and thermal stability assessment, with potential for future point-of-care diagnostic workflows.
authors: Kailiang Zhang; Wei Xiang; Anbin Hu

title: A Single‐Capillary Open Microfluidic Probe for Robust and Versatile Spatial Multi‐Omics Using Ambient Mass Spectrometry Imaging
abstract: High‐resolution spatial mapping of tissue molecular architecture—from metabolites and lipid isomers to native proteins—remains a central challenge for ambient mass spectrometry imaging (MSI). Existing methods typically rely on multi‐capillary, alignment‐sensitive liquid‐extraction probes, compromising robustness and compatibility with structure‐resolved spatial omics. We mitigate this trade‐off by introducing a monolithic, knot‐shaped open microfluidic probe (Knot‐probe) fabricated from a single capillary. Knot‐probe achieves 40 µm scan‐direction spatial resolution and acquisition throughput up to 0.16 mm s −1 , yet can be fabricated in ∼30 min with standard laboratory tools and operated reliably for over one month. Without sacrificing conventional spatial lipidomics and metabolomics, Knot‐probe enables structure‐resolved spatial omics, delivering high‐resolution imaging of phosphatidylcholine sn ‐positional isomers via tandem MS and, in a pneumatically‐assisted variant, native MSI of proteins and proteoforms with higher throughput and enhanced sensitivity than with probes lacking pneumatic assistance. These capabilities arise from the integrated knot geometry, which ensures a stable micro‐liquid junction for localized extraction with a minimized sampling footprint and efficient mass transfer, while eliminating intricate probe alignment for robust operation. Readily integrated with standard electrospray ionization MS, Knot‐probe bridges conventional ambient MSI and emerging structural spatial omics, offering a broadly accessible approach across diverse biological and chemical applications.

title: A Staged Reaction Optimisation Workflow for Fragment-to-Lead Elaboration
abstract: Here, we present a reaction optimisation workflow that integrates data mining to generate unbiased, data-led starting points, high-throughput experimentation (HTE) to narrow the reaction parameter space, and closed-loop flow experiments guided by multi-objective Bayesian optimisation for fine-tuning. Designed for early-stage medicinal chemistry, particularly fragment-based drug discovery (FBDD), the workflow was demonstrated in two direct two-step syntheses of potent fragment-derived protein kinase C inhibitor precursors, involving sequential C–C and C–X bond formations. Quantum-mechanical (QM) reactivity prediction was used to inform route redesign improving synthetic efficiency and safety. HTE identified promising categorical starting points, which were subsequently refined within 20-40 autonomous continuous flow experiments per campaign, across 4 reaction steps. The workflow improved reaction yields in both syntheses while minimising simple E-factor and incorporating selectivity as an additional optimisation objective to facilitate downstream purification. An accelerated variant identified comparably productive conditions within a single working week, reducing substrate consumption by approximately 60%. This work demonstrates how staged, data-informed optimisation can accelerate material delivery in early-stage drug discovery while reducing experimental burden and providing valuable insights for subsequent process optimisation.
authors: Sebastian Soritz; Zhen Guo; Nicholas A. Jose; Rachel Grainger; Alexei A. Lapkin

title: A VERSATILE FLUIDIC DEVICE DESIGNED FOR CARTILAGE TISSUE-ENGINEERED PRODUCTS AND NATIVE CARTILAGE CULTURES
abstract: Introduction: Osteoarthritis is the most prevalent degenerative joint disease worldwide. However, no effective cure currently exists. Therefore, the development of more relevant in vitro models for modeling joint diseases is necessary for advancing new therapeutics. By taking advantage of the development of microfluidic technologies and cell/tissue models, combining both technologies appear as a promising route to better mimic joint. The versatility offered by fluidic based chip technologies enable the integration of tissue-engineered products (TEP) or native tissues into fluidic culture chambers disregarding their dimensions.Objectives: The objective of this study is to evaluate a 28-day culture in fluidic devices of native cartilage and cartilage TEP and specifically to assess the preservation of the extracellular matrix's integrity in native cartilage tissues and the chondrogenic potential of mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs) in TEP integrated into fluidic devices.Methods: The native cartilage was collected from knee arthroplasty of patients with advanced osteoarthritis. The TEP used are collagen sponges seeded with MSCs differentiated toward a chondrocyte-like phenotype by TGF-β1. The native tissue and TEP stimulated with TGF-β1 were maintained in fluidic devices in comparison with static cultures in well-plate. Both native cartilage and TEP were cultured for 28 days in fluidic devices made in polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS). The cell viability was monitored twice a week by conducting LDH assay. After four weeks, extracellular matrix components were characterized by histological and immunohistochemical techniques.Results: We developed a fluidic system that showed neither leakage nor contamination up to 28 days of culture. Cell viability of native cartilage is important during the 28-day culture and the extracellular matrix's integrity of native cartilage is maintained between the D0 and D28. Cell viability in TEP in fluidic devices is higher and more homogeneous during the time than TEP in static condition. The MSCs with chondrogenic induction in TEP cultured in fluidic device demonstrated a good extracellular matrix (ECM) synthesis with global collagens, collagen II, and proteoglycans. For TEP, global collagen synthesis was similar in cultures performed in fluidic devices and in well-plate cultures, but collagen II and proteoglycan synthesis remain more important in well-plate cultures than in fluidic devices at D28.Conclusion: Fluidic device seems to be an innovative tool to improve in vitro joint model. It should be interesting to evaluate the ECM synthesis and the phenotype’s stability after 56 days.Acknowledgments: This research has received financial support from the CNRS through the MITI interdisciplinary programs through its exploratory research program and was funded in part by the French National Research Agency (ANR) as part of the project ANR-25-CE19-7413-01”.
authors: Nicolas Potier; Christel Henrionnet; Laurent Grossin; Didier Mainard; Pierre Gillet; Laurent Galois; Halima Alem; Astrid Pinzano

title: A Water Compartment Cell Culture Lid Enables Stable Longitudinal Recording of Neuronal Networks In Vitro
abstract: Longitudinal electrophysiological recordings of neuronal networks are essential for studying network maturation, plasticity, and pharmacological responses. Yet, current microelectrode array (MEA) approaches are limited by evaporation-induced drift in culture conditions, exacerbated by heat dissipation from active recording electronics on CMOS-based high-density MEAs. We present a cell culture lid featuring a water compartment at its interface that eliminates evaporation whilst maintaining gas exchange. Combined with a custom incubator that uses independent temperature control of the MEA to prevent condensation, the system enables stable, uninterrupted recordings for weeks. We show that perturbations in firing rate and functional connectivity following medium exchange are significantly reduced by suppressing evaporation. We demonstrate continuous 35-day recordings of patterned human iPSC-derived neuronal networks with a single half-medium exchange, revealing multiple spatiotemporal firing patterns that are held concurrently and evolve over weeks. All design files are provided, enabling adoption across culturing platforms for longitudinal studies of development within individual cultures, and establishing the conditions required for studies of plasticity and chronic pharmacology.
authors: Benedikt Maurer; Fabio Fischer; Giulia Amos; Vaiva Vasiliauskaitė; János Vörös

title: A critical review of microfluidic dielectrophoresis technology in microparticle separation chips
abstract: In recent years, dielectrophoresis (DEP) technology based on microfluidic chips has become a key method for the efficient manipulation of particles, owing to its advantages of being non-contact, highly precise and highly controllable. This paper reviews the latest advancements, fundamental principles, mixing mechanisms, application fields, and future challenges associated with DEP particle separation technology. It provides a detailed overview of the structural design, separation efficiency, voltage, frequency and other parameters of electrode-based and insulator-based DEP, and discusses the challenges currently facing this technology. Furthermore, the paper proposes a novel classification scheme for synergistic strategies combining DEP with other separation mechanisms. These are categorized into sequential separation, synergistic separation, and multi-stage separation, with a discussion of the respective advantages and limitations of each approach. Finally, the paper summarizes recent progress in the application of DEP particle separation across fields such as biological cell identification, environmental particle monitoring, and chemical particle analysis. It concludes by outlining future directions for the development of DEP and hybrid separation technologies, thereby offering theoretical and technical references for achieving high-precision, high-throughput, and multifunctional capabilities within the field of microfluidic separation.
authors: Yu Liu; Wenbo Han; Haoyu Yue; Xinran Wang; Siqi Zhang; Guo Wenxuan; Xiaotong Mu; Wei Li; H.O.N.G.P.E.N.G. Zhang

title: A hybrid CoordAttention model with focal loss for handling visual similarity in gastrointestinal endoscopic images
abstract: Gastrointestinal (GI) diseases represent a major global health challenge that requires timely and accurate diagnosis for effective treatment. Deep learning has shown promise in endoscopic image analysis. However, challenges such as class imbalance and visual similarity among classes degrade the prediction performance. This study proposes a hybrid deep learning framework that combines ResNet50 and VGG16 architectures with the Coordinate Attention (CoordAttention) mechanism to enhance feature representation and improve classification accuracy. Both architectures were individually optimized with CoordAttention before concatenating them into a feature-level hybrid model, which was further refined using focal loss to address class imbalance. Experiments on the 22-class GastroVision dataset showed that the proposed hybrid with CoordAttention achieved higher scores than the baseline and the compared state-of-the-art models, with a macro F1-score of 0.718, a micro F1-score of 0.897, and a Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) of 0.886. The hybrid model without CoordAttention obtained a macro F1-score of 0.657, a micro F1-score of 0.835, and an MCC of 0.816 with the focal loss function. Focal Loss mitigates the effects of class imbalance by emphasizing difficult and underrepresented samples. The proposed approach did not apply any synthetic technique to handle imbalance, which may make it applicable to datasets with different class distributions. Although standard data augmentation was applied uniformly to improve the diversity of datasets, no specific class-balancing strategy was used to artificially balance class distributions. These findings suggest that the proposed framework is a useful approach for jointly addressing class imbalance and visual similarity in GI endoscopy image classification.
authors: Saba Akram; Bushra Zafar; Muhammad Kashif Hanif; Muhammad Murad Khan

title: A microfluidic mother machine for high-throughput single-cell analysis of human leukemia T cells
abstract: We present a mother machine-like microfluidic device tailored for high-throughput, long-term tracking of non-adherent T-cell proliferation via live-cell microscopy. Our platform consists of an array of microchannels whose geometry was optimized through computational fluid dynamics simulations, facilitating single-cell capture and ensuring a continuous nutrient supply, enabling cell proliferation over multiple generations under controlled growth conditions. We demonstrate the device efficacy by characterizing the growth dynamics of human leukemia T-cells. Specifically, our findings reveal that these cells undergo slightly asymmetric volume division, employing a sizer-like strategy to compensate for stochastic fluctuations in cell size.
authors: Simone Scalise; Giovanna Peruzzi; Davide Caprini; Giorgio Gosti; Giancarlo Ruocco; Mattia Miotto

title: A novel liquid mixing injection process control method incorporating both continuous and high-frequency modes
authors: Pengcheng Gao; Kun Ren; Chentao Ke; Jian Chen; 方涛; 良茗; Shiwen Yi; Jiaomei Luo; Jiabo Cheng; Qiqi Shen

title: A practical guide to vascularized microphysiological systems
abstract: Microphysiological systems (MPS) are emerging as human-relevant models for pharmaceutical research, reducing reliance on animal testing. Despite progress in reproducing organ-specific features, integrating functional microvasculature remains challenging. Advances have expanded the number of available options, making it difficult to identify the most suitable one for a specific MPS. Here, we provide a guide to designing vascularized MPS by comparing current vascularization strategies according to key design drivers, including the microfluidic platform, organotypic vascular architecture, matrix properties, and coculture with perivascular cells. We highlight trade-offs between biological fidelity, engineering control, and translational needs, while considering approaches widely adopted in commercial MPS. Finally, we discuss how close the field is to delivering physiologically accurate vascularized MPS and how emerging omics technologies may redefine vascular identity and functionality.
authors: Alice Salvadori; Mina Petrovic; Laia Gifre-Renom; Aleksandr Ovsianikov

title: A reinforcement learning framework for goal-directed stimulation of engineered neuronal networks
abstract: Systematically perturbing neuronal circuits under controlled conditions offers a promising route to understanding how they encode and process information, yet remains methodologically demanding. In vitro neuronal networks can be cultured on microelectrode arrays (MEAs) that allow stimulation and recording, and microfluidic patterning can constrain network topology to yield stable stimulation-evoked responses. Yet, the space of possible spatiotemporal stimulation patterns remains too large for exhaustive exploration. Additionally, the evoked responses depend on prior stimulation history. Here, we present an open-source framework that sustains closed-loop reinforcement-learning (RL) control of engineered neuronal networks, sending electrical stimuli to the MEA and evaluating the evoked responses to identify stimulation patterns that drive specific target activity motifs. We extend inkube, a low-cost, open-source electrophysiology system from off-the-shelf components, with closed-loop electrophysiology. This enables reliable delivery of stimulation at single-sample precision with millisecond-range round-trip times. It also allows independent RL agents to control multiple networks simultaneously. As a proof-of-principle application, we benchmarked different agents on the task of identifying stimulation patterns that maximise the length of clockwise-circular firing sequences. We first demonstrated that stimulation-evoked responses in engineered recurrent networks were stable and separable across the action space over hours of continuous operation. We characterised the dependency of responses on prior stimulation history, finding state dependence in a subset of stimulus pairs. The agents learned to improve reward during training with respect to random stimulation. Agents converged on non-trivial stimulation patterns that span the full action space rather than mirroring the target motif. All hardware designs and software are publicly available, providing an accessible platform for goal-directed functional characterisation of engineered neuronal networks at single-spike resolution.
authors: Benedikt Maurer; Vaiva Vasiliauskaitė; Julian Hengsteler; Gino Cathomen; Tobias Ruff; Cédric Schmid; János Vörös; Stephan J. Ihle

title: A stopping rule for completing computed phase diagrams with generative models
abstract: Phase diagrams constructed using known phases misjudge stability when key phases are missing. Generative models supply as many structures as needed, but how many structures to generate and which diagrams will change are unknown. We add 10,000 MatterGen structures per system, relaxed with a machine learning interatomic potential, to Materials Project (MP) data for six Li–transition-metal–O ternaries and track the hull convergence. The responses fall into two groups: Li–Ru–O, Li–Hf–O, and Li–Zr–O (70–107 MP structures) gain 4–9 stable candidates and exhibit total convex-hull shifts of 59.9–62.9 meV/atom, whereas Li–Mn–O, Li–Co–O, and Li–Ni–O (240–609) exhibit a minimal hull shift. When reduced to 70 MP structures, the latter gain a similar number of stable candidates by rediscovering removed hull phases. The hulls converge within 5,000–8,000 structures. After generating 8,000 structures, a stopping rule, tested using Li–Ir–O, decides whether more are needed. Density functional theory places seven Li–Ru–O compositions 5–83 meV/atom below the MP-only hull but rejects the potential’s false positives in well-explored systems. This gives a stopping rule and early diagnostic for incomplete phase diagrams.
authors: Seungbae Kim; Juo Kim; 박재휘; Yerim Jung; Kyoungmin Min

title: AI Agents as supporting infrastructure for all-solid-state battery development
abstract: Materials discovery increasingly depends on a multiscale ecosystem of simulations, experiments, and shared facilities, yet advances in individual AI tools do not by themselves connect the decisions that link these components. This gap is especially severe in all-solid-state batteries (ASSBs), whose development couples electrochemical performance to interfacial stability, mechanics, processing, manufacturability, reliability, safety, and cost. Here we argue that AI agents could support ASSB development toward commercial viability by maintaining a shared decision–evidence state that links materials discovery and optimization to cell-level validation and manufacturing constraints. We develop this argument through three complementary dimensions of scientific agency: coordination across heterogeneous resources, method augmentation across models and scales, and project-level adaptation over time. Cross-domain demonstrations establish several relevant capability primitives, including stateful tool planning, task execution, and delegated analysis. Agents should therefore be evaluated as supporting infrastructure for concurrent ASSB engineering rather than as autonomous replacements for scientific expertise. Their value ultimately lies in driving materials development in the context of interfaces, cell architectures, and manufacturing processes toward the performance, reliability, safety, and cost requirements of ASSB commercialization. context & scale Commercializing all-solid-state batteries (ASSBs) requires more than identifying high-performing materials: ion transport, interphase chemistry, mechanics, processing, cell architecture, reliability, safety, and cost impose coupled constraints that can invalidate otherwise promising candidates. This Perspective argues that AI agents could serve as auditable infrastructure, maintaining a decision-evidence state that connects objectives, specimen histories, models, uncertainties, actions, and validation to support ASSB development. Such infrastructure could broaden research across instruments and engineering stages, strengthen validation by linking atomistic, mesoscale, continuum, and experimental descriptions, and preserve evidence and revisions throughout development cycles. Future efforts should move beyond task-level demonstrations toward systematic ASSB development, establishing whether agents can contribute to the development of reliable and economically viable ASSB systems.
authors: Chu-Liang Fu; Xuewen Ning; Yanzi Shi; Feilong Wang; Xiang Zhao; Fucheng Ren; Weihan Li; Jiamin Fu; Xiaona Li; Jianwen Liang; Huanli Sun; Xueliang Sun; Shuo Wang

title: AI for Biologists: The Knowledge Boundaries of Foundation Models in the Age of Agentic Systems
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing how biological research is done. Biological foundation models trained on millions of nucleotides, protein, and single-cell measurements predict protein structures, mutation effects, and cellular responses to genetic perturbations. Agentic systems, AI assistants built on large language models, can run multistep analyses from plain-language requests and increasingly call foundation models as tools. Yet it is often unclear when these models' outputs can be trusted. We frame this as a model's knowledge boundary: the range of inputs, tasks, and conditions over which its outputs are reliable. This review explains how foundation models are built and proposes that five design elements (data, architecture, training scheme, evaluation scheme, and post-analysis) define this boundary. We examine evidence on where current models succeed or fail and present standardized descriptions of model limits so that researchers, and the agents acting for them, can use these tools reliably.
authors: Tian Cai; Andrew Kleist; Jaimin Patel; Duccio Malinverni; Alexander K. Taylor; Malvika Sharan; Renato Umeton; M. Madan Babu

title: AI for Science in Space: Orbital Laboratories, Planetary Fieldwork, and Embodied Autonomy
abstract: Artificial intelligence for science (AI4S) is extending from interpretation of existing data to the design and execution of experiments. Space offers distinctive scientific opportunities while restricting physical support. Microgravity and extraterrestrial environments expose phenomena that terrestrial experiments cannot fully reproduce; finite samples, constrained resources, and limited opportunities for intervention complicate sustained investigation. This critical review examines orbital laboratories and planetary in situ science across biology, materials, fluid and thermal physics, and adaptive exploration. We distinguish learning from space-derived data, selecting scientific actions, executing them, and preserving experimental validity. Terrestrial self-driving laboratories provide complementary evidence on optimization, dedicated automation, robotic manipulation, and the support needed for unattended operation. The synthesis connects scientific gains already demonstrated by bounded AI systems to gaps in observation, executable actions, and continuity of valid evidence. Space robots can expand the attainable scope of autonomous science when necessary interventions exceed validated instrument capabilities and timely human support is unavailable. Their value must be established against dedicated mechanisms, redundancy, and human-supported operation. We develop a framework connecting sample history, scientific decisions, physical execution, and claim-specific validity. A worked orbital design, a planetary extension, and matched evaluation schemes separate the contributions of sensing, decision policies, and physical actions. The resulting agenda measures autonomy through valid scientific return, task coverage, intervention costs, and evidence integrity across complete campaigns.
authors: Zizhe Wang; Jia Deng; Xin Lü; Zehao Jia; Yi Huang; Yao ZHU; Jianing Li

title: AI in neuro-oncology: An overarching review
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being applied across neuro-oncology domains to analyze complex, high-dimensional, multimodal data. Despite major advances in the biological understanding and classification of CNS tumors, clinical outcomes for many of them remain poor, reflecting intra- and inter-tumor heterogeneity and limitations of conventional reductionist approaches. AI offers a paradigm shift to capture this heterogeneity and provide quantitative, reproducible diagnostic, predictive, and prognostic insights. This article describes a joint effort across the Response Assessment in Neuro-Oncology (RANO) working groups to provide an overarching review of the AI use across six key domains of neuro-oncology: neuroimaging, neuropathology, laboratory medicine, neurosurgery, drug discovery, and clinical trials. Applications closest to clinical use include imaging segmentation and quantification, AI-assisted image reconstruction, DNA methylation-based classification, and workflow optimization. Radiogenomics, WSI-based molecular prediction, AI-guided surgical targeting, liquid biopsy interpretation, AI-guided drug discovery, digital twins, and in silico trials remain promising but require stronger prospective validation. Key challenges include limited availability of large diverse datasets, variability in data acquisition and reference standards, and limited external validation. This review provides a unifying framework for understanding the role of AI across neuro-oncology and highlights key considerations for its responsible implementation, emphasizing standardization, reproducibility, multi-institutional validation, and human oversight.
authors: Carla Pitarch-Abaigar; Philipp Lohmann; Patrick Aloy; Fátima Al‐Shahrour; Omar Arnaout; Wenya Linda Bi; Norbert Galldiks; Jason T. Huse; Philipp Karschnia; MacLean P. Nasrallah; Areeba Patel; Rifaquat Rahman; Felix Sahm; Timothy R Smith; Joerg-Christian Tonn; Renato Umeton; Manuel Valiente; Mark Zarella; Raymond Y. Huang; Spyridon Bakas

title: AI-Driven Approaches in Pyridine-Based Drug Discovery: Implementation, Challenges and Future Perspectives
abstract: Pyridine is a heterocyclic scaffolds in medicinal chemistry and serves as a key structural component in many approved drugs used to treat cancer, viral infections, bacterial diseases, inflammatory disorders, and neurological conditions. Owing to its biological activities, pyridine continues to attract significant attention in drug discovery research. However, approaches for the identification and optimisation of pyridine-based drug candidates are often labour-intensive, time-consuming, and costly. In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a tool capable of transforming the drug development process by accelerating the discovery of novel agents and improving decision-making throughout stages of research. This chapter explores the role of AI technologies, including machine learning, deep learning, and generative models, in the discovery and development of pyridine-based therapeutics. Particular emphasis is placed on AI-assisted virtual screening, quantitative structure–activity relationship (QSAR) modelling, molecular property prediction, de novo molecular design, and ADMET evaluation. The integration of AI with computational techniques such as molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations, and network-based analyses has enhanced the identification of pyridine derivatives with improved biological activity and safety profiles. Additionally, applications and success stories demonstrating the practical implementation of AI in pyridine drug discovery are highlighted. The chapter further discusses limitations, including challenges related to data quality, model transparency, and experimental validation. Finally, developments such as explainable AI, foundation models, autonomous laboratories, and personalised medicine are examined as opportunities for advancing pyridine-based drug discovery. these advances underscore the potential of AI to reshape the development of pyridine-derived therapeutics and facilitate the discovery of safer, more effective medicines.
authors: Pratima Katiyar; Kalpana Kushwaha; Suprabha Nishad

title: AI-driven entropy analysis of Sutterby tetra-hybrid nanofluid energy conversion for electromagnetic peristaltic flow
abstract: Predicting nano-blood transport in electromagnetically actuated peristaltic microchannels requires solving coupled nonlinear equations for momentum, energy, mass, and microorganism conservation a computationally expensive task when Hall and ion-slip effects, thermal radiation, viscous dissipation, entropy generation, and Sutterby non-Newtonian rheology are all included, limiting real-time clinical use. This study addresses that bottleneck by developing a Levenberg-Marquardt optimized artificial neural network (ANN-LM) trained on 2,400 high-fidelity datasets generated from the governing Multiphysics equations, to predict velocity, temperature, concentration, and microorganism distributions for a Sutterby tetra-hybrid nanofluid. The ANN-LM achieves mean absolute errors below 0.3% and correlation coefficients near unity across all fields, while reducing computational cost by more than two orders of magnitude relative to direct numerical solution. By coupling deep learning with electromagnetic-rheological-bioconvective modeling for the first time in this configuration, the framework enables millisecond-scale parametric exploration and inverse design previously infeasible with conventional solvers offering a practical route toward real-time, patient-specific control in magnetically guided drug delivery, cardiovascular interventions, and microfluidic diagnostic platforms.
authors: Nahid Fatima; Nouman Ijaz; Ahmed Zeeshan; Abdinn Albadri; Yamen El Touati; Kamal Barghout; Nidal Abu-Libdeh; Imran Ejaz

title: AI‐Guided Intrinsic and Extrinsic Photocorrosion Inhibition of III–V Semiconductors for Durable Photoelectrochemical Water Splitting
abstract: Group III–V semiconductors are suitable for solar‐driven hydrogen production due to precise lattice matching (for tandem device combinations), high carrier mobilities (>10 3 cm 2 V –1 s –1 ), tunable bandgaps (1.1–2.5 eV), strong absorption coefficients (>10 5 cm –1 ), and a large range of doping possibilities. GaInP 2 , GaAs, and InP have a theoretical solar‐to‐hydrogen efficiency of more than 20%. Still, their high susceptibility to chemical and photochemical corrosion during prolonged photoelectrochemical water splitting (PEC‐WS) is a major industrial hurdle. This review comprehensively covers critical strategies to enhance the photostability of group III–V semiconductors for industrial‐scale PEC‐WS, emphasizing artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) support. We discuss three main intrinsic and extrinsic strategies that include (i) AI‐driven crystal structure modification and faceted growth control, (ii) physical and chemical surface passivation coupled with machine learning for passivation material screening strategies, and (iii) combining III–V semiconductors with appropriate band‐aligned materials via preferable heterojunctions, utilizing algorithms to select optimal compositions. We examine the underlying mechanisms of each strategy and conclude with perspectives on achieving optimal materials for PEC‐WS using advanced AI and ML screening tools. Implementing these effective modification strategies, the wide commercial potential of III–V photoelectrodes for PEC‐WS technology can be unlocked.
authors: Nafeesa Sarfraz; Ibrahim Khan; Muhammad Ibrar Ahmed; Muhammad Nawaz Tahir; Ajayan Vinu; Sanghyuk Wooh

title: ART of PIV: Agentic Real-Time Particle Image Velocimetry for Active Flow Control
abstract: Particle image velocimetry (PIV) measures fluid motion from images of tracer particles, but its accuracy depends on choices throughout the estimation pipeline, including image preprocessing, flow estimation, and postprocessing. These choices are typically left to expert tuning, and a fixed configuration can become less accurate as conditions change. This matters especially when PIV supplies feedback for real-time control, where measurements must be both accurate and fast, and flow conditions vary. We introduce ART of PIV -- short for Agentic Real-Time and also a nod to the art of tuning a PIV pipeline -- which automates pipeline choice for each image pair. A learned agent selects a configuration according to a chosen measurement objective from a library assembled for a specified speed budget. Across cross-correlation, classical optical-flow, and learning-based estimators, ART of PIV reduces average end-point error (AEPE) by 12.2-22.4 % relative to the best single estimator at matched speed, with gains extending to 1000-4000 image pair/s. In a simulated local velocity regulation task, it reduces mean normalized closed-loop cost by 13.24-13.59 percentage points relative to a tuned fixed estimator, with the same classical controller in both cases. In a tabletop water channel, we illustrate two ways to tune ART of PIV for a fluidic pinball of three rotating cylinders: selecting between complementary optical-flow tunings for accuracy, and selecting regions of interest with coherent rotation or shear using a common flow estimator. For the first variant, we train a DreamerV3 reinforcement learning controller directly in the physical world and demonstrate tracking of a prescribed flow field in the wake of a fluidic pinball.
authors: Antonio Terpin; Francesco Banelli; Alan Bonomi; Raffaello D’Andrea

title: ARTGEL: A temperature-regulated gel electrophoresis platform for quantitative studies of reversible association
abstract: Here we present ARTGEL, an actively regulated-temperature gel electrophoresis platform designed for quantitative studies of temperature-sensitive reversible biomolecular association. Existing literature describes electrophoretic mobility shift assays in which biomolecular reactions are suppressed during electrophoresis through dilution, the use of competitors, or reduced temperature. These approaches can alter temperature-sensitive equilibria and may cause the gel to report a state different from that of the original bulk solution. Rather than attempting to quench reactions, ARTGEL enables electrophoresis to be performed at the same temperature as complementary bulk measurements, allowing reversible association to be quantified directly in the gel and compared with matched measurements in solution. The ARTGEL platform integrates feedback-controlled thermoelectric regulation of gel temperature, a large, heated, and continuously circulated buffer reservoir to help maintain ionic strength, and automated electrode-wiping to mitigate electrode fouling and maintain stable electrophoresis current during long-duration electrophoresis. During electrophoresis, ARTGEL maintained the gel temperature at 30°C setpoint with a temporal variation of 0.03°C and a spatial range of 0.6°C. With periodic automated electrode wiping, the electrophoresis current remained at 139.5 ± 2.5 mA during the 24-h experiment. Using DNA origami assemblies, we further show that ARTGEL preserves distinct temperature-dependent association states, resolves reaction-dependent distortions of migrating bands, and supports extraction of in-gel kinetic and thermodynamic parameters from reaction–diffusion–advection modeling.
authors: Rupam Saha; Seth Fraden

title: ASPIRE improves protein binder prioritization through cross-target priors and sparse preference feedback
abstract: Generative protein design supplies vast candidate libraries, but experimental throughput and sparse feedback constrain binder discovery. We introduce Active Selection with Prior-Informed Ranking for Experiments (ASPIRE), which learns transferable target-conditioned priors from within-assay pairwise preferences and adapts through lightweight Bayesian updates. Cold-start selection achieves 12.7–25.0-fold top-1% enrichment across interaction benchmarks. Combining prior initialization with preference updating reaches the top 0.0355% of the held-out 149,361-variant GB1 landscape within 12 simulated measurements. In VISTA peptide discovery, cold-start selection identifies three binders among four tested candidates. Historical-feedback adaptation promotes a 10.2 µM lead into the four-peptide selection, improving the best measured affinity 2.19-fold over cold start. ASPIRE integrates transferable experimental knowledge and small-batch feedback into a practical framework for discovering stronger binders with limited experiments.
authors: M Ingjun Chen; Liping Huang; Yuxue Guo; Yue Peng; Yihui Yang; Yuhong Li; Wen Li; Zhonghua Liu; Gang Logan Liu; Wenjun Hu

title: Accelerating Iterative Data-Driven Hotspot Protein Engineering Using Annealed Oligos and Cell-Free Expression
abstract: Protein engineering increasingly leverages data-driven strategies to navigate complex fitness landscapes, but conventional high-throughput screening workflows mainly capture sequence-function data for only high-performing variants, producing limited datasets for learning. Recent approaches retaining full sequence-function information frequently rely on laborious cell-based cloning and expression or broad sequencing, which slows iterative design. This problem has been partly addressed through the rapid cell-free assembly and expression of predefined variants from gene fragments. However, gene fragments present limitations for hotspot engineering, where their size can prevent closely spaced mutations from being independently swapped, and the limited quantities typically supplied do not readily support multiple screening rounds. We extend this approach to hotspot engineering using short (∼20−40 bp) annealed oligo fragments to rapidly screen predefined variants in <9 h while preserving complete sequence-function data. Bulk-prepared oligos provide sufficient material for repeated screening rounds without cloning or amplification. Their small size also facilitates the independent swapping of hotspot mutations. This workflow is validated by screening 3 to 10 fragment assemblies for two proteins. Its utility for high-iteration protein engineering is demonstrated with an additive model-guided screening campaign, which identified variants with >100% increase in fitness.
authors: Ryan Godin; Sepehr Hejazi; Bret Lange; Basmala Aldamak; Nigel Forest Reuel

title: Acceleration of Materials Insertion in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: How the Materials Genome Initiative Got Us Here, and Where Does the Field Go Now?
abstract: While concepts around applying artificial intelligence to materials R&D have become commonplace, the road to this ubiquity has been decidedly uneven. Here we explore this evolution from the foundational ideas captured in the Materials Genome Initiative to the implications of autonomous laboratories (self-driving laboratories, SDLs) for the research enterprise. Realizing the promise of SDLs will also require a long, ongoing conversation about standards, as the interoperability of research tools is central to successful SDL implementation. Standards development can take years, and the incentives are often diffuse at best. However, the advent of large language models (LLMs) and associated tools may help to overcome the barriers to interoperability.
authors: James A. Warren

title: Accounts on Synthetic Cells
abstract: Frontiers of Life is a research network of the University of Bordeaux focused on the re-engineering of living systems, starting from the construction of a synthetic cell. In this article, we present our motivation to build a cell from scratch and the elementary building blocks we worked on over the past four years. While the final objective regarding the construction of a synthetic cell remains a long-term target, the reconstruction of living cells provides both a methodology and experimental approaches to improve our understanding of living systems with potential to become the next generation of biotechnologies.

title: Acoustic emission-based monitoring for size-controlled robotic powder grinding
abstract: Controlling particle size is essential in solid-state synthesis, yet powder grinding remains a critical and largely unresolved challenge in self-driving laboratories. Here, we present a robotic mortar-based grinding system integrated with structure-borne acoustic emission (AE) sensing for autonomous powder processing. By measuring high-frequency elastic waves transmitted through the mortar, the proposed approach enables robust AE acquisition in standard laboratory environments without specialized acoustic facilities and provides a practical basis for particle-size-dependent feedback and autonomous stopping. We model AE-derived total spectral power as a monotonic function of particle size using monotone Bernstein polynomial regression, enabling size-dependent threshold design for grinding termination. Using this threshold-based stopping strategy, autonomous grinding experiments on NaCl and citric acid demonstrate reliable size-controlled processing. In contrast, monosodium glutamate exhibits degraded threshold reliability at intermediate target sizes, where AE fluctuations approach the noise floor. These results reveal material-dependent regimes in which AE-based feedback is effective only when sufficient signal-to-noise ratio is maintained, thereby clarifying the intrinsic limitations of AE-driven autonomous powder processing in solid-state self-driving laboratories.
authors: Yusaku Nakajima; Ryusei Takamoto; Yasuo Takeichi; Kanta Ono

title: Acute loss of PLIN5 in brown adipocytes reveals its indispensable role in maintaining mitochondrial function and cold tolerance.
abstract: Cold exposure induces adaptive molecular and mitochondrial remodeling in brown adipose tissue (BAT) of mice to sustain thermogenesis. We previously showed that the lipid droplet protein Perilipin 5 (PLIN5) is strongly induced in BAT by cold exposure and promotes thermogenic gene expression, mitochondrial remodeling, and uncoupled respiration. However, constitutive BAT-specific PLIN5 deletion impaired mitochondrial function without causing cold intolerance, suggesting physiological compensation, likely via induction of thermogenic genes in white adipose tissue (WAT). To test this possibility, we generated mice with doxycycline-inducible BAT-specific PLIN5 deletion. Acute PLIN5 deletion in adult mice during cold exposure reduced BAT thermogenic gene expression, mitochondrial cristae density, and uncoupled mitochondrial respiration, which resulted in cold intolerance. Unlike constitutive PLIN5 knockout mice, mice acutely rendered PLIN5-deficient in BAT failed to mount a compensatory thermogenic response in inguinal WAT. Together, these findings demonstrate that PLIN5 is required for mitochondrial homeostasis in brown adipocytes and for adaptive thermogenesis during cold exposure. Notably, by cell fractionation and protease protection assay, we observed that PLIN5 enriches on the outer mitochondrial membrane in BAT during cold exposure. We also observed that the absence of PLIN5 in BAT is not associated with reduced contacts between lipid droplets and mitochondria, thereby suggesting that the role of PLIN5 in adaptive thermogenesis may depend on its translocation to the mitochondrial outer membrane for a purpose unrelated to the formation of contacts between lipid droplets and mitochondria.
authors: Violeta I Gallardo Montejano; Chaofeng Yang; Hannah Hurtado; Perry E Bickel

title: Adaptive reinforcement learning-driven personalized training plan generation and effect evaluation for college students’ physical fitness tests
abstract: Conventional college fitness training in China relies on uniform schedules that ignore between-student variability, producing marginal gains for many and elevated risk for those pushed beyond their adaptive ceiling. We propose an adaptive reinforcement learning framework that generates and revises individualized training plans aligned with the National Student Physical Health Standard. The framework binds five layers—input ingestion, adaptive feature extraction, an improved Proximal Policy Optimization decision module, plan rendering, and dual-rate feedback—into a closed loop that ingests fitness scores, demographic descriptors, and longitudinal training logs to issue weekly prescriptions across endurance, strength, and flexibility components. Because no agent may experiment on students, we treat the historical records as an offline decision problem: a validated student-response model supplies the state transitions, and returns for prescriptions the records never contain are estimated only inside the support of the teaching policy that generated them. Three design elements distinguish the system: a slowly refreshed adaptive state representation that absorbs cohort drift; a four-component reward with deficit-driven scalarization balancing fitness gain, safety, adherence, and plan rationality; and a bounded-staleness prioritized buffer with importance-sampling correction, paired with cosine-annealed learning rates, for stable convergence under noisy educational signals. Experiments on 4128 students from four cohorts, partitioned so that no student ever spans two folds, returned a composite fitness improvement of 14.6% in held-out cross-validation. A 16-week randomized field study with 312 participants produced a 13.8% gain against 7.1% in the control arm; the prespecified intention-to-treat mixed model places the adjusted between-arm effect at 4.71 composite points (95% CI 3.92–5.50), or roughly six percentage points of relative improvement. Plan rationality reached 91.7% and adherence 87.3%, with the largest absolute gains accruing to initially failing students. Adaptive reinforcement learning therefore offers a workable—though not yet longitudinally proven—path toward precision physical education in higher education settings.
authors: Qian Zhou; Jin Gao

title: Advanced cell-instructive bio-inks: Engineering multiscale niches for functional tissue formation
abstract: Three-dimensional bioprinting has transformed tissue fabrication by enabling the precise spatial organization of living cells and biomaterials into biomimetic tissue constructs. However, advances in manufacturing have outpaced the development of bio-inks capable of actively directing tissue formation. Most existing bio-inks remain optimized for printability, rheological behaviour, and structural fidelity, while providing limited control over the biological processes that govern tissue morphogenesis, functional maturation, and regeneration. This review examines the emerging paradigm of cell-instructive bio-inks, which integrate biological regulation directly into material design to recreate the cellular microenvironments that guide tissue development. We present a unifying framework that classifies these bio-inks according to three complementary regulatory dimensions: biochemical niches that regulate cell fate through molecular signalling and regenerative matrices; architectural niches that direct tissue organization through spatial and structural cues; and metabolic niches that modulate oxygen availability, redox homeostasis, and cellular metabolism. We further discuss strategies for integrating these instructive functions within multifunctional bio-inks, together with scalable manufacturing, and artificial intelligence-assisted bio-ink design. By redefining bio-inks as active regulators of cellular behaviour, this review establishes a conceptual framework for engineering next-generation bio-inks capable of orchestrating tissue development, functional maturation, and regenerative outcomes.
authors: Wei Long Ng; Yan Xu; Fengyuan Liu; Paulo Bártolo

title: Advances in algorithm‑driven tomographic volumetric (bio)printing toward an AI‑led future
abstract: Tomographic volumetric printing (TVP) is an emerging three-dimensional (3D) technique that enables rapid, layer-free fabrication of sophisticated structures via multi-angle light projection. While tomographic volumetric bioprinting (TVBP) extends to print with living cells, allowing for fast fabrication of cell-laden 3D constructs. Our continuous work and the rapid developments on TVP/TVBP (TV(B)P) encourage us to review the current challenges faced by TV(B)P and the recent trend in algorithm-based optimization vs AI-based optimization. This review summarizes recent algorithmic advances in TV(B)P, with emphasis on algorithmic strategies for improving printing resolution and fidelity, including optimization of light refraction, scattering, and iterative reconstruction. Then, we further explore increasing attention on the emergence of AI-based TV(B)P, enabling automatic parameter optimization, adaptive exposure control, accelerated slicing, and automated quality assessment. Further, we compare the differences between algorithm-based and AI-based strategies, as well as the difference between AI-driven TV(B)P, by which the system is granted autonomous decision-making power at critical stages of manufacturing; and AI-assisted TV(B)P, by which efficiency, robustness, and interpretability are enhanced without replacing existing physical or algorithmic models. In summary, this review offers insights into the future directions of AI-based TV(B)P in materials science, biomedical engineering, and advanced manufacturing.
authors: Dan Ye; Yunhai Lin; 呼新荣 Hu Xinrong; Jinpeng Chen; Liming Lian; Jiaqi Lv; Zhuo Xiong; Guoxi Xie; Maobin Xie

title: Advancing Rural Health Through Nursing Education, Community Partnerships, Research, and Workforce Development
abstract: BACKGROUND: Rural populations experience healthcare disparities, including workforce shortages, geographic isolation, limited access to specialty services, and adverse social determinants of health. These challenges are particularly evident in South Dakota, where nearly half of the population resides in rural or frontier communities. Because of these challenges, preparing nurses to work in rural America is critical to building a workforce capable of meeting this population's unique healthcare needs. METHODS: This article is an experience-based institutional case essay describing an integrated approach to how South Dakota State University College of Nursing, located within a rural land-grant institution, has developed and adapted educational programs, workforce initiatives, community partnerships, and research programs to address rural health challenges across the state and region. The College of Nursing (CON) includes three campus locations-Brookings, Sioux Falls, and Rapid City-and includes undergraduate and graduate nursing education. Nursing education is designed to allow students to blend their nursing education with South Dakota's unique rural environment. RESULTS: The CON offers multiple pathways into the profession, including traditional and accelerated Bachelor of Science in Nursing (BSN) programs, an online BSN option utilizing a train-in-place model, master's-level nursing education and administrator programs, Doctor of Nursing Practice (DNP) programs, and PhD education. Through strategic academic-practice partnerships and federally funded workforce initiatives, the college prepares nurses for rural practice across primary care, acute care, long-term care, and underserved settings. Additional initiatives support Native American student success, rural workforce recruitment and retention, oral health outreach, care coordination for children and youth with special healthcare needs, and research focused on workforce well-being, workplace violence, and healthcare access. CONCLUSIONS: A multi-pronged approach by rural colleges of nursing may improve rural healthcare access, strengthen the nursing workforce, and address the complex health needs of rural and frontier populations. South Dakota State University CON demonstrates how innovative educational delivery models, community partnerships, targeted workforce initiatives, and research can contribute to sustainable rural healthcare solutions and rural health.
authors: Lea Niederbaumer; Michelle Lichtenberg; Danielle M. Schievelbein; Abby O. Seydel; Nicole Carlson; Theresa Garren-Grubbs; Danielle Currier; Brian Williamson; Amanda Mehlhaff; Marie Schmit; Sarah Mollman

title: Advancing the Translational Pipeline: From In Vivo and In Vitro 2D Models to Next-Generation Cell Culture Models for Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis Modelling and Drug Discovery
abstract: Background: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is still a global health challenge, as there is no effective treatment due to the inadequacy of conventional experimental platforms for comprehending pathogenic mechanisms and developing therapy. Objectives: This review details the recent progress and clinical utility of next-generation iPSC-derived 3D in vitro systems integrated with microfluidics, CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing, multi-omics readouts, and AI-based machine learning, which are emerging as transformative platforms for recapitulating key ALS pathological hallmarks. Methods: A literature search was performed using PubMed and Web of Science, including only English-language publications. All the published papers collected covered the period from January 2015 to June 2026. Results: Human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) cerebral organoids, assembloids, and organ-on-a-chip technologies are revolutionizing research into ALS by providing a way to model the complex spatial organization, cellular heterogeneity, and neural network dynamics of the human brain. Moreover, recent bioengineering advancements enable the inclusion of functional neurovascular units, the integration of resident immune cells (microglia), and the use of 3D bioprinting to accelerate the functional maturation of age-related phenotypes. CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing, OMICS, and machine learning improve tools for studying ALS and identifying therapeutic targets. Conclusions: Novel cell culture models may bridge the gap between preclinical animal models and human clinical trials and reduce the duration and costs of translation. Future work is likely to integrate bioprinting with organ-on-chip microfluidics, CRISPR-based genetic editing, and multi-omics readouts to build increasingly faithful, patient-specific ALS models for both basic research and precision therapeutics.
authors: Elisabetta Carata; Stefania Mariano; Bernardetta Anna Tenuzzo; Elisa Panzarini

title: Agent-Pilot: A Visual Hybrid Intelligence Closed-Loop Framework for Supervised Autonomous eVTOL Landing
abstract: Achieving safe and precise supervised autonomous landing of eVTOL (electric vertical take-off and landing) aircraft in environments lacking special infrastructure remains a critical challenge. Existing approaches either rely on specific cooperative visual markers (which perform poorly in unstructured settings) or on highly precise global navigation satellite system (GNSS) data and multiple sensors. Meanwhile, large vision-language models (VLMs) excel at high-level semantic reasoning yet lack accurate 3D perception and stable control – leading to a spatial grounding problem. Therefore, this study proposes Agent-Pilot, a modular hybrid-intelligence framework that enables supervised autonomous landing without requiring specialized infrastructure. We propose a purely monocular vision-based approach that integrates classical Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID)-based feedback control, 3D spatial perception, real-time video-based depth estimation, and VLM-driven decision-making into a unified pipeline. The approach requires no pre-training on specific landing markers. Finally, we introduce a decoupled safety agent to monitor internal and external anomalies and alert the pilot in the event of an abnormality. The framework is evaluated in a flight simulation through online testing in Microsoft Flight Simulator (MSFS) 2024, realized through a self-developed toolbox, the MSFSDevKit, which is open-sourced in this study. Results demonstrate that Agent-Pilot achieves high success rates across 16 challenging scenarios and maintains attitude stability and glide-path accuracy superior to those of trained human pilots in both clear and fog conditions at the urban vertiport. All necessary code and tools used in this study are open-sourced to enable researchers to replace components modularly to improve the framework.
authors: Chenglin Liu; Yuxin Du; Yufan Chen; Dengbo He; Yingcong Chen; Hai Yang

title: Agentic cryo-EM structure determination with CryoPilot
abstract: Single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) relies on mature computational tools, but experts must still inspect intermediate results, choose among alternative processing routes, and decide when earlier choices should be revised. Here we present CryoPilot, a system of two language-model agents that carries cryo-EM data from raw micrographs through three-dimensional reconstruction to validated atomic models. Rather than executing a predefined pipeline, its reconstruction agent evaluates intermediate images and quantitative diagnostics, selects and parameterizes CryoSPARC jobs, tests alternative strategies, compares their outcomes, and retains, revises, or reverts decisions accordingly. A persistent programming environment and session database preserve the complete processing history, making each decision traceable and allowing multi-day workflows to proceed with minimal human intervention. Its modeling agent determines map handedness, builds atomic models with CryoZeta, removes regions the density does not support, and optimizes each model by testing refinement steps against map fit, geometry, and DAQ, a measure of local model-map agreement. Across nine public EMPIAR datasets, eight reconstructions reached 2.61-3.51 Å resolution, and refined models from seven maps agreed with reference structures to within 0.4-4.9 Å Cα RMSD. For a challenging α-latrocrustotoxin dataset, a single change of particle-picking strategy that we suggested enabled CryoPilot to improve the reconstruction from 5.9 to 4.15 Å. CryoPilot establishes an adaptive and auditable framework for agent-driven cryo-EM structure determination.
authors: Pranav Deep Punuru; Thomas Klose; Daisuke Kihara

title: An Ethical Framework for Safety and Governance in Biomedical Self-Driving Laboratories: Challenges and Perspectives
abstract: Self-driving laboratories close the loop between hypothesis generation, experimental execution, and analysis, removing the human from the inner cycle of discovery. Their migration from chemistry and materials science into biomedicine introduces ethical problems that the chemistry literature does not encounter: experiments run on human-derived material, generate data about identifiable people, produce candidates intended for patients, and act on living systems whose variability can masquerade as signal. We argue that biomedical self-driving laboratories defeat the categorical triggers on which biomedical oversight depends, because what an autonomous platform will do is determined at runtime by a model rather than at review time by an investigator. We propose Proportionate Autonomy Governance, a framework that replaces protocol review with envelope review: oversight bodies approve a formally specified and machine-checkable region of experiment space together with the invariants that constrain search within it. Five duties, bounding, tracing, controlling, verifying, and answering, scale jointly with a platform’s autonomy level and consequence tier, and we specify what each requires at each position in that grid. We work the framework through a hypothetical induced pluripotent stem cell differentiation campaign, giving its envelope, autonomy annex, and accountability register, and we state what the framework costs and what it does not fix. We map current instruments onto this framework and identify where they fail to bind, and we relate the proposal to operational design domains, runtime assurance, and safety cases in established safety-critical practice. We report a search for documented safety incidents in autonomous laboratories, which returned none, and we are explicit about the limits of what that absence supports. We close with an implementation agenda.
authors: Nura Brimo; Tolga Tarkan Ölmez; Dilek Çökeliler Serdaroğlu

title: An In-Line Dynamic Light Scattering-Based Exploratory Approach for Time-Resolved Nucleation and Particle Growth Kinetics in Solvent-Antisolvent Nanoprecipitation of Poorly Water-Soluble Drugs
abstract: A deep understanding of nucleation and growth mechanisms in solvent-antisolvent nanoprecipitation is critical to achieve nanoparticles with the desired properties. However, real-time monitoring remains challenging. This work aims to demonstrate the feasibility of dynamic light scattering (DLS) as an in-line process analytical technology (PAT) for the time-resolved monitoring and characterization of scattering changes associated with nucleation and particle growth during the solvent-antisolvent nanoprecipitation of active pharmaceutical ingredients. Dexamethasone serves as a poorly water-soluble model drug. Thermodynamic solubility and metastable zone width are determined experimentally. The in-line DLS assessment reveals a characteristic four-stage profile, consistent with prenucleation clustering in supersaturated solutions, the onset of detectable nanoscale entities associated with nucleation, a postnucleation growth-dominated stage, and late-stage aggregation. Controlled supersaturation is examined by computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations and milli-fluidic mixing in a 3D-printed Y-mixer for kinetic assessment. A Python algorithm enables automated extraction of DLS-derived induction times (tind) data. Noteworthily, this combined computational, milli-fluidic, and DLS-based approach minimizes user bias and enhances the detection of subtle nucleation variations under various hydrodynamic and nominal final relative supersaturation regimes. Overall, the findings presented here position in-line DLS as a powerful PAT approach for (nano)precipitation process understanding and optimization. This approach follows recent trends in automation and continuous flow preparation at early stages of nanoparticles development.
authors: Luis Castillo-Henríquez; Andrés Castillo-Henríquez; Pauline Chavrier; Bruno Saubaméa; Benoît Maxit; Khair Alhareth; Karine Andrieux; Nathalie Mignet; Yohann Corvis

title: An Integrated Artificial Intelligence Framework for Nanomedicine Engineering
abstract: The translation of nanomedicines is frequently bottlenecked by trial-and-error optimization. Integrating artificial intelligence (AI) transforms this process into a closed-loop, experimentally grounded discovery ecosystem. This Review provides a roadmap for this paradigm, demonstrating how AI, high-throughput testing, and nanoscale design converge to generate clinically translatable nanotherapeutics. We emphasize the necessity of standardized multimodal data-spanning pharmacokinetic, biodistribution, and drug-release profiles-anchored strictly to validated biological phenomena. Furthermore, we evaluate an algorithmic spectrum, ranging from classical machine learning to physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) and reinforcement learning (RL), to align models with specific formulation objectives. To bridge computational design and empirical reality, we examine how high-throughput technologies, such as robotic laboratories and in vivo DNA-barcoding multiplexing, operationalize the "Design-Make-Test-Analyze" (DMTA) cycle for dynamic model recalibration. Ultimately, this review demonstrates how integrating AI, physical constraints, and automated validation accelerates the rational design of next-generation nanomedicines.
authors: Meichen Dong; Qin Luo; Xinyi Ding; Chaoqi Lu; Ru Zhang; Qingqing Tan; Zhiqing Pang; Defang Ouyang; Dongsheng Li; Jiaxuan Xia; Jianxin Wang

title: An open-source, 3D-printable droplet microfluidics platform with strobe-enhanced microscopy
abstract: Droplet microfluidics underpins many single-cell, precision biomedical, and nanomaterial techniques. However, implementing these methods reproducibly remains challenging outside specialised laboratories due to high equipment costs, operational inflexibility, mechanical impracticality at the microscope stage, as well as open-source pumping solutions that are inadequately validated for low-flow stability. We present an accessible, research-grade, open-source droplet microfluidics platform integrating a compact, microfluidics-optimised microscopy stage with networked syringe-pump control. Designed for local digital fabrication, primarily 3D printing, and widely available components, the platform supports reproducible builds across diverse settings. This setup enables stable droplet generation, observation of rapid droplet dynamics, and automation-ready networked workflows. The microscopy module uses a Raspberry Pi camera and microsecond stroboscopic illumination to capture sharp images of fast-moving droplets without the need for a high-speed camera. A modular hardware interface and extensible, web-accessible software stack provide a path to integrate additional modules and laboratory automation beyond the configuration evaluated here. For infusion, we introduce an open-source syringe pump optimised for low reliable flow rather than maximum rates, combining gearbox-assisted stepper mechanics with workflow-centric control that enables manual intervention (keypad control) and remote operation (web interface and automation hooks). We benchmark droplet regimes, size tuning, and time-stability under low-flow conditions (between 25 and 2500 µL/h) relevant to advanced assays and demonstrate biomedical readiness through the encapsulation and incubation of cells, beads, and bacteria in monodisperse droplets. The platform has been replicated across laboratories in Latin America and globally, including independent builds, supporting reproducibility. All design files, firmware/software, analysis notebooks, and benchmark datasets are openly released.
