title: Analysis of sperm processing and cryopreservation procedures in the common marmoset ( Callithrix jacchus ) to reduce fragmentation and maximize total and progressive motility
abstract: The marmoset has emerged as an ideal species for studying complex neurodevelopmental diseases, and IVF is required for gene-editing success. Reliable sperm processing is paramount to several IVF techniques, including traditional insemination. If not used immediately, thermal stress from cryopreservation diminishes sperm quality, requiring improved processing methods. Swim-up and gradient methods may limit adequate sperm quality, and the lack of a standardized freezing protocol often results in impaired post-thaw motility. Thus, reliable standards for sperm processing and cryopreservation in the marmoset are needed to support vital IVF processes. Collected semen underwent one of four pre-processing incubation steps before processing by swim-up, sucrose gradient, or a microfluidics assay. Sperm parameters were assessed using a Hamilton Thorne Computer Assisted Sperm Analysis (CASA) system. To evaluate cryopreservation, microfluidics-processed sperm were subjected to five protocols using different cryoprotectants and cooling methods. After thawing, sperm samples were analyzed with the CASA system and a DNA fragmentation assay. Incubation for 30 minutes at 38°C in TYH media decreased sperm aggregation, and subsequent microfluidics resulted in a higher percentage of motile and progressively motile sperm than swim-up or gradient methods. Our optimized cryopreservation protocol consistently achieved at least 20% progressive motility, a key benchmark for usable marmoset sperm, while previously published or commercial methods were less consistent. The cryopreservation protocol outperformed other published methods, having the least significant change in post-thaw motility without causing DNA damage. These findings establish standardized methods for reliably procuring and storing sperm samples for IVF or husbandry in the common marmoset.

title: Analytical perspectives on RNA aptamer switch-based biosensors
abstract: RNA aptamer switches are programmable tools that enable ligand-responsive control of gene expression, making them valuable as genetically encoded biosensors in synthetic biology, diagnostics, and therapeutic applications. RNA aptamer switch functionality is often evaluated through changes in reporter gene expression following ligand recognition; however, analytical methods used to characterize RNA aptamer switch activity vary across studies, making it difficult to compare between platforms. This review examines analytical approaches to evaluate RNA aptamer switch-based biosensors, highlighting how each method captures different aspects of switch performance and how molecular, cellular, and experimental factors shape output. We also discuss considerations for experimental design, including normalization, controls, assay context, and sensitivity. By comparing the strengths and limitations of different analytical readouts, we provide suggestions for selecting appropriate measurement methods. Finally, we discuss current challenges in standardization, with the goal of improving quantitative and predictive evaluation of RNA aptamer switch-based biosensors.
authors: Jiawen Liu; Maureen McKeague

title: Application of skin organoids in radiation-induced skin injury
abstract: Radiation-induced skin injury (RISI) is a severe and intractable complication of tumor radiotherapy and nuclear exposure; however, traditional research models fail to accurately recapitulate the underlying human skin physiology and pathology. As an advanced 3D culture system, skin organoid technology has emerged as a revolutionary platform to overcome these translational barriers. This review highlights the pivotal applications of skin organoids in RISI research. First, they serve as robust in vitro models to elucidate dynamic pathophysiological mechanisms, ranging from acute DNA damage to chronic dermal fibrosis. Second, they function as high-throughput screening platforms that accelerate the discovery of novel radioprotective therapeutics and the validation of advanced drug delivery systems. Most importantly, we emphasize their immense translational potential as functional, patient-specific tissue-engineered grafts for the personalized regenerative repair of extensive RISI. Furthermore, by integrating advanced bioengineering strategies, such as microfluidic chips and immunocompetent models, skin organoids promise to bridge the gap between bench and bedside, offering a paradigm shift in RISI management.
authors: Ranran Dong; Ce Zhang; Chuxuan Fang; Lingzhi Zhang; Caiying Song; Zehua Zhou; Long Yang; Daojiang Yu

title: Aptamers as a sandbox for lab-in-the-loop agentic molecular discovery
abstract: Despite breakthroughs in AI-driven molecular generation, existing discovery pipelines operate largely in silico, with wet-lab feedback reserved for validation rather than iterative improvement. Whether large language model (LLM)-based reasoning agents can accelerate de novo discovery by iterating with lab data remains unproven. Here we use protein-binding aptamer design as a sandbox (1-2 week cycles, \$1-\$3 per candidate) to demonstrate a wet lab in a closed loop with AI systems. We tasked agentic pipelines with developing aptamer binders against $α$-thrombin and myoglobin across three design-test-improve cycles ($\sim$1,000 candidates per round; $\sim$4,400 constructs). Statistically significant, bead-corrected on-target hit rates among new candidates rose across rounds from 0.0% in Round 1 to 26.0% in Round 2 and 42.1% in Round 3 on $α$-thrombin (37.1% excluding literature motif descendants), and from 10.2% in Round 1 to 3.7% in Round 2 and 33.5% in Round 3 on myoglobin. Single-clone bead-binding titrations of eight full-length $α$-thrombin candidates confirmed concordance with pooled sequencing enrichment (Pearson $r = 0.90$). In these assays, literature-derived motifs engineered by the agents to reduce off-target reactivity in the pooled screen reached apparent affinities of $K_D = 24.6$--$133$ nM, whereas de novo scaffolds showed low-micromolar binding ($K_D > 1\ μ$M). We also report how our pipelines used myoglobin binding data to exploit the G-quadruplex binder space, diagnose cross-reactivity as on-target specificity dropped from 75.0% to 19.1%, and recover by developing strategies that restored specificity to 72.4%. We demonstrate that empirical lab data is more valuable than existing computational proxies, showing how iterative experimental feedback enables AI agents to diagnose assay artifacts and refine molecular designs across rounds.
authors: Zachary Cutts; John Coller; Rachel Chen; Hua Tang; Mathias M. J. Bellaiche; Ryder Easterlin; Dina Zverinski; Petar Sirkovic; Avinatan Hassidim; Yossi Matias; Pooja Rao; Annalisa Pawlosky

title: Aqueous Two-Phase Systems for the Extraction of Cell-Free DNA from Plasma : Process Development and Application in Liquid Biopsy
abstract: Molecular diagnostics based on circulating biomarkers have become increasingly important in precision medicine, especially in oncology, where there is an ongoing need for minimally invasive methods of disease detection and monitoring. In this context, liquid biopsy has gained significant attention as a technique that enables analysis of tumor-related material directly from body fluids. Unlike conventional tissue biopsies, it allows repeated sampling and facilitates the monitoring of disease progression and treatment response over time. Among the accessible analytes, circulating cell-free DNA (cfDNA) is particularly relevant, as it reflects tumor-associated genetic alterations and supports various clinical applications, including early diagnosis, therapeutic decision-making, and longitudinal disease monitoring. In addition, its rapid turnover in circulation provides a dynamic snapshot of disease status, making it suitable for real-time clinical assessment. However, the analytical use of cfDNA is associated with several challenges. The concentration of cfDNA in plasma is typically low, rarely exceeding a few nanograms per milliliter, and varies by cancer type and stage. Furthermore, cfDNA consists of short, fragmented molecules with a characteristic length of approximately 167 bp and often exhibits a nucleosomal structure. These molecules are found within a complex biological environment with a high abundance of proteins, as well as high-molecular-weight genomic DNA (gDNA) potentially released during blood processing. These factors complicate sample preparation for sequencing-based analytical methods, such as droplet digital PCR and next-generation sequencing (NGS), which require highly efficient and selective extraction techniques. Therefore, the isolation of cfDNA is considered a crucial step in the pre-analytical phase of liquid biopsy procedures. Current state-of-the-art cfDNA extraction predominantly relies on solid-phase adsorption to silica membranes or functionalized magnetic beads using strong chaotropes. Although these methods are widely adopted for their robustness and high purity, they present several drawbacks. Most kits involve time-consuming bind-wash-elute protocols with repeated manual handling and vacuum or centrifugation steps, which can increase the risk of sample loss and cross-contamination. Automated platforms can mitigate these risks and improve throughput and ease of use, but high reagent costs and the need for specialized equipment remain limitations that may restrict flexibility and scalability. Furthermore, incomplete adsorption or elution and contamination with gDNA can reduce the detection of rare tumor-derived variants. Short DNA fragments may also be recovered less efficiently, introducing a size bias that can affect downstream analysis. These issues highlight the need for alternative cfDNA extraction methods that can simplify workflows while maintaining high performance. Aqueous two-phase systems (ATPS) represent a promising liquid–liquid extraction method for biomolecule separation and purification. These systems consist of two immiscible aqueous phases formed by mixing polymers and salts above a critical concentration threshold, within which biomolecules distribute according to their physicochemical properties. This enables selective separation without the need for denaturing agents. Besides their mild operating conditions and cost-effectiveness, ATPS offer advantages in scalability and process simplicity, as phase separation can be achieved quickly by centrifugation. Although ATPS are well established for a variety of biomolecules, including proteins and nucleic acids, their application to short DNA fragments relevant to liquid biopsy has not been systematically studied. In particular, the partitioning behavior of cfDNA-like fragments in polymer–salt systems remains poorly understood, especially in the presence of plasma, a complex biological matrix that may influence phase properties. Furthermore, the integration of ATPS capture into a complete extraction workflow compatible with downstream molecular analyses has only been superficially addressed to date. Therefore, linking partitioning behavior to process design is essential for the development of an efficient ATPS-based separation strategy. Supported by relevant literature, Chapter 1 offers a comprehensive overview of the theoretical background, current research status, and remaining challenges within the field. As outlined in Chapter 2, this thesis presents the development of an ATPS-based extraction workflow for cfDNA-like fragments from plasma, integrating fundamental insights into phase partitioning with a practical, analytically compatible process. The three presented studies progress from investigations in well-defined model systems to application in a complex biological matrix and, ultimately, the creation of an integrated workflow. To enable systematic investigation, PCR-generated 160 bp DNA fragments were used as cfDNA-like surrogates in most experiments. The results provide new insights into the partitioning behavior of short DNA fragments in ATPS and demonstrate that the developed process yields sequencing-compatible DNA. The first study (Chapter 3) examined the partitioning behavior of 160 bp DNA fragments in well-defined polymer–salt ATPS, addressing the limited availability of systematic data for molecules in the size range relevant to cfDNA. Considering the complex interaction of factors affecting solute distribution, a comprehensive experimental approach was used to investigate how key system parameters, including polymer molecular weight, salt type, tie-line length, phase volume ratio, and the addition of neutral salts, influence DNA partitioning and recovery. High-throughput screening with a liquid-handling platform and automated routines for binodal and tie-line determination enabled efficient testing of many system compositions. The results revealed consistent trends in DNA distribution and identified conditions that allowed high recovery. More generally, it was demonstrated that short DNA behaves similarly to plasmid DNA in PEG/phosphate ATPS, with overall partitioning trends mainly driven by PEG molecular weight. For example, DNA fragments were primarily found in the top phase when PEG was below 600 g/mol, whereas they accumulated in the bottom phase with PEG 600 and 1000. Additionally, it was confirmed that adding a neutral salt, such as NaCl, to a PEG 400 system shifted the DNA distribution from the top to the bottom phase. Preliminary experiments in a simplified synthetic plasma matrix containing human serum albumin and immunoglobulin G showed that partitioning behavior could, to some extent, be transferred to more complex systems. These experiments also indicated that the NaCl-induced phase shift is selective for DNA, achieving 88% recovery while removing 99% of proteins. These findings improved the understanding of short DNA partitioning in ATPS and laid the groundwork for selecting optimal conditions for future extraction studies. Building on this foundation, the second study (Chapter 4) investigated the use of ATPS to capture cfDNA-like fragments from human plasma. Unlike the model systems described in Chapter 3, the presence of proteins and other plasma components introduces additional interactions that can affect phase behavior and solute partitioning. Therefore, the study assessed the recovery and distribution of these fragments, as well as phase formation, in plasma-containing PEG/phosphate ATPS. The selective NaCl-induced shift observed in PEG 400 systems proved less effective due to the formation of an interphase consisting of reversibly aggregated plasma proteins present in excess. Consequently, PEG 1000 ATPS were preferred, enabling DNA recoveries of up to 90% in the salt-rich bottom phase while reducing protein concentrations from 60–80 mg/mL in plasma to below 3 mg/mL, corresponding to over 95% removal. This study also confirmed the robustness of the ATPS capture step across plasma samples from different donors and collection tubes, both of which introduce variability. To address practical limitations caused by sample dilution from phase-forming components pre-dissolved in water, a system was designed in which solid PEG and salts were added directly to the plasma. This modification increased the plasma input from 38% (w/w) to 67% (w/w) without affecting DNA or protein partitioning. The scalability of this approach was verified by processing up to 4 mL of plasma at once, which is equivalent to the volume obtainable from a single blood tube. Additionally, reverse elution was implemented as a purification step to desalt and increase protein removal to above 99%, while reducing flow-through volume and thereby concentrating the DNA-rich extract, ultimately improving suitability for downstream sequencing-based analyses. The results confirmed that DNA can be efficiently recovered from plasma while separating it from the main protein fraction, yielding extracts with substantially reduced matrix complexity. This work established key process elements required for an integrated workflow and provides a basis for further process optimization. The third study (Chapter 5) focused on integrating individual process steps into a cohesive, optimized ATPS-based extraction workflow and evaluating its compatibility with downstream analyses. First, the effect of different lysis methods on DNA recovery and protein removal was examined. The results indicated that a lysis step might not be necessary, as the high salt content of the DNA-containing bottom phase may be sufficient to separate DNA from most proteins and possibly dissociate the nucleosomal complex, streamlining the entire process. The system composition was then optimized to increase DNA concentration while minimizing losses by adjusting the phase volume ratio and tie-line length. title: Artificial Intelligence and the Scientific Method: A Theoretical Examination of Discovery, Explanation and Reproducibility in AI-Driven Science
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing the conduct of science. Models predict protein structures and propose materials, generate hypotheses, design and execute experiments, and increasingly assist in writing the papers that report the results. This paper examines the effect of these developments on the scientific method, drawing on the philosophy of science, the research-integrity and reproducibility literatures, and recent work on AI-driven discovery across the natural, engineering and social sciences. It distinguishes three functions of science that AI affects differently: discovery, the identification of what is the case; explanation, the account of why it is the case; and reproducibility, the possibility of independent confirmation. The paper argues that AI substantially accelerates discovery, threatens explanation, because predictive success without mechanistic understanding is now attainable at scale, and complicates reproducibility, since AI-driven results depend on models, data and computing conditions that are seldom reported in full or readily reproduced. It sets out a corresponding division of epistemic labour between human scientists and AI systems and a set of reporting and verification standards for AI-assisted research, and it considers the particular implications for scientific institutions in Africa, which may gain access to discovery capacity previously beyond their means while facing acute risks of irreproducibility and of dependence upon others. It argues that these three effects pull in different directions rather than reinforcing one another, so that the governance of AI-assisted research cannot treat acceleration, understanding and confirmation as a single problem. The paper sets out propositions on where predictive models may stand in for mechanistic explanation and where they may not, and proposes that African scientific institutions adopt explicit standards for the reporting and verification of AI-assisted results as a condition of building research capacity that is independent rather than dependent.
authors: Emmanuel Usulor Nwogboji; Atolagbe Umar Kawu; Igwe Emmanuel Sunday

title: Artificial Intelligence for Precision Agriculture: Applications and Future Directions
abstract: Agriculture is increasingly challenged by climate variability, declining natural resources, population growth, and the need to improve crop productivity while minimizing environmental impacts. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers promising opportunities to address these challenges through data-driven monitoring, predictive modelling, and automated decision-making. This review examines the applications of AI in precision agriculture, with particular emphasis on machine learning, deep learning, computer vision, remote sensing, Internet of Things (IoT), and agricultural robotics. The literature synthesis covers major application areas, including crop health monitoring, disease and pest detection, yield prediction, soil characterization, irrigation scheduling, nutrient management, weed identification, and autonomous farm operations. The reviewed evidence indicates that integrating multisource agricultural data with AI-based predictive models can improve the timeliness and spatial precision of farm management decisions. Convolutional neural networks and other deep learning architectures are particularly useful for image-based crop diagnosis, whereas ensemble learning and recurrent neural networks provide opportunities for yield forecasting and environmental prediction. Furthermore, AI-integrated sensor networks facilitate real-time monitoring and site-specific management of water and nutrients. Despite these advancements, practical implementation remains constrained by limited representative datasets, model transferability, infrastructure costs, inadequate rural connectivity, data ownership, and insufficient field validation. Future developments should prioritize explainable AI, multimodal data integration, edge computing, autonomous agricultural systems, and accessible decision-support platforms. This review highlights the importance of integrating technological innovation with agronomic knowledge to develop sustainable, economically viable, and climate-resilient precision agriculture systems.
authors: Arshad; Susheel Kumar; Kamardeen Mohamed Aafir; Muhammad Zahid Rashid; Amina; Plosha Khanum; Maryam Anwar

title: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Discovery and Autonomous Optimization of Perovskite Photovoltaics: From Materials Design and Property Prediction to Self-Driving Laboratories
abstract: Artificial intelligence is transforming perovskite photovoltaics from empirical development toward data-driven and increasingly autonomous research. This review critically examines this transition across multiple scales, connecting materials prediction with device engineering, stability analysis, and experimental decision-making. Machine learning (ML) strategies for bandgap and crystal-structure prediction, synthesizability assessment, and high-throughput materials screening are first evaluated, with particular attention to emerging graph-based models and ML force fields that extend predictive capability toward complex structural and dynamical phenomena. At the device level, recent advances in performance and operational-lifetime prediction, degradation analysis, defect and ion migration modeling, phase stability assessment, and data-driven passivator discovery are systematically discussed. The review further examines the progression from retrospective modeling toward active experimentation through robotic fabrication and characterization, and self-driving laboratories. Particular attention is also given to ML-assisted perovskite tandem photovoltaics, where coupled materials, architectural, spectral, and environmental variables require multidimensional optimization, as well as to AutoML frameworks that reduce the expertise and manual intervention required for model development. Finally, the major challenges limiting the broader application of AI in perovskite photovoltaics are critically discussed, and future research directions toward more reliable, transferable, and experimentally integrated AI frameworks are outlined.

title: Artificial intelligence for protein engineering: From prediction and generation to evidence-centred design cycles
abstract: Artificial intelligence now supports mutation ranking, structure modelling, inverse folding, generative design and experiment selection in protein engineering. These tools can propose far more candidates than laboratories can test. This critical review examines data resources and benchmarks, computational roles and objective-specific workflows, and appraises the quality and limits of the experimental evidence supporting their use. It covers enzymes, binders, stability and developability, therapeutic and membrane proteins, assemblies, biosensors and genome editors. Across these applications, structural self-consistency, model likelihood and docking scores can help prioritise candidates but do not establish function. Prospective experimental success is distinguished from demonstrated improvement in candidate selection, which requires relevant comparators. We apply six domains to the prospective campaigns surveyed here: objective–assay alignment; data provenance and generalisation; calibrated computation and selection; prospective and orthogonal validation; reproducibility and traceability; and governance and translation. We recommend coupling context-aware models to experiments that test their hypotheses and inform the next design decision.
authors: Yugeng Liu; Heng Wang; Xiaojian Zhang; 茶桂宏
venue: Artificial Intelligence in the Life Sciences

title: Artificial intelligence in 3D bioprinting: From predictive modeling to autonomous biofabrication
abstract: Three-dimensional bioprinting is shifting from empirically tuned fabrication toward workflows that integrate quantitative data on materials, printing, structure, and biology. This review summarizes how artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning are being used across these areas, with particular attention to studies that include experimental validation. We first discuss conventional measurements such as rheology, filament formation, shape fidelity, and biological assays because these measurements define the inputs and labels used by AI models. We then examine how data from materials, processes, structures, and biology can be linked within the same experiment. Representative studies are compared with respect to the models used, the amount and type of data, validation methods, and whether model outputs were tested in new experiments. Current evidence is strongest for printability prediction, structural quality assessment, and image-based monitoring, while several studies have also demonstrated cell-viability prediction, parameter optimization, transfer learning, Bayesian optimization, and closed-loop correction. We also discuss inverse design, active learning, uncertainty-aware optimization, physics-informed learning, and biological feedback as approaches to reducing the experimental burden. Finally, we use a five-level maturity framework to distinguish AI-assisted analysis, AI-driven recommendations, adaptive control, and autonomous biofabrication. AI is increasingly influencing experimental planning and process control, but fully integrated autonomous workflows remain uncommon. Further progress will depend on validation across materials and platforms, longer-term biological readouts, traceable data, and the reliable integration of experimental feedback.
authors: Jooyoung Lee; Hyungseok Lee

title: Artificial intelligence in mental health: benefits and challenges of electronic health records
abstract: A incorporação de novas tecnologias de inteligência artificial aos electronic healthcare records (EHRs) tem proporcionado um forte aumento na capacidade de acumular e analisar dados dos pacientes. E a área de saúde mental tem sido uma das beneficiárias deste potencial de melhorias, proporcionando aos seus profissionais ganhos de tempo e eficiência na gestão de informações médicas. Entretanto, há relatos de problemas que estão surgindo na medida em que a utilização das tecnologias de IA se intensifica. Este quadro inclui questões referentes à gestão de informações sensíveis dos pacientes, à falta de padronização dos dados de saúde mental, prejudicando a interoperabilidade dos mesmos, o receio de que o relacionamento terapêutico paciente-profissional seja prejudicado, além da preocupação que os profissionais estão tendo pela possibilidade de serem substituídos pelas tecnologias de IA. Considerando este contexto, o presente artigo tem por objetivo identificar e analisar a dinâmica de incorporação das tecnologias de IA à área de saúde mental. Para realizar este objetivo, foi realizada uma revisão de literatura envolvendo publicações sobre o tema dos últimos seis anos. Ao final, são oferecidas algumas sugestões para desenvolvimento de futuras pesquisas que possam explorar mais possíveis soluções para os problemas identificados, ao longo do processo de adoção de novas tecnologias de IA na área de saúde mental que está em curso.

title: Artificial intelligence in the in vitro fertilization laboratory: A scoping review and SWOT-based evaluation of emerging applications
abstract: Objective: Artificial intelligence (AI) represents a potentially transformative tool in assisted reproductive technology (ART), particularly in vitro fertilization (IVF), for gamete assessment, embryo selection, non-invasive genetic testing, and laboratory automation. This scoping review synthesized recent evidence on AI applications in IVF laboratories and evaluated their translational maturity using an evidence maturity framework and a strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats (SWOT) analysis. Methods: This scoping review followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) Extension for Scoping Reviews guidelines. PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched for peer-reviewed studies published from January 2020 to February 2025. Eligible studies evaluated AI, machine learning, or deep learning in laboratory components of ART. Data were charted on AI methods, dataset characteristics, validation strategies, clinical endpoints, and performance metrics. Results: Ninety-four studies were included. Most applications addressed embryo grading and implantation prediction using convolutional neural networks and were evaluated through internal cross-validation. Reported areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve ranged from 0.75 to 0.92, depending on the endpoint and dataset size. AI applications in sperm analysis and oocyte assessment showed greater reproducibility than manual evaluation. Non-invasive genetic prediction models displayed promising but heterogeneous sensitivity and remained predominantly limited to internal validation. Few studies reported prospective evaluation or external validation using multicenter datasets. Conclusion: AI applications in IVF are expanding, but most remain at early stages of clinical translation. Standardized datasets, external validation, interpretable algorithms, and regulatory oversight remain necessary for safe, equitable clinical integration. AI should function as a decision-support tool that supplements, rather than replaces, embryologists' expertise.

title: Artificial intelligence-enhanced microbial synthesis, functionalization, and applications of bio-based nanomaterials: advances, challenges, and future perspectives
abstract: As demand for sustainable nanotechnology grows, microbial synthesis has emerged as an environmentally friendly alternative to conventional nanoparticle production methods. Microorganisms, including bacteria, fungi, algae, cyanobacteria, and actinomycetes, can synthesize metallic, metal oxide, and hybrid nanomaterials through enzymatic and metabolite-mediated pathways. Unlike conventional physicochemical approaches, microbial synthesis generally operates under mild conditions and reduces the reliance on hazardous chemicals and energy-intensive processes. These biologically synthesized nanomaterials exhibit excellent biocompatibility, enhanced surface functionality, and reduced environmental impact, making them attractive for biomedical, environmental, and industrial applications. This review comprehensively discusses recent advances in microbial nanomaterial biosynthesis and functionalization, and their applications in antimicrobial therapy, cancer treatment, wound healing, drug delivery, wastewater treatment, pollutant degradation, biosensing, food packaging, and sustainable catalysis. It also highlights current challenges, including reproducibility, process optimization, scale-up, and regulatory acceptance, that limit large-scale commercialization. A key focus of this review is the emerging integration of artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and data-driven materials informatics with microbial nanotechnology. These computational approaches enable predictive modeling, synthesis optimization, high-throughput screening, intelligent functionalization, process control, and safety assessment. Consequently, they can reduce experimental effort and accelerate nanomaterial discovery. Finally, the review discusses future opportunities arising from the convergence of microbial biotechnology, AI, automation, and synthetic biology. This integration could enable autonomous, self-optimizing nanomanufacturing platforms for the production of next-generation bio-based nanomaterials.
authors: Anisha Salim; Jouharsha Afthab

title: Artificial intelligence‐driven bioinformatics: From analytical pipelines to model‐centered biological discovery
abstract: Traditional bioinformatic pipelines, which focus on predefined statistical analyses, are increasingly inadequate for handling high‐dimensional, heterogeneous, and context‐rich multi‐omics, spatial, and clinical datasets. Artificial intelligence (AI) is extending modern bioinformatics from predefined analytical pipelines toward learned biological representations, intervention‐oriented modeling, and more automated discovery workflows. This review comprehensively summarizes AI advances across genomic interpretation, single‐cell and spatial transcriptomics, multi‐omics integration, structural bioinformatics, disease stratification, precision medicine, and drug discovery. We categorize underlying AI technologies, including classical machine learning, deep representation learning, generative foundation models, and executable AI agents, and highlight their complementary use cases alongside inherent limitations and failure modes. Building on rather than claiming priority for the model‐centered paradigm described in recent literature, this review contributes a cross‐domain, failure‐aware evaluation framework organized around six unified axes: representation validity, task‐specific incremental value, robustness under biological and technical distribution shift, causal support, resource requirements, and validation/governance readiness. We further discuss key technical and social barriers and hierarchically prioritize future research directions. We conclude that AI complements rather than replaces conventional bioinformatic tools, extending the capacity for hypothesis generation and mechanism‐driven validation. This review provides structured and practical guidance for robust, interpretable, and clinically translatable AI‐driven biological discovery.
authors: Songming Chen; Wei Zhang; Luohuan Dai; Zujian Xiong; Sicen Lai; Haitao Xu; Jia Gu; Kang Peng; Nian Jiang; Liu Hong; Xuejun Li

title: Automated Materials Data and Knowledge Extraction using Machine Learning and Large Language Models
abstract: Over the past decade, substantial efforts have been devoted to developing machine learning (ML) methods for extracting materials data and, where possible, materials knowledge directly from the scientific literature. This review traces the evolution of these methods from heuristic, rule-based pipelines through natural language processing (NLP) models and transformer-based encoders to, lastly, large language models (LLMs) and agentic systems capable of extracting materials information across multiple modalities, including text, tables, and figures. Beside construction of large, queryable materials databases and knowledge graphs that support downstream materials discovery, we discuss how these advances have enabled new capabilities, such as, generic question answering across materials science, AI co-scientists and chatbots for research assistance, and closed-loop optimization and discovery when integrated with autonomous laboratories. We critically assess the datasets generated using these approaches, their extraction accuracy and computational costs, and the respective strengths and limitations of different methodologies, and even provide practical guidelines for developing more reliable and scalable materials data extraction pipelines. Finally, we identify key open challenges, including the extraction of full materials structure-property-processing-performance tetrahedron at the sample level, the scarcity of reliable benchmark datasets for systematic evaluation, and the resolution of non-standard materials terminology across different document modalities.
authors: Arjun Sundaram; B. Pabitramohan Prusty; Rohit Batra

title: Automated Perovskite Film Fabrication with High-Resolution Data Acquisition and Machine Learning Analysis
abstract: Lead halide perovskite solar cells have emerged as promising candidates for next-generation photovoltaics; nevertheless, fabrication of the perovskite photoactive layer remains highly intricate with film formation strongly modulated by various processing and environmental factors. Here, we report an environment-controlled, robot-assisted platform for automated thin-film fabrication designed to quantify and visualize perovskite crystallization in situ. Beyond precise control of each processing step, the system captures dynamic phenomena spanning subsecond color evolution and millisecond antisolvent droplet behavior while simultaneously recording slower environmental parameters (temperature, humidity/moisture, and concentrations of oxygen and volatile organic compounds). For optoelectronic assessment, we implemented time-resolved microwave conductivity (TRMC) measurements together with photoluminescence intensity quantification by using a complementary automated evaluation system. By combining machine-learning regression with SHAP (Shapley additive explanations) analysis, we identify the environmental parameters that most impact film properties and propose a feedback strategy to refine data and extract precise effects of process factors. A comparative study of a two-cation perovskite, (FAPbI3)0.87(MAPbBr3)0.13, and a three-cation perovskite, FA0.85MA0.10Cs0.05PbI3, further reveals markedly different sensitivities to environmental factors (FA, formamidinium; MA, methylammonium), in particular, temperature and resultant phase transition kinetics during thermal annealing. Based on the ML analysis and feedback, we tuned the antisolvent droplet velocity and obtained the maximized power conversion efficiency of 24.4%. Notably, this manual device fabrication was consistent with the results obtained by the automated system. This work establishes a practical route to stable, quantitative, and mechanistically informed investigation of solution-processed photovoltaic films.
authors: Ryosuke Kado; Fumiya Iwai; Ryosuke Nishikubo; Fumitaka Ishiwari; Akinori Saeki

title: Autonomous Experimentation Enables Rapid Optimization of Photochemical Continuous-Flow Synthesis of Diazaxanthilidene Fluorophores
abstract: Photoconvertible diazaxanthilidene dyes enable optical labeling and tracking in live cells, but the batch photocyclization that generates them requires days of irradiation and analog-specific optimization. Here we report a closed-loop continuous-flow platform that uses Bayesian optimization to tune light intensity, temperature, flow rate, and concentration. In campaigns on the parent diazaxanthilidene and four analogs, the platform improved throughput for four of five compounds. For the parent diazaxanthilidene, photoconversion yield rose from approximately 69% in batch to 79%, while throughput increased from 0.52 to 87 nmol min-1. The platform autonomously performs >40 optimization experiments to turn a multiday, analog-specific batch synthesis into a same-day flow synthesis.
authors: Joao Luiz P. de Albuquerque; Scott Laverty; Mao Niimura; Ari Bortman; David M. Chenoweth; Andrew F. Zahrt

title: Autonomous Nanomedicine: Closing the Biological Validation Gap
abstract: Although nanomedicines offer advanced formulation control and physicochemical characterization, clinical translation has been limited. Delivery meta-analyses and late-stage attrition indicate biological validation is often a bottleneck. It must account for context-dependent processes such as protein corona formation, immune recognition and cell/tissue barrier effects, which standard preclinical testing cannot always assess adequately. To address this, we propose a Design-Make-Test-Biology-Learn (DMTBL) workflow that separates biological validation from physicochemical testing and feeds human-relevant biological results back into formulation design. We assess the capabilities required for end-to-end autonomy using an author-assigned technology-readiness evaluation with explicit criteria adapted for biomedical translation. Many of the required technologies are approaching practical deployment, including high-throughput robotic formulation, automated physicochemical assays, predictive models for biodistribution and toxicity, and patient-derived organoids with growing human relevance. But no closed-loop DMTBL system has yet been demonstrated: integration sits at technology readiness level 2-3 against components at levels 3-8. The Learn step also requires a different computational stack from the Analyze step it replaces, handling imaging and multi-parametric phenotypes rather than scalar physicochemical metrics. Three practical barriers remain: mismatched timescales between formulation and biological testing, heterogeneous data combining quantitative measurements with imaging and biological variability across platforms and donors. We set out near-term engineering and standardization priorities within a staged roadmap that separates plausible short-term milestones from longer-horizon goals.
authors: Yi-Chan Lin; Izabella Komperda

title: Autonomous Quantum Measurement with Agentic AI
abstract: Quantum materials exhibit diverse electronic and functional phenomena, but their characterization requires extensive experimental expertise, iterative decision-making and accumulated laboratory knowledge that is difficult to document and transfer. Here we introduce Quantum Agent (QUANTA), an agentic artificial intelligence (AI) framework for autonomous quantum-materials characterization. Using a widely adopted Physical Property Measurement System (PPMS) as an experimental platform, QUANTA combines retrieval augmentation using scientific literature, experimental protocols and prior measurements with specialized agents for experimental planning, troubleshooting, and data interpretation. A separate deterministic control layer validates instrument actions. Guided by incoming data, QUANTA evaluates measurement quality, revises experimental plans and selects subsequent measurements. We demonstrate these capabilities through transport measurements of the topological Weyl semimetal TaP, as well as investigations of nonlinear responses in magnetic material Co2MnGa. These results establish QUANTA as a generalizable framework for evidence-driven, safeguarded and closed-loop quantum-materials characterization.
authors: Eunbi Rha; Abhijatmedhi Chotrattanapituk; Mouyang Cheng; Chung-tao Chou; Shenyong Ye; Ashley S. Dale; Long Ju; Luqiao Liu; Mingda Li

title: Autonomous Science Bench: Evaluating AI Agents for Autonomous Scientific Discovery
abstract: AI agents for autonomous scientific discovery must decide which experiments to run under a limited budget. Most benchmarks for science agents provide fixed datasets, while others that support active experimentation largely rely on simulation. We introduce Autonomous Science Bench, an initial release comprising six budgeted design-build-test-learn campaigns grounded in published experiments across biology, chemistry, and materials science. Agents select batches of designs, receive measurements from a lab service, and use the results to guide subsequent experiments before delivering a predictive model. Success requires passing two calibrated gates: a discovery gate, which evaluates the designs the agent measured, and a learning gate, which evaluates its model's ranking of held-out designs. In a pilot evaluation of ten agent-model configurations and 180 trials, the best configuration succeeds in 72% of trials, while the hardest campaign is solved in only five of 30 attempts. The two gates reveal different weaknesses: some agents build accurate rankings but find too few promising designs, while others find promising designs but fail to predict which unseen designs will perform well. These differences are obscured by overall success rates alone. We release version 0.1 of the campaigns, lab runtime, and public leaderboard at https://asb.open-ssi.org/.
authors: Yibo Wen; Han Liu

title: Autonomous adaptive spectral analysis with an LLM agent for self-driving laboratories
abstract: Self-driving laboratories accelerate materials exploration through autonomous closed-loop integration of synthesis, characterization, and next-experiment selection. However, characterization does not always directly provide the target property; measured spectra or images often require automated analysis to extract quantitative descriptors based on physically motivated assumptions and predefined criteria. Such procedures can fail for measurements outside these criteria, requiring a decision on whether a reliable value can be recovered or no numerical value should be reported. Here, we implemented an autonomous adaptive spectral-analysis agent using a large language model (LLM) to supervise a deterministic numerical-analysis routine. For each spectrum, the agent executes the predefined analysis script and assesses the result using the measured spectrum and fitting diagnostics. Valid results are accepted unchanged, recoverable failures are reanalyzed through bounded adjustments of predefined fitting parameters, and NaN (not a number) is returned when no scientifically defensible value can be obtained. We evaluated the workflow on optical transmittance spectra from 203 epitaxial beta-Ga2O3 films grown during a previously reported self-driving thin-film growth campaign. The predefined optical analysis script returned Urbach energy, an optical-quality metric, for 183 spectra and failed for 20. The agent retained those 183 values and evaluated 20 exception cases, recovering 16 through bounded parameter adjustments and returning NaN for 4 when the spectral evidence did not support a reliable Urbach tail. The audit records captured spectral features, parameter changes, and rationale for each decision. These results demonstrate autonomous scientific exception handling by an LLM agent while leaving quantitative property extraction to deterministic numerical analysis.
authors: Yuki K. Wakabayashi; Yui Ogawa

title: BEAKER: An Expert-Curated Benchmark for Embodied Brains in Self-Driving Chemical Laboratories
abstract: Self-Driving Chemical Laboratories (SDCLs) are moving chemical experimentation toward embodied automation, where machines must perceive laboratory scenes, reason about experimental states, and act under physical, procedural, and safety constraints. Although Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly considered as embodied brains for such systems, existing laboratory benchmarks mainly focus on safety, anomaly detection, or general scientific understanding, leaving their execution-oriented embodied capabilities underexplored. To fill this gap, we introduce BEAKER, a Benchmark for evaluating Embodied Actionability, Knowledge, Experimentation, and Reasoning in SDCLs. BEAKER contains 1,000 expert-curated question-answer samples across 11 image and video task types, covering key judgments required for chemical laboratory execution, including affordance grounding, trajectory planning, equipment, state, and safety recognition, apparatus setup, operation and step reasoning, and temporal procedure reasoning. All questions and annotations are manually created and reviewed by chemistry and embodied Artificial Intelligence (AI) experts, without AI-assisted generation or annotation. We evaluate 28 general-purpose, science-oriented, chemistry-specialized, and embodied MLLMs in an offline, single-turn setting. Results show that current models can follow coarse experimental procedures in videos, but still struggle to ground actions into operable regions and feasible trajectories, to recognize fine-grained laboratory apparatus, states, and safety norms, and to order steps in mid-length procedures. BEAKER thus reveals a clear gap between coarse procedural understanding and the precise, action-grounded perception required for laboratory execution, providing a diagnostic benchmark for future MLLMs in SDCLs.
authors: Fei Lin; Tengchao Zhang; Ziyang Gong; Xiaotong Yu; Bohan Zhang; Yifan Zhou; Qihao Yang; Ji Dai; Dong Li; Yining Jiang; Qinghua Ni; Jun Huang; Qiang Zhang; Yue Zhou; Zhihang Zhong; Yonglin Tian; Fei-Yue Wang; Xue Yang

title: Best Practices for Unsupervised Learning in Molecular Systems
abstract: Unsupervised learning is used throughout computational molecular science on unlabeled data such as molecular dynamics trajectories and conformer ensembles. Some questions admit no predefined labels at all: how many conformational states a molecule visits, whether a virtual library covers chemical space, or which structures are unlike anything else in the set. Clustering, dimensionality reduction, and density estimation serve both cases. They are easy to apply, and their output generally appears like a discovery, whether or not it is one. Establishing a new discovery is difficult, because there is no held-out target to check against. This guide is a prescriptive companion to the review literature: it sets out what to do at each stage of the pipeline these analyses share (curate, split, represent, scale, reduce, group, validate), why each step matters, and what goes wrong when it is skipped, with a checklist for each stage. The representation, the distance metric, and the scaling usually decide the outcome, not the chosen algorithm. An apparently structured low-dimensional map is not evidence that structure exists, and null models, stability analysis, and cheap baselines should be used. Statistical practice in molecular machine learning is not widespread, so we give a comparison protocol covering resampling variability, dependence between repeated estimates, multiple comparisons, and post-selection effects. Leakage and splitting are treated in depth, and we provide accompanying notebooks to run each recommendation on molecular data.
authors: Rhyan Barrett; Arnav Brahmasandra; Bingqing Cheng; Grégory Fonseca; Ivan Gilardoni; Rocío Mercado; T. Oestereich; Max Pinheiro; Hessam Yazdani

title: Beyond Candidate Generation: A Validation-First Protocol for AI-Assisted Transition-State Discovery
abstract: Machine-learned models can now propose three-dimensional transition-state (TS) geometries in seconds, but a candidate geometry is not a validated TS. The gap between a plausible structure and a mechanistically meaningful barrier—one imaginary frequency, the intended atom pair, the correct connectivity, and a consistent electronic state—remains the bottleneck in AI-assisted computational chemistry. We present a validation-first protocol that separates candidate generation from physical validation. The protocol combines (i) a chemical preflight that fixes reactive pairs, spin surfaces, connectivity, and conformers; (ii) a per-point independent scan that localizes the barrier without fragile collective scans; (iii) a constrained reference calculation that produces the Hessian; (iv) an OptTS stage that reuses that Hessian; and (v) a validation stage based on imaginary-mode localization, key bond lengths, IRC endpoints, spin diagnostics, and energy-convention checks. The protocol is implemented as a portable, open-source skill package for local ORCA/xtb and Gaussian/Slurm execution. Case studies from Ni/Fe catalysis illustrate the failure modes the protocol is designed to catch: a generative model produced candidates with 3.6–4.4 Å heavy-atom RMSD for an 84-atom broken-symmetry organometallic system, a collective scan failed three times where a per-point strategy completed 16/16 points, and a single-conformer R/S comparison would have misread a conformerdominated difference. The reported gains of multi-sampling and conformer enumeration are taken from the published benchmark, not measured here. We argue that the near-term role of AI is not to replace electronic-structure judgment but to shrink the search space before it and to make the validation layer reproducible.
authors: Haofan Li

title: Beyond Conventional Culture: Integrating Rapid Molecular Diagnostics, Proteomic Technologies and Artificial Intelligence for Pathogen Identification in Clinical Microbiology
abstract: This research aims to optimize in vitro propagation techniques for ginger (Zingiber officinale Rosc.) by investigating the effects of plant growth regulators (PGRs) on shoot induction, root formation, and callus proliferation. Ginger is an economically valuable crop with medicinal, culinary, and industrial applications, but its conventional propagation through rhizomes is slow, prone to disease, and limits large-scale production, necessitating improved tissue culture techniques. The highest shoot induction (4.9 shoots) occurred at 3.0 mg·L⁻¹ BAP, while optimal shoot length (5.9 cm) was observed at 2.0 mg·L⁻¹ BAP. Root induction was most effective at 3.0 mg·L⁻¹ IAA, producing the highest root count (7.1), with the longest root length (5.3 cm) achieved at 4.0 mg·L⁻¹ IAA. Callus formation was optimized using 1.0 mg·L⁻¹ 2,4-D combined with 0.5 mg·L⁻¹ Kinetin and 0.750 mg·L⁻¹ IAA, leading to the quickest callus initiation (10 days), highest fresh weight (3.5 g), and largest diameter (2.3 cm). Acclimatization trials demonstrated high survival rates, with 93% in the growth chamber, 78% in the shade house, and 81% in open conditions. This study provides an efficient and reproducible tissue culture protocol for the mass production of disease-free, genetically uniform ginger plants, offering a sustainable alternative to traditional propagation methods and significantly improving cultivation practices, ensuring higher yields, better plant quality, and increased availability of superior planting material for agricultural and commercial applications.
authors: Bushra Iqbal; Maham Javaid; Shajeeha Zainab; Sidra Qaisar; Aiman Fatima; Mehwar Batool; Esha Khalil; Sana Shabbir; Muhammad Hasnain Raza
venue: Kashmir Journal of Academic Research and Development

title: Beyond structural complexity: functional validation of vascularized and immune-integrated organoid-on-a-chip models
abstract: Organ-on-a-chip (OoC) platforms combine the self-organizing capacity of organoids with microfluidic control to model tissue environments in vitro . Vascularization and immune-cell integration have expanded the range of tissue features these platforms can reproduce, but the presence of these components does not necessarily indicate functional maturity. This review examines vascularized and immune-integrated OoC models, covering vascular network formation, immune-cell co-culture, and the effects of fluid shear stress, cyclic stretch, and extracellular matrix mechanics. A central challenge is the gap between structural features and functional evidence. Endothelial networks, for example, do not necessarily demonstrate effective perfusion, barrier integrity, or molecular transport. Similarly, the presence or infiltration of immune cells does not establish appropriate trafficking, sustained function, or relevant immune responses. Differences in cell sources and limited standardization further complicate reproducibility. These limitations highlight the need to evaluate OoC models against clearly defined functional criteria rather than structural complexity alone. Functional assays should be comparable across platforms and selected according to the intended application, while reproducibility and scalability remain important considerations. Such validation will help establish the reliability of OoC models for disease modeling and drug evaluation.
authors: Qixiu Jiang; Lin Zhou; Haiqing Bai; Xin Xie

title: Bioengineering strategies for next-generation female reproductive organoids: A roadmap to clinical translation
abstract: The human female reproductive system is characterized by highly dynamic tissue remodeling, cyclical endocrinology, and the precise orchestration of maternal–fetal immune tolerance. Historically, deciphering reproductive pathologies ranging from infertility to obstetric complications and malignancies has been hampered by the fundamental physiological and interspecies disparities inherent in 2D cultures and animal models. While three-dimensional (3D) organoid technology has initiated a paradigm shift, conventional static cultures relying on poorly defined, xenogeneic matrices (e.g., Matrigel) introduce profound immunogenic confounding factors and severe bioengineering bottlenecks. To bridge this gap, this review comprehensively delineates the advanced bioengineering strategies driving the next-generation of female reproductive models. We first outline foundational engineering pillars, highlighting the transition toward intelligent biomaterials, deterministic 3D bioprinting, and microfluidic microenvironments. Subsequently, we critically evaluate state-of-the-art organoid models across the ovary, fallopian tube, the maternal–fetal interface containing endometrium and placenta, cervix, and vagina. We emphasize how multi-lineage “assembloids” and multiorgan microphysiological systems successfully recapitulate transient implantation events and bidirectional endocrine crosstalk. Finally, we propose a strategic roadmap for the field, demonstrating how the integration of materials science, genetics, multi-omics, and engineering methods will overcome current limitations, ultimately accelerating the transition from benchtop in vitro models to standardized clinical diagnostics and reproductive regenerative therapeutics.
authors: Bowen Gao; Jianing Gao; 魏文博; Yixuan Hu; Chengran Hu; Wentao Su; Shuo Chen; Li Wang

title: Biofabrication of osteochondral composite scaffolds: advances in multi-material bioprinting, functional microenvironment engineering and orthopedic translation
abstract: evaluation approaches and major translational barriers such as mechanical mismatch, long-term stability, scalability, and regulatory issues. The integration of multimaterial bioprinting, adaptive biomaterials, and programmable microenvironments may facilitate the development of osteochondral implants with improved tissue integration and translational potential. Future studies should prioritize long-term osteochondral integration, vascular coordination, manufacturing reproducibility, and clinically relevant validation.

title: Biological-Digital-Twin-Driven Microrobotic Sampling Decisions at the Limit STARLI Research Institute XXIX — Flagship Research Monograph 10 What if the next scientific sample could be selected not merely to collect more data, but to distinguish between competing explanations of biological behavior? Biological-Digital-Twin-Driven Microrobotic Sampling Decisions at the Limit explores a prospective research architecture combining versioned biological digital twins, active learning, microrobotic sampling, uncertainty quantification, and mechanistic model discrimination. The central question is whether a computational twin can identify safe, informative sampling actions that distinguish competing biological mechanisms more effectively than conventional experimental schedules, while retaining the ability to recognize model inadequacy and abstain from unsupported decisions. The proposed framework treats biological digital twins as revisable scientific models rather than exact replicas of living systems. Its reference environment is a controlled, nonclinical microfluidic platform containing two declared dynamical mechanisms and a third withheld mechanism reserved for evaluating open-world uncertainty and model failure. The research architecture is organized around five interconnected layers: versioned biological modeling, explicit prior assumptions and knowledge gaps, physically constrained predictive interrogation, comparative adaptive experimentation, and independent requalification. The manuscript develops thirty candidate mathematical research plates covering Bayesian mechanism inference, conditional information gain, experimental identifiability, observation uncertainty, transport dynamics, calibration, model discrepancy, and decision safety. These mathematical structures are connected to eighty-two research chapters, five independently paginated investigation sections per chapter, two hundred detailed Research Gates, and thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos. Each Research Gate is intended as a transferable research question that future investigators may test, challenge, refine, or reject. The proposed evaluation compares twin-guided sampling against optimized fixed schedules, established experimental-design approaches, and alternative active-learning policies under matched physical constraints and experimental budgets. Particular attention is given to blinded mechanism identification, probabilistic calibration, out-of-distribution rejection, specimen integrity, model-version accountability, and explicit stopping conditions. The volume includes DOI-linked methodological literature and a staged nonclinical verification pathway. Scientific status and limitations: This manuscript presents a conceptual methodological research program, not completed experimental validation. Its integrated hypotheses, mathematical proposals, and experimental architectures remain subject to independent technical review and empirical testing. The manuscript does not establish clinical efficacy, diagnostic reliability, therapeutic benefit, or proven superiority of microrobotic digital-twin systems. The work also acknowledges remaining editorial limitations, including recurring methodological language that requires further substantive review before the manuscript can be regarded as a fully refined scientific monograph. The broader purpose of this research is to develop scientific systems that can remain useful even when their initial models are incomplete. Rather than demanding certainty from a digital twin, the proposed framework asks whether future autonomous research tools can become more transparent, corrigible, experimentally accountable, and capable of recognizing the boundaries of their own knowledge. Within the STARLI research continuum, this volume is intended as an evolving research inheritance for future human and artificial-intelligence investigators. title: Biology-informed virtual staining enables label-free detection of cell state transitions at the single-cell level
abstract: Assessing cell viability and death pathways is central to biomedical research, yet conventional fluorescence-based live/dead assays are invasive, labour-intensive, and limited in capturing dynamic transitions. Deep learning-based virtual staining has emerged as a noninvasive alternative, but its accuracy remains restricted by the inconsistencies and artifacts inherently present in chemically stained training datasets. Here, we introduce a biology-informed augmented staining framework that integrates human-in-the-loop curation with generative adversarial networks to translate phase-contrast microscopy images into reliable virtual fluorescence representations. By imposing biologically motivated constraints — such as replacing unreliable labels with controlled synthetic noise — we mitigate biases in conventional datasets and improve the representation of live, unhealthy (early apoptotic), and dead cells. Using human endothelial cells subjected to oxidative stress in microfluidic devices, we demonstrate that our approach recapitulates population-level fluorescence viability dynamics while also enabling analysis at single-cell resolution. Transition points between viability states are automatically detected by comparing smoothed intensity traces and quantifying change points with associated transition bands. In an independent experiment comprising 20 cells and 2000 frames, assessed by three annotators blinded to the predictions, biology-informed training increased the macro-averaged F1 score from 0.57 to 0.78 and Cohen’s kappa from 0.34 to 0.65 compared with training on raw fluorescence labels. This analysis also reveals substantial heterogeneity in apoptotic onset and progression, consistent with morphological cues. Our results establish biology-informed virtual staining as a strategy to extend the scope of image translation methods, enabling label-free, longitudinal, and accurate single-cell monitoring of viability states. This approach addresses the key bottleneck of training data reliability and provides a framework for integrating domain knowledge into machine learning methods for biological imaging.
authors: Sergi Masó-Orriols; Jesús Pineda; Zofia Korczak; Benjamin Midtvedt; Jesús A Dominguez; Montse Masoliver; J. Bertrán; Giovanni Volpe; Carlo Manzo; Caroline B. Adiels

title: Biomaterials and biofabrication in the Netherlands: state of the art in 2026
abstract: Biomaterials and biofabrication are multidisciplinary and rapidly evolving fields that enable innovations that are crucial for addressing current healthcare challenges. The Netherlands has a broad, active, and collaborative research community that is developing advanced biomaterials and cutting.edge biofabrication methods, with applications in tissue engineering, regenerative medicine, in vitro disease modeling, and biomedical devices. Dutch researchers have pioneered advanced biofabrication, supramolecular and inorganic chemistry for creating biomaterials, organoids and organ-on-chip in vitro platforms, and regenerative medicine. This paper presents recent work on biomaterials and biofabrication and their applications from 11 prominent research institutions across the Netherlands, and it describes joint initiatives that target broader goals within the field. Contributors from each institution provide insights into recent progress, key scientific contributions, and forward-looking perspectives. By presenting the state-of-the-art research landscape, this article serves as a reference for scientists actively engaged in or planning to initiate biofabrication or biomaterials-related research, offering guidance on technology selection, experimental design, academic collaboration, and translational development.
authors: Jing Nie; Eric Farrell; Matthew B. title: Biomedical properties and emerging translational potential of bovine milk extracellular vesicles
abstract: Extracellular vesicles have garnered significant attention in the biomedical field due to their potential as therapeutic agents and diagnostic tools. Bovine milk extracellular vesicles (BMEVs), in particular, have emerged as a promising tool in biomedical research due to their unique biocompatibility, stability, and ease of isolation. As an alternative to extracellular vesicles sourced from human cells, such as stem cells or blood, these naturally occurring nanovesicles are increasingly recognized for their dual role as potential therapeutic carriers and diagnostic candidates. To map the evolution and knowledge structure of the field, we conducted a CiteSpace analysis that reveals how BMEVs research has expanded beyond nutritional science to emerge as a versatile biomedical platform with rapidly broadening applications. Also, this review systematically examines the biogenesis, isolation techniques, and structural features of BMEVs, while highlighting their applications in drug delivery, disease therapy, and diagnostics. Current preclinical studies provide preclinical evidence supporting potential therapeutic applications. However, clinical safety, therapeutic efficacy, reproducibility, dosing, biodistribution, immunogenicity, large-scale manufacturing, and regulatory acceptance remain to be established. Future research should focus on optimizing drug-loading strategies, enhancing targeted delivery, and exploring novel biomedical applications.
authors: Xiaoqi Guan; Xinxin Hou; Wanting Meng; Hai-dong Guo

title: Bioprinting-Enabled Customization of Biohybrid Actuators: Scaling Dimensions and Functional Complexity
abstract: Biohybrid actuators integrate living contractile cells with engineered materials, combining biological force generation with the structural and functional control offered by synthetic components. However, translating engineered muscle tissue into reproducible, high-performance biohybrid robots remains limited by tissue organization, matrix degradation, force transmission, and long-term functional stability. This review analyzes how biofabrication parameters and material properties influence tissue maturation and actuator-level performance, with particular emphasis on bioprinting. We compare muscle cell sources; extrusion-based, embedded, and light-assisted fabrication strategies; and scaffold biomaterials using reported structural and functional outcomes. We also evaluate electrical and optical activation and mechanical conditioning, distinguishing their roles in controlling contraction and promoting maturation. The comparison highlights a gap between architectural control during fabrication and reproducible robotic performance: methods that produce complex muscle constructs do not necessarily yield integrated devices with validated force transmission or locomotion. Tissue maturation, tissue-material interfaces, and nutrient transport emerge as closely coupled priorities for scaling functional constructs. We conclude with a framework for standardized benchmarking and discuss multimaterial printing, data-driven design, and feedback control as complementary routes toward more reproducible and capable biohybrid actuators.

title: Boundary Genesis Omega v43: Universal Null–Void Ceiling, Recoverability-Constrained Meta-Science, and Terminal Material Closure
abstract: Boundary Genesis Omega v43 presents an executable research-governance architecture for distinguishing mathematical closure, evidentiary sufficiency, scientific uncertainty, and terminal material closure within a recoverability-constrained research system. The edition introduces a Universal Null–Void Ceiling that prevents unsupported conclusions from being promoted into scientific, clinical, legal, or operational authority. It provides explicit classification of evidence states, scope-bounded closure rules, deterministic audit procedures, reopening conditions, and human-first safeguards. The architecture extends the available Boundary Genesis Omega v41–v42 research components and incorporates the Null–Void Ceiling as a governing constraint on formal reasoning and research claims. Its primary application context is the evaluation of scientific hypotheses and causal assumptions associated with human vision restoration, including biological mechanisms, neural pathways, implantable technologies, computational models, and human-machine research systems. The edition does not claim that human vision restoration has been achieved, that a novel biological mechanism has been experimentally demonstrated, or that all scientific possibilities have been exhausted. 1. Research problem Complex scientific and computational systems may generate large numbers of hypotheses, combinations, mathematical derivations, simulations, and apparent discoveries. However, formal completeness within a specified model does not establish completeness of physical reality. A system may exhaust a finite combination space while leaving fundamental questions unresolved concerning biological mechanisms, experimental reproducibility, measurement validity, causal identification, patient-specific variation, and clinical effectiveness. Boundary Genesis Omega v43 addresses the risk of confusing these different forms of closure. It establishes explicit conditions under which a claim must remain open, may be provisionally closed within a defined scope, or must be reopened following new material evidence. 2. Universal Null–Void Ceiling The Universal Null–Void Ceiling defines the limit beyond which the system cannot legitimately assert conclusions from its available records. The architecture distinguishes six evidentiary states: NULL: No evidence is recorded. VOID: No admissible successor exists within the declared model. UNKNOWN: Evidence is available, but it is insufficient to justify a definite conclusion. CONTRADICTORY: The available evidence contains unresolved conflicts. REFUTED: Explicit counterevidence is recorded. SUPPORTED: The record explicitly documents adequate evidence, validated measurement, and independent replication. These classifications concern the contents and sufficiency of supplied research records. They are not independent certifications of external scientific truth. The Null–Void Ceiling prevents absence of evidence, unmeasured conditions, or computational silence from being interpreted as proof of nonexistence, biological failure, clinical effectiveness, or consent. 3. Terminal material closure Terminal material closure is defined as a scope-bounded determination rather than universal scientific finality. A record may be materially closed only when its required information is present and its documented scope meets one of the permitted terminal conditions: VOID, REFUTED, or SUPPORTED. Records containing unresolved uncertainty or contradictory evidence remain open. Every materially closed record remains reopenable when new evidence changes the relevant distinction. The architecture explicitly rejects the assertion that all scientific possibilities have been exhausted. 4. Recoverability-constrained governance The framework applies human-first governance requirements to research classification, computational inference, scientific communication, and possible future clinical applications. Its safeguards include: Silence must not be interpreted as consent. Unknown biological states must not be classified as intact. Absence of evidence must not be interpreted as proof of nonexistence. Simulations must not be represented as clinical demonstrations. No automatic authorization for human intervention is permitted. Mathematical enumeration must not be represented as exhaustive biological knowledge. Conclusions must remain bounded by their documented scope. Counterexamples and contradictory records must be preserved. Clinical claims require human expert review. Material new evidence must permit reopening. These principles preserve the distinction between scientific exploration and authorized intervention. 5. Scientific and interdisciplinary scope The research architecture identifies material evidence gaps across twelve domains: Mathematics and formal models Meta-laws and foundational assumptions Derivations and proof obligations Biological mechanisms Neural and visual pathways Implantable and assistive technologies Artificial intelligence and computational systems Clinical evidence Governance and authorization Ethics and informed consent Measurement and experimental validation Scientific novelty and independent verification The architecture is intended to support structured scientific scrutiny rather than substitute for experimental investigation. 6. Executable software components The distribution includes Python research engines, executable tests, documentation, and a machine-readable material-gap register. The v43 component provides commands for: Displaying the supported research domains. Generating a structured research-record template. Auditing an input record against the Null–Void evidence classification. Producing a machine-readable audit result. Verifying the integrity of an audit record. Running deterministic software tests. The included v41 and v42 components are preserved as earlier research layers. The archive does not contain every historical Boundary Genesis Omega edition. 7. Formal closure versus scientific discovery The software implements deterministic evidence-state classification and scope-bounded closure rules. Successful execution establishes behavior of the implemented program under its tests. It does not independently establish the truth of the submitted evidence, the validity of an experimental hypothesis, or the effectiveness of a medical intervention. In particular, the archive does not demonstrate a new treatment capable of restoring human vision. Any proposed biological or technological breakthrough requires appropriate experimental evidence, independent replication, functional outcome assessment, and applicable ethical and regulatory authorization. 8. Non-circular stopping and reopening The architecture introduces a non-circular stopping principle. A research branch should stop when the same evidence, assumptions, and predictions are repeated without producing a material distinction. The branch may reopen when new observations, independent replication, counterexamples, distinct falsifiable predictions, or relevant changes in human needs and preferences become available. The stopping condition therefore limits unsupported recursive assertion without permanently prohibiting future discovery. 9. Relationship to Recoverability-Constrained Systems and Continuity Science Boundary Genesis Omega v43 is presented as a domain-specific research-software contribution within the wider Recoverability-Constrained Systems and Continuity Science corpus associated with Noelia Sanchez and Interval Studio. Its Null–Void Ceiling is intended to connect finite successor-space reasoning, recoverability-constrained admissibility, recursive governance, evidentiary distinction, and terminal closure. The edition operationalizes the principle that computational closure must remain separate from scientific certainty and human authorization. 10. Reproducibility The archive provides executable Python components and deterministic tests. Users can generate research templates, evaluate structured records, inspect audit outcomes, and verify recorded audit integrity. Reproducibility of the software is distinct from independent reproduction of biological or clinical findings. 11. Limitations The distribution is a research-governance and methodological software artifact. It is not a medical device, a clinically validated diagnostic system, an autonomous laboratory, or an authorization framework for human experimentation. It does not establish universal scientific completeness, experimentally verified biological discoveries, or regulatory approval. Evidence classifications depend on the supplied records and the implemented rules. 12. Terminal material-closure determination The edition reaches a defined software-level stopping boundary. The declared evidence states, classification procedures, and closure conditions are implemented within the available research package. Unresolved scientific evidence gaps remain open. The system must not promote unsupported conclusions beyond the available evidence. The recorded stopping reason is the absence of a new material distinction sufficient to justify stronger claims. Future research remains admissible when genuinely new evidence, reproducible counterexamples, independent experiments, or meaningful changes in human needs arise. Final determination: Formal software closure within the declared scope; scientific and clinical discovery remain open.
