While optical methods remain indispensable for visualizing cellular behavior, their limitations in long-term, multi-parameter, and quantitative monitoring have increasingly motivated the integration of sensors directly within MPS. This review focuses on the engineering strategies underlying sensor fabrication and integration in MPSs. We first highlight representative examples of physiological parameters that have been measured using sensor-integrated MPSs. We then summarize recent advances ranging from micro electromechanical system (MEMS)-based microfabrication approaches to emerging additive fabrication techniques, as well as the direct incorporation of commercially available sensors. Key engineering considerations for sensor fabrication and integration are discussed to provide practical guidance for the design of sensor-integrated MPSs. By providing a fabrication- and integration-focused overview of sensor-enabled MPSs, this review aims to inform the rational design of next-generation platforms capable of high-precision, multimodal, and in situ biological monitoring. These advances are expected to accelerate the translation of MPS technologies toward more predictive disease models, improved drug screening platforms, and broader applications in translational biomedical research.
authors: Minseung Shin; Jun Sang Choi; Namgu Kang; Song Ih Ahn

title: Engineering antimicrobial peptides through the design–build–test–learn framework
abstract: The rapid emergence of antimicrobial resistance has intensified the need for alternative anti-infective strategies. Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) offer diverse mechanisms of action, but their translation remains constrained by poor physiological stability, host toxicity, and manufacturing costs. This review examines AMP development within a design-build-test-learn (DBTL) framework that connects computational discovery, peptide production, experimental evaluation, and iterative optimization. Proteome mining and generative artificial intelligence expand the accessible sequence space, while solid-phase synthesis, engineered microbial hosts, and cell-free systems convert selected sequences into testable molecules. Chemical modification and formulation provide complementary routes to improve stability and delivery. Standardized screening and in vivo studies then establish the evidence needed to prioritize candidates and inform subsequent design and production decisions. Throughout this cycle, activity must be optimized together with toxicity, stability, manufacturability, and delivery rather than treated as the sole measure of success. This review discusses applications in medicine, agriculture, food preservation, and biotechnology, and identifies remaining limitations in data quality, assay comparability, scale-up, and translational support. The DBTL framework provides a basis for coordinating these activities, although its practical value depends on experimentally validated feedback and application-specific development criteria.
authors: Xu Yinbiao; Jingbo Xu; ZHU Wanting; Wenhao Zhang; Peizhao Yang; Rui Chen; Xuanzheng Li; Haosheng Lin; Junhao Luo; Yongjie Ma; Kangjia Jiang; Jinyuan Hu

title: Engineering ex vivo T-cell expansion for CAR-T therapy: bridging biological fidelity and bioprocess scalability through platforms, functional consumables, and integrated closed manufacturing
abstract: Background: Chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR-T) cell therapy has changed the treatment of relapsed or refractory B-cell malignancies and multiple myeloma, but manufacturing time, cost, variability, and access remain major barriers. Scope: In this critical narrative review, we position ex vivo T-cell expansion at the interface of biological signaling and engineering design and dissect how each unit operation-from selection and activation to harvest and formulation-influences the final therapeutic product. Key advances: Static gas-permeable culture, rocking-motion and stirred-tank bioreactors, hollow-fiber and perfusion systems, biomaterial scaffolds, microcarriers, and defined activation nanoparticles offer distinct routes to scalable expansion. Closed automated platforms now integrate multiple unit operations, while microfluidic systems, rapid manufacturing, and process analytical technologies (PAT) create new possibilities for monitoring and control, with data-driven and AI-assisted prediction emerging as supporting tools rather than established capabilities. Challenges: Expansion remains constrained by the trade-off between cell number and preservation of memory phenotype, metabolic fitness, and potency. Donor variability, raw-material quality, consumable dependence, limited interoperability, and incomplete potency assays complicate standardization. Outlook: Future progress will depend on coordinated development of defined raw materials, functionally designed consumables, closed-system engineering, interoperable automation, and data-driven process control. The goal is not simply to expand more cells, but to reproducibly manufacture the right cells at an acceptable cost.
authors: Qingzhi Wu; Menghui Jiang; Yuanyuan Li; Hui Huo; Haoyuan Cheng; Tian Jia; Yushu Wang; Ziwei Wang; Mengdie Ji; Jingjing Lin; Deyue Jiang; 张娜; Fuliang Chen

title: Engineering multifunctional materials and smart recognition probes for holistic electrochemical affinity biosensing
abstract: Affinity-based electrochemical biosensing evolves from conventional molecular detection platforms toward intelligent, multifunctional, and decentralized systems capable of making decisions in near real time based on comprehensive biochemical information. This transformation has been driven by advances in multifunctional materials and smart recognition probes that improve sensitivity, selectivity, signal transduction, robustness, analytical versatility and decentralized applicability. Multifunctional materials, including sustainable and functional hybrid nanomaterials, enable interface engineering, affinity bioassays, and signal amplification, while smart probes comprise structure-changing, multiblock, multifunctional, multivalent, and fully synthetic recognition elements. This review highlights representative strategies that integrate these innovations to develop simple, cost-effective, reagent-free, fully integrated, and adaptive biosensor platforms for continuous, multiplexed, and real-time analysis, expanding their capabilities beyond conventional detection. Finally, current challenges and future perspectives are discussed, emphasizing how advances in materials and probe engineering are driving the development of intelligent, adaptive, autonomous electrochemical biosensors for personalized, sustainable, and decentralized healthcare and environmental monitoring.
authors: Susana Campuzano; María Gamella; Víctor Ruiz‐Valdepeñas Montiel; Rebeca Magnolia Torrente-Rodríguez; Verónica Serafín; María Pedrero; José Manuel Pingarrón

title: Engineering signal transduction for closed-loop gene and cell therapies
abstract: Chronic diseases are still treated largely with interventions that are constitutive, intermittently administered and poorly aligned with real-time physiology. Synthetic biology is changing this paradigm by treating gene circuits as programmable genetic software that can be deployed across cellular therapeutic hardware spanning from prokaryotic to eukaryotic systems, including probiotic cells, designer cells, immune cells and stem‑cell‑derived platforms. In this framework, engineered systems can sense disease-associated signals, compute them through synthetic or repurposed transduction pathways and adjust therapeutic output to maintain physiological variables within a desired range. Closed-loop therapeutics therefore begin to merge diagnosis, treatment and prevention within the same living platform. Across metabolism, inflammation, infection, cardiovascular regulation and cancer, early mammalian systems show that endogenous sensing, intracellular computation and therapeutic actuation can be combined in clinically relevant architectures. The emerging concept of setpoint medicine captures the clinical ambition of these systems: not simply to deliver a dose, but to keep physiology within an interpretable and therapeutically desirable range. Realizing this vision will require durable and modular control circuits, hardware-aware delivery strategies, interpretable safety frameworks, controller-style performance metrics and increasingly AI-assisted design, calibration and oversight. If these challenges can be met, the future of therapy may be defined less by intermittent dosing than by the continuous control of physiology.
authors: Haifeng Ye; Martin Fussenegger

title: Enzyme-Immobilized Nanomaterials for Endocrine Disorders: Therapeutic Innovation and Translational Challenges
abstract: Endocrine disorders result from chronic disturbances in the hormonal regulation and feedback control, which cause metabolic, reproductive, and systemic complications. Despite the advances in disease management with current therapies such as hormone replacement or multi-pathway pharmacological therapies, problems with variable patient response, side effects and the need for continuous monitoring and dose adjustment remain. To overcome some of these limitations, enzyme-immobilized nanomaterials have become attractive platforms for providing controlled biochemical interactions, catalytic activity and enzyme stability for therapeutic and diagnostic purposes. Enzymes can be immobilized using adsorption, covalent binding, cross-linking and entrapment to minimize denaturation, enhance reusability and improve operational performance. At the nanoscale level, other advantages of having high surface area and tunable interfacial chemistry are the better orientation of the enzyme, mass transfer and control over enzyme activity. There are other benefits for magnetic and field responsive nanomaterials in recovery, re-use, scalable processing and regenerable biosensing systems. In this review, the therapeutic potential of enzyme-immobilized nanomaterials for endocrine diseases has been discussed, focusing on the concepts of nanobiocatalyst design, biosensing for endocrine diseases, and the promise of biomanufacturing in the same field. It also points to some of the main hurdles facing the clinical translation of these technologies, such as problems with enzyme leaching, diffusion limitations, loss of interfacial activity, reproducibility issues, long-term stability, and safety evaluation requirements.
authors: Bingya Zhang; Jun Zhang; 何扬芳

title: EnzymeRSI: A dual-loop recursive self-improvement system for enzyme design
abstract: Enzyme engineering usually optimises which candidates to assay within a fixed model and workflow; when the bottleneck is a mismatched method or a failing workflow, that route is hard to escape. We present EnzymeRSI, a dual-loop system for recursive self-improvement (RSI). The outer loop evolves harness assets without changing model weights; the inner loop develops prediction and selection algorithms under controlled conditions; a cloud laboratory system is specified for closing the physical loop with quality-controlled feedback. The outer loop raised the mean development-set Spearman correlation on ProteinGym by 0.044 across five assays, reaching 0.335 on CD19 and 0.683 on OPSD (rhodopsin); of the two first places, only CD19 was produced by the outer loop itself. In ThermoMPNN self-improvement the inner loop reached a PCC of 0.849, and on TadA-Bench a Spearman correlation of 0.307 in 1.13 h. We examined the system's experimental decision-making in three enzyme systems. For the luciferase RLuc, 10 of the 32 nominated substitutions not pre-specified reached at least twice wild-type activity in a single round. For the cytidine deaminase A3A, a variant selected by a rule that caps loss of unmodified C raised 5mC conversion in the weaker CT context from 11.4% to 46.5% and reversed the substrate preference in both contexts. For the DNA polymerase KOD-E, 189 single-substitution variants defined a landscape on which different objective functions selected divergent next steps from the same parent; one assayed combination reached 31.1 times the parent on a modified substrate. By treating the organisation of research and the development of algorithms as separately scored objects of evolution, and linking a frozen decision record to a physical measurement, this work offers an evolutionary paradigm for moving beyond the blind spots of a fixed method and for autonomous enzyme engineering.
authors: Genoria AI Team; 侯曰杰; Lixiang Yang; Yisi Liu; Weiting Tang; Yueyuxiao Yang; Meng Yang

title: Enzymes can activate and mobilize dense biomolecular condensates across scales
abstract: Biomolecular condensates have so far been studied in terms of their structural, compositional, and functional properties. However, condensate enzymatic activity - a key aspect of cellular metabolism - remains unexplored due to the complexity of the system. In this study, using a combination of experimental, computational and theoretical techniques, we have discovered that the non-equilibrium activity which originates from catalytic reactions couples with the environment through various feedback mechanisms across five orders of magnitude of length scales. We observe that condensed enzymes catalyze more rapidly in the presence of crowding proteins and show that the increased enzymatic activity within these droplets stems from the emergence of lower-energy protein conformations induced by the highly crowded environment. Despite the crowding in the environment of the droplet, which might suggest an effective increase in its overall viscosity, we find that it becomes more agile, as evidenced by the observation of enhanced diffusion and macroscopic flow, due to the enzymatic activity. These findings shed light on the dynamic interplay between enzymatic activity, composition and crowding in condensates, and their roles on the mobility and accessibility of various functional units in these environments, expanding our understanding of liquid-liquid phase separation in metabolically active conditions.
authors: Mirco Dindo; Jakob Metson; Weitong Ren; Michalis Chatzittofi; Kiyoshi Yagi; Alessandro Bevilacqua; Erika Fukuhara; Yuji Sugita; Ramin Golestanian; Paola Laurino

title: Establishment of a Responsive Tooth‐on‐a‐Chip Platform for the Assessment of Regenerative Factors in Dental Tissue Regeneration
abstract: Tooth formation relies on reciprocal signaling between embryological dental epithelial (DE) and mesenchymal (DM) cells, orchestrating the formation of enamel, dentin, and vascularized pulp. Current regenerative strategies aim to recreate DE-DM signaling, yet responsive in vitro platforms that faithfully reconstruct this interface and enable benchmarking of candidate cues are unavailable. Herein, a tooth-on-a-chip with a reconstructed DE-DM interface was tested for cue-specific tissue maturation in vitro. The platform comprises a polydimethylsiloxane microfluidic device integrating a fibrin-based mesenchymal compartment with an overlying epithelial layer. The system was exposed to two developmental inducers, sequential fibroblast growth factor 10 (FGF10) and bone morphogenetic protein 4 (BMP4), and BMP2, as well as the clinically used enamel matrix derivative Emdogain, to emulate distinct inductive environments. The platform robustly supported interface formation and revealed cue-specific maturation trajectories with high experimental reproducibility. Notably, Emdogain induced enamel organ-like structural maturation, revealing a previously unrecognized pro-enamel (amelogenic) activity of a biomaterial that has been used clinically for over three decades. Together, these findings validated the tooth-on-a-chip system as a biologically relevant in vitro test platform, providing a translational framework for benchmarking regenerative cues and guiding the development of dental regenerative therapies.
authors: Chong Huang; Wei Ji; Fang Yang; X. Frank Walboomers

title: Experimental reasoning in large language models
abstract: Scientific reasoning requires interaction with the physical world: designing experiments, interpreting outcomes, and deciding what experiment should come next. Here we show that general-purpose large language models (LLMs) already possess substantial capabilities for experimental reasoning. We connected LLMs to a liquid-handling robot and camera through PEARL, which provides perception, action, and persistent state. Given objectives rather than prescribed workflows, the system designed and successfully executed experiments, interpreted observations, and revised its approach as evidence accumulated. When information was insufficient, PEARL autonomously designed and performed intermediate experiments to acquire it. In quantitative enzyme characterization, it judged whether measurements were sufficient, new data were required, or conditions needed to change. Across eight scenarios, these behaviors were reliable with limited agent scaffolding and no supplied scenario-specific recovery recipes. More broadly, general-purpose LLMs may provide a reasoning layer between scientific objectives and physical experimentation, shifting laboratory automation from executing predefined procedures toward AI systems that participate directly in the experimental process.
authors: Jeongyheon Kim; Philip Romero

title: Expert consensus on neuro‐musculoskeletal functional reconstruction for post‐stroke spastic hemiplegia
abstract: Persistent motor dysfunction in post-stroke spastic hemiplegia may result from impaired voluntary motor control, abnormal muscle overactivity, fixed structural restriction, muscle force imbalance, or their combination. Advances in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs), peripheral nerve surgery, and tendon and soft-tissue reconstruction have expanded therapeutic options, yet optimal indications and sequencing remain unclear. A multidisciplinary expert panel reviewed current evidence, addressed key clinical questions, and developed consensus recommendations for noninvasive BCI, diagnostic motor nerve block (DNB), selective or hyperselective peripheral nerve surgery, and reconstructive procedures. The consensus emphasizes evaluation of four major components: central voluntary motor impairment, dynamic abnormal muscle overactivity, fixed structural limitations, and muscle force imbalance. Treatment should be guided by the patient's functional goals and the primary factor restricting performance. Task-oriented motor training remains fundamental when voluntary motor control is impaired, with BCI-based closed-loop training as a potential adjunct in selected patients. Focal, functionally significant muscle overactivity caused by abnormal neural drive may be considered for selective or hyperselective peripheral nerve surgery, with DNB assisting patient selection. Fixed structural restrictions may require tendon or soft-tissue procedures, while muscle force imbalance may benefit from tendon transfer or other dynamic reconstruction. When multiple impairments coexist, combined reconstruction followed by targeted motor retraining and comprehensive reassessment may be appropriate. Overall, neuro-musculoskeletal functional reconstruction should follow an individualized pathway linking functional goals, dominant pathophysiology, treatment targets, and outcomes. Given the variable evidence quality, no universal treatment sequence or combination strategy is currently supported.
authors: Peng Wen; Y.-Z. Wang; Zhongzheng He; Zhizhong Zhu; Chunbing Chen; Kaifeng Wu; Xiaohong Fu; Guoguang Zhao; Liu‐Lin Xiong

title: Explore or Confirm? LLM Agents Misallocate Measurements Under Noise
abstract: As model reasoning gets cheaper, the physical experiment becomes the slow and costly step in discovery. Each experiment returns a noisy reading: a high value can mean a good candidate or a lucky draw. With a fixed budget, an AI agent must keep choosing between exploring a new candidate and confirming a promising one by re-testing it. We measure that choice in Wellocate, a simulated assay campaign with known true values. It is built on a generated landscape and on two real protein datasets, GB1 and PhoQ, scrambled so no model can answer from memory. We test five language models as minimal agents, with no tools and no memory beyond the history in each prompt. They misallocate in both directions. Three over-confirm, spending most of the budget re-testing. On the generated landscape one under-confirms, trusting single readings, and there every model ends with a worse final pick than a basic scripted strategy. Each failure has its own cause. The over-confirmers run short of new candidates worth trying: a list of untried candidates cuts their re-testing and, on real protein data, makes two of them pick much better. A running summary of their readings or a description of the landscape changes it by at most five percentage points. For the under-confirmer, re-testing its top candidates in a final round, replayed on its own campaigns, recovers only about a quarter of what it loses by picking the wrong candidate. This suggests confirmation has to run through the whole campaign. We release Wellocate as a benchmark and reinforcement-learning environment with frozen splits and scripted baselines. With it, anyone can measure how an agent splits its budget before trusting it with real experiments, and train agents to split it better. Code, data and the environment are available at https://github.com/Xstendyl/wellocate.
authors: Abdul Karim; Matt Keon

title: Exploring the Implementation Potential of Integrating Diabetes Care Into Tuberculosis Services in Pakistan: A Qualitative Case Study
abstract: BACKGROUND: The co-occurrence of diabetes and tuberculosis (TB) worsens outcomes for both conditions, increasing mortality risk and treatment failure. Despite the need for integrated care for the two conditions, evidence on feasible and context-specific implementation strategies remains limited. This study explored the implementation potential of contextually designed implementation strategies to integrate diabetes within TB care in Pakistan, using the Optimised TB and Diabetes (Opt-TBD) package. METHODS: This qualitative case study was conducted from October 2023 to June 2024, across four TB facilities representing primary, secondary and tertiary levels of care in Pakistan. Using a qualitative design, we conducted in-depth interviews with TB patients with comorbid diabetes (n = 12) at 3 and 6 months after implementation, while healthcare providers (n = 6) were interviewed towards the end of the implementation period. We applied the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR) alongside Proctor's implementation outcomes framework to explore implementation processes and six implementation outcomes: acceptability, appropriateness, feasibility, adoption, penetration and sustainability. RESULTS: Several contextually tailored implementation strategies, including structured staff training, standardised screening protocols and strengthened referral mechanisms, were employed to integrate diabetes care within routine TB services. Overall, the intervention aligned well with existing TB workflows, provided that adequate resources, clearly defined referral pathways and ongoing staff training were ensured. Despite logistical challenges-such as delays in obtaining HbA1c test results and patient privacy concerns-healthcare providers reported adopting diabetes screening and counselling practices beyond the initial study participants. Strong leadership engagement and consistent programmatic support facilitated early implementation; however, sustaining these efforts long-term will require securing dedicated financial resources and formal integration into policy frameworks. CONCLUSION: This qualitative study indicates promising implementation potential for integrating the Opt-TBD care package within routine TB services in Pakistan. Participants generally perceived the package as acceptable and workable within routine TB services, while laboratory delays, referral challenges and dependence on external financing remained important barriers to wider implementation. These findings informed refinement of the Opt-TBD package and the subsequent broader RE-AIM evaluation. LIVED EXPERIENCE OR PUBLIC CONTRIBUTION: To develop a more inclusive and contextually relevant integrated TB-diabetes care pathway, we gathered input from both service providers and service users, including patients with TB-diabetes multimorbidity. The Opt-TBD care package was co-designed with relevant stakeholders, and this qualitative study was undertaken to capture the experiences and insights of patients and healthcare providers during implementation. Participation was sought across different genders, age groups, provinces and levels of care to ensure a broad range of perspectives. This approach helped ensure that the views of those directly affected by and involved in service delivery informed the refinement of the care package and its implementation strategies.
authors: Saima Afaq; Syeda Fatima Jamal; Aliya Rehman; Umair Ashfaq; Zala Zala; Muhammad Asim; Farman Ullah Khan; Suneel Gill; Haroon Latif Khan; Mariyam Sarfraz; Zohaib Khan; Kamran Siddiqi; Hannah Maria Jennings

title: FROM DISPLACEMENT PHYSICS TO INTELLIGENT AND SUSTAINABLE EOR: MULTISCALE EVOLUTION OF ENHANCED OIL RECOVERY MECHANISMS, TECHNOLOGIES, AND STRATEGIES ALIGNED WITH THE SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT GOALS (2000–2026)
abstract: Enhanced Oil Recovery (EOR) is a fundamental approach for increasing oil production from mature reservoirs, in which a significant fraction of the oil remains trapped due to capillary forces, unfavorable mobility ratios, heterogeneity, and preferential flow. This review analyzes the evolution of physics applied to EOR between 2000 and 2026, highlighting the transition from methods based on the optimization of isolated properties toward integrated, multiscale, and reservoir-specific strategies. The main mechanisms associated with low-salinity water and smart water, polymers, surfactants, ASP processes, miscible CO₂ and CO₂-foam, nanotechnology, microfluidics, and digital rock physics are discussed. The analysis demonstrates that mobility, capillarity, wettability, interfacial tension, miscibility, rheology, and transport act in a coupled manner, making it inadequate to evaluate any technology based on a single performance parameter. The development of microfluidics, computed tomography, and digital rock reconstructions has expanded the ability to directly observe pore-scale phenomena and relate them to macroscopic responses. More recently, physics-informed machine learning, Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), neural networks, and neural operators have been used to integrate experimental data and physical laws for the prediction and optimization of recovery processes. Parallelly, it is demonstrated that the evolution of contemporary EOR extends beyond production maximization by directly aligning with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) of the 2030 Agenda, highlighting resource optimization in mature fields (SDG 12 - Responsible Consumption and Production), digitalization and AI innovation (SDG 9 - Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure), permanent geological carbon storage via CCUS (SDG 13 - Climate Action), and transitional energy efficiency (SDG 7 - Affordable and Clean Energy). It is concluded that the main frontier of contemporary EOR does not lie in the search for a universal technology, but rather in the combination of physical mechanisms, experimental characterization, computational modeling, artificial intelligence, and global sustainability guidelines. This integration establishes the foundations for intelligent, adaptive, multiscale, sustainable EOR guided by the characteristics and uncertainties of each reservoir. It is concluded that the main frontier of contemporary EOR does not lie in the search for a universal technology, but rather in the combination of physical mechanisms, experimental characterization, computational modeling, and artificial intelligence. This integration establishes the foundations for intelligent, adaptive, multiscale EOR guided by the characteristics and uncertainties of each reservoir.
authors: Landson Soares Marques; Geruza Iolanda Aparecida Capovilla Mendes; Michel da Costa

title: Faceted Photocatalytic Microswimmers for Adaptive Navigation and Cargo Transport via Structured Illumination
abstract: Precise navigation of photocatalytic microswimmers typically requires external fields, physical confinement, chemical gradients, or feedback control, limiting their operation in dynamically changing environments. Here, light‐programmable faceted BiVO 4 microswimmers are introduced, where structured illumination provides both the energy for propulsion and the spatial information required for navigation. While uniform illumination activates self‐propulsion without directional guidance, patterned illumination defines light–dark interfaces that the microswimmers autonomously follow through continuous reorientation. Fluorescence mapping, EPR spectroscopy, tracer‐particle experiments, facet‐distribution controls, and numerical simulations support a mechanism in which partial illumination creates asymmetric photocatalytic activity, generating local chemical gradients and associated flow fields around the particle. These local imbalances allow microswimmers to remain coupled to projected boundaries, adapt to static and dynamically reconfigured geometries, and follow independently programmed trajectories within the same field of view. The same strategy enables light‐controlled cargo capture, transport, and release along confined and serpentine pathways. Overall, this work establishes an all‐optical strategy to activate, direct, and reprogram photocatalytic microswimmer motion, enabling adaptive navigation and cargo transport along complex pathways.
authors: Angie J. Bolaños; Shang Gao; Majid Basharat; Katherine Villa

title: Fallopian Tube Organoid-Integrated Microfluidic Platform for Real-Time Imaging and Outflow Analysis
abstract: The fallopian tube is a dynamic, hormonally regulated epithelial conduit whose luminal microenvironment governs oocyte transport, fertilisation, early embryo development, and the initiation of gynaecological diseases including ectopic pregnancy, hydrosalpinx, and serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma (STIC), yet existing models such as 2D monolayers, intact organoids, and static Transwell systems fail to recapitulate a polarised epithelium lining a perfused lumen under physiological fluid shear while preserving native organoid secretory function. We present a robust and accessible workflow integrating mechanically opened fallopian tube organoids into a custom-designed polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) microfluidic device, in which organoid fragments form epithelial sheets and re-establish luminal-like architecture under controlled perfusion. The focus of this study is organoid integration and the characterisation of the resulting organoid-derived epithelium, rather than establishing chip cultures from individual cell lines. As this epithelium is built from expandable organoid stock rather than primary tissue, which typically survives only a few days in culture, the approach removes a major bottleneck to establishing organ-on-chip models, and we maintain viable cultures for up to 10 days. Epithelial sheets reproducibly covered more than 90% of the channel area by day 6 (n = 5 devices) and formed continuous ZO-1-positive tight junctions. The platform supports longitudinal brightfield and fluorescence microscopy at subcellular resolution, continuous collection of conditioned flow-through for ELISA, and quantitative analysis of cell coverage and health using CellProfiler software. We characterise the organoid-derived epithelium by benchmarking against tissue culture (TC) formats, comparing nuclear morphology on-chip with conventional well culture, and showing that the damage-associated cytokine interleukin-1α (IL-1α) was detectable in organoid lysates but below the assay limit of detection in both chip outflow and intact-organoid secretions. These findings indicate that culturing mechanically opened organoids on-chip did not produce a detectable increase in IL-1α release relative to intact organoids. Computational flow modelling characterises perfusion through the device and predicts how factors secreted by healthy epithelium and by tumour cells are distributed along the channel. The feasibility of tumour– epithelium co-culture was explored using OVCAR3 ovarian cancer spheroids as a proof-of-concept model to investigate interactions between tumour cells and the fallopian tube epithelium. Together, these results establish the technical feasibility of the platform and support its further development as an accessible system for studying reproductive health conditions affecting the fallopian tube, including tubal damage from infection, endometriosis, STIC lesions, and occlusion.
authors: Dolan Evans; Heidi Savey-Bennett; Kimberley Perkins; Alice Thompson; Daniel Joseph Netherwood; Eleanor A. Doman; Christine K. Schmidt; Peter T Ruane; Raveen K. J. Tank

title: Fast antibiotic susceptibility test-integrated microfluidic chips for detection of carbapenem/colistin-resistant bacteria using smartphone-based analysis
abstract: Although many phenotypic methods have been developed for the detection of antibiotic-resistant bacteria, this emerging field still requires more rapid, practical, and economic approaches. Herein, we report a colorimetric phenotypic antimicrobial susceptibility test integrated into a microfluidic chip (mc-AST) for the detection of carbapenem (Car)- and colistin (Col)-resistant bacteria. A key component of the mc-AST is anthocyanin, a natural pH indicator that changes color based on the pH of the reaction environment. The mc-AST contains corresponding antibiotics to suppress the growth of susceptible bacteria. The color changes in the mc-AST can be detected by the naked eye and through image processing using a smartphone. The novelty of this study lies in the first ever integration of an anthocyanin-based antibiotic susceptibility test into a microfluidic chip. This integration provides a resistance profile for multiple doses of antibiotics on a single chip. Ultimately, the mc-AST reduces the workload and delivers results within 2 hours.
authors: Cagla Celik Yoldas; Nilay Ildız; Pinar Sagiroglu; Mustafa Altay Atalay; Naim Yağız Demir; Memed Duman; Barbaros Çetin; Ender Yıldırım; Gülten Can Sezgin; Yusuf Kenan Genc; Erhan Yoldas; İsmail Öçsoy

title: Feedback control via H3K9 methylation and siRNA biogenesis autonomously maintains RNAi heterochromatin through continuous low-level transcription
abstract: The logic of RNA-based silencing involves nascent RNA molecules that serve as scaffolds to recruit proteins that repress transcription. Despite transcription and silencing being antagonistic, RNA-based recruitment mechanisms have been widely adopted in organisms ranging from yeast to humans. In fission yeast ( Schizosaccharomyces pombe ), the nuclear RNAi pathway that establishes heterochromatin at pericentromeric repeats to silence transcription exemplifies this paradox. Current models propose that cells reconcile these opposing activities by confining pericentromeric transcription to S phase while maintaining silencing during the rest of the cell cycle. Here, using strand-specific single-molecule RNA FISH (smFISH), we detect forward and reverse pericentromeric transcripts with high sensitivity and single-cell resolution. We find that repeat-associated transcription is rare, heterogeneous and happens independently of cell-cycle control. Instead, transcript production is governed solely by feedback involving small RNA biogenesis and H3K9 methylation. By combining mathematical modeling with experiments, we show that low levels of H3K9me or siRNAs prevent heterochromatin establishment, whereas high levels of H3K9me cause stochastic switching. Our work reveals that the same RNA-based feedback architecture can sample distinct transcriptional regimes, with feedback strength determining how often cells produce transcripts without any external regulatory inputs.
authors: Sumanth Kumar Maheshwaram; Amith Z. Abdulla; Serena Chiu; Dionysus Morris-Evans; Jané Kondev; Kaushik Ragunathan

title: Fermentative valorization of edible algae: nutritional potential, food applications, safety considerations, and industrial challenges
abstract: Edible algae, including microalgae and macroalgae, are recognized as sustainable aquatic bioresources for future food systems, with high areal productivity, low reliance on arable land and freshwater, and rich nutrients including proteins, polyunsaturated fatty acids, pigments, minerals, vitamins and functional polysaccharides. Yet their wider application in mainstream foods is limited by low digestibility, rigid cell walls, marine off-flavors, variable safety and high processing costs. This review examines the nutritional potential, food applications, fermentation strategies, safety considerations and industrial bottlenecks of edible algae, focusing on fermentation-mediated valorization as an enabling strategy beyond conventional preservation. Lactic acid, alcoholic and mixed-culture fermentation can boost shelf stability, release intracellular nutrients, modulate sensory attributes, generate bioactive metabolites, and support circular use of residual algal biomass. Meanwhile, advanced technologies like enzyme-assisted extraction, non-thermal extraction, microfluidics and nanoencapsulation help enhance ingredient functionality and bioactive delivery. The review also notes that the future value of algae-based foods relies on matrix-specific formulation, standardized safety control for heavy metals and iodine, strain improvement, biorefinery integration and consumer-oriented sensory design. Overall, fermentative and precision-processing strategies offer a promising route to transform algae from niche supplements into safe, palatable, multifunctional ingredients for sustainable food innovation.
authors: Donglin Ma; Chaokang Xia; Aiming Jia; Guilan Zhang; Yuzong Zhao; Haiwei Ren; Xiaogang Liu; Fengjun Li; Lilang Li; Rui‐Bo Jia; Kuntai Li

title: Ferroelectric nematic liquid crystals as a new paradigm in polar soft matter: a review
abstract: Ferroelectric nematic liquid crystals (FNLCs) constitute a newly established and rapidly evolving class of soft materials in which long range orientational order coexists with the spontaneous macroscopic polarization (P). Unlike conventional apolar nematics (N), ferroelectric nematic (FN) phase breaks inversion symmetry, leading to exceptionally strong electro-optic (EO), dielectric, mechanical and nonlinear optical (NLO) responses at ultra-low driving fields. The present work surveys and contextualizes major experimental, theoretical and materials advances in FN, covering molecular design, phase behavior, interfacial alignment, elasticity, dielectric dynamics, NLO and emerging device concepts. Studies on highly polar rod like and bent core mesogens reveal spontaneous polarization values of 2–7 µC cm -2 , dielectric permittivity approaching 10 4 –10 5 , NLO coefficients up to ~ 25 pm V -1 and voltage controlled switching behavior. The studies also report that such behavior of FN arises from the interplay of strong dipole–dipole correlations, flexoelectric effects, coupling between polarization and director fields, elastic constant softening and electrostatic interactions at surfaces and interfaces. These properties enable transformative applications of FN in low power EO devices, photonics, actuators, adaptive optics, microfluidics and soft ferroelectric technologies. Despite the rapid progress, significant challenges remain including ionic effects, viscosity, surface anchoring control, defect management and stabilization of room temperature FN phases. Overall, FNLCs open a fundamentally new paradigm bridging soft condensed matter physics, molecular engineering and next generation functional devices.
authors: Chinky Jaggi; Parul Malik; Pankaj Kumar

title: Flow-Stabilized Microfluidic Sensing of Thermally Induced Changes in Red Blood Cell Aggregation During Closed-Loop Circulation
abstract: Red blood cell (RBC) aggregation is a sensitive indicator of hemorheological alterations, but conventional methods generally rely on intermittent or end-point measurements. This study presents a flow-stabilized closed-loop microfluidic platform for continuous measurement of the RBC aggregation index (AI) during controlled circulation and thermal exposure. The system integrates a peristaltic pump, hydraulic flow stabilizer (FS), microfluidic aggregation sensor, and thermal mixer to suppress flow pulsation and RBC sedimentation. The FS increases the characteristic flow-response time by approximately 17.6-fold, markedly attenuating pump-induced fluctuations. Under stabilized conditions, flow rates in the main channel and test chamber remain highly linear with the imposed flow rate, while stable AI measurements are maintained for at least 30 min. The platform also resolves dextran-dependent changes in RBC aggregation during continuous circulation. During thermal exposure from 25 to 47 °C, main-channel image intensity (Imc) and AI remain nearly constant up to 43 °C, whereas exposure at ≥45 °C causes a progressive increase in Imc and a marked decrease in AI. These results demonstrate continuous detection of thermally induced changes in RBC aggregation at a fixed measurement temperature of 25 °C without interrupting circulation and provide a versatile framework for investigating progressive changes in aggregation behavior under controlled and reproducible in vitro conditions.
authors: Yang Jun Kang

title: FluOpti: an open-source system for programmable whole-plate optogenetics and multi-fluorescence imaging
abstract: Bacteria are able to self-organize into complex spatial communities, such as colonies, biofilms and swarms. Probing cells and gene networks with dynamic stimuli while preserving their spatial organization is therefore essential for understanding how bacterial communities organize across spatial and temporal scales. Optogenetics offers a powerful approach for such a task given the precise control of stimulus delivery without the perturbations normally associated with the addition of liquid inducers. However, most optogenetics devices have been developed to work with liquid cell cultures or to deliver a spatial pattern without the concurrent recording of gene responses and colony growth. Here, we describe FluOpti, an open source, low-cost device for controlling gene expression, through programmable light inputs, and recording multi-fluorescence responses and colony growth across whole petri dishes. White light LEDs are used for brightfield imaging while green and red LEDs are used as optogenetic inputs to activate and inactivate target genes via the CcaS/R two component system in E. coli. Low cost blue and orange acrylic are used as excitation and emission filters for fluorescence imaging, respectively. We developed custom software to analyze colony growth and optogenetic responses from 72-hour time-lapse experiments. A mathematical model was developed to predict gene expression levels in response to green-to-red light ratio stimuli. We use FluOpti to reveal a spatially structured response to optogenetic stimuli, with gene activation rates differing in cells located at the center and edge of colonies. to validate its use at a whole petri dish scale, FluOpti was used to depict how Voronoi territories can act as predictors of colony size, in congruence with previous studies. Together, these results demonstrate the utility of the device for studying gene networks at multiple spatio-temporal scales, from individual colonies to the whole petri dish. Performing optogenetics studies in whole petri dishes while preserving spatial arrangements could offer valuable insights into the spatial biology of gene networks in microbial populations.
authors: Isaac Nuñez; Tamara Matúte; Alejandro Aravena; Wladimir Araya; Daniel Nuñez; Severine Cazaux; Valentina Ferrando; Patricio Obregón; Francisco Javier Quero; Gustavo Düring; Timothy Rudge; Fernán Federici

title: Fluid-driven robotic micromanipulation for assembloid fabrication
abstract: The assembly of cellular spheroids into spatially organized assembloids represents a transformative paradigm for modeling complex biological systems. However, the lack of standardized fabrication strategies fundamentally limits the precision and reproducibility of these models, hindering their widespread application. Here, we present a robotic micromanipulation platform-Fluid-Driven Tweezer with Visual Servo Control (FDT-VSC). By integrating multidimensional visual perception with microfluidic control, our system enables the gentle and programmable assembly of diverse cellular spheroids. Leveraging this platform, we achieve the bottom-up construction of structurally defined, heterogeneous multicellular tissues, and the programmed orchestration of multilineage models that recapitulate the complex microenvironments of early organogenesis. Crucially, the system improves consistency during the scalable fabrication of tumor-stroma assembloids, supporting reliable drug screening. These results demonstrate that FDT-VSC advances assembloid-based applications across modular tissue engineering, developmental biology, and drug discovery.
authors: Yang Wu; Gang Huang; Songlin Zhuang; Xinghu Yu; Wenqi Jia; Zhitai Liu; Zhan Li; Mingsi Tong; Li Zhang; Huijun Gao

title: Forensic Drug Analysis for Toxicologists: From Crime Scene to Court
abstract: The field of forensic drug analysis is rapidly advancing, driven by innovations in technology and analytical instrumentation. These advancements have significant implications for forensic science and criminal justice. Forensic Drug Analysis for Toxicologists serves as a guide for toxicologists in forensic science, law enforcement, and the legal system, highlighting methodologies, best practices, and the integration of science within legal frameworks. This book describes advanced analytical techniques, such as instrumental methods of analysis, electromagnetic spectrum, spectrophotometry, stringent quality control protocols, and cutting-edge technologies that enhance the accuracy and reliability of toxicological assessments. By bridging technical insights with procedural requirements, this account offers a holistic understanding of forensic drug analysis and its applications. Key Features: • Provides fundamental insights and basic knowledge in forensic science, forensic medicine, and toxicology in a clear and accessible manner. • Includes an introduction to narcotic and psychotropic drugs, drug of abuse, classification and properties of NDPS, and conventional methods of analysis. • Reviews the legal framework and regulatory standards and provides tips for court testimony.
authors: Sachil Kumar; Shipra Rohatgi; T.R. Baggi

title: Foundations and Evolution of AI-Integrated Microfluidic and Biosensing Technologies
abstract: Healthcare measurement is increasingly moving beyond the central laboratory and toward the body, with testing distributed across point-of-care devices, wearable sensors, and implantable systems. This chapter establishes the conceptual foundations for the convergence of biosensing, microfluidics, and artificial intelligence (AI) that has enabled this transition, and traces the historical development through which three independently maturing fields became increasingly interdependent. The foundational introduction defines the core functions of the three technologies and the historical discussion then follows each field along its own trajectory: biosensing from target-specific detection toward multiplexed and data-rich measurement; microfluidics from miniaturized assay formats toward an enabling infrastructure for controlled sample preparation and integration; and computation from chemometric calibration and pattern recognition toward adaptive models for biomedical interpretation and decision support. Their convergence is presented as an integrated pathway from question to sample, signal, interpretation, and action, enabling point-of-care, wearable, implantable, and closed-loop systems. Within this framework, AI is a structural component that shapes how signals are calibrated, interpreted, validated, and translated into action. AI-integrated biosensing requires coordinated design across intended use, sampling, transduction, modeling, and validation, so that distributed measurements preserve biological meaning, remain interpretable, and support timely action in personalized healthcare.
authors: Aleksandr Simonian

title: From AI-Generated Sequences to Therapeutic Peptide Candidates: A Disease-First Perspective on Computational Design, Developability, and Application
abstract: Therapeutic peptides bridge the gap between small-molecule drugs and biologics, offering high target selectivity and broad opportunities for chemical and structural optimization. However, their clinical translation remains constrained by proteolytic instability, limited bioavailability, delivery barriers, safety concerns, and manufacturing challenges. Artificial intelligence (AI) expands the generation and prioritization of peptide hypotheses through language models, target-conditioned design, structure-aware modeling, and multi-objective optimization. Experimental testing of disease-relevant activity, exposure, safety, and developability determines which hypotheses warrant further development. This review examines AI-enabled therapeutic peptide discovery from a translational and disease-oriented perspective, with particular emphasis on the transition from computationally generated sequences to experimentally supported and developable candidates. We summarize major computational paradigms for peptide generation, structural design, and candidate prioritization, and discuss how stability, permeability, toxicity, chemical modifiability, synthesis feasibility, and manufacturability should be incorporated into early-stage design. We further propose a disease-first framework in which clinical indication, target biology, delivery requirements, disease microenvironment, and acceptable safety profiles define the design space before sequence generation. To distinguish computational promise from translational maturity, we propose a four-level evidence framework, which has not been independently validated, spanning in silico nomination, in vitro validation, in vivo support, and preclinical development. Purposively selected examples across infectious diseases, oncology, metabolic disorders, neurological diseases, and autoimmune or inflammatory diseases illustrate disease-specific translational barriers; they do not represent a systematic sample of the field. Finally, we highlight the need for standardized benchmarking, negative-data retention, closed-loop experimental feedback, synthesis-aware modeling, and regulatory-ready evidence generation to advance AI-designed peptides toward clinically credible therapeutics. A) Disease context and clinical need. Bullet list: Clinical unmet need. Disease barriers and target accessibility. Target selection and biological context. Indication-defined design constraints. B) Developability optimization. Bullet list: Early filtering and prioritization. Exposure, permeability and stability. Safety and selectivity. Chemical modification and manufacturability. C) Disease-oriented translational applications. Labeled icons: Infectious diseases. Oncology. Metabolic diseases. Neurological disorders. Autoimmune or inflammatory diseases. D) AI design paradigms. Bullet list: Sequence and structure learning. Protein language and diffusion models. Constraint-guided generation. Multimodal and structure-aware design. E) Evidence maturation and translation. Four stacked levels connected by downward arrows: Level 1, in silico. Level 2, in vitro. Level 3, in vivo. Level 4, preclinical development. F) Challenges and future outlook. Bullet list: Evidence gap from sequence generation to therapeutic translation. Standardized data, negative evidence and reproducible benchmarks. Disease-relevant validation and patient stratification. Developability, manufacturability and CMC constraints. Closed-loop and agent-driven discovery systems. Regulatory-oriented translational evidence framework. A horizontal timeline arrow runs left to right beneath the sections, with dotted vertical connectors from each section to a circular marker on the line.A process diagram of six themes for therapeutic design and translation, arranged on a timeline arrow.
authors: Zhixin Wang; Hui Deng; Ziao Hu; Zirui Han; Haipeng Wen; Bing Zeng; Dai Weiwei; Min Hu; Yedi Zhou

title: From Algorithm Performance to Laboratory Deployment: A Critical Review of Artificial Intelligence in Clinical Chemistry
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being applied in clinical laboratories to support laboratory processes and interpretation of test results. Recent developments in machine learning, deep learning, and large language models have expanded the potential applications of AI across different stages of laboratory testing. However, the use of AI in clinical laboratories also raises important questions regarding validation, analytical performance, and transferability between laboratories. This narrative review examines recent applications of AI across the total testing process in clinical chemistry. Recent English-language scientific literature published from 2023 to 18 August 2026 was identified through searches of PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar. It describes AI-assisted test utilization; specimen handling and quality assessment; detection of laboratory errors; patient-based quality control; interpretation of complex analytical outputs, including signals from emerging AI-integrated biosensors and nanomaterial-based analytical platforms; result verification; and laboratory-report interpretation. The review also discusses major implementation challenges, including analytical variability, data quality, sensor and platform reproducibility, model generalizability, interoperability, and limitations of large language models. Particular attention is given to external validation, transportability, and real-world implementation. Among the studies considered in this review, many applications remain supported mainly by retrospective or internally validated studies, while prospective and operational evaluations are less common. Finally, practical considerations for validation, local verification, quality assurance, and performance monitoring are discussed. AI has considerable potential to support clinical chemistry laboratories, but safe use requires appropriate evaluation and continued involvement of laboratory professionals.
authors: Abdelraheem A. Bani Ahmad; Sulieman Bani‐Ahmad

title: From Multiscale Emergence to Testable Intervention
abstract: Precision chemistry requires more than accurate prediction: it requires a traceable chain from measurement to representation, mechanism, design, and reproducible intervention. We argue that, within a declared operating envelope, a small set of physically meaningful coordinates and explicit relations can reduce multiscale prediction and design to a closed model that can be evaluated within specified error and computational budgets. We formulate five requirements for such coordinates─predictive sufficiency, dynamical closure, interventional stability, identifiability, and reachability─and organize them in a representation–closure–search–intervention (RCSI) cycle. Its central object is an input–output description mediated by physical variables whose relations can be examined and revised. Analytic, numerical, learned, and hybrid solvers are selected according to accuracy, cost, and latency. Uncertainty and provenance are retained at every stage, and models are evaluated by extrapolation, mechanism discrimination, and intervention success. Examples from catalytic interfaces, electronic and atomistic models, polymer field theory, microscopy, active matter, biomolecular design, and quantum-control planning illustrate both the opportunity and the limits. We conclude with prospective tests that can falsify each stage and a reporting standard for closed-loop scientific AI.
authors: Sulei Hu; Xingao Gong; Duyu Chen; Jingguo Li; Qiyu Kang; Yongliang Jiang; Chenhui Peng; Shoucong Ning; Qiangqiang Gu; Jinzhe Zeng; Chao Wang; Fuli Feng

title: From Static Classrooms to Living Systems
abstract: This chapter explores how Digital twins (DTs) are changing in their roles across the educational spectrum. DTs play both theoretical and practical roles, facilitating immersive, feedback-intensive and personal experiences beyond traditional simulations. DTs in life sciences and agricultural engineering enable safe, repeatable and data-rich learning environments where learners can practice realistic simulations of poultry farm management, disease control and performance analytics without endangering living animals in the laboratory. DTs have been applied to reinvent introductory programming education in computing education. DTs have been identified as potential solutions for schools in developing countries such as Mozambique and Rwanda that lack physical laboratory facilities. In chemical engineering education, virtual reality twins of extraction columns enable interactive manipulation of flow parameters and AI-based image analysis to optimize droplet size, introducing students to the fusion of process control and data analytics in an accessible, hardware-light format.
authors: Marwa M. EID

title: From conventional monitoring to agentic AI: integration of data streams and computational tools for real-time microalgal surveillance
abstract: Microalgal cultivation generates continuous and diverse data streams, including physicochemical sensor measurements, optical and spectroscopic signals, and episodic molecular tests. Together, these data characterize cultivation conditions at different biological scales. Existing AI/ML frameworks can interpret these streams independently; however, human intervention is required to translate predictions into cultivation decisions, adding delays and limiting adaptability across strains, reactors, and environmental conditions. This mini-review describes the transition from conventional monitoring to agentic AI as the progressive integration of sensing, interpretation, and action. The real-time sensing modalities that constitute an agent's perceptual field include AI/ML models and genome-scale metabolic models, which serve as callable tools in the proposed agentic architecture for coordinated data-model integration in algal systems biology. Emerging evidence from agentic systems in microbiome research and precision oncology supports the conceptual and technical plausibility of a multi-agent, tool-enabled framework for autonomous microalgal cultivation and management. However, the proposed integrated architecture holds significant potential for microalgal cultivation systems, it has not yet been implemented and requires experimental validation.
authors: H. L. Lekhana; K. S. Mukunthan; S. Balaji

title: From deterministic to adaptive magnetic micro-robots
abstract: Robotics has long pursued the development of systems that can control physical objects remotely and precisely in diverse environments. With ongoing miniaturization, micro-robots have emerged as promising platforms for a wide range of applications. In particular, magnetic micro-robots are compelling because external magnetic fields provide a wireless and biocompatible means of actuation, overcoming the constraints of on-board power sources in confined and complex settings. Despite extensive studies, the classification of magnetic micro-robots has often remained indistinct. This review seeks to contribute a more systematic understanding by defining four major categories—rigid, reconfigurable, shape-changing, and swarm—while also discussing emerging hybrid systems that bridge these paradigms. We synthesize the fundamental actuation principles and representative designs of each category. By examining the capabilities and limitations of each paradigm, we identify challenges and outline future directions for the advancement of adaptive and intelligent magnetic micro-robotic systems.
authors: 조은화; Seungyeon Kim; Koohee Han

title: From medical to pedagogical care: A bibliometric review of AI agent research in education
abstract: BACKGROUND: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) agents, including chatbots and virtual tutors, into education has expanded rapidly; however, systematic quantitative analysis of research trends in this field remains limited. Notably, the intellectual foundations of AI agent research lie not in education but in medicine, where AI agents were first extensively deployed and studied in clinical, experimental, and pedagogical contexts. METHODS: In this study, a bibliometric analysis of 377 records retrieved from the Web of Science was conducted using VOSviewer to map the evolution, thematic focus, and collaborative networks within this field. RESULTS: The study showed AI agent research originated strongly in healthcare, with educational applications emerging more recently. Key research themes encompassed AI technologies, human-computer interaction, pedagogical applications, and ethical considerations. Collaborative efforts were led by the USA and China, supported by active European and Asian research hubs. The findings revealed a dual narrative of significant benefits for personalized learning and learner well-being alongside persistent challenges such as algorithmic bias and accessibility gaps. CONCLUSION: To realize the transformative potential of AI in education, future research should prioritize the development of adaptive algorithms, robust ethical frameworks, inclusive design, and interdisciplinary collaboration. By focusing on these areas, the field can work toward overcoming technical, ethical, and logistical barriers, thereby ensuring that AI acts as a sustainable force for equity and excellence in education.
authors: Xinhuang Tang; Shukun Chen; Jinyan Chen

title: From prediction to creation: How AI-driven design is reshaping microbial biocatalysis
abstract: Enzyme engineering has long relied on rational design and directed evolution, yet both remain bounded by natural enzyme space - a constraint felt acutely across the largely uncharacterised microbial world. The 2021 advent of accurate structure prediction marked an inflection point, catalysing AI methods that now extend far beyond folding. These tools are organism-agnostic; the microbial domain is their proving ground because it supplies both the uncharacterised sequence space and the expression hosts. Here we examine three stages: mining microbial sequence space; generative design, whether conditioned on structure or sequence; and machine learning-guided directed evolution. We trace the trajectory from reading the protein universe toward writing it, asking where each has delivered for microbial biocatalysis. Because published claims are hard to compare, we propose a tiered framework - catalysis, selectivity, producibility, process fit - for judging whether an AI-designed enzyme is a useful biocatalyst rather than merely a functional protein.
authors: Gregory G. Y. Guirimand; Raghvendra Mall; Chirag Patel; Hisashi Kudo; Mami Matsuda; Vincent Courdavault; Tomohisa Hasunuma

title: From smart sensing to adaptive remediation: artificial intelligence and Internet of Things for persistent organic pollutants
abstract: Persistent organic pollutants (POPs) remain a major environmental challenge because of their persistence, long-range transport, bioaccumulation, and resistance to degradation. Conventional monitoring and remediation systems provide reliable analytical performance but are largely fragmented, laboratory dependent, and unable to deliver the continuous, predictive, and adaptive management required for complex, dynamic contamination scenarios. Recent literature reports substantial advances in biosensors, Internet of Things (IoT)-enabled sensing, machine learning (ML), and artificial intelligence (AI) for pollutant detection, forecasting, source identification, and remediation optimization. However, these developments often operate separately, with limited coordination between environmental sensing, data analytics, treatment processes, and decision-making. The literature further highlights persistent barriers to field deployment, including limited and geographically heterogeneous datasets, inconsistent sensor performance and calibration, restricted model transferability, insufficient independent validation, uncertainty in AI predictions, and the lack of mature regulatory frameworks for AI-assisted environmental assessment. From our perspective, the next advance in POP management should move beyond isolated AI applications toward integrated, closed-loop AI-IoT architectures that continuously connect sensing, prediction, remediation, and feedback control. Such systems could transform POP management from reactive assessment to proactive and adaptive environmental governance. Future progress will depend on standardized, Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable (FAIR) environmental datasets, explainable and uncertainty-aware AI, robust field validation, and interoperable sensing infrastructures.
authors: Khaled Chawraba; Abrar Hussain; Obaid A. Alharbi; Amal Abdelhaleem

title: From stretchable materials and functional fibers to intelligent textile sensing systems
abstract: Wearable sensors that offer significant adaptability and comfort demonstrate substantial potential for discrete, seamless integration into garments, enabling diverse applications for remote monitoring. The transformation of rigid electronic devices into flexible and stretchable sensors, achieved by integrating conductive materials with compliant dielectrics, has enabled the development of robust sensors. However, several factors must be addressed to enable widespread adoption, including garment integration, wireless communication, data pipelines, signal processing, multimodal fusion, privacy and security concerns. Addressing these challenges is essential for establishing the technological and social infrastructure necessary for the widespread adoption of wearable technologies. This review highlights innovations in material and mechanical design strategies that have shaped the current landscape of wearables, and points out some remaining challenges.
authors: Maria Papaefstathiou; Mohamed Elgendi; Carlo Menon

title: Gap Analysis and Recent Advances in HPLC and UPLC
abstract: Objective: To systematically review the advances of High-Performance Liquid Chromatography (HPLC) and Ultra-Performance Liquid Chromatography (UPLC) since the year of 2020 in the fields of analytical performance, sustainability, automation, and emerging technologies. Data Sources: Databases were searched for all literature related to HPLC and UPLC published from 2020 to 2026 using Scopus, PubMed, Web of Science, and Google Scholar as resources. Study Selection: A total of fifty-five peer-reviewed papers were chosen based upon predefined eligibility criteria to be included as part of this literature surveythese comprised fifteen reviews, twenty-nine articles, and eleven abstracts. Summary of Contents: Advances in the following areas are reviewed: Sub-2 µm and superficially porous columns, Q-TOF MS, green analytical chemistry metrics, automated processes, AI, and miniaturized sample preparation. Challenges include limited transfers of existing methods, lack of open access databases, and inadequate validation of AI-assisted method development by regulatory bodies. Conclusion: HPLC and UPLC have the potential to evolve into faster, more eco-friendly, and innovative analytical platforms. Addressing current limitations will allow for further integration of HPLC and UPLC with nanotechnology, microfluidics, and sustainable analytical chemistry.
authors: Snehal Shete; Deotale Kiran; Gayatri Katole; Vinod Thakre
venue: Asian Journal of Pharmaceutical Research and Development

title: GeONet: Geometry-Encoded Operator Network for Predicting Flow in Heterogeneous Porous Media
abstract: Rapid prediction of pressure-driven flow in microfluidic porous media is important for experimental design, tracer-test interpretation, and digital-twin development for subsurface energy and critical mineral applications. High-fidelity simulations resolve geometry-controlled flow but are computationally expensive across large geometry ensembles. Here, we introduce GeONet, a Geometry-Encoded Operator Network that predicts steady-state pressure fields by jointly representing material properties, spatial coordinates, and solid--void geometry. GeONet extends the Branch--Trunk architecture with a dedicated Leaf Network encoding the binary domain mask through multiscale features. The Branch Network represents porosity and permeability, the Trunk Network combines coordinates with local geometric descriptors and random Fourier features, and a gated DeepMixer integrates these representations to predict pressure. GeONet was trained and evaluated using 5,000 PFLOTRAN simulations of heterogeneous Reduced Complexity Platform domains, comprising nearly 30 TB of data. Comparisons with pore-scale Stokes solutions across three geometries yielded Pearson correlations of 0.987--0.991 and $R^2$ values of 0.974--0.982, supporting PFLOTRAN as reference data. Under matched partitions and two-stage hyperparameter optimization, GeONet substantially outperformed a boundary-condition-aware DeepONet baseline. Across three held-out domains, GeONet achieved NRMSE of 0.0381--0.0500, MAPE of 1.76--2.59%, and $R^2$ of 0.9673--0.9822, versus 0.1483--0.2040, 7.81--10.45%, and 0.5658--0.7126 for DeepONet, respectively. On three additional unseen geometries, GeONet achieved NRMSE of 0.0448--0.0676 and $R^2$ of 0.9511--0.9770. These results demonstrate improved accuracy, pressure-range preservation, and cross-geometry generalization through explicit geometry encoding.
authors: Md Lal Mamud; Maruti Kumar Mudunuru; Yucheng Fu; Aramy Troung; Satish Karra; Ivani Patel; Arunima Bhattacharjee; Tamás Varga; Pratanu Roy; Michael Penwarden; Rajesh K. Singh; Arjun Chakrawal; Kalyana Babu Nakshatrala; Christof Meile; Erin Rooney; Glenn Hammond

title: Graphene-oxide-microfiber aptasensor for dynamic neutrophil monitoring: Bridging cytokine release syndrome and point-of-care sepsis diagnosis
abstract: Neutrophil granule release is critical for host defense, yet its dysregulation underpins cytokine release syndrome (CRS) in both acute (such as sepsis) and sustained inflammatory states. Distinguishing these phases requires real-time monitoring of early markers like neutrophil elastase (ELANE) and lactoferrin (LF), but conventional assays lack requisite sensitivity. Here, we developed a graphene-oxide-functionalized optical microfiber biosensor with high-affinity DNA aptamers (NE-AP and LF-AP) to quantify ELANE and LF via aptamer-protein binding-induced spectral red shifts. The sensor achieved ultralow detection limits (3.57 × 10 −20 M for ELANE and 1.28 × 10 −19 M for LF), eight orders below ELISA, with excellent selectivity. In a lipopolysaccharide-induced murine model, it resolved distinct temporal release profiles of ELANE and LF, and in clinical validation, it showed distinct spectral responses between septic patients and healthy controls in a preliminary clinical cohort. This platform provides a highly sensitive, real-time tool for decoding neutrophil dynamics, with preliminary translational potential for early sepsis diagnosis.
authors: Zhiheng Yu; Han Dong; Xiaolin Chen; Mengjiang Xu; Ren Liu; Jin Wang; Cunliang Yang; Ke Wang; Xianyuan Zhao; Hao Jia; Jijun Feng

title: Gynecological cancers on a chip: status, advances, and future
abstract: Gynecological cancers, including cervical cancer, ovarian cancer, and endometrial cancer, negatively influence women's physical and mental wellbeing. Modeling disease progression could enable new therapeutic interventions. The development of microfluidic technology has led to the creation of gynecological cancer-on-a-chip (CoC) models. Since the tumor microenvironment (TME), along with other physiological variables such as microvasculature, shear stress due to blood flow, and biological barriers, can be simulated in a chip setup, these factors can be used to model how tumor cells cross blood vessels and migrate to invade other organs. Therefore, fluidic chips, integrating organoids and other biofabrication concepts, provide a fresh approach to elaborate tumor molecular mechanisms and treatment strategies since physiological variables (signaling and cellular processes) can be controlled. Although gynecological cancer chips have many advantages, the number of related studies is limited. Currently, the research landscape is primarily focused on TME reconstruction and drug screening, while the incorporation of tissue-derived samples and organoids has yet to gain traction. This review summarizes the current status of research, along with technical progress and future challenges, thus providing a comprehensive reference for further research in this field.
authors: Yantao He; Venkatram Prasad Shastri

title: Hemin Triggers Cytoprotective Lipid Droplet Formation in Pulmonary Microvascular Endothelial Cells.
abstract: Sickle cell disease (SCD) is characterized by chronic and episodic hemolysis, inducing endothelial cell dysfunction and death. Lipid droplets (LDs) accumulate intracellularly in response to stress but the role of LDs in hemin-stressed pulmonary microvascular cells remain unexplored. We hypothesized that LD formation is an adaptive response that improves endothelial cell survival during hemin-induced stress. We utilized cultures of human lung microvascular endothelial cells (hLMVECs) to test this hypothesis. Hemin alone was able to induce LD biogenesis in culture. In response to hemin treatment, we found an increase in cellular death by lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) assay when LD biogenesis was inhibited with a small molecule inhibitor of diacylglycerol acyltransferase 1 (DGAT1), A922500. Induction of LDs by treatment with oleic acid (OA) coupled with hemin resulted in improved endothelial cell survival. Hemin treatment was able to activate p-JNK and p-P38 signaling, while treatment with OA alone could not induce either signaling pathway. Hemin treatment combined with DGAT1 inhibition resulted in an increase in endothelial cell secreted IL-6 and IL-8 levels as measured by enzyme linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), demonstrating an increase in endothelial cell dysfunction and stress. Induction of LD formation with oleic acid (OA) treatment resulted a reduction in secreted IL-6 and IL-8. Mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) production was decreased by OA treatment, as evidenced by MitoSOXRed assay. These data suggest that hLMVECs are protected from hemin-induced inflammation and death by the presence of LDs. Further studies are needed to explore the Hemin-LD-Cell Death axis for translational therapeutic use.
authors: Alan de Brito Carneiro; Robert W Wysocki; Xu Zhang; Victor R Gordeuk; Roberto F Machado
venue: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology

title: HiSpoT: a novel one-tube dual-barcode PCR method for NGS spoligotyping amplicon library preparation in Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex
abstract: Tuberculosis remains one of the leading infectious causes of death globally, making rapid, accurate, and affordable strain typing essential for effective outbreak tracking and epidemiological surveillance. To address the limitations and high costs of current typing methods, we developed a novel one-tube, dual-barcode PCR method for preparing targeted next-generation sequencing (NGS) amplicon libraries for spoligotyping of Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC), which we termed HiSpoT (High-throughput Spoligotyping by Targeted next generation sequencing). The assay targets 43 conserved spacer oligonucleotides in the CRISPR direct repeat (DR) region and is presented here together with the previously unpublished, difficult-to-design dual-barcode primer set needed to multiplex 96 samples in a single tube. HiSpoT is accurate, fast, high-throughput, and low-cost, eliminating the need for a commercial NGS library preparation kit. Because HiSpoT is PCR-based, the resulting spoligotypes remain directly comparable with the large PCR-based spoligotype databases accumulated over decades, enabling rapid outbreak tracking and biogeographic characterization of a country’s tuberculosis burden while higher-resolution whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data are obtained. Analysis of 288 clinical MTBC isolates from Israel (2020-2022) demonstrated a broad range of genetic lineages, and comparison of 79 isolates analyzed by both HiSpoT and WGS showed 70% full concordance, with essentially all discrepancies attributable to single-spacer insertion-element disruptions of PCR primer sites. We also present two open-source Google Colab Python tools, Spoligotyping_MTBC_gcl and its condensed HiSpoT_Spoligotyping_v8_ready VIBE variant, freely available on GitHub, which automatically process Illumina paired-end fastq output from HiSpoT or WGS and report binary and octal spoligotypes, spoligo international types (SIT), and MTBC family assignments with accompanying quality-control reports. IMPORTANCE Tuberculosis, caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis , is the leading cause of death from a single infectious agent worldwide, and rapid, accurate, and affordable strain typing is essential for tracking outbreaks and directing limited public health resources. The decades-old laboratory method for spoligotyping, a widely used genetic fingerprint for this bacterium, is slow, labor-intensive, and hard to read. Newer sequencing-based approaches solve these problems but usually still need an expensive, time-consuming commercial kit to prepare samples for sequencing. This work describes HiSpoT, a simplified, low-cost, one-tube method that prepares samples for sequencing without a commercial kit, cutting turnaround from about a week to about two days while testing many samples together. Because HiSpoT results agree with results obtained from older typing methods, laboratories anywhere with basic sequencing equipment can compare results to decades of stored international data. Two free, open-source computer programs are also provided so laboratories with limited bioinformatics expertise can analyze their sequencing data automatically.
authors: Paul Jeffrey Freidlin; Mor Rubinstein; Ephraim Fass; Inna Kutikov; Gal Zizelski Valenci; Yelena Losev; Zeev Dveyrin; Efrat Gavrieli Rorman; Israel Nissan

title: High‐Q Photonic Crystal Nanobeam Cavities for Resonantly Enhanced Mid‐IR Photothermal Spectroscopy in Microfluidic Environments
abstract: Label‐free chemical sensing in liquids using integrated photonic resonators at telecom wavelengths (∼1.55 µm) is limited by Q‐factor degradation in asymmetric liquid‐cladding environments and by the lack of molecular specificity in refractive index (RI)‐based sensors. Here, we introduce a compact (100 × 10 µm 2 ) silicon nitride (Si 3 N 4 ) photonic crystal nanobeam cavity (PhCNC) as a resonant transducer for liquid‐phase photothermal spectroscopy (PTS).
