The nanobeam supports a localized resonant defect mode providing strong optical confinement and liquid interaction. Simulations predict intrinsic Q‐factors exceeding 10 6 , while foundry‐fabricated devices operated under liquid cladding exhibit loaded Q‐factors on the order of 10 4 . Integrated with microfluidics, the PhCNC enables flow‐through refractometric sensing and stop‐flow mid‐infrared (∼6 µm) PTS. Molecular absorption of a modulated mid‐IR excitation is transduced by the cavity resonance into an optical intensity modulation of a telecom probe. The device achieves a bulk RI sensitivity of ∼233 nm/RIU with a LoD of ∼5 × 10 −6 RIU. Spectrally resolved stop‐flow mid‐IR PTS is demonstrated forDIW‐IPA mixtures and caffeine‐EtOH solutions, yielding LoDs of 0.5% and 0.4 mg/mL, respectively. The measured PTS spectra reproduce characteristic FTIR absorption features. These results establish Si 3 N 4 PhCNCs as compact, liquid‐compatible resonant transducers for spectrally selective on‐chip PTS and chip‐scale mid‐infrared chemical sensing.
authors: Jesús Hernán Mendoza-Castro; Daniela Tomasetig; Artem S. Vorobev; Simone Iadanza; Savda Sam; Frédéric Sovannara Prum; Laurent Markey; Giovanni Magno; Liam O’Faoláin; Bernhard Lendl; Marco Grande

title: How the fruit fly connectome can help autonomous materials discovery
abstract: Autonomous laboratories for two-dimensional semiconductors pair a recipe planner with instruments that return in situ spectra every few seconds. Some decisions are too fast for the planner: stop a failing selenization anneal, flag a flake that is not the logged material, or end an ion irradiation at a set vacancy density, from a few examples, on a small computer at the instrument. The fruit fly takes decisions of this form with two structures whose wiring is measured at synapse level: the mushroom body, a one-shot memory for odours, and the ventral nerve cord, which turns a few descending commands into local reflexes. We asked which instrument jobs models wired from these connectomes do better than engineered tools. A mushroom-body model of 685 projection neurons and 5,177 Kenyon cells read one Raman band per glomerulus; over 20 paired seeds, on simulated selenization Raman streams and on Ar + irradiation anchored in published in situ spectra, it lost the fewest flakes when one failed run taught a stop rule (3.3 of 30, against 3.9 for a nearest neighbour), read vacancy density from its sparse code with less error than from the raw spectrum (5.5 % against 6.4 %), and ran in 0.30 ms on a Raspberry Pi 5 within 152 kB. A stop decided at the furnace, as the nerve cord decides reflexes, prevented the losses of a planner that needed 60 s per turn (0.15 against 10.7 flakes of 30). It did not choose recipes. In three animals and after training, measured wiring matched a degree-preserving shuffle, and the nerve-cord wiring matched a ridge regression: the connectome contributes an architecture and wiring statistics, not a partner map. As hardware, the fixed wiring can be binary and each plastic synapse needs about 64 levels. The connectome supplies a low-cost reflex layer under the planner, not a replacement.
authors: Ka Chun WONG; Taylor D. Sparks

title: Humanistic Care Profiles among Medical Postgraduate Students: Associations with AI Risk Anxiety and Ethical Sensitivity
abstract: Background Humanistic care is an essential component of medical professionalism. This study aimed to identify distinct profiles of humanistic care among medical postgraduate students and examine their associations with AI risk anxiety and ethical sensitivity. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted in August 2026 among 661 professional-degree master's and doctoral medical postgraduate students studying at three tertiary Grade-A general hospitals in Changsha, Hunan Province, China. Humanistic care was assessed across seven dimensions: altruism, honesty, courage, trust, patience, humility, and hope. Latent profile analysis (LPA) was used to identify distinct humanistic care profiles. Differences in demographic characteristics, AI-related experiences, AI risk anxiety, and ethical sensitivity across profiles were examined. Pearson correlation and pairwise binary logistic regression analyses were further performed. Results The mean total humanistic care score was 3.67 ± 0.47. LPA identified three profiles: low (19.67%), moderate (63.54%), and high (16.79%). Age, weekly AI use frequency, AI-related training, and AI ethics education differed significantly across profiles (all P < 0.05). In multivariable analyses, older age, more frequent AI use, AI-related training, AI ethics education, and higher ethical sensitivity were associated with higher humanistic care profiles, whereas higher AI risk anxiety was associated with lower profiles. AI risk anxiety decreased progressively across profiles, whereas ethical sensitivity increased (both P < 0.001), and AI risk anxiety and ethical sensitivity were negatively and positively correlated with humanistic care, respectively (all P < 0.001). Conclusions Medical postgraduate students showed heterogeneous patterns of humanistic care, with higher profiles associated with lower AI risk anxiety and higher ethical sensitivity. Postgraduate medical education should consider differentiated support according to students’ humanistic care needs. AI education should be integrated with humanistic care, ethical reasoning, patient-centred communication, and professional responsibility, with greater emphasis on reflective practice, ethical case-based learning, and responsible AI use. This integrated approach may better prepare future physicians for technologically advanced yet human-centred healthcare.
authors: Ping Zhang; Jiawen Liu; Yana He; Ying Zhang; Huanwen Luo

title: Hyperbolic neural networks for biologically informed classification of white blood cells and hematopoietic cell states in peripheral blood smears
abstract: Automated white blood cell (WBC) classification in peripheral blood smears supports morphological assessment of hematological disorders, but most deep learning classifiers treat cell categories as independent labels and do not account for hematopoietic maturation. We propose a hyperbolic classification framework that combines a ResNet-18 feature extractor with a prototype-based classifier in the Poincaré ball, allowing biologically related cell states to be represented in a geometry suited to hierarchical structure. The model was evaluated on a curated dataset of 129,174 annotated single-cell images mapped to 14 blood cell classes, including leukocyte subtypes, hematopoietic precursor states, and multiple stages of granulocytic maturation. To reduce acquisition-level information leakage, we used a grouped evaluation protocol that keeps linked multi-focus acquisitions within the same subset. Across the six top-ranked grouped-split configurations, the hyperbolic model improved macro-averaged F1-score from 0.812 ± 0.005 to 0.819 ± 0.004 relative to the Euclidean baseline, while overall accuracy remained slightly lower (0.826 ± 0.002 vs 0.830 ± 0.006). Recall gains were most pronounced for promyelocytes, immature WBCs, and metamyelocytes. These results suggest that hyperbolic representation learning can improve class-balanced classification of WBCs and related hematopoietic cell states while maintaining competitive overall accuracy.
authors: Lukáš Jochymek; Markéta Vašinková; Petr Gajdoš

title: Improved Diagnostics Through Understanding Living Systems: Rethinking Biomarker Discovery
abstract: This book tackles the challenge of biomarker discovery. The lack of new effective biomarkers contributes to medical errors, emphasizing the need for solutions. Rochat explores new solutions based on a reassessment of our understanding of life and diseases. He challenges traditional views from standard academic training to highlight the unique nature of each individual’s biological dynamics. The text proposes a new strategy for biomarker discovery taking advantage of a state‑of‑the‑art technology, i.e., high‑resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS), to perform comprehensive analyses of patient blood samples. This new strategy is feasible and involves not knowing which biomarker to determine prior to non‑targeted HRMS analysis. Comparison of compounds found in the patient’s plasma with plasma from healthy individuals could reveal outlier compounds and biomarker(s) indicative of the patient’s symptoms. As part of an individualized vision of healthcare, this strategy aims to identify unexpected patient‑specific biomarkers indicative of pathology. This could revolutionize diagnostic practices, reducing medical errors and the diagnostic odyssey.
authors: Bertrand Rochat

title: In Vitro and In Vivo Drug Screening for Breast Cancer Using 3d Engineered Tissues
abstract: Breast cancer remains a prevalent and complex malignancy affecting a vast population in the world, characterized by its varied histological, molecular, and microenvironmental features. This comprehensive review research findings from 2010 to 2024, emphasizing the significant role of the tumor microenvironment and the advancement of innovative in vitro and in vivo models in breast cancer research and treatment. It delves into the biological mechanisms underlying breast cancer progression, particularly the interactions between cancer cells and surrounding stromal components, including immune cells, fibroblasts, adipocytes, and the extracellular matrix, which collectively impact disease progression and therapeutic responses. Additionally, the review highlights the emergence of advanced three-dimensional (3D) models, such as spheroids, organoids, and tumor-on-chip systems, as groundbreaking tools that closely mimic the native tumor environment, thereby enhancing our understanding and treatment of this multifaceted disease. Tumor-on-chip systems represent a significant advancement in cancer research, effectively mimicking the native tumor architecture and heterogeneity, which enhances their predictive value for drug screening and personalized medicine. Patient-derived organoids (PDOs) and xenografts (PDXs) have demonstrated promising correlations between genomic profiles and therapeutic outcomes, providing valuable insights into treatment resistance and sensitivity across various breast cancer subtypes. Furthermore, incorporating microfluidic and nanotechnology-based platforms has improved the physiological relevance of preclinical testing, thereby narrowing the translational gap. However, the review also critically examines the limitations of these models, such as the incomplete recapitulation of tumor heterogeneity in organoids and the high cost and complexity of PDX models, which must be addressed to fully realize their potential in personalized oncology. This review highlights the essential role of biomimetic modeling in the progression of breast cancer diagnostics, drug development, and precision oncology, affirming its critical importance in modern medical research.
authors: FATEMEH MIRI; Dhiya Altememy; Fatemeh Keshavarzian; SABA NAZEMI; YEGANEH MIRHAJ; Maliheh Gharibshahian; Akram Alizadeh; Elham Saffarieh

title: Inductively proprioceptive liquid crystal elastomers with unified sensing and actuation
abstract: Liquid crystal elastomers (LCEs) are promising artificial-muscle materials for soft robotics, yet their closed-loop control often relies on external sensors that introduce hardware complexity and limit compact integration. Resistance-based self-sensing offers an integrated alternative, but strong temperature-strain coupling renders the readout susceptible to thermal drift and viscoelastic effects. Here, we report inductively proprioceptive LCE artificial muscles in which a single embedded copper coil serves as both the Joule-heating element and a deformation-dependent inductive feedback element. Time-domain switching separates heating from inductive readout and suppresses drive-induced interference. Coil geometry dominates the inductive readout. At fixed geometry, its normalized thermal sensitivity was approximately one-sixth that of the resistive readout. In matched tests, independent laser measurements showed better position retention with inductive feedback. To manage the path-dependent hysteresis of thermal actuation, we adopt separate heating/cooling calibration maps. The length-inductance calibration was repeatable across the tested voltages and loads. The tubular actuator achieved approximately 36% reversible axial contraction (35 mm). In closed-loop tests, the maximum steady-state displacement error was below 0.28 mm, and the ramp-and-hold root-mean-square error (RMSE) was below 0.51 mm. An antagonistic spinal actuator extends this approach to bidirectional angle feedback over ±60°, with a loaded tracking RMSE of approximately 0.92°. We further demonstrate inductive feedback control in a droplet transport platform, a contact-aware gripper, and a bioinspired lizard robot. This unified actuation-sensing architecture offers a compact proprioceptive strategy for closed-loop LCE soft robots, with potential applications in microfluidic manipulation, adaptive gripping, and soft locomotion.
authors: Hongtai Ren; Jiandong Huang; Tianxi Jiang; Shuaishuai Sun; Shiwu Zhang

title: Information coding strategies in biological reservoir computing for multiclass time-series classification
abstract: Physical reservoir computing (RC) using biological neural networks (BNNs) offers a framework for probing how high-dimensional dynamics arising from multicellular systems support complex information processing in the brain. However, how electrical inputs and extracellular readouts should be designed to suit different task demands remains unclear. Here, using primary rat cortical neurons cultured on a high-density microelectrode array, we investigated how input encoding and spike detection methods influence neural representations and the resulting RC performance in BNNs. Comparison of pulse amplitude modulation and latency coding revealed that the latter exhibited superior performance in demanding multiclass conditions, including a 10% improvement in a 10-class spoken digit classification task. Spike sorting further improved classification performance by enhancing class separability, while largely preserving the low-dimensional structure of population activity. These findings highlight the importance of designing information coding strategies according to task difficulty.
authors: Yusei Nishi; Hideaki Yamamoto; Yuichi Katori; Shigeo Sato

title: Integrated Droplet Microfluidic Platform for Single-Spheroid Photothermal Nanotherapy and Morphology-Driven Response Prediction.
abstract: Photothermal therapy (PTT) is a promising cancer treatment modality, but its evaluation remains limited by the lack of physiologically relevant and quantitatively controlled in vitro platforms. Here, we present a droplet-based microfluidic platform that enables single-spheroid formation, programmable nanoparticle delivery, and in situ laser irradiation with real-time thermal monitoring. The platform enables temperature multiplexing within a single experiment, allowing construction of single-spheroid dose-response relationships and the definition of a temperature-based inhibitory metric (IT50). This provides a direct and physically meaningful quantification of photothermal efficacy. In parallel, a label-free, spheroid morphology-based machine learning approach predicts treatment response across cell types, nanoparticle incubation conditions, and therapeutic regimes while preserving intrinsic single-spheroid variability. Despite a limited dataset size and biological heterogeneity, the system achieves robust and reproducible predictive performance. Overall, this work establishes a scalable and versatile microfluidic framework for quantitative photothermal nanotherapy screening, integrating controlled thermal dosing, 3D tumor models, and morphological data-driven analysis within a single-spheroid platform.
authors: Hasti Honari; Léo Dancert; Caroline Parent; Guilhem Bousquet; Jean-Louis Viovy; Claire Wilhelm

title: Integrating Artificial Intelligence with High-Throughput Biological Testing for Antimicrobial Drug Discovery
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance is eroding the effectiveness of existing antibiotics, while conventional discovery continues to yield few clinically useful chemical classes. This critical narrative review evaluates how artificial intelligence (AI) has been integrated with high-throughput screening (HTS) and prospective biological testing in antibacterial discovery. Graph-based and generative models have produced prospectively confirmed active compounds, pathogen-selective candidates and structures outside familiar antibacterial scaffolds. Where studies included suitable comparators, AI-guided selection also showed experimental enrichment. The strongest programs confirmed selected candidates through concentration-response testing, host-cell counter-screening, mechanism or resistance studies and, in some cases, animal infection models. Most workflows, however, trained a model once and tested a limited shortlist. Documented experimental feedback that changed a later model or selection decision was uncommon, and sustained design-test-learn optimization was rarer still. Comparisons were constrained by small or imbalanced datasets, chemically overlapping splits, inconsistent assay conditions and activity definitions, and limited prospective benchmarking. Most candidates also lacked comprehensive toxicity, pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic, formulation and resistance evaluation. AI-HTS integration has therefore produced useful preclinical starting points and demonstrated enrichment in selected controlled comparisons, but improved clinical productivity has not been established.
authors: Surbhi Sharma; Fadi Shehadeh; Jacob K. McPherson; Paul Peter Sotiriadis; Eleftherios E Mylonakis

title: Integrating advanced pharmaceutical manufacturing with life cycle assessment to promote eco-efficient drug development and sustainable therapeutic innovation
abstract: A holistic approach that connects pharmaceutics, manufacturing technologies and Life-Cycle Assessment (LCA) for the sustainable development of pharmaceuticals is highly significant in the current era. In this review, how advanced manufacturing technologies, namely, Process Analytical Technology (PAT), Continuous Manufacturing (CM), Artificial Intelligence (AI), and digital twins can be implemented to improve product quality and at the same time reduce energy consumption, wastage of materials, and environmental consequences has been analyzed. Sustainability indicators such as Process Mass Intensity (PMI), the improved Green Aspiration Level 2.0 and carbon emission factors have been explored for correlation with processes and the features identified as highlighting environmental sustainability. Other circular strategies like solvent recovery, water reuse and sustainable packaging are also stated. The key result of this investigation is the Sustainable Pharmaceutical Integration Framework (SPIF) enabling the integration of modern manufacturing, LCA measurements, digital decision tools and Circular Economy (CE) strategies in a single decision-making pathway. This approach will enable identification of potential environmental problems at an early stage and will optimize production to meet all product requirements. Further research needs include expanded API toxicity databases, larger and more harmonized LCA standards, and Techno-Economic Analysis (TEA). In a nutshell, sustainability means complete integration of the sustainability concept into the pharmaceutical to achieve eco-friendly and sustainable drug development.
authors: Milon Selvam Dennison; Sarad Pawar Naik Bukke; M. Abisha Meji; P. Sathish Kumar

title: Intelligent Agriculture for Plant Disease Management: A Critical Review of Operational Value, Field Reliability, Adoption Barriers, and Research Priorities
abstract: Plant disease management increasingly integrates artificial intelligence (AI), Internet of Things (IoT) sensing, remote and proximal sensing, disease forecasting, robotics, cloud–edge computing, and decision-support systems (DSS). This critical narrative review evaluated their operational value, reliability under production conditions, barriers to adoption, and priorities for improving field performance. An initial 99-record bibliography was screened, yielding 45 eligible sources; targeted searches of DOI/indexing services and publisher databases from 2010 to July 2026, while retaining earlier foundational studies, identified 35 additional DOI-verified sources, producing an 80-reference corpus. Evidence was appraised across five deployment-oriented domains: field representativeness, diagnostic ground truth, comparator quality, uncertainty and failure reporting, and operational outcomes. Intelligent tools provide three main benefits: earlier or more scalable detection, continuous and spatially explicit risk assessment, and targeted intervention. Field evidence is strongest for established disease-warning systems and selected precision-spraying applications, whereas image classifiers, foundation models, and autonomous robots remain more commonly validated in curated or crop-specific settings. Distribution shift is a major reliability concern, with commercial-field studies showing substantial performance losses under open-set conditions. Wider adoption is constrained by interoperability, cost, maintenance, connectivity, data governance, trust, liability, and unequal access. The most credible near-term pathway is supervised, context-sensitive autonomy. Future progress requires multi-farm and multi-season validation, explicit uncertainty reporting, FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) data architectures, economic evaluation, climate-adaptive hybrid models, and end-to-end comparisons with best conventional practice. Intelligent agriculture should therefore be developed as accountable plant-health infrastructure that keeps plant pathologists, advisers, and farmers in the decision loop.
authors: Emna Bouazizi; Yâakoub Gharbi

title: Intelligent drone-based biosensor for the detection of dengue virus antigen towards smart unmanned aerial-vehicle platform-based virus diagnosis
abstract: In the current work, we established a smart system for dengue diagnosis that enables on-site detection while removing the need for human intervention and continuous monitoring in difficult-to-reach areas. The system comprises of 4-smart technologies: i) drone, ii) biosensor, iii) Yolov5 AI-module, iv) a QR-code-derived digital website linked patient E-Prescription barcode, where the biosensor acts as a smart detector, and the drone as a vehicle for transporting the biosensor to the testing zone. Deep learning analysis was done by an expert using an artificial intelligence module; additional QR-code-based websites were added to the system, allowing users to scan the code and send detection data to laboratory authorities, and the patient got a medical e-prescription from the doctor. The proposed system has lightweight materials, optimized power sources, and weather-resistant housing to ensure reliable on-site diagnostics. However, practical challenges associated with drone-based diagnostic deployment, including environmental conditions, flight stability, battery capacity, payload constraints, and reliable operation in remote settings, should be considered when evaluating the field applicability and scalability of the proposed system. The suggested detection platform used the instrument-less lateral flow colorimetric approach, enabling naked-eye detection of dengue virus antigen with an LOD of 0.91 µg/mL within 5 s. As a consequence, the Drone-based approach allows clinicians to monitor the dengue virus antigen in remote populations. Accordingly, governments and non-profit organizations can utilize this technology to monitor the red alert zone, receiving precise and reliable data for informed decision-making.
authors: Mohd. Rahil Hasan; Sameer Khan; Dakshita Naithani; Pradakshina Sharma; Yashomita Mehta; Samra Ansari; Sushil Kumar; Ubaid Mushtaq Naikoo; Anupam Baliyan; Mohamed Abbas; Muneer Parayangat; Shaeen Kalathil; Jagriti Narang

title: Introduction to Devices, Circuits and Applications
abstract: This chapter lays the cornerstone for understanding the complex architecture of modern technology: electronic devices and circuits. We’ll begin by dissecting their fundamental classifications and then venture into the cutting-edge realms of nanoelectronics and quantum devices, exploring the future of computation. We’ll also examine the intricacies of circuit design, particularly for high-frequency applications, crucial for wireless communication. A significant focus will be on the Internet of Things (IoT), exploring its architecture and applications with smart cities as an example. Mastering these foundational concepts is key to grasping larger technological trends and innovations. This knowledge will help the reader navigate and contribute to the rapidly evolving landscape of electronics, providing a critical advantage in fields ranging from engineering and computer science to everyday technological use and innovation.
authors: Sangeeta Nakhate; Priti Lokhande; Gaurav Tiwari; Abhinandan Nakhate Jain

title: Isothermal Strand Displacement Amplification for Chemical Sensing: From Molecular Design to Integrated and Intelligent Platforms.
abstract: Strand displacement amplification (SDA) provides a versatile isothermal framework for chemical and biosensing, coupling polymerase-driven strand displacement with programmable nucleic-acid signal generation. Its analytical scope now extends beyond direct nucleic-acid detection because aptamers, DNAzymes, antibodies, and responsive probes can convert diverse recognition events into amplifiable DNA triggers. This review develops a unified view of SDA from molecular design to practical implementation, with particular emphasis on programmable amplicon generation, recognition-to-DNA transduction, interfacial confinement, cascaded amplification, and CRISPR coupling. The review follows SDA across biomedical, food, and environmental applications, including RNA biomarkers, liquid biopsy, genetic and epigenetic targets, proteins, enzymes, small molecules, and viruses. It also considers how these assays are being transferred into microfluidic, paper-based, lateral-flow, self-powered, regenerative, and intelligent systems. The important distinction is that analytical sensitivity does not necessarily predict practical performance. Extremely low detection limits often depend on cascaded processing beyond SDA itself, whereas real samples expose weaknesses in matrix tolerance, background suppression, reagent stability, fluid control, assay duration, and manufacturing reproducibility. Comparison with commercially established isothermal methods further shows that wider adoption will depend on converting flexible molecular chemistry into robust, standardized, sample-to-answer systems.
authors: Chia-Chun Lee; Wei-Ting Hsueh; Chin-Chung Tseng; Lung-Ming Fu

title: Knowledge Graph-Based Hypothesis Generation and Experimental Validation in Yeast
abstract: Integrating biological knowledge with automated experimentation enables the generation and testing of hypotheses for scientific discovery. However, identifying promising hypotheses from heterogeneous biological data remains challenging. Here, we present a knowledge graph-based approach to prioritising gene-chemical interactions associated with decreased chemical stress resistance in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae. We combine information from biological databases and ontologies with a hierarchy-aware graph neural network to rank candidate interactions for experimental testing. We selected 35 gene-chemical hypotheses involving six chemical stressors and evaluated them using automated growth assays. Ten hypotheses were supported after correction for multiple testing, including nine of the 30 highest-ranked candidates for the six target chemicals and one involving a poorly characterised gene. Experimental support varied across the six chemical stressors, highlighting differences in the outcomes of the tested gene-chemical interactions. These findings demonstrate how knowledge graph predictions can be evaluated experimentally to identify gene-chemical interactions for further investigation. Finally, we extended the Revisions for Improvements of Models in Biology Ontology (RIMBO) to represent knowledge graph updates alongside experimental evidence and provenance, retaining records of both supported and unsupported hypotheses. This approach connects knowledge graph-based prediction, experimental evaluation, and traceable updates to biological knowledge.
authors: Filip Kronström; Erik Y. Bjurström; Ievgeniia Tiukova; Ross D. King

title: LabCompiler: A Framework for Verifiable Human-Machine Laboratory Execution from Imperfect Protocols
abstract: Closing the loop of AI-driven science requires reliably translating natural-language protocols into executable laboratory workflows despite protocol defects and heterogeneous hardware. Existing approaches often couple scientific interpretation with device-specific code generation, making errors difficult to localize and limiting reuse across laboratory platforms. We introduce LabCompiler, a robust protocol-to-execution framework that transforms imperfect natural-language protocols into verifiable human-machine workflows. Its protocol firewall diagnoses and repairs defects before compilation while preserving unaffected content, guided by troubleshooting knowledge accumulated through perturbation-guided self-evolution. A two-level, device-agnostic graph representation separates experimental semantics from hardware-specific implementation and supports capability-based device assignment with coordinated human execution. We further introduce a protocol recovery benchmark covering four controlled perturbation types and naturally occurring errors collected from protocols written by iGEM participants. Experiments show that LabCompiler outperforms frontier LLMs in protocol error correction while enabling coordinated human-machine execution across heterogeneous, partially automated laboratory settings.
authors: Jingyuan Li; Dongzhan Zhou; Minting Pan; Yujie Liu; Yuan Gao; Yankai Jiang; Xinyu Gu; Zhe Liu; Yang Li; Bo Zhang; Lei Bai; Tong Si; Weinan Zhang

title: Labference: Benchmarking the Reasoning-Action Connection in Robotic Laboratories
abstract: Realizing Embodied AI for Science requires robots to translate experimental goals into reliable physical procedures, reducing hazardous and repetitive human work while generating evidence for scientific discovery. Although language-based planning and learned manipulation provide complementary capabilities, their integration requires robots to adapt subsequent operations to actual execution outcomes. For example, an unsuccessful placement changes what must be done next, even when the experimental goal remains unchanged. Existing benchmarks assess planning, manipulation, and laboratory workflows through task completion and reasoning or execution metrics; however, aggregate performance leaves the connection between outcome-dependent choices and physical execution unresolved. To address this evaluation gap, we introduce Labference, a benchmark for evaluating how observed physical outcomes guide subsequent choices and how those choices translate into robotic laboratory actions. Its evaluation protocol is designed to test outcome-dependent behavioral adaptation through controlled evidence variations, while independently measuring operation selection, physical execution, and task completion. Matched Oracle-assisted continuations from shared checkpoints then assess which forms of support improve subsequent choices and task completion. Initial weighing evaluations reveal target-selection errors in the tested VLA policies despite successful object transfers, whereas GPT-driven control achieves correct selection but encounters execution failures and substantial computation costs. Together, these findings highlight the need to connect task-appropriate reasoning with reliable, timely action. By making this connection measurable and diagnosable, Labference supports targeted improvements toward autonomous experimentation for Embodied AI for Science.

title: Lifecycle tissue engineering: An AI-enabled multimodal sensing and digital twin roadmap
abstract: The clinical translation of tissue engineering (TE) is critically hampered by the absence of real-time, non-invasive monitoring throughout the entire lifecycle of tissue fabrication and repair. Current reliance on end-point assessments obscures dynamic biological events, making early detection of deviations and failures challenging. While multimodal sensing offers rich data streams, inherent issues such as long-term drift, noise accumulation, and difficulties in cross-modality comparability impede their transformation into reliable process metrics and actionable insights. This review introduces a novel, comprehensive four-layer framework consisting of Problem, Data, Model, and Application Evidence, to systematically integrate artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled multimodal sensing across the full TE lifecycle. The Problem Layer delineates critical biological uncertainties and monitoring requirements. The Data Layer surveys diverse in vitro and in vivo observables, sensing modalities, and readout strategies. The Model Layer bridges data acquisition with decision-making, emphasizing AI's role in signal processing, feature extraction, data fusion, and predictive analytics for early failure identification and outcome prediction. The Application Evidence Layer synthesizes current evidence, showcasing AI and sensing applications in donor or cell screening, in vitro process optimization, post-implantation quantitative readout, longitudinal assessment, and diagnostic prediction. This framework moves beyond fragmented approaches by proposing a unified architecture for lifecycle TE, addressing a significant gap in existing literature. We further delineate a strategic roadmap for clinical translation, underscoring the imperative for standardization, long-term reliability, unified evaluation protocols, and responsible AI development. By distinguishing demonstrated technologies from integration steps that remain conceptual or require TE-specific validation, this review outlines a structured roadmap for moving TE monitoring from isolated readouts toward more predictive, traceable, and verifiable translational workflows.
authors: Xing Liu; Yitao Zhou; Cuiyi Wang; Lewei Tu; Xiaoxuan Zhao; Jingjing Gu; Qiuhua Sun; Malcolm M. Q. Xing; Yeqin Yang

title: Long-term natural aging alters the mechanical and thermal response of PDMS for microfluidic applications
abstract: Polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) is widely used in microfluidics; however, its long-term natural aging under routine storage conditions remains insufficiently characterized. PDMS was classified by curing age and compared across two macro-groups: young PDMS ( < 30 days) and aged PDMS ( > 3000 days). Specimens were evaluated by uniaxial compression, hyperelastic fitting, Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR), and thermogravimetric analysis (TGA). The average small-strain modulus rose from 0.65 MPa in young samples to 2.01 MPa in aged samples, a threefold increase ( p = 4.5 × 1 0 − 11 ). The large-strain tangent modulus did not differ significantly (119.6 versus 125.0 MPa), whereas Poisson’s ratio ν remained close to the incompressible limit in both groups (0.499 versus 0.497). Seven phenomenological hyperelastic models were compared using R 2 and the normalized root mean square error. The Mooney–Rivlin five-parameter model gave the lowest residual error, but its coefficients are not identifiable from a single deformation mode, so the three-parameter Yeoh formulation is recommended ( R 2 = 0.9940 young, 0.9890 aged). FT-IR spectra retained the characteristic PDMS bands, and the Si–CH 3 to Si–O–Si band-area ratio, the most diagnostic of methyl loss, differed by 0.3% between groups (one specimen each). TGA showed a degradation onset shifted from approximately 300 to 350 °C, a derivative thermogravimetric (DTG) peak from 423.8 to 503.3 °C, and residual mass reduced from 63.31% to 41.66%. At 10 kPa, a compliance analysis indicates that an aged microchannel deforms 67% less than a young one of identical geometry. Curing age is therefore an experimentally relevant material-state variable: aged PDMS remains chemically the same material but becomes mechanically and thermally distinct.

title: MICROROBOTIC SAMPLING AND QUANTUM BIOSENSING CO-DESIGN AT THE LIMIT An Exploratory Engineering Monograph on Sample Handling, Reference Control, and Biological Risk Boundaries This research monograph examines whether controlled micromanipulation can improve the positioning, transport, recovery, and reproducibility of biological research samples without increasing sample alteration, cross-contamination, thermal exposure, or misleading biosensor signals. The guiding three-coupling is Sample Handling × Reference Control × Biological Risk Boundary. Its guiding question is not whether an autonomous microrobot can move a sample, but whether the resulting measurement remains traceable to an authentic, independently verifiable sample state. The work synthesizes three mother research architectures: (S) Swarm Manufacturing and Robotic Matter at the Limit, particularly chapters 9–16 and 33–40, for embodied manipulation and collective transport; (QH) Autonomous Quantum Health Infrastructure at the Limit, especially chapters 9–24 and 67–74, for raw-to-result lineage, uncertainty-aware decisions, human authority and recovery; and (QB) Self-Calibrating Quantum Biosensing Networks at the Limit, particularly chapters 57–73, for fabrication variation, reference transfer, calibration, drift and measurement integrity. These sources contribute methods rather than evidence that the cross-domain integration is already demonstrated. Across 82 chapters and 12 single-section research studies per chapter, the monograph examines non-clinical microfluidic sample environments, magnetic and acoustic micromanipulation, optical and electrokinetic methods, nanoscale surface chemistry, quantum-enabled and classical biosensing, correlated uncertainty, sample-to-signal provenance, authorized closed-loop control, physical damage and carryover detection, interlaboratory replication, lifecycle burden, and successor reconstruction. Thirty mathematical and physical derivation plates introduce assumptions and validity boundaries. Every chapter presents a distinct candidate engineering relation and a geometric three-dimensional research portrait. The validation approach prioritizes synthetic phantoms and permitted ex-vivo research standards in closed non-clinical environments. It calls for blinded comparison of skilled manual pipetting, passive microfluidics, and robotic operation under matched sample identity, measurement time, contamination constraints, and independent calibration. A perceived improvement in robotic throughput or algorithmic readout quality does not establish improved sample authenticity. Any claim of quantum advantage must be compared against an appropriate, strong classical sensing baseline end to end. The research architecture closes with 200 independently framed Research Gates and 33 provisional Phoenix Answer Embryos, each accompanied by one of 233 indexed equation eggs. Gates specify questions, comparators, pass criteria, and veto conditions; answer embryos can be challenged, decomposed, recombined or retired. An accompanying Research Gates spreadsheet maps these questions to chapters, physical relations, evidence packets and future experiments. The study is explicitly exploratory and non-clinical. It does not establish the existence of mature autonomous in-body nanorobotic medicine, grant permission for diagnosis or therapy, or imply that quantum-enabled detection is intrinsically superior. Candidate indices and equations are design hypotheses unless identified as established physical relations; many passages use a recurring structured research grammar and require independent experiments, domain expert review, and peer assessment. The aim is to leave a reproducible and falsifiable research architecture that subsequent investigators are free to revise, reject, or extend. abstract: 微型機器人採樣與量子生物感測協同設計的極限 關於樣品處理、參考控制和生物風險邊界的探索性工程專著 本研究專著探討了可控微操作能否在不增加樣品改變、交叉污染、熱暴露或誤導性生物感測器訊號的前提下,改善生物研究樣品的定位、運輸、回收和可重複性。其核心三要素耦合為:樣品處理 × 參考對照 × 生物風險邊界。其核心問題並非自主微型機器人能否移動樣品,而是由此產生的測量結果是否能追溯到真實、可獨立驗證的樣品狀態。 這項工作綜合了三個母體研究架構:(S)群體製造與極限機器人物質,特別是第9-16章和第33-40章,涉及具身操控和集體運輸;(QH)極限自主量子健康基礎設施,特別是第9-24章和第67 -74章,涉及從原始資料到最終結果的溯源、不確定性感知決策、人類權威和恢復;以及(QB)極限自校準量子生物感測網絡,特別是第57-73章,涉及製造偏差、參考轉移、校準、漂移和測量完整性。這些來源提供的是方法,而非跨領域整合已被驗證的證據。 這部專著共82章,每章包含12個獨立研究部分,探討了非臨床微流控樣品環境、磁性和聲學微操控、光學和電動力學方法、奈米級表面化學、量子和經典生物感測、相關不確定性、樣品到訊號的溯源、授權閉環控制、物理損傷和殘留檢測、實驗室間重複性、相關不確定性、樣品到訊號的溯源、授權閉環控制、物理損傷和殘留檢測、實驗室間重複性、生命負擔以及後續重建等生命週期。書中包含30個數學和物理推導圖,闡述了相關假設和有效性邊界。每章都呈現獨特的候選工程關係和一個幾何三維研究圖。 驗證方法優先考慮在封閉的非臨床環境中,使用合成模型和允許的離體研究標準。它要求在匹配的樣本身份、測量時間、污染限制和獨立校準條件下,對熟練的手動移液、被動微流控和機器人操作進行盲法比較。機器人處理量或演算法讀出品質的提升並不能證明樣本真實性的提升。任何關於量子優勢的說法都必須與適當的、可靠的經典感測基線進行端到端的比較。 研究架構包含 200 個獨立建構的研究門和 33 個暫定的鳳凰答案胚胎,每個答案胚胎對應 233 個索引方程式卵中的一個。研究門規定了問題、比較器、通過標準和否決條件;答案胚胎可以被質疑、分解、重組或棄用。配套的研究門電子表格將這些問題映射到章節、物理關係、證據包和未來實驗。 本研究明確屬於探索性研究,而非臨床研究。它並未證實成熟的自主體內奈米機器人醫療技術的存在,也未授權用於診斷或治療,更未暗示量子檢測技術本質上優於其他技術。除非明確指出是已確立的物理關係,否則候選指標和方程式均為設計假設;許多段落採用重複出現的結構化研究語法,並要求進行獨立實驗、領域專家評審和同行評估。本研究旨在建構一個可重複且可證偽的研究框架,以供後續研究者自由修改、否定或擴展。 馮承恩(33)× Starli STARLI | 奈米-量子三耦合研究系列 | 旗艦13 Support STARLI Research Gates ☕ If you find value in our open research, scientific explorations, and technological blueprints for the future, you are warmly invited to support our continued creative journey. title: Machine Learning–Assisted Fluorescent Eu@ZnMOF for the Enoxacin and Glyphosate Detection in Food by Suppressing Sensitization and Ligand–Metal Charge Transfer
abstract: The antibiotics and pesticides in the ecosystem environment, owing to their extensive application in veterinary medicine and insecticides, present a significant hazard to public health. Herein, we developed a novel bimetallic metal‐organic framework (MOF) as a ratiometric fluorescent sensor for the simultaneous monitoring of enoxacin (ENX) and glyphosate (GLY). To fabricate a dual‐responsive probe, we synthesized the ZnMOF by reacting Zn 2+ ions with the ligands (2,2′‐bipyridine‐5,5′‐dicarboxylic acid, 8‐hydroxyquinoline, and 2‐aminoterephthalic acid). Subsequently, the bimetallic Eu@ZnMOF was synthesized by loading europium (Eu 3+ ) ions into the ZnMOF based on the coordination with the 2,2′‐bipyridine‐5,5′‐dicarboxylic acid sites. The Eu@ZnMOF‐based detection system exhibits a distinct green emission due to the suppression of excited‐state intramolecular proton transfer in 8‐hydroxyquinoline by Zn 2+ ions. In the detection system, ENX enhances the red emission of Eu@ZnMOF by sensitizing Eu 3+ ions. Accordingly, the ENX fluorescent sensing system was fabricated. Moreover, ENX‐modified Eu@ZnMOF was fabricated. Upon the addition of GLY, suppression of sensitization and ligand‐to‐metal charge transfer (LMCT) occurs, which quenches the red emission of Eu 3+ and boosts the blue emission, resulting in a distinct color transition from red to blue. The ratiometric fluorescent sensor allows detection limits of 0.05 and 0.10 mg/L for ENX and GLY, respectively. Moreover, we integrated this material into a microfluidic chip. By combining this platform with smartphone imaging and machine learning algorithms, we constructed a rapid detection protocol capable of simultaneous multi‐sample analysis. These results demonstrate the promising application potential of Eu@ZnMOF for advanced environmental and food‐safety testing.
authors: Ze Li; Yan Man; Qingju Liu; Jilong Han; Zhikun Zhang

title: Machine learning-based Taylor cone analysis for electrospinning process-window identification and cell-laden nanofiber scaffold fabrication
abstract: Electrospinning is a powerful biofabrication technique for constructing fibrous scaffolds that mimic extracellular matrix architectures. However, the process is highly nonlinear and involves strongly coupled parameters, making fiber architecture and biological performance difficult to control empirically and limits reproducibility. Most ML studies still focus on static correlations between processing parameters and outcomes rather than on dynamic modeling of electrospinning evolution and regulation, thereby hindering real-time, precise process control. Here, we establish a data-driven framework that links process parameters, Taylor cone geometry, and nanofiber/cell outcomes through high-speed imaging and ML. A custom image-processing pipeline is developed to automatically extract cone angle, height, and width from in situ images with improved accuracy via a rotating-ray–based geometric algorithm. Using datasets collected from three representative polymer systems PVDF, PVB, and PEO, RF models outperform SVM and MDL, achieving moderate-to-good prediction of Taylor cone descriptors ( R 2 ≈ 0.57-0.83) across varied voltages, flow rates, and needle–collector distances. We further extend this framework to PEO-based cell electrospinning. By correlating predicted cone geometries with experimentally measured viability of 293 T cells and umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cells, we identify a Taylor cone ‘safe window’ that simultaneously stabilizes jet formation and preserves cell survival (>95%). Guided by this window, a bilayer cell-laden scaffold comprising a PVB support layer and a PEO–cell layer is fabricated with improved process robustness. This enables stable delivery of high-density, highly viable cells and facilitates the fabrication of three-dimensional cell-laden nanofiber scaffolds. Overall, this ML-guided Taylor cone analysis strategy provides a quantitative framework for process-window identification in polymer and cell electrospinning, and may support future integration with real-time monitoring, online inference, and closed-loop control in intelligent biofabrication.
authors: Huazhen Liu; Kaidi Luo; Jiayao Gu; Wenbin Sun; Xiaoyi Wang; Yongjun Zheng; Zhijian Li; Su Xiao; Yuanyuan Liu

title: Magnetic Field-Based Intervention in Cardiovascular Diseases: Biological Basis, Therapeutic Strategies, and Translational Challenges
abstract: Cardiovascular diseases remain the leading cause of death worldwide, and their burden continues to rise. As a noninvasive physical intervention, magnetic fields offer deep tissue penetration, remote programmability, and favorable spatiotemporal controllability, making them uniquely valuable for modulating cardiovascular function. This review systematically summarizes the biological basis of magnetic field actions on the cardiovascular system, including multi-scale effects on cardiac electrophysiology and ion channels, vascular endothelial function and microcirculatory perfusion, and cardiac autonomic regulation. On this basis, we synthesize therapeutic advances in three areas: electrophysiological intervention in arrhythmias, cardiac autonomic neuromodulation, and cardiac repair and regeneration. Preclinical evidence indicates that magnetic fields can mediate nonpharmacological intervention in arrhythmias, myocardial infarction, and heart failure, although clinical validation to date is limited to a single small randomized trial. Finally, we analyze translational bottlenecks (standardization of stimulation parameters, long-term in vivo safety assessment, and intelligent closed-loop control) and outline future directions integrating magnetic fields with regenerative medicine and artificial intelligence, aiming to provide new strategies for precision cardiovascular care.
authors: 孔德汶; 唐杨烽

title: Making Self-Driving Laboratories Auditable:A Unified Framework for Hybrid Actions,Measurements, and Safe Execution
abstract: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) are laboratory systems that couple experimental planning, automated execution, and measurement feedback in a closed loop. Integrating flexible robot control with the typed application programming interfaces (APIs) and continuous measurements exposed by laboratory instruments remains an execution-interface challenge. To address this challenge, we propose a traceable framework comprising four components: LAM (Lab Action Model), OpenSDL, Safe-SDL, and L3-Bench. LAM is a proposed measurement-conditioned policy architecture that extends vision-language-action paradigms to generate both continuous robot trajectories and typed instrument API calls. OpenSDL is an execution substrate with an initial control implementation, designed to map role-level operations to heterogeneous devices, coordinate execution, and record timestamped causal events. The proposed Safe-SDL runtime gate combines pre-dispatch schema and resource checks with signal temporal logic monitoring during execution, including extended waiting periods. L3-Bench (Level-3 Laboratory Benchmark) specifies an episode-level evaluation protocol covering physical outcomes, timing, reproducibility, safety violations, and fault recovery. Together, these components provide an end-to-end design for linking hybrid action generation, monitored device execution, measurement feedback, and experimental evaluation, addressing coordination and traceability challenges in SDL workflows.
authors: Zihan Zhang; Zeyu Wu; Xin Zhang; Mingyu Luo; Haohui Que; Tong Zhu

title: Management of acute necrotizing pancreatitis: Current evidence, controversies and future perspectives
abstract: Acute necrotizing pancreatitis affects 10%-20% of patients with acute pancreatitis and carries substantial morbidity and mortality, ranging from 15% in sterile necrosis to 30-40% in infected necrosis.Over the past two decades, management has shifted from early aggressive intervention to a delayed, minimally invasive "step-up" approach, though several aspects remain non-standardized.This narrative review synthesizes evidence from randomized controlled trials, systematic reviews, meta-analyses and current guidelines across diagnosis, supportive care, antibiotics, intervention indications, step-up strategies, minimally invasive and open necrosectomy.Initial management should favor moderate fluid resuscitation, early oral/enteral feeding, and appropriate intensive care unit triage.Antibiotic prophylaxis is unsupported by evidence and therapy should be reserved for confirmed or strongly suspected infected necrosis, guided by clinical/radiological reassessment.When intervention is needed, step-up remains standard of care.Endoscopic and surgical step-up show broadly comparable survival, though not uniformly across anatomical patterns and settings, with endoscopy favoring fistula rates and length of stay.Minimally invasive necrosectomy is associated with lower mortality and fewer complications than open necrosectomy.However, these findings are largely observational and prone to confounding by indication.Based on this evidence, we propose a risk-adapted algorithm separating risk stratification from treatment escalation.
authors: Matteo Matteucci; Riccardo Masserano; Daniele Tesoro; Andrea Colombo; Luca Portigliotti; Giampaolo Formisano; Paolo Pietro Bianchi

title: Mapping Skill Demand and Occupational Interdependencies in Online Job Postings: A Sentence-BERT and Vector Space Approach
abstract: The accelerating pace of technological change, automation and artificial intelligence is profoundly restructuring global labour markets, shifting the focus of demand-side analyses from static occupational titles toward dynamic and multifaceted skill portfolios. Traditional macroeconomic monitoring instruments, such as employer surveys and administrative registries, frequently suffer from significant reporting latency, aggregate oversimplification and rigid taxonomic classifications that fail to capture emerging competencies in real time. This study investigates the structural interdependencies and statistical dispersion of demanded skills across nine major occupational groups by analyzing a massive repository of web-scraped job postings from leading commercial recruitment platforms in Poland (SOJO dataset, 2019–2023). Leveraging Natural Language Processing, raw vacancy descriptions were embedded using a deep contextual Sentence-BERT architecture and mapped into the European Skills, Competences, Qualifications and Occupations (ESCO) taxonomy via Facebook AI Similarity Search (FAISS) dense vector indexing at a strict similarity threshold. In addition, the distribution, concentration and dispersion of 74 medium-level skill concepts were assessed through box-plot parameters, interquartile ranges and outlier analyses. The empirical findings confirm that skill demand varies significantly across occupational categories in both type and frequency, while revealing strong cross-occupational penetration of digital literacy, operational coordination and transversal capabilities into traditionally manual occupations. These results provide actionable insights for technological forecasting, curriculum modernization and data-driven active labour market policies.
authors: Karolina Bolesta

title: Mapping artificial intelligence for science with open metadata reveals shifting evidence regimes across scientific domains
abstract: Artificial intelligence for science (AI4S) is often discussed as a unified transformation, although scientific domains differ markedly in how model outputs are tested, validated, and justified. We map an audited corpus of N=2,784 records (2014–2025) retrieved from Crossref and screened with a frozen, versioned rulebook, and compare evidence regimes in protein science, materials design, drug discovery, closed-loop experimentation, and mathematical reasoning. Using term co-occurrence, reference co-citation, burst detection, growth models, and collaboration networks, we identify three robust patterns: (i) rapid but decelerating growth (Poisson rate 1.381, 95% CI 1.361–1.402, declining from 1.537 in 2014–2019 to 1.320 in 2019–2025); (ii) a coherent term-co-occurrence structure (75 nodes, modularity Q=0.404 ) organized around four measured streams—representation learning, generative and inverse design, closed-loop experimentation, and neuro-symbolic reasoning—with the generative stream acting as the connecting hub; and (iii) a right-boundary rise in large language model terminology (burst state 3) that a year-by-year backtest shows is not a last-observation artefact. The maps are sensitive to metadata availability: abstract coverage is 50.6%, reference coverage 84.3%, and a title-only variant changes the network partition substantially (adjusted Rand index 0.762), so the maps describe the screened open-metadata corpus rather than the total AI4S literature. Cross-domain analysis shows that AI most consequentially shifts scientific bottlenecks from representation and candidate generation toward experimental or formal validation, provenance, and responsibility for claims. We contribute an auditable, open-metadata science-mapping workflow designed for reproducibility and an evidence-regime framework for analysing how epistemic labour is redistributed across models, instruments, formal verifiers, infrastructures, and human experts.
authors: Fengchang X, Ge L, Xinliang W, Na Z.

title: Mapping the technology–demand interface: how brain organoid evolution is reshaping the translational landscape of stroke
abstract: Stroke research faces a dual modeling barrier: interspecies divergence and oversimplified 2D cultures have contributed to the failure of many neuroprotective trials. Brain organoids, which provide human genetic backgrounds and 3D neural networks, offer a promising but incomplete solution. Existing reviews often address isolated technological aspects without linking them to stroke-specific demands. This narrative review establishes a "technological iteration-clinical demand" mapping matrix (Figure 1). We trace organoid evolution from static oxygen-glucose deprivation models to vascularized, assembloid, and microfluidic chip-integrated systems, and toward multi-organ coupling. We highlight how these advances may uncover human-specific neuroinflammation, proposed PANoptosis-like spatiotemporal cascades, and synaptic deficits mediated by human-specific genes such as SRGAP2C. We argue that the inability of animal models to resolve certain human-specific targets is driving organoids from static endpoint models toward dynamic platforms with perfusable vasculature and immune integration, although current systems remain at an early stage. We critically evaluate the preclinical role of organoids, defining scenarios where they may partially replace animal testing and where they cannot. Major bottlenecks include fetal-like organoid maturity (transcriptome approximately equivalent to gestational weeks 12-20) versus the average stroke onset age of about 70 years, and the absence of peripheral immune infiltration, which mediates a large fraction of secondary injury. We outline potential solutions including multi-omics integration, inducible aging, gene editing, and multi-organ chip coupling, and emphasize that standardized evaluation frameworks are needed to translate organoid findings into personalized stroke therapy.
authors: Caohang Qiu; Ning Sun; Jun Yang; Ling Tan; Maoyu Zhao; Yuyao Fu; Gonghong Liu; Zhifu Song; Wenyou Wu
