title: Matrix-Based Specific T-Cell Activation Reporter for Nearly-Digital Mapping of Antigen-Specific T Cells via Heterotypic Cell Micro-Communities and Digital Microfluidics.
abstract: Antigen-specific T cells constitute a low percentage of peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) and require antigen presentation by autologous antigen-presenting cells for activation and cytokine secretion. Conventional interferon-γ release assay (IGRA) averages rare activation events beyond cellular resolution, while single-cell compartmentalization disrupts the intracellular synapses for T cell immunity. Here, we developed mSTAR (matrix-based Specific T-cell Activation Reporter), an active-matrix digital microfluidic platform that partitions microliters of PBMCs into a nanoliter-scale matrix of 16 cell microcommunities (CMCs), each retaining tens to hundreds of PBMCs in their native heterotypic composition to preserve the natural physiological immune response. In a proof of concept, mSTAR executes parallel IGRA for a tuberculosis disease model, including CMC stimulation and magnetic-bead-based immunofluorescence assay. The IGRA of the mSTAR system achieves a limit of detection of 3.70 pg/mL, yielding 16 interferon-γ quantification readouts and ratios between CMCs incubated with different stimulants (negative, positive, or specific antigen). This enables the mapping and reporting of activated antigen-specific T cells in the matrix, thereby achieving functional phenotyping of each CMC. Poisson-based modeling of the droplet matrix converts rare T-cell activation events into a nearly digital estimation, and the positive CMCs encapsulating target cells can be retrieved for further characterization without loss. By bridging functional phenotyping and molecular features without prior cell sorting or engineering, mSTAR provides a programmable immunoanalytical infrastructure for broad downstream applications such as antigen-specific immunotherapy development or T-cell receptor discovery.
authors: Hangjia Tu; Mengxing Mou; Chenxuan Hu; Jinxin Fu; Xiaotian Tan; Yuzhong Xu; Ji Huang; Wenxin Yan; Wenjuan Wu; Peijin Wang; Tianyuan Zhao; Jianheng Huang; Binmao Zhang; Chengbin Yang; Hanbin Ma; Siyi Hu; Yujuan Chai

title: Measurement of multiple rheological properties of oil–water emulsions using a rotating device and machine learning
abstract: Rapid and non-intrusive measurement of the rheological properties of non-Newtonian fluids is crucial for applications such as the development of autonomous experimental systems. Herein, we propose a technique that utilizes machine learning to sequentially predict surface tension, contact angle, and viscosity characteristics based on flow images. Flow images were obtained by rotating oil–water emulsion samples in a cuvette by 90°. The extracted interface positions were used as features to train a random forest algorithm. The 1 mL emulsion sample remained entirely unconsumed, and the measurement was completed in 6 s. We demonstrated that the surface tension and contact angles of eight emulsion samples could be predicted with a NRMSE = 27.7% or less using training data from only two samples.
authors: Kazuhiro ITOH; 沙優 橋本; Mehak Jain; Masakazu Morimoto

title: Mechanical Versus Kinematic Alignment in Total Knee Arthroplasty: Relationship Between Postoperative Alignment and Short-Term Functional Outcomes
abstract: Background/Objectives: Mechanical alignment (MA) has traditionally been the reference alignment strategy in total knee arthroplasty (TKA), whereas kinematic alignment (KA) has emerged as an individualized alternative intended to approximate patient-specific knee anatomy. However, the relationship between postoperative mechanical-axis alignment and functional recovery remains incompletely understood. This study aimed to compare short-term functional outcomes and postoperative mechanical-axis alignment between MA and KA following primary TKA and to investigate the relationship between measured postoperative alignment parameters and functional outcomes. Methods: This single-center retrospective comparative cohort study included 120 patients who underwent primary unilateral TKA for end-stage knee osteoarthritis (KOA) between January 2022 and December 2024; 51 underwent MA and 69 underwent KA. Radiographic assessment included the hip–knee–ankle (HKA) angle, mechanical-axis deviation (MAD), residual varus deformity, and radiographic knee extension deficit. Functional outcomes were assessed using the Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS), the Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC), and the Knee Society Score (KSS). Preoperative, postoperative, and change-from-baseline (Δ) functional scores were evaluated. Analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) was used to assess associations between alignment strategy and postoperative functional outcomes after adjustment for baseline functional scores and relevant covariates. Associations between postoperative radiographic parameters and functional outcomes were additionally assessed. Results: Both alignment groups demonstrated substantial preoperative-to-postoperative functional improvement. MA achieved postoperative HKA alignment closer to the neutral mechanical axis than KA (179.63 ± 1.23° vs. 178.24 ± 2.32°; p < 0.001; FDR-adjusted p < 0.001). Absolute HKA deviation from neutral was lower with MA (0.97 ± 0.83° vs. 2.42 ± 1.62°; FDR-adjusted p < 0.001), as was postoperative absolute MAD (5.19 ± 4.53 mm vs. 7.86 ± 6.76 mm; p = 0.011; FDR-adjusted p = 0.018). KA was associated with a higher unadjusted postoperative KOOS score than MA (84.04 ± 12.33 vs. 77.12 ± 15.65; p = 0.010), whereas postoperative WOMAC (p = 0.206) and KSS (p = 0.843) did not differ significantly between groups. Between-group differences in change from baseline were not statistically significant for KOOS (p = 0.227), WOMAC (p = 0.130), or KSS (p = 0.427). After multivariable adjustment, no statistically significant between-group associations were observed for postoperative KOOS (adjusted β = 2.42; 95% CI, −0.93 to 5.77; p = 0.155), WOMAC (adjusted β = −2.80; 95% CI, −6.73 to 1.14; p = 0.162), or KSS (adjusted β = 1.09; 95% CI, −2.05 to 4.24; p = 0.492). Associations between the postoperative radiographic parameters and functional outcomes were negligible to weak, with none remaining statistically significant after FDR correction. Conclusions: Both MA and KA were associated with substantial short-term functional improvement, with no significant between-group differences in the magnitude of improvement from baseline. MA achieved postoperative alignment closer to the neutral mechanical axis, while the higher unadjusted postoperative KOOS score observed with KA was not statistically significant after adjustment for baseline characteristics and potential confounders. No significant postoperative differences in WOMAC or KSS were observed. The generally weak associations between measured postoperative mechanical-axis parameters and functional outcomes suggest that mechanical-axis alignment alone may not adequately explain short-term functional recovery. Because patient-specific coronal alignment parameters and achievement of the individualized KA target were not quantitatively assessed, the present findings cannot determine whether restoration of patient-specific anatomy was associated with functional outcomes.
authors: Giada Baroni; Elena Lucchesini; Dan Fruja; Ioana Teodora Floarea; Ana-Liana Bouroș-Tataru; Laura Ioana Bondar; Nicoleta Anamaria Paşcalău; Corina Dalia Toderescu; Georgeta Lucia Piscoi; Alexandru Pop

title: Methods of studying monocyte transmigration in norm and pathology
abstract: The aim of the work is to analyze modern methods of studying the migration of monocytes from blood vessels to tissues. Material and methods. 59 sources were selected in the Pubmed database by key queries related to the migration of monocytes and leukocytes. The selection criterion was the description of the process of the movement of monocytes (transmigration) through the endothelial barrier in vitro or in vivo . Results and discussion. The mechanisms of monocyte transmigration are summarized. A comparison of in vitro (Boyden chamber, µ-slides, microfluidic systems) methods of studying migration was carried out according to a number of criteria. The Boyden chamber is the simplest and most common method, widely used to test the effect of therapy on monocytes. Real-time transmigration observation is possible using real-time cell assay migration cells and µ-slides with a viewing field, which is widely used to evaluate cell morphological properties. Microfluidic systems have enabled the creation of complex systems capable of mimicking the circulatory system; however, this method is not standardized and is complex to manufacture in laboratory conditions. To assess the representativeness of the experimental models, data on the study of in vivo migration are presented – fluorescent labeling of cells, nuclear tomography, bioluminescence. Conclusions. The review combines modern ideas about the mechanisms of monocyte migration and their modeling in vitro and in vivo . The criteria for evaluating model systems, their advantages, disadvantages, and possibilities of application in research and in therapy of diseases are described.
authors: Vadim Solntzev; R. V. Plotnitskii; V. A. Markelov; Ksenia Vladimirovna Danilko

title: Micro Shock Waves
abstract: Shock waves occur in many different ways. They are widespread in nature and present in science and technology. If one disregards shock wave generation in high-energy-density experiments such as with laser-produced plasmas (LPP), nearly all shock waves can be considered as macroscopic, even though phenomena on microscale may play a role. In particular, shock wave research makes use of macroscopic shock tubes with inner diameters typically ranging from centimeters up to more than a meter. However, supersonic flows may behave differently, when generated and propagated in microtubes where the inner diameter may be as small as ten to a few hundred micrometers. This topic of shock waves at micro scale is totally new and may be regarded as a new area of fluid mechanics. Not only is downscaling not necessarily trivial, but novel physical phenomena also are encountered to offer numerous opportunities for in-depth study. This includes the access for shock wave research in regimes not accessible with macroscopic shock tubes. This chapter reviews the subject of “guided” supersonic flows, namely shock (and blast) waves in microtubes or capillaries, simply termed as “micro shock waves”. It lays emphasis on experimental work, including the discussion of novel methods of shock generation and well-adapted special diagnostics for the investigation of the shock propagation. However, theoretical issues and accompanying computational fluidic dynamics (CFD) simulations are covered as well. At the end of the present chapter, potential future applications are presented. They may come to the fields of microfluidics, physical chemistry, or biology/medicine. This includes opportunities for multidisciplinary physics approaches, for example, experiments with free electron lasers performed at high repetition rate may be mentioned. Thus, overall, micro shock waves may offer many surprises.
authors: Ulrich Teubner

title: Microcapillary-assisted acoustoelectric platform for selective single-cell isolation and in situ transfection
abstract: Single-cell transfection technologies hold tremendous promise for precision cell and immunotherapies. However, monolithic integration of cell isolation with targeted intracellular delivery remains technically challenging, especially within complex biological matrices. Herein, we present a microcapillary-assisted acoustoelectric single-cell selective isolation and sonoporative transfection platform (μC-ASSIST), which seamlessly sequences microcapillary-assisted dielectrophoresis (μC-DEP) for deterministic single-cell trapping with high-frequency surface acoustic waves (SAWs) for transient membrane poration within a unified workflow. We demonstrate the label-free, high-efficiency extraction of human non-small cell lung cancer (A549) cells from a complex white blood cell (WBC) background with a capture efficiency of 95%. Furthermore, we validate the highly efficient, contact-free intracellular delivery of diverse cargoes ranging from small dyes (PI) to functional small interfering RNA (siRNA) and large plasmid DNA (mRFP-C3), maintaining a high cell viability of 83.7% alongside a 78.1% transfection efficiency. Crucially, the targeted delivery of siBcl-xL significantly suppressed target mRNA expression and profoundly inhibited tumor cell motility. By circumventing off-target effects and cumbersome manual handling, the μC-ASSIST platform establishes a highly versatile, streamlined paradigm for precision single-cell engineering, holding immense potential for advancing functional genomics and next-generation gene therapies.
authors: Xuefeng Xu; Ziqiao Zhou; Guangyang Li; Jie Liang; Jianhui Wu; Jiaqi Lu; Fang Shen; Shengjun Wu; Zhi Ruan; Shurong Dong; Jikui Luo; Zhen Cao

title: Microdroplet Generator Surrogate Enhancement and Inverse Design Through an Uncertainty-Guided Framework
abstract: Microfluidic droplet generation is critical for many applications, yet efficient device design in high-dimensional parameter spaces remains computationally prohibitive due to complex multiphase flow dynamics. This work presents a unified methodology that couples adaptive surrogate enhancement with simulation-driven inverse design. High-fidelity Volume-of-Fluid simulations provide ground-truth data, while neural network ensembles predict flow regimes and droplet diameters. Ensemble-based uncertainty quantification identifies epistemic uncertainty using consensus levels for regime classification and the coefficient of variation for diameter prediction, revealing that uncertainty concentrates near regime transition boundaries where physics is highly sensitive to parameter perturbations. A physics-informed enrichment strategy targets these critical zones and addresses class imbalances by deploying additional targeted simulations and retraining the surrogates forming the ensembles. A framework that integrates Particle Swarm Optimization for constrained inverse design, balancing accuracy with predictive confidence and physical consistency is therefore proposed. Validation on independent test datasets demonstrates that the enriched ensembles achieve higher accuracy, with the fraction of predictions within the 0-3% error range on droplet diameter nearly doubling, and high-error cases (above 10%) dropping substantially. The inverse design procedure reliably identifies physically realizable configurations meeting target droplet sizes. This approach significantly reduces computational costs while ensuring reliable predictions, offering a framework with potential applicability to the optimization of a broad range of microfluidic systems.
authors: David Gabriel Harispe; Matías Gerard; Pablo A. Kler

title: Microfluidic Chips in Food Science: From Principles to Applications and Beyond
abstract: The microfluidic has emerged as a promising platform to manipulate the fluid in micro scale. It has been widely used in multiple fields, e.g ., biomedical engineering, analytical chemistry, environment detection, and drug screening. Recently, the application of microfluidic chip has been extended to the food science. The microfluidic chip can be used to fabricate food delivery systems, e.g ., emulsions, lipid vesicles, microparticles, and microcapsules. These systems encapsulate the bioactive substances that are highly nutritious but sensitive to environmental factors. Another application of microfluidic chip in food science is to detect food hazards. It has exhibited several advantages, such as portability, ease to manipulate, low cost, and low sample consumption. Moreover, the nutrition delivery systems show excellent performances in monodispersity, size uniformity, and also stability. The microfluidic chip for food science has attracted considerable attention and is still developing rapidly. To make this novel technique well-known to the researchers in this field, we summarized the advances of microfluidic technology in food science, including the design of microfluidic chips, and the detailed applications. At the end, we proposed the current challenges and possible solutions, and prospected the future development.
authors: Yuqing Dong; Wenyuan Kang; Yuting Yin; Qingzhen Yang

title: Microfluidic Fabrication of Functional Micro-/Nanoparticles: From Structural Regulation to Scalable Integration.
abstract: Functional particles play critical roles in biomedicine, sensing, catalysis, energy storage and conversion, and environmental remediation. Conventional bulk synthesis can provide limited control over local reaction environments when narrow size distributions, complex morphologies, or hierarchical architectures are required. Microfluidic synthesis addresses these limitations by confining reactions within microscale channels, droplets, or flow segments, thereby enabling controlled multiphase flow, rapid heat and mass transfer, and precise regulation of local reaction conditions. This review is organized around a particle formation/process control/particle properties/scale-up framework, linking microfluidic design and operating parameters to nucleation, growth, phase separation, interfacial assembly, and solidification, and subsequently to particle size, morphology, dispersity, and hierarchical structure. Representative strategies, including droplet microfluidics, hydrodynamic focusing, co-flow systems, structured microchannels, and integrated microreactors, are critically compared in terms of particle-quality control and manufacturing feasibility. Particular attention is given to scalability, productivity, process robustness, clogging, downstream processing, and internal and external integration. Although microfluidic processing can improve control and reproducibility, many reported systems remain at the proof-of-concept or laboratory scale. Future development therefore requires quantitative process-structured relationships, robust device engineering, in-line monitoring, feedback control, and validated scale-up strategies.
authors: Ran Tian; Jiani Liu; Tao Liu; Hanyu Du; Geng Dou; Juan Tong; Xinyu Qiu; Linqian Hou; Xiaoju Lu; Yuting Su

title: Microfluidic engineering for organoid formation, cultivation, and sensing
abstract: models for studying tissue morphogenesis, organogenesis, and disease mechanisms. However, they are typically generated and maintained in static culture without perfusion, a configuration that imposes fundamental biophysical constraints and thereby restricts their physiological relevance. This review examines how microfluidic engineering addresses these limitations across the entire organoid workflow, from formation and long-term culture to integrated biosensing. First, we analyze how material selection, flow actuation, and channel hydrodynamics define the engineering basis for controlled microenvironments. We then classify microfluidic architectures by function: geometric confinement and droplet microfluidics for organoid formation; mechanical stimulation, vascularization, co-cultivation, and gradient control for long-term culture; and on-chip imaging with physical and biochemical sensors for real-time monitoring. By mapping these engineering solutions onto specific biological bottlenecks-diffusion-limited transport, the absence of vasculature, and sparse inter-tissue crosstalk-we identify persistent challenges in reproducibility, standardization, and sensor integration. Finally, we discuss the path toward regulatory qualification of such platforms and their potential to advance personalized medicine while reducing reliance on animal testing.
authors: I. A. Kushnir; K. O. Salina; Y. A. Bogolubova; T. M. Mushegian; M. A. Dragun; D. D. Volegova; L. Y. Polynkin; A. A. Kopylova; A. B. Salmina; S. O. Yurchenko

title: Microfluidic platforms for Enzymatic assays: advances, challenges, and clinical applications
abstract: Enzymatic assays are fundamental tools in clinical diagnostics and biomedical research owing to their high specificity and sensitivity for biomarker quantification. However, their translation from centralized laboratories to point-of-care (POC) and resource-limited settings remains limited by lengthy assay procedures, high reagent consumption, and reliance on conventional analytical instrumentation. Microfluidic technologies address many of these limitations by enabling precise fluid handling, reducing sample and reagent volumes, and integrating multiple analytical processes within miniaturized platforms. In this review, we critically examine recent advances in enzymatic microfluidic systems for biomarker analysis, with particular emphasis on their applicability to POC diagnostics. Rather than providing a descriptive overview, we systematically compare pressure-driven, centrifugal, droplet-based, and digital microfluidic platforms with respect to device architecture, reaction kinetics, detection strategies, analytical performance, system integration, and clinical applicability. We further discuss how microscale factors, including thermal regulation, mass transfer, surface interactions, and enzyme immobilization, influence the performance of enzymatic assays across different platforms. In addition, we critically assess the current level of experimental and clinical validation, highlighting persistent challenges related to reproducibility, standardization, scalability, and clinical translation. By linking microfluidic design principles with enzymatic assay performance, this review provides a conceptual framework for the rational development and future clinical implementation of next-generation microfluidic enzymatic assays.
authors: Bahareh Mohammadi Jobani; Esmail Pishbin; Amin Dehghan; Siamak Salami; Amid Rahi; Zahra Shahsavari

title: Microfluidic-Based Molecular Diagnostics for Pathogen Detection in Urine Samples for Resource-Limited Settings: A Review
abstract: Urine is a convenient, noninvasive specimen for molecular diagnostics, offering advantages in scalability, patient compliance, and suitability for decentralized testing. However, its clinical adoption for molecular pathogen detection remains limited by intrinsic physicochemical variability, low target abundance, and the presence of inhibitors of enzymatic nucleic acid amplification that may seriously compromise assay sensitivity and reproducibility. In this review, we introduce a urine-first design paradigm in which device architecture and assay chemistry are codesigned around the unique biochemical constraints of urine rather than adapted from conventional blood-based workflows. This paradigm is built on three interdependent principles: matrix-aware sample processing with efficient inhibitor removal and multifraction nucleic acid capture; amplification chemistry with built-in tolerance to pH fluctuations, ionic variability, and residual urinary inhibitors; and closed, integrated microfluidic architectures that minimize contamination risk. We compare on-chip amplification strategies, including PCR, isothermal amplification methods such as LAMP and RPA, digital PCR, and CRISPR-assisted detection, and evaluate trade-offs in sensitivity, inhibitor tolerance, and deployability. Detection modalities, including fluorescence, colorimetric, electrochemical, and lateral-flow readouts, are assessed for analytical performance and compatibility with resource-limited settings. By integrating biological insight with engineering design, this review provides a practical roadmap for developing accessible, field-ready urine-based diagnostic platforms.
authors: E. Alperay Tarim; Natish Kumar; Michael Mauk; Mohamed El‐Tholoth

title: Microfluidics Lab‐on‐a‐Chip Approaches to Decipher Atherosclerosis Pathogenesis
abstract: Atherosclerosis is a complex, multifactorial disease driven by intricate cellular and molecular interactions within the vascular microenvironment. While conventional experimental models have provided important insights into disease progression, they often fail to recapitulate the coupled mechanical and biochemical stimuli that govern vascular pathology in vivo. Lab-on-a-chip technologies offer a powerful platform for reconstructing key cellular and tissue-level features of atherosclerosis within controlled microscale environments, enabling the study of processes such as endothelial dysfunction, inflammatory signaling, cell-matrix interactions, and vascular remodeling. The integration of microfluidics further enhances these models by enabling precise control of flow-derived mechanical cues, including shear stress, vascular geometry, and pulsatile pressure. This review highlights recent advances in microfluidic lab-on-a-chip models for atherosclerosis research, with a focus on their ability to replicate human-relevant pathophysiological conditions. We discuss pioneering studies that have employed these paltforms to investigate endothelial barrier dysfunction, monocyte recruitment, foam cell formation, vascular remodeling, and plaque instability across different stages of disease progression. Collectively, these microfluidic systems provide powerful, physiologically relevant tools for dissecting the mechanisms underlying atherosclerosis and evaluating therapeutic strategies under controlled, biomimetic vascular conditions.
authors: Fahima Akther; Hang Thu Ta

title: Microfluidics to assess the impact of transfused blood components
abstract: Assessing the function of transfused blood components within the dynamic environment of the vascular system remains challenging, as conventional assays are largely static and poorly represent the dynamic mechanical and biochemical interactions between blood cells and the vessel wall. Microfluidic approaches, which study blood flow within small-scale channels, provide an opportunity to bridge this gap by introducing physiologically relevant flow and shear rates into experimental models. This review synthesises the current literature describing the application of microfluidic technologies to the assessment of transfused blood components, with particular emphasis on platelet concentrates, red cell concentrates and plasma-derived products. Across existing studies, microfluidic models have demonstrated differences in component function related to storage conditions, manufacturing methods and emerging transfusion products that are not always detected using conventional bulk assays. These approaches have provided new insights into platelet haemostasis at defined shear rates, red cell deformability and gas exchange, and plasma-mediated coagulation in trauma and critical illness. However, substantial diversity in device design, experimental conditions and analytical endpoints limits direct comparison between studies and constrains translation into routine practice. The development of more standardised platforms, alongside integration with endothelialised and organ-on-a-chip models, may help to overcome these challenges. Overall, microfluidics represents a promising tool for improving functional assessment of blood components and supporting future advances in transfusion medicine research and personalised transfusion strategies.
authors: Edward John Sayers; Jamie Nash; E. M. Davies; Christine V. Saunders; Chloë E. George

title: Microwell-based nDEP multifunctional microfluidic system for single-cell capture and analysis
abstract: Microfluidic systems have revolutionized biological and clinical analyses, offering precise control over fluid manipulation at a microscale. In recent years, significant advancements have been made by integrating these systems with lab-on-a-chip technologies and expanding their applicability in various biotechnological and diagnostic fields. This work presents the development of a multifunctional lab-on-a-chip device that combines microwell structures with negative dielectrophoresis (nDEP) to enable both single-cell capture and in situ single-cell analysis. The proposed device was first validated using commercially available polystyrene microparticles (beads) and human embryonic kidney (HEK) 293 cells. Impedance analysis and real-time fluorescence microscopy was used to confirm nDEP-mediated high-efficiency single-cell capture within the device's microwells. Finally, single-cell lysis was performed to demonstrate in situ analysis inside the microwells. One of the key advantages of nDEP is its ability to function effectively in physiological media, which typically has high conductivity to model in vivo conditions. nDEP is compatible with high-conductivity environments which allows for optimization across a range of biomedical and clinical studies. In summary, our device provides a platform for a low-cost, miniaturized, and automated single-cell analysis which can be adapted to numerous applications, such as single-cell sequencing, protein analysis, and electrophysiological studies.
authors: Tianxiang Jiang; Zuyuan Tian; Mohamed NF Shaheen; Xuanjie Ye; Ahmed A. Khorshed; Bingxuan Li; Yiwei Feng; Daniel To; Xihua Wang; Jie Chen

title: Minimal essentials for humanized vessel-on-a-chip model for vascular research
abstract: AIMS: During the last decade, in vitro 3D models based on organ-on-a-chip technology have been developed, representing a biotechnology research advance towards more physiologically relevant models that aim to provide more predictable and less costly preclinical models. We aimed to develop a vessel-on-a-chip using a biocompatible microfluidic device co-cultured with human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVEC) and vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMC). MATERIALS AND METHODS: VSMC and HUVEC were isolated from umbilical cords and co-cultured in a polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) chip using specific growth media and tropoelastin-enriched media to favour extracellular matrix (ECM) synthesis, which was measured by gene expression (quantitative polymerase chain reaction) and deposition (immunofluorescence), to establish an organized structure. Then, using a microfluidic pump system, the functional relevance of the model was evaluated by fluidic and permeability studies after a 9-day- cell growth period. KEY FINDINGS: Our vessel-on-a-chip model showed a bilayer structure, cell specific morphology and biomarkers phenotypes, and cell integrity. Gene and protein expression demonstrated the presence of ECM components, providing structural support and microenvironment control. It was observed that shear stress closer to the physiological range provided stability to the model and control of the permeability function. SIGNIFICANCE: Our 3D model may serve as a promising preclinical research tool that closely mimics the structural conformation of blood vessels and reflects essential physiological parameters, including cell maturity, shear stress, and functional permeability. Consequently, it could potentially be applied to cellular and molecular research to further elucidate vascular biology in cardiovascular diseases.
authors: Amparo Romero; Laura Vázquez‐Vázquez; Diana Rodríguez-Suárez; Simón Rodríguez-Moar; Bruno K. Rodiño‐Janeiro; Carmen Bao; Sonia Eiras; José Ramón González‐Juanatey; Rosa María Agra-Bermejo; Ezequiel Álvarez

title: Minimally Invasive In Vivo Fabrication of Multiscale Biohybrid Systems
abstract: Multiscale biohybrid systems integrating living materials with minimally invasive in vivo fabrication offer new opportunities for precise diagnosis, physiological monitoring, and tissue regeneration. This review provides a unified perspective on their design and therapeutic integration, organizing recent advances across multiscale material design, minimally invasive fabrication, spatiotemporal co-engineering, and functional applications. Three emerging principles are identified: multiscale coupling bridges material architectures with cellular and tissue responses; spatiotemporal coordination integrates precise in vivo construction with dynamic material and biological evolution; and sensing-regeneration feedback extends biohybrid systems from passive repair toward responsive therapeutic regulation. Building on these principles, we highlight machine learning-assisted material discovery, multi-site fabrication, and intelligent feedback control as key directions for developing adaptive, closed-loop therapeutic systems. Together, these insights provide design guidance for translating minimally invasive multiscale biohybrid systems toward next-generation patient-centered healthcare.
authors: Zhixing Ge; Yuji Gao; Elgene Chng Junyuan; Truong‐Son Dinh Le; Liang Lanfeng; Yu Zhang; Chwee Teck Lim

title: Modeling long-range human nigrostriatal connectivity in vitro reveals striatal target-dependent maturation of dopamine neurons
abstract: The human nigrostriatal pathway, comprising dopaminergic neurons in the ventral midbrain that project to the dorsolateral striatum, is essential for motor control and selectively vulnerable in Parkinson's disease. How this circuit assembles during human development remains poorly understood, and in vitro models capturing its long-range connectivity and spatial organization have been lacking. Here, we establish a compartmentalized, human stem cell-based model of the nigrostriatal pathway by integrating ventral midbrain and striatal organoids within a custom-engineered microfluidic device that confines cell bodies while guiding axonal growth to recapitulate key aspects of in vivo topography. Functional connectivity was confirmed by retrograde rabies tracing, and optogenetic and pharmacological stimulation. Single-nucleus transcriptomic analysis reveals that axonal target engagement with spatially separated striatal neurons promotes maturation of human dopaminergic neurons and activates transcriptional programs associated with neurotransmitter secretion. Our study establishes a biologically relevant in vitro system for investigating how long-range connectivity regulates neuronal assembly in the nigrostriatal circuit and for modelling key pathological features of Parkinson's disease.
authors: Sara Corsi; Edoardo Sozzi; Andreas Bruzelius; Giorgio Scordo; German Ramos Passarello; Clara Zannino; Samuel T. da S. Maraschin; Surangrat Thongkorn; Arto Heiskanen; Janko Kajtez; Jenny Emnéus; Malin Parmar

title: Modeling the Human Stomach In Vitro: Gastric Organoids in Development, Disease, and Therapy
abstract: Gastric organoids are advanced three-dimensional models generated from adult or pluripotent stem cells. By reproducing key structural, cellular, and functional features of gastric tissue, they overcome several limitations of conventional two-dimensional cultures and animal models. Gastric organoids provide physiologically relevant platforms for studying stomach development, cellular differentiation, and the molecular mechanisms underlying gastric diseases. This review summarizes the principal cell sources and protocols used to generate gastric organoids and discusses recent advances in culture systems, including two-dimensional organoid-derived monolayers, air–liquid interface cultures, co-culture systems, and organoid-on-a-chip technologies. Particular attention is given to the application of gastric organoids in modeling Helicobacter pylori infection, SARS-CoV-2 infection, and gastric cancer, as well as in evaluating therapeutic responses. Their roles in developmental biology, the investigation of congenital disorders, drug screening, potential precision-medicine application, biobanking, and regenerative medicine are also discussed. Despite their considerable potential, current gastric organoid models remain limited: conventional epithelial organoids lack stromal, immune, neural, and vascular components; PSC-derived organoids contain only a limited mesenchymal population; and more complex engineered multicellular tissues still depend largely on in vivo engraftment for maturation. Variable maturation, dependence on poorly defined extracellular matrices, and insufficient standardization further limit their translation.
authors: Zahra Enteshari Najafabadi; Ireneusz Ryszkiel; Hossein Baharvand; Amir Sadeghi; Agata Stanek; Anna Meyfour

title: Models and Tools for Evaluating the Safety and Efficacy of Emerging CAR-T Cell and Nanoparticle Cancer Therapies, with a Perspective on Societal Implications
abstract: Adoptive cell therapy (ACT), particularly using chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells, has led to major advances in the treatment of hematological malignancies. However, its efficacy against solid tumors remains limited, though this challenge may be addressed through nanoparticle (NP)-based approaches. Evaluating the safety of ACT and nanomedicines in parallel with their antitumor efficacy is essential to balance therapeutic benefit with potential adverse effects. In this Review, we provide a comprehensive practical guide by describing the advantages, limitations, and perspectives of several tools and models, from animal-free systems, such as spheroids, tumor-on-chips, ex vivo tissue slice models, and organoids, to different preclinical animal models. In addition, we present advanced technologies, such as single-cell transcriptomics, enabling in-depth characterization of cellular interactions, supporting the optimization of CAR-T cell functionality, and providing insights into the impact of NPs on cells. There is a critical need of developing predictive models to anticipate and mitigate the potential toxic effects of NPs and ACT. In this regard, the integration of bioinformatics and machine learning technologies holds great promise for predicting the therapeutic efficacy of ACT and nanomedicines, thereby refining strategies and facilitating more rational combination choices. Besides, we highlight that ethical considerations are essential in ACT and nanomedicine, as public concerns about the safety and long-term effects of ACT and NP-based therapies can limit acceptance despite its therapeutic promise. Transparent communication and active engagement with stakeholders are therefore crucial to build trust and ensure that technological progress aligns with societal values and ethical standards. Finally, we discuss the challenges of the technical and methodological developments shaping current approaches to the safety and efficacy evaluation of CAR-T cell and NP-based cancer therapies. We also highlight their immediate practical relevance and potential to advance this emerging field.
authors: Daniel Rieger; Shayamita Ghosh; Μαρία Αντωνίου; Tatiana Bobrova; Erica Frostegård; Lorena García‐Hevia; Wilder Ruíz; Ayush Shukla; Yassen Abbas; Antreas Afantitis; Renate Baumgartner; Emmanuel Donnadieu; Tomasz M. Kostrzewski; Mónica L. Fanarraga; Juha Rantala; Michiel Van Oudheusden; Cécilia Ménard‐Moyon

title: Modular construction of osteochondral organoids: Recapitulating gradients and microenvironment
abstract: In recent years, bone and cartilage organoid technology has attracted increasing attention and undergone rapid development, offering emerging approaches and broad prospects for osteoarthritis (OA) treatment, tissue engineering, regenerative medicine, and related fields. Despite the documented progress of bone and cartilage organoid models in structural biomimetic design, their limitation in the holistic reproduction of osteochondral unit, including interface gradient and physiological functions, remains a challenge for clinical application. Based on cutting-edge research, this review summarizes modular construction strategies of bone and cartilage organoids, targeting three types of signals in the osteochondral unit microenvironment: mechanical, metabolic, and immune. First, this review analyzes the microenvironment characteristics of the osteochondral unit, including the interface gradient and major signal pathways, then discusses the essential requirements for construction of osteochondral organoid. Then, based on different emphases, various osteochondral or cartilage organoid examples are classified and reviewed. Furthermore, this paper analyzes their advantages, bottlenecks, and feasibility, thereby outlining a design framework for modular organoids. Next, the technical pathways for functional coupling between modules are discussed, mainly including 3D bioprinting, organoid assembly, and microfluidic chips, in an attempt to provide solutions to the integrated challenge of osteochondral organoids. Then, the monitoring of multidimensional signals in organoids culture system is discussed. Finally, feasibility of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning in this field is discussed, with the aim to establish a closed-loop system for intelligent organoid culture.
authors: Zihan Xu; Yixing Ren; Xiaoming Li

title: Molecular point-of-care testing for infectious diseases and antimicrobial resistance: integrated biosensing technologies, evidence maturity, and clinical and one health translation
abstract: Effective infectious-disease management requires diagnostic results early enough to inform isolation, referral, and antimicrobial treatment. Molecular point-of-care testing (POCT) addresses this need, but analytical sensitivity alone does not establish readiness for clinical use. This critical narrative review examines molecular POCT as an integrated sample-to-answer biosensing system. It connects CRISPR-Cas recognition, isothermal amplification, microfluidic sample handling, nanomaterial-assisted preparation and transduction, and smartphone readout with contamination control, matrix tolerance, multiplexing, calibration, and reagent stability. Respiratory infections, sexually transmitted infections, and antimicrobial-resistance (AMR) testing illustrate different clinical decision windows. We propose a five-domain framework distinguishing mechanistic feasibility, analytical characterization, clinical accuracy, usability and operations, and clinical utility and implementation. A structured comparison of representative primary studies applies the framework while separating authentic clinical specimens from contrived samples and reaction time from complete workflow time. The framework is an interpretive reporting aid, not a validated readiness score. Clinically evaluated cartridge systems provide stronger evidence of diagnostic accuracy and intended-user operation than many emerging prototypes; however, randomized evidence shows that rapid pathogen identification does not necessarily reduce antibiotic prescribing. Genotypic resistance detection is therefore distinguished from phenotypic susceptibility testing and from host-response or antimicrobial-residue measurements. A focused One Health section examines transferable engineering constraints in foodborne-pathogen detection, irrigation-water surveillance, and antimicrobial-exposure monitoring. Priorities for translation include internal process controls, transparent invalid-result reporting, prospective evaluation in intended-use settings, reproducible manufacturing, affordability, secure connectivity, and explicit links between a test result and an appropriate action.
authors: Zhe Chen; Ruitao Yang; Xiaoxue Huang; Jie Wang; Jing Yan

title: Monitoring the Metabolic Microenvironment of Insulin-Secreting and Insulin-Responsive Cells: Sensing Technologies, Byproduct Dynamics, and Culture-Health Prediction
abstract: Insulin-secreting and insulin-responsive cells are central in vitro models for metabolic disease. Yet, the phenotypes they report, glucose-stimulated insulin secretion, insulin sensitivity, and downstream signalling, are sensitive to the chemical state of the surrounding culture medium. Cellular metabolism continuously alters oxygen tension, pH, substrate availability, and the accumulation of byproducts such as lactate, ammonia, and reactive species, and endpoint assays cannot resolve these dynamics. This narrative review maps the real-time sensing of the metabolic microenvironment for insulin-secreting and insulin-responsive cell models, with the aim of distinguishing genuine metabolic dysfunction from artefacts of the culture system. The cell-type scope, basal media composition, and the distinction between two-dimensional and three-dimensional culture are defined as determinants of byproduct accumulation and sensor interpretation. The principal metabolic byproducts and their concentration windows are described, followed by the four recognition paradigms that dominate real-time measurement: electrochemical enzymatic biosensors, optical and luminescence-based sensors, and vibrational spectroscopy with chemometric modelling, with electrochemical aptamer-based sensing extending coverage to enzyme-inaccessible analytes. Commercial monitoring systems and multi-analyte signal-integration strategies are then surveyed. Throughout the culture matrix, in particular serum-borne growth factors and diffusion-limited gradients, emerge as the dominant constraint. No current approach provides continuous, in situ, multi-analyte inference of culture health for insulin-secreting and insulin-responsive models, which remains an open challenge.
authors: Saiyyna Stepanova; Kayla Howard; Kiara Boodhoo; Thendo I. Mabuda; L. Witthauer; Marí van de Vyver

title: Multi-Agent Scheduling of Instrument-Time for High-Throughput Palladium-Catalysed Cross-Coupling
abstract: NMR time and a shared liquid-handling robot are scarce, noisy and only partially observable, so the practical question is which experiment to run next on which instrument. Existing reaction-optimisation benchmarks measure budgets in experiments rather than instrumenthours, and they learn chemical feasibility only by paying for infeasible runs. We present CHASE, a centralised-training decentralised-execution scheduler with three coupled modules: a belief encoder (PEB) infers per-instrument throughput and channel health from local event histories and exchanges only low-bandwidth summaries; a chemistry feasibility gate (CFG) masks chemically impossible actions with a four-layer compatibility graph; and a counterfactual attribution module (CFA) converts delayed campaign reward into per-step credit through leave-one-experiment-out surrogate scoring. On the Buchwald–Hartwig (3,955 reactions) and Suzuki–Miyaura (5,760 nanomole-scale conditions) HTE datasets, the ten Olympus benchmarks and a plant-wide Tennessee Eastman process, CHASE reaches 94.1% best-found yield under a shared 60 instrument-hour budget, +3.3 points over the strongest same-setting baseline, attains 90% of the attainable optimum with 25.6% fewer experiments, and cuts infeasible actions to 0.7–1.6% across plate, flow and fault-injection settings.
authors: Yuhang Shao; Siqi Meng; Yutian Luo; Jiawei Tan; Chengyu He
