title: Multimodal wearable biosensors in sports: integrating physical and chemical sensing for performance and health
abstract: Wearable technologies have emerged as essential tools for monitoring athletes’ performance and physiological states in real time. This review systematically examines advances in biosensing and wearable systems for sports applications, highlighting their design, sensing modalities, and integration strategies. Athlete tracking and data acquisition form the foundation for personalized training, injury prevention, and performance optimization. Biopotential sensors, including electrocardiography (ECG), electromyography (EMG), electroencephalography (EEG)/electroneurogram Electroneurography, and biopotential electrodes, provide insights into cardiac, muscular, and neural activity. Physical sensors, such as temperature, piezoresistive, piezoelectric, balance and acceleration, pressure, optical, and galvanic skin response (GSR) sensors, enable real-time assessment of movement, mechanical load, body posture, stress, and environmental interactions. Chemical sensors, including sweat and glucose sensors, facilitate non-invasive metabolic monitoring, supporting hydration and energy management. Integrated and hybrid biosensor systems combine multiple sensing modalities, offering comprehensive real-time feedback and personalized analytics for athletes. Despite these advances, challenges remain in sensor miniaturization, power efficiency, data accuracy, wireless communication, and user comfort. Future directions focus on artificial intelligence-driven data analysis, flexible and durable materials, multi-modal integration, and fully personalized wearable platforms. Collectively, wearable biosensing technologies present a transformative approach to sports monitoring, enabling enhanced performance evaluation, injury prevention, and long-term health management.
authors: Burhan Adıgüzel; Mansour Ghorbanpour; Begüm Sarac; Seydanur Yücer; Fatih Çiftçi

title: Multiscale computational modeling of photoacoustic generation from micrometer-size polymeric bead suspensions in liquid media
abstract: Photoacoustic sensing has emerged as a promising technique for detecting polymeric particles suspended in liquids through the conversion of absorbed optical energy into acoustic signals. Here, we present a multiscale computational study of the photoacoustic response of polystyrene (PS) beads suspended in water under pulsed optical excitation. The framework combines particle-resolved simulations of individual beads with point-particle descriptions of randomly distributed multi-particle suspensions. The results reveal a rapid acoustic transient followed by a residual pressure field persisting in the liquid. As particle concentration increases, the residual pressure level progressively rises and exhibits an approximately square-root dependence on the number of photoacoustic sources. The point-particle study further shows that the pressure response is closely related to the effective number of irradiated particles rather than to the nominal suspension concentration, while the induced particle motion remains negligible. Overall, the present results provide a physically grounded basis for interpreting photoacoustic signals from PS bead suspensions in water and support future developments of photoacoustic sensing strategies for applications ranging from microplastic detection in aqueous media to polymer-bead-based microfluidic and bioanalytical platforms.
authors: Felice Alberto Sfregola; Federico Pizzi; Stefania Caragnano; Raffaele De Palo; Annalisa Volpe; Pietro Patimisco; Lluís Jofre

title: Nanomaterials in Solid-State Physics and Engineering: Synthesis Strategies, Structure-Property Relationships, and Emerging Applications
abstract: Nanomaterials often deliver impressive laboratory metrics, yet translation is weakened when the path from synthesis to operating-state behavior is poorly documented. This review asked whether performance claims could be traced consistently from controllable processing to verified structure, mechanism, function, and a stated translation boundary. Peer-reviewed literature published mainly from 2021 to 31 March 2026 was examined through a narrative review. During major revision, a structured OpenAlex and Crossref audit was added for operando and active-state characterization. The literature showed that size alone rarely determined performance. Surface chemistry, defects, interfaces, and process history often changed the outcome, and in many systems the functional state differed from the pristine or post-mortem structure. Translation problems were most visible when these changes were not connected to realistic measures of loading, yield, stability, or manufacturing compatibility. Stronger studies combined controlled processing with complementary characterization and measurements made under relevant operating conditions. They also made clear where the evidence stopped. Comparison across application areas showed markedly different levels of readiness, from manufacturing-scale evidence in a few device platforms to predominantly laboratory demonstrations in others. On this basis, the review treats the evidence chain as a practical traceability tool rather than a new materials theory and translates it into a domain-adaptable minimum evidence package for engineering claims.
authors: Thanh Van Nguyen
venue: Indonesian Journal of Modern Science and Technology

title: Next-Generation Liposomes for Drug Delivery: Engineering Strategies and Therapeutic Applications
abstract: Liposomes are versatile nanocarrier systems widely investigated for pharmaceutical drug delivery because of their biocompatibility, biodegradability, and ability to encapsulate both hydrophilic and lipophilic drugs. Since their discovery in the 1960s, liposomes have evolved into advanced nanomedicine platforms with applications in cancer therapy, antimicrobial treatment, gene delivery, vaccines, and personalised medicine. Advances in lipid chemistry, nanotechnology, and pharmaceutical engineering have enabled the development of long-circulating, targeted, stimuli-responsive, and multifunctional liposomal formulations. Several liposome-based products have received regulatory approval, demonstrating their clinical and translational potential. However, challenges related to formulation stability, encapsulation efficiency, large-scale manufacturing, storage, and regulatory requirements remain. Emerging approaches, including microfluidics, artificial intelligence-assisted formulation development, precision nanomedicine, and personalised drug delivery, are expected to address these limitations. This review discusses the historical development, structural characteristics, classification, preparation methods, therapeutic applications, clinical status, and future perspectives of liposomal drug delivery systems, with particular emphasis on recent innovations driving the development of next-generation liposomal therapeutics. Keywords: Liposome, Nanomedicine,Drug Delivery System, Phospholipid Vesicles, Targeted Drug Delivery, Nanotechnology, Lipid Nanocarriers, Controlled Drug Release.
authors: Shubham Sachdeva; Vikramjit Singh; Kaur Harwinder; Fairy Fairy; Jitender Singh
venue: Journal of Drug Delivery and Therapeutics

title: Next‐Generation Electrochemical Analytical Systems: A Critical Review of Biosensing Technologies, Miniaturized Platforms, and Future Intelligent Diagnostics
abstract: Electrochemical analytical systems have evolved from conventional sensing devices into advanced platforms capable of real-time monitoring, multiplexed analysis, and decentralized diagnostics. Progress in biosensing technologies, nanomaterials, microfluidics, wearable devices, and artificial intelligence has significantly improved analytical performance and expanded potential applications in healthcare, environmental monitoring, and food safety. This review critically evaluates recent advances in next-generation electrochemical analytical systems, focusing on biosensing technologies, nanomaterial-enabled platforms, miniaturized devices, precision diagnostics, and emerging intelligent analytical systems, and identifies the major barriers to their practical implementation. Advanced electrochemical biosensors, including enzymatic, immunosensors, aptasensors, nucleic acid sensors, and molecularly imprinted polymer-based platforms, have demonstrated remarkable sensitivity and selectivity. Nanomaterials such as graphene, carbon nanotubes (CNTs), MXenes, and metal nanoparticles have further enhanced signal amplification and electron-transfer efficiency. In parallel, miniaturized technologies, including screen-printed electrodes (SPE), paper-based devices, microfluidic systems, and wearable sensors, have accelerated point-of-care diagnostics. However, persistent challenges related to matrix effects, biofouling, reproducibility, standardization, long-term stability, clinical validation, and manufacturing scalability continue to hinder widespread translation. The future of electrochemical analytical systems lies in developing robust, standardized, and clinically validated intelligent diagnostic ecosystems that integrate advanced sensing technologies with artificial intelligence, digital connectivity, and automated data analysis. Achieving successful clinical translation will require greater emphasis on reproducibility, regulatory compliance, multicenter validation, and real-world applicability, rather than solely on achieving ever-lower detection limits.
authors: Hemn A.H. Barzani; Rebaz Anwar Omer; Sarbast Naser Ahmad; Hazha Omar Othman; Ali Sedeeq Noaman; Kovan Dilawer Issa; Seerwan Hamadameen Sulaiman

title: Nonreciprocal multibody interactions activate liquid state of acoustically levitated particle ensembles
abstract: Nonreciprocal forces are often a consequence of asymmetry in the properties of the interacting objects. However, even if all objects are identical and isotropic, and the pairwise interactions between two objects are completely reciprocal, nonreciprocal forces can still appear when an arrangement of many objects breaks configurational symmetry in the presence of nonpairwise, multibody interactions. Here, we demonstrate that such emergent nonreciprocity can activate a particle ensemble to behave like a liquid, albeit with unique traits. In our experiments, passive microspheres are acoustically levitated in air, where they form a freely floating monolayer containing up to a couple hundred particles and collectively behave like a two-dimensional liquid droplet. The particles interact via nonreciprocal multibody forces that arise from the combination of acoustic scattering and sound-induced viscous microstreaming. We find that these forces drive superdiffusive particle motion with non-Gaussian tails in the particles’ speed distribution. Using probes that reach laterally into the levitation plane, we perform liquid pendant drop and pinch-off experiments. Compared to ordinary liquids, the droplets are found to have a kinematic viscosity similar to that of water, but in combination with an extremely low interfacial tension. The pinching-off is driven by nonreciprocity-induced active fluctuations and exhibits the self-similar double-cone neck profile seen also in liquid nanojets close to rupture, however, here characterized by power law behavior with a scaling exponent that is anomalously small.
authors: Nina M. Brown; Heinrich M. Jaeger

title: ORCHID-SAGE: Fully Reproducible CALPHAD Assessment from Evidence to Phase Diagram
abstract: Knowledge of phase stability is the first requirement for materials design, and predicting the conditions under which new materials can be synthesized has become a key capability of self-driving laboratories (SDLs). For inorganic materials, notably alloys, these predictions come from thermodynamic databases built with the CALPHAD method. Building a database, however, requires expert judgment at many steps, and because these decisions are rarely recorded, others can use a database but cannot regenerate or update it. Machines can already collect the data, build a first model with machine-learned interatomic potentials and refine it against experiments. The assessment itself, the sequence of judgments that turns these parts into a reliable database, is still carried out by human experts. We argue that it can be automated reproducibly only if the expert knowledge behind an assessment is encoded in formal protocols, so that an assessment delivers a record of its construction and not only its parameters. We introduce ORCHID-SAGE, a standard that organizes this record into reproducible and automatable protocols. In this first attempt, applied to Cr-Ni, the database was regenerated from its record by a script on a second machine, by an AI agent working only through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and by a refit from public sources only, with the same predictions. Recorded in this way, a database need no longer be fixed at publication but can be updated by AI agents as SDLs and other sources provide new evidence, while the judgment remains with people and on the record.
authors: Raymundo Arróyave

title: Oculomics and artificial intelligence in cardiovascular risk prediction: Ocular biomarker assessment and perspectives for precision medicine
abstract: Oculomics uses ocular characteristics as potential biomarkers of systemic health. Combined with artificial intelligence (AI), it offers new opportunities for cardiovascular risk assessment. This study aims to analyze the applications of oculomics and AI in identifying ocular biomarkers associated with cardiovascular risk, highlighting their potential and limitations. This literature review examines retinal biomarkers, fundus photography, optical coherence tomography (OCT), optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA), and AI-based computational models. The available evidence indicates that AI algorithms can identify retinal vascular and structural patterns associated with hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and cardiovascular conditions, supporting their potential use in risk stratification. However, detecting existing disease must be distinguished from predicting future cardiovascular events. Limited external validation, algorithmic interpretability, population representativeness, implementation costs, and data privacy remain sig nificant challenges. In conclusion, oculomics combined with AI represents a promising noninvasive approach to cardiovascular assessment and precision medicine. Nevertheless, further prospective studies and independent validation are required to establish its clinical utility and support broader implementation.
authors: Jéssica Lara Anjos; Camila Nayara da Silva Anjos; Gabriela de Melo Branco; Isaque de Oliveira Costa; Matheus Pedro Rossini; Felipe Fraga Schneider

title: On-board International Space Station Verification of Autonomous Emulsification Lab-on-Chip Payload: TIGERS-X Project
abstract: Sustained deep-space exploration under space programs places critical constraints on pharmaceutical and nutritional resupply, motivating fluid-processing systems, including emulsification, that can operate reliably in microgravity. Conventional terrestrial emulsification relies on high-shear, buoyancy-assisted processes unavailable in free fall, while passive, capillary-driven static mixers offer a compact, low-power alternative better suited to spaceflight constraints. This paper reports the design, ground verification, and on-orbit validation of TIGERS-X, a low-cost, teleoperated lab-on-chip experiment cube for the International Space Station (ISS). Ground testing, including chemical safety, electromagnetic compatibility, and structural verification, confirmed compliance with ISS pressurized-payload requirements. TIGERS-X uses multi-channel Tesla-valve microfluidic devices and optical diagnostics to observe oil-water mixing and emulsification behavior, operating under ground control via YAMCS-based command and telemetry with no astronaut interaction required beyond installation and removal. Across a 10-day flight campaign, TIGERS-X returned near-real-time video of fluid behavior under sustained microgravity, resolving a duration and environment inaccessible to prior parabolic-flight studies. Quantitative colorimetric analysis revealed substantial, geometry-dependent oil-water phase redistribution within short microfluidic channel lengths, extending prior ground- and parabolic-flight-based findings to realistic orbital conditions. These results establish TIGERS-X as a validated, accessible platform for microgravity fluid science, with potential extension to more complex biological applications such as cell culture systems in future missions.
authors: Saran Seehanam; Thakdanai Sirisombat; Rattanawalee Tobsri; Warisara Boonrueng; Potiwat Ngamkajornwiwat; Witsaroot Sripumkhai; Pattaraluck Pattamang; Wares Chancharoen

title: Ontology-enabled neuro-symbolic closed-loop control of laser powder bed fusion
abstract: A geometry-conditioned, neuro-symbolic closed-loop architecture is proposed for laser powder bed fusion, in which an ontology aligned with established standards and domain vocabularies operates inside the control loop and couples symbolic reasoning with statistical learning to set the targets of a constraint-aware predictive controller. The ontology links the process objectives and constraints to the signals a controller can observe. A description-logic reasoner selects the active constraints, which are converted into references and bounds enforced on each scan. The demonstrated case is overhang dross: a quality limit on the melt pool depth, which governs quality but is not measured in the present formulation, is mapped through a geometry- and power-dependent depth-to-width ratio onto a bound on the observable width. The ratio and its empirical uncertainty are estimated by a neural ensemble. The reasoner classifies each upcoming feature and selects the active constraints, adding a lack-of-fusion floor at overhangs and an extrapolation guard when the overhang angle falls below the calibrated range or uncertainty is high. It runs only when the symbolic context changes, and the inferred classification remains cached between changes. In an Eagar–Tsai surrogate calibrated to the NIST AM-Bench benchmark for IN625, the architecture reduced the mean total defect count at 45° from 6.0 to 6.2 tracks for the geometry-conditioned baselines to 3.2 per build and avoided their shift from dross to lack of fusion. Ablation attributed the ontology contribution to explicit representation of constraint applicability, inference, and consistency checking rather than separate numerical gains. The results establish architectural feasibility. Machine-specific calibration of the depth-to-width relation and physical validation are the principal next steps.
authors: Gisuk Hong; Jaebong Cho; Hyunbo Cho

title: On‐Chip Biomimetic Intelligence: Integrating Adaptive Molecular Sensing With Longitudinal Proteomic Profiling for Advanced Disease Diagnostics
abstract: Biological, molecular, and functional states evolve across multiple timescales, limiting the utility of conventional diagnostics based on isolated measurements. This Perspective introduces on-chip biomimetic intelligence as an integrated approach combining biomimetic molecular recognition and signal transduction with dynamic sensing, adaptive local computation, and longitudinal interpretation of molecular changes. It focuses on multiplexed molecular-affinity measurements of selected disease-associated protein panels, coupled with event-driven signal processing to reduce redundant data generation. Where appropriate, sensing outputs may inform patient-specific digital twin models and dynamically update PBPK or PK-PD models. Rather than treating intelligent biosensors, neuromorphic biosensing, edge AI, and digital twins as isolated technologies, it integrates their functions and describes architectural and functional requirements for chip-level biomimetic intelligence. Implementation requires regenerable molecular-recognition interfaces, reliable molecular-to-signal transduction, and computational methods capable of estimating protein states and temporal trajectories. Causal validation and constrained closed-loop control may support clinically relevant decision-making when sufficient evidence is available. However, complete architecture has not yet been demonstrated as a single clinically validated system. Its realization requires advances in sensing stability, biocompatibility, antifouling performance, calibration, drift control, and clinical validation. Thus, biosensing shifts from static biomarker detection to longitudinal, adaptive, and clinically interpretable monitoring of changes in biological state.
authors: Bakr Ahmed Taha; Ali J. Addie; Khansaa Basem Fadhil; Adawiya J. Haider; Ahmed Jamal Jasim; Norhana Arsad

title: Optimal strategies for the growth of dual-seeded lattice structures
abstract: Optimal growth of structures governed by spatially stochastic dynamics arises in many scientific settings, for example in processes such as solution-based crystallization and the formation of microbial biofilms on patterned substrates or microfluidic networks. In this work, we investigate lattice growth using a two-dimensional, zero-temperature stochastic model of short-range spin interactions. Our goal is to determine how external perturbations can be optimized to steer the system efficiently toward the uniformly positive state, starting from two initial clusters of positive sites. To achieve this, we cast the problem as a Markov decision process adapted for a two-dimensional Ising model with zero-temperature dynamics. Within this framework, we compare alternative growth geometries and identify the structure of optimal strategies across three representative regimes.
authors: Maike de Jongh; Cristian Spitoni; Emilio N. M. Cirillo

title: Optimisation of Topical and Transdermal Pharmaceutical Formulations: Methods, Challenges and Opportunities
abstract: Topical and transdermal pharmaceutical formulations are a large and diverse class of products, yet their optimisation remains a complex, resource‐intensive challenge. Statistical design‐of‐experiments approaches have long provided the methodological backbone for this process and have shown broad effectiveness across topical and transdermal formulation systems, but face growing demands as formulation complexity and the number of variables increase. Classical machine learning offers more flexible modelling of nonlinear formulation–performance relationships; adaptive sequential design adds uncertainty‐aware experiment selection; high‐throughput screening platforms address the data‐generation bottleneck and self‐driving laboratories integrate automated execution with model‐guided decision‐making. However, their application in topical and transdermal formulation remains uneven, and their advantages over established methods depend strongly on data quality, validation design and experimental context. This review examines optimisation approaches applied to topical and transdermal formulation development, from classical factorial designs and response surface methodology through machine learning and adaptive sequential design to high‐throughput screening and self‐driving laboratories.
authors: Yongrui Xiao; Yu Zhang; Chunlin Chen; Dimitrios A. Tsaoulidis; Kai Yang; Tao Chen

title: Optimiser Repairs for Living-Cell Self-Driving Laboratories: Performance and Redundancy under Experimental Constraints
abstract: Living-cell self-driving laboratories must optimise experiments despite delayed readouts, changing responses and limited sample availability. In simulations, we evaluate when optimiser repairs improve closed-loop performance and when platform constraints make them redundant, separating consumption of a sample from permanent loss of the ability to repeat its condition. We prove that exclusions and confirmation requests produce exactly the baseline trajectory when they act only on conditions already forbidden by the platform, share the same posterior and selection procedure, and release infeasible requested slots. This result covers the evaluated pending-exclusion, previous-batch and confirmation rules under permanent condition retirement; it does not cover arbitrary selection interventions. We then conduct 33,900 simulated policy runs with 200–300 paired campaign seeds per setting. A public PBMC reference supports characterisation of the target-label readout, while condition-response landscapes remain synthetic. Across 27 landscape, assay-size and kernel settings, previous-batch exclusion changes final normalised performance by −0.004 to +0.283, with positive differences surviving Holm adjustment in 13 settings. Effects are small on the rugged landscape. Permanent retirement can be harmful under noisy rugged responses. All three subsumed interventions reproduce every saved baseline event on 200 of 200 paired seeds. These results establish the importance of explicit availability constraints and evaluation across experimental regimes when assessing optimiser repairs.
authors: Nura Brimo; Han Zhang; Dilek Çökeliler Serdaroğlu

title: Optimization of Scheduling Algorithms for Modular Medical Laboratory Automation Lines
abstract: As in vitro diagnostics (IVD) equipment develops toward high throughput, multi-assay capability, modularization, and flexibility, the processes of sample transport, pipetting, mixing, incubation, detection, washing, and result output in medical laboratory automation lines have increasingly exhibited strong coupling, multi-resource coordination, and concurrent multi-task execution. Traditional centralized control architectures typically rely on a mid-level controller to perform unified scheduling of all execution units. In scenarios involving increased sample volumes, complex combinations of testing items, or frequent module expansion, such architectures are prone to task response delays, resource conflicts, increased communication load, and global operational impact caused by single-point failures. To address these issues, this paper proposes a distributed event-driven scheduling algorithm for modular medical laboratory automation lines. Based on autonomous functional units, the algorithm decomposes the sample processing workflow into configurable event-task sequences and realizes parallel scheduling and coordinated execution of sample tasks across multiple functional modules through a local event engine, a publish-subscribe event communication mechanism, and a dynamic priority scheduling strategy. This paper establishes a scheduling model for modular laboratory automation lines, designs a hybrid scheduling algorithm based on event triggering, resource locking, task priority, and rolling-window optimization, and proposes evaluation metrics in terms of task waiting time, equipment throughput, module utilization, communication load, and fault isolation capability. The study shows that the distributed event-driven scheduling method can effectively reduce the system bottleneck of centralized scheduling and improve the operational efficiency and system reliability of modular medical laboratory automation lines under concurrent multi-sample and multi-assay scenarios.
authors: Yanfeng He
venue: European Journal of AI Computing & Informatics

title: Optoelectronically Enabled Simultaneous and Decoupled Navigation and Selective Pairing of Electrically Driven Janus Particles for Multi-Agent Microrobotics
abstract: Self-propelled Janus particles are promising active agents for microscale manipulation and microrobotic applications. However, when powered by a global external energy source, such as an electric, magnetic, or optical field, all particles respond simultaneously, preventing their independent and concurrent control. Achieving parallel, decoupled control without continuous particle-specific feedback, while preserving intrinsic self-propulsion, remains a significant challenge. Here, we present an optoelectronic (OE) strategy for simultaneously and independently controlling electrically driven, self-propelled metallo-dielectric Janus particles (JPs) using spatially programmable virtual electrodes. These electrodes are generated by projecting a single predefined illumination pattern from a digital micromirror device onto a photoconductive surface. The resulting confinement landscape enables multiple JPs to follow distinct trajectories without continuous monitoring, feedback, or pattern reconfiguration. We demonstrate controlled pairing of JPs with passive polystyrene particles and biological cells. For automated multi-agent operation, an image-based assignment framework identifies optimal agent-target pairs, excludes intersecting trajectories, and generates a single composite pattern for simultaneous, selective pair formation without real-time updating. Finally, we demonstrate independent manipulation of multiple magnetically rolling JPs under a globally applied magnetic field. Overall, this programmable open-loop strategy provides a versatile framework for multi-agent microrobotic manipulation, with potential applications in in-vitro micromanipulation and microfluidic systems.
authors: Srikanta Debata; Ido Rachbuch; Gilad Yossifon

title: PARAFAC-Assisted Excitation–Emission Matrix Fluorescence for Minimal-Preparation Co-Determination of Norfloxacin and Metoclopramide in Human Urine: Overcoming Severe Concentration Imbalance Without Chromatography
abstract: Direct simultaneous determination of norfloxacin (NOR) and metoclopramide (MET) in human urine is severely complicated by intense biological autofluorescence, spectral overlap, and an extreme concentration disparity arising from clinical co-administration (400 mg NOR vs. 10 mg MET; dose ratio 40:1). Multiway chemometrics offers a chromatography-free approach to resolving fluorophores, but biological background and extreme concentration disparities can complicate global PARAFAC modeling. Herein, we demonstrate that this limitation can be completely overcome using a dual-submatrix excitation–emission matrix (EEM) PARAFAC strategy in human urine after a simple 10-fold dilution with pH 3.0 aqueous buffer, omitting extraction, derivatization, and organic solvents. By partitioning the measured EEM array into two dedicated sub-arrays (XNOR: λex 260–310 nm, λem 440–500 nm; XMET: λex 260–310 nm, λem 380–410 nm), rank deficiency is circumvented, rotational ambiguity is eliminated, and trilinearity is fully preserved. External calibration in spiked urine yielded linear dynamic ranges of 1000–6000 ng mL−1 for NOR (R2 = 0.9981) and 15–80 ng mL−1 for MET (R2 = 0.9995). Validation across independent test mixtures showed excellent mean recoveries of 100.79 ± 4.57% for NOR and 101.86 ± 4.06% for MET, with root mean square errors of prediction (RMSEP) of 144.65 and 2.38 ng mL−1, respectively. Net analyte signal figures of merit demonstrated high sensitivity and limits of detection of 119.87 ng mL−1 (NOR) and 3.16 ng mL−1 (MET). The validated method was successfully applied to urinary excretion monitoring in five healthy volunteers following oral co-administration of commercial tablets (Noracin® 400 mg and Primperan® 10 mg), recovering 24.89 ± 4.63% (NOR) and 13.59 ± 9.27% (MET) of the administered dose over 72 h. Multi-metric greenness and practicality assessments (AGREE: 0.68, ComplexMoGAPI: 69, CaFRI: 63.1, BAGI: 75.0) confirmed substantial sustainability advantages over conventional chromatographic workflows. This study revitalizes PARAFAC as an ultra-green, chromatography-free tool for modern pharmaceutical bioanalysis.
authors: Mahmoud M. Elkhoudary; Randa A. Abdel Salam; Mohamed S. Abdel‐Maksoud; Ghada M. Hadad

title: PV-WTConv: a parallel network for abnormal white blood cell classification based on wavelet transform convolution
abstract: In the field of cell detection research, the detection of abnormal white blood cells is not only central to the early diagnosis of malignant haematological diseases such as leukaemia and myelodysplastic syndromes, but also serves as a key indicator for assessing infectious diseases, immunodeficiencies and the efficacy of chemotherapy. The use of computer-aided techniques to accurately classify white blood cells in microscopic images can assist clinicians in diagnosing and detecting various blood-related diseases more promptly and accurately. However, the accurate identification and classification of white blood cells remains challenging due to the blurred boundaries between abnormal white blood cells and normal white blood cells-or even those exhibiting physiological variations-the lack of uniform and fixed morphological criteria for different types of abnormal cells (such as leukaemic cells and hyperplastic cells), and interference from factors such as the complexity of cell imaging and staining techniques. Therefore, this paper proposes a parallel classification network for abnormal white blood cells based on wavelet transform convolution, designed to enhance the accuracy of recognising and classifying different categories of abnormal white blood cells. This study utilised the AWBC-LZWH dataset of abnormal white blood cell images, provided by the Department of Clinical Laboratory Medicine at Liuzhou Workers' Hospital, for the main training, validation and testing phases, and conducted supplementary experiments using the PBC_dataset of peripheral blood cell images, which was collected and publicly released by the Hospital Clínic de Barcelona. PV-WTConv achieved an accuracy of 94.4% on AWBC-LZWH, compared with 56.9% for the convolutional baseline and 91.4% for ResNet50, corresponding to absolute differences of 37.5 and 3.0 percentage points, respectively. The results of this study indicate that PV-WTConv demonstrates good classification performance on the evaluated white blood cell image datasets; however, its clinical diagnostic value still requires further validation through prospective, multicentre studies.
authors: Xiangsuo Fan; Xipeng Song; Borui Sun; Zhenxing Yao; Jie Meng

title: Photo-Programmable Temporal Uncoupling Enables One-Pot Isothermal Enrichment and Detection of Low-Abundance Single-Nucleotide Variants.
abstract: Sensitive detection of low-abundance single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) remains challenging because rare mutant alleles are frequently masked by overwhelming wild-type DNA backgrounds. Herein, we develop a photo-programmable temporally uncoupled one-pot isothermal sensing platform (PTU-One-Pot) for sensitive enrichment and detection of the EGFR L858R mutation. The platform integrates restriction endonuclease-mediated wild-type DNA digestion with recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA) in a closed tube. To resolve the intrinsic kinetic conflict between relatively slow wild-type DNA digestion and rapid RPA amplification, RPA primers are modified with a photocleavable 6-nitropiperonyloxymethyl (NPOM) group. During the initial phase, NPOM-caged primers suppress RPA amplification, allowing MlsI restriction endonuclease to selectively digest wild-type templates. Subsequent brief ultraviolet irradiation removes the NPOM protection and activates RPA amplification of remaining mutant-type templates. Mechanistic studies confirm RPA photo-programmable trigger and sequence-selective wild-type template cleavage. Droplet digital PCR, high-resolution melting, Sanger sequencing verify that PTU-One-Pot can effectively eliminate wild-type templates and convert the final products from wild-type-dominated to mutant-enriched. Under optimized conditions, fluorescence readout achieves a limit of detection of 0.05% variant allele frequency, showing high specificity to EGFR L858R mutation. Lateral flow assay integration enables low-instrument visual detection at 1% variant allele frequency. Evaluation using 23 formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded patient samples demonstrates that both fluorescence and lateral flow readouts are consistent with next-generation sequencing and droplet digital PCR reference results. Overall, this PTU-One-Pot strategy provides a rapid and sensitive isothermal platform for low-abundance mutation enrichment and analysis.
authors: Zhijin Li; Min Qing; Jianbo Wang; Chao Yu

title: Physicochemical rule-embedded generative modeling for constrained peptide therapeutics
abstract: Constrained peptides couple covalent topology, stereochemistry, three-dimensional structure, conformational dynamics and developability. We review physicochemical rule embedding across chemical-language, target-conditioned structural, geometric, atom-bond, ensemble and property-guided generative models, distinguishing generated molecular objects from downstream inference and predictions from prospective evidence. We identify limitations in chemical coverage, applicability, uncertainty and pipeline attribution, and routes towards identity-preserving, environment-aware and experimentally calibrated design.
authors: Yuzhou Wang; Dongsheng Cao; Xiangzheng Fu; Xiangxiang Zeng; Xiaojun Yao

title: Physics-informed neural network with ADAM–LBFGS optimizer for modeling of TDF bioconvection nanofluid with gyrotactic microorganisms in microfluidics systems
abstract: This work presents an investigation of a physics-informed neural network (PINN) for simulating two-dimensional, time-dependent flow (TDF) bioconvection nanofluid flow between two parallel plates. The model involves a set of nonlinear equations that describe fluid motion, heat transfer, nanoparticle movement, and microorganism migration. Unlike classical numerical solvers, the proposed PINN framework provides a continuous physics-informed representation of the solution within the prescribed parameter configurations considered in this study. By incorporating the equations and boundary conditions into the loss function of the neural network, a mesh-free solution is obtained that satisfies the physical laws. In this work, the impact of various parameters, namely, squeezing parameter β, Lewis number Le, Brownian motion Nb, thermophoresis Nt, Péclet number Pe, and Schmidt number Sc, on the solution is investigated. It has been found that an increase in the squeezing parameter β enhances the wall shear stress and Nusselt number, and reduces the microorganism concentration in the core region. Also, nanoparticle concentration decreases with an increase in Le and Nt, but Brownian motion enhances it. In addition, microorganism concentration is influenced by both Pe and Nt; an increase in these parameters results in a higher concentration of microorganisms. In this work, the accuracy of the PINN framework is high for all the field variables, with an absolute velocity error of the order of 10 −6 . This work shows the potential of physics-informed neural networks (PINN) to act as a computational tool for simulating complex fluid flow problems.
authors: Hassan Azari; Sepehr Behrouzifar; Mehdi Mahboobtosi; Davood Domiri Ganji

title: Plasmonic metasurface microfluidic accelerates redox reactions for rapid phenotypic antibiotic susceptibility testing
abstract: Electron-accepting chain reactions play crucial roles in diagnostics for bacterial infections, from nucleic acid amplification for bacterial identification to metabolic assays for phenotypic antibiotic susceptibility testing. When coupled with redox mediators, these reactions can be interrogated using an electroanalytical method. We demonstrate kinetic acceleration of loop-mediated isothermal amplification-based identification and resazurin-based phenotypic antibiotic susceptibility profiling through enhanced electromagnetic fields and modulated hot electron injection at the multilayered plasmonic metasurface-fluidic interface. We systematically investigate rounded versus sharp-apex plasmonic architectures, quantifying near-field magnitude and decay to identify geometries that maximize kinetic amplification under electrochemical readout. This approach is further combined with machine learning-assisted Gaussian fitting to improve data quantification and interpretation. Across diverse bacterial species, we achieved rapid identification with no cross-reactivity and phenotypic antibiotic susceptibility testing without overnight culture. In a prospective pilot clinical study of urine specimens directly from patients with suspected urinary tract infections, we observe high accuracy and strong essential and categorical agreement with standard clinical microbiology assays for bacterial identification and antibiotic susceptibility testing.
authors: Roozbeh Siavash Moakhar; Mahsa Jalali; Tamer AbdElFatah; Sripadh Guptha Yedire; Max Petkun; Carolina del Real Mata; Ziwei He; Hamed Shieh; Geoffrey A. McKay; Rachel Corsini; Grace Reszetnik; Seyed Vahid Hamidi; Sahar Sadat Mahshid; Cédric P. Yansouni; Dao M. Nguyen; Sara Mahshid

title: Point-of-Care Testing for Aquatic Animal Disease Diagnosis: A Socio-Technical Review of Technologies Enabling Sustainable Aquaculture and Blue Food Security
abstract: Disease outbreaks are among the principal constraints on the sustainability of global aquaculture, yet diagnostic capacity remains concentrated in centralized laboratories far from the point of production. Point-of-care testing (POCT)-immunochromatographic strips, isothermal amplification (LAMP, RPA/RAA), CRISPR-Cas assays, microfluidics and biosensors-can compress the diagnosis-to-intervention window from days to about an hour. This structured narrative review draws on a documented search of the Web of Science Core Collection, Scopus, PubMed and the China National Knowledge Infrastructure (2000-2026), with explicit inclusion criteria and a three-tier evidence-grading scheme (Section Review Methodology and Evidence Grading). We synthesize the evidence in the following three tiers: the technical landscape, comparing eight representative platform classes on sensitivity, turnaround, instrument dependence and deployment maturity; the application geography, tracing how POCT has entered pond-side screening, hatchery biosecurity, border inspection of live aquatic trade and IoT-based surveillance networks across East Asian freshwater, Indo-Pacific shrimp and North Atlantic salmonid systems, with markedly uneven evidence of routine adoption; and the bottlenecks that determine whether analytical performance becomes a sustainability outcome-sample-matrix interference, cold-chain dependence, the absence of unified field-performance standards (with WOAH diagnostic-kit registration suspended from May 2024 to May 2027), ambiguous legal status of POCT results, and smallholder affordability. Adopting a sustainability-transition perspective, we argue that the binding constraint is no longer assay chemistry but socio-technical governance, and that POCT should be positioned as enabling infrastructure for antimicrobial stewardship (SDG 3), loss avoidance and trade resilience (SDG 2/12), and aquatic ecosystem protection (SDG 14). We close with coordinated action imperatives for researchers, standard setters, policymakers and industry, including field-validation-first study designs and use of the 2024-2027 standards window to establish graded performance claims for on-site aquatic diagnostics.
authors: Na Jiang; Yukun Zhang; 于欢欢; Xiaoxiao Zhang

title: Point-of-care testing in the diagnosis of infectious diseases
abstract: Point-of-care testing (POCT) has emerged as an indispensable diagnostic strategy for addressing the increasing global burden of infectious diseases and the worsening threat of antimicrobial resistance. Owing to prominent advantages such as rapid detection of infectious agents, portability, and ease of accessibility, POCT can effectively address the inherent limitations of traditional laboratory diagnostic workflows. This review summarizes the core technical platforms that underlie current POCT technologies, including lateral flow assays, chemiluminescence immunoassays, isothermal amplification systems, CRISPR/Cas-based diagnostic systems, and microfluidic chip technologies. Furthermore, we describe the key clinical scenarios in which POCT can be applied, including respiratory tract, bloodstream, gastrointestinal, urinary tract, and sexually transmitted infections. We also comprehensively discuss the technical characteristics and clinical applicability of mainstream POCT modalities, including immunochromatography and molecular diagnostics. Despite limitations associated with detection sensitivity, quality control, cost efficiency, and clinical integration, POCT technology continues to undergo consistent improvements. Advances in nanomaterials, microfluidic engineering, and artificial intelligence and continuous improvements in industry standardization have led to increased performance, systematic integration, and intelligent detection in POCT. Given these technological advancements and optimizations, POCT shows promising applicability and is therefore expected to become a core diagnostic tool for both precision clinical management and epidemic prevention and control in public health.
authors: Quan Fang; Yuyan Lin; Guiqi Hu; Jiangjie Hu; Jun Cheng; 戴玉柱; Li Yan; Xiaohong Wu

title: PolyJet 3D-printed microfluidic device that integrates hydrodynamic focusing of red blood cells and detection of ATP release
abstract: a chemiluminescence reaction by introducing luciferin/luciferase mixture into the sheath flow side channels, mixing with any released ATP, and the resulting emitted light was captured with a PMT under the device. The dimensions of the 3D printed focusing/mixing channel were optimized downstream to increase the residence time of the RBCs over the PMT, leading to improvements in calibration sensitivity and the limit of detection for both flow rates. The optimized device was used to detect the ATP release from RBCs as a function of differing focusing widths. Finally, the effect of inhibiting ATP release from RBCs was also determined using diamide and glibenclamide. This PolyJet 3D printing approach clearly provides a method to modulate deformation forces on RBCs and measure the subsequent ATP release in near real-time.
authors: Mariama Singhateh; Samuel Azibere; Randy S. Sprague; Ajith Karunarathne; Sashima Liyanage; R. Scott Martin

title: Precision Injection‐Compression Molding and Functional Integration of Hollow Microneedle Microfluidic Chips for Minimally Invasive Continuous Health Monitoring
abstract: Real-time biomarker monitoring through interstitial fluid (ISF) sampling using hollow microneedle (HMN) arrays is crucial for personalized precision medicine and chronic disease management. However, clinical translation faces a critical bottleneck: the absence of stable, cost-effective, scalable high-precision manufacturing technologies. This work systematically establishes a comprehensive end-to-end solution encompassing precise molding and functional integration. We employed injection-compression molding with multi-objective optimization algorithms to elucidate relationships between critical process parameters and HMN array molding quality. The results demonstrate that positioning the HMN array at the far-gate locations enhances filling quality and reduces core-pin impact force by 15%, revealing the underlying physical mechanisms governed by shear heating effects and pressure transmission dynamics, which enriches conventional micro-injection molding theory. The optimized process achieves >6.8% filling ratio improvement and 10% injection pressure reduction. Furthermore, we established a complete design and fabrication workflow for ISF extraction chips, developed patterned microelectrode bonding technology for complex microchannel sealing, and validated in situ detection platform advantages. In vitro testing validated safe and efficient ISF extraction with a 95% success rate while maintaining exceptional portability for wearable health monitoring applications. This work provides theoretical and practical guidance for scalable HMN manufacturing, establishing a foundation for commercializing next-generation continuous health monitoring systems.
authors: Baishun Zhao; Dimitrios Kontziampasis; Mingyong Zhou; Wangqing Wu; Zhiyu Yang; Bingyan Jiang; Dou Zhang

title: Precision immunopharmacology in xenotransplantation: integrating genome-engineered donors, organoid testbeds, and AI-guided translation.
abstract: Xenotransplantation is moving from isolated proof-of-concept procedures toward an engineered biotechnology platform for organ replacement. This review examines how genome-designed donor pigs, recipient-directed immunopharmacology, human-relevant in vitro testbeds, and data-driven decision systems can be integrated to address the remaining barriers to clinical translation. CRISPR-Cas-based engineering enables deletion of dominant carbohydrate xenoantigens, insertion of human complement- and coagulation-regulatory genes, modulation of innate and adaptive immune checkpoints, control of donor-organ growth, and inactivation of porcine endogenous retrovirus sequences. However, donor engineering does not eliminate residual T-cell, B-cell, antibody, complement, natural killer (NK) cell, macrophage, and inflammatory responses. Contemporary immunopharmacological strategies therefore increasingly combine costimulation blockade with complement inhibition, lymphocyte-directed therapy, and selected cytokine- or innate-immune interventions, with future regimens requiring closer integration of pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic monitoring with donor genotype and organ-specific risk. Organoids and microfluidic vascular systems may provide an intermediate testing layer by quantifying antibody binding, complement activation, endothelial injury, coagulation, leukocyte transmigration, cytokine responses, and tissue-specific function under controlled conditions before escalation to large-animal studies. Artificial intelligence may further support xenoantigen discovery, genome-editing design, donor-recipient matching, multimodal rejection surveillance, and ultimately clinician-supervised immunopharmacological decision support. We propose that these components should be connected through a traceable design-build-test-learn workflow linking computational prediction, donor construction, standardized functional testing, non-human-primate validation, and early human data. Durable translation will depend not on any single technological advance, but on reproducible donor manufacturing, precision immune control, validated human-relevant test systems, standardized longitudinal data, pathogen surveillance, organ-specific management, and transparent regulatory governance.
authors: Tao Ren; Gongbo Fu; Shichao Duan; Min Zeng; Yi Gao

title: Precision weeding and spraying robot vehicle integrating spatial perception and closed-loop control
abstract: To address the problems of unstable target positioning, accumulated end-effector errorsand insufficient dynamic operation response in traditional pesticide application equipment in complex field environments, this study proposes a target-oriented weeding robot vehicle with dynamic spatial compensation for precision spraying, achieving autonomous perception, spatial correctionand precise intervention against weeds. The system addresses the spatial uncertainties of agricultural robots during continuous movement by constructing a multi-source information fusion architecture integrating high-precision satellite positioning, inertial attitude perception, structural error compensationand edge intelligent control. The real-time nozzle spatial pose calculation model is established to uniformly describe the robot's motion state, suspension mechanism changesand nozzle installation geometry, enabling continuous estimation of the spraying end position under dynamic conditions. Simultaneously, a nonlinear structural compensation mechanism based on Gaussian process regression is introduced to jointly model and correct suspension mechanism motion errors, mechanical connection deviations, structural deformationand random disturbances, improving the stability and environmental adaptability of nozzle spatial positioning. Furthermore, the dynamic deposition prediction model integrating robot motion state, droplet motion patternsand target spatial distribution information is constructed. By predicting the spatiotemporal relationship between the spray landing point and the target area, the nozzle response strategy is adjusted in advance to achieve precise triggering and targeted coverage of the target area. This research breaks through the limitations of traditional agricultural spraying systems that rely on fixed geometric relationships, static compensation parametersand preset triggering rules. It deeply integrates spatial perception, error compensation, motion predictionand spraying control, providing a new technical path for the development of agricultural robots from mechanized operations to intelligent precision operation systems with environmental understanding and autonomous decision-making capabilities.
authors: Ruipeng Tang

title: Predicting droplet landing in angle-controlled surface acoustic wave jetting
abstract: Nozzle-free droplet generation eliminates the need for a dispensing orifice, but useful printing also requires control over where droplets are deposited. Here we demonstrate predictable droplet deposition using a nozzle-free, angle-controlled surface acoustic wave jetting platform. Opposing focused interdigital transducers steer droplets from a pendant parent drop toward a collection substrate, with the ejection angle set by the time-integrated acoustic acceleration imbalance. The overall acceleration ratio identifies the operating window for single-droplet ejection and separates it from no-ejection, satellite-droplet, and multiple-droplet regimes. We then connect ejection angle to landing position through a geometric deposition model referenced to a balanced shot in each experiment. At a 5.2 mm parent-drop-to-substrate spacing, 80 steered shots across twenty experiments show strongly anisotropic relative placement scatter: 0.59 mm in the steering direction and 0.06 mm transverse to it. In tests conducted independently over several days, a model calibrated on six earlier collection dates predicted landing positions on two later dates with a root-mean-square error of 0.71 mm; boot-strap resampling placed the 95% confidence range for this error between 0.41 and 1.01 mm. The results establish a practical framework for predicting relative droplet landing in angle-controlled surface acoustic wave jetting and identify the limits imposed by steering angle, separation distance, and actuation regime from an orifice-free, clog-free droplet ejection method.
authors: Md Aminul Islam; Sara Adibi; James Friend

title: Predictive Design of Greener Ultrafast Chromatography for Accelerated Discovery and Development Chemistry
abstract: Liquid chromatography (LC) is the analytical workhorse of pharmaceutical research and, at the same time, one of its largest sources of organic solvent waste and energy consumption. High-throughput experimentation amplifies this burden by generating thousands of samples per campaign, each conventionally analyzed by methods that consume milliliters to liters of solvent per system and keep instruments running for hours. Because solvent consumption and instrument energy demand scale directly with run time, accelerating these analyses is both a throughput and a sustainability priority. Routine implementation of ultrafast LC, however, has been limited by two related barriers: the experimental effort required to identify high-speed conditions that retain decision-critical selectivity, and the solvent-intensive nature of method development itself. Herein, we introduce a predictive in silico framework that transforms ultrafast LC assay development from empirical screening into a model-driven design workflow. Experimental retention data are used to model chromatographic selectivity across temperature, gradient slope, flow rate, and column geometry, enabling rapid identification of the fastest separation conditions that preserve the information required for decision-making. Retention modeling is further combined with fit-for-purpose resolution criteria and in silico peak clustering to selectively resolve critical components while intentionally grouping noncritical analytes to maximize throughput. The approach is demonstrated across closely related isomers, chiral analyses, and high-throughput reaction screening, where model-predicted separations translated directly into reliable experiments, substantially shortened analysis cycle times, and required minimal manual intervention. The resulting methods give lower analytical method greenness scores, in some cases by more than 10-fold. Together, this framework establishes a general strategy for systematically deploying greener ultrafast chromatographic assays while reducing method-development burden, solvent consumption, and energy demand, with broad applicability to biocatalysis, natural products, metabolomics, high-throughput experimentation, and modern synthesis.
authors: Devin M. Makey; Rodell C. Barrientos; Andrew McGrath; Dan Lehnherr; Andrew N. Singh; Eli J. Larson; Emmanuel Appiah‐Amponsah; Erik L. Regalado

title: ProTEUS: A mutation-resolved world model for closed-loop protein evolution
abstract: Protein engineering requires navigating rugged fitness landscapes, where small sequence changes can produce large functional differences, but experimental screening can only sample a small fraction of sequence space. Thus, a central challenge is to efficiently traverse the large combinatorial space of mutations in silico. We introduce ProTEUS, a mutation-resolved world model for closed-loop protein evolution. Pretrained on deep mutational scanning assays, ProTEUS learns a joint representation of sequence, evolutionary, and structural information using MutationFormer, a mutation-biased attention architecture. Variants are represented as states in this joint latent space, and mutations define actions whose functional consequences are predicted. To support exploration of many mutants, we developed a fast, physics-constrained all-atom predictor that utilizes explicit geometric constraint enforcement to achieve >10 fold increase in speed than AlphaFold3 with guaranteed physical validity. Lastly, ProTEUS refines its prediction and understanding of protein activity through closed loop experimental feedback to guide evolution toward a desired phenotype. ProTEUS surpasses established models in both zero-shot and supervised fine-tuning mutation prediction tasks. We experimentally demonstrate its utility in two closed-loop multi-objective engineering campaigns on aldehyde dehydrogenase and levansucrase, yielding variants with >10 fold higher activity than wild type. ProTEUS provides a world-model framework that connects virtual evaluation of mutational outcomes with experimental learning for efficient protein evolution.
authors: Yikun Zhang; Minghao Guo; Guangxue Xu; Peter Yichen Chen; Wojciech Matusik; Wengong Jin; Jingjing Chai; Kaiyi Jiang

title: Programmable Axial–Radial Multichannel Nickel Microtubes Fabricated by Core-Filament Jet Electrodeposition
abstract: Programmable hollow metallic microdevices with lateral outlets are attractive for distributed fluid handling, but integrating an axial lumen, side channels, and a sealed distal tip remains fabrication-intensive. Here, a core-filament jet electrodeposition (CF-JED) strategy combines segmented electrolyte-jet operation with sacrificial nylon-fiber templating to fabricate multichannel nickel microtubes. An 80 μm nylon core defines the axial lumen, whereas 50 μm transverse and helical fibers prescribe lateral channels. Interrupting the jet creates the in situ assembly interval for template placement; resumed localized electrodeposition encapsulates the fibers and can close the distal tip, and physical pull-out releases the channels without chemical dissolution or drilling. Stable growth was obtained at 2.5 mA with an axial growth rate of approximately 15 μm·min−1. Micro-computed tomography revealed a 50 ± 5 μm radial channel and a 76 ± 6 μm axial lumen interconnected within the sealed-tip structure. SEM/EDS confirmed open lateral apertures and nickel-rich walls, while water-immersion gas testing provided qualitative evidence of channel interconnectivity. CF-JED therefore provides a template-defined route to programmable multichannel hollow-metal microstructures; direct liquid-flow, mechanical, and biological validation remain necessary for application-specific use.
authors: Wei Wang; Hongtao Qian; Pengju Liu; Zhonghe Li; Yulong Li; Xiaohong Yang

title: Programmable DNA Nanotechnology as a paradigm shift in targeted therapeutics, molecular diagnostics, and emerging nanotechnologies
abstract: DNA nanotechnology has become a programmable platform for building precise nanoscale architectures with applications across biomedicine and materials science. This review examines recent advances in the design, synthesis and biological evaluation of DNA nanomaterials, including DNA origami, tetrahedral DNA nanostructures and DNA hydrogels. We survey established and emerging fabrication routes, among them chemical synthesis, enzymatic methods, hybridization, microfluidics and machine learning-guided design, and what each offers for scalability and cost. Structural strategies such as scaffold-staple folding are reviewed alongside surface chemistries including PEGylation and lipid bilayer encapsulation, with attention to their effect on stability and biological efficacy. Behavior in vivo is covered in detail: nuclease-mediated degradation, intracellular trafficking, clearance, and the biological interactions set by protein corona formation and physicochemical properties. For targeted therapeutics we cover aptamer functionalization and aptamer-drug conjugates; for molecular diagnostics, aptamer-based electrochemical biosensing and point-of-care formats. Immunogenicity and safety are treated in detail, including innate immune stimulation through TLR9 and cGAS-STING, complement activation and cytotoxicity. By setting out the preclinical evaluation frameworks that matter, among them pharmacokinetic characterization and toxicity testing, the review connects design decisions to biological safety and to what clinical translation of DNA nanomedicines will require.
authors: Pranjal Agarwal; Bhagyesh Parmar; Sakshi Soni; Sunny Rathee; Dhiraj Bhatia

title: Programmable Droplets as Active Matter in a Reconfigurable Environment
abstract: Exploring systems that bridge the gap between non living and living matter requires a reconfigurable environment coupled to synthetic systems capable of autonomous motion, adaptive behaviour and persistent dynamics. Self propelled droplets provide a minimal platform for such life like behaviour, but quantitative measures capturing both persistence and adaptability to enable closed loop reconfiguration remain lacking. Here we introduce an autonomous closed loop robotic platform to characterise and dynamically program the autonomous behaviour of multicomponent oil in water droplets. We explored two chemical composition spaces, with and without external pH perturbations, analysing droplet behaviour in real time and iteratively selecting formulations. To quantify this behaviour, we introduce two descriptors, persistence and diversity. Persistence is quantified by mapping temporal dynamics in a speed shape complexity space, where we identify a persistence domain that distinguishes active from inactive droplets. Diversity captures spontaneous or environmentally induced variation in motion and the propensity of droplets to reorient or adapt under perturbation. We show that persistence and diversity are constrained by a behavioural trade off: high persistence limits diversity, whereas high diversity reduces persistent activity. Our results provide a quantitative framework for navigating and programming life like behaviours in active droplets and show how closed-loop experimentation can uncover organising principles in complex active matter.
authors: Ivan Shmarov; Abhishek Sharma; Michael Jirásek; Kristine Laws; Leroy Cronin

title: Protruding Geometry Provides Potential Homing Sites of Circulating Tumor Cells
abstract: Circulating tumor cells (CTCs) must adhere to the vascular endothelium to initiate metastasis, yet the role of vessel wall topography remains unclear. We present an integrated microfluidic platform combining defined protruding geometries, live-cell imaging, and controlled perfusion to study CTC homing. Using a multiscale device that reproduces hierarchical vascular branching, we show that CTCs accumulate preferentially at locations with protruded geometry, including bifurcations, sharp corners and positively curved segments. At these hotspots, a viscoelastic, polymer-like network assembles, capturing CTCs and accompanying progressive multicellular aggregation. This network undergoes stretching and elastic recoil even under laminar flow. Mechanistically, knockdown of DSG2 and ITGB3 reduces retention, suggesting a potential anti-metastasis strategy targeting molecular–mechanical coupling. Computational fluid dynamics simulations indicate that hotspots coincide with pronounced velocity and pressure perturbations. Our experiments identify local geometry as a critical determinant of CTC arrest and provide a platform for studying the physical mechanisms of metastatic homing.
authors: Yeqing Leng; Bo Li

title: QUANTUM-INSPIRED SWARM MICROROBOTICS AND SAFE AUTONOMY FAMILY 14 | F066-F070 | The independent long-form scientific technical notebook A 4D biomedical microrobot x quantum-inspired computation x BCI x stroke rehabilitation RESEARCH DESIGN. Prospective, nonclinical, reconstructable and falsifiable. No completed clinical experiment or quantum hardware advantage is asserted. 33 x STARLI | White Rainbow Era THE SECOND SCIENTIFIC VOICE: WHY THE SWARM MUST BE ALLOWED TO FAIL Perhaps the most attractive image in microrobotics is a swarm moving as a single body. What the image does not reveal is what the particles know, which fields act upon them, which unit was lost, and which commanding intelligence had authority to decide the next motion. This notebook follows the scientific difficulty that starts where the visualization ends. It asks how a candidate local rule becomes a physically identifiable mechanism rather than a label assigned to any coherent animation. A convincing answer would need an independently metered actuation field, a sealed task definition, a tracked population and a competing ordinary explanation that could win. F066 begins with the neighbor graph. It asks whether local exchange can account for coordination after controlling for a common magnetic field. F067 asks whether an optimizer has delivered the work it was assigned, or quietly reduced the roster of obligations. F068 treats contact avoidance as a physical permission boundary rather than a penalty term in a solver. F069 examines the unit that never returned after a fault, even when throughput recovered. F070 holds the entire argument in a contest with well-tuned classical algorithms, full input and output timing, energy use and a separate laboratory. These five subjects cannot be collapsed into a single optimization metric without losing their causal differences. All five topics share a strict nonclinical boundary. Inert microrobots or calibrated substitutes in sealed microchannels can be used to develop hypotheses about coordination and actuation. An ex-vivo specimen requires separate authorization and does not establish implanted-device safety. A controller can generate physically interesting robot motion without helping a person who has experienced stroke. Evidence of neural intention decoding, effective assistance and unaided recovery belongs to separate, properly governed experiments. The integration imagined here is a research roadmap; it is not a report of achieved human benefit. The phrase five-stage parallel spacetime reasoning describes a plural research method, not a physical capability. We begin with a physical origin, encode a candidate model, step into an adversarial alternative world, stress the proposed mechanism at a bounded extreme, and converge only on the evidence that another laboratory can reconstruct. Each stage prevents a preferred algorithm from becoming immune to disagreement. The most important gain may be that a scientist can close one research round with a precise unanswered question, rather than polishing an unsupported claim into apparent completeness. A quantum-inspired controller often runs on ordinary classical machinery. Binary energy functions, quantum-like annealing vocabularies and Ising encodings do not establish access to quantum processors. Nor does a shorter internal solver time prove a faster physical task. Encoding, task ingestion, movement authorization, magnetic actuation, field calibration and retrieval all consume resources. Classical consensus, auctions, mixed-integer programming and model-predictive methods can be exceptionally strong competitors when carefully tuned. The design must let them win and must say so without embarrassment. The most severe oversight in long research works is not merely verbal repetition; it is a loss of the difference between hypotheses. Here the 82 chapters therefore have specific mechanisms, measured quantities, rival explanations and hidden stressors. Their six pages move from physical identification to mathematics, independent observation, fair competition, bounded adverse worlds and successor handoff. The technical notebook uses those same six obligations in a different form: three long arguments about mechanism, measurement and refutation. A successor should find not a perfect manuscript, but an actionable next experiment. The cited literature on magnetic microrobotics and swarm autonomy provides essential background, including Yang and Zhang, Motion Control in Magnetic Microrobotics (DOI 10.1146/annurev-control-032720-104318); Jiang, Yang and Zhang, An Overview of Micro/Nanorobot Swarm Control (DOI 10.1109/TMECH.2024.3449393); and Li et al., Automated Magnetic Microrobot Control (DOI 10.3390/math12142180). These references are not citations proving the original integrated architecture in this volume. Their contribution here is the physical plausibility of the questions and the methodological necessity of feedback, control and realistic uncertainty.

An independent blind experiment should conceal a junction obstacle and randomize sensor lag while counting every near miss and collision. The strongest ordinary baseline is a conventional reciprocal-velocity obstacle method, local reactive barrier controller and resource-matched centralized collision planner. Its observation contract requires frame-synchronized contact witness, robot radii [um], channel geometry [um], relative velocity [um/s] and aged-position logs [ms]. No apparatus or treatment benefit is asserted to have been demonstrated. The family-level interface is the same traceable inert-swarm test platform, but each flagship measures and can falsify a different mechanism. title: Quality monitoring in extrusion-based bioprinting: From defect formation to AI-driven detection and correction
abstract: Extrusion-based bioprinting is widely used to fabricate cell-laden three-dimensional constructs, yet its structural integrity remains difficult to ensure because interactions among bioink rheology, process parameters, hardware and construct design produce defects that compromise the dimensional accuracy and cell viability of the bioprinted samples. This review organizes the structural defects along a causal chain, from root-cause factors to nozzle-level failures (clogging and buckling-induced filament curling), filament-level defects (size inconsistency, fusion, delamination, sagging, collapse and breakage) and construct-level inaccuracy. It then maps each defect class to the sensing modalities that have been shown to observe it, spanning surface imaging (optical and machine-vision imaging, microscopy, thermography, video-based vibrometry and laser profilometry), volumetric analysis (optical coherence tomography, X-ray computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging and ultrasound) and process sensing (dielectric impedance spectroscopy and flow sensing). The methods are compared in terms of processing stage, reported resolution and target object. The evidence linking each defect class to each method is also mapped. Machine learning is assessed as an interpretation layer on these data, distinguishing classification, segmentation, anomaly scoring, open-loop prediction, and assisting corrective measures in printing. Key open challenges include the scarcity of shared, standardized datasets, limited external validation and regulatory frameworks, the absence of standardized defect definitions and the coupling between structural fidelity and cell viability, which together define the requirements for quality-assessment frameworks that can support clinical translation. Collectively, this review aims to provide a structured foundation for developing quality assessment frameworks capable of supporting the translation of extrusion-based bioprinting from laboratory research toward consistent, clinically viable fabrication.
authors: Md Asif Hasan Khan; Md Anisur Rahman; Jinki Kim

title: Quantitative KRAS ctDNA Dynamics Predict Early Recurrence After Neoadjuvant Therapy and Surgery in Pancreatic Cancer
abstract: Early recurrence remains prevalent in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) despite multimodality treatment. Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) is an emerging prognostic biomarker showing promise in detecting minimal residual disease (MRD). Using a high-sensitivity digital droplet PCR (ddPCR) assay, we evaluated KRAS- mutant ctDNA as a marker of MRD associated with early recurrence (< 12 months) in patients with localized PDAC receiving neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC), surgery, and adjuvant chemotherapy (AC). KRAS G12D, G12V, and G12R mutations found in cell-free DNA were detected and quantified with maximum variant allele frequency (mVAF). Of 130 enrolled patients, 55 completed NAC and resection. ctDNA was detected a median of 7.6 months before imaging-confirmed recurrence. Postoperative detection KRAS ctDNA was independently associated with worse recurrence-free survival (RFS) (aHR 3.30, 95% CI 1.33–8.21, p = 0.010), and ctDNA clearance after NAC and surgery was independently associated with improved RFS (aHR 0.23, 95% CI 0.06–0.90, p = 0.035). Median cohort mVAF was 0.03%; patients with mVAF above the median had shorter RFS (12.8 vs. 26.3 months) and more frequent early recurrence (p = 0.027). ctDNA-positive patients who received AC remained with worse outcomes than ctDNA-negative patients, suggesting persistent chemotherapy resistance. These data indicated that persistent KRAS ctDNA after NAC and surgery reflects MRD and support sensitive postoperative ctDNA testing to stratify high risk patients for early recurrence, guiding quantitative, longitudinal monitoring. Future studies in adaptive treatment settings may further extend these findings toward ctDNA-guided clinical decision-making.

title: Quantum-Inspired Graph Neural Digital Twins for the sub-microsecond topological co-design and temporal degradation modeling of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin smart gels.
abstract: The clinical translation of lignocellulosic smart gels is constrained by empirical formulation screening, complex structure-property relationships, and uncertainty in degradation and therapeutic-release behavior. This study aims to determine whether a unified computational digital-twin framework can (i) optimize the crosslinking topology of cellulose-, hemicellulose-, and lignin-based matrices, (ii) predict their mechanical and temporal degradation behavior, and (iii) translate optimized formulations into real-time control parameters for microfluidic synthesis. To address these objectives, we develop a Quantum-Inspired Graph Neural Digital Twin (Q-GNDT) that represents molecular interactions as dynamic non-Euclidean graphs and formulates topological optimization as a Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) problem. A temporal graph-decay model couples pH-dependent hydrolysis, enzymatic cleavage, percolation loss, and drug diffusion to predict time-resolved degradation and release. The computational architecture is integrated with an edge-AI control model designed for sub-microsecond microfluidic actuation. Retrospective cross-validation against published experimental datasets from three independent studies yielded mean absolute errors of 2.1% for pore size, 2.9% for storage modulus, and 1.5% for drug-release kinetics, with an overall RMSE of 0.74%. An in-silico targeted-delivery case study further produced 4.1% initial burst release, 98.0% cumulative delivery, and near-linear release kinetics (R2 = 0.991). These results indicate that Q-GNDT can serve as a computational design and screening framework for narrowing the experimental search space of programmable lignocellulosic biomaterials. Prospective synthesis, biological testing, and in vivo validation remain necessary before clinical translation.
authors: Krishna Bajpai

title: RPA-primed droplet-partitioned CRISPR/Cas12a assay for low-copy detection of Candida albicans in vaginal specimens
abstract: Candida albicans is a major cause of vulvovaginal candidiasis, and sensitive detection of low-abundance fungal DNA remains challenging in clinical specimens. In this study, we developed a two-stage assay combining rapid recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA) with droplet-partitioned CRISPR/Cas12a fluorescence detection. Target DNA was first amplified by RPA for 10 min and subsequently analyzed in vortex-generated polydisperse droplets without microfluidic chip fabrication. Using predefined NTC-based analytical criteria, the operational LoDs were 10 copies/μL for the bulk RPA-Cas12a assay and 1 copy/μL for the droplet-partitioned format under the tested conditions. No cross-reactivity was observed with the tested non-target organisms, including additional clinically relevant non- albicans Candida species. In a preliminary evaluation of 28 residual vaginal swab specimens, the assay showed complete concordance with a routine composite clinical reference using an exploratory cohort-derived droplet-count cutoff. Because the comparator was not species-specific for C. albicans , these findings represent preliminary concordance rather than definitive diagnostic accuracy. The complete workflow was performed within approximately 1 h using basic laboratory equipment. These findings demonstrate that droplet partitioning can improve the low-copy analytical readout of RPA-Cas12a detection and provide a practical approach for qualitative identification of C. albicans DNA in vaginal specimens.
authors: Ju Long; Juan Xie; Fang Liu; Jie Peng; Wenfei Xu; Xu-Hui Li
