title: Real-time estimation of high-resolution flow fields and reduced-order coordinates from event-based imaging velocimetry
abstract: A data-driven framework is proposed to estimate high-resolution (HR) velocity fields and reduced-order flow coordinates from coarse real-time event-based imaging velocimetry (rt-EBIV) measurements. Low-resolution (LR) data are retrieved through fast event analysis on a coarse grid. During offline training, the LR/HR mapping and a linear dynamical model in a proper orthogonal decomposition (POD)-based reduced-order space are identified. Online, each incoming LR snapshot is projected onto the LR basis, and the corresponding HR reduced-order coordinates are estimated and temporally regularized. Three estimators are proposed and compared: a direct Kalman filter (KF), a linear stochastic estimation (LSE) combined with Kalman filtering, and a variance-rescaled implementation (LSE+VR). The full HR velocity field is then reconstructed from the estimated reduced-order coordinates using the retained POD basis. The framework is assessed on two turbulent flows acquired by pulsed event-based imaging velocimetry (EBIV): a submerged water jet and a channel flow over a square rib. All three estimators outperform direct cubic interpolation of the LR fields, recovering physically consistent HR flow states with improved estimation of turbulent kinetic energy, spectral content, reduced-order dynamics, and temporal coherence. The linear stochastic estimator yields the lowest overall reconstruction error, while its variance-rescaled implementation provides nearly identical values and improves the recovery of fluctuation energy and higher-order content. The direct KF formulation remains highly efficient in terms of computational cost and provides the closest agreement with the HR reference in the temporal and spatial spectral analyses. The bulk of the computational cost lies in the full-field HR reconstruction, whereas the reduced-order coordinate estimation alone is negligible compared with the cost of the LR processing itself. The framework enables deliberately coarse real-time EBIV processing to be combined with reduced-order refinement, extending the effective real-time operating range towards higher update frequencies while still providing richer and dynamically more consistent HR flow representations. This makes the approach attractive for high-quality real-time flow diagnostics and as a first step towards future observer-based and closed-loop flow-control applications.
authors: Luca Franceschelli; Enrico Amico; C. Willert; Marco Raiola; Gioacchino Cafiero; Stefano Discetti

title: Reasoning in the loop: antibody lead optimization by probing mechanism and measurement
abstract: Lab-in-the-loop systems, in which a model proposes molecules, automated assays measure their properties and the results retrain the model, are a popular approach to antibody lead optimization. These systems optimize for a specification defined with metrics computed from instrument signals, so their success depends on how well those metrics serve as proxies for the properties a drug candidate needs. When a metric is a poor proxy, neither a better model nor more data will fix it, and identifying the problem usually requires expert review. We report two campaigns run on BigHat Biosciences' Milliner platform, one on an anti-albumin nanobody (VHH) and one on an anti-mesothelin single-chain variable fragment (scFv), in which a research team and a general-purpose AI agent, Claude, brought scientific reasoning into the loop. Over seven rounds and about 1,010 design variants we built libraries from antibody lineage, structure and biophysics, and found from the raw curves that on each scaffold one thermal metric did not measure what its name implied. The libraries were built as controlled comparisons, so the results also show what each mutation contributes to each property. We fit a physical model of the curves, used it to choose metrics suited to each scaffold, and changed the experimental protocol, varying protein concentration and heating rate, to test the model against pre-registered predictions. Both leads improve on their parents in affinity, thermal stability and aggregation while improving or maintaining yield and purity.
authors: Samuel Stanton; Aaron Solomon; Emily Delaney; Melanie Montgomery; Crystal Humphries; Timothy Acker; Ryan Henrici; Charbel Eid; Eddie Abrams; Peyton Greenside

title: Recent Advances in Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning in Pharma Drug Discovery, Physiotherapy Practice, and Personalized Medicine: A Comprehensive Review
abstract: The convergence of artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and deep learning (DL) architectures has established a paradigm shift across the continuum of modern bio-medicine.Historically, biomedical innovation operated within isolated silos: pharmaceutical research grappled with exorbitant attrition rates and extended development timelines; physical rehabilitation relied on subjective observational assessments; and clinical medicine administered standardized therapeutic regimens to heterogeneous patient cohorts.Today, generative deep learning, geometric graph neural networks (GNNs), computer vision algorithms, and multi-omics integrative frameworks bridge these domains into a unified ecosystem.In drug discovery, modern AI models execute high-throughput virtual screening, predict three-dimensional macromolecular target structures, and design optimized lead compounds with precise pharmacokinetic properties.In physical therapy and rehabilitation, vision-based motion tracking, wearable sensor fusion, and smart robotics enable continuous, quantitative bio-feedback and dynamic intervention tailoring.Concurrently, in personalized medicine, transformer-based genomic language models and multi-modal clinical decision support systems (CDSS) aggregate multi-omics data, longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs), and real-world evidence (RWE) to optimize treatment strategies for individual patients.This comprehensive review synthesizes the cross-disciplinary advances, underlying mathematical architectures, clinical validation pipelines, regulatory challenges, and future trajectories of AI and ML across pharmaceutical discovery, physical rehabilitation, and precision therapeutics.
venue: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology

title: Recent Advances in Closed-Loop Control Techniques for Additive Manufacturing: A Review
abstract: Additive manufacturing (AM) has transformed modern manufacturing by enabling the layer-by-layer fabrication of complex components directly from digital models. However, variations in process parameters, material behavior, thermal conditions, and machine dynamics can significantly affect product quality, dimensional accuracy, and process stability. This review examines advanced closed-loop control techniques for additive manufacturing, emphasizing real-time monitoring, feedback control, and intelligent process regulation. The AM process, major printing technologies, and conventional closed-loop control concepts are first discussed to establish the fundamental framework. In-situ monitoring techniques, including imaging and acoustic sensing, are examined for real-time defect detection and process validation. Advanced control strategies such as Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) control, Adaptive Control, Gain Scheduling, Model Reference Adaptive Systems (MRAS), and fuzzy logic-based control are then reviewed. These approaches enable dynamic adjustment of printing parameters in response to process deviations, thereby improving manufacturing consistency and reducing defects. The review also highlights an integration of AI with closed-loop systems to support predictive and autonomous control. Finally, current challenges and research opportunities are identified, emphasizing intelligent sensing, adaptive algorithms, and data-driven control for reliable and autonomous additive manufacturing.

title: Recent advances in fluorescent probes for diagnostics and targeted therapeutics at the biomedical frontier
abstract: Fluorescence probes have contributed immensely to the understanding of cellular dynamics, pathology, and complex molecular interactions of biomolecules in living systems. There has been a resurgence in fluorescence imaging field mainly due to breakthroughs in advanced high-resolution techniques, thus propelling the development of innovative probes with superior therapeutic potential. This review emphasizes the design of fluorescent probes and the significant advancements in diagnostic modalities over the last five years.
authors: Pinaki Bhattacharjee; Malliga R. Iyer

title: Recent advances in nanofabrication strategies for biosensors: from precision nanopatterning to scalable, flexible, and AI-assisted manufacturing
abstract: Nanofabrication has become central to the development of high-performance biosensors by enabling precise control over sensing interfaces, enhanced signal transduction, and integration across optical, electrochemical, microfluidic, and wearable platforms. This review examines the evolution of biosensor nanofabrication from deterministic top-down patterning toward scalable and integrated manufacturing strategies. Top-down approaches, including electron-beam lithography, focused ion beam milling, nanoimprint lithography, reactive ion etching, and laser-based fabrication, are discussed alongside replication and transfer processes, soft lithography, lithography-free plasmonic structuring, and additive three-dimensional fabrication. Bottom-up strategies based on nanoparticle assembly, DNA nanotechnology, block-copolymer and nanoporous templating, and stimuli-responsive materials are further considered as routes to programmable nanoscale organization and functional biointerfaces. Particular attention is given to flexible and wearable biosensors, where substrate mechanics, conductive-interface fabrication, textile integration, epidermal microfluidics, packaging, power management, and wireless communication introduce manufacturing requirements beyond conventional rigid devices. Across these approaches, the review emphasizes that analytical sensitivity alone is insufficient for translation; nanoscale precision must be accompanied by reproducibility, scalable processing, stable biofunctionalization, antifouling performance, packaging, storage stability, and device-level quality control. Emerging AI-assisted fabrication and process optimization strategies are also discussed as tools for linking manufacturing parameters with structural and analytical performance. Overall, the review provides a manufacturing-oriented perspective on how hybrid nanofabrication strategies can bridge high-performance laboratory biosensors with reproducible, scalable, and application-ready sensing systems.
authors: Meryem Beyza Avci; Furkan Kocer; Seda Nur Topkaya; Konstantinos Papatryfonos; Arif E. Çetin

title: Reconfigurable acoustic tweezers based on a programmable droplet array
abstract: Conventional acoustic manipulation relies on either direct acoustic radiation force acting on particles or indirect methods using acoustic streaming generated by acoustic pressure fields to manipulate particles. While acoustic devices generating standing waves can create patterned arrangements of particles and cells, these methods are typically limited to producing regular arrays in static configurations. This study introduces a dynamic acoustic field modulation method to overcome these limitations, significantly enhancing manipulation flexibility. Crucially, the propagation of acoustic energy varies substantially at liquid-solid interfaces or gas-solid interfaces due to differences in acoustic impedance matching. To exploit this, we use a digital microfluidic chip (DMF) to manipulate droplets and generate a programmable droplet array via the electrowetting-on-dielectric effect. By utilizing the programmable droplet array, we dynamically alter the spatial distribution of the acoustic field from a bulk acoustic wave (BAW) device in real time and demonstrate this technique's capability for capturing and manipulating particles on demand. We believe this is a unique method to create acoustic tweezers with great flexibility and reconfigurability, which holds promising potential for advanced applications in micromanipulation, micro-assembly, and beyond.
authors: Zhen Wang; Menglei Zhao; Kangfu Chen; Yao Lu; Haopu Wang; Zongliang Guo; Zonghao Li; Meiyi Zhou; Huiliang Cao; Kaiqiang Cao; Xiaoyi Wang; Rongxin Fu; Hang Li; Zhichao Ma; Jiafang Li; Huikai Xie; Xicheng Zhang

title: Regular exercise augments gut-brain communication and visceral feedback control of appetite
abstract: OBJECTIVES: Regular exercise is widely accepted to support long-term body weight management; however, the neurobiological adaptations that contribute to the beneficial effects of habitual physical activity beyond increases in energy expenditure per se remain unclear. Here, we investigated whether regular exercise alters gut-brain communication and visceral feedback control of feeding. METHODS: Mice were subjected to regular voluntary wheel running. Energy expenditure and feeding were assessed under basal conditions and following an overnight fast. Nutrients were delivered directly into the stomach by intragastric infusion. Brain-wide responses to intragastric nutrient delivery were assessed using positron emission tomography (PET). Single-cell sequencing and histological analyses were used to determine nutrient-responsive neuronal populations in the caudal brainstem. Genetic associations with body weight were evaluated using GWAS data. RESULTS: Intragastric nutrient delivery suppressed feeding more strongly in exercising mice. Brain-wide PET revealed enhanced responses to intragastric nutrients in various brain regions. Single-cell sequencing identified several nutrient-responsive caudal brainstem populations, including a previously unrecognized population marked by expression of fibrinogen C domain containing 1 (FIBCD1). Regular exercise selectively enhanced the nutrient-evoked activation of FIBCD1 neurons. Histological analyses demonstrate that FIBCD1 neurons are also present in the human brainstem, and GWAS data suggest a potential relevance of this neuron population to body-weight regulation. CONCLUSIONS: Regular exercise enhances behavioral and brain responses to intragastric nutrient delivery and sensitizes FIBCD1 neurons in the brainstem of mice. These findings reveal an exercise-associated adaptation of gut-brain communication that may contribute to improved matching of caloric intake to energy expenditure.
authors: Diba Borgmann; Dylan M. Rausch; Sofia Hult Lundh; Sahar Hassan; Cansu Tokgöz; Annika Glatzel; Leonie Cabot; Malou Cajsa ten Voorde; Cecilie Bæch‐Laursen; Paula Sanchís; Claus Brandt; Heiko Backes; Tune H. Pers; Henning Fenselau

title: Regulatory and scientific frameworks for AI-driven biosensor technologies in antimicrobial resistance monitoring
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) diagnostics require evidence matched to the intended clinical or surveillance use. This narrative review synthesizes biosensor research, artificial intelligence (AI) analytics, and device oversight through a regulatory-scientific lifecycle perspective. Electrochemical and optical transduction are distinguished from microfluidic sample handling and nanomaterial enhancement. Pathogen identification, resistance-gene detection, phenotypic antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST), minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) prediction, and population surveillance are compared by output, reference standard, and validation requirement. Representative Raman-machine-learning and microfluidic studies illustrate both analytical promise and limitations in independent clinical validation. The review maps these findings to US and European device pathways, software controls, interoperability, cybersecurity, and data governance. Its proposed five-phase framework adapts established total-product-lifecycle, quality-management, and risk-management principles to AMR-specific challenges, including emerging resistance mechanisms, breakpoint revisions, specimen shifts, and algorithm changes. The framework is a conceptual implementation tool, not a new regulatory pathway or an empirically validated model. Safe translation requires claim-specific validation and controlled updates rather than extrapolation from isolated prototype performance.
authors: Anjanasree Murali; Priyanka Thakor; Shivani Shah; Manav Singh; Om V. Singh

title: Remimazolam versus propofol for general anaesthesia in children undergoing laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair: a propensity score- matched retrospective cohort study
abstract: Background Remimazolam is an ultra-short-acting benzodiazepine with a favourable safety profile, but comparative evidence against propofol in paediatric surgery remains limited. We compared remimazolam-based and propofol-based general anaesthesia in children undergoing laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair. Methods In this single-centre retrospective cohort study, children aged 3–12 years with American Society of Anesthesiologists physical status I–II who underwent elective laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair between April 2024 and May 2025 were identified from routinely collected clinical records. Children receiving remimazolam or propofol were matched 1:1 by nearest-neighbour propensity score matching with a 0.05 caliper. Emergence time was the primary outcome; secondary outcomes included airway-device removal time, intraoperative haemodynamic instability, adverse events within 24 h, postoperative recovery, length of stay and Pediatric Quality of Life Inventory 4.0 scores. Continuous and categorical variables were compared using appropriate parametric or non-parametric tests, chi-square or Fisher’s exact tests, and mixed-effects analysis for repeated quality-of-life measurements. Results After matching, 120 children were analysed in each group. Remimazolam was associated with shorter emergence time (median 11.5 vs 18.2 min) and airway-device removal time (13.2 vs 20.4 min; both P < 0.001), less intraoperative haemodynamic instability (15.0% vs 25.8%; P = 0.034), and fewer adverse events within 24 h (8.3% vs 35.8%; P < 0.001). Emergence agitation occurred in 3.3% versus 26.7%, and nausea or vomiting in 4.2% versus 18.3%. Oral intake, ambulation and hospital discharge occurred earlier in the remimazolam group. PedsQL scores were higher at 1 week and 1 month after surgery, with between-group differences exceeding the reported minimal clinically important difference. Conclusions In this propensity score-matched retrospective cohort of children undergoing laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair, remimazolam use was associated with shorter emergence and airway-device removal times and a lower observed incidence of selected postoperative adverse events than propofol. Higher postoperative PedsQL scores were also observed in the remimazolam group at follow-up. These findings should be interpreted cautiously because of the retrospective, single-centre design, the possibility of residual confounding, and limitations in the assessment of patient-reported outcomes. Prospective studies are needed to confirm these associations and evaluate their clinical significance.
authors: Jianmin Tian; Jun Liu; Teng Fan; Zhijie Jia; Junna Sun; 李晓芳

title: Remote‐Controlled Genetic Circuits: Light, Ultrasound, and Magnetic Fields for Programmable Gene Regulation
abstract: Remote-controlled genetic circuits use externally applied physical signals to regulate gene expression and cellular functions with spatial and temporal precision. Light, ultrasound, and magnetic fields provide complementary advantages in controllability, tissue accessibility, and biological compatibility, but their performance depends on both physical-field propagation and efficient conversion of external energy into intracellular signals and predictable gene-regulatory outputs. This review presents a unified framework of physical transduction, biological sensors, signal processors, and genetic effectors for comparing prokaryotic and eukaryotic systems. Core genetic circuits are distinguished from delivery and auxiliary platforms that support cargo release, cellular uptake, or energy conversion without directly regulating genes. Representative systems are compared by circuit architecture, transduction mechanism, stimulus parameters, dynamic range, basal leakage, response kinetics, reversibility, in vivo actuation, delivery requirements, and safety. The evolution from inducible switches toward multi-input logic, tunable regulation, genetic memory, and feedback control is discussed. An end-to-end codesign workflow and modality-specific reporting framework are proposed to integrate physical inputs, transducers, genetic circuits, delivery strategies, and stimulation devices. Quantitative benchmarking and standardized safety evaluation are essential for advancing these systems toward predictable and clinically translatable therapeutic platforms.
authors: Xinming Yu; Yi Lu; Xiaomiao Yu; Shang Jia; Yuru Ma; Ruicun Liu; Xin Ni Mu; Yanfang Su; Xingwen Sun; Yefeng Shen; Xin Li; Xiuyun Liu; Zhiyuan Shi

title: Reprogramming Protein Function by Expanding Chemical and Combinatorial Space: Integrating Chemical and Computational Strategies
abstract: Proteins are biological macromolecules that perform critical functions, including catalysis, molecular recognition, and cellular regulation. Natural evolution has generated remarkable protein diversity, leaving vast opportunities for engineered molecular innovation. Protein engineering has evolved from the rational design of proteins over the last few decades to approaches based on directed evolution and computational methods to enhance their properties. Protein engineering is shifting from optimization-based approaches to an integrated approach, which includes rational design, directed evolution, computational and generative modeling, synthetic chemistry, synthetic biology, and laboratory automation. These strategies widen the scope of experimentally accessible chemical and structural toolboxes in proteins without sacrificing the physicochemical constraints, cellular compatibility, evolutionary processes, and experimental validation. Meanwhile, synthetic chemistry is extending the natural abilities of proteins by incorporating noncanonical amino acids, novel cofactors, and modified metal centers and catalytic environments. These technologies enable the creation of artificial enzymes, programmed molecular binders, synthetic receptors, molecular machines, and biomaterials that have functions beyond those of their natural counterparts. This review introduces advances in the protein engineering field, from past methods of modifying proteins to present-day opportunities for generating proteins with artificial intelligence, and explains how the fields of computation, chemistry, and biology are driving the future of programmable proteins.
authors: Mohsin Shad

title: Research Progress on Multimodal Physiological Sensing and System Integration of Flexible Bioelectronic Devices
abstract: Flexible bioelectronic devices provide mechanically compliant interfaces for acquiring, processing, and modulating physiological information across skin, organ, and neural systems. Their development has moved from single-parameter wearable sensors toward integrated platforms that combine electrophysiological, mechanical, thermal, and biochemical measurements with wireless communication, soft power modules, and algorithm-assisted interpretation. This review summarizes recent progress in the material basis, interface construction, multimodal sensing mechanisms, and system-level integration of flexible bioelectronics. Emphasis is placed on conductive hydrogels, elastomeric composites, liquid metals, laser-induced graphene, organic electrochemical transistors, porous soft structures, and adhesive interfaces that support low-impedance coupling, strain tolerance, and long-term operation. The review further discusses device designs for electrocardiography, electromyography, electroencephalography, pressure, strain, temperature, sweat metabolites, electrolytes, and inflammatory biomarkers, followed by integration strategies for crosstalk control, energy supply, wireless data transfer, intelligent analysis, and closed-loop feedback. It is demonstrated by current evidence that clinically oriented flexible bioelectronics require coordinated optimization of biointerface mechanics, signal fidelity, biochemical selectivity, manufacturing reproducibility, and data reliability. Future research is anticipated to focus on standardized validation, durable encapsulation, patient-specific algorithms, and therapeutic systems capable of linking continuous sensing with adaptive intervention.
authors: Mingyang Yuan

title: Research platforms and recent advances of mechanoimmunology
abstract: Unlike most tissue-resident cells that inhabit relatively homeostatic mechanical microenvironments, immune cells encounter diverse mechanical cues as they circulate throughout the body and transmigrate across tissue barriers. Mechanical stimuli have emerged as fundamental upstream regulators of both innate and adaptive immune responses. Mechanotransduction processes governed by core biomechanical sensors and effectors, including Piezo1, TRPV4, and YAP/TAZ, have recently attracted escalating research attention across immunological and mechanobiological fields. Notably, cellular mechanosensing is intrinsically context-dependent, shaped by the interplay between local mechanical properties and biochemical cues within tissue microenvironments. As a result, mechanoregulated immune phenotypes and functional outputs are highly sensitive to the experimental configurations of preclinical models. In contrast to previous reviews that mainly outline mechanotransduction signaling cascades, this review systematically categorizes prevalent biomechanical research platforms, detailing their technical specifications and key parametric characteristics, while contextualizing the mechanical regulation of immune behaviors within specific experimental frameworks. STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE: Mechanoimmunology has revealed that mechanical forces are fundamental regulators of immune cell function, yet the field is plagued by contradictory findings arising from inconsistent platform parameterization. This review provides the first systematic classification of five major biomechanical research platforms - 2D hydrogel systems, 3D matrix models, microfluidic devices, single-molecule force spectroscopy, and in vivo genetic models - detailing their technical specifications, parametric boundaries, and experimental contexts. By anchoring immune mechanobiological conclusions to specific platform parameters, we establish a framework for resolving apparent phenotypic contradictions and standardizing cross-study comparisons. This context-aware approach directly informs the rational design of immunomodulatory biomaterials with tunable mechanical properties, bridging biomaterials engineering and immune cell biology for applications in tissue repair, cancer immunotherapy, and regenerative medicine.
authors: Yuhuan Su; Zipeng Zhang; Li Jian; Tianhao Yan; Yiran Shi; Xuanxu Piao; Zhuoyuan Xin; Jinghua Li; Chunyan Zhao; Xiaoni Ai; Qian Peter Su; Lanfen Chen; Yongzheng Li

title: Research progress of artificial intelligence applications in obstetrics
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being applied across obstetrics, with applications spanning electronic medical record analysis, prenatal ultrasound, fetal monitoring, prediction of pregnancy complications, labor management, postpartum care, and telemedicine. The evidence reviewed in this article indicates that AI can improve automated information extraction, image and signal interpretation, and risk discrimination across multiple obstetric tasks, with particularly consistent advances in fetal ultrasound analysis, cardiotocography (CTG) interpretation, and early prediction of gestational diabetes, preeclampsia, and preterm birth. However, model performance is heterogeneous and is often reported using discrimination or classification metrics rather than patient-centered clinical outcomes. In CTG research, models differ substantially in whether they classify interpretation categories, detect fetal hypoxia or acidemia, or predict neonatal outcomes, making direct comparison difficult. Similarly, high predictive accuracy for pregnancy complications does not establish that AI implementation itself improves maternal or neonatal outcomes, and the clinical benefit of treatment should not be attributed to the predictive model without intervention studies. Across obstetric applications, limited external validation, dataset shift, class imbalance, calibration, interpretability, workflow integration, and data governance remain major barriers to clinical translation. This review therefore emphasizes the distinction between technical model performance and demonstrated clinical utility, and highlights the evidence required to move AI applications from retrospective development toward prospective, clinically integrated obstetric care.
authors: Liping Zhang; Yuqin Liu; Yongting Zhao; Jing Ma; Lijie Pan; Liehong Wang

title: Research progress on precision screening and high-density cultivation technologies for probiotics: from multi-omics and high-throughput to intelligent fermentation

title: Research progress on the application of multi-scale computational methods in the research and development of anti-tuberculosis infection drugs
abstract: Tuberculosis (TB), driven by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), remains a leading cause of mortality from infectious disease worldwide.​ The global dissemination of multidrug-resistant (MDR) and extensively drug-resistant (XDR) strains—coupled with protracted treatment regimens and the persistence of latent infection—has not only compromised first-line chemotherapies but also underscored the stagnation of conventional drug development pipelines. In this review, we systematically synthesize how multi-scale computational strategies are reshaping anti-TB drug discovery and explicitly delineate their hierarchical integration—a cohesive framework that, to our knowledge, has yet to be comprehensively mapped in the existing literature.​ We survey four interconnected computational layers: (i) systems and network pharmacology for macroscopic target and pathway prioritization; (ii) machine learning (ML) for mesoscopic virtual screening, resistance classification, and ADMET prediction; (iii) molecular docking for microscopic elucidation of ligand–target binding modes; and (iv) molecular dynamics (MD) simulations for atomic-level validation of binding poses and assessment of complex stability. Representative studies demonstrate that this workflow has pinpointed pivotal TB vulnerabilities (e.g., MmpL3, InhA, DprE1, ATP synthase, and FtsZ), enabled ML models to predict drug resistance from genomic data with high fidelity, and identified promising candidates such as vazabitide A (predicted binding affinity of −85.8 kcal/mol against Pks13) alongside repurposed agents (e.g., aldoxorubicin, quarfloxin). Critically, these computational predictions are reinforced by orthogonal experimental validation spanning in vitro enzymatic and phenotypic assays, in vivo infection models, clinical pharmacokinetic profiling, and multi-omics corroboration. We conclude that the top-down pipeline-spanning network pharmacology to ML, docking, and MD-integrated with bottom-up feedback constitutes a closed-loop paradigm that accelerates lead identification while addressing emergent drug resistance.​ Nevertheless, inherent limitations in predictive reliability and cross-layer error propagation necessitate rigorous downstream experimental validation. Looking forward, generative artificial intelligence, self-driving laboratories, and standardized cross-method benchmarking are poised to consolidate this multi-scale pipeline into a robust engine for next-generation anti-TB therapeutics.
authors: yajing ZHAO; Chao Wang; Wenjing Shang; Xun Peng; Mingyu Zhang; Chuanxi Zhao

title: Responsible AI in Public-Serving Institutions: Advances, Challenges, and Future Directions
abstract: Public-serving institutions (government agencies, courts, health systems, social-welfare bodies, and regulators) are adopting artificial intelligence (AI) to triage caseloads, allocate resources, detect fraud, and personalize services. Because these institutions exercise coercive and distributive authority over citizens who cannot easily exit the relationship, the stakes of getting AI wrong are qualitatively different from those in commercial settings. This paper surveys the advances, challenges, and future directions of responsible AI in the public sector, synthesizing scholarship on AI in government, algorithmic fairness, transparency, and AI ethics with practitioner-facing governance instruments. We first delimit what makes public-serving institutions distinctive: statutory mandates, due-process obligations, and diffuse accountability. We then map the state of the art across four dimensions (use cases, governance and policy instruments, fairness/transparency/accountability practices, and organizational capacity and procurement) and consolidate representative advances in a described table. We argue that the field has matured from principle proliferation toward operational risk management, exemplified by the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and the OECD AI Principles, yet a persistent gap remains between high-level commitments and verifiable practice on the ground. Core challenges include bias and equity harms, threats to legitimacy and due process, opacity and contestability, thin institutional capacity, and fragmented accountability. We conclude with a research and practice agenda emphasizing contestable-by-design systems, sociotechnical evaluation, procurement as governance, participatory oversight, and workforce capability. Responsible AI in public service is less a technical property of models than an institutional achievement sustained over time.
authors: Uchechi Mary-Linda Unamma; Ifeanyichukwu Jeffrey Okwesa; Abubakar Umar Abdulmalik; Serif Oyindamola Oyesiji

title: Robotic arm-assisted droplet-based additive manufacturing via acoustic levitation: process implementation and experimental optimization
abstract: This paper presents the concept, implementation and process optimization of a robotic arm-assisted additive manufacturing system using acoustic levitation for droplet-based deposition of photocurable resin. By integrating acoustic levitation and robotic manipulation, the tank-free material deposition approach has the potential to overcome the limitations inherent in conventional 3D printing - such as fixed build directions, planar layers and the reliance on resin tanks. The focus of this study is on experimental characterization and process optimization. Necessary aspects of implementing the additive manufacturing system were investigated, including the ultraviolet (UV) light profile characterization, resin curing characterization and contact angle measurement. A Taguchi experiment- based process optimization further revealed the optimal combination of process parameters for surface quality on continuously deposited droplets. Implementation of the system was demonstrated using a commercial photocurable resin. This work paves the way for the development of a multi-material contactless and tankless additive manufacturing platform that supports multi-directional deposition.
authors: Ye Li; Umamaheswara Ra Datla; Noah Negron

title: Robots as lab partners: chemists’ perspectives for informing the design of robot-assisted experimentation
abstract: Experimental laboratory work involves repetitive, labour-intensive manual procedures and strict safety protocols, making it an attractive area for Robotics and Artificial Intelligence (RAI). With research currently focused on technical innovation, there has been little work investigating the human factors of chemist-robot collaboration, and how these technologies will change the nature of work in chemistry. Understanding chemists’ requirements and perspectives is vital to the successful deployment and acceptance of RAI in laboratories. We examined the potential for robot-assisted chemistry experimentation through the perspective of future users by conducting contextual inquiries and semi-structured interviews with nine experimental chemists at various career levels with and without laboratory automation experience. Reflexive thematic analysis was used to gain a situated understanding of how their work could benefit from automation, as well as their perspectives and opinions on working alongside robots. We found that our participants are open to robot-assisted experimentation and have clear ideas for human-robot partnerships in the lab. We identified eight themes characterising chemists’ desired applications, the implementation requirements, and the perspectives on the adoption of robot-assisted experimentation. These findings show that successful acceptance of robot-assisted experimentation depends not only on technical innovation, but also on addressing the practical barriers and concerns of the chemists who will work alongside these systems. The key concern being that RAI should not constrain, but rather complement the role of the chemist in knowledge discovery. The findings contribute to a set of initial design considerations covering hardware, software, and interaction design for successful integration of RAI in experimental laboratory work.
authors: Adrian Vecina Tercero; Praminda Caleb-Solly; Nikhil Deshpande

title: Rotationally Symmetric Lattice Boltzmann Pseudopotential Methods for Porous Media Applications
abstract: Pseudopotential models are a well established approach for multiphase and multicomponent simulations using the lattice Boltzmann method. Although not the most accurate, they are often chosen for ease of implementation and adaptability. A drawback of the models are spurious currents at the interfaces and particularly at solid walls which introduce numerical artifacts. An improved lattice Boltzmann pseudopotential model is presented. The discrete fluid density gradients in the coupling force are computed with rotationally symmetric gradient operators formulated as a convolution. As a result, spurious currents are reduced in settings where solid walls are unaligned with the lattice directions. Additionally, variations of introducing fluid-solid interaction either equally through both fluids or through a single fluid only are compared. Presented model variants are compared using droplets on walls as a common benchmark, analytically solvable capillary rise experiments (Jurin's law), and porous media imbibition as a practical application. Rotationally symmetric operators outperform the classical lattice weights approach in all tests in terms of accuracy, while avoiding extending the lattice to compute higher order gradients. The choice of the fluid-solid interaction variant depends on the problem under consideration and the desired properties of the resulting model.
authors: Benjamin Kellers; Arnulf Latz; Timo Danner

title: SEA-Lab: Experiment-grounded recursive self-improvement in an automated laboratory
abstract: AI scientists can generate hypotheses, plans, and protocols. Translating these outputs into reliable experiments requires adapting them to local equipment and resources using feedback from observed outcomes. A key challenge is to retain laboratory execution feedback as reusable knowledge for subsequent planning. We present SEA-Lab ( S elf- E volving A utonomous Lab), which combines an environment-grounded Dry-Lab Harness that generates protocols and machine-readable procedures, a wet-lab execution harness that coordinates heterogeneous devices and records execution traces and experimental measurements, and a recursive self-improvement mechanism that uses physical feedback to revise reusable execution policies and experimental strategies. Across three rounds of review on 219 tasks, protocol-review pass rates reached 90.41%. On 66 automation-eligible tasks, mean virtual-validation pass rates increased from 16.7% to 87.7% after two revisions. On two liquid handlers, runtime fell by 45.8% for plate replication, 34.1% for well rearrangement, and up to 68.6% for sample normalization. We demonstrated the system in a phage-display experiment linking four automated experimental steps: molecular cloning, phage titration, sample normalization, and ELISA screening. Of 96 starting samples, 93 yielded a sequence-correct clone, and primary ELISA screening identified ten candidates. These results illustrate how laboratory feedback can guide planning around local resources, refine execution on different laboratory instruments, and inform method revision based on experimental results.
authors: Yuliang Jiang; Ruijie Gong; He Chen; Xin Wang; Bin Zhang; Qiujun Wang; Tengfei Zhang; Mengya Fan; Xueya Mao; Zhenling Hou; Yang Hu; Yuan Gao; Chengzhi Wang

title: SPARC: Evidence-guided adaptive model composition for materials discovery
abstract: Closed-loop experimentation requires more than selecting the next experiment. It must also determine which existing measurements and model-derived relationships are sufficiently supported to influence that decision. Here we introduce SPARC (Sparse Predictive Aggregation of Regression Components), a framework that continually revises this support as experimental evidence accumulates. Competing model families are evaluated through out-of-fold predictions, so that each model is tested on observations not used in its corresponding fit. Sparse posterior composition assigns model influence according to predictive contributions supported by the out-of-fold evidence, retaining complementary contributions from several model families. Candidate-dependent predictive dispersion and residual variability define trust, which modulates exploration alongside the predicted response. Independent diagnostics also prioritize existing measurements for prospective verification, with model-derived trust reported alongside them. Across eight published materials datasets, SPARC achieved higher $R^2$ than the corresponding literature-reported values in six, with relative gains of up to 77% without the density-functional-theory- or experiment-derived descriptors used by several published pipelines. In an automated alkaline oxygen-evolution-reaction campaign, 8 of 11 SPARC-selected experiments reached overpotentials below 300 mV, with a best value of 242 mV, compared with 18 of 125 initial experiments. Measurements prioritized for verification before repetition subsequently deviated by 76 mV on average, compared with 27 mV for matched controls. SPARC therefore turns experimental evidence into a basis for revising model influence, directing exploration and identifying measurements that warrant verification.
authors: Sissi Feng; Yuchen Han; Runze Zhang; Jiaru Bai; Brandon Sutherland; Ali Shayesteh Zeraati; Jason R. Hattrick-Simpers; Varinia Bernales; Alán Aspuru‐Guzik; Yang Bai

title: STaSBO: LLM-Guided Strategy Planning and Configuration Selection for Bayesian Optimization
abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) enables sample-efficient search for expensive black-box problems, but its performance depends strongly on surrogate-acquisition configurations whose suitability varies across problems and optimization states. We take a significant step toward LLM-driven strategic management of BO with STaSBO, a task-agnostic meta-controller that plans search behavior and jointly selects surrogate-acquisition configurations, while numerical BO retains responsibility for probabilistic modeling and candidate generation. STaSBO comprises two coordinated stages: strategy planning and strategy-guided configuration selection. A structured memory system connects prior plans, configuration selections, and candidate behaviors to optimization states, allowing the controller to revise its trajectory summary and behavioral plans during planning. To navigate the large joint configuration space, the selection stage shortlists configurations using surrogate fit evidence. Prospective BO-action diagnostics then expose the candidate behaviors, supporting final joint selection against the behavioral plans. Across 12 synthetic mathematical and 10 scientific and engineering application tasks, STaSBO achieves the best average rank against 11 baselines: 2.17 and 2.60, compared with 4.08 and 4.10 for the strongest baseline in each suite, respectively.
authors: Youngseok Yoon; Peng Li

title: Scalable Arrayed T‐cell CRISPR Screening in Autologous Tumor Co‐cultures to Prioritize Combination Partners for T‐cell Engagers
abstract: T-cell-engaging therapies (TCE) have shown clinical promise in hematologic malignancies, but the T-cell-intrinsic determinants of TCE-mediated cytotoxicity remain incompletely defined. This is in part because functional studies in patient-derived primary samples have been technically challenging. Here, we describe a flow cytometry-based arrayed CRISPR knockout screening platform to prioritize regulators of TCE-mediated cytotoxicity in suspension tumor cells using patient-derived, autologous chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) samples. The principal advantage of this system is the use of matched T cells and tumor cells from the same patient, retaining patient-matched effector-target pairings that are not captured in donor-mismatched or cell line-based assays. In this workflow, CD3+ T cells isolated from viably frozen CLL peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) are expanded and edited for 2 days using arrayed Cas9 ribonucleoprotein nucleofection. TCE-mediated cytotoxicity was assessed in a 72-hr, feeder-supported co-culture assay using patient-matched CLL tumor cells in the presence of CD20×CD3 TCE. In the current implementation, the workflow is organized into modules that accommodate up to 96 arrayed perturbations, with technical replicates evaluated under TCE and control conditions. Because perturbations remain physically indexed in an arrayed format, the workflow is amenable to parallelization and laboratory automation, providing a path toward substantially larger targeted screens. This platform therefore provides a scalable framework for mechanistic studies and combination-target discovery for TCE therapies. © 2026 The Author(s). title: Scalable Fabrication of Chemically Stabilized Gelatin Hydrogel Fibers by Thermal Drawing
abstract: Gelatin represents a promising hydrogel fiber matrix for drug delivery, tissue engineering, and neural interfaces due to its inherent biocompatibility, biodegradability, and mechanical adaptability. Yet, existing soft‐material fabrication methods typically constrain fiber length, aspect ratio, throughput, and structural complexity, thereby restricting the capabilities of these fibers. Here, we introduce a multimaterial thermal drawing platform capable of continuously producing gelatin hydrogel fibers with lengths reaching tens of meters. Instead of relying on conventional synthetic crosslinkers, we leverage the Maillard reaction—adapted from food engineering—to induce in situ crosslinking under the heat generated during drawing. Guided by comprehensive rheological analyses, a moderate incubation step ensures a stable viscous flow regime essential for uninterrupted fiber production. This approach enables control over swelling and mechanical properties of hydrogel formulations, which exhibit elastic moduli in the tens to hundreds of kilopascals range and ultimate strains exceeding 100%. The hydrogel fibers can incorporate and gradually release therapeutic agents and generate low‐molecular‐weight species following collagenase exposure in vitro. By relying exclusively on naturally derived or naturally occurring constituents, the method circumvents the biocompatibility concerns associated with synthetic crosslinkers. The scalability and versatility of this fabrication platform open new design opportunities for hydrogel fibers tailored to diverse biomedical applications.
authors: Chaoqun Dong; Bastien Schyrr; Stella Laperrousaz; Hritwick Banerjee; Andreas Leber; Fabien Sorin

title: Scaling Science: Toward a Chain Reaction of Discovery
abstract: Scientific discovery advances when evidence from different investigations is brought into contact. Yet paper-centric communication leaves experimental results fragmented, delayed, or unreported, creating a "scientific memory wall" between growing computational capabilities and the evidence accessible to AI systems. Breaking this wall requires a paradigm shift in AI for Science: moving from passively mining questions out of existing datasets to actively generating and recombining experimental data around unresolved scientific questions. In a network of intelligent laboratories, a failed or overlooked experiment in one domain could trigger a hypothesis in another, whose testing generates fresh evidence that stimulates further investigations. To enable these evidence-driven chain reactions, we propose Evolving Scientific Intelligence (ESI), an architectural blueprint that connects shared scientific memory with distributed experimental loops. ESI preserves experimental records -- including negative and anomalous results -- in computable representations, allowing models to recombine evidence across domains into testable hypotheses. Rather than following fixed screening pipelines, the system jointly selects candidates and evaluation methods according to scientific value, reliability, and cost, directing distributed laboratories to produce the exact evidence needed next. Their physical feedback revises both hypotheses and evaluators, while slower meta-control reassesses research objectives and decision criteria to guard against self-reinforcing errors and misguided optimization. We call for an Information Manhattan Project to build this infrastructure for scaling science through experimentally grounded chains of discovery.
authors: Yuheng Ding

title: Self-Attention-Based Deep-Learning Model Using Multimodal MRI to Predict Ki-67 Expression and Recurrence-Free Survival in Hepatocellular Carcinoma
abstract: Purpose: To assess multimodal gadolinium-enhanced MRI-based deep learning fusion schemes for preoperative Ki-67 expression estimation in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and clarify their correlation with recurrence-free survival (RFS). Patients and Methods: This retrospective study enrolled 297 patients with pathologically confirmed HCC. All patients underwent preoperative 3.0-T multimodal gadolinium-enhanced MRI, including T1- and T2-weighted, arterial, portal venous, delayed and hepatobiliary phases. Single-sequence models were developed using a 3D ResNet-50 network. Three fusion models were developed: Deep Learning Image Fusion model (DL-IF), Decision Fusion model (DL- DF ), and Self-Attention Feature Fusion model (DL-SAFF). Univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses identified independent clinical predictors, which were subsequently used to build the Deep Learning–Clinical Self-Attention Feature Fusion model (DLC-SAFF). Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) and Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analyses were applied to visualize model spatial attention and quantify feature contributions. Prognostic value was assessed using follow-up data. Results: Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) and hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) were identified as independent indicators linked to elevated Ki-67 expression in HCC. DL-SAFF reached a validation area under the curve (AUC) of 0.816, surpassing results from DL-IF (AUC: 0.735) and DL- DF (AUC: 0.792). The DLC-SAFF model further improved performance (AUC: 0.828, 95% CI: 0.74– 0.92). Decision curve analysis indicated higher net benefit for DLC-SAFF across thresholds of 0.11– 0.71. SHAP analysis demonstrated that hepatobiliary phase and delayed phase features were the dominant contributors to model prediction. The DLC-SAFF model identified high Ki-67 patients with a shorter median RFS (18.59 vs 47.73 months, p = 0.0011). Conclusion: The DLC-SAFF model enables noninvasive prediction of Ki-67 expression in HCC using multimodal MRI and shows potential for risk stratification, offering a promising tool to guide preoperative biological assessment and individualized treatment planning.
authors: Jiayi Li; Xiyu Wu; Jingyi Lin; Xinze Xiong; Hemin Chen; Hui Ma; Yifan Pan; Yueming Li

title: Self-Supervised In-Context Operator Learning for Optimal Mixing in Incompressible Flows
abstract: We develop a self-supervised operator-learning framework for optimal mixing in incompressible flows, aimed at overcoming the computational limitations of classical PDE-constrained optimal control. The objective is to design velocity fields that efficiently homogenize a passive scalar while minimizing kinetic energy, quantified through the $\dot H^{-1}(Ω)$ mix-norm. Classical methods solve a separate optimal control problem for each initial condition using iterative forward-adjoint procedures, leading to substantial computational costs and limited scalability. In contrast, we propose to learn the solution operator that maps initial scalar fields to optimal mixing controls directly. The proposed self-supervised method does not require access to supervised labels, thereby significantly reducing the data-generation burden of supervised operator-learning methods. Our framework integrates a Lagrangian reformulation of the transport equation with a transformer-based neural operator architecture. The transport dynamics are represented through characteristic ODEs, enabling particle-based Monte Carlo optimization, while the learned velocity field is parameterized in a divergence-free spectral basis enforcing incompressibility and no-penetration conditions exactly. Numerical experiments on parametric families of initial conditions in two and three spatial dimensions demonstrate robust generalization to unseen regimes and approximately exponential decay of the mix-norm. The learned controls also transfer consistently to independent Eulerian finite-volume simulations, validating the physical fidelity of the learned operator. To the best of our knowledge, this work provides the first self-supervised operator-learning framework for optimal mixing and among the first data-driven approaches for optimal mixing in fully three-dimensional incompressible flows.
authors: Weiwei Hu; Rongjie Lai; Ziqian Li

title: Semantic Representation for Agentic Self-Play in Automated Laboratories
abstract: Navigating complex, high-dimensional biological search spaces necessitates scalable physical and computational intelligence to explore beyond local optima through iterative self-play across ideation, experimentation, and automation. Translating experimental designs into reliable physical execution remains bottlenecked by static laboratory automation and unmodeled physical variability. To address this, we introduce VERified Infrastructure for Discovery Laboratories, or VERID, a foundational infrastructure designed to bridge the gap between the high-level reasoning of artificial intelligence (AI) agents and complex, error-prone physical realities of wet labs. VERID is a persistent, high-fidelity semantic digital twin of the laboratory workcell that provides four core services: queryable introspection for agentic reasoning, time-compressed simulation for protocol validation, comprehensive trace persistence for a complete scientific record, and a framework for safe execution. We present three case studies using aqueous dye and deionized water mixtures to validate the optical and fluidic foundations of VERID. These studies demonstrate how VERID enables pre-emptive detection of critical errors in experimental protocols, stateful mid-run error recovery and post-hoc identification of subtle physical failures. The simulation functions as a discrete accounting engine, allowing agents to safely and inexpensively explore experimental designs in silico and refine experimental strategies through iterative self-play. VERID also captures structured multimodal experimental data for downstream analysis, knowledge mining and agent training. We argue that this semantic layer is an essential prerequisite for deploying autonomous agents in the biochemical and biomedical sciences, ensuring data integrity, operational safety, and paving the way for tackling previously intractable grand challenges in biology.
authors: Yves Delley; John Coller; Zachary Cutts; Alexander Daryin; Mathias M. J. Bellaiche; Jun Woo Kim; Oscar Donosa; Srinidhi B. Seshadri; Tanner Clary; Sandy Klemm; Avinatan Hassidim; Yossi Matias; Pooja Rao; Petar Sirkovic; Annalisa Pawlosky

title: Silicon Photonics and Optically Controlled Microrobotics at the Limit English Introduction and Research Abstract This monograph asks whether silicon-photonic chips can create, observe, communicate, and close control around microscale agents with lower total burden than magnetic, wired, mechanical, microfluidic, or external-optical alternatives. It replaces impressive motion with a complete evidence chain from the commanded chip field to terminal task quality, thermal and photochemical exposure, recovery, and independent replay. Scientific position The candidate objective is O_ctrl = B_control P_track - L_couple - Delta T_abs - C_align. Optical control is valuable only when usable control bandwidth and tracking success remain meaningful after coupling loss, absorbed heat, alignment, compute, calibration, packaging, missed agents, and failed recovery are counted. Unsafe exposure, runaway motion, lost identity, irreversible material change, corrupted command ancestry, or missing evidence are hard vetoes. Research architecture The PDF contains thirty gold derivations, eighty-two chapters with five single-page sections each, and two hundred detailed one-page Research Gates. Every derivation links to chapter, experiment, and Gate corridors. Every chapter opens with its governing formula. Fixed quotas for Easter-Egg Equations and Phoenix Answer Embryos are not used. Five research layers Function and burden contract: Define terminal tasks control bandwidth eligible agents external infrastructure strong baselines and hard vetoes. Photonic field and sensing plane: Calibrate power phase polarization spatial fields pose information and coordinate ancestry. Mechanism-resolved actuation: Separate optical momentum electrokinetic thermal fluidic acoustic chemical adhesion and surface effects. Closed-loop multi-agent qualification: Join estimation latency constrained control identity occlusion collision recovery and independent task readout. Reliability portability and succession: Count exposure aging packaging foundry variation economics security transfer redesign safe stop and retirement. Minimum demonstrator A silicon-photonic test chip generates calibrated fields over an inert microfluidic workspace. Randomized agents carry independent visual or spectral references. The experiment compares integrated optical, external optical, magnetic, and wired control on identical path following, sensing, transport, and safe-stop tasks. Hidden phase, alignment, occlusion, latency, and absorption faults test the controller. Independent thermometry and post-mission surface assays challenge the claimed mechanism and safety. Central deliverable The Photonic Microrobot Control Plane binds circuit genealogy, source-to-agent power, phase and polarization commands, field maps, agent identity and material history, mechanism evidence, raw observations, state estimates, control actions, thermal and photochemical exposure, task outcomes, failures, recoveries, cost, and successor authority. Another team must be able to reproduce, refute, simplify, fork, repair, or retire the claim.

title: Silk Fibroin-Based Flexible Electronics: A Mesoscopic Pathway Toward Human–Machine Interconnection
abstract: Silk fibroin, a natural textile material spun by silkworms over millennia, is emerging as a transformative platform for integrating human intelligence with artificial intelligence. Its core innovation lies in the meso-functionalization strategy, which precisely programs protein refolding and hierarchical assembly. This strategy groundbreakingly resolves the long-standing performance paradox among biocompatibility, mechanical compliance, and high-fidelity signal acquisition in bioelectronic interfaces, thereby providing a solution that is difficult to achieve with other material systems. This transformation elevates the traditional fiber into a programmable electronic material, capable not only of conformal and seamless skin contact but also of constructing dynamic conductive networks, and even pioneering the fabrication of neuromorphic memristors that emulate synaptic plasticity. Furthermore, silk fibroin systems, reshaped through meso-engineering, are poised to catalyze a novel paradigm for deep integration between biological systems and artificial intelligence. When coupled with AI-driven intelligent analytics and closed-loop feedback control, the system can decode human physiological states in real time into machine-interpretable command signals, while simultaneously delivering adaptive regulatory responses back to the body. This bidirectional interface breaks through the conventional boundaries of human–machine interaction, with application prospects spanning frontier domains such as wearable health monitoring, invasive brain–computer interfaces, and cognitive augmentation technologies. Ultimately, while honoring its heritage as a natural textile, silk fibroin opens a pathway toward deep biointegration that is both sustainable and exceptionally biocompatible. Along this pathway, ancient material wisdom collides with future artificial intelligence to spark synergistic innovation, ultimately empowering human intelligence to reach new heights through human–machine co-evolution.

title: Sliding rail-enabled capillary flow control on μPADs for programmable fluid delivery.
abstract: Precise control of fluid transport is critical for paper-based microfluidic analytical devices (μPADs), especially in point-of-care testing (POCT) applications involving multistep reactions and timed reagent delivery. Here, we propose a simple yet versatile strategy to regulate capillary flow on μPADs by overlaying a film above a paper strip as a sliding rail for liquid samples. By systematically investigating the surface wettability of the sliding rail and its distance (0.1-2.4 mm) from the NC paper strip, we demonstrate that flow velocity on μPADs can be efficiently modulated through geometric control and surface modification. The influence of the width of sliding rails is also investigated. For hydrophilic sliding rails, increasing the width of film will accelerate flow velocity, whereas for hydrophobic sliding rails, narrower film widths yield higher flow velocity. Furthermore, we use a three-branch μPAD to show that both sequential and synchronized fluid arrival can be achieved by fine-tuning gap distance and paper strip width. In addition, a proof-of-concept delay valve implemented by introducing a continuous hydrophilic sliding rail above the segmented NC paper strips is successfully validated. A 1 mm interval located at various positions of μPADs will lead to different time delays. Beyond flow control, the sliding rail also enables localized droplet delivery and transport using a Janus hydrophobic-hydrophilic film with defined apertures. This platform supports sequential and parallel reagent delivery, allowing chemical reactions on-chip. The feasibility of this approach is validated through precipitation reactions, colorimetric reactions, and an enzymatic colorimetric glucose assay, which exhibits a strong correlation (R2 = 0.9980) between gray intensity and glucose concentration under controlled laboratory conditions, suggesting its potential for quantitative applications in high-concentration samples. Overall, this work introduces a highly adaptable and fabrication-friendly μPAD platform with rapid flow tuning and multifunctional reaction capability. The mechanical support and alignment structure (3D-printed frame and spacers) are reusable across experiments, while the paper strips and surface-modified films are single-use consumables to ensure reproducible flow performance. This offers a powerful solution for efficient POCT applications and paper-based microfluidic systems.
authors: Shi Y, Zhong J, Li H, Chen H, Zhang H, Chu LT, Lin M, Guo W.

title: Smart microneedle platforms: Integrating biosensing, artificial intelligence, and targeted drug delivery for better therapeutic outcome
abstract: Smart microneedle platforms are innovative biomedical systems that integrate biosensing, artificial intelligence (AI), and targeted drug delivery into a single minimally invasive technology. These micro-scale needle arrays can painlessly penetrate the outer skin layer to access interstitial fluid, enabling continuous and real-time monitoring of key biochemical markers such as glucose, metabolites, and disease-related biomarkers. Recent advancements in nanomaterials, microfabrication techniques, and biofunctional coatings have significantly improved their sensitivity, stability, and multifunctional performance. The incorporation of AI further enhances these systems by enabling advanced data analysis, pattern recognition, and predictive health monitoring, which supports early disease detection and personalized treatment strategies. In addition to diagnostics, smart microneedles are highly effective for controlled and targeted drug delivery, including insulin, vaccines, and anticancer therapeutics, thereby improving treatment efficiency while minimizing systemic side effects. Stimuli-responsive materials also allow these devices to release drugs in response to physiological changes such as pH, temperature, or glucose levels, enabling feedback-controlled therapy. Despite their significant potential, challenges such as large-scale manufacturing, long-term biocompatibility, regulatory approval, and data security must still be addressed. Overall, smart microneedle platforms represent a powerful convergence of biosensing, AI, and precision therapeutics, offering a promising pathway toward next-generation personalized, real-time, and minimally invasive healthcare systems.
authors: Akshay Kumar; Mohit Agrawal; Syed Mahmood; Kajal Ghosal; Mohit Kumar; Neeraj Choudhary; Dinesh Kumar; Ravindran Jaganathan

title: Smartphone-based flow-controlled μPAD for automated nitrite determination.
abstract: We report a smartphone-based microfluidic platform for automated nitrite determination using a paper colourimetric assay. The system combines a V-shaped microfluidic paper-based analytical device (μPAD), a wireless electronic module for capacitive flow monitoring and thermal actuation, and a custom Android application that coordinates the measurement sequence and processes the captured image. Fluid arrival at the sensing zone is identified from changes in capacitance, which trigger the heating step required to collapse a NIPAM-based hydrogel reservoir and release sulfanilic acid from the hydrogel reservoir. Images are acquired under ambient lighting conditions and analysed by an image-processing algorithm that includes circle detection, saturation-value (SV)-based pixel selection, and colour correction using in-frame black and white references. Calibration with standard nitrite solutions showed that the platform achieved a limit of detection (LOD) of 7.63 × 10<sup>-6</sup> M (0.35 mg L<sup>-1</sup> as NO<sub>2</sub><sup>-</sup>) after colour correction, improving by about 17% with respect to the uncorrected response. The platform also showed good repeatability (CV < 6% at 10<sup>-4</sup> M) and consistent behaviour when tested with two different smartphones and several lighting conditions. Analysis of tap water and marine samples gave results in agreement with the reference method at the 95% confidence level. The platform combines automated fluid handling, thermally triggered reagent release, and adaptive image-based quantification in a portable format for nitrite analysis outside the laboratory.
authors: Escobedo P, Torres-Molina MA, Ruiz-García I, Carvajal MA, Erenas MM, Martínez-Olmos A, Pérez de Vargas Sansalvador IM, Capitán-Vallvey LF, López-Ruiz N, Palma AJ.

title: SphereChip attaches spheroids and organoids to planar multielectrode arrays with microfluidics
abstract: Human cardiac and neuronal stem cell-derived spheroids and organoids are emerging models for drug discovery and drug safety studies. Their electrical properties are frequently investigated by means of multielectrode arrays (MEAs). However, it is difficult to establish adequate electrode contacts between planar MEAs and these round, 3D cell models. Contractions of cardiac 3D models and movement artefacts during the application of test solutions can also disrupt the recordings. As a solution, we present a microfluidics device (hereinafter referred to as SphereChip) that enables quick and stable attachment of free-floating spherical cell models such as cardiospheres, cardioids and neurospheres to conventional planar MEAs. The device reduces motion artifacts and enables complete solution exchange. It was successfully used with two different MEA designs for field potential measurements and simultaneous imaging using fluorescent probes on small cardio- and neurospheres (diameter 300 to 500 μm) and larger cardioids (800 to 900 μm). We observed concentration-dependent prolongation of action and field potentials of cardiospheres by the potassium channel (Kv1.11) inhibitors E4031 and dofetilide. In neurospheres, application of a potassium channel (Kv7.2/7.3) activator ML213 reduced spiking and bursting. We present these results as proof of concept for the microfluidics device as a means to enable organ-on-a-chip studies combining field potential measurements with simultaneous imaging on spherical cell models using planar MEAs. The method is applicable to different MEA formats and holds promise as a workable platform for drug testing and toxicity studies.
authors: Clara Hoebart; Manuel Lux; Stanislav Beyl; Bozhidar Baltov; Steffen Hering

title: Strategies for Enhancing the Performance of 3D ‐Printed Flexible Sensors and Their Applications
abstract: In recent years, 3D printing technology has emerged as a promising approach for the fabrication of flexible sensors, owing to its advantages of low cost, high design flexibility, and simplified construction processes. The rapid progress of flexible electronics, smart wearable technologies, and soft robotics has driven the demand for flexible sensors with enhanced sensitivity, improved stability, and higher levels of system integration. However, existing 3D‐printed flexible sensors still face certain challenges in terms of sensing performance, long‐term reliability, and versatility. Consequently, developing effective performance improvement strategies has become a key area of research in this field. This paper provides a review of recent research progress in 3D‐printed flexible sensors. The discussion focuses on performance enhancement strategies, including microstructure design, embedded integration, and emerging auxiliary enhancement strategies. In addition, this article provides a systematic summary of the specific applications of these sensors, including soft robotics, human health monitoring, and human motion detection. It also analyzes the challenges and trends facing current technology, providing valuable guidance for bridging the gap between research and practical application and helping to accelerate the design and manufacturing of high‐performance, intelligent flexible sensors.
authors: Junru Wu; Xiaotong Zhang; Bin Wang; Yuping Bu; Weixin Dai; Minghao Zhu; Tianyi Gao; Linjun Huang; Jianguo Tang

title: Surface‐Enhanced Raman Spectroscopy Aptasensors for Nucleic‐Acid Detection: Advances, Challenges, and Future Perspectives
abstract: Nucleic-acid biomarkers play pivotal roles in disease diagnosis, therapeutic monitoring, and precision medicine, creating an urgent demand for analytical platforms combining high sensitivity, molecular specificity, and rapid detection. Surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS) integrated with aptamers, short single-stranded DNA or RNA oligonucleotides, has attracted considerable attention by coupling programmable molecular recognition with ultrasensitive plasmon-enhanced Raman detection. This review evaluates recent advances in aptamer-based SERS biosensors for nucleic-acid analysis, systematically examining sensing mechanisms, plasmonic substrate engineering, aptamer immobilization, signal-transduction pathways, and amplification approaches, including catalytic hairpin assembly, hybridization chain reaction, rolling circle amplification, and CRISPR-assisted systems. Recent developments in microfluidics, artificial intelligence-assisted spectral analysis, portable Raman instrumentation, and point-of-care platforms are assessed while distinguishing true aptamer-mediated sensing from conventional hybridization-based DNA detection. Rational hotspot engineering, deterministic nanogap architectures, and advanced amplification strategies have enabled detection from femtomolar to attomolar levels with improved selectivity, multiplexing, and reproducibility. Challenges including substrate variability, quantitative standardization, aptamer stability, biosafety, and clinical translation are discussed. Future directions toward standardized, intelligent, clinically deployable SERS platforms for next-generation molecular diagnostics and precision healthcare are proposed.
authors: MK Alam; Kazi Mohammed Mehedi Hassan; Monika Tarafdar; Mohammad Imran Hossain; Mohammad Anwar Parvez; Mostafizur Rahaman; Mohammad A. Hasnat

title: Surrogate Verifiers Shape Decisions in Closed-Loop Experimental Design
abstract: High throughput, automated screening has revolutionized biological experimentation and prompted predictions of AI-enabled "self-driving" labs. Deployed autonomous lab systems typically use a learned surrogate to predict new experimental candidates and rank which conditions deserve expensive follow-up. Determining whether a computational surrogate verifier can substitute for an experimental assay's ground truth requires an understanding of model accuracy, uncertainty, and extrapolation. In this work, we present surrogate verifiers trained on N=7,688 Lacticaseibacillus growth curves exploring a 10-dimensional media component experimental design space. We train surrogate models across six distinct families including polynomial, Gaussian-process, tree-ensemble, neural, and Monod-kinetic forms to predict maximum optical density (OD600). Surrogates ranked by the most commonly reported accuracy metrics (held-out R^2; MAE; RMSE) disagree sharply on which experiments to test next and the best achievable yield. We evaluate models in a Bayesian optimization loop and find that the model used as the active learning oracle matters more than the acquisition function or batch size. We apply conformal calibration to build a model-agnostic assessment criterion of uncertainty and model coverage. We end by evaluating model accuracy and calibration under transfer to an unseen related bacterial strain, and confirm on a prospective validation plate that the transferred verifier's intervals fail in the direction and region our retrospective analysis predicts. This work explores the surrogate verifier within the loop as a previously underexplored axis of closed-loop design and points towards best calibration practices.
authors: Charlotte Merzbacher; Jannus Goecke; Jacob Cohen; Martin Patz

title: Surveying Experimentally-Validated Components for DNA-Based Molecular Communication
abstract: Molecular communication is a novel paradigm for the design of nanonetworks. It uses molecules as information carriers and enables communication between nanodevices. DNA-based molecular communication is a promising approach for medical applications, such as in-body networks for diagnostics and drug delivery. However, the transition from theoretical models to practical experiments is still in its early stages. This survey reviews experimentally validated DNA-tiles, nanocarriers, and biosensors relevant to implementing DNA-tile-based nanonetworks in vitro. We evaluate these components based on their stability, compatibility, cost-effectiveness, and overall suitability for wet-lab implementation. Based on this analysis, we identify promising component combinations and derive a blueprint for a minimal proof-of-concept experiment. The resulting framework provides researchers with both a structured overview of experimentally relevant design choices and a concrete starting point for implementing and validating DNA-based nanonetworks in the wet lab.
authors: A. WALDNER; Regine Wendt; Nils Stumpf; Sarah Scheer; Christian Hyttrek; Stefan Fischer; Florian-Lennert Adrian Lau

title: Survival of the fittest tool: choosing between open and closed artificial intelligence in pharmaceutical science
abstract: Three years ago, this journal published the editorial Technological Darwinism , urging pharmaceutical scientists to adapt to artificial intelligence (AI) rather than resist it. Since then, the question has shifted from whether to use AI to which AI to use, under what circumstances, and with what evidence. This review addresses that question by mapping current AI tools across the five canonical stages of drug development, from discovery to post-market pharmacovigilance. It is a narrative review, not a systematic one, and it treats openness as a spectrum rather than a binary. It compares two broad categories: open systems free, often open source or open weight, inspectable, and locally deployable and closed systems, which are proprietary, commercial, and delivered as a service. The central conclusion is pragmatic. For routine laboratory, educational, and research tasks, capable open tools now exist for almost every application, including manuscript drafting, literature review, reference management, statistical analysis, pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic modelling, calibration and standard-curve fitting, chemical structure drawing and SMILES handling, image and figure generation, and prediction of physicochemical, ADMET (absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity), formulation, and excipient compatibility properties. Free web services, however, may require confidential structures to be uploaded to a third party, so openness is distinguished here from private deployment, and independent head to head evidence against commercial tools is uneven. In contrast, integrated end to end drug discovery and validated regulatory workflows remain dominated by proprietary platforms. During the period covered by this review, the first generative AI-designed molecule targeting a generative AI-derived protein reported positive Phase IIa results and entered Phase III in July 2026; protein structure prediction was recognized with the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, shared by Hassabis, Jumper and Baker and became partly open; an autonomous frontier language model improved a longstanding medicinal chemistry reaction through thousands of wet-laboratory experiments; and regulatory agencies issued their first guidance on AI credibility.
