The review argues that the most enduring competency is not mastery of any single AI platform but the ability to select appropriate tools, critically validate their outputs, and document their credibility in proportion to the decisions they inform. Accordingly, open AI systems should be the default for routine, low-risk, and educational applications, whereas proprietary platforms currently retain advantages for integrated discovery and regulated development. Credibility is defined operationally, human oversight is treated as a condition of use, and the review states where comparative evidence is lacking.
authors: Neal M. Davies; Raimar Löebenberg

title: THE AUTONOMOUS CLINICAL LABORATORY: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE, ROBOTICS, DIGITAL PATHOLOGY, AND THE FUTURE OF PRECISION DIAGNOSTICS AND EMERGENCY CARE CRITICAL NARRATIVE REVIEW
abstract: The autonomous clinical laboratory is often described as the convergence of artificial intelligence, robotics, and digital diagnostics, yet technical integration does not by itself establish clinical safety or benefit. This critical narrative review examines how these technologies can be combined into a clinically accountable laboratory service. Initial targeted searches of publicly accessible scholarly records and official guidance were completed on September 5, 2026, with a focused emergency-care update on October 20, 2026, prioritizing recent original investigations, implementation studies, and authoritative standards. Evidence was interpreted according to study design, population, reference standard, external validation, workflow effects, and the distinction between predictive performance and patient benefit. Selected investigations demonstrate faster microbiological reporting, reduced immunohistochemistry use in a small prospective pathology study, and promising classification of acute leukemia and influenza from routine laboratory parameters. However, historical controls, selected populations, simulated errors, limited prospective evaluation, and heterogeneous endpoints constrain claims of generalizable autonomy. Foundation models expand opportunities for whole-slide analysis and multimodal integration, but benchmark scale should not be mistaken for validation of unattended clinical reporting. A practical framework is proposed in which specimen identity, analytical quality, model eligibility, authorized actions, human escalation, and post-deployment surveillance form a controlled diagnostic pathway. Particular attention is given to calibration, abstention, interoperability, cybersecurity, economic evaluation, and implementation in Saudi Arabia. The most defensible near-term objective is bounded, auditable automation with accountable specialist oversight. Progress should be judged by reliable clinical decisions and equitable service delivery, rather than the proportion of tasks performed without human involvement.
authors: Hanadi Fahad Lafi Alruwaili; Mashael Samah Al-Harbi; Gharam Faleh Altalib; Rahaf Hulayel Al-Mutairi; Bashayer Abdullah AlZuraiq; Mohammed Hamoud Alosaimi; Ramadan Juma’an Alzahrani; Shafi Fiyadh Kasb Alshammari; Mabkhoutah Mufaq Almari; Meshari Abdullah Wasl allah Alharbi

title: Temperature-Resolved Coding for Highly Multiplexed Digital PCR Using MeltArray.
abstract: Digital PCR enables sensitive absolute nucleic acid quantification, but its broader application remains constrained by limited multiplexing capacity. Here we report digital MeltArray (dMeltArray), a temperature-resolved endpoint decoding strategy that transfers MeltArray mediator-probe chemistry to a static droplet-imaging digital PCR system. In dMeltArray, target-specific mediator products generate fluorescent reporter duplexes with programmed melting temperatures. Post-amplification imaging at discrete temperatures progressively erases lower-T<sub>m</sub> signals while retaining higher-T<sub>m</sub> signals, allowing target-specific concentrations to be recovered from Poisson-corrected cumulative counts within each fluorescence channel. This strategy converts melting temperature into a programmable readout dimension requiring no real-time tracking or full-curve acquisition, addressing key trade-offs between multiplexing capacity, workflow simplicity, and cost. dMeltArray can be combined with 5'-hydrolysis probes, adding an orthogonal persistent-signal readout in the same optical framework. As proof-of-concept applications, we developed a 13-plex assay for post-transplantation viruses, an 11-plex assay for KRAS/BRAF hotspot mutations, and a 14-plex assay that integrates a 5'-hydrolysis probe into the 13-plex panel. These findings establish temperature-resolved endpoint decoding as a scalable route to multiplex digital PCR and support multidimensional target encoding by combining spectral, thermal and hydrolysis-probe readouts without requiring full melting-curve acquisition.
authors: Chen X, Yang Z, Wu X, Lai M, Shao W, Huang W, Liu Y, Xu Y, Li Q.

title: Temporary Uterine Artery Clamping During Laparoscopic Myomectomy and Perioperative Hemoglobin Decline: A Retrospective Single-Center Comparative Study
abstract: Background/Objectives: The aim of this study was to evaluate the adjusted association of temporary uterine artery clamping with the absolute and percentage decreases in hemoglobin during the perioperative period in women undergoing laparoscopic myomectomy, and to evaluate this association after multivariable adjustment for patient and leiomyoma characteristics. Methods: This single-center, retrospective, comparative observational study included 118 patients who underwent elective laparoscopic myomectomy for uterine leiomyomas between January 2021 and January 2026 (65 with temporary uterine artery clamping and 53 controls). The decision to perform clamping was based on the surgeon’s intraoperative assessment. The primary outcome measures were defined as absolute hemoglobin drop and percentage hemoglobin drop. The adjusted association of clamping with these measures was examined using multivariable linear regression models simultaneously adjusting for age, body mass index (BMI), and tumor burden (evaluated as dominant diameter in Model 1 and specimen weight in Model 2), with baseline hemoglobin additionally adjusted in absolute decline models. Results: No significant differences were found between the two groups in terms of baseline clinical and leiomyoma characteristics (age, BMI, number of pregnancies, preoperative hemoglobin level, leiomyoma size, and weight) (all p > 0.05). Although the difference in postoperative hemoglobin levels did not reach statistical significance (9.59 ± 1.70 vs. 10.01 ± 1.45 g/dL; p = 0.153), both the absolute hemoglobin decline (controls vs. clamping: 2.20 ± 0.90 vs. 1.83 ± 0.88 g/dL; p = 0.027) and the percentage hemoglobin decline (controls vs. clamping: 18.84 ± 7.77% vs. 15.24 ± 6.61%; p = 0.008) were significantly lower in the clamping group. Evaluated as a composite safety outcome across all 134 surgical patients (transfusion or conversion to laparotomy), procedural safety events occurred in 18.5% (12/65) of controls compared with 5.8% (4/69) of clamping cases, demonstrating a statistically significant reduction in composite major surgical morbidity in the clamping cohort (Fisher’s exact test p = 0.033; Relative Risk = 0.31, 95% CI: 0.11 to 0.92). In both the primary and sensitivity multivariable models, temporary uterine artery clamping demonstrated a significant adjusted association with lower values of approximately 0.38 g/dL in absolute hemoglobin decline (p = 0.015–0.016) and approximately 3.6 percentage points in percentage hemoglobin decline (p = 0.007–0.008). Furthermore, while the preoperative hemoglobin level was independently and positively associated with the absolute decrease in hemoglobin (p < 0.001 in both absolute decline models), age, BMI, leiomyoma size, and weight showed no independent association. Conclusions: Temporary uterine artery clamping demonstrated a significant multivariable adjusted association with a modestly attenuated perioperative hemoglobin decline during laparoscopic myomectomy. The finding that static postoperative hemoglobin levels alone did not differ significantly between groups underscores the importance of using dynamic hemoglobin parameters in the assessment of surgical blood loss. Although the retrospective design limits causal inferences, temporary uterine artery clamping appears to be a feasible surgical adjunct associated with reduced perioperative hemoglobin decline in experienced hands; however, prospective trials evaluating operative duration, clamping intervals, and long-term reproductive safety are warranted before broader clinical safety can be definitively established. Temporary uterine artery clamping demonstrated a significant multivariable adjusted association with a modest attenuation in perioperative hemoglobin decline (approximately 0.38 g/dL) during laparoscopic myomectomy, whereas static postoperative hemoglobin levels alone did not differ significantly between groups. Given the modest clinical magnitude of this difference, the lack of a significant difference in standalone transfusion rates, and the potential for residual confounding by indication in this retrospective cohort, temporary clamping should be considered a feasible adjunctive measure in experienced hands rather than a definitive routine intervention, and prospective randomized trials are warranted.
authors: Engin Korkmazer; Rulin Deniz; Alihan Tığlı; Oğuzhan Karakoç; Yasemin Ercan Değirmenci; Nazlı Şener; Güzide Ece Akıncı; Yasemin Albayram; Esra Söylemez; Kübra Dilşad Sönmez Özgür; Mehmet Ali Aydin; Yakup Baykuş

title: Test Automation in Wireless Hardware Engineering: A Comprehensive Review of Scripting Frameworks and Instrument Control Strategies
abstract: The accelerating complexity of wireless hardware systems, driven by the proliferation of multistandard radios, multi-band front-ends, and highly integrated system-on-chip platforms, has made manual RF test methodologies increasingly inadequate for the validation workloads of modern hardware engineering laboratories. Test automation, the systematic use of scripting frameworks and programmable instrument control interfaces to execute RF measurement sequences without manual intervention, has emerged as a foundational engineering discipline that determines the throughput, repeatability, and traceability of wireless hardware characterization workflows. This paper presents a comprehensive review of test automation architectures, scripting frameworks, and instrument control strategies applicable to wireless hardware engineering. The review examines the evolution of automation approaches from early GPIB-based sequential scripting to modern Python-based asynchronous measurement orchestration, covering standard communication protocols including SCPI, LXI, and VISA, scripting environments including Python, MATLAB, and LabVIEW, specialized RF test frameworks including Keysight PathWave and National Instruments TestStand, and emerging approaches based on cloud-connected measurement architectures and machine learning-assisted measurement optimization. The paper synthesizes design principles for constructing automation frameworks that maximize measurement throughput while maintaining calibration traceability, and identifies the key challenges of timing synchronization, instrument state management, error recovery, and data provenance that differentiate professionally engineered automation systems from ad hoc scripts. A structured taxonomy of automation approaches is presented according to test complexity, measurement speed requirement, and deployment context. The review concludes by identifying the most significant open challenges in wireless hardware test automation, including automated calibration verification, uncertainty-aware measurement pipelines, and the integration of AI-based anomaly detection into production test workflows.
authors: Robert Quainoo
venue: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ENGINEERING AND MODERN TECHNOLOGY

title: The Cyber-Physical Attack Surface of Legacy Scada Networks: A Systematic Review of Vulnerabilities, Threats, and Detection Gaps in Critical Infrastructure
abstract: Legacy Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) networks remain the operational backbone of the electric power, water treatment, and oil-and-gas sectors, yet they were engineered in an era that prioritized deterministic availability and physical safety over information security. The progressive convergence of information technology (IT) and operational technology (OT) has dissolved the air gaps that once isolated these systems, exposing an attack surface for which their aging protocol stacks were never designed. Field-level communication standards such as Modbus and DNP3 typically transmit control directives without encryption, authentication, or message integrity, allowing an adversary who reaches the network to forge, replay, or manipulate commands at will. The defining hazard of this domain is the cyber-physical attack, in which a purely digital intrusion is translated into tangible physical damage, service disruption, or threats to human life. Against this class of threat, conventional signature- and rule-based intrusion detection is structurally inadequate, missing novel and stealthy manipulations while generating unsustainable false-alarm volumes. This review systematically synthesizes the vulnerability landscape, a taxonomy of cyber-physical threats, landmark incidents including Stuxnet, the 2015 Ukrainian grid attack, TRITON, and Maroochy, the protocol-level weaknesses of legacy assets, and the resulting detection gap. Drawing together the industrial-control and applied cybersecurity literature, it argues that intelligent behavioural anomaly detection offers the most credible path toward resilient protection of critical infrastructure
authors: Chukwunenye Amadi
venue: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF COMPUTER SCIENCE AND MATHEMATICAL THEORY E-ISSN

title: The Foundations of Immersive Reality in Life Sciences
abstract: Spatial computing establishes an operational bridge between physical biopharmaceutical environments and synthetic digital spaces, structured systematically along the Milgram-Kishino Reality-Virtuality Continuum. The integration of Augmented Reality, Virtual Reality, and Mixed Reality into pharmaceutical workflows addresses long-standing visualization constraints, transitioning molecular modeling and shop-floor execution from planar representations into interactive three-dimensional spaces. Optical See-Through waveguides and Video See-Through display architectures dictate the optical delivery of synthetic visual data, balancing ambient physical awareness against absolute digital occlusion. Kinesthetic force-feedback exoskeletons and cutaneous tactile actuators introduce mechanical resistance into virtual manipulation, rendering steric clashes and instrument calibrations with physical fidelity. The spatial registration underpinning these environments relies on Visual-Inertial Odometry and Simultaneous Localization and Mapping algorithms that process multi-camera and depth-sensor feeds to ground digital coordinates onto physical machinery without drift. At the software layer, specialized development kits including Unity 3D, Vuforia, and ARKit convert macromolecular structural databases and industrial telemetry into responsive meshes, supporting markerless model tracking across cleanroom perimeters. Moving beyond localized workstations, browser-based WebAR frameworks leveraging WebGL and WebGPU, alongside cloud-rendered remote pixel streaming, democratize access across commodity mobile devices while preserving intellectual property containment. Looking forward, the deployment of Multi-Access Edge Computing and emergent sub-terahertz 6G telecommunication networks compresses motion-to-photon latency beneath critical human vestibular thresholds. This convergence of spatial infrastructure, localized edge compute, and ambient sensing establishes a unified, low-latency foundation for autonomous laboratories and connected Pharma 4.0 operations.
authors: Mrudula Raj Vanga

title: The Microglial Lipid-Immune Axis in Brain Aging: Adaptive Lipid Handling and Metabolic Dysfunction in Lipid-Droplet-Accumulating Microglia.
abstract: Microglia in the aging brain process lipids released during membrane and myelin turnover. Lipid droplets can buffer this demand, but lipid retention also accompanies defective phagocytosis and inflammatory responses. This review critically compares the substrates, perturbations, and functional endpoints underlying these observations. We examine cholesterol esterification and export, fatty-acid activation and triacylglycerol synthesis, and lipid mobilization through lipolysis and lipophagy in relation to TREM2-TYROBP/DAP12-SYK signaling, APOE genotype, and local substrate supply. Physiological-aging studies are distinguished from demyelination, Alzheimer's disease, and Parkinson's disease models. Quantitative comparisons show why inhibiting storage can improve selected amyloid-associated phenotypes while impaired storage can compromise myelin repair. We use the established distinction between lipid pools and metabolic flux to assess what each experiment demonstrates: altered droplet abundance, a specific processing defect, or recovery of a cellular task. We propose a reporting framework covering droplet burden, transcriptional state, metabolic function, and cellular performance, with missing measurements retained explicitly and no claim of validated diagnostic thresholds. Intervention evidence is assessed by the reaction perturbed, dose and duration, target validation, delivery route, and measured benefit. The resulting synthesis identifies supported mechanisms and unresolved causal steps, providing a practical basis for selecting and evaluating interventions without treating droplet reduction as a universal therapeutic endpoint.
authors: Xintong Wang; Anran Lv; Yu Tian; Dongna Li; Xueji Fan; Yuqian Wang; Pengwei Zhuang; Yanjun Zhang

title: The Sperm Rheotaxis Index for Assessing Sperm Function and Male Infertility Using a Microfluidic Platform
abstract: Background: Male infertility accounts for nearly half of infertility cases worldwide. Conventional semen analysis provides limited information about sperm function. Sperm rheotaxis, the ability of sperm to swim against fluid flow, is a distinctive form of sperm motility that contributes to natural fertilization. Objective: To establish the Sperm Rheotaxis Index (SRI) using a microfluidic platform and evaluate its potential as a functional biomarker for assessing sperm function and male infertility. Methods: A bioinspired microfluidic platform was developed to mimic the mucosal folds of the female reproductive tract and generate physiologically relevant shear stress, enabling real-time visualization and quantitative assessment of sperm rheotaxis. SRI was calculated using image analysis to quantify directional sperm motility under controlled flow conditions. In a cohort of 86 participants, associations between SRI, conventional motility parameters, and the DNA fragmentation index were evaluated. Receiver operating characteristic analysis was used to assess the discriminatory performance of SRI relative to conventional motility parameters, including among men with normal sperm motility. Results: SRI showed strong positive correlations with several sperm motility parameters and a negative correlation with the DNA fragmentation index. Lower SRI values were observed in individuals with male infertility-related conditions. SRI demonstrated better discriminatory performance than conventional motility parameters, with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.77. Among men with normal sperm motility, SRI also distinguished fertile from subfertile individuals (AUC = 0.70). These findings support the potential of SRI as a functional biomarker that complements conventional semen analysis in the assessment of male fertility.
authors: Boyang Zhang; Hui Zhang; Guanyu Ren; Chenghua Yang; Jian Xu; Xun Wang; Weihao Sun; Shuguang Piao; Wenjie Chen; Xinyu Yang; Jiaxin Liu; Lei Wang; Zhiyong Liu

title: The Unbearable Lightness of Prompting: A Critical Reflection on the Environmental Impact of genAI use in Design Education
abstract: Design educators are finding ways to support students in skillfully using GenAI tools in their practices while encouraging the critical scrutiny of the ethical and social issues around these technologies. However, the issue of environmental sustainability remains unaddressed. There is a lack of resources to grasp the environmental costs of genAI in education, but also, and foremost, a lack of shared practices for engaging with the issue. This article critically reflects on the energy costs of using genAI in design education, using a workshop held in 2023 with 49 students as a springboard for reflection. Through this reflection, we develop a set of five alternative stances: acceptance, shift, moderation, friction, and refusal. Each of these, and the related actions, can support a conscious use of genAI in design education. The work contributes to the field of design and HCI by bringing together ways for educators to reflect on their practices, informing the future development of educational programs around genAI.
authors: Maria Luce Lupetti; Elena Cavallin; Dave Murray-Rust
venue: ACM Journal on Computing and Sustainable Societies

title: The Verification Wall in Microbial Metabolomics
abstract: Computational methods now propose structures for gut microbial metabolites faster than any laboratory can confirm them. We argue that verification, not generation, is the binding constraint, and that better models will not relieve it. Confirming a structure to the field's own standard means having the molecule in hand. Automation can lower what that costs per compound, but the cost stays proportional to the number of structures and never amortizes across them. Two substitutes are on offer and neither removes that requirement. In-silico spectral prediction ranks candidates instead of confirming one, and the strongest current model puts the right structure first 33.5% of the time on a scaffold-split benchmark. Any assignment resting on spectral similarity is, by the field's own definition, made without a reference standard. Microcrystal diffraction does return a structure, but it needs the compound to crystallize out of a trace mixture, which is a different problem rather than an easier one. We sorted 10,645 computationally inferred metabolite structures by what verifying each would take. Between 5% and 37% have no verification route identified under our analysis. That spread reflects where the thresholds are set rather than a measured count of unverifiable compounds, and the inaccessible ones cluster among the most speculative entries. Those figures understate the problem, because the gut makes far more compounds than any database records. HMDB holds only what someone has already thought worth cataloguing, and structure generators are bounded by nothing at all. The claim is easy to disprove. Show a route that confirms structures as fast as they are proposed. Until someone does, two problems stay unsolved. Nobody knows how to spend a verification budget that will always be too small, or what a biologist may conclude from a structure that was never confirmed.
authors: Takahiko Koyama

title: The intelligence loop and value creation in the age of AI agents
abstract: Research Summary Artificial intelligence (AI) is moving from generating outputs to executing work. An agent that executes work autonomously produces something generative AI does not: operational experience that can raise its future intelligence. Prior research on AI emphasizes value creation through demand‐side feedback, notably data network effects, in which user data improve prediction and reinforce adoption. We develop the supply‐side counterpart, the intelligence loop: delegated usage generates operational experience, agentic capability converts it into future intelligence, and the resulting value maintains or expands usage. The loop cannot operate until autonomous execution is viable, a threshold we call minimum viable intelligence (MVI). Crossing MVI does not guarantee rising intelligence. Comparable deployments of AI agents can diverge as their loops decay, sustain, or accelerate. Three implications follow. Competitive advantage may depend more on the loop than on installed base. An above‐MVI agent supplies scarce expert skill as a non‐rival, replicable resource, so productive capacity can grow faster than expert headcount, with the one‐person company as a limiting case. And a venture with adequate demand, capital, and a capable team can still fail because its loop never functions or later deteriorates. Managerial Summary Artificial intelligence (AI) agents can execute work, and the experience generated through execution can raise their future intelligence, a feedback process we call the intelligence loop. An agent crosses a workflow's minimum viable intelligence (MVI) when it executes reliably without step‐by‐step direction, autonomous execution creates at least as much net value as the best alternative after oversight and correction costs, and governance arrangements keep residual risk acceptable and accountability clear. Investment belongs where one of these conditions keeps a valuable workflow below MVI. Deployment can begin with narrow, feedback‐rich workflows near MVI that ideally lead to harder workflows, since base model upgrades can match gains on simple work. Even above MVI, the loop is not automatic: it stalls when feedback is not timely and diagnostic, experience yields little intelligence gain, gains add little user value, or value does not maintain or expand usage. Human involvement shifts from executing work to specifying goals, evaluating outputs, governing execution, and supplying tacit knowledge. When the loop sustains or accelerates, productive capacity can grow faster than expert headcount. With capable base models widely available, advantage depends less on access to AI than on building and governing the loop, controlling proprietary operational experience, and converting it into intelligence more effectively than rivals. A venture with adequate demand, capital, and a capable team can fail because its loop never functions or later deteriorates. Cutting evaluation or oversight to scale faster may increase output in the short run but weaken the loop even while revenue remains healthy.
authors: Yong Li; Ming Zeng; Alexis Li

title: The microglial lineage: from molecular states to context-dependent functions
abstract: Microglial states are now being cataloged far faster than their associated cellular functions can be tested, widening the gap between molecular description and causal understanding of tissue impact. The gap becomes especially apparent as microglial biology moves beyond the rodent central nervous system (CNS). Peripheral nervous system (PNS) microglia, identified in human and other large-vertebrate ganglia, share major molecular features with CNS microglia and contribute to neuronal growth, yet their adult maintenance and responses to injury and disease remain unresolved. TREM2 exposes a second limit of state-based interpretation. The receptor supports recurring cellular processes, including myeloid fitness, lesion-associated accumulation and cargo handling, but their tissue consequences vary with the substrate, model and disease stage. This review separates population identity, molecular state, cellular function and tissue outcome, and outlines an experimental path that combines state-informed genetic screens, direct functional assays, multicellular human models and temporally controlled in vivo validation to connect molecular discovery with context-dependent function.
authors: Cuihua Li; Zhisheng Wu; Xianyuan Xiang; Hanjie Li

title: The role of artificial intelligence in urological malignancies: an overview of systematic reviews
abstract: OBJECTIVES: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has the potential to transform clinical medicine by enhancing diagnostic precision, prognostic accuracy, and personalized decision making. In urological oncology, AI technologies are increasingly integrated across diagnostic, prognostic, and therapeutic pathways. This overview of systematic reviews aims to synthesise the current evidence on the performance and clinical utility of AI applications in urological malignancies. METHODS: A systematic search was conducted of major bibliographic databases from 1974 to October 2024 to identify systematic reviews (SRs) evaluating AI-based models in urological cancers. We followed the Cochrane methodology of Overviews of Reviews. Outcomes of interest included diagnostic accuracy metrics (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUC-ROC], sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy) and predictive performance for treatment-relatedoutcomes. RESULTS: A total of 67 SRs encompassing 1139 primary studies were included. RoB was assessed as low in 21 reviews, high in 41, and unclear in 5. Forty-five SRs evaluated AI in prostate cancer (PCa). AI models demonstrated high accuracy (88-93%) in distinguishing benign from malignant lesions, and outperformed human interpretation alone in predicting clinically significant PCa (AUC: 0.933 vs. AUC: 0.82-0.87). Performance in Gleason score classification was also very strong (AUC: 0.72-0.99, Accuracy: 70.8-93.0%). Sixteen SRs assessed AI in Renal carcinoma (RCa), reporting accurate subtype classification and tumor grade prediction, with some models exceeding 90% accuracy. Sixteen SRs focused on Bladder Cancer (BCa), showing improved detection of muscle-invasive disease and recurrence risk prediction compared with the conventional approach. Key limitations included heterogeneity in validation strategies, overlap of primary studies across reviews, and potential oversampling due to synthetic or augmented data. CONCLUSIONS: AI-based models consistently demonstrate improved diagnostic and predictive performance across urological malignancies and hold promise for enhancing clinical decision-making and patient outcomes. At present, AI tools should be regarded as decision-support systems that complement, rather than replace, clinical expertise. Future research should emphasize prospective validation, standardized outcome definitions, and evaluation of real-world clinical impact. Robust and harmonized evaluation frameworks are also essential to address challenges related to data quality, privacy, generalizability, and ongoing regulatory and legal uncertainty, thereby enabling safe and equitable integration of AI into routine urological cancer care.
authors: Vasileios I. Sakalis; Eftichia Chatzigriva; Karl H. Pang; Bhavan Prasad Rai; Isaak Filippidis; Lisa Moris; Maria Chalkidou; Yuhong Yuan; Michael Bussmann; Dimitrios Papanikolaou; James N’Dow; Muhammad Imran Omar

title: Theranostic Imaging Agents: Integrating Molecular Diagnostics, Precision Therapeutics, and Artificial Intelligence
abstract: Theranostic imaging agents combine molecular diagnosis, targeted therapy and monitoring of treatment response into a single paradigm of precision medicine. This review summarizes the current development and translational landscape of theranostic imaging agents, covering molecular targets, imaging platforms, principles of agent design, nanotheranostics, radiotheranostics, and disease-specific applications. Particular emphasis is given to clinically validated and emerging targeting strategies using prostate-specific membrane antigen, somatostatin receptors, fibroblast activation protein, C-X-C Chemokine Receptor 4 (CXCR4), Human Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor 2 (HER2) and other disease-associated biomarkers. Moreover, the review addresses Positron Emission Tomography (PET), Single-Photon Emission Computed Tomography (SPECT), Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), optical, photoacoustic, Raman and multimodal imaging approaches, therapeutic payloads, stimulus-responsive systems, and pharmacokinetic optimization. Moreover, emerging applications of artificial intelligence, radiomics, radiogenomics, spatial and single-cell multiomics, liquid biopsy, digital pathology, personalized dosimetry, and digital twins are evaluated for their potential to improve patient stratification, treatment selection, response assessment and adaptive therapy. Despite tremendous progress, clinical translation is hampered by target heterogeneity, off-target accumulation, radionuclide availability, manufacturing complexity, dosimetric uncertainty, regulatory requirements, limited clinical validation, data interoperability, cost and unequal access. This review, overall, emphasizes the convergence of molecular imaging, targeted therapeutics, nanotechnology, and artificial intelligence in the development of next-generation theranostic platforms, and outlines critical priorities for their clinical translation.
authors: Shrestha Sharma; Syed Arman Rabbani; Mohamed El-Tanani; Mohamed Anas Patni; Rakesh Kumar; Manita Saini

title: Thermomechanical Noise Dilution by Low‐Q Cavity for Nanoparticles Detection
abstract: Phonon laser sensors offer powerful label‐free detection, yet their sensitivity remains bounded by noise for which robust suppression strategies are still lacking. Here we introduce a technique for diluting thermomechanical noise that counter‐intuitively selects lower‐Q optical modes to suppress thermal fluctuations of phonon‐laser frequency, followed by active feedback locking for frequency stabilization. The combined approach enables real‐time detection of single 10 nm‐radius polystyrene particles based on a microbubble cavity with a 38 MHz phonon mode, estimating a mass limit of . We further apply the platform to study iron–oxide uptake and reaction dynamics in cells.
authors: Gui‐Wen Zheng; Rui Niu; Yi‐Wen Huang; Tian Tian; Yu‐Xuan Chen; Yu Wang; Hao Tian; Fang‐Wen Sun; Xi‐Feng Ren; Guo G; Zhen Shen; Chun‐Hua Dong

title: Toward Self-Improving MEMS Research Agents through Experience-Informed Procedure Refinement
abstract: Microelectromechanical systems (MEMS) research requires translating device concepts into geometries with physically meaningful behavior under specified structural constraints. Although research agents increasingly automate scientific workflows, successful numerical execution alone does not establish operating-mode identity and dynamic behavior, identify loss mechanisms, or verify geometric compliance. Here we introduce the MEMS Research Agent Framework, which brings agent-based research and experience-informed procedure refinement into an expert-guided MEMS workflow. Agents execute investigations using reusable instructions and scripts, while experts define objectives, assess physical interpretations, and review methodological changes. In a researcher-guided study of a silicon double-ended tuning-fork resonator, the proposed framework carries a literature-derived thermoelastic-dissipation hypothesis through geometry construction, coupled-field simulation, and operating-mode identification. The selected segmented-slot design achieves a modeled thermoelastic quality factor approximately 5.2 times the baseline at a resonant frequency 20% lower. The slotting mechanism is consistent with a published experimental study reporting a 5.9-fold increase in measured quality factor in a different geometry. Development histories trace a procedural route toward self-improvement: recorded failures inform expert-reviewed changes to research instructions and diagnostic checks reused in subsequent runs. A registered comparison across 25 runs evaluates research outcomes and evidence completeness under five frozen configurations. The final author assessment gives 1/5 successful runs without the proposed framework and 5/5 with it; the initial model-judge assessment gives 1/5 and 2/5, respectively, reflecting differences in evidence acceptance. These studies demonstrate the feasibility of delegating parts of MEMS inverse-design iterations to agents, laying a foundation for self-improving research automation in device design and discovery.
authors: Ruiqi Guo; Xinrong Ouyang; Yuan Wang; Zishen Dai; Pan Zhang; Pui‐In Mak; Rui Paulo Martins; Jiawei Xu

title: Toward a lab-in-the-loop AI platform for RNA therapeutics
abstract: RNA therapeutics, spanning messenger RNA vaccines, small interfering RNAs, antisense oligonucleotides, and aptamers, are advancing rapidly, yet the design space that governs whether an RNA drug succeeds remains difficult to navigate. Its principal determinants, namely sequence, chemical modification, secondary structure, delivery vehicle, and tissue tropism, are strongly coupled, and together they constitute a combinatorial space far too large for human heuristics or isolated experiments to explore effectively. Here, we envisage a platform that brings two complementary advances into concert. First, RNA and molecular foundation models can compress this design space into a learnable representation that generalizes across RNA molecules and the carriers that deliver them. Second, a lab-in-the-loop architecture narrows the gap between prediction and biological function by coupling model-generated proposals to automated wet-laboratory experiments, allowing the model to be continually recalibrated against domain-specific feedback. Calibrated uncertainty connects these components: it enables the loop to prioritize candidates whose measurement is expected to be most informative. A platform built on these principles could support joint optimization of sequence and modification, co-design of payload and delivery vehicle, off-target prediction and in silico candidate ranking, and could ultimately bring the rational design of personalized therapies within reach.
authors: Gen Li; Bowen Li

title: Toward full-cycle automation of closed-loop molecular discovery – a case study on JAK targets
abstract: Combining AI and self-driving laboratories unlocks closed-loop molecular discovery by automation across all stages of the Design-Make-Test-Analyze (DMTA) cycle.
authors: Jannis Born; Carlo Baldassari; Doriela Grabocka; Antonio Cardinale; Oliver Tobias Schilter; Alessandro Castrogiovanni; Artem Leonov; Filip Skogh; Jeeven Singh; Yaoyao Xiong; John Evans; Thomas Fleming; Teodoro Laino; Matteo Manica

title: Towards Intelligent Membrane Systems: A Critical Analysis of Digital Twin–ML Integration for Real–Time Process Optimization, Fouling Management, and Autonomous Design
abstract: Membrane separation is central to potable water production, wastewater reclamation, desalination, gas separation, and decarbonization, yet its economics remain constrained by fouling and by a gap between process data and timely operating decisions. Digital twins (DTs) offer live, bidirectionally coupled virtual representations of physical assets, while machine learning (ML) extracts predictive and prescriptive insights from operational data. Together, they are promising computational approaches for membrane systems. However, their applications have largely evolved independently across fouling prediction, DT development, and ML-based materials discovery. This review argues that these are converging strands of a single trajectory toward self-sensing, self-predicting, and eventually self-designing membrane systems, and that treating them separately obscures key interdependencies. The contributions are threefold. First, applying the digital model/digital shadow/digital twin taxonomy, it shows that most published membrane DTs are digital shadows (DSs). Second, it proposes a five-level autonomy framework, inspired by vehicle automation taxonomies, providing a unified scale for comparing applications ranging from LSTM-based fouling forecasting and reinforcement learning dosing control to autonomous materials laboratories. Third, it integrates autonomous materials design, including self-driving laboratories, inverse design, generative models, and Bayesian search, into the upper levels of this ladder. Evidence is synthesized across reverse osmosis, nanofiltration, ultrafiltration, microfiltration, membrane bioreactors, membrane distillation, and gas separation membranes, with emphasis on critically assessing model performance and generalizability. The study concludes with a roadmap for overcoming data limitations, poor interpretability, interoperability gaps, cybersecurity risks, techno-economic barriers, and regulatory trust deficits that block autonomous membrane systems.
authors: Olawumi O. Sadare; Samuel P. Alonge; A. O. Akinyemi; Abass A. Adesina; Shukrah Adesola-Olabiyi; Lanrewaju Ibrahim Fajimi

title: TransBiolab: A Real-World Multi-View Dataset of Cluttered Transparent Biomedical Objects
abstract: Autonomous biomedical laboratories increasingly rely on visual perception to recognize, localize, and manipulate transparent plasticware, yet high-quality real-world datasets for this setting remain limited. The scarcity of domain-relevant data is particularly restrictive in cluttered multi-object scenes, where mutual occlusion and view-dependent appearance changes remain challenging even for contemporary visual foundation models. Existing transparent-object datasets have advanced segmentation, depth, and pose estimation, but they usually do not evaluate the combined setting of multi-object clutter, occlusion, and calibrated multi-view capture that characterizes real laboratory manipulation scenes. To address this gap, we present TransBiolab, a real-world RGB-D dataset of cluttered transparent biomedical objects captured as calibrated multi-view sequences. TransBiolab contains 161,315 frames from 98 scenes and 1.03M instance annotations over 15 laboratory object types, including 6D poses, full and visible masks, depth, and per-frame camera calibration. The dataset is organized along three axes that reflect operational difficulty: object category, the total number of objects in a frame, and camera viewpoint. We further define dataset-centric benchmarks for segmentation, depth estimation and completion, and 6D pose estimation, and report a system-level robot manipulation evaluation enabled by the released annotations and calibrations. By focusing on repeated transparent instances, clutter, and multi-view laboratory capture, TransBiolab provides a resource for segmentation, depth estimation, 6D pose estimation, and multi-view reasoning in autonomous laboratory manipulation. Project page: https://dualtransparency.github.io/TransBiolab/.
authors: Ke Ma; Yifei Wang; Meng Wang; Tian Xia
venue: ACM International Conference on Multimedia (ACM MM)

title: Transforming Biomedicine for Future Health: Roles, Technological Convergence, Translational Prospects, and Governance Challenges
abstract: Biomedical science is undergoing rapid transformation through the convergence of cell and molecular biology, genomics and multi-omics, immunology, gene editing, organoids, mRNA technology, bioinformatics, and artificial intelligence. This article aims to analyze the strategic role of biomedical science in modern health, review the prospects for biomedical technology development in future healthcare services, and identify challenges in translation, ethics, governance, infrastructure, and access equity. The study uses a qualitative literature review approach with a narrative-integrative synthesis of reputable journal articles mainly published from 2020 to 2026. The results show that biomedical science is increasingly shifting healthcare from a reactive and one-size-fits-all approach toward earlier diagnosis, risk stratification, precision therapy, accelerated drug development, continuous monitoring, and public health preparedness. The greatest value comes from the convergence between technologies, such as integrating multi-omics data with AI, validating biomarkers through advanced biological models, and translating genomic findings into gene and cell therapies. However, these benefits are limited by infrastructure gaps, bias and representation in data, technology costs, the need for clinical validation, privacy protection, and uneven access. In the context of Indonesia, strengthening genomic capacity, laboratories, biomedical data, multidisciplinary human resources, and translational governance is a priority. The article concludes that the future of biomedicine depends on the ability to connect basic discoveries, technology platforms, clinical evaluation, and health system implementation in a safe, effective, inclusive, and sustainable way
authors: Loso Judijanto
venue: International Journal of Natural and Health Sciences

title: Transforming pharmaceutical education and research through artificial intelligence
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has now become an important tool in the pharmaceutical industry and it is connected with many foundational as well as applied areas. In this review, we first discuss the basic concepts of AI, which includes Machine Learning (ML), Deep Learning, Natural Learning Processing, and Reinforcement learning, and we try to explain in simpler and more Understandable terms how these technologies actually work and operate. The review also looks at some of the major innovations that happened in the past and shows hoe AI has helped in accelerating breakthroughs in drug discovery and development, while also changing many of the traditional methods which were used earlier. One important part of this review is about the role of AI in pharmaceutical education. It discusses different tools and platforms which can help in improving learning, including virtual simulation environments and adaptive systems that can personalize the training according to the needs od students and professionals. These technologies can help in better knowledge retention and also support skill development, especially when the pharmaceutical curriculum includes complex concepts and practical areas. The review also includes different AI tools that are being used for research, such as software related to molecular modeling, predictive analytics, Virtual screening and lead optimization. These tools can improve the R&D processes by making the work faster, reducing the time required in different stages, and improving the accuracy in areas such as toxicity prediction and data analysis. In this way, what we put forth in the present study is to combine these different aspects and shows the potential of AI in supporting innovation, ethical education, and more efficient research. The study also provides practical suggestions for pharmaceutical educators, researchers, and industry leaders so that they can adopt AI-driven strategies in their respective areas, while also considering challenges related to integration and governance. Overall, readers can understand how AI-based tools and approaches can be used to support pharmaceutical education and also help in advancing drug discovery and research.
authors: Neha Yadav; Arpita Kasliwal
venue: International Journal of Pharmacy and Pharmaceutical Science

title: Ultrasound and surface acoustic wave powered transdermal drug delivery: Mechanisms, technological advances, and future perspectives
abstract: Transdermal drug delivery (TDD) offers a unique non-invasive route for therapeutic administration, but its widespread application is constrained by the barrier function of the stratum corneum (SC) of the skin layer. Ultrasound and surface acoustic wave (SAW) technologies have emerged as promising physical approaches for enhancing skin permeability and facilitating transdermal transport of therapeutic agents. Acoustic stimulation generates a range of biophysical effects, including acoustic radiation, cavitation, acoustic streaming, and localised thermal modulation, which collectively perturb the structural integrity of the SC layer and effectively promote molecular transport across the skin. This paper reviews fundamental ultrasound and acoustic TDD mechanisms and recent advances in biomedical acoustics, microfabrication, materials engineering technologies, and diverse acoustic-mediated delivery platforms, which include focused ultrasound systems, microbubble-assisted sonoporation, ultrasound-responsive nanocarriers, microneedle (MN)–acoustic hybrid systems, and SAW enhancing technologies. Despite significant progress, several challenges are identified, including the precise control of acoustic bioeffects, efficient delivery of macromolecules or therapeutic biomolecules, and establishment of standardised treatment parameters and safety guidelines. Future innovations are highlighted in the fields of integration of multimodal delivery strategies, wearable acoustic devices, and intelligent feedback-controlled systems, which can improve the efficacy, safety, and clinical translatability of ultrasound- and SAW-mediated TDD.
authors: Jikai Zhang; Xiaoyan Zhang; Zhushan Han; Zenan Wang; Zhishan Yuan; Ran Tao; Chen Fu; Jingting Luo; Xin Yang; Yongqing Fu

title: Ultrasound as a Multifunctional Physical Platform for Whole‐Grape Valorization: From Field Management to Green Extraction, Quality Modulation, and Intelligent Scale‐Up
abstract: The grape and wine industry faces prolonged barrel aging, microbial spoilage, protein haze, chemical additives, and inefficient by-product valorization. These challenges motivate nonthermal technologies that reduce chemical inputs. Ultrasound operates in two mechanistically distinct regimes: sensing, based on acoustic propagation, reflection, and echo detection, and processing, driven mainly by acoustic cavitation and its physical and chemical effects, including microjets, shock waves, localized hotspots, and reactive radicals. These complementary modes provide a versatile physical platform. This review covers ultrasound across the grape-wine continuum: acoustic imaging for precision viticulture; postharvest preservation with green activated water; green extraction enhanced by natural deep eutectic solvents; grape protein modification for ingredient assembly; modulation of wine color, aroma, and colloidal stability; selected aging-associated reactions involving 1-hydroxyethyl radicals; selective microbial inactivation and fermentation modulation; and scale-up based on energy characterization, continuous-flow reactors, and data-driven modeling. Current evidence indicates that ultrasound is evolving from an empirically optimized unit operation toward a mechanistically informed and quantitatively characterized physical-field platform. Reported effects include accelerated aging-related transformations, modified protein structure and stability, and selective microbial responses, although they depend on treatment conditions and matrix properties. Absorbed energy density supports quantitative comparison of treatments, but reliable scale-up also requires acoustic-field distribution, residence time, temperature, and reactor geometry. Future progress will require standardized energy reporting, pilot- and continuous-flow validation, physics-informed data-driven modeling, and integration of process analytical technologies with closed-loop control. These advances would support more reproducible, scalable, and sustainable ultrasound processing in the grape and wine sector.
authors: Xian Li; Rongjun Xu; Qirui Peng; Junhe Wang; Wenchao Li; Xuanming Liu; Tingrui Luo; Yiqun Yang; Yishan Zhang; Xinhui Liu; Jiang Jiao; Yi Qin; Yanlin Liu; Yuyang Song
venue: Comprehensive Reviews in Food Science and Food Safety

title: Understanding and Mitigating Charge‐Trapping Induced Transfer Curve Drift in Electrolyte‐Gated Graphene Field‐Effect Transistors
abstract: Electrolyte-gated graphene field-effect transistors (EG-gFETs) have great potential for chemical and biosensing applications and are increasingly attractive platforms for synaptic or memristive elements in neuromorphic computing. However, EG-gFETs exhibit drift in their electrical response, a phenomenon that remains poorly understood. An in-depth understanding of EG-gFETs' responses is essential for fully exploiting their behavior in applications and to open a much-needed discussion and standardization of practices within the community. In this work, we show that drift is ubiquitous across all tested devices and experimental conditions, and present evidence indicating that it is driven by progressive charge trapping in the insulating layer beneath the graphene channel. We then discuss potential strategies to mitigate drift, including alternative interrogation schemes and fabrication processes. Additionally, we propose approaches to enhance signal readability and facilitate discrimination of the signal from noise and false-positive responses in biosensing applications.
authors: João Mouro; Tiago Pereira; Tiago Dias; Mohammadmahdi Faraji; Rui Campos; Jérôme Borme; Pedro Alpuim

title: VISION-BASED DRY-MATERIAL INVENTORY ESTIMATION IN AUTONOMOUS LABORATORIES: RGB SEGMENTATION VERSUS RGB-D SURFACE RECONSTRUCTION
abstract: Reliable dry-material inventory monitoring is needed for autonomous laboratory operation, but the suitability of a non-contact method depends on material behaviour, optical access, calibration requirements and the quantity to be estimated. We compared two vision-based approaches—material-specific RGB/YOLO level estimation and visible-surface reconstruction from an Intel RealSense D405—across three materials (black polypropylene pellets, wood powder, and microcrystalline cellulose fine powder) in small transparent laboratory tubes representative of common dosing instruments, with the aim of informing a practical, evidence-based framework for choosing between such methods in laboratory automation and similar industrial contexts. Software-coordinated records linked the two camera channels to a nominal mass-fraction inventory reference and a manual-height baseline. Across six runs and 133 paired, reference-eligible material states, D405 achieved lower error than YOLO in every run (mean absolute error of 3.26 vs. 7.14 percentage points), though YOLO offered higher valid-result coverage (97.2% vs. 95.1%). Both methods showed increased error under repeated surface disturbance, with YOLO degrading more sharply than D405. An exploratory correction fitted using the first observation at each mass level substantially improved YOLO but did not surpass D405’s uncorrected accuracy, while a single global correction worsened both methods—indicating that simple corrections do not transfer robustly across conditions. The results support a method-selection framework based on error, availability, viewing geometry, calibration-state representativeness and total resource requirements. Conclusions are limited to the tested materials and setups, and the mass-fraction reference is an operational inventory proxy rather than a direct measurement of true occupied volume.
authors: Mostafa Abd Al Kader; Miguel Hernández‐del‐Valle; Maciej Harańczyk

title: Vision-Guided Closed-Loop Autonomous Navigation of Light-Driven Janus Microbots
abstract: Artificial microbots capable of precise and autonomous navigation could provide versatile platforms for microscale transport, manipulation, and task execution in complex environments. However, reliable navigation becomes increasingly challenging at the micrometre scale, particularly when the surrounding environment changes dynamically. Here, we develop a vision-guided closed-loop navigation framework for light-driven cube-shaped hematite/TiO2 Janus microbots with a characteristic size of approximately 3 μm. Real-time visual localization using a custom-trained YOLOv11 object-detection model is integrated with discretized waypoint-based magnetic steering to enable precise navigation along complex prescribed trajectories, with more than 90% of the measured trajectory deviations remaining below 6 μm across the tested path geometries. The framework further enables arbitrary user-defined free-hand trajectories and autonomous navigation through a physically confined maze. In dynamically changing environments, A* path planning enables real-time path replanning while avoiding multiple independently swimming 5 μm spherical Janus micromotors. Finally, the microbot selectively captures multiple cargo particles and autonomously transports and delivers them to a predefined location while simultaneously avoiding dynamic obstacles. These results establish an integrated platform combining programmable trajectory control, autonomous path planning, real-time environmental adaptation, and task execution within a single light-driven Janus microbot system.
authors: Kanhu Charan Andia; Harsh Prashant Katole; Parth Nitinkumar Bhosale; Hemant Kumar; Dhruv Pratap Singh

title: Vision-derived stability indicators from melt pool and wire dynamics in laser hot-wire directed energy deposition
abstract: Laser hot-wire directed energy deposition (LHW-DED) improves process performance by enhancing wire preheating. Reliable in situ assessment of process stability remains challenging because the melt-pool behavior and wire transfer are commonly evaluated separately. This study develops vision-derived stability indicators by jointly characterizing melt-pool geometry and wire dynamics during the deposition of stainless steel 316LSi under varying laser power and hot-wire power. Optical videos were analyzed using multi-Otsu segmentation for melt-pool area extraction and the Segment Anything Model 2 for temporal wire segmentation. Melt-pool area was used to characterize the energy input, while frame-to-frame Intersection over Union (IoU), IoU volatility, and angle variability were evaluated as indicators of wire stability. Low energy conditions produced smaller melt pools and greater wire flutter, whereas sufficient energy inputs produced larger melt pools and more consistent wire behavior. Parameter-level correlations showed that melt-pool area for single beads was related to penetration depth and total cross-sectional area measured by optical microscopy. Melt-pool area was also associated with wire stability during the single-bead laser-power sweep. These results establish melt-pool geometry and wire dynamics as complementary indicators of LHW-DED stability and support future process qualification and in situ feedback control.
authors: Mario Rodriguez-Parra; Miguel Hoffmann; Mithulan Paramanathan; Thomas A. Feldhausen; Eric MacDonald

title: Wearable Devices in Clinical Trials: Technologies for Continuous Patient Monitoring
abstract: Wearable devices are transforming clinical research by enabling continuous, remote, and real-world monitoring of physiological and behavioural parameters. Conventional clinical trials frequently rely on intermittent assessments obtained during scheduled site visits, which may provide only a limited representation of a participant’s health status. Wearable technologies-including smartwatches, smart rings, sensor-embedded patches, continuous glucose monitoring systems, electrocardiographic patches, and activity monitors can generate high frequency longitudinal data in participants’ everyday environments. These data can be processed into digital measures and, when appropriately validated, digital biomarkers or digital clinical outcome assessments. Recent evidence indicates rapid growth in usage of wearable- derived measurements into interventional clinical trials. A 2026 analysis identified 1,021 interventional trials registered between 2001 and 2025 that incorporated wearable- derived data, demonstrating the increasing role of wearables in drug development. Wearables can support assessment of physical activity, mobility, gait, sleep, heart rate, cardiac rhythm, glucose, respiratory parameters, temperature, medication adherence and treatment-related changes. Their incorporation may reduce dependence on site-based assessments, improve ecological validity, and enable more frequent measurement of treatment effects. However, technological variability, sensor accuracy, missing data, participants’ burden, interoperability, cyber security, privacy, algorithmic bias, and insufficient clinical validation remain important barriers. Regulatory agencies have consequently emphasized fit-for-purpose technology selection, analytical and clinical data validation, data integrity, and patient protection. This review discusses the technologies underlying wearable monitoring, their applications in clinical trial, the development of digital end points, considerations, limitations, and prospective directions. The integration validated wearable-derived measures with conventional clinical endpoints has the potential to create more continuous, patient-centred, and decentralised approaches towards clinical research.
authors: Aditya Malleboina; Bhavani Estarla; Sri Krishna Raja Kiran Kalepu; Satish Kumar Vemavarapu
venue: International Journal of Pharmaceuticals and Health Care Research

title: Wearable Surface EMG Biofeedback for Neuromuscular ReEducation in Upper Limb Overuse Tendinopathies: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
abstract: Background: Upper limb overuse tendinopathies, including lateral elbow tendinopathy (LET) and rotator cuff tendinopathy (RCT), represent major causes of pain, occupational disability, and functional impairment. Pathophysiological cascades involve not only tendon structural disorganization but also maladaptive central nervous system reorganization, altered motor unit recruitment, and aberrant muscle co-activation patterns. Wearable surface electromyographic (sEMG) biofeedback has emerged as a targeted digital health intervention to restore motor control by transforming internal electrical muscle activity into real-time visual, auditory, or vibrotactile sensory cues. Objectives: To systematically evaluate the effectiveness of wearable sEMG biofeedback in reducing pain, restoring functional capacity, and correcting neuromuscular activation patterns during rehabilitation in patients with upper limb overuse tendinopathies. Methods: Systematic searches were modeled across MEDLINE (PubMed), EMBASE, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), Web of Science, CINAHL, and IEEE Xplore through early 2026. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and controlled clinical trials comparing sEMG biofeedback (alone or alongside conventional physical therapy) against control interventions (sham biofeedback, exercise alone, or standard care) were included. Primary outcomes were pain intensity (Visual Analog Scale [VAS] or Numeric Pain Rating Scale [NPRS]) and upper limb functional status (e.g., Patient-Rated Tennis Elbow Evaluation [PRTEE], Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand [DASH]). Secondary outcomes encompassed pain-free grip strength, maximum voluntary isometric contraction (MVIC), agonist-antagonist co-activation ratios, and adverse events. Standardized mean differences (SMD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated using random-effects models. Results: Twenty-two studies comprising 1,184 participants met the eligibility criteria. Meta-analysis demonstrated that wearable sEMG biofeedback combined with therapeutic exercise yielded significant reductions in short-term pain intensity compared to exercise alone (SMD = -0.74, 95% CI: -0.98 to -0.50, p < 0.001) and medium-term pain intensity (SMD = -0.58, 95% CI: -0.81 to -0.35, p < 0.001). Significant functional recovery was observed across standardized functional scores (SMD = 0.81, 95% CI: 0.59 to 1.03, p < 0.001) alongside improvements in pain-free grip strength (SMD = 0.69, 95% CI: 0.44 to 0.94, p < 0.001). Electrophysiological analyses revealed marked normalization of the extensor carpi radialis brevis (ECRB) to flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS) co-contraction ratios in LET cohorts, as well as enhanced periscapular activation timing in RCT cohorts. Conclusions: Wearable sEMG biofeedback provides clinically meaningful adjunctive benefits over standard exercise therapy alone in upper limb overuse tendinopathies. By modulating maladaptive neuroplasticity, downtraining excessive compensatory recruitment, and optimizing kinematic coordination, wearable biofeedback systems represent an effective modality for neuromuscular re-education.
authors: Jitendra Kumar Shriwas; Navkiran Virk; Rekha Kothiyal; Amit Gupta; Japinderjit Kaur; Richa Uniyal
venue: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology

title: Wearable acoustic bioelectronics for health monitoring and therapy
abstract: Wearable acoustic bioelectronics (WABEs) are an emerging class of body‐coupled acoustic systems that integrate ultrasound transducers with miniaturized electronics, spanning skin‐conformal wearable patches, conformal probes, and ultra‐miniaturized implantable nodes for continuous sensing and therapy. Compared with conventional ultrasound systems, WABEs reduce reliance on bulky instrumentation and operator‐dependent scanning by enabling ambulatory monitoring, mechanical adaptability, and improved user comfort, although current platforms still face trade‐offs among aperture size, channel count, imaging quality, power consumption, and thermal management. Despite rapid progress, current developments remain fragmented, often focusing on isolated aspects such as piezoelectric material optimization or device structure, while critical challenges–including acoustic performance, system miniaturization, long‐term biocompatibility, energy management, and clinical translation remain insufficiently addressed. This review provides a comprehensive and multidisciplinary overview of WABEs, spanning key material constituents, device architectures, and system‐level integration strategies that enable wireless operation, data processing, and scalability. We further highlight emerging biomedical applications, including bedside and daily ultrasound imaging, cardiovascular and musculoskeletal monitoring, and ultrasound‐assisted therapies such as targeted drug delivery, wound healing, and neuromodulation. By bridging material innovation, device engineering, and biomedical utility, this review identifies key knowledge gaps and outlines future directions toward intelligent, autonomous, and clinically deployable wearable acoustic healthcare systems.
authors: Jinli Tang; Zhongwei Li; Wenzhe Lu; Long Li; Lingling Huang; Wenhui Ji; Jumei Liu; Ruijie Xie; Weiwei Zhang; Huiming Ye; Xiaoqian Su

title: What makes a laboratory self-driving? Mapping the SDL terminology landscape and introducing the FLEx categorization framework
abstract: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) are increasingly used to accelerate experimentation across chemistry, materials science, biotechnology, and related fields. Yet, the rapid development of autonomous experimentation has produced a fragmented terminology landscape in which overlapping terms, including autonomous laboratories, materials acceleration platforms, and robot scientists, are applied inconsistently. This complicates comparisons between systems and obscures what constitutes scientific autonomy. Here, we examine the definitions, historical development, disciplinary associations, and usage patterns of SDLs and related concepts. We further review existing approaches to categorizing autonomous laboratory systems and show that many rely on characteristics such as hardware complexity, system architecture, or human involvement that are difficult to apply consistently across disciplines and technologies. To provide a technology-independent alternative, we introduce the Feedback Loop Extent (FLEx) framework. FLEx classifies systems according to how far experimental feedback reaches into the scientific process, progressing from scripted execution without a scientific feedback loop to parameter optimization, autonomous experiment planning, hypothesis formulation, and scientific goal formulation. Applying FLEx to representative published systems shows that most contemporary SDLs autonomously plan experiments within human-defined objectives, whereas few demonstrably formulate hypotheses and none unambiguously reformulate broader scientific goals. FLEx provides a common language for distinguishing automation from different forms of autonomy and enables more transparent comparison and reporting of current and future SDLs.
authors: Alexander Böser; Kjell Kochale; Patrick Courtney; Thorsten Teutenberg; Florian Boser; Guangqi Wu; Nikhil Deshpande; Christian P. Haas; K. Cheung; Shuyuan Zhang; Radhika Gudipati; Alexei Lapkin; Frank Glorius; Stefan Braese

title: When Can a Learned Design Surrogate Be Trusted in a Self-Driving Microfluidics Laboratory? An Offline Closed-Loop Framework Built and Tested on Six Public Tables
abstract: Self-driving laboratories couple a learned design surrogate to an instrument, and on every new target domain it must answer four questions: when it can be trusted, how many target measurements it needs, which to make first, and when to stop adapting, switch models or escalate. We state a framework making each measurable (a competence ratio, a budget $k^*(\varepsilon)$, a time-to-target and a priced decision) and instantiate it without wet experiments on six public droplet-microfluidic and liposome tables as offline laboratories: 107 leave-one-group tiers whose rows are hidden labels. A sealed, pre-registered programme (two sealed negative validations and a pre-registered test on three more tables) and seven frozen closed-loop protocols, each run twice, yield 23 findings. Shift cost is stratified by shift type; no label-free statistic certifies individual candidates; random-split model-family rankings predicted neither the sealed nor the loop rankings. Warm-start residual boosting returns a surrogate to $1.25\times$ its development reference within 20 target rows in 94% of chemistry tiers (27% under a strict noise-floor reading), 90% of laboratory and 40% of device tiers, and a budget planned from the shift type on other tables is not measurably worse on a new one. In the loop, one gain survives drift and shuffled-label controls on all tiers, carried by the sparsely sampled ones: proposing at once and warm-starting on every measurement reaches a 10% target in 2.80 measurements against 3.31 for the reference, and in 5.72 against 11.35 for random proposals on 301 hard units at a 3% tolerance. No label-free acquisition rule survives the shuffled-label control, no interval-aware proposal or other model family does better, and no threshold rule on the tested diagnostics beats always continuing once escalation is priced. No wet-lab validation is claimed.
authors: Zhiyuan Zhang

title: [Research progress of microfluidic technology in competitive sports].
abstract: Aiming at the practical requirements of point-of-care testing, dynamic functional monitoring of athletes, precise diagnosis and treatment of sports injuries, and rapid anti-doping screening for competitive sports, microfluidic technology, with the prominent advantages of miniaturization, high throughput, low sample consumption and fast response, has become a critical interdisciplinary technical tool for advancing the scientization of competitive sports. This review systematically summarizes recent research progress and typical applications of microfluidic technology in key fields of competitive sports, including anti-doping detection, monitoring of athletes' physiological and psychological status, management of sports injuries, development of intelligent sports equipment, and bionic research of exercise physiology. The technical characteristics and scenario adaptability of diverse microfluidic systems are further compared and analyzed. The development paths and application prospects of the integration between microfluidic technology and competitive sports are discussed. This review intends to provide theoretical basis and technical references for the scientific development of competitive sports in China.
authors: Chun Hu; Chao Zhang; Zhenmin Fan; Xiaoyan Deng; Ming Liu

title: chain to loop: cost-aware value-of-information scheduling for cyclic-peptide discovery
abstract: Drug discovery screens candidate molecules through a cascade of assays rather than a single test — from cheap property predictors through docking, molecular dynamics and free-energy perturbation to synthesis and a wet-lab measurement — whose costs differ by orders of magnitude. As these pipelines become automated, a platform must decide not only which candidate to test next but which assay to spend the next unit of budget on — a scheduling question that is usually ignored. What little evidence exists is measured across repeated runs of a single method rather than across the laboratories or targets to which a result must generalise. Here we ask whether a cost-aware value-of-information (VOI) policy can do better: at each step it chooses the candidate-and-assay pair that most reduces advance-or-kill uncertainty per unit of cost. The preliminary experimental results are promising. On two real cyclic-peptide discovery cascades — PAMPA permeability for 715 molecules across 27 laboratories, and Kᵢ binding affinity for 1,964 compounds across 40 targets — VOI scheduling beat the standard cascade that runs each candidate from the cheapest assay to the dearest, raising cost-weighted top-decile yield by 0.201 for permeability and by a positive margin for binding (0.080), each beating a random baseline. Significance is judged across whole laboratories and targets rather than individual molecules, so the gains reflect whether the advantage carries over to new laboratories and targets. Choosing what to measure next, not only what to make, turns a fixed validation cascade into an adaptive one — and as discovery moves toward self- driving laboratories, deciding where to spend each experiment may come to matter as much as the molecules proposed.

title: НЕЙРОКОМП’ЮТЕРНІ ІНТЕРФЕЙСИ: ОГЛЯД СУЧАСНОГО СТАНУ, ПЕРСПЕКТИВ ТА ДОСТУПНИХ АПАРАТНО-ПРОГРАМНИХ ПЛАТФОРМ
abstract: У статті розглянуто сучасний стан нейрокомп’ютерних інтерфейсів – інтерфейси «мозок–комп’ютер» (ІМК), які забезпечують прямий канал обміну інформацією між центральною нервовою системою людини та зовнішніми технічними пристроями без залучення периферичних нервових шляхів і м’язів. Метою огляду є узагальнення сучасних уявлень про принципи функціонування, методи реєстрації сигналів, парадигми керування та клінічні застосування ІМК, а також аналіз можливостей побудови доступних систем на основі відкритого апаратного та програмного забезпечення. Розглянуто еволюцію технології від перших експериментів з електроенцефалографією до двонаправлених замкнених контурів із сенсорним зворотним зв’язком і коадаптацією користувача та алгоритмів. Проаналізовано неінвазивні, напівінвазивні, судинні та інвазивні методи реєстрації нейрофізіологічних сигналів, а також матеріалознавчі підходи до підвищення біосумісності електродів. Детально описано нейрофізіологічне підґрунтя класичних парадигм, таких як уявний рух, потенціал P300, стійкі зорові викликані потенціали і повільні кіркові потенціали, а також перспективи гібридних ІМК. Висвітлено застосування методів глибокого навчання і просторової фільтрації для декодування сигналів, а також досягнення у моторній реабілітації та мовленнєвих нейропротезах. Запропоновано концепцію розподіленої бюджетної системи, у якій мікроконтролер ESP32 виконує функції периферійного вузла збору та бездротової передачі даних, а одноплатний комп’ютер Raspberry Pi – центрального вузла обробки, декодування та керування зовнішніми пристроями. Показано, що поєднання відкритих сенсорних рішень, бібліотек BrainFlow і MNE-Python та протоколу MQTT створює технологічну основу для навчальних і дослідницьких нейроінтерфейсів з реєстрацією електроенцефалограми, електроміограми та електроокулограми.

title: Functional double-emulsion droplets enable multiplexed CRISPR quantification of cancer-related miRNAs.
abstract: Accurate, multiplexed microRNA detection is critical for early cancer diagnosis. We present a droplet-based digital CRISPR/Cas13a platform for simultaneous, amplification-free detection of multiple miRNAs. By integrating double emulsion (DE) microfluidics with programmable crRNAs, the system achieves orthogonal, interference-free readouts, enabling precise absolute quantification in complex biological samples. The assay demonstrates high sequence specificity, robust orthogonality, and consistent performance across target combinations and matrices. Fluorescence-positive droplet counts correlate linearly with input concentrations, allowing quantification of miRNA-21, miRNA-29a, and miRNA-92a with 10 copies/μL representing the lowest concentration experimentally evaluated in this study. The applicability of the platform is further evaluated in a small proof-of-concept cohort of plasma samples from healthy controls and colorectal cancer (CRC) patients. This platform provides an amplification-free approach for multiplexed miRNA quantification and supports further development for clinical biomarker analysis.
authors: Yang Zhang; Fei Deng; Rui Sang; Ling Liu; Tracie J Barber; Ewa M Goldys; Ming Li

abstract: Soft Pressure Sensors In Research Article e75582, Min-gu Kim and co-workers present gallium-based liquid-metal multilevel dome-on-dome microstructures for artificial robotic skin. A hybrid lithography combining photolithography, soft lithography, and selective wetting enables high-density (>72,500 ea/cm2), wafer-scale fabrication on curved or nonplanar surfaces with >98% yield. Integrated into a humanoid hand, the skin quantifies and maps arterial pulses in real time for robotic palpation.
