title: A Novel Hemizygous ARX Variant in an Infant with Global Developmental Delay
abstract: An ARX variant is a genetic change in the ARX (aristaless related homeobox) gene located on the X chromosome (Xp21.3). ARX encodes a transcription factor involved in early brain development, and pathogenic variants are associated with a broad spectrum of X-linked neurodevelopmental disorders. Interpreting a rare ARX variant can be challenging when acquired perinatal injury may also contribute to the phenotype. We describe a 12-month-old boy with profound global developmental delay, spastic quadriplegia, laryngomalacia, and neonatal seizures that were resolved during the neonatal period. His history suggested perinatal asphyxia, while routine brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed no major structural abnormalities. Initial metabolic investigations, including a positive urinary glycosaminoglycan spot test, did not establish a metabolic diagnosis; mucopolysaccharidosis was excluded by lysosomal enzyme assays. Clinical exome sequencing identified a hemizygous ARX missense variant, NM_139058.3:c.634G>A (p.Gly212Ser), which was absent from the population databases. Conflicting computational predictions and the available ACMG/AMP evidence supported classification as a variant of uncertain significance (VUS), rather than a definitive molecular diagnosis. Independent review also identified an erroneous automated domain annotation. Parental segregation testing and Sanger confirmation remain pending. This case illustrates the importance of integrating phenotype, variant - level evidence, and careful annotation review while avoiding premature attribution of causality.
authors: Chandrashekha Indoria; Vikram Mahendra Baid; Divakar Rangari

title: A Qualitative Examination of Perceptions Surrounding Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation Preferences in Head, Neck, and Lung Cancer Survivors
abstract: Purpose Head and neck cancer (HNC) and lung cancer (LC) survivors smoke at elevated rates at the time of diagnosis compared to other cancer survivors, and standard cessation interventions show suboptimal efficacy in this population. Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) is FDA-cleared for smoking cessation, and it may also address co-occurring depressive symptoms undermining cessation in cancer survivors. No studies have examined TMS acceptability for smoking cessation in cancer populations. Objective To examine HNC/LC survivors’ perceptions of TMS for smoking cessation as part of the assessment phase of the ADAPT-ITT framework. Methods HNC/LC survivors diagnosed within six months who currently smoked were recruited, and semi-structured interviews (45–60 minutes) were conducted via videoconference. Participants viewed a two-minute TMS educational video midway through the interview. Interview transcripts were analyzed using content and thematic analysis. Results Nine participants (7 head and neck cancer, 2 lung cancer survivors) provided data for this qualitative study. Smoking history ranged from 16 to 87.6 pack-years. Cancer diagnosis increased quit motivation, yet cessation was elusive. Despite no prior TMS knowledge, all nine participants expressed willingness to try TMS after the educational video, citing its non-invasive nature and independence from medications. The primary barrier was the six-week time commitment, with participants open to flexible, shorter treatment protocols. Facilitators included intrinsic motivation, family support, and structured accountability of clinic-based treatment. Participants recommended co-locating TMS with cancer care and providing educational materials through oncology providers. Conclusions HNC/LC survivors were receptive to TMS for smoking cessation after brief education. Findings support proceeding to subsequent ADAPT-ITT phases.
authors: Gopalkumar Rakesh; Kimberly L. Haney; Jean Edward; Vilma Bursac; Tia Weber; Jessica L. Burris

title: A Review of Strip Shape Prediction Methods Transitioning From Mechanistic Models to Interpretable Deep Learning
abstract: Strip shape prediction is a core task in rolling process control, and its accuracy directly impacts product quality and production efficiency. However, complex multivariable nonlinear couplings, dynamic operating conditions, and strong environmental disturbances severely challenge the accuracy and adaptability of traditional mechanistic models. In recent years, machine learning (ML) has provided new pathways to overcome these limitations. Although research achievements are increasingly abundant, the field still lacks a systematic review that integrates technological evolution with industrial application experience. This paper systematically reviews the research progress of ML in strip shape prediction, tracing the evolution from mechanistic modeling to data‐driven approaches. By detailing the core modeling stages and using strip crown, flatness, and key influencing factors as specific contexts, we systematically categorize the functional positioning and applicable scenarios of various ML algorithms. Crucially, we outline their structural limitations in practical deployment, such as “black‐box” unreliability and a lack of physical consistency. Based on this synthesis, the paper explores current industrial bottlenecks and future development directions, specifically highlighting interpretable deep learning, mechanism‐data fusion, and causal inference. Ultimately, this review aims to provide valuable references and insights for academia and industry professionals striving to advance intelligent steel production and enhance process efficiency.
authors: Fei Shang; Zhijie Zheng; Huilin Chen; Jipeng Zhao; Yonhao Ma; Sifang Wang; Ruilin Miao; Xuegang Zhou; Chunwei Xing; Pengpeng Zhang

title: A Three-Year Generalizability Study of Clinical Skills Assessment: Improvement in Reliability Following Expansion of Clinical Reasoning Tasks
abstract: Background As competency-based education has expanded among health professionals, greater emphasis has been placed on teaching and assessing clinical skills as a domain distinct from knowledge. Given that clinical skills assessments involve multiple facets, establishing their validity and reliability is crucial. This study evaluated the validity and reliability of a summative clinical skill assessment (S-CSA) at a single college over three consecutive years (2023–2025). Methods The S-CSA consists of clinical performance examinations (CPX) using patient-encounter cases and objective structured clinical examinations (OSCE) using clinical skill cases. Data from three years were analyzed, with 47, 46, and 56 examinees in 2023, 2024, and 2025, respectively. The analyses included descriptive statistics, correlations among CPX domain scores, CPX total scores, and OSCE total scores, and estimation of generalizability coefficients using generalizability theory (G-theory). Results Descriptive analyses showed a consistent tendency for CPX scores to be lower than OSCE scores. In particular, the history-taking and physical examination domains tended to show lower achievement levels across the years. Correlations among CPX domains were modest to moderate, whereas correlations between OSCE and CPX total scores remained low, suggesting that the CPX and OSCE assessed distinct constructs. The G-coefficients ranged from 0.534 to 0.850. Reliability estimates varied across cohorts but became more stable over time, with fewer poorly functioning stations identified in later years. Sensitivity analyses demonstrated that the exclusion of underperforming stations substantially improved reliability estimates in earlier cohorts. Conclusions Over three years, repeated analyses of the reliability of the clinical skills assessment showed that the examination ultimately reached a level generally considered acceptable for high-stakes assessment. This improvement may have been supported by the identification of stations that undermined the overall reliability and by the increasing number of CPX stations emphasizing clinical reasoning. Continued case development and further refinement are required. Future studies should include item-level reviews and analyses with larger sample sizes.
authors: Soo-Hyun Lee; Seong-Eun Kwon; Man-Suk Hwang; Minna Hong; Eui-Hyoung Hwang; Jihwan Kim; Aram Jeong; Hye-Yoon Lee

title: A Translational Approach for Treatment of Posterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries: From Foundational Anatomic and Biomechanical Studies to Validated Surgical Outcomes.
abstract: Posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) injuries were historically managed nonsurgically or with primary repairs, owing to limited anatomic knowledge, subjective diagnostic techniques, and nonvalidated reconstructions that frequently failed. We describe a two-decade, bench-to-bedside PCL research pyramid that progressively addressed these deficiencies. Foundational cadaveric work characterized the quantitative anatomy of the PCL, including the anterolateral and posteromedial bundles, yielding reproducible femoral and tibial osseous landmarks for tunnel placement. Robotic biomechanical testing established the codominant contribution of both bundles, optimal graft fixation angles, and the destabilizing influence of posterolateral corner injuries and flat tibial slope. Objective diagnostic methods, such as kneeling PCL stress radiography and posterior tibial translation on MRI, were validated to quantify laxity and detect chronic tears. These insights informed an anatomically grounded double-bundle reconstruction, complemented by multiligament tunnel convergence-avoidance strategies, evidence-based tensioning sequences, and a refined rehabilitation and bracing treatment protocol. Prospective outcome studies confirmed restoration of stability comparable to anterior cruciate ligament reconstructions, demonstrating how integrated translational research transformed treatment of this challenging injury.
authors: Robert F LaPrade; Luke V Tollefson; Lars Engebretsen; Nicholas I Kennedy; Jorge Chahla; Christopher M LaPrade; Gilbert Moatshe; Nicholas N DePhillipo; Jill K Monson; Andrew S Bernhardson

title: A causal decision framework for selecting industry 4.0 technologies to overcome open innovation barriers in construction
abstract: The construction industry has long struggled to embrace open innovation, not for lack of intent, but because of deeply embedded financial, organizational, and cultural barriers that resist change. This study responds to that challenge by building an integrated decision-support framework that identifies which Industry 4.0 technologies are best positioned to address these barriers. The research followed a three-stage design. Following a systematic literature review and expert content validation, 11 open innovation barriers and 7 technologies were retained. Then, a two-method analytical sequence combining Pythagorean Fuzzy DEMATEL (PF-DEMATEL) with Grey MABAC applied. PF-DEMATEL mapped the causal structure among the barriers, identifying inadequate support from top management and their risk attitude (C2; weight = 0.1119, D + R = 4.566) as the central systemic mediator, while difficulty in finding suitable human resources for R&D (C6; D − R = 1.730) and market uncertainty regarding innovative products (C4; D − R = 1.023) emerged as the dominant root causes driving the broader barrier network. Grey MABAC then ranked the seven technologies by their weighted mitigation potential, placing Building Information Modelling well ahead of the field, followed by the Internet of Things and Artificial Intelligence. The findings offer construction practitioners a sequenced, evidence-based roadmap for digital transformation that targets the most influential barriers first and builds collaborative innovation capacity from the ground up.
authors: Payam Shojaei; Amin Nikbakht

title: A new semi-automated, motility-based screening assay for discovery of compounds with activity against the juvenile stage of Fasciola hepatica
abstract: Fasciola hepatica is a trematode parasite responsible for fasciolosis, a liver disease that affects humans and livestock worldwide. Together with other food-borne trematode infections, fasciolosis is considered a neglected tropical disease. Further, it imposes substantial agricultural losses due to infections in ruminants. No vaccine is currently available, and control heavily relies on drug treatment, especially with triclabendazole (TCBZ). However, the intensive use of TCBZ over the past four decades has led to increasing rates of treatment failures and the emergence of drug-resistant parasites. Therefore, the identification of new treatment options is an urgent priority. The currently available toolset for drug screening, however, is limited. To address this need, we established a novel, semi-automated, standardized, and objective screening assay based on motility monitoring of newly excysted juveniles using microscopic live imaging. The assay was validated by testing a panel of ten compounds with known anthelmintic properties, amongst them TCBZ (IC 50 : 1.5 µM) and the new activator of the F. hepatica transient receptor potential melastatin (TRPM PZQ ) ion channel, benzamidoquinazolinone (IC 50 : 1.05 µM). In addition to these two compounds with known activity against F. hepatica , three compounds were identified as particularly promising with a fast onset of action and IC 50 values in the nanomolar range: the salicylanilides MMV665807 (IC 50 : 44 nM), niclosamide (IC 50 : 32 nM), and its ethanolamine salt, niclosamide ethanolamine (IC 50 : 9 nM). Complementary live/dead staining revealed that only TCBZ displayed parasiticidal activity, while the other compounds, although leading to parasite paralysis, did not lead to parasite death within 72 hours. Scanning electron microscopy of drug treated parasites did not reveal any significant damage at concentrations corresponding to the IC 50 s, but strong phenotypes were visible at 20 µM. The presented motility assay provides a robust method for the discovery of novel anthelmintic compounds and facilitates the ongoing effort to combat fasciolosis.
authors: Alice Bernal; Diana S. Gliga; Giulia Colangeli; Matías Preza; Rossitza N. Irobalieva; Caroline F. Frey; Andrew Frederick Hemphill; Britta Lundström‐Stadelmann; Natalie Wiedemar

title: A portable biomedical device for post-stroke spasticity assessment: preliminary validation study
abstract: Purpose This preliminary validation study investigated the feasibility of a portable biomedical device equipped with force and motion sensors for objectively quantifying resistance to passive movement in individuals with chronic post-stroke hemiparesis. The study examined associations between device-derived measurements and clinical spasticity scores obtained using the Modified Ashworth Scale (MAS). Methods Twenty-one individuals with chronic post-stroke hemiparesis were evaluated. MAS grading and device-based measurements were performed simultaneously during the same passive stretch to ensure comparable biomechanical conditions. Synchronized resistance-force and angular-displacement data were recorded during assessments of the shoulder adductors, elbow flexors, and wrist flexors. Associations between device measurements and MAS scores were analyzed using Spearman's rank correlation. Results Strong positive correlations were observed between device-derived resistance measurements and MAS scores for the shoulder adductors (ρ = 0.79, p < 0.001) and elbow flexors (ρ = 0.80, p < 0.001). A moderate correlation was found for the wrist flexors (ρ = 0.47, p = 0.003). Conclusion The findings provide preliminary evidence of concurrent associations between quantitative resistance measurements and MAS scores, supporting the device's feasibility as an adjunct tool for objective biomechanical assessment of post-stroke spasticity. However, larger studies incorporating independent blinded examiners, repeated measurements, and formal reliability analyses are necessary to establish its measurement properties and clinical applicability.

title: A reproducible safety assessment model for concurrent transcranial magnetic stimulation with implanted intracranial electroencephalography electrodes
abstract: BACKGROUND: Concurrent transcranial magnetic stimulation and intracranial EEG (TMS-sEEG) offers a powerful approach for interrogating human brain circuits with high spatiotemporal resolution. However, standardized safety testing procedures for TMS in the presence of implanted electrodes are lacking. OBJECTIVE: To establish and validate a reproducible methodological framework for assessing TMS safety with sEEG hardware, addressing potential risks of electrode displacement, heating, and secondary current induction. METHODS: A conductive agarose phantom implanted with clinical-grade platinum sEEG electrodes was exposed to single-pulse TMS (0.4 Hz), repetitive TMS (1-50 Hz), and intermittent theta burst stimulation. Electrode displacement was quantified via high-speed video and motion tracking. Temperature changes were measured with fiber-optic thermal probes positioned at stimulated electrode contacts. Induced voltages were recorded using an oscilloscope and intracranial EEG hardware, and secondary current and charge density were calculated from oscilloscope outputs and impedance measurements. RESULTS: sEEG lead displacement remained micrometer-scale across stimulation conditions, with a maximum transient displacement of 10.99 μm and a maximum 1-s mean displacement from the pre-TMS position of 16.27 μm. Temperature changes remained well within the 2°C safety threshold across all tested conditions; in the primary temperature series, the maximum observed increase was 0.073°C. Induced voltages and charge densities remained below established safety limits, exhibiting consistent exponential decay with increasing distance from the coil. All stimulation conditions, including those exceeding typical clinical ranges, remained well within safety margins. CONCLUSIONS: Under the tested conditions in a controlled phantom environment, TMS exposure produced micrometer-scale transient and longer-timescale displacement, temperature changes within established safety thresholds, and charge densities within established safety thresholds. This validated methodological pipeline provides a standardized framework for future safety experiments involving TMS and implanted devices and supports continued development of TMS-sEEG as a tool for studying human brain circuitry and neuromodulation.

title: A scenario-adaptive AHP-FCE framework for lithium-ion battery thermal management: Optimal strategy selection in energy storage, supercars, and marine propulsion
abstract: The suitability of lithium-ion battery thermal management strategies (TMSs) varies substantially across operating conditions and engineering constraints, limiting the effectiveness of single-metric or fixed-weight evaluation methods. This study develops a scenario-adaptive framework integrating the Analytic Hierarchy Process and Fuzzy Comprehensive Evaluation (AHP-FCE). The framework comprises four primary criteria (technical performance, economic viability, environmental safety, and sustainability) and 15 secondary indicators, with scenario-specific weights and evaluation boundaries established for energy storage systems (ESS), electric supercars (ESC), and electric propulsion ships (EPS). Among the evaluated candidates, single-phase immersion cooling, two-phase immersion cooling, and single-phase cold-plate cooling rank first for ESS, ESC, and EPS, with adaptability scores of 0.894, 0.930, and 0.885, respectively, highlighting the scenario dependence of TMS selection. Robustness analyses confirm the overall stability of these recommendations, although the ESC ranking is more sensitive to the weighting method. An external techno-economic benchmark further supports the engineering plausibility of the ESS recommendation. The proposed framework provides a transparent and interpretable quantitative basis for preliminary TMS screening and scenario-specific engineering decision-making.
authors: Xiaoyu Wang; Yanshun Yu; Zhihang Wang; Tengfang Chen

title: A story for Pepper and Nao: applying the learning by teaching paradigm in children with patterns of neuromotor impairment
abstract: Background Social robots are increasingly used in educational and clinical contexts to enhance engagement and learning, particularly in children with neurological and neurodevelopmental disorders. The Learning by Teaching paradigm, in which children actively teach social robots, promotes cognitive and metacognitive processes such as planning, self-efficacy, and executive functioning; however, controlled and systematic evidence supporting its effectiveness remains limited. Children with neuromotor disorders frequently present with closely intertwined motor and cognitive planning difficulties, which significantly impact learning and everyday functioning. In this context, social robot–mediated interventions based on the Learning by Teaching paradigm may represent a promising approach. The current multicenter randomized controlled trial (RCT) explores the feasibility and effectiveness of this approach to enhance cognitive and motor planning in children with neuromotor impairments, and to examine potential generalization effects on other cognitive domains and engagement. Methods The main aim of this RCT study is to evaluate the feasibility and effectiveness of a social robot-mediated Learning by Teaching intervention in children aged 7–16 years with neuromotor impairments. Eighty participants will be randomly assigned to an Experimental Group (EG) receiving social robot training or to a Control Group (CG) continuing standard care. The intervention consists of 20–25 sessions in which children teach a humanoid social robot (Pepper or NAO) to order picture-based stories of increasing complexity. Assessments will be performed at baseline (T0), post-intervention or control period (T1), and follow-up/post-treatment (T2). Primary outcomes include planning abilities assessed through picture arrangement and an ad hoc motor planning task. Secondary outcomes encompass executive functions, visuo-spatial memory, attention, inhibition, narrative production, visual-perceptual skills, and reading comprehension. Engagement will be measured using a multimodal approach integrating behavioral, cognitive, emotional, and physiological indicators derived from video, audio, and wearable sensors. Results The study will examine improvements in planning and motor programming abilities and potential generalization effects on executive functions and reading comprehension. Additionally, the predictive and mediating role of engagement in intervention effectiveness will be reported. Conclusions This research protocol proposes an innovative, engagement-focused rehabilitation approach integrating cognitive, motor, and narrative processes through social robotics. Findings are expected to inform the development of evidence-based, personalized interventions for children with neuromotor disorders and to advance methodological approaches for assessing engagement in human–robot interaction. title: A virtual tool for the rehabilitation of patients based on the developed heart rate measurement model
abstract: Relevance.The development of intelligent information and measurement systems for patient rehabilitation is an important area of modern biomedical engineering.Particular attention is paid to synchronizing physiotherapeutic interventions with individual physiological processes to improve the effectiveness of rehabilitation procedures for patients with peripheral circulatory disorders.Aim of the study.The aim is to develop a heart rate measurement model and a virtual hardware-software device for synchronizing electrical stimulation with the natural rhythm of peripheral blood flow.Objectives.The objectives include developing a model for determining the arrival time of the arterial pulse wave at the affected limb area, implementing a virtual measurement and stimulation system, and experimentally evaluating its functionality and effectiveness.Methods.The study applies methods of cyber-physical systems design, biomedical signal acquisition and processing, mathematical modeling, virtual instrumentation, and automated feedback control.The hardware-software system was implemented using multifunctional data acquisition equipment and the LabVIEW programming environment.Scientific novelty.A model and an approach to controlling electrical stimulation are proposed that enable the generation of stimulation pulses synchronized with the actual propagation of the arterial pulse wave.Unlike conventional approaches with predefined stimulation intervals, the developed system dynamically adjusts stimulation timing according to individual changes in the patient's heart rhythm and peripheral blood flow characteristics.Practical significance.The developed virtual device provides automated monitoring of physiological signals, real-time generation of synchronized stimulation pulses, and assessment of rehabilitation effectiveness using indicators of limb temperature and peripheral blood circulation.The proposed solution can support the development of adaptive physiotherapeutic equipment and personalized rehabilitation technologies.Results.Experimental investigations confirmed the functionality of the developed virtual device and demonstrated stable synchronization of electrical stimulation pulses with t he patient's physiological rhythm.The rehabilitation procedures were accompanied by increased limb temperature and improved peripheral blood supply, indicating positive changes in the monitored physiological parameters.Conclusions.The developed heart rate measurement model and virtual rehabilitation device provide a technological basis for adaptive electrical stimulation synchronized with natural blood flow dynamics.The obtained results demonstrate the feasibility of integrating virtual instrumentation, biomedical signal processing, and automated control into intelligent rehabilitation systems.

title: ANOMALY FUEL FRAUD DETECTION TECHNIQUES AND FUEL MONITORING IN LOGISTICS
abstract: The logistics and trucking industry continues to face significant operational challenges due to high fuel costs, which typically constitute 20-30% of total operational expenses. Fuel fraud, including fuel draining, side fueling, and unauthorized diversions, further escalates these costs, particularly for Uzbekistan-based IT Park companies managing dispatching and back-office operations for North American heavy-duty trucking fleets. Traditional rule-based monitoring systems often fail to detect sophisticated and subtle fraud patterns hidden within normal operational day. This thesis proposes a hybrid anomaly detection framework that integrates Isolation Forest and Autoencoders for effective real-time fuel fraud detection. The model leverages telematics data, fuel purchase transactions and Transport Management System (TMS) records. Autoencoders are employed to learn complex normal consumption patterns and temporal dependencies in time-series data, while Isolation Forest efficiently isolates anomalous instances in the learned feature space. This hybrid approach enables accurate identification of common fuel theft scenarios, including gradual fuel drainage over multiple stops, side fueling, and unauthorized tank transfers.

title: ARM-01: an open-source reversible 2-DOF upper-limb rehabilitation robot with internal cable routing and intrinsic safety
abstract: The rising global incidence of stroke necessitates accessible and effective upper-limb rehabilitation solutions. However, the widespread adoption of commercial rehabilitation robots is often hindered by prohibitive costs, complex setups, exposed wiring hazards, and the financial burden of requiring dedicated left- or right-arm systems. This paper presents ARM-01, a cost-effective, open-source, 2-degree-of-freedom (DOF) rehabilitation robot engineered for passive range-of-motion and predefined trajectory tracking of the shoulder and elbow joints. Built using highly accessible off-the-shelf (OTS) components, 3D-printed parts, standard aluminum profiles, and SUS304 stainless steel, the hardware is specifically designed for straightforward replication. To maximize economic viability and clinical adaptability, the ARM-01 features a tool-free reversible mechanism, allowing a single unit to seamlessly alternate between left- and right-side upper-limb rehabilitation. Furthermore, the system incorporates a hollow-shaft internal cable-routing strategy that reduces exposed wiring and associated entanglement risks. Biomechanical alignment between the robot and the user's glenohumeral joint is facilitated through a combination of a mobile base and a motorized lifting column, enabling convenient adjustment of the robot's position relative to the user. The system's hierarchical control architecture integrates a ROS2-based backend with an intuitive Unity 3D human-machine interface (HMI), facilitating tailored trajectory execution, real-time spatial monitoring, and multi-layered safety protocols. Comprehensive kinematic modeling, workspace simulation, and static load analyses theoretically evaluate the system's actuator torque adequacy and safety boundaries. Successful operational testing in a controlled laboratory setting demonstrates the prototype's basic operational feasibility under non-clinical conditions, offering the research community an adaptable and reproducible platform for further development of upper-limb rehabilitation technologies.
authors: Tien-Lap Vu; Cao-Long Vu; Thanh-Dat Nguyen; Hoang-Hiep Ly; Xuan-Thuan Nguyen; Dinh-Ba Bui; Thi-Thoa Mac

title: AS-ULDAR: a ROS 2-based collaborative robotic platform for upper-limb rehabilitation — systems integration and pilot usability evaluation in a clinical environment
abstract: Robotic rehabilitation can increase the intensity and personalization of upper-limb therapy, but its clinical translation is hindered by the difficulty of integrating individually validated technical components into a single clinician-ready platform. This paper presents a platform which is intended to be an Auto-calibrating System for Upper Limb Disability Assessment and Rehabilitation (AS-ULDAR), a ROS 2-based platform built around a Franka Emika Panda robot that unifies motor/cognitive assessment, sensorless force estimation, and Cartesian and Human Joint-based Trajectory Tracking within a clinician-oriented GUI. While these functionalities were individually validated in prior work, the present contribution lies in their systems-level integration and in identifying the operational barriers that emerge when deploying such a platform in a real clinical workflow, targeting adult patients with chronic neurological conditions (stroke, Parkinson’s, ALS, MCI) and mild-to-moderate upper-limb impairment. The platform was evaluated through a formative usability study: the standalone GUI by five naïve users, and the complete system by seven physiotherapists performing the full clinical workflow (no patients were involved; clinical efficacy is outside this scope). The system was technically stable throughout. Usability (SUS) was high for the GUI (87.5 ± 1.8) but markedly lower and more heterogeneous for the complete platform (54 ± 16), with feedback pointing to robot setup and workflow operation—not interface design—as the main friction points for clinical staff. These results show that integrating multiple rehabilitation functionalities is technically feasible, but that usability must be treated as a system-level property, and they provide concrete operational lessons for the clinical translation of cobot-based rehabilitation platforms.
authors: Chiara Alessi; Nikolas Sacchi; Cira Fundarò; Antonella Ferrara

title: Adaptive material assembly by Brucella pituitosa in response to interfacial stress
abstract: Oil–water interfaces provide hydrocarbon-utilizing microorganisms access to carbon substrates while exposing them to physicochemical conditions that may challenge cellular fitness. However, the relationships between interfacial properties, microbial physiology, and extracellular material assembly remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated Brucella pituitosa BU72, a non-motile hydrocarbonoclastic bacterium isolated from oil-contaminated sediment that produces exopolysaccharide-based surfactants. We examined whether differences in interfacial physicochemistry were associated with BU72 viability and extracellular material assembly, using interfacial film formation and mechanical properties as functional outcomes. BU72 was exposed to hexadecane–water and squalene–water interfaces, representing saturated and unsaturated hydrocarbon environments with distinct interfacial tensions and chemical compositions. BU72 accumulated at both interfaces, reduced interfacial tension, and formed stable films that resisted droplet coalescence. At the hexadecane–water interface, characterized by higher interfacial tension, BU72 exhibited lower cell viability and formed films with greater elastic responses and distinct carbohydrate compositions. In contrast, the squalene–water interface, characterized by lower interfacial tension, supported higher cell viability and softer films, with greater carbohydrate partitioning into the aqueous phase. These findings reveal distinct physiological and material responses associated with the two interfacial environments, suggesting a potential relationship between cellular fitness, extracellular material distribution, and interfacial mechanics. Collectively, our results identify interfacial physicochemistry as an important factor to understand microbial material assembly and establish BU72 as a model for investigating microbial responses at hydrocarbon–water interfaces, with potential implications for hydrocarbon bioremediation.
authors: Shakira M. Martínez Vásquez; Tianyi Liu; Li Tan; Chang‐Hyeock Byeon; Luis González Menéndez; Mouna Mahjoubi; Parastoo Azadi; Ameur Cherif; Ümit Akbey; Tagbo H. R. Niepa

title: Advancements in Clinical Applications of Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation Using Different Coil Configurations: A Review
abstract: The effects of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) are jointly determined by coil geometry, intracranial electric-field distribution, stimulation target, and pulse parameters, with coil design directly governing stimulation depth, spatial focality, and brain tissue coverage. This review compares circular, figure-of-eight, double-cone, and H-coils in terms of geometry, electric-field distribution, effective depth, focality, and current clinical use. Figure-of-eight coils provide high superficial focality and are suited to anatomically defined cortical targets such as the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, primary motor cortex, and supplementary motor area. Double-cone and H-coils extend effective electric-field coverage to medial and relatively deep networks but reduce spatial selectivity, illustrating the depth-focality trade-off. The maturity of clinical evidence varies across disorders. Conventional repetitive TMS, intermittent theta-burst stimulation, and H1-coil deep TMS have comparatively established evidence in depression, whereas stroke and migraine remain heterogeneous in terms of target selection, dose, and patient selection. Key challenges are to match individualized intracranial electric-field dose, disease-network targets, pulse sequences, and brain state. This work offers valuable guidance for researchers in related fields and professionals engaged in the clinical management of neuropsychiatric disorders.
authors: Wentao Zhang; Mai Lu

title: Advances in integrated surgical and rehabilitation treatment for cerebral palsy.
abstract: Cerebral palsy (CP) is a group of motor disorders caused by non-progressive brain injury during development, often accompanied by sensory, cognitive, and behavioral impairments. It remains one of the most common causes of childhood disability. In recent years, the coordinated integration of surgical intervention and rehabilitation has transitioned from a conceptual framework to clinical practice, becoming a core strategy for improving patient function. However, integrated treatment still faces major bottlenecks: insufficient bridging between treatment phases, lack of individualized protocols, and inconsistent outcome measures. This review examines recent advances in integrated surgical and rehabilitative care for CP, covering four core domains: spasticity management (selective dorsal rhizotomy, botulinum toxin injection) with sequential rehabilitation; deformity correction (tendon lengthening, osteotomy) with biomechanically guided individualized rehabilitation; neuromodulation (deep brain stimulation, transcranial magnetic stimulation) with neuroplasticity-targeted training; and emerging technologies including robotic-assisted therapy, artificial intelligence, and digital therapeutics. Surgery creates the anatomical foundation for function; rehabilitation determines the ultimate functional value of surgery. The temporal coordination and strategic synergy between the two are critical for maximizing functional improvement. Future efforts should focus on establishing unified outcome measures for integrated treatment, promoting early intervention combined with regenerative medicine, and leveraging AI to shift from experience-driven to data-driven precision therapy.

title: An Identification Method for Upper Limb Spasticity Based on IDATC in Rehabilitation Training: A Preliminary Study
abstract: During rehabilitation training, real-time monitoring and accurate identification of whether spasticity is occurring at the moment are crucial. This serves as the prerequisite for rehabilitation devices or robots to promptly implement interventions to alleviate spasticity, ensure patient safety, and ensure therapeutic efficacy. However, research on the real-time identification of the moment when the spasticity occurs by rehabilitation robots during training remains limited. In this paper, through clinical manifestations of spasticity and theoretical analysis, an index based on the divergence of acceleration and external torque changes (IDATC) and an IDATC-based method for identifying spasticity onset are proposed. A combined experiment was conducted to collect the kinematic, interaction force, and electromyography (EMG) data of stroke patients during spasticity provocation. The proposed spasticity identification method was validated using upper limb spasticity data collected from stroke patients. Preliminary results of the experiment demonstrate that the negative peak of the IDATC is highly consistent with the EMG peak of the corresponding spastic muscle, so it has potential to identify spasticity onset using the proposed IDATC-based spasticity identification method. Furthermore, provided that the threshold is appropriately selected, the proposed IDATC-based method may achieve an exceptionally high identification F1 score.
authors: Zemiao Fang; Yungang Hao; Shuoyu Wang; Tao Liu

title: An augmented reality and robotic rehabilitation platform with prognostic modeling for post-stroke hand spasticity
abstract: Post-stroke hand impairment can limit manual dexterity and daily activities. We evaluated Rehabotics, an integrated augmented reality (AR) and robotic finger-stretching platform, in a 5-week single-arm intervention. Eighty patients with hand spasticity (time since stroke, 4.53 ± 1.04 months; baseline Ashworth Scale (AS), 2.28 ± 0.62) completed three supervised 30-minute sessions per week, consisting of AR serious-game training followed by robotic finger stretching. Clinical outcomes were assessed at baseline and post-intervention using the AS, Box and Block Test (BBT), and Active Range of Motion (AROM), expressed as Total Active Motion (TAM). We developed a novel exploratory prediction framework using linear mixed-effects models to derive task-specific features from first-session AR task performance, relative to patterns learned from repeated training-cohort data. These AR-derived digital markers were combined with baseline clinical variables in ridge regression to predict post-intervention outcomes. Internal validation used patient-level 5-fold grouped cross-validation (CV), with leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) CV performed as a sensitivity analysis. Following the intervention, AS scores decreased from 2.28 ± 0.62 to 1.34 ± 0.48 ( p = 3.22·10 − 15 ), BBT scores increased from 39.14 ± 2.45 to 45.14 ± 1.57 blocks ( p = 3.47·10 − 50 ), and AROM increased from 147.98 ± 19.27° to 224.61 ± 7.58° ( p = 3.37·10 − 62 ). Our findings reflect within-group pre–post changes in a single-arm cohort and do not establish superiority over conventional physiotherapy. The prediction model achieved R² = 0.615 ± 0.397 for BBT and 0.661 ± 0.271 for AROM, while AS classification achieved 0.850 ± 0.034 accuracy and quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) of 0.608 ± 0.187. LOSO CV yielded pooled R² values of 0.636 for BBT and 0.750 for AROM, with AS accuracy of 0.900 and QWK of 0.768, suggesting that early AR-derived markers may provide short-term prognostic information.
authors: Pantelis Syringas; Iοannis Kakkos; Georgios Papagiannis; Athanasios Triantafyllou; Orestis N. Zestas; Nikolaos D. Tselikas; Stavros-Theofanis Miloulis; Ioannis Vezakis; George K. Matsopoulos

title: Anatomic Anterolateral Ligament Reconstruction Using the Iliotibial Band Results in Less Internal Rotation Constraint and Lateral Compartment Joint Loading As Compared With the Modified Lemaire Procedure: A Robotic Biomechanical Study.
abstract:
Background

While current anterolateral complex knee procedures have been demonstrated to reduce anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) graft failures, concerns about potential lateral compartment overload are present.

Purpose

To compare lateral compartment pressures and knee laxity between an anterolateral ligament reconstruction (ALLR) using the iliotibial band and the modified Lemaire lateral extra-articular tenodesis (LET) procedure by biomechanically testing for anterior tibial translation, a simulated pivot shift, and internal rotation (IR).

Study design

Controlled laboratory study.

Methods

Seven paired cadaveric knees were utilized for this study. A 6 degrees of freedom robotic system was used to measure anterior tibial translation with an 88-N anterior drawer load, IR with a 5-N·m torque, and a simulated pivot-shift test using 5-N·m IR and 10-N·m valgus torques. Force sensors inserted under the lateral meniscus measured lateral compartment pressure during the simulated pivot shift. All specimens were tested in 3 states: intact, anterior cruciate ligament cut, and ACLR. The specimen pairs were then randomized to either an anatomic ALLR technique or a modified Lemaire LET.

Results

When compared with the ALLR cohort, the modified Lemaire LET cohort had significantly increased lateral compartment peak pressure at 30° (P = .047) and significantly decreased IR at all flexion angles (all P < .05). For the modified Lemaire cohort, lateral compartment peak contact pressures were significantly increased versus the intact and ACLR states at 30° of flexion, and IR was significantly decreased as compared with the intact state at 30°, 45°, and 90° during IR testing (all P < .05). For the ALLR cohort specifically, lateral compartment peak contact pressures were not significantly different from intact and ACLR states, and IR was significantly increased relative to the intact state at 30°, 45°, and 60° during IR testing (all P < .05).

Conclusions

Lateral compartment peak contact pressure was restored to near intact values with an ALLR using the posterior third of the iliotibial band, while the modified Lemaire LET led to significantly increased pressures. Additionally, the modified Lemaire LET led to decreased IR at all flexion angles, while the ALLR had significantly increased IR between 30° and 60° of flexion.

Clinical relevance

Reconstruction of the anterolateral ligament using the posterior third of the iliotibial band is an option for knees requiring an anterolateral complex procedure. Modified Lemaire LET leads to increased lateral compartment pressures and decreased IR; however, no negative long-term outcomes of overconstraint have been agreed on in the literature.
authors: Tollefson LV, Slette EL, Shoemaker EP, Carlson MR, Rasmussen MT, Lee DR, Kennedy NI, LaPrade CM, LaPrade RF.

title: Aperiodic neural activity predicts cortical excitability in TMS-EEG
abstract:
Background

Fluctuating cortical excitability states are inherent to and critical for brain function. They can be probed non-invasively using transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) combined with electroencephalography (EEG) by measuring early local TMS-evoked potentials (EL-TEPs). Pre-stimulus periodic neural activity can predict fluctuating excitability states. To what extent aperiodic neural activity represents a marker of cortical excitability has not been explored.

Objectives

We investigated the relationship between pre-stimulus aperiodic and periodic neural activity and EL-TEP amplitude in both the primary motor cortex (M1) and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC).

Methods

Single-pulse TMS was delivered to the left M1 or left DLPFC in 29 and 11 healthy adults, respectively, while EEG was recorded simultaneously. Pre-stimulus EEG was parameterized into aperiodic and periodic components to extract the aperiodic exponent (slope of 1/f-like activity), alpha power (8–13 Hz), and beta power (13–30 Hz). EL-TEP peak-to-peak amplitudes were extracted from approximately 20-65 ms after the TMS pulse.

Results

Aperiodic exponent showed a strong negative relationship with EL-TEP amplitude in both M1 and DLPFC, with steeper 1/f-like slopes associated with smaller EL-TEP amplitudes. Inconsistent relationships were found between alpha and beta power with EL-TEP amplitude across the two regions.

Conclusions

These findings indicate that pre-stimulus aperiodic neural activity influences cortical excitability in both motor and prefrontal areas. Notably, the aperiodic exponent exhibited stronger associations with cortical excitability compared to periodic alpha or beta power. Brain-state-dependent protocols may benefit from real-time extraction of aperiodic exponent as a target feature to improve the precision and efficacy of TMS.

Highlights

Pre-stimulus aperiodic exponent predicts EL-TEP amplitude in M1 and DLPFC. Larger aperiodic exponent is associated with smaller EL-TEP amplitudes. Periodic alpha and beta power do not consistently influence EL-TEP amplitude. Aperiodic exponent may inform brain-state-dependent and closed-loop TMS.
authors: van Hattem T, Hougland JR, Gogulski J, Gordon PC, Belardinelli P, Ziemann U.

title: Application of Functional Alignment Principles and Stepwise Gap Balancing in Staged Bilateral Total Knee Arthroplasty for Severe Varus Knee Osteoarthritis With Lateral Femoral Bowing Using Conventional Instrumentation: A Case Report
abstract: Severe varus deformity with apparent lateral femoral bowing can complicate component alignment and soft-tissue balancing during total knee arthroplasty (TKA) performed with conventional instrumentation. Functional alignment principles emphasize restoration of balanced soft tissues and stable knee kinematics rather than rigid correction to neutral mechanical alignment. We report a case of bilateral Grade IV osteoarthritis with severe varus deformity managed using conventional jig-based TKA and rectangular gap balancing principles. A 70-year-old female presented with bilateral knee pain for more than 25 years associated with progressive deformity, difficulty in ambulation, and limitation of daily activities. Clinical examination revealed fixed varus deformity of approximately 20° on the right side and 15° on the left side, fixed flexion deformity of 20° bilaterally, medial soft tissue contracture, and relative lateral laxity. Flexion was preserved up to 110° and 115° in the right and left knees, respectively. Radiographs demonstrated bilateral Grade IV osteoarthritis with severe medial compartment degeneration and radiographic evidence of lateral femoral bowing. The patient, therefore, underwent staged bilateral TKA using conventional instrumentation, with the left knee replaced first, followed by the right knee during a subsequent admission after satisfactory recovery from the initial procedure. Femoral preparation was performed using a conventional intramedullary alignment guide. A 5° distal femoral valgus resection was performed on the left knee, while a 6° distal femoral valgus resection was used on the right knee. The resection angle was individualized according to the deformity characteristics and intraoperative assessment of coronal alignment and soft-tissue balance rather than applying a uniform valgus angle to both knees. Sequential balancing consisting of osteophyte excision, selective medial release, posteromedial release, and medial reduction osteotomy was performed to achieve balanced rectangular flexion and extension gaps. Postoperative radiographs demonstrated satisfactory component positioning and restoration of acceptable coronal alignment. Complex varus knee morphology and lateral femoral bowing may be successfully managed using functional alignment principles even when advanced technologies are unavailable. Careful deformity assessment and stepwise soft tissue balancing remain critical to achieving stable ligament tension and satisfactory knee kinematics. Functional alignment and rectangular gap balancing can be successfully achieved in severe bilateral varus knees with lateral femoral bowing using conventional instrumentation. Individualized balancing strategies may facilitate improved postoperative range of motion, Oxford Knee Scores (OKS), and clinically stable knees on examination without the need for robotic or navigation-assisted systems.
authors: Anurag S Sekhon; Basant Rai; SK Julfikar Hossain

title: Applications of Single-Atom Alloys in Thermal, Electro, and Photo Catalysis
abstract: Single-atom alloys (SAAs) are an emerging class of heterogeneous catalysts that maximize atom efficiency by embedding isolated reactive metal atoms within a host metal surface, creating well-defined active sites. Atomic isolation imparts unique catalytic properties, including high selectivity, resistance to poisoning, coking, and sintering, and in some cases the ability to circumvent conventional scaling relationships that limit traditional catalysts. This article focuses on progress in the SAA field since our 2020 review (Chem. Rev.2020, 120, 12044-12088.), while incorporating earlier foundational studies where relevant. We first examine the fundamental principles governing SAA formation, stability, electronic structure, reactivity, and selectivity, drawing on insights from experimental single-crystal model systems and theoretical studies. We then review the application of SAAs in a wide range of industrially important reactions, including hydrogenation, dehydrogenation, selective oxidation, water-gas shift, Fischer-Tropsch synthesis, and dry reforming, among others. Beyond thermal catalysis, SAAs demonstrate great promise in electrocatalysis and plasmon-driven chemistry. Their structurally simple active sites have also enabled the rational design of novel catalysts and promoters that challenge conventional catalytic intuition. Looking ahead, recent advances in computing, including machine-learning potentials, offer the opportunity to explore vast compositional spaces and discover new alloy chemistries for challenging reactions using the SAA concept.
authors: Nima Rajabi; 김동범; Yicheng Wang; Emma Hollis; Dennis Meier; Toghrul Azizli; M. M. Montemore; Adam Holewinski; Dayne F. Swearer; Phillip Christopher; E. Charles H. Sykes

title: Applications of non-invasive brain stimulation in the treatment of children with cerebral palsy: a narrative review
abstract: Noninvasive brain stimulation has emerged as a promising adjunctive strategy for pediatric neurorehabilitation, particularly for children with cerebral palsy. This narrative review, informed by a structured literature search, summarizes current evidence on transcranial direct current stimulation and repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation in children with cerebral palsy, with emphasis on neurophysiological mechanisms, brain network targets, clinical outcomes, safety, and future translational directions. Cerebral palsy is a heterogeneous neurodevelopmental condition characterized by persistent motor impairment and frequent sensory, cognitive, communicative, behavioral, and musculoskeletal comorbidities. Although multidisciplinary rehabilitation remains the foundation of clinical management, improvements in higher level motor control, cognition, communication, and real world participation are often constrained by training intensity, adherence, developmental heterogeneity, and resource availability. Neuroimaging and electrophysiological studies indicate that children with cerebral palsy may present with corticospinal tract impairment, altered cerebellar thalamic cortical circuitry, interhemispheric inhibitory imbalance, and atypical development of frontoparietal executive control and language related networks. These findings provide a rationale for targeting the primary motor cortex, dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, and selected language related cortices with neuromodulatory interventions. At the mechanistic level, transcranial direct current stimulation and repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation may influence cortical excitability, NMDA receptor mediated long term potentiation and long term depression like plasticity, interhemispheric inhibition, and functional connectivity within distributed neural networks. Current evidence from small to moderate sized randomized trials and recent systematic reviews suggests that these techniques, when combined with task specific rehabilitation, may provide additional benefits for gross motor function, gait, balance, upper limb dexterity, spasticity, and selected cognitive, dual task, and communication outcomes. Available data also suggest acceptable short term safety and tolerability when appropriate pediatric screening and recommended stimulation parameters are applied. This review summarizes the current research progress on noninvasive brain stimulation in children with cerebral palsy and highlights its potential value for optimizing individualized neurorehabilitation strategies and improving motor, cognitive, and communication related outcomes.
authors: Ce Wang; Yuqiu Jia; Xiaoyan Ding; Dandan Wang; Qing Shi; 詹莎莎; Zhicheng Bao; Lei Huang

title: Artificial Intelligence Adoption in Facility Management Procurement: A Systematic Literature Review and Research Agenda
abstract: Facility management (FM) procurement faces increasing complexity due to globalised supply chains, regulatory pressures, and demands for cost optimisation and transparency. Although artificial intelligence (AI) offers transformative potential for procurement efficiency, its adoption in FM contexts remains underexplored, as research on AI in procurement and on digital technologies in FM has developed largely in parallel. This systematic literature review examines AI adoption in FM procurement by addressing four research questions concerning readiness factors, adoption strategies, framework components and theoretical foundations, and the research gaps that justify the development of an expert-consensus AI adoption framework. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, 12 databases were searched across six evidence streams for studies published from 2000 to 2026. From 3,245 identified records, 994 unique records remained after deduplication, 500 underwent full-text assessment, and 180 studies met the inclusion criteria. Quality appraisal employed CASP, JBI, MMAT, ROBINS-I, and conceptual quality checklists, and thematic synthesis was used to integrate the evidence. The review identified 33 readiness factors across five dimensions (organisational, technological, human resource, data, and external readiness), with top management support, data quality, and IT infrastructure emerging as the most critical. Twenty-four adoption strategies were categorised into five groups, with phased implementation and executive sponsorship most frequently recommended. The Technology-Organisation-Environment (TOE) framework emerged as the most suitable theoretical lens. Only 18 of 180 studies (10%) specifically addressed AI in FM procurement, revealing a significant domain-specific research gap, while publication output has grown exponentially since 2018. The findings reveal a fragmented research landscape and provide a foundation for developing context-specific AI adoption frameworks for FM procurement. Seven critical research gaps are identified, including the need for domain-specific frameworks, empirical validation through expert consensus methods, and studies in Southeast Asian contexts, offering actionable insights for FM organisations, procurement professionals, technology vendors, and policymakers.
authors: Nor Hazlin Md Gharip; Norliana Sarpin; Roshartini Omar
venue: International journal of research and scientific innovation

title: Artificial Intelligence Adoption in SMEs: Linking Adoption Conditions to Entrepreneurial Competitiveness
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming how small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) operate, innovate, and compete. However, AI adoption remains uneven because SMEs often face limitations in technological capability, managerial expertise, financial resources, and access to skilled employees. This theoretical paper develops an integrated framework explaining both the conditions shaping AI adoption and how adoption may contribute to entrepreneurial competitiveness. Drawing on the Technology–Organisation–Environment (TOE) framework and a resource-based perspective, the paper synthesises recent literature on AI adoption, SME digital transformation, organisational capability, and competitiveness. The framework proposes a two-stage process. First, perceived benefits, digital/AI capability, top management support, resource constraints, and competitive pressure shape the extent to which SMEs integrate AI into organisational activities. Second, AI adoption can contribute to entrepreneurial competitiveness through improved innovation, market responsiveness, decision-making, operational efficiency, and opportunity identification. The paper argues that adoption alone does not automatically generate competitive advantage. Competitive value depends on SMEs' ability to combine AI with complementary organisational knowledge, capabilities, and managerial commitment. By linking adoption conditions with strategic outcomes, the framework moves beyond research focused primarily on adoption intention and provides a basis for future empirical examination of how SMEs translate AI investment into competitive value.
authors: Ahmed Abdelkader
venue: Proceedings of the International Conference on AI Research.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Peroral Endoscopic Myotomy: Current Evidence, Limitations, and Future Directions
abstract: Peroral endoscopic myotomy (POEM) is an established treatment for achalasia and selected spastic esophageal motility disorders, but several aspects of care remain highly operator-dependent. These include early diagnosis, patient selection, procedural planning, myotomy length, intra-procedural safety, training assessment, and prediction of post-procedure reflux. Artificial intelligence (AI) may help address these limitations by integrating endoscopic video, high-resolution manometry, timed barium esophagram, EndoFLIP, clinical variables, procedural data, and follow-up outcomes into more personalized decision-support tools. This narrative review critically examines the evidence for AI across the POEM pathway and distinguishes direct achalasia or POEM evidence from adjacent and conceptual applications. Early AI applications are most likely to emerge in achalasia detection during diagnostic endoscopy, automated motility interpretation, video-based procedural assessment, and prediction of clinical response or post-POEM reflux. More ambitious applications, such as real-time tunnel orientation, vessel recognition, mucosal injury alerts, and personalized myotomy planning, remain largely investigational. Most AI-specific POEM applications remain at an early or conceptual stage and require multicenter validation, standardized outcomes, and careful clinical governance. AI should support, rather than replace, expert judgment, and an AI-derived reflux estimate cannot replace standard follow-up or objective reflux assessment.
authors: MD Ahmed Abdallah Salman; Ahmed Abdallah

title: Artificial Intelligence in the Assessment and Management of Spasticity: A Scoping Review
abstract: Spasticity is a prevalent and disabling consequence of upper motor neuron disorders, yet its assessment and management remains clinically challenging. Artificial intelligence (AI) may offer opportunities to enhance the objective assessment, prediction, and management of spasticity; however, the current evidence base has not been comprehensively characterised. This review systematically mapped evidence on the application of AI across the continuum of spasticity care and identified key evidence gaps to inform future research. PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, and Web of Science were searched for peer-reviewed English-language studies evaluating AI in adult spasticity. Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed methodological quality using NHLBI tools and PROBAST + AI. This scoping review was prospectively registered with the Open Science Framework Registries. The search yielded 1832 records, of which 21 studies were included after screening. One additional study was identified through citation searching, bringing the total to 22 studies involving 1114 participants. Applications spanned four clinical domains: discrimination between spastic and healthy individuals (n = 2), severity assessment (n = 18), risk prediction (n = 1), and treatment response prediction (n = 1). Most studies focused on post-stroke upper limb spasticity. Surface electromyography was the most frequently used input modality, often integrated with kinematic or kinetic sensors. Conventional machine learning predominated, with reported accuracies of 74–96% and the Modified Ashworth Scale as the most common reference standard. All 22 studies were at high overall risk of bias on PROBAST + AI, and none performed external validation, highlighting substantial methodological limitations that constrain clinical translation.
authors: Ruoxi Cao; Ruojin Li; Joon Sin Ser; Yeow Leng Tan; Jing Chen

title: Assistive and rehabilitative effects of non-weight bearing wearable robots for gait improvement in neurological conditions
abstract: Gait impairment substantially limits mobility and functional independence in individuals with neurological conditions. Portable, non-weight bearing lower-limb wearable robots may address residual gait deficits during voluntary overground walking and support repeated gait training. However, these devices have only recently gained attention, and their effects have not been synthesized or compared across neurological conditions. This review examines wearable robotic interventions for ambulatory individuals with stroke, cerebral palsy, Parkinson’s disease, multiple sclerosis, and incomplete spinal cord injury, focusing on target gait deficits, target joints, and assistive and rehabilitative effects. Target joints and intervention strategies varied across conditions, with the clinical rationale not always clear. In stroke and cerebral palsy, both assistive and rehabilitative effects have been reported, but their underlying mechanisms and the relationship between the two effects remain insufficiently understood. Studies in Parkinson’s disease, multiple sclerosis, and incomplete spinal cord injury were limited, precluding definitive conclusions highlighting the need for further investigation that accounts for the characteristics of each condition. Interpretation of intervention effects was further complicated by variability in outcome selection and how meaningful gait improvement was defined. Future research should better align gait deficits, intervention objectives, and outcome interpretation while addressing inter-individual heterogeneity through personalized strategies. Community-based implementation also warrants further investigation. Ultimately, continued research in this field may help translate improvements in gait into meaningful gains in daily life use.
authors: Sooyeon Choi; Seungjoo Noh; Minjong Kim; Junyeop Lee; Cheolhee Lee; J. Kim

title: Association Between Final Intraoperative Medial Joint Laxity and One-Year Patient Satisfaction After ROSA-Assisted Medial Unicompartmental Knee Arthroplasty
abstract: Background Robotic-assisted unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (UKA) provides intraoperative measurements of joint laxity, but the relationship between final medial joint laxity and postoperative patient satisfaction remains unclear. This study investigated the associations of medial joint laxity measured at 0° and 90° of knee flexion with one-year patient satisfaction after ROSA-assisted medial UKA. Methods This retrospective, single-center study included patients who underwent ROSA-assisted medial UKA between January 2024 and May 2025. The primary outcome was the Patient Satisfaction domain of the 2011 Knee Society Score (KSS) at one year postoperatively. Multivariable linear regression was performed in patients with complete data, with medial joint laxity at 0° and 90° included simultaneously and preoperative Patient Satisfaction included as a covariate. Heteroscedasticity-consistent HC3 robust standard errors were used. The difference between the regression coefficients at the two angles was also assessed. Secondary analyses examined the Symptoms, Patient Expectations, and Functional Activities domains. Results Ninety-five patients were included in the primary analysis. Greater medial joint laxity at 0° was associated with lower one-year Patient Satisfaction (regression coefficient, − 1.19 points/mm; 95% confidence interval [CI], − 2.09 to − 0.29; P = .009). Laxity at 90° was not significantly associated with Patient Satisfaction (− 0.66 points/mm; 95% CI, − 2.47 to 1.14; P = .473). The difference between the regression coefficients at 90° and 0° was not statistically significant (0.53 points/mm; 95% CI, − 1.70 to 2.77; P = .640). No statistically significant associations were observed between laxity at either angle and the secondary KSS domains. Conclusions Greater final intraoperative medial joint laxity at 0° was associated with lower one-year Patient Satisfaction after ROSA-assisted medial UKA. However, the association did not differ significantly between measurements obtained at 0° and 90°. These findings suggest a potential relationship between extension-position medial laxity and patient satisfaction, but further prospective studies using standardized measurements are needed to confirm the findings and establish their clinical significance. Trial registration Not applicable. This study was a retrospective observational study and did not involve a clinical trial.
authors: Matsumoto K, Ishimaru D, Sohmiya K, Terabayashi N.

title: Atomic cluster expansion potentials for screw dislocations in BCC refractory metals
abstract: Accurate atomistic modeling of screw dislocations in body-centered cubic (BCC) metals remains challenging because their plasticity is governed by complex dislocation glide behavior due to their compact threefold symmetric core structure and a strongly temperature-dependent flow stress induced by the large Peierls barrier. In the context of group 5 (V, Nb, and Ta) and group 6 (Mo and W) refractory metals (RMs), both classical interatomic potentials and some machine-learning potentials consistently fail to reproduce density functional theory (DFT) Peierls barriers and the glide plane. Here, we developed an array of atomic cluster expansion (ACE) potentials for these RMs by extending an existing DFT database. The developed ACE potentials significantly improve the description of screw dislocation properties, showing good agreement with the DFT references for Mo and W and substantial improvement for V, Nb, and Ta. The results show that transferability to screw dislocation behavior depends sensitively on both database composition and element-specific energetics and that achieving a single-humped Peierls barrier alone is not a sufficient validation metric for accurate prediction of dislocation glide. For Nb, Mo, and W, the developed ACE models also enable reliable calculation of kink-pair activation enthalpies, which are well described by both Kocks' law and a line-tension model.
authors: Lei Zhang; Francesco Maresca

title: Attenuated motor neuroplasticity after tongue-muscle training in older adults: A proof-of-concept study
abstract: PURPOSE: Low tongue pressure contributes to dysphagia by compromising safe swallowing. While tongue-lift training consistently induces corticomotor plasticity in younger individuals, neuromuscular efficacy and motor neuroplasticity in older adults remain unclear. This proof-of-concept study aimed to investigate central and peripheral motor adaptations following brief tongue-lift training in older adults with low tongue pressure. METHODS: Thirteen older adults (8 women, mean age ± SD: 81 ± 4 years) with low tongue pressure (<30 kPa) underwent 41-minute standardized daily tongue-lift training over 5 consecutive days. Maximal tongue pressure was measured daily pre- and post-training. Transcranial magnetic stimulation was administered on days 1 and 5 to evaluate the resting motor threshold (MT) and motor-evoked potential (MEP) map areas of the tongue as measures of corticomotor excitability. Friedman tests were conducted to examine effects of time on outcome parameters. RESULTS: The 5-day tongue training induced a significant increase in maximal tongue pressure (33.0%; P = 0.005) with a significant decrease in its coefficient of variation (-51.5%, P = 0.030), accompanied by a significant decrease in the tongue MT (-11.3%, P < 0.001). However, the tongue MEP cortical map area did not change significantly (P = 0.853). CONCLUSIONS: These findings provide preliminary evidence for attenuated motor neuroplasticity following tongue-muscle training in older adults. Nevertheless, improved tongue motor function and corticobulbar excitability indicate that the potential for neurophysiological and functional adaptation remains intact. A better understanding of these age-related differences may contribute to the development of rehabilitation strategies for older adults with oral hypofunction.
authors: Yukako Matsuda; 裕紀 森岡; Takayuki Kusunoki; Takashi Iida; Peter J. Svensson; Kazuya Takahashi; Akiko Shimada

title: Automated and noninvasive in vivo mapping of brain functions in the human cortex
abstract: Mapping forms the basis for understanding the functional organization of the brain and for developing targeted interventions in neurological and psychiatric disorders. Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) is a non-invasive tool that allows causal mapping of cortical functions involved in motor control, speech, and connectivity. Since manual mapping procedures limit standardization, we present an automated cortical mapping method that integrates electronically controlled multi-locus TMS with a Bayesian optimization algorithm for identifying stimulation targets efficiently and objectively through a closed-loop framework. We localized individual motor representation area peaks with high accuracy (average 2.4 mm and 5° deviation from the optimum) in only approximately 4 minutes. This represents a substantial advancement over current mapping approaches, providing the means to greatly accelerate and standardize both research and clinical protocols while maintaining high reliability. We anticipate that our approach can further extend to map other cortical functions that cannot be easily analyzed online by a human operator.
authors: Ida Granö; Olli‐Pekka Kahilakoski; Mikael Laine; Miriam Kirchhoff; Oskari Ahola; Ana Maria Soto; Renan H.
