title: Availability-Aware Historical Feedback Learning for Electric Arc Furnace Temperature and Chemical Composition Prediction
abstract: Electric arc furnace (EAF) steelmaking plays an increasingly important role in recycled and lower-carbon steel production. However, variability in charged materials, energy input, and operating conditions makes accurate prediction of molten steel temperature and final chemical composition challenging. Intermittent or delayed measurements limit the information available for timely prediction. This study develops an availability-aware historical-feedback learning framework for predicting EAF endpoint temperature and the final concentrations of twelve chemical elements. Eight industrial data sources are integrated into three progressively enriched predictor representations comprising 19 static, 39 temporal, and 47 history-informed features. Historical outcomes are incorporated only when eligible under an assumed 60-minute measurement-release delay. Using 19,738 temperature heats and 3,341 chemistry heats, twelve tuned regression algorithms are evaluated through chronological forward validation. The proposed historical-feedback representation reduces root mean squared error (RMSE) in 147 of 156 matched algorithm-target comparisons. For temperature prediction, ExtraTrees achieves an RMSE of 12.290 degrees C, representing a 5.54 percent reduction compared with its temporal-only counterpart. Historical-feature ablation and feedback-delay sensitivity analyses demonstrate the importance of recent outcome information and its availability. In a separate retrospective later-period evaluation, lightweight adaptive residual correction reduces temperature RMSE from 12.502 to 12.275 degrees C without retraining the underlying model. Exploratory deep learning comparisons and target-specific feature-attribution analyses provide additional insights into predictive behavior. The results establish historical outcome availability and sequential feedback as important considerations for EAF endpoint prediction.
authors: Ahmed Shoyeb Raihan; Farzana Islam; Ashish Nimbarte; Imtiaz Ahmed

title: Axonic-Revive Spasticity Reset and Regeneration Multi-Phasic Integrative Strategy for Functional Neural Repair after Complete Traumatic Spinal Cord Transection
abstract: Chronic complete spinal cord injury remains a major challenge in regenerative neurobiology due to the formation of an inhibitory microenvironment that limits spontaneous axonal regeneration. This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of a sequential three-phase therapeutic strategy combining modulation of glial scarring, neurotrophic stimulation of axonal growth, and brain-computer interface-controlled neuromodulation for motor recovery after chronic spinal cord injury. The study involved 69 male Sprague-Dawley rats with complete spinal cord transection at the T9–T10 thoracic level. After an eight-week period for the development of chronic spasticity, the animals were allocated to standard rehabilitation (n=13), Phase I (n=14), Phase I+II (n=15), Phase I+II+III (n=14), or Phase III only (n=13). Functional, electrophysiological, molecular, and histological outcomes were assessed over 24 weeks. The complete protocol led to a 50.2% reduction in pathological reflex responses and an improved locomotor function to 13.7 points, representing a 15.2-fold increase compared with controls. The regenerating axon density increased 7.8 times, the synaptic density 5.8 times, and reinnervated motor units 17.9 times. Neurotrophic factors increased 3.3–3.7 times, while pro-inflammatory cytokines decreased by 52%. The full protocol was also associated with ectopic sprouting (2.4±1.1 points) and a lower mechanical withdrawal threshold (2.1±0.5 g), indicating greater mechanical hypersensitivity. Regression analysis showed that 91% of the functional recovery variability was explained by structural and molecular predictors. The findings suggest an improved locomotor recovery with sequential multimodal treatment in this rat model, while the safety findings and lack of large-animal validation limit direct clinical extrapolation.
authors: Ireneusz Siemionkowicz

title: BanglaBBQ: A Bias Benchmark for Question Answering in the Bangladeshi Context
abstract: This paper presents BanglaBBQ, a question-answering bias benchmark designed to capture stereotypes grounded in the Bangladeshi context, in both Bangla and English. Following KoBBQ and PakBBQ, BanglaBBQ adapts the original Bias Benchmark for Question Answering (BBQ) by classifying its templates into three groups: directly translated (DT), modified to align target groups or contexts with Bangladesh (TM), and removed when deemed unsuitable for the Bangladeshi context (SR). This process retains 140 templates across six categories, comprising 76 DT and 64 TM templates. Five newly authored (NA) categories, based on stereotypes common in Bangladeshi society, are then added: marital status, age and political perception, regional origin, educational background, and mental-health status. Native Bangladeshi annotators judged all 466 newly authored templates, and 372 were retained because a strict majority of English annotators identified the intended target and rated the attitude as common enough. Each newly authored template is linked to a documented source and a verbatim quote from it. Each evaluated template also has a counter-stereotypical version of its disambiguated context. The dataset was evaluated using two open-weight models (Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B) and two closed models (GPT-4.1-mini and Gemini 2.5 Flash). All four lean towards the stereotyped person when the context is ambiguous, in both languages, and the effect of language differs by model, so English results do not predict behaviour in Bangla. On the adapted BBQ templates, both Qwen3 models are also less accurate when the context contradicts a stereotype than when it confirms it. On the newly authored templates, the closed models follow counter-stereotypical evidence almost perfectly, and all four models are more biased on the templates that annotators validated than on those they rejected.
authors: Sumit Anthony Gomes; Yasin Rahman; Taeeba Tasnia; Faiza Nooren Suhita

title: Bayesian adaptive design for neural recruitment curves
abstract: Nonlinear response models remain ubiquitous across disciplines with recruitment curves describing muscle response to neural stimulation. Conventional acquisition methods typically rely on static uniform sampling, requiring many stimuli, while adaptive threshold-hunting designs such as ML-PEST forfeit accurate characterization of the overall curve. We present a Bayesian adaptive design that uses posterior uncertainty over curve parameters to propose stimuli that maximize information gain across the full recruitment curve. We additionally implement a focused acquisition method that can target arbitrary subset of curve parameters, which we use to evaluate and interpret our design. In simulations, our design outperforms uniform sampling in recovering threshold while matching ML-PEST, and outperforms ML-PEST in predictive curve accuracy while matching uniform. It likewise matches our threshold-focused acquisition, suggesting our design doesn't trade off threshold estimation for recovering the curve. We further show data collected using our design yields greater power when detecting a change in threshold in intervention studies. Our design proposes the next stimulus within 5 seconds, making it feasible for transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) experiments. Finally, we validate our design in TMS experiments and provide a library for Python, called onMEP, for online acquisition of neural recruitment curves.
authors: Vishweshwar Tyagi; Saihari S. Dukkipati; Daniel Twili; Jonas M. Mikhaeil; Andrew Gelman; Jason B. Carmel; James R. McIntosh

title: Bio-inspired open ligamentous knee joint with extended pitch and yaw range of motion
abstract: This study presents a bio-inspired open knee joint for biofidelic robots with an anatomically correct range of motion. Bio-inspired joints contribute to robot performance and understanding living organisms by providing dynamic motion data as the real-world physical twin. The proposed joint structure features the integration of the open joint and ligamentous constraint. In particular, the spherical envelope of the condyles contributes to the rotation other than pitch rotation. By applying a bio-inspired ligament arrangement, the developed knee joint performed pitch and yaw motion. The relationship between the ligament length and joint orientation was derived by forward kinematics and the ligament wrapping. The arrangement of the bio-inspired collateral ligaments was determined with the iterative calculation method considering the object wrapping, which predicted the yaw range of motion. Verification of the proposed approach includes the evaluation of the range of motion on the robotic knee joint equipped with the motor-driven tendons. The robot validation tests include the rotational motions around the pitch and yaw axes. The tests showed that the proposed joint structure can be a relevant approach for replicating the range of motion of a human knee joint. Future work includes the motion control of the joint system and integration into a real robot.
authors: Shinsuke Nakashima; Yilun Sun; Julius Ambros; Robin Schregle; Christoph Rehekampff; Qi An; Atsushi Yamashita; Tim Christian Lueth

title: Bivariate Multiscale Sample Entropy of Frontoparietal-Subgenual ACC Dynamics in Depression During Accelerated TMS at 7 T
abstract: Objective: To examine whether longitudinal changes in frontoparietal (FP) - subgenual anterior cingulate cortex (sgACC) joint temporal complexity differ between sgACC hemispheres in patients undergoing accelerated TMS (aTMS) and untreated healthy controls. Methods: Twenty-four patients with current depressive episodes and fifteen healthy controls underwent 7T resting-state fMRI at baseline and follow-up. Patients received aTMS localized to the left DLPFC using Beam-F3. The same bilateral FP time series was paired separately with left and right sgACC time series. Bivariate multiscale sample entropy (bMSE) across scale factors a1-a10 was summarized by trapezoidal integration as a complexity index (bMSE-CI). The primary test was the Group x Time x sgACC Hemisphere interaction in a mixed repeated-measures ANOVA. Scale-specific interactions and clinical Spearman correlations were evaluated with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction. Change scores were follow-up minus baseline. Results: The bMSE-CI Group x Time x Hemisphere interaction was significant (F(1,37) = 6.043, p = 0.0188, partial Eta squared = 0.140). Mean left/right bMSE-CI changes were -0.286/+0.124 in patients and +0.323/+0.112 in controls. Of ten scale-specific three-way interactions, only a2 survived FDR correction (q = 0.0435). No baseline or change-score bMSE-MADRS association survived the specified FDR corrections. A random-intercept-only mixed-model sensitivity analysis did not reach statistical significance for the three-way interaction (p = 0.0718). Conclusion: FP-sgACC joint temporal complexity showed hemisphere-dependent longitudinal differences between patients undergoing aTMS and healthy controls. These exploratory findings motivate further evaluation of bMSE as a candidate measure of longitudinal neural change in depression. Independent replication, more precise reliability estimates, and prospective validation of clinical relevance are needed.
authors: Niklaus Denier; Matthias Grieder; Kay Jann; Pascal Borel; Stefan Dendorfer; Gianluca Andri Florineth; Kristina Adorjan; Andrea Federspiel; Roland Wiest; Leila Maria Soravia; Sebastian Walther; Tobias Bracht

title: Blockchain in the digital value creation chain of a retail enterprise
abstract: The digital transformation of retailing increasingly affects not only individual operations but the architecture of value creation, delivery, capture, and reproduction. The article develops a conceptual approach to managing the digital value creation chain within the retail enterprise business model and examines blockchain as a cross-cutting mechanism for transparency, traceability, and trusted data exchange. The study systematizes the stages of the digital value creation chain, including product identification and data capture, demand analytics and personalization, order processing, procurement and inventory replenishment, warehousing and fulfilment, sales and delivery, and post-purchase relationship management. The proposed model integrates CRM, SRM, WMS, TMS, omnichannel interfaces, artificial intelligence, data analytics, and blockchain into a unified digital platform. Particular attention is paid to reducing information asymmetry, verifying product provenance, supporting smart-contract-based interaction, and coordinating participants across the retail ecosystem. The findings substantiate that blockchain creates managerial and economic value when embedded in a broader business-model configuration rather than introduced as an isolated technology. The paper formulates practical implications for retail enterprises redesigning value creation around reliable data, customer experience, and platform-based coordination.
authors: Kravchenko E.S.
venue: Economy and business: theory and practice

title: Botulinum toxin type a within function-oriented management of post-stroke spasticity: a narrative review
abstract: Post-stroke spasticity (PSS) is a heterogeneous complication of stroke that affects motor recovery, care needs, pain, positioning, and participation in daily life. Current management frameworks commonly stratify patients by time since stroke, but disease duration alone does not capture differences in neural mechanisms, residual voluntary control, functional priorities, or response to intervention. This narrative review searched PubMed, the Cochrane Library, and Wanfang databases from inception to May 2026, prioritizing randomized controlled trials, prospective cohort studies, systematic reviews, real-world studies, Goal Attainment Scaling research, the Upper Limb International Spasticity cohort series, best-practice guidance, and clinical trials including BEST and InTENSE. We synthesize evidence that PSS heterogeneity can be understood across central and peripheral mechanisms, temporal trajectories, and active versus passive functional consequences. Available studies suggest that active and passive functional goals differ in baseline functional profiles, outcome assessment, treatment response, and intervention requirements. However, patients sharing a functional goal type may still differ in residual voluntary control, neural and non-neural contributors to movement restriction, pain, mobility, and care dependency. Botulinum toxin type A is well aligned with focal tone reduction and passive goals, including pain relief, hygiene, and limb positioning. It may also support contracture-prevention strategies when modifiable neural muscle overactivity remains, whereas active functional gains usually require preserved motor potential and integration with task-oriented training, rehabilitation, and adjunctive modalities. We propose that functional goal type should complement time-based staging as a decision dimension rather than serve as a complete clinical phenotype. This combined framework may better align patient selection, intervention matching, outcome assessment, and longitudinal treatment planning. Prospective goal-stratified studies and standardized assessment tools are needed to test its clinical utility.
authors: Baoling Su; Yating Huang; Xiaotong Li; Kun Wang; Bing Bao

title: Brief Trains of Closed-loop TMS Induce Controllable Power in FM-theta Oscillations
abstract:
Objective

Frontal-midline theta (FM-theta; 4–8 Hz) oscillations are thought to support cognition. Brief trains of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) can probe these oscillations with high temporal precision but have rarely changed theta power. One possible reason is that prior studies ignored the instantaneous phase of the oscillation, which strongly shapes the cortical response to TMS. We tested whether brief TMS trains triggered at specific FM-theta phases in real time directionally modulate post-train FM-theta power.

Approach

Six healthy adults received TMS over dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (Fz) with concurrent electroencephalography during a whole-report working memory task. A beamformer and real-time phase-estimation pipeline triggered four-pulse 6 Hz trains (110% of resting motor threshold) at FM-theta peaks (0°) or troughs (180°), randomized trial by trial. Post-train spectral power was decomposed into total, induced (non-phase-locked) and evoked (phase-locked) components.

Main results

Trough-triggered trains transiently increased post-train FM-theta power relative to peak-triggered trains; task performance did not differ. Cluster-based permutation tests showed trough−peak differences in total (4.6–7.1 Hz) and induced (5.0–7.8 Hz) power ∼50–440 ms after the train, suggesting amplification of the oscillation . No evoked effect was detected. The total-power effect was robust at the subject level (Cohen’s dz = 1.32, p = 0.023). Within-train theta power did not differ between conditions, suggesting a cortical origin.

Significance

To our knowledge, this is the first study to lock brief rhythmic TMS trains to the real-time phase of an ongoing oscillation, and to show phase-dependent modulation of FM-theta power after individual trains on timescales relevant to behavior. Open-loop brief-train protocols may have missed such effects by mixing facilitatory and suppressive phases. Phase-locked brief trains offer a precise tool for testing the causal role of oscillations in cognition.
authors: Erickson B, Kim B, Degenhart A, Stenroos M, Rich R, Medaglia J.

title: Burning Questions in Neuropsychology
abstract: This book is an indispensable resource for students and teachers of clinical and experimental neuropsychology. It does not replace standard textbooks but complements them by addressing questions and perspectives often overlooked in conventional introductions. Rather than presenting material to be memorized, it encourages readers to reflect, question, and remain curious. Psychometric testing has its place, but scores alone never tell the whole story. Burning Questions in Neuropsychology looks beyond numbers to the human realities they represent. In doing so, the book will ignite curiosity, which is essential for opening newer perspectives.
authors: Peter Brugger

title: Cannabis-based product use in multiple sclerosis: a Swiss nationwide, registry-based observational study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Cannabis-based products are commonly used to manage multiple sclerosis (MS) symptoms such as spasticity and pain. However, the prevalence of cannabis-based product use, types of products used and factors associated with use remain unexplored in the Swiss MS population. OBJECTIVE: To estimate the prevalence of cannabis-based product use, identify factors associated with use and characterise use patterns among people with MS enrolled in the Swiss Multiple Sclerosis Registry (SMSR). Additionally, we explored trends in cannabis-based product types, prescription status and insurance reimbursement over time. METHODS: This exploratory observational study analysed self-reported data collected between 2016 and 2024. Prevalence estimates and associated factors were assessed using descriptive statistics and multivariable logistic regression on participants’ baseline responses. Follow-up data from cannabis-based product users were analysed descriptively to evaluate temporal trends. RESULTS: Of the 2193 participants, 330 (14.4%) reported current cannabis-based product use at baseline. Use varied by year of baseline questionnaire completion, ranging from 12.2% in 2016 to 25.6% in 2022. Cannabis-based product use was positively associated with reporting five or more symptoms (odds ratio [OR]: 2.41, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.19–5.24), presence of dysphagia (OR: 2.02, 95% CI: 1.27–3.17), spasms (OR: 1.59, 95% CI: 1.13–2.23), pain (OR: 1.48, 95% CI: 1.07–2.05) and greater gait disability (OR: 2.05, 95% CI: 1.39–3.01 for moderate; OR: 2.76, 95% CI: 1.56–4.85 for severe vs mild). Male sex (OR: 1.44, 95% CI: 1.06–1.96) was associated with higher odds of cannabis-based product use, while older age (OR: 0.98 per year, 95% CI: 0.96–0.99) and use of disease-modifying therapies (OR: 0.68, 95% CI: 0.49–0.95) were associated with lower odds. Follow-up data from 469 cannabis-based product users, providing 876 responses, showed cannabidiol was the most frequently used product between 2018 and 2022 but declined from 40% of reported use in 2019–2020 to 25% in 2023. In contrast, nabiximols use increased from 20% in 2018 to 30% in 2023, becoming the most commonly used product. The proportion of prescribed cannabis-based products rose from approximately 30% to 40%, while insurance reimbursement increased from 76% to 93% over the follow-up period. CONCLUSIONS: Cannabis-based product use among people with MS exceeded rates seen in the general population in Switzerland. Higher symptom burden and greater disability may be key drivers of use. Increasing prescription and reimbursement rates over time suggest a shift towards more regulated, medically supervised use, likely influenced by evolving policy.
authors: Gábor Horváth; Mina Stanikić; Claude Vaney; Sabin Ammann; Claudia Baum; Pasquale Calabrese; Andrew Chan; Christian P. Kamm; Patrick Roth; Chiara Zecca; Viktor von Wyl

title: Case report and literature review of spastic paraplegia type 5: a patient with two heterozygous CYP7B1 nonsense variants
abstract: Background Hereditary spastic paraplegia type 5 (SPG5) is a rare autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder associated with biallelic CYP7B1 variants and altered oxysterol metabolism. The relationship between genotype and clinical severity remains uncertain. Case Presentation We describe a 55-year-old woman evaluated at age 55 years for progressive spastic paraplegia. Sequencing identified two heterozygous CYP7B1 nonsense variants, c.1162C>T and c.334C>T, but their allelic phase was not established. An exploratory pooled analysis included 131 patients, of whom 80 had classifiable ambulatory status. In univariable mean bias-reduced cumulative logit regression, the presence of at least one truncating variant was associated with lower odds of worse ambulatory status (odds ratio [OR], 0.30; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.12–0.78; P = 0.013). The univariable Firth binary sensitivity analysis showed a similar association with wheelchair dependence or no functional ambulation (OR, 0.31; 95% CI, 0.09–0.99; P = 0.048). After adjustment for disease duration, the genotype estimate remained in the same direction but was imprecise (OR, 0.35; 95% CI, 0.12–1.04; P = 0.059), while longer duration was associated with worse ambulatory status (OR per 10 years, 2.22; 95% CI, 1.51–3.26; P < 0.001). Conclusion The clinical findings and two heterozygous CYP7B1 nonsense variants support SPG5 as the leading diagnosis, although their phase and combined functional effect remain unconfirmed. In pooled cross-sectional data, truncating-variant status showed a consistent univariable association with less severe ambulatory impairment, but the adjusted estimate was uncertain. Larger cohorts with standardized outcomes are needed to assess this genotype–phenotype association.

title: Challenges of implementing Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) systems in Bangladesh
abstract: Goal: This study examines why Bangladeshi companies struggle to adopt ERP systems, looking at organizational, technical, and human hurdles. By combining the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and Critical Success Factors (CSF) frameworks, it shows how user acceptance and organizational readiness directly drive ERP success. Methodology: A sequential exploratory mixed-method design was used. First, a PRISMA-guided literature review mapped out key ERP challenges to shape the survey. Questionnaires were then gathered from 30 professionals across multiple Bangladeshi sectors with hands-on ERP experience. Finally, the data was analyzed using descriptive statistics, Cronbach’s alpha, one-sample t-tests, and Cohen’s d to evaluate reliability, significance, and practical effect size. Results: Cronbach’s alpha was 0.560, indicating moderate internal consistency. All seven ERP challenges were statistical significant. Budget limitations, lack of training and support, shortage of skilled personnel and maintenance costs demonstrated strong practical effects, whereas data migration, employee resistance and weak top management support also emerged as significant barriers. Limitations: The study is exploratory, cross-sectional, and based on a small sample. Practical implications: Organizations should focus on training, budgeting, skilled teams, leadership support, change management, and data governance. Originality/Value: The study adds Bangladesh-based ERP evidence using an integrated TAM-CSF perspective.

title: Characterising cortical perturbation-recovery dynamics using TMS-EEG: The Brain Dynamic Metric Toolbox
abstract: Objective To adapt dynamical measures used in computational and experimental perturbation models to human transcranial magnetic stimulation-electroencephalography (TMS-EEG) and determine whether analysis of the extended post-stimulation trajectory reveals additional features of the cortical response to long-interval intracortical inhibition (LICI). Methods Single-pulse and paired-pulse LICI TMS-EEG responses from the bilateral dorsolateral prefrontal cortex were re-analysed in 16 healthy adults. At the stimulation site, 75 single-pulse and 75 paired-pulse trials were delivered; paired pulses comprised conditioning and test stimuli separated by 100 ms. Responses from 20 frontocentral EEG channels were analysed from 50–950 ms following TMS using the open-source Brain Dynamic Metric Toolbox. Perturbative Integration Latency Index (PILI) indexed cortical resilience via response energy and recovery, Autocorrelation Function Width (ACFW) captured temporal memory, and Lyapunov Exponent (LE) indicated the dynamical stability. Linear mixed-effects models examined temporal, spectral, and time-frequency effects from the measured metrics. Results LICI altered the temporal evolution of the dynamical measures. PILI distinguished conditions in the earliest post-stimulation window before converging, whereas ACFW differences persisted across a broader early interval. LE showed weaker and less consistent discrimination. Spectral effects were most evident for ACFW, while time-frequency analyses revealed later, frequency-specific LICI effects for PILI and ACFW but not LE. Conclusions The extended post-stimulation trajectory revealed LICI-related differences in cortical resilience and temporal memory with distinct temporal and spectral profiles, while effects on dynamical stability were less consistent. Significance The Brain Dynamic Metric Toolbox provides a reproducible framework for quantifying perturbation-recovery dynamics in TMS-EEG and demonstrates that the extended perturbational response contains information about LICI not captured by discrete early response measures. Graphical Abstract Responses to single-pulse transcranial magnetic stimulation with electroencephalography (TMS–EEG) and paired-pulse stimulation using long-interval intracortical inhibition (LICI) were compared in 16 healthy adults following stimulation of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. Three dynamical metrics, the Perturbative Integration Latency Index (PILI), Autocorrelation Function Width (ACFW) and Lyapunov Exponent (LE), characterised the post-stimulation response across temporal, spectral and time-frequency domains over 950 ms. Inhibitory conditioning was associated with early alterations in cortical resilience, more persistent changes in temporal memory and later frequency-specific effects. LE differences were less consistent. Together, these measures provide complementary characterisation of the evolving response to inhibitory conditioning and are implemented in the user-friendly, open-source Brain Dynamic Metric Toolbox to support reproducible analysis and further physiological and clinical validation. Highlights Dynamical metrics quantify a perturbation-recovery framework for inhibitory TMS-EEG Analysis beyond 300 ms post TMS revealed additional dynamics of paired-pulse inhibition Dynamical metrics captured distinct temporal and spectral inhibitory responses Extended dynamics may help characterise inhibitory processes in brain disorders Open-source toolbox enables reproducible perturbation-recovery analysis

title: Cholinergic inputs to motoneurons in the spinal cord augment focal muscle spasticity in rodents
abstract: Background and Purpose Cholinergic premotor inputs to motoneurons support high levels of motor output when required. However, the possible role of these inputs in pathologically elevated muscle tone has not been characterised. To address this, we examined the modulatory effect of spinal acetylcholine (ACh) on experimental spastic paralysis. Experimental Approach Rats were injected with tetanus neurotoxin (TeNT, 33–100 pg, im) into gastrocnemius to induce sustained rigid hind‐paw extension and resistance to passive ankle flexion. The effects of spinal ACh on experimental hypertonia were probed by lumbar intrathecal application of the AChE inhibitor neostigmine (NEO) or a muscarinic M 2 receptor antagonist (AQ‐RA 741). Effects of NEO on extracellular ACh were measured in the facial nucleus after TeNT (33 pg) or botulinum toxin A (BoNT/A, 2 U) injection into the rat whisker pad. The intensity of TeNT‐evoked hindlimb hypertonia (10 pg, im) was assessed in mice with genetic ablation of cholinergic C bouton source interneurons (V0 C interneurons). Key Results NEO augmented the severity of TeNT‐evoked hypertonia, whereas AQ‐RA 741 attenuated it. Local perfusion of NEO caused a BoNT/A‐sensitive increase in extracellular ACh concentration. The involvement of cholinergic C boutons was corroborated by reduced hypertonia following TeNT challenge (10 pg, im) in V0 C ‐ablated mice. Conclusions and Implications Our results suggest that spinal cholinergic transmission, associated with vesicular ACh release and M 2 signalling at C boutons, exacerbates experimental spastic paralysis. We reveal a new role for endogenous spinal ACh, with implications for developing new therapeutic approaches to treat spasticity and hyperkinetic movement disorders.
authors: Patrik Meglić; Petra Šoštarić; Eirini Tsape; Melpomeni Galani; Ana Knezović; Laura Restani; Marco Pirazzini; Ornella Rossetto; Gareth Brian Miles; Laskaro Zagoraiou; Ivica Matak

title: Clinical-priority task orchestration and verified safety supervision for a physician-directed ward-rounding robot: a simulation-based feasibility study
abstract: Introduction A ward-rounding robot that accepts orders at the level of clinical intent becomes a shared clinical resource: several clinicians may hold outstanding requests of differing urgency, and execution is punctuated by confirmation gates at which the robot waits on a human and by engagement steps that cannot safely be interrupted. This paper formalizes the resulting scheduling problem together with the safety layer that it necessitates. Methods We present (i) a task model in which an intent-level order expands into primitives carrying resource locks, physician confirmation gates, and an explicit interruptibility partition; (ii) the Clinical-Priority Scheduler (CP-Sched), which combines urgency weighting, aging, travel awareness, and class-relative escalation and preempts only at safe interruption points; and (iii) a safety supervisor specified as a network of timed automata and verified exhaustively for a single robot serving one order at a time, with independent reproduction in the TLA+ model checker TLC. All task timings in the 1,590 discrete-event simulation runs are modeling assumptions, not hardware measurements. Results Across 1,080 runs spanning two ward sizes and three utilization levels, CP-Sched reduced the 95th-percentile time for urgent orders to bedside from 347 s to 215 s at moderate utilization, a 38% reduction relative to the strongest of four baselines; all comparisons survived Holm’s correction at p < 0.0001 under both the paired Wilcoxon signed-rank and unpaired Mann–Whitney tests (rank-biserial effect sizes: 0.93–1.00 paired, 0.66–0.93 unpaired). A further 510 runs showed that aging alone cannot bound the waiting time and that escalation at a fixed absolute horizon restores a guarantee only by inflating the urgent tail at saturation. All five clinical invariants hold under the supervisor and each is violable without it, so none is vacuous. Runtime enforcement eliminated all 757 unsafe interruptions observed in the unshielded ablation at a cost of 2.1–35.4 s in the median urgent tail. Discussion The enforcement cost is small but systematic at light and moderate loads and undetectable at saturation, which supports keeping the safety layer independent of the scheduling policy. The formal guarantee covers a single-order model, and absolute timings require calibration on a physical platform.
authors: Cheng Hang; Safaa Najah Saud Al-Humairi; Ahgalya Subbiah

title: Cloud computing adoption model for financial services implementation: An integrated TAM–TTF approach in a developing-country contextExploratory Case Study: Unified Network for Money – Aden
abstract: Cloud computing is a scalable, flexible, pay-per-use model for delivering IT services that can substantially improve how financial institutions process data, scale operations, and serve customers. Yet its adoption in developing and post-conflict economies remains limited. This paper aims to explore the factors that influence the adoption of cloud computing in the financial-services sector as an alternative to costly on-premises infrastructure. Building on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and Task–Technology Fit (TTF), two influential theories in technology adoption research, this study develops an integrated hierarchical model. Data were gathered using a structured questionnaire administered to a census of 40 managerial and technical staff employed at the Unified Network for Money (UNMoney), a payment institution in Aden, Yemen, and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM). In this exploratory case study of a single payment institution, the proposed model accounted for 48.7% of the variance in cloud-computing adoption. Among the statistically significant formative relationships, cloud knowledge and top-management support were the strongest organizational components, whereas perceived usefulness was the strongest component of individual perceptions. Given the small census sample, the findings are interpreted as exploratory. The study contributes an integrated TAM–TTF adoption model for financial services in a developing-country context and offers guidance for raising organizational readiness for cloud adoption.
authors: Rana Khaled Al-Sayed Ali; Ali Balaid; Omaima Bahaidara

title: Community-based RoboGym training improves gross motor function in ambulatory children with cerebral palsy
abstract: Children with cerebral palsy (CP) require sustained, intensive, task-specific rehabilitation, yet conventional community-based rehabilitation (CBR) is often limited by insufficient training dose and lack of assistive technologies. In this pragmatic randomized controlled trial, 60 children with CP (mean age 10.4 ± 1.4 years; Gross Motor Function Classification System levels II–III) were allocated 1:1 to a community-based RoboGym (CRG) integrating five robotic modalities in a task-oriented circuit, or to conventional CBR. Both groups received 90-min sessions twice weekly for 6 months. The primary outcome was the Gross Motor Function Measure-66 (GMFM-66); secondary outcomes were the Pediatric Balance Scale (PBS), Functional Independence Measure (FIM), and Pediatric Quality of Life Inventory (PedsQL). Significant Time × Group interactions favored CRG for GMFM-66 ( p = 0.048), PBS ( p = 0.048), and the PedsQL emotional ( p = 0.039) and social functioning ( p = 0.015) domains; differences in FIM ( p = 0.065) and PedsQL physical functioning ( p = 0.076) also favored CRG but were not statistically significant. The CRG mean GMFM-66 percentile advanced from the 36th to the 48th (individual effect size (iES) = 1.14, large), whereas CBR remained near baseline (iES = 0.29). A higher proportion of CRG participants exceeded the minimal detectable change threshold (37–63% vs. 17–27%), a difference that was statistically significant for GMFM-66, PBS, and FIM. Multi-modal robotic circuit training may offer a scalable community-based approach to CP management, although confirmation in larger multicenter trials is required. title: Comparison of joint laxity measured using 60- and 80-N distraction forces and manual stress during robot-assisted total knee arthroplasty.
abstract:
Background

Appropriate intraoperative soft-tissue balance is essential for achieving successful outcomes following total knee arthroplasty (TKA). However, the optimal distraction force for evaluating joint laxity remains unclear. This study aimed to compare joint laxities measured using specific distraction forces with those obtained under manual varus-valgus stress and assess the interobserver variability.

Methods

A total of 55 bi-cruciate-stabilized TKAs were performed using a robotic system. Medial and lateral joint laxities were evaluated using a force-controlled tensioner device under a distraction force of 60 and 80 N at 10°, 30°, 60°, and 90° of flexion and under manual varus-valgus stress using the robotic system. To assess interobserver differences, all measurements were performed independently by the senior surgeon and one of the assistant surgeons.

Results

In the medial compartment, no statistically significant differences were detected between joint laxity under manual stress and that measured using a distraction force of 80 N at 10° and 30° of flexion. At 90° of flexion, no statistically significant difference was detected between JLR and JLT60N. In the lateral compartment, no statistically significant differences were detected between joint laxity under manual stress and that measured using 80 N at 10° and 90° of flexion, whereas joint laxity under manual stress was significantly greater than that measured using 80 N at 30° and 60° of flexion. Interobserver variability was greater in the lateral compartment than in the medial compartment, especially at higher flexion angles.

Conclusions

The differences between joint laxity measured under manual stress and that measured using a tensioner device varied depending on the compartment and knee flexion angle. The lateral compartment showed greater measurement variability, suggesting the need for careful assessment and standardization of intraoperative joint laxity evaluation during robot-assisted TKA.

title: Correlation of Postural Control with Gross Motor Function in Children with Spastic Cerebral Palsy: An Analytical Cross-Sectional Study
abstract: Background: Poor postural control limits gross motor function in children with spastic cerebral palsy (CP), the most common subtype. In Pakistan, many children reach rehabilitation services at Gross Motor Function Classification System (GMFCS) levels III–V, yet local data on gross motor change during postural-control-focused physiotherapy are scarce. This study assessed the association between postural-control-focused physiotherapy and gross motor function in children with spastic CP. Methods: This analytical cross-sectional study reviewed clinical records from four pediatric rehabilitation centers in Karachi, Pakistan. Through purposive sampling, records of 60 children aged 4–14 years with spastic CP (GMFCS III–V) and two Gross Motor Function Measure-88 (GMFM-88) assessments six months apart were analyzed. Pre–post change was tested with a paired-samples t-test, and its association with clinically meaningful improvement (>40%) with point-biserial correlation. Results: Of the 60 children, 32 (53.3%) were boys. The mean GMFM-88 score increased from 11.40 ± 11.27 to 44.90 ± 20.24 (mean change 33.49; 95% CI 29.40–37.59; p < 0.001; d = 2.11). GMFM-88 change correlated positively with improvement >40% (r = 0.370; p = 0.004). Overall, 41 children (68.3%) improved by more than 40%, with no significant difference between age groups (62.9% vs 76.0%; p = 0.281). Conclusion: Children with spastic CP receiving postural-control-focused physiotherapy made large gross motor gains over six months, and these gains were moderately associated with clinically meaningful improvement regardless of age. Controlled studies with direct postural control measures are needed.
authors: Ebad ur Rehman Khan Ghouri; Syed Wasif Ali; Misbah Shareef; Saira Bano; Hafsa Batool

title: Corticospinal excitability depends on hemodynamic brain state: A study using optical neuroimaging-triggered, brain-state-dependent stimulation
abstract: Background This study aimed to investigate whether a neural interface, which utilizes functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) to trigger transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) based on real-time hemodynamic signals, can modulate corticospinal excitability more effectively than brain-state-independent stimulation. Methods We developed an fNIRS-TMS interface that acquired oxyhemoglobin concentrations from the supplementary motor area (SMA) during kinesthetic motor imagery (KMI). In the brain-state-independent condition, participants performed continuous KMI while TMS pulses were delivered irrespective of their brain state. In the fNIRS-guided state-dependent condition, TMS was triggered to elicit motor evoked potentials (MEPs) only when real-time fNIRS signals from the SMA exceeded a predetermined activation threshold. MEP amplitudes were compared between conditions in both healthy and post-stroke participants. Results In 20 healthy participants, a generalized estimating equation adjusted for VAS revealed that SMA-fNIRS-guided TMS produced significantly larger MEP amplitude compared to the brain-state-independent TMS ( p = 0.010). Parameter estimates indicated that MEP amplitude was lower in the brain-state-independent condition compared to that collected during the brain-state-dependent condition ( B = −0.109, SE = 0.042, 95% CI: [−0.192, −0.026]). However, no significant difference between the two conditions was observed in the included eight patients with subcortical ischemic stroke. Above the individual activation threshold, higher hemodynamic signal levels were associated with lower MEP amplitude ( r = −0.15, p = 0.027). Conclusion The fNIRS-TMS interface shows preliminary technical feasibility for developing brain-state-dependent stimulation to probe and modulate brain function. Whether the absence of brain-state-dependent facilitation of SMA in post-stroke participants reflects impaired SMA-to-M1 facilitatory connectivity, and whether restoring such facilitation is clinically beneficial, warrant further investigation. Clinical trial registration NCT07088107.

title: Critical Success Factors for AI Training Robot Adoption in Accounting SMEs: An Integrated Delphi–DEMATEL–ANP Approach
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Robotic Process Automation (RPA) are transforming accounting services toward intelligent, data-driven professional services. However, small and medium-sized accounting firms (SMEs) face barriers to AI adoption, including limited resources, technological capabilities, employee skills, and regulatory uncertainty. This study identifies and prioritizes the critical success factors (CSFs) influencing AI training robot adoption in Taiwanese accounting SMEs. The framework integrates the Technology–Organization–Environment (TOE) framework, Task–Technology Fit (TTF), Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), Human–Computer Trust (HCT), and Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI). We used a two-round Delphi process with 15 experts to refine the CSFs, followed by DEMATEL to identify causal relationships and ANP to assess their relative priorities. The DEMATEL results indicate that the Technological dimension is the strongest causal driver (D−R = 1.355), followed by the Organizational dimension (D−R = 0.435), whereas Decision Making is the principal effect dimension (D−R = −1.781). The findings further emphasize task–technology alignment, AI maturity, regulatory conditions, top management support, employee AI competence, and human–computer trust. Overall, AI adoption represents an integrated organizational transformation rather than merely a technological investment. The proposed Delphi–DEMATEL–ANP framework provides systematic decision support for resource prioritization, organizational readiness, capability development, and sustainable AI-enabled digital transformation in accounting SMEs. JEL classification numbers: M15, M41, O33, C44. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, AI Training Robots, Accounting SMEs, Task-Technology Fit, DEMATEL, Analytic Network Process, Digital Transformation.
