title: Evaluation of high-dose alerts in computed tomography using an automated dose monitoring system: a retrospective institutional study
abstract: Radiation dose monitoring software (DMS) tools are increasingly used to support automated monitoring of radiation dose in medical imaging. This study evaluated the frequency and causes of high-dose events detected by a DMS in computed tomography (CT). All CT examinations performed at one hospital across three CT scanners over a one-year period were retrospectively analysed to establish the frequency and causes of high-dose alerts. Descriptive statistics summarized alert frequency and distribution, and multivariable logistic regression identified factors independently associated with high-dose alerts. Of 11,865 CT examinations, 851 (7%) exceeded predefined dose thresholds. High-dose alerts occurred most frequently in spine (17%), musculoskeletal joint (14%), abdomen/pelvis (8%), vascular angiography (8%), chest/lung (5%), and head/face (4%) examinations. Reasons for high-dose alerts included high body mass index (29%), scan repetition (25%), additional scans (15%), patient malpositioning (12%), excess scan range (11%), and orthopaedic hardware (6%). Multivariable analysis showed that overweight status, scanner model, spine and joint examinations, and patients aged 45-74 years were independently associated with high-dose alert occurrence (P < .05). DMS is an effective tool that enables imaging facilities to automatically identify high-dose events, facilitating investigation of their causes, protocol review, and identification of opportunities for dose optimisation.
authors: Mohammed Sadon Alanazi; Peter L. Kench; Seyedamir Tavakoli-Taba; Matthew Russell; Ernest Usang Ekpo

title: Experts' and AI perspectives on the environmental sustainability of tensile membrane structures
abstract: Purpose With increasing demands for sustainable construction, there is growing interest in enhancing the environmental performance of tensile membrane structures (TMS). This study aims to investigate the environmental sustainability challenges and opportunities of TMS across their lifecycle stages by integrating expert insights and advanced AI-generated perspectives. Design/methodology/approach A qualitative methodology was employed using semi-structured interviews with 16 experienced professionals including architects, engineers, contractors, builders, environmental sustainability experts and researchers. To enhance the reliability of findings and address potential gaps, the study also utilised artificial intelligence (AI) tools (ChatGPT and DeepSeek) to compare human expert insights with AI responses. Thematic analysis was conducted to categorise the results into core environmental sustainability themes. Findings Five interrelated themes were identified: (1) material innovation and environmental sustainability, (2) structural efficiency and lightweight design, (3) construction techniques and environmental sustainability alignment, (4) life durability management and (5) accessibility, inclusivity and waste management. These themes highlight critical performance indicators such as energy use, structural behaviour, material optimisation, user experience and maintenance strategies. The integration of AI insights helped highlight both consensus and gaps in expert knowledge. Originality/value This study provides a systematic qualitative investigation of environmental sustainability in TMS from an expert-practice perspective and is among the first to compare expert insights with AI-generated assessments of environmental sustainability within the TMS domain. The research contributes to the growing field of environmentally responsive structural design by offering actionable strategies for embedding environmental sustainability assessment practices into TMS planning and implementation. The findings provide valuable guidance for architects, engineers and policymakers seeking to enhance low-carbon design decisions in membrane architecture.
authors: Sarah Elattar; Xiancun Hu; Mike Louw

title: Explainable AI-driven neural activity analysis in Parkinsonian rats under electrical stimulation
abstract: Parkinson’s disease (PD) is characterized by motor dysfunction and abnormal neural oscillations. This study combined graphene-based cortical stimulation with an explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) framework to investigate spatial and frequency-related features contributing to pre- and post-stimulation classification in Parkinsonian rats. Electrocorticogram (ECoG) signals were recorded before and after stimulation and classified using EEGNet and DeepConvNet. Layer-wise relevance propagation (LRP) and DeepLIFT were applied to identify frequency bands and recording channels contributing to the classification. The anatomical locations of these channels were mapped onto a cortical map. XAI analyses were performed separately for each animal to examine individual attribution patterns. Our XAI analysis revealed frequency-band- and region-specific contributions to pre- and post-stimulation classification in Parkinsonian rats. Our approach provided complementary insights into the features contributing to pre- and post-stimulation ECoG classification alongside PSD-based analyses. These findings highlight the potential of combining graphene-based cortical stimulation with explainable deep learning to identify classification-relevant features across frequency bands and cortical areas in pre- and post-stimulation recordings.
authors: 최한슬; Gaeun Kim; Sunggu Yang; Eunha Baeg; Donggue Kim; Seongwon Jin; Sangwon Byun; Jibum Kim

title: Exploring collaborative problem-solving in AI-assisted robotics education
abstract: Prompt engineering (PE) involves creating, improving, and deploying prompts to improve large language model (LLM) performance. Despite its increasing importance, many students lack skills in this area. Although frameworks for prompt design and process exist, theory-based instructional tools for improving prompt engineering skills are uncommon for developing collaborative problem-solving (CPS) skills in Robotics Education. This study adopted a PE strategy in AI-assisted robotics education, particularly for developing CPS. PE has four scaffolding stages: Alignment, Adaptation, Autonomy, and Innovation, and was analysed through four PE codes: Alignment Specification, Adaptive Refinement, Auditing, and Innovation. This study adopted a non-randomised, multi-site, criterion-group comparative design, with 243 undergraduate students categorised according to their ability group. This study used epistemic network analysis (ENA) to identify the co-occurrences of PE and CPS skills and examine the differences in conversation patterns among ability groups. The findings revealed distinct PE–CPS discourse configurations across ability groups. These results underscore the pedagogical value of scaffolding in developing PE skills and fostering students’ productivity in a synergetic learning environment.
authors: Christian Basil Omeh; Elias Oupa Mashile

title: Exploring the Critical Success Factors for the Implementation of Intellectual Capital Management in the Organization: A Structured Literature Review
abstract: The purpose of this paper is to present a structured literature review to identify the critical success factor for Intellectual capital management implementation in the organization. A structured literature review is carried out on the subject of ICM research (2013-2026) on success factors affecting implementation of ICM in an organization. After primary review of the articles, 55 research papers were identified for further review. The articles selection process followed like identification, screening, eligibility, inclusion and exclusion. 20 most CSFs were compiled using content analysis methodology and an inductive coding technique and categorized into four groups. The two of the most highly cited frequency CSFs were Top management and leadership support and organization culture, knowledge management and infrastructure, human capital development, technical integration and digital transformation and performance alignment and alignment.There is a small amount of research papers in conducting systematic literature review and this study did not use a specific organizational or sector to identify relevant CSFs because different types of organization and sectors which might be influence the CSFs of intellectual capital management in the organization. This study contributes in preventing failure for implementing KM in the organizational environment. This study may benefit and contributes in preventing failure for implementing ICM in the organization.The authors call for researchers to consider helping public sector practitioners implement IC frameworks and models through interventionist research. In keeping with the performative third-stage IC research agenda, interventionist research makes it possible for academic researchers to act as a catalyst for implementing IC frameworks and models in practice.

title: Factores críticos y estrategias para la implementación de la logística integral en centros de distribución en Panamá
abstract: Panama combines an interoceanic position with distribution centers whose operational integration was uneven, and studies that explain this gap are scarce. The objective was to determine the critical factors that conditioned the implementation of integrated logistics in Panamanian distribution centers and the strategies that can be adapted to the local context. A qualitative systematic review was carried out following PRISMA 2020, with searches in Scopus, Web of Science, EBSCO, SciELO and Redalyc and with institutional grey literature published between 2019 and 2026; the process identified 200 records, and 30 documents (23 scientific articles and 7 technical reports) passed screening, full-text reading and bibliographic verification. Content analysis, organized into five categories, showed that the best supported benefits were lower distribution costs, better supply chain performance and energy efficiency. Barriers were distributed across organizational, technological and human capital dimensions, with resistance to change, staff reskilling and the cost of digital infrastructure standing out. Warehouse management systems, transport management systems and the Internet of Things offered the best balance between evidence and feasibility, and no adoption figures specific to Panama were located. A gradual four-phase roadmap anchored in Latin American experiences was formulated, and the results indicated that the main gap was organizational and related to human talent, and that pilot projects and coordination among academia, industry and government offered the most viable path to close it.
authors: Pompilio Alexis Campos Portugal; M. Tejedor; B. Rodríguez; Alcides Torres Achurra; Franklin Cerrud Álvarez; Zoraya Paola Jiménez Jordán

title: Femoral rotation and medial flexion gap tightness in functional alignment robotic total knee arthroplasty for varus knees
abstract: Functional-alignment (FA) robotic total knee arthroplasty (TKA) combines component positioning and soft-tissue management. This study described the association between medial flexion-gap tightness and surgeon-selected femoral rotation, together with release grades and intraoperative gap asymmetry in varus knees. This observational single-surgeon study included the 65 varus knees in an 89-knee database. Medial tightness was defined as lateral minus medial preoperative flexion gap. Correlation and ordinary least-squares regression used 63 complete observations. Recorded preoperative, planned and final trial gaps were analysed with endpoint-specific denominators. An exploratory model considered tibial coronal positioning and posterior slope. Selected rotation was associated with medial tightness (Spearman ρ = 0.571; p < 0.001). The univariable fit was rotation = 1.93° + 0.343°/mm × tightness (R² = 0.257; slope 95% CI, 0.194-0.492). The adjusted slope was 0.296°/mm (95% CI, 0.131-0.460; n = 60). Release was mild in 64/65 and moderate in 1/65 knees. Mean absolute final asymmetry was 0.38 mm in extension and 0.29 mm in flexion. Asymmetry <1 mm occurred in 50/60 (83.3%) and 55/59 (93.2%), respectively; 53/58 (91.4%) met ≤1 mm in both positions. Greater medial flexion tightness was associated with greater selected femoral rotation. Predominantly mild release and small final mean asymmetry accompanied the combined workflow. The equation describes one surgeon's decisions and is not a validated surgical rule. These observations do not establish an independent release-sparing effect, clinical superiority of submillimetre symmetry, patellofemoral safety or long-term benefit.
authors: Eduardo Frois Temponi; Pedro Henrique Oliveira Gomes; Alexandre Leite de Andrade; Miguel Jourdain Alipio do Vale; Matheus Braga Jacques Soares; Luiz Fernando Machado Soares; Lúcio Honório de Carvalho

title: From Task Affinities to Optimal Allocations: Probabilistic Graphical Modelling for Supervised Finetuning
abstract: Supervised fine-tuning over a large pool of heterogeneous tasks is often computationally expensive, leading practitioners to train language models on a fixed training budget of carefully chosen SFT tasks. Thus, achieving strong downstream performance hinges on selecting an effective subset of tasks, or equivalently, identifying an optimal task mixture under a fixed budget constraint. In practice, supervised finetuning mixtures are often determined using simple heuristics (e.g., uniform or size-proportional sampling) that ignore task interactions, which can hurt transfer and waste budget on redundant task sources. We introduce TASKMIXPGM, a framework for learning continuous task mixtures through energy-based modelling over SFT tasks. Each task forms a node in a Markov random field, with unary potentials capturing task utility and pairwise potentials modelling inter-task relationships via behavioral divergences between predictive distributions of single-task fine-tuned models. Optimizing this objective yields task mixtures that balance utility, coverage, and redundancy. We further show that the induced set function defined over the set of such tasks is weakly submodular under budget constraints, enabling approximation guarantees for discrete task selection. Empirically, we provide a fixed, benchmark-independent mixture that improves over heuristic mixing across multiple model families and different training budgets. TASKMIXPGM also uncovers interpretable structure in task interactions, revealing complementarities and redundancies that inform effective SFT mixtures.
authors: Prateek Chanda; Saral Sureka; Krishnateja Killamsetty; Ganesh Ramakrishnan

title: Functional and structural neuroplasticity of motor system in hemiplegic cerebral palsy
abstract: Hemiplegic cerebral palsy results from a unilateral prenatal or perinatal brain injury and causes motor impairments in the contralateral side of the body. Variable functional outcomes among children with hemiplegic cerebral palsy despite similar lesion extent suggest that developmental neuroplasticity and brain reorganization contribute to motor function. By using multimodal neuroimaging, we characterize the structural and functional reorganization of the motor system and examine its associations with lesion characteristics and upper-limb performance. We examined 26 children with hemiplegic cerebral palsy and 26 typically developing controls using electromagnetic source imaging to map the primary motor cortex and characterize movement-related oscillations across physiologically relevant frequency bands, navigated transcranial magnetic stimulation to assess motor cortical excitability and lateralization, and functionally guided diffusion-weighted MRI to evaluate the structural integrity of descending motor and motor commissural fibers. We further assessed upper-limb function using Melbourne Assessment 2 and examined multimodal relationships using correlation, cross-validated latent-variable, and mediation analyses. Children with hemiplegic cerebral palsy showed microstructural abnormalities in the descending motor and motor commissural fibers, characterized by lower fractional anisotropy and higher mean, axial, and radial diffusivity (all P < 0.05). The navigated transcranial magnetic stimulation identified ipsilateral corticospinal projections from the less affected hemisphere in 17 of 22 children (77%) with hemiplegic cerebral palsy, accompanied by reduced contralesional primary motor cortex lateralization (P < 0.05). The hemiplegic cerebral palsy group also exhibited hemisphere-specific abnormalities in movement-related oscillations, including reduced theta synchronization in the contralesional hemisphere and attenuated mu- and beta-band desynchronization in the ipsilesional hemisphere (all P < 0.05). Larger lesions were associated with poorer motor performance (Rho = -0.74 to -0.57, P < 0.05). Reduced descending motor fiber integrity was associated with impaired dexterity and attenuated mu- and beta-band desynchronization (Rho = -0.51 to 0.62, P < 0.05), while motor commissural fiber integrity was associated with corticospinal motor lateralization (Rho = -0.45 to 0.41, P < 0.05). A cross-validated multimodal structural-functional model predicted motor function (Q^2 = 0.42, P < 0.001) more accurately than structural measures alone (Q^2 = 0.25). Beta-band desynchronization mediated the association between descending motor fiber integrity and motor performance (indirect effect = 0.12 SD, 95% CI 0.03-0.24). Developmental motor neuroplasticity in hemiplegic cerebral palsy reflects an integrated structure-physiology-behavior process rather than the direct consequence of lesion burden alone. Multimodal biomarkers may improve prognostication and support individualized rehabilitation and neuromodulation.
authors: Sadra Shahdadian; Yanlong Song; Alireza Vaysi; Regan Christian; Madhan Bosemani; Fernando Acosta; Brooke Kimbrell; Warren Marks; Christos Papadelis

title: Functional vision assessment in virtual reality: A structured narrative review with an illustrative seated O&M case study
abstract: Functional vision assessment aims to evaluate how vision supports daily activities, but conventional methods remain limited by subjectivity, low reproducibility, or restricted control of testing conditions. Virtual Reality (VR) offers a flexible way to simulate diverse environments and capture behavioral data, making it a promising platform for developing more ecological and standardized assessment methods. In this review, we provide a structured narrative overview of VR-based functional vision assessment. We trace the progression from questionnaire-based and physical assessments to immersive VR protocols, and discuss task design, technical implementation, performance metrics, behavioral data, and validation challenges. In addition, we present our seated VR-based Orientation and Mobility (O&M) test as an illustrative case study. This review aims to offer a concise reference for researchers working across ophthalmology, VR applications, behavior analysis, and computer science.
authors: Yujie Huang; Alexandre Bruckert; Patrick Le Callet

title: Getting REAL balance: a simple and reproducible method for imageless robotic TKA.
abstract:
Background

In imageless robotic-assisted total knee arthroplasty (RA-TKA), intraoperative assessment of ligament balance may be influenced by asymmetric cartilage wear, potentially misrepresenting true soft-tissue behavior. Functional alignment (FA) aims to restore constitutional alignment while respecting the native ligament envelope. Using the unworn compartment as the primary reference for intraoperative balancing may reduce the effect of asymmetric wear and improve mediolateral symmetry.

Methods

A retrospective analysis was performed on 180 knees (176 patients) undergoing femur-first imageless RA-TKA with a functional alignment strategy at a single-volume center. All procedures were performed using the ROSA Knee System with a medial congruent implant. Intraoperative balancing prioritized the unworn or less affected compartment, targeting a 19-mm implant space with near-symmetric medial-lateral laxity in extension and flexion. Medial and lateral laxities were recorded robotically before implantation and after final component placement and classified using the Robotic Evaluation of Articular Laxity (REAL).

Results

Preoperatively, lateral laxity exceeded medial laxity in both extension and flexion. Following implantation, mediolateral symmetry was restored with a significant reduction in medial-lateral laxity differences (p < 0.001). At final assessment, 178 knees (98.9%) were classified as REAL 1A. Soft-tissue releases were required in 14 knees (7.8%), with no intraoperative instability, additional bone recuts, or device-related complications.

Conclusions

In femur-first imageless RA-TKA performed according to functional alignment principles, unworn-compartment-based balancing enables reliable restoration of mediolateral ligament symmetry with balanced REAL phenotypes and a limited need for soft-tissue releases, representing a refinement of robotic ligament assessment in knees with asymmetric osteoarthritis during contemporary robotic surgery.
authors: Rossi SMP, Sangaletti R, Muci C, Capitani P, Benazzo F, Andriollo L.

title: Global Burden of Post-Stroke Wrist Extension Weakness Due to Wrist Extensor Muscle Inactivity: Pathophysiology, Functional Implications, and Rehabilitation Challenges- Systematic review.
abstract: Most stroke survivors experience upper-limb dysfunction, making stroke one of the major causes of long-term disability globally.One of the main causes of chronic hand dysfunction and decreased functional independence Wrist extension recovery has gotten less attention than general upper-limb rehabilitation, despite its vital role in regaining grasp, object manipulation, and activities of daily living.This review will thoroughly examine the global burden of post-stroke wrist extension weakness linked to wrist extensor muscle inactivity.The evidence that is currently available indicates that delayed wrist extension recovery results from a complex interaction between neural and musculoskeletal impairments that compromises the selective activation of the wrist extensor muscles.Conventional rehabilitation methods that improve upper-limb function generally include task-oriented training, strengthening exercises, functional electrical stimulation, mirror therapy, robotic-assisted therapy, and biofeedback; however, recovery of specific wrist extensor activity often fails.Additionally, the lack of studies that specifically target wrist extensor muscle inactivity and the variety of rehabilitation protocols impede the development of standardized, evidence-based interventions.Wrist extension weakness following a stroke is still a major but little-known cause of upper-limb impairment.Selective wrist extensor activation and functional recovery may be improved by placing more of an emphasis on impairment-specific rehabilitation, objective evaluation of wrist extensor function, and the incorporation of cutting-edge technologies like wearable electromyography, intelligent biofeedback, and robotic-assisted rehabilitation.
venue: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology

title: Gut and nasal microbiome trajectories shape respiratory disease severity in calves exposed to antibiotic and pathogen challenge
abstract: Bovine respiratory disease complex (BRDC) is a multifactorial syndrome resulting from interactions among pathogens, host responses, and environmental stressors. However, substantial variation in disease severity persists among animals exposed to similar infectious challenges. To assess the contribution of the respiratory and gut microbiota to BRDC severity, we experimentally inoculated 28 calves with Mycoplasma bovis , bovine coronavirus (BCoV), and influenza D virus (IDV), with half receiving metaphylactic tilmicosin. Clinical trajectories were classified into mild, moderate, and severe phenotypes using unsupervised clustering of longitudinal health scores. Severe BRDC was associated with higher and more persistent nasal IDV loads, yet pathogen burden alone failed to explain the marked inter-individual variability in clinical outcomes. Tilmicosin-treated calves developed substantially milder disease despite comparable pathogen loads, coinciding with lower systemic inflammation, suggesting that host-pathogen interactions, rather than pathogen replication alone, influenced disease severity. Neither nasal nor faecal microbiota diversity consistently explained BRDC severity. However, calves that later developed severe disease displayed a more homogeneous nasal microbiota before infection, indicating that early microbial community structure may influence susceptibility. In contrast, the strongest disease-associated microbial signatures were observed in the faecal microbiota. Gut antibiotic-induced dysbiosis revealed associations between BRDC severity, specific intestinal bacterial taxa, systemic inflammation, and faecal short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) profiles. Notably, Chlamydia was strongly associated with disease severity, while several other taxa were linked to inflammatory biomarkers and SCFA concentrations. Collectively, these findings support a holobiont-driven model of BRDC in which disease severity emerges from interactions among pathogens, host inflammatory responses, and microbiota-associated functions. The stronger associations observed in the intestinal microbiota, along with links between gut bacteria, SCFAs, and disease outcomes, provide evidence for a functional gut-lung axis in calves and highlight microbial metabolism as a potential target for strategies to improve respiratory health and reduce antibiotic use. Implications Bovine respiratory disease is one of the most costly health and welfare problems in cattle production. This study shows that disease severity is not determined only by pathogen infection but is also linked to changes in the gut microbiome and its metabolic activity. Calves with different microbiome profiles developed markedly different clinical outcomes despite similar pathogen exposure. The findings provide new evidence for a gut-lung connection in cattle and identify microbial functions associated with disease resilience. These results may support the development of microbiome-based strategies to improve animal health, reduce production losses, and decrease reliance on antibiotics in livestock systems.
authors: Maverick Monié--Ibanes; Thomas Peyret; Guenaelle Derolez; Marie Corbin; Florence Mompart; David Bars; Fatima Sikht; Christine Citti; Laurent‐Xavier Nouvel; Éric Baranowski; Gilles Meyer; Mariette Ducatez; Núria Mach

title: Heart rate deceleration tracks antidepressant response to accelerated dorsomedial prefrontal intermittent theta-burst stimulation in major depression
abstract: Identifying accessible, low-cost biomarkers of treatment response remains a key challenge in personalizing transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) therapy for major depressive disorder (MDD). We tested whether stimulation-evoked heart rate deceleration (HRD) predicts antidepressant response to accelerated intermittent theta-burst stimulation (iTBS) of the dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (dmPFC). Thirty-two patients with MDD received accelerated bilateral dmPFC-iTBS delivered with a double-cone coil. Heart rate was sampled continuously at 1-second intervals using a low-cost chest-strap sensor, and HRD was quantified as the relative change from a 1-minute pre-stimulation baseline to the mean heart rate across the stimulation window. Response was defined as a 50% or greater reduction in 17-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale score. Response and remission rates were 65.6% and 56.3%, respectively. Responders showed greater HRD than non-responders (Cohen’s d = 1.40). HRD discriminated responders with an area under the curve of 0.905; a 2% cutoff yielded 90.5% sensitivity and 81.8% specificity. Each 1% increase in HRD was associated with approximately 2.5-fold higher odds of response. Stimulation-evoked HRD tracked antidepressant response and is compatible with modulation of a prefrontal-autonomic network; it warrants evaluation in larger sham-controlled studies as a pragmatic, bedside-accessible candidate marker of response. The trial was registered retrospectively at ClinicalTrials.gov (identifier NCT07615387 first posted 29/05/2026).
authors: Ali Tarık Altunç; Yusuf Çiçek; Ahmet Torun; Sarp Yoldaş; Melike Nur Altunç; Halil Aziz Velioğlu; Burç Çağrı Poyraz

title: Higher body mass index is associated with lower patient-reported outcomes, whereas alignment and soft-tissue balance remain comparable following imageless robotic-assisted functional alignment total knee arthroplasty: A retrospective analysis from the Brescia Knee Research Group.
abstract: Obesity is common among patients undergoing total knee arthroplasty (TKA) and may increase technical difficulty, complications and patient dissatisfaction. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the influence of body mass index (BMI) on component alignment, soft-tissue balancing and postoperative patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) following primary imageless robotic-assisted TKA performed using a functional alignment (FA) strategy. This retrospective analysis of a prospectively maintained database included 364 consecutive patients who underwent primary imageless robotic-assisted TKA between January 2021 and December 2024 at a single high-volume arthroplasty centre. Patients were stratified according to World Health Organization BMI classes. Radiographic alignment (mechanical hip-knee-ankle angle, medial proximal tibial angle, lateral distal femoral angle, posterior tibial slope), intraoperative robotic soft-tissue laxity (final medial and lateral extension/flexion laxity in mm) and postoperative PROMs (Knee Society Score function, Forgotten Joint Score-12 [FJS-12], Oxford Knee Score, anterior knee pain scale, visual analogue scale pain) were compared across body mass index (BMI) categories at a mean follow-up of 38.4 months. Postoperative coronal and sagittal alignment did not differ significantly across BMI categories. Final extension and flexion gaps were comparable among groups, except for a small difference in final medial flexion laxity (p = 0.046), which was below the threshold of clinical relevance. Patient-reported outcomes declined progressively with increasing BMI. The largest BMI-related effect was observed for the FJS-12 (p = 0.008), with lower scores in patients with class II and III obesity. In this cohort, component alignment and soft-tissue balance after imageless robotic-assisted TKA using an FA strategy were comparable across BMI categories, with no detectable group differences. However, higher BMI remained associated with lower PROMs, suggesting that extra-articular, biological and biomechanical factors related to obesity may continue to influence subjective recovery even when technical precision is maintained. Level III.
authors: Guglielmo Miele; Angelo Carosini; Emanuele Sica; Lorenzo Elia; Giulio Calandra; Rudy Sangaletti; Francesco Benazzo; Luca Andriollo

title: How Can Talent Managers Create Organizational Value Throughout the Hype Cycles of Emerging and Innovative Industries?
abstract: Talent managers in emerging industries face a distinctive challenge: they must build and reconfigure talent management (TM) systems to build organizational value while stakeholder expectations, legitimacy, regulation, and capital availability continually fluctuate. Drawing on interviews with 14 experienced executives across the emerging Canadian recreational cannabis and solar industries, media and scholarly related industry research, we examine how TM challenges and responses vary across hype cycle inflection points. Extending Makram et al.’s (2017) talent value framework into a dynamic industry context, we theorize hype cycle inflection points as an organizing mechanism for talent architectures in emerging industries. Our findings show that TM value processes are temporally reweighted as industries move from innovation trigger to inflated expectations, through disillusionment, and toward stabilization. We contribute to HRM/TM scholarship by showing that talent architectures in hype‐driven emerging industries are not best understood as fixed bundles of best practices or as universal organizational stages, but as contingent configurations that must be rebalanced as external expectations, legitimacy, regulation, and resource availability change. We further identify stage‐specific talent logics: rapid capability acquisition, accelerated scaling, defensive stabilization, capability consolidation, and strategic optimization. The findings advance research on contextualized TM, temporal dynamics, and organizational value by explaining when and why different forms of talent become strategically valuable in emerging industries.
authors: Francine K. Schlosser; Márcia Carvalho de Azevedo; Deborah M. McPhee

title: Hubungan Antara Tingkat Spastisitas dengan Kemampuan Motorik Anak Cerebral Palsy Spastik di Pusat Rehabilitasi Harapan Jaya Pematang Siantar
abstract: Spastic cerebral palsy (CP) is a prevalent neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by velocity-dependent muscle hypertonia, which severely hinders motor execution and functional independence in pediatric populations. This study aimed to analyze the correlation between the level of spasticity and gross motor function among children with spastic CP at the Harapan Jaya Rehabilitation Center in Pematang Siantar, Indonesia. A quantitative observational study with a cross-sectional design was conducted involving 33 pediatric patients aged 4–12 years selected through purposive sampling. Spasticity was evaluated using the Modified Ashworth Scale (MAS), while gross motor capacity was classified via the Gross Motor Function Classification System (GMFCS). The cohort was predominantly characterized by spastic quadriplegia (81.8%), elevated spasticity grades (MAS Grade 4: 42.4%; MAS Grade 3: 36.4%), and severe motor limitation (GMFCS Level V: 72.7%). Spearman’s rank correlation test demonstrated a statistically significant, strong positive correlation between spasticity level and gross motor function impairment (r = 0.710, p < 0.001). These findings confirm that higher degrees of muscle hypertonia correlate directly with increased severity of gross motor limitation. This study contributes empirical evidence from a community-based rehabilitation setting, emphasizing the clinical necessity of combining spasticity-reduction strategies with task-specific gross motor functional training to optimize mobility and independence in children with severe spastic CP
authors: Lusianti Simanjuntak; Mustafa Al Haris; Sulaiman

title: INFLUÊNCIA DO MÉTODO HALLIWICK NO CONTROLE POSTURAL E NA FUNCIONALIDADE DE CRIANÇAS COM PARALISIA CEREBRAL ESPÁSTICA: UMA ANÁLISE TERAPÊUTICA
abstract: Este estudo analisou a influência do Método Halliwick no controle postural e na funcionalidade de crianças com paralisia cerebral espástica. Trata-se de pesquisa quantitativa, quase-experimental, com avaliações pré e pós-intervenção, realizada com cinco crianças de 4 a 12 anos. O protocolo compreendeu 12 sessões de terapia aquática. Foram utilizadas as escalas Gross Motor Function Measure (GMFM-66), Pediatric Balance Scale (PBS), Avaliação das Atividades Funcionais Estáticas (AFE) e Ashworth Modificada. Sexo e GMFCS foram descritos por frequências absolutas e relativas; as variáveis numéricas, por média ± desvio-padrão e mediana (IIQ). A normalidade das diferenças foi verificada pelo teste Shapiro-Wilk. Utilizaram-se o teste t pareado (GMFM-66, PBS e AFE) e Wilcoxon (Ashworth). O tamanho de efeito foi estimado pelo d de Cohen, classificado em pequeno (≈ 0,2), médio (≈ 0,5) ou grande (≥ 0,8). Adotou-se significância de 5% (p ≤ 0,05). Houve aumento significativo na GMFM-66 (p = 0,0016; d = 3,42), PBS (p = 0,0275; d = 1,52) e AFE (p = 0,0036; d = 2,75). A espasticidade permaneceu inalterada (p = 1,000). Conclui-se que o método esteve associado a melhorias motoras e posturais, embora a amostra reduzida e a ausência de grupo controle limitem a interpretação.
authors: Ana Laura Baseggio Fontes; Rafaela Maria Souza Farias; Alexssandro Pereira Furtin
venue: Revista Ibero-Americana de Humanidades, Ciências e Educação

title: Immediate transcranial magnetic stimulation‐evoked potentials reveal short‐latency intracortical inhibition
abstract: Short-interval intracortical inhibition (SICI) is the most widely used neurophysiological index of GABAergic inhibition in the human cortex. However, it is an indirect measure, inferring synaptic inhibition from suppression of peripherally recorded motor-evoked potentials (MEPs) elicited by transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). In the standard protocol, a subthreshold conditioning pulse suppresses the MEP evoked by a suprathreshold test pulse delivered 1-5 ms later. Interpretation is further complicated by temporal overlap with short-interval intracortical facilitation (SICF), reflecting excitatory interactions at interstimulus intervals of ∼1.5 and 2.7 ms. To overcome these limitations, we recorded immediate TMS-evoked EEG potentials (iTEPs; 1-10 ms post-stimulus) as a more direct measure of motor cortical activity in 16 healthy volunteers (20-35 years; seven male). The conventional SICI protocol suppressed only later components of the iTEP, probably corresponding to late corticospinal volleys previously identified in epidural spinal recordings after suprathreshold TMS, while the earliest iTEP component was unaffected. Importantly, later iTEPs were suppressed to a similar extent whether conditioning-test intervals coincided with SICF peaks or troughs, and the magnitude of iTEP suppression correlated with concurrently recorded paired-pulse MEP suppression. SICI also reduced an early TEP component (N15; 10-20 ms), but paired-pulse N15 suppression showed a different dependence on stimulus intensity and did not correlate with MEP suppression. These findings demonstrate that SICI measured via MEPs does not reflect a global index of cortical GABAergic motor cortical inhibition but instead reflects inhibition within specific cortical circuits that can be investigated more directly with iTEPs. KEY POINTS: Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) over the primary motor cortex evokes high-frequency activity in the corticospinal tract, which can be measured directly with invasive, epidural recordings or indirectly as a time-locked, compound EMG response [i.e. motor evoked potential (MEP)]. GABAergic intracortical inhibition can be indexed as the MEP suppression caused by a subthreshold TMS pulse preceding the suprathreshold pulse by 1-5 ms. Combining TMS with artifact-minimized EEG allows the assessment of paired-pulse inhibition of immediate and early peaks of TMS-evoked EEG potential (TEP). Both immediate TEP (iTEP) and early TEP peaks display paired-pulse inhibition but only iTEP suppression relates to MEP suppression. iTEPs enable investigations of intracortical interactions non-invasively at the cortical level, which enables assessment of cortical and corticospinal physiology with TMS even in the absence of MEPs.
authors: Lasse Christiansen; Yufei Song; Ditte Haagerup; Mikkel Malling Beck; Kora T Montemagno; John C. Rothwell; Hartwig Roman Siebner

title: Improvements in Rail Traffic Management Systems (TMS) for More Efficient Operation of Trains with Connected Driver Advisory System (C-DAS)
abstract: Connected driver advisory systems (C-DAS) improve railway operations through tighter connection between drivers and traffic controllers, enabling optimized speed profiles with maximal traffic flow and minimized energy consumption. The benefits from C-DAS depend on having a high-quality real-time traffic plan (RTTP). The traffic controller creates the RTTP in the Traffic Management System (TMS). Today, many TMS lack advanced functionality to facilitate the maintenance of a high-quality RTTP. This has shown to drastically limit the benefits of C-DAS systems and increase the workload of the traffic controller, in particular on single-track lines with traffic consisting of both trains that are equipped with C-DAS and trains that are not equipped. This paper introduces a support tool for assisting the traffic controller in maintaining a high-quality RTTP. The tool estimates the runtimes of non-C-DAS-trains using Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT) models, as well as finetunes the timing details of the RTTP through a mixed-integer optimisation that simultaneously minimizes delays and energy consumption and maximize the robustness of the traffic. The prototype is validated on the single-track corridor Kalmar – Alvesta in southern Sweden, a section with mixed passenger and freight traffic.
authors: Martin Joborn; Zohreh Ranjbar; Oskar Rune; Rebecka Haraldsson; Peter Olsson

title: In Vivo Validation of Automated Knee Arthrometry: What Do These Measurements Really Represent?
abstract:
Background

Objective assessment of anterior knee laxity (AKL) is important for evaluating graft integrity after anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction. Automated arthrometers, such as the GNRB, provide reproducible measurements; however, the in vivo biomechanical meaning and validity of these measurements remain unclear.

Hypothesis/purpose

The primary purpose was to validate GNRB-derived AKL measurements against biplanar videoradiography (BVR)-derived metrics under in vivo postoperative conditions. It was hypothesized that GNRB measurements would differ significantly from BVR-derived measures of tibiofemoral translation and ACL graft elongation. A secondary, exploratory purpose was to examine the relationships between GNRB- and BVR-derived laxity measures.

Study design

Cohort study (Diagnosis); Level of evidence, 2.

Methods

Twenty patients (6 months post-ACL reconstruction) underwent simultaneous AKL testing using a GNRB arthrometer and BVR. Six BVR-derived laxity metrics were calculated, including tibiofemoral translation, tibial tuberosity displacement, and ACL graft elongation. Arthrometer accuracy was assessed using a repeated-measures analysis of covariance, and linear regression analyses were used to evaluate relationships between GNRB- and BVR-derived measures.

Results

GNRB-derived laxity differed significantly from all BVR-derived measures (P < .001). Compared with BVR-defined tibiofemoral and graft-based metrics, the GNRB consistently overestimated AKL (bias: 3.4-6.1 mm). The strongest relationship to GNRB was observed in BVR-derived tibial tuberosity displacement expressed in the world coordinate system (r = 0.93), whereas associations with ACL graft elongation were weakest (r = 0.51-0.66). Differences between tibial tuberosity displacement expressed relative to the femur versus the world coordinate system indicated a substantial contribution of femoral motion during arthrometric testing.

Conclusion

This study provides the first in vivo validation of GNRB-derived AKL measurements following ACL reconstruction. Using BVR as the reference standard, the GNRB consistently overestimated AKL and showed the weakest correlation with ACL graft elongation. These findings highlight the need to better understand how arthrometry relates to knee motion and ACL graft elongation to improve the reliability and clinical interpretation of postoperative AKL assessments.
authors: Bugajski T, Figueroa A, Gregory BP, Lowe WR, Zandiyeh P.

title: Induction of interhemispheric visual plasticity by paired associative stimulation
abstract: Unveiling the plastic mechanisms of the primary visual cortex (V1) is crucial for understanding how visual processing can change and adapt, ultimately informing interventions to promote functional recovery following visual system damage. Paired associative stimulation (PAS) protocols can induce associative plasticity within the human V1. However, previous paradigms used full-field visual stimulation, engaging both hemispheres simultaneously, leaving unclear whether plasticity can be selectively targeted to a single visual pathway and whether it can modulate the non-stimulated hemisphere. Across three experiments in healthy participants, we investigated the neurophysiological, behavioural, and interhemispheric outcomes of a novel lateralized visual PAS protocol (vPAS). Pattern-reversal checkerboards were presented in a single visual hemifield and time-locked to transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) pulses delivered over the contralateral V1. Experiment 1 assessed neurophysiological effects by recording hemifield-lateralized visual-evoked potentials (VEPs) and testing three inter-stimulus intervals (ISIs: 75, 100, and 125 ms) between vPAS-paired stimuli. Experiment 2 evaluated perceptual changes in contrast detection, while Experiment 3 examined vPAS hemispheric specificity and aftereffects on interhemispheric visuomotor transfer. Only the 75-ms ISI consistently modulated visual processing in the non-conditioned hemisphere, reducing N75 amplitude and improving contrast detection for visual stimuli presented contralateral to the TMS side. Longer ISIs were not effective. Furthermore, this protocol altered interhemispheric transfer exclusively when the left, but not the right, V1 was targeted during vPAS. In conclusion, lateralized vPAS induces timing-dependent changes beyond the stimulated cortex, suggesting that associative plasticity can engage contralateral visual circuits and modulate visual processing.
authors: Francesca Crespi; Giacomo Guidali; Eleonora Arrigoni; Nadia Bolognini

title: Integral resonant filter-based chattering reduction in switched human-robot interaction with hybrid admittance-adaptive impedance control
abstract: Physical human-robot interaction (pHRI) is a type of interaction that implies that robots should demonstrate dynamic and compliant behavior that is dependent on the interaction environment. A prominent solution is compliant control, which includes either Admittance Control in the case of soft contact or Impedance Control for stiff contact. However, if the nature of the environment is unknown or dynamic, then a hybrid control scheme that switches between the admittance and impedance regimes is adopted. However, switching from admittance to impedance and vice versa results in discontinuity in the control signal. The discontinuity inherent in the abrupt switching mechanism causes high-frequency oscillations (chattering) in the control signal. The effect of this phenomenon is poor performance of the system, mechanical stress, and high energy consumption. To effectively attenuate this chattering and its negative effects, this work proposes an Integral Resonant Control (IRC) command filter, which is incorporated into the switching loop of the hybrid admittance and adaptive impedance control. The IRC filter, normally employed to damp structural vibrations, is designed here to act as a command filter for robust signal smoothing by damping the high-frequency components of the control signal introduced by the switching action. The proposed hybrid controller is compared to a standard hysteresis (dead-zone) chattering mitigation strategy. Comparative simulation results indicate that the proposed filtering technique can reduce the Chattering Index on average by over 76% for both joints of a planar rehabilitation robot while maintaining trajectory tracking accuracy. The results obtained indicate that the proposed switched hybrid control is Lyapunov stable and can be employed to achieve effective, energy-efficient, and compliant robotic rehabilitation in uncertain environments.
authors: Ado Haruna; Auwalu Muhammad Abdullahi; Ronnapee Chaichaowarat

title: Integrated, adaptive decarbonization strategies for last mile delivery
abstract: The aim of this study is to identify and assess the importance of selected decarbonization instruments in shaping integrated, adaptive, and low-emission last-mile delivery strategies, taking into account consumer behavioural determinants. The study utilised a modelling approach, developing a conceptual model integrating regulatory, organisational, and behavioural factors, which was then subjected to preliminary empirical verification. The obtained results indicate that the decarbonization process is nonlinear and systemic, based on interdependencies between the regulatory, strategic, and consumer levels. Regulatory pressure and enterprise adaptation strategies play a key role, significantly determining operational efficiency and the implementation of low-emission solutions, while the influence of behavioural factors remains relatively limited. Consequently, the research hypothesis was partially confirmed, indicating an asymmetry in the interactions between ”top-down” and ”bottom-up” mechanisms. A limitation of the study is the need for further in-depth empirical verification, particularly using operational data and a broader consideration of the demand side. Practical implications include the need to develop integrated adaptation strategies, intensify digitalisation processes, and apply behavioural economics tools to logistics demand management. In the social dimension, the importance of strengthening the role of consumers in the low-carbon transition process is emphasised. The study's originality lies in its integration of systems and behavioural approaches in the analysis of last-mile delivery decarbonization, which significantly complements existing research, which focuses primarily on technological and regulatory aspects.
authors: Urszula Motowidlak

title: International Multi-Centre Validation of Unsupervised Domain Adaptation for Precise Discrimination between Normal and Abnormal Retinal Development
abstract: Arrested retinal development can cause childhood visual impairment, but grading optical coherence tomography scans is difficult to standardise across devices and centres. We developed and evaluated an unsupervised domain adaptation model to classify normal and abnormal retinal development across different OCT systems. This retrospective multicentre study used OCT scans from five centres in four countries and the UK Biobank. Data covered four OCT devices, including table mounted and handheld systems. A ResNet50 based Domain Adversarial Neural Network was trained using labelled images from a source device and unlabelled images from a target device. We evaluated six source to target pairings and compared model performance with seven clinician graders. A separate Heidelberg Spectralis dataset was reserved for external evaluation. Across validation sets, accuracy ranged from 87.75% to 96.06%, sensitivity from 88.68% to 98.38%, and specificity from 78.00% to 98.02%. The best performing model, adapted from TM OCT1 to HH OCT1, achieved 96.06% accuracy and an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.994, with a 95% confidence interval from 0.981 to 0.999. Several models also maintained discrimination on the unseen Heidelberg device. Unsupervised domain adaptation enabled OCT classification across devices without labelled target device data. The approach may support more consistent assessment of retinal development and large scale analysis of existing imaging datasets.

title: Intravenous midazolam alters short-interval paired-pulse TMS responses differently in younger and older adults
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Aging is associated with changes in cortical excitability and altered responsiveness to benzodiazepines, but the effects of benzodiazepine challenge on motor cortical paired-pulse physiology in older adults remain incompletely understood. We examined whether intravenous midazolam differentially modulates corticospinal excitability and short-interval paired-pulse transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) responses in younger and older adults. METHODS: Sixteen younger adults (18-35 years) and sixteen older adults (50-69 years) underwent single-pulse and paired-pulse (conditioning stimulus: 110% motor threshold; test stimulus: 143% motor threshold) TMS of the left primary motor cortex at baseline and during intravenous midazolam administration. Single-pulse motor evoked potential (MEP) amplitude was used to assess corticospinal excitability. Short-interval paired-pulse responses were quantified as the ratio of conditioned to unconditioned MEP amplitude. RESULTS: At baseline, younger adults showed greater corticospinal excitability than older adults, reflected by larger single-pulse MEP amplitudes (adjusted p = 0.04). Younger adults demonstrated paired-pulse inhibition at baseline, reflected by a conditioned/unconditioned MEP ratio below 1.0 (ratio = 0.73; adjusted p < 0.01), whereas older adults did not show inhibition and instead had a mean ratio above 1.0 (ratio = 1.25). Midazolam reduced single-pulse MEP amplitudes in both groups. During midazolam administration, paired-pulse inhibition was no longer observed in younger adults, and older adults continued to show no evidence of inhibition. CONCLUSIONS: Younger and older adults differed in baseline corticospinal excitability and in short-interval paired-pulse TMS responses. Intravenous midazolam reduced corticospinal excitability and altered paired-pulse response patterns, eliminating baseline paired-pulse inhibition in younger adults while producing little measurable change in older adults. These findings suggest that aging may modify the net motor cortical response to benzodiazepine challenge. The results should be interpreted in relation to the paired-pulse stimulation parameters used and support further studies using complementary approaches to characterize age-related differences in inhibitory and facilitatory motor cortical circuits.
authors: Keith McGregor; Seyed A. Safavynia; Thomas Novak; Ashton Weber; Jessica Wang; Joe R. Nocera; Anna Woodbury; Bruce Crosson; Paul S. García

title: Investigation into Multi-Timestamp High-Resolution Faulting Measurements for Jointed Concrete Pavements Using 3D Pavement Surface Data
abstract: As 3D laser imaging systems have become mainstream among highway agencies for automated pavement condition assessment, obtaining high-resolution joint faulting measurements along the full length of each transverse joint in surveyed jointed concrete pavement segments has become feasible. Leveraging this newly available sensor-based data is essential to improve the understanding of faulting behavior, characterizing deterioration mechanisms, and establishing consistent reporting practices at both the joint and segment levels. This study conducts a detailed investigation of faulting behavior using multi-timestamp high-resolution measurements from a 9.2 mi undoweled jointed plain concrete pavement section on Georgia’s Interstate 16 near Macon, U.S., surveyed from 2013 to 2018 by the Georgia Tech sensing van. The analysis includes zone-based spatial analysis along the joint, examination of how representative faulting metrics influence condition reporting, assessment of negative faulting occurrences, and deterioration analysis at both the joint and segment levels. Findings show that faulting varies substantially along the transverse joint and cannot be characterized reliably by a single location such as the right wheel path. The choice of a representative faulting metric therefore plays a significant role in determining reported condition and shaping observed trends across survey cycles. A notable portion of joints exhibited partial or complete negative faulting, underscoring the need for guidance on how these cases should be treated for assessment and how they should be aggregated at the segment scale. Segment-level results showed consistent increases in faulting, while joint-level trends varied depending on factors such as slab cracking and base support conditions.
authors: Ryan Salameh; Amirreza Parsaei; Anna He; Yichang James Tsai

title: Issue Information
abstract: Brain stimulation interventions transfer energy directly to brain tissue, administering electrical, magnetic, or sonic stimulation to alter brain function.These therapies may require neurosurgery to implant electrodes in the nervous system or they may be totally noninvasive.Over the last 25 years, there has been a dramatic increase in the scientific study of these interventions and in the number of FDA clearances of safe and effective therapies for multiple neuropsychiatric disorders.This review summarizes the therapeutic use and challenges of five classes of brain stimulation intervention and discusses opportunities for additional breakthroughs in treatment development.

title: Life-Mimicking Adaptive Coacervates Mediated by Nanoparticles
abstract: Life-mimicking adaptive coacervates mediated by nanoparticles Chapter 1 introduces liquid–liquid phase separation (LLPS) as key principle underlying cellular organization and biomimetic compartmentalization. It outlines the formation mechanisms, encapsulation capabilities, and interfacial properties of coacervates, emphasizing their relevance as simplified models of artificial cells. This chapter then highlights the role of nanoparticles as structural and active modulators, both through internal encapsulation and interfacial stabilization, enabling enhanced control over coacervate properties. Moving beyond passive systems, the integration of active components is discussed as a strategy to endow coacervates with life-mimicking behaviors, including dynamic mass exchange, metabolism, and adaptive responses. Finally, the chapter defines the central objective of this thesis: to engineer adaptive, life-like coacervate systems by incorporating functional nanoparticles, thereby overcoming the limitations of static coacervates and advancing synthetic biology and functional materials research. Inspired by our previously prepared photothermal peptide-based nanoparticles, in Chapter 2, we described a light-driven and hierarchical artificial cell platform that enables programmable anisotropic encapsulation of photothermal nanoparticles within amylose-based coacervates. Through self-assembly, fluorescent and photothermal peptide-based nanoparticles were formed and subsequently encapsulated into coacervates via strong electrostatic interactions. The system was further stabilized by the introduction of a terpolymer membrane. A stable three-dimensional anisotropic photothermal cluster structure within terpolymer-stabilized coacervates was formed. Upon laser irradiation, localized light-activated heating imparted autonomous motility to the system. Furthermore, the nanoparticles exhibited multi-stimuli responsiveness to pH, ionic strength, and redox conditions, enabling dynamic modulation of their spatial distribution within the coacervate droplets—and thereby tuning the degree of structural anisotropy. The motile behavior of the hierarchical coacervates was further shown to be governed by this internal anisotropy. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that rationally engineered asymmetry within coacervate-based artificial cells provides a robust design principle for achieving controllable motility. In chapter 3, we introduced photothermal modules to the interface of coacervates by physically anchoring gold nanoparticles (AuNPs)-coated PEG-PDLLA stomatocyte nanomotors at the coacervate interface in combination with a terpolymer membrane. The positively charged coacervates promoted the assembly of negatively charged nanomotors on their surface via electrostatic interactions. By costabilizing the coacervates with a terpolymer membrane, patches of nanomotors were firmly immobilized on the coacervates’ surface. The distribution of nanomotors shifted from spotted distribution, patchy distribution, to almost full coverage upon increasing nanomotor concentration. Optimal motile behavior was found when achieving a patchy coverage of nanomotors at the interface, which enabled the system to become a light-driven micromotor platform through the surface plasmon thermal effect of the AuNPs. The motion dynamics of these coacervate droplets could be modulated by tuning nanomotors’ density on the surface, coacervate size, and laser light intensity. This study provides a first example of a coacervate system, which is stabilized by nanomotors, of which their motility is effectively transferred to the artificial cell structure. In Chapter 4, building on Chapter 3, we further explored other life-mimicking properties of patchy membrane-stabilized coacervate systems. We present a novel strategy for controllable multiphase separation using patchy membranes, where multiphase separation behavior is governed by the membrane’s composition, and subcompartments form near the membrane interface. The nanomotors embedded within the terpolymer matrix enabled precise control over multiphase separation upon introducing succinylated bovine serum albumin (suc-BSA), a second negatively charged component. By modulating the nanomotor density at the coacervate interface, we could fine-tune the size, position, and quantity of BSA-rich subdroplets. Full coverage of the coacervate interface by nanomotors increased the areal density of negative charge, enhancing the stability of the multiphase system, which showed improved resistance to salt and pH variations, as well as higher storage stability. Furthermore, the system was dynamically tuned through ionic strength and temperature variations. As a practical demonstration, we showed how this custom-designed multiphase structure near the membrane, with an expanded interfacial area, significantly accelerated the uptake rate of cargo molecules. These findings provide new insights into the design of membrane-based systems with precise control over multiphase behavior and enhanced functional performance. In Chapter 5, we report programmable, light-driven fusion dynamics of membrane-stabilized coacervates, by employing the nanomotor-decorated coacervates developed in Chapter 3. Upon two-photon (TP) light irradiation, nanomotors escaped from the interface, which led, together with the inherent membrane fluidity, to the fusion of two closely contacting membrane-stabilized coacervates. Moreover, under higher intensity laser irradiation, we achieved fusion of non-contact coacervate droplets, as well as continuous, cascade-like fusion events within droplet swarms. Systematic pairwise fusion analysis showed that the presence of a sufficient number of nanomotors on one droplet at the contact interface is the key determinant for fusion. Furthermore, fusion of membrane-stabilized multiphase coacervates under TP laser stimulus was confirmed. Controllable modulation of both fusion initiation and fusion rate was also demonstrated. This strategy establishes a general platform for achieving programmable fusion in membrane-stabilized coacervates, thereby offering new opportunities for the design of dynamic, artificial cell-like systems.
authors: Siwen Sun

title: Lingering Guilt and Cautious Adoption: Examples of Post-Secondary Instructors’ Perception of Generative Artificial Intelligence
abstract: Instructors play a unique role in today's university setting, straddling the line between practicing teachers and professors in academia, specifically in the College of Education. This perspective helps bridge the gap between academic professors and practicing teachers in public schools. Therefore, we investigated five instructors' experiences with generative artificial intelligence (genAI) to better understand its effects on today's teachers. While their experiences with genAI varied slightly, the exploratory study highlights the instructors' progress from initial skepticism and experimentation to evaluation, reflection on emotional response, and, finally, cautious adoption. We present this data not to generate generalizable results, but to show how instructors use these tools and how they respond to the development of this technology. Here, we present their stories to understand their experiences.
authors: Dan Sawyer; Liz Ochoa; Amanda Gantt Sawyer; Bonnie Yoder; Jen Dameron; Alicia Berry
