title: Longitudinal Gait Improvement With Multimodal Treatment and Repeated Hybrid Assistive Limb Gait Training in Hereditary Spastic Paraplegia: A Case Report
abstract: Hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by lower-limb spasticity and gait impairment. Although spasticity management, including botulinum toxin injections, intrathecal baclofen therapy, and orthopedic surgery, can reduce spasticity and improve limb alignment, translating these improvements into meaningful gains in walking remains challenging. Robot-assisted gait training with wearable exoskeletons, such as the Hybrid Assistive Limb (HAL), may facilitate task-specific gait practice by assisting voluntary movements based on the user's motor intention. We report the case of a 64-year-old man with spastic paraplegia type 4 (SPG4), a subtype of HSP associated with pathogenic variants in the SPAST gene, who underwent stepwise spasticity management combined with repeated HAL-assisted gait training over long-term follow-up. Botulinum toxin injections were initiated at presentation, followed by intrathecal baclofen therapy during follow-up and tendon lengthening surgery. HAL-assisted gait training was performed repeatedly from Month 29 to Month 49. Over the course of treatment, walking speed and 2-minute walk distance gradually improved, whereas cadence remained relatively stable. These functional gains persisted despite a temporary decline. These sequential interventions may have provided a therapeutic foundation for subsequent gait reconstruction through repeated task-specific gait training using the HAL. Although the individual effects of each intervention cannot be determined from a single case, this clinical course suggests that integrating impairment-oriented interventions with repeated HAL-assisted gait training can optimize functional walking outcomes in patients with HSP.
authors: Taiyo Kawaguchi; Takatoshi Hara; Yuta Miyazaki; Ayano Matsui; Yuki Hara; Keiko Sone; Takeshi Matsuura; Yuji Takahashi; Tetsuya Tsuji; Masahiro Abo

title: MIRROR THERAPY COMBINED WITH REHABILITATION INTERVENTIONS FOR POST-STROKE UPPER LIMB MOTOR DYSFUNCTION: CURRENT EVIDENCE, MECHANISMS, AND FUTURE DIRECTIONS
abstract: Post-stroke upper limb motor dysfunction is a common cause of long-term disability. Mirror therapy (MT) is a generally safe, accessible, and low-cost rehabilitation intervention, and its combination with other rehabilitation modalities has attracted growing clinical interest. This narrative review synthesized targeted literature available up to September 2026 on MT combined with electrical stimulation, non-invasive brain stimulation, task-oriented training, acupuncture, robot-assisted therapy, and electromyographic biofeedback. Higher-level clinical evidence and relevant mechanistic studies were prioritized, while no PRISMA-style systematic screening, de novo risk-of-bias assessment, or meta-analysis was undertaken. Across the six combined approaches, evidence suggests potential additional benefits for upper limb motor function and activities of daily living (ADL), but certainty varies substantially. Moderate-quality evidence supports major motor and ADL outcomes for robot-assisted MT, whereas evidence for several electrical stimulation outcomes remains low-certainty. Recent meta-analyses also support potential benefits of MT combined with tDCS and acupuncture, although protocol heterogeneity remains substantial. Patient selection, intervention dose and sequencing, and adverse-event reporting remain inconsistent across studies. MT combined with other rehabilitation interventions is a promising adjunctive strategy for post-stroke upper limb recovery, but current evidence does not support uniform superiority across all modalities or patient groups. Future studies should prioritize standardized reporting, stronger comparative trials, patient stratification, safety monitoring, and clinically meaningful outcome measures.
authors: GaoQiang Chen; JianMing Fu; Ya Sun
venue: Journal of Pharmaceutical and Medical Research

title: Machine Learning Detection of Peritoneal Entry from Vibroacoustic Signals During Veress Needle Insertion
abstract: Background/Objectives: Establishing access is a hazardous step of laparoscopic surgery, and the widely used Veress needle offers only subjective tactile and auditory cues for peritoneal entry. Proximal vibroacoustic (VA) sensing captures needle–tissue interaction non-invasively and is known to contain a characteristic peritoneal puncture signature, which could help surgeons to precisely identify peritoneal entry. However, the VA signature has been evaluated only by retrospective, video-anchored and manual signal analysis. We investigate whether peritoneal entry can instead be detected automatically. Methods: Cavity entry is framed as a binary classification of VA signal segments, and four model families are benchmarked under a single unified protocol: a one-dimensional convolutional neural network (1D CNN), a multilayer perceptron, a bidirectional long short-term memory network (LSTM), and a support vector machine (SVM) with a radial basis function kernel. All models were trained, selected, and threshold-tuned on a synthetic abdominal phantom (996 segments) and tested once on an independent porcine cadaver dataset (154 cavity, 462 non-cavity signals) so that every test result measures generalisation across a phantom-to-porcine domain shift. Results: The 1D CNN performed the best (accuracy 0.869, AUROC 0.904, macro F1 0.833, cavity recall 0.818), closely followed by the SVM (AUROC 0.900, AUPRC 0.878). Conclusions: These results establish the feasibility of automatically detecting peritoneal entry across a phantom-to-porcine domain shift and extend the descriptive cadaveric characterisation of the puncture signature toward the automated machine learning-based detection of peritoneal entry in laparoscopic access with a Veress needle.
authors: Moritz Spiller; Mohammad Rezapourian; Axel Boese; Alfredo Illanes Manríquez; Thomas Neumuth; Nazila Esmaeili

title: Making Smell Actionable in Design: Lexicon, Movement Patterns, and Gesture Cards
abstract: Smell is powerful in design, yet it often remains vague and difficult to work with in studios and classrooms. While olfactory HCI has produced devices, toolkits, and scenario-based applications, designers still lack teachable, shareable resources that link smell to bodily action. This paper presents a three-phase research program that makes smell actionable by moving from lived smell experiences to movement patterns and, finally, to gesture resources. We study olfactory-motor mappings and package the results as teachable design representations through a progressively narrowing method: (1) extracting smell-verb-intent relations from user narratives; (2) capturing and clustering embodied enactments into standardized upper-limb trajectory families; and (3) translating these trajectories into gesture card representations for design teaching and ideation through design workshops. We present a three-phase translational framework and empirically derived smell-gesture correspondences that structure the smell-intent-trajectory-gesture pathway, together with reusable assets (lexicon, trajectory atlas, gesture tables, and cards) that support teaching, reuse, and adaptation across contexts.
authors: Anran Feng; Shengyu Gao; Xingyu Zhao; Zhenyu Qian; Jingrui An

title: Mapping the current evidence on mirror therapy, soft robotic gloves, and their combined use in upper limb rehabilitation after stroke: a scoping review
abstract: Background Upper-limb impairment after stroke can restrict hand use, activities of daily living, and functional independence. Mirror therapy (MT) and soft robotic glove (SRG)-based rehabilitation represent technology-enabled approaches to upper-limb rehabilitation. The extent and characteristics of evidence examining these approaches individually and in combination have not been mapped. Objective To map the literature on MT, SRG-based rehabilitation, and their combined use after stroke, with emphasis on study characteristics, intervention dosage, outcome measures, technological integration, safety reporting, and evidence gaps. Methods This scoping review followed Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology and the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and CENTRAL were searched in the original review. The Scopus strategy was rerun using OR between the MT and SRG concept blocks, and IEEE Xplore was searched to improve engineering-literature coverage. Eligible interventional studies involved adults with stroke receiving MT, SRG-based rehabilitation, a direct MT + SRG combination, or a direct MT-versus-SRG comparison. Data were charted using a standardized form and synthesized descriptively; study-level fields were rechecked against accessible full-text articles or primary records to resolve classification and reporting discrepancies. Results The evidence map included 84 studies reporting 2,634 stroke participants. Fifty-four studies were MT-only (64.3%), 27 were SRG-only (32.1%), two directly combined MT + SRG (2.4%), and one directly compared MT with SRG (1.2%). Randomized controlled/clinical trials accounted for 53 studies (63.1%) and pilot/feasibility studies for 16 (19.0%). Chronic stroke was explicitly represented in 31 studies (36.9%), subacute stroke in 15 (17.9%), acute stroke in five (6.0%), and mixed acute/subacute populations in two (2.4%); stage was unspecified/other in 31 (36.9%). FMA was charted in 35 studies (41.7%), ARAT in 12 (14.3%), and ADL/independence outcomes in 19 (22.6%). Safety was not reported in 52 studies (61.9%); 23 (27.4%) explicitly reported no serious/adverse safety signal. Conclusion The evidence base is substantially larger for MT or SRG studied separately than for their direct combination. Considerable heterogeneity exists in study design, stroke stage, intervention dosage, outcome selection, technology integration, and safety reporting. The review provides an evidence map and identifies areas requiring further investigation without making claims of comparative treatment superiority.
authors: Mohammed Hindi Alwatifi; Wafaa Abd Ali Hattab
venue: Bulletin of Faculty of Physical Therapy

title: Matching Corticospinal and Cortical Excitability along the motor cortex: TMS-EMG-EEG study
abstract:
There is still no consensus on how to choose intensities for transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). The resting motor threshold (RMT)—the intensity needed to evoke muscle contractions in the contralateral limb muscles—is a robust muscle-specific index of corticospinal excitability. RMT from one of the hand muscles is commonly used as a reference for TMS neuromodulation interventions and TMS-electroencephalography (TMS-EEG) studies. However, it only provides an indirect measure of cortical excitability, and even for the primary motor cortex (M1), we do not understand how cortical and corticospinal excitability correspond to each other. Indeed, it remains unclear whether cortical responses to TMS follow similar location-dependent patterns along the M1 as RMTs, and whether subthreshold stimulation can reliably engage cortical circuits relevant to motor output. Combining TMS with electromyography (EMG) and EEG—TMS-EMG-EEG—enables simultaneous assessment of corticospinal and cortical excitability to answer these questions. We investigated how cortical excitability thresholds (CETs, measured with EEG), relate to corticospinal excitability thresholds (RMTs, measured with EMG) at the hand, arm, and leg hotspots along the M1 in 24 healthy subjects. RMTs and CETs were strongly correlated, and both increased from hand to arm to leg. CETs were generally lower than RMTs, indicating that subthreshold stimulation was enough to evoke robust early TMS evoked potentials (TEPs). Within subjects, CETs differed from the corresponding RMTs at all three M1 hotspots, and this difference increased from hand to leg representations. The findings of the present study argue against using a default hand-muscle RMT to set cortical excitability dosage along the M1 and beyond. Online TMS–EEG can enable real-time dosing and could improve stimulation precision, efficiency, and generalizability, but the site-specific variability calls for adaptive control.

Dictionary

TMS-EMG-EEG

A multimodal neurophysiological approach, combining EMG and EEG recording during TMS, to assess corticospinal and cortical excitability simultaneously.

Corticospinal Excitability

Responsiveness of the corticospinal motor pathway to stimulation, reflecting the combined excitability of cortical and spinal motor circuits.

Cortical Excitability

Responsiveness of cortical neuronal circuits to external stimulation, including electrical and magnetic stimulation.

EMG-EEG Compound Hotspot

The stimulation site that elicited clear and consistent early TEPs and reliable MEPs for the target muscle.

MEP (motor evoked potential)

Electrical activity recorded from the peripheral muscle via EMG, in response to TMS stimuli.

RMT (resting motor threshold)

A measure of corticospinal excitability.

TEP (TMS-evoked potential)

Electrical potentials recorded from the scalp via EEG, in response to TMS stimuli.

CET (cortical excitability threshold)

The early peak-to-peak deflection at an electrode near the stimulation site, quantified in real-time.
authors: Nazarova M, Higdon M, Rouste J, Mutanen T, Nikulin V, Ukharova E, Vaalto S, Ilmoniemi RJ, Lioumis P, Renvall H.

title: Mechanical Digitorum Sensory Stimulation Enhances Hemiplegic Upper Limb Motor Function in Stroke Patients by Increasing Cortical Excitability and Functional Connectivity
abstract: Background Relieving flexor spasticity, enhancing extensor strength, and improving hand function in patients with stroke remain significant clinical challenges. Mechanical Digitorum Sensory Stimulation (MDSS), a novel therapy that applies precise mechanical pressure to the affected fingers, may address these issues; however, its effects and mechanisms have not been thoroughly studied. Methods Sixty convalescent patients with post-stroke hemiplegia were randomly assigned to a Control group (conventional rehabilitation + sham MDSS) or an MDSS group (conventional rehabilitation + MDSS) for 3–4 weeks. Muscle spasticity, strength, upper-limb motor function, and activities of daily living were assessed using the Modified Ashworth Scale (MAS), Manual Muscle Testing (MMT), Fugl-Meyer Assessment–Upper Extremity (FMA-UE), and Modified Barthel Index (MBI), respectively. Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) was used to measure oxyhemoglobin (HbO) concentrations in regions of interest (ROIs) during the resting state (RS) and task state (TS; i.e., MDSS) to evaluate cortical excitability and functional connectivity (FC) by calculating correlations of HbO concentration changes between specific ROIs. Results After the intervention, the MDSS group showed significantly lower MAS scores for all finger flexors ( P < 0.001) and significantly higher MMT scores for all finger extensors, as well as higher FMA-UE and MBI scores ( P < 0.01) compared with the Control group. Regarding cortical excitability, increases in HbO concentration were higher in most ROIs in the MDSS group than in the Control group, including 10 ROIs (83.33%) during RS and 11 ROIs (91.67%) during TS. Moreover, increases in FC across all ROI-to-ROI pairs were greater in the MDSS group than in the Control group during both RS and TS. Conclusions MDSS effectively alleviates flexor spasticity, enhances extensor strength, and improves upper-limb motor function in patients with stroke. These effects are associated with enhanced cortical excitability and strengthened functional connectivity, supporting MDSS as a promising rehabilitation strategy for hemiparetic hand recovery. Trial registration The study protocol was registered in the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (Website https//www.chictr.org.cn/showproj.html?proj=176575 Registration Number ChiCTR2200063792)
authors: Wei Huang; Heyan Zhang; Jinqiang Yu; Yuan Ma; Qiqi Li; Rui Wu; Yuyou Yao; Shuting Zhang; Yongfeng Hong

title: Mediolateral Joint Balance Assessment Is Reproducible Between Surgeons, Under No Standardized Varus-Valgus Stress, During Robot-Assisted Total Knee Arthroplasty.
abstract: Objective: To evaluate inter-surgeon variability in mediolateral joint balance assessment during robotic-assisted total knee arthroplasty (TKA) using the robotic surgical assistant (ROSA) Knee System, and to determine whether such variability influences the surgical planning generated by this system. Methods: An observational study was conducted including 101 patients undergoing primary robotic-assisted TKA. Two experienced surgeons independently assessed intraoperative mediolateral laxity by manually applying varus-valgus stress across six predefined flexion angles (0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°, and 120°). Measurements of medial and lateral gaps (mm) and varus-valgus alignment (°) were recorded using the ROSA Knee System. Inter-observer differences were analysed using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, and reliability was assessed using the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC). The impact of inter-surgeon variability on surgical planning, including bone resection and compartmental space measurement parameters, was also evaluated. Results: No statistically significant inter-observer differences were observed in mediolateral gap measurements or varus-valgus alignment across all flexion angles (p > 0.05). Inter-observer reliability for varus-valgus measurements was good to excellent in extension and early flexion (ICC 0.86-0.91), decreased to moderate at 90° (ICC 0.68-0.74) and was poor for varus assessment at 120° (ICC 0.46, 95% CI 0.29-0.60). For gap measurements, reliability was excellent for the medial gap and good for the lateral gap in extension (ICC 0.93 and 0.89, respectively), and moderate for both gaps at 90° (ICC 0.71-0.74). No significant inter-observer differences were found in cut or space measurements, with excellent agreement for cut parameters (ICC > 0.95). Conclusions: Inter-surgeon assessment of mediolateral joint balance during robot-assisted TKA showed good-to-excellent reproducibility in extension and early flexion, with reduced reproducibility in deep flexion. Statistically significant inter-observer differences were not observed in the resulting cut and space measurements.
authors: Grillo G, Coelho Leal A, Martí D, Tortajada MP, Gil-Gonzalez S, Peñalver Matamoros JM, Pelfort Lopéz X.

title: Mirror Skin: In Situ Visualization of Robot Touch Intent on Robot Skin
abstract: Effective communication of robot touch intent is essential for safe and predictable physical human-robot interaction. While intent communication has been widely studied, existing approaches lack the spatial specificity and semantic depth necessary to efficiently convey robot touch intent. We present Mirror Skin, a cephalopod-inspired concept that mirrors in-situ visual representations of a human’s body parts onto the corresponding robot’s touch region to communicate who shall initiate touch, where it will occur, and when it is imminent. We informed the design of Mirror Skin through a structured design exploration with experts and demonstrate the real-world feasibility of Mirror Skin with a proof-of-concept prototype. User studies in VR and with the physical prototype showed that Mirror Skin significantly improves accuracy and response times for interpreting touch intent and improves the user experience during physical human-robot interactions.

title: Modeling blockchain adoption in the United Kingdom’s banking: an empirical study using technology-organization-environment framework
abstract: Introduction Blockchain technology (BCT) has the ability to significantly change the financial services industry by making transactions faster, cheaper, safer, as well as more transparent. Therefore, the current paper seeks to investigate and empirically validate the variables, which are affecting the adoption of Blockchain in the UK’s banking system. Methods For this purpose the study collected secondary data through reviewing literature for the period January 2015 and June 2025 from well indexed journals, conference proceedings, books, white papers, and industry reports, those are related to blockchain technology and the banking sector. However, primary data for this study were collected from banking and financial services employees in London between the period January 2025 and July 2025 using a structured questionnaire. A non-probability purposive sampling technique was adopted and Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) was used to examine the relationships among the proposed technological, organizational, and environmental determinants of blockchain adoption. The Technology Organizational Environmental framework served as the model for the scale used for measuring BCA enablers. Results Consequently, the study found that perceived Compatibility, relative advantage, learning culture, top management, consumer readiness, and competitive pressure significantly affects the adoption of blockchain, whereas perceived cost limits this adoption process. Additionally, the results reveal that perceived compatibility, relative advantage, learning culture, top management support, customer readiness, and competitive pressure positively influence blockchain adoption, whereas perceived cost negatively affects adoption. Discussion Moreover, the findings indicated that Blockchain might therefore be viewed as an emerging disruptive force in digital technology that is transforming business models and is becoming as an essential element on a global scale.

title: Motor Cortex Disinhibition Is Dissociated from Clinical Motor Features in Parkinson's Disease: Longitudinal Evidence
abstract: Background In Parkinson's disease, motor dysfunction largely reflects dopamine‐dependent pathophysiological alterations and compensatory mechanisms that progress over time and are partially reversible with dopaminergic treatment. Our recent cross‐sectional observations suggest that disinhibition of the primary motor cortex—assessed with short‐interval intracortical inhibition (SICI) using transcranial magnetic stimulation—does not correlate with clinical motor features, does not progress across disease stages, and instead correlates with olfactory dysfunction, a common prodromal and dopamine‐independent feature. Objective We aimed to provide longitudinal evidence for or against the hypothesis that motor cortex disinhibition is dissociated from clinical motor features in Parkinson's disease. Methods We compared SICI across three cohorts (total n = 95 patients): (1) baseline and 2‐year follow‐up (n = 43), with concurrent motor assessment and 18 F‐DOPA positron emission tomography (PET) imaging (n = 24); (2) before and after levodopa administration (n = 30); and (3) before and after focused ultrasound subthalamotomy (n = 22). We also included a pooled healthy control group (n = 75) from two previously published studies. Bayesian statistics was applied to formally assess evidence for the presence or the absence of an effect. Results SICI was expectedly reduced, with very strong to extreme Bayesian evidence, in patients compared with control subjects. We found evidence that cortical disinhibition did not worsen with clinically evident disease progression confirmed with 18 F‐DOPA PET and did not improve following a clinically effective dose of levodopa or subthalamotomy. Moreover, changes in SICI did not correlate with changes in motor features across cohorts. Conclusions These findings provide longitudinal evidence that motor cortex disinhibition is largely dissociated from clinical motor features in Parkinson's disease. © 2026 International Parkinson and Movement Disorder Society.

title: Motor Evoked Potentials in Preclinical Models of Spinal Cord Injury and Stroke in Rodents: A Systematic Review
abstract: Motor Evoked Potentials (MEPs) serve as an invaluable tool for assessing corticospinal tract (CST) integrity and motor pathway function in preclinical models of spinal cord injury (SCI) and stroke. Despite their diagnostic and prognostic utility, substantial methodological variability persists across studies, complicating interpretation and cross-study comparisons. This systematic review synthesizes MEP acquisition and interpretation protocols from 83 rodent SCI and stroke studies published since 2015, aiming to outline common practices, identify sources of variability, and highlight methodological gaps. Our analysis reveals a predominance of SCI models and a focus on hindlimb MEPs, employing diverse stimulation protocols including transcranial electrical stimulation (TES), direct cortical stimulation (DCoS), and transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). Anesthetic approaches are notably heterogeneous, representing a potentially large source of variability in MEP acquisition. Amplitude and latency, often measured jointly, emerged as the most frequently reported MEP parameters. Critically, MEPs bridge cellular and molecular changes to observable behaviour by reflecting the integrated functionality of neural cell populations and their circuits. However, a lack of standardization in reporting, particularly for secondary electrophysiological features and stimulation intensity, hinders reproducibility. We emphasize the necessity for standardized protocols for stimulation, electrode positioning, and data analysis, particularly the use of comprehensive recruitment curves. Adopting these best practices will enhance the transparency, comparability, and translational potential of MEP methodology in advancing our understanding and treatment strategies for neurological disorders. Graphical abstract Motor evoked potentials (MEPs) in rodent models of spinal cord injury (SCI) and stroke. This review focuses on various brain stimulation techniques (orange) and electromyographic approaches employed to quantify MEPs (green) and factors affecting MEP recording and analysis (blue). Future directions include greater standardization of stimulation, recording-electrode placement, and data-analysis practices; such as the potential use of recruitment curve features and high-density EMG recordings such as Myomatrix. Recruitment curves provide a more comprehensive characterization of evoked responses than single-pulse stimulation. While a single pulse only offers a snapshot of a subject’s motor threshold, recruitment curves yield a dynamic, S-shaped (sigmoidal) function that reflects the net excitability of upper and lower motor pathways across a range of stimulation intensities. This enables better control over sources of variability, such as stimulation and recording electrode placement, anesthetics dose, that can alter amplitude-based features. Because recruitment curves quantify the relationship between stimulus intensity and response rather than relying solely on absolute amplitude, the derived features are less susceptible to these artifacts (e.g., slopes, S50—stimulation intensity to reach half of the maximum amplitude). In addition, high-density recordings make it possible to better characterize the evoked activity of multiple motor units within the same target muscle and to identify the innervation zones of the motor units under study. title: Multidimensional Electrophysiological Responses to TMS on the Primary Motor Cortex: A TMS-EEG Characterization of Immediate Cortical Responses
abstract: Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) combined with electroencephalography (EEG) enables millisecond-scale characterization of cortical responses, but direct multidimensional comparisons across stimulation protocols remain limited. In a randomized within-subject crossover study, 17 healthy adults received 10 Hz repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), 1 Hz rTMS, and intermittent theta-burst stimulation (iTBS) over the left primary motor cortex in separate sessions. TMS-evoked potentials (TEPs), power spectral density (PSD), and EEG microstate dynamics were assessed before and immediately after stimulation. Following 10 Hz rTMS, group-level P30 amplitude increased from 0.17 to 0.89 μV, while N45 became less negative from −1.73 to −0.82 μV; PSD increased significantly across 15.5–45 Hz. In contrast, 1 Hz rTMS reduced P30 from 0.68 to 0.39 μV and increased P60 from 0.31 to 1.65 μV, with significant PSD reductions at 12.7–31.7 Hz and 32.2–45 Hz. iTBS reduced the magnitude of N45 from −2.76 to −1.93 μV and decreased P60 from 1.41 to 0.47 μV. These findings demonstrate protocol-specific multidimensional electrophysiological profiles across temporal and spectral measures. This framework facilitates systematic comparison across stimulation protocols and provides a basis for further investigation of TMS-induced cortical responses and individualized neuromodulation.
authors: Yuyao He; Wei Wang; Dechen Kong; Jiayu Chen; Hongying Li; Haoyang Xing; Hongmei Zhang

title: Muscle Activation Timing and Synergies During End-Effector Robot-Assisted Gait: A Surface EMG Study
abstract: Surface electromyographic (SEMG) patterns during robot-assisted walking are still poorly documented. This study aimed to characterize the timing and synergies of muscle activations of the lower extremities during locomotion assisted with an end-effector robot. Healthy subjects walked at 1.8 km/h under two modes: passive and active with a full body weight load. The robotic gait cycle (RGC) was identified by detecting the flexion-extension phases of the right lower limb. SEMG signals were recorded from eight lower limb muscles, time-normalized with respect to the RGCs and averaged across 10 RGCs. Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF) identified three basic waveforms (factors) explaining 90.6% of the variance in the dataset of SEMG waveforms corresponding to three distinct muscle synergies: rectus femoris-vastus lateralis-vastus medialis (extension phase), gastrocnemius medialis-soleus-peroneus longus (mid-flexion phase), and tibialis anterior-biceps femoris longus (transition between extension and early flexion phases). Cluster analysis on the cosine distance matrix of the NMF factor coefficients further validated the three distinct muscle groupings. Temporal activation patterns were seemingly preserved between passive and active conditions, suggesting similar underlying neuromuscular organization. This study supports the use of clinical gait analysis, particularly with SEMG, to assess neuromuscular patterns of neurological patients before, during, and after robotic rehabilitation.
authors: Matteo Cioni; Maria Stella Valle; Laszlo Kovacs; Daniela Vorazzo; Caterina Sergi; Gianfranco Bosco

title: NESTApp: A GUI-Based MATLAB Application for Auditable TMS-EEG Preprocessing with EEGLAB
abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) preprocessing determines signal quality and interpretation, particularly for transcranial magnetic stimulation combined with EEG (TMS-EEG), where recordings are affected by large and complex stimulation-related artifacts. Several preprocessing approaches have been developed, but substantial variability remains in how pipelines are implemented, documented, and evaluated across recordings, limiting reproducibility and comparability across studies. We developed NESTApp, a MATLAB-based graphical interface built on EEGLAB, to provide an accessible and reproducible framework for implementing and evaluating TMS-EEG preprocessing pipelines. Rather than prescribing a specific pipeline, NESTApp allows users to construct and consistently apply customisable workflows incorporating established EEGLAB and TMS-EEG processing tools, while automatically documenting processing decisions and parameters. Integrated quality-control procedures track data removal and flag recordings based on user-defined criteria, facilitating systematic evaluation across participants. The application also supports group-level visualisation and export of processed TMS-EEG measures for subsequent analyses. Applied to 29 recordings from 16 participants, NESTApp processed 27 and identified those requiring further inspection. By integrating pipeline implementation, documentation, quality control, and group-level evaluation within a single interface, NESTApp provides a transparent framework for TMS-EEG preprocessing that may improve reproducibility, facilitate consistent processing across cohorts, and lower technical barriers to the implementation of established preprocessing approaches.
authors: Aref Pariz; Wesley Dunne; Jeremie Lefebvre; Sara Tremblay

title: Navigating how Transformational Leadership, Creative Engagement, and Green Innovation impact SME Performance and Growth: The Mediating and Moderating Role of Top Management Support
abstract: This study investigated the relationships among green transformational leadership, creative process engagement, green innovation (product and process), and firms' innovative performance, focusing on small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in South Africa.Unlike previous studies that examined these factors in isolation or across developed and Asian economies, this study presents a comprehensive model explaining how green leadership influences creativity, innovation, and business growth in an emerging-economy context.The research followed a positivist philosophy and employed a quantitative approach.Data were collected through a structured survey distributed to 321 managers from manufacturing SMEs in Cape Town, Western Cape province, South Africa, using simple random sampling.SmartPLS software version 4.0.9.5 was utilised to analyse both the measurement and structural models.The results indicate strong positive relationships between green transformational leadership and creative process engagement, which in turn lead to green product and process innovation.Both types of green innovation significantly contribute to firms' innovative performance, ultimately positively impacting SME business growth.A significant contribution of this study is the identification of the dual role of top management support: both a mediator and a moderator in the relationship between innovative performance and SME business growth, thereby elucidating the organisational mechanisms through which innovation drives sustained growth.The findings offer practical recommendations for SME owners, managers, and policymakers seeking to utilise green leadership and top-management commitment to promote innovation, competitiveness, and long-term growth.

title: Navigation-Assisted and Robotic Total Hip, Knee, and Unicompartmental Arthroplasty: Reconciling Positioning Accuracy with Biomaterial Performance and Long-Term Implant Survival
abstract: Navigation-assisted and robotic systems improve component positioning in total hip (THA), total knee (TKA), and unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (UKA), but whether this improves biomaterial performance and implant survival is unclear. This structured narrative review asks for which bearing materials and fixation interfaces positioning accuracy plausibly alters the degradation and fixation pathways that govern survival, and how strong the evidence is for each link. We propose a conceptual model linking positioning to the local mechanical environment, material-specific degradation, biological response, and survival, and grade each link's evidence by study design. Enabling technologies consistently reduce outliers. Position-dependent degradation is well documented for conventional polyethylene, ceramic-on-ceramic, and metal-on-metal bearings, mainly from simulator, retrieval, and cohort studies. Highly cross-linked polyethylene appears to attenuate the wear penalty of malposition, although rim fatigue and impingement remain position-sensitive and vitamin E stabilization has no proven additional clinical benefit. In cementless TKA, varus alignment is associated with greater early tibial migration, a validated surrogate for loosening. Clinical translation remains limited: trials and registries show no consistent reduction in all-cause revision after TKA or THA, with lower dislocation after THA and a more favorable UKA signal as exceptions. Precision may matter most for position-sensitive bearings and cementless interfaces.

title: Neuroengineering Approaches in Rett Syndrome: Eye Tracking, Virtual Reality, Brain–Computer Interfaces, and Non-Invasive Brain Stimulation
abstract: Rett syndrome (RTT) can restrict the motor and verbal responses needed for conventional assessment and rehabilitation. This non-systematic critical narrative review examines human RTT evidence on eye tracking, virtual reality (VR), electroencephalography (EEG), brain–computer interfaces (BCIs), wearable sensing, and non-invasive brain stimulation, with an evidence horizon of 25 August 2026. The searches were non-exhaustive, and the selected evidence inventory does not constitute a systematic census of all eligible studies. In the author’s interpretation of heterogeneous evidence, eye-gaze augmentative and alternative communication has the clearest implementation experience in selected individuals; this does not constitute a comparative efficacy grade. Gaze-adapted assessment requires task-specific validation. Small VR studies provide feasibility and outcome-specific controlled findings, without established durable participation benefits. EEG studies support candidate biomarkers and task-state measurement, rather than demonstrated therapeutic benefit. No peer-reviewed RTT-specific study demonstrating clinical efficacy of real-time EEG command control was located by the stated searches; programme reports, conference material, and registry eligibility are distinguished from such evidence. Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) remains a physiological probe, transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) an experimental adjunct supported by limited controlled evidence, and transcranial photobiomodulation a therapeutic hypothesis. A proposed multimodal framework separates documented component uses from unvalidated integration and adaptive links.

title: Next-generation control strategies for lower-extremity exoskeletons: State-of-the-art, limitations, and future directions.
abstract: Wearable powered exoskeletons are emerging rehabilitation tools for restoring gait in individuals with neurologic or motor impairments, including stroke, spinal cord injury, myopathy, and cerebral palsy. Lower-extremity exoskeleton-assisted walking can improve motor function, gait parameters, balance, and independence. Exoskeleton use has also been associated with secondary health benefits, including reduced spasticity and improvements in autonomic functions such as bladder and bowel control. However, despite these clinical benefits, exoskeleton control systems remain a central bottleneck limiting functional gains and widespread clinical adoption. The majority of clinically approved lower-extremity devices rely on weight shift triggers, predefined gait phase controllers, impedance-based assistance, or simple electromyographic signal activation. These approaches often feel unintuitive and require substantial user training. As a result, persistent challenges remain in detecting user intent, reproducing a user's expected dynamic behaviors, adapting to variable gait patterns and changing environmental conditions such as uneven terrain or inclines, and minimizing cognitive burden during everyday use. This review focuses on control strategies for lower-extremity exoskeletons used in gait rehabilitation and restoration of motor function. It summarizes current approaches in commercial and research systems and outlines why existing methods remain insufficient for seamless, user-driven assistance. We also examine emerging approaches for determining user intent, including brain-computer interfaces, peripheral nerve interfaces, novel biosignals such as ultrasound and mechanomyography, and regenerative surgical approaches. Together, these advances may help bridge the gap between human intent and robotic assistance, enabling more natural and autonomous mobility.
authors: Victoria Vespa; Stephen W P Kemp; Deanna Gates; R Brent Gillespie; Paul S Cederna; Theodore A Kung

title: No difference in patella mobility between conventional mechanically aligned and robotic-assisted functionally aligned total knee arthroplasty.
abstract: Robotic-assisted (RA) surgery allows for higher accuracy in total knee arthroplasty (TKA) and for better standardization of alignment concepts. It was hypothesized that the more personalized component placement in functional robotic-assisted total knee arthroplasty (RA-TKA) would show an impact on patella mobility and clinical outcome. Prospective study was performed on 80 patients who received TKA (Triathlon; Stryker). In 51 patients, the prosthesis was implanted using MAKO robotic assistance (RA-TKA), while 29 patients underwent conventional implantation (conventional total knee arthroplasty [C-TKA]). Patella mobility was compared pre- and postoperatively after three months. Medial and lateral translation was measured in extension by using a patellostabilometer (PSM), which measures medio-lateral patella mobility under a force of 10 N. Clinical assessment was based on Oxford Knee Score (OKS), Knee Society Score (KSS), Kujala and Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Arthritis Index (WOMAC) scores. The medio-lateral patella mobility was 31 ± 9 mm before and 34 ± 7 mm (p < 0.01) after surgery. There was no significant difference in mediolateral patella mobility between the two groups (p = 0.282). Patella mobility increased by 3 mm in both groups after surgery. The medial and lateral shift ranged between 14 and 18 mm. All clinical scores (OKS, KSS, Kujala and WOMAC score) improved significantly from before to after surgery (p ≤ 0.001) without difference between the groups. RA-TKA did not result in changes in patella mobility when compared to conventional implantation. Other factors, such as general joint laxity or implant design and component placement, may have a more significant impact on patella mobility and clinical outcome. Level II prospective designed study.
authors: Krzysztof Lachowski; Karim Mustapha Naja; Robert Prill; Andreas Niemeier; Mikhail Salzmann; Roland Becker

title: Novel ExoTMS Technology for the Improvement of Self-Control and Food Cravings: 1-Month Preliminary Results
abstract: Higher levels of self-control or willpower are associated with greater mental health and favorable life outcomes. Despite its importance, strategies to enhance self-control remain limited. This randomized, single-blinded, sham-controlled study aims to assess the impact of the ExoTMS technology on enhancing self-control, using changes in food cravings as a behavioral indicator of self-regulation. 37 subjects were included in this interim analysis (n = 37, 24–74 years, BMI 20.2–58.8 kg/m2) and assigned to either active (n = 29) or sham (n = 8) group. The active group received treatment intensity up to 70% of MT and the sham group received 5% of MT. The Brief Self-Control Scale (BSCS) and Food Cravings Questionnaire–Trait (FCQ-T) were used to evaluate changes in self-control and food cravings, respectively. At one month, the active group showed an improvement of 6 points in BSCS scores and 38.1 points in FCQ-T scores. Within the active group, BSCS improvement was associated with FCQ-T reduction (R² = 0.215, p = 0.011). These preliminary findings suggest that ExoTMS may enhance self-control, and reduce food cravings.

title: OS EFEITOS DA ESTIMULAÇÃO TRANSCRANIANA NO EEG NO AUTISMO EM CRIANÇAS: UMA REVISÃO SISTEMÁTICA
abstract: O transtorno do espectro autista (TEA) apresenta heterogeneidade clínica e neurobiológica, o que tem estimulado a investigação de técnicas de neuromodulação associadas a medidas neurofisiológicas. Este estudo analisou os efeitos da estimulação transcraniana não invasiva, particularmente da estimulação magnética transcraniana repetitiva (EMTr) e da estimulação transcraniana por corrente contínua (ETCC), sobre parâmetros eletroencefalográficos e desfechos comportamentais em crianças e adolescentes com TEA. Realizou-se revisão sistemática conforme o PRISMA 2020, com buscas em seis bases de dados até junho de 2023. Dez ensaios clínicos randomizados foram incluídos, sendo sete sobre EMTr e três sobre ETCC. Os estudos identificaram modificações em oscilações cerebrais, coerência, conectividade funcional e efetiva, complexidade da atividade elétrica e microestados do EEG, além de alterações comportamentais em parte das investigações. Entretanto, houve ampla heterogeneidade quanto aos protocolos de estimulação, métodos de análise e instrumentos clínicos, além de preocupações relacionadas ao risco de viés. Conclui-se que as técnicas apresentam potencial para modular a atividade cerebral, mas as evidências ainda não permitem estabelecer um padrão eletroencefalográfico de resposta terapêutica ou um protocolo ideal.

title: OUCH: Objective, Uniform, Controlled Haptic Stimulation for Automated Neurological Assessment
abstract: Motor responses evoked by noxious stimulation are used to assess neurological function in hospitalized patients with disorders of consciousness. In standard bedside assessments, these stimuli are applied manually, resulting in substantial variation in force, duration, frequency, and location. Here, we present OUCH (Objective, Uniform, Controlled Haptic stimulation), a wrist-worn device that uses pneumatic actuation to deliver noxious mechanical stimuli. OUCH combines stacked pneumatic pouch actuators, a rigid indenter, and a compliant spacer designed to buckle at a set load, so that the indenter contacts the skin only during actuation. We characterize the device using blocked force tests, clinician evaluation, finite element analysis, and a deformable pressure testbed, and benchmark it against a commercially available handheld pressure algometer. At 200 kPa pouch inflation pressure, our indenter concentrated its load into an estimated contact pressure of 18,500 kPa, over 25 times that of the algometer tip, while requiring less total force. On the deformable testbed, it localized deformation near the surface, while deformation at depth remained comparable to the algometer. As a result, in preliminary perceptual testing, our indenter elicited discomfort at approximately 89% lower applied force than the algometer, demonstrating the feasibility of evoking discomfort with a compact, wearable soft actuator. These results show that combining pneumatic actuation with designed contact geometry enables controlled, repeatable noxious stimulation at the wrist, providing a foundation for objective neurological assessment.
authors: Sherry Choi; Sitao Sunny Li; Joseph Romero; Lillian Chin; Ashwin G. Ramayya; Allison M. Okamura; Ava Chen

title: One placement, many fields: robust voxel-wise mapping with multichannel TMS
abstract: Understanding the human brain at the individual level is central to understanding its function and a prerequisite for personalized therapy. Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) can map structure–function relationships at high resolution by regressing trial-wise variation in the TMS-induced electric field (E-field) against a response such as motor evoked potentials (MEPs). This requires distinct E-fields across pulses at different cortical locations, which single-coil TMS (sTMS) achieves by physically repositioning the coil—increasingly reliant on robotic guidance and capped by the coil geometry. Multichannel TMS (mTMS) instead steers the E-field electronically via independent currents in several coils, opening a design space of high variability without physical repositioning. We adapt determinant-based sequence optimization from discrete sTMS coil-placement sets to the continuous mTMS current space (D-optimal design), identifying pulse sequences whose induced cortical E-fields are as mutually dissimilar as biophysical constraints allow. We benchmarked optimized mTMS sequences against random baselines and optimized sTMS placements in virtual motor mapping across multiple head models, assessing three mTMS array geometries (5-channel planar, 6- and 12-channel spherical), two figure-of-eight sTMS coils, and varying pulse counts, response noise, and cortical depth. D-optimal mTMS currents substantially outperformed random currents and optimized sTMS at matched pulse counts. The gain was modest without noise but increased significantly with it: at the highest noise level, optimized sTMS failed to converge after 100 pulses (∼20–22 mm error), whereas all mTMS arrays reached median errors at or below 6 mm. mTMS also recovered deep targets better than sTMS (up to 35 mm skin–cortex distance, versus 25 mm) and performed uniformly across the region of interest. In addition, we found that a coil-space scheme based only on the magnetic vector potential, precomputable once per array without per-subject MRI, captured most of the benefit, matching subject-specific optimization at 100 pulses. mTMS thus makes voxel-wise mapping robust throughout a region of interest without coil repositioning.
authors: Ole Numssen; Renxiang Qiu; Victor Hugo Souza; Mikael Laine; Renan H. Matsuda; Lena Buchberger; Carla W. Martin; Nico Scherf; Konstantin Weise; Thomas R. Knösche

title: Outcomes of Minimally Invasive versus Open Surgery for Incarcerated or Strangulated Abdominal Wall Hernia Repair
abstract: Emergency repair of acutely incarcerated or strangulated abdominal wall hernias requires prompt reduction, assessment of bowel viability and definitive repair, with the operative approach influenced by the patient's physiological condition, the degree of contamination and the need for bowel resection. This narrative review examines outcomes of minimally invasive surgery (MIS) compared with open repair, focusing on feasibility, postoperative outcomes, patient selection, mesh use and surgical expertise. The available literature suggests that laparoscopic repair, particularly transabdominal pre-peritoneal (TAPP) repair for groin hernias, is feasible in selected patients and may be associated with shorter hospital stays and fewer wound complications. MIS can also permit direct assessment of bowel viability and, in appropriately equipped and experienced centres, bowel resection when required. However, suspected ischaemia or the need for resection demands careful assessment, and perforation, generalised peritonitis, extensive contamination, haemodynamic instability or inadequate laparoscopic access may favour open surgery or prompt conversion. Mesh may reduce recurrence in selected emergency repairs, although infection risk becomes more relevant with bowel resection and contamination. Interpretation of comparative outcomes is limited by predominantly retrospective evidence, selection bias, variation in hernia types and operative techniques, and inconsistent long-term follow-up. Current evidence therefore supports MIS as a selective option rather than a universally superior approach. Prospective multicentre studies with standardised definitions and long-term assessment of recurrence, reoperation, chronic pain and functional recovery are needed.
authors: Arjun Jay Prakash; Ahmed Elgohary; Shamika Sumanathissa; Filiza Koya; Sylvie Marie Regine Etienne; Mohamed Sadek; Mir Saad Ahamed

title: P32 Delayed phenylketonuria diagnosis in a 60-year-old male: a case report of a phenotype mimicking hereditary spastic paraplegia
abstract: Phenylketonuria (PKU) is an autosomal recessive metabolic disorder caused by phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH) deficiency. Newborn screening programmes in the UK have largely eliminated its severe presentations, however a tiny fraction of patients, especially those born before the introduction of newborn blood spot screening, may have escaped early diagnosis. We discuss the WGS findings of a 60-year-old British caucasian male who presented with a 10-15-year history of progressive spastic tetraparesis affecting the legs, brisk reflexes, hypertonia of the upper limbs and muscle spasms. WGS analysis yielded two variants in the PAH gene classified as pathogenic and likely pathogenic for which the phase was unknown. Following clinical discussion, a history of mild learning difficulties was uncovered and metabolic workup revealed a severely elevated serum phenylalanine concentration, confirming the diagnosis of PKU and highlighting the importance of biochemical follow up. This case demonstrates that PKU can present uniquely in late adulthood as progressive spastic paraplegia without severe childhood intellectual disability and shows the importance of complete phenotypic information. Clinical scientists should not rule out the possibility of inborn errors of metabolism when analysing WGS in adults presenting with atypical neurodegenerative phenotypes and multidisciplinary discussion is critical in such cases.
authors: J Jaudzemaite; L Cobbold; A Haworth; M McQueen-Mencias

title: P34 Identification and automated phenotypic characterisation of putative autosomal dominant RELA variants in patients with inflammatory bowel disease
abstract: Background RELA encodes the p65 subunit of the NF-kB complex, regulating transcription of inflammatory response genes. Autosomal dominant RELA variants cause autoinflammation and immune dysregulation, including inflammatory bowel disease(IBD). Methods Southampton genetics of IBD study(n=1,291), and Mt Sinai Crohn’s and Colitis cohort(n=1,038), were interrogated. Phenotype and whole-exome data were used to identify patients with likely-pathogenic variants in RELA. GenePy, a method to integrate rare and common functionally impactful variants was used to generate whole-gene RELA scores for all. Human phenotype ontology (HPO) terms were extracted from clinical records and standardised using HPOMapper v1.0. Association for Clinical Genomic Science(ACGS) criteria were applied to assess variant pathogenicity. Results 44 patients with non-zero GenePy in RELA were found in these cohorts(n=2,329). Literature review identified 35 HPO terms associated with RELA. Of these 35 terms, raised CRP, increased faecal calprotectin, and increased eosinophil count were found in >50% of patients. 10/44 patients were identified as having a matching phenotype and in-silico variant predictions suggesting functional impact. One variant (observed in two patients) was classified as likely-pathogenic using ACGS guidelines. Conclusions We identified one likely-pathogenic variant in two patients with IBD suggesting RELA haploinsufficiencymay be an underlying cause of disease in a proportion of cases.

title: Performance Measurements from split Timed Up and Down Stairs test in Cerebral Palsy with and without Ankle Foot Orthoses
abstract: The dataset presented was collected during split Timed Up and Down Stairs tests of a novel, robotic ankle foot orthosis (AFO) with adjustable stiffness and manually variable neutral angle for seven individuals with spastic cerebral palsy (CP). Tests were conducted between May 2025 - October 2025 at Northern Arizona University. Test conditions included nine combinations of stiffness and neutral angle for the robotic AFO, a solid AFO, and shoes alone. Outcomes included TUDs time, peak ankle dorsiflexion and plantarflexion, knee range of motion, soleus and vastus lateralis integrated electromyography, perceived exertion, balance confidence, 3-axis trunk acceleration, and robotic AFO power and torque. These outcomes, conditions, and participant characteristics are reported in this dataset. These data may contribute to 1) further development of robotic ankle foot orthoses and 2) understanding stair ambulation biomechanics in CP.

title: PhenX Toolkit: a knowledgebase that enables consistent data collection and facilitates cross-study analysis and data reuse
abstract: The PhenX (consensus measures for Phenotypes and eXposures) Toolkit (https://www.phenxtoolkit.org/) is a publicly available knowledgebase of well-established, broadly validated measurement protocols recommended for use in genomic, clinical, translational, and epidemiological research involving human participants. Consistent use of PhenX protocols, including questionnaires, bioassays, and physical assessments, improves the rigor, transparency, reproducibility, and comparability of research data. The Toolkit was recently highlighted in the National Institutes of Health (NIH) implementation plan, "Leading in Gold Standard Science," as an example of efforts to advance reproducible biomedical research. The Toolkit currently includes 1010 protocols spanning a wide range of diseases, exposures, and study designs. Content development is guided by the scientific community through a consensus-based process involving expert Working Groups, community input, and strategic oversight from the PhenX Steering Committee. Collaborations with NIH Institutes have expanded Toolkit content in priority areas, including substance use and cardiovascular disease. The PhenX Toolkit enhances study design and supports implementation of selected protocols. PhenX also collaborates with resources that facilitate data collection (REDCap), data standards (LOINC), and data repositories to promote interoperability and cross-study analyses. To date, the Toolkit has been recommended in 711 NIH funding opportunities and cited in >1300 publications. Future directions are discussed.

title: Physical Ergonomics in Robotics
abstract: With the emergence of embodied intelligent systems like collaborative robots (cobots), the landscape of physically demanding work is changing. Indeed, robotic devices can augment human strength, optimize performance, and minimize the physical demands associated with a job or a task. These achievements of human-robot interaction (HRI) surely match the objectives of physical ergonomics: making physical interactions between humans and other elements of a system more efficient, more gratifying, and safer. One of the key goals of physical ergonomics certainly is to prevent work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSDs). Therefore, a cobot must have insight into the effect of physical stress on the human body. One of the most common ways to provide that is to use the established ergonomics look-up tables that indicate which working configurations and conditions may cause WMSDs based on experience. Another approach is to use musculoskeletal models to get real-time estimates of key internal body parameters, such as joint torques, muscle forces, and muscle fatigue. A cobotic or, in general, robotic system can then use these ergonomic indexes and variables to guide a human co-worker to more favourable configurations and conditions. In this chapter, we examine physical human-robot interactions (pHRIs) to have an introductory overview of possible scenarios and constraints. We then look into the fundamentals of physical ergonomics such as anthropometry, biomechanics, and environmental factors, including important ergonomic assessment tools and innovative indicators developed in robotics. Subsequently, concrete examples of methods that address physical ergonomics with collaborative robotics are examined in terms of design and control methods.

title: Physics-informed neural operators for rapid electric field prediction in transcranial magnetic stimulation of healthy and tumor subjects
abstract: Accurate and rapid prediction of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS)-induced electric fields is essential for personalized clinical applications, from individualized therapy in major depressive disorder to presurgical functional mapping in neuro-oncology. Yet conventional finite element methods are often too computationally expensive for interactive use. Existing deep learning surrogate models partly address this limitation but are largely constrained to fixed voxel-grid representations that cannot naturally accommodate the irregular geometry of subject-specific head meshes. We present the first physics-informed neural operator (PINO) for subject-specific prediction of vector TMS electric fields, built on a mesh-native dual-encoder architecture that jointly encodes head anatomy and coil configuration. By incorporating a curl-based regularization term aligned with the curl-free nature of the TMS secondary field, the PINO model promotes physical consistency as a soft regularizer alongside data-driven supervision. Trained on 75 subjects from the IXI dataset, the framework was evaluated across four independent held-out test datasets, including healthy subjects from two additional MRI cohorts and, for the first time in learning-based TMS electric-field prediction, tumor patients. The resolution-agnostic formulation generalizes across subjects, coil types, and spatial resolutions without retraining, predicting vector electric fields on approximately 300,000 gray matter volume nodes in under 100 ms on a consumer-grade GPU. Across all test datasets within the focality-50% region, the PINO model achieved median center-of-gravity errors of 0.39–0.43 mm, RMSE of 0.12–0.16 V/m, and mean angular deviations of 6.7°–7.3°, with performance within or below the error ranges reported by recent deep-learning approaches. At the selected 5% physics-loss weighting, curl loss decreased by 9.1% relative to the data-only model, while RMSE and MAD increased by only 1.6% and 1.3%, respectively. These results suggest that physics-informed neural operators provide a scalable technical foundation for rapid gray-matter electric-field approximation, supporting future studies on real-time electric-field-guided TMS workflows

title: Posterior cruciate ligament biomechanics in pediatric finite element knee models: Validation against cadaveric posterior tibial translation and coupled rotational loading
abstract: BACKGROUND: Pediatric posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) biomechanics remain poorly characterized, and validated computational models are limited. The purpose of this study was to evaluate whether pediatric knee finite element models could reproduce intact cadaveric posterior tibial translation under PCL-dominant loading. METHODS: Twenty-two pediatric knee models were generated from computed tomography scans using a previously established juvenile modeling workflow. Model predictions were benchmarked against published intact cadaveric data for two loading conditions: a 134 N posterior tibial load at 30° flexion and a coupled 100 N posterior tibial load with 5 Nm external rotation at 0° of flexion. Posterior tibial translation was compared using Welch's two-sample t-tests and confidence intervals. FINDINGS: Under isolated posterior loading at 30°, the models predicted 9.4 ± 1.4 mm of posterior tibial translation compared with 10.8 ± 3.7 mm in the cadaveric benchmark (p = 0.15). No significant difference was found under the coupled posterior loading with external rotation between the models predicted posterior translations of 6.9 ± 0.6 mm and the experimental translation at 6.5 ± 3.1 (p = 0.56). INTERPRETATION: These findings support the use of specimen-specific pediatric knee models as an externally benchmarked platform for studying PCL biomechanics. Accurate reproduction of cadaveric posterior laxity under clinically relevant loading provides a foundation for future analyses of pediatric injury mechanisms and surgical and rehabilitation strategies.
authors: Alexandria Mallinos; Richard P Steiner; Kerwyn C. Jones

title: Predicting Robot-Based Tracking Performance After Stroke Using Lesion Features and Clinical Assessments: A Pilot Study
abstract: Background: Following stroke, motor and cognitive impairments often limit functional independence. Personalized rehabilitation requires comprehensive clinical assessments, which are costly and time-consuming. Imaging scans are routinely collected, but their predictive value in determining post-stroke function remains unclear. Objectives: To determine the ability of clinical assessments, lesion features with medical chart information, and a combined clinical and biomedical model to predict kinematic outcomes from a robot-based tracking task in chronic stroke individuals. Methods: Eighteen participants (70±6 years) completed a robot-based tracking task and a battery of motor and cognitive assessments. Three elastic net regression models were developed: 1) clinical assessments only; 2) lesion metrics and chart information only; and 3) a combined model. Models were evaluated using leave-one-subject-out cross-validation, bootstrapping, and permutation testing with false discovery rate correction. Robot-based outcomes included tracking error, normalized distance, velocity error response, and delay. Results: =0.11). The imaging model did not significantly predict any outcome. Box and Blocks Test and Color Trails 1 were stable features. The right dorsal attention network was a stable predictor in several combined models. Conclusion: Clinical assessments outperformed lesion features in predicting tracking performance after chronic stroke. Attention- and motor-related measures were the strongest predictors, highlighting the importance of cognitive-motor interactions in function. A larger sample and more granular lesion features may improve prediction from imaging biomarkers.
authors: Reem M. Azar; Erica L. Waters; Joana Opong-Duah; Rochelle J. Mendonca; Pamela Z. Cacchione; Michelle Jillian Johnson

title: Predictors of 6-month clinical change in primary progressive aphasia following language therapy and transcranial magnetic stimulation
abstract: Primary progressive aphasia (PPA) is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive language impairment. Available treatments and information on factors associated with clinical change and treatment response remain limited. This study is a post hoc analysis of a randomized controlled trial and aimed to identify baseline demographic, cognitive and neuroimaging factors associated with clinical change in a subanalysis of a double-blind, randomized, parallel clinical trial of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) and language therapy in PPA. Fifty-seven patients diagnosed with PPA received 6 months of lexical retrieval treatment, 40 with active TMS and 17 with sham TMS. All participants underwent comprehensive cognitive and language assessments before treatment and were evaluated using the Mini Linguistic State Examination (MLSE), naming task, words per minute, the Interview for Deterioration in Daily Living Activities in Dementia (IDDD), the Neuropsychiatric Inventory (NPI) and fluorodeoxyglucose-PET scans before and after treatment. Predictors of clinical change were analysed using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) and Elastic Net regression models, and unsupervised k-means clustering was applied to identify response profiles. Models for MLSE (LASSO: R2 = 0.52; Elastic Net: R2 = 0.57), naming (LASSO: R2 = 0.42; Elastic Net: R2 = 0.41), IDDD (LASSO: R2 = 0.46; Elastic Net: R2 = 0.58) and NPI (LASSO: R2 = 0.81; Elastic Net: R2 = 0.77) demonstrated good predictive accuracy. TMS treatment consistently emerged as the strongest predictor of clinical improvement across all outcomes. Higher metabolism in several brain regions (left hippocampus, posterior cingulate and orbitofrontal cortex) predicted greater clinical improvement. Cluster analysis identified two subgroups: responders and non-responders, with 77.5% of patients receiving active TMS in the responder cluster and 82.4% of the sham group in the non-responder cluster. Among patients receiving active TMS, a positive effect was associated with the non-fluent and semantic variants and with better cognitive performance in non-language domains. In conclusion, TMS treatment emerged as the main factor associated with clinical improvement on cognitive-linguistic and functional measures. Better cognitive performance and preserved brain metabolism in key regions were linked to more favourable clinical outcomes. These findings underscore the potential of TMS in combination with language therapy and pave the way for precision medicine approaches in PPA, emphasizing the need to identify individual profiles that predict optimal treatment response.

title: Preliminary Design of Hybrid Aircraft Thermal Management System (Tms) Experimental Test Campaign in Cira Icing Wind Tunnel (IWT)
abstract: Within the EU-funded AMBER project [1], CIRA (Italian Aerospace Research Centre) is responsible for the experimental validation of the Thermal Management System (TMS) for a hybrid aircraft. To support this activity, CIRA is upgrading its Icing Wind Tunnel (IWT) [8], taking advantage of its large test section and its ability to reproduce realistic flight conditions, including altitude, temperature, and mass flow rates ranging from 1.5 to 55 kg/s. The upgraded facility will enable full-scale testing of TMS units with power levels up to approximately 0.5 MW, providing realistic operating conditions for accurate performance evaluation and optimization. This paper presents the ongoing upgrades to the IWT, including the required equipment, subsystems, and experimental requirements for TMS characterization. A preliminary numerical performance characterization of a realistic TMS for an hybrid aircraft has been performed leading to a better definition of the facility operating envelope. Once completed, the upgraded IWT will provide a unique capability for testing thermal management systems under representative hybrid aircraft operating conditions, supporting the development and validation of advanced thermal performance solutions.

title: Preoperative coronal phenotype is associated with the initial balance state but only weakly with final balance in robot‐assisted TKA
abstract: PURPOSE: To determine how preoperative coronal phenotype and structural remodelling relate to initial and final intraoperative balance in robot-assisted total knee arthroplasty. METHODS: Initial analyses included 429 knees; final/change analyses included 389. Preoperative phenotype was characterised by hip-knee-ankle angle (HKA), arithmetic HKA (aHKA), functional knee phenotype (FKP), and categorical aHKA-joint-line obliquity (JLO) components. Structural factors included medial and lateral osteophyte burden and coronal tibiofemoral subluxation. Medial and lateral gaps and coronal laxity ranges were recorded in extension and flexion before and after balancing. Signed mediolateral gap difference was defined as lateral minus medial, and change as final minus initial. Initial extension signed gap difference was the primary outcome; corresponding initial flexion, final, and change outcomes were secondary. Compartment-specific gaps, laxity ranges, and varus-valgus analyses were exploratory. Multivariable linear regression adjusted for age, sex, and body mass index, with patient-level cluster-robust standard errors and Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction. RESULTS: values of 0.234 and 0.122, respectively. In exploratory comparisons, valgus knees had greater initial extension and flexion signed gap differences than varus knees (adjusted mean differences, 3.10 mm [95% confidence interval, 2.39-3.81] and 2.98 mm [2.23-3.74], respectively; both false discovery rate-adjusted p values were < 0.001). CONCLUSIONS: Preoperative coronal phenotype and structural remodelling explained only modest variability in the initial intraoperative balance state and changes between assessments, and little variability in final balance, particularly in flexion. These findings support direct intraoperative assessment. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, retrospective cohort study.

title: Preresection hyperextension is associated with greater initial extension laxity and site‐specific reductions in bone resection without substantial joint‐line lowering in robot‐assisted cruciate‐retaining total knee arthroplasty
abstract: PURPOSE: Associations of preresection hyperextension with intraoperative laxity, bone resections, joint-line height and clinical outcomes were examined in cruciate-retaining (CR) robot-assisted total knee arthroplasty (TKA). METHODS: In this retrospective single-surgeon cohort, knees were classified by initial intraoperative extension angle as control (0° to +5°), mild hyperextension (-5° to <0°) or greater hyperextension (<-5°). Intraoperative balance, surgical adjustments, joint-line height, 6-week clinical extension and 1-year Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score for Joint Replacement (KOOS-JR) outcomes were evaluated. Adjusted associations were assessed using regression models. RESULTS: Among 258 knees (149 control, 76 mild and 33 greater), greater initial extension laxity was observed in both hyperextension groups versus controls, with adjusted differences of 1.1° (95% CI, 0.4-1.9) and 2.4° (1.1-3.7), respectively. Postoperative hip-knee-ankle angle differences versus controls (n = 256) were 0.1° (95% CI, -0.9 to 1.0) and -0.6° (-1.8 to 0.7), respectively. Among 109 hyperextension knees, each 5° greater hyperextension was associated with smaller distal lateral femoral and proximal medial tibial resections (adjusted β, -1.0 mm [95% CI, -1.6 to -0.3] and -1.2 mm [-1.7 to -0.6]; false-discovery-rate-adjusted p = 0.016 and p < 0.001). Mean joint-line lowering was 0.3 mm (95% CI, 0.02-0.60), without a significant association with hyperextension magnitude. No significant differences were detected in final extension imbalance or 6-week extension. Paired KOOS-JR scores were available for 208 knees, without significant group differences in scores or improvement. Greater hyperextension was associated with higher adjusted odds of patient acceptable symptom state (PASS) failure versus combined control and mild-hyperextension groups (OR, 2.69; 95% CI, 1.02-7.08; p = 0.045). CONCLUSIONS: Greater preresection hyperextension was associated with greater initial extension laxity, smaller selected resections and higher adjusted odds of PASS failure. Minimal average joint-line change was observed. Using initial sagittal assessment to individualise resection planning is supported. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, retrospective cohort study.
authors: Yugo Morita; Jonggu Shin; Mohammed El-Hassan; Ittai Shichman; Skylar Lewis; John M. Dundon; William John Long; Peter Keyes Sculco

title: Principles of use of tensile J-curve materials in antagonistic arrangements
abstract: Natural ligaments are soft connective tissues that provide high stretchability for dexterous flexibility but switch to high stiffness to protect the musculoskeletal system from excessive deformation. These two functions cannot be independently tuned in conventional engineering materials with linear or hyperelasticity. Biological materials achieve this tailored behavior through a highly nonlinear tensile response characterized by a J-shaped curve, featuring an extended "toe region" of low force up to intermediate strains followed by an inflection, called the "heel region" which marks the onset of nonlinear stiffening. Here, we aim to study the characteristics of J-curves to establish principles for their use in robotic mechanisms. We define and measure the J-curve features responsible for protectiveness and mobility, describe the effective stiffness and the level of nonlinearity as a function of pre-stretch, and elucidate how the J-curve decouples flexibility from damage protection. Experimental measurements reveal the performance advantages of twisted and coiled elastomeric J-curve materials in engineered antagonistic arrangements and highlight their unique design space compared with linear elastic systems. Furthermore, we present a conceptual analysis of exploiting J-curve materials in energy-efficient running as an outlook toward their use in bioinspired robots.

title: Proceedings del XXVI Congresso SIAMOC 2026
abstract: FROM RESEARCH TO PRACTICE: ASSESSMENT AND REHABILITATION OF MOVEMENT DISORDERS IN ADULT AND PEDIATRIC POPULATIONS Il congresso annuale della Società Italiana di Analisi del Movimento in Clinica (SIAMOC) giunge alla sua XXVI edizione e nel 2026 si terrà a Genova: una città che invita al movimento, fatta di salite e discese, percorsi che cambiano prospettiva e traiettorie che si intrecciano tra mare e alture. Genova è da sempre luogo di scambio e connessione, in cui esperienze e competenze diverse si incontrano e si trasformano in dialogo. Il suo carattere, fatto di passaggi, incroci e relazioni, rappresenta una cornice particolarmente adatta per ospitare una comunità come quella SIAMOC, che fonda la propria identità sull’incontro tra competenze differenti e sulla costruzione di un linguaggio comune. In questi anni l’analisi del movimento ha ampliato il proprio ruolo nella clinica, diventando uno strumento sempre più trasversale nei percorsi di valutazione, riabilitazione e assistenza. Dalla valutazione strumentale del cammino e della postura all’analisi del movimento nei contesti di diverse patologie, nella vita quotidiana e durante il sonno, dalla definizione degli obiettivi riabilitativi alla quantificazione degli esiti e alla personalizzazione del trattamento, l’analisi del movimento contribuisce oggi a rendere la decisione clinica più precisa, riproducibile e condivisa. Il messaggio scientifico di questa edizione è racchiuso nel suo titolo: From Research to Practice. Il congresso vuole valorizzare il percorso che porta dalle evidenze scientifiche alla pratica clinica quotidiana, promuovendo strumenti, metodi e linguaggi condivisi per la valutazione, la riabilitazione e l’assistenza nei disturbi del movimento nelle popolazioni adulta e pediatrica. L’obiettivo ultimo è rendere la valutazione sempre più utile nelle decisioni cliniche e nella vita di tutti i giorni, migliorando autonomia, partecipazione e qualità di vita. In un ambito per sua natura multidisciplinare, SIAMOC rappresenta un punto di riferimento per il confronto e il lavoro in team tra professionisti: medici, fisioterapisti e terapisti della riabilitazione, ingegneri biomedici, psicologi, scienziati motori, ricercatori, tecnici e studiosi del movimento umano. Il congresso è il luogo in cui queste competenze si incontrano non solo per presentare risultati, ma soprattutto per discutere metodi, definire standard, costruire una visione e messaggi comuni capaci di tradursi in pratica clinica.
