title: TMS timed to interictal epileptiform discharges
abstract: Interictal epileptiform discharges (IEDs) are pathological hypersynchronous bursts of electrical brain activity that occur between seizures in patients with epilepsy. IEDs are caused by transient brain states that are difficult to predict, making them a challenging neurophysiological and technological case for brain-state-dependent stimulation. Administering stimulation at IED onset may provide insight into the epileptic network and optimize neurostimulation therapies. Here, we assessed the feasibility of IED-triggered transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) in two children with self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes (SeLECTS), a common pediatric epilepsy in which IEDs emerge from the motor cortex. A convolutional neural network (CNN) was trained on the participants’ pre-recorded electroencephalography (EEG) data with IEDs annotated by an epileptologist. The CNN was integrated into an EEG-processing pipeline that classified EEG segments as “IED” or “non-IED” in real time. With this pipeline, TMS pulses were administered during IED or non-IED periods in an interleaved, randomized design. We stimulated both the motor cortex generating the IEDs and the contralateral motor cortex and tested the impact of IEDs on TMS-evoked potentials (TEPs). Our study demonstrated that TMS can be timed to IEDs and that there is a site-specific increase in TEP amplitude when stimulating during IEDs. Out of the TMS pulses aimed at an IED, 19% and 39% were successfully delivered during an IED for the two participants, respectively. For future research, we propose ways to address the methodological challenges of IED-timed TMS, enabling brain-state-dependent TMS for epilepsy research and treatment.
authors: Matilda Makkonen; Olli‐Pekka Kahilakoski; Miguel Menchaca; Ivan Zubarev; Oula Siljamo; Umair Hassan; Xiwei Shé; Wendy Qi; Tuomas P. Mutanen; Risto Juhani Ilmoniemi; Pantelis Lioumis; Fiona Mitchell Baumer

title: TMS-EEG Investigation of Cortical Activity Induced by Individualized rTMS in Patients with Prolonged Disorders of Consciousness
abstract: Objective To establish an individualized repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) target selection protocol based on resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) directed functional connectivity for patients with prolonged disorders of consciousness (pDoC), and to explore the underlying electrophysiological mechanisms using transcranial magnetic stimulation combined with EEG (TMS-EEG). Methods We enrolled 42 pDoC patients and randomly assigned to an individualized rTMS group, a conventional rTMS group, and a sham stimulation group. The individualized rTMS group selected the target with stronger directed functional connectivity between F3 and Pz as the stimulation site based on Granger causality analysis. The conventional rTMS group received random stimulation at either F3 or Pz. Both active groups received 10 sessions of high-frequency rTMS over 10 consecutive days, while the sham group underwent sham stimulation. Behavioral improvement and cortical connectivity were assessed before and after treatment using the Coma Recovery Scale-Revised (CRS-R) and TMS-EEG, respectively. Results CRS-R scores significantly increased in both the individualized and conventional rTMS groups ( p < 0.05), whereas no significant improvement was observed in the sham group ( p > 0.05). TMS-EEG analysis demonstrated that the amplitudes of N100 and P180 components significantly increased post-treatment in both active groups ( p < 0.05), with no statistically significant changes in the sham group ( p > 0.05). Global mean field amplitude (GMFA) significantly increased post-treatment in both active groups ( p < 0.05). Specifically, significant increases were found in the 1-100 ms and 101–200 ms time windows post-treatment in both active groups ( p < 0.05). Additionally, the individualized rTMS group showed a significant increase in the 201–300 ms window ( p < 0.05), which was not observed in the conventional group ( p > 0.05). No significant differences were found in the sham group across any time windows (1-100 ms, 101–200 ms, 201–300 ms, 301–400 ms, 401–500 ms; p > 0.05). Correlation analyses indicated that the change in CRS-R score positively correlated with the change in N100 amplitude in both the individualized ( r = 0.82, p < 0.001) and conventional ( r = 0.79, p = 0.001) treatment groups. Similarly, the change in CRS-R score positively correlated with the change in P180 amplitude in the individualized ( r = 0.77, p = 0.0002) and conventional ( r = 0.62, p = 0.025) groups. Conclusion Individualized rTMS based on resting-state EEG directed functional connectivity is more effective in promoting consciousness recovery in pDoC patients. Compared to conventional rTMS, this approach may better facilitate the sustained propagation of post-stimulation cortical activity along residual consciousness networks and promote integration during middle-to-late stages. This study provides preliminary evidence supporting the transition of neuromodulation therapy for pDoC from fixed-target interventions to individualized precision regulation. Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05682248. Ethics approval : Ethics Committee of Xuanwu Hospital, 2022[022].
authors: Ye Zhang; Xiao Yan; Zilong Zhu; 杜巨豹; Lei Cao; weiqun Song; Yong Wang

title: Targeting Tumour Microtubes to Disrupt Glioma Networks
abstract: Glioma cells form multicellular communication networks through tumour microtubes (TMs), integrating tumour–tumour and neuron–tumour connectivity to sustain growth and therapy resistance. Underlying molecular regulation of TMs and potential targeting strategies have proven elusive. Here, we demonstrate that glioma stem cells (GSCs) preferentially grow TMs, which locally synthesize neurotransmitter receptors and metabolic enzymes to support network communication. Coordinated proteomics and functional screening of TMs identified inner mitochondrial component, FASTKD2, as essential to local protein synthesis. Targeting FASTKD2 attenuates tumour stemness and growth, disrupting coordinated mitochondrial RNA metabolism in TMs, which sustains intercellular communication and tumour proliferation. Structure-function screening revealed antibiotic linezolid inhibited FASTKD2 interactions with mitochondrial RNA, thereby disrupting tumour network communication and augmenting efficacy of therapies targeting neuronal stimulation of tumour cells. Collectively, tumour cells coopt features of neuronal cell biology, including localized protein synthesis, to reinforce TM-mediated glioma network communication, generating therapeutic vulnerabilities.
authors: Tengfei Huang; Po Zhang; Suchet Taori; Shuai Wang; Shuai Wang; 陈志晔; Huairui Yuan; Xujia Wu; Tingting Duan; Tingting Duan; Weichi Wu; Rui Wang; Huan Li; Huan Li; Deguan Lv; Deobrat Dixit; qiulian wu; Jeremy Rich; Frank Winkler

title: Teamknitt: Configuring, Observing and Intervening in LLM-Agent Teams through the Lens of Dynamical-Systems and Human-Team Theory
abstract: Most frameworks for teams of large language model (LLM) agents fix the team's shape inside the software: who talks to whom, how much is passed along, and what a human can do once a run has started. Human-team research has long asked those questions: where team phenomena live (in members or in their interaction), how team-level properties arise, and what separates what a team does from how a team is. I propose using that theory as the organizing lens for configuring, observing and intervening in LLM-agent teams, without assuming its findings transfer. I introduce teamknitt, a framework and open reference implementation in which a user configures a team of 1-16 AI agents for task completion, solution generation, achieving a goal or a research mission; selects one of fourteen deterministic routing topologies or a custom directed graph; chooses a sharing profile that limits what may travel along permitted routes; and binds sources, representations, work dependencies, handoffs and an expertise directory. The recorded process can be observed through non-system views (member reports and behavior) and system views (distributed problem-solving, differentiated transactive memory, interactive coordination, team dynamics). Interventions are explicit and human-led: reviewed reconfiguration between runs, planned disturbances, and private feedback, pause, resume or stop applied at dependency-wave boundaries, with "queued", "applied", "assembled", "understood" and "improved" kept as separate claims. Emergent states such as trust and shared understanding are declared unmeasured. This is an idea and system-description paper with falsifiable hypotheses on topology, information flow and intervention timing, including whether the fractal scaling of communication output between members, and between members on different models, relates to task and team performance. No comparative result is reported.
authors: Goran Mitevski

title: Temporomandibular Joint Arthrocentesis and Prolotherapy
abstract: Temporomandibular joint disorders (TMD) comprise a heterogeneous group of conditions characterized by pain, restricted mandibular movement, joint sounds, and functional impairment. Among minimally invasive treatment modalities, temporomandibular joint (TMJ) arthrocentesis and prolotherapy have emerged as valuable options for patients who do not respond adequately to conservative management. Arthrocentesis primarily involves lavage and hydraulic distension of the superior joint space to remove inflammatory mediators, disrupt intra-articular adhesions, and improve mandibular mobility. In contrast, prolotherapy involves the injection of an irritant solution, commonly dextrose, to stimulate a localized reparative response in periarticular tissues and may be particularly relevant in patients with ligamentous laxity, joint hypermobility, instability, or recurrent subluxation. This chapter reviews the historical evolution, relevant anatomy, indications, contraindications, procedural techniques, potential complications, and current clinical applications of TMJ arthrocentesis and prolotherapy. Particular emphasis is placed on understanding the differing mechanisms of action and therapeutic objectives of these interventions. Arthrocentesis is primarily directed toward intra-articular pathology and mechanical restriction, whereas prolotherapy targets periarticular tissue dysfunction and instability. Understanding these distinctions can assist clinicians in selecting an appropriate minimally invasive approach based on the underlying pathology, clinical presentation, and treatment objectives. By integrating current concepts and practical considerations, this chapter provides a clinically oriented framework for the application of arthrocentesis and prolotherapy in the management of TMDs.
authors: Atapol Yongvikul

title: The Discovery Gap: Why Artificial Intelligence Must Learn to Change Its Mind "Rethinking Human–AI Collaboration from Molecule to Market"
abstract: Scientific discovery requires the revision of belief: giving up a claim when the evidence turns against it, and knowing what else must change with it. Artificial intelligence (AI) has transformed research - predicting protein structures, generating molecules, screening billions of candidates - but it does not do this. Autonomous agents traverse the discovery loop end to end without holding the beliefs that loop exists to revise. I use dynamic scientific intelligence for the class of system this requires, one that holds hypotheses as persistent objects with provenance, uncertainty and explicit dependencies. Its distinguishing condition is that a system can identify what supports each commitment and what depends on it, and so revise one without disturbing the rest. Because no architecture can revise beliefs on evidence it never receives, the problem is jointly architectural and infrastructural. Using drug development from molecule to market as the test case, I identify where evidence generated downstream should revise commitments made upstream and does not, and three decision points at which the non-delegable human act is adjudication rather than generation. I propose a revision test - an evaluation distinct in kind from any predictive benchmark - and a minimum reporting standard for claims of AI-assisted discovery. Until AI learns to change its mind well, it will remain a tool rather than an infrastructure in which discovery accumulates.
authors: Silvano Coletti

title: The Effects of Robotic Rehabilitation on Spasticity in Spinal Cord Injury: Current Evidence and Methodological Limitations
abstract: In this Letter to the Editor, Bayraktar critically examines the conflicting evidence regarding the effects of robot-assisted gait training (RAGT) on spasticity in patients with spinal cord injury. Drawing on recent meta-analyses and clinical studies, the author highlights inconsistencies in reported outcomes and identifies methodological limitations associated with conventional spasticity assessments, particularly the Modified Ashworth Scale. The letter advocates incorporating the Modified Tardieu Scale, Spasm Frequency Score, and patient-reported outcomes to better capture the multidimensional nature of spasticity. Importantly, it emphasizes that reduced muscle tone does not necessarily translate into functional improvement and that clinical factors influencing spasticity must be considered. This timely contribution underscores the need for standardized, comprehensive outcome assessments in future randomized controlled trials of robotic rehabilitation.
authors: Handan Elif Nur Bayraktar
venue: European Journal of Innovative Medical Research

title: The Evolution of Brain-Computer Interfaces Towards Collaborative Intelligence
abstract: Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) are evolving from unidirectional control toward deeper integration of biological and machine intelligence. This transition is constrained by two complementary bottlenecks: Intent Mismatch, or Brain-to-Machine Underreach, in which user intentions cannot be sufficiently decoded, represented, or executed by the machine; and State Mismatch, or Machine-to-Brain Overload, in which system demands exceed the user’s current cognitive, affective, or neural resources. This review uses these two mismatches as an organizing framework for examining the evolution of BCIs toward brain-machine collaborative intelligence, while distinguishing non-invasive and invasive modalities according to their signal characteristics and translational constraints. We review neural decoding, generative artificial intelligence, and shared control as approaches for reducing Intent Mismatch, and passive BCIs, adaptive interaction, neurofeedback, and neuromodulation as approaches for reducing State Mismatch. By integrating these solution paths, this review outlines a pathway toward adaptive, bidirectional, and human-centered BCI systems.
authors: Yang Yu; Yingxin Liu; Zhipeng Fan; Zongtan Zhou; Ling‐Li Zeng; Dewen Hu

title: The GenAI Who Knew Too Little: Revisiting Transactive Memory Systems in Human GenAI Collaboration
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly transforming knowledge work, creating new collaborative dynamics that challenge tradi-tional human-human interaction patterns. This study investigates how Transactive Memory Systems (TMS) manifest in human-GenAI collabora-tion. Through qualitative interpretive interviews with 14 knowledge work-ers and thematic analysis, we identified distinct TMS manifestations across its three main dimensions: (1) regarding specialization, expertise recogni-tion exhibited asymmetry. Humans developed awareness of GenAI capabili-ties while GenAI demonstrated only temporary recognition of human exper-tise; (2) in terms of credibility, humans formed ambivalent trust relation-ships with GenAI, simultaneously attributing expertise to the latter while implementing additional verification processes; and (3) concerning coor-dination, where humans primarily directed more passive GenAI systems lacking initiative, resulting in hierarchical interaction patterns and unidi-rectional information flow. Our findings reveal that TMS manifests differ-ently in human-GenAI compared to human-human collaboration, necessitat-ing theoretical adaptations including trust markers, acknowledging GenAI's absent metamemory, and identifying its temporary memory.
authors: Christian Meske; Tobias Hermanns; Florian Brachten

title: The Impact of Selected Physical Factors on Neurogenesis—What Do We Know?
abstract: New discoveries are constantly being made regarding cognitive processes, pain perception, the development of degenerative diseases, brain aging, and many other functions of the nervous system. Neurogenesis plays a significant role in all of these processes. As a manifestation of brain plasticity, neurogenesis continues throughout life, and its intensity can vary depending on internal and external factors. The process by which neurons are generated can be disrupted. This depends, among other things, on age and represents one of the potential targets for interventions aimed at improving cognitive function. Inhibition of neurogenesis increases the risk of neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and other conditions that lead to dependence on others in their advanced stages. The status of the neurogenesis process can be monitored by measuring the levels of mediators in the blood. The state of the brain can be influenced by providing stimuli that increase the concentration of mediators stimulating neurogenesis. People are exposed to physical factors that can inhibit the neurogenesis process, but there are also phenomena that stimulate it. Magnetic stimulation, ultrasound, electrostimulation, light therapy, normobaric and hyperbaric oxygen therapy, whole-body cryotherapy, as well as touch and vibrations, can have a significant impact on neurogenesis and accelerate this process. The aim of this study is to present the impact of physical factors on the process of neurogenesis in humans and animals, which can significantly influence the course of this process. The review uses the wording originally used in the source articles.
authors: Adam Lipski; Kamil Koszela; Julia Pingot; Michał Słupiński; Robert Irzmański; Marta Woldańska-Okońska

title: The Reality Gap in Automated Driving Systems Testing: Landscape, Challenges, and Research Directions
abstract: Simulation is essential for testing automated driving systems (ADS), but discrepancies between simulation and reality can undermine testing conclusions. It remains unclear which discrepancies the literature addresses and what evidence supports correspondence claims. We present a systematic mapping of 235 primary studies that measure or mitigate the reality gap in ADS testing, selected from 4,195 publications. We characterise objectives, targets, approaches, experimental setups, and evaluation evidence. Our classification distinguishes simulated and real-world execution across six ADS test components, separately for each approach and its evaluation reference. This distinguishes real-world information used to construct an approach from evidence used to evaluate its claims. Of the included studies, 76% address mitigation, primarily targeting scenario and actor realism and perception, while 94% report validation or measurement procedures. Only 61 studies report metrics from multiple families covering sensor/perception correspondence, ADS behaviour, vehicle dynamics, or safety outcomes; this coverage does not establish causal links between discrepancies and test verdicts. The synthesis highlights that real-world content and physical execution must be interpreted against the claim evaluated. The findings motivate claim-specific evaluation and component-level reporting to establish which discrepancies affect testing conclusions and when simulation evidence supports conclusions about real-world ADS behaviour.
authors: Stefano Carlo Lambertenghi; Oliver Weißl; Johannes Betz; Andrea Stocco

title: The Role of Panca Cinta-Based Instructional Supervision in Supporting the Pedagogical and Professional Competencies of Arabic Language Teachers
abstract: This study examines the implementation of Panca Cinta-based instructional supervision and its contribution to supporting the pedagogical and professional competencies of Arabic teachers. Employing a qualitative case study approach, the study involved 7 informants, consisting of specify the informants roles, such as the head of the madrasah, vice principal for curriculum, Arabic teachers, and students. Data were collected through interviews, classroom observations, and document analysis, including lesson plans and supervision assessment forms. The data were analyzed descriptively to identify supervision practices and their contributions to teacher competencies. The findings show that supervision included scheduled pre-observation, classroom observation, post-observation evaluation, and follow-up, with Panca Cinta values integrated into lesson planning and classroom activities. In developing pedagogical competence, supervision contributed to teachers' ability to simplify learning materials, diversify instructional strategies, select appropriate visual and audio media, and adapt teaching approaches to students' learning needs and emotional conditions. In developing professional competence, supervision encouraged teachers to strengthen digital literacy, participate in professional development training, and explore artificial intelligence to create learning media. These findings suggest that humanistic and value-oriented supervision can support teacher development beyond performance evaluation. However, the study is limited to one madrasah and a small number of Arabic teachers, restricting the transferability of its findings to other educational contexts. The study offers an integrated perspective on Panca Cinta-based supervision as a humanistic approach to developing both pedagogical and professional competencies among Arabic language teachers.
authors: Siti Marya Ulpah; Sofyan Sauri; Mad Ali

title: The Role of Physicians and Caregivers in the Implementation of a Surgical Treatment Strategy for Hip Subluxation and Dislocation in Children with Cerebral Palsy
abstract: Introduction . Hip joint pathology is one of the most common and serious orthopedic complications in cerebral palsy. We conducted a study to identify the reasons for delays in surgical treatment of spastic hip instability from the perspective of parents’ roles and attitudes toward this issue. Aim : to determine the reasons for delays in surgical treatment for spastic hip instability in children with cerebral palsy and to examine parents’ perceptions of information provided by healthcare professionals. Materials and methods. An anonymous survey was conducted among parents of children who had undergone hip surgery. The study group included parents of 50 children with hip dislocation. The control group consisted of parents of 50 children who had undergone surgery for hip subluxation. Results . The average age of children at the time of surgery was 7.2±3.1 years (study group) and 5.8±2.9 years (control group); the differences were not statistically significant (p=0.12). Among parents of children with hip dislocation, 86% believed that the surgery was performed too late (compared to 55% in the subluxation group). Sixty-four percent of respondents attributed the primary responsibility for the delay to healthcare professionals. In the dislocation group, 60% of parents indicated that they completely rely on healthcare professionals regarding their child’s health, compared to only 29% of parents in the control group (p=0.003). In the dislocation group, 78% of parents reported being informed of the presence of hip pathology at least 3 years prior to surgery, but 82% believed that doctors did not provide them with complete and understandable information. In the control group, the corresponding figures were 52% and 36%, respectively (p <0.01). The study revealed a significant gap between the objective information provided by healthcare professionals and parents’ subjective perceptions of it. Parents tend to shift responsibility to healthcare professionals, which, in the absence of clear guidelines, leads to uncertainty and reliance on the doctor’s decision, which, however, is not always clear. Conclusion . Improving communication between the doctor and the family is an important condition for implementing a general rehabilitation program for children with cerebral palsy, who are at high risk of progression of musculoskeletal pathology, and should be considered an integral part of the prevention of orthopedic complications.
authors: Vladimir Markovich Kenis; T. I. Kiseleva; I. Yu. Klychkova; Andrey V. Sapogovskiy; Evgenii V. Melchenko; Stanislav V. Ivanov; Федосеева Александра Сергеевна

title: The effect of high-intensity magnetic therapy combined with robot-assisted gait training in post-stroke patients
abstract: AIMS: To assess whether adding high-intensity magnetic therapy (HIMT) to robot-assisted gait training (RAGT) with a ReoAmbulator produces greater improvement in spasticity and gait than RAGT with standard inpatient care in chronic stroke patients with residual spasticity. METHODS: We conducted a two-arm quasi-randomised controlled trial (No. EK 24/01), in which 29 of 30 enrolled patients were analysed per protocol. The experimental group (EXP, n=18) received 15 sessions of HIMT applied to the paretic lower limb, starting 1-2 weeks before RAGT, together with 10 RAGT sessions and standard care, whereas the control group (CON, n=11) received 10 RAGT sessions and standard care only. The primary outcomes were the Modified Ashworth Scale (MAS) of knee extensors and plantar flexors and the Timed Up and Go test (TUG), and the secondary outcomes were RAGT walking speed, session duration and distance. Within-group changes were tested with the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, between-group differences in delta values with the Mann-Whitney U test, and effect sizes were quantified using Cohen's d and Cliff's δ. RESULTS: Baseline characteristics were comparable between groups (all P>0.05), and both groups improved in all outcomes (Wilcoxon P ≤0.031). Between-group deltas favoured EXP, with TUG improving by -7.9 vs -4.7 s (P<0.001, d=1.51), RAGT distance by +512 vs +324 m (P<0.001, d=1.55), MAS of knee extensors by -0.61 vs -0.27 (P=0.010, d=1.12) and MAS of plantar flexors by -0.56 vs -0.27 (P=0.008, d=1.15). Cohen's d exceeded 1.0 in five of the six outcomes. CONCLUSION: Our findings suggest that adding HIMT to RAGT may produce greater improvements in spasticity and gait than RAGT with standard care alone in chronic stroke patients. The observed effect sizes (Cohen d>1.0 for the key outcomes) are consistent with the international literature on the antispastic action of repetitive peripheral magnetic stimulation. Because of the limited sample size and the quasi-randomised design, these results should be regarded as preliminary and require confirmation in a larger randomised controlled trial with long-term follow-up.

title: The influence of premotor cortices on primary motor cortex excitability
abstract: Le mouvement volontaire nécessite des interactions coordonnées entre le cortex moteur primaire (M1) et le cortex prémoteur (PMC), incluant ses sous-régions dorsale (PMd) et ventrale (PMv). Bien que ces deux régions soient reconnues pour influencer l’excitabilité du M1 dans l'hémisphère opposé, leur contribution respective demeure incomplètement comprise. Cette thèse a examiné l'influence de la PMd et de la PMv sur le M1 controlatéral à l'aide de mesures de stimulation magnétique transcrânienne (TMS) dans deux études menées chez des adultes en bonne santé. La première étude a examiné l'influence interhémisphérique de la PMd et de la PMv à l'aide de la période de silence ipsilatérale (iSP) déclenchée par une stimulation monophasique et de l'inhibition interhémisphérique (IHI) évaluée par stimulation de deux sites. Trente jeunes adultes y ont participé. L'iSP évoqué à partir du PMd, du PMv et du M1 montre que la PMd et la PMv exercent une influence inhibitrice sur le M1 controlatéral, l’inhibition étant la plus forte pour M1, suivie du PMd puis du PMv. L'IHI à deux sites a examiné la signalisation PMd-M1 et PMv-M1 à trois intervalles interstimulus (ISI) : 0, 10 et 50 ms. Les résultats ont montré que le PMd exerce une inhibition sur le M1 controlatéral à tous les ISI, avec l'inhibition la plus forte à 0 ms. En revanche, la PMv a montré des effets inhibiteurs à 0 et 50 ms, sans effet à 10 ms. Ces résultats indiquent que la PMd et la PMv ont une influence distincte sur le M1 controlatéral. La deuxième étude a examiné comment, et par quels mécanismes, la modulation du PMd et du PMv affecte l’excitabilité du M1 controlatéral et la signalisation interhémisphérique par l’IHI. Vingt-deux jeunes participants ont reçu une stimulation thêta en rafales continue (cTBS), une TBS intermittente (iTBS) ou une stimulation placebo (sham) appliquées sur la PMd et la PMv. L'excitabilité de M1 (dans les deux hémisphères) et l'IHI ont été mesurées avant et après la TBS. Comme dans l'étude 1, l'IHI a été évaluée aux ISI de 0, 10 et 50 ms. La cTBS sur la PMd a augmenté l'excitabilité du M1 controlatéral et réduit l'IHI PMd-M1 aux ISI de 10 et 50 ms. L'iTBS sur la PMv a diminué l'excitabilité du M1 controlatéral sans modifier l'IHI PMv-M1. De plus, l'excitabilité de M1 ipsilatérale a été modulée de manière spécifique à chaque sous-région : la cTBS et l'iTBS sur la PMd ainsi que l'iTBS sur la PMv ont augmenté l'excitabilité dans le même hémisphère, tandis que la cTBS sur la PMv l'a diminuée. Ces résultats montrent que la PMd et la PMv peuvent moduler de manière bidirectionnelle le M1 controlatéral et ipsilatéral selon des mécanismes spécifiques à chaque sous-région. En résumé, cette thèse démontre que la PMd et la PMv influencent le M1 controlatéral par des mécanismes distincts. Ces résultats enrichissent notre compréhension de la signalisation prémotrice-motrice. Ces deux sous-régions peuvent être considérées comme des cibles neuromodulatrices potentielles, avec des implications possibles pour les stratégies de réadaptation impliquant le cortex prémoteur.
authors: Elnaz Allahverdloo

title: The restricted 4D inverse kinematic alignment workflow: A patient‐specific approach integrating both bony and laxity phenotypes for total knee arthroplasty planning
abstract: PURPOSE: Two standardized total knee arthroplasty (TKA) balancing goals exist-equal gaps or a larger lateral flexion gap. Applying either without considering preoperative laxity phenotypes may alter native laxity and post-operative kinematics. This study proposes a restricted inverse kinematic alignment (iKA)-based technique to integrate bony and laxity phenotypes in three dimensions and evaluates its performance using a TKA simulator. METHODS: The restricted 4D-iKA technique and its boundaries were described and validated in 80 knees using the Knee-CAT simulator (MDA). Preoperative MPTA, LDFA, HKA and PTS were entered into the simulator and reevaluated after TKA. All simulated resections, including posterior condylar offset (PCO), were measured in millimetres. The individual laxity phenotype was defined by first recreating the bony functional knee phenotype (B-FKP) and then classifying each knee into one of nine laxity phenotype types (L-FKP). L-FKP restoration and correction were assessed, together with the reconstruction of CPAK and B-FKP types. RESULTS: = 2.6° [95% CI = 0.9-4.3°]; p < 0.01), consistent with the predefined boundaries. PCO exceeded the predefined ±2 mm reconstruction limit in 45% of cases, compared to the preoperative state. The predefined target L-FKP IV or V was achieved in all cases, except one. In 60% of knees, the lateral flexion gap was larger than the medial flexion gap, while in 40% of cases the gaps were equal. CONCLUSION: This first restricted iKA-based technique incorporates patient-specific L- and B-FKP to personalize TKA planning. However, balancing flexion and extension required increasing PCO by ≥2 mm in 45% of cases. This suggests that knee anatomical adjustments should be expected when laxity targets are considered. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV, retrospective, non-comparative study.
authors: Heiko Graichen; Michael Tobias Hirschmann; George Mihai Avram; Pieter-Jan Vandekerckhove; Philip Winnock de Grave; Pier Francesco Indelli; Alexander Aichmair; Rüdiger von Eisenhart-Rothe

title: The role of emotional intelligence and empathy as personal resources in enhancing employee performance in the IT industry: a job demands-resources perspective
abstract: This study investigates the relationships among Organisational Ethics (ETH), Interpersonal Relationships (IR), Job Autonomy (AUT), Support from Top Management (STM), Job Demands, Job Resources, Emotional Intelligence (EI) and Empathy (EMP) and Employee Performance (EP) within the IT (Information Technology) Industry through the JD-R (Job Demands-Resources) theory. This study examines how organisational and job-related factors are associated with Job demands and Job resources which are subsequently associated with Emotional Intelligence, Empathy and Employee Performance. Given the limitations from the previous empirical studies on EI and EMP as personal resources in IT industry context, this research aims to fill this gap by investigating the association of these personal resources with EP with a special focus on the IT industry. A quantitative research design was adopted using a structured questionnaire administered through a survey among IT employees working in different management and technical positions in Bengaluru, India. Around 318 valid responses were collected and analysed using SPSS and Jamovi. Structural Equation Modelling (SEM) was used to analyse the relationships among the constructs. The findings indicate that Emotional Intelligence and Empathy are significantly positively associated with Employee Performance in the IT industry. Further, the significant association of Job demands and Job resources with EI and EMP indicates the significance of workplace conditions in shaping employees’ emotional capabilities. This study applies the JD-R framework to examine EI and EMP as personal resources connecting job characteristics with employee performance outcomes in the IT industry. These research findings contribute to the literature of EP by providing practical insights for the IT industry seeking to enhance employee performance by developing emotional competencies and creating a supportive work culture.
authors: V. Lakshmi Voleti; Meenakshi Verma

title: The role of shape and local features in human object recognition and learning
abstract: An object’s shape is an important visual cue, critical for both perception and cognition. However, the current best models of human vision, Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), do not prioritize shape, but instead, they rely on texture-like local visual features. This raises the question: Could shape be less important for human perception than previously believed? In seven experiments with both adults ( N = 300) and 5-year-old children ( N = 100), we tested the role of shape and local features in visual object recognition and learning. We found that humans could identify common objects as accurately using local visual features as they could using shape. This finding suggests that, like DNNs, local features may be sufficient for everyday visual recognition and that shape may not be necessary. However, we found that shape played a crucial role in novel object learning, allowing participants to even accomplish one-shot object categorization. Together, these findings force us to reconsider the role of shape in visual recognition and suggest that DNNs, despite not using shape, may nevertheless capture an important aspect of human visual processing. Significance Computational models have long sought to emulate the visual recognition and learning abilities of humans. Yet, the current best models neglect a crucial aspect of human vision: shape perception. Instead, models overwhelmingly rely on texture-like local features. Here, we investigated whether local features may play a more important role in human visual recognition than previously believed. We found that adults and children could accurately identify common objects using only local features, and shape was not needed. However, shape played an especially important role when participants needed to learn new object categories. These findings shift our current understanding of the role of shape and local features in visual perception, and reconcile longstanding debates regarding the alignment of machines to humans.
authors: Allan Raymond Schneider; Olivia Maltz; Vladislav Ayzenberg

title: The use of innovative decision-making systems in Ukrainian enterprises
abstract: The purpose of this study is to analyze the procedures for implementing innovative decision-making systems in Ukrainian enterprises and to identify the key organizational and technical factors influencing the nature and effectiveness of their application. Research methods: a mixed-methods approach was employed, integrating both quantitative and qualitative data collection and analysis techniques. The quantitative component involved a structured survey of 50 managers from enterprises across ten industries, using an adapted instrument based on the UTAUT2 framework. The qualitative component consisted of 15 in-depth semi-structured interviews with practitioner experts. Statistical data processing was conducted using Pearson correlation analysis and multiple linear regression, while qualitative data were analyzed through thematic analysis following the Braun and Clarke procedure, with the support of NVivo 12 Plus software. Results: the findings indicate the dominance of business intelligence systems (76% of enterprises) and performance management systems (62%). The constructed regression model explains 61% of the variance in the effectiveness of decision support systems (R² = 0.61; F (5, 44) = 13.82; p < 0.001). The most significant predictors of effectiveness are top management support (β = 0.35; p < 0.001), the level of organizational digital maturity (β = 0.28; p < 0.01), and staff qualifications (β = 0.21; p < 0.05). Qualitative analysis identified four key themes: adaptation of international solutions to local needs, implementation challenges under resource constraints, the role of organizational culture, and the specifics of Ukrainian business practice. Practical implications: the findings can be utilized by practitioners to substantiate digital transformation strategies, as well as by regulators and public authorities in shaping policies to support the implementation of innovative management technologies in Ukrainian enterprises. Conclusions: the effectiveness of innovative decision-making systems is determined primarily by the quality of organizational leadership rather than the scale of financial investment; the identified practices of phased implementation, the use of cloud-based solutions, and the development of a data-driven decision-making culture are recommended as effective strategies for the digital transformation of Ukrainian enterprises
authors: І. В. Гуцал

title: Tibial spine fracture in children - a retrospective cohort study with clinical results and sports participation
abstract: Background In Norway, no previous studies have investigated the incidence or mechanism of injury of tibial spine fractures in children. The aim of this study was to describe the treatment outcomes of patients treated for a tibial spine fracture at Akershus University Hospital between 2010 and 2020. Methods This was a retrospective cohort study with cross-sectional follow-up including children (boys ≤ 16 years and girls ≤ 14 years old at time of injury) treated for tibial spine fractures at Akershus University Hospital between 2010 and 2020. The included patients were invited to a clinical follow-up visit with clinical examination of knee laxity testing (Lachman test and portable Rolimeter arthrometer measurements) and assessment of patient reported outcome measures (PROMs), including Pediatric International Knee Documentation Committee Subjective Knee Evaluation Form (pedi-IKDC) and Hospital for Special Surgery Pediatric Functional Activity Brief Scale (HSS Pedi-FABS). The primary outcome of this study was to describe outcomes after a tibial spine fracture while secondary observations included injury mechanisms, additional injuries, treatment, reinjuries and clinical examination of knee laxity. Results Twenty-four patients were included in this study. 17 (70.8%) were male and median age was 12 years old (range 6 to 16 years). Alpine skiing was the injury mechanism in 33.3% of cases. 14 of the patients were treated surgically. 6 patients (25%) had additional intraarticular injury at baseline, 3 patients later developed an anterior cruciate ligament injury, and 2 patients sustained a contralateral tibial spine fracture. The median pedi-IKDC score was 92,9, and the median HSS pedi-FABS score was 14,5. Most of the patients had differences in Rolimeter measurements between the injured and uninjured knee, with the largest side-to-side difference being 5 mm and a median difference of 1 mm. Conclusion We found increased laxity measurements with Rolimeter, but the clinical significance of this finding is uncertain. In our patient cohort, PROMs were acceptable compared with normative values. Due to the rarity of this type of injury, there is a need for a multicenter prospective study on tibial spine fractures in children. Level of evidence Level 4.
authors: Maren Gundersen; Asbjørn Årøen; Jan Harald Røtterud; Guri Ranum Ekås

title: Training and workforce development for robotic surgery in the United Kingdom
abstract: Robotic-assisted surgery is now being established across multiple specialties in the United Kingdom, but the systems that train surgeons have developed more slowly than the technology itself, resulting in training variables, resource dependence, and concentration among senior surgeons. This review synthesises current evidence from the United Kingdom on robotic surgery training and workforce development, examining trainee experience, learning curves, curriculum standardisation, service and delivery models, and the barriers to equitable competence. Most trainees value greater access to robotic training and believe it should be part of formal curricula; however, structured exposure in early training has been limited and access is perceived as inequitable across trusts. Learning curves are real but poorly standardised, and automatically captured metrics such as console time indicate exposure and participation rather than competence; thus, validated, programmatic assessment within a competency-based framework is still needed. A multi-specialty consensus curriculum, built on device, basic skills, and procedural training, revealed that structured training is safe, feasible, and deliverable beyond tertiary centres. Funding, protected console time, and unequal access across centres remain the principal constraints. National data on the number, regional distribution, credentialing, and staffing of the trained robotic workforce are largely absent, which represents a research and policy gap. The United Kingdom is moving from ad hoc apprenticeship toward standardised, competency-based robotic training, and realising this shift depends on sustained investment, protected console time, equitable access across centres, and national data to monitor training, workforce, and outcomes.
authors: Gloria C. Okoye; Sheila Marinze; Damilola Akinsulire; Sukanya Lakshmi Mahendran; Emmanuel Ojeabuo Oisakede; David B. Olawade

title: Transcranial magnetic stimulation to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex modulates single-neuron activity in humans
abstract: Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) is an established treatment for depression, yet the fundamental question of how cortical stimulation influences single neurons in deep brain circuits critical for mood regulation remains unanswered. Using a rare opportunity to record from intracranial microelectrodes while TMS was delivered in four neurosurgical patients, we evaluated the responses of 185 single neurons. Artifact cleaning enabled single-neuron spikes to be resolved as early as 8 ms after stimulation. We found that single-pulse TMS to the left dlPFC elicited time-locked firing responses in 46% of neurons (26% facilitated only, 19% suppressed only, 1% both). These responses occurred within deep bilateral cortical and subcortical structures, including the putamen and thalamus. Single-pulse TMS tended to facilitate spiking in striato-thalamic putative inhibitory neurons from ~8 ms, peaking at ~80 to 100 ms, and decaying until ~600 ms. In contrast, putative excitatory neurons and limbic areas were suppressed with a slower time course lasting to ~1,000 ms. TMS-evoked potentials recorded from intracranial depth macroelectrodes to quantify network activity revealed that the modulation of responsive neurons was positively correlated with cortico-striato-thalamic network activity and anticorrelated with limbic network activity in one participant with sufficient network and unit sampling. These results suggest that dlPFC TMS recruits a high percentage of neurons spanning cortical and subcortical brain regions bilaterally. The recruitment pattern selectively involves increasing the firing rate of inhibitory neurons in executive control networks while suppressing limbic excitatory drive, providing a candidate cellular mechanism for how cortical stimulation modulates distributed brain networks.
authors: Charles W. Dickey; Umair Hassan; Hiroto Kawasaki; Ariane E. Rhone; Christopher C. Cline; Matthew A. Howard; Nicholas T. Trapp; A. J. Boes; Joel Isaac Berger; Corey J. Keller

title: Transcranial temporal interference stimulation combined with soft robotic glove training improves upper-limb motor function after subacute stroke: a randomized controlled pilot trial
abstract: Background Upper-limb dysfunction, particularly impaired distal hand function, remains one of the most disabling sequelae following a stroke. Soft robotic glove (SRG) training can provide repetitive and task-specific hand practice; however, its therapeutic effects may be limited by insufficient modulation of the damaged motor network. Transcranial temporal interference stimulation (tTIS), a novel non-invasive neuromodulation approach capable of targeting deeper neural circuits, may enhance post-stroke motor recovery by engaging cerebellar-related motor pathways and promoting network-level plasticity. Objective This study investigated whether cerebellar tTIS combined with SRG training improves upper-limb motor function in patients with subacute stroke and explored the associated changes in cortical activation and resting-state functional connectivity (FC) using functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS). Method In this prospective, single-center, randomized, sham-controlled pilot trial, 46 patients with first-ever subacute stroke were randomized 1:1 to the tTIS-SRG group ( n = 22) or the SRG group ( n = 22). Both groups received conventional rehabilitation and SRG training. The tTIS-SRG group additionally received active cerebellar tTIS, whereas the SRG group received sham stimulation, delivered once daily, 5 days per week, for 2 weeks. The primary outcome was the upper-limb motor function assessed by the Action Research Arm Test (ARAT), and the secondary outcome was activities of daily living (ADL) assessed by the modified Barthel Index (MBI). fNIRS was used to evaluate task-related cortical activation and resting-state functional connectivity before and after the intervention. This trial has been registered with the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR2500107031). Results Of the 46 randomized participants, 44 completed the trial and were included in the final analysis (22 per group). One participant in the tTIS-SRG group withdrew from the study due to hospital discharge, and one participant in the SRG group declined the final assessment for personal reasons. Participants in both groups showed improvements in ARAT and MBI scores following treatment. The tTIS-SRG group demonstrated a significantly greater improvement in ARAT scores than the SRG group ( Z = −2.955, p = 0.003), whereas the between-group difference in MBI change was not significant ( Z = −1.706, p = 0.088). fNIRS analysis revealed that false discovery rate (FDR)-corrected channel-level analysis identified greater oxyhemoglobin (HbO) changes in the tTIS-SRG group than in the SRG group in two channels located in the ipsilateral frontal pole area (FPA) and ipsilateral somatosensory cortex (SSC). No region of interest (ROI)-level comparison remained statistically significant after FDR correction. Although several channel-level comparisons reached nominal significance before correction, only two channels remained statistically significant after FDR correction. Conclusion In this pilot trial, cerebellar tTIS combined with SRG training provided a more significant improvement in upper-limb motor recovery compared with SRG training alone in patients with subacute stroke. The observed clinical improvement was accompanied by enhanced task-related cortical activation and changes in motor-related functional connectivity. Larger multicenter trials with longer follow-up are needed to confirm the efficacy, durability, and underlying mechanisms of this combined intervention. Clinical trial registration https://www.chictr.org.cn/searchprojEN.html , identifier ChiCTR2500107031.
authors: Ailipinai Yasen; Xiaoyu Liao; Conghui Wei; Xinyu Zhang; Jun Lu; Xumiao Peng; 苗渝梓; Dan Zhen; Zhaodan Gan; Guangxu Xu

title: Transient and Immediate Motor Effects of Endurance Training in People With Multiple Sclerosis: The Exploratory TIME Study
abstract: Background: People with multiple sclerosis (MS) occasionally report deterioration of motor function after endurance training. Endurance training is recommended to help manage MS symptoms, but its immediate impact on functional mobility and spasticity is not well understood. Therefore, the aim of this exploratory pre/post analysis was to investigate the immediate effects of a single bout of endurance training on a bicycle ergometer on functional mobility and lower extremity spasticity in people with MS. Methods: Forty people with MS (21 men and 19 women; Expanded Disability Status Scale score ≤ 6.0) were randomly assigned to perform either a single bout of high-intensity interval training (HIIT) or moderate continuous training (MCT) on a bicycle ergometer. Functional mobility and spasticity were assessed using the Timed Up and Go (TUG), Numeric Rating Scale for Spasticity (NRS-S), and Modified Ashworth Scale (MAS) at 5 timepoints: before exercise, up to 5 minutes after exercise, at 60 minutes, 180 minutes, and 300 minutes after exercise. Results: = .01), were observed immediately after exercise in both groups. However, within 1 hour, TUG reverted to baseline, whereas NRS-S and MAS improved beyond baseline at 180 minutes post exercise. Conclusions: The findings of this study can be used to reassure patients that acute, exercise-related symptom worsening is short-lived and to inform them about the time course to performance and symptom recovery to baseline, or even beyond.
authors: Isa Slotboom; Sean A. Collings; Marie Kupjetz; Roger Hilfiker; Daniel Riese; Ramona Sylvester; Marit Lea Schlagheck; Roman Rudolf Gonzenbach; Jens Bansi

title: Uma Aplicação para Monitoramento de Progresso em Terapias de Reabilitação Pós-AVC por meio de Visão Computacional
abstract: This study aimed to develop and technically validate a markerless computer-vision-based mobile telerehabilitation prototype for post-stroke kinematic monitoring. An incremental software lifecycle was adopted, with requirements elicited through an integrative literature review. The accessible interface (WCAG 2.1 AA) was developed using Flutter, while the kinematic analysis service was implemented in Python using MediaPipe and OpenCV to analyze three exercises: elbow flexion, squat, and pinch grip. NumPy was used for numerical calculations and movement metrics, while ReportLab supported automated PDF report generation. Technical bench verification was conducted by the developers to calibrate the kinematic rules. The system supports automated repetition counting, detection of postural compensations, bilateral symmetry calculation, and analytical PDF report generation, while meeting contrast and accessibility standards. In conclusion, the preliminary verification demonstrated that the proposed application is a viable, accessible, and low-cost solution with the potential to decentralize post-stroke rehabilitation, establishing the technical baseline for future clinical trials.
authors: Carla Gabriela Cavalcante Ribeiro; Thiago Amaral Guarnieri

title: Understanding Advances in Computational Cognitive Neuroscience Over the Past Ten Years: A Scoping Review
abstract: Computational Cognitive Neuroscience (CCN) is an interdisciplinary field that uses computational models to understand how the brain gives rise to cognition. Although the field has grown substantially over the past ten years, no review has systematically mapped the major advances achieved during this period. This review therefore aims to map advances in CCN over the past ten years by analyzing the most frequently used computational models, the cognitive domains investigated, and the computational tools employed, and by determining the predominant emphasis of the studies, whether theoretical, translational, or integrated. This scoping review was conducted in accordance with the methodology proposed by the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) and reported following PRISMA-ScR. Searches were performed in PubMed, Embase and IEEE Xplore between 24 and 28 April 2025, and were complemented by a supplementary relevance-ranked Scopus search and by expert-informed identification of additional records. A total of 104 studies were included. Recent progress in CCN was found to be predominantly theoretical, with research focused on memory, learning, language and communication, and decision-making. Recurrent neural networks and Bayesian models emerged as the most widely adopted frameworks. Although CCN has advanced rapidly over the past ten years, the field continues to face critical challenges, notably concerning neurobiological plausibility, model integration, limited external generalizability, and a pressing need for more translational research. Beyond the reviewed corpus, the review discusses emerging AI paradigms, transformers, foundation models, large language models, and neuromorphic computing, as prospective directions informed by complementary literature.
authors: Tiago Schimit Rocha; Sabrina Souto; Aline Macedo Brito; Thaynara Paiva Barbosa; João Pedro Pinheiro Alves; Marcella Viana da Silva Lins; EDNA DE QUEIROZ MACIEL; Lauriston Medeiros Paixão

title: Understanding blockchain adoption in supply chains through institutional forces, fashion waves, and leadership mediation
abstract: Although blockchain has been widely promoted as a transformative technology for supply chains, its widespread adoption has not met expectations. High-profile initiatives such as TradeLens were ultimately discontinued, highlighting persistent challenges and limited industry-wide adoption. To better understand this pattern, we examine blockchain adoption through a different theoretical lens—framing it as a bandwagon process shaped by institutional forces and management fashion and exploring how top management support translates external pressures into firm-level decisions. Based on survey data from 320 U.S. managers with direct blockchain experience and strategic decision-making roles, the study offers insights from those directly involved in the adoption process. The structural equation modeling results indicate that coercive pressure, mimetic pressures, fashion setters’ influence, and perceived technological progressiveness all significantly influence adoption decisions. Top management support partially mediates coercive and fashion-driven pressures but does not mediate mimetic or normative pressures. These findings suggest that during early adoption stages, legitimacy-seeking and symbolic motivations often outweigh efficiency-driven considerations. This study contributes in two important ways. First, it is the earliest effort to integrate social contagion and management fashion perspectives to explain blockchain adoption in supply chains. Second, it reconceptualizes top management support as a mediating mechanism rather than a straightforward antecedent. Overall, the study enriches theory on technology diffusion under uncertainty and underscores the need for practitioners to carefully evaluate hype-driven pressures while leveraging leadership commitment to convert symbolic adoption into meaningful, value-creating implementation.
authors: Md. Golam Kibria; Benjamin George; Bassam Hasan

title: Understanding the determinants of embracing e-HRM in the hospitality industry
abstract: This research examines the factors influencing E-HRM implementation in the hospitality industry and their effects on adoption intention. Drawing on prior research, the study developed a theoretical framework for E-HRM adoption. The study collected data through a self-administered questionnaire completed by 276 HR managers at tour operations and hotel enterprises. The study used partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) to analyze associations among the factors and behavioral intentions. The results show that compatibility, top management support, relative advantage, regulatory support, competitive pressure, organizational readiness, and firm size influence E-HRM implementation in the study area. These findings can inform strategic decisions and resource allocation in organizations implementing E-HRM systems. Complexity and cost were not significant at the 0.05 level. Although these factors may not directly affect adoption intention in this context, examining them adds depth to the analysis and supports a more nuanced understanding of E-HRM system dynamics. Overall, this study contributes to the growing body of knowledge on E-HRM adoption, particularly in the hospitality industry, and offers actionable insights for industry stakeholders.
authors: Mohinder Chand Dhiman; Ashish Dahiya

title: User Understanding of Robot Learning Evaluations through Task Success Rates and Beyond
abstract: Robot Foundation Models (RFMs) and related robot learning techniques represent a promising approach to developing general-purpose home robots. Given the broad capabilities of RFMs, users will inevitably ask an RFM-based robot to perform tasks that the RFM was not trained or evaluated on. In these cases, it is crucial that users understand the risks associated with attempting novel tasks due to the relatively high cost of failure. Furthermore, an informed user who understands an RFM’s capabilities will know what situations and tasks the robot can handle. In this paper, we study how non-experts interpret performance information from RFM and similar robot learning evaluations. These evaluations typically report task success rate (TSR) as the primary performance metric. While TSR is intuitive to experts, it is necessary to validate whether novices also use this information as intended. Toward this end, we conducted a study in which users saw real evaluation data, including TSR, failure case descriptions, and videos from multiple published robot learning projects. The results highlight that non-experts use TSR in a manner consistent with expert expectations and highly value other information types, such as failure cases that are not often reported in RFM evaluations. Furthermore, we find that users want access to both real data from previous evaluations of the RFM and estimates from the robot about how well it will do on a novel task.
authors: Isaac S. Sheidlower; Jindan Huang; James Staley; Bingyu Wu; Qicong Chen; Reuben M. Aronson; Elaine Schaertl Short

title: Validation of a single-detector radiostereometric analysis setup for biomechanical research
abstract: Introduction Radiostereometric analysis (RSA) enables direct three-dimensional tracking of radiopaque markers placed in internal structures that are inaccessible to external optical measurement systems. The objective was to evaluate the agreement of a custom single-detector RSA system with a validated robotic reference and to compare its measurement performance with that of established optical and tactile measurement systems. It was hypothesized that RSA would show low trial-to-trial variability and measurement performance comparable to the comparator systems. Methods In this controlled laboratory study, programmed translational displacement of 5.00 mm in the anterior (AT), lateral (LT), and superior (ST) directions was performed in a synthetic knee model by a six-degree-of-freedom industrial robot. Ten displacement trials were performed in each direction. Evaluable trial counts were 10 for RSA and a stereo-optical measuring system (SOMS), 7–10 for a tactile measuring system (TMS), and 8–9 for an infrared measuring system (IRMS). Agreement between each system and the robotic reference was characterized by the mean bias with its 95% confidence interval, error standard deviation, 95% fixed-reference error limits, root mean square error (RMSE), and the proportion of errors within ±0.10 mm. Equivalence of the mean bias to zero within ±0.10 mm was assessed using two one-sided tests. Results RSA demonstrated biases of −0.083 mm for AT, −0.133 mm for LT, and −0.028 mm for ST. Error standard deviations ranged from 0.015 to 0.071 mm, and RMSE values ranged from 0.031 to 0.149 mm. Mean-bias equivalence was established for AT and ST, but not for LT. SOMS showed error standard deviations of 0.017–0.029 mm but systematically underestimated displacement in ST. TMS and IRMS showed direction-dependent variability, with error standard deviations of 0.093–0.125 mm and 0.112–0.367 mm, respectively. Discussion The presented RSA system measured static translations with low variability and measurement performance comparable to the established comparator systems. Mean-bias equivalence within ±0.10 mm was demonstrated for AT and ST, but not for LT. These findings support the use of the RSA system for static in vitro biomechanical experiments assessing macroscopic translations.
authors: Matthias Klimek; Moritz Martinovic; Alina Albert; Klemens Horst; Michael David Huelskamp; Jens Wermers; Christian Peez; Christoph Kittl; Adrian Deichsel

title: Validez y fiabilidad de la Escala del Escritor Frustrado en la educación superior
abstract: La frustración en la escritura académica se identifica como una experiencia en estudiantes de educación superior, asociada a exigencias institucionales, dificultades lingüísticas y procesos formativos. El objetivo del estudio fue diseñar y obtener evidencias de validez y fiabilidad de la Escala del Escritor Frustrado en estudiantes universitarios. Se realizó una investigación instrumental con una muestra no probabilística de 243 estudiantes de educación superior con una media general de edad de 20.87 años, 83.13% fueron mujeres, 15.24% hombres, 0.82% no binario y 0.82% prefirió no decirlo. La versión inicial del instrumento fue sometida a una evaluación de evidencias de validez de contenido mediante juicio de expertos y, posteriormente, a un análisis de componentes principales (ACP) con rotación oblicua Robust Promin. Asimismo, se evaluó la adecuación muestral mediante el índice Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin (KMO) y la prueba de esfericidad de Bartlett, y se estimó la consistencia interna mediante el coeficiente omega de McDonald. La estructura final quedó integrada por 22 ítems agrupados en tres componentes determinados mediante análisis paralelo. La adecuación muestral fue satisfactoria (KMO = .888; prueba de esfericidad de Bartlett = 2098.1, p < .001). Los componentes explicaron el 48.3% de la varianza acumulada. La escala presentó un coeficiente omega de McDonald de .901, mientras que los tres componentes mostraron valores entre .807 y .826. Se concluyó que la Escala del Escritor Frustrado presentó evidencias preliminares de validez de contenido y estructura interna, así como de fiabilidad para evaluar experiencias de frustración asociadas con la escritura académica en educación superior, con utilidad potencial para el estudio de la dimensión emocional de la escritura académica.

title: Varying Lateral Extra-articular Tenodesis Femoral Fixation Points and Fixation Flexion Angles Do Not Affect ACL Graft Force and Tibiofemoral Motion After ACL Reconstruction.
abstract:
Background

The addition of lateral extra-articular tenodesis (LET) to anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction (ACLR) has been shown to reduce rotational laxity and improve graft survivorship. Despite the increased utilization of LET with ACLR, there remains a lack of consensus on the ideal location of the femoral attachment site of LET.

Purpose

To compare ACL graft force and tibiofemoral motion in cadaveric specimens undergoing ACLR with the addition of LET at varying fixation angles and fixation points.

Study design

Controlled laboratory study.

Methods

A total of 10 fresh-frozen cadaveric knees were tested in 6 conditions, including LET fixation at 2 anatomic locations. Location 1 was defined as 8 mm proximal and 4 to 5 mm posterior to the lateral femoral epicondyle, at the insertion of the anterolateral ligament. Location 2 was defined as 31 mm proximal to the lateral femoral epicondyle, at the insertion of the distal Kaplan fibers. The testing conditions were as follows: (1) native; (2) ACLR; (3) ACLR + LET at location 1, fixed at 30°; (4) ACLR + LET at location 2, fixed at 30°; (5) ACLR + LET at location 1, fixed at 60°; and (6) ACLR + LET at location 2, fixed at 60°. Specimens were mounted on a 6 degrees of freedom robotic system to assess tibial internal rotation and anterior tibial translation at 0°, 30°, 60°, and 90° of knee flexion. A load cell was utilized to assess ACL graft force.

Results

There were no differences between the 4 LET states in any outcome. In internal rotation, the addition of LET demonstrated reductions in ACL graft force in all 4 configurations, ranging from -14.9 N (14%) to -19.5 N (20%) at 0°, -19.7 N (51%) to -21.4 N (55%) at 30°, and -3.9 N (30%) to -4.6 N (35%) at 60° (all P < .05). The addition of LET also demonstrated reductions in internal rotation range of motion in all 4 configurations, ranging from -1.86° (15%) to -2.45° (19%) at 0°, -4.87° (18%) to -5.75° (20%) at 30°, and -4.70° (19%) to -5.92° (23%) at 60° (all P < .05).

Conclusion

Variations in LET fixation location and fixation flexion angle did not alter its effect on ACL graft force reduction or tibiofemoral motion in the cadaveric knee. The addition of LET had a protective effect on the ACL graft in internal rotation while demonstrating overconstraint compared to the native knee.

Clinical relevance

The findings suggest that surgeons may have flexibility in selecting the femoral fixation location and knee flexion angle for LET without substantially altering its biomechanical effect on ACL graft loading or tibiofemoral kinematics. However, because LET reduced internal rotation beyond the native state, care should be taken to avoid excessive constraint when performing the procedure.
authors: Kruckeberg BM, Brady AW, Cinque ME, Sidrak JP, Kanakamedala AC, Hackett TR, Vidal AF, Godin JA.

title: Vibrotactile Stimuli For Functional Rehabilitation In Neurological Individuals
abstract: Background: Neurological disorders such as Spinal Cord Injury (SCI), Cerebral Palsy (CP), and stroke pose significant challenges to sensorimotor function in affected individuals, with traditional therapies often yielding incomplete recovery. This thesis investigates Focal Muscle Vibration (FMV) as a non-invasive intervention to enhance motor and sensory rehabilitation in neurological diseases, addressing gaps in mechanistic understanding, functional performance and clinical efficacy. Objective: The overarching aim of this thesis is to investigate FMV's role in sensorimotor rehabilitation by understanding its neurophysiological impacts following its use as an exercise intervention in people suffering from neurological diseases. Three specific research objectives were pursued: Objective 1 (OB1) — Device Engineering: To engineer a wearable FMV device capable of delivering precise and reproducible vibrations suitable for neuromuscular and sensory rehabilitation. Objective 2 (OB2) — Neurophysiological Effects: To investigate the specific effects of prolonged FMV exposure on motor function, spasticity, and brain activity in individuals with SCI and CP, and how these effects vary with different vibration frequencies. Objective 3 (OB3) — Device Feasibility: To evaluate the feasibility, usability, and short-term clinical effects of a co-designed wearable FMV device on spasticity and upper limb function in stroke survivors. Methods: An FMV device was developed using ERM vibration motor and characterized for frequency output using accelerometers. An electronic circuitry using was designed to operate the device at the desired frequencies (60-120 Hz) after the frequency characterization. This device was then used for the experimental studies. Experimental evaluations included three cohort studies investigating the neurophysiological impacts and usability of the FMV device in CP, SCI and stroke cohorts as detailed below: CP: Effects of 8 weeks of FMV applied to quadriceps at 80 Hz and 100 Hz was assessed via EEG and EMG in a cohort of 65 CP children. Resting-state functional connectivity (FC) and movement related cortical potentials (MRCPs) were used to see the cortical impacts of FMV through the EEG assessments. Muscle activations, fatigue and co-contraction metrics were assessed through EMG assessments. SCI: Three weeks of FMV to the Achilles tendon was delivered to 10 SCI patients, and their EEG FC was investigated. Stroke: An FMV device usability study in stroke (n= 12) was also conducted using a specifically modified commercial FMV device, with a view to establish for its potential for translation from laboratory to home-based use. Patient feedback was collected to update the original device design. After the updated device design, a single 30-minute dose of FMV was delivered to the arms, and clinical assessments of Fugl-Meyer Upper Extremity (FMUE) and modified Ashworth scores (MAS) were conducted. Results: OB1 — Fully Met: A wearable FMV device was designed and developed, delivering vibration frequencies at four levels (60, 80, 100 and 120 Hz) with a mean accuracy of 96.83%. The device was wearable, lightweight (65 g), and low-cost (under £100), meeting all pre-specified engineering requirements. OB2 — Fully Met (CP); Partially Met (SCI): In CP, FMV demonstrated frequency-dependent enhancements in beta-band functional connectivity, reduced movement-related cortical potentials, improved muscle activation, and delayed fatigue, with 100 Hz yielding superior motor outcomes. In SCI, significant alpha- and beta-band EEG connectivity changes in central-parietal regions were observed, suggesting neuroplasticity; however, clinical spasticity reductions were modest and the sample size (n = 10) precluded definitive conclusions, making this objective partially met for the SCI cohort. OB3 — Partially Met: The co-designed device was found to be comfortable and easy to use by stroke patients and clinicians. A single session of FMV produced improvements in FMUE scores but no significant changes in spasticity (MAS). Given the feasibility-study design with a small cohort (n = 12) and a single-session protocol, the clinical effectiveness component of OB3 is considered partially met, warranting further investigation in powered randomised trials. Conclusion: Findings support FMV's role in modulating cortical and neuromuscular pathways, with implications for personalised, accessible rehabilitation. OB1 was fully met through the development of a characterised, wearable, low-cost FMV device. OB2 was fully met for the CP cohort, demonstrating cortical and neuromuscular benefits, while SCI findings remain promising but preliminary, partially meeting OB2 for that population. OB3 was partially met, confirming device usability and short-term upper limb gains in stroke, with further powered trials needed to confirm clinical efficacy. Limitations include small samples and short follow-up periods, warranting larger trials. This work advances wearable FMV therapy toward evidence-based practice, bridging engineering innovation and clinical application for improved neurological outcomes.

title: What Drives Successful FinTech and Intelligent Workflow Automation in Banking? The Roles of Organisational Readiness, Integration Capability, and Regulatory Governance
abstract: The growing adoption of financial technology (FinTech) and intelligent workflow automation is transforming banking operations, yet the organisational and technological capabilities required to integrate these technologies successfully remain insufficiently understood. Drawing on the Technology–Organisation–Environment (TOE) framework and the Resource-Based View (RBV), this study examines the effects of technological compatibility, digital infrastructure readiness, top-management support, employee digital competence, organisational change readiness, and regulatory pressure on integration capability, as well as the relationship between integration capability and automation success in banking sector of Pakistan. The relationships were examined using partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM). The results indicate that all six antecedents have significant positive relationships with integration capability. Technological compatibility demonstrates the strongest association followed by top-management support digital infrastructure readiness organisational change readiness employee digital competence and regulatory pressure Furthermore, integration capability exhibits a strong positive relationship with automation success. These findings highlight the importance of technological compatibility, managerial commitment, digital infrastructure, employee capabilities, organisational adaptability, and the regulatory environment in developing effective integration capabilities for banking automation. The study contributes to the literature by integrating technological, organisational, and environmental determinants into a unified framework for understanding FinTech and intelligent workflow automation. The findings also offer practical guidance for banking managers seeking to strengthen technology integration and improve automation outcomes.
authors: Syed Asim iqbal Hussaini; Tayyab Dilshad

title: When Agent Memory Needs to Compute: Evidence Access and Executable Aggregation
abstract: Questions about an agent's history often require aggregating events, which retrieval alone does not resolve. We combine source-preserving evidence access with executable aggregation. Trajectory Memory (TM) retains the original trajectory and constructs a source-addressable reading view at question time. TallyMem augments it with a reusable event ledger, model-generated event specifications and deterministic execution. With a commit-specific adaptation on 776 questions from 99 held-out MINTEval repositories, TallyMem raises Qwen3-32B exact match from 35.2% to 49.0%, a 13.8-point gain over TM; gains span 12.8-13.9 points across three readers. A controlled probe with event sets parsed independently from raw logs shows an 11.0-point gain, from 82.8% to 93.8%, without routing. On full AMA-Bench, the routed system yields a smaller 1.3-point gain, from 69.8% to 71.1%. These results support executable aggregation on tasks that require combining events, with benefits dependent on the task and event specification, the largest residual system-error category in our diagnostic analysis.
authors: Zerui Yang; Quan Xue; Chaorui Zhang; Xueyan Niu; Xuanyu Zheng; Xiyuan Wang; Haolin Ruan; Guangcheng Song; Weixi Zhang; Wei Han; Bo Bai

title: When Does AI Capability Pay Off in SMEs? Strategic decision quality and top management support in a moderated mediation model
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) capability is increasingly treated as a strategic resource, yet small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) often obtain uneven returns from similar AI investments. We explain this variation by focusing on how AI-enabled information is converted into strategic judgment and organizational performance. Drawing primarily on organizational information processing theory (OIPT), we propose that AI capability improves strategic decision quality, which in turn enhances SME business performance. We further argue that top management support strengthens both the conversion of AI capability into decision quality and the conversion of decision quality into performance, producing a dual-stage moderated mediation process. Consistent with the final research design, AI capability and top management support are measured at T1, strategic decision quality at T2, and SME business performance at T3, with waves separated by three months. Results of this study indicated that all hypotheses were significantly supported. This study provided a significant mediation role of strategic decision quality in the relationship between AI capability and SME performance. In addition, moderation effect of TMS was significant at three level of study. The study contributes by reframing AI value creation as an information-processing and managerial implementation problem rather than a technology-possession effect.
