title: A RESEARCH PAPER ON THE DESIGN AND DEVELOPMENT OF A WEB-BASED BLOOD BANK DONOR MANAGEMENT SYSTEM
abstract: The Blood Bank Management System is a Python-based application developed to simplify and automate the management of blood bank activities. The system provides a centralized platform for managing donor information, blood group details, blood inventory, patient requirements, blood requests, and distribution records. It helps maintain accurate information about the availability of different blood groups and makes it easier to manage blood collection and supply. The system reduces manual paperwork, minimizes human errors, and provides quick access to important blood bank records. It can store donor and patient details securely and allows authorized users to add, update, search, and retrieve information whenever required. Database connectivity helps maintain organized and reliable records of blood donations and transactions. The proposed system improves the efficiency, accuracy, and reliability of blood bank operations. Overall, the Blood Bank Management System provides a simple and user-friendly solution for managing blood resources and ensuring that required blood information can be accessed quickly when needed.
authors: K ADISESHA; Pruthvi Gowda

title: A fully-automated high-throughput DNA extraction protocol for human microbiome samples
abstract: Microbial DNA extraction is a critical step in metagenomic analyses and a major source of technical bias. With the rapidly increasing demand for large-scale metagenomic studies, there is a growing need for robust and high-throughput DNA extraction workflows. Here, we developed a fully automated microbial DNA extraction pipeline inspired by the International Human Microbiome Standards (IHMS) integrating liquid-handling robots, automated sample management, and a dedicated data-handling suite. This pipeline, named “epsilon”, enables the processing of up to ten times more samples compared to the standard, with a throughput capacity of approximately 30,000 samples per year with two technicians. To assess the impact of automation, we applied this pipeline to 11 fecal samples and compared its performance to the corresponding semi-automated protocol. No significant differences were observed in DNA yield or overall quality. In conclusion, we present a fully automated microbial DNA extraction pipeline that substantially increases throughput and reduces both costs and carbon footprint, while preserving DNA quality and compatibility with international standards. This workflow provides a reliable reference for large-scale microbiome studies and represents a step toward a modern, high-throughput DNA-extraction standard for both academic and industrial settings.
authors: Christian Morabito; Marine Gilles; Mamadou-Gabou Thiam; Théo BATARDIERE; Elliot Mathieu; Benoît Quinquis; Florian Plaza-Onãte; Joel M. Dore; Patrick Veiga

title: A large audit of Cobas CT/NG screening and Xpert CT/NG supplemental testing reveals low confirmatory rates in oropharyngeal samples with evidence of commensal cross-reactivity with an isolate of <i>Neisseria lactamica</i>.
abstract: Sensitive and high-throughput testing for Neisseria gonorrhoeae (NG) is widely underpinned by automated commercial solutions using nucleic acid amplification tests. We outline our experience of using Roche Cobas 8800 CT/NG (Cobas NG) for primary testing of NG at scale. Over 360000 specimens were tested over a three-year period. A disproportionate number of 'indeterminate' oropharyngeal swabs (25%) tested positive by Cobas NG but failed to confirm by Xpert CT/NG, significantly higher than genital samples (4%) (chi-square p-value <0.05). Such samples are highly problematic, as they fail to provide a definitive result for the patient. To investigate this non-specificity, publicly available sequences for Cobas NG DR-9 targets were aligned with Neisseria genome databases. We found a strain of Neisseria lactamica (PubMLST 49718), isolated from a throat swab, which was predicted to cross-react with Cobas NG. We subsequently confirmed a Cobas NG false-positive result with this isolate. BLAST analysis showed the target gene NG DR-9 was rare among available non-NG Neisseria whole genome sequences. This may suggest the existence of an as-yet unknown and difficult to cultivate oral commensal that contains NG DR-9. Our findings further highlight the need for NG confirmatory testing of oropharyngeal samples screened with Cobas NG.

title: A mosaic RBD-nanoparticle pan-sarbecovirus vaccine elicits nanobodies that target highly conserved epitopes
abstract: SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes COVID-19, continually mutates, producing new variants of concern (VOCs). Substitutions in the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein receptor-binding domain (RBD) have resulted in reduced efficacies of vaccines and therapeutic monoclonal antibodies. Indeed, since the emergence of Omicron and earlier VOCs, most previously approved anti-RBD therapeutic monoclonal antibodies are no longer authorized as therapeutics. To address VOC substitutions effects on therapeutic antibody efficacy, we sought to identify single-domain nanobodies (VHHs) targeting RBD regions (class 4, class 1/4, portions of class 3 and class 5 RBD epitopes) that are more conserved across VOCs, reasoning that the smaller size of camelid nanobodies compared with conventional two-domain antibody combining sites would facilitate access to occluded RBD epitopes. We used a Beacon optofluidic platform to isolate and characterize single memory B cells from a llama immunized with a mosaic RBD-nanoparticle immunogen that elicits broad antibody responses across sarbecoviruses. Using multiplex binding assays, we identified nanobodies that bind to spike RBDs from diverse sarbecovirus strains. Competition ELISAs and crystal structures of VHH-RBD complexes showed that isolated nanobodies recognize broadly conserved epitopes, including those on the RBD that are inaccessible to analogous conventional two-domain antibodies. Promising VHH-Fcs neutralized SARS-CoV-2 variants of concern and zoonotic sarbecoviruses, demonstrating potential therapeutic utility for current and future outbreaks.

title: A simplified pre-bronchoscopy risk stratification model for patients with suspected lung cancer based on age, smoking status, and serum CEA
abstract: Background Bronchoscopy is commonly used in the diagnostic work-up of patients with suspected lung cancer, yet clinicians often lack a simple tool to estimate malignancy risk before the procedure in patients already being considered for bronchoscopic evaluation. Most existing prediction models focus on the malignant potential of pulmonary nodules and rely heavily on imaging features, limiting their applicability to the pre-bronchoscopy setting. This study aimed to develop and internally validate a simplified pre-bronchoscopy risk stratification model using routinely available clinical variables. Methods This single-center retrospective cohort study included 336 patients undergoing evaluation for suspected lung cancer. Candidate predictors were restricted to variables available before bronchoscopy and selected based on clinical relevance, routine availability, and data completeness. From 32 candidate predictors, LASSO regression retained 18 variables, which were entered into a multivariable logistic regression model followed by elimination based on statistical and clinical criteria. A simplified model was then constructed and presented as a nomogram. Model performance was assessed in the full cohort, with bootstrap internal validation using 1,000 resamples; the post-LASSO elimination steps were not repeated within bootstrap samples. Results Three independent predictors were identified: age (odds ratio [OR] = 1.045, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.017–1.073, P < 0.001), smoking status (OR = 3.216, 95% CI: 1.847–5.598, P < 0.001), and serum carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) [ln(CEA + 1), per unit increase] (OR = 4.989, 95% CI: 3.095–8.043, P < 0.001). After bootstrap optimism correction, the model demonstrated a corrected C-statistic of 0.837 and a calibration slope of 0.972, with acceptable discrimination and calibration. In biomarker analysis, serum CEA at a cut-off value of 4.57 ng/mL showed high specificity (94%) but moderate sensitivity (52%), whereas bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) CEA at 22.6 ng/mL showed higher sensitivity (71%) but lower specificity (57%). Mediation analysis indicated that serum CEA partially mediates the association between smoking and lung cancer (indirect effect: 0.09, 95% CI: 0.02–0.15, P = 0.004). Restricted cubic spline analysis showed a linear association between serum CEA and lung cancer risk, with no nonlinearity ( P = 0.514). Conclusions We developed a simplified clinically oriented pre-bronchoscopy risk stratification model based on age, smoking status, and serum CEA levels. The model estimates malignancy probability within a selected bronchoscopy population and does not determine procedural appropriateness or the optimal diagnostic pathway. For patients already being considered for bronchoscopic evaluation because of suspected lung cancer, this model may serve as an adjunctive tool for estimating malignancy risk and informing clinical prioritization. Given the sample size relative to the number of candidate predictors, the model should be regarded as exploratory and supportive rather than determinative. External validation in broader and more diverse populations is required before clinical implementation.
authors: Shuling Wang; Guofu Lin; Jiefeng Huang; Lifang Fu; Yuehua Chen; Aiming Zeng; Biying Wang

title: Adequacy of tissue acquired by shape-sensing robotic bronchoscopy for molecular profiling of non-small cell lung cancer
abstract: Introduction and Objectives Shape-sensing robotic bronchoscopy (ssRAB) is increasingly utilised to obtain tissue diagnosis of pulmonary nodules. Data on tissue adequacy for comprehensive molecular profiling via ssRAB are, however, limited.1 We evaluated tissue acquired for diagnosis, PD-L1 testing and next generation sequencing (NGS) in patients with suspected lung cancer. Methods Retrospective analysis of 206 patients undergoing ssRAB-guided biopsy with a combined total of 212 pulmonary nodules between 01/2024 and 01/2025. Patient demographics, nodule characteristics, diagnostic outcomes, and molecular adequacy were analysed. ssRAB was performed in conjunction with radial endobronchial ultrasound (rEBUS) and fluoroscopy alone (no cone-beam CT). Results The cohort included 98 males and 108 females with 157 ever smokers and 49 never smokers. Median nodule size was 22.5mm (IQR 14.5-32mm). Overall diagnostic yield of all nodules was 77.8% with 121/212 nodules (57.1%) confirming lung cancer (figure 1). Adenocarcinoma was the most common histological diagnosis in 82 of the 121 nodules confirming lung cancer (67.8%). Reflexive testing for PD-L1 and NGS was performed in 110 and 89 cases respectively. PD-L1 was completed in 99/110 cases (90%), and complete DNA and RNA NGS in 70/89 cases (78.7%) with partial sequencing in 5/89 (5.6%). 58 gene mutations were detected, the most common being KRAS 31/58 (53%) and EGFR 14/58 (24.1%). Additional alterations were identified in MET, BRAF, HER2, ALK, RET and ROS1. Mean NGS processing time was 26.4days. Complete NGS was more frequently achieved in nodules demonstrating concentric rEBUS views (82.8% vs 50%). Insufficient NGS samples were more frequent in part-solid versus solid nodules (27.3% vs 13.1%). Cryobiopsy was performed in 104 cases of confirmed lung cancer and yielded the diagnosis in 97 cases (93.3%). Conclusions We demonstrated that fluoroscopy-guided ssRAB biopsy provides high diagnostic and molecular profiling adequacy for pulmonary nodules, particularly in solid nodules with concentric rEBUS view and when cryobiopsy is utilised. Reference Lee-Mateus AY, Sawal N, Hartley C, et al. Efficacy of robotic bronchoscopy for molecular marker analysis in primary lung cancer. Clin Lung Cancer. 2024;25(1).

title: Alzheimer's Disease Biomarkers Measured by Capillary Blood Collection Versus Venous Plasma and Cerebrospinal Fluid
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Blood biomarkers are increasingly critical for non-invasive Alzheimer's Disease (AD) diagnostics and research but typically require on-site processing. Remote point-of-care collection methods could enhance biomarker testing in clinical and research settings. We evaluated the safety and accuracy of blood collection via venous blood and two capillary blood collection devices (Tasso+ and TAPII) for measurements of amyloid-beta 42/40 ratio (Aβ42/40), phosphorylated-tau-217 (pTau217), neurofilament-light (NfL), and glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) from capillary plasma to simultaneously collected venous plasma and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). METHODS: Patients seen at the Johns Hopkins Center for CSF Disorders (N = 192) underwent diagnostic lumbar punctures and venipuncture. Warming packs were held to the skin for 5 min before collecting capillary blood (via TAPII or Tasso+ device) and numeric pain scores. CSF, venous, and capillary plasma were analyzed using Quanterix SIMOA immunoassays. Statistical analysis included Pearson/Spearman correlations, Lasso regression, and quantitative comparisons using Bland-Altman plots. RESULTS: 86 TAPII and 126 Tasso+ plasma samples were collected (77 M, 115 F; mean age 61 ± 18.3 years, range 16-91). Tasso+ devices were 90.3% successful in collecting > 50 μL whole blood, and TAPII devices were 86% successful. Mean pain scores were significantly higher in venous than capillary collections (Venous 2.24/10, TAPII 0.73/10, Tasso+ 0.2/10, p < 0.001). Capillary Aβ42/40, NfL, and GFAP strongly correlated with venous plasma analytes (Tasso+: Aβ42/40 r = 0.75, NfL r = 0.91, GFAP r = 0.80, all p < 0.001; TAPII: Aβ42/40 r = 0.74, NfL r = 0.86, GFAP r = 0.84, all p < 0.001). Tasso+ capillary pTau217 weakly correlated with venous (r = 0.23, p = 0.04). Capillary NfL and GFAP correlated modestly with CSF NfL and GFAP (TAPII NfL r = 0.74, GFAP r = 0.6, all p < 0.0001; Tasso+ NfL r = 0.69, GFAP r = 0.59, all p < 0.0001). Capillary Aβ42/40 and pTau217 did not significantly correlate with CSF measures. Lasso regression identified age and GFAP as significant predictors of AD across capillary and venous samples (Tasso+ AUC = 0.87, TAPII AUC = 0.75, Venous AUC = 0.83). INTERPRETATION: Neurodegeneration biomarkers Aβ42/40, NfL, and GFAP in capillary plasma (Tasso+, TAPII) strongly correlated with venous plasma measures. Capillary and venous pTau217 correlated weakly, indicating further assay refinement is needed. Tasso+ collection was less painful and caused less hemolysis compared to TAPII.

title: An Autonomous Robotic Phlebotomy Device: Extended Analytical Validation and Real-World Hemolysis Assessment
abstract: Background/Objectives: Automated phlebotomy may improve preanalytical quality and access to venous blood testing. Prior work evaluating the Aletta Autonomous Robotic Phlebotomy Device (ARPD) demonstrated analytical equivalence. This study expanded the initial analytical validation to additional blood collection tubes and analytes and also assessed real-world hemolysis rates. Methods: The study was conducted in three hospital outpatient phlebotomy departments, including a site with a high prevalence of (hemato-)oncology patients. The within-subject analytical validation study included Greiner VACUETTE (Cohort 1) and BD Vacutainer (Cohort 2) serum, lithium heparin, and EDTA tubes. Equivalence of potassium, lactate dehydrogenase, hemolysis index, and complete blood count (CBC) with differential between paired ARPD-collected and manually collected samples was assessed using Passing–Bablok regression. Real-world ARPD hemolysis (>0.5 g/L free hemoglobin) rates were determined in a separate cohort (Cohort 3) and compared with site-specific manual hemolysis rates. Results: In the analytical validation study, 119 patients were included in the analysis (Cohort 1, n = 52; Cohort 2, n = 67). All tests met the predefined acceptability criteria. The hemolysis index was statistically significantly lower in ARPD-collected lithium heparin samples in Cohort 1. In real-world use (1368 ARPD venipunctures), the ARPD hemolysis rate was 0.0% (95% CI: 0.0–0.3%), significantly lower than manual phlebotomy (1.6%, p = 0.025). Conclusions: The study demonstrated analytical equivalence in a clinically complex population and found reduced ARPD hemolysis rates. The results further substantiate that the ARPD could improve patient care by reducing preanalytical errors.

title: An Exceptional Mobility Group Among Older Adults: Protocol for the Super Movers Study
abstract: Background Gait dysfunction is a preclinical marker of Alzheimer disease (AD) and related dementias (ADRD), often emerging years before clinical diagnosis. While much of the existing literature has focused on the pathological mechanisms driving motor and cognitive decline, the neural and biological substrates that confer resilience against such decline remain poorly understood. Individuals who maintain exceptional gait performance into advanced age, termed Super Movers, represent a unique phenotype of resilient aging. Understanding the biological profile of these individuals offers a unique and largely untapped window into the mechanisms underlying healthy aging and resilience to dementia. Objective This study aims to identify the structural, functional, neurophysiological, and molecular brain characteristics that distinguish older adults with exceptional mobility from their usual and slow-moving peers, and to determine whether these characteristics predict cognitive and physical decline over time. We hypothesize that the interplay between protective and pathological mechanisms in aging gives rise to structural, functional, neurophysiological, and molecular brain changes that manifest along a continuum from resilient gait to gait dysfunction. Methods We aim to enroll 350 adults aged 65 years and older from community and clinic settings. Participants will be classified by gait speed into fast, usual, and slow movers using age- and sex-specific thresholds; fast movers aged 80 years and older will be designated as Super Movers. All participants will undergo comprehensive assessments at baseline, including brain imaging, mobile electroencephalogram (EEG) recorded during walking, multisensory integration (MSI), comprehensive blood profiling, blood-based markers of neurodegeneration, epigenetic and proteomic aging clocks, and detailed cognitive testing. Follow-up assessments will be conducted annually in person and every 6 months by telephone. Results This study was funded by the National Institute on Aging (R01AG089096; PI: Joe Verghese) and has received Institutional Review Board (IRB) approval from Stony Brook University. Enrollment is currently underway. Conclusions Fast and Super Movers are expected to demonstrate distinct neural substrates, EEG activation signatures, and favorable biomarker profiles relative to usual and slow movers. By shifting the scientific focus from the biology of gait decline toward the biology of gait resilience, this protocol is uniquely positioned to advance our understanding of healthy aging and inform novel strategies for dementia prevention.
authors: Chathathayil Mohammedali Shafeeque; Kelly Cotton; Sanish Sathyan; Emmeline I. Ayers; Valerie Nunez; Uroš Marušič; Erica F Weiss; Daliah Ross; Jie Yang; Helena M. Blumen; Jeannette R. Mahoney; Joe Verghese

title: An online, open-access, cost comparison tool for presumptive tuberculosis testing using low complexity, automated, nucleic acid amplification tests (LCaNAAT) versus near point-of-care (NPOCs) molecular tests
abstract: The world is far from achieving universal access to rapid tuberculosis (TB) diagnostics that align with the World Health Organization (WHO) TB diagnostic standard. Although WHO-recommended molecular rapid diagnostics (mWRDs), including low-complexity automated nucleic acid amplification tests (LCaNAAT), have significantly improved TB detection, high capital, maintenance, and consumable costs have constrained scale-up. Recently, lower-cost, near-point-of-care nucleic acid amplification tests (NPOCs) have emerged offering the potential to expand access to rapid TB diagnosis while reducing the financial burden. To better understand the budget impact of using newer NPOCs as the initial TB diagnostic compared with established mWRDs, we developed a flexible cost calculator. Developed in Microsoft Excel, key parameters were organized in a structured input sheet using standardized labels. Separate worksheets defined diagnostic scenarios and performed calculations, with results summarized in an overview covering various costs. After validation, the model was converted into R (version 2025.09.1 + 401). The app (app.R), developed with Shiny, is available here for free global access. Using two hypothetical countries, we compared current LCaNAAT- based testing strategies with scenarios in which NPOCs were implemented as the initial diagnostic test. In hypothetical Country A, there were cost savings of 56.4% in Scenario 1 (based on current testing trends) and 60.5% in Scenario 2 (based on ambitious testing goals). In hypothetical Country B, the corresponding cost differences were 44.2% in Scenario 1 and 59% in Scenario 2. The analysis showed that countries can reach ambitious TB testing targets over 3 years using NPOCs at roughly the same total cost as implementing one year of current LCaNAAT testing. This highlights the potential of cheaper molecular diagnostics to significantly improve access to mWRDs. By reducing capital and maintenance costs, NPOC platforms let TB programs test and detect more cases within existing budgets, accelerating progress toward universal rapid TB diagnosis.
authors: Pushpita Samina; Puneet Kumar Dewan; Chase Mertz; Mikashmi Kohli; Madhukar Pai

title: Andes virus molecular diagnosis and viral RNA kinetics using a research use only RT-PCR assay: Experience from a Spanish tertiary hospital.
abstract:
Objectives

To evaluate the clinical performance and qualitative agreement of a commercially available Research Use Only (RUO) real-time RT-PCR assay for Andes virus (ANDV) detection and longitudinal molecular monitoring during the first imported ANDV outbreak managed in Spain.

Methods

Fourteen repatriated individuals exposed to an ANDV outbreak underwent molecular screening using whole blood and serum specimens. Confirmed cases were prospectively monitored with serial whole blood, serum, oropharyngeal swab, urine, and rectal swab specimens collected every 72 h. Clinical specimens were inactivated in a Biosafety Level 3 facility before automated RNA extraction and testing with the RealStar® Hantavirus-HPS RT-PCR assay (Altona Diagnostics, Hamburg, Germany). All specimens were also analyzed at the Spanish National Reference Laboratory using a hantavirus-specific real-time RT-PCR reference method. Qualitative agreement, Ct value correlation, and viral RNA kinetics were assessed.

Results

A total of 185 clinical specimens were analyzed, including 124 screening specimens from exposed individuals and 61 specimens collected during longitudinal follow-up of two confirmed cases. All 124 screening specimens were negative by both assays (124/124, 100% agreement). Among follow-up specimens, overall qualitative agreement was 93.4% (57/61; κ=0.837), and Ct values showed a strong correlation between assays (Pearson's r = 0.965). Four discordant results occurred in specimens with high Ct values (≥34-35), consistent with low concentrations of detectable viral RNA. Whole blood showed the lowest Ct values and the longest persistence of detectable viral RNA among the specimen types evaluated.

Conclusions

The RealStar® Hantavirus-HPS RT-PCR assay showed high qualitative agreement with the reference method in the clinical specimens evaluated and provided timely molecular information during outbreak investigation and longitudinal follow-up. Whole blood may be useful for longitudinal detection of ANDV RNA; however, these findings are descriptive and do not establish generalized viral shedding kinetics or infectivity. Further analytical and clinical studies are required to establish the assay's performance and clinical utility.

title: Apport de la bronchoscopie assistée par robot en pneumologie
abstract: The increasing number of CT scans performed is leading to the detection of a growing number of pulmonary nodules, creating a need for accurate and minimally invasive diagnostic methods. Robot-assisted bronchoscopy is a platform that allows for precise access to small peripheral lesions. Its performance is comparable to transthoracic needle biopsy, with fewer complications, especially when combined with imaging and sampling tools. It also enables marking of nodules before surgical resection, mediastinal lymph node assessment and could, in the future, be used for endobronchial ablative treatments. It helps accelerate the diagnosis of lung cancer at an earlier stage but its widespread adoption remains limited by its cost, the expertise required, and the lack of robust health economic data.
authors: Gokul Ramakrishnan; Anna Schiller; Benoît Bédat; Romain Messe

title: Assessment of breakage resistance of Improvacuter® venous blood collection tubes under standardised drop testing conditions
abstract: Blood collection tubes are integral to diagnostic workflows but are routinely exposed to mechanical stress during handling, transportation, and routine laboratory processing. Structural failure of these tubes may result in specimen loss and pose potential biohazard risks to healthcare personnel. This standards-based verification study evaluated the breakage resistance of six categories of IMPROVACUTER® venous blood collection tubes. A total of 108 tubes from three independent manufacturing lots were filled to their nominal draw volumes and subjected to a standardised 1 m drop test, with three consecutive drops per tube onto a concrete surface. Following testing, tubes were inspected for visible cracks, leakage, breakage, or cap dislodgement. Evaluation criteria were based on ISO 6710:2017 and ISO 2859-1 (AQL 1.5), with a predefined practical acceptance criterion of at least 90% passing per tube category. The overall pass rate was 94.4% (102/108; 95% CI, 88.3%–97.9%). Citrate tubes achieved a 100% pass rate, while Gel & Clot Activator, EDTA K2, Heparin, and Glucose tubes each demonstrated a 94.4% pass rate. Clot Activator tubes showed a pass rate of 88.9%. These findings indicate high breakage resistance under the standardised drop-test conditions evaluated; other performance characteristics were not assessed.

title: Asymptomatic carriage of Streptococcus pyogenes and other potentially pathogenic microorganisms among children and staff in day-care facilities in Varna municipality
abstract: Introduction: Scarlet fever is an acute infection caused by group A β-hemolytic streptococcus, Streptococcus pyogenes. Childcare settings are an important environment for the circulation of pathogens causing upper respiratory tract infections, with asymptomatic carriage playing a significant role in epidemiological control.Aim: To investigate the asymptomatic carriage of S. pyogenes and other potentially pathogenic microorganisms in nasal and throat swabs among children and staff in two childcare facilities in the municipality of Varna.Materials and Methods: The study was conducted in 2025 in connection with Project No. 23013 funded by the Science Fund of the Medical University of Varna, entitled “Investigation of Group A Streptococcus pyogenes Carriage among Children and Staff in Childcare Facilities in the Varna Region,” and in accordance with the decision of the Research Ethics Committee (REC) at the Medical University of Varna, No. 142/18.04.2024. A total of 131 individuals were included in the study—112 children and 19 staff members. A nasal swab and a throat swab were collected once from each participant. Identification of the isolated microorganisms was performed using the Phoenix 100 automated system (BD). Fisher’s exact test was used for comparative analysis, while Fisher’s exact test with Monte Carlo simulation was applied to analyze nasal carriage by age.Results: S. pyogenes was not isolated from any of the samples examined. Resident microbiota was detected in nasal swabs from 99/131 participants (75.6%). Staphylococcus aureus was isolated in 20 participants (15.3%), Streptococcus pneumoniae in 8 (6.1%), and Moraxella catarrhalis with heavy growth in 3 participants (2.3%); a combination of S. aureus and S. pneumoniae was identified in 1 participant (0.8%). In throat swabs, resident microbiota was detected in 129/131 participants (98.5%), while Staphylococcus aureus was isolated in 2 children (1.5%). No statistically significant difference was found between children and staff with regard to nasal carriage (p = 0.157) or throat carriage (p = 0.987). Among the children, no statistically significant differences were observed according to sex or childcare facility. Analysis of nasal carriage by age showed a trend toward differences, although statistical significance was not reached (p = 0.061).Conclusion: The results provide regional data on the microbial colonization of the upper respiratory tract in the childcare settings studied. The absence of isolated S. pyogenes should be interpreted in the context of the specific study sample and sampling period and does not allow for the conclusion that the pathogen is absent from circulation in the community.

title: Automatic milking systems as a tool for mastitis control in dairy cow herds – a review
abstract: The size of dairy cow herds continues to grow all over the world. At the same time, the amount of available manpower decreases. This results in an increased adoption of robotic milking systems worldwide. The use of milking robots typically increases milk yield, largely due to higher milking frequency, averaging around three milkings per day. Automatic milking systems (AMSs) minimize the need for manual labor by automating udder preparation, milking procedures, and real-time monitoring, whereas conventional milking systems rely entirely on human execution for all milking-related tasks. Regular udder health monitoring is crucial for early mastitis diagnosis, which is challenging in large herds. AMS provides comprehensive data for mastitis detection through sensors measuring milk parameters, such as somatic cell count (SCC), electrical conductivity, color, temperature, and lactate dehydrogenase activity. Mastitis – most often caused by microorganisms – is diagnosed mainly through the SCC. Early mastitis detection and treatment improve cow welfare, support faster recovery, and reduce economic losses associated with treatment, discarded milk, decreased yield, culling, and pathogen transmission. This review examines the role of AMS as a tool for rapid mastitis detection and control in dairy herds. Data collected from milking robots provide valuable insights for analysis, supporting both the farmer and the veterinarian in effective herd management and health monitoring.
authors: SANDRA KUNDA; K. Siatka; Roland Kozdrowski

title: BNCT Triggers Immunogenic Cell Death in B16 Melanoma Without Accompanying T-Cell Infiltration—Implications for Combination Immunotherapy
abstract: Objective Boron neutron capture therapy (BNCT) is a targeted radiotherapy with highly selective tumor killing; its potential to induce immunogenic cell death (ICD) and modulate the tumor immune microenvironment has attracted attention. However, whether BNCT-induced immune activation can overcome the T-cell exclusion barrier of immunologically “cold” tumors and translate into intratumoral effector T-cell infiltration remains unclear. Methods A B16 melanoma model was established in C57BL/6 mice. Mice were assigned to CK, N10/N20 (neutron irradiation alone for 10 or 20 min), BPA, and BNCTN10/BNCTN20 groups (BPA 500 mg/kg plus 10 or 20 min irradiation) to evaluate tumor suppression and survival. In a separate cohort (CK, N20, and BNCTN20), the most efficacious regimen (BNCTN20) was compared with CK on days 3 and 7: H&E staining; immunohistochemistry/immunofluorescence for γH2AX, HMGB1, cleaved caspase-3, PD-L1, CD8⁺, and granzyme B; ELISA for cytokines and chemokines; and ICP-OES for ¹⁰B distribution. Results BNCT significantly suppressed tumor growth. When CK tumors reached the humane endpoint (≈2000 mm³), N20 tumor volume was half that of CK (TGI ≈ 49.8%), whereas BNCTN20 reached only one tenth (TGI ≈ 88.9%, p < 0.001), with prolonged survival (p < 0.001). BNCT induced γH2AX-associated DNA damage, HMGB1 release, and cleaved caspase-3-mediated apoptosis; upregulated PD-L1; induced a Th1-type response (elevated IFN-γ/TNF-α, reduced IL-10); and enhanced CXCL9/10 signaling. However, intratumoral CD8⁺ T-cell infiltration and granzyme B expression did not increase, indicating that this activation was not translated into a local effector T-cell response. Conclusions BNCT inhibited tumor growth and prolonged survival while inducing ICD and a systemic Th1 response; nevertheless, systemic activation failed to translate into local CD8⁺ T-cell infiltration, while PD-L1 was upregulated—a “strong direct killing but blocked immune translation” profile in the B16 cold tumor. PD-L1-associated adaptive immune resistance may limit this conversion, providing rationale for combining BNCT with immune checkpoint blockade.
authors: Rui Quan; Hefa Huang; Lili Zhang; Chengyu Zhang; Shuyu Chang; Menglin Wu; Shixu Zhang; Xingkang Su; Lu Zhang; Zhongying Dai; Long Gu

title: Battery-free ingestible electronic capsule with programmable high-output soft actuation for active gastrointestinal interventions
abstract: Ingestible capsules have garnered considerable attention due to their high gastrointestinal (GI) transitability and minimally invasive nature. However, constrained by pill-sized dimensions (approximately 2 to 4 cubic centimeters), current ingestible capsules face persistent challenges in achieving both controllable high mechanical output and sufficient onboard power delivery, limiting their capacity for effective in vivo therapeutic interventions. Here, we present a wirelessly powered ingestible electronic capsule that integrates programmable soft phase-change actuation within a rigid-soft architecture to enable programmable, high-output mechanical operations. Leveraging bidirectional thermoelectric regulation and guided rigid-soft coupling, the capsule delivers a peak force of 3.8 newtons and a volumetric stroke of ∼250 cubic millimeters within a confined geometry based on the phase-change actuation. To power this actuation, we implemented a compact wireless power transfer system that achieved a maximum load-received power per unit receiver-coil volume of 9.15 watts per cubic centimeter at a 5-centimeter transfer distance under the tested conditions. The structural adaptability of the soft actuator allows modular integration of functional end-effectors, supporting high-output tissue acquisition, site-directed delivery of model liquid or gel payloads, and active biofluid sampling under magnetic navigation. In vivo experiments in beagles demonstrated the feasibility of mechanical interventions in physiological environments. By overcoming the long-standing power and actuation constraints of capsule architecture, this work establishes a physical framework for high-output ingestible robotics and advances the development of minimally invasive robotic platforms for complex GI interventions.

title: Blood Availability in Nigeria: Fragmentation, Supply Gaps, and the Case for National Coordination
abstract: Nigeria faces a reported shortfall in blood collection alongside challenges in timely access to suitable blood. This narrative review and policy analysis explores evidence from within Nigeria, combined with publications from the World Health Organization, relevant legislation and blood safety standards, as well as reports from departments and organizations. The experience of a number of multicentre studies reveals the variability between centers for the preparation of blood components, the use of testing for blood-borne infections, recording of blood issues, and other aspects of blood transfusion. The paper discusses the use of electronic reporting, subnational haemovigilance, and an evolving National Blood Management System. Local studies point to cost barriers to care, and the facility-level studies continue to report commercial donation. Blood availability is a system property: safely collected and clinically appropriate blood must be able to be identified, verified, allocated, transported, and delivered to the patient who needs it in time. Rather than establishing entirely new institutions, blood systems can be strengthened in a phased manner, with the option of expansion depending on local ‘operational readiness’ and their subsequent performance. However, there is uneven coverage of studies, conflicting data on collection figures, and a lack of data on the implementation and cost of different strategies to increase blood availability, which limits analysis of the national situation and of cause and effect.
authors: Ogorchukwu Ochem

title: Brazilian Society of Surgical Oncology Guideline for Bloodless Surgery. (Part 2: Intraoperative Strategies)
abstract: INTRODUCTION: The Brazilian Society of Surgical Oncology (SBCO) developed evidence-informed consensus recommendations for intraoperative blood conservation and the rational use of blood components in surgical patients. METHODS: Between June and December 2024, a multidisciplinary panel of 40 experts developed 48 clinical questions covering three perioperative phases: preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative care. This second article of the series addresses 16 questions related to intraoperative blood conservation. Expert working groups conducted structured literature reviews and drafted preliminary recommendations, which were subsequently reviewed by the project coordinators and submitted to an online consensus vote. Because high-quality oncology-specific evidence was limited for some questions, evidence from other surgical populations was considered when clinically applicable, with indirectness reflected in the wording and grading of the recommendations. An adapted evidence-classification system was used to determine the level of evidence and grade of recommendation. CONCLUSION: Intraoperative blood conservation requires an individualized, multimodal, and multidisciplinary approach. The selection of anesthetic, pharmacological, surgical, and blood-conservation interventions should consider the quality and directness of the available evidence, patient characteristics, surgical complexity, expected blood loss, and patient preferences.

title: Bridging the gap in One Health: challenges at the diagnostic interface – laboratory insights on sample quality and stewardship
abstract: BACKGROUND: The aim was to conduct an interface analysis to assess the sources and frequency of errors in the diagnostic workflows involved in handling human and animal microbiological samples. METHODS: A web-based cross-sectional survey was conducted among German-speaking healthcare workers in human and veterinary medicine between 7th October 2022 and 14th July 2023. The data evaluated in this study focus on perceptions of microbiology laboratory staff responsible for specimen reception, processing, and interpretation (sample recipients, SR) in human and veterinary laboratories across both outpatient and inpatient settings in German-speaking countries. Based on the questionnaire sent out using the snowball method, 20 of the 166 questions were tailored to recipients of diagnostics and used for descriptive and statistical (t-tests, chi-square tests) data analysis. RESULTS: A total of 2,464 valid responses were analysed; 372 (15.1%) were identified as SR, with the largest group working in human medicine (HM) (n=166, 44.6%). Respondents estimated that 18.5 samples per 100 were incorrectly requested by HM, compared with 15.4 by veterinarians and 14.8 by medical technicians (MT). All professional groups consistently cited swabs as the most error-prone material. Respondents with over 10 years of experience more frequently reported that requests took over 60 minutes of post-processing time per day. However, this was not statistically significant. CONCLUSIONS: SR face substantial challenges due to insufficient information, communication gaps, and inconsistent sample quality. Effective diagnostic stewardship requires addressing these issues through interprofessional education, digital decision-support, and standardised test-requesting processes.

title: Bronchial branch tracing with cone-beam CT tool-in-lesion confirmation for peripheral pulmonary nodules
abstract: Peripheral pulmonary nodules (PPNs) are increasingly detected through lung cancer screening. Conventional navigation techniques like bronchial branch tracing with radial endobronchial ultrasound (r-EBUS), lack ‘tool-in-lesion’ confirmation, limiting diagnostic yield. Cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) addresses this gap. This study aimed to evaluate the feasibility of integrating CBCT into an established bronchial branch tracing and r-EBUS workflow as a targeted tool-in-lesion confirmation strategy This prospective, single-centre observational study compared standard bronchial branch tracing with r-EBUS against the same workflow with CBCT used for tool-in-lesion confirmation. Consecutive patients undergoing bronchoscopy for PPNs under general anaesthesia were enrolled with allocation determined by CBCT availability. Feasibility was determined by the primary endpoint of navigational success. Secondary outcomes included diagnostic yield, procedural time, radiation exposure and safety. Forty patients were analysed (n = 20 CBCT, n = 20 standard of care). Demographic and nodule characteristics were similar between groups. In the CBCT arm, navigational success with bronchial branch tracing alone was 75% increasing to 90% with CBCT guided re-navigation. Strict diagnostic yield was 70% in CBCT with diagnostic accuracy of 80% upon completion of the follow-up period. This compared to a strict diagnostic yield of 60% (p = 0.51) in standard of care and 65% diagnostic accuracy (p = 0.29). Procedure suite time was modestly increased (51.00 vs 46.00 min, p = 0.03) while anaesthesia and procedure times were similar. No complications occurred in the CBCT arm. Radiation exposure was higher with CBCT (median total dose 3.9 mSv vs 0.35 mSv). Selective use of CBCT as a tool-in-lesion confirmation modality is feasible and may enhance navigational success and diagnostic yield when added to a conventional bronchial branch tracing and r-EBUS workflow with minimal impact on procedural time. Despite an increase in radiation exposure, these findings support CBCT as a practical means of strengthening existing bronchoscopic workflows.

title: Calibrated multiview inverse finite-element identification of heterogeneous lung mechanics with screened physics auditing
abstract: Mechanics-aware lung models need tissue stiffness, which CT cannot measure and must be estimated from deformation under load. Sparse surface tracks from a few calibrated views leave stiffness, contrast, inclusion size, and load magnitude hard to separate. Learned regressors are fast but unverified against mechanics; inverse finite-element (FEM) search verifies but is costly and initialization-sensitive. We propose screened inverse-FEM identification, in which physics decides whether a learned stiffness estimate is refined or kept. A calibrated regressor converts the multiview tracks, applied loads, and mesh into a two-level stiffness field with conformal uncertainty. A first round of finite-element probes tests this estimate; refinement proceeds only if they lower a prior-weighted misfit by a fixed margin, and each decision is reported. Modeling choices are frozen before testing, and CT-derived anatomies are split by subject. A prior-matched all-frame extended Kalman filter serves as a sequential reference. On 50 held-out synthetic cases, the initial estimate reached 3.82% median background-modulus error; the screen accepted 4/50 refinements (8%; final 4.11%); without it, background error rose to 8.81% and median evaluations from 7 to 64. On 120 scenes from six held-out CT-derived geometries with synthetic mechanics, the calibrated hybrid initializer lowered ratio error from 26.95% (raw MeshGNN) to 17.77%, while screened refinement raised background error from 8.55% to 11.70% (73/120 accepted). The screen did not reveal model mismatch; started from the same initializer, the sequential filter reached 2.73% (synthetic) and 4.74% (CT) and carries the identification evidence. All material targets were synthetic; clinical validity is untested.

title: Capillary self-blood collection for centralized testing – a pan-European cross-sectional pilot study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Self-collection of capillary blood allows study participants to provide samples without in-person healthcare contact and to return them by mail to a central laboratory. We evaluated the feasibility and analytical agreement of internationally mailed self-collected capillary blood in a pan-European setting. METHODS: In this cross-sectional pilot study, adults attending the INFORM EU plenary meeting in Hannover, Germany provided two capillary blood samples: one sample was mailed from their country of residence (capillary mail-in sample, CMS); the other was analyzed within 24 h (capillary comparison sample, CCS). Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), C-reactive protein (CRP), creatinine, and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) were measured. Agreement was assessed with correlation coefficients, Deming and Passing-Bablok regression, and Bland-Altman analysis. RESULTS: Of 66 participants, 49 (74.2%) returned a mailed sample after a median transit of 8 days (Q25-Q75: 5-12). Analytically valid pairs were available for 17 (TSH), 16 (ALT), 16 (creatinine), and 19 (CRP) participants. Agreement was high for CRP (r and CCC = 1.00) and good for TSH (r = 0.90; CCC = 0.88). Creatinine showed a strong correlation but low concordance (r = 0.85; CCC = 0.19) with a proportional bias, and ALT showed the weakest agreement (r = 0.54; CCC = 0.21) and largest bias. Longer transit was associated with higher ALT differences (ρ = 0.57). CONCLUSIONS: International postal return of self-collected capillary blood was achievable, and the main constraint was insufficient plasma volume rather than delivery. CRP, and to a lesser extent TSH, reached acceptable agreement, whereas ALT and creatinine did not. Given the small number of valid samples and healthy study population, these findings need further confirmation. GERMAN CLINICAL TRIALS REGISTER IDENTIFIER: DRKS00033172 on January 30th, 2024.

title: Capsule biopsy and targeted sampling techniques: current status and future perspectives
abstract: Early screening and definitive diagnosis of gastrointestinal (GI) diseases remain major clinical challenges. Although wireless capsule endoscopy enables patients to undergo minimally invasive imaging of the GI tract, it cannot obtain tissue or fluid samples; therefore, a separate invasive endoscopic procedure is still required when a suspicious lesion is identified. The next logical step is to develop capsule systems capable of both visualizing and sampling lesions during a single swallowable examination. This review summarizes recent advances in smart GI sampling capsules, categorized according to the type of specimen collected (solid tissue vs. luminal fluid or microbiome) and the mode of device control. Miniaturized electromechanical systems (MEMS), stimuli-responsive materials, and magnetic actuation have substantially expanded the technical capabilities of sampling capsules; however, most active tissue-biopsy platforms remain at the preclinical stage. In contrast, several passive or environment-responsive luminal-sampling systems have progressed to early human evaluation. Major barriers to clinical translation include reliable lesion targeting, adequate and reproducible specimen acquisition, prevention of cross-contamination, device miniaturization, and demonstration of procedural safety. Artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted and autonomous targeting remain areas for future investigation rather than established clinical practices.
authors: Yixin Wan; Zichuan Han; Yuan Tian; Long Rong

title: Cerebral Air Embolism After Navigational Bronchoscopy Treated With Aspiration Thrombectomy: A Case Report
abstract: Systemic arterial air embolism is a rare but potentially devastating complication of bronchoscopic lung biopsy. A 68-year-old man with severe emphysema developed abrupt bradycardia, hypotension, and failure to regain consciousness after navigational bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia. Computed tomography demonstrated air within the left middle cerebral artery, and angiography confirmed proximal large-vessel occlusion. Urgent aspiration thrombectomy achieved complete reperfusion after one pass, with retrieved material compatible with thrombus. Despite technically successful reperfusion, major neurological deficits persisted. This case highlights haemodynamic collapse and delayed emergence as warning signs and supports rapid neuroimaging with selective endovascular treatment when an accessible large-vessel occlusion is present.

title: Circulating Tumour DNA is Enriched as long Fragments Associated with Nanoparticles that can be Rapidly Isolated by Autonomous Microfluidic Filtration
abstract: Introduction: Circulating tumour-derived DNA (ctDNA) is an increasingly important marker of minimal residual disease. Although generally referring to short, histone-bound fragments, the term ctDNA can describe any length of DNA in diverse macromolecule complexes. Despite extensive clinical analysis of short ctDNA, it is not currently known how ctDNA is most likely to present in blood. Moreover, patient-centric blood drop processing has the potential to improve the resolution and sensitivity of cancer therapy monitoring by increasing access to ctDNA analysis.

title: Clinical Artificial Intelligence in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer: From Early Detection and Computational Pathology to Precision Oncology
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is being developed to analyze radiological, histopathological, molecular, and clinical data across the non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) pathway. This narrative review examines representative applications through August 2026, focusing on intended clinical use, validation, and the evidence required to influence care. Studies were selected purposively for clinical relevance and methodological importance. Imaging models support investigation of nodule detection, malignancy estimation, and future lung cancer risk, although predictive performance does not establish the benefit of changing screening or diagnostic pathways. In computational pathology, models classify tissue, quantify morphological features, and estimate selected molecular alterations. Foundation models extend these capabilities, but their evaluation requires attention to pretraining provenance and independence of downstream testing. Histology-based molecular prediction does not currently justify replacing validated molecular assays; prioritization of testing requires prospective workflow evaluation. Models evaluated in immunotherapy-treated cohorts can predict response or survival, but these associations do not establish differential benefit between treatments. The principal limitations include selected retrospective populations, incomplete assessment of calibration and clinically relevant thresholds, uncertain transportability, and limited evaluation of model-guided care. Evidence should therefore be interpreted at the level of the individual system and intended decision. Prospective evaluation, appropriate comparators, explicit failure procedures, and post-deployment monitoring are required before technical performance can be translated into clinical benefit.

title: Clinical performance evaluation of a high-throughput real-time PCR platform for congenital cytomegalovirus screening on saliva swabs with quantitative reporting thresholds
abstract: Background Congenital cytomegalovirus (cCMV) is typically diagnosed using nucleic acid amplification testing on saliva followed by urine confirmation if positive. Major challenges in saliva screening include low positive predictive value (PPV) and throughput constraints. We validated the cobas CMV assay on the cobas 8800 high-throughput real-time polymerase chain reaction (PCR) platform as a lab-developed test for newborn saliva swabs and urine, and evaluated its clinical performance characteristics for cCMV screening. Methods From April 2023 to January 2026, saliva swabs and urine from infants ≤21 days were tested in a cCMV screening program. Qualitative results were reported, with viral loads recorded offline. Urine PCR served as the reference standard to classify saliva results. Results CMV PCR was positive in 50/6559 (0.76%) saliva swabs meeting study inclusion criteria, with 29 (58%) confirmed by urine. Among 28 saliva-negative infants who had urine testing, all were negative. Median saliva viral load was significantly lower in false-positives than true-positives (below lower limit of quantitation at <35 IU/mL vs. 4.09 ×10 6 IU/mL, p<0.001). Using urine PCR as the gold standard, saliva PCR performance varied by reporting threshold (from detected at any value up to 100 IU/mL) with sensitivity 93.1-100%, specificity 57.1-100%, PPV 58.0-100%, and negative predictive value (NPV) 96.1-100%. Conclusion The cobas CMV assay as validated in our laboratory demonstrated acceptable clinical performance characteristics for saliva-based cCMV screening. Clinical specificity and PPV are further improved through application of a viral load threshold for positivity reporting or an “equivocal” range.
authors: Anfal Marafie; Aya Aboulhosn; Sarah E. Worley; Mary Kathryn Doud; Julia Tanzo; Frank P. Esper; Hannah Wang

title: Clinically Suspected Systemic Arterial Gas Embolism during Robotic-Assisted Bronchoscopy: a Case Report
abstract:
Background: Systemic arterial gas embolism (SAGE) is a rare but potentially catastrophic complication of robotic-assisted bronchoscopy with lung biopsy. During general anesthesia, the earliest manifestations of SAGE may be limited to transient electrocardiographic or hemodynamic abnormalities. The absence of visible intracranial gas on subsequent imaging does not exclude the diagnosis. We report a case of clinically suspected SAGE during robotic-assisted bronchoscopy in which intraoperative sentinel signs preceded delayed emergence and focal neurologic injury. Case presentation: A 78-year-old woman underwent robotic-assisted bronchoscopy under general anesthesia for biopsy of a 4.6-cm right middle lobe ground-glass opacity using transbronchial needle aspiration and cryobiopsy. Significant airway bleeding occurred after sampling. Immediately after biopsy, she developed transient tachycardia, hypertension, bradycardia, and ST-segment elevation in lead V5. Although these abnormalities resolved, she was unresponsive shortly after extubation and developed right gaze deviation, facial twitching, abnormal movements, and absent right upper-extremity withdrawal to pain. Head computed tomography showed no acute abnormality, and brain magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated left frontal and precentral cortical diffusion restriction without visible intracranial gas. Because SAGE was strongly suspected, she received 100% oxygen, levetiracetam, endotracheal reintubation, and hyperbaric oxygen therapy at 2.8 atmospheres absolute approximately 4 hours after bronchoscopy. High-sensitivity troponin I peaked at 5,116 ng/L and left ventricular ejection fraction improved from 45-50% to 60% the following day. She was extubated on post-procedure day 10 with persistent neurologic deficits. On post-procedure day 18, she experienced hypoxic cardiac arrest associated with bilateral pulmonary emboli and an acute aortic dissection and died the following day after transition to comfort-focused care.

Conclusions:

During bronchoscopic biopsies under general anesthesia, unexplained ST-segment changes, hemodynamic instability, or delayed neurologic recovery should prompt immediate consideration of SAGE, even when initial neuroimaging is negative. Administration of 100% oxygen, airway and hemodynamic support, minimization of airway pressures, and urgent consultation for hyperbaric oxygen therapy should not be delayed while awaiting radiographic confirmation.
authors: Hom BM, Rosenberg B, Xu NY, Szokol JW, McCarthy M.

title: Comparative Clinical Impact of Transbronchial Cryobiopsy and Forceps Biopsy Utilizing Radial EBUS Guidance for the Diagnosis of Peripheral Pulmonary Lesions
abstract: BACKGROUND: The prevalence of peripheral pulmonary lesions (PPLs) is increasing; however, their diagnosis remains challenging despite the availability of various modalities. Transbronchial cryobiopsy (TBCB) offers an additive benefit in diagnostic yield. Combining radial endobronchial ultrasound (R-EBUS)-guided transbronchial forceps biopsy (TBFB) with cryobiopsy may enhance tissue acquisition. METHODS: This retrospective study reviewed 197 patients with pulmonary lesions who underwent bronchoscopy-guided biopsy between January 1, 2023, and December 31, 2023. Strict diagnostic yield and diagnostic accuracy were calculated according to the predefined definition, and the additive impact of cryobiopsy was further analyzed. RESULTS: The cohort comprised 117 patients in the TBFB group and 80 in the TBCB group. The overall mean age was 68 years and 60% were male; baseline lesion characteristics were comparable across groups, with lesions <20 mm in 45% and 44% of the TBFB and TBCB groups, respectively, and a positive CT bronchus sign in 82% and 85%. Compared with TBFB alone, the TBCB group achieved a higher strict diagnostic yield (76.2% vs. 63.2%) and diagnostic accuracy (86.8% vs. 80.4%), respectively. Among the 33 patients in whom R-EBUS-guided TBFB was followed sequentially by cryobiopsy, the addition of cryobiopsy further increased diagnostic yield and accuracy by 21.6% and 13.5%, respectively. Procedure-related severe bleeding and severe hypoxia occurred in 2.5% and 1.3% of patients in the TBCB group, both significantly higher than the corresponding rates in the TBFB group (p < 0.05). CONCLUSION: R-EBUS-guided TBCB demonstrated efficacy for diagnosing PPLs, offering superior diagnostic yield and accuracy than conventional R-EBUS-guided transbronchial lung biopsy alone.
authors: Rong Lih Ho; Jung Ho Han; So Yeon Kim; Junsu Choe; Sun Hye Shin; Byeong‐Ho Jeong; Sang‐Won Um; Kyungjong Lee

title: Comparative Evaluation of two Automated Magnetic-bead cell free DNA Extraction Workflows in Early Colorectal Cancer
abstract: Introduction: Reliable extraction of cell-free DNA (cfDNA) from plasma is a critical step in liquid biopsies and depends on the standardization of pre-analytical processes. In this study, a paired comparison was conducted between two automated magnetic particle-based extraction methods—the Maxwell RSC ccfDNA LV Plasma Kit (standard) and the Maxwell RSC Rapid ccfDNA Kit—using EDTA plasma from 48 patients with early-stage colorectal cancer. For each patient, 4 mL of plasma was divided into two 2 mL aliquots, which were processed in parallel on the same instrument according to the manufacturer's instructions.

title: Comparative analysis of operative cost in lung resection: preoperative robotic navigational bronchoscopy (Nav) vs. intraoperative wedge biopsy.
abstract: Evaluate differences in operative cost in pulmonary resection between patients who had preoperative biopsy via robotic navigational bronchoscopy versus an intraoperative diagnostic wedge. We performed a retrospective cohort study of patients who underwent standard lobectomy at our institution between January 2024 and July 2025. We identified patients who had a preoperative robotic navigational bronchoscopy (Nav) prior to lung resection and those who had no preoperative biopsy (NPB) and had intraoperative diagnostic wedge. We then examined operative time, stapler load quantity, stapler cost, robotic cost, and overall operative cost. 128 patients were identified, 53 in the NPB cohort and 75 in the Nav cohort. The mean age of the cohort was 68. The average surgical cost of the non-preoperative biopsy (NPB) cohort was $10,258.68 and $9,249.36 in the Nav cohort (P = 0.007). The average stapler loads used, total stapler cost, total robotic I&A costs, and surgical supply costs were higher in the NPB cohort (P < 0.001). The average technical cost of performing a frozen specimen was $65.35. There was no statistically significant difference in operative time between cohorts, however the NPB cohort had a longer operative time on average (187.83 min vs. 174.63 min, P = 0.161). We found that on average, surgical cost, operative time, robotic cost, and OR charges were higher in patients who had undergone intraoperative frozen section (NPB) compared to those with preoperative biopsy (Nav). This data suggest that the use of preoperative robotic bronchoscopy is associated with decreased cost of robotic lung resection.

title: Comparing MiniDock MTB, chest radiography, and symptoms for tuberculosis screening: a community-based evaluation in Karachi, Pakistan
abstract: Background Community-based active case finding (ACF) for tuberculosis (TB) is constrained by limited access to chest X-ray (CXR) and reliance on sputum-based diagnostic testing. Recently, WHO recommended near point-of-care testing which offers a non-sputum alternative, tongue swab (TS). We evaluated the feasibility and screening performance of MiniDock MTB on TS compared with WHO four-symptom screening (W4SS) and CXR in Pakistan. Methods We conducted 49 screening camps in underserved communities of Karachi. All adolescents and adults (> 10 years) underwent screening via W4SS, CXR, and TS collection. Individuals screening positive by any method were asked to provide sputum for Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra, sputum swab testing on MiniDock MTB, and mycobacterial culture. A microbiological reference standard (MRS) was defined as a positive Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra and/or mycobacterial culture. Results Overall, 4,303 individuals were screened (median age 28 years [IQR 16–40]); 38% were female. All participants had CXR and W4SS screening results, while 3,432 (79.8%) had valid TS results. Overall, 752 participants were screen-positive for TB, including 606 with valid TS results. TS was positive in 19/3,432 (0.4%), CXR in 302/4303 (7.0%) and W4SS in 522/4,303 (12.1%). Sputum was collected from 243 (32%) of 752 screen-positive participants, including 225 (37%) with valid TS results; Among 30 MRS-positive individuals, 29 had abnormal CXR, 14 had symptoms and 13 a positive TS result. CXR showed the highest sensitivity (96.7%; 95% CI 82.8–99.9), compared with W4SS (46.7%; 95% CI 28.3–65.7) and TS testing (46.4%; 95% CI 27.5–66.1). Conclusion TS testing, although feasible, was not sufficiently sensitive to function as a standalone TB screening test. Further optimization of specimen collection, assay performance, and evaluation in diverse settings is needed to better define the role of TS testing in community-based TB screening.
authors: Kinz ul Eman; Yves Laurent Jackson; Samreen Ashraf Qureshi; Usman Rasool Lodhi; Beatrice Kirubi; Jacob Creswell; Sabira Tahseen

title: Comparison of QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus results using ELISA and automated CLIA detection: a 39,000-sample real-world study
abstract: QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus (QFT-Plus) is a widely used interferon-γ release assay (IGRA) for the diagnosis of Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection. Recent advances introduced fully automated chemiluminescence immunoassay (CLIA) platforms as alternatives to conventional enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), potentially improving analytical performance and laboratory workflow. This study compared ELISA- and CLIA-based QFT-Plus assays using both lyophilized and liquid conjugate formulations in routine clinical practice. This retrospective study included 39,604 QFT-Plus assays performed during three distinct 1-year periods: 2019 (ELISA), 2023 (CLIA with lyophilized conjugate), and 2024 (CLIA with liquid conjugate). Test results were classified as positive, negative, or indeterminate. Indeterminate results were further categorized as due to low mitogen response (LMR) or high Nil value (HNV). Indeterminate results significantly decreased from 6.5% (777/11,885) with ELISA to 3.1% (394/12,690) with CLIA test using lyophilized conjugate and 3.1% (470/15,029) of CLIA tests using the liquid conjugate ( P < 0.0001). Positive results accounted for 10.6 (1,254/11,885), 10.3 (1,312/12,690), and 9.0% (1,355/15,029) of tests, respectively. Among indeterminate results, LMR accounted for 97.3% (756/777) with ELISA, whereas HNV accounted for 27.4 (108/394) and 16.8% (79/470) with the lyophilized- and liquid-conjugate CLIA methods, respectively. Agreement between TB1 and TB2 responses was consistently high across all methods (98.5–98.8%; κ = 0.92). CLIA-based QFT-Plus assays were significantly associated with a lower proportion of indeterminate results while maintaining an excellent TB1/TB2 concordance compared with ELISA. These findings support fully automated CLIA platforms as a robust and efficient alternative to conventional ELISA for high-throughput tuberculosis screening and routine clinical diagnostics. IMPORTANCE This study provides a large real-world evaluation of QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus testing across different analytical platforms, including more than 39,000 tests performed in routine clinical practice. The transition from conventional enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) to automated chemiluminescence immunoassay (CLIA) was associated with an approximately 50% decrease in indeterminate results from 6.5 to 3.1%, with similarly low rates observed using both lyophilized and liquid conjugate formulations. Beyond documenting this substantial reduction, our study reveals a marked difference in the causes of indeterminate results: low mitogen response predominated with ELISA, whereas high Nil values accounted for a larger proportion of indeterminate results with CLIA. These findings, interpreted together with our previous paired-sample comparison, indicate that differences in quantitative IFN-γ measurement across platforms may affect how samples are classified against fixed decision thresholds.
authors: Federica Sorella; Vincenzo Ferraro; Paolo Caiazza; Miriam Ciccarelli; Giuliana Germinario; Alessia Cantiani; Giulia Lombardi; Francesco Bisognin; Paola Dal Monte

title: Comparison of remimazolam total intravenous anesthesia versus sevoflurane inhalational anesthesia on emergence agitation in patients undergoing laparoscopic surgery for gastric or colorectal cancer: study protocol for a randomized controlled trial
abstract: Background Emergence agitation (EA) remains a common, potentially harmful complication after general anesthesia for prolonged laparoscopic oncologic surgery. Sevoflurane, a widely used inhalational anesthetic, is associated with higher EA risk. Remimazolam, an ultra-short-acting benzodiazepine, may reduce EA owing to favorable hemodynamic stability and a distinct recovery profile compared with sevoflurane. We aim to test whether remimazolam-based total intravenous anesthesia (RTIVA) decreases EA incidence versus sevoflurane-based inhalational anesthesia (SINH). Methods This single-center, assessor-blinded, randomized controlled trial will enroll 108 adults (≥18 years, ASA II–III) scheduled for elective laparoscopic radical resection of gastric or colorectal cancer with expected duration ≥2 h. Participants will be randomized 1:1 to RTIVA (remimazolam infusion + remifentanil) or SINH (sevoflurane + remifentanil). Perioperative management is standardized across groups. The primary outcome is incidence of EA in the post-anesthesia care unit (PACU), defined as Riker Sedation-Agitation Scale (RSAS) ≥5, assessed by blinded observers from PACU arrival to discharge. Secondary outcomes include severe agitation (RSAS = 7), extubation time, time to BIS ≥80, time to full emergence, PACU length of stay, analgesic/antiemetic needs, use of flumazenil, postoperative nausea/vomiting within 24 h, postoperative delirium during hospitalization, QoR-15 on postoperative day 1, perioperative TNF-α and IL-6, intraoperative hemodynamics, hospital length of stay, and safety events (hypotension, bradycardia, resedation, hypoxemia, intraoperative awareness). Discussion This study will contribute to evaluating the efficacy and safety of remimazolam for reducing the incidence of EA in patients undergoing laparoscopic radical resection for gastric or colorectal cancer. The results may provide preliminary clinical evidence informing evidence-based anesthetic practice for this high-risk patient group. authors: Wenjie Mao; Binbin Yang; Fan Huang; Cui Ping Chen; Suying Li; Huide Wang

title: Cone-beam computed tomography augmented-fluoroscopy-guided center-strike targeting during peripheral bronchoscopy: robotic vs. manual catheters.
abstract: Computed tomography (CT)-to-body divergence and tool-tissue divergence (TTD) limit bronchoscopic access to peripheral pulmonary lesions (PPLs). Fixed cone-beam CT (CBCT) with augmented fluoroscopy (AF) enables intraprocedural target segmentation, live fluoroscopic overlay, and confirmation of tool position. We describe three CBCT AF-guided spatial targeting techniques as a targeting workflow and compare manual pre-curved and shape-sensing robotic catheters using center strike as the primary technical endpoint. This retrospective single-center study included 200 consecutive patients with 219 biopsied PPLs. The first 100 patients underwent biopsy with manual pre-curved catheters (Medtronic; 106 lesions), followed by 100 patients who underwent biopsy using a shape-sensing robotic catheter (Intuitive; 113 lesions). All procedures used fixed CBCT-AF, a ventilation protocol with apneic breath-holding, needle targeting with traditional two-angle, slow-sweep, and/or center-datum techniques, and CBCT tool-position confirmation. Center strike was defined as needle position in the middle third of the lesion on axial, sagittal, and coronal CBCT images. The primary outcome was center-strike tool position; diagnostic yield and 1-year diagnostic accuracy were secondary outcomes. Robotic catheters achieved a higher center-strike rate, the primary endpoint, than manual catheters {66% [75/113; 95% confidence interval (CI): 57-74%] vs. 42% (45/106; 95% CI: 33-52%), P<0.001}, as well as a higher tool-in-lesion (TIL) rate [100% (113/113; 95% CI: 97-100%) vs. 91% (96/106; 95% CI: 83-95%), P<0.001]. Diagnostic yield was 91% (95% CI: 84-95%) vs. 80% (95% CI: 72-87%) (P=0.02), and 1-year diagnostic accuracy was 96% (95% CI: 91-99%) vs. 86% (95% CI: 78-91%) (P=0.01). Dose-area product (DAP) was higher with robotic catheters [median 13,251 [interquartile range (IQR), 8,683-18,264] vs. 11,114 (IQR, 6,336-15,199) µGy·m2, P=0.04], without significant differences in fluoroscopy time or number of CBCT spins. Two pneumothoraces occurred in the robotic cohort, one requiring chest tube placement. A CBCT AF-guided targeting workflow combines real-time needle-vector alignment with intraprocedural confirmation of tool position before tissue sampling. Within this workflow, robotic catheters achieved higher center-strike and TIL rates and were associated with improved diagnostic performance. Reliable intraprocedural spatial confirmation may become increasingly important as bronchoscopy evolves toward precision transbronchial therapies.
authors: Krish Bhadra; Pranjal Patel; Amit K Mahajan; D Kyle Hogarth; Ajay A Wagh

title: ConeBeam-CT-gestützte bronchoskopische Herdnavigation – Schritt für Schritt
abstract: The assessment of peripheral lung lesions (PPH) is gaining increasing importance with the introduction of lung cancer screening using low-dose CT. Bronchoscopic navigation techniques, such as electromagnetic or virtual navigation bronchoscopy or robot-assisted bronchoscopy, are used for histological evaluation and have improved diagnostic accuracy. Navigation to the lesion using a preoperative chest CT scan can be inaccurate, particularly for small lesions or those in the lower lobe, due to CT-to-body divergence. Intraoperative 3D imaging using cone beam CT (CBCT) can significantly improve diagnostic accuracy. The combination of modern navigation techniques and CBCT is non-inferior to CT-guided transthoracic biopsy in terms of diagnostic accuracy and has a significantly more favorable risk profile. This article provides a detailed step-by-step description of how to perform CBCT-guided bronchoscopy.
