title: Current Approaches to the Storage, Processing, and Quality Assessment of RBC and Platelet Components: A Narrative Review
abstract: This narrative review summarizes current findings regarding the storage, processing, and quality assessment of red blood cell, platelet components, and whole blood. Particular attention is given to technologies aimed at preserving cellular and functional properties during storage, such as cold storage, cryopreservation, hypoxic and anaerobic storage, modified gas environments, inert gases, leukoreduction, ionizing irradiation, and pathogen-reduction methods. The literature search was conducted in PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus and eLibrary.ru; it included experimental and clinical studies, reviews, guidelines, and regulatory or technical documents published from 1958 to 2026. Evidence demonstrates that various storage and processing strategies offer distinct advantages and limitations, influencing cellular metabolism, membrane and cytoskeleton organization, morphology, mechanical properties, and hemostatic function. While conventional quality-control parameters provide essential information, they may not adequately capture early structural, biomechanical, and molecular changes associated with storage lesions. Consequently, advanced analytical techniques, including atomic force microscopy, scanning ion-conductance microscopy, Raman spectroscopy, metabolomics, and proteomics, are receiving increased attention. These methods facilitate detailed analysis of cell morphology, membrane nanostructure, mechanical properties, hemoglobin status, metabolic changes, and molecular markers of storage-induced damage. Integrating conventional quality-control parameters with biophysical and molecular approaches may enable a more comprehensive evaluation of blood-component quality. Future research should prioritize standardization of emerging storage and analytical technologies, multicenter validation, and identification of parameters associated with post-transfusion recovery and functional efficacy.
authors: Snezhanna Kandrashina; Mikhail Shvedov; Ekaterina A. Sherstyukova

title: DNA metabarcoding samples from nest soil and beaks outperform samples from talons and faeces when identifying diversity of white-tailed eagle diet in South Greenland
abstract: DNA metabarcoding is an emerging approach to study diets across a broad range of species but requires careful optimisation of the sample collection method and substrate used. The suitability of different sample types to identify the diet of the target species remains under investigated. Here, we address these knowledge gaps by collecting four different sample types - faeces, beak swabs, talon swabs, and soil samples - during nest visits of white-tailed eagles ( Haliaeetus albicilla ) during the 2025 breeding season in South Greenland. We further investigated whether some eagle dietary taxa could act as vectors for microplastic pollution. Our analyses revealed a broad diet, with 25 dietary taxa for white-tailed eagles. Lumpfish ( Cyclopterus lumpus ) was the most frequently detected dietary taxon in the diet, which was composed of 75 % fish, 19 % birds, and 7 % mammals. Our findings indicate that diets varied strongly between nesting sites. Although each sample type was efficient in capturing diet, soil and beak swabs were most promising for eagles and gave comparable results. On the other hand, faeces provided a distinct dietary profile with a reduced detection of fish, while requiring an increased sample size, and talon swabs missed rare food items. Finally, we recovered microplastic contamination in 33 % of our samples, but no dietary taxon was associated with microplastic pollution. Taken together our results underline the overlooked value of soil from nests to provide dietary information and highlight the necessity to deepen our knowledge of Arctic food webs and their microplastic contamination.
authors: Mael Perroud; Kay Lucek; Knud Falk; Nicholas Per Huffeldt

title: DeGenRESOLVE : An offline GUI ‐based automated nanopore sequencing pipeline for viruses with custom rule‐based indel and degeneracy resolution
abstract: Sequencing methods based on Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) have revolutionized the field of viral genomics. However, available analysis tools are often internet-dependent, have complex installation requirements, or lack graphical user interfaces (GUIs), limiting their use in laboratories with restricted internet access or limited bioinformatics expertise. Here we present DeGenRESOLVE, a pipeline designed for amplicon-based ONT resequencing where a reference genome is available. This pipeline does not perform de novo assembly but processes raw base-called ONT viral sequencing data offline in an easy-to-use GUI. The pipeline combines existing tools with a rule-based algorithm that applies user-defined criteria to positions the variant caller reports as ambiguous and to the insertions and deletions (indels) it proposes, logging every decision with its statistics. The application works with both segmented and non-segmented viral genomes. Tested on eight influenza A isolates with Illumina-derived genomes, the consensus agreed at 99.97% of positions with each isolate's own genome as reference, and 36 of 37 resolved positions agreed. With close genomes as references, 99.98% of called positions agreed. However, agreement decreased as the reference diverged. Where the hemagglutinin cleavage site differed in length from the reference, indel adjudication reproduced it in four of five isolates, against none without it. In known mixtures, an ambiguity code was retained only when the minor allele exceeded ~40%. In essence, the refined sequence is a dominant consensus, not a record of within-sample variation. Therefore, DeGenRESOLVE facilitates offline, reproducible, and auditable sequencing analysis, reducing ambiguity in consensus generation and minimizing reproducibility errors.
authors: Shoaib Saikat; Mohammad Enayet Hossain; Jenifar Quaiyum Ami; Rehana Parvin; Mohammed Ziaur Rahman

title: Delayed-centrifugation blood collection tube for remote blood biomarker assessment
abstract: Introduction: Plasma phosphorylated tau 217 (p-tau217) and amyloid-β 42 (Aβ42) are advancing toward clinical use for Alzheimer's disease (AD), but their reliability can be impacted by preanalytical handling. Although alternative collection tubes with distinct stabilization strategies-P100 (protease inhibitor) and HEMAcollect (hemolysis/platelet-activation minimization)-have been developed to stabilize plasma proteins, how well they preserve these markers remains unresolved; we therefore compared both against fresh standard EDTA tubes. Methods: In 40 participants, plasma p-tau217 and Aβ42 were measured (Lumipulse) in paired fresh EDTA, P100, and HEMAcollect samples after 5-day ambient storage. We assessed concentration change, rank-order preservation (Spearman ρ), percentage difference, and diagnostic classification under the p-tau217/Aβ42 ratio and p-tau217 alone. Results: P100 preserved p-tau217 favorably, with high rank-order correlation (ρ=0.98) and a modest median change (+12.1%), and its classification agreement with fresh EDTA reached 97.5% using p-tau217 alone. HEMAcollect showed greater p-tau217 signal loss (-57.5%). Aβ42 was reduced in both tubes (-72.8% P100; -95.5% HEMAcollect) with loss of rank order, so neither preserved the p-tau217/Aβ42 ratio. Discussion: Stability was tube- and analyte-specific, and P100 consistently outperformed HEMAcollect-preserving p-tau217 rank order while HEMAcollect reduced signal across analytes. Although neither tube preserved the Aβ42-dependent ratio, P100 shows potential for p-tau217-based workflows. Preanalytical stability must be established analyte by analyte before alternative tubes enter clinical AD diagnosis.
authors: You‐Rim Lee; Anurag Raj; Oscar Lopez; Xuemei Zeng; Thomas K. Karikari

title: Dense Endoluminal Mapping and Localisation from Monocular Bronchoscopy
abstract: Bronchoscopy inserts a camera through the airways to diagnose endoluminal disease. Locating the camera along the airway usually requires additional equipment, such as an electromagnetic tracker and a preoperative CT scan. In this paper, we investigate the use of the monocular camera stream to localise the bronchoscope without requiring additional sensing. We introduce a monocular SLAM system that localises the tip of a bronchoscope and reconstructs the airway surface around it from RGB video alone. A Depth Anything 3 backbone, fine-tuned on over a million photorealistic airway renderings, returns metric per-pixel depth and is the system's only source of scale. DINOv3 features routed through a custom cross-attention matcher supply sub-pixel correspondences on mucosa where classical descriptors fail. Both enter a factor graph alongside a dense constraint from projective iterative closest point (ICP) registration against the system's own running reconstruction, so surface evidence stabilises the directions the visual factors leave weakly observable. On six airways rendered from patient CT scans, the system reaches 26.1 mm mean absolute trajectory error and 77.5% mean surface F-score. Its mean surface accuracy exceeds that of five recent monocular SLAM and feed-forward baselines. MASt3R-SLAM, which fits a free scale to the ground truth, has a lower mean trajectory error (22.0 mm). ORB-SLAM3 completes only two of the six airways, whereas our system completes all six and also reconstructs two ex vivo specimens.
authors: Salvatore Esposito; Matías Mattamala; Daniel Rebain; Liang Zhao; K. Dhaliwal; Mohsen Khadem; Subramanian Ramamoorthy

title: Detection of Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) in Black-Horned Capuchin Monkeys, Brazil
abstract: We carried out a viral surveillance study on 30 black-horned capuchin monkeys (Sapajus nigritus) in Rio Doce State Park, a protected area in the Brazilian Atlantic Forest. Samples were tested for orthopoxviruses, flaviviruses, coronaviruses, influenza viruses, and a wide range of other respiratory viruses using molecular and serological methods. RT-qPCR detected the respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) genome in oral swabs from two asymptomatic juvenile females sampled in an area with high human interaction. This finding indicates a possible exposure of an population to RSV, a contagious human pathogen, and highlights the importance of increased surveillance at the human-wildlife interface.

title: Detection of the pqsA Gene and Histological Changes Induced by Pseudomonas aeruginosa
abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa uses quorum-sensing systems to coordinate activities regulated by specific genes, such as metabolic and environmental responses. The pqsA gene is a key component of the pqs pathway (quinolone signaling in Pseudomonas aeruginosa).This study focused on applying a mouse model to some local isolates of P. aeruginosa and identifying those carrying the pqsA gene. The study included isolating 150 samples for analysis, which resulted in confirmation of the presence of 58 isolates of P.aeruginosa. The specimens including wound swabs, burn samples, urine samples, middle ear swabs, and sputum were collected from different hospitals. The presence of the pqsA gene was confirmed molecularly using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) on 19 selected isolates, all of which showed positive amplification (448 bp). The experimental mouse model consisted of Swiss albino mice, divided into a control group and two treatment groups with low (1×10⁴ CFU) and high (1×10⁸ CFU) concentration of bacteria. We evaluated body weight before and after exposure and also performed histological examinations of the liver and lung tissue. The results showed that increased bacterial concentrations led to increased weight loss and extensive histological changes. In contrast, low concentrations produced only minor tissue changes. Statistical analysis (results are presented as means ± SE calculated using one-way ANOVA) confirmed these findings as statistically significant (p ≤ 0.05). Based on the above information, it can be concluded that the pqsA gene is highly conserved in local isolates of P. aeruginosa and that the presence of this gene leads to significant effects in host tissue in controlled in vivo studies. Therefore, this research contributes to understanding of the bacterial quorum sensing mechanism, the pathogenicity of bacterial species and their ability to interact with host bacteria in in vivo studies

title: Development of a Rapid Automated Point-of-Care Test for <i>Mycobacterium tuberculosis</i> Detection From Tongue Swabs and Sputum Specimens on the DASH® Rapid PCR System.
abstract:
Background

Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB) disease is a global health threat with most cases occurring in low-and middle-income countries (LMIC) with limited healthcare infrastructure. Near-point-of-care testing deployed at peripheral clinical settings is needed to start treatment earlier and thereby improve treatment outcomes.

Methods

We developed a rapid MTB detection assay for the DASH® Rapid PCR System with cartridge-based sample prep and dual target qPCR multicopy MTB insertion sequences IS6110 and IS1081 amplification. The limit of detection and analytical specificity of the RUO (research use only) DASH MTB assay were evaluated. Two clinical evaluations were performed using 110 (70 positive and 40 negative) de-identified blinded tongue swab specimens and 100 (49 positive and 51 negative) de-identified blinded sputum specimens from South African symptomatic clinic attendees.

Results

The DASH assay demonstrated a limit of detection of 2.5 MTB cells/swab with no detection of 10 non-tuberculosis Mycobacterium strains. The clinical sensitivity of tongue swab specimens was 91%, and the specificity was 100% as compared to Xpert Ultra results on paired sputum specimens. The overall clinical sensitivity of sputum specimens was 96% (100% for smear-positive and 88% for smear-negative samples) and the specificity of 88% when compared to sputum culture. The DASH test is compatible with peripheral LMIC settings via external battery operation and cartridge stability at 45°C for one year.

Conclusions

The DASH MTB's assay demonstrated high sensitivity and specificity, rapid time to result, and compatibility with environments that lack air conditioning and consistent electricity make this assay suitable for diverse clinical settings.
authors: Butzler MA, Reed JL, Olson AM, Wood RC, Cangelosi GA, Luabeya AK, Hatherill M, Chiwaya AM, Rockman L, Theron G, McFall SM.

title: Development, validation and clinical implementation of cellular swab materials for quality assurance of pharmacogenomic point-of-care testing
abstract: Background Pharmacogenomic point-of-care testing (PGx POCT) enables genotype-informed prescribing at the bedside, but implementation is limited by the lack of suitable reference materials for clinical verification and standardised external quality assessment (EQA). Methods Fixed lymphoblastoid cell lines were formulated as swab-based materials at defined cellular inputs for MT-RNR1 POCT. Materials were evaluated using Genedrive® assays, quantitative PCR, acceptance quality limit batch release, workflow-perturbation testing and stability studies, then deployed for clinical verification and in an international EQA programme. Results Materials were homogeneous, workflow compatible and reproducible, with 100% correct genotype calls at the lowest intended manufacturing cell load. Clinical verification of 11 Genedrive® systems across five neonatal units demonstrated 99% concordance with expected genotype classifications (232/234 results). Seven EQA surveys yielded 253 participant results, with full-mark rates of 87.5–100%, and six test failures. Most failures occurred with low cell-input materials near the assay limit of detection. The materials supported genotype concordance, performance monitoring and identification of workflow and sample-related variability. Conclusions Workflow-compatible cell-based reference materials combined with EQA provide a scalable framework for quality-assured PGx POCT beyond specialist laboratories. Clinical verification of Genedrive® systems within neonatal units using the cell-based swab materials, together with deployment of an International MT-RNR1 PGx POCT EQA programme, demonstrated their suitability for supporting both pre-implementation testing and ongoing quality assurance in decentralised healthcare settings. The framework may provide a model for the implementation, clinical verification and ongoing quality assessment of PGx POCT services. Further evaluation across platforms, analytes, settings and participant groups is required to establish broader applicability.
authors: Henry Thomas; John Henry McDermott; William G. Newman; Shaun Ainsworth; Gino Miele; Simon J. Patton; Rosa Morra

title: Diagnostic Efficiency of Sequential Tissue Acquisition During Shape-Sensing Robotic-Assisted Bronchoscopy in a Thoracic Surgery Setting: A Biopsy-Level Analysis
abstract: Background: Shape-sensing robotic-assisted bronchoscopy (ssRAB) enables precise navigation to peripheral pulmonary lesions, while intraprocedural imaging can improve assessment of biopsy tool positioning relative to the target. However, successful lesion localization does not necessarily translate into diagnostic tissue acquisition, and little is known about the diagnostic contribution of individual sequential biopsy specimens. This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic yield and sequential tissue acquisition during ssRAB at both the lesion and individual specimen level, with particular emphasis on the number of biopsies required to establish a diagnosis. Methods: We performed a retrospective single-center analysis of consecutive thoracic surgical ssRAB procedures using the ION™ Endoluminal System (Intuitive Surgical, Sunnyvale, CA, USA) between August 2024 and March 2026. Procedures performed exclusively for bronchoscopic lesion marking without diagnostic tissue acquisition were excluded. Intraprocedural imaging was performed using cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) or C-arm fluoroscopy. Primary outcome measures included specimen-level diagnostic yield, lesion-level diagnostic yield, the biopsy number at which the first diagnostic specimen was obtained, and the diagnostic-to-total specimen ratio per lesion. Results: Eighty-four patients with 118 pulmonary nodules were included. Median lesion diameter was 9.0 mm, and 94 lesions (79.7%) were solid, 10 (8.5%) were subsolid, and 14 (11.9%) were pure ground-glass opacities. CBCT was used in 111 lesions (94.1%) and C-arm fluoroscopy in seven (5.9%). A diagnostic bronchoscopic result was obtained in 101 lesions, corresponding to a lesion-level diagnostic yield of 85.6%. A total of 794 individual biopsy specimens were obtained, of which 487 (61.3%) were diagnostic. The mean diagnostic-to-total specimen ratio per lesion was 0.59 ± 0.39. Among diagnostically successful lesions, the first biopsy specimen was diagnostic in 68/101 cases (67.3%). A diagnosis was established within the first three biopsy specimens in 91/101 lesions (90.1%) and within the first five specimens in 99/101 lesions (98.0%). In two lesions, the first diagnostic specimen was obtained with the eighth biopsy. Conclusions: Although ssRAB achieved a high lesion-level diagnostic yield, diagnostic performance at the individual specimen level was substantially lower. Most successful diagnoses were established within the first three biopsy specimens, while additional sampling continued to provide incremental diagnostic information. These findings highlight the distinction between successful lesion localization and successful tissue acquisition and support a sequential, rather than single-sample, approach to tissue acquisition during ssRAB.
authors: Hruy Menghesha; Philipp Feodorovici; Joachim Schmidt; Donatas Zalepugas

title: Diagnostic Performance and Safety Profile of Shape-Sensing Robotic-Assisted Bronchoscopy in Peripheral Pulmonary Lesions: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract:
Introduction

Shape-sensing robotic-assisted bronchoscopy (ssRAB) has emerged as a promising modality for diagnosing peripheral pulmonary lesions. This meta-analysis evaluated its diagnostic performance and safety profile.

Methods

PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Library were searched from inception to December 2025. Study quality was assessed using the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies-3. Random-effects model was used to estimate the pooled diagnostic yield, sensitivity for malignancy, and complication, with rates (%) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) when the I2 index exceeded 50%. Cumulative meta-analysis was performed to assess the temporal stability and evidence saturation of the pooled diagnostic yield. Publication bias was evaluated using funnel plots and Egger's test.

Results

A total of 3,678 lesions from 18 studies were included. Notably, diagnostic yield varied significantly by outcome definition, with pooled diagnostic yield of 82.5% (95% CI: 78.3%-86.0%) under strict definition vs. 88.1% (95% CI: 82.8%-92.0%) under the intermediate definition (p = 0.036). The pooled sensitivity for malignancy of 90.0% (95% CI: 86.4%-92.8%). Cumulative meta-analysis showed stabilized diagnostic performance after approximately 1,500 lesions for the strict definition and 500 lesions for intermediate definition. Moreover, the safety profile was favorable, with pooled rates of pneumothorax of 1.8% (95% CI: 1.3%-2.3%), chest tube placement of 1.1% (95% CI: 0.7%-1.5%), and severe bleeding of 0.0% (95% CI: 0.0%-0.3%). Subgroup analyses showed consistent performance across study designs, region, and nodule characteristics. Diagnostic yield was significantly influenced by publication year and lesion size (p < 0.05).

Conclusion

ssRAB was associated with favorable, definition-dependent diagnostic yield (82.5%-88.1%) with exceptional safety, supporting ssRAB as an attractive first-line minimally invasive diagnostic option in appropriately selected patients, especially for small nodules (<2 cm) and patients at elevated procedural risk.
authors: Hu X, Wang L, Shi J, Fernandez-Bussy S, Liu D.

title: Diagnostic Yield and Safety Profile of Shape-Sensing Robotic-Assisted Bronchoscopy in Peripheral Pulmonary Nodules 8 mm or Smaller.
abstract:
Purpose

Lung cancer screening guidelines generally recommend imaging surveillance rather than tissue sampling for nodules measuring ≤8 mm. Evidence regarding the feasibility, diagnostic performance, and safety of tissue biopsy in this lesion size remains limited. We evaluated the diagnostic performance and safety of shape-sensing robotic-assisted bronchoscopy (ssRAB) for biopsy of peripheral pulmonary nodules measuring ≤8 mm.

Methods

We conducted a retrospective single-center study of consecutive patients who underwent ssRAB between June 2020 and December 2025 for biopsy of nodules measuring ≤8 mm on pre-procedural CT imaging. The primary outcome was strict diagnostic yield, as defined by the American Thoracic Society/American College of Chest Physicians. Secondary objectives included intermediate diagnostic yield, diagnostic distribution, procedural outcomes, and complications. Diagnostic performance according to lesion size (≤ 6 mm vs. 6.1-8 mm) was evaluated separately as a subgroup analysis.

Results

A total of 195 nodules were included in the study. Median lesions diameter was seven mm (IQR 6-8). Strict diagnostic yield was 70.2% (137/195), while intermediate diagnostic yield was 77.4% (151/195). Malignancy was identified in 104 lesions (53.3%). The median ssRAB procedure time was 59 min (IQR 45-83). Pneumothorax occurred in six patients (3.3%), with chest tube placement required in two (1.1%).

Discussion

Shape-sensing robotic-assisted bronchoscopy demonstrated meaningful diagnostic performance and a favorable safety profile for peripheral pulmonary nodules measuring ≤8 mm, including lesions ≤6 mm. In this selected, higher-risk cohort, our findings suggest that earlier tissue diagnosis can be feasible and may benefit some patients.
authors: Fernandez-Bussy S, Murillo-Torres RM, Yu Lee-Mateus A, Rojas-Zapata TA, Karki D, Evans L, Alqawasma MA, Chadha RM, Khoor A, Vu LH, Abia-Trujillo D, Husta BC.

title: Diagnostic Yield of Endometrial Sampling by Age in Premenopausal Women with Abnormal Uterine Bleeding: A Retrospective Cross-Sectional Study
abstract: Background: An age of 45 years is often used to guide endometrial assessment in abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB), but age is only one component of clinical risk. We described the relationship between age and histopathological yield among premenopausal women who had undergone endometrial sampling. Methods: This single-centre retrospective cross-sectional study analysed the index sampling episodes of 824 women with AUB documented as premenopausal or perimenopausal (January 2022–May 2026). The clinically more consequential endpoint was endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia (EIN)/atypical hyperplasia or carcinoma; the primary statistical outcome was a broader composite that also included hyperplasia without atypia. Modified Poisson regression estimated the adjusted association between age ≥45 years and the primary outcome. Discrimination of age alone and of an exploratory model using variables available before biopsy was compared in 776 complete cases with bootstrap internal validation. Results: EIN/carcinoma occurred in 4/361 (1.1%) women aged <45 years and 25/463 (5.4%) aged ≥45 years (crude RR 4.87, 95% CI 1.71–13.88). The broad outcome occurred in 24/361 (6.6%) and 57/463 (12.3%), respectively (absolute difference 5.7 percentage points, 95% CI 1.6–9.6; adjusted RR 1.62, 95% CI 1.01–2.61; p = 0.047). Results were similar across sensitivity analyses (adjusted RRs 1.52–1.68). With age coded as ≥45 years in both models, the optimism-corrected AUC was 0.686 for the exploratory pre-biopsy model and 0.575 for age alone (difference 0.111, 95% CI 0.060–0.196). Conclusions: Among premenopausal women selected for endometrial sampling, histopathological yield increased with age, and most EIN/carcinoma cases occurred at age ≥45 years, but the adjusted association for the broad outcome was imprecise, and age alone had limited discrimination. Model performance was assessed only internally and only in sampled women; this study cannot establish a biopsy rule for all women with AUB because women not sampled were not observed.
authors: Izabella Erdelean; Dragos Erdelean; Răzvan Roșca; Andrei Pescaru; Cosmin Cîtu; Denis Mihai Șerban; Victor Bogdan Buciu; Anca Raluca Dinu; Nilima Rajpal Kundnani; Sebastian Ciurescu

title: Diagnostic performance of an automated qRT-PCR assay using a peripheral blood host 5-mRNA signature for active tuberculosis: a single-center prospective cohort study and external validation in public databases
abstract: BACKGROUND: Tuberculosis remains a major global public health concern. Current sputum-based etiological assays have limited diagnostic performance in patients with smear-negative tuberculosis, atypical clinical manifestations, or restricted access to specimens containing Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB). Novel molecular tools for clinical triage in healthcare settings are urgently needed. METHODS: A total of 438 participants were enrolled and classified into five groups based on comprehensive clinical data: confirmed active tuberculosis (Group 1), suspected tuberculosis after antibiotic treatment (Group 2), undetermined diagnosis (Group 3), non-tuberculous infectious disease controls (Group 4), and non-infectious controls (Group 5). mRNA expression levels of FCGR1A, FCGR1B, GBP5, GBP6, and CXCL10 in peripheral blood were measured, and the TB active score (TBA-Score) was calculated to identify TB infection. Multiple public microarray and RNA-seq datasets were used for external validation of the diagnostic performance of this 5-host-gene signature for tuberculosis infection. RESULTS: The TBA-Score was significantly elevated in patients with active tuberculosis and effectively discriminated active tuberculosis from non-tuberculous infectious and non-infectious controls. The AUC for Group 1 versus Group 4 was 0.905 (95% CI, 0.850-0.959), with a sensitivity of 83.6% and specificity of 95.1%; the AUC for Group 1 versus Group 5 was 0.916 (95% CI, 0.869-0.962), with a sensitivity of 83.6% and specificity of 90.6%. During external validation, this 5-mRNA signature retained robust discriminative ability across six public transcriptomic datasets, with AUC values ranging from 0.824 to 0.970 for distinguishing active tuberculosis from latent tuberculosis infection. CONCLUSIONS: This automated qRT-PCR system enables rapid detection using peripheral-blood-derived 5-mRNA TBA-Score. The signature shows cross-platform and multi-ethnic population reproducibility, supporting its further evaluation for non-sputum near-point-of-care TB testing.
authors: Xiaocheng Luo; Zhenxing Wang; Xianzhen Huang; Yuliang Huang; Shunda Luo; Jinfeng Lu; Chaoyong He; Xiayan Meng; Yanqun Lan; Fengmei Zhu; Jin Liu; Zixuan Huang; Bo Zhang; Liang Zhang; Guohui Sun

title: Diagnostic yield and predictors of complications in CT-guided percutaneous lung biopsy: an analysis based on ATS/ACCP criteria.
abstract: CT-guided percutaneous lung biopsy (CT-PLB) remains a cornerstone for the diagnosis of pulmonary nodules (PNs), although several alternative techniques, including robotic-assisted bronchoscopy, are increasingly adopted. This study aimed to evaluate CT-PLB in a real-world cohort, focusing on predictors of diagnostic yield and complications. We retrospectively evaluated patients who underwent CT-PLB between 2020 and 2024. The diagnostic yield was defined according to the recently published ATS/ACCP criteria. Clinical, radiological, and periprocedural variables were assessed as predictors of diagnostic outcome and complication [pneumothorax (PNX) and pulmonary hemorrhage]. Six hundred fifty-seven patients were included (mean age 69 ± 11 years; 54% male). The diagnostic yield was 84% with higher yield observed for nodule size (diameter ≥ 10 mm), density (solid), and location (peripheral). Increasing subcutaneous fat thickness was independently associated with a modest but significant reduction in diagnostic yield. PNX was radiologically present in 44.4% of cases; however, only 5.9% required hospitalization, and 4.7% required chest-tube placement. Greater parenchymal depth, trans-fissural needle passages, pleural tags and supine and left-lateral decubitus positions were associated with increased PNX extent, while intraparenchymal lesion and greater chest-wall thickness showed a protective effect. Radiological pulmonary hemorrhage >2 cm occurred in 38% of patients, whereas only 1.5% experienced major bleeding requiring intervention. Greater parenchymal depth and non-solid density were associated with increased hemorrhage severity. In a contemporary diagnostic landscape, CT-PLNB still demonstrates high diagnostic yield and an acceptable safety profile when strict diagnostic criteria are applied. These findings support its continued role as a primary diagnostic approach for PNs.

title: Diagnostic yield and safety of CT-guided lung biopsy performed following multi-disciplinary triage of robotic navigational bronchoscopy referrals
abstract: Introduction National lung cancer screening has increased the detection and work-up of small pulmonary nodules. As a tertiary referral centre with a robotic-assisted navigational bronchoscopy (RAB) biopsy service, referrals for robotic-assisted lung nodule biopsy have risen substantially from across the region. In December 2024, a multidisciplinary triage meeting involving bronchoscopists and radiologists was introduced to direct patients towards surveillance, CT-guided biopsy (CTB), or RAB. This study evaluated all CTB outcomes over a 12-month period and compared diagnostic yield and complication rates between patients initially referred from external institutions for RAB but re-directed to CTB (group 1) and those referred directly for CTB (group 2) from both internal and external referral sources. Methods Biopsy outcomes were classified as positive, true negative, false negative, or indeterminate according to table 1, following review of the electronic patient record and PACS. Mediastinal, chest wall and pleural biopsies were excluded from the analysis. Outcomes and complication rates, including pneumothorax (PTX), chest drain insertion requiring admission, haemoptysis, and air embolism were compared between groups. A secondary analysis compared maximum nodule size (mm) between groups. Results A total of 208 CT-guided lung biopsies were performed: 47/208 (22.6%) in group 1 and 161/208 (77.4%) in group 2. Positive or true negative results were achieved in 41/47 (87.2%) of group 1 and 138/161 (85.7%) of group 2 (p=0.79). PTX occurred in 8/47 (17.0%) of group 1 and 41/161 (25.5%) of group 2 (p=0.24). Chest drain insertion requiring admission was required in 4/47 (8.5%) and 17/161 (10.6%) respectively (p=0.68). One air embolism occurred in group 2. Median nodule diameter was 18 mm (range 7–50 mm) in group 1 and 21 mm (range 6–142 mm) in group 2. Conclusions Patients redirected to CT-guided biopsy following initial navigational bronchoscopy referral and triage had comparable diagnostic yield and complication rates at biopsy compared to those referred directly for CTB. Multidisciplinary triage may therefore support efficient management of a high-volume tertiary referral pathway for lung nodule biopsy.

title: Digital connectivity in plateletpheresis collections improves productivity and workflow efficiency without compromising donor safety.
abstract:
Background and objectives

Blood banks face pressure to meet the growing demand for platelet components while improving operational efficiency and maintaining donor and patient safety. This study describes a data-driven strategy using connectivity tools to reduce data transfer errors, optimize workflow, and safely implement high-yield platelet collections.

Materials and methods

This retrospective observational study analyzed plateletpheresis procedures performed with Trima Accel™ Automated Blood Collection System between January 2022 and November 2025 at Fundação Pró-Sangue, São Paulo. In November 2022, the Terumo Operational Medical Equipment Software (TOMEs™) middleware was implemented to establish a bidirectional interface between apheresis devices and the blood bank information system. Data-driven simulations identified donors eligible for high-yield collections, enabling the introduction of triple-dose plateletpheresis in October 2024. Variables included donor data discrepancies, adverse events, procedure duration, platelet yield, predicted post-procedure platelet counts, anticoagulant use, inter-donation intervals, and workflow efficiency. Outcomes before and after implementation were compared.

Results

Integration of the bidirectional interface reduced donor data discrepancies from 47% to 3%, and decreased manual interactions by 30%, improving data reliability and operational efficiency. Simulations showed that 30% of donors met Brazilian regulatory criteria for triple-dose plateletpheresis. After implementation, plateletpheresis productivity increased 16%. Adverse event rates remained low and comparable before and after implementation (8.2% vs. 7.9%). Predicted post-procedure platelet counts in triple donors remained within the device safety threshold recommended by Brazilian policies.

Conclusion

Digital integration and data-driven decision-making enable the safe implementation of triple-dose plateletpheresis, improving productivity without compromising donor safety. This approach may serve as a practical model for blood centers, particularly in resource-limited settings.

title: Distribution and Age Dynamics of Respiratory Mycoplasmosis in Birds on Farms of the Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic
abstract: Experiments revealed that 1- to 60-day-old chickens are more susceptible to respiratory mycoplasmosis. Those chickens that contracted the disease experienced developmental delays. Serological studies revealed that the serum droplet agglutination test (SDR) in chickens testing positive for mycoplasmosis resulted in high infection rates in 1- and 20-day-old chickens, amounting to 57.5% and 62.5%, respectively. Respiratory mycoplasmosis infection was recorded in 35.5% of 40-day-old chickens and 6.6% of 60-day-old chickens. Thus, during the study, the percentage of infected chickens did not fall below 50.0% in the RSPN, with the infection peaking at 7 and 10 months of age, amounting to 91.6% and 80.0%, respectively. According to the hemagglutination test, 100% antibodies to mycoplasma were detected at all age periods. At the same time, the maximum average titer (5286±932) was also recorded during the period of intensive egg production. With age, a decrease in the average titer to 3171±428 was recorded. Bacteriological examination of throat swabs taken from healthy laying hens revealed M. gallisepticum cultures in 26.6%–53.3% of all age groups. Detection of the causative agent of respiratory mycoplasmosis in embryos and one-day-old chicks indicates that the infection is transmitted transovarially. The highest mycoplasma carriage rate (53.3%) was detected in 10-month-old hens. Among 12-month-old roosters, the mycoplasma carriage rate was 64.0%.

title: Drill with Confidence: Real-Time Automated Drilling Fluid Testing and Dynamic Hydraulic Modeling for Drilling Optimization
abstract: Manual drilling fluid measurements typically conducted 2–4 times per day, lack the resolution required for precise hydraulic calculations and management in high-performance wells. This paper details the implementation of a closed-loop workflow involving an inline automated fluid testing device and real-time hydraulics simulation and monitoring across two wells in the field. The primary objective was to replace intermittent manual sampling with high-frequency data integrated into a live hydraulic and hole-cleaning simulator to monitor and optimize drilling performance parameters such as Rate of Penetration (ROP), tripping speeds, and circulation times. The technology utilized an inline dual-sampling drilling fluid characterization device to continuously analyze mud properties in the circulating system. The automated system achieved a significant increase in data density, providing 46 rheology tests and 1,920 density readings per day, a massive improvement over the conventional 2–4 rheology tests and 48 density readings. These real-time parameters (Density, PV, YP, and 6-speed readings) and drilling parameters were streamed to a Real-Time Center where a hydraulics modelling software was used for real-time monitoring and optimization. This allowed for the continuous monitoring of the Hole-Cleaning Index (HCI), Cuttings Bed Height (CBH), and Equivalent Circulating Density (ECD) against planned pressure and fracture gradients and identify opportunities for drilling parameter optimization. The integration of real-time data into predictive simulations yielded substantial operational efficiencies as follows: Drilling Performance: The system enabled a maximum ROP of 400 ft/hr while maintaining good hole cleaning. A field-best 24-hour footage of 3,945.68 feet was achieved in the 6-inch section at this time.Circulation Optimization: While the original plan was six bottom-up cycles, predictive simulations suggested optimizing this sequence to just two (a potential saving in circulation time of 67% whilst ensuring a clean wellbore)Tripping Efficiency: Real-time surge/swab monitoring enabled potential tripping speed increases of nearly 100% over previous rig KPIs, offering 15–25% time savings compared to the best-performing rigs in the region.Data Accuracy: Comparative analysis showed a high correlation between simulated ECD and actual annular pressure while drilling (APWD) data, confirming the reliability of automated fluid inputs for pressure management. This work demonstrates that automating the fluid-data-to-simulation loop moves the industry from reactive monitoring to proactive drilling management. It quantifies the specific "time-savings" value of high-frequency rheology data, proving that automated testing is a critical precursor to fully autonomous drilling systems.

title: Dual-Wield: An Observational Study of Utilization and Outcomes of Cryobiopsy and Intraoperative CT scan During Navigational Bronchoscopy
abstract: Background Pulmonary nodules are common incidental imaging findings, and distinguishing malignant from benign etiologies frequently requires invasive sampling. CT-guided transthoracic needle biopsy offers high yield but carries pneumothorax rates of 15–45% and precludes concurrent mediastinal staging. Shape-sensing navigational bronchoscopy, intraprocedural cone-beam CT (CBCT), and transbronchial cryobiopsy have each independently improved bronchoscopy performance, but integration of all three into one workflow remains poorly characterized. We describe real-world utilization and outcomes of these modalities at a large volume community tertiary care center. Research Question What is the real-world utilization, diagnostic performance, and complication rate of navigational bronchoscopy for lung nodule sampling with the addition of CBCT and cryobiopsy? Study Design and Methods We conducted a retrospective cohort study of navigational bronchoscopy procedures performed at a single community tertiary care center between January 1, 2024, and January 1, 2026. Two physician investigators independently abstracted procedure reports, imaging, and pathology from the electronic health record, recording cryobiopsy use, CBCT use, target nodule size, pathology, and complications. Diagnostic yield was determined using the strict ATS/ACCP consensus definition. Results Among 199 navigational bronchoscopy procedures, 229 lesions were sampled. Mean nodule size was 22.4 ± 17.7 mm overall, smallest with cryobiopsy plus CBCT (17.4 ± 13.7 mm) and largest with no adjunctive modality (29.8 ± 20.3 mm). Overall diagnostic yield was 78.0%: 83.9% with cryobiopsy plus CBCT, 75.0% cryobiopsy alone, 70.4% CBCT alone, and 73.2% no adjunctive modality. The complication rate was 3.5% (7/199). Diagnostic yield trended higher in cases with both cryobiopsy and CBCT. Conclusion Integrating navigational bronchoscopy with CBCT and cryobiopsy achieved the highest diagnostic yield while sampling the smallest nodules with an acceptable safety profile. Prospective randomized studies are warranted to define the independent contribution of each adjunct and to detect any true incremental harm.
authors: Naman Garg; Maria Haseem; Sina Rahesh; Kunal Jain; Ross Charles Schumacher

title: Early applications of apple vision pro in clinical medicine and medical education: a scoping review
abstract: The Apple Vision Pro (AVP), a next-generation spatial computing device, has demonstrated potential applications in multidisciplinary clinical diagnosis, treatment, and medical education, by leveraging its unique technical architecture and performance advantages. In clinical practice, its fundamental advantages of three-dimensional (3D) visualization, real-time image integration, and immersive interaction have been preliminarily employed in disease diagnosis and treatment, surgical planning, precise operations, and postoperative rehabilitation across multiple disciplines. In medical education, AVP surpasses the limitations of conventional models, offering a novel methodology for anatomy education, clinical skills development, specialized practical training, and collaboration of distance learning, thereby alleviating persistent challenges such as unequal distribution of teaching resources, low efficiency in skills and specialized training, and the high cost of distance education. However, AVP faces some limitations, including limited hardware portability, insufficient system compatibility, a lack of specialized medical applications, high costs, and incomplete medical certification. Currently, most evidence derives from feasibility studies, case reports, and opinion pieces. Only two Stage 2b confirmatory studies were identified. Thus, high-level evidence for clinical benefit remains scarce. Readers should interpret all reported benefits as preliminary technical demonstrations rather than established clinical outcomes. Future advancements necessitate iterative development of lightweight hardware design, development of specialized medical software, cross-system optimization, and establishment of standardization protocols. Moreover, more randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and multicenter studies are urgently needed to fully explore and validate its intrinsic value in precision medicine and the equitable allocation of medical resources.

title: Effect of Early Tourniquet Release on Hemolysis in Emergency Department Phlebotomy: The TOURNI-ED Randomized Trial
abstract: Background and Objectives: Hemolysis is the most common preanalytical error in emergency department samples and can compromise diagnostic reliability. Evidence on tourniquet-release timing under standardized pressure is limited. We assessed whether initiating cuff deflation when blood enters the first tube and completing it as that tube fills reduces hemolysis. Materials and Methods: In a single-center, parallel-group, 1:1 randomized trial (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT07617103), 792 adults triaged as Emergency Severity Index (ESI) 3 to 5 underwent venipuncture with stasis applied at 60 mm Hg by sphygmomanometer. Cuff deflation was initiated when blood entered the first tube and completed as that tube filled (n = 396) or after the last tube filled (n = 396). The primary outcome was the proportion of serum separator gel tubes with a hemolysis index of 1+ or greater, assessed by personnel blinded to allocation. The primary complete-case analysis included 790 participants analyzed as randomized. Results: Hemolysis occurred in 68 of 395 patients (17.2%) with early release and 103 of 395 (26.1%) with late release (absolute risk reduction 8.9 percentage points; 95% confidence interval (CI), 3.1–14.5; p = 0.003; number needed to treat (NNT) 11.3). The adjusted odds ratio in the prespecified model was 0.58 (95% CI, 0.41–0.82), and the ordinal distribution also favored early release (p = 0.002). No early-release patient exceeded 60 s of stasis, versus 29.0% with late release. Complication estimates were imprecise (8.1% vs. 5.6%; risk difference +2.5 points; 95% CI, −1.0 to 6.1). Conclusions: In adult emergency department patients presenting with non-critical acuity (ESI 3–5) undergoing direct 21-gauge venipuncture under standardized 60 mm Hg cuff pressure, early cuff release significantly reduced specimen hemolysis (NNT 11.3 for preventing one laboratory-defined hemolyzed sample). These findings cannot be generalized to resuscitated patients (ESI 1–2), intravenous catheter blood draws, winged collection devices, or uncalibrated elastic tourniquets.

title: Effective and ineffective teamwork in robotic-assisted surgery: operating room professionals’ accounts
abstract: BACKGROUND: Robotic-assisted surgery (RAS) has transformed modern surgical practice and introduced unique challenges to teamwork and communication. While prior research has examined human factors integration, barriers, and interventions in RAS, we explore operating room (OR) professionals' experiences of teamwork across all operative phases. OBJECTIVE: This study aims to give voice to OR professionals actively performing RAS and to understand what they perceive as effective and ineffective teamwork in their experiences. METHOD: Using an interpretivist paradigm, we conducted critical incident-based, semi-structured interviews with 21 OR professionals across multiple roles and specialties at two teaching hospitals using a closed-console RAS system. We analyzed the data using reflexive thematic analysis and employing an inductive, semantic coding strategy in which the content of the data was coded as explicitly described by the participants. RESULTS: We organized the results across three operative phases. In the pre-operative phase, deliberate planning, including team briefings, equipment checks, procedural steps, and patient and robot positioning, was reported as more important for teamwork in RAS. During the intraoperative phase, effective and ineffective teamwork was, respectively, described as the presence or absence of explicit verbal communication (closed-loop communication, real-time narration, anticipation in tandem with verbal prompts), team reflexivity, centralized coordination through a bedside assistant, psychological safety, and shared mental models. In the post-operative phase, participants linked teamwork quality to patient safety and operative efficiency in a cascading effect. CONCLUSION: Teamwork in RAS requires a more deliberate, structured team approach than in open or laparoscopic surgery. We provide best practices for effective teamwork and pitfalls to avoid in RAS. Targeted training emphasizing teamwork and communication may enhance team effectiveness and patient safety in robotic surgical environments.

title: Effectiveness of ultraviolet–C robots in isolation room disinfection: Impact of dose, distance, and direct exposure on environmental surface decontamination
abstract: BACKGROUND: To minimize environmental services staff's exposure to pathogens, ultraviolet-C (UV-C) disinfection robots were applied before terminal manual environmental disinfection. This study aimed to evaluate the disinfection efficacy of the UV-C robot and to assess the effects of ultraviolet-C dose, distance, and direct exposure (line-of-sight irradiation) on disinfection outcomes. METHODS: This before-after study was conducted in a negative-pressure isolation ward comprising 17 single-patient rooms at a medical center in Taiwan between August 24, 2024, and January 3, 2025, yielding a total of 270 paired samples. An ultraviolet-C-emitting robot with a wavelength of 254 nm was sequentially positioned on both sides of the patient bed and operated for 5 minutes on each side before routine manual environmental disinfection. Total aerobic colony counts (ACC) and bacterial culture positivity rates were obtained from high-touch environmental surfaces (e.g., bed rails, call bells and bedside chairs) before and after UV-C disinfection. The effects of UV-C dose, distance between the robot and surfaces, and the presence of direct exposure (line-of-sight irradiation) versus indirect exposure on disinfection efficacy were analyzed using multivariate binary logistic regression, performed using SPSS version 27.0. The results of the regression analysis were expressed as odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). RESULTS: The median ACC and bacterial culture positivity rates on surfaces significantly decreased after UV-C disinfection (0.76 vs. 0.08 CFU/cm²; 83% vs. 57.4%, P < 0.001). A weak negative correlation was observed between ACC and UV-C doses after disinfection (rs = -0.281, 95% CI: -0.390 to -0.164, P < 0.001), while no correlation (rs = 0.040, 95% CI: -0.083 to 0.162, P = 0.510) and weak correlation (rs = 0.317, 95% CI: 0.202 to 0.424, P < 0.001) were found between ACC at short and long irradiation distances. The ACC on environmental surfaces with direct UV-C exposure were significantly lower than those in shadowed areas [median: 0.00 (IQR: 0.00 to 0.44) vs. median: 0.16 (IQR: 0.00 to 0.80); P < 0.001]. Multivariate logistic regression identified direct exposure (line-of-sight irradiation) as the strongest predictor of negative bacterial culture results, reducing the odds of bacterial culture positivity by 79.5% compared to indirect exposure (OR = 0.205, 95% CI: 0.083 to 0.508, P < 0.001) in the layout of the negative pressure isolation room in this study. CONCLUSIONS: Ultraviolet-C robots serve as an effective disinfection intervention for hospital environments. Their efficacy is most pronounced when direct exposure (line-of-sight irradiation) is achieved in the isolation rooms. Therefore, aligning movable items toward the UV-C robot prior to disinfection, alongside subsequent manual environmental disinfection and physical debris removal, remains essential, particularly in shadowed areas.

title: Effects of Immersive Virtual Reality and Relaxation Video on Symptom Severity, Distress, and Quality of Life in Lung Cancer Patients During Initial Chemotherapy Cycles: A Three-Arm Randomised Controlled Trial
abstract: BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: To examine the effects of immersive virtual reality (VR) and a theme-matched relaxation video (RV) on symptom severity, distress, and quality of life in lung cancer patients. METHODS: = 105) group. During the first two chemotherapy cycles, the VR and RV groups were assigned two 20 min sessions of immersive nature-themed VR or theme-matched RV, while the CG received routine care alone. The primary outcome domain was symptom severity, assessed through within-session changes in ten individual Edmonton Symptom Assessment Scale (ESAS) symptom scores; distress and quality of life were secondary outcomes. Data were analysed with linear mixed models, and between-group differences are reported with Bonferroni-adjusted 95% confidence intervals (CI). RESULTS: Compared with the CG, the within-session improvement was greater for eight of the ten ESAS symptoms with VR and for five with RV; the largest differences were for well-being (VR 1.26 points, 95% CI 0.98 to 1.53; RV 0.76, 0.49 to 1.03), with smaller differences for tiredness, depression, and anxiety. Distress also decreased more with VR (1.04, 0.73 to 1.34) and RV (0.73, 0.42 to 1.03) than in the CG. VR improved more than RV for well-being (0.50, 0.22 to 0.77), tiredness (0.47, 0.16 to 0.79), and distress (0.31, 0.002 to 0.62). No intervention-specific effect emerged for nausea, lack of appetite, or quality of life. CONCLUSIONS: Compared with routine care, two sessions of VR or RV improved acute symptoms, mainly well-being, tiredness, depression, and anxiety, and reduced distress, with no intervention-specific effect on quality of life. The additional benefit of VR was small and, for the ESAS symptoms, below the minimal clinically important difference, so RV may be a practical and accessible option. title: Effects of Sample Matrix, RNA Extraction Method, Carrier RNA, and Storage Conditions on RT-qPCR Detection of Foot-and-Mouth Disease Virus
abstract: Reliable molecular detection of foot-and-mouth disease virus (FMDV) depends on RT-qPCR performance and pre-analytical factors, including sample matrix, RNA extraction method, carrier RNA supplementation, and storage conditions. This study compared silica membrane- and magnetic bead-based RNA extraction workflows for detection of FMDV serotypes O, A, and SAT2 in serum, PBS-based swab suspension, and tissue homogenates at three virus dilutions, with and without carrier RNA. FMDV RNA stability in serum stored at room temperature or -20 °C for up to 60 days and following five freeze-thaw cycles was also evaluated using serotype O. Extraction performance was matrix-dependent. In serum, silica-based workflow yielded significantly lower Ct values than magnetic bead-based extraction. In tissue homogenates, magnetic bead extraction yielded significantly lower Ct values with carrier RNA, whereas carrier RNA impaired silica-based extraction. No significant differences were observed for PBS-based swab suspension samples. FMDV RNA detectability remained stable at -20 °C for 60 days, whereas room-temperature storage caused progressive signal loss, which was reduced by carrier RNA. Five freeze-thaw cycles did not progressively affect RNA detectability. These findings demonstrate that the effects of extraction workflow and carrier RNA supplementation on FMDV RT-qPCR detectability differed according to the sample matrix and experimental conditions, highlighting the importance of matrix-specific optimization of pre-analytical procedures.

title: Effects of Standardized Ileal Digestible Lysine to Crude Protein Ratio on Growth Performance of 163 to 214 lb Pigs
abstract: Recent evidence in late nursery and finishing pigs has suggested that nitrogen may become limiting for synthesis of nonessential amino acids in low-protein, amino acid-fortified diets. A previous experiment by Navales et al.2 using finishing pigs of various stages of growth observed that cubic models provided the best fit for body weight (BW) ranges of 100 to 153 lb, 121 to 172 lb, and 228 to 275 lb to estimate standardized ileal digestible lysine to crude protein (SID Lys:CP) ratios to optimize F/G based on the local minimum. However, for pigs weighing 187 to 238 lb, the requirement was estimated to be below 5.13%, the lowest SID Lys:CP ratio tested based on the linear model. Therefore, a 21-d study was conducted using a total of 693 pigs (241 × 600 DNA; initially 163.3 ± 1.46 lb) to determine the effect of SID Lys:CP on growth performance and blood urea nitrogen (BUN) of 163 to 214 lb pigs using ratios of 77.5 to 107.5% of the NRC (2012) rather than the 85.0 to 115.0% tested by Navales et al.2. Pens of pigs were blocked by BW and randomly assigned to one of five dietary treatments in a randomized complete block design. There were 9 to 10 pigs per pen and 14 replications per treatment. Dietary treatments were corn-soybean meal-based and formulated to contain 0.71% SID Lys. Treatments provided SID Lys:CP ratios of 77.5, 85.0, 92.5, 100.0, and 107.5% of requirement estimates calculated from NRC (2012) resulting in SID Lys:CP ratios of 4.68, 5.13, 5.58, 6.03, and 6.49%, respectively. Intermediate SID Lys:CP levels were achieved by blending diets with the lowest and highest SID Lys:CP ratio. Pen weights, number of pigs per pen, and feed deliveries were recorded to calculate ADG, ADFI, and F/G. Blood samples were collected on d 14 after a 10-h fasting period from one gilt and two barrows per pen and analyzed for serum BUN. Dose-response curves were evaluated using linear, quadratic polynomial, cubic polynomial, and broken-line linear (BLL) models. Overall (d 0 to 21), increasing SID Lys:CP had no effect on ADG or final BW. A cubic response was observed (P = 0.004) for ADFI, where ADFI decreased when increasing SID Lys:CP from a ratio of 4.68 to 5.13%, then increased up to a SID Lys:CP ratio of 6.03%, followed then by a slight reduction in ADFI at the highest SID Lys:CP treatment of 6.49%. A similar response was observed for F/G (cubic, P < 0.001), where F/G improved when SID Lys:CP ratio was increased from 4.68 to 5.13%, followed by a worsening of F/G as the SID Lys:CP ratio increased further to 6.03%, with a slight improvement in F/G at the highest SID Lys:CP ratio of 6.49%. Increasing SID Lys:CP decreased (cubic, P ≤ 0.004) N intake per day and per kg gain, as well as reduced (linear, P < 0.001) blood urea nitrogen. In conclusion, increasing SID Lys:CP worsened F/G and decreased BUN in 163 to 214 lb pigs. Based on the local minimum determined using the cubic model, the estimated SID Lys:CP ratio to optimize F/G for pigs weighing between 163 to 214 lb is 4.98%, which is below the estimate calculated from NRC (2012).

title: Efficient and Enhanced Automated Extraction of Circulating Cell-free DNA Across Research and Clinical Workflows Using Maxwell® Rapid ccfDNA Kits.
abstract: Introduction: Circulating cell-free DNA (ccfDNA) is a valuable biomarker in both clinical and research settings, playing a key role in non-invasive clinical applications such as cancer monitoring, prenatal testing, and organ transplant assessment. However, extracting ccfDNA from plasma and other biological fluids can be labor-intensive and prone to variability. The Maxwell® Rapid ccfDNA workflow addresses these challenges with a simplified, rapid, and automated approach to ccfDNA extraction.

title: Efficient bronchoscopy image triaging via distilled cascaded deep networks: a lightweight framework for pulmonary pathology classification
abstract: Tuberculosis (TB) and lung cancer are major pulmonary diseases that contribute substantially to morbidity and mortality worldwide. Differentiating these diseases from bronchoscopic images can be challenging because some of their visual features overlap. In this study, we developed a knowledge-distilled cascaded convolutional neural network for classifying bronchoscopic images into three categories: normal, tuberculosis, and lung cancer. The framework uses two sequential binary classifiers. The first classifier separates normal from abnormal bronchoscopic images, and the second classifies abnormal images as either TB or lung cancer. DenseNet-121 was used as the teacher network. Smaller student networks were then developed through knowledge distillation by removing the fourth Dense Block and optimizing the depth of the third Dense Block using the Neural Network Intelligence (NNI) framework. NNI was also used to optimize the training hyperparameters of both the teacher and student networks. The method was evaluated using 515 bronchoscopic images from 81 normal subjects, 76 patients with pulmonary tuberculosis, and 277 patients with lung cancer. Since several patients had more than one image, primary five-fold cross-validation was carried out at the patient level, ensuring that images from the same patient were not included in both the training and test sets. The distilled network achieved an accuracy of 91.5%, compared with 90.5% for the teacher network, with sensitivities of 92.2% for lung cancer, 80.3% for TB, and 98.8% for normal cases. Although the distilled network achieved a higher accuracy in the primary five-fold cross-validation evaluation, the difference between the teacher and student models was not statistically significant in the repeated paired hold-out analysis (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p = 0.4378). In the 30 repeated hold-out experiments, the teacher and student models achieved mean accuracies of 0.8890 ± 0.0325 and 0.8568 ± 0.0839, respectively, with a 95% confidence interval of [-0.0214, 0.0857] for the paired teacher–student accuracy difference. Compared with the teacher network, the distilled model reduced the number of trainable parameters by 54.1%, the model size by 54.1%, and the FLOPs by 14.6%. The inference time was also reduced from 0.0920 s to 0.0567 s per image. The results indicate that architectural reduction combined with knowledge distillation and automated hyperparameter optimization can substantially reduce model complexity and computational requirements, while no statistically significant difference in classification accuracy was detected between the student and teacher models. The reduced model provides a basis for future evaluation in bronchoscopy computer-aided diagnosis systems.

title: Electrochemical Detection of PFAS Contaminants Across Environmental and Pharmaceutical Matrices:Sensing Mechanisms, Nanomaterial Platforms, Biological Monitoring, and Regulatory Convergence
abstract: PFAS are a class of over 14,000 synthetic compounds characterized by a stable carbon-fluorine bond that confers resistance to thermal and biological degradation, resulting in common contamination of various aquatic matrices at concentrations ranging from sub-parts per trillion to parts per billion.Demand for directly deployable sensitive quantification methods has been spurred by increasingly stringent regulatory responses such as the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) proposed maximum contaminant levels of 4 ppt for PFOA and PFOS in 2024 under its third Fourth Unregulated Contaminant Monitoring Rule and sub-parametric values recommended by the EU Drinking Water Directive.Conventional liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry provides the required sensitivity but is still limited by centralized infrastructure and slow sample preparation that prevents point-of-care or real-time surveillance.Another critically understudied dimension includes pharmaceutical matrices, where PFAS can act as formulation excipients or derive from the synthesis of fluorinated active pharmaceutical ingredients and pharmacokinetically interfere with albumin binding and hepatic CYP450 activity in exposed populations.The current review summarized the existing electrochemical sensing strategies, including molecularly imprinted polymers, aptasensors, and CRISPR-Cas12a biosensors, and state-of-the-art electrode structures, including metal-organic frameworks, MXenes, and covalent triazine frameworks, for targeting PFAS in environmental and biological matrices.While some of these can be implemented analytically with detection below 1 ppt, critical benchmarking using regulatory thresholds reveals that 10% of sensor studies validate their performance in non-spiked field or clinical matrices.This highlights the need for multi-analyte array development to allow standardized sensor validation frameworks across environmental and pharmaceutical quality monitoring.
venue: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology

title: Electromagnetic bronchoscopy versus computed tomography for pulmonary nodule localization
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Electromagnetic navigational bronchoscopy (NAVIB) and CT-guided transthoracic marking (CTI) are two possible methods for preoperative marking. We have conducted a study to determine whether one technique performs better in a selected patient population. METHODS: In a single-center, 1:1 randomized controlled trial we compared NAVIB using indocyanine green and CTI with Technetium-99m during uniportal wedge resections of lung nodules. Primary endpoint was the duration of surgery. Secondary endpoints included wedge resection time, complication rates, surgical margin, and surgeon satisfaction questionnaires. RESULTS: 63 patients were randomized, with 32 assigned to the NAVIB and 31 to the CTI group. Surgeries' duration was similar, with a median of 52.5 minutes (IQR:40-70) for NAVIB and 45 minutes for CTI (IQR:30-60;p= 0.664). The median wedge time for NAVIB was 15.5 minutes (IQR: 13-20), while for CTI it was 12 minutes (IQR: 9-15;p=0.0007). Grade II or higher complication rates were 9.4% for NAVIB vs 12.9% for CTI; (p = 0.144) and lesion's distance to staple line was 5.7mm (CI:4.2-7.2) vs. 7.0mm (CI:4.3-9.9) respectively (p = 0.355). In the questionnaire from 0 (not helpful) to 3 (very helpful), CTI received a median score of 3 (IQR;3-3), while NAVIB's was 2.5 (IQR;2-3;p = 0.045). After Bonferroni correction, questionnaire differences were not significant. CONCLUSIONS: The randomized trial failed to demonstrate a significant difference in overall surgery duration between electromagnetic navigational bronchoscopy and computed tomography-guided transthoracic marking.

title: Elevated Maternal Glycated Albumin is Associated with Large for Gestational Age Infants: Results from a Prospective Longitudinal Study
abstract: Aims/hypothesis Glycated albumin (GA) has been shown to be a moderate predictor of gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM), while evidence supporting its role in predicting adverse pregnancy outcomes remains limited. Here, we aimed to perform a comparative study of GA and haemoglobin A1c (HbA 1c ) for predicting GDM and large-for-gestational-age (LGA) infants in a prospective cohort. Methods We developed a rapid liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry method for measuring site-specific albumin glycation. GA was quantified at two glycation sites, GA (KQT) and GA (KLV), as well as their sum, GA-total. GA was measured in stored serum samples collected at 11-14 and 23-31 gestational weeks from 465 participants in the single-centre observational cohort. HbA 1c was measured routinely at each visit. Linear mixed-effects models were used to compare GA between participants with and without GDM (n=100) or LGA (n=57). Logistic regression was used to estimate odds ratios (ORs) for GDM and LGA according to GA and HbA 1c . Results GA was lower in women who developed GDM during early pregnancy compared to non-GDM controls (GA-total; p =0.004), while in mid-late pregnancy, only GA (KQT) was lower in women with GDM ( p =0.036). In contrast, HbA 1c was higher in women with GDM at both timepoints compared to non-GDM controls ( p <0.001) and higher HbA 1c was associated with increased odds of GDM (OR=2.20, p <0.001; OR=2.30, p <0.001, respectively). GA was higher in the LGA group, in both early (GA-total; p =0.032) and mid-late pregnancy (GA-total; p =0.030) and associated with increased odds of LGA (GA-total; OR=1.59, p =0.009; GA-total; OR=1.46, p =0.019, respectively). HbA 1c was not associated with LGA at either timepoint. Conclusions/interpretation Higher GA in early and mid-late pregnancy were associated with an increased risk of LGA, whereas no significant association was observed for HbA 1c . GA may therefore provide risk assessment beyond HbA 1c for identifying pregnancies at risk of fetal overgrowth. Research in Context What is already known about this subject? Glycated albumin (GA) has been proposed as a biomarker for GDM, LGA, and other adverse pregnancy outcomes. HbA 1c is an established marker of chronic glycaemia outside pregnancy, but its role in the routine diagnosis and monitoring of GDM during pregnancy remains limited. Both GA and HbA 1c are markers of glycaemic exposure; however, they capture different time frames and are influenced differently by the physiological changes of pregnancy. What is the key question? Are GA and HbA 1c measured during pregnancy associated with GDM and LGA? What are the new findings? HbA 1c and GA showed opposing associations with GDM development. Higher GA in early and mid-late pregnancy were associated with an increased risk of LGA. HbA 1c showed limited association with LGA. How might this impact clinical practice in the foreseeable future? GA and HbA 1c may serve as complementary biomarkers for assessing glycaemia and predicting pregnancy complications, with potential utility for improving risk stratification during pregnancy.
