title: Enhancing Adolescent HIV Screening: A Quality Improvement Approach Using Point-of-care Testing in an Outpatient Pediatric Setting
abstract: Introduction: Routine HIV testing remains poorly implemented nationwide, despite national recommendations. Half of adolescents who are HIV positive do not know their status. This quality improvement project aimed to increase the rate of routine HIV screening during well-child checks (WCCs) for eligible adolescents 15-18 years of age with no prior lifetime HIV test to greater than 50% within 1 year through implementation of point-of-care (POC) oral swab HIV testing at a pediatric outpatient clinic affiliated with Loma Linda University in Moreno Valley, Calif. Methods: All adolescent patients 15-18 years of age presenting for WCC who had not yet been tested once in their lifetime for HIV were eligible. We conducted 6 plan-do-study-act cycles from August 2023 to September 2025, including initial and subsequent implementation cycles. Key drivers included standardizing the process to facilitate HIV testing in the clinic, improving provider awareness, providing standardized information on patient eligibility, and providing patient and family education on HIV screening. The primary intervention was implementing oral swab POC testing during WCC visits. Other interventions included creating an educational curriculum for physicians on HIV screening guidelines, developing multilingual resources for families on the importance of HIV screening, and using a multidisciplinary team to integrate testing into clinic workflow. The primary outcome measure was the monthly percentage of adolescents 15-18 years of age who were screened for HIV via the POC swab during their WCC. Results: Before implementation, the average percentage of eligible patients screened from January 2023 to July 2023 was 29%. Screening rates increased from 29% to 51% among eligible adolescents over the first eight months. With implementation of the POC oral swab HIV test, screening rates increased from 51% to 56% over an additional 8 months. During the later implementation cycles (December 2024 to September 2025), monthly screening rates generally exceeded the project goal of 50%, averaging 64%. Eligibility was based on age, visit type, and prior lifetime HIV testing status. No reactive or positive HIV test results were identified during the study period. Potential balancing measures included additional time needed during clinical visits, false-positive results, and the potential workflow burden on clinical staff. Conclusions: Improving HIV screening among adolescents is feasible through a multicomponent quality improvement strategy that incorporates POC rapid antibody testing. This type of testing is painless, can be performed quickly during clinic visits, and improves patient confidentiality because results are available at the time of the visit rather than by phone or email. Medicaid covers POC testing for HIV. This makes this form of testing feasible in many clinics.
authors: Graydon Dietrich; Natasha Thomas; Alexandria Grellmann; Gabrielle Pina; Rachel Davidge; Jerard Tambunan; Mona Abutouk

title: Environmental biosurveillance in commercial poultry beyond clinical signs: the case for continuous environmental biosurveillance in commercial poultry production
abstract: Commercial poultry production in the United States is threatened by infectious disease, with highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) H5N1 alone responsible for the destruction of more than 206 million birds and more than $1.4 billion in federal outbreak response and indemnity costs since 2022. Despite the scale of these losses, disease detection in commercial operations generally remains reactive, relying on the recognition of clinical signs, increased mortality, and production declines before diagnostic testing is initiated. This delay in diagnosis also creates an unnecessary urgency to begin treatment, leading some operators to apply blanket treatments before diagnostic results have been returned. Transitioning to proactive biosurveillance presents a promising alternative but introduces two new fundamental challenges: which individual birds should be selected for sampling from largely asymptomatic flocks, and which pathogens should be targeted for testing? Environmental sampling approaches-including drag swabs, litter grab samples, boot sock swabs, air samples, and water samples -offer one solution to the first challenge by aggregating pathogen shedding signals from an entire production unit into a single composite sample. While multiplexed PCR and metagenomics methods offer target-agnostic approaches to the second challenge by simultaneously characterizing some or all of the diversity of microbial taxa present in a sample without prior specification of which organisms may be causal. The objective of this review is to present (1) current flock health monitoring practices, (2) the promise and limitations of continuous environmental surveillance, (3) the range of environmental sample types available for poultry barns, and (4) how emerging multi-target testing approaches may address the lack of symptomatic guidance for what pathogens should be assessed. Together, this information represents a scientifically grounded path toward shifting commercial flock health management from reactive disease control to proactive prevention, though significant technical and operational work remains before routine commercial deployment is feasible.
authors: Cassandra L. Ettinger; Natalie J. Urie; Elena G. Olson; Casey E. McGinley; Michael B. Rhys; Steven C. Ricke; Jake Byrnes

title: Ethanol improves RNase P stability in nasopharyngeal samples stored at room temperature for SARS-CoV-2 RT-qPCR diagnosis.
abstract: Despite the end of the global health emergency, COVID-19 and its etiological agent, SARS-CoV-2, remain topics of high scientific and public health relevance due to the continued circulation of the virus, the emergence of new variants, and the persistent risk of outbreaks. RT-qPCR is the gold standard procedure for SARS-CoV-2 detection, but its reliability depends on preserving viral RNA and the human Ribonuclease P (RNase P; internal control) target during sample storage and transport. This study aimed to evaluate the effect of different preservation conditions on nucleic acid stability for SARS-CoV-2 detection by RT-qPCR: samples maintained in 0.9% saline and samples supplemented with absolute ethanol to reach a final concentration of 70% (v/v), under different storage temperature conditions. Nasopharyngeal swab samples, initially collected and transported in 0.9% saline and previously classified into different viral load categories, were pooled and redistributed into the experimental storage conditions: ethanol or saline under refrigerated conditions (4°C) or at room temperature. RNA was extracted using an automated magnetic bead-based method and analyzed by RT-qPCR targeting the SARS-CoV-2 E gene and the human RNase P internal control, with nucleic acid stability monitored over a 12-day storage period. Viral RNA detection remained stable in both storage media; however, RNase P detection progressively declined in saline, particularly during room temperature storage, while ethanol maintained consistent amplification. These findings indicate that 70% ethanol better maintains the stability of the human internal control (RNase P) than saline during room temperature storage of nasopharyngeal samples for up to 12 days.
authors: Lia Ayumi Umezawa; Fabiana Barcelos Furtado; Gabriela Boni Poli; Leonardo Nazario de Moraes; Maércio José De Oliveira Alho; Flavia Hebeler-Barbosa; Guilherme Targino Valente; Rejane Maria Tommasini Grotto

title: Evaluating robotic-assisted bronchoscopy for bronchus-unconnected peripheral pulmonary nodules: diagnostic efficacy and safety.
abstract: Bronchus-unconnected peripheral pulmonary lesions (PPLs) pose diagnostic challenges due to lack of direct airway access and computed tomography (CT)-to-body divergence (CTBD). We evaluated robotic-assisted bronchoscopy (RAB) combined with the intraprocedural CT-guided navigation with ventilatory strategy for atelectasis (ICNVA) strategy. This prospective, single-arm study enrolled patients (18-75 years) with pulmonary nodules (6-30 mm) lacking a bronchus sign. All underwent RAB with the ICNVA strategy, integrating preoperative mapping, intraprocedural breath-holds to minimize atelectasis, and real-time CT confirmation. The primary endpoint was tool-in-lesion (TIL) rate. Secondary endpoints included diagnostic yield, center strike rate, CTBD, and safety. Thirty patients were enrolled (mean age 55.6±10.7 years). Lesions had a mean diameter of 14.0±4.3 mm and a median distance to the nearest bronchus of 18 mm. The ICNVA strategy resulted in a mean CTBD of 13.4 mm. We achieved a 100% (30/30) navigational success rate (TIL) and a 66.7% (20/30) center strike rate. The overall diagnostic yield was 90% (27/30), with 90.9% (20/22) sensitivity for malignancy. Pneumothorax occurred in 2 patients (6.7%) and mild hemorrhage in 7 (23.3%), with no severe adverse events occurred. RAB combined with the ICNVA strategy demonstrates high diagnostic yield and safety for bronchus-unconnected PPLs. This approach effectively mitigates CTBD, enabling precise localization and sampling of lesions traditionally considered difficult to access.
authors: Shaohua Dai; Wei Zuo; Bentong Yu

title: Evaluation of Gene Xpert Xpress System for Detecting SARS-CoV-2 in Suspected Clinical Samples
abstract: Background: The emergence of SARS-CoV-2 caused a global COVID-19 pandemic, necessitating rapid and accurate diagnostic tools, especially in resource-limited settings. Materials and methods: This cross-sectional study evaluated the diagnostic performance of the fully automated Gene Xpert Xpress SARS-CoV-2 assay compared to conventional real-time RT-PCR (Gold standard) using nasopharyngeal swabs from 105 suspected COVID-19 patients at BITID, Bangladesh from December 20 to December 21. Results: Of the 105 samples, 65 (61.9%) were RT-PCR positive and 40 (38.1%) were negative. The Gene Xpert Xpress detected 62/65 positives (sensitivity 95.4%) and 32/40 negatives (Specificity 80.0%) yielding an overall accuracy of 89.5%. Discordant results were mainly attributed to differences in limit of detection and Ct value interpretation. Conclusion: The Gene Xpert Xpress system demonstrated high sensitivity, rapid results (~45 minutes) minimal training requirements and suitability for decentralized settings, making it a valuable tool for timely SARS-CoV-2 detection and clinical decision-making in emergency situations and low-resource environments. authors: Md Shakeel Ahmed; Md Zakir Hossain; Md Rakibul Bulbul Hassan; Md Zahirul Islam; Md Fazle Rabby; Mahabubul Mowla; Md Shamiul Islam

title: Evaluation of an automated device for fingertip blood collection by comparing test results with venous blood.
abstract: BackgroundCapillary blood collection offers a less burdensome alternative to venous sampling and may improve access to laboratory testing in resource-limited settings. However, manual procedures can yield pre-analytical variation, resulting in the need for skilled personnel. To address these limitations, we developed a prototype device that automates fingertip blood collection.MethodsThe device automatically punctures a fingertip using a disposable lancet, applies intermittent compression to the fingertip using a cuff, sequentially collects blood into two microtubes, and completes hemostasis with gauze. We evaluated the device in 58 healthy volunteers aged 20-60 years by comparing capillary blood collected with the device to venous blood via standard phlebotomy. Paired samples were processed and analyzed under hospital laboratory quality control. Measurements included 8 CBC parameters, glucose and HbA1c in whole blood, 3 electrolytes, and 15 biochemical analytes in serum. Agreement was assessed using Deming regression, and bias with 95% confidence intervals at medical decision levels (MDLs) was calculated.ResultsMost analytes exhibited biases within the allowable limits defined by the Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments (CLIA), except for white blood cell count (WBC), potassium (K), lactate dehydrogenase (LD), and glucose. Compared with the BD MiniDraw™, which involves manual finger compression, our device showed greater biases in WBC and K, likely due to the margination effect and hemolysis, respectively-both enhanced by stronger compression.ConclusionThe device demonstrated acceptable analytical performance for most parameters. Optimizing compression strength and duration may reduce bias. Automated capillary collection could support decentralized testing and reduce phlebotomy workload.
authors: Hiroki Doi; Takashi Irie; Kei Takenaka; Sakuichiro Adachi; Taku Sakazume; Taku Kato; Hiroyasu Ito

title: Evaluation of carry-over, product quality and cleaning validation following a batch campaign manufacturing of benzydamine hydrochloride spray 0.15%
abstract: Introduction: Campaign manufacturing reduces equipment downtime, water and cleaning-agent use, and production cost but must be scientifically justified to protect product quality and patient safety under EU GMP. Consecutive same-product batches remove cross-contamination risk between different APIs, yet residue build-up, degradation in poorly drained areas, and microbial proliferation remain relevant quality risks. Benzydamine hydrochloride is a topical NSAID with analgesic and anti-inflammatory action, used for inflammatory conditions of the oral cavity and pharynx. Methods: Ten consecutive commercial-scale batches were produced using the same equipment and approved manufacturing process without intermediate cleaning or sanitization, only standardized drain-down and line-clearance after every batch. A full automated CIP cycle was executed only after completion of batch 10. Risk-based swab sampling targeted highest residue-retention potential locations. Validated, stability-indicating RP-HPLC with UV detection at 232 nm was used for analysis. MACO derivation was based on toxicology data applying LOEL/LOAEL approach and PDE calculations. Results: Method validation showed high specificity, linearity, and precision suitable for monitoring trace-level benzydamine residues. Residue levels stayed below the calculated MACO with no cumulative build-up across the campaign. Standardized drain-down and line-clearance were effective after each batch. Full CIP cycle was only needed after batch 10, followed by cleaning validation swabbing confirming restoration of a validated clean state. Conclusion: Ten consecutive batches of benzydamine HCl spray 0.15% can be manufactured without intermediate cleaning while maintaining product quality, microbiological control and GMP compliance. Residues stayed below MACO with no cumulative build-up. Post-campaign CIP cleaning validation confirmed full restoration of a validated clean state. Findings provide scientific justification for a 10-batch campaign manufacturing strategy.
authors: Elena Petrovska Kostadinoska; Irena Slaveska Spirevska; Kateřina Kochová; Kristina Grncaroska; Silvana Janevikj; Jana Micevska; Milena Prculovska

title: Evaluation of the Hologic Aptima® Vaginitis and Seegene Allplex™ assays for microbiological diagnosis of bacterial vaginosis and Candida vaginitis in women in France, relative to Nugent score and culture
abstract: Introduction. Molecular assays such as the Hologic Aptima ® Vaginitis Panel and Seegene Allplex ™ Vaginitis assay offer improved sensitivity and multiplex detection for the diagnosis of vaginitis compared with the non-molecular standard of care. Gap Statement. Evidence comparing the relative performance of Aptima versus Seegene is limited, as is knowledge of Aptima’s compatibility with non-proprietary swabs. Aim. This prospective study assessed the diagnostic performance of the Aptima BV (bacterial vaginosis) and Aptima CV/TV assays ( Candida vaginitis/ Trichomonas vaginitis) alongside the Seegene Allplex assay in symptomatic women (≥18 years) presenting for vaginitis testing in primary care in France. Methodology. Two vaginal swabs were taken per patient: one Aptima Multitest Swab and one non-proprietary Σ-TRANSWAB liquid Amies collection swab. Aptima swab data were used solely to confirm performance of the Aptima assays under current test conditions, while all primary assay comparisons were performed using Σ-TRANSWAB samples. These comparisons were performed for each assay relative to Nugent score (for BV) or culture (for CV), as well as Aptima relative to Seegene. Results. In total, 500 women underwent vaginitis testing between July and August 2024. When using non-proprietary Σ-TRANSWAB collection methods, sensitivity and specificity values for the Aptima BV assay were 96.7 and 89.7% relative to Nugent score, and 89.9 and 90.6% for Seegene Allplex relative to Nugent score. Among ‘intermediate BV’ samples ( n =66), agreement between Seegene Allplex and Nugent score was 1.5%. Sensitivity and specificity values for the detection of CV were 88.6 and 90.8% for the Aptima CV/TV assay, and 90.2 and 93.7% for Seegene Allplex. Assay detection of TV could not be validated due to an insufficient number of TV-positive samples ( n =1). These findings were consistent with Aptima’s performance when using proprietary collection methods. Conclusion. Overall, the Aptima Vaginitis Panel demonstrated comparably high diagnostic performance to Seegene Allplex for the detection of BV and CV when using a non-proprietary sample collection method. TV prevalence was too low in this cohort to permit meaningful assay evaluation for this pathogen.
authors: Cécile Martaresche; Florian Scherrer

title: Evaluation of the Sysmex UF-5000 automated urine flow cytometer for detection of urethral inflammation and clinical urethritis in men.
abstract:
Objective evidence of urethral inflammation is required to diagnose urethritis in men. Clinically, this is established by confirming urethral discharge on examination in symptomatic patients. Alternatively, laboratory approaches rely on identifying polymorphonuclear neutrophils (PMNs) from a urethral swab specimen or leukocyte esterase (LE) activity in urine. However, physical examination-based diagnosis may be subjective, collection of a urethral swab is invasive, and often painful, and LE has poor sensitivity. To address these limitations, we evaluated the white blood cell (WBC) parameter of the Sysmex UF-5000 automated urinary flow cytometer for the detection of urethral inflammation and clinician-diagnosed urethritis. Using 1,000 remnant male urine specimens from a sexual health clinic, we measured urinary WBC counts (WBC/μL) using the UF-5000, LE by urinalysis, and abstracted corresponding clinical data and urethral Gram stain results from the electronic medical record. Urinary WBC counts measured by the UF-5000 were significantly higher in men with urethral symptoms, LE ≥1+ status, a clinical diagnosis of urethritis, and strongly correlated with elevated and increasing urethral Gram stain PMN density. The UF-5000 demonstrated excellent diagnostic discrimination, yielding areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.86 for Gram stain-defined urethral inflammation, and 0.90 for clinician-defined urethritis. Optimized thresholds provided >95% sensitivity for ruling out infection and >95% specificity for ruling it in, outperforming standard LE testing. In conclusion, the UF-5000 automated urine flow cytometer offers a robust, non-invasive alternative for male urethritis diagnosis. This approach could expand diagnostic reach-particularly for men who decline urethral swab collection-and warrants prospective clinical validation.

Importance

Male urethritis diagnostics are limited by the poor sensitivity of leukocyte esterase (LE) testing or the invasive nature of urethral swab collection for Gram stain microscopy. These limitations may create barriers to patient care and delay urethritis diagnosis. Automated urinary flow cytometry may overcome these limitations, but few studies exist. We analyzed 1,000 remnant male urine specimens to evaluate the Sysmex UF-5000 white blood cell (WBC) parameter for detecting urethral inflammation. Elevated urinary WBC counts strongly correlated with elevated WBCs on urethral Gram stain smear microscopy and positive LE. The UF-5000 outperformed LE for ruling in and ruling out urethral inflammation and clinical urethritis. Automated urinary flow cytometry is a powerful, non-invasive diagnostic approach that warrants prospective evaluation in point-of-care clinical studies.
authors: Toh E, Modi IK, Ardizzone CM, Zhang X, Alrebdi WM, Ren J, Nelson DE, Jordan SJ.

title: Evaluation of whole genome sequencing protocols and target-capture panels for detection of respiratory viruses in clinical specimens
abstract: Respiratory viruses are major contributors to global morbidity and mortality. When viral mutations compromise detection by conventional diagnostic assays, identifying cases and tracing transmission becomes challenging. Whole genome sequencing (WGS) improves on conventional diagnostics as it can detect viruses with novel mutations. This study evaluated the performance of the ePlex, a rapid multiplex polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assay (RMPA), an in-house real-time reverse transcription PCR assay (RT-qPCR) and WGS for detecting respiratory virus infections in clinical specimens. Sixty-one sequence libraries were prepared, and bait enriched from nasopharyngeal swabs, collected in 2021, which were negative for SARS-CoV-2 but positive for co-infections of respiratory viruses detected by the ePlex. An in-house bioinformatics pipeline enabled a metagenomic analysis approach to be compared with the ePlex and RT-qPCR. In most swabs, respiratory viruses were detected by WGS (average genome recovery: 85.9%) or RT-qPCR which concurred with the ePlex result, but as single viruses rather than co-infections. WGS recovered respiratory syncytial viruses (80%) and metapneumoviruses (70%) most often. This study demonstrates the power of WGS and bait capture in resolving the genomes of respiratory pathogens from limited clinical material. Detection of a single virus, rather than co-infections, in this instance could highlight the targeted nature of bait capture technology or competition between viruses during bait hybridization. The number of respiratory syncytial viruses detected (16/20) could be due to a spike in activity detected after the alleviation of non-pharmaceutical interventions in the COVID-19 pandemic.
authors: Daniel Kelly; Ketharani Yogananthan; Priya Subramaniam; Tiina Talts; Carmen F. Manso; Beatrix Kele; David Bibby; Mark A. Zuckerman; Jean Lutamyo Mbisa

title: Exo2EgoPose: Leveraging Exocentric Demonstrations for Vision-Language guided Egocentric 3D Hand Pose Forecasting
abstract: Perceiving multimodal cues and forecasting fine-grained actions from an egocentric (Ego) perspective is vital for applications like robot manipulation. However, previous studies either rely mainly on under-informed visual inputs to predict coarse human motions or follow the VRM/VLA paradigm, which suffers from insufficient robot data and the gap between human and robot embodiments. We observe that 3D hand pose naturally serves as a unified representation to bridge human-robot actions. Hence, we investigate an under-explored Vision-Language guided Egocentric 3D Hand Pose Forecasting (VL-EHPF) task, which aims to predict future Ego 3D hand poses from visual observations, a language instruction, and pose states. To overcome the limited field-of-view and highly dynamic motions in the Ego view, we propose a framework dubbed Exo2EgoPose, which innovatively leverages holistic and stable exocentric (Exo) demonstrations as guidance to compensate for partial and dynamic Ego-view cues. Specifically, we introduce a Dual-level Exocentric Reconstruction Module (DERM), which incorporates the paired Exo videos as supervision to reconstruct their video-level and chunked frame-level representations, thereby modeling spatial contexts and temporal dynamics. Then, the Global-to-Local Modulation Module (GLMM) utilizes the reconstructed hierarchical Exo representations for progressive feature refinement via attention mechanisms and adaptive modulation, enabling comprehensive Exo guidance for accurate Ego hand pose forecasting. Extensive experiments on AssemblyHands, Ego-Exo4D, and our newly constructed EgoMe-pose benchmarks show the superiority of our method, which outperforms state-of-the-art methods by a large margin. Moreover, it demonstrates an effective human-to-robot transfer capability and yields improvements on the CALVIN dataset. Code is available at https://github.com/ZhaofengSHI/Exo2EgoPose.
authors: Zhaofeng Shi; Heqian Qiu; Lanxiao Wang; Xiang Li; Hongliang Li
venue: ACM International Conference on Multimedia (ACM MM)

title: Expert operating skills learning-based intelligent shared control method for a CT-guided percutaneous biopsy robot
abstract: Accurate and minimally invasive percutaneous biopsy is critical for early lung cancer diagnosis, yet conventional manual procedures suffer from repeated radiation exposure, high reliance on doctor expertise, and risk of tissue injury. This study presents a 5 degree-of-freedom robotic system combined with an intelligent shared control framework guided by expert skills learning. Expert skills were modeled using a variational autoencoder-hidden Markov model to segment latent procedural phases, and dynamic motion primitives reconstructed representative expert trajectories. These learned skills were integrated into a phase-adaptive shared controller, enabling online modulation of impedance and trajectory parameters. Both phantom and in vivo porcine experiments validated the system's feasibility, safety, and accuracy, with animal experiment studies confirming minimal tissue trauma and stable physiological responses. Compared with manual, leader-follower, and admittance control methods, the intelligent shared control substantially reduced force fluctuations and trajectory deviations.
authors: Shuang Wang; Guoliang Zhang; Wei Chen; Han Zhang; Wenlong Zhang; Guang‐Zhong Yang; Qing Yun Li; Jieming Qu; Le Xie

title: Exploring phenotypic, nutritional and metabolic traits associated with early sexual development in young Nelore (Bos indicus) heifers.
abstract: This study explored the associations among phenotypic, reproductive, nutritional, and metabolic traits with early sexual development in Bos indicus heifers. A total of 443 prepubertal Nelore heifers (11.1 ± 0.07 mo old) were evaluated during a feedlot (automated feeders) period from day -70 to day 0. Parameters assessed on day -70 (beginning of the feedlot period) included body weight (BW), body condition score (BCS), presence of CL, uterine (UT) and largest follicle (LF) diameters, as well as blood collection for LC-MS/MS metabolomics (subset of 139 heifers). On day 0 (end of the feedlot period), all heifers were submitted to a timed artificial insemination protocol (TAI). In addition, on that day, ribeye area (REA) and rump fat thickness (RFAT) were assessed by ultrasound. Residual feed intake (RFI), average daily gain (ADG), and dry matter intake (DMI) during the feedlot period were calculated. Pregnancy diagnosis was performed on day 39 and heifers confirmed as pregnant were classified as early-conceiving (EC; n = 212), while those non-pregnant were classified as late-conceiving (LC; n = 231). Parameters evaluated on days -70 and 0 were compared between these groups. On day -70, no differences in BW (P = 0.30), BCS (P = 0.11), UT (P = 0.32) and LF (P = 0.39) diameters, and presence of CL (P = 0.98) were observed between groups. On day 0, no difference between groups were observed in BW (P = 0.46), BCS (P = 0.82), LF (P = 0.56) diameter, and REA (P = 0.19). However, EC heifers had greater UT diameter (P = 0.05), RFAT (P = 0.02) and presence of CL (P = 0.04). Additionally, although no differences between groups were observed in DMI (P = 0.15) and ADG (P = 0.40) during the feedlot period, EC heifers had higher RFI (P = 0.05) than LC heifers. Metabolomic analyses of samples collected on day -70 indicated a marked separation between LC and EC heifers, with an accuracy of 0.74. Significant pathways altered were alanine, aspartate and glutamate metabolism, TCA cycle, and pyruvate metabolism. In conclusion, none of the phenotypic traits assessed on day -70 reliably predicted early sexual development in heifers. By day 0, EC heifers demonstrated increased fat deposition and uterine development. Moreover, feed efficiency was negatively associated with early sexual development in yearling Bos indicus heifers. Metabolomic analyses revealed key changes in amino acids and energy metabolism and provided moderate predictive accuracy between EC and LC heifers. Collectively, the phenotypic, nutritional, and metabolic traits evaluated in this study contribute to a more integrated understanding of the physiological mechanisms underlying sexual development in Nelore heifers.

title: Factors Associated With Moderate‐to‐Severe Pain After Paediatric Laparoscopic Pyeloplasty: Implications for Nursing Care
abstract: BACKGROUND: Moderate-to-severe pain remains a clinically relevant concern after paediatric laparoscopic pyeloplasty and may interfere with early recovery. Identifying children at increased risk may support more timely and individualized perioperative pain management. AIMS: To investigate factors associated with moderate-to-severe pain after laparoscopic pyeloplasty in children and to inform targeted nursing and perioperative management strategies. METHODS: This single-centre retrospective observational study included children undergoing laparoscopic pyeloplasty. Postoperative pain was assessed at 2, 6, 12 and 24 h using either a Faces Pain Scale or the Face, Legs, Activity, Cry and Consolability (FLACC) scale according to age and communication ability. Moderate-to-severe pain was defined as a score ≥ 4 at any assessment within 24 h. Demographic, disease-related, surgical and perioperative variables were analysed. Multivariable binary logistic regression was used to identify factors independently associated with moderate-to-severe pain, and repeated-measures analysis of variance was used to assess changes in pain scores over time. This study was reported in accordance with the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guidelines. RESULTS: Among 258 children, 65 developed moderate-to-severe postoperative pain, corresponding to an incidence of 25.2%. Multivariable analysis showed that age < 3 years, significant preoperative anxiety, operative time ≥ 120 min and the absence of a regional block were independently associated with moderate-to-severe pain. Sex, severe hydronephrosis and postoperative drainage tube placement were not independently associated with the outcome. Pain scores were highest at approximately 6 h after surgery, with significant group, time and group-by-time interaction effects. CONCLUSION: Moderate-to-severe pain is relatively common during the early postoperative period after paediatric laparoscopic pyeloplasty. Early risk identification, preoperative psychological support, appropriate regional analgesia and intensified pain assessment during the first 6-12 h may improve perioperative pain management. Prospective multicentre studies are warranted to validate these findings and develop clinically applicable risk-stratification strategies.

title: Factors Associated with Diagnostic Yield of Transbronchial Biopsy for Suspected Lung Cancer
abstract: Background: Transbronchial biopsy (TBB) is an important diagnostic approach for identifying peripheral lung lesions in suspected lung cancer patients. As is known, the lesion characteristics and radiological findings may influence its diagnostic yield. Therefore, this study aimed to identify factors associated with TBB diagnostic yield to help optimize patient selection and improve diagnostic success. Method: This cross-sectional study included 77 adults with suspected lung cancer who underwent TBB at Persahabatan Hospital between September and December 2024. Factors associated with TBB diagnostic yield, including tumor size, bronchus sign, and lesion location, were assessed. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis was performed to determine the optimal tumor-size cutoff. A parsimonious multivariable logistic regression model including tumor size and bronchus sign was used to identify independent factors associated with a positive TBB result. Results: The overall diagnostic yield of TBB was 63.6%. In bivariate analysis, tumor size ≥2.95 cm and the presence of a bronchus sign were significantly associated with a positive TBB result. ROC analysis demonstrated modest discrimination for tumor size (AUC=0.693; 95% CI=0.562–0.824; P=0.005), with a cutoff of 2.95 cm yielding 87.8% sensitivity and 53.6% specificity. Lesions ≥2.95 cm had a higher diagnostic yield than lesions <2.95 cm (76.8% vs. 28.6%; OR=8.27; 95% CI=2.67–25.65; P<0.001). In multivariable analysis, tumor size ≥2.95 cm remained independently associated with a positive TBB result (aOR=6.33; 95% CI=1.91–20.83; P=0.002), whereas bronchus sign was not independently associated (aOR=0.36; 95% CI=0.07–1.77; P=0.206). Conclusion: Tumor size ≥2.95 cm was independently associated with a higher diagnostic yield of TBB in patients with suspected lung cancer. Tumor size may therefore be useful in identifying peripheral lung lesions more likely to yield a diagnostic transbronchial biopsy.

title: Fatty acid characteristics of high-fat diet-induced tumor tissue in the liver of mice
abstract: Recent studies have highlighted the potential involvement of hepatic lipid characteristics in the development of liver cancer. Using a non‑invasive approach that integrates near‑infrared hyperspectral imaging (HSI) with machine learning, we previously established a method to visualize total lipid concentration, saturation level, and hydrocarbon chain length of fatty acids within a three‑dimensional feature space in mouse liver tissue. In the present study, to further elucidate the mechanisms underlying tumorigenesis, we expanded our dataset by adding eight additional tumor‑bearing mouse samples and separately analyzed cancerous and non‑cancerous regions within each hepatic lobe. Both gas chromatography and HSI consistently demonstrated that cancerous tissues exhibited elevated total lipid concentrations and were characterized by a notably higher abundance of oleic acid.

title: Feasibility Of a Multi-Modal Sensing Guidewire for Tissue Interaction Awareness in Bronchoscopic Lung Cancer Intervention: A Conceptual Architecture and Validation Roadmap
abstract: Bronchoscopic access to peripheral pulmonary lesions has been transformed by navigation, robotic, and imaging-assisted platforms, yet the physical interaction between an instrument tip and airway tissue remains difficult to quantify directly. Conventional guidewires provide push ability, torque transmission, and mechanical steering, but generally do not return a direct quantitative signal describing tissue interaction. This paper presents a literature-grounded feasibility framework that reimagines the guidewire as a multi-modal sensing platform rather than a purely mechanical component. Four complementary sensing channels—force, localized pressure, electrical impedance, and temperature—are proposed within a guidewire-centred architecture. The methodology comprises channel calibration and signal conditioning, temporal synchronization, feature extraction, lightweight edge-assisted sensor fusion, confidence estimation, and human-in-the-loop clinician feedback. Artificial intelligence is deliberately positioned as a supporting interpretation layer for procedural interaction states rather than as an autonomous cancer-diagnosis mechanism. The study analyses the principal mechanical, electrical, miniaturization, packaging, safety, and manufacturing constraints and defines a staged validation pathway from component calibration and bench testing through tissue-mimicking phantom evaluation, AI validation, preclinical feasibility, and eventual clinical feasibility. No prototype measurements or clinical diagnostic performance are claimed in the present work. The principal outcome is a coherent, experimentally testable architecture and validation roadmap that identifies how quantitative instrument–tissue information could complement existing bronchoscopic navigation while preserving clinician control. Advanced technologies are retained as future extensions outside the present scope.

title: Field evaluation of the Automated Hematology Analyzer XN-31 using blood samples from asymptomatic residents in a malaria-endemic area of Thailand: importance of sample transport and temperature control
abstract: Background The Automated Hematology Analyzer XN-31 can readily quantify the number of malaria parasite–infected red blood cells (MI-RBCs) within approximately one minute using flow cytometry technology, and it has already demonstrated clinical utility for malaria patients in both endemic and non-endemic settings. Recently, asymptomatic carriers with low-density parasitemia in endemic regions have been identified as significant reservoirs contributing to ongoing malaria transmission. Therefore, field-based malaria surveys in endemic areas, including epidemiological investigations of asymptomatic infections, are important for malaria control. Methods To evaluate the feasibility and limitations of the XN-31 use under real-world field conditions, we collected a total of 1,799 blood samples from asymptomatic residents in a malaria-endemic area along the Thailand–Myanmar border during five field trips conducted between January 2021 and May 2022. Samples were transported within the same day to a central laboratory in Bangkok. XN-31 measurements were performed after transport, together with microscopy and rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs). Dried blood spots were also sent to Japan for PCR analysis. Results Microscopy detected one P. vivax –positive case. In contrast, PCR identified 2 P. falciparum and 4 P. vivax infections, whereas all RDT results were negative. The XN-31 detected 5 MI-RBC–positive samples, of which only one was confirmed as P. vivax –positive by both microscopy and PCR. Among the XN-31 measurements, 176 samples were flagged as “MI-RBC Abn Scattergram,” indicating the presence of unidentified particles in the scattergram that prevented proper interpretation. Following protocol adjustments for the transport of whole blood samples to Bangkok, the MI-RBC Abn Scattergram rate in XN-31 decreased from 23.8% (first trip) to 4.6% (fifth trip). Lower frequencies of MI-RBC Abn Scattergram results were observed following modifications to collection-to-analysis time, transport procedures, cooling methods, and transport temperature management. Conclusions In conclusion, although several operational challenges were encountered during field application, the XN-31 may be applicable to malaria surveys in endemic areas when appropriate sample handling and transport conditions are ensured.

title: First Korean experience with shape-sensing robotic-assisted bronchoscopy integrated with mobile cone-beam CT: Results from the prospective ULSAN-ION study.
abstract:
Introduction

Shape-sensing robotic-assisted bronchoscopy (ssRAB) integrated with mobile cone-beam CT (mCBCT) has emerged as a promising platform for the diagnosis of peripheral pulmonary nodules (PPNs), with high diagnostic yield and low complication rates. However, no data have been reported in a Korean population. We evaluated the diagnostic yield and safety of ssRAB integrated with mCBCT in a Korean cohort.

Methods

This prospective, single-center cohort (the ULSAN-ION study) enrolled patients undergoing ssRAB with integrated mCBCT from July 2025 to April 2026 (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT07057648). Diagnostic yield was assessed using the strict ATS/ACCP definition at the per-nodule and per-patient levels.

Results

A total of 111 patients with 140 PPNs were enrolled. Median age was 64.0 years (IQR, 55.5-69.5), and 51.4 % were male. Median nodule size was 14.0 mm (IQR, 10.0-19.2), and nodule morphology included solid (57.9 %), part-solid (28.6 %), and pure ground-glass opacity (13.6 %). A CT bronchus sign was absent in 70.7 % of nodules. mCBCT was performed in 88.6 % of nodules, with tool-in-lesion confirmation in 77.9 % and an overall tool-to-lesion rate of 99.1 %. Per-nodule diagnostic yield was 85.0 % (119/140) and per-patient diagnostic yield was 90.1 % (100/111). A malignant diagnosis was established in 75.7 % of patients, most commonly adenocarcinoma, and a specific benign diagnosis in 14.4 %. Pneumothorax occurred in 4.5 % of patients, with chest tube insertion required in 2.7 %. Airway bleeding (Nashville Grade ≥ 2) occurred in 1.8 %, with no Grade ≥ 3 events.

Conclusion

This first prospective Korean experience demonstrates that ssRAB integrated with mCBCT achieves high diagnostic yield with an acceptable safety profile for PPN diagnosis.
authors: Chae G, Park C, Kim JH, Ra SW, Seo KW, Jegal Y, Cha HJ, Lee T.

title: Flexible Sensing for Embodied Robotics: From Materials and Devices to System Integration and Closed-Loop Control
abstract: Flexible sensors that bend, stretch, and conform to curved surfaces are being integrated into robotic bodies with increasing frequency, allowing robots to acquire contact, deformation, and near-field environmental information on curved and large-deformation structures. High-sensitivity devices, however, do not automatically produce reliable task-level perception. This review is organized along a traceable evidence chain from observable, transduction, body integration, signal interpretation, and closed-loop control to task outcome, and compares five transduction mechanisms (piezoresistive, capacitive, piezoelectric, triboelectric, and optical) together with material platforms such as liquid metals and hydrogels. It further examines how structural assembly, stretchable interconnects, calibration and drift compensation, multimodal fusion, and feedback control affect system performance. Using dexterous manipulation, deformation and posture estimation, and human-robot interaction as the three task domains, the review separates device metrics, robot-integration demonstrations, and closed-loop task evidence, and applies this evidence grading consistently across all layers. Current work shows that contact tactile sensing has formed a relatively complete real-robot closed loop under limited objects and operating conditions, whereas environmental sensing, cross-platform transfer, and long-term whole-body deployment still lack unified validation. Future priorities should shift from isolated sensitivity improvement toward comparable evaluation under unified conditions, reporting of end-to-end latency and maintenance costs, and perception-decision-action loops with fail-safe fallback.

title: Fulminant Emphysematous Hepatic Abscesses Due to Clostridium perfringens With Massive Intravascular Hemolysis: A Case Report
abstract: Clostridium perfringens is a gram-positive, anaerobic, gas-forming bacterium that can cause fulminant sepsis. Its alpha-toxin may induce massive intravascular hemolysis, and gas-forming hepatic infection with this organism often progresses to death within hours. An 80-year-old man presented to the emergency department with acute epigastric pain radiating to the back, tachycardia, hypertension, and fever. Triple-phase computed tomography demonstrated two gas-forming hepatic abscesses in segments 7 and 8 with portal venous gas, while the gallbladder appeared normal. He developed a severe high anion gap metabolic acidosis, hyperkalemia, and indirect hyperbilirubinemia with a low haptoglobin and a rapid hemoglobin drop, consistent with massive intravascular hemolysis. Percutaneous drainage could not be performed because of rapid hemodynamic deterioration. He suffered a cardiac arrest with transient return of spontaneous circulation, followed by a second, fatal arrest two hours and 11 minutes after presentation. Blood cultures drawn at presentation grew C. perfringens, Enterococcus faecalis, and Serratia marcescens, and post-mortem examination with culture of the gallbladder wall identified the gallbladder as the primary source of infection. This case illustrates that gas-forming hepatic abscesses combined with unexplained hemolysis should immediately raise suspicion of C. perfringens sepsis and that a radiologically normal gallbladder does not exclude it as the source. Given the extremely compressed clinical course, early recognition and emergent source control are critical.
authors: Ritchie Mulleman; Annelies Truyen; Koen Monsieurs

title: Future‐ready blood services: Building strategic foresight for the blood supply chain
abstract: BACKGROUND: Blood is an irreplaceable resource in the healthcare system, and ensuring its safe and timely delivery from donors to patients is the core function of the blood supply chain (BSC). Managing the BSC is increasingly challenging given the uncertainty surrounding interconnected factors such as demographic shifts, technological advances, and evolving clinical practices. Conventional planning approaches are insufficient to capture these complexities, motivating the development of narrative scenarios. STUDY DESIGN AND METHODS: We developed narrative scenarios for the BSC using a decomposition-based scenario development framework. Through a systematic literature review and expert consultations, we identified 10 key uncertainty factors and defined four development paths for each. We elicited pairwise consistency ratings between development paths from BSC experts and used them to select four internally consistent and maximally diverse scenarios. RESULTS: Four internally consistent scenarios were developed: Strained Resilience, Thriving Transformation, Adaptive Automation, and Regulatory Rigidity. Cross-scenario analysis reveals three structural findings: (i) where synthetic blood alternatives emerge, they complement rather than replace voluntary donation, (ii) apparent stability can mask underlying fragility, and (iii) long-term resilience is determined by social and institutional conditions rather than operational capacity alone. CONCLUSION: Our findings identify donor engagement, institutional trust, cybersecurity resilience, and regulatory agility as robust strategic priorities for the BSC across a wide range of possible futures. The scenarios reveal that factors conventionally excluded from BSC analytical models, such as civic trust and regulatory flexibility, are among the most consequential drivers of long-term system resilience.
authors: Marina De Amorim; Eeva Vilkkumaa; Fabrício Oliveira; Mikko Arvas; Jarkko Ihalainen

title: GPU-resident Execution for Timing-predictable Sensor Processing Systems
abstract: Real-time embedded systems increasingly place GPU-accelerated processing of high-bandwidth sensor streams inside closed-loop systems, but the CPU (the host) remains the primary orchestrator of each iteration. The host observes sensor inputs, submits CUDA work, waits for completion, and commits actuation. This host-mediated path exposes the closed-loop end-to-end latency to I/O interrupts, host scheduler decisions, and CUDA API overheads even after common host-side mitigations such as GPU-memory RDMA or CPU core isolation. This paper presents GPU-resident Execution, a new execution model for real-time sensor processing pipelines that keeps I/O and GPU execution in a long-lived device-resident loop. Sensor inputs arrive in GPU memory, trigger GPU-side processing, and reach GPU-visible output endpoints without any host wakeups. We implement the model in the NVIDIA Holoscan C++ framework and provide reference components for building GPU-resident applications. We evaluate our system on NVIDIA GPUs and SoCs with inference, host-contention, multi-loop, and streaming camera workloads. On an industry-grade 1080p, 60 Hz real-time camera-to-display application, GPU-resident Execution reduces photon-to-display jitter from 4.83 ms to 0.66 ms (7.3x) relative to a CPU-driven GPU-memory RDMA baseline and reduces software-processing jitter from 1.70 ms to 0.01 ms (170x).
authors: Soham Sinha; Rahul Choudhury; Shekhar Dwivedi; Gregory Lee; Gigon Bae; Anisha Goel; Elena Agostini; Patrick O'Grady; Yosi Levi; Mahdi Azizian

title: Genomic tracking of Campylobacter jejuni along poultry and pig value chains in Northeast India: Implications for food safety
abstract: Campylobacter jejuni is the predominant causative agent of human campylobacteriosis. A total of 864 samples (poultry cloacal swabs, chicken intestine, chicken meat, pig rectal swab, pig intestine, pork) were screened for the presence of C. jejuni using standard methods. A total of 27 isolates were confirmed with PCR with an overall occurrence rate of 3.13%. Highest isolation rates were from chicken intestine samples (9.72%), followed by pork (7.64%) and chicken meat (1.39%). Resistance levels were high towards nalidixic acid, tetracycline, ampicillin and ciprofloxacin. Multidrug-resistance and biofilm formation featured in 30.77% and 53.84% isolates, respectively. Genomic characterization identified the highest presence of T86I mutation in gyrA and cmeABC system. The isolates were abundant with important virulence genes such as cdtABC, wlan, neuABC and cstIII . The isolates belonged to diverse Penner serotypes and MLST types with ST 353 complex being the predominant clonal complex. Phylogenetic analysis indicated tendency of the genomes with similar ST/CC to cluster together and indicated wide genetic diversity . To the best of our knowledge, this serves as the first genome submission of C. jejuni from porcine sources of India. Further, this study underscores the need for exploiting modern technologies, including genomics, to study various food-borne pathogens.

title: Haemato-Biochemical Characterisation with Reference to Dental Affections and Oral Bacterial Flora in Managed Asian Elephants (Elephas maximus)
abstract: Dental abnormalities in elephants may interfere with mastication and feeding efficiency, while microorganisms associated with the periodontal region may represent normal commensal flora or opportunistic pathogens. Haematological and serum biochemical investigations provide complementary information on the physiological and systemic health status of managed elephants. The present study was undertaken to characterise selected haemato-biochemical parameters in managed Asian elephants examined for dental affections in Madhya Pradesh, India, with reference to their dental findings and associated bacterial flora. The study was conducted from July 2023 to January 2024 and included 30 elephants maintained in four tiger reserves and private facilities. Dental examination and periodontal swab assessment were performed in all 30 elephants, while blood samples for laboratory investigations were available from 21 animals. Haematological and serum biochemical parameters were estimated using automated and semi-automated analysers, respectively. Dental observations included plaque, tartar, caries, cracked teeth, tusk abnormalities and tooth loss. Of the 30 periodontal swab samples examined, bacterial growth was obtained from 26, whereas four samples showed no growth. Various Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacterial organisms were identified. The mean erythrocyte count, total leucocyte count, packed cell volume and haemoglobin concentration were 3.38 ± 0.12 × 10⁶/µL, 18.28 ± 1.11 × 10³/µL, 42.29 ± 1.90% and 13.79 ± 0.56 g/dL, respectively. The mean serum total protein, ALT, AST, BUN and creatinine values were 8.21 ± 0.31 g/dL, 23.63 ± 1.43 U/L, 39.44 ± 2.53 U/L, 23.15 ± 2.01 mg/dL and 1.82 ± 0.24 mg/dL, respectively. Although the group mean values of the biochemical parameters remained within the cited reference intervals, variations were observed in selected individual haematological and biochemical parameters. The study provides descriptive information on the haemato-biochemical profiles of managed Asian elephants in relation to their dental affections and periodontal bacterial flora. The findings highlight the importance of integrating dental examination, microbiological assessment and laboratory investigations in routine health monitoring. However, further controlled studies with individual-level correlations are required to clarify the possible associations between dental conditions, periodontal bacterial flora and systemic physiological responses.
authors: Babita Singh Kushwah; Somesh Singh; Bhavana Gupta

title: Humoral Immunity and Variant Cross-Reactivity Following Asymptomatic and Symptomatic SARS-CoV-2 Infection and Vaccination in Young Adults (The ACE Cohort)
abstract: Purpose Asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection was a driving force of the COVID-19 pandemic, acting as a silent transmitter of the virus. The question of whether asymptomatic immunity differs from symptomatic immunity remains, as existing studies fail to recruit ‘well-defined’ asymptomatic individuals. Here, we conducted a longitudinal cohort study to evaluate humoral responses to infection and vaccination in asymptomatic predominantly young adults identified as part of the Asymptomatic COVID-19 in Education [ACE] cohort. Methods Asymptomatic testing services, located at three UK universities, identified asymptomatic adults who were subsequently recruited with age- and sex-matched symptomatic and uninfected controls. Blood and saliva samples were collected after SARS-CoV-2 Wuhan infection, and again after vaccination. Over 500 participants were recruited, and their IgG and IgA titres were measured in response to 5 Variants of Concern. Results Pre-vaccination, asymptomatic individuals exhibit significantly lower IgG responses to four of the tested variants; Wuhan, Alpha, Beta, and Delta, compared to symptomatic individuals; these differences diminished post-vaccination. In addition, there were key differences in terms of IgG cross-reactivity, where symptomatic individuals displayed stronger IgG cross-reactivity than asymptomatic and uninfected individuals, alluding to better protection from emerging variants. Individuals without prior natural infection displayed reduced IgG responses compared to symptomatic individuals, to all variants, post-vaccination. Despite their low IgG, salivary IgA levels in uninfected individuals were high, pre-vaccination. Conclusion This work demonstrates the requirement of vaccinations to enhance weaker IgG responses but also highlights that vaccines need to be constantly adapted to overcome viral evolution, particularly with more done to improve mucosal delivery options for respiratory viruses to enhance IgA responses.

title: Hyperelasticity as an efficient regularizer for 2D-3D thoracic motion models
abstract: Patient-specific motion models enable real-time volumetric imaging of the thorax from a single x-ray projection, but most existing approaches require hours of training. The VM-DS framework trains in minutes, yet its image-space self-consistency regularizer accounts for 40% of the motion-model fitting time and does not prevent the fitted fields from folding. In this paper, we explore a range of regularization approaches including scaling-and-squaring, bending energy, diffusion, first-order inverse consistency, isotropic total variation, a negative-Jacobian hinge, |log det J|, a control-point injectivity bound and hyperelastic regularization. Hyperparameters were selected on two development cases from the public DIR-Lab 4D dataset under rules fixed in advance, and the regularizers were tested on eight held-out cases. At a fixed number of training steps, the hyperelastic term trained in 5.6 against 8.4 min and gave a lower held-out TRE (2.5 mm). With a quarter of the motion-model budget it matched the baseline (2.7 mm), and at every budget from 2 to 17 min its mean TRE was lower by 0.3-0.5 mm. Hyperelastic fields had no folded voxel in any held-out view, whereas baseline fields folded in 83 % of views, with image similarity unchanged. A hyperelastic volume penalty can therefore replace image-space self-consistency, matching accuracy with 3-5 minutes of training and removing folding, bringing on-the-day motion models closer to routine use in image-guided interventions. Code will be available at https://github.com/Image-X-Institute/Voxelmap/tree/hyper

title: Hypoxia‐Guided Magnetic Catheter for Localization and Minimally Invasive Intervention in Early‐Stage Lung Cancer
abstract: To enable the precise localization and minimally invasive treatment of early-stage pulmonary lesions, we developed a magnetic catheter system integrating magnetic navigation, hypoxia fluorescence imaging, and multifunctional minimally invasive intervention. The distal end of the system incorporates multiple permanent magnets, a miniature camera equipped with an optical filter, multiple fiber-optic channels, and a flexibly switchable multifunctional working channel. Under a 40 mT magnetic field applied perpendicular to the initial catheter axis, the catheter incorporating 2.0 mm-diameter magnets achieved a bending angle of 39.63° ± 2.47° and successfully navigated to multiple designated branches in the bronchial phantom. A proof-of-concept model was established using A549 lung cancer spheroids labeled with hypoxia-responsive fluorescent probes, enabling fluorescence-guided localization of simulated hypoxic lesions. In the bronchial phantom, the system successfully identified simulated hypoxic lesions and subsequently performed biopsy sampling, simulated drug delivery, and localized laser irradiation. The system was further evaluated in porcine lungs to demonstrate its navigation and localized intervention capabilities. This magnetic catheter system provides a new technological strategy for the precise localization and in situ treatment of early-stage lung cancer.
authors: Jiatian Chen; Yaxuan Jiao; Lei Li; Shengchang Zhang; Xianbing Zeng; Juncai Song; Yujing Li; Guanghao Wu; Yubing Guo

title: Immunogenicity of the Foldon trimerization domain and efforts to shield it
abstract: Protein subunit and mRNA vaccines encoding viral glycoprotein antigens fused to the bacteriophage T4 fibritintrimerization domain are increasingly being tested in human clinical trials. AREXVY and ABRYSVO®, subunit vaccines composed of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) prefusion F glycoprotein(s) fused to Foldon, are now FDA-approved and regularly administered. However, administration of vaccine antigens containing the Foldon domain has the potential to elicit off-target antibody responses. Here, we demonstrate that protein subunit vaccine antigens RSV F Foldon and influenza hemagglutinin (HA) Foldon elicit antibodies against the Foldon domain. To dampen Foldon-induced antibody responses, we engineered influenza computationally optimized broadly reactive antigen (COBRA) HA proteins with N-glycosylation motif mutations at three different sites in Foldon. Mass spectrometry analyses confirmed partial occupancy of N-glycosylation modifications at two of the three intended sites. Two of the three COBRA HA Foldon mutant antigens demonstrated reduced binding by anti-Foldon monoclonal and polyclonal antibodies compared to the wild-type COBRA HA Foldon. However, mice immunized with the COBRA HA Foldon mutant antigens did not have a significant reduction in the elicitation of anti-Foldon antibodies. Further analysis suggested that some of the observed differences in antibody binding to mutant Foldon antigens can be attributed to differences in protein sequence alone. Altogether, these data suggest that while the N-glycosylation modifications may partially shield the Foldon from reactive antibodies, this shielding does not significantly reduce its immunogenicity in a naïve setting. Importantly, these data highlight that the Foldon trimerization domain is immunogenic, which should be considered during clinical trials of vaccines that contain Foldon.
authors: John V. Dzimianski; Spencer R. Pierce; Sara M. O’Rourke; Ian Kunkel; Kevin Delgado-Cunningham; Aaron D. Gingerich; Jarrod J. Mousa; Ted M. Ross; Rebecca M. DuBois

title: Impact of Nasopharyngeal Swab Freezing Storage on the De-tection of Common Respiratory Viral Molecular Targets
abstract: Archived respiratory specimens are valuable for retrospective diagnostic studies, although long-term storage may affect viral RNA detection. This study evaluated nasopharyngeal swabs (NPS) stored at −80 °C for at least one year and retested using automated molecular assays with different multiplexing formats. Qualitative agreement with initial results and changes in cycle threshold (Ct) values were assessed, with discordant results investigated using an independent assay. SARS-CoV-2 showed the highest stability (positive percent agreement, PPA: 97.1–98.6%; mean Ct increase: 2.8–3.4), followed by respiratory syncytial virus (RSV; PPA: 88.4–97.1%; mean Ct increase: 1.75–4.50) and influenza virus (PPA: 80.0–92.9%; mean Ct increase: 5.48–7.92). Ct increases were significant for all viral targets. Differences across assay configurations suggested that assay formulation and target characteristics may influence post-storage detection. NPS aliquots stored at −80 °C remain useful for retrospective molecular testing, although target- and assay-dependent signal loss should be considered when interpreting results from archived specimens. title: Indocyanine Green and Technetium-99m: CT-Guided Marking of Lung Nodules Before Robotic-Assisted Lung Resection
abstract: Background/Objectives: For stage I non-small cell lung cancer, surgery remains the cornerstone of treatment and the use of minimally invasive techniques is desirable. The lack of tactile feedback in RATS is a well-known drawback of this approach, so precise identification of the disease is crucial for performing lung resection. Methods: We present our retrospective case history, accounting for 83 patients, which were divided into two groups based on marking technique: 99mTc-MAA (99mTechnetium Albumin Macroaggregates) only (Tech group) (22 cases, 26.5%) and 99mTc-MAA + Indocyanine Green (Tech + ICG group) (61 cases, 73.49%). Results: In the Tech group, there were 11 males (50%) ad 11 females (50%), the median nodule diameter was 21.5 mm (IQR 16), and the median distance of the nodule from the visceral pleura was 18 mm (IQR 21). Eighteen out of 22 nodules (81.82%) were subsolid. Three conversions were reported, all due to failure to identify the nodule (13.63%). The mean operative time was 111.6 ± 45.6 min. The histopathological examination resulted in 13 lung adenocarcinomas, one squamous cell carcinoma, two minimally invasive lung adenocarcinomas, two lung adenocarcinomas in situ, three metastases from another tumor, and one benign nodule. In the Tech + ICG group, there were 27 males (44.26%) and 34 females (55.73%), the median nodule diameter was 18 mm (IQR 14), and the median distance of the nodule from the visceral pleura was 24 mm (IQR 15). Forty-six out of 61 nodules were subsolid (75.4%). Four conversions were reported, due to failure in nodule identification (6.55%). The operative time was 105.6 ± 36.8 min. The histopathological examination resulted in 12 lung adenocarcinomas, seven squamous cell carcinomas, nine minimally invasive lung adenocarcinomas, 12 lung adenocarcinomas in situ, one typical carcinoid, seven atypical adenomatous hyperplasias, seven metastases from another tumor, and six benign nodules. The two groups are homogeneous in terms of median nodule diameter (p = 0.676), the median distance from visceral pleura (p = 0.114), SUV max (p = 0.894), operative time (p = 0.512), and nodule characteristics (solid vs. subsolid) (p = 0.724). The conversion rate was lower in the Tech + ICG group (6.55% vs. 13.63%), but the difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.375). Conclusions: Both techniques appear to be safe and reproducible. Further standardized studies are needed to validate and confirm the results obtained from our case series.

title: Integrated Microfluidic CRISPR-Based Diagnostic Device for Rapid Testing of HPVs.
abstract: Screening for high-risk human papillomavirus (HR-HPV) is a pivotal strategy for the prevention of invasive cervical cancer, particularly in resource-constrained settings. In this study, we developed a CRISPR-based compact automated real-time detection system, termed Ccard, for rapid testing of HPV16, HPV18, and the internal reference gene GAPDH through a streamlined workflow. A simple room-temperature treatment efficiently releases nucleic acids directly from swab samples, bypassing the need for extraction. The mixture was driven through the channels and loaded into the reaction chambers on the microfluidic chip by a vacuum pump. The lyophilized reagents in the reaction zone of the microfluidic chip were redissolved. The system subsequently performs a single-step RPA-CRISPR/Cas13a reaction, with real-time detection enabled by an Internet of Things device. The assay achieved detection within 30 min, with a limit of detection (LOD) of 5 copies/µL for both HPV16 and HPV18. Validation with clinical samples demonstrated high sensitivity (96.8% for HPV16 and 100% for HPV18) and 100% specificity. These results highlight the reliability, precision, and strong potential of the Ccard system for rapid testing of HR-HPVs.
authors: Tianci Wang; Lingyun Li; Yunxiang Wang; Yongjun Han; Teng Li; Chaoran Yu; Yufeng Lou; Zhen Rong; Kai Lin; Shengqi Wang

title: Intratumoral Therapeutic Injections for Lung Cancer: Current Evidence, Personalized Therapeutic Approaches, and Future Directions
abstract: Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide despite significant advances in surgery, radiation therapy, targeted therapies, and immunotherapy. Although systemic therapies have improved outcomes across all stages of disease, treatment efficacy is often limited by inadequate intratumoral drug delivery, systemic toxicities, treatment resistance, and disease heterogeneity. Intratumoral therapeutic injections (ITIs), including intratumoral chemotherapy (ITC), have emerged as a promising locoregional therapeutic strategy designed to overcome these limitations through direct delivery of antineoplastic agents into tumor tissue. Advances in bronchoscopic technologies, particularly endobronchial ultrasound-guided transbronchial needle injection (EBUS-TBNI), robotic bronchoscopy, electromagnetic navigation bronchoscopy, and cone-beam computed tomography guidance, have expanded the feasibility of delivering therapeutic agents to central and peripheral pulmonary lesions. Most of the evidence for ITI comes from case reports, prospective or retrospective studies with small sample sizes, and non-randomized, single-arm clinical trials. While further evidence is needed, especially in the form of randomized controlled trials, the current literature shows promise in the areas of malignant airway obstruction and isolated mediastinal and hilar recurrence. Studies have also assessed the utility of novel formulations, including large surface area microparticle paclitaxel (LSAM-PTX). Potential future applications of ITI include use as neoadjuvant therapy, as part of combination therapy with radiation and immune checkpoint inhibitors, and in cases of oligoprogressive disease and medically inoperable tumors. Novel formulations, including large surface area microparticle paclitaxel (LSAM-PTX), sustained-release drug delivery systems, and the potential use of immunomodulatory agents, have further enhanced the therapeutic potential of local drug administration. Furthermore, advances in radiomics, artificial intelligence, computational drug distribution modeling, and biomarker-driven patient selection have positioned ITI within the broader framework of personalized cancer therapy. This review summarizes the biological rationale, technical approaches, clinical evidence, and future directions of ITI in lung cancer, emphasizing its evolving role as a precision therapeutic platform capable of providing effective cancer treatment alongside established therapeutic paradigms.
authors: Tatiana Maser; Moath Bani Salem; Osama Al Zoubi; Alexandria Iakovidis; Miguel Castro; Jingjing Chen; Pankit Patel; Karthik Vijayan; Hiren J. Mehta

title: Isolation and Identification of Aerobic Bacteria from the Dental Region of Managed Asian Elephants (Elephas maximus)
abstract: Aims: This study aimed to isolate and identify aerobic bacteria from dental swab samples collected from Asian elephants (Elephas maximus) managed at different Tiger Reserves in central India. Study Design: Observational microbiological investigation involving dental examination, bacterial culture, Gram staining, and automated bacterial identification. Place and Duration of Study: Samples were collected from elephants managed at Pench, Bandhavgarh, Kanha, and Satpura Tiger Reserves and privately managed elephants in central India. Laboratory investigations were conducted at the School of Wildlife Forensic and Health, Nanaji Deshmukh Veterinary Science University, Jabalpur, from July 2023 to January 2024. Methodology: Thirty Asian elephants were included in the study. Dental swab samples were cultured in brain heart infusion broth and subsequently inoculated onto nutrient agar, MacConkey agar, and brain heart infusion agar supplemented with 5% blood. Following incubation at 37°C for 18–24 hours, bacterial colonies were examined, subjected to Gram staining, and identified using the BD Phoenix M50 automated identification system. Results: Fourteen bacterial taxa were identified: Klebsiella pneumoniae, Klebsiella oxytoca, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Enterobacter cloacae, Enterobacter aerogenes, Citrobacter freundii, Serratia marcescens, Acinetobacter spp., Staphylococcus aureus, Enterococcus faecalis, Enterococcus faecium, Rothia mucilaginosa, Streptococcus mitis and Streptococcus mutans. Klebsiella pneumoniae had the highest reported isolation frequency (45.45%), followed by Pseudomonas aeruginosa (18.18%) and Enterobacter cloacae (13.63%). Conclusion: The study documents a range of aerobic bacteria in dental swab samples from managed Asian elephants in Madhya Pradesh. These findings provide preliminary information on the dental bacterial flora of this species and support further investigations linking microbiological findings with oral health, clinical examination, and molecular identification.
authors: Babita Singh Kushwah; Somesh Singh; Amol Rokde; Sumit Kumar Patel; Poonam Sharma

title: Isolation and Identification of Bacterial Pathogens from Hemodialysis Patients at Zliten Dialysis Center and Evaluation of Their Antibiotic Susceptibility Patterns
abstract: A B S T R A C T Background: The most complication that Hemodialysis patient suffer from is get infected by microorganisms awhile they do the treatment these infections cause serious complications for dialysis patient especially catheter related bloodstream infection (CRBSIs). Aims: This study amid to isolate isolation and identification of bacterial pathogens associated with bloodstream infections and bacterial colonization of venous catheter sites from hemodialysis patients in Zliten City Libya., Then determine the major bacterial species and test their antimicrobial susceptibility patterns. Methods: A total of 124 clinical specimens were collected, comprising 62 catheter-site swab samples from peripheral venous catheter sites were conducted from hemodialysis patients and processed using standard microbiological procedures. The samples were cultured on appropriate selective and differential culture media and incubated under suitable conditions. The bacteria were examined based on colony morphology, microscopic characteristics, and Gram staining. Identification was performed using a series of conventional biochemical tests. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing was carried out to determine the susceptibility patterns of the isolated bacterial strains to commonly used antibiotics for hemodialysis patients. Results: The results a total of 124 clinical specimens, comprising 62 catheter-site swab samples and 62 blood samples. 62 swab sample .93.55% (58 samples) showed bacterial growth, While 6.45% (4 sample) no bacterial growth. Among the 62 blood samples, showed result 22 bacterial growth. show the presence of several bacterial species associated with catheter sites and bloodstream infections. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing showed varying degrees of resistance among the bacterial isolates, with some strains exhibiting resistance to multiple classes of antibiotics. The results suggest the presence of multidrug-resistant bacterial strains and the potential risk of antimicrobial resistance within the hospital environment. Conclusion: catheter-related infections are the most concern for hemodialysis patients. Infection prevention and control practices, particularly appropriate catheter insertion, aseptic techniques, sterilization, and catheter care, is essential to reduce the risk of infection. In addition, antimicrobial therapy should be done by laboratory-based antimicrobial susceptibility testing. Continuous microbiological surveillance and rational antibiotic use are recommended to reduce the emergence and dissemination of antimicrobial-resistant bacteria among hemodialysis.
