title: Just-in-time volumetric imaging: Learning 2D-3D thoracic motion models during image-guided interventions
abstract: Despite two decades of innovation, cutting-edge bronchoscopic techniques still fail to yield clear diagnostic decisions in 30% of cases and miss malignancies in 20% of cases. Intraprocedural 3D imaging drastically improves both tool positioning and diagnostic yield. However, each 3D spin represents a static snapshot of an anatomy that is continuously evolving as the patient is ventilated throughout the procedure. Here, we propose just-in-time volumetric imaging, in which a patient-specific 2D--3D motion model is trained on pre-intervention scans before it is needed and then supplies volumetric images from single fluoroscopic projections during sampling. Given the inspiration-hold CBCT already acquired for navigation and an additional motion-inclusive CBCT, our optimization regime named VoxelMap-DualScan (VM-DS), solves a low-rank motion model by alternating least squares and then amortizes it into a projection encoder trained on synthesized projections with known motion, all within a 10-minute window. On eight held-out cases from the public DIR-Lab 4DCT dataset, VM-DS achieved a mean landmark target registration error of 2.8 mm, a structural similarity index of 0.95 and a peak signal-to-noise ratio of 37.7 dB. Accuracy was maintained when reducing the number of projections used for training from 227 to 23. Inference takes 1.5 ms per projection, making the framework suitable for real-time use during image-guided interventions. Code will be made available at https://github.com/Image-X-Institute/Voxelmap/tree/VM-DS
authors: Nicholas Hindley

title: Limited efficacy of enrofloxacin against Mesomycoplasma ovipneumoniae infection in domestic lambs
abstract: Mesomycoplasma ovipneumoniae is an important respiratory pathogen in sheep that leads to pneumonia and reduced productivity, commonly upon co-infection with other opportunistic microbes. Whether M. ovipneumoniae infection can be successfully treated with antibiotics is unclear. Our pilot study evaluated the efficacy of enrofloxacin (Baytril ® ) for treating experimental M. ovipneumoniae infection in domestic lambs. Ten 3-month-old specific-pathogen-free lambs were randomly assigned to a treatment and an untreated control group. Lambs were inoculated with fresh nasal wash fluids from M. ovipneumoniae- positive sheep. After 4 weeks, the treatment group received enrofloxacin at 0.5 mg/kg in 200 mL of saline intranasally and 5 mg/kg subcutaneously on five consecutive days. Lambs were observed for an additional 4 weeks, with daily health scoring, weekly assessment of weight gain, and weekly nasal swab quantitative (q)PCR analysis for M. ovipneumoniae and Mannheimia haemolytica . Successful M. ovipneumoniae infection of all lambs was confirmed by qPCR 1 week after inoculation. While overall health scores and average daily weight gains were statistically similar between groups, enrofloxacin administration significantly accelerated the rate of body temperature decline over the post-treatment period ( P = 0.007). Interestingly, all treated lambs tested negative for M. ovipneumoniae by qPCR 1 week after treatment. However, there was a re-emergence of M. ovipneumoniae infection 2 weeks after treatment with 1/5 lambs testing positive, and 3/5 lambs tested positive 4 weeks after treatment. Co-infection with Mannheimia haemolytica was detected in all lambs, with a similar temporary suppression after enrofloxacin treatment. Endpoint tissue swab samples revealed variable qPCR detection of M. ovipneumoniae , with a trend for reduced infection of the lower respiratory tract in the treated lambs. However, middle ear swabs from all lambs tested qPCR-positive for M. ovipneumoniae , suggesting that the middle ear is a potential reservoir of this pathogen. Tissues collected after euthanasia showed reduced histopathological lung lesions in the enrofloxacin-treated group (Mann–Whitney U test, P = 0.032 ). Amongst four M. ovipneumoniae isolates recovered from the lung of one enrofloxacin-treated lamb, one isolate showed reduced susceptibility to enrofloxacin in vitro . Overall, our study showed that enrofloxacin treatment was only partially successful in reducing M. ovipneumoniae infection in domestic lambs.
authors: Sobha Sonar; Michael Throolin; Stephen Smith; Jonathon Sago; Eli T. Selong; Noah Adams; Jessica Dibbert; McKenna D. Quirk; Nathan J. Schaff; Helen Schwantje; Christian J. Posbergh; Diane Bimczok

title: Low-Cost IoT-Based Smart Blood Collection Bag Monitoring and Agitation System for Real-Time Hemovigilance
abstract: This paper presents the study, design, and development of a comprehensive, low-cost blood collection system. The proposed system is based on IoT technology and aims to improve the efficiency, safety, and standardization of blood donation procedures in clinical settings, while providing continuous monitoring, automated alerts, and centralized oversight. More specifically, the system consists of two components: the blood collection station and the information system. The blood collection station consists of two parts. The first part is a device that includes a load cell weighing unit which accurately measures the mass of a blood collection bag during collection. The device then continuously converts the measured weight into an estimated blood volume, thereby allowing for accurate monitoring of the progress of the blood donation. The second section consists of a mechanism for gently agitating the collected blood with the anticoagulant solution, with the aim of reducing the risk of clot formation during the procedure. The information system consists of a server that includes a database and web-based visualization software. The Wi-Fi protocol was used for data transmission. The heart of the system is a microcontroller that includes Wi-Fi connectivity and is responsible for collecting, processing, and transmitting data to the database. This enables simultaneous real-time monitoring of multiple blood collection stations through a central monitoring system. It can provide alarm notifications; for example, when the volume of collected blood reaches a predetermined threshold (e.g., 400 mL), the system can trigger both audible and visual alerts, ensuring an immediate response from medical and nursing staff. Through the visualization software, it is possible to monitor and record data, which can improve workflow coordination in blood donation centers and hospital settings. This approach achieves both a reduction in human error and the optimization of blood collection procedures.

title: Machine Learning–Integrated Surface-Enhanced Raman Spectroscopy for Analysis of Petroleum-Derived Environmental Contaminants
abstract: Surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS) is a highly sensitive technique that enhances the Raman scattering of molecules supported by some noble metal nanostructured materials. The development of SERS allows to detect of fingerprints of molecules at very low concentrations of analyte through the plasmonic effect and magnification of electro magnetic fields by nanoparticles. The high sensitivity is critical in environmental and safety applications, including the detection of toxic naphthenic acids in oil sand wastewater, the removal of petroleum-based agrochemical residues in the environment. The primary objective of this project is the development of the SERS based analytical frame-work for the rapid and sensitive detection and quantification of petroleum-derived contaminations. First, a sample-preparation platform is developed to address the low, uneven analyte loading that limits SERS sensitivity in dilute aqueous samples. Dispersive liquid–liquid microextraction(DLLME) is coupled with controlled droplet evaporation on an omniphobic, nano/micro-structured porous microfiber membrane, concentrating extracted analytes into a small, reproducible hotspot region. This improves signal enhancement and yields more uniform, repeatable spectra than direct deposition, providing a practical front end for trace detection in real water matrices. Second, a SERS–ML approach is established for multiplex profiling of naphthenic acids (NAs) in water, a major class of toxic constituents in oil sands process-affected water. Using colloidal silver nanoparticles, the characteristic SERS fingerprints of structurally similar NAs are resolved and classified with ML model, achieving quantification and identification for a multi-component matrix. This shows that machine learning can disentangle overlapping vibrational signatures that defeat conventional univariate analysis, enabling simultaneous identification and concentration estimation of multiple NAs from a single measurement. Third, the framework is extended from aqueous samples to solid product surfaces for pesticide-residue screening. A simple cotton-swab sampling step lifts residues from chili pepper and apple surfaces and transfers them onto a reproducible, optically transparent Ag–PDMS plasmonic film, after which ML classification identifies and quantifies target pesticides. The transparent, flexible Ag–PDMS substrate provides uniform enhancement across the film, and the swab-and-transfer workflow converts an irregular, non-flat real surface into a standardized SERS measurement. Fourth, the framework addresses the performance gap between low-cost handheld instruments and benchtop confocal systems through deep-learning spectral translation, supported by an automated acquisition platform. A two-actuator stage with vision-based screen-state detection drives the handheld device through a hands-free measurement cycle, removing operator variability and yielding reproducible spectra for data-driven modeling. A concentration-conditioned generative model (CcGAN) then translates noisy, low resolution handheld spectra into confocal-quality spectra, recovering peak sharpness and signal-to-noise while preserving the concentration-dependent features required for quantification. Together, the automated stage and the translation model provide a data-driven route to laboratory-grade spectra from a portable device, extending SERS–ML measurement to field-deployable use without sacrificing analytical fidelity. Overall, this work provides a coherent, experimentally validated SERS–ML frame work that improves signal reliability through substrate and sample-preparation design, extracts quantitative multiplex information through machine learning, extends trace detection from water to food surfaces, and makes portable measurement automated and laboratory-comparable through deep learning, supporting the practical deployment of SERS for trace chemical detection outside the laboratory.

title: Magnetic microrobots for precision medicine: From locomotion mechanisms and advanced materials to clinical translation
abstract: As minimally invasive surgery (MIS) ventures into increasingly confined and delicate anatomical regions, conventional tethered instruments encounter inherent limitations in miniaturization and maneuverability. Untethered magnetic microrobots, characterized by precise navigation, deep tissue penetration, and highly efficient propulsion in low-Reynolds-number fluids, have emerged as a transformative platform for targeted diagnostics and therapeutics with sub-millimeter accuracy. This review systematically examines the state-of-the-art breakthroughs and the clinical translation landscape of magnetic microrobotic systems. Specifically, we first categorize and analyze four distinct propulsion modalities-translation, swimming, tumbling, and jumping-alongside their adaptive strategies for navigating unstructured physiological environments. Subsequently, the core technological framework is detailed, encompassing material selection (ranging from functional to bio-integrated materials) and cross-scale fabrication techniques such as two-photon polymerization and microfluidics. Finally, the discussion underscores recent milestones in vascular interventions, gastrointestinal diagnostics, and oncology, while exploring emerging frontiers such as ophthalmic surgery and tissue engineering.
authors: Gongxin Li; Yuting Mao; Fei Liu; fangmei an; Qiang Zhan

title: Management of Persistent Air Leak and Bronchopleural Fistula in Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome: A Systematic Review With Narrative Synthesis
abstract: Persistent air leak (PAL) and bronchopleural fistula (BPF) can complicate acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), prolong mechanical ventilation, and delay liberation from extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO), yet evidence guiding intervention selection is limited. This systematic review with narrative synthesis, conducted in accordance with Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020, searched four major databases for reports evaluating bronchoscopic interventions or autologous blood pleurodesis for PAL or BPF in mechanically ventilated or ECMO-supported patients. Heterogeneity and the scarcity of comparator arms precluded meta-analysis. The only comparative ARDS-specific study evaluated autologous blood pleurodesis. Evidence for endobronchial valves and related devices consisted mainly of observational cohorts, case series, and case reports, including patients on venovenous ECMO. Successful bronchoscopic therapy depended on accurate localization of the leak, whereas large, multiple, infected, or complex fistulas often required multimodal or surgical management. Certainty of the evidence was low, and no study directly compared blood pleurodesis, endobronchial valves, and surgery. The available low-certainty evidence supports an individualized, physiology-based approach to management; however, comparative evidence is insufficient to establish the superiority of any intervention. Management should minimize fistula flow while ensuring pleural drainage and infection control. Blood pleurodesis or bronchoscopic occlusion may facilitate air-leak resolution and liberation from mechanical ventilation or ECMO in selected patients, whereas surgical management may be required for patients with large, complex, infected, or refractory defects.
authors: Mustafa Ahmed Akmal; Jasnoor Kaur Chatrath; Sarah Ahmed Akmal; Karanjot Singh Chatrath; Rashid N Nadeem

title: Metabolic responses, body reserve mobilization, productive performance, and reproductive recovery of sows managed under manual and automated thermal control during late gestation and lactation
abstract: This study evaluated the effect of thermal control systems on body reserve mobilization and metabolic responses in sows during late gestation and lactation. A total of 140 sows (Yorkshire × Landrace) were evaluated under commercial conditions with either manual (MTC) or automated thermal control (ATC) systems. Temperature–humidity index (THI), daily feed intake (DFI), and productive performance were recorded. Blood metabolites including glucose, urea, β-hydroxybutyrate (BHB), and non-esterified fatty acids (NEFA) were determined. Associations among environmental variables, DFI, and metabolic indicators were analyzed using correlation and linear regression models. During lactation, DFI was higher under ATC (5.78 vs. 4.52 kg/day; p = 0.0011), accompanied by reduced body weight loss (8.34 vs. 14.70 kg; p < 0.0001) and fat mass loss (9.22 vs. 13.17 kg; p < 0.0001). Concentrations of glucose (73.05 vs. 66.8 mg/dL), NEFA (0.36 vs. 0.30 mmol/L), BHB (0.59 vs. 0.48 mmol/L), and urea (33.9 vs. 23.8 mg/dL) were higher under MTC (p < 0.05). Under MTC conditions, THI was positively correlated with glucose (r = 0.66), NEFA (r = 0.64), and BHB (r = 0.73; p < 0.0001), whereas DFI showed negative correlations (r = − 0.78 to − 0.63; p < 0.0001). THI was a significant predictor of NEFA (β = 0.18) and BHB (β = 0.23). Furthermore, ATC increased the number of weaned piglets and weaning weight, and reduced the weaning-to-estrus interval (p < 0.05). These results demonstrate that ATC reduced lipolytic activation and improved productive efficiency, confirming the regulatory role of thermal load on maternal metabolism.
authors: Gerardo Ordaz; Ericka Ramírez Rodríguez; Tércia Cesária Reis de Souza; Gerardo Mariscal Landín

title: Microbiological contamination in an anatomy laboratory: comparison of cadaveric materials and environmental surfaces
abstract: This study investigated the distribution of microbial contamination in an anatomy laboratory to determine whether contamination was primarily associated with cadaver-related materials or with the general laboratory environment. Although cadaver dissection is an essential component of medical education, anatomy laboratories may represent potential sources of biological exposure because microorganisms can persist on cadavers, laboratory equipment, and frequently touched surfaces. The study aimed to compare microbial growth among human tissues, cadaver-related surfaces, and commonly used laboratory areas. A total of 88 swab samples were collected from human tissues, cadaver-contact surfaces, and areas without direct cadaver contact. Samples were cultured using standard microbiological techniques, and microbial identification was performed with an automated identification system. Microbial growth was detected in more than half of the collected samples. The highest contamination levels were observed on laboratory surfaces without direct cadaver contact, particularly laboratory coats, student desks, door handles, and electrical switches. Lower contamination rates were identified in samples obtained from formaldehyde-preserved cadavers and frozen cadavers, suggesting that preservative methods reduce but do not completely eliminate microbial survival. Dry bone materials demonstrated comparatively higher microbial colonization. Frequently isolated microorganisms included Staphylococcus aureus , Staphylococcus epidermidis , Bacillus subtilis , Enterococcus faecalis , and several enteric bacteria, while fungal species such as Candida albicans and Aspergillus flavus were also identified. These findings demonstrate that microbiological contamination in anatomy laboratories extends beyond cadavers and may spread through environmental surfaces and shared materials. Regular disinfection, appropriate ventilation, and consistent use of personal protective equipment are therefore critical for maintaining biosafety in anatomy education environments.
authors: Elif Emre; Zülal Aşçı Toraman; Murat Ögetürk; Yasemin Bulut

title: Microfluidic Extraction of Extracellular Vesicle-Associated Nucleic Acids for Downstream Molecular Analysis
abstract: Aim To develop a microfluidic workflow for extracting extracellular vesicle (EV)-associated nucleic acids (NAs) from biofluids, such as blood plasma and serum, for downstream molecular analysis. Methods Healthy serum and plasma samples were spiked with EVs obtained from Hec-1-A cells carrying defined mutations and characterized in accordance with MISEV guidelines. The spiked samples were then processed using either the standard centrifugation-based ExoGAG protocol or a microfluidic workflow. The latter combines ExoGAG mediated aggregation of EVs with mechanical entrapment of the resulting EV aggregates in a microfluidic filtration device (EVNA-chip). The retained material was washed and on-chip lysed to release its NA cargo. NAs were subsequently purified using a commercial silica column, producing an output suitable for molecular analysis through droplet digital PCR (ddPCR). Results The EVNA-chip recovery yield was 42.0 ± 4.28% and 38.1 ± 1.46% for double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) and microRNA respectively. The recovered dsDNA remained compatible with ddPCR detection of the KRAS p.G12D variant (c.35G>A) and with the assessment of MSI-associated alterations using BAT25, BAT26, NR21, NR24, and MONO27. The method was demonstrated for pilot cohort of patients with endometrial cancer. The RNA workflow supported reverse transcription and was demonstrated for the quantification of miR-X, a potential marker of Fabry disease, using patient samples and healthy controls. Conclusion Although recovery was lower than with the standard protocol, the centrifugation-free EVNA- chip workflow demonstrates the compatibility of the method with downstream NA molecular analyses and is advantageous for the development of an integrated, automated platform for EV-based liquid biopsy applications.

title: Mitochondrial background and tissue-specific heteroplasmy in relation to clinical features of patients with diabetes
abstract: Introduction Mitochondrial diabetes is a rare syndromic form of monogenic diabetes whose clinical presentation resembles that of the more common, polygenic forms of diabetes. We characterized the mitochondrial genetic background, clinical spectrum and tissue-specific heteroplasmy in Polish patients with suspected monogenic diabetes. Methods Next-generation sequencing of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) was performed in 496 patients referred with suspected monogenic diabetes and negative nuclear DNA testing. The clinical analysis included 53 individuals from 31 families. In 30 m.3243A>G carriers, heteroplasmy was quantified in urine sediment and buccal swabs, and longitudinally, at two time points, in peripheral blood. Results Pathogenic mtDNA variants were identified in 21/496 patients (diagnostic yield 4.23%), most frequently m.3243A>G (17/21). Three further probands carried rare mitochondrial tRNA variants of uncertain clinical significance, two of them in MT-TL2 . No significant association between heteroplasmy in any tissue and specific clinical features was demonstrated, although statistical power was limited. A clear tissue hierarchy was observed (p < 0.0001): mean heteroplasmy was highest in urine sediment (60.7%), followed by buccal swabs (39.1%) and blood (21.6%). Blood heteroplasmy decreased with age by 0.58% per year (linear mixed-effects model, p < 0.0001). Conclusions Urine sediment appears to be the most informative material for assessing heteroplasmy. Analysis of blood alone may be insufficient to establish the genetic basis of mitochondrial diabetes, particularly in older patients. The recurrent identification of rare MT-TL2 variants in patients with diabetes warrants further functional studies of this gene. These findings have direct implications for diagnostic algorithms, genetic counseling, and clinical follow-up.
authors: Sebastian Skoczylas; Tomasz Płoszaj; Ewa Zmysłowska-Polakowska; Katarzyna Piekarska; Julia Grzybowska-Adamowicz; Agnieszka Zmysłowska

title: Molecular Detection of Human Cytomegalovirus in Patients with Recurrent Respiratory Tract Infections
abstract: Recurrent LRTIs are a recurring clinical and diagnostic conundrum in paediatric and adult pulmonary medicine, often leading to chronic, progressive decreases in respiratory function and/or cumulative parenchymal damage. Human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) is well known as an opportunistic pathogen in classical immunosuppressed conditions but recently, local reactivation of the virus in the lower respiratory tract of patients with chronic pulmonary inflammation without the presence of the classical type of immunodeficiency is increasingly suggested as a possible mechanism. This prospective cross-sectional observational study was carried out to assess the molecular detection and viral load of HCMV DNA in lower respiratory tract specimens in relation to matched plasma specimens, quantify local inflammatory markers (interleukin 6 and tumor necrosis factor alpha) and detect co-infecting viral/bacterial pathogens. One hundred and twenty (120) patients with documented recurrent lower respiratory tract infection (LRTI) were evaluated by diagnostic bronchoscopy or deep tissue samples of lower respiratory tract. Alongside the quantitative microbiology and cytokine immunoassays, automated nucleic acid extraction and real-time quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) were done. HCMV DNA was identified in 41.7% (50/120) of lower respiratory tract specimens, while plasma DNAemia was only found in 12.5% (15/120); this is characteristic of a compartmentalized pulmonary shedding profile. Local interleukin 6 levels were significantly elevated in endobronchial HCMV detection as compared to HCMV negative patients. The present study results suggest that HCMV shedding in the lungs is common during recurrent RTIs and that the use of direct molecular quantification of HCMV in lower respiratory samples should be considered as a tool to make clinical decisions, not only serological and plasma based.
authors: Suad Hammood Al Bashar
venue: European Multidisciplinary Journal of Modern Science

title: Molecular detection of lumpy skin disease virus in cattle nasal swabs using P32 gene-targeted PCR in Cauvery Delta region, Tamilnadu
abstract: Lumpy skin disease (LSD) poses a considerable challenge to cattle health and livestock production. Reliable laboratory diagnosis is essential for the investigation of suspected cases and effective disease monitoring. The present investigation focused on the molecular identification of lumpy skin disease virus in nasal swab samples obtained from cattle in the Cauvery Delta region of Tamil Nadu, India by targeting the P32 gene. A total of 25 nasal swab samples were processed for genomic DNA isolation using the DNeasy Blood & Tissue Kit (QIAGEN, Germany). The extracted DNA was subsequently examined by conventional polymerase chain reaction (PCR) employing primers specific to the selected P32 gene region which was expected to produce an amplicon of approximately 192 bp. The amplification products were subjected to agarose gel electrophoresis for the detection of the target fragment. Among the 20 specimens tested, 18 exhibited amplification at the expected product size accounting for 90% PCR positivity. The findings demonstrate the presence of P32-targeted gene in suspected samples collected from cattle in the study area.
authors: Azhagarasi Shanmugam; Lurthu Reetha Thomas; Manickam Ramasamy; Selvaraj Jayaraman; Shanmuganathan Subramaniyan
venue: International Journal of Advanced Biochemistry Research

title: Molecular detection of respiratory viruses from breath samples: Evaluation of nucleic acid extraction systems and PCR panels
abstract: Background Reliable and scalable molecular testing is essential for risk assessment and monitoring of respiratory viruses with epidemic or pandemic potential. The AveloMask Kit (Avelo) is a non-invasive sampling device that collects exhaled breath aerosols (XBA) using a high-performance filter, which can be released into a stabilizing buffer for nucleic acid preservation. Detection of viral nucleic acids in breath samples remains challenging, as viral loads are typically lower than in conventional upper-respiratory swabs. Therefore, optimizing extraction and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) workflows is critical to maximizing analytical sensitivity. Methods In this proof-of-concept study, we compared the nucleic acid extraction efficiency of ELITe InGenius® (ELITech) and QIAsymphony (Qiagen) automated platforms in combination with an in-house real-time quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) panel and a commercial PCR panel (RespiFinder® 2Smart, Pathofinder). Using synthetic ribonucleic acid (RNA) standards, we determined the limit of detection (LOD) for severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), influenza A, influenza B, and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) as a performance indicator for both extraction platforms and PCR panels. As proof-of-concept, we analyzed seven XBA samples from infected individuals, eight from healthy controls, and one from a person recovering from a cold. Results Our results demonstrate that ELITe InGenius and QIAsymphony provide comparable extraction efficiencies without negatively impacting downstream RT-qPCR. The combination of QIAsymphony and RespiFinder 2Smart achieved LODs below 100 viral copies/mL and detected all pathogens in clinical XBA samples (7/7) that were also detected in matched swabs. Conclusions These initial findings suggest the compatibility of high-throughput extraction systems and PCR panels with XBA samples collected using AveloMask and warrant further investigation of XBA sampling as a non-invasive method for respiratory virus detection.

title: Multicentre Evaluation of Loop-Mediated Isothermal Amplification (LAMP) for Environmental Monitoring of Nosocomial Pathogens in Italian Hospitals.
abstract:
Background

Environmental contamination of hospital surfaces, especially in high-risk clinical areas, partly sustains healthcare-associated infections. The detection of microbiological contamination in hospital settings using culture-based methods remains fundamental, even though these methods are not rapid, show moderate sensitivity in areas with low microbial loads, and are unsuitable for some microbial species. This multicentre study evaluated the performance of loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) for the rapid detection of major nosocomial pathogens on hospital surfaces.

Methods

A multicentre observational method-comparison study was conducted in three Italian hospital centres. Overall, 298 environmental surface samples were collected from clinical areas included in local infection-prevention monitoring plans. For each sampling point, LAMP swab sampling was paired with an adjacent contact plate culture. LAMP assays targeted Staphylococcus aureus, Acinetobacter baumannii, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Manual and automated nucleic acid extraction workflows were analysed separately. Diagnostic performance, agreement metrics, and discordant paired results were assessed using a contact plate culture as the microbiological comparator.

Results

No LAMP-negative/RODAC-positive pairs were observed. Positive percent agreement (PPA) relative to contact plate culture was therefore 100% in the subgroups evaluated. Relative specificity ranged from 90.9% to 98.6%, while overall accuracy ranged from 93.8% to 98.6%. Discordant results were exclusively LAMP-positive/contact plate-negative and were more frequent for S. aureus and P. aeruginosa. Selective culture verification supported several LAMP-positive findings not recovered by routine contact plates.

Conclusions

LAMP showed high negative agreement, high specificity, and rapid target-specific detection of selected nosocomial pathogens on hospital surfaces. It may complement conventional cultures in environmental surveillance, particularly when timely feedback is needed to guide infection-prevention and sanitation-monitoring strategies.

title: Multidimensional Tracing of Error Sources and Structured Corrective Strategies for Leukocyte Count and Differential on Automated Hematology Analyzers
abstract: Leukocyte count and differential are core indicators for clinical infection assessment, hematological disease diagnosis, and therapeutic monitoring. Currently, clinical testing heavily relies on automated hematology analyzers. Influenced by factors such as specimen characteristics, limited analyzer recognition capability, and improper manual operations, automated testing often produces unreliable results, interfering with clinical decision-making and threatening patient safety. Existing studies remain fragmented, lacking a multidimensional error-tracing framework and practical corrective strategies covering the entire testing workflow. A narrative review was conducted to summarize the causes, identification methods, and corrective strategies for unreliable leukocyte results. Relevant literature up to August 2026 was searched in PubMed/MEDLINE and CNKI. We categorized multidimensional error sources into specimen-related interferents, leukocyte morphological and developmental abnormalities, and preanalytical or systematic factors, and established a practical diagnostic workflow spanning from anomaly recognition to result reporting. By incorporating both legacy and current analytical systems, we compared the characteristic scattergram patterns of various interferents across analyzers with different detection principles, broadening the applicability to diverse clinical laboratories. To better ensure the reliability of corrective strategies and provide diverse alternative options, we not only summarized widely accepted routine practices but also included case-based experimental methods. The proposed multidimensional error-tracing system and practical diagnostic workflow significantly improve analytical accuracy and reduce clinical risks. However, current hematology analyzers cannot automatically identify or correct complex interferences. Future systems must integrate multi-platform advantages, optimize complex cell recognition capabilities, and enrich multidimensional scattergram information to overcome existing analytical limitations. Furthermore, integrating artificial intelligence technology holds immense potential to drive automated hematology analysis toward a more intelligent and precise direction.
authors: Ping Deng; Lianhui Yu; Haoting Zhan; Lin Zheng; Yipei Jing; J. Fang; Min Zhang; Wei Wu

title: Nanomedicine-Enhanced CAR-Engineered Immunotherapy for Lung Cancer: Focusing on Multimodal Strategies and Precision Therapy
abstract: Lung cancer remains a major therapeutic challenge because of its molecular and antigenic heterogeneity, rapid evolution, treatment resistance, and immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). Although chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy has transformed the treatment of hematological malignancies, its efficacy in lung cancer remains constrained by antigen heterogeneity, poor tumor trafficking and infiltration, T-cell dysfunction, suppressive stromal and myeloid compartments, manufacturing complexity, and pulmonary on-target off-tumor toxicity. Nanomedicine offers a versatile platform to address these barriers by improving CAR-T manufacturing and functional fitness, enabling targeted delivery of nucleic acids and immunomodulators, remodeling the TME, enhancing local accumulation and controlled activation, and supporting transient in situ generation of CAR-engineered immune cells. This review integrates these advances within a Route-Antigen-Microenvironment-Programming (RAMP) framework and emphasizes the mechanistic interdependence among delivery route, target selection, local tumor ecology, and CAR generation and control. We examine the antigen landscapes of non-small-cell and small-cell lung cancer and propose a quantitative framework for antigen selection that incorporates antigen density, spatial and temporal heterogeneity, normal-tissue safety, and engineering compensability. We further discuss nanotechnology-assisted manufacturing, cell-surface nanobackpacks, tumor preconditioning, local biomaterial reservoirs, in vivo CAR programming, pulmonary delivery, multimodal therapy, and theranostic monitoring. Most nano-enabled approaches are still supported primarily by preclinical studies or evidence from non-lung-cancer settings, underscoring the need for standardized assessment of biodistribution, reproducibility, immunogenicity, pulmonary safety, and long-term material fate. Integrating quantitative antigen profiling with biodegradable and controllable materials and lung-relevant translational models may help advance CAR-engineered immunotherapy toward a spatially controlled, dynamically monitored, and personalized therapeutic platform for lung cancer.
authors: Xianye He; Jiao He; Zhongsong Zhang; Yuanyin Teng; Bing Wang; Hao Sun; Xiang Deng; Junjun Xiong; Yuzhuo Huang

title: Needle-based Confocal Laser Endomicroscopy (nCLE) for Tool-in-Lesion Confirmation in Cone-Beam CT-guided Navigation Bronchoscopy: a Prospective Concordance Study
abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE: Positioning sampling instruments within pulmonary nodules remains a challenge during navigation bronchoscopy. Cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) and needle-based confocal laser endomicroscopy (nCLE) enable tool positioning feedback. However, access to CBCT systems is limited and associated with radiation exposure. To date, no direct comparison between these two modalities has been reported. This study compares CBCT and nCLE for sampling tool position in navigation bronchoscopy for peripheral pulmonary nodules (PPNs). METHODS: Twenty-five patients with PPNs scheduled for CBCT-guided navigation bronchoscopy were prospectively enrolled. nCLE imaging, CBCT image acquisition and needle aspiration were performed twice for each nodule, followed by (cryo)biopsies. nCLE videos were evaluated using validated criteria and categorized as tool-in-lesion (TIL) or tool-out-lesion (TOL). CBCT scans were classified as TIL, tool-in-contact (TIC), or TOL. RESULTS: nCLE imaging was performed in 24 patients (nodule was not reached in one), with a median nodule diameter of 19 mm, yielding good-quality images in 22/24 patients (92%). In 77% of these cases, there was an agreement between nCLE and CBCT on the needle position. There were no cases in which CBCT confirmed TIL while nCLE did not. From the five discrepant cases, four were TIC on CBCT, while nCLE was TOL. In one case, there was a complete discrepancy between the techniques with nCLE as TIL and CBCT TOL. CONCLUSION: nCLE and CBCT offer complementary tool position information, with nCLE delivering microscopic-level insights and CBCT providing three-dimensional anatomical context. In environments where CBCT is not available, nCLE may serve as an alternative.
authors: Saskia van Heumen; Onno M. Mets; Daniel M de Bruin; Peter I Bonta; Johannes M A Daniels; Marjolein A. Heuvelmans; Jouke T Annema

title: Non-Diagnostic Does Not Mean Non-Malignant: Outcomes and Predictors of Malignancy Following Nondiagnostic Robotic-Assisted Bronchoscopy.
