title: Non-Imaging Optical Tactile Sensors for Robotics: Transduction Principles, System Integration, and Robotic Applications
abstract: Non-imaging optical tactile sensors encode contact through changes in optical intensity, wavelength, spectra, or photon counts, offering diverse architectures for robotic touch. Their usefulness depends on whether contact variables can be reliably distinguished from coupled mechanical and environmental effects, and whether the resulting information can be delivered in time to guide action. This review develops a unified framework linking mechanical load transmission, optical encoding, readout, and tactile inference to robotic task requirements. It examines reflective and waveguide-based devices, micro/nanofibers, fiber gratings, interferometric and resonant structures, and mechanoluminescent composites. Three considerations emerge across these approaches. First, high optical sensitivity supports accurate tactile estimation only when target variables remain identifiable under the relevant contact and calibration conditions. Second, spatial coverage and feedback timing must be assessed at the system level, accounting for multiplexing, acquisition, demodulation, and inference. Third, device characterization, offline recognition, and closed-loop robotic performance provide distinct levels of evidence and require different evaluation criteria. Representative studies illustrate how these considerations shape force estimation, contact localization, slip correction and distributed interaction. This review concludes with priorities for calibration transfer, reliable interfaces, scalable readout, and task-based validation, providing a basis for selecting and developing non-imaging optical tactile architectures for robotics.
authors: Hao Wu; Yu Feng; Haotian Guo; Huichan Zhao; Changsheng Wu; Jianshu Zhou

title: Optimizing cfRNA Liquid Biopsy Analysis: Systematic Evaluation of Blood Collection Tubes and Small RNA-seq Workflow for Cell-free RNA Profiling
abstract: Introduction: Liquid biopsy is a powerful, minimally invasive approach for the detection of multiple biomarkers in blood – including cell-free RNA (cfRNA) from plasma. An important aspect of reproducible cfRNA research is managing preanalytical variability that is highly dependent on sample collection and stabilization conditions.
authors: Markus Wolf; Ioanna Andreou; Samuel J. Rulli; Anita Davla; Thorsten Voß

title: Patient Experience with Phlebotomy and Laboratory Testing at a University Hospital: A Mixed-Methods Exploratory Study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Patient satisfaction with the phlebotomy center or the laboratory in general is often only infrequently measured in single touchpoint surveys. In addition, patient complaints are scarce and patients rarely proactively provide feedback by themselves. The aim of this single-center study was to explore patient satisfaction and perceived improvement opportunities regarding phlebotomy and laboratory testing at a university hospital phlebotomy center. METHODS: We conducted a mixed-methods study combining survey data (including Net Promoter Score [NPS] and Customer Effort Score [CES], n = 109) and semi-structured interviews with 8 patients frequently visiting the phlebotomy center. RESULTS: In the survey, 34.9% of the respondents were promoters, 53.2% were passives, and 7.3% were detractors, resulting in an NPS of 27.6%. The median CES was 1 (interquartile range 1-2), indicating low perceived effort. Interview findings suggested that while the service was considered well-organized, "waiting"-rather than the phlebotomy procedure itself-emerged as the most important theme. Key recommendations included reducing waiting times, improving the waiting area, providing more instructions on the phlebotomy process, offering reliable online information on laboratory tests and results, and facilitating phlebotomy close to home. While most recommendations addressed functional needs, some also targeted emotional needs (e.g., free coffee, private seating). CONCLUSIONS: This mixed method study illustrates how involving patients in examining the laboratory-related patient journey can yield concrete, patient-reported insights and suggestions for improvement. Implementing recommendations derived by open-ended survey responses and interviews is likely to improve the patient journey, on both functional and emotional levels.
authors: Wendy P. J. den Elzen; Maurits C F J de Rotte; Marjorie G G Rosheuvel; Helena Chon; Judith M. E. P. Gillis; Wilfred Achthoven; Róbert de Jonge
venue: The Journal of Applied Laboratory Medicine

title: Persistent gut microbiota alterations after ischemic stroke are modifiable by probiotic intervention
abstract: SUMMARY The gut-brain axis has emerged as a critical modulator in neurological diseases, including stroke. While acute post-stroke dysbiosis is well established, it remains unclear whether these alterations persist long-term and can be therapeutically modulated. This study addresses this gap through integrated metagenomic and metabolomic profiling in two independent clinical stroke cohorts, complemented by experimental models. Experimental stroke induced persistent changes in gut microbiota composition and altered short-chain fatty acid profiles. In patients, microbiota composition remained distinct from controls up to three months after ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack (TIA), accompanied by persistent reductions in propionic and valeric acid and reduced abundance of Prevotella -associated microbial signatures. We performed a randomized, double-blind interventional trial (PRISE) testing a multispecies probiotic versus placebo, using household members as additional controls. Probiotic intervention led to microbiome compositional changes with increased abundance of beneficial taxa and significantly improved functional recovery. The tested probiotic strains showed anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects in vitro. These findings suggest that targeted modulation of the microbiome represents a promising therapeutic avenue to improve chronic stroke recovery, warranting validation in larger Phase III clinical trials.
authors: Philip William Melton; Adam Sorbie; Velma Tea Essi Aho; Christina Haslinger; Maili Zimmermann; Wiola Marut; Christian Jaeger; Paul Wilmes; Corinne Benakis; Arthur Liesz

title: Pilot Evaluation of Saliva Samples as An Alternative to Blood for Large-scale Whole-genome Sequencing Studies
abstract: Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) studies have traditionally relied on blood as the primary DNA source and manual workflows. As population-based genomics studies expand, minimally invasive and easily deployable biospecimen collection methods compatible with high-throughput automation are increasingly needed. In this pilot study, we established a real-world, end-to-end automated WGS workflow, encompassing robotic DNA extraction, library preparation, sequencing and quality control. We compared saliva- and blood-derived WGS across key analytical parameters, including performance at each step of the workflow, overall cost, and feasibility for future large-scale implementation. First, germline variant calls from saliva and blood samples showed high concordance, reaching 97% genome-wide and over 99% in high-confidence genomic regions. Second, key workflow metrics, including DNA quality and sequencing quality, were comparable between saliva and blood samples, while saliva samples had a lower per-sample cost. We compared three commercially available saliva collection kits and found that all achieved at least 95% genome-wide concordance with matched blood samples, with differences primarily driven by cost. Finally, automated saliva processing produced sequencing and short variant calling metrics broadly comparable to manual processing in a small paired comparison. Collectively, these results provide a practical and scalable solution for incorporating saliva into future large cohort sequencing studies. Larger and more diverse studies are needed to further validate the robustness and generalizability of this pilot study.
authors: Susu Qu; Ruijun Meng; Ran Wu; Yi Shao; Xinshuang Zhang; Yi Wei; Jingxuan Zhang; Lu Yang; Min Li; Li Zhang

title: Platelet-Based Blood Products in Bovine and Equine Medicine: A Systematic Scoping Review of Blood Collection, Preparation Methods, and Reporting Completeness
abstract: Platelet-based blood products, including platelet-rich plasma, platelet concentrate, and platelet lysate, are increasingly investigated in veterinary medicine as biological preparations with proposed regenerative, anti-inflammatory, and immunomodulatory properties. In bovine and equine medicine, their use has expanded across several clinical fields, but blood collection and product preparation methods have not been systematically synthesized. This systematic scoping review aimed to describe the literature on platelet-based blood products in bovine and equine medicine, summarize methodological characteristics of blood collection and preparation methods, and analyze studies addressing bovine mammary disorders. Searches were performed in Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, CAB Abstracts, and PubMed on 25 August 2026, with no publication-year or start-date restriction. Eligible studies were original peer-reviewed articles in English; fibrin- or gel-based preparations were excluded when the corresponding liquid platelet-based product could not be separately characterized or evaluated, as were scaffold or combined constructs when the platelet-based component could not be evaluated separately. No formal review protocol was registered or published. Studies providing eligible bovine and/or equine data and reporting at least one methodological aspect related to collection, preparation, activation or lysis, storage, characterization, or administration were eligible. A total of 191 studies were included. Studies contributing equine data only among the target species predominated (161/191; 84.3%), whereas 29 studies (15.2%) contributed bovine data only and one study (0.5%) included both bovine and equine data. The PRP family, including PRP and related PRP-type preparations, was the most frequently investigated product group (134/191; 70.2%), followed by platelet lysate (46/191; 24.1%) and platelet concentrate (19/191; 9.9%); categories were not mutually exclusive. Methods varied in donor source, collection site, blood volume, anticoagulant, collection system, centrifugation workflow, activation or lysis, storage, and characterization. The main blood collection and preparation workflow was reconstructable in 111 studies (58.1%) and partially reconstructable in 80 studies (41.9%). Methodological reporting was frequently incomplete, particularly for leukocyte concentration, activation or lysis procedures, storage conditions, and product-level sterility or microbiological quality control. Product-level sterility or microbiological quality control was explicitly reported in 7 studies (3.7%) and partially reported in one study (0.5%). Only five studies addressed bovine mammary disorders and investigated methodologically distinct products. More complete and consistent methodological reporting is needed to improve reproducibility and comparability across studies.
authors: Filippo Rigo; Caterina Marcon; Margherita Soncin; Flaviana Gottardo

title: Portable Hand Vein Finder System Based on Near-Infrared Illumination
abstract: Vein visualisation is critical in medical procedures such as venipuncture, where accurate identification of superficial veins can help reduce patient discomfort and procedural failure. However, conventional vein identification relies largely on visual inspection and palpation, which may be challenging in cases of difficult venous access. Near-infrared (NIR) imaging provides a non-invasive approach to enhancing the visibility of superficial veins beneath the skin. This study presents the development of a portable NIR vein visualisation system using a 64-bit Raspberry Pi, a modified HBVCAM GC0308 camera, twelve 850 nm NIR LEDs, and a TFT LCD. The system captures NIR images of the hand, processes them using image enhancement techniques implemented on the Raspberry Pi, and displays the resulting vein patterns in real time. A rechargeable 5 V power bank provides portable power. Experimental evaluation demonstrated that the system successfully visualised superficial veins in different anatomical regions and among participants with different skin pigmentation conditions. Higher vein contrast was generally observed in participants with light skin, while vein patterns remained distinguishable, although with relatively lower contrast, in participants with dark skin. The system achieved real-time image acquisition and processing, producing clear vein images without noticeable processing delays. The developed prototype demonstrates the feasibility of a compact and portable NIR-based approach to superficial vein visualisation. Its relatively simple hardware configuration and use of commercially available components offer potential for a cost-effective solution to assist venipuncture procedures. Further improvements in camera technology and image processing could enhance its performance and support future clinical and educational applications.
authors: Najat Boufa; Aboubakr Ammar; Aziza Qashout; Salma AlKadaa
venue: AlQalam Journal of Medical and Applied Sciences

title: Potassium EDTA Contamination Causing Preanalytical Errors in Canine and Feline Serum Samples.
abstract:
Background

Contamination of serum samples with the anticoagulant potassium ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (kEDTA) constitutes a critical pre-analytical error in veterinary diagnostics and can lead to potentially life-threatening misinterpretation of biochemical test results.

Objectives

To develop and validate a method for quantifying EDTA in canine and feline sera. A second aim was to evaluate the effect and prevalence of kEDTA contamination in canine and feline serum samples.

Methods

A copper-PAN-based automated method for quantifying EDTA in canine and feline sera was developed. Canine and feline serum samples admitted together with EDTA tubes were analyzed for kEDTA contamination.

Results

The measuring range was set to 0.03-0.4 mM, with a coefficient of variation of < 13.1% and acceptable linearity upon dilution (75%-118%). Spiking experiments demonstrated that kEDTA caused a dose-dependent increase in potassium and decreases in calcium, magnesium, iron, and zinc, with iron and zinc most profoundly affected. The allowable total error was exceeded at low kEDTA concentrations, even when analytes remained within reference intervals. A prevalence study of 1065 serum samples submitted with kEDTA tubes revealed contamination rates of 1.1% in dogs and 1.8% in cats.

Conclusions

These findings emphasize that even small amounts of kEDTA can compromise diagnostic accuracy. This underscores the importance of strict compliance with recommended blood collection order and highlights the value of direct EDTA measurements in veterinary laboratory diagnostics.
authors: Strage EM, Larsson A, Hillström A, Eriksson G, Olausson J.

title: Pre-analytical Performance of TAG FLEX-LB Tubes in Detecting and Stabilizing Proteins Compared to Standard Blood Collection Tubes
abstract: Background & Aim: Pre-analytical variability remains a critical bottleneck in liquid biopsy workflows, affecting the integrity of both circulating nucleic acids and protein-based biomarkers. While specialized blood collection tubes (BCTs) are increasingly optimized for circulating cell-free DNA (cfDNA), maintaining protein stability and preventing cellular lysis—which leads to endogenous protein contamination such as hemoglobin—is vital. This study aims to evaluate whether the proprietary TAG FLEX-LB (TFLB) stabilization reagent can successfully detect and stabilize proteins like hemoglobin, IL-6, TGF-β1, and Bradykinin compared to standard BCT alternatives.
authors: Emily Medina; Tony Baker

title: Precision of the Advia 2120 for the complete blood count of African elephants (Loxodonta africana)
abstract: Elephant leukocytes exhibit distinctive morphologic features, including unique heterophils and monocytes, which pose a particular challenge for automated CBC analysis. Therefore, most automated analyzers cannot correctly identify elephant leukocytes. Many zoologic institutions have turned to manual methods for elephant leukocyte differential count, but these methods are prone to error and are time-consuming. The Advia 2120, a flow cytometry automated hematology analyzer, has the advantage of offering preprogrammed species-specific cell-gating parameters that should allow for correct cell differentiation. This study aimed to evaluate the precision (within run and between run) of the Advia 2120 for use in captive African elephants (Loxodonta africana). Whole blood samples were collected in K2 EDTA from three healthy adult female African elephants. Repeatability and reproducibility were excellent for most variables. Coefficients of variation were >10% for absolute reticulocyte counts, eosinophil counts, and basophil counts, which is expected with cell types that appear in low numbers in peripheral blood. Future studies investigating the accuracy of the Advia 2120 in elephants are necessary.
authors: Samantha J. Cohen; Francisco O. Conrado; Joyce S. Knoll; Marjorie Bercier
venue: Journal of Zoo and Wildlife Medicine

title: Protocol for the Assessment of Endogenous Platelet-Associated Tissue Factor-Dependent Thrombin Generation in Human Platelets Using the Calibrated Automated Thrombogram.
abstract: Platelet-associated Tissue Factor (TF) is increasingly recognized as a functionally active determinant of platelet procoagulant activity, enabling platelets to initiate and sustain thrombin generation beyond their established role as a phospholipid surface for coagulation factor assembly. However, its specific functional assessment remains challenging, as conventional Calibrated Automated Thrombogram (CAT) assays rely on exogenous TF to trigger thrombin generation, thereby masking the endogenous contribution of platelet-associated TF. Here, we describe a Calibrated Automated Thrombogram (CAT)-based workflow that enables the selective assessment of TF-dependent thrombin generation in isolated intact human platelets under conditions that preserve the contribution of endogenous platelet-associated TF. The protocol integrates key methodological steps, including inhibition of contact pathway activation through the use of microvesicle-free plasma pool containing a contact pathway inhibitor, normalization of the procoagulant membrane surface by exogenous phospholipids, and functional validation through neutralizing antibodies against TF and Tissue Factor Pathway Inhibitor (TFPI). The workflow also addresses key pre-analytical variables related to blood collection and platelet-rich plasma (PRP) preparation. Under these controlled conditions, thrombin generation kinetics -particularly LagTime- reflect the functional activity of platelet-associated TF, as demonstrated by their modulation upon TF and TFPI inhibition and their association with TF<sup>pos</sup>-platelets levels measured by flow cytometry. By avoiding the addition of exogenous TF, this approach overcomes key methodological limitations that have contributed to the ongoing controversy surrounding platelet-associated TF, providing a functional readout that complements antigen-based measurements. This protocol therefore represents a robust and reproducible framework for investigating platelet-associated TF in both mechanistic and clinical studies.
authors: Camera M, Becchetti A, Brambilla M, Valle PD, Giesen PLA, Tremoli E.

title: Pulmonary Sarcoidosis Mimicking Multifocal Adenocarcinoma: An Atypical Radiologic and Diagnostic Dilemma
abstract: Known as “the great mimic,” sarcoidosis often poses a diagnostic challenge. Although common radiological manifestations include hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy and micronodules, atypical patterns can also be encountered, requiring awareness of the disease’s potential radiological manifestations to allow for prompt diagnosis and management. We report a case of sarcoidosis presenting with predominant ground-glass opacities (GGOs) on high-resolution CT (HRCT) of the chest, mimicking adenocarcinoma in situ. The diagnosis was established by histopathology after other causes of pulmonary GGOs had been excluded. This report highlights the importance of maintaining a high degree of clinical suspicion and pursuing a comprehensive workup, including tissue diagnosis, even in minimally symptomatic patients.
authors: Aya Gohar; Alaa Hmeedan; Ashraf Saeed; JEHAD J AZAR; Muhammad Naeem

title: Real-time Volumetric Imaging for Minimally-Invasive Thoracic Interventions: A Deformable Phantom Study
abstract: Objectives This study aimed to evaluate the ability of VoxelMap, a deep learning framework for 3D respiratory motion estimation, to generate volumetric images in real-time from 2D projections acquired for two deformable lung phantoms on a clinical interventional C-arm angiography system. Materials and Methods VoxelMap was evaluated using the PixelPrint 4D and Casper deformable physical thoracic respiratory phantoms. Four-dimensional cone-beam CT (4D CBCT) images acquired on a clinical fixed-room C-arm angiography system were used for network training and volumetric ground truth. Prediction accuracy was evaluated on withheld respiratory phases using structural similarity index measure (SSIM) and peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR). Model inference time was measured to assess suitability for continuous real-time processing. Deep ensembles were also used to assess model uncertainty. Correlation between ensemble uncertainty and prediction error was evaluated for both phantoms. Results VoxelMap achieved high prediction accuracy across withheld respiratory phases in both physical phantoms. SSIM values exceeded 0.92 in all experiments, with a higher performance observed for the Casper phantom (0.969-0.973) than for the PixelPrint 4D phantom (0.927-0.943). Model inference times were less than 15 ms for both phantoms which is compatible with real-time processing. Ensemble uncertainty was positively correlated with prediction error in both phantoms, indicating that higher uncertainty was associated with less accurate volumetric predictions. Conclusions Our study demonstrated that VoxelMap generates accurate volumetric deformations of respiratory anatomy from projections acquired on a clinical interventional C-arm system, with computational inference times compatible with continuous processing. By deriving volumetric information directly from two-dimensional fluoroscopic projections, VoxelMap has the potential to augment continuous fluoroscopic guidance with continuously updated volumetric information. Ensemble uncertainty may provide a potentially useful indicator of prediction reliability. Further studies using clinically representative training data and patient studies is required to establish clinical utility. Our code is available at https://github.com/Image-X-Institute/Voxelmap .
authors: Alexander S Lin; Alen Biju; Allen R. Goode; Jessica Y. Im; Peter Benjamin Noël; Magdalena Bazalova‐Carter; Tess Reynolds; Nicholas Hindley

title: Real-world outcomes of navigational bronchoscopy for peripheral pulmonary lesions: a single centre analysis of demographics and PDL1 specimen adequacy
abstract: Background Electromagnetic navigational bronchoscopy (ENB) is a minimally invasive technique that improves diagnostic access to peripheral pulmonary lesions (PPLs) while maintaining a favourable safety profile. Recent evidence has demonstrated non-inferior diagnostic accuracy compared with transthoracic needle biopsy,1 with significantly fewer complications. However, real-world data on diagnostic performance, safety, and suitability for molecular testing remain limited. Aim To evaluate the diagnostic yield, safety profile, and molecular adequacy of ENB for PPLs in a tertiary referral centre. Methods A retrospective review was performed of all ENB procedures undertaken using the Medtronic Illumisite™ navigation platform between 2023 and 2025. Data collected included patient demographics, lesion characteristics, diagnostic outcomes, complications, and adequacy for ancillary molecular studies. Results Fifty-two ENB procedures were performed. Most patients (86.5%, n=45) underwent ENB for suspected primary lung cancer. Lesions were predominantly located in the upper lobes (58%, n=30), with a mean diameter of 2.7cm ± 1.4SD. Overall diagnostic yield was 69.2% (36/52). Malignancy was diagnosed in 29 cases (55.8%), comprising 25 primary lung cancers and 4 other malignant lesions. Diagnostic yield was higher for lesions >20 mm than for lesions ≤20 mm (77.4% vs 60.9%). The overall complication rate was 5.8% (n=3), including Pneumothorax (3.8%), with one requiring chest drain insertion (1.9%) and one episode of bronchospasm (1.9%). No major procedure-related mortality occurred. 80% (n=20) of the primary lung cancers were non-small cell lung carcinoma (NSCLC), with adequate tissue for PD-L1 testing obtained in 90% of NSCLC cases (18/20). Six initially negative cases were subsequently confirmed as malignant following image-guided biopsy or surgical resection, yielding a sensitivity of 79.3%. Diagnostic performance improved over the study period, with diagnostic accuracy increasing from 66.7% in year 1 to 72.2% in year 3. Conclusion ENB demonstrated favourable diagnostic yield, low complication rates, and high molecular adequacy for PD-L1 testing. These findings support ENB as a safe and effective alternative to TTNB for the diagnosis of PPLs and its role in facilitating biomarker-driven lung cancer care. Reference Lentz RJ, et al. Navigational bronchoscopy or transthoracic needle biopsy for lung nodules. N Engl J Med. 2025;392:2100-2112. DOI: 10.1056/NEJMoa241405.
authors: EF Foley; DT Thong; DB Breen

title: Repurposing a commercial artificial intelligence vision platform for automated surgical instrument identification: a proof-of-concept study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Retained surgical items are classified as never events but continue to occur, and the count meant to prevent them is often recorded as correct even when an item is retained. Computer vision could provide an independent check on what is on the instrument table, but purpose-built surgical systems are scarce. Industrial vision platforms offer a faster route, although their surgical performance is unknown. METHODS: In a prospective experimental study, a commercial artificial intelligence vision platform developed for industrial inspection was applied to 19 surgical instruments and 3 suture items, each presented once in 100 runs (2,200 experiments). No software redesign was required, but the classifier had been trained on this item set, making this a supervised rather than a zero-shot setting. Two outcomes were recorded: whether the platform assigned the exact item identity, and whether it registered an item as present at the packing step irrespective of type, termed count-presence detection. Because experiments are clustered within items and runs, the primary estimate is the mean per-item accuracy with cluster-adjusted intervals. RESULTS: The correct instruments were identified in 2,036 of 2,200 experiments (92.5%). The mean per-item accuracy was 92.5% (95% confidence interval 88.4 to 96.7; cluster-adjusted 87.7 to 95.6). Count-presence detection was 99.1% (98.7 to 99.4). Performance was reproducible across runs (intraclass correlation 0.02), whereas variance clustered by item (0.12). Accuracy ranged from 64% (suture needle 6-0) to 100% (six items). Errors were directional and almost always within visually near-identical sub-types. CONCLUSIONS: An industrial vision platform detected item presence with high reliability and identified item type with high accuracy, however, with a residual error rate of 7.5%. The errors were predictable and confined to visually similar classes, pointing to correctable mitigations rather than a fundamental limit. These figures represent an upper bound under highly controlled conditions rather than expected intraoperative performance. Such a system is intended to support rather than replace the perioperative team. This study establishes feasibility rather than clinical benefit; a prospective intraoperative study is the necessary next step.
authors: Simon Stoerzer; Klinto Xhemo; Felix Gronau; Linda Feldbruegge; Philipp Felgendreff; Maximilian Kaltenecker; Jacques Hahn; Gerrit Grannas; Moritz Schmelzle

title: Risk-aware optimization in truck–drone humanitarian logistics: A systematic review and future research agenda
abstract: Humanitarian crises are escalating globally, with disaster-affected populations increasing by 23% annually. Yet traditional single-vehicle logistics systems fail catastrophically when infrastructure is compromised, creating life-threatening delays in critical supply delivery. While emerging truck-drone integrated systems show promise, existing research remains fragmented across disciplines, lacking systematic analysis of risk-aware optimization approaches and their real-world applicability. This study addresses two primary research objectives: (1) to develop a comprehensive taxonomy of mathematical models and solution methodologies for truck-drone humanitarian logistics, and (2) to quantify performance improvements and identify implementation barriers. A systematic review of 132 peer-reviewed papers from Scopus (2020–2026) was conducted using PRISMA methodology, complemented by bibliometric analysis of citation networks. The analysis reveals that hybrid solution approaches dominate the field (67 studies), with emergency response applications showing the strongest research focus (36 studies), though only about 40% report validation beyond purely simulated experiments. This review identifies three main contributions: a structured taxonomy of 15 distinct problem formulations and 8 solution categories, a quantitative benchmarking framework revealing performance trade-offs, and identification of critical research gaps in uncertainty modelling and stakeholder coordination. The results inform policy frameworks for regulatory approval while offering practitioners evidence-based counsel for decisions about technology adoption. This analysis lays the groundwork for more robust humanitarian logistics networks by advancing both theoretical knowledge and actual application of risk-aware truck-drone systems.
authors: Armin Mahmoodi; Kelechi C. Umeaka; Seyed Mojtaba Sajadi; Said M. Easa

title: Robot-Assisted Radical Cystectomy with Intracorporeal Urinary Diversion: Perioperative Management and Operative Technique
abstract: Radical cystectomy with bilateral pelvic lymphadenectomy and urinary diversion remains the standard of care for muscle-invasive bladder cancer and selected high-risk non-muscle-invasive disease. The procedure carries substantial morbidity, in part because the typical patient is elderly and burdened by cardiorespiratory comorbidity. Robot-assisted radical cystectomy (RARC) was developed to attenuate this morbidity, and RARC with intracorporeal urinary diversion (iRARC) avoids the laparotomy that earlier randomized trials required for extracorporeal reconstruction. In this technical narrative review, we present a single-institution operative approach to iRARC, distinguishing institutional practice from evidence-based recommendations. We describe patient selection, preoperative optimization and enhanced recovery, and provide a step-by-step account of our operative technique for male and female radical cystectomy, pelvic lymph node dissection template, and totally intracorporeal ileal conduit and orthotopic neobladder reconstruction. We also summarize the perioperative, oncological, and functional outcomes of iRARC, which support its role as a safe option with specific perioperative advantages in experienced, high-volume centers.
authors: Cristofer Zillo; Ashti M. Shah; Agustín Pérez-Londoño; Jinlei Li; Zyad James Carr; Fady Ghali; Wei Shen Tan

title: Robotic bronchoscopy delivery of optical ultrasound imaging for transbronchial lung biopsy guidance.
abstract: Accurate guidance for transbronchial pulmonary nodule biopsy requires visualisation of targets and tools beyond the airway wall, yet radial endobronchial ultrasound provides only a cross-sectional image orthogonal to the probe axis, and must be withdrawn before a tool is passed, leaving tissue acquisition unguided. Optical ultrasound (OpUS) imaging offers a miniaturised, fibre-based alternative that may enable image guidance from within the narrow distal bronchi. In this study, we evaluated the feasibility of OpUS imaging for endobronchial guidance by deploying a side-viewing, linearly actuated OpUS probe through a clinically available robotic bronchoscopy catheter, and assessed the corresponding imaging performance in separate bench-top experiments within an anatomically correct lung phantom containing airway structures and inclusions. Robotic integration was successful: the 1.8 mm outer-diameter OpUS probe could be delivered through the robotic catheter without visibly impairing catheter navigation, platform operation and probe delivery. The >2 m long probe maintained distal linear actuation through the catheter and tolerated catheter bending down to an estimated bend radius of approximately 5 mm before probe failure. The bench-top experiments confirmed how real-time OpUS imaging (4 Hz) could visualise the inclusion within the lung phantom from inside the airway lumen using a robotic bronchoscopy catheter. In addition, bench-top experiments on image guidance of needle insertions into phantoms confirmed that OpUS imaging is capable of clearly visualising the needle trajectory in settings matching the confined space of endobronchial interventions, supporting the great potential for OpUS image guidance of endobronchial lung biopsies.
authors: Shaoyan Zhang; Semyon Bodian; Nyma Nassren; Ashley K Hooi; Helena L Y Lam; Efthymios Maneas; Edward Z Zhang; Paul C Beard; Neal Navani; Ricky Thakrar; Richard J Colchester; Adrien E Desjardins; Erwin J Alles

title: Robotic bronchoscopy following prior non-diagnostic biopsy: diagnostic yield and malignancy detection in a salvage diagnostic cohort
abstract: Background Robotic-assisted bronchoscopy (RAB) is increasingly utilised for diagnosis of peripheral pulmonary nodules. However, its performance following prior unsuccessful or non-diagnostic biopsy remains poorly defined. We evaluated the diagnostic performance of RAB in lesions with previous failed biopsies and its effectiveness in detecting malignancy. Methods A retrospective analysis was performed of the first 271 RAB procedures over a three-month period at a tertiary interventional pulmonology centre, comprising 310 pulmonary nodules after exclusion of therapeutic procedures. Nodules were stratified into those with one or more prior failed or non-diagnostic biopsies (prior biopsy), and biopsy-naïve lesions. Primary outcomes were diagnostic yield per nodule determined using the American Thoracic Society DELPHI strict definition, and sensitivity for malignancy. Secondary outcomes included need for repeat biopsy following index RAB. Categorical variables were compared using chi-squared testing; continuous variables are presented as median (IQR). Results Twenty-five nodules (8.3%) underwent RAB following a prior non-diagnostic CT-guided transthoracic needle biopsy (n=22) or navigational bronchoscopy (n=3). Compared with biopsy-naïve lesions, nodules in the prior biopsy cohort were more frequently located in the outer third of the lung (76.0% vs 44.0%, p=0.009) and demonstrated a lower prevalence of malignancy (60.0% vs 72.9%, p=0.17). Diagnostic yield was lower following prior biopsy (64.0% vs 80.9%, p=0.046); however, sensitivity for malignancy remained high and comparable between groups (93.3% vs 94.6%, p=0.842). Among lesions undergoing repeat RAB after a prior non-diagnostic RAB (n=8), diagnostic yield was 75% with 100% sensitivity for malignancy and no subsequent biopsies required. Conclusion RAB maintains high sensitivity for malignancy following prior failed or non-diagnostic biopsy while minimising further invasive procedures. Although strict diagnostic yield was lower in the prior biopsy cohort, lesions were more peripheral and demonstrated lower malignancy prevalence, which may contribute to the reduced yield given the greater challenge of establishing definitive benign diagnoses. Similar findings were observed in the repeat-RAB subgroup. These findings suggest that RAB effectively identifies missed cancers in this difficult-to-diagnose population and support its use as an effective salvage diagnostic strategy for technically challenging and previously non-diagnostic pulmonary nodules.
authors: BP Patani; HT Trainer; JP Panaguiton; OV Volhina; AK Karir; Anand Tana; Justin L. Garner; James Tonkin; Christopher Michael Orton; Pallav L. Shah

title: Robotic bronchoscopy in early lung cancer: a biomarker-driven platform for genomic profiling and immunotherapy-oriented decision-making.
abstract: Robotic bronchoscopy is increasingly used to sample peripheral pulmonary lesions as lung cancer screening detects more small, distal, subsolid and ground-glass nodules. Most evidence has assessed the technology by diagnostic yield and safety, but these endpoints only partly capture clinical value. In early lung cancer care, the relevant question is whether bronchoscopy provides information that is sufficient for diagnosis, staging, molecular profiling and treatment-ready decision-making. This state-of-the-art review examines robotic bronchoscopy as a potential diagnosis-to-treatment platform rather than an isolated navigation device. We summarise evidence on distal airway access, procedural stability, CT-to-body divergence, tool-in-lesion confirmation, cone-beam CT, mobile cone-beam CT and radial endobronchial ultrasound. We also discuss tissue stewardship, rapid on-site evaluation, cell block preparation, next-generation sequencing, PD-L1 testing and same-session endobronchial ultrasound-guided transbronchial needle aspiration (EBUS-TBNA) and, when appropriate, endoscopic ultrasound with bronchoscope-guided fine-needle aspiration (EUS-B-FNA) as determinants of molecular adequacy and clinical actionability. We propose clinically actionable yield as a pragmatic, complementary, and currently unvalidated reporting construct linking lesion access, confirmed targeting, pathological diagnosis, molecular adequacy, staging completeness, and management decisions. For prospective evaluation, Level 5 (treatment decision informed or changed) should be assessed within 30 days after the index bronchoscopic procedure or before definitive therapy, whichever occurs first. Bronchoscopic ablation is considered as a future therapeutic extension, but current evidence remains early and does not establish equivalence with surgery, stereotactic body radiotherapy or percutaneous ablation. Future studies should evaluate decision-centred and patient-centred endpoints, including molecular-testing success, repeat biopsy avoidance, time to treatment, local control, pulmonary function, quality of life and cost-effectiveness.
authors: Dengxia Zhang; Yahui Han; Haonan Zhang; Chaoyang Yu; Shiqian Zhang; Teng Li

title: Robotic systems in cranial surgery: a systematic review of accuracy, clinical outcomes, and adverse events
abstract: Robotic-assisted surgery is becoming more prevalent in neurosurgery. Many studies have classified the advantages and disadvantages, particularly in spinal robotic surgeries. However, the use of robotics in cranial procedures has been limited to individual studies without large-scale review of the different modalities. This study is a comprehensive systematic review of the major robotics utilized in cranial neurosurgical procedures and their respective outcomes. Following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, a systematic review was conducted over PubMed, Cochrane, and Embase for articles published between January 2000 to February 2025. EndNote and Rayyan were utilized to organize the 1,409 identified studies and conduct a blinded multiphase process for including and excluding studies. Originally, studies were intended to be run as a meta-analysis to compare robotic modalities, but the existing data was too heterogeneous to statistically contrast outcomes. Overall, 51 studies were included, with six robots being discussed in more than one study. The use of robotics in cranial neurosurgery stretches mostly across functional neurosurgery, with different applications in brain tumor biopsies and resection, hemorrhage drainage, and endoscopic surgeries. Cranial neurosurgical procedures primarily apply robotics in the world of functional neurosurgery. Outside of this subspecialty, robotic-assisted cranial surgery remains sparse in the literature. As technology evolves, more use cases may be realized.
authors: Alison E. Burgess; Bailey D. Lupo; Luke P. Landry; Ben V. Peco; Nadia V Haik; Zack Karzoun; Norris C Talbot; James R. Bridges; Michael S. Folse; Ryan Diaz; Jamie Toms

title: Robotic-Arm Assisted versus Conventional Total Hip Arthroplasty via the Direct Anterior Approach: Acetabular Cup Positioning, Limb-Length Discrepancy, and Offset Restoration
abstract: Background Robotic-arm assisted total hip arthroplasty (THA) aims to improve the precision of acetabular cup placement and limb-length restoration. Whether these radiographic advantages translate into clinically meaningful benefits over conventional THA via the direct anterior approach (DAA) remains incompletely characterized. Methods We retrospectively reviewed 330 consecutive patients who underwent primary unilateral THA via the DAA by a single surgeon-led team between January 2021 and January 2025 at a tertiary referral center. In total, 165 patients received MAKO robotic-assisted THA and 165 underwent conventional THA. Indications included osteonecrosis of the femoral head, developmental dysplasia of the hip, rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, and femoral neck fracture. All postoperative radiographic measurements were performed independently by two attending radiologists using a picture archiving and communication system. Primary outcomes comprised acetabular anteversion and inclination, leg-length discrepancy (LLD), and hip offset parameters. Secondary outcomes included Lewinnek and Callanan safe-zone compliance, rates of absolute LLD exceeding 5 mm and 10 mm, total intraoperative blood loss, operative time, complications, and Harris Hip Scores (HHS) at a maximum follow-up of 3 years. Results Baseline demographics were well matched between groups (all P > 0.05). The robotic group demonstrated significantly greater accuracy in acetabular cup placement, with 94.6% of cups within the Lewinnek safe zone versus 84.2% in the conventional group (P = 0.004; OR = 3.24). The proportion of patients with absolute LLD > 5 mm was markedly lower in the robotic group (15.8% vs. 38.2%; P < 0.001; OR = 0.30). No between-group differences were observed for the Callanan safe zone, severe LLD (> 10 mm), or individual offset parameters. Robotic-assisted THA was associated with longer operative time (118.5 vs. 97.8 min; P < 0.001) and greater total intraoperative blood loss (285.6 vs. 160.3 mL; P < 0.001). HHS at final follow-up was comparable between groups (90.5 vs. 90.1; P > 0.05). Conclusions Robotic-arm assisted DAA THA improves the precision of acetabular cup positioning within the Lewinnek safe zone and reduces the incidence of moderate limb-length discrepancy compared with conventional THA. These radiographic gains are achieved at the expense of longer operative time and greater blood loss, with no detectable difference in short-term functional outcomes. Long-term studies are needed to determine whether these improvements translate into reduced dislocation rates and improved implant survivorship.
authors: Yilun Yao; Dongyang Chen; Zhihong Xu; Minghui Sun; Qing Jiang

title: Robotic-Assisted Bronchoscopic Lung Cryobiopsy Is Associated With Higher Diagnostic Yield in Diffuse Parenchymal Lung Disease: A Multicenter Retrospective Cohort Study
abstract: Background Transbronchial lung cryobiopsy (TBLC) is increasingly used to obtain tissue for the diagnosis of diffuse parenchymal lung disease (DPLD). However, diagnostic performance and complication rates vary with procedural technique and institutional experience. Robotic-assisted bronchoscopy (RAB) with cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) may improve target localization and parenchymal sampling. Methods We conducted a multicenter retrospective cohort study of 65 adults who underwent TBLC for suspected DPLD at three Mayo Clinic sites between January 2025 and June 2026. Patients underwent FB-TBLC with a 1.1-mm cryoprobe ( n = 26), FB-TBLC with a 1.7-mm cryoprobe ( n = 19), or RAB-TBLC with a 1.1-mm cryoprobe ( n = 20). We compared specific histopathologic diagnostic yield and procedure-related complications among biopsy approaches. Results Specific histopathologic diagnostic yield was 61.5% with FB-TBLC using a 1.1-mm cryoprobe, 73.7% with FB-TBLC using a 1.7-mm cryoprobe, and 95.0% with RAB-TBLC ( P = 0.032). After adjustment for radiographic fibrosis and maximum biopsy dimension, RAB-TBLC remained associated with higher diagnostic yield than FB-TBLC using a 1.1-mm cryoprobe (adjusted OR, 11.15; 95% CI, 1.76–219.95). Diagnostic yield did not differ between the two FB-TBLC groups. Complication rates were 34.6%, 42.1%, and 10.0%, respectively ( P = 0.065). Conclusion RAB-TBLC using a 1.1-mm cryoprobe was associated with a higher specific histopathologic diagnostic yield than FB-TBLC, without a detectable increase in procedure-related complications. Prospective studies are needed to validate these findings and determine which components of the RAB sampling strategy contribute to diagnostic performance.
authors: Azar J, Khattar G, Zein J, Naeem M, Gotway MB, Azadeh N, Benzo RP, Butt YM, Fernandez-Bussy S, Larsen BT, Lee AS, Reid MM, Alqalyoobi S, Ryu JH, Khoor A, Yi ES, Smith ML, Swanson KL, Tazelaar HD, Vaszar LT, Ibraheem M, Mohamed H, Sakata KK.

title: Robotic-assisted bronchoscopic biopsy and EBUS-TBNA in lung cancer: An outcome comparison between clinical and pathological staging.
abstract: Accurate mediastinal staging of suspected lung cancer is critical for guiding treatment and determining prognosis. While computed tomography (CT) and positron emission tomography (PET) are integral to initial staging, both modalities have limitations for detecting nodal metastases. Endobronchial ultrasound-guided transbronchial needle aspiration (EBUS-TBNA) provides a minimally invasive option for obtaining tissue confirmation. This study evaluates the impact of adding EBUS-TBNA at the time of lung tumor biopsy on mediastinal staging accuracy. We conducted a retrospective study of patients who underwent shape-sensing robotic-assisted bronchoscopy (ssRAB) with concurrent EBUS-TBNA between June 2020 and December 2025. Preprocedural CT and PET findings were compared with EBUS-TBNA cytopathology to assess their diagnostic performance and to evaluate stage migration in patients with primary pulmonary malignancies. A total of 1,234 patients underwent ssRAB with EBUS-TBNA, of whom 123 (10.0 %) had malignant lymph nodes on cytopathology. Among these, 23 patients (18.7 %) had no suspicious lymphadenopathy on preprocedural CT and/or PET imaging. The sensitivity of CT and PET for detecting malignancy at specific lymph node stations was 44.5 % and 68.5 %, respectively. In the clinical-to-EBUS staging analysis, 66 (74.2 %) demonstrated no major stage change, while 23 (25.9 %) experienced stage migration. Concurrent EBUS-TBNA identified occult nodal involvement and resulted in stage migration. These findings underscore the critical role of EBUS-TBNA in identifying clinically occult nodal disease and optimizing lung cancer treatment.
authors: Sebastian Fernandez-Bussy; Regina M Murillo-Torres; Tatiana A Rojas-Zapata; Alejandra Yu Lee-Mateus; Paola Gutierrez-Gallegos; David Abia-Trujillo; Linh H Vu; Ryan M Chadha; Kelly S Robertson; Bryan C Husta

title: Robotics in neurosurgery: past, present, and future
abstract: Background Robotics has progressed from stereotactic positioning and instrument guidance toward integrated platforms combining navigation, intraoperative imaging, immersive visualization, and computer-assisted control. However, technical accuracy and clinical benefit are not interchangeable, and the maturity of evidence differs markedly across neurosurgical indications. Objective To critically synthesize the historical development, contemporary applications, supporting evidence, implementation constraints, and research priorities of robotic and complementary augmented-reality (AR)/virtual-reality (VR) technologies in neurosurgery. Methods This is a critical narrative review and technology-focused synthesis, informed by the literature and reference set of the original manuscript (which described searching PubMed, Google Scholar, and ScienceDirect through January 2021), supplemented by selected contemporary publications and the two VOSTARS studies suggested during peer review. No new reproducible systematic search, dual-reviewer screening, formal risk-of-bias assessment, or quantitative synthesis was performed; therefore, PRISMA study counts are not reported. Synthesis Cranial robotic systems facilitate trajectory planning and reproducible positioning for stereotactic biopsy, stereoelectroencephalography, deep brain stimulation, and related interventions. Spine robotics can support pedicle screw placement, although comparative estimates depend on platform, comparator, experience, and outcome definition. Endovascular and microsurgical robotics remain heterogeneous, with many applications at feasibility or early clinical stages. Wearable AR systems such as VOSTARS illustrate the convergence of visualization and navigation but require validation under real operative conditions. Acquisition and maintenance costs, registration error, line-of-sight constraints, human factors, training, and cybersecurity are distinct adoption barriers. Conclusions The most defensible current contribution of robotics is task-specific assistance within surgeon-led workflows, not universal superiority or autonomy. Future studies should prioritize patient-important outcomes, transparent technical reporting, prospective comparisons, and context-sensitive economic evaluation.
authors: Hosam Maher Al-Jehani; Ahmed Hafez Mousa

title: RynnWorld-Latent: A Cross-Embodiment World Model Conditioned on Universal Latent Actions
abstract: Learning controllable world dynamics from heterogeneous interaction videos is challenging because robot embodiments use incompatible action spaces, while human videos lack native control labels. We present RynnWorld-Latent, a cross-embodiment video world model that uses the 3D-grounded latent actions introduced by RynnLAM as a shared conditioning interface. This representation enables joint pretraining on human interaction videos, robot demonstrations, and simulation rollouts without requiring a common native action space. Built on a pretrained video transformer, RynnWorld-Latent combines global action tokens with an identity-initialized local pathway that aligns actions with future video latents. We pretrain on 23 datasets comprising approximately 553.5M frames and adapt the model to target robots through post-training. The framework supports two data-generation routes: digital teleoperation uses target robot commands to generate action-video demonstrations, while latent-action synthesis transfers source motion to an edited initial frame and pairs the resulting rollout with retargeted pseudo robot actions. Experiments show improved video prediction metrics on public benchmarks and two real-robot platforms, alongside qualitative action following when different action sequences share the same initial observation. Synthetic mid-training improves policy success rates on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, and both generation routes improve real-world policy success rates over real-demonstration-only training in the evaluated settings. These results support universal latent actions as a scalable interface for learning controllable visual dynamics across heterogeneous embodiments.
authors: Haoyu Zhao; Yinzhou Tang; Zixuan Wang; Minghao Zhu; Dongchi Huang; Xingyue Zhao; Qin Zhao; Kehan Li; Siteng Huang; Xin Li; Zhenyu Zeng; Mingxiu Chen; Deli Zhao; Zhongyu Li

title: STEAM and educational robotics in the development of statistical literacy
abstract: In primary school, the teaching of mathematics and natural sciences should promote meaningful, context-based learning that enables students to apply knowledge in real-life situations. Interdisciplinary approaches such as STEAM foster 21st century competences through active and collaborative methodologies, while educational robotics (ER) supports the development of computational thinking and social skills. This study analyses the influence of a STEAM practice, incorporating ER on the development of statistical literacy and learning about ocean plastic pollution among 4th grade students. The research adopted a mixed-methods, interpretative action research design. Data were collected by the trainee teacher as participant researcher through performance tasks, field notes, photographs and audio recordings, later used to construct multimodal narratives. Findings reveal statistically significant improvements in global level of knowledge and global performance. The study concludes that steam practices incorporating ER and grounded in real-world problem-solving constitute an effective strategy for fostering statistical literacy.
authors: Vanda Santos; Ana Silva; Filipa Pinto; Marisa Alexandra Maia Machado; Fernando Martíns
venue: Eurasia Journal of Mathematics Science and Technology Education

title: Safety and Efficacy of Endobronchial Ultrasound
abstract: Purpose of review The use of bronchoscopy with endobronchial ultrasound (EBUS) to aid in lymph node and lung biopsy is relatively new. This review will summarize the literature surrounding the efficacy of bronchoscopy with EBUS. Safety of bronchoscopy with EBUS is not markedly different that procedure with EBUS and is impacted by patient features including co-morbidities as well as different sedation modalities. This paper reviews the impact on both safety and diagnostic yield. Recent Findings The yield from using EBUS guided biopsy varies with the diagnosis but is high with linear EBUS. Recent data incorporating other technologies (electromagnetic navigation, robotic assistance) with bronchoscopy has potential to increase diagnostic yields, appears to be equivalent to transthoracic needle biopsies performed by radiology. Different sedation modalities are utilized, including the use of dedicated anesthesia providers, for bronchoscopy with EBUS but do not appear to significantly affect the diagnostic yield. Summary Bronchoscopy with EBUS (both linear and radial) is a safe procedure with acceptable yields. The type of sedation does not appear to affect the diagnostic yield or the safety of the procedure. Further research into incorporation of other technologies may provide for higher diagnostic yields.
authors: Travis Yamanaka; Kevin P. Haas

title: Sample Adequacy PD-L1 and NGS in NSCLC: Shape-Sensing Robotic Assisted Bronchoscopy Versus CT Guided Lung Biopsy.
abstract:
Background

Routine assessment of programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression and comprehensive next-generation sequencing (NGS) is recommended to guide treatment selection in patients with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Obtaining adequate tissue for biomarker and molecular analyses is therefore essential. This study compared sample adequacy for PD-L1 and NGS testing between shape-sensing robotic-assisted bronchoscopy (ssRAB) and computed tomography-guided transthoracic lung biopsy (CTTB) in patients with NSCLC.

Methods

We conducted a single-center retrospective study of patients with NSCLC who underwent biopsy of PPL by ssRAB or CTTB between June 2020 and December 2025. Demographic, procedural, pathological, biomarker and molecular data were extracted from electronic medical records, and descriptive statistics analysis and multivariable logistic regression were performed.

Results

A total of 402 patients were included, comprising 198 in the ssRAB cohort and 204 in the CTTB cohort. ssRAB demonstrated significantly higher sample adequacy rates than CTTB for both PD-L1 (98.8% vs. 90.6%, p < 0.001) and NGS testing (92.3% vs. 79.1%, p = 0.005). In multivariable logistic regression analyses, ssRAB was independently associated with higher odds of PD-L1 sample adequacy (adjusted OR 11.48, 95% CI 2.89-78.30; p = 0.002) and NGS sample adequacy (adjusted OR 4.01, 95% CI 1.64-11.40; p = 0.004) compared with CTTB. In a separate model evaluating biopsy tools, cryobiopsy use was independently associated with higher odds of PD-L1 adequacy (adjusted OR 16.54, 95% CI 2.92-317.65; p = 0.010) and NGS adequacy (adjusted OR 5.83, 95% CI 1.93-25.39; p = 0.006) compared with non-cryobiopsy sampling.

Conclusions

ssRAB-acquired specimens were associated with higher rates of PD-L1 and NGS sample adequacy than CTTB-acquired specimens in patients with NSCLC. Future prospective studies are needed to better understand the procedural and specimen-related factors underlying these differences.

title: Sample-to-answer automated centrifugal microfluidics with computer-vision readout for point-of-care molecular diagnostics
abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic exposed how unprepared the world is to respond to an infectious disease outbreak at scale. Conventional diagnostic testing relies on centralized laboratories, and when testing demand surges during an outbreak, these facilities become strained for resources and personnel, a problem compounded in low- and middle-income countries with less developed health and transport infrastructure. Decentralized, point-of-care diagnostics offer a path around this bottleneck, but automated platforms capable of true sample-to-answer operation remain limited. Here we report a fully automated centrifugal microfluidic platform that combines loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) with computer-vision-based readout, demonstrated using SARS-CoV-2 detection as a model application. The integrated platform performs the complete assay protocol, including heating, rotation, and optical detection, at the push of a single button, without user intervention, processing 26 samples in 40 minutes. Using RNA fragments spiked into water and artificial saliva, the platform consistently detected amplification down to approximately 1000 copies per 10 µL reaction. This platform architecture is broadly applicable beyond SARS-CoV-2 and offers a template for rapid, decentralized molecular diagnostics for future infectious disease outbreaks.

title: Sclerosing Pneumocytoma Diagnosed by Robotic Bronchoscopy Fine Needle Aspiration (FNA) Cytology: An Unusual Case Crossing the Major Fissure
abstract: Introduction/Objective Sclerosing pneumocytoma (SP) is a rare benign tumor of pneumocytic origin characterized by a dual population of surface cuboidal cells and underlying round stromal cells. The variability in architectural patterns and heterogenous cell population can make cytologic diagnosis challenging, particularly in atypical radiologic presentations. Methods/Case Report A 50-year-old woman presented with dyspnea. Chest CT revealed a 3.9 cm circumscribed mass along the left major fissure, involving both left upper and lower lobes. The radiologic differential was broad, including solitary fibrous tumor, carcinoid, and atypical pulmonary hamartoma. Initial navigational bronchoscopy FNA was non-diagnostic. Repeat sampling by ION-assisted robotic bronchoscopy FNA demonstrated papillary fragments of cuboidal epithelium overlying a proliferation of cytologically bland round cells. Immunohistochemistry showed co-expression of TTF-1 and EMA in both populations. Surface cells were positive for CK7 and pancytokeratin, while round cells were negative. The cytology diagnosis was papillary fragments of bland pulmonary tissue and favored SP. Subsequently, a limited wedge resection of left upper and lower lobes confirmed a 4.5 cm SP with negative margins. Results NA Conclusion SP is a potential cytologic diagnostic pitfall that can mimic papillary adenocarcinoma. Accurate diagnosis requires recognition of its dual cell population and characteristic immunoprofile, and integration with clinicoradiologic findings to avoid misdiagnosis and overtreatment.

title: Selected interleukins, soluble TNF-α receptors, c-reactive protein and cortisol as biomarkers of surgical trauma-induced inflammation in children
abstract: PURPOSE: To evaluate the influence of surgical trauma-induced inflammation and surgery type or presence of appendicitis on the levels of the studied cytokines, CRP and cortisol as biomarkers. METHODS: A prospective study was performed of pediatric patients undergoing laparotomy or laparoscopy. The concentrations of cytokines were assessed using Luminex xMAP technology, CRP by immunoturbidimetric method, and cortisol by ELISA. Their levels were determined twice at four time points: at baseline, after 6-12 h postoperative (cortisol), 12-24 h (other markers apart from CRP), and 36-48 h (CRP). RESULTS: Significant increases were observed in IL-6 (p = 0.001) and IL-10 (p = 0.034) in non-inflammatory patients undergoing laparotomy, and in IL-6 in inflammatory (p = 0.035) and non-inflammatory (p < 0.001) groups receiving laparoscopy. Significant increases in IL-8 (p = 0.020) and sTNFRII (p = 0.004) were demonstrated in patients with inflammation undergoing laparoscopy. Significant increased CRP levels were noted in all four examined subgroups (p = 0.003, p = 0.01, p < 0.001, p < 0.001). CONCLUSION: sTNFRII, CRP and IL-6 are sensitive biomarkers of surgical trauma-induced inflammation. sTNFRII and CRP are reliable indicators of the presence of appendicitis. Laparotomy resulted in a greater increase in sTNFRII levels, whereas laparoscopy stimulated CRP production more strongly. The open surgery is characterized by earlier mechanical tissue injury than laparoscopy.

title: Semi-Automatic Cleaning in the Pharmaceutical Industry
abstract: This presentation examines semi-automatic cleaning of shared production equipment in the pharmaceutical industry within the framework of Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) and cleaning validation. It defines semi-automatic cleaning as a hybrid approach that combines manual gross-soil removal with controlled, automated wash cycles, and introduces the T.A.C.T. model (Temperature, Action, Chemistry, Time) as a basis for process parameter optimization and reproducibility. The work describes the principal equipment used, including pressure wands, ultrasonic baths and Clean-Out-of-Place (COP) washers. It provides a comparative analysis of manual, semi-automatic and fully automatic cleaning in terms of reproducibility, operator dependency, capital investment and validation complexity, and discusses the advantages and limitations of the semi-automatic approach. The second part addresses the verification of cleaning effectiveness through residue analysis. It covers sampling techniques (swab sampling and rinse sampling) and analytical detection methods, namely Total Organic Carbon (TOC) analysis and High-Performance Liquid Chromatography (HPLC). It then presents the establishment of acceptance criteria, including the calculation of the Maximum Allowable Carryover (MACO) from the Acceptable Daily Exposure (ADE) or Permitted Daily Exposure (PDE), supported by a worked example, together with legacy limits (10 ppm and 0.1% of the minimum daily dose). This material is intended for students, researchers and professionals in pharmaceutical engineering, quality assurance and GMP compliance.

title: Sensor design and development for autonomous devices for disease diagnosis and therapy
abstract: (English) This doctoral research addresses key challenges in diabetes management by integrating sustainable materials, non-invasive sensing, and advanced insulin delivery technologies into a unified framework. Diabetes mellitus is a chronic metabolic disorder that requires continuous glucose monitoring and precise insulin administration to maintain glycemic control and reduce complications. Responding to these needs, the thesis is structured around three major contributions. First, the work advances the development of a previously created non-invasive glucose-monitoring device by incorporating recycled low-density polyethylene (LDPE) into the sensor design. The use of recycled LDPE improves sustainability, cost-efficiency, and environmental compatibility while maintaining reliable sensing performance. This demonstrates the feasibility of repurposing plastic waste in biomedical technologies without compromising functionality. Second, the research explores new strategies for controlled insulin delivery through stimuli-responsive hydrogels. Hydrogels based on poly(γ-glutamic acid) and multi-armed polyethylene glycol (PEG) were engineered to achieve sustained and tunable insulin release. The incorporation of poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene) (PEDOT), a biocompatible conducting polymer, enables electrically triggered and on-demand insulin delivery. This approach offers a minimally invasive alternative to conventional injection-based therapies and highlights the potential of electro-responsive materials in smart drug-delivery systems. Finally, the thesis investigates the nanomechanical properties of multi-armed PEG hydrogels using a microcantilever-based optomechanical sensor. This analysis provides essential insights into the structural behavior, stability, and long-term performance of the hydrogels, contributing to the optimization of their mechanical robustness and responsiveness. Together, these contributions form a comprehensive strategy for improving diabetes care. By integrating non-invasive monitoring, environmentally conscious materials, and intelligent delivery platforms, the research promotes more sustainable biomedical solutions while advancing patient-centered therapeutic tools. La diabetis mellitus és un trastorn metabòlic crònic que requereix monitoratge continu de la glucosa i una administració precisa d’insulina per mantenir el control glucèmic i reduir complicacions. Responent a aquestes necessitats, la tesi es divideix en tres aportacions principals. L’ús de LDPE reciclat incrementa la sostenibilitat, l’eficiència econòmica i la compatibilitat ambiental sense comprometre’n el rendiment, demostrant la viabilitat de reutilitzar residus plàstics en tecnologies biomèdiques. La incorporació del polímer conductor PEDOT permet un alliberament elèctric i sota demanda, oferint una alternativa mínimament invasiva als mètodes tradicionals. Finalment, s’investigaren les propietats nanomecàniques dels hidrogels de PEG multibraç utilitzant un sensor optomecànic amb microcantilever, aportant informació clau sobre el seu comportament estructural, estabilitat i rendiment a llarg termini. En conjunt, aquestes aportacions constitueixen una estratègia completa per avançar en la gestió de la diabetis mitjançant solucions biomèdiques sostenibles i plataformes intel·ligents d’alliberament terapèutic. La diabetes mellitus es un trastorno metabólico crónico que requiere una monitorización continua de glucosa y una administración precisa de insulina para mantener el control glucémico y reducir complicaciones. En respuesta a estas necesidades, la tesis se articula en tres aportes principales. En primer lugar, el trabajo mejora un dispositivo previo de monitorización no invasiva de glucosa incorporando polietileno de baja densidad (LDPE) reciclado en el diseño del sensor. El uso de LDPE reciclado aumenta la sostenibilidad, la eficiencia económica y la compatibilidad ambiental sin afectar el rendimiento. Esto demuestra la viabilidad de reutilizar residuos plásticos en aplicaciones biomédicas. En segundo lugar, la investigación explora nuevas estrategias para la liberación controlada de insulina mediante hidrogeles sensibles a estímulos. Se desarrollaron hidrogeles basados en ácido poli(γ-glutámico) y polietilenglicol (PEG) multibrazo para lograr una liberación sostenida y modulable. La incorporación del polímero conductor PEDOT permite una liberación de insulina eléctrica y bajo demanda, ofreciendo una alternativa mínimamente invasiva a los métodos convencionales. Finalmente, se estudiaron las propiedades nanomecánicas de los hidrogeles de PEG multibrazo utilizando un sensor optomecánico basado en microcantilever. Este análisis proporciona información clave sobre su comportamiento estructural, estabilidad y rendimiento a largo plazo. En conjunto, estas contribuciones conforman una estrategia integral para mejorar el tratamiento de la diabetes mediante soluciones biomédicas sostenibles y plataformas de administración inteligente.

title: Shape sensing of viscoelastic structures using the inverse finite element method: numerical and experimental validation
abstract: The inverse Finite Element Method (iFEM) is well established for shape sensing of elastic structures, but its performance under time-dependent viscoelastic deformation remains insufficiently assessed. This work presents, to the authors' knowledge, the first combined numerical and experimental assessment of iFEM under creep and recovery conditions within the small-deformation regime. The objective is to determine whether time-dependent displacement fields can be reconstructed directly from strain histories without introducing a viscoelastic constitutive law, material parameters, load histories, or internal variables into the inverse analysis. Two complementary case studies are considered. First, a viscoelastic abdominal-patch model is analysed under sustained pressure, with a calibrated Generalised Maxwell model used only in the forward finite element simulation to generate reference strain and displacement fields. Second, an SLA-manufactured NACA 0016 airfoil beam is experimentally tested under loading and unloading, using measured strain histories as iFEM input and LVDT measurements for validation. In the numerical case, the maximum error in central transverse displacement is 2.46%, while the field-based normalised RMSE remains below 2.26%. In the experimental case, the reconstructed tip displacement differs from the LVDT measurements by less than 5% for most of the test, with larger discrepancies during unloading. The results show that the kinematics-based iFEM formulation can reconstruct creep and recovery histories directly from measured strains, while the material time dependence is conveyed through the strain data rather than through a constitutive model within the inverse analysis.

title: Silent travelers: the potential of migratory birds and their ticks to introduce emerging viruses into Switzerland
abstract: Switzerland hosts over 400 bird species, many of which are migratory. Through diverse movement patterns, ranging from short distances to almost global migrations, these birds can introduce zoonotic viruses, such as West Nile virus (WNV) or avian influenza virus (AIV), as well as unknown and potentially emerging viruses. Furthermore, they facilitate the global dispersal of infected ectoparasites, particularly ticks, risking the introduction of novel tick-borne diseases. To assess this risk, we sampled 42 bird species (39 migratory, 3 resident) over seven months in 2023 at the Bolle di Magadino nature reserve and the Piano di Magadino area in the canton Ticino (Switzerland). This region, because of its transitional climate, serves as an important resting and breeding ground for migratory birds. In total, 496 oropharyngeal-cloacal swabs, 164 sera, and 22 associated ticks were collected. While RT-qPCR of the swabs detected no active WNV or AIV infections, ELISA testing identified Orthoflavivirus antibodies in 15 of 164 sera, indicating prior exposure. Metagenomic next-generation sequencing revealed a viral landscape spanning 33 families (29 of which were identified in birds). Within this virome, DNA viruses, predominantly Circoviridae, Genomoviridae, and Parvoviridae , dominated in abundance but exhibited low diversity. In contrast, the highly diverse RNA virome primarily reflected the birds’ dietary habits and the local habitat at the nature reserve. Notably, we report the first detection of Bole tick virus 4 (BoTV4) in Switzerland, identified in several ticks ( Rhipicephalus turanicus ) associated with long-distance migrants. This member of the newly established Pestiviridae family is already established in parts of Asia, Africa, and Europe. This study provides the first active surveillance of the wild bird virome in Switzerland. Our findings establish a framework for the early detection of emerging viruses and underscore the role of migratory birds as dispersal vectors for ticks and novel tick-borne viruses.
authors: Corinne Manuela Gerber; Giulia Zezza; Valeria Guidi; Michele Wyler; Claudia Bachofen; Jakub Kubacki

title: Simulator-Limb Training in Phlebotomy among Health Science Students: Implications for Technique-Related Preanalytical Errors—A Systematic Review
abstract: Introduction: Phlebotomy is an essential skill that health science students need to develop for future clinical practice. Proper phlebotomy technique can help prevent technique-related preanalytical errors that may compromise specimen quality and patient safety. Simulator-limb training gives students opportunities to practice venipuncture in a controlled environment before performing procedures on actual patients. This study examined the effectiveness of simulator-based limb training in phlebotomy and its potential to minimize technique-related preanalytical specimen errors. Methods: A systematic review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 reporting guidelines to examine simulator limb training in phlebotomy among health science students and its implications for technique-related preanalytical specimen errors. Google Scholar, PubMed, and EBSCOhost were searched for English-language studies published from January 2016 to September 2026. Eligible studies evaluated simulator-limb training in phlebotomy among health science students and reported outcomes related to procedural competency or preanalytical specimen errors. Methodological quality was assessed using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT), version 2018. Due to heterogeneity in study designs, populations, and outcome measures, the findings were synthesized narratively and organized into three themes: clinical competency and learner readiness; safe, repetitive, and experiential learning; and implications for patient safety and the prevention of technique-related preanalytical errors. Results and Discussion: The reviewed literature showed that simulator-limb phlebotomy training improved venipuncture competency, confidence, and psychomotor skills while providing a safe environment for repetitive practice, error recognition, and feedback. However, no included studies directly measured the potential effect on reducing technique-related preanalytical specimen error rates before and after simulator-limb training; improved procedural competency and consistent phlebotomy performance may contribute to specimen quality and patient safety. Lastly, challenges include equipment and maintenance costs, limited funding, faculty training, curriculum integration, and limited clinical authenticity in integrating simulator-limb training for health science students practicing phlebotomy. Conclusion: Simulator-limb training may complement phlebotomy competency development among health science students. Further research directly measuring preanalytical errors and specimen rejection rates is needed to establish its effectiveness in reducing technique-related preanalytical errors.

title: Simultaneous dual cryobiopsy using two bronchoscopes for multiple peripheral lung lesions: a novel case report
abstract: Introduction Bronchoscopic biopsy of multiple pulmonary lesions is typically performed sequentially, often requiring repeated imaging confirmation during cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT)–guided procedures. Case presentation We report a novel technique using simultaneous dual cryobiopsy with two bronchoscopes to sample separate lesions during a single CBCT acquisition. A patient with multiple lesions in the left upper lobe underwent bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia. Two bronchoscopes were inserted simultaneously through a 9 mm endotracheal tube: an Ambu aScope 5 Broncho (4.2 mm outer diameter, 2.2 mm working channel) with a 1.9 mm reusable cryoprobe and an Olympus MP190F bronchoscope with a 1.1 mm cryoprobe. A single CBCT spin confirmed simultaneous tool-in-lesion positioning for both cryoprobes. Cryobiopsies were obtained successfully from both lesions. Histopathological examination revealed squamous cell carcinoma. Conclusion This case demonstrates the technical feasibility of simultaneous dual cryobiopsy and suggests a potential strategy to improve procedural efficiency and reduce imaging requirements during CBCT-guided bronchoscopy.

title: Single-Step Sample-Activated Alternating Sequential Flow Enables Autonomous Multistep Electrochemical Lateral Flow Detection of Mpox Virus DNA.
abstract: The 2022 multinational mpox virus (MPXV) outbreak and continued cross-border transmission have highlighted limitations of laboratory-confined PCR diagnostics. Here, we report an alternating lateral flow architecture (ALFA) that transforms traditional single-pass lateral flow into a programmable platform for autonomous multistep electrochemical nucleic acid detection following a single prepared-sample introduction. By regulating passive fluid delivery, ALFA enables sequential molecular processing and in situ signal generation without external intervention. Coupled with Ag(I)-mediated mismatch DNA nanocomplexes (MDNs), the system provides electrochemical signal amplification without nucleic acid amplification. ALFA detected MPXV DNA with a limit of detection (LOD) of 1.55 pM and a linear range of 101-105 pM. In urine and saliva spiked with structurally intact viral particles, the lowest statistically distinguishable concentration was 10 copies mL-1. Clinical evaluation of 50 PCR-characterized lesion swab samples yielded 92.11% sensitivity, 100% specificity, and 94.0% accuracy. The platform also maintained stable performance over an estimated 112 days. ALFA therefore provides a programmable lateral flow framework for rapid, amplification-free, decentralized nucleic acid diagnostics.
