title: Single-cell dissection of immune-state architecture across diverse human population cohorts
abstract: The extension of human lifespan is accompanied by a growing burden of chronic disease and multimorbidity. The immune system, whose functional state is continuously remodelled by ageing, environmental exposures, infection history and disease, is pivotal to respond to these challenges. However, how these factors jointly influence immune variation, regulatory mechanisms and disease susceptibility across populations remains poorly understood. Here we present an outline and first results of the CARDINAL (Cellular Architecture of immune-state Regulation, Disease, and Immune Networks across the Adult Lifecourse) project. We generated a new population-scale single-cell atlas of peripheral blood comprising almost 10 million immune cells from 6,003 individuals across two UK cohorts with integrated genomic and longitudinal electronic health record data: the UK Biobank (predominantly European ancestry British) and Genes & Health (British Bangladeshi and British Pakistani). We identify immune-state architectures, shared across cohorts, associated with ageing, chronic viral exposure, inflammatory activation and premalignant conditions. We show that demographic and lifestyle factors induce largely conserved immune programmes, while chronic cardiometabolic diseases are associated with cohort-dominant cellular programmes and transcriptional states. Disentangling of genetic and clinical influences reveals coordinated regulatory programmes associated with metabolic, inflammatory and infectious remodelling. These programmes are observed in specific disease contexts and immune states, such as those induced by chronic viral exposure, often independently of genetic differences. Together, our findings support a model of immune-state architecture shaped by ageing, environment, disease history and genetic variation, which can be read from population-specific regulatory landscapes.

title: Single-session robotic bronchoscopy diagnoses histologically discordant synchronous lung lesions.
abstract: Histologically discordant synchronous pulmonary lesions in a previously treated patient may represent independent primaries, intrapulmonary metastasis, or histologic transformation. A 74-year-old woman with previously treated right upper lobe adenosquamous carcinoma developed two new, spatially separate, solid fluorodeoxyglucose-avid lesions. Both were sampled during one anaesthetic using shape-sensing robotic-assisted bronchoscopy with radial-probe endobronchial ultrasound confirmation. The peripheral right upper lobe lesion was small cell carcinoma; the left upper lobe lesion was non-small cell carcinoma, not otherwise specified, with patchy TTF-1 and p40 expression compatible with adenosquamous differentiation. Comparative clonality testing was not performed, so their relationship remained unproven. Both lesions received stereotactic ablative radiotherapy (50 Gy in five fractions); the small cell carcinoma was also treated with carboplatin and etoposide, with consolidation durvalumab planned. Bilateral sampling revealed clinically consequential histologic heterogeneity and enabled histology-directed therapy without assuming a common origin.
authors: Venkatkiran Kanchustambham; Swetha Saladi; Alexey Hodkoff

title: Skill Erosion and Identity Shifts under AI Delegation in Imaging-based Medicine
abstract: This paper reports on a qualitative study with 12 experts across dermatology and radiology about the risk of AI-induced skill erosion. Integrating AI tools (e.g., visual diagnosis, generative scribes) into medical workflows introduces the risk of AI-induced skill erosion among experts despite short-term efficiency gains. While existing literature focuses on short-term behavioral phenomena like automation bias and real-time accuracy, it fails to capture how continuous AI integration alters what clinicians consider essential skills and reshapes professional identity over time. We conducted 12 semi-structured interviews and speculative design workbook activities with expert radiologists and dermatologists. From this study, we derived the Human-AI Clinical Skill Framework, which maps how modular, unitary, and dynamic skill philosophies intersect with mechanical, integrative, and translational skill tiers, and what it means for clinical expertise in an AI-powered practice. We conclude with design principles for integrating AI into medical tools to mitigate skill erosion.
authors: Thitaree Tanprasert; Tim Miller; Tapani Rinta-Kahila; Ida Someh

title: Stage-Specific Associations of Automated RPR With Treponema pallidum qPCR Positivity and Cycle Threshold in Early Symptomatic Syphilis: A Multicenter Study Using Specimens Collected During Routine Care
abstract: Background Treponema pallidum quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) positivity and cycle threshold (Ct) by rapid plasma reagin (RPR), disease stage, and other characteristics are poorly characterized in routine-care specimens, leaving it unclear when qPCR of such specimens is informative for diagnosis. Methods This Japanese multicenter cross-sectional study explored qPCR positivity and Ct by these characteristics. Nonblood specimens collected during routine care underwent qPCR at a central laboratory for this study. Bayesian logistic and normal regressions modeled positivity and mean Ct of TP0574 and polA with stage-specific continuous automated RPR terms, patient characteristics, collection site, and facility random intercepts. Estimates were standardized over the analyzed specimens. Population-group predictions were instead averaged within each group. Results Among 154 nonblood specimens from 145 patients (71.7% non-MSM men and women) at 14 facilities, 109 (70.8%) were qPCR positive. At RPR 1, adjusted positivity was 72.2% (95% credible interval, 60.9%–82.9%) in primary and 43.8% (16.7%–69.9%) in secondary syphilis. Positivity showed a modest downward trend with RPR in primary but increased in secondary syphilis, reflecting a stage-by-RPR interaction (secondary-to-primary ratio of odds ratios, 1.78; 1.25–2.65). Predicted positivity showed an upward trend with RPR values among MSM; adjusted positivity was relatively high for genital/urethral/urinary and anal/perianal/rectal specimens. Adjusted mean Ct increased with RPR in primary and followed an inverted-U pattern in secondary syphilis. Conclusions In primary syphilis, nonblood qPCR positivity was high even at low RPR. When serologic findings remain inconclusive in this stage, qPCR is highly recommended for securing an early diagnosis. Summary In nonblood specimens collected during routine care, Treponema pallidum qPCR positivity was high even at low automated RPR values in primary syphilis, potentially supporting earlier diagnostic confirmation when serology is inconclusive. In secondary syphilis, positivity increased with RPR.

title: State-of-the-art in automated image-based species identification systems
abstract: Accurate and rapid species-level identification of bacteria and fungi from culture plates are longstanding challenges in diagnostic microbiology. Visual assessment of colony morphology lacks sufficient specificity for definitive identification, while biochemical profiling is often too slow for routine clinical use. Matrix assisted laser desorption ionization - time of flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF MS) has largely replaced biochemical identification in high-income settings because of its speed and accuracy; however, its cost and infrastructure requirements limit accessibility in most low resource settings. Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs), offers a promising alternative by enabling growth detection and presumptive identification direct from digitalized macroscopic images of culture plates. This review summarizes key aspects of visual identification from agar cultures and recent advances in image-based microbial analysis using CNNs, Siamese networks, object detectors, and Vision Transformers. Automated growth detection and whole-plate interpretation achieved sensitivities of 99.8-100%, specificities of approximately 63-90%, and within-institution AUCs of ≥0.98, although cross-institution performance decreased to ≥0.90; reported workflow benefits included 3-5-hour reductions in time to result and up to 80% less hands-on review of negative cultures. Species-level bacterial classification ranged from a mean sensitivity of 66.2% in an early 18-species model to 90.6% top-1 and 97.6% top-3 accuracy with the contextual DeepColony framework. Fungal models achieved a mean accuracy of 89.7% with FungID and an AUROC of 92.7% with smartphone-based MoldVision, whose F1 score increased from 38.8% during days 1-2 to 92.1% during days 3-5, highlighting the influence of colony maturity, dataset composition, and validation setting. We further discuss the integration of AI image analysis in commercial laboratory automation systems, including Copan WASPLab™, BD Kiestra™ MLA, APAS™ Independence by Clever Culture Systems, as well as the potential of smartphone-based tools in resource-limited settings. Overall, AI-based image analysis can support high-sensitivity screening, workflow triage, colony enumeration, and presumptive identification, but robust external validation, standardized imaging and reporting, regulatory approval, and continued expert oversight remain essential.

title: Swab-based molecular testing near the point-of-care for childhood tuberculosis: a prospective diagnostic accuracy study
abstract:
SUMMARY

Background

Swab-based molecular testing for tuberculosis (TB) could provide a near point-of-care (nPOC) diagnostic for children. We evaluated the accuracy of two swab-based nPOC platforms to detect pediatric pulmonary TB.

Methods

We prospectively enrolled children under 15 years with presumptive TB in Uganda and South Africa. They completed TB evaluation including sputum molecular testing and culture. Two tongue swabs were collected and tested with MiniDock MTB (Pluslife Biotech, China) and Truenat MTB Ultima (Molbio Diagnostics, India), and one swab was dipped in sputum for testing with MiniDock MTB. We calculated the sensitivity and specificity of each index test against a culture-based standard and compared them with sputum molecular testing and smear microscopy.

Findings

We included 335 children, among whom median age was 3 years (IQR 1-6), 53% were female, 11% were living with HIV, and 16% had microbiologically confirmed TB. Tongue swabs were collected in all children, with invalid test rates of less than 3%. Against a culture-based standard, the sensitivities of tongue swab MiniDock MTB and MTB Ultima were 50% (95% CI 33.4-66.6) and 50% (95% CI 28.2-71.8), respectively, and specificities were ≥98% for both. Sputum swab MiniDock MTB had similar sensitivity to sputum Xpert Ultra (85.7% vs. 75.0%, p=0.45), but substantially higher sensitivity than tongue swab MiniDock MTB (+23.1%, p=0.03) and sputum smear microscopy (+46.4%, p<0.001).

Interpretation

Sputum swab testing had similar accuracy to sputum Xpert Ultra in children. Tongue swab testing had moderate accuracy, and has value to identify microbiologically confirmed cases when sputum is not available.

Funding

National Institutes of Health, United States Department of State Bureau of Global Health Security and Diplomacy, and South African Medical Research Council

RESEARCH IN CONTEXT

Evidence before this study

We evaluated the literature from October 2021 to October 2026 for studies in any language on oral swab molecular testing for M. tuberculosis (MTB). We included diagnostic accuracy studies and excluded work on extrapulmonary TB, screening and early assay development, and searched PubMed and Google Scholar with the terms “swab” AND “tuberculosis” AND “diagnosis.” Manual quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) testing on tongue swabs has high accuracy to detect pulmonary TB in adults (80-93% sensitive and >98% specificity), with similar accuracy to sputum samples. Translation to semi-automated PCR assays such as Xpert Ultra have had high specificity but variable sensitivity (59-76%). Newer assays have been developed that are designed specifically for swab testing, and are small, portable, and can be used near the point-of-care (nPOC). Studies in adults have found that nPOC tongue swab testing is feasible, sensitive (75-86%), and specific (>96%). Testing can also be performed by dipping a swab in sputum, offering higher accuracy than tongue swabs and similar performance to sputum Xpert Ultra. However, the evidence in children has been limited to Xpert Ultra tongue swab testing, with low sensitivity (7-19%).

Added value of this study

To our knowledge, this is the first assessment of two swab-based nPOC assays for childhood TB: MiniDock MTB and MTB Ultima. In two high TB-burden settings of South Africa and Uganda, we prospectively enrolled children with presumptive TB and determined the accuracy of tongue and sputum swab testing. We found that tongue swab testing detected about half of children with culture-confirmed TB; sputum swab testing had substantially higher sensitivity than tongue swabs, and similar performance to sputum Xpert Ultra, meeting the World Health Organization (WHO) target accuracy for an nPOC sputum molecular TB test.

Implications of all the available evidence

The recent WHO guidelines endorsed sputum swab testing in adults and adolescents, and tongue swabs if sputum is not available. Similarly, we found that a single platform can enable nPOC molecular testing for TB among children, with sputum swab accuracy comparable to Xpert Ultra when sputum is available, and tongue swabs providing a simple, non-invasive approach to increase microbiological confirmation and potentially reduce delays in treatment when sputum is not available.

title: Swab-based recovery of simethicone emulsion at different concentrations in gastroscope biopsy channels: an experimental study
abstract: Simethicone is widely used during endoscopy but raises concerns about residue retention. This study quantitatively evaluated swab-recoverable simethicone residues in endoscope channels under clean and contaminated conditions, and assessed standard reprocessing effectiveness. Thirty-six gastroscopes with nominal 2.8-mm instrument channels were divided into clean (Olympus GIF-HQ290, n = 18) and contaminated (SonoScape 580, n = 18) arms. Three simethicone concentrations (0.1, 0.2, 1.0 mg/mL) were tested. The contaminated arm received defibrinated sheep blood containing Escherichia coli (10⁶ CFU/mL) before simethicone. Residues were measured by ¹H-nuclear magnetic resonance before and after standard reprocessing (manual cleaning plus automated orthophthalaldehyde disinfection). A linear mixed-effects model (LMM) was fitted to log-transformed residue mass with arm, phase, concentration, and their interactions as fixed effects, and endoscope as a random intercept. In clean endoscopes, pre-reprocessing swab-recoverable residue increased with concentration (F = 12.842, P < 0.001), decreasing significantly after reprocessing to 0.22–0.33 mg ( P < 0.001). In contaminated endoscopes, no concentration-response relationship was observed, and residues did not decrease significantly after reprocessing ( P = 0.134). A linear mixed-effects model confirmed that the pre-to-post reduction in residue differed significantly between clean and contaminated endoscopes (arm × phase interaction: coefficient = 0.597, 95% CI: 0.092 to 1.102, P = 0.021). ​Residues did not decrease significantly in the contaminated arm ( P = 0.134), although this comparison had only 32.3% statistical power. Standard reprocessing effectively reduced swab-recoverable simethicone residue in clean endoscopes. The pre-to-post change differed between the two study arms; however, because endoscope model and contamination condition were collinear, this difference cannot be attributed exclusively to biological contamination. Whether standard reprocessing definitively fails in soiled endoscopes remains inconclusive and warrants larger model-controlled studies using validated absolute-quantification methods.

title: TRAJECTORY PLANNING OF ACUPUNCTURE ROBOTS
abstract: For the clinical demand of sequential needling at multiple facial acupoints, needles already inserted and retained in the tissue become static obstacles to subsequent insertions. Planning a collision-free, smooth and efficient insertion path for each new needle inside the narrow facial workspace is therefore a key problem in the automation of acupuncture robots. This paper takes an acupuncture robot system composed of a UR5e six-degree-of-freedom manipulator and a self-developed acupuncture end effector as the research object, formulates multi-acupoint sequential needling as a constrained motion planning problem in which the obstacle set grows with the needling sequence, and proposes an improved APF-RRT* algorithm. The algorithm combines a bidirectional growth mechanism and goal-biased sampling on the RRT* framework to improve the convergence of the two trees, introduces Informed ellipsoidal subset sampling to reduce ineffective exploration, constructs an improved artificial potential field to alleviate the goal-unreachable and local-minimum problems, and designs a dynamic adaptive step-size strategy based on the ratio of attractive to repulsive force together with a bidirectional greedy path-pruning strategy. Simulation results in two- and three-dimensional environments show that, under the same maximum number of nodes, the proposed algorithm converges faster and yields a lower path cost than RRT* and APF-RRT*: in the 2D environment the runtime is reduced from 44.702 s to 9.538 s and the path cost from 792.702 to 750.477, while in the 3D environment the runtime is reduced from 84.594 s to 32.796 s and the path cost from 933.077 to 822.857, verifying the effectiveness and engineering applicability of the algorithm.

title: Teaching strategies in higher education in OECD member countries (2021–2025) and their effects on learning, motivation, and competence development: a PRISMA systematic review
abstract: Teaching strategies in higher education have gained increasing prominence in recent years, alongside the expansion of active, collaborative, and technology-supported pedagogies. This systematic review analyzed recent scientific evidence on teaching strategies in higher education institutions across Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) member countries, describing their methodological characteristics and their effects on learning, motivation, and competence development. A structured search was conducted in Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, ERIC, and PubMed. Peer-reviewed empirical studies published between 2021 and 2025 in English or Spanish, addressing teaching strategies in higher education within OECD countries, were included. Eligibility criteria were defined using the PCC framework; study selection followed the PRISMA 2020 guidelines; methodological quality was assessed using MMAT-2018 at the item level, without an overall quality score. Of the 564 records identified, 121 studies met the inclusion criteria and were incorporated into the qualitative synthesis. The findings showed a predominance of quantitative designs, mainly non-randomized studies and randomized controlled trials, complemented by mixed-methods and qualitative research. The teaching strategies were grouped into two main pedagogical families: student-centered active learning and technology-mediated or hybrid learning, together with an intermediate mixed category. Across the three groups, formative assessment and structured feedback emerged as shared pedagogical dimensions rather than as independent strategic categories. Most studies were conducted in European contexts and focused on health sciences, education, engineering, and related fields. These strategies were associated with improvements in academic performance, motivation, engagement, self-regulation, and the development of professional and socio-emotional competences. However, recent evidence remains fragmented by discipline, type of intervention, and assessment method, limiting a comprehensive understanding of their impact on university students. Furthermore, the concentration of studies in health sciences and education restricts the generalizability of the findings to other fields such as engineering, the humanities, and the social sciences. Overall, the evidence suggests that higher education systems in OECD countries are progressively adopting more active, hybrid, and technology-enhanced pedagogical models.
authors: Karla I. Pedraza-Maquera; Caroll J. U. Lévano-Villanueva; KARIN YANET SUPO GAVANCHO; José Luis Morales-Rocha; Ruthy Merla Pilco Velásquez; Jesús Alfredo Chacaltana García

title: The Collection of a Real-World, Large-Scale Dataset for Automated Skill Evaluation in Central Line Dressing Change
abstract: Central line-associated bloodstream infections (CLABSIs) remain a major source of preventable morbidity and mortality in healthcare settings. Proper execution of the central line dressing change (CLDC) procedure is essential for infection prevention, yet current approaches to competency assessment rely primarily on manual ob- servation by clinical educators, making evaluation time-intensive, difficult to scale, and limited in consistency and granularity. These challenges highlight the need for AI-assisted skill evaluation methods that can support more objective, reproducible, and scalable assessment of clinical performance. However, progress in this area has been constrained by the lack of broad-scale, clinically grounded datasets for developing and evaluating such methods. In this work, we present the collection process of a large-scale video dataset for CLDC skill evaluation, comprising 365 recordings of registered nurses collected during the 2026 annual competency exam at Houston Methodist Hospital. Each video is paired with subtask-level temporal annotations and clinical performance assessments spanning 17 subtasks of the procedure. We describe the data collection and curation pipeline, including pilot testing of record- ing configurations, annotation protocol design, and post-collection processing. We further establish the feasibility of video-based skill assessment through benchmark experiments with spatiotemporal deep learning models. This dataset provides a foundation for future research on automated clinical skill assessment, feedback generation, and AI-assisted training in nursing education.
authors: Ummey Tanin; Shannan K. Hamlin; Hsin-Mei Chen; Peizhu; Qian

title: The Living Lab at Home as an innovative platform for equitable and accessible study of families across a diverse developmental spectrum
abstract: Living lab platforms have gained increasing attention over the past two decades as an innovative approach to enhance engagement in research. These models emphasize co-development with participants, encourage knowledge exchange, and facilitate real-world data collection. Living labs have been applied to study health problems in older adults where research participation for vulnerable groups has been constrained by social, economic, or system-level barriers. Applying the living lab to children’s health is emerging as an innovative approach to foster more accessible research, which is especially important for children living with neurodevelopmental disorders, psychiatric conditions and chronic diseases, as well as social-environmental vulnerability. In this Expert Review Article we introduce the Living Lab at Home (LLAH) as an iterative, co-designed multi-method approach to developmental research. The LLAH offers an ethical, accessible, and equitable research platform for health research in underrepresented populations across a developmental spectrum. It allows for application of a variety of data collection methods such as smartphone-based microlongitudinal self-report, wearables, and non-invasive biomarkers to study everyday life in children with chronic pain and complex conditions. Co-development that supports the balance between scientific rigor and flexibility is key for capturing data that is of high quality and relevance. Based on our review we suggest that the LLAH holds potential for reducing inequities in research and health care systems, and opens new possibilities to individualize care, harness digital technology, and optimize health and well-being where children and youth live every day.
authors: Katelynn E. Boerner; Veronica Dudarev; Tim F. Oberlander

title: The STABLE Trial: Sustained Breath-Hold During Tissue Acquisition in Robotic Bronchoscopy—A Randomized Controlled Trial
abstract: Background: Respiratory motion and anesthesia-associated atelectasis may contribute to CT-to-body divergence and reduce the precision of peripheral pulmonary lesion sampling. Breath-hold ventilation has been proposed to stabilize the target and biopsy tool during robotic bronchoscopy, but prospective randomized evidence is limited. We evaluated whether sustained breath-hold during tissue acquisition improves diagnostic yield or tool-lesion positioning during imaging-integrated robotic bronchoscopy. Methods: The STABLE ( S tudy of T ool-lesion A lignment and B reath-hold Ventilation in Robotic Bronchoscopy for Peripheral Lung LE sions) Trial was a prospective randomized study of patients undergoing robotic bronchoscopy for peripheral pulmonary lesions using the Noah Galaxy system with integrated augmented fluoroscopy and C-arm-based tomosynthesis. Patients were randomized to standardized sustained breath-hold during tissue acquisition or conventional ventilation during tissue acquisition; both groups underwent brief breath-holds during AF/CABT image acquisition. The primary endpoint was strict diagnostic yield according to ATS/ACCP definitions, independently adjudicated by a pulmonologist blinded to ventilation assignment. Secondary endpoints included successful lesion localization, tool-in-lesion (TIL), tool-touching-lesion (TTL), no tool in lesion (NTL), radiation exposure, and complications. Standardized mean differences (SMDs) assessed baseline balance. Results: Among 117 randomized patients, 53 underwent breath-hold and 64 conventional ventilation. Mean age was 67.5±10.0 versus 66.3±10.4 years, and mean lesion diameter was 1.7±0.7 versus 1.9±0.8 cm, respectively. Most baseline characteristics were similar; the largest imbalances involved bronchus sign (34.0% vs 51.6%; absolute SMD 0.35) and left-upper-lobe location (28.3% vs 45.3%; SMD 0.35). Overall strict adjudicated diagnostic yield was 89.7% (105/117). Diagnostic yield was 86.8% with breath-hold and 92.2% with conventional ventilation (OR 0.56, 95% CI 0.17–1.87, p-value 0.34). With greater than 1 year of ongoing follow-up, overall diagnostic accuracy was 97.4% (114/117). Nearly all procedures achieved TIL or TTL (98.1% vs 96.9%). TIL occurred in 62.3% versus 64.1% (OR 0.93, 95% CI 0.44–1.97). Localization, tool-position distribution, sampling intensity, radiation exposure, and complications showed no clear between-group differences. Two pneumothoraces requiring chest-tube placement occurred (2/117; 1.7%), both in the conventional ventilation group. Across both groups, diagnostic yield increased from 0% with NTL to 85.0% with TTL and 95.9% with TIL. Conclusions: Sustained breath-hold during tissue acquisition did not improve diagnostic yield or tool-lesion positioning during imaging-integrated robotic bronchoscopy. Diagnostic yield varied according to imaging-confirmed tool-lesion position, supporting procedural strategies that prioritize accurate real-time positioning rather than breath-hold alone. Trial registration: International Standard Randomised Controlled Trial Number (ISRCTN) Registry, ISRCTN11802169; retrospectively registered (01/09/2026).
authors: Mathew R, Danilevskaya O, Cherian S, Meena N.

title: The impact of experience on radiation dose and procedure duration in shape-sensing robotic-assisted bronchoscopy
abstract: Introduction Shape-sensing robotic-assisted bronchoscopy (ssRAB) is increasingly used for the diagnosis of peripheral pulmonary lesions, but data describing operator learning beyond diagnostic yield remains limited. Procedural efficiency and radiation exposure are important markers of technical development and patient safety, yet their evolution during early operator experience is poorly characterised. We evaluated changes in procedure duration and radiation dose across the first 100 diagnostic cases of three staggered operators at a tertiary referral centre. Methods We conducted a retrospective analysis of prospectively collected data. Three operators performing ssRAB were included, with staggered start dates. Operator 1 commenced first, followed sequentially by Operator 2 after 7 cases and operator 3 after 124 total cases. The first 100 consecutive diagnostic cases per operator were analysed. Procedure time per nodule and radiation dose per nodule were calculated for each case. Cases were divided into quartiles of 25 and median values with interquartile ranges (IQR) reported. Differences between groups were assessed using the Mann-Whitney U test. A p-value <0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results Significant reductions in procedure time per nodule and radiation dose per nodule were demonstrated across the cohort. Results are presented in table 1. Conclusion All three operators demonstrated reductions in radiation dose per nodule across their first 100 cases (Op 1: -63.2%, p<0.001; Op 2: -38.0%, p=0.050; Op 3: -44.3%, p=0.003). Operator 3, who commenced after Operators 1 and 2 were established, started with the lowest baseline procedure duration and radiation dose, suggesting later operators benefit from the accumulated experience of their predecessors. These findings support a structured, staggered operator introduction model during ssRAB programme development.
authors: HJ Trainer; BP Patani; JP Panaguiton; Ola Volhina; A Karir; Anand Tana; James Tonkin; Justin L. Garner; Pallav L. Shah; Christopher Michael Orton

title: The impact of scenario-based simulation learning on clinical self-efficacy among pre-licensure nursing and midwifery students: A systematic review of design features and educational outcomes
abstract: AIM: To systematically review how scenario-based simulation learning (SBSL) shapes clinical self-efficacy among pre-licensure nursing and midwifery students and how simulation design, context and assessment timing influence educational and clinical translation. BACKGROUND: Scenario-based simulation learning (SBSL) is widely used in nursing and midwifery education, yet evidence on its effect on clinical self-efficacy and how simulation design moderate outcomes remains fragmented. DESIGN: A systematic review following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. METHODS: A PRISMA 2020-compliant review searched eight databases. Eligible studies measured task-specific clinical self-efficacy via validated tools in pre-licensure cohorts. Two reviewers independently screened records, extracted data on scenario complexity, theoretical integration, debriefing structure and outcome timing and appraised risk of bias. RESULTS: Fifty-two studies (N = 4774; 46 nursing, 6 midwifery) were included. SBSL broadly correlated with self-efficacy gains, yet only 55.8% (n = 29) demonstrated statistically significant between-group superiority. Psychomotor skill (54.1%), knowledge (61.9%) and cognitive reasoning (62.5%) improvements were documented. Studies embedding explicit theoretical frameworks, calibrated scenario difficulty ("Goldilocks Zone") and structured debriefing showed the most consistent benefits. Immediate post-simulation assessments were frequently distorted by acute simulation anxiety; self-efficacy crystallized only after cognitive consolidation. CONCLUSION: SBSL shows promise for building clinical self-efficacy, but effects are inconsistently captured and methodologically constrained by reliance on subjective self-report. Pedagogical architecture-progressive scaffolding, discipline-sensitive scenario design and rigorous debriefing-matters more than technical fidelity. Sustained efficacy requires longitudinal follow-up beyond immediate post-intervention windows. Faculty pedagogical preparedness, rather than equipment investment, is the decisive lever for translational impact. REGISTRATION: A Systematic Review.
