title: The transformative power of artificial intelligence and machine learning in blood banking/transfusion medicine: A vein‐to‐vein approach from blood collection to transfusion services: On behalf of the AABB Foundation
abstract: BACKGROUND: Artificial intelligence (AI)/machine learning (ML) are poised to transform transfusion medicine across the vein-to-vein continuum, from donor recruitment to recipient outcomes. Large datasets generated from millions of donations and transfusions create opportunities for predictive modeling, precision medicine, improved safety, and operational efficiency. This review outlines key applications of AI in blood banking and transfusion medicine using a comprehensive vein-to-vein framework. METHODS: The review synthesizes perspectives from blood services and hospital-based transfusion practices. Applications are discussed across donor recruitment, collections, testing, inventory management, hospital transfusion services, and education. Finally, AI safety, including ethical, regulatory, privacy, and implementation challenges, is addressed. This is a narrative, non-exhaustive review; given the rapidly evolving pace of AI/ML capabilities, this synthesis should be interpreted as a framework for ongoing surveillance rather than a fixed inventory of applications. RESULTS: Donor-focused applications include personalized recruitment, individualized iron management, and fairness auditing to reduce inequities. In supply chain operations, ML can improve demand forecasting, minimize waste, and optimize inventory. Federated learning may support multi-institutional collaboration without sharing raw data. Omics and genomic applications can enable high-throughput analysis, phenotype prediction, and precision transfusion support for rare blood types and alloimmunized patients. In hospitals, AI can augment hemovigilance by identifying/predicting adverse transfusion reactions, while large language models and retrieval-augmented generation may enhance decision support, patient blood management, and education through adaptive learning. CONCLUSION: AI holds substantial promise to improve transfusion safety, efficiency, equity, and sustainability. Realizing this potential will require robust governance, model validation across diverse populations, privacy safeguards, bias mitigation, reproducibility, regulatory oversight, and human-in-the-loop implementation.
authors: Ruchika Goel; Sheharyar Raza; W. Alton Russell; Jansen N. Seheult; Tho D. Pham; Angelo D’Alessandro; Rounak Dubey; Celina Montemayor; David B. Daniel; Cliff Numark; Brian Custer; Jason Sapia; Tony Casina; Jerry A. Holmberg; Aaron A.R. Tobian; Na Li

title: Time to Positivity of Blood Culture in an Automated Bact/Alert 3D System and Its Association with Procalcitonin Levels and Organism Type: A Retrospective Observational Study
abstract: Background Bloodstream infections (BSIs) are life-threatening conditions frequently encountered in critical care, where early identification of infection and timely initiation of appropriate antimicrobial therapy are essential for reducing morbidity and mortality. Although blood culture remains the reference method for microbiological conformation, automated blood culture systems provide rapid and standardized detection of microbial growth. Time to positivity (TTP) may provide additional information regarding the infecting organism and microbial burden. While procalcitonin (PCT) is widely used as an adjunctive biomarker in the assessment of suspected bacterial infection and sepsis. In this study to determine the TTP of clinically significant blood cultures processed using the automated Bact/Alert 3D system and evaluate its relationship with serum procalcitonin levels. The study also assessed organism-specific differences in TTP and relevant demographic associations. Methods A retrospective observational study was conducted in the Department of Microbiology, SRM Medical College Hospital and Research Centre, Kattankulathur, Tamil Nadu, from September 2025 to August 2026. All blood culture samples received during the study period were included. Samples were collected under strict aseptic conditions and processed using the automated Bact/Alert 3D system. TTP was recorded in hours. Available serum PCT values were correlated with TTP, and organism-specific differences were statistically analyzed. Results Of the total suspected blood stream infection culture samples analyzed, 8,726(90.2%) showed no growth after five days, 514(5.3%) yielded skin commensals, and 434(4.5%) yielded clinically significant organisms. A valid TTP was obtained for 259 positive cultures. The mean TTP was 14.36 ± 13.67hours, with a median of 9.21 hours (IQR 6.00–16.28). Overall, 62.9% of cultures became positive within 12 hours, 82.6% within 24 hours, and 95.8% within 48% hours. Gram-negative organisms predominated (59.1%), followed by Gram positive organisms (30.9%) and Candida species (8.1%). Candida showed the longest median TTP (32.01 h; p < 0.001). PCT showed a significant inverse correlation with TTP (p = -0.270, p < 0.001). Conclusion TTP varied significantly by organism and showed an inverse correlation with PCT. Combining TTP and PCT may support early risk assessment and clinical management of sepsis in critical care settings.
authors: Sandhiya R; Leela K V; Jayaprakash T; Rahul H L

title: Time-Dependent Analysis of Blood Glucose Stability in Sodium Fluoride Versus Plain Blood Collection Tubes
abstract: OBJECTIVES: Sodium fluoride (NaF) tubes are routinely recommended for blood glucose estimation because of their glycolysis-inhibiting properties. However, NaF inhibits enolase, a downstream glycolytic enzyme, and does not immediately prevent glucose consumption by blood cells. This raises the following questions: How does glucose stability compare between NaF plasma and plain serum over time? Does NaF offer better glucose preservation than plain serum? Does prompt separation of blood cells improve glucose stability? This study aimed to compare glucose stability in NaF plasma and plain serum at different time intervals and assess the effect of prompt cell separation on glucose preservation under routine laboratory conditions. Materials and methods: This prospective observational study included 172 paired blood samples collected simultaneously in NaF and plain serum tubes. Samples were categorized into three groups: Group 1, plasma from NaF tubes; Group 2, serum from plain tubes; and Group 3, serum separated after centrifugation(using LabTop centrifuge at 3000 rpm for 10 minutes) and aliquoted into microcentrifuge tubes. Groups 1 and 2 were analyzed (using clinical chemistry analyzer Bonavera Chem 200, Biogeny Diagnostics Pvt. Ltd., Beacon Group, Surat, India) at <4 hours (baseline), four to six hours, 12-14 hours, and 24-26 hours after collection while stored at room temperature. Group 3 samples were analyzed after 24 hours. Percentage variation in glucose concentration from baseline was calculated. RESULTS: The mean difference between plain serum and NaF plasma within four hours of collection was 0.44%, with individual variation ranging from -0.62% to 3.36%. In NaF plasma, the mean decline in glucose concentration from baseline was 2.47% at four to six hours, 4.31% at 12-14 hours, and 9.97% at 24-26 hours. Corresponding individual variations ranged from 0.46% to 5.12%, 2.99% to 8.56%, and 3.96% to 17.47%, respectively. By contrast, the mean glucose decline in unseparated serum samples was 8.69%, 45.94%, and 75.59% at the respective time intervals. Glucose concentrations in aliquoted serum remained stable after 24 hours, showing <1% variation from baseline. CONCLUSION: The consistent and substantial decline in glucose concentrations over time in both serum and plasma samples that remain in contact with blood cells highlights the critical importance of prompt cell separation to minimize pre-analytical glycolysis and ensure reliable glucose measurements. Notably, even when blood is collected in NaF tubes, delayed centrifugation and separation of plasma from blood cells may still permit considerable glucose loss. This raises concerns about the presumed advantage of fluoride-containing tubes over plain tubes when prompt sample processing is not ensured. In a hospital-based lab or referral lab with a rapid processing workflow, the use of a single plain serum tube can yield accurate glucose results, along with other biochemical tests, although it is not universally recommended as for peripheral collection centers. This can prevent the extra cost burden of fluoride vials for diagnostic labs and also decrease the extra burden of blood samples on patients. This also decreases the burden of biomedical waste generated in the form of fluoride vials, making it more sustainable and environmentally friendly. Further multicenter studies are warranted before recommending changes to existing specimen collection guidelines.
authors: Kuldeep K Gupta; Tabassum Yasmin; Farhat Khan; Priyanka Asia

title: Tissue-specific virome variation and diversity of the Himalayan marmot on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau
abstract: The Qinghai-Tibet Plateau harbors unique extreme habitats and diverse natural foci of infectious diseases. The Himalayan marmot is a key reservoir and amplification host for various pathogens; however, its viral carriage spectrum remains largely unexplored. In this study, 745 specimens were collected from 70 wild Himalayan marmots, including nasopharyngeal swabs, parasitic fleas, blood, rectal feces, and tissues from the heart, liver, spleen, lung, kidney, and brain. Viral metagenomics was used to characterize viral community composition and diversity across tissues. Alpha diversity differed significantly among tissues, with the highest diversity in heart and brain and the lowest in liver and kidney. Blood and flea samples showed significantly higher diversity than rectal samples, whereas no significant difference was observed between blood and flea samples. Principal coordinates analysis based on Bray-Curtis distances revealed significant tissue-specific clustering at family, genus, and species levels (PERMANOVA, all P = 0.001). Differential abundance analysis identified distinct viral enrichment patterns: Peduoviridae and Retroviridae in blood, Microviridae in feces, Polyomaviridae and Microviridae in heart, Retroviridae and Orthoherpesviridae in respiratory and lung tissues, and Circoviridae and Streblomastigidae in nasopharyngeal swabs. These findings reveal niche differentiation and spatial heterogeneity of viral communities across marmot tissues, organs, and transmission vectors, and provide baseline data for zoonotic disease surveillance on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau.These findings reveal niche differentiation and spatial heterogeneity of viral communities across marmot tissues, organs, and transmission vectors, and provide foundational data for understanding virus-host interactions and zoonotic disease prevention on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau.
authors: Haisheng Wu; Wenxuan Peng; Danni Zhou; Qingwen Zhang

title: Towards more personalized approach in rectal cancer
abstract: Rectal cancer treatment has evolved substantially over recent decades, resulting in improved oncological outcomes. However, treatment-related morbidity and its impact on quality of life remain important challenges. Traditionally, treatment decisions have largely been based on clinical and radiological staging. But increasing opportunities to tailor treatment to individual tumor characteristics, treatment response, and patient-related factors are driving a shift toward more personalized care. This thesis explores different strategies to support this transition, ranging from translational biomarkers and prediction models to patient-reported outcomes and individualized treatment strategies in clinical practice. The first part of this thesis investigates approaches to improve patient selection for treatment. Liquid biopsy techniques are explored as potential biomarkers to predict response to neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy and to guide postoperative chemotherapy based on circulating tumor DNA. In addition, a machine-learning model based on clinical characteristics was developed to predict pathological complete response after chemoradiotherapy. The thesis subsequently examines health-related quality of life after minimally invasive rectal cancer surgery. Longitudinal analyses demonstrate largely comparable quality-of-life outcomes between robotic and conventional laparoscopic surgery and show that most differences associated with neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy diminish during postoperative follow-up, while the presence of a stoma particularly affects body image. Finally, this thesis evaluates personalized treatment strategies in clinical practice. Nationwide implementation of watch-and-wait demonstrates that organ preservation can be achieved in a substantial proportion of patients following neoadjuvant treatment. Furthermore, differences in presentation and survival between male and female patients emphasize the potential relevance of sex-related factors in rectal cancer care. In patients with local re-recurrent rectal cancer, aggressive treatment may provide meaningful survival in carefully selected patients despite the complexity and morbidity of treatment. Together, these studies support a continued shift from standardized treatment pathways toward a more personalized approach in rectal cancer, integrating tumor biology, treatment response, patient characteristics, quality of life, and individual preferences to provide treatment that is as intensive as necessary, but as limited as possible.
authors: David M Mens

title: Transport revolutions and urban development: Historical trajectories and possible futures
abstract: The configuration of cities has experienced profound changes over time, and one of the lenses through which these shifts can be interpreted is the emergence of successive transport technologies and systems, giving rise to major transport revolutions. Most of the first six of such revolutions have historically contributed to shaping urban morphology. This paper addresses this via the “one-hour city” hypothesis that combines the Travel Time Budget (TTB) assumption with the average travel distance and the speed allowed by the prevailing transport technology. Today, a seventh transport revolution is potentially unfolding, propelled by decarbonization, autonomous driving, and the introduction of digital mobility services. This ongoing transition holds the potential to reshape both the spatial and functional dimensions of cities, although overall effects are still unpredictable. These changes have been widely researched in recent years but often with reference to specific features. This paper presents research results in a holistic view, proposing two extreme, opposing scenarios. The first is based on a model of car ownership similar to the present, only based on autonomous cars. This scenario will be labelled as the “autonomous-car city.” Research results suggest an increase in car demand and congestion, as well as a decrease in public transport ridership. Conversely, the “post-car city” scenario shifts from ownership to a “car-as-a-service” paradigm using shared, electric autonomous fleets. This transition drastically reduces parking footprint, enabling urban space reclamation and better separation between motorized and active transport modes. In both scenarios, public transit and individual mobility blur into Demand-Responsive Mobility Services. As for city dimensions, the analytical model would suggest that, given that the commercial speed of future services is arguably comparable to the present, spatial dimensions will depend on the value of average TTB. This paper concludes with some policy recommendations to steer future cities toward more sustainable trajectories.
authors: Ennio Cascetta; Marilisa Botte; Anna Limmatola
venue: Journal of Transport and Land Use

title: Ultrasound-Guided Percutaneous Placement of Indocyanine Green-Dyed Coils for Intraoperative Localization of Subpleural Lung Tumors
abstract: Accurate localization of peripheral pulmonary lesions is a prerequisite for lung-sparing minimally invasive resection. Indocyanine green (ICG)-dyed coils have emerged as an effective multimodal marker, detectable by near-infrared fluorescence, fluoroscopy, palpation, and ultrasound, but their placement currently relies on CT or cone-beam CT guidance, with the associated radiation exposure and logistical demands. For subpleural lesions, transthoracic ultrasound offers real-time, radiation-free guidance. We present our initial experience with ultrasound-guided percutaneous placement of ICG-dyed coils. Of 33 patients scheduled for ICG-coil marking between July 2025 and March 2026, eight were assessed for ultrasound-guided marking, and three (37.5% of those assessed; 9% of all scheduled) had a lesion with a suitable acoustic window. In these three patients (aged 52-67 years), an ICG-dyed coil was placed adjacent to the tumor under real-time transthoracic ultrasound guidance in the operating room under general anaesthesia, immediately before uniportal or biportal video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS). The lesions measured 17-19 mm and were located 2-4 mm below the visceral pleura in the left upper, right lower and right upper lobe. Coil placement was technically successful in all patients, with a median procedure time (first ultrasound contact to needle removal) of 12 minutes (range 11-13 minutes) and a median total added time, including preparation, of 33 minutes. The marker was identified by near-infrared fluorescence in every case, and all lesions were resected with R0 margins. Histology showed squamous cell carcinoma in two patients and metastatic adenocarcinoma of colorectal origin in one. No bleeding or other immediate complications were observed at thoracoscopy. Because the lung was collapsed for resection immediately after puncture, delayed pneumothorax and marker migration could not be assessed. In selected patients with solid subpleural lesions and an adequate acoustic window, ultrasound-guided placement of ICG-dyed coils was technically feasible and enabled fluorescence-guided localization at thoracoscopy. However, due to the small series, the safety of the technique or its added value over intraoperative palpation or thoracoscopic ultrasound cannot be established. Larger prospective studies, including marking with delayed resection, are needed to define patient selection and to compare the technique with CT-guided and bronchoscopic marking.
authors: Sammy Onyancha; Hasnain Saifee Bawaadam; Peter Hollaus; Gernot Rohde; W Schreiner

title: Unlocking microbiome secrets: a systematic review of microbiome-derived biomarkers for early colorectal cancer detection
abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is a leading cause of cancer-related death worldwide, and established non-invasive screening tools such as the guaiac fecal occult blood test and the fecal immunochemical test have limited sensitivity for early-stage disease. Microbiome-derived biomarkers have emerged as a promising alternative for early, non-invasive CRC detection. This systematic review evaluated the diagnostic performance of microbiome-derived biomarkers - including 16S rRNA gene sequencing, metagenomic shotgun sequencing, and co-metabolomic profiling - for detecting early-stage colorectal cancer and its precursor lesions. A systematic search of PubMed and EMBASE (via OVID) covering the ten years up to May 3, 2024 was conducted following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, with triplicate ASReview-assisted screening and two-of-three reviewer consensus for full-text selection; risk of bias was assessed using QUADAS-2. Of 3,859 records identified in the primary search, 26 studies met all eligibility criteria; following a post-hoc bibliographic verification and a subsequent targeted search update, the final set comprised 28 studies, drawn from East Asia, South Asia, Europe, and North America and predominantly using fecal samples, with a minority also using oral swab or serum samples. Reported diagnostic performance varied widely across studies (area under the curve 0.28-0.98; sensitivity 18-100%; specificity 39-97%), with the highest accuracy reported for panels derived from oral swab samples. Most studies carried a high or unclear risk of bias in the index-test domain, and no included study reported independent external validation of its biomarker panel in a separate cohort. Microbiome-derived biomarkers show promising but highly heterogeneous and largely unvalidated diagnostic performance for early CRC detection. Standardized sample-collection and analytic protocols, together with externally validated, multi-center studies in populations not yet represented in the evidence base - including South America - are needed before these biomarkers can be considered for clinical or population-level screening use.
authors: Juliana Victoria Martinez Janne; Mabel Bohorquez Lozano; Shehnaz K. Hussain; Luis G. Carvajal‐Carmona

title: Unsupervised surface defect detection and localization of transparent vacuum blood collection tubes using region-aware reconstruction and expert fusion
abstract: Automated inspection of transparent vacuum blood collection tubes is complicated by specular reflections, heterogeneous endpoint structures and highly elongated regions of interest. An unsupervised region-aware reconstruction framework is developed using native-coordinate patches, three jointly trained reconstruction experts and region-prior-guided soft fusion. A Regional Multiscale Excess Score (RMES) calibrates normal regional residual tails for image-level detection while preserving the original pixel anomaly map. Evaluation on 100 abnormal ROIs and a reserved pool of 145 normal ROIs across three training seeds yielded Image AUROC of 0.9868 ± 0.0027, macro Pixel AP of 0.8358 ± 0.0710 and micro fixed-threshold Pixel F1 of 0.2499 ± 0.0052. Controlled fusion comparisons and same-map scoring experiments further assess the contributions of expert reconstruction and regional anomaly-score calibration.
authors: Zhanmin Zhao; Pengxiang Zhao; Bingyu Bai; Xuemei Shi; Han Wang

title: Utility and performance of robotic-assisted bronchoscopic fine-needle aspiration compared with robotic-assisted bronchoscopic cryo-biopsy for the evaluation of pulmonary lesions.
abstract: Few studies have compared robotic-assisted bronchoscopic (RAB) fine-needle aspiration (FNA) with RAB cryo-biopsy (CB) for the evaluation of peripheral pulmonary lesions. We compared performance between RAB-FNA and RAB-CB in the evaluation of peripheral pulmonary lesions. From our pathology database, we identified patients who underwent RAB-FNA with rapid on-site evaluation and concurrent RAB-CB between January and December 2024. We recorded patient and lesion characteristics, RAB-CB and RAB-FNA diagnostic categorization (non-diagnostic, benign, atypical, suspicious, malignant), and specimen type used for molecular studies. RAB-FNA and RAB-CB results were compared with those of surgical resection and clinical follow-up as the gold standard. For both procedures, we evaluated diagnostic performance for establishing the diagnosis of the pulmonary lesion. We identified 240 cases including 148 malignant, 1 neoplasm with undetermined malignant potential and 91 benign diagnoses, based on the gold standard. The male-to-female ratio was 23:25; median patient age, 69 years; and median lesion size, 1.8 cm. Touch preparation of RAB-CB was performed in 26 (11%) cases. Compared with RAB-CB, RAB-FNA had lower sensitivity for malignant tumors (89% versus 91%) but higher sensitivity for metastasis (73% versus 70%) and lymphoma (86% versus 71%), and it was used less often for molecular testing (99% versus 1%). The RAB-FNA and RAB-CB diagnoses were discordant in 44 cases (18%). RAB-CB provided superior diagnostic performance overall compared with RAB-FNA for peripheral pulmonary lesions. However, the use of rapid on-site evaluation to evaluate RAB-FNA tissue yield guided the procurement and preservation of CB without touch preparation. Our findings support an integrated dual-sampling approach combining RAB-FNA and RAB-CB, as FNA aids in real-time confirmation of lesional targeting, thereby optimizing procedural adequacy while preserving cryobiopsy material for downstream studies.
authors: Saroja Devi Geetha; Dianna Klippel-Almaraz; Neda Kalhor; Anthony Rowe; Saad Farooq; George Eapen; Savitri Krishnamurthy
venue: Journal of the American Society of Cytopathology

title: VLM-based multi-agent architecture for multifunctional robotic health attendant (RHA) using phase-prompt task design
abstract: Introduction: Healthcare robots are increasingly needed to support clinicians whose work involves diverse tasks and frequent task switching. However, most healthcare robots developed to assist clinicians either perform a single function or implement multiple functions as fixed task pipelines that are difficult to adapt to different patients, rooms, or care teams. This study presents a vision language model (VLM) based multiagent architecture for a multifunctional Robotic Health Attendant (RHA). Methods: In this architecture, each task can be designed by writing natural language phase specifications that describe how available tools should be used during task execution. A main agent interprets natural language requests from clinicians or patients and routes each request to the appropriate task agent. During execution, the VLM uses language, visual input, and contextual information to select tools and interpret their results. A shared Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool layer provides elemental robot functions such as navigation, manipulation, and perception across tasks. The architecture was implemented on a TIAGo Pro robot and evaluated in an unoccupied patient room across five tasks including object delivery, documentation, visual monitoring, patient education, and medication reminders. Results: The case study demonstrated the feasibility of the proposed architecture as a reasoning core for a multifunctional healthcare robot by executing multiple tasks and adapting task behavior by editing natural language phase specifications. The comparison across three VLMs showed that longer tool-call sequences led to skipped steps and, in some cases, false reports of task success, which is a key reliability concern for healthcare robots performing long, multi-step tasks. Discussion: The study also identified technical limitations and future research needs that must be addressed to make the architecture more robust in realistic care settings.
authors: Kyungki Kim; John R. Windle; Tom Windle; Melissa Christian; Christian Haas; Bethany Lowndes

title: Validation of a deep neural network workflow for fully automated dicentric chromosome analysis in biological dosimetry
abstract: Artificial intelligence has recently found its way into biological dosimetry. This study validated the initial version of a deep neural network (DNN) workflow implemented by MetaSystems to detect dicentric and polycentric chromosomes in microscopy images. This was performed through parameter optimisation, calibration curve generation and independent testing. Optimisation of thresholds for the class score parameter defining the aberration classes was performed and brought DNN scoring closer to manual scoring ( 60 Co dataset) for low doses by reducing the number of false-positive dicentrics, while balancing the influence of false-negative detections, especially for higher doses. Although slightly higher, the DNN achieved an acceptable yield of dicentrics for the control. A comparison of the calibration curves showed that the DNN curve was between manual and semi-automatic curves. DNN curves based on two independent test datasets (X-ray) from different laboratories showed very good agreement, with dose estimations matching the reference doses for all 12/13 test samples precisely, even for low doses and for triage scoring. This DNN-workflow enables the establishment of calibration curves for different radiation qualities and successfully performs dose estimations. It could replace semi-automated scoring and enhance the capacity of biological dosimetry laboratories in the event of large-scale radiological or nuclear incidents.
authors: Martin Bucher; Andreas Brown; Siegfried Hänselmann; Jayne Moquet; Stephen G. R. Barnard; Ursula Oestreicher; David Endesfelder

title: Antimicrobial susceptibility patterns of Group B Streptococcus isolates recovered from pregnant individuals in Greece.
abstract: Group B Streptococcus (GBS) remains an important pathogen in pregnancy and a major cause of neonatal morbidity and mortality. This study aimed to investigate the antimicrobial susceptibility profile of GBS isolates recovered from pregnant individuals in Greece. A retrospective observational study was conducted, including 89 non-duplicate GBS isolates recovered from vaginal and rectal swab specimens during routine antenatal screening at a maternity clinic in Athens, Greece, between 2021 and 2025. Bacterial identification was performed using the VITEK 2 automated system, and antimicrobial susceptibility testing was conducted by determining the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) according to the European Committee on Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing (EUCAST) criteria. High resistance rates were observed for erythromycin and clindamycin, with 58.62% and 54.55% of tested isolates classified as resistant, respectively. Tetracycline showed the highest resistance rate (89.77%), while most isolates remained susceptible to benzylpenicillin (97.75%) and vancomycin (98.86%). Multidrug resistance was detected in 50% of isolates. These findings underscore the need for susceptibility-guided prophylaxis and ongoing surveillance of antimicrobial resistance in Greece.
authors: Karolina Akinosoglou; Maria Gavatha; Panayotis D Ziakas; Alexandros Psarris; Christina Vogiantzi; Eleni Polyzou; Aristotelis Tsiakalos

title: A Large Language Model-Driven Embodied Conversational Agent for Patient Education in Virtual Reality: Mixed Methods Usability Study (Preprint)
abstract: BACKGROUND Clinicians routinely distribute printed patient education materials at the point of care. Tutorials covering all relevant information are rarely feasible within clinical time constraints and ongoing educational support is commonly needed. Patients reading these materials on their own cannot ask questions or have passages explained, and a pamphlet does not adjust to a patient’s educational needs. Embodied conversational agents (ECAs) powered by large language models could take on the role of a clinician or health educator, guiding a patient through educational materials they were given. Virtual reality (VR) additionally affords spatial grounding of anatomical references and use of attentional cues from the patient, such as gaze and pointing, as human educators do while teaching. Whether patients find such a system usable and acceptable in VR is unknown. OBJECTIVE We evaluated an agentic workflow that transforms static patient education pamphlets into structured learning sessions delivered by an ECA in VR. We conducted a formative evaluation of the usability and acceptability of the VR learning experience, including pre-post knowledge change. METHODS We conducted a mixed methods usability study. Healthy adult volunteers (N=22 enrolled; N=21 analyzed) completed a VR learning session (mean duration 18.0 minutes, SD 3.5) in which the ECA delivered a multimodal walkthrough of standardized patient education materials on colonoscopy, appendectomy, or kidney cancer, supported open-ended questions, and reinforced understanding through summaries and brief multiple-choice review questions (flashcards). Measures included overall satisfaction, perceived quality of the education material using an adapted version of the Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool, pre- and post-session knowledge tests, and semi-structured interviews. RESULTS Satisfaction with the VR learning session was positive (mean 6.35, SD 0.92 on a 7-point scale, significantly above the scale midpoint), as was perceived content quality (mean 6.21, SD 0.88 on a 7-point scale). Knowledge test scores increased significantly from mean 23.45 (SD 8.82) before the session to 34.90 (SD 7.56) after, on a 0-50 scale (paired t test, t20=5.40; P<.001). Interview themes included immersion and spatial visualization of anatomy, the agent’s supportive manner, and interactive feedback. Participants also reported headset weight and discomfort, unfamiliarity with VR controls, and problems with the ECA’s synthesized voice. CONCLUSIONS In a single-session formative evaluation with healthy, predominantly highly educated volunteers, an ECA powered by a large language model delivering a guided walk-through of patient education material in VR was usable and well accepted, and knowledge scores increased significantly from pre- to post-session. These findings suggest that patient education may be augmented with an embodied agent, though specific hardware and speech-synthesis barriers need additional adaptation before evaluation with clinical populations.
authors: Chongyang Wang; Mina Fallah; Akilan Baskar; Michael K. Paasche‐Orlow; Timothy Bickmore

title: A Persian Vision-Language-Action Dataset and Benchmark for Ambiguity- and Infeasibility-Aware Instruction-to-Plan Grounding
abstract: Converting natural-language instructions into executable action plans conditioned on a scene image is a core capability for embodied human-robot interaction, but existing benchmarks target English, simulated or video-grounded environments, and largely assume instructions are clear and executable. We introduce the first Persian vision-language-action dataset for this task: 258 instances over 230 real household/office photographs, annotated with reference plans, deliberate ambiguity and infeasibility labels, disambiguating question-answer pairs, and an auto-generated chain-of-thought rationale for training. Using this resource, we ablate retrieval-augmentation, chain-of-thought prompting, and an agentic disambiguation step, evaluated with an LLM-as-judge protocol and a new metric, PGOS-FA, extending prior work (PG2S) with step-order sensitivity, an over-generation penalty, and Persian-adapted embeddings. Paired statistical testing across 36 comparisons shows retrieval-augmentation is a large, robustly significant effect, while finer-grained additions are directionally consistent but not statistically distinguishable from noise at this scale, and the LLM-judge metric has near-zero power where PGOS-FA succeeds. A blind human-correlation study on 79 real outputs shows PGOS-FA tracks human judgment at least as closely as the LLM-judge. Testing generalization beyond the ablation's single backbone, we find that most of the gap between an open-weight and a substantially stronger closed planner is attributable to open-weight model generation rather than to the closed model's capability specifically, and that our best configuration significantly outperforms an independently reproduced external baseline despite a weaker backbone. The dataset, PGOS-FA implementation, and evaluation code will be made available upon reasonable request.
authors: Abdollah Pourasghari; Saeedeh Sadat Sadidpour; Mohammad Roustaei

title: A Self-Evolving Agent for Longitudinal Personal Health Management
abstract: Medical large language models and agents show strong single-encounter question answering and evidence interpretation but struggle to accumulate and govern experience across encounters. We present HealthJev, an open-source agent separating shared safety rules and medical knowledge from a private longitudinal memory and distilling lessons from completed cases. To filter out erroneous lessons before they affect future behaviour, we self-train JevGate, a lightweight System-One model that decides which lessons enter memory; each decision takes a median of 86 milliseconds and about 1,000 input tokens, sustaining experience accumulation at negligible run-time overhead. On a longitudinal benchmark of 90-day simulated daily interactions for 20 users built from real MIMIC-IV trajectories, HealthJev outperformed a memory-free ReAct agent and three memory-augmented frameworks, with all paired comparisons significant. Across six tasks spanning clinical records, medical imaging, genomics and clinical text, HealthJev improved every task with a mean gain of 13.3 percentage points over the base condition, surpassing all baselines. The frozen library transferred to six further backbones with macro-average gains of 6.8 to 15.1 percentage points, and one task's library brought gains on other tasks. These results indicate that governed, self-evolving memory supports longitudinal personal health management beyond single encounters. HealthJev is publicly available at https://github.com/HC-Guo/Self-Evolving_HealthJev.
authors: Hongcheng Guo; Haoran Li; Jiangli Deng; Tong Jin; Jinghong Han; Yuxin Wang; Zexin Wang; Jinyu Sun; Qingyi Si; 庄吓海; Xiahai Zhuang; Jia You; Wei Cheng; Jianfeng Feng

title: A systematic review of embodied intelligence: concepts, technologies, applications, evaluation and challenges
abstract: Embodied intelligence extends artificial intelligence from information processing in the digital domain to autonomous interaction with the physical world. Despite rapid progress, the field still faces challenges such as ambiguous conceptual boundaries, fragmented technical frameworks, and insufficient alignment between application requirements and evaluation standards. This review presents a systematic framework for understanding embodied intelligence from five perspectives: conceptual foundations, key technologies, representative applications, evaluation methodologies, and future challenges. We first distinguish embodied intelligence from teleoperation and conventional automation, and establish an evolutionary framework spanning disembodied intelligence, spatial intelligence, physical intelligence, and embodied intelligence. Then we summarize key technologies in embodiment, the cerebellum, brain architectures, data acquisition, and training approaches, with particular emphasis on the evolution from traditional hierarchical modular architecture to large-model-driven modular architecture, Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model architecture, world model architecture, and world action model architecture. Representative applications are categorized into structured-environment manipulation, unstructured-environment interaction, and high-risk open-domain exploration. To bridge technological development and real-world deployment, we further review three evaluation paradigms which include data-based evaluation, simulation-based testing and real-world testing. Finally, we identify eight major challenges which cover data quality, long-horizon planning, multimodal fusion, edge deployment, safety and trustworthiness, continual learning, unified navigation and manipulation, and multi-agent collaboration. This review provides a systematic perspective on embodied intelligence and highlights key directions for advancing embodied systems toward reliable deployment in complex real-world environments.
authors: Yixiang Liang; He Ma; Yong Chen; Xuan Huang; Bichun Li; Linglong Lin; Lei Sun; Shengchao Zhen; Shuai Zhang; Biao Yu; 陈池来

title: Advancing Clinical Trials and Precision Medicine in Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy Using Machine Learning‐Based Trajectory Modeling and MRI Radiomics
abstract: Given heterogeneous progression of Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), accurately characterizing individual disease trajectories is critical for effective clinical trials and therapeutic development. In this study, we applied machine learning (ML) approaches leveraging disease progression models and baseline magnetic resonance (MR)‐derived radiomic features to quantify individual‐level DMD progression trajectories and support quantitative characterization of disease progression. Radiomic features were extracted from segmented soleus (SOL) and vastus lateralis (VL) fat‐fraction maps, generating 810 features per individual, with additional functional and demographic measures incorporated as covariates following feature selection. Multiple ML regressors were trained and validated to estimate MR‐spectroscopy fat‐fraction trajectory descriptive parameters: DPT 50 (age at half‐maximal increase), DP max (extent), γ (rate), S 0 (extrapolated measure at age 0). Key radiomic features were identified through feature importance analyses, followed by downstream analyses, including unsupervised clustering. The tree‐based XGBoost regression model demonstrated best future longitudinal fat‐fraction trajectories (SOL: mean absolute error (MAE) = 0.04, R 2 = 0.94; VL: MAE = 0.06, R 2 = 0.95). Subsequent downstream analyses highlighted potential key biomarkers clinically associated with DMD progression. Clustering analysis revealed clinically meaningful slow‐ and fast‐progression subgroups with interpretable decision criteria (SOL: DPT 50 = 12.21 vs. 14.83; γ = 8.07 vs. 7.54, VL: 10.37 vs. 14.21; γ = 7.72 vs. 7.09) that can inform clinical trial designs and therapeutic effects within homogenous groups. Individual‐level feature importance interpretation further shows the possibility of tailoring personalized intervention strategies. These findings highlight the potential of ML‐based trajectory modeling approaches leveraging baseline MRI radiomics for advancing AI‐assisted clinical trial development and precision medicine, charting a new direction for MRI‐guided disease modeling in neuromuscular disorders.
authors: Hyun-Jae Jeong; Rebecca J. Willcocks; Glenn A. Walter; Robert A. Mueller; Fiorella M. Sanabria; William T. Triplett; Krista Vandenborne; Sarah Kim

title: Airway collapse in small breed dogs and its association with clinical and anatomic variables
abstract: OBJECTIVES: The objective of the study was to evaluate associations between clinical and anatomic variables in small breed dogs with lower airway collapse. MATERIALS AND METHODS: One hundred and fifty dogs with chronic cough presenting between July 2017 and July 2023 were retrospectively included. Bronchoscopy recordings were reviewed to identify presence, location and severity of airway collapse. Anatomic variables were measured on computed tomography images. Cardiac variables were assessed with echocardiography or thoracic radiographs. RESULTS: Decreasing thoracic height:width ratio (Estimate: -51.75; 95% CI: -82.54 to -20.96), increasing body condition score (BCS) (Estimate: 6.45; 95% CI: 3.35 to 9.55) and presence of left atrial enlargement (Estimate: 21.97; 95% CI: 7.02 to 36.92) were associated with increasing cumulative bronchial collapse scores. Decreasing thoracic height:width ratio (OR: 0.02; 95% CI: 0.0004 to 0.63), increasing age (OR: 1.02; 95% CI: 1.01 to 1.03) and increasing body condition score (OR: 1.41; 95% CI: 1.04 to 1.92) were associated with increasing bronchomalacia scores. Decreasing thoracic height:width ratio (OR: 0.001; 95% CI: 0.00000758 to 0.08), increasing body condition score (OR: 1.63; 95% CI: 1.18 to 2.29), presence of left atrial enlargement (OR: 4.89; 95% CI: 1.19 to 21.65) and presence of airway neutrophilic inflammation (OR: 3.98; 95% CI: 1.10 to 17.39) were associated with increasing left principal bronchus collapse scores. Decreasing thoracic height:width ratio (OR: 0.003; 95% CI: 0.0001 to 0.07), increasing body condition score (OR: 1.54; 95% CI: 1.20 to 1.99) and presence of left atrial enlargement (OR: 4.85; 95% CI: 1.38 to 18.99) were associated with increasing left caudal lobar bronchus collapse scores. CLINICAL SIGNIFICANCE: Variations in thoracic conformation might be involved in the aetiopathogenesis of airway collapse and reduced thoracic height:width ratio is associated with increasing airway collapse scores. Increasing body condition score is a modifiable variable associated with increasing airway collapse scores. Left atrial enlargement is associated with increased bronchial collapse scores but might directly contribute only to pre-existing collapse of the left caudal lobar bronchus.
authors: Darren Kelly; J. Labrador; Kerry Peak; Eliana Doyle; S. Calleja; M. Vecin; T. Lomp; Alexander Smith; B. Rasmussen‐Clark; Danica Pollard

title: Artificial Intelligence in Pancreatic Resection: Current Evidence, Surgical Applications, and a Framework for Clinical Translation
abstract: Introduction: Pancreatic resection remains technically demanding, with clinically relevant postoperative pancreatic fistula (CR-POPF) a major source of morbidity. Artificial intelligence (AI) may support risk stratification, operative planning, intraoperative assessment, and postoperative decision support. This focused narrative review evaluates current AI applications in pancreatic resection and their translational maturity. Methods: A structured PubMed/MEDLINE search with an evidence cutoff of 24 July 2026 was supplemented by backward and forward citation tracking. Seventy eligible primary reports were synthesised by clinical task, information timing, and validation maturity. Results: Evidence is dominated by CR-POPF prediction after pancreatoduodenectomy, with additional studies in distal pancreatectomy, other perioperative outcomes, tissue and margin assessment, three-dimensional anatomical planning, and intraoperative video and anatomy recognition. Performance varied with patient selection, predictor timing, data modality, and validation strategy. External validation often changed reported discrimination, while calibration and clinical utility were inconsistently reported. Most studies were retrospective or technical; overlapping cohorts limited independence, and no included study demonstrated improved patient-centred outcomes. Conclusions: AI in pancreatic resection is expanding across prediction, planning, and guidance, but technical performance should not be equated with clinical readiness. Independent validation, prospective workflow and human-factors evaluation, and clinical-impact studies are needed. AI should augment, rather than replace, specialist surgical judgement.
authors: Karim Heiba; Ambareen Kausar

title: Artificial intelligence-assisted art therapy in digital psychiatry: Clinical applications, mechanisms, and ethics
abstract: Artificial intelligence-assisted art therapy should be understood as a therapistmediated extension of creative practice rather than an autonomous treatment.This structured narrative review synthesizes eleven directly relevant publications, including preliminary patient studies and adjacent creative-activity research, alongside transferable evidence from art therapy, conversational artificial intelligence, digital psychiatry, immersive technologies, affective computing, social robotics, and health-care artificial intelligence ethics.Direct patient-level evidence remains limited and heterogeneous, with mixed, domain-specific findings that do not establish general efficacy, comparative effectiveness, or safety; clinicianperspective evidence is limited, and most proposed applications and mechanisms derive from conceptual or transferable evidence.We therefore distinguish artificial intelligence used in visual creation, therapeutic dialogue or documentation, behavioral or emotional inference, and immersive or embodied interaction, and separate professional art therapy from broader digital creative activity.Supervised image-making, reflective preparation, patient-selected monitoring, and recoveryoriented follow-up are candidate uses for prospective research.The proposed taxonomy, pathway, risk framework, mechanisms, and safeguards are conceptual, research-oriented, provisional, and non-validated; they are not clinical guidance or a validated practice standard.Key risks include privacy loss, culturally stereotyped imagery, hallucinated feedback, misinterpretation, uncertain authorship, dependency, and image-specific provenance and secondary-use concerns.Future research should test clearly defined therapist-mediated protocols using explicit risk stratification, adverse-event monitoring, and transparent data governance.
authors: Ke Meng; Mingzhi Hou; Heeju Chae

title: Audit-first rollback semantics for safety–critical deployment pipelines
abstract: Deployment runtimes for safety–critical embodied agents keep two records: the live state components execute and the audit chain operators and regulators read. When an upgrade crashes mid-flight, a runtime that fails open keeps the partial deployment running, so the audit chain misstates what runs. We propose audit-first rollback semantics: the revert is attempted before any terminal record is written, and the record states what it did. Provisional state machines with a rollback closure and a bounded soak budget realize the rule; a protocol design extends it to coordinated bridges. We implemented it in a robot-manipulator deployment runtime and compared it with fail-open at 23 enumerated fault sites plus a control and over 10 runs of a 12-point crash grid. The sweep exposed two writes the first implementation left outside its guard and a fallback that lost the divergence flag. With the guard widened, every audit-first trial ended in the specified state; under our stricter coherence check fail-open did so at 5 sites, the ones needing no revert. Over the guarded trials that ended ROLLED_BACK, a terminal record followed within 35.7 ms at the 99th percentile. A terminal record then states what is running or flags that it must be reconciled.
authors: Xue Qin; Simin Luan; Cong Yang; Zhijun Li

title: Big data and AI for decision-making purposes in the metaverse: A cross-domain review of architectures, applications, and governance
abstract: This review examines how big data and artificial intelligence are being mobilized to support decision-making in metaverse and metaverse-adjacent environments. Rather than treating the metaverse as an interface novelty, the paper frames it as a decision environment in which persistent interaction, embodied participation, and multimodal sensing tighten the loop between observation and intervention. Using a transparent narrative review approach, the synthesis applies a consistent decision-making taxonomy across nine domains (industrial and manufacturing operations, smart cities, healthcare, retail and commerce, supply chain and logistics, energy and utilities, finance, education, tourism). For each domain, evidence is organized around decision level, decision mode, time requirements, data context, and action type, enabling comparability without collapsing domain-specific consequences into a single maturity scale. Across domains, the most salient pattern is that decision value depends less on immersion itself and more on the integration of digital representations (often via digital twins), AI inference, and bounded action pathways. The review highlights metaverse-specific constraints that shape decision reliability: measurement validity challenges in multimodal signals, proxy gaming when engagement metrics substitute for decision impact, identity and consent boundaries that constrain permissible inference, and latency/edge limits that compress feasible action sets. Building on these observations, the paper proposes a reference architecture organized as a data–AI–simulation–action loop with explicit fast and slow paths, emphasizing safe-state behavior, fallback logic, and escalation rules as architectural requirements for real-time decisions. A compact cross-domain synthesis consolidates recurring gaps as testable absences in current work, including unclear decision objects, weak semantic and identity alignment, limited uncertainty communication, under-specified constraint handling, insufficient audit trails, and inadequate robustness to drift and adversarial manipulation. The paper concludes with governance and ethics considerations anchored in established regulatory and standards frameworks, and outlines research directions aimed at decision-centered evaluation protocols, contestable immersive interfaces, and governance-ready metaverse decision systems.
authors: Leonidas Theodorakopoulos; Alexandra Theodoropoulou; Aristeidis Bakalis

title: Blood‐ and Liver Stiffness‐Based Non‐Invasive Tests for Clinically Significant Portal Hypertension in Patients With cACLD and HCC
abstract: BACKGROUND AND AIMS: The applicability of non-invasive tests (NITs) for clinically significant portal hypertension (CSPH) in patients with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is controversial. We performed a head-to-head comparison of various NITs for CSPH and evaluated rule-in/-out criteria. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective study including 283 patients with HCC undergoing hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG) measurement at the Vienna Hepatic Haemodynamic Lab with available, same-day data on NITs (i.e., liver stiffness measurement [LSM], platelet count [PLT], von Willebrand factor antigen [VWF:Ag], and the ratio of VWF:Ag and PLT [VITRO]). For the subsequent analysis, we focused on patients with compensated advanced chronic liver disease (cACLD). RESULTS: Among 164 patients with cACLD, most were BCLC 0/A (50.6%) and CSPH prevalence was 46.3%, the median LSM was 20.0 kPa (IQR: 13.3-37.9), and mean VWF:Ag/VITRO was 266 ± 119%/2.30 ± 1.81. The VITRO score yielded the highest discriminative ability to detect CSPH (AUROC: 0.834), followed by ANTICIPATE ± NASH (AUROC: 0.822), PLT (AUROC: 0.803), LSM (AUROC: 0.779), and VWF:Ag (AUROC: 0.707). The application of the Baveno VII criterium (LSM ≤ 15 kPa & PLT ≥ 150G/L) and the VITRO score (≤ 1.0) individually showed an excellent performance for ruling-out CSPH (sensitivities: ≥ 95%, NPV: 100%/87.9%). For ruling-in CSPH by individual criteria, the VITRO score provided the highest PPV (≥ 2.5, specificity/PPV: 89.8%/83.0%), followed by the Baveno VII criteria (specificity/PPV: 81.8%/74.6%). When sequentially applying Baveno VII criteria and VITRO, the grey zone could be significantly reduced to 16% (sensitivity/NPV: 94.7%/92.2%; specificity/PPV: 73.9%/84.4%). CONCLUSION: The discriminative ability in patients with cACLD and HCC was comparable to patients without HCC. However, PPVs of established criteria were < 90%, which may be explained by the comparatively low prevalence of CSPH in this context.

title: CASSIEA: Calibrated Anthropomorphism as Social Scaffolding for Interactions with Embodied Agents
abstract: Humanoid Social Robots are entering various avenues of society, including healthcare, yet clinical paediatric deployment poses a challenge unresolved by existing Child-Robot Interaction (cHRI) literature: the dynamics of children encountering an embodied Socially-Assistive Robot (SAR) for the first time in a busy hospital, with no social schema in place, often anxious and medically vulnerable. We summarise CASSIEA: Calibrated Anthropomorphism as Social Scaffolding for Interactions with Embodied Agents, a novel five-construct framework as proposal for supporting children’s first SAR encounter in clinical settings. An in-the-wild cHRI study with N=273 children (across 8 days: 90 sessions, 9,611 conversation turns) at a hospital attempts to practically illustrate CASSIEA’s feasibility for real SAR deployment and lay foundations for a scientific discourse towards a validated conceptual framework in future.

title: CD49f identifies stem-like memory T cells with enhanced therapeutic potency
abstract: The efficacy of adoptive cell therapies depends on the presence of T cells with durable self-renewal, proliferative capacity, and differentiation potential, yet heterogeneity within starting cell populations remains a major barrier to consistent clinical outcomes. Here, we identify CD49f as a marker of a unique subset of human memory T cells with stem-like characteristics. CD49f Hi memory CD8 + and CD4 + T cells exhibited transcriptional and phenotypic features associated with T cell stemness, including elevated LEF1, TCF1, CCR7, CD27, and CD28, while CD49f Lo cells exhibited effector-like transcriptional programs. Clinical evaluation of solid-organ transplant recipients treated with virus-specific T cells for cytomegalovirus complications demonstrated that autologous T cell therapies manufactured from CD49f Hi -enriched T cells were associated with superior immune reconstitution and greater in vivo expansion of CMV-specific T cells. Functional assays further revealed that CD49f Hi memory T cells possessed enhanced proliferative capacity and transcriptional plasticity following activation. Consistent with these findings, CD19 CAR T cells engineered from CD49f Hi memory T cells demonstrated improved persistence and conferred superior survival in a preclinical lymphoma model. Together, these findings establish CD49f as a marker of a stem-like memory T cell subset with enhanced therapeutic potential and identify CD49f Hi enrichment as a practical strategy to improve the consistency, durability, and clinical efficacy of both virus-specific and CAR T cell therapies.

title: Canine gonadal tissues-derived mesenchymal stem cell therapy for early myxomatous mitral valve disease in dogs: the SPRING study, a prospective comparative pilot study
abstract: Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) are multipotent stromal cells that can promote tissue repair and exert immunomodulatory and anti-inflammatory effects. Myxomatous mitral valve disease (MMVD) is primarily degenerative, and routine pharmacological treatment is not recommended at stage B1. This exploratory study assessed changes in serum transforming growth factor-β1 (TGF-β1) following systemic administration of allogeneic canine gonadal tissue-derived MSCs (GD-MSCs) in client-owned dogs with stage B1 MMVD, with N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) and echocardiographic measurements as secondary outcomes. The analyzed cohort comprised ten dogs, allocated according to owners’ treatment choices (MSC, n = 5; control, n = 5). Treated dogs received intravenous allogeneic GD-MSCs (1 × 10 6 cells/kg) at monthly intervals for four administrations and were followed for 6 months. Compared with controls, MSC-treated dogs showed greater decreases from baseline to six months in serum TGF-β1 ( p = 0.0317), NT-proBNP ( p = 0.0079), and body weight-normalized anterior mitral leaflet area ( p = 0.0079; Holm- and Bonferroni-adjusted p = 0.0238). The NT-proBNP mean-change difference was − 530.38 pmol/L (Welch 95% confidence interval − 846.19 to − 214.57), although absolute concentrations did not differ significantly between groups at either visit. Changes in body weight-normalized left ventricular end-diastolic internal diameter (LVIDDN) ( p = 0.0397) and vertebral left atrial size (VLAS) ( p = 0.0079) also decreased to a greater extent in the MSC group. GD-MSC administration was associated with six-month changes in circulating biomarkers and selected cardiac imaging measurements in dogs with stage B1 MMVD. These prospective comparative observations support further evaluation of MSCs in early MMVD, with larger randomized studies needed to determine whether the initial signals translate into sustained clinical benefit.
authors: So-Young Jeung; Ga‐Hyun Lim; Sun-Hye Song; 정유진; Sohee Lim; Sung‐Soo Kim

title: Cell‐Based Micro/Nanorobots: From Living Carriers to Living Therapeutic Specialists
abstract: Cell‐based micro/nanorobots (CMNRs) integrate intrinsic biological functions with engineered capabilities, constituting an emerging class of biohybrid robotic platforms. Unlike fully synthetic micro/nanorobots, whose functions depend entirely on artificial materials, CMNRs are constructed from living cells or cell‐derived components and can exploit unique biological capabilities. Over the past decade, CMNR research has progressed from the development of simple delivery carriers toward therapeutic specialists capable of performing diagnostic and therapeutic tasks within distinct organs. Although the complex and highly heterogeneous physiological environments of different organs impose formidable barriers, CMNRs possess intrinsic organ‐specific compatibility shaped by evolution, offering a promising strategy for improving their performance in specialized medical tasks. Here, we propose a novel framework for constructing organ‐specific therapeutic platforms. Guided by this framework, we systematically review and critically assess the biological properties, robotic functions, and recent in vivo applications of CMNRs. Despite substantial progress, a considerable gap remains between laboratory prototypes and clinical translation. This Review identifies key translational barriers that must be addressed to ensure the safety, controllability, and functional reliability of CMNRs in clinical use. Overall, a future trajectory toward organ‐specific theranostic systems is outlined to provide a conceptual basis for the clinical development of next‐generation CMNRs.
authors: Junfeng Wu; Zhaoyu Zhang; Ke Xu; Enkuo Li; Yuting Cui; Yuting Zhou; Huanyu Zhou; Beipei Zhang; Shuai Jiang; Xiaodong Wang; Jialin Jiang; Lianqing Liu; Niandong Jiao

title: Clinical versus pathological staging in prostate cancer: insights from a retrospective cohort study
abstract: Background Prostate cancer (PCa) is the most commonly diagnosed cancer in men worldwide. This cohort study evaluates agreement between clinical and pathological T and N staging in PCa, examining patterns of understaging and overstaging and associated clinical factors. Method This retrospective study included 97 patients who underwent radical prostatectomy at King Hussein Cancer Center (2006–2021). Data collected included age, diagnosis date, PSA, clinical and pathological T and N stages, Gleason score, PI-RADS score, lesion characteristics, extracapsular extension, and prostate volume. Concordance between clinical and pathological staging was assessed, and associations with clinical and radiological predictors were analyzed. Patients were categorized as correctly staged, understaged, or overstaged for T stage; only clinical understaging was observed for N stage. Analyses were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics 26.0. Results Ninety-seven patients (mean age 67.7 years; mean PSA 20.9 ng/mL) were included. Clinical and pathological T staging agreed in 61.9% of cases, with 28.9% understaged and 9.3% overstaged (κ = 0.41, p < 0.001). N-stage concordance was 94.8%, with 5.2% understaging (κ = 0.79, p < 0.001). In exploratory regression analysis, larger prostate volume was associated with both T-stage understaging (OR = 1.04, p = 0.04) and overstaging (OR = 1.06, p = 0.04), while PSA, lesion size, Gleason grade, and PI-RADS score were not significantly associated with T-stage discrepancy. Given the small number of N-stage discrepancies, predictor analysis was not performed. Conclusion Clinical and pathological concordance was fair for T stage and substantial for N stage. T-stage discrepancies were linked to larger prostate volume and cT3b status, while N-stage errors were rare and limited to understaging. Improved standardization and advanced imaging may enhance staging accuracy in prostate cancer.

title: Clinical-scale manufacturing of CD137+ enriched tumor-reactive T cells for glioblastoma in the CliniMACS Prodigy
abstract: Background: Most tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) studies and therapies have focused on tumors with high T-cell infiltration and mutational burden. Glioblastoma (GBM) represents a challenging indication for TIL therapy because of its limited T-cell infiltration and low mutational burden. We investigated whether targeted enrichment of tumor-reactive T cells using CD137-based selection could enable robust, clinical-scale production of TIL products from GBM. Methods: Ultrasonic aspirates (UAs), routinely collected during GBM resections, were evaluated as a source of TILs for clinical manufacturing. TILs were generated from GBM UAs under GMP-like conditions at clinical scale using the closed, automated TRT Process on the CliniMACS Prodigy. Matched TRT products that were enriched for CD137+ cells, depleted of CD137+ cells, or left unselected were generated in parallel at full manufacturing scale. Products were characterized by cellular and transcriptomic analyses and evaluated in functional assays for cytotoxicity against autologous and non-autologous patient-derived GBM cell lines. Results: Cellular and transcriptomic analyses revealed that UA-derived CD137+ (4-1BB/TNFRSF9) T cells were clonally expanded, exhibited activated and memory phenotypes, and displayed transcriptional profiles associated with tumor reactivity. The closed manufacturing process preserved phenotypic features previously associated with clinical benefit in other TIL indications. Functional assays demonstrated potent, tumor-reactive cytotoxicity of CD137-enriched TRT products against autologous GBM cell lines compared with TILs generated in parallel without selection. Discussion/Conclusions: These findings establish the feasibility of a clinical-scale TIL manufacturing approach using the CliniMACS Prodigy that enables production of clinically relevant quantities of TILs from GBM while enriching for cells with tumor-reactive characteristics. This approach may broaden the application of TIL therapy to immunologically cold tumors with limited T-cell infiltration or low mutational burden that have historically been challenging to manufacture using conventional TIL production methods.

title: Closed Measurement, Open Interpretation: A Four-Layer Behaviour-Classification Architecture and a Grounded Subconscious Reasoner for Companion-Animal Perception from Consumer Video
abstract: Companion-animal products that speak in the animal's voice make factual claims about a living subject every few seconds. The characteristic failure of such systems is not measurement error but fabrication: an assertion that no admitted measurement supports. We present a production architecture that separates measurement from interpretation by construction — closed measurement, open interpretation — so that no path exists from absence of evidence to assertion. Every two seconds, a structured camera read is projected onto a fixed, version-controlled vocabulary of 19 channels and 216 classes with explicit abstention classes; out-of-vocabulary output is discarded at parse time. A 39-keypoint markerless pose engine and a facial-landmark channel supply measured channels as peers. Four layers classify: closed per-frame measurement; a salience-gated behaviour stream; 13 composite signatures and 18 named state transitions; and sequence models admitted to the user path only through a provenance gate that certifies trained status, on a declared dataset, for a declared species. Two principles organise the design: an admissibility principle — a claim may be asserted only if admitted evidence supports it, at sufficient confidence, recently, for the same animal in the same session — and a taxonomy of fabrication modes for percept-to-speech systems, each closed by a named architectural guard. A pain index mapped to the Glasgow Composite Measure Pain Scale — Short Form is bias-invariant by construction: in a demographic-invariance probe, varying demographics across 23 groups while holding behaviour fixed changed the score by at most 0.00. The measured channels include a gated kinematic engine whose false-locomotion rate on a seated animal is 1.8% of frames. A Reasoner, confined to a digest of sensor-derived facts and a strictly validated decision set, maintains the system's state record off the speech path; welfare and clinical language bypasses it entirely and is rendered deterministically. The first sensor-grounded utterance arrives 3–7 s after connection, and the transport layer sustains 100 concurrent sessions with zero failures. The validation is organised claim-first, in three evidence types: a demographic-invariance probe, a failure-mode taxonomy in which every mode carries its own guard check, and a latency and load characterisation of the production transport. The separation, and the guard catalogue, transfer to any embodied agent that speaks about a living subject.
