title: Comparison of different transplantation routes and timing for stem cell therapy in stroke
abstract: BACKGROUND: Stem cell transplantation holds therapeutic promise for stroke, yet its clinical translation is hindered by unresolved challenges in administration routes, timing, and poor cell engraftment and survival. METHODS: This is a narrative (non-systematic) review. Registered clinical studies were identified in ClinicalTrials.gov, the European Union Clinical Trials Register and the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry, and were supplemented by targeted PubMed searches for the preclinical and mechanistic literature. Records were eligible if they evaluated stem cell transplantation for ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke and reported the delivery route and/or the transplantation time window; records reporting neither were excluded. Because direct head-to-head clinical comparisons of routes and time windows are scarce, registry data and selected preclinical studies were synthesised descriptively rather than pooled, and no meta-analysis was performed. RESULTS: Each administration route presents a distinct profile. Intravenous injection is minimally invasive and simple but limited by pulmonary sequestration, low cerebral engraftment, and high cell dose requirements. Intra-arterial infusion offers improved targeting but shares similar limitations. Intrathecal delivery allows direct central nervous system access with concentrated doses but carries risks of cerebrospinal fluid leakage and an inflammatory microenvironment. Intracerebral implantation ensures high local engraftment and long-term survival with minimal cell numbers but is invasive and poses risks of hemorrhage and further tissue injury. Intranasal administration is non-invasive with a wide therapeutic window yet exhibits extremely low delivery efficiency. Regarding timing, intravenous and intra-arterial routes are primary in the acute phase; in the subacute phase these routes remain common, alongside intrathecal administration; for chronic stroke, intracerebral and intrathecal transplantation are the predominant strategies in clinical trials. CONCLUSION: This review synthesizes two decades of progress and persisting challenges in stem cell therapy for stroke, focusing on delivery strategies and timing. Successful clinical translation will require further large-scale, multicenter prospective studies to optimize these critical parameters.
authors: Qingdong Meng; Hao Deng; Ziqian Zhang; Yongxu Wei; Mingjian Liu; Bin Chen; Yijun Cheng; Hanbing Shang

title: Cumulative and Audited Guardrail Tool Evolution for LLM Agent Safety
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly operate in open-world environments where safety risks cannot be fully predefined. However, most existing guardrail mechanisms remain static, relying on fixed rules, prompts, or classifiers that generalize poorly to emerging risks. Here we present EVOLVE, a tool-level self-evolving defense framework that formulates agent security as a process of cumulative security evolution. Inspired by how human societies transform experiences into transferable protective knowledge, EVOLVE externalizes security knowledge into executable guardrail tools that are continuously inherited, independently audited, and iteratively refined through lifelong interaction. Across multiple benchmarks, backbone models, and embodied environments, EVOLVE consistently outperforms existing defenses across diverse risk scenarios with +22\% average F1 score. We further validate the framework in real-world robotic and autonomous agent systems. Our results suggest that scalable agent safety may require continuously evolving defense systems rather than static guardrails.
authors: Xiao Yang; Aishan Liu; Siyuan Liang; Zonghao Ying; Le Wang; Jiakai Wang; Xianglong Liu; Dacheng Tao

title: Cytogenetic and epigenetic determinants of leukemogenesis: clinical implications for clonal evolution in hematologic malignancies
abstract: Leukemogenesis is a dynamic evolutionary process driven by interactions between cytogenetic lesions, epigenetic dysregulation, clonal selection, and the bone marrow microenvironment. Although recurrent chromosomal abnormalities and somatic mutations have transformed diagnosis and risk classification, conventional genomic approaches often incompletely resolve subclonal architecture, lineage plasticity, treatment resistance, and measurable residual disease (MRD). This narrative review examines how genetic and epigenetic alterations cooperate to initiate and sustain hematologic malignancies and how their temporal evolution shapes disease progression and therapeutic response. Particular emphasis is placed on recurrent cytogenetic abnormalities, DNA methylation, histone modification, chromatin remodeling, non-coding RNA regulation, clonal hematopoiesis, and interactions between leukemic cells and their microenvironment. Contemporary multi-omic technologies, including single-cell DNA and RNA sequencing, integrated single-cell multi-omics, spatial transcriptomics, and optical genome mapping, are critically evaluated for their capacity to resolve founder clones, cooperating lesions, subclonal trajectories, and lineage plasticity. The review further considers evolutionary mechanisms of resistance involving FLT3 , TP53 , BCL2 -dependent survival, KMT2A –menin signaling, and BCR :: ABL1 kinase-domain alterations, alongside emerging targeted therapies. Particular attention is given to MRD interpretation, including the distinction between persistent preleukemic clones and clinically relevant residual leukemia. Integrating longitudinal genomic, epigenetic, transcriptomic, and spatial information may enable more precise evolutionary monitoring and individualized treatment. This framework positions leukemogenesis as an adaptive ecosystem and supports precision hematology strategies designed to anticipate clonal escape, therapeutic resistance, disease progression, and relapse while improving molecularly informed clinical decision-making prospectively.
authors: Emmanuel Ifeanyi Obeagu

title: DEVELOPMENT AND CONTENT VALIDATION OF A MOBILE APPLICATION FOR CLINICAL ASSESSMENT AND DIABETIC FOOT PREVENTION IN PRIMARY HEALTH CARE
abstract: Diabetic foot is one of the most severe chronic complications of type 2 diabetes mellitus and is associated with high rates of ulceration, amputation, hospitalization, and mortality. Early identification of risk factors and systematic clinical foot assessment are essential strategies for preventing these complications, particularly in the context of Primary Health Care. This study aimed to develop and validate a mobile application for clinical assessment, risk stratification, and prevention of foot lesions in individuals with type 2 diabetes mellitus receiving care in Primary Health Care settings. This methodological study focused on the development and validation of a health technology and was conducted between August 2024 and August 2026. The application was developed based on scientific evidence and national and international clinical guidelines and subsequently submitted to content validation by a panel of 34 healthcare professionals experienced in diabetes care. The tool was organized into three integrated modules: user profile, clinical assessment and risk stratification, and multidisciplinary intervention and health education. Experts demonstrated a high level of agreement across all evaluated criteria, with no inadequate ratings recorded. The highest levels of agreement were observed for items related to the relevance of the application for healthcare practice (97.1%). Content Validity Index values ranged from 0.84 to 1.00, while the overall Content Validity Coefficient was 0.86, confirming satisfactory content validity. Following refinement, improvements related to usability, social determinants of health, user monitoring, and offline functionality were incorporated. The application demonstrated satisfactory evidence of content validity and potential to support clinical assessment, risk stratification, and diabetic foot prevention in Primary Health Care, representing an innovative tool for improving healthcare quality and supporting clinical decision-making within the Brazilian Unified Health System.
authors: Tatiana Cristina Dias de Oliveira; Laila de Castro Araújo; Valéria de Castro Fagundes; Alana Ferreira de Oliveira; Maria Pantoja Moreira de Sena; Luann Wendel Pereira de Sena

title: Deployment of a Multilingual, Embodied, Holographic Artificial Intelligence Concierge in Ambulatory Care: Early Implementation Lessons From the Artificial Intelligence Responsive Interactive Agent.
abstract: Health care environments can be difficult to navigate, particularly for individuals with limited language proficiency, hearing impairment, low digital literacy, or unfamiliarity with the facility. Conversational artificial intelligence (AI) systems may support accessibility and navigation, although descriptions of real-world implementation in health care settings remain limited. As a descriptive, single-site quality-improvement pilot, this report characterizes the experience of implementing a conversational AI agent in the lobby of a large, outpatient, academic practice. The Artificial Intelligence Responsive Interactive Agent (ARIA) is a multilingual, 3-dimensional, holographic conversational AI concierge developed to provide real-time assistance with navigation, digital onboarding, and information regarding amenities and services. ARIA leverages natural language processing and large language model technology to provide voice-enabled interactions in English, Spanish, Mandarin, and Arabic, with real-time closed captioning. The system can also generate quick response codes that push information directly to users' smartphone devices. Piloted in a large ambulatory lobby from October 21, 2025, to February 2, 2026, ARIA recorded 1429 device-activation sessions. Of these, 689 sessions (48%) contained analyzable user interaction data. Wayfinding and general information requests were the most common use cases. Deployment surfaced operational challenges, including audio capture, network reliability, interaction timing, workflow integration, quick response transfer, and content governance. As the use of AI in clinical settings expands, there may be a role for an embodied agent serving as a digital concierge if these barriers can be addressed. Future evaluations should prospectively define implementation outcomes, use systematic utilization denominators, and assess user experience and operational impact with validated measures.
authors: Ellen C Meltzer; Jared T Staal; Alyssa B Chapital; Pete J Pallagi; Katelyn M Cheetham; Haley Wang; Qiuyu Jin; Rafael Fonseca; Aman Anand; Mark R Stemler; Chris S Jaeckel; Danielle M Stricker; Jacob M Dison; Cherish D Caputo; Tharana Maran; Beverly Hansen; Praneetha R Elugunti; Biju T Samkutty; Anjali Bhagra

title: DiabAgent: Toward Agentic Physiological Control
abstract: As pretraining scales, medical language models have advanced rapidly in clinical question answering. Their ability to achieve effective physiological control through sustained intervention still lacks systematic quantitative evaluation. Type 1 diabetes provides a concrete setting: impaired insulin secretion creates dependence on exogenous insulin, with dosing continually adjusted using information about meals, exercise, illness, and glucose measurements. We introduce DiabAgent, a research suite for agentic physiological control comprising the Agentic Physiological Control (APC) framework, the DiabetSim simulator, and the SweetBench benchmark. APC controls glucose through medical-device tools, using ongoing observations to infer individual states, accumulate personal experience, and choose treatment actions. We build DiabetSim to simulate different patients, events, and device conditions for scalable virtual testing and training. Using DiabetSim, we construct SweetBench by instantiating 32 scenario designs as 212 glucose-control tasks. With Claude Opus 5.5 and a fixed decision interval of one hour, APC achieves a COGI of 73.5, compared with 71.2 for the open-source closed-loop baseline OpenAPS. Ablations further show that individual adaptation and contextual information improve glucose control. Combining high-frequency rule-based control with lower-frequency agent decisions shows potential for balancing control performance and computational cost. Our work provides a framework, simulator, and evaluation foundation for agents to participate in human physiological control.

title: Diagnostic accuracy and inter-observer variability of cardiac and left atrial radiographic measurements in cats with and without cardiomyopathies
abstract: Inroduction Radiographic assessment of cardiac size and left atrial enlargement (LAE) can be challenging in cats with suspected heart disease. Several radiographic indices, including vertebral heart size (VHS) and left atrial-specific indices, such as left atrial vertebral heart size (LA-VHS), vertebral left atrial size (VLAS), and radiographic left atrial dimension (RLAD), have been proposed to assess LAE. However, their reproducibility, repeatability and diagnostic accuracy in cats have not been fully established. The aims of this study were to evaluate the inter-observer reliability, agreement and intra-observer repeatability of VHS, LA-VHS, VLAS, and RLAD in cats and to assess their diagnostic accuracy for identifying moderate-to-severe LAE. Methods In this retrospective, multicenter study, right lateral thoracic radiographs of cats of any age, sex, or body weight were retrieved from the medical databases of two institutions. Only cats that underwent radiographic and echocardiographic examinations during the same clinical evaluation were included. Echocardiography was used to diagnose feline cardiomyopathies (FCMPs) and grade the severity of LAE. Results A total of 86 cats were included, comprising 33 cardiologically healthy controls and 53 cats with FCMPs. Of these, 33 cats (38.4%) had no LAE, 12 (13.9 %) had mild LAE, 6 (7%) had moderate LAE, and 35 (40.7%) had severe LAE. Each radiograph was independently evaluated by three observers with different levels of clinical expertise in veterinary radiology and cardiology. Inter-observer reliability, intra-observer repeatability and agreement of the radiographic measurements, correlations between radiographic indices and echocardiographic assessment of LAE, and their diagnostic accuracy for detecting moderate-to-severe LAE were evaluated. All radiographic indices showed good-to-excellent inter-observer reliability, with intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) ranging from 0.85 to 0.97 and median coefficients of variation (CVs) ranging from 3% to 11%. Intra-observer repeatability was generally good to excellent, with ICCs ranging from 0.70 to 0.99 and median CVs ranging from 0.7% to 9.3%. However, significant differences in VHS and RLAD measurements were observed among observers (both p < 0.001). Diagnostic accuracy for detecting moderate-to-severe LAE was consistent across observers, with areas under the curve ranging from 0.73 to 0.83. The VHS, LA-VHS, VLAS and RLAD showed moderate-to-good diagnostic accuracy in cats. Conclusion These indices may therefore serve as useful supportive tools for screening and initial clinical assessment when LAE or underlying cardiac disease is suspected, although their diagnostic accuracy remains insufficient for use as stand-alone diagnostic tests in clinical practice.
authors: Carlotta Valente; Nicolò Mastromattei; Carlo Guglielmini; Helen Poser; Tommaso Banzato; David Chiavegato; Roberto Venturini; Barbara Contiero; Alessandro Zotti

title: DobotTrack: Target-Grounded Vision-Language-Action Learning for Embodied Person Tracking
abstract: Language-guided embodied person tracking requires a mobile agent to identify a target from a referring description and consistently follow the target under egocentric observations. We present DobotTrack, a target-grounded vision-language-action (VLA) framework that integrates auxiliary grounding supervision with efficient temporal modeling. We systematically investigate five auxiliary tasks---person segmentation, bounding-box grounding, visual-spatial classification (VSC), future DINO feature prediction, and future-frame prediction---and adopt complementary mask and bounding-box supervision to enhance target delineation and localization. We introduce Q-identity, a target-conditioned historical visual compression module that leverages target-grounding predictions to selectively preserve identity-discriminative appearance features and spatial cues in compact historical tokens. On EVT-Bench, our 0.8B-parameter model achieves an average success rate of 77.9%, exceeding OmTrackVLA by 16.9 percentage points across the three tasks. We further construct a real-world person-tracking dataset collected using a quadruped robot, comprising 126 episodes and 596,323 mask-annotated frames. The target masks enable automatic derivation of bounding boxes and visual-spatial labels encoding horizontal position and apparent image scale, providing additional grounding supervision without separate manual annotation of these labels. Together, our framework and annotation pipeline support learning target-grounded tracking policies from simulated and real-world data. Code is available at https://github.com/Dobot-Team/dobot_track.
authors: Shengjun Deng; Yinghan Zhang; Chengrui Wei; Liu Liang; Songyuan Liu; Pengkun Zheng; Yajun Zheng; Ying Zhang; Yuan Tian; Xi Li; Teng Wang

title: Driving Intelligence: The Amber Book
abstract: Driving Intelligence examines artificial intelligence through the lens of autonomous driving, using driving as a real-world test case for intelligence. At a time when expectations of artificial general intelligence are rising, the book challenges how intelligence is defined and measured, arguing that current benchmarks saturate, leak, and can be gamed. The book develops a framework for understanding intelligence through the concept of real-world agency, with autonomous driving as its central case study. It argues that driving uniquely combines scale, open-ended environmental complexity, and continuous multi-agent interaction under uncertainty. Unlike most AI benchmarks, which are static or isolated, autonomous driving unfolds in a dynamic physical and social world that cannot be exhaustively specified in advance. The book analyzes failure modes in perception, prediction, planning, and interaction, showing how these limitations reveal a deeper gap between statistical learning from large-scale data and genuine agency. This volume, Amber, benchmarks today's autonomous driving systems against real-world performance data and tracks the shift from language-based AI toward Vision-Language-Action (VLA) systems in robotics. The book's central contribution is to reframe autonomous driving as a benchmark for intelligence grounded in real-world agency. It identifies systematic limitations in current AI approaches and clarifies what is missing for genuine autonomy, providing a concrete framework for evaluating progress in Real-World AI and Physical AI. The book will be essential reading for professionals, academics, and students working and researching AI and autonomous vehicles, as well as the interested general reader.
authors: Gabriel Seiberth; J. Mark Bishop

title: Embodied Science Agents: Making Embodied Experimental Design Learnable
abstract: Recent advances in large models have accelerated AI for Science toward agentic science, where AI agents autonomously conduct scientific discovery. Realising this vision requires closing the loop between computational reasoning and physical experimentation, positioning self-driving laboratories (SDLs) as critical enablers. However, existing SDLs exhibit a fundamental paradox: foundation model integration has increased linguistic sophistication while severing physical grounding. By treating models as disembodied planners that output symbolic workflows for separate robotic systems, current architectures inherently block the development of embodied experimental intuition. We argue that overcoming this paradox requires embedding \emph{learnability} along three interdependent axes: cognitive learnability (learning what to investigate), experimental learnability (learning where to search), and embodied learnability (learning how to act). Building on this view, we introduce the Embodied Science Agent (ESA), which unifies digital intelligence with physical embodiment through three synergistic components: a Digital Agent that provides cognitive and experimental learnability via memory-based reasoning and Bayesian optimisation, an Embodied Agent that provides embodied learnability via generalisable instrument control, and an Embodied Unified Interface for seamless coordination. We validated ESA in autonomous wastewater treatment experiments, navigating over 200 million possible conditions. Through 15 continuous rounds, ESA raised the final solution transmittance from 82\% to 99.7\%, corresponding to a 98.5\% reduction in residual dye concentration and near-complete decolourisation, while its learned visuomotor policies generalised across varying instrument placements, a promising step toward next-generation SDLs for autonomous scientific discovery.
authors: Yihang Che; Zhongwei Yu; Yang Li; Xingyu Lu; Hongxia Yu; Jun Wang

title: Endothelial VCAM1 links oncogenic KRAS signaling to myeloid inflammation and hemorrhagic instability in brain arteriovenous malformations
abstract: BACKGROUND: Hemorrhagic conversion is the most devastating complication of brain arteriovenous malformations (bAVMs). However, endothelial mechanisms promoting macrophages (Mφ) recruitment, microglia (MG) activation, and bAVM lesion instability remain unclear. We investigated vascular cell adhesion molecule-1 (VCAM1) as a mediator linking oncogenic endothelial signaling to myeloid cell responses and hemorrhagic progression in bAVMs. METHODS: We performed integrated transcriptomic analysis of human bAVM and epilepsy-control brain tissues, with validation in local bAVM specimens. Transcriptomic and proteomic analyses of bAVM lesions and intact brain tissues from mutant KRAS-induced bAVM mice were followed by histological validation. Using AAV-BR1-KRASG12V-injected Cx3cr1-gfp;Ccr2-rfp mice, we performed intravital imaging to assess Mφ/MG responses to VCAM1 neutralization. Hemorrhage and myeloid cell responses were also evaluated following endothelial-specific VCAM1 deletion. Plasma soluble VCAM1 (sVCAM1) was measured in patients with unruptured and ruptured bAVMs and unruptured aneurysm controls. Effects of sVCAM1 on MG activation were examined in vitro. RESULTS: Integrated human endothelial bulk and single-cell RNA-sequencing and tissue validation identified VCAM1 upregulation in bAVMs, including unruptured lesions. Plasma analyses showed increased sVCAM1 in unruptured and ruptured bAVM patients compared with unruptured aneurysm controls. In mutant KRAS-induced bAVM mice, transcriptomic and proteomic analyses demonstrated increased VCAM1 expression, with endothelial localization confirmed histologically. In vitro, mutant KRAS increased sVCAM1 production, while recombinant sVCAM1 stimulated inflammatory mediator expression in MG. Both MG and Mφ expressed VLA-4, a major VCAM1 receptor. Intravital imaging showed that VCAM1 neutralization reduced Mφ accumulation and MG activation, while early VCAM1 neutralization reduced hemorrhagic burden. Consistently, endothelial-specific VCAM1 deletion reduced Mφ accumulation, MG activation, and hemorrhage volume in bAVM mice and improved behavioral performance. CONCLUSIONS: These findings identify endothelial VCAM1 as an upstream mediator linking mutant KRAS signaling to myeloid cell responses and hemorrhagic progression in bAVMs. This study establishes endothelial VCAM1 as a potential therapeutic target for attenuating hemorrhagic progression.
authors: Eun Su Park; Jung-Eun Park; Hyejin Park; Ohnmar Myint; Sung Wook Kang; Xian Chen; Zhongming Zhao; Jong Min Choi; Sung Yun Jung; Shuning Huang; Jakob Körbelin; Huimahn Alex Choi; Jaroslaw A Aronowski; Peng Roc Chen; Eunhee Kim

title: Exercise reshapes cellular immunity toward anti-inflammation and diminishes CCR4 levels on LFA-1α high CD4 + T cells in multiple sclerosis
abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) represents a multifaceted neuroinflammatory disease for which regular exercise is now recommended by many healthcare institutions. Although preclinical studies indicate robust immunomodulatory effects of exercise, evidence from human studies is lacking. In this randomized controlled trial, persons with MS (pwMS) were assigned to three months of high-intensity interval training or a passive control condition, with outcomes assessed at baseline, after intervention, and a four- week follow-up. Additionally, a healthy matched control group was included. Besides exercise-induced sustained increases in physical fitness, systemic inflammation was diminished and the T reg -to-T H 17.1 ratio improved after exercise. Untargeted proteomic analysis of peripheral blood mononuclear cells covering >7000 proteins revealed an exercise-induced decrease in proteins implicated in inflammatory diseases (i.e., MTHFD2). This was supported by inferred transcription factor activity analysis, which indicated enhanced polarization of immune cells toward anti-inflammatory phenotypes at follow-up. Using flow cytometry, we identified an LFA-1α high CD4 + T-cell subset that was associated with disease biomarkers and exhibited increased CCR4 expression compared to healthy matched subjects which was reduced after exercise. Our findings significantly expand knowledge of how exercise training exerts immediate and sustained immunomodulatory effects in pwMS and thereby strengthens the mechanistic rationale for exercise recommendations made by healthcare professionals. One Sentence Summary Using multiparametric flow cytometry and state-of-the-art mass spectrometry, we demonstrate that exercise training promotes an anti-inflammatory state at both the systemic and immune-cell proteomic levels and ameliorates dysregulated CCR4 expression on disease-associated LFA-1α high CD4 + T cells in multiple sclerosis patients.
authors: Sebastian Proschinger; Tiffany Y. title: ExplaiNavility: Interpretable Vision-and-Language Navigation with Reasoning Supervision
abstract: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) requires embodied agents to follow natural language instructions while grounding their decisions in complex visual environments. Despite recent progress, most VLN agents remain difficult to interpret, providing limited insight into why a navigation action is selected. In this work, we introduce ExplaiNavility, an interpretable VLN framework that augments navigation with explicit reasoning supervision. Our model combines a visual scene encoder with a multimodal LLM, using structured prompts to jointly condition on the instruction, the navigation history, and the candidate viewpoints available at each step. Beyond predicting the next navigable location, the model is trained to produce human-readable explanations of its decisions and descriptive low-level action labels, such as turning left, turning right, moving forward, or stopping. To supervise these outputs, we augment R2R trajectories with speaker-style action explanations generated from consecutive observations, together with action labels obtained from the simulator. By fine-tuning the embodied multimodal agent with these auxiliary reasoning objectives, ExplaiNavility encourages more transparent decision-making while preserving strong navigation ability. Experiments on the R2R benchmark show that our approach improves over prior explainable VLN methods on unseen environments, while producing interpretable rationales that make the agent's behavior easier to inspect. These results suggest that explicit reasoning supervision can benefit both navigation performance and interpretability in embodied instruction-following agents.
authors: William Raccagni; Niyati Rawal; Marcella Cornia; Lorenzo Baraldi; Rita Cucchiara
venue: IRIS UNIMORE (University of Modena and Reggio Emilia)

title: Exploiting the Nanoparticle–Protein Corona for Advanced Biomedical Applications
abstract: Nanoparticles have significant potential to improve medicines, diagnostics and other healthcare technologies, but their behaviour in the body can differ substantially from how they are designed or perform in the laboratory.This is largely because proteins from biological fluids rapidly attach to nanoparticle surfaces, forming a protein corona that changes how the nanoparticles interact with cells, tissues and the immune system.Understanding and controlling this process is therefore important for translating nanomaterials into effective and reliable biomedical technologies.This Review highlights a shift in how the protein corona can be viewed: rather than being an unavoidable barrier to nanoparticle performance, it can potentially be used as a functional biological interface.We examine how nanoparticle properties can influence corona formation and how the resulting protein layer can be characterised, exploited and deliberately engineered for applications including targeted drug delivery, disease diagnosis, biosensing, molecular recognition and nanotoxicology.This approach could enable nanoparticles with improved therapeutic efficacy, more accurate diagnostics, and enhanced safety.Downloaded from https://www.cambridge.org/core.06 Nov 2026 at 19:15:19, subject to the Cambridge Core terms of use.Realising these benefits at scale will require greater standardisation of protein-corona analysis, reproducible manufacturing and characterisation of nanoparticles, and improved understanding of how coronas evolve across different biological environments and between individuals.Integration of advanced analytical methods, computational modelling and rational materials design will be important for translating laboratory findings into robust and clinically relevant technologies.By bringing together emerging approaches to understand and engineer the nanoparticle-protein interface, this Review highlights opportunities to develop more predictable, effective and biologically informed nanomaterials for future healthcare applications.
authors: Emma Cooper; James C. Reynolds; Amanda Kate Pearce

title: From AI-Enabled Remote Patient Monitoring Toward Agentic Robotics: Embodiment, Governance, and Care Integration
abstract: AI-enabled remote patient monitoring is evolving beyond passive data collection toward agentic AI systems that interpret patient states, coordinate care, and initiate action across domestic and clinical settings. This structured scoping review finds that mature agentic care has not yet emerged: Most systems remain human led, while stronger decision-action coupling and embodied AI remain largely confined to prototypes and pilots. Healthcare robotics makes the transition from monitoring to action especially visible by translating AI-generated recommendations and decisions into speech, movement, prompting, physical assistance, escalation, and care coordination, making embodiment, clinical integration, human oversight, and governance fundamental design requirements. Further progress requires safe and interoperable care architectures in which intelligent components operate through clinically validated and accountable workflows. We propose agentic robotics as a future direction for supervised systems embedded in the care ecosystem, connecting AI agents and robots with clinicians, caregivers, and patients through auditable workflows that can be interrupted and remain subject to human oversight and explicit AI governance.
authors: Ivana Ragusa; Lorenzo Guiducci; Filippo Cavallo

title: From Programmed Machines to Generalist Agents: Enabling Technologies and the Future of Service Robotics
abstract: Service robots are leaving the caged, deterministic world of industrial automation and entering unstructured, human-centred environments. This survey argues that the central transition of the next decade is from machines programmed for fixed tasks to systems that perceive, reason and adapt, and that the pace of this transition is limited less by algorithms than by robustness, safety certification and economics. Introducing the IFR/ISO classification and a short market snapshot, review the enabling technologies (3D perception, learning-based control and sim-to-real transfer, vision-language-action models, dexterous manipulation, navigation, human-robot interaction and safety standards, hardware, and cloud/teleoperation infrastructure), and analyse two sectors in depth (agriculture and healthcare) and several more briefly. We then discuss economic, regulatory, social and ethical factors, with emphasis on the European regulatory landscape, and close with a critical 5-to-10-year outlook that separates what is probable, what is plausible, and what is currently hype.
authors: Marina Antolinez Cabrero

title: From clinic to living room:Wearable sensors for home-based upper extremity stroke rehabilitation
abstract: Stroke is a major cause of long-term disability, with upper extremity impairments frequently limiting independence and participation in daily life. At the same time, increasing healthcare demands, workforce shortages, and rising costs challenge the delivery of upper extremity stroke rehabilitation. This thesis investigates the design and evaluation of home-based upper extremity telerehabilitation supported by wearable sensor technology. The research focused on two overarching aims: first, to design a telerehabilitation solution for stroke patients that facilitates motivation for upper extremity exercise therapy, while accounting for the home context; and second, to evaluate the validity, feasibility, and potential efficacy of home-based telerehabilitation solutions with wearable sensors for stroke patients. The studies demonstrated that successful home-based rehabilitation requires more than technology alone. Using a user-centred design approach, key requirements for telerehabilitation were identified, highlighting the importance of personalised, goal-oriented programmes that integrate daily activity monitoring with task-oriented, high-repetition exercises. Furthermore, a blended-care approach with adaptive feedback and motivational support was found to be important for tailoring interventions to individual patient needs. The findings also showed that motivation for home-based upper extremity rehabilitation is strongly influenced by factors related to the basic psychological needs of autonomy, competence, and relatedness, with themes such as curiosity, choice, and trustworthiness being particularly important in the home setting. In addition, wearable sensor technologies showed promising potential for home-based stroke rehabilitation. A sensor-based feedback device was found to be feasible and acceptable for stimulating daily arm activity, while inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensors demonstrated promising validity and reliability for capturing upper extremity kinematics during exercise. Finally, this thesis showed that prognostic targeting can substantially improve the efficiency of upper extremity stroke rehabilitation trials by reducing the number of participants required to detect clinically meaningful treatment effects, providing an important methodological foundation for future evaluation studies of home-based telerehabilitation interventions. Overall, this thesis demonstrates the potential of wearable sensors to support accessible, personalised, and home-based upper extremity rehabilitation after stroke. The findings provide important directions for the further development, evaluation, and implementation of telerehabilitation solutions in clinical practice
authors: Nienja Langerak

title: Functional precision medicine in leukemias: current applications, challenges, and future directions
abstract: Functional precision medicine represents a promising approach to address the biological heterogeneity and therapeutic complexity of leukemias. By integrating direct functional assessment of drug response with molecular and clinical information, this strategy provides a more comprehensive framework for individualized therapy selection. Although important challenges remain, including methodological standardization, limited viability of primary leukemic cells, high infrastructure costs, and the need for prospective clinical validation, ongoing technological and computational advances are expected to facilitate broader clinical implementation. Ultimately, functional precision medicine may become a central component of modern hematologic oncology, enabling more dynamic, biologically informed, and patient-centered therapeutic strategies.
authors: Samara de Sousa Mariano; Mateus Milani; José Andrés Yunes

title: GazeAct: A Human-Gaze-Annotated Manipulation Dataset for Attention-Regularized Policies
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies must ground language instructions in the right objects, contact points, and target locations for reliable manipulation. Human gaze provides a natural signal for this grounding, but existing robot datasets rarely pair real human gaze with the multi-camera observations used by modern policies. We introduce GazeAct, a gaze-equipped real-robot manipulation dataset and training framework for multi-view VLA policies. Using screen-based teleoperation, we record gaze directly on the robot camera feed viewed by the operator, yielding 12000 demonstrations across 40 tasks and five domains with 300 Hz gaze synchronized with images, proprioception, and actions. We transfer gaze from the operator-selected view to the remaining synchronized cameras, producing spatially consistent targets across the policy's visual inputs. We then use these gaze-derived targets to regularize language-conditioned visual attention during training while keeping inference gaze-free. Across 18 real-world tasks, our method improves average success from 48.1% to 58.6%, with gains up to 25 percentage points. Ablations show that gaze works best as soft supervision and that real human gaze provides stronger attention targets than generic attention-shaping priors. The gains transfer to LIBERO-Spatial (57.9% to 69.6%) and different VLA backbones.These results show that gaze collected in the robot observation space can provide effective training-time targets for improving visual grounding in VLA manipulation.
authors: Anupam Pani; Wang Yuan; Qifan Wang; Yanchao Yang

title: Gemini Robotics in Agriculture: Applications, Models, Fruit Industry, and Future Perspectives
abstract: Agricultural robotics is progressing from task-specific automation toward embodied systems that integrate multimodal perception, language, reasoning, and physical action. This chapter reviews Gemini Robotics and closely related vision-language model (VLM) and vision-language-action (VLA) developments in the context of agriculture, with particular emphasis on fruit production. It first presents a conceptual agricultural architecture linking sensing, cognition, decision and control, actuation, connectivity, power and safety. It then examines emerging evidence from language-guided agricultural navigation, spatial-memory systems, occlusion-aware harvest planning, VLA-based strawberry harvesting, obstacle separation and text-prompted multi-fruit picking. The reviewed studies show growing capability in navigation, semantic reasoning and closed-loop manipulation, but also expose important limitations in agricultural validation, cross-crop generalization, action datasets, real-time computing, safety and commercial readiness. For fruit systems, the principal technical challenges remain occlusion, maturity and accessibility assessment, three-dimensional localization, delicate detachment and adaptation across cultivars, canopies and seasons. The chapter therefore proposes a future pathway centered on multimodal agricultural foundation models, edge VLA inference, soft and tactile manipulation, continual learning, natural-language human-robot collaboration and coordinated UAV-UGV-manipulator systems. The Gemini Robotics provides a promising foundation for moving agricultural robots from isolated perception-action pipelines toward general-purpose embodied intelligence, although extensive field validation is required before broad deployment.
authors: Mustafa Mhamed; Zhao Zhang

title: Generative AI chatbots and mental health: A critical narrative review of benefits, risks, and clinical implications
abstract: The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence chatbots has repositioned these systems from productivity tools to interlocutors used for emotional support, companionship, and mental health guidance. This critical narrative review has three aims: to give mental health professionals a concise technical account of large language models; to separate the evidence and risks attached to four distinct system classes, protocolized therapeutic chatbots, clinically bounded generative systems, general-purpose large language models used as informal therapy, and companion platforms; and to examine clinical, ethical, and regulatory implications. Literature was identified through non-systematic, iterative database and preprint-server searches between March and July 2026, supplemented by citation tracking and policy documents. No prespecified eligibility or screening protocol was used; the comparative claims are therefore provisional. Protocolized and clinically bounded systems carry the strongest evidence, including a meta-analysis of generative and hybrid chatbots reporting modest short-term symptom reduction and a randomized trial of an expert-fine-tuned therapeutic chatbot; these trials are brief, predominantly waitlist-controlled, and reliant on self-report. General-purpose models and companion platforms may deliver immediate validation and temporary reductions in loneliness, but that evidence is largely observational, qualitative, or short-term experimental and does not establish sustained benefit. Concerns include emotional dependence, social substitution, sycophantic reinforcement, unsafe responses to suicidal or psychotic content, commercial manipulation, and delusional beliefs temporally associated with sustained use. These systems are not a single intervention class. Their effects appear contingent on clinical structure, relational design, user vulnerability, duration and centrality of use, commercial incentives, and safeguards.
authors: Bruno da Silva Santos; Arthur Dolberth; Giovanni Gonçalves De Toni; Carlos Eduardo Freitas Dantas; Matheus de Lima Ruffini; Flávio Pereira Kapczinski; Jaime E. C. Hallak; Ives Cavalcante Passos; Thiago Henrique Roza

title: Genotoxic safety and long-term engraftment dynamics of efficient translational CRISPR/Cas9 therapeutics for β-haemoglobinopathies from bench to clinical trials
abstract: BACKGROUND: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing targeting the BCL11A erythroid enhancer has transformed therapeutic approaches for transfusion-dependent β-thalassemia (β-thal) and sickle cell disease (SCD). Even though clinical efficacy is well demonstrated, translating these therapies to global patient populations requires a strong evidence-based framework to address critical concerns regarding long-term genotoxic safety and long-lasting engraftment dynamics. METHODS: Following the 2020 PRISMA guidelines, we conducted a systematic review of 21 key clinical and preclinical studies (published during 2014-2026) to evaluate CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing in β-thal and SCD. The inclusion criteria focused on studies reporting foetal haemoglobin (HbF) induction, transfusion independence (TI) and safety outcomes. RESULTS: Clinical data indicate high efficacy, with exagamglogene autotemcel (exa-cel) achieving TI in 91% of β-thal patients and a vaso-occlusive crisis (VOC)-free status in 97% of SCD patients. Safety profiling confirmed that severe adverse events, including febrile neutropenia and stomatitis, are primarily associated with busulfan-based myeloablation rather than gene editing. Gene-editing safety and conditioning toxicity are interlinked because conditioning is part of the process, and edited clones might interact with stress pathways during long-term repopulation. Preclinical benchmarks substantiate molecular reliability, with negligible off-target activity reported in most validated platforms. However, rare instances of complex structural rearrangements and intergenic off-target indels highlight the necessity for in-depth, unbiased long-term genomic surveillance. CONCLUSION: CRISPR/Cas9 therapeutics for β-thal and SCD treatment constitute a treatment option within current clinical frameworks. These therapies need continuous surveillance. Rather than establishing a perfect plan, this systematic review highlights that while current platforms are thought to have short-term molecular precision, the use of Multilayer Safety Risks Screening and Surveillance for pretransplant conditioning is critical. This approach helps address long-term genotoxic concerns and ensures the safety and scalability of gene-editing therapies for global β-thal and SCD patient care.
authors: Abeer M. Al‐Subaie; Jesu Francis Borgio

title: Gobernanza clínica para humanizar sin revictimizar el embarazo en niñas y adolescentes: revisión de alcance
abstract: Objective: To identify the clinical, relational, protective, and organizational components of humanized, non-revictimizing care during pregnancy, childbirth, and postpartum among girls and adolescents, and translate them into clinical-governance responsibilities. Materials and methods: A scoping review followed JBI and PRISMA-ScR. Primary studies on perinatal care for people aged 10–19 years were searched in PubMed, SciELO, and Academic Search Ultimate, with regional verification in BVS/LILACS and SciELO. Eligibility decisions were documented by pathway. Results: A total of 3,567 records were screened. Of 130 reports sought in the main databases, 16 were not retrieved; of 114 assessed, 22 were excluded and 92 corresponded to 90 unique studies. Regional verification added five non-duplicate studies after excluding three of eight reports. The final corpus comprised 97 reports from 95 unique studies. Evidence was grouped into four domains: clinical safety; relationships, information, and autonomy; privacy and protection; continuity, coordination, and networks. Conclusions: Humanized care depends on the clinical encounter and the service capacity to sustain privacy, participation, protection, and continuity. HUM-ENA organizes these responsibilities into a review-derived conceptual-operational framework requiring adaptation and validation before use as a guideline or assessment instrument. Keywords: Pregnancy in Adolescence; Adolescent Health Services; Prenatal Care; Patient-Centered Care; Humanization of Assistance.
authors: Luis Miguel Álvarez Luna; Jehiel Abiezer Jimenez Coba

title: Gym-Anything for Robotics: Scaling physical simulations with digital agents
abstract: Realistic, fast robotics simulations could enable large-scale training of embodied AI models that transfer to the real world. However, despite decades of progress, available simulations cover only a narrow range of real-world tasks and physical phenomena. The core bottleneck is that creating better simulations requires significant expert effort and therefore does not scale. To address this, we introduce Gym-Anything for Robotics, a framework in which coding agents create realistic robotics simulations. Our core insight is that simulation creation is a coding agent task, so improvements in coding agents translate directly into richer and more faithful simulations. We select simulations based on U.S. GDP data to cover economically valuable physical work, define what makes a good simulation and a good task, and develop an adversarial creation-audit loop that checks each simulation and task against these definitions. Using this pipeline, we build RoboWorld, a set of 25 simulations with 25 test and 175 training RL environments of varying difficulty. Even the best frontier models fail on every RoboWorld test task, achieving an average reward of only 0.06. Building on RoboWorld, we introduce several new ways for frontier models to improve, including in-context learning across repeated attempts, a privileged teacher that reads the simulator state and teaches a student in context, self-assisted learning from the model's own privileged experience, and code policies that generate demonstrations across varied scenes to train vision-language-action models (VLAs) such as $π_{0.5}$. Each of these substantially improves performance. We release our pipeline, RL environments, and benchmark to facilitate future research. Code and data are available at https://gym-anything.github.io/robotics
authors: Pranjal Aggarwal; Sean Welleck

title: Health-seeking behaviour and treatment preferences among women reporting symptoms suggestive of female genital schistosomiasis in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa: A facility-based cross-sectional study
abstract: Female Genital Schistosomiasis (FGS), a neglected manifestation of Schistosoma haematobium infection, affects 20-56 million women in sub-Saharan Africa and is associated with elevated HIV risk. In a Schistosoma haematobium-endemic area of KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa, 32% of girls aged 10-12 years reported a history of genital symptoms, yet awareness is low, and the proportion seeking appropriate care is undocumented. This study quantified healthcare-seeking behaviour and treatment preferences for FGS-suggestive symptoms across biomedical, traditional, and combined care pathways. A facility-based cross-sectional survey was conducted at eight primary healthcare clinics in iLembe District between June and August 2025, using REDCap. Of 713 women surveyed, 694 were included, and the analyses focused on 318 who reported at least one symptom suggestive of FGS, without microbiological, serological, or gynaecological confirmation. Multivariable logistic regression identified predictors of healthcare-seeking; among all symptomatic women, treatment preference was examined across biomedical-only, traditional/CAM-only, and combination pathways, with logistic models identifying predictors of preferring any traditional/CAM care. Analyses used Stata/SE 19. Mean age was 30.6 years (SD 8.0). Of the 318 women, 78.3% preferred only biomedical care. Women in informal employment had 4.12 times the odds of preferring traditional/CAM care compared with unemployed women (aOR = 4.12; 95% CI: 2.35-7.23; p < 0.001). In the multinomial analysis, informal employment was most strongly associated with preferring traditional/CAM care alone, carrying nearly nine times the relative risk relative to biomedical care (RRR = 8.89; 95% CI: 2.74-28.90; p < 0.001), whereas water-contact activity other than bathing was associated with a preference for combination care (RRR = 3.28; 95% CI: 1.44-7.47; p = 0.005). These findings support policies that integrate FGS screening and referral into primary healthcare, sexual and reproductive health, HIV, and antenatal services, as well as health worker training, community awareness, and coordinated referral pathways.
authors: Sinegugu Nosipho Shongwe; Chester Kalinda; Khumbulani Hlongwana; Themba G. Ginindza

title: Hierarchical causal construction for semantic-granularity-aligned counterfactual medical image generation
authors: Zhizhong Fu; Wei Zhou; Zhaoyang Jiang; Yudong Lin; Gaoming Li; Yuke Cao; Yifu Hou; Ding Xiaorong; Qiang Yan; Yifan Chen

title: Higher Blood Eosinophil Counts During Acute Preschool Wheeze Are Associated With School‐Age Asthma: A Retrospective Cohort Study
abstract: Aim To assess whether blood eosinophil counts (BEC) measured during acute preschool wheeze were associated with asthma after age five and added predictive information to clinical factors. Methods We reviewed the records of 1373 children aged 1–5, hospitalized for wheezing at a tertiary centre (2013–2024). Clinical predictors and BEC were obtained from the earliest available complete blood count during the index wheezing hospitalization. Respiratory outcomes were assessed for 323 children with available hospital and affiliated outpatient records after their fifth birthday. We used logistic regression and ROC analysis to assess whether BEC predicted later asthma. Results Persistent wheeze/asthma was identified in 115 children (35.6%). Median BEC was higher in children with persistent wheeze/asthma than in those without asthma (0.30 [0.10–0.66] vs. 0.14 [0.03–0.30] × 10 3 /μL; p < 0.001). BEC alone showed modest discrimination (AUC 0.673) and improved prediction when combined with five clinical predictors (AUC 0.789). A BEC threshold of 0.57 × 10 3 /μL identified a high‐specificity subgroup (sensitivity 30.4%, specificity 92.8%). Conclusion BECs during acute wheezing hospitalization were independently associated with later asthma and provided modest incremental predictive information when combined with clinical features. BEC may help identify hospitalized preschool children with wheeze who warrant closer follow‐up. External validation is required before clinical implementation.
authors: Aleksander Adamiec; Katarzyna Moliszewska; Aleksandra Marchwińska-Pancer; Paweł Kukiełka; Marek Kulus; Wojciech Feleszko

title: Holtercare-Bench: A Multimodal Benchmark for Evaluating Long-Term Dynamic ECG Analysis
abstract: While multimodal large language models (MLLMs) excel in medical applications, most of them favor static images or short-term signals. In the critical field of dynamic electrocardiograms (ECG), models struggle with complex temporal reasoning and diagnostic report generation due to a lack of high-quality datasets and benchmarks. To address this, we introduce (i) Holtercare-23K, a large-scale multimodal dynamic ECG dataset comprising 22,980 QA pairs derived from 788 clinical Holter records and featuring a novel signal--video--text tri-modal alignment. Based on this dataset, we present (ii) Holtercare-Bench, a multimodal benchmark that evaluates models on temporal localization, clinical diagnosis, and global summarization. Zero-shot evaluations of leading MLLMs reveal a significant performance gap in processing ultra-long pathological sequences. However, fine-tuning representative models yields substantial improvements. This work illuminates the limitations of current MLLMs in electrophysiology and provides a foundational benchmark for long-term medical MLLMs. Our project is available at https://github.com/ZJU4HealthCare/Holtercare-Bench.
authors: Yihan Xie; Hanwen Cui; Runze Ye; Juekai Lin; Haoyang Wang; Jinhao Mao; Bo Zhang; Xiaogang Guo; Jun Xiao; Lei Zhang
venue: ACM International Conference on Multimedia (ACM MM)

title: HospitalBench: Diagnosing Where and Why Embodied Agents Fail on Long Hospital Task Chains
abstract: Long-horizon embodied tasks fail in ways that end-task success cannot see. HospitalBench is a diagnostic benchmark of ten hospital chores in NVIDIA Isaac Sim, each two unscored warm-up steps followed by a causal chain of five scored sub-tasks in one continuous simulation: the state one step leaves (an object pose, a choice, a fact seen once) determines what the next step must do, unlike benchmarks that place sub-tasks side by side. Vision-language agents act through skill-level tools from camera images. A scripted robot that makes only the calls a model gets is the solvability check of a chore. From each trajectory the benchmark reads where a chain breaks, what the agent did after a failed call, and how far its own position estimate drifts from the true one. This version reports first results only: 15 of 60 planned runs (three models at high effort, one run each on chores T1 and T10 from both start states and T3 from one), with scripted-robot proofs on three of the ten chores. Of the 15 runs, 2 passed all five sub-tasks. Runs still going after sub-tasks 1 to 5 were 15, 8, 4, 2, 2. Of 189 failed calls, 168 were followed by a different call and 111 by a call that did not fail. These are first results and not a full benchmark. We will release the scenes, task chains, scripted robot, evaluation harness and trajectories.
authors: Gaytri Jena; Kapil Wanaskar; Aman Chadha; Vasu Sharma; Vinija Jain; Amitava Das

title: Identifying adverse event clusters and treatment effects in randomised trials using latent class analysis: an application in the COV-BOOST trial
abstract: Background Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) are essential for evaluating treatment efficacy and safety, particularly in vaccine trials, where adverse events are systematically collected and assessed. The high volume of reported adverse events often presents challenges in discerning meaningful associations between treatments and adverse events. Traditional analytical approaches rely on multiple pairwise treatment comparisons of individual adverse events, which can be difficult to interpret. This study explores the use of latent class analysis (LCA) to identify adverse event profiles and estimates the average treatment effects (ATE) for these in an RCT setting. Methods Data from the COV-BOOST trial (ISRCTN registration 73765130), which assessed the safety and efficacy of seven COVID-19 booster vaccines, was used. This trial monitored a predefined set of 17 adverse events, graded by severity, over a 7-day period following immunisation. LCA was applied to classify participants into adverse event subgroups based on shared event profiles. After identifying these classes, the ATE was estimated for each identified adverse event profile to quantify the causal impact of different vaccine boosters. This was achieved by regressing treatment on the latent adverse event class membership outcome. Results Fatigue, pain, and headache were commonly reported adverse events across all vaccine arms. LCA identified three distinct adverse event profiles among participants: (class 1) minimal AEs, (class 2) mild AEs, and (class 3) severe AEs reports. Four vaccines, ChAd after BNT/BNT primer, Ad26, CVn, and MOD after both primer vaccines, were associated with higher reactogenicity, with most recipients falling into class 2 or 3. Conclusion This study demonstrates the utility of LCA in identifying adverse event profiles within an RCT and uniquely integrates the latent adverse event class membership of participants as an outcome for ATE estimation. By examining the varying effects of booster vaccines in the COV-BOOST trial, this method advances the understanding of these vaccines’ safety. The successful application of this innovative approach in this study could pave the way for its adoption by researchers in future clinical trials across various medical domains. More broadly, integrating LCA with ATE estimation provides a novel framework for enhancing vaccine pharmacovigilance and improving safety assessments for medical interventions.

title: Interpretable Ensemble Pipeline for Early Identification of Diabetic Kidney Disease Using Augmented Clinical Data
abstract: OBJECTIVES: Early detection of diabetic kidney disease (DKD) is difficult in semi-urban healthcare settings where diagnostic resources are limited and comorbidities overlap. This study developed and evaluated an interpretable ensemble learning pipeline that combined hybrid resampling and high-performance computing to predict DKD early in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). METHODS: Data from a retrospective cohort of 210 adults with T2DM were analyzed using 35 demographic, lifestyle, and biochemical variables. Missing values (<7%) were imputed with the median or mode. Class imbalance (DKD:non-DKD = 1:2.6) was addressed by combining the synthetic minority oversampling technique with Tomek link cleaning and random undersampling. A stacking ensemble of logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost was evaluated using accuracy, recall, specificity, F1-score, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) were used to interpret the features. RESULTS: The ensemble achieved an AUC of 0.948 and an F1-score of 0.947. Data augmentation increased recall from 0.83 to 0.95 but reduced specificity from 1.00 to 0.89. SHAP identified urea, albumin, and diabetes duration as the most influential predictors, with better detection among patients with a longer diabetes duration. Using histogram-based XGBoost reduced training time by approximately 63%, and inference latency was below 0.02 seconds per patient record. CONCLUSIONS: The ensemble classifier pipeline discriminated DKD well and provided interpretable predictions in this moderate-sized cohort. Hybrid resampling improved sensitivity at the cost of lower specificity. External validation and longitudinal evaluation are needed before wider clinical use.
authors: Reena Mol V U; M Pushpalatha; Meenakshi V. Patel

title: LIBERO-RIG: A Hardware-Setup Robustness Benchmark for Vision-Language-Action Models
abstract: Robot policies are expected to generalize across deployment environments, including variations in the robot itself: cameras are bumped and remounted, calibrations drift, controllers run at different rates, and end-effector pads wear down. We present LIBERO-RIG, a benchmark that perturbs only the robot's hardware and setup while holding every LIBERO task fixed. The benchmark spans eleven perturbation axes, including camera mounting and optics, camera-to-arm calibration, actuation gain, control rate, proprioceptive noise, base pose, table height, and gripper pads. Each axis has five severity levels, yielding 210 conditions across the four LIBERO suites. We evaluate nine recent vision-language-action models using 500 episodes per condition and substantiate each finding with rigorous statistical tests. Pooled success falls from 0.932 to 0.767 at the middle severity and 0.509 at the highest severity. Performance degradation varies substantially across perturbation axes and action interfaces, and training on visual perturbations does not mitigate faults that leave camera images unchanged. We release the benchmark together with manifests specifying the fixed perturbation parameters for each episode.
authors: Andrea Yaoyun Cui; Hanyu Wang; Xinyi Wang; Bangzheng Li; Lin Zhang; Zhenggang Tang; Shyamal Buch; Dejia Xu; Matthew Tancik

title: Listening and Mirroring: The Effects of Verbal Attunement and Behavioral Mimicry on Social and Empathic Perceptions of Embodied AI Agents in VR
abstract: As embodied agents take on increasingly social and relational roles in VR, visual realism and embodiment alone may be insufficient; users must also perceive these agents as emotionally attuned, supportive, and humanlike. Prior work suggests that verbal attunement and nonverbal mimicry can each improve users’ social evaluations of embodied agents. However, behavioral mimicry has largely been studied outside of real-time, conversational AI interactions, leaving limited understanding of how users respond when an agent simultaneously generates contextually responsive dialogue and adapts its nonverbal behavior during an immersive conversation. To address this gap, we developed an embodied AI counselor that combines conversational AI with real-time facial-expression and posture mimicry, while producing either verbally attuned or neutral responses. We evaluated the system in a 2 × 2 within-subjects study with 20 participants, manipulating verbal attunement and behavioral mimicry. Results showed that verbal attunement was the most reliable driver of perceived empathy. Behavioral mimicry showed a marginal relationship with perceived humanness, while greater mimicry exposure showed preliminary, exploratory positive associations with empathy, positivity, and humanness, particularly among female participants. Together, these findings show that multimodal synchrony is not a simple additive strategy for designing empathic conversational agents in VR and underscore the need to consider how verbal and nonverbal behaviors are combined during real-time interaction.
authors: Nathalia Gomez; Haig Shamlian; Omar Khan; Tiffany D. Do

title: MASH Cirrhosis: A Stage‐Specific Framework for Care and Clinical Trial Design
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) is an increasingly important cause of cirrhosis, yet no pharmacological therapy is approved specifically for MASH cirrhosis. Completed trials indicate that this therapeutic gap reflects limitations in biological targeting, population definition, treatment duration, and endpoint selection rather than evidence that established disease is immutable. Most agents evaluated in compensated MASH cirrhosis did not meet their prespecified primary endpoints; aldafermin met an enhanced liver fibrosis endpoint without establishing histological benefit, and later assessment of efruxifermin suggested that structural change may require longer exposure. MASH cirrhosis should therefore not be investigated as a simple extension of precirrhotic MASH. Disease stage, clinically significant portal hypertension, metabolic comorbidity, and frailty influence both prognosis and treatment tolerance. Selected invasive and cross-sectional studies suggest heterogeneity in the relationship between hepatic venous pressure gradient and clinical events in advanced MASLD or MASH, but prospective data confirm that hepatic venous pressure gradient remains prognostic; these observations do not establish a universally distinct hemodynamic phenotype. Mechanistic findings involving sinusoidal endothelium, bile handling, and canalicular architecture are translational leads rather than validated clinical markers. We propose a stage-specific framework that separates current care from trial design; prioritizes clinical outcome endpoints in compensated disease with portal hypertension and in decompensated disease; and treats biopsy, liver stiffness, enhanced liver fibrosis, hemodynamic, and frailty measures according to their context and level of validation. Prospective MASH-cirrhosis cohorts and competing-risk-aware trials are now required.
authors: David Shengyang Zhang; Tsubasa Tsutsumi; Mark Dhinesh Muthiah

title: Machine-oriented Visual Media Quality Assessment
abstract: With the development of Embodied AI, machines have replaced humans as the main consumers of visual media, yet existing Image Quality Assessment (IQA) metrics remain focused on humans and overlook machine preference (a domain where quality depends on task utility rather than perceptual fidelity alone). To address this gap, we introduce the Machine-oriented Image Quality Assessment (MoIQA) Challenge, emphasizing simulation comprehension and real-world execution. The challenge comprises three tasks: 1) MoIQA-Absolute, primarily evaluating the consistency between IQA models and the performance of mainstream Vision-Language Models (VLMs) in simulation software; 2) MoIQA-Relative, measuring the consistency between IQA models and the variance of VLM inference after distortion, also in simulation; and 3) MoIQA-Real, focusing on whether IQA models match the results of the latest Vision-Language-Action Models (VLAs) in the Real-world. This challenge aims to advance reliable image understanding for machine preference and support robust Embodied AI applications. This grand challenge attracted 142 high-level teams around the world, and the relevant resources are open-sourced at: Homepage: https://m-vqa-challenge.github.io/M-VQA/ Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/AIBench/M-VQA
authors: Chunyi Li; Rui Qing; Jianbo Zhang; Yufei Han; Shiyu Liu; Yuanzhong Zhang; Zicheng Zhang; Huiyu Duan; Wei Zhou; Roger Zimmermann; Weisi Lin; Guangtao Zhai
