title: MedEvo: Medical Reasoning Evolution through Knowledge Navigation
abstract: Medical multimodal reasoning models are typically trained on teacher-generated rationales, discarding the valid reasoning in students' own failed trajectories, while general-domain correction methods offer little guidance for errors in image reading, anatomical context, or differential diagnosis. We propose MedEvo, which uses medical knowledge, namely a tag taxonomy and error-type diagnosis, to navigate both trajectory repair and data selection. For each failed rollout, a gold-blind auditor locates the first consequential error and provides a minimal, answer-free hint; the same student retains the valid prefix and regenerates the erroneous suffix. After each round, MedEvo identifies capability gaps across medical tags on a held-out feedback set and prioritizes related questions for new rollouts and repairs. With supervised fine-tuning (SFT) alone, MedEvo raises Qwen3.5-9B mean accuracy across seven benchmarks from 65.57% to 69.12% (47.40% to 54.50% on the multimodal track of MedXpertQA (MedXpertQA-MM)), surpassing teacher-distillation SFT (66.93%). It also raises Qwen3.5-35B and Qwen3.5-397B mean accuracy from 67.91% to 73.04% and from 71.83% to 74.95%, respectively. Our analyses show that failed trajectories contain reasoning worth preserving, that repair success does not imply learning value, and that independent feedback is key to sustained improvement.
authors: Xiaoliang Wang; Zhuo Chen; Chuanyang Zheng; Quanbin Wang; Jiangwei Lao; Yingao Liu; Jiajia Liu; Jinming Cao; Honglin Lin; Zhihong Lu; Hao Jin; Jian Wang; Lijun Wu; Lijun Wu

title: MedHarnessBench: A Unified Benchmark for Healthcare Agent Evaluation
abstract: Healthcare agents must transform longitudinal clinical evidence into reliable actions through heterogeneous tools and stateful workflows, conditions under which model-centric systems may lose context, misuse tools, fail to verify consequential transitions, or cross authorization boundaries. Existing medical-agent benchmarks primarily emphasize terminal task outcomes, making it difficult to determine whether execution failures arise from the agent model, the runtime harness, or their interaction. We present the Medical Harness Protocol, an outcome-preserving framework that independently evaluates seven healthcare-specific process dimensions: Care Action Fulfillment, Clinical Resource Competence, Patient-Evidence Alignment, Clinical Workflow Continuity, Clinical Auditability, Closed-Loop Verification, and Clinical Conduct Boundaries. A normalized intervention trace further tracks whether runtime support is available, activated, delivered, adopted by the agent, and propagated into subsequent behavior. We instantiate the protocol as MedHarnessBench, comprising 342 executable tasks across FHIR/EHR operations, healthcare-administration interfaces, and multimodal clinical tools. Across more than 16,000 controlled task executions, MedHarness yields broad improvements in terminal task success, intermediate subtask completion, and healthcare-specific process quality. We further evaluate MedHarness against multiple general-purpose harnesses and use controlled single-fault perturbations to verify the sensitivity and discrimination of the seven-dimensional evaluation. These results demonstrate that healthcare-specific runtime support can substantially improve both task completion and execution quality, while revealing failures that terminal outcomes alone cannot capture. Code and resources are available at https://github.com/Tomry1114/Awesome-Agent-Harness-for-Healthcare.
authors: Rui Tang; Hongqiu Wang

title: Medical Embodied Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare Delivery and Clinical Workflows
abstract: Medical embodied artificial intelligence (AI) closes the loop between sensing, action and feedback in clinical and care tasks, from procedures and examination to rehabilitation and hospital logistics. Its clinical value therefore depends not only on what a system can do, but on how its action loop fits the task, the people who supervise it and the service responsible for recovery. In this structured narrative Review, we trace the field from image-guided and teleoperated robots to learned policies and foundation models, and survey its technical foundations along the action loop, from perception and task reasoning to planning, control, vision–language–action and world models and safety monitoring, together with data and simulation resources and applications across eight clinical task categories. A 96-source evidence map and targeted technical searches underpin the synthesis, and a separately defined subset of 40 direct empirical studies characterises the settings in which embodied systems have been validated. Evidence in this subset remains predominantly preclinical or feasibility-based and does not establish clinical superiority or long-term safety. We argue that the principal translational bottleneck is not insufficient autonomy alone but a mismatch among task boundaries, machine authority, evidence maturity and health-service readiness. To address this mismatch, we propose a task-bounded framework that links the operational design domain and allocated authority to the evidence required, the conditions for implementation and the mechanisms for monitoring, revalidation and rollback, and we identify technical priorities in grounded foundation models, shared data, uncertainty-aware autonomy and verifiable safety. The framework prioritises clinically relevant comparators, effective clinician takeover and evaluation of the complete workflow, including preparation, supervision and recovery, and offers a basis for appraising deployment claims; its decision value and effects on care now require prospective evaluation.
authors: Chen Z, Cong Z, Fan W, Han Z, Gong H, Liao C, Liu X, You G, Wang W, Wang C.

title: Multimodal tactile–posture capture enables physically grounded annotation of human demonstrations
abstract: Learning dexterous manipulation from human demonstrations requires records of physical interactions that video alone cannot fully capture. Here we present tactile-motion capture (TaMoCap), a portable physical interaction tracking system that records multimodal tactile–posture information during natural human demonstrations, reconstructs physical interaction states of human-object interaction, and converts them into structured semantic annotations. The system integrates a smart textile glove with distributed three-axis force, triboelectric and strain sensors. The synchronized multimodal sensing streams are processed to reconstruct three-axis contact forces, strain-derived joint-angle estimates, and triboelectricity-based contact-transition states, yielding physically interpretable representations that characterize sustained loading, transient interaction events, and hand posture during natural manipulation. A tactile semantic translation framework integrates synchronized visual observations, reconstructed physical interaction states, and task context to generate action annotations, which are verified against multimodal evidence for physical consistency and source traceability. In a descriptive evaluation of four selected massage cases, the full visual–tactile–semantic input achieves a mean composite score of 94.75/100 in model-based assessment, 33.5 points higher than the video-only input. In a long-horizon noodle-cooking demonstration, TaMoCap preserves temporal alignment between multimodal sensing evidence and structured semantic annotations throughout the action sequence. TaMoCap provides a systematic approach for constructing physically grounded human demonstration records for tactile-enhanced embodied agents and robotic manipulation systems.
authors: Lin Fan; Herong Wang; Yong Tian; Yiyang Li; Xiaojian Rao; Yue Xiao; Yuzhou Wang; Weiguan Zhang; Jindong Tian; Ning Li; Gaojie Chen

title: Multiple sclerosis relapse following gamma knife radiosurgery for meningioma in a patient treated with natalizumab: case report
abstract: Objectives: We describe a case of a patient with multiple sclerosis (MS) stable on natalizumab who developed widespread gadolinium-enhancing lesions and clinical relapse seven and eight months after gamma knife radiosurgery (GKRS) for left cerebellar convexity meningioma. We explore how increased blood-brain barrier (BBB) permeability post-GKRS could potentially interfere with the lymphocyte anti-trafficking effect of natalizumab and result in new central nervous system (CNS) inflammation distant from the radiation site. Methods: Comprehensive analysis of the patient's chart, brain and spine imaging, serum and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) profiles was conducted. We compiled a graphical representation of treatment changes, radiologic findings, and GKRS initiation within one timeframe. We conducted a structured literature review to support the discussion of this case and hypothesize possible pathophysiological mechanisms contributing to clinical and radiological findings. Results: Seven months after GKRS, follow-up brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated multiple gadolinium-enhancing lesions in both cerebral hemispheres, and repeat imaging one month later revealed new gadolinium-enhancing lesions, correlating with the patient's clinical relapse. Alternative causes of disease progression, including radiation-induced demyelination, radionecrosis, opportunistic infections, progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML), and development of anti-natalizumab antibodies, were explored and considered less likely. The patient was switched to ofatumumab with subsequent clinical and radiological stability. Discussion: Given extensive new inflammatory lesions far from the GKRS site, it seems unlikely that the sole mechanism was radiation-induced neurotoxicity. We hypothesize that late delayed radiation side effects caused by GKRS may have enabled peripheral lymphocytes to enter the CNS, counteracting the effects of natalizumab on blocking lymphocyte trafficking through the BBB and possibly contributing to MS relapse.
authors: Maryna Turbinska; Nabeela Nathoo; Penelope S. Smyth

title: NI-ACT: A Neural Intent Interface for Brain-Embodied Manipulation
abstract: Intracortical brain-computer interfaces can drive robotic arms, but they keep the user inside the fast sensorimotor loop: every approach, correction, and grasp must be neurally specified. Whether intracortical population activity can instead serve as a task-level condition for a learned embodied policy, without symbolic commands or hand-designed skill libraries, remains unknown. NI-ACT addresses this question with a hierarchical brain-embodied framework: a brief motor-cortical signal is read once as a persistent intent, and a visuomotor policy then closes the perception-action loop from vision and proprioception. In a counterfactual grasping task where the scene cannot specify the target, the neural intent alone determined which object the robot grasped; replacing the intent changed the behavior accordingly. Passing the full population latent as a dedicated intent token, rather than a one-hot decoded direction, raised grasp completion from 69% to 81% over 132 held-out scenes, whereas a continuous direction alone did not improve on a one-hot label. Where the signal was read also mattered: in one dual-array session, with the readout window matched, premotor (PMd) intent completed more grasps than primary motor (M1) intent (77% vs. 53%), and the conventional post-cue M1 readout reached 42%. Preparatory activity was itself sufficient: in a center-out task, intent read only from PMd before the go cue (that is, before any movement) drove complete grasps, and in one recording it completed more grasps than the same animal's post-cue readout. These results show that how a neural signal is represented, and where and when it is read, jointly determine how effectively it conveys movement goals to an embodied agent.
authors: Yinghao Li; WeiHsien Lee; Zeyu Zhang; Canyang Zhao; Ke Fang; Xing Li; Bing Liu

title: Post-hoc Epistemic Uncertainty for Vision-Language-Action Policies
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies need to recognize gaps in their training knowledge to request useful demonstrations or assistance in new situations, especially when failures are costly. Disagreement within an ensemble of independently trained policies can guide these decisions, but requires training and running multiple policies. We propose post-hoc kernel-variance heads that estimate epistemic uncertainty from the embeddings of a single policy. Each head computes the conditional variance of a Gaussian process conditioned on embeddings from the training demonstrations. Fitting requires no regression targets or gradient updates and leaves the policy unchanged. In experiments with SmolVLA on LIBERO-10, the kernel variance heads perform competitively with two-policy ensemble scores in task-level correlation with task success, in demonstration acquisition during active learning, and in referral to a stronger supervisor policy as a proxy for human assistance. For SmolVLA, the head on the vision-language backbone reduces uncertainty-scoring time by up to approximately a factor of 50 compared with ensemble scores, while also substantially reducing setup costs. We also show that the established evaluation protocol on LIBERO-10 primarily rewards recognition of coverage differences between tasks, while execution variability weakens assessment of within-task rankings. Thus, controlled perturbations provide a complementary evaluation: modality-specific heads identify unfamiliar camera, instruction, or state inputs, while fused heads can detect unfamiliar combinations of individually familiar inputs. With a supervisor proxy trained on the evaluated perturbation families, the decoder head improves within-task referral over ensemble disagreement. These findings show that useful uncertainty estimates for adaptive robot learning can be obtained from a single policy.

title: RAISE: A Novel Approach to Assure the Safety of Vision–Language-Action-Based Driving Systems
abstract: Vision–Language–Action (VLA)–based driving systems represent a significant paradigm shift in autonomous driving since, by combining traffic scene understanding, linguistic interpretation, and action generation, these systems enable more flexible, adaptive, and instruction-responsive driving behaviors. However, despite their growing adoption and potential to support socially responsible autonomous driving as well as understanding high-level human instructions, VLA-based driving systems may exhibit new types of hazardous behaviors. For instance, the integration of open-ended natural language inputs (e.g., user or navigation instructions) into the multimodal control loop may lead to unpredictable and unsafe behaviors that could endanger vehicle occupants and pedestrians. Hence, assuring the safety of these systems is crucial to help build trust in their operations. To support this, we propose a novel safety case design approach called RAISE. Our approach introduces novel patterns tailored to instruction-based driving systems such as VLA-based driving systems, an extension of Hazard Analysis and Risk Assessment (HARA) detailing safe scenarios and their outcomes, and a design technique to create the safety cases of VLA-based driving systems. A case study on SimLingo illustrates how our approach can be used to construct rigorous, evidence-based safety claims for this emerging class of autonomous driving systems.
authors: Gerhard Yu; Fuyuki Ishikawa; Oluwafemi Odu; Alvine Boaye Belle
venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Symposium Series

title: RESCUE: Is This Alarm Worth Acting On? Counterfactual Evaluation of VLA Runtime Monitors
abstract: Runtime failure monitors for robot policies are typically evaluated by how accurately they distinguish failed from successful executions. Yet an accurate alarm may arrive too late for recovery, while an unnecessary intervention may disrupt an execution that would otherwise succeed. We introduce RESCUE, a counterfactual framework for evaluating whether a monitor's alarms enable useful interventions. By restoring simulator and policy states at execution checkpoints, RESCUE compares alternative actions, identifies the latest checkpoint satisfying a specified recovery criterion, and evaluates whether acting on alarms reduces expected task-completion cost. We evaluate RESCUE with OpenVLA-OFT and $π_{0.5}$ over LIBERO-Spatial and LIBERO-Plus using 128,340 counterfactual branches. Recoverability depends on the state--intervention pair rather than on robot state alone: at $τ=0.5$, 14 of 66 OpenVLA-OFT/LIBERO-Plus failures contain a recoverable checkpoint under continuation, compared with 34 of 66 under continuation or scripted recovery, while recovery reduces recoverability in other conditions. On the primary strong-policy conditions, favourable detection scores do not establish lower intervention cost. Under the evaluated stop-and-reset model, even an idealised detector can afford only a 2.0--3.3% false-alarm rate before unnecessary resets outweigh the savings from stopping failures early. These results show that monitor value depends jointly on the intervention available and the workload in which it is deployed.

title: Random Is Almost Enough? Stable and Low-Cost Benchmark Compression via BestRand
abstract: Benchmark compression reduces the often prohibitive time and cost of model evaluation by evaluating models on a small benchmark subset that closely matches full-benchmark results. To quantify estimation error, we derive an accurate analytical approximation to the error distribution when estimating full-benchmark scores from a subset, showing that most subsets yield small errors, while a few produce much larger errors, resulting in a long-tailed distribution. This means random sampling alone can achieve surprisingly strong performance with high probability, but remains unstable due to rare large errors. We further show that this instability is inherent to modern foundation models and persists even as more models are evaluated. Based on these findings, we introduce BestRand, a stable and low-cost benchmark compression method that preserves the efficiency of random sampling while substantially reducing its high-error tail. We validate BestRand on 70+ text, multimodal, and agent benchmarks, and further extend it to VLA evaluation. Compared with competitive methods, BestRand reduces high-error risk by 50.2% and estimation error by 16.4% on average, while requiring only 51.3% of the construction cost. It further reduces OOD estimation error by 21.8% on average across score-range, model-family, and temporal shifts. Together, our theory provides practical guidance for understanding and predicting the accuracy and reliability of benchmark compression, while BestRand enables stable and accurate compression at low cost. The code and data are publicly available onhttps://github.com/George-Ling3/BestRand.
authors: George Ling; Shanshan Zhong; Lijin Yang; Hao Yang; Nanxiang Li; Zhongzhan Huang

title: Reaching for Mental Wellbeing via Reachy Mini
abstract: Continuous assessment of patient psychological well-being remains a critical challenge in clinical inpatient care, where demanding workloads limit manual psychiatric evaluations and static surveys induce patient fatigue. In this paper, we present an embodied, agentic bedside framework targeting deployment on the Reachy Mini robotic companion to support the global AI-ready nursing workforce. The system integrates a real-time, tri-modal emotion recognition pipeline tracking vision (facial tracking and dynamics), acoustic prosody (voice-activity-driven speech emotion recognition), and transcribed semantic text. Complementing continuous emotion tracking, the robotic agent administers an adaptive 11-question conversational screening protocol that evaluates psychological trajectories across the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) and Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7) clinical tests, incorporating targeted probing to decouple somatic illness from primary affective distress. Synchronized interaction analytics and automated safety alerts are rendered on a clinician-facing nursing dashboard to facilitate proactive triage without inflating administrative overhead. We evaluate the perception models on a standard emotion benchmark and the conversational screener on a synthetic clinical cohort spanning the full range of depression and anxiety severity. The screening study shows that a single merged interview recovers both a depression and an anxiety item from one prompt on most shared questions, that item-level scores stay close to ground truth even when patients describe symptoms indirectly, that severity-band classification under natural, indirect dialogue falls to near-chance accuracy despite this item-level agreement, and that the strictness of the blind scorer governs a clear tradeoff between self-harm recall and false alarms. Together these results position the framework as a feasibility step toward continuous, interpretable psychological telemetry at the bedside.
authors: Aarat Satsangi; Sara Lahourpour; Sumira Allamraju; Apurva Narayan
venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Symposium Series

title: Reinforcement Learning with World Models in the Era of Scale: From Online Imagination to World Action Models
abstract: In World Model Reinforcement Learning (WM-RL), agents learn a parameterized model of environmental dynamics that serves as the basis for planning, imagination-based policy training, or synthetic data generation in decision making tasks. From 2019 to 2026, a drastic phase transition took place within this field. Initially started as an effort to improve efficiency in visual control tasks, WM-RL has become the core of interdisciplinary AI infrastructure. Today, internet-scale video-based generative world foundation models allow the autonomous vehicle pipeline to learn generalist policies from unlabeled human video, facilitating applications in medical therapy and molecular dynamics. To review the entire trajectory of WM-RL research, it is necessary to synthesize key sources that summarize the advances made throughout the years. Three prominent paradigm shifts are observed during this period. These include the shift from online Model-Based Reinforcement Learning (MBRL) to pretrain-first imagination-only policy training; architecture integration from decoupled worlds and policies to unified World Action Models; and the generalization of specific algorithms to physical AI infrastructure for all MBRL applications. Regarding architecture, WM-RL follows several generations of innovations. They include PlaNet, Recurrent State-Space Model (RSSM), the Dreamer family, value-equivalent implicit models, Transformer-based world models, diffusion dynamics, and the abstract-space Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) predictor. In this review, we examine WM-RL from multiple aspects, ranging from general model-based reinforcement learning, robotic manipulation, navigation, autonomous driving, multi-agent systems, large language model agents, healthcare, and games. The usage of world models varies widely depending on the application areas, while the validated architectures are discussed accordingly.
authors: Wojciech Dąbrowicki; Andrzej Rusiecki

title: Relevance of sprint interval and repeated sprint training protocols to the physiological and kinematic demands of 25 and 50-m swimming: A randomized experimental case study
abstract: Purpose To compare the physiological and kinematic responses of sprint interval training (SIT) and repeated sprint training (RST) with the demands of maximal 25- and 50-m freestyle swimming in a national-level sprint swimmer. Methods A 19-year-old male national-level freestyle specialist completed maximal 25 and 50 m freestyle time trials, a SIT protocol (2 × 4 × 25 m, 40 s recovery), and a RST protocol (2 × 8 × 12.5 m, 20 s recovery) on separate testing days. Blood lactate ([La − ]) concentration, blood glucose (BG), maximal lactate concentration rate (VLa max ), swimming speed (SS), stroke number (SN), stroke length (SL), stroke rate (SR), and stroke index (SI) were assessed to determine the physiological and biomechanical relevance of each training protocol. Results [La − ] reached 10.7 mmol·L −1 after the 50 m trial, compared with 11.8 and 13.4 mmol·L −1 following the SIT and RST protocols, respectively. BG demonstrated a similar pattern, with the highest values observed after completion of the RST protocol. Also, the RST protocol better maintained stroke mechanics across repetitions, whereas the SIT protocol elicited greater changes in stroke rate. Conclusions Both SIT and RST reproduced the high anaerobic demands of 50 m freestyle swimming. However, the proposed RST protocol induced the greatest glycolytic response while maintaining swimming velocity and race-specific stroke characteristics, suggesting that short repeated maximal efforts may provide a more event-specific stimulus for sprint swimmers.
authors: Konstantinos Papadimitriou; Daniel Almeida Marinho; Henrique Pereira Neiva
venue: International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching

title: Repercussões psicossociais da oncologia pediátrica para crianças e adolescentes, familiares e profissionais: revisão integrativa
abstract: Objective: To describe the psychosocial impacts of pediatric oncology on children and adolescents. Methodology: This is an integrative literature review comprising six methodological stages: formulation of the core question using the PICo strategy, definition of inclusion and exclusion criteria, search of the SciELO, BVS-BDENF-LILACS, and PubMed Central databases and Google Scholar, screening of articles by title and abstract, analytical reading of the selected texts, and categorization of the results. The search utilized DeCS and MeSH descriptors, combined with the Boolean operator “AND.” The studies were categorized through content analysis. Results: Sixteen articles on the psychosocial perspective of pediatric oncology were analyzed, yielding the following categories: Psychoemotional aspects for children and adolescents in cancer care; Family members’ experiences with pediatric oncology; and Repercussions of pediatric oncology care for healthcare professionals. Conclusion: The study demonstrated that pediatric oncology poses significant challenges that extend beyond clinical boundaries. Children face emotional distress, isolation, and changes in routine, while family members suffer from overload and the fear of loss. Healthcare professionals are also emotionally impacted due to the bonds formed with patients. The scarcity of studies on children’s subjective perspectives is revealed, and the need for comprehensive care and psychological support for all those involved is highlighted.
authors: Alana Rocha da Silva Rodrigues; Evilly Carneiro Almeida; Iara Neves Alves; Ravena dos Santos Lopes; Márcio Costa de Souza; Aisiane Cedraz Morais

title: Robo-MLT: Dual-System Robotic Manipulation for Long-Horizon Medical Laboratory Tasks
abstract: Reliable medical laboratory automation requires robots to complete entire workflows in protocol order while handling changes during execution. A robot may execute each motion correctly yet fail the workflow by confusing visually similar stages or stalling after human intervention. We present Robo-MLT, a dual-system framework that couples explicit workflow monitoring with learned action generation. A vision--language planner composes an ordered atomic-skill sequence from the protocol and the initial workspace observation. A multiframe execution monitor detects when the active skill has completed or become infeasible, then advances the workflow or triggers replanning. A skill-conditioned vision--language--action policy generates the manipulation trajectories, and an asynchronous runtime coordinates it with the monitor. We evaluate Robo-MLT against four policy baselines and a VLM-based monitor baseline on blood gas analysis and blood sample tube sorting, with 50 nominal configurations per method and 20 sample-removal configurations. Robo-MLT achieves task success rates of 82\% and 70\%, exceeding $π_{0.5}$ by 30 and 22 percentage points, respectively. After an operator removes the sample being handled, the system revises the remaining plan and continues processing the other samples. These results indicate that, under the evaluated conditions, explicit workflow monitoring makes long-horizon laboratory manipulation more reliable and recoverable.
authors: Zequan Zeng; Kai Wang; Delvin Ce Zhang; Huaping Liu; Zhipeng Yuan; Junqin Yang; YunLong Zhang

title: Robotic Assistants in the Operating Room: A Systematic Review of Vision‐Based Systems for Nonoperative Tasks
abstract: Nonoperative tasks in the operating room, such as instrument handling, sterile packaging, and logistics, are demanding yet have received less robotics attention than autonomous surgery. This review, the first to synthesize this literature, maps the perception methods, autonomy levels, methodological quality, and clinical readiness of vision‐based robotic assistants for scrub nurse, circulating nurse, and OR logistics roles. Searches of PubMed, IEEE Xplore, Scopus, ACM Digital Library, Web of Science, and Google Scholar returned 465 records; 20 publications describing 11 robotic system families met inclusion criteria. Most evidence, 17 publications across eight system families, concerns scrub nurse assistance; circulating nurse support, OR logistics, and dental assistance are each represented by one system. Vision methods have moved from classical image processing and predefined gestures toward deep learning, multimodal perception, and vision–language–action models, but autonomy has not kept pace: one system family reaches LoA 1, seven LoA 2, and three LoA 3, with Technology Readiness Levels spanning TRL 4 to TRL 6. Reported success rates are often high but rarely comparable and mostly generated in laboratory or simulated settings. Closing that gap requires stronger evidence on safety, sterility, failure recovery, workflow integration, execution speed, reproducibility, and, notably absent, manipulation of deformable sterile materials.
authors: Eugenia Mawuenya Akpo; Pietro Falco; Nicholas Tobias Johannes Raison; Christos Bergeles; Letizia Gionfrida

title: RobustRLlib: A Unified Library and Benchmark for Robust Reinforcement Learning Algorithms
abstract: Robust reinforcement learning (RL) is critical for reliable real-world deployment, where policies may fail under diverse shifts and disruptions. Existing robust RL algorithms offer a rich set of mechanisms and principles, yet two major barriers limit their broader potential: limited algorithm reusability and an unclear empirical capability boundary. We introduce RobustRLlib, an algorithm-centric library and benchmark that addresses both challenges. It integrates 17 representative robust online, offline, and safe RL algorithms under a unified interface for substantially improved reusability, together with an enhanced evaluation platform spanning diverse real-world shifts and advanced humanoid and vision-language-action tasks. Systematic evaluation over 273 perturbation configurations provides an up-to-date capability map of current robust RL algorithms, revealing where they remain effective and where substantial robustness gaps persist. As an open-source, user-friendly platform, RobustRLlib offers a reproducible and extensible codebase for applying existing methods to new problems and developing new robust RL algorithms.
authors: Xi Chen; Fengqi Hu; Zeyu Shen; Jiaying Xu; Shangding Gu; Pan Xu; Anqi Liu; Laixi Shi

title: SCALP COOLING EFFICACY IN PREVENTING CHEMOTHERAPY-INDUCED ALOPECIA IN BREAST CANCER PATIENTS: A PROSPECTIVE OBSERVATIONAL STUDY
abstract: Vchodiska: Ztrta vlas spojen s cytostatickou lbou pedstavuje ast nedouc inek vznamn ovlivujc kvalitu ivota pacientek. Jednou z monost prevence je chlazen pokoky hlavy, kter me pomoci pedchzet chemoterapi indukovan alopecii. Cl: Clem studie je zhodnotit innost chladc terapie u pacientek s karcinomem prsu podstupujcch cytostatickou lbu. Metodika: Studie mla charakter prospektivn observan studie a zahrnovala celkem 29 pacientek. U 75,9 % z nich byla podvna lba antracykliny. Pro zhodnocen mry alopecie bylo pouito hodnocen dle Deanov, piem za spnou terapii byla povaovna alopecie ≤ 50 %. Vsledky a diskuze: Vsledky ukzaly, e chlazen pokoky hlavy me sniovat riziko alopecie. authors: Eliška Kolajová; Aneta Hujová

title: SHRIMP: Iterative Refinement of Robot Task Plans
abstract: As collaborative robots have entered domains such as manufacturing, agriculture, and healthcare, programming or adapting robot behavior typically requires robotic expertise that most end users lack. Natural language lowers this barrier. Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) have made it feasible to translate natural language into robot task plans. However, language-based task specification can suffer from semantic ambiguity, and generative models lack transparency for how language instructions are translated into robot actions, making it difficult for users to validate plans before execution. To address these issues, we introduce SHRIMP: Simulation-driven Human-in-the-loop Refinement Interface for Manipulation Planning. SHRIMP allows users to automatically generate a hierarchical robot primitive plan using natural language and iteratively revise their plan through re-prompting and explicit correction. At each revision, SHRIMP allows users to validate their plan in simulation, and once satisfied, execute it on the physical robot. Through a user study involving participants planning tabletop kitchen tasks (N = 35), we validate that SHRIMP improves perceived control and enhances robot transparency. System videos and source code are available at https://wisc-hci.github.io/SHRIMP.
authors: Mya Schroder; Yuna Hwang; Callie Y. Kim; Leqian Cheng; Jeffrey Li-cheng Liu; Chenchen Zheng; Xinning He; Bilge Mutlu
venue: ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)

title: SLA: Scaling Spatial-Language-Action Model via Continual Pre-training
abstract: Reliable robotic manipulation requires both semantic understanding and precise control in three-dimensional space. However, vision-language-action (VLA) foundations largely inherit visual representations from 2D vision-language pre-training, while spatial supervision is often introduced only during task-specific adaptation. Developing spatial understanding as a transferable foundation-model capability therefore calls for learning from broader robot experience. We present SLA, a Spatial-Language-Action Model that scales implicit spatial alignment to continual pre-training and maintains it during downstream post-training. Initialized from a pretrained pi05 policy, SLA jointly optimizes action prediction and alignment between intermediate visual embeddings and spatial representations from a frozen 3D perception model. We curate and unify heterogeneous robot datasets to support spatial learning across diverse embodiments, tasks, and scenes. To accommodate this diversity, we introduce feature-dependent gates that adaptively aggregate visual embeddings from multiple VLA layers for spatial supervision. The teacher further exploits partially available depth and camera calibration alongside RGB observations, enabling effective use of heterogeneous geometric annotations. Probabilistic state dropout encourages reliance on visual cues and mitigates overfitting to demonstration trajectories. All auxiliary components are used only during training, allowing direct reuse of pretrained VLA weights and preserving the original inference architecture.
authors: Fuhao Li; Wenxuan Song; Qizhou Huang; Ziyang Zhou; Jingbo Wang; E Junwu; Pengwei Wang; Yan Wang; Shunbo Zhou; Haoang Li

title: See No Evil: Aligning Vision-Language Agents with Multimodal Contextual Integrity via Adversarial Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Vision-Language Agents (VLAs) that operate graphical user interfaces (GUIs) face a distinctive privacy-alignment problem: sensitive information is embedded in screen regions and interaction targets, so failures can arise through both textual disclosure and grounded actions. Existing text-centric safety guardrails are poorly matched to this setting because they treat privacy as a fixed property of an entity type, rather than as a context-dependent information-flow constraint. We formulate this problem as Multimodal Contextual Integrity (M-CI), where legality depends on the current contextual relation among actors, attributes, and transmission principles. To operationalize M-CI, we propose the Visual-Agent Guardian (VAG), which represents each interaction state using a contextual tuple together with a region-level authorization map over GUI elements. VAG combines a context-conditioned inverse rendering pipeline for counterfactual supervision, an M-CI-CoT module for contextual tuple and authorization inference, and a Visual-Semantic Reward Model (V-SRM) that scores both textual and spatial actions against the inferred CI state. We train the agent under a privacy budget using Constrained Group Relative Policy Optimization (C-GRPO), a critic-free constrained reinforcement learning method with PID-Lagrangian updates, and further improve robustness through automated adversarial self-play. Experiments on privacy-critical benchmarks demonstrate that VAG fundamentally shifts the privacy--utility Pareto frontier: it reduces visual privacy leakage to under 5% across all three benchmarks while averaging over 80% task success, and reduces the average multimodal social-engineering attack success rate to below 4%.
authors: Runshan Hu; Jia Bi; Chenyang Zhu
venue: ACM International Conference on Multimedia (ACM MM)

title: Simulation and Learning for Autonomous Surgical Robotics: From Language-Guided Blood Suction to End-to-End Suturing
abstract: Robot-assisted surgery has become increasingly common because it provides surgeons with improved precision, visualization, and dexterity. Existing surgical robots can reduce hand tremor and translate a surgeon's movements into precise instrument motion. However, these systems still depend heavily on direct human control, and their level of autonomous assistance remains limited. Increasing this assistance could reduce surgeons' workload and allow robots to handle repetitive or time-sensitive tasks. Achieving surgical autonomy is inherently more challenging than performing general robotic tasks because surgical environments are highly dynamic, involving deformable tissues and fluids, and require long procedures in which even a small mistake early on may affect everything that follows. Traditional motion-planning approaches can work well in carefully defined settings, but adapting them to a wide range of procedures would require extensive task-specific tuning, making them difficult to scale. Robot learning can reduce this dependence on hand-crafted techniques by learning from demonstrations or experience. However, it is limited by scarce real-world data, costly demonstrations, and the risks of trial-and-error training on physical tissue. This thesis therefore focuses on extending realistic surgical simulators and applying robot learning methods within these environments. The work considers blood suction in a changing soft tissue and fluid environment and suturing through deformable tissue. The first part investigates language-guided blood suction using vision-language-action (VLA) policies trained in simulation. The policies generate suction trajectories from natural-language instructions without requiring separate controllers for each command. The simulator is further extended to include deformable tissue, cutting, blood flow, and suction, enabling comparison between VLA models and a language-conditioned ACT policy. Results are promising, although the cutting and blood-flow scenarios still require physical validation. The second part builds on the existing GPU-accelerated CRESSim-MPM soft-tissue engine by adding a PBD suture model and two-way coupling between the suture and MPM tissue. Reinforcement-learning agents trained entirely in the resulting environment learn needle insertion, driving, and extraction, achieving 80\% success for insertion and 68\% for extraction under the strictest evaluation threshold. These results demonstrate the extended simulator's potential as a platform for robotic suturing research. The final part further extends this platform to autonomous end-to-end suturing using a hierarchical five-phase framework. Comparing ACT with asymmetric Residual Fine-Tuning (aResFiT), aResFiT completes 38 of 50 phase trials, compared with 29 of 50 for the original imitation-learning policies, while reducing entry and exit errors. Initial transfer to a physical da Vinci Research Kit also demonstrates that simulation-trained policies can transfer to real hardware, while still some sim-to-real challenges remain. Overall, this thesis contributes extensions to surgical simulation environments and learning frameworks for language-guided blood suction and multi-phase suturing. The results support simulation-first development while showing that physical validation, broader randomization, improved calibration, and learning methods that correct motion are required before clinical usage.
authors: Tleukhan Mussin
venue: ERA: Education and Research Archive (University of Alberta)

title: Study protocol for a retrospective cohort study of real-world effectiveness of the VLA1553 (IXCHIQ®) chikungunya vaccine during an epidemic among healthcare workers in Reunion Island.
abstract:
Background

Real-world effectiveness data for the live-attenuated chikungunya vaccine VLA1553 (IXCHIQ®) remain limited because licensure relied primarily on immunogenicity and safety. The 2025 vaccination campaign at the University Hospital of Réunion offers an opportunity to evaluate effectiveness during an outbreak.

Objectives

HO-VLA-CHIK aims to estimate vaccine effectiveness against symptomatic chikungunya among hospital employees. Secondary objectives address laboratory-confirmed symptomatic infections, hospitalizations, chronic chikungunya, sick leave duration, adverse events following immunization, and determinants of vaccine uptake.

Methods

This retrospective exposed-unexposed cohort study involves approximately 700 vaccinated and unvaccinated employees across two hospital sites. Structured electronic questionnaire data will be supplemented by occupational health registries, laboratory results, and medical records. A marginal Cox model with stabilized inverse probability of treatment weighting will estimate vaccine effectiveness, using calendar time and time-dependent vaccination status. Vaccinated person-time will begin 15 days after vaccination. Adjustment will use prespecified baseline confounders.

Results

Ethical approval was obtained in May 2026. Recruitment and data collection are scheduled to end in December 2026. Analyses will follow data validation. Expected findings include estimates of vaccine effectiveness and descriptions of reported adverse events, persistent symptoms, and work absence. These findings may inform vaccination strategies and hospital workforce preparedness during future chikungunya outbreaks.
authors: Mosnier E, Benhard J, Badia V, Galmiche S, Perrault E, Moiton MP, Zossoungbo J, Ducrot YM, Desmoulin A, Kuli B, Keranflec'h M, Castel T, Manaquin R, Hellencourt FL, Ferdynus C, Gérardin P, Nguyen LBL.

title: SuperGlance: Driving at a Glance with a Vision-Language Model
abstract: Autonomous driving is turning to vision-language-action models (VLAs). They answer and plan by decoding, one step at a time. Each step is another forward pass, so a plan can take over a second of GPU time. Embodied AI often pairs such a slow, reasoning System 2 with a fast System 1 that acts. Human drivers plan at a glance, with System 1. Faster designs usually put System 1 outside the vision-language model (VLM), in a planner without its abilities. Yet before a VLM writes its first token, it has already read the scene into one hidden state. We show that, once trained, this hidden state is enough to drive and to answer questions about what the model sees. SuperGlance reads it to turn a decoder-only VLM into an encoder-style driving policy. Its linear head scores a fixed set of 5,273 candidate trajectories. With the set fixed, rewards are computed offline, so supervised targets can be reward-weighted and reinforcement learning maximizes the exact expected reward. Before and during policy training, multiple-choice training keeps the VLM's visual abilities in one pass, so the policy still answers questions about driving scenes. Training questions are built against shortcuts. Each must be answered right in two option orders. Against drift, a KL term keeps each stage near its starting model. One pass offers VLAs a more plausible path to System 1. SuperGlance answers visual multiple-choice questions as well as its base VLM does by decoding. It plans in 84 ms of GPU time, six times faster than Qwen-Drive-1.0, and at least as well on NAVSIM, PAI-AV and WOD-E2E. In AlpaSim closed loop, km per at-fault incident holds for both planners up to a 300-ms delay and drops beyond. With GPU time charged as delay, SuperGlance's lead over Qwen-Drive-1.0 grows from 2.8 to 3.9 times. Delayed by 1.2 s, our model falls below Qwen-Drive-1.0 at its own 518 ms.
authors: Jieyuan Pei; Xin Yan; Mingwei Xu; Haiyi Zhang; Siyu Zou; Zhangyi Hu; Zhuoxuan Li; Yuguang Yang; Rongjunchen Zhang; Cheng Chi; Hui Xiong; Yan Wang

title: SurgTAP-3D: A Large-Scale Cross-Surgery Video Dataset with Contact-Aware 3D Motion Tracking
abstract: Understanding 3D scene dynamics in minimally invasive surgery (MIS) is a fundamental step toward physically intelligent and autonomous surgical systems. However, existing public datasets offer limited scalability and diversity in real-world clinical scenarios. Moreover, annotations typically focus on either tissue or instruments alone, overlooking tool-tissue interactions. This gap limits applications such as augmented reality guidance and autonomous surgery driven by vision-language-action (VLA) models or world models, which demand large-scale, high-quality 3D supervision. In this work, we construct SurgTAP-3D, a large-scale in-vivo pseudo-3D surgical motion tracking dataset and benchmark, comprising 520K frames, 4,549 action clips, and 1.4M 2D/3D point trajectories from diverse robotic and manual procedures under unified action categories. To make annotation scalable, we design a unified framework for surgical 3D point tracking that converts uncalibrated monocular surgical videos into structured 4D annotations through contact-region prompting, active-tool segmentation, dynamic bundle adjustment, and global 4D refinement. This pipeline adapts foundation priors to surgical videos and produces temporally consistent trajectories, pseudo-scale geometry, camera poses, and instrument masks. The dataset captures realistic challenges inherent to surgical environments, including occlusions, smoke, bleeding, and rapid instrument motion. We establish a comprehensive benchmark on SurgPose, SurgT, and STIR, covering both instrument and tissue tracking. We demonstrate instrument displacement estimation, deformable surface reconstruction, and foundation-model fine-tuning. Extensive experiments and analysis demonstrate the effectiveness of our dataset and annotation framework for 3D surgical point tracking, reconstruction, and surgical action understanding. Homepage: https://wrld.github.io/surgtap-3d/
authors: Jiaxin Guo; Wenzhen Dong; Taoyu Wu; Haomin Kuang; Mengya Xu; Kejian Shi; Ziyi Wang; Tongfan Guan; Mingkai Jia; Yue Wang; Qi Dou; Yun-Hui Liu

title: SurgiCLAW: An Interpretable Atomic-Skill Agent for Precision Robotic Micromanipulation
abstract: Recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs) and vision--language--action models have provided robots with new capabilities for long-horizon task understanding and planning. In surgical robotics, however, end-to-end prediction of low-level actions remains limited by insufficient precision, opaque decisions, and scarce data. This paper presents SurgiCLAW, a hierarchical skill-based framework for precision surgical manipulation. SurgiCLAW confines an MLLM to intraoperative visual understanding, structured explanation, and atomic surgical-skill selection, while delegating physical execution to verifiable deterministic control programs. For brain--machine-interface implantation, a representative high-precision surgical task, we construct a state-to-skill invocation dataset and expand it through visual and state perturbations. The model first learns structured skill invocation through supervised fine-tuning and is then optimized using three rewards for action correctness, operation prerequisites, and format validity, improving action selection, operational safety, and output parseability. We evaluate subtask success, offline model comparison, real-robot performance, and ablations. On a fixed test set, SurgiCLAW achieves 94.6% skill-selection accuracy and 93.0% macro-averaged F1 (Macro-F1). Across 50 closed-loop real-robot implantation trials, it achieves an 88.0% task success rate.
authors: Angen Ye; junjie xie; Yujia Song; Junkai Huang; Dapeng Zhang

title: Surgical Intelligence Labs: a technical feasibility study of smartphone-based egocentric data capture and computational retargeting for robotic surgery
abstract: Surgical robotics could benefit from demonstrations of manual operating-room work, yet most existing surgical datasets emphasize endoscopic video or robot kinematics. We developed and evaluated a smartphone-based method for capturing first-person video, head pose, device motion and hand motion in a non-clinical simulation. Surgical Intelligence Labs is an iPhone application that records first-person video with synchronized ARKit camera pose and device motion. Apple Vision provides 21 two-dimensional hand keypoints per hand; an articulated model fits these keypoints in three dimensions and maps the fitted motion computationally to humanoid and bimanual robot models. Testing used two author-made, non-clinical recordings, including a 63-s bare-hand suturing simulation. The manuscript distinguishes implemented local capture functions from planned operating-room collection and de-identification workflows. In the 63-s suturing simulation, ARKit reported normal tracking for all 1,877 video frames and the phone pointed a mean 55° below the horizon. Both hands were detected in 97% of sampled frames and 99% of tracked hand observations retained a three-dimensional fit. These frame-level proportions describe a single temporally correlated sequence, not independent trials. Position-based retargeting reproduced median thumb-to-fingertip gaps within 2 mm of the fitted human-hand gaps; because gap matching is included in the position-based retargeting objective, this is a fitted-model geometric consistency check rather than independent validation. Numerical inverse kinematics solved all 300 G1 + and 200 WidowX deliberately reachable test targets (median position errors 1.1 and 0.35 mm, respectively). A consumer smartphone can capture synchronized first-person video, head pose, device motion and hand landmarks and map fitted hand motion to robot models computationally. This single-operator, non-clinical study establishes technical feasibility of the capture and processing pipeline; it does not establish absolute hand accuracy, generalizable performance, physical robot execution, policy learning or clinical readiness.
authors: Mustafa Khan; Joao Bombardelli

title: TP-JSCC: Efficient Token Pruning and Joint Source-Channel Coding for LVLMs-based 3D-VQA in Cloud-Edge Collaboration
abstract: Deploying large vision-language models (LVLMs) on resource-constrained embodied agents for 3D visual question answering necessitates cloud-edge collaboration. However, offloading massive visual data to the cloud over bandwidth-limited and noisy channels introduces severe latency and transmission distortion. To address this, we propose TP-JSCC, an efficient token pruning and joint source-channel coding method for LVLMs-based 3D-VQA in Cloud-Edge Collaboration. First, we develop a Local and Global Semantics-based Hybrid Token Pruning (LGS-HTP) module to significantly reduce the visual token count. By decoupling foreground-background tokens and jointly selecting local and global semantics, LGS-HTP effectively reduces redundancy while preserving reasoning-critical tokens. Second, we introduce a lightweight Token Joint Source-Channel Coding (T-JSCC) module to further compress the pruned tokens and ensure their robust transmission over error-prone channels. By employing lightweight cascaded linear layers and Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR)-adaptive mechanism, this module adapts to fluctuating channel conditions while maintaining minimal computational overhead. Extensive experiments on ScanQA and SQA3D datasets indicate the exceptional efficiency and robustness of our approach. Specifically, on ScanQA validation set, the LGS-HTP module could achieve 90% pruning ratio while incurring less than a 1% CIDEr loss. Building on this, the T-JSCC further compresses the tokens by 18 times, resulting in an overall 180 times data volume reduction for robust transmission, while saving 90% in computational complexity for LVLM deployment. Our code is available at https://github.com/yuanhui0325/TP-JSCC.
authors: Zhengxin Li; Chongzhen Tian; Hui Yuan; Hao Liu; Sam Kwong

title: The Right Amount of “Human Touch”: The Curvilinear Effect of Embodied AI Agent Anthropomorphism on Consumer Usage Intention under Social Intrusiveness
abstract: Anthropomorphic design in embodied AI agents often evokes ambivalent consumer responses, yet it remains a key strategy for enhancing users’ intention to use such agents. Based on three video-based scenario experiments with 438 participants, this study examines how anthropomorphism shapes consumers’ usage intentions. The results confirm an inverted-U-shaped relationship between anthropomorphism of embodied AI agents and usage intention. Further analyses reveal that likability and eeriness jointly mediate this curvilinear relationship: anthropomorphism exerts an inverted U-shaped effect on likability, which in turn positively influences usage intention, whereas anthropomorphism exerts a U-shaped effect on eeriness, which negatively influences usage intention. In addition, social intrusiveness functions as a boundary condition by (1) strengthening the curvilinear relationships between anthropomorphism and both likability and eeriness, and (2) moderating the indirect effects of likability and eeriness. These findings provide empirical support for applying social information processing theory to human–AI interaction and extend uncanny valley theory from emotional responses to usage intention. The study also offers practical implications for deploying embodied AI agents in customer service contexts.
authors: Du Chen; Lin Hui Sun

title: The epidemiology of frailty in urban and rural KwaZulu Natal, South Africa; a cross-sectional study
abstract: Introduction We investigated the prevalence and clinical risk factors associated with frailty, and frailty’s relationship with health-related quality of life (HRQoL) in urban and rural South Africa. Methods In a population-based cross-sectional study, using age- and sex-stratified random sampling of adults aged ≥40 years, researcher-administered questionnaires collected socio-demographic and clinical data. Physical assessments included body mass index (BMI), grip strength, short physical performance battery (SPPB), vision and hearing, and EuroQol 5-Dimensions 5-Levels measured HRQoL. A modified Fried’s Frailty Phenotype defined frailty. Multivariable logistic regression calculated the odds of frailty for associated risk factors, and logistic and quantile regression examined HRQoL by frailty status. Results Amongst 1,893 participants, median age 60 years [IQR 50-70], 54% female, the overall study prevalence of frailty was 16.4%. Frailty was more common in those ≥70 years than those 40–49-years old (32.5% vs. 7.5%; OR 6.0 [95%CI 3.7,8.4], p < 0.001), and in females compared to males (19.2% vs. 13.1%; OR 1.6 [1.2,2.0], p < 0.001). Older age (≥60 years), urban residence, low educational attainment, moderate to severe food insecurity, visual and hearing impairments, self-reported disability, BMI<18kg/m 2 , and impaired SPPB were all independently associated with frailty. Compared to being robust, frailty was associated with a lower HRQoL utility score (median 0.81(IQR 0.71-0.86) in frail vs. 0.86 (0.83-0.90) in robust/prefrail, β -0.05 ([95%CI -0.07,-0.03], p < 0.001). Conclusion Frailty is common and associated with poorer HRQoL. The identified clinical risk factors can be used to prioritise individuals for referral for clinical assessment of frailty in SA.
authors: E. I. Y. Madela; Celia Louise Gregson; Anya J. Burton; Farhanah Paruk; Rita Patel; Hannah Wilson; Bavumile Mbanjwa; Fundile Habana; Anthony Muchai Manyara; Lucy Gates; Camille M. Pearse; Chris Grundy; Kate A Ward; Bilkish Cassim

title: The future of robotic surgery in the age of artificial intelligence.
abstract: Patient outcomes after robotic surgery vary widely, often reflecting differences in surgical performance. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers new ways to address this variability, with applications spanning automated skills assessment and feedback, intraoperative guidance and autonomous surgery. The most credible short-range advances of AI in this space consist in generating assistive systems that enhance perception, anticipate risks and standardize feedback while remaining under surgeon control. Results from early studies suggest that AI can influence decision-making, reduce errors and shorten learning curves, particularly in areas such as augmented navigation, anatomy recognition, error detection and telesurgery support. Long-term directions include emerging vision-language-action interfaces capable of programming task-specific support through natural language. In addition to technical performance, translation of AI into clinical practice will require robust datasets, systems designed around human users, regulatory alignment and clear accountability. Ultimately, the measure of surgical AI will be patient outcomes, including reduced complications, fast proficiency acquisition and improved outcome consistency across diverse settings.
authors: Ludovica Cella; Jasmine Lin; Mitchell G Goldenberg; Andrew J Hung

title: Toward Mathematically Grounded Boundary Optimization for Image Segmentation
abstract: Image segmentation models are predominantly optimized using region-based objectives such as IoU and Dice, which aggregate pixel-wise agreement to evaluate mask quality. While effective for estimating object extent, these objectives provide no theoretical guarantee on boundary alignment. This limitation is critical in practice, as such predictions can still produce unusable boundaries, as commonly observed in medical image segmentation. This work investigates the disconnect between region overlap and boundary quality, and proposes a boundary-centric formulation that incorporates explicit topological constraints. The core hypothesis is that boundary errors can be controlled through a differentiable penalty that jointly models false positive and false negative regions with respect to boundary distance. Preliminary results on camouflaged object segmentation benchmarks show that the proposed formulation significantly improves boundary quality (up to +86% BF-score) while maintaining competitive region-based metrics. Ongoing work focuses on extending this formulation to large-scale models and boundary-critical applications such as medical imaging and robotic manipulation.
authors: Nguyen Ngoc Huynh
venue: ACM International Conference on Multimedia (ACM MM)

title: Toward Verifiable Medical Imaging World Models: An Engineering Framework for Evaluating Simulation Fidelity, Roll-Out Stability, and Clinical Plausibility
abstract: Medical world models simulate how a patient's imaged state evolves over time and, in some systems, under clinical interventions. Their value comes from multi-step, action-conditioned roll-outs, yet evaluation is still dominated by perceptual or single-step metrics. We treat assessment of these models as a verification problem, distinct from later evidence of clinical benefit, and organize it around three axes. Simulation fidelity asks whether predicted states are correct at the level claimed by the model. Roll-out stability asks whether that correctness is maintained over multiple steps; we summarize this using an effective planning horizon, defined as the last step before a stated loss quantile first exceeds a clinical tolerance under the observed action policy. Clinical plausibility and reliability ask whether simulated responses are counterfactually consistent, calibrated, and adequate across patient subgroups. We also propose a claim-proportionate reporting standard and a reproducible procedure for estimating the horizon from retrospective data. Applying the framework to a purposively selected sample of nine imaging world models, we find that reported evidence is uneven across capability tiers. Under the proposed standard, every model claiming action-conditioned prediction or above omits at least one applicable item: none reports an explicit counterfactual-consistency check or a clinically meaningful subgroup analysis of the type specified in Item 7, and none reports an effective planning horizon at a stated clinical tolerance. Because the effective planning horizon is estimated on-policy, it should not be interpreted as evidence of off-policy counterfactual reliability.
authors: Chathura Wimalasiri
venue: Journal of Imaging Informatics in Medicine

title: Utility of the Heart-to-Single Vertebra Ratio Compared with Artificial Intelligence-Derived Vertebral Heart Score for Detecting Cardiomegaly in Dogs with Myxomatous Mitral Valve Degeneration
abstract: The heart-to-single vertebra ratio measured at the seventh thoracic vertebra (HSVR-T7) is a recently described radiographic method used to assess heart size in dogs. Our study evaluated the diagnostic performance of HSVR-T7 for identifying echocardiographically defined cardiomegaly in dogs with myxomatous mitral valve disease (MMVD). Its correlation with vertebral heart score (VHS) and vertebral left atrial size (VLAS), and as its discriminatory performance compared with artificial intelligence (AI)-derived VHS and VLAS measurements were investigated. Radiographs of 93 dogs with echocardiographically confirmed myxomatous mitral valve disease were included; 35 were classified as ACVIM stage B1 and 58 as stage B2 or C. Among the 35 stage B1 dogs, five (14.3%) had isolated left atrial enlargement and two (5.7%) had isolated left ventricular enlargement. The HSVR-T7 scores were significantly higher in dogs with echocardiographically confirmed cardiomegaly (stage B2 or C) than in dogs without cardiomegaly (stage B1): 11.65 ± 1.13 versus 10.47 ± 1.08 (p < 0.001). At the optimal cut-off value of ≥11.15, HSVR-T7 yielded an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.769 of the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve, with 70.7% sensitivity and 74.3% specificity. The HSVR-T7 showed a very strong positive correlation with VHS (r = 0.890; p < 0.001). Artificial intelligence-derived VHS showed the highest diagnostic performance at an optimal cut-off value of ≥11.35 (AUC, 0.861; sensitivity, 75.9%; specificity, 82.9%), whereas AI-derived VLAS yielded an AUC of 0.765, with 62.1% sensitivity and 85.7% specificity at an optimal cut-off value of ≥2.65. Overall, HSVR-T7 was less sensitive and specific in detecting cardiomegaly in dogs with myxomatous mitral valve disease than VHS, and it cannot replace echocardiographic, VHS or VLAS measurements.
authors: Berfin Eftelya Guder; Zeynep Nurselin Kot; Viktor Szatmári

title: VISTA: Active Exploration for Self-Improvement in Embodied Agents
abstract: Agentic embodied intelligence plays a foundational role in open-ended, dynamic physical environments. Rather than treating policy learning as an end-to-end mapping from instructions to actions, recent studies reveal that embodied systems depend not only on pre-trained foundation models, but also on harness. Prior approaches largely treat rollouts as static logs for post-hoc reflection, producing harness updates without autonomously testing and refining them through subsequent embodied interaction. To address this challenge, we propose VISTA, a meta-agent framework that transforms post-hoc rollout reflection into active self-exploration for embodied harness improvement. Specifically, VISTA maintains a harness graph that records the lineage of proposed harnesses, which enables the meta-agent to retrieve prior hypotheses, build on effective mechanisms, and avoid repeatedly exploring failed directions. Each iteration begins from a retained harness version and its execution evidence. Rather than directly committing an update from these historical trajectories, the meta-agent actively explores in the environment. It autonomously generates new rollouts, probes execution failures and recovery behaviors, and iteratively modifies the harness based on the resulting evidence. The refined harness is then evaluated afresh and added to the harness graph. We evaluate VISTA on the LIBERO-Pro, RoboCasa, and RoboTwin benchmarks. Experimental results demonstrate that VISTA progressively improves task success and is more rollout-efficient than static reflection, achieving higher success rates with fewer simulator rollouts.
authors: Zhang Zhang; Shengjun Zhang; Simin Huang; Min Chen; Chong Xia; Xin Fei; Yueqi Duan

title: VirtualTrialHarness: Coordinating Agentic Operationalization of Virtual Trial Protocols Across Complex Clinical Schemas
abstract: Virtual trials use routinely collected clinical data to evaluate treatment strategies, but translating a study protocol into an executable analysis requires determining how clinical concepts and study requirements should be represented in the available data and applied consistently across the workflow. These decisions depend on local data representations and operational conventions and can involve source selection, patient and encounter identity, linkage, and temporal interpretation. Here we introduce VirtualTrialHarness (VTHarness), an agent framework that coordinates virtual-trial operationalization by selecting reusable procedural skills for each workflow stage and uses explicit contracts to maintain consistent study decisions across stages. We also introduce VTBenchmark for evaluating source selection and cohort construction. Across three complex synthetic environments, VTHarness successfully produced all required cohort outputs matching the references in 95.1% of workflows after requirement clarification, compared with 60.4% using retrieval from the same procedural corpus. Procedural skills improved source recovery across three language models and increased source overlap with analyst code in 13 Mayo Clinic cases. Site-specific adaptation enabled reference-matched cohort execution across eight MIMIC-IV tasks. Within the Mayo Clinic Virtual Trials Program, the framework supported investigator review of cohort construction and endpoint analysis. These findings support coordinating procedural guidance with workflow decisions to improve virtual-trial implementation across complex clinical schemas.
authors: Pengze Li; Jingna Feng; Yue Yu; Yining Wu; Xinyue Hu; Jie Lin; Avanti Bhandarkar; Cui Tao

title: Wellness Robots and the Path to Full Autonomy
abstract: This paper introduces the autonomous wellness robot as a distinct category of socially assistive system, defined by its capacity to continuously assess and respond across the seven ICAA dimensions of wellness (see Figure 2). We propose the Care Robot Autonomy Scale (CRAS): a six-level taxonomy (L0-L5) modeled on the automotive automation standard SAE J3016 and evaluated across four wellness-aligned dimensions. We present Ryan, developed initially at the University of Denver and commercialized by DreamFace Technologies, as a case study. NIH/NIA-funded longitudinal evidence (N = 18; 887 hours) shows statistically significant cognitive improvement (SLUMS +2.61, p = 0.015) and a clinically meaningful directional reduction in depressive symptoms (PHQ-9 -2.50, p = 0.073), with no novelty effect. We position Ryan today at CRAS Level 1-2, with emerging Level 3 capabilities in some dimensions, and outline a three-phase roadmap to L5 (full autonomy) by the early 2030s.
authors: Mohammad H. Mahoor; Matthew Hessler; Chileshe Lombe; Ola Alsaadi; Eshrat Emamian; Kerstin S. Haring; Richard M. Voyles

title: Where Should Models Run? A Collaborative Inference Framework for Embodied Intelligence in 6G
abstract: Embodied intelligence systems rely on fast and reliable inference to enable real-time perception, reasoning, and control. Recent advances in large-scale artificial intelligence (AI) models, including Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, have significantly enhanced the capabilities of embodied agents in complex environments. However, deploying these models remains challenging due to the limited computational resources and energy budgets of robotic platforms. A fundamental question is where inference should be executed. Collaborative inference, which partitions models across end devices, edge servers, and the cloud, has emerged as a promising solution. Yet determining the optimal partitioning point remains an open problem, as it depends on wireless network conditions, model structure, and privacy requirements. This article reviews the state of the art in collaborative inference for embodied intelligence and proposes an edge-centric framework in which the edge coordinates model partitioning and execution. Through both simulation and real-world experiments over WiFi and 5G networks, we demonstrate that the optimal partitioning strategy varies with network conditions and model structure. We further identify latency-minimizing partition points for ResNet-101, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and OpenVLA-7B in collaborative inference between NVIDIA Jetson Nano or AGX Xavier devices and an AGX Thor edge server under varying wireless conditions. Finally, we discuss the future directions for collaborative inference in 6G-empowered embodied intelligence systems.
authors: Wanlu Sun; Zhenhui Yuan; Xiang Ji; Yi Han; Qing Li; Gan Zheng

title: Why Large Language Models will Never be Embodied: A Categorical, Not Engineering, Impossibility
abstract: A persistent ambition in artificial intelligence research holds that large language models (LLMs) will eventually become embodied—through attachment to robots, augmentation with multimodal sensors, integration into vision–language–action architectures, or sheer scale until grounding emerges from training data. This ambition rests on a misunderstanding of embodiment. Embodiment is a constitutive condition of being a self-producing, self-maintaining living system whose continued existence is genuinely at stake in its couplings with the environment. Adding sensors, actuators, or physical instantiation to a computational substrate yields engineered coupling, which is something else entirely. We identify five conditions that any genuinely embodied system must satisfy—autopoietic closure, precariousness, constructive self-determination, intrinsic temporality, and mereological closure—and show that no computational artifact can satisfy any of them, let alone all five. The barrier is categorical incompatibility: the same property that makes a system computational (heteronomous design and maintenance through external specification) is the property that precludes it from being embodied. Coupling artifacts to environments through transducers achieves engineered interaction. Having a body and being a body are different conditions. We close by examining why the embodiment-equivalence claim persists despite its categorical impossibility, and by arguing that the confusion sustains two harms—overselling AI systems for tasks they cannot perform, and misdirecting public concern toward speculative futures while the actual harms of deployed systems accumulate without being addressed. Clarifying the categorical distinction is a precondition for taking the genuine stakes of AI deployment seriously rather than as a philosophical aside.
authors: Madhur Mangalam
